title: CktHGVAE: A Symmetric Design/State Heterogeneous Graph Variational Autoencoder for Transistor-level Analog/Mixed-signal Circuit Design and Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.19508v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose CktHGVAE, a heterogeneous graph variational autoencoder for transistor-level analog/mixedsignal CMOS circuits that takes not only design variables but also state variables as its inputs and outputs. With a single hyperparameter configuration without topology-specific tuning, comparison between model-generated and SPICE-simulated circuit operational states gives median R2 values above 0.9 for typical single-ended voltage amplifiers and the CMOS inverter, and 0.81-0.96 for differential amplifiers with larger datasets. Latent-space optimization in the PCA-reduced latent space with Bayesian optimization, evolutionary search, random search, and quasi-exhaustive search is demonstrated for a common-source voltage amplifier with NMOS input and resistive load, where the objective function is defined as a penalty for deviation from required circuit specifications. For each search strategy, 93.3 - 100% of all design candidates suggested by the model satisfy the required circuit specifications at the decoder output, and SPICE simulations verify that 90 - 100% of them indeed satisfy the requirements. The model pretrained on a batch of topologies can be transferred to unseen topologies without retraining at all, with zero-shot reconstruction median R2 values of 0.72-0.90 in three of four scenarios, including transfer from single-ended to differential topologies, although the transfer fidelity depends on the choice of pretraining topologies. Our demonstrations suggest that the proposed model can potentially serve as a basis for AMS CMOS circuit design automation.

title: Long-horizon Video Generation with Slot Memory Addressed By Region Tokens
description:
arXiv:2610.19257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.

title: Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
description:
arXiv:2610.19783v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naively training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method, Advantage Guidance, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model's ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.

title: React and TypeScript Best Practices: Build Reliable Applications
description:
React and TypeScript are a powerful combination for building maintainable, scalable frontend applications. React makes it easier to create reusable user interfaces, while TypeScript catches many common mistakes before your code reaches production.

However, simply adding TypeScript to a React project does not automatically make the codebase reliable. The real benefits come from defining precise types, designing reusable components, handling asynchronous states correctly, and avoiding unnecessary complexity.

In this guide, we will explore practical best practices for React and TypeScript, using JavaScript examples to demonstrate the underlying patterns. These concepts help developers write more predictable components, simplify debugging, and build applications that remain manageable as requirements evolve.

1. Practical Best Practices for React and TypeScript

Define Explicit Types for Component Props

Well-defined component props make component contracts easier to understand and maintain. Instead of passing loosely structured objects, describe the required properties, optional values, and callback signatures using TypeScript interfaces or type aliases.

For example, a reusable button component might accept a label, a disabled state, and an event handler. Explicit types help prevent missing properties and incompatible callback arguments during development, while keeping the component's public API clear.

Avoid Using Any and Prefer Unknown for Untrusted Data

The any type disables most useful type checking, allowing mistakes to spread throughout a codebase. Prefer unknown when handling values from APIs, external libraries, or other untrusted sources, and validate those values before using them.

TypeScript types disappear at runtime, so declaring an API response as a particular interface does not verify that the server actually returned the expected structure. Runtime validation is important whenever data crosses an application boundary, especially when dealing with user input or third-party services.

Model UI States Explicitly

React applications frequently handle loading, success, empty, and error states. Representing these states explicitly prevents contradictory combinations, such as showing an error and a successful result simultaneously.

Discriminated unions are particularly useful because TypeScript can narrow the available properties based on a shared literal field. This approach makes state transitions easier to reason about and helps ensure that each UI state contains the information it actually needs.

Keep Components Small and Focused

A component should have a clear responsibility, whether that means displaying a product, handling a form, or presenting an error message. Extracting repeated behavior into custom hooks can reduce duplication without forcing every small piece of logic into a separate abstraction.

Keep business logic separate from presentation when doing so improves clarity or makes behavior easier to test. Avoid excessive abstraction, however, because a simple component does not need multiple layers of indirection to become maintainable.

Use Type-Safe Event Handlers and Immutable State Updates

React event handlers should use appropriate event types when working with inputs, forms, and other interactive elements. Functional state updates are especially useful when the next state depends on the previous state, because React can apply the update against the latest queued value.

Treat arrays and objects in state as immutable values. Create updated copies with methods such as map, filter, and object spread instead of modifying existing state directly, so React can reliably detect changes and render the correct UI.

Understand What TypeScript Cannot Guarantee

TypeScript provides compile-time checks, but it does not replace runtime validation, application testing, or accessibility checks. A correctly typed component can still contain a logic bug, render an inaccessible interface, or mishandle a failed network request.

Combine static typing with focused tests, linting, strict compiler settings, and clear error handling. A strong React and TypeScript codebase uses these tools together rather than relying on a single layer of protection.

const assert = require('node:assert/strict');

// This runnable JavaScript example demonstrates patterns that can be
// modeled with TypeScript in a real React application.
// JavaScript itself does not enforce TypeScript interfaces or unions.

console.log('Step 1: Define the application's data contract');

// In TypeScript, define this with an interface or type alias.
// interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string; }
function createUser(id, name, email) {
  return { id, name, email };
}

const initialUser = createUser(1, 'Ansh', 'ansh@example.com');
console.log('User created:', initialUser);
assert.equal(initialUser.id, 1);

console.log('\nStep 2: Validate untrusted API data at runtime');

// TypeScript annotations alone cannot validate a JSON response.
function parseUser(value) {
  if (typeof value !== 'object' || value === null) {
    throw new TypeError('User must be an object');
  }

  if (!Number.isInteger(value.id) || value.id <= 0) {
    throw new TypeError('User id must be a positive integer');
  }

  if (typeof value.name !== 'string' || value.name.trim() === '') {
    throw new TypeError('User name must be a non-empty string');
  }

  if (typeof value.email !== 'string' || !value.email.includes('@')) {
    throw new TypeError('User email must be valid');
  }

  return {
    id: value.id,
    name: value.name.trim(),
    email: value.email.trim(),
  };
}

const apiResponse = {
  id: 2,
  name: '  Priya  ',
  email: 'priya@example.com',
};

const validatedUser = parseUser(apiResponse);
console.log('Validated API user:', validatedUser);
assert.equal(validatedUser.name, 'Priya');

console.log('\nStep 3: Model UI states with a discriminated union pattern');

// A TypeScript version can use a union of loading, success, and error types.
// This JavaScript function demonstrates the same runtime branching.
function describeRequestState(state) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'loading':
      return 'Loading users...';
    case 'success':
      return `Loaded ${state.users.length} users.`;
    case 'error':
      return `Request failed: ${state.message}`;
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unknown status: ${state.status}`);
  }
}

const loadingState = { status: 'loading' };
const successState = {
  status: 'success',
  users: [validatedUser],
};
const errorState = {
  status: 'error',
  message: 'Unable to reach the server',
};

console.log(describeRequestState(loadingState));
console.log(describeRequestState(successState));
console.log(describeRequestState(errorState));
assert.match(describeRequestState(successState), /Loaded 1 users/);

console.log('\nStep 4: Update collections immutably');

const products = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Soap', price: 99, active: true },
  { id: 2, name: 'Shampoo', price: 199, active: true },
  { id: 3, name: 'Oil', price: 149, active: false },
];

// Never modify an existing React state array directly.
// map creates a new array and spread creates a new product object.
const updatedProducts = products.map((product) =>
  product.id === 2
    ? { ...product, price: 179 }
    : product
);

const activeProducts = updatedProducts.filter(
  (product) => product.active
);

console.log('Original shampoo price:', products[1].price);
console.log('Updated shampoo price:', updatedProducts[1].price);
console.log('Active products:', activeProducts);
assert.equal(products[1].price, 199);
assert.equal(updatedProducts[1].price, 179);

console.log('\nStep 5: Use predictable state transitions');

// This reducer can be shared by UI logic and unit tests.
function cartReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return {
        ...state,
        items: [...state.items, action.product],
      };
    case 'remove':
      return {
        ...state,
        items: state.items.filter(
          (item) => item.id !== action.id
        ),
      };
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unsupported action: ${action.type}`);
  }
}

const emptyCart = { items: [] };
const cartWithProduct = cartReducer(emptyCart, {
  type: 'add',
  product: { id: 10, name: 'Neem Soap', price: 99 },
});

console.log('Cart after adding product:', cartWithProduct);
console.log('Original cart remains unchanged:', emptyCart);
assert.equal(cartWithProduct.items.length, 1);
assert.equal(emptyCart.items.length, 0);

const emptyCartAgain = cartReducer(cartWithProduct, {
  type: 'remove',
  id: 10,
});

console.log('Cart after removing product:', emptyCartAgain);
assert.equal(emptyCartAgain.items.length, 0);

console.log('\nStep 6: Handle asynchronous operations safely');

// In React, manage loading and error states explicitly and consider
// AbortController or effect cleanup when a component unmounts.
async function loadUsers(fetchImplementation) {
  try {
    const response = await fetchImplementation();

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP error: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const payload = await response.json();

    if (!Array.isArray(payload)) {
      throw new TypeError('Expected an array of users');
    }

    return {
      status: 'success',
      users: payload.map(parseUser),
    };
  } catch (error) {
    return {
      status: 'error',
      message: error instanceof Error
        ? error.message
        : 'Unexpected error',
    };
  }
}

async function main() {
  const result = await loadUsers(async () => ({
    ok: true,
    status: 200,
    json: async () => [
      { id: 4, name: 'Riya', email: 'riya@example.com' },
    ],
  }));

  console.log('API operation result:', result);
  assert.equal(result.status, 'success');
  assert.equal(result.users.length, 1);

  const failedResult = await loadUsers(async () => ({
    ok: false,
    status: 503,
    json: async () => ({}),
  }));

  console.log('Handled API failure:', failedResult);
  assert.equal(failedResult.status, 'error');

  console.log('\nAll examples completed successfully.');
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error('Unexpected example failure:', error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Conclusion

React and TypeScript work best when types communicate clear contracts, components have focused responsibilities, and state transitions remain predictable. Runtime validation is equally important because external data can violate the assumptions expressed by your TypeScript definitions.

Start by enabling strict TypeScript checks, typing component props and event handlers, avoiding unnecessary any types, and modeling asynchronous states explicitly. Add runtime validation where data enters the application, and test business logic independently from component rendering whenever practical.

The goal is not to add types everywhere simply to satisfy the compiler. It is to make incorrect states harder to represent, make component behavior easier to understand, and help your team deliver changes with confidence as the application grows.

title: Test-Time Forecasting: Recurrent Depth Enables In-Context Dynamics Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19552v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Foundation models for dynamical systems can forecast unseen partial differential equations (PDEs), ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and time series during inference. However, it remains an open question whether these foundation models truly learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies. We show that looped transformers are capable of emulating propagators for dynamical systems in-context by first establishing a link between linear attention and (extended) dynamic mode decomposition. We then generalize this insight into the $\textit{Test-Time Forecasting}$ (TTF) framework in which a one-step forecaster leverages iterations of gradient descent as recurrent depth. We demonstrate that lightweight TTF models trained on ODEs and PDEs generalize to out-of-distribution system dynamics during autoregressive rollout after being trained for one-step prediction. Our results reinforce TTF as a theoretically motivated framework for designing recurrent depth models capable of forecasting unseen dynamical systems at test-time.

title: Go 1.26 Lets new() Take an Expression. Delete Your Pointer Helpers
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

In April 2021, Rob Pike opened golang/go#45624, "spec: expression to create pointer to simple types", as an alternative to an older proposal, #9097. Getting a pointer to a struct was always easy: &S{a: 3}. Getting a pointer to the number 3 was not. When Alan Donovan closed the issue in October 2025, he signed off with a joke: "All done, in only eleven years since #9097. ;-)"

That fix shipped in Go 1.26, released on February 10, 2026. The built-in new now accepts an expression, not only a type. new(42) compiles. So does new(time.Now()).

If your codebase has a ptr[T], a StringPtr, an IntPtr, or a utils/pointer.go file that every package imports, you can likely delete most of it now, and go fix will do the bulk of the work.

Why every Go codebase grew a pointer helper

Go has no Optional[T]. When a field can be absent, and absent has to mean something different from zero, the usual answer is a pointer. The Go 1.26 release notes call this out directly: the feature is "particularly useful when working with serialization packages such as encoding/json or protocol buffers that use a pointer to represent an optional value."

The trouble was always the write side. You cannot take the address of a constant or of a function call's result, so &42 and &time.Now() do not compile. Teams kept writing the same one-line escape hatch, and the ecosystem shipped its own copies: proto.String and proto.Int64 in protobuf-go, ptr.To in k8s.io/utils, ToPtr in samber/lo. The protobuf ones are a single line each: func String(v string) *string { return &v }.

Here is the pattern you probably have today. A settings payload where "retries not set" and "retries set to 0" are different instructions:

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func ptr[T any](v T) *T { return &v }

type Settings struct {
    Theme   *string    `json:"theme,omitempty"`
    Retries *int       `json:"retries,omitempty"`
    Beta    *bool      `json:"beta,omitempty"`
    Updated *time.Time `json:"updated,omitempty"`
}

func main() {
    s := Settings{
        Theme:   ptr("dark"),
        Retries: ptr(0),
        Beta:    ptr(false),
        Updated: ptr(time.Now()),
    }
    b, err := json.Marshal(s)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(b))
}

Retries: ptr(0) is the whole reason the pointer exists. omitempty drops a nil pointer, but a non-nil pointer to 0 is kept, so the JSON says "retries":0 instead of saying nothing.


The helper was always a detour: take a value, park it in a variable, hand back the address.

The same code on Go 1.26

Delete ptr and call the built-in:

func main() {
    s := Settings{
        Theme:   new("dark"),
        Retries: new(0),
        Beta:    new(false),
        Updated: new(time.Now()),
    }
    b, err := json.Marshal(s)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(b))
}

The behavior is the same as the helper. The spec's Allocation section now reads: "If the argument is an expression x, then new(x) allocates a variable of the type of x initialized to the value of x." new(int) still gives you a pointer to 0. new(123) gives you a pointer to 123. Both are *int.

For this to compile, the module (or the file, through a build constraint) has to declare Go 1.26 or later. If your go.mod still says go 1.25, bump it:

go mod edit -go=1.26

That raises the minimum Go version for anyone who imports your module. For an application that is usually fine. For a library, it is a decision, and it is the first case where the old helper wins (more on that below). Go 1.27 has been out since August 19, 2026 and its release notes make no change to new(expr), so either current release works.

The sweep: go fix -newexpr

You do not have to hunt the call sites by hand. Go 1.26 also rewrote go fix into the home of Go's modernizers, built on the same analysis framework as go vet. One of them, newexpr, targets exactly this pattern. Alan Donovan's post on the Go blog shows the command to run only that fixer:

# preview first
go fix -diff -newexpr ./...

# apply
go fix -newexpr ./...

# read the analyzer's own docs
go tool fix help newexpr

What it does, according to the analyzer docs and its source:

  • It finds "new-like" functions: one non-variadic parameter, one pointer result, and a body that is a single return &param. Reading the source, a generic ptr[T] should qualify too: the match is on the parameter itself rather than its type, and the call-site check carries a comment saying it is formulated that way "to support generics."
  • It rewrites the helper's body to return new(x) and adds a //go:fix inline directive, so the source-level inliner can treat calls to it as inlinable.
  • It rewrites call sites like ptr("dark") to new("dark").
  • It only touches files that already require Go 1.26, so bump go.mod first or the diff comes back empty.
  • The helper's own body is only rewritten when its file requires Go 1.26 as well. Whether calls to helpers from other modules, like proto.String, get rewritten depends on the analyzer recognising them as new-like, so check the -diff output instead of assuming either way.

The blog also advises running go fix "more than once until it reaches a fixed point; twice is usually enough." So run the apply step twice.

Then delete the helper and run go build ./.... Whatever the fixer left behind shows up as compile errors, and that list is your manual review queue. I haven't run this sweep myself, so treat the -diff output as the source of truth for your repo.


go fix rewrites the safe calls and leaves the ones it cannot prove are equivalent.

The calls go fix leaves alone

The fixer refuses a rewrite when the new code would change the type. The check in the source compares the call's result type against a pointer to the argument's default type, and skips the call if they differ. That one rule explains most of what survives the sweep.

Untyped constants with a non-default type. The spec says an untyped constant passed to new is first converted to its default type. new(42) is *int. new(1.5) is *float64. So for a field typed *int64, new(42) does not compile, and ptr[int64](42) is not rewritten. Your hand-written version needs a conversion:

type Job struct {
    TimeoutMs *int64   `json:"timeout_ms,omitempty"`
    Ratio     *float32 `json:"ratio,omitempty"`
}

j := Job{
    TimeoutMs: new(int64(5000)),
    Ratio:     new(float32(0.25)),
}

That works, and the type is explicit. But if a protobuf message has twenty int64 fields, proto.Int64(5000) reads better than new(int64(5000)), and keeping it is a defensible call.

Shadowed new. If a package declares its own new (a constructor, a local variable), the fixer skips calls in that scope. Rename the local first.

Untyped composite literals. The analyzer's source skips arguments like {1, 2} because new({1, 2}) is a compile error. For structs you already had the better tool: &Config{Port: 8080}.

Where the helper is still the clearer choice

The fixer handles the mechanical part. These are judgment calls, and the old helper wins in each one.

You need a function value. The spec's built-in functions section says built-ins "can only appear in call expressions; they cannot be used as function values." So new cannot be passed where a func(T) *T is expected:

func mapSlice[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U {
    out := make([]U, 0, len(s))
    for _, v := range s {
        out = append(out, f(v))
    }
    return out
}

names := []string{"a", "b"}
ptrs := mapSlice(names, ptr[string]) // compiles
// mapSlice(names, new)              // does not compile

A closure works too (func(s string) *string { return new(s) }), but at that point the named helper is shorter.

Your library supports Go versions before 1.26. new(expr) is a language change, gated by the go directive. If your go.mod promises 1.24 compatibility, you keep the helper until you drop that promise.

The read side. new(expr) only helps you build pointers. Reading an optional field with a default still needs a helper, like ptr.Deref in k8s.io/utils (func Deref[T any](ptr *T, def T) T). Delete ptr[T], keep deref[T].

new(x) is not &x. It allocates a fresh variable holding a copy of x, exactly like the helper did:

n := 1
p := new(n) // copy of n
q := &n     // address of n
n = 2
// *p is 1, *q is 2

If you wanted aliasing, you still want &.

A five-minute checklist

  1. Bump go.mod to go 1.26 or later (applications only, or libraries ready to drop older versions).
  2. Run go fix -diff -newexpr ./... and read the diff.
  3. Apply with go fix -newexpr ./..., twice.
  4. Delete the helper, run go build ./..., and fix what is left by hand: add conversions like new(int64(5000)), or keep a typed helper on purpose.
  5. Keep any helper you pass as a function value, and keep your deref helper.

Run step 2 on your repo first. The diff tells you how big the job really is.

If this was useful

If the tricky part of this post was the language underneath it, The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers that ground: pointers and zero values, why built-ins like new behave differently from ordinary functions, how untyped constants pick their default type, and the standard library packages such as encoding/json that lean on pointers for "absent". It is the reference to keep open when a release like 1.26 changes a rule you thought was settled.

title: Quicken iPhone App: A Companion, Not a Source of Truth
description:
AI Mode Answer
The Quicken iPhone app has improved, with a 4.6 average rating on the App Store and regular updates, but sync issues are still reported, including a known problem where the mobile budget doesn't update after new transactions. It works best as a companion to the desktop app: build the budget on the desktop, then use the phone to check balances and capture spending. When sync keeps failing, an independent Quicken consultant can review the setup.

Quick Answer

  • The app can show your budget and transactions and accept new entries on the go.
  • Sync complaints continue, so treat the desktop as the source of truth.
  • Verify important numbers on the desktop before acting on them.

A recent question on Reddit's Quicken community asked whether the iPhone app has finally been fixed. The poster wanted Quicken on the go, mainly to get a grip on their budget.

It's a good question to look at the way an engineer would, because most of the frustration with a companion app is really about sync, not about the app itself.

This reflects information available in mid-October 2026. Check the current App Store listing and Quicken's support pages before relying on it.

What the app is designed to do

According to the App Store listing, the app lets you see spending trends and check your budget, view balances, accounts and transactions, enter transactions even when offline, and sync automatically with the desktop. Quicken's mobile help page describes the same pattern: create the budget on the desktop and check it on the phone. (That page was last updated in 2020, so treat its details with caution.)

What the evidence says

Signs of improvement

  • A 4.6 out of 5 average from about 15,000 ratings on the App Store
  • Regular "improvements and bug fixes" releases, with dark mode added in 8.4.0

Signs of remaining problems

  • Sample reviews on the same listing mention edits not carrying over between desktop and mobile
  • A Quicken community thread on the iOS companion app budget not updating describes budget totals that don't change after new transactions are entered, even after refreshing. A reported workaround is logging out and back in. Quicken said it escalated the issue, and as of mid-May 2026 it was still marked ongoing with no estimated fix date.

So "fixed" overstates it. A more accurate summary is: usable, actively maintained, with a known sync issue on budgets.

A mental model that helps

This is my own framing, not a description of Quicken's internal design: think of the setup as a primary store with a sync client.

Desktop file  <--sync-->  Cloud  <--sync-->  Phone app
(primary)                                    (companion)

When two copies of data can be edited in more than one place, you get the usual distributed-data headaches: stale reads, delayed updates, and the occasional conflict. A few habits keep those under control.

Habits that make it reliable

  1. Build and edit the budget on the desktop. Treat the phone as a viewer and a quick-entry tool.
  2. Let the desktop finish syncing first. Then open the phone app. Letting both run at once is an easy way to create mismatches.
  3. If the budget looks stale, try the known workaround. Log out of the mobile app and back in. It's a workaround, not a fix.
  4. Cross-check important numbers on the desktop. If the two disagree, trust the desktop and look for the cause.
  5. Keep both apps current. Version mismatches can cause odd behavior.
  6. Back up the desktop data file before changing sync settings or troubleshooting.
  7. Watch for duplicates. A transaction entered by hand on the phone can also arrive from the bank. Review the downloaded transactions list and accept or match items carefully.

Debugging checklist when it still doesn't match

  • [ ] Desktop fully synced?
  • [ ] Phone app updated?
  • [ ] Logged out and back in?
  • [ ] Budget category matches on both sides?
  • [ ] Duplicate or unaccepted transactions on the desktop?
  • [ ] Recent Quicken or iOS update that could explain the change?

If all of that checks out and the mismatch continues, the issue may lie in your specific setup, such as the version, the account connections, or how the data file syncs.

Getting a second pair of eyes

Quick Advisors Hub is an independent advisory service for Quicken users. You send a description of the problem, the scope and fee are confirmed in writing before you pay, and you receive written, prioritized steps. It doesn't use remote access or ask for passwords. For billing, subscription or Quicken ID matters, go to Quicken directly through its official website.

Takeaway

The iPhone app is worth another look if you treat it as a companion to the desktop. Keep one place as the source of truth, sync in a consistent order, and verify the numbers that matter.

title: Model vs. User: Whose Values Prevail? Inference-Time Value Alignment in Multi-Turn Conversations
description:
arXiv:2610.19817v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human values shape how we expect language models to behave. Dominant alignment approaches treat values as global objectives, although the appropriate value orientation is personal and contextual. Training-free alignment can steer models toward target values at inference time, yet has been largely evaluated in single-turn settings and with a single steering direction (e.g., toward safety). We evaluate four prompt- and activation-based steering methods in multi-turn conversations, where user and assistant models push toward the same or opposing, equally desirable values. We track alignment with a linear probe across three models and two value trade-offs. When assistant and user pull in opposite directions, the side matching the assistant's baseline bias often prevails, and effects that look successful early often fade or reverse after a few turns. Steering should therefore be evaluated over full conversations and in both directions of a value trade-off.

title: NEPSEE: A Double-Annotated Benchmark for Nepali Sentiment Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.19190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many sentiment datasets use one annotator for each item, so the test labels show the conventions of that person. We build a Nepali benchmark from two annotators who labelled the same sentences blind. They labelled 5,614 sentences from tweets of Nepali public figures on a five-point scale. We keep only the 3,189 sentences where both give the same polarity. On the three-class benchmark, NepBERTa with a fixed tokenizer gets a macro-F1 of 0.877 and IndicBERTv2 0.867. Three commercial large language models (LLMs) get 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot, and these differences are not significant. On the five-point scale, 766 sentences have two adjacent labels, for example Pos and SPos. We accept both labels and train on both. On this task, Claude Opus 5.5 beats the best encoders by 0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1. A tokenizer audit adds a second result. The default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models delete the non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama. When we restore the marks, macro-F1 increases by 0.084 for NepBERTa but decreases by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.

title: Infant Fingerprints: Quality Assessment & Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.20432v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Infant fingerprint recognition is hindered by a combination of physiological characteristics, such as small ridge width and spacing, and acquisition challenges that include involuntary motion, skin residue, and uneven fingertip pressure. These factors undermine fingerprint quality standards originally designed for adults, which assume feature distributions that do not hold for infants. To address this gap, this paper evaluates ten fingerprint quality assessment methods on a longitudinal dataset that spans six age groups from newborns to three months, alongside a parameter tuning routine that uncovers age-specific fingerprint characteristics to recalibrate methods with domain-dependent assumptions. Both default and tuned configurations are compared through recognition experiments assessing the effectiveness of quality-guided gallery selection. Template-fusion strategies and latent fingerprint recognition technologies are further examined to identify the best possible matching rates achievable by the top-performing method. Results show that tuned parameter sets outperform default configurations for the majority of methods and age groups, indicating that targeted recalibration of existing frameworks improves gallery utility and contributes to more reliable infant fingerprint recognition.

title: Knowledge transfer between simple discrete worlds
description:
arXiv:2610.15081v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adapting to a new world and reasoning correctly about which outcomes are possible under rules one has not met before is a basic capacity underlying general intelligence. We study it in small discrete worlds: sets of grid configurations consistent with a shared set of rules, concretely Sudoku-like puzzles built from a common base and a handful of extra rules. We train a single depth-recurrent model on many combinations of rules and test it at four levels of novelty: a new puzzle, a new combination of known rules, a pairing of rules never seen together, and a rule instance not seen at all during training. The model receives the active rules either as a symbolic description or as two solved examples, and a model that gets no rule information is used as a baseline. At recombining rules it was trained on, the description matches or exceeds examples ($99\%$ against $95\%$ on new combinations). On rule instances whose components never co-occurred in training, the description falls below the no-information baseline while examples stay above it. The framework allows us to test many such generalization regimes in more systematic way than benchmarks such as ARC-AGI and provides new ground for evaluating depth-recurrent reasoning models, which are typically tested on saturated Sudoku benchmarks.

title: Your Test Didn't Flake. Your UI Moved While Nobody Was Looking.
description:
A test clicks Save. The app saves the record. A green toast appears, hangs around for two seconds, and blocks the next button.

The test fails.

Someone adds a three-second sleep. The test passes. Everyone moves on.

Two weeks later, the toast takes four seconds to disappear on a busy CI machine. Same failure. Different Monday.

I think this is one of the most expensive habits in frontend testing: treating every unpredictable UI event as a timing problem. Sometimes the timing is fine. The application has changed which element is actually available for interaction.

A small UI change can be a big state change

Modern apps throw a surprising amount of stuff at a browser: notifications, loading masks, drawers, dropdowns, permission prompts, confirmation dialogs, and third-party widgets. Any of these can alter where focus goes or which control is on top.

Imagine this sequence:

  1. A user changes a billing address.
  2. A confirmation dialog opens.
  3. Clicking Confirm triggers a loading overlay.
  4. A toast slides across the bottom of the page.
  5. The test tries to click Continue.

If Continue is behind the toast, clicking it isn't a legitimate user action at that moment. Retrying the same coordinates is no better. A useful test should wait for an actionable state, then locate the button again.

This is why I like the idea behind this benchmark for testing toast interference and modal stacking. It separates completing the flow from recovering sensibly when the interface gets noisy. Those are different abilities.

A test that passes after twenty silent retries isn't automatically better than one that fails immediately with a screenshot showing the obstruction.

The DOM can be ready while the experience isn't

React and Next.js introduce a variation of the same problem. The server sends HTML. The browser paints it. Hydration begins. Something changes.

The button you found on the first render might be replaced, disabled, or wired to behavior only after hydration. This creates a particularly irritating failure: everything looks fine in the screenshot, but the click happens at the wrong stage.

Blanket rules such as "fail the build for every hydration warning" are tempting. They also make it hard to distinguish a harmless discrepancy from a broken purchase button.

A more useful approach is to reproduce the mismatch, identify the affected component, and assert the interaction the user actually needs. There's a focused walkthrough of testing React and Next.js hydration mismatches without treating every warning as fatal.

The key question isn't whether the console is immaculate. It's whether the page ended up usable and correct.

Focus bugs are the quiet cousin of click bugs

Custom comboboxes are a great trap for overconfident tests. You type into the box, see an option, click it, and assume the widget works.

Now try the same thing without touching the mouse.

Does Arrow Down move the active option? Does Escape close the list? Does focus remain where it should? Does aria-activedescendant point to a real option? Does Enter choose the highlighted item rather than the first item in the DOM?

A click-only test can happily pass through a component that fails for keyboard users. The combobox and typeahead testing guide is worth using as a checklist when you're dealing with custom widgets.

I'd add one rule: check the resulting value and focus state, not merely whether a dropdown was visible.

Please stop screenshotting every pixel

The same mistaken obsession with implementation details shows up in layout testing.

A grid can reflow because content grows, a font changes, or the viewport narrows. That doesn't necessarily mean the user experience is broken. Meanwhile, a footer button can become inaccessible with only a tiny visible change.

For CSS subgrid and intrinsic sizing, I'd rather assert things like:

  • Key elements don't overlap.
  • Important controls remain inside the viewport or reachable by scrolling.
  • Text isn't clipped.
  • Reading and tab order still make sense.

Use screenshots for visually meaningful regressions, not as the only definition of correctness. The practical examples in this piece on testing CSS subgrid and layout reflows make that distinction nicely.

A better way to debug the next "flaky" failure

When the next intermittent click failure appears, resist the immediate urge to increase a timeout. First find out what was actually on screen. Was the button covered? Was it disabled? Did the page re-render? Where was keyboard focus? Which state was the app in immediately before the action?

Then create a small, repeatable version of the problem. Force the toast to appear. Delay the hydration step. Stack the dialogs. Navigate with the keyboard.

A test that fails consistently under a known bad state is easier to fix than a test that passes inconsistently after a random sleep.

The funny part is that teams often spend more time arguing about locator syntax than asking whether the element was genuinely available to the user. The second question is usually where the bug lives.

title: How to add a like animation in React (and play it in reverse)
description:
When you come across something you like in an app, a great article, a funny video, a photo that catches your eye, you want to respond, so you hit the like button. If the heart just switches from an outline to a solid icon, it's kind of meh. Okay, I clicked it, but did anything really happen? If the heart fills up and bounces a little, it feels like your tap actually meant something.

I'm not a coder, I'm a motion designer. I create animations like this in After Effects, and I was curious to see how they'd work in a real interface, so I built this button from scratch. This is what I figured out along the way.

Building that bounce in CSS takes keyframes, a scale curve, a color transition and a second set of rules for un-liking. With Lottie, you take the motion a designer made in After Effects as a small JSON file, and React only has to tell it when to play and in which direction.

Here's the whole thing, step by step.

What you need

  • A React app (React 18.2 or newer)
  • A like animation in Lottie format. You can use mine: like.json for light-on-dark UIs, or like-light.json for dark-on-light. It's 3.5 KB and free to use in your projects.

1. Install lottie-react 

npm i lottie-react

This installs lottie-react v3, which brings lottie-web (the player) with it.

2. The component 

import { useState } from "react";
import { useLottie } from "lottie-react";
import likeAnimation from "./like.json";

export function LikeButton() {
  const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false);
  const lottie = useLottie({ src: likeAnimation, autoplay: false, loop: false });

  const toggle = () => {
    lottie.setDirection(liked ? "reverse" : "forward");
    lottie.play();
    setLiked(!liked);
  };

  return (
    <button
      onClick={toggle}
      aria-pressed={liked}
      aria-label={liked ? "Unlike" : "Like"}
      style={{ background: "none", border: 0, padding: 0, cursor: "pointer" }}
    >
      <div ref={lottie.setDisplayRef} style={{ width: 48, height: 48 }} />
    </button>
  );
}

That's it. Drop <LikeButton /> anywhere.

3. How it works

The animation goes from "not liked" on its first frame to "liked" on its last frame. So:

  • autoplay: false and loop: false keep it parked on the first frame until someone taps.
  • On like, we set the direction to "forward" and call play(). The heart fills and bounces.
  • On unlike, we set the direction to "reverse" and call play(). The same motion runs backwards and the heart empties.

The logic is three lines: pick a direction, play, flip the state. Everything else is markup.

aria-pressed tells screen readers the button is a toggle, and the label changes with it, so the animation isn't the only way to know the state.

The easy mistake: restarting instead of reversing

The tempting way to un-like is to jump to the start and play a separate "unlike" animation, or to reset the animation to frame 0. It looks fine when you tap slowly. Now tap twice quickly: the second tap lands while the heart is still bouncing, the animation snaps to its start, and the heart visibly jumps.

Playing in reverse doesn't have this problem. If you tap while the heart is still moving, in either direction, setDirection turns the animation around from exactly where it is, so it always moves smoothly. Try tapping fast in the demo: it never jumps.

One more thing if you're copying from older tutorials. Many of them are written for lottie-react v2, which used animationData and setDirection(-1). In v3 the prop is src and the direction is a word, "forward" or "reverse". If your copied snippet throws or does nothing, that's usually why.

Make it yours: change the color

The heart is orange in my file. Lottie stores colors as numbers inside the JSON, so you can swap them before you pass the animation in:

type Hex = `#${string}`;
const toRgb = (hex: Hex) => [1, 3, 5].map((i) => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255);

export function recolor<T>(animation: T, colors: Record<Hex, Hex>): T {
  const swaps = Object.entries(colors).map(([from, to]) => [toRgb(from as Hex), toRgb(to as Hex)]);
  const copy = structuredClone(animation);
  const walk = (node: any): void => {
    if (Array.isArray(node)) return node.forEach(walk);
    if (!node || typeof node !== "object") return;
    const k = node.c?.k;
    if ((node.ty === "fl" || node.ty === "st") && Array.isArray(k) && typeof k[0] === "number") {
      const hit = swaps.find(([from]) => from.every((v, i) => Math.abs(v - k[i]) < 0.01));
      if (hit) node.c.k = [...hit[1], k[3] ?? 1];
    }
    Object.values(node).forEach(walk);
  };
  walk(copy);
  return copy;
}

Then, once at the top of your file (outside the component):

const pinkLike = recolor(likeAnimation, { "#FF4A1C": "#E11D48" });

and pass src: pinkLike. The animation uses only two colors, the line (#F2F1ED, or #121212 in the light version) and the accent (#FF4A1C), so two entries are enough to match any brand.

Wrapping up

A like that lands instead of flipping is a small thing, but it's the kind of small thing people feel without being able to name it. With lottie-react it costs you a 3.5 KB file and three lines of logic.

The animation in this post is from Zeltrium, my pack of Lottie UI micro-interactions. Get 5 more free at zeltrium.com.

title: Building a Decentralized Mesh Network in Rust: GhostWire
description:
Building a Decentralized Mesh Network in Rust: GhostWire

GhostWire is an open protocol and reference implementation for resilient peer-to-peer communication. It is built in Rust with libp2p, XChaCha20-Poly1305, X25519/ML-KEM hybrid post-quantum key exchange, delay-tolerant networking, and AI-assisted routing.

Why GhostWire exists

Most communication systems assume a working internet, centralized servers, and stable identities. GhostWire assumes the opposite: intermittent connectivity, untrusted infrastructure, and real physical threats. It is built for disaster responders, rural communities, privacy advocates, and developers who need communication that still works when the normal stack fails.

What works today

  • Encrypted P2P messaging over libp2p
  • Forward secrecy with a symmetric ratchet
  • Peer discovery with mDNS, DHT, and bootstrap peers
  • Delay-tolerant store-carry-forward routing
  • Post-quantum key encapsulation (ML-KEM)
  • Terminal UI and Axum-based REST API
  • 200+ passing tests

Protocol stack 

Application: messaging, knowledge ark, ghost channels
API: REST, WebSocket, CLI, TUI
Services: block store, mailbox, social, Sphinx
AI routing: LightGBM -> Gemma 4 -> GNN -> PRoPHET
Crypto: XChaCha20-Poly1305, X25519, ML-KEM-768
Transports: TCP, WebRTC, BLE, LoRa, obfs4, Reticulum
Mesh: libp2p GossipSub, Kademlia DHT, DTN

Quick start 

git clone https://codeberg.org/PHANTOMOJO/GhostWire-secure-mesh-communication.git
cd GhostWire-secure-mesh-communication/ghostwire
cargo run --release

The node starts on http://127.0.0.1:8080. Mesh networking activates with --mesh-port.

Build on it

GhostWire is a protocol, not just an app. Use it as a Rust crate, REST API, or implement the spec in another language.

Read the spec: docs/spec/
GitHub/Codeberg: https://codeberg.org/PHANTOMOJO/GhostWire-secure-mesh-communication
Website: https://www.ghostwire.cc/

Contribute

We welcome code, tests, docs, security review, and field testing. Good first issues and help-wanted labels are being prepared now. If you work on mesh networking, privacy, DTN, or Rust crypto, your review would help.

title: Synthetic reaction data from transformation rules for graph-to-sequence pretraining in biodegradation pathway prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The scarcity of observed biodegradation reactions constrains the training of product and pathway predictors. We present enviGraph, a framework that generates and curates synthetic reaction data, uses these data to pretrain a graph-to-sequence predictor, and fine-tunes the predictor on observed environmental reactions for product and recursive pathway prediction. Applying inherited environmental transformation rules to structures from PubChem, NORMAN SusDat and EPA DSSTox, followed by curation, produces 776,851 canonical parent-product pairs for pretraining. We compare this dataset with three United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) reaction datasets: USPTO-50K, USPTO-MIT and USPTO-Stereo. We evaluate enviGraph and the sequence-based enviFormer using ten folds split by pathway on the EAWAG Biocatalysis/Biodegradation Database (BBD), regulatory pesticide biodegradation data (Soil) and activated-sludge biodegradation data (Sludge). For both predictors, synthetic pretraining gives the highest BBD mean precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) among the evaluated pretraining datasets for single-generation and multi-generation prediction. enviGraph achieves BBD single-generation PR-AUC of $0.202 \pm 0.050$ with synthetic pretraining, compared with $0.169 \pm 0.065$ for the retrospectively selected strongest USPTO condition, USPTO-Stereo (mean $\pm$ sample standard deviation across folds). Its exact BBD top-1 and top-5 accuracies with synthetic pretraining are 0.355 and 0.594. The strongest USPTO conditions give higher PR-AUC means than synthetic pretraining in most Soil and Sludge comparisons. enviGraph has higher Soil multi-generation PR-AUC means than enviFormer under each of the four main pretraining datasets, and with synthetic pretraining it also leads enviFormer on BBD single-generation PR-AUC and exact top-1 and top-5 accuracy.

title: Event Cameras versus Frame Cameras for Synthetic-Aperture Imaging: A Simulation Study
description:
arXiv:2610.20309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthetic-aperture imaging (SAI) removes occluders such as foliage by integrating many views of a scene along a camera path. It has so far been used mainly with frame cameras. We ask whether an event camera has advantages for SAI, and answer the question in simulation, where both sensors see exactly the same scene and the same camera movement. A densely rendered Blender sequence is turned into frames with an EMVA~1288 noise model of an industrial global-shutter camera, and into an event stream with the v2e simulator parameterized like a Sony IMX636. The frames are integrated with the existing airborne optical sectioning renderer. For the events we add a new integration path that projects every single event onto the focal plane at its own interpolated pose, so no events have to be binned into frames. We compare the two sensors in three main runs and an additional dark high-speed test. In a bright scene at 25,m/s the frame camera records only three images on the path and cannot remove the occluder, while the event camera reconstructs the target, even after an event-rate controller drops most of its events to fit the camera link. At the same speed in a 5,lux scene the event camera no longer resolves the target either. In a 5,lux scene at 5,m/s both sensors reconstruct the target at similar quality. We also compare the data one traversal of the aperture costs. At high speed the capped event stream still shows the target at the same data volume as the three frames. At 1,m/s we compare both cameras at two matched data budgets, and there the event camera has no advantage over the frame camera in reconstruction quality. The data rate of the event camera depends on the scene and is highest exactly in the fast bright scenes where it is needed most.

title: The Impact of Detector Architecture, Model Scale, and Scene Density on Multi-Pedestrian Tracking
description:
arXiv:2610.19369v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pedestrian tracking in video is important for applications such as surveillance and scene analysis, but it becomes more challenging in crowded scenarios with frequent occlusions and rapid motion. This paper analyzes how detector architecture, model scale, scene density, and inference regime affect the tracking of multiple pedestrians. We compare the YOLO11, RT-DETR, and YOLO26 detector families with the ByteTrack and BoT-SORT trackers on sequences from the MOT17, MOT20, and SOMPT22 benchmarks. For YOLO26, we also compare traditional overlap filtering via Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) with end-to-end inference. The RT-DETR family achieved the highest mean scores on the HOTA tracking quality metric across all three benchmarks with both trackers, with a more pronounced advantage on MOT20, albeit at a higher computational cost. On MOT17 and SOMPT22, YOLO26 variants, especially YOLO26-L with NMS, offered favorable combinations of quality and speed compared with RT-DETR. In the YOLO26 inference comparison, the end-to-end mode did not yield consistent tracking gains over the NMS-based regime. Taken together, these results provide a practical guide for selecting detectors and trackers for this task based on application priorities.

title: A background refresh must not move the row under your cursor, so our table renders the snapshot it loaded with
description:
Nakodo finds creators on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok for a brand, scores each one and emails the good fits. The part of the app this post is about is the boring part: the table of what it has found so far, which the owner of the campaign reads, sorts, filters and ticks boxes in while the pipeline behind it is still adding rows.

The page is a server component. A small client component polls an endpoint for a fingerprint of the campaign's data and calls router.refresh() when it changes:

export function AutoRefresh({ campaignId, every = 30_000 }: { campaignId: string; every?: number }) {

Thirty seconds on the campaign's own pages, five on the outreach page while a draft is being written. Each quiet check doubles the wait, and the timer stops while the tab is hidden. (That endpoint and its fingerprint were their own post; this post is about what the refresh does to the page it lands on.)

router.refresh() is lovely. It re-renders the server component, keeps client state, and the new rows appear. It is also, in a sorted table, a small act of violence: the pointer is over row 14, a creator two rows up finishes being scored, the sort is by score, and row 14 is now a different creator. The checkbox you were about to tick belongs to someone else.

The list is not rows

The component takes rows as a prop and never renders it directly. On first render it captures a Map of the two fields the list sorts on:

type Snapshot = Map<string, { score: number | null; stage: string }>;

const snapshotOf = (rows: ResultRow[]): Snapshot =>
  new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.channelId, { score: r.score, stage: r.stage }]));

Then the list it renders is built from rows and the snapshot together:

const { shown, changed } = useMemo(() => {
  const shown: ResultRow[] = [];
  let changed = 0;
  for (const r of rows) {
    const s = snapshot.get(r.channelId);
    if (!s) {
      changed++;
      continue;
    }
    const same = s.score === r.score && s.stage === r.stage;
    if (!same) changed++;
    shown.push(same ? r : { ...r, score: s.score, stage: s.stage });
  }
  return { shown, changed };
}, [rows, snapshot]);

Three things fall out of that loop.

A row the snapshot has never seen is not rendered. It is counted.

A row whose score or stage has moved is rendered with the old score and stage. Every other field is the fresh one: a name, an avatar, a thread status, a view count. Only the two values the order depends on are held back, because they are the two that can move a row.

Everything else about the refresh still works. Counts in the header update, the "waiting on you" box updates, a creator whose conversation has advanced shows its new badge. The row simply stays where it is.

The banner is the whole feature 

{changed > 0 && (
  <div role="status" className="...">
    <span>{plural(changed, w.one, w.many)} found or updated since this list loaded.</span>
    <Button
      size="xs"
      variant="outline"
      onClick={() => {
        setFresh(new Set(rows.filter((r) => !snapshot.has(r.channelId)).map((r) => r.channelId)));
        setSnapshot(snapshotOf(rows));
      }}
    >
      Show them
    </Button>
  </div>
)}

Two setState calls in that order. fresh is the set of ids that were not in the old snapshot, so it has to be computed before the snapshot is replaced. Re-snapshotting is what admits the new rows, because shown is derived from the snapshot.

The rows in fresh arrive with a highlight and a mark:

@keyframes row-arrive {
  0% { opacity: 0; background-color: var(--selected); box-shadow: inset 2px 0 0 var(--color-cyano-600); }
  12%,
  40% { opacity: 1; background-color: var(--selected); box-shadow: inset 2px 0 0 var(--color-cyano-600); }
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .row-arrive {
    animation: row-arrive 2.4s ease-out calc(var(--i, 0) * 50ms) backwards;
  }
}

--i is the row's index in the visible list, Math.min(i, 10), so twelve new rows stagger over half a second instead of over six. backwards is what makes the delay work: without it a row with a 500ms delay is fully visible for 500ms, then starts its own fade-in from nothing. The mark next to the name is labelled "New since this list loaded", so the highlight is not the only way to know.

The banner's role="status" costs one attribute and means the count is announced instead of appearing silently.

Two things that look like mistakes

A setState during render.

const [snapshot, setSnapshot] = useState(() => snapshotOf(rows));
if (snapshot.size === 0 && rows.length > 0) setSnapshot(snapshotOf(rows));

That is React's own documented pattern for adjusting state when props change, not a mistake, and it is here because of a real sequence: a campaign's page opens seconds after it was created, when the first search has not returned anything, so rows is empty and so is the snapshot. The first batch to arrive would otherwise be twenty rows of "found since this list loaded" against an empty table, with a button to see them. An empty snapshot is not a snapshot, so it takes whatever arrives next. An effect would do the same thing one paint later, which is one paint of an empty table with a full banner over it.

useOptimistic over the derived list, not over the prop.

const [optimistic, setOptimistic] = useOptimistic(shown, (state, change: { ids: string[]; skipped: boolean }) => {
  const ids = new Set(change.ids);
  return state.map((r) => (ids.has(r.channelId) ? { ...r, skipped: change.skipped } : r));
});

Setting a creator aside is a server action. The optimistic layer sits on top of shown, so while the action is in flight the row greys out immediately, and when the action settles and the page refreshes, the optimistic state is dropped onto a list that still has the same ordering. If useOptimistic wrapped rows, the row would grey out and then jump.

Paging works the same way, without an effect:

const [page, setPage] = useState({ key: "", limit: PAGE });
const limit = page.key === fromParam ? page.limit : PAGE;

fromParam is the serialized filters. If they differ from the key the limit was raised under, the limit is PAGE again. Changing a filter resets paging to the first fifty by arithmetic rather than by a useEffect watching the filters.

What it costs

The table is deliberately stale, and the banner is the only signal. If you walk away with the tab open and come back, the list is as it was, with a count over it. We think that is the right trade for a table you work in with a pipeline running underneath, but it is a trade: there are two values for a creator's score in the client for as long as you leave the banner alone.

The other cost is that "changed" conflates two events: a new creator, and a creator whose score moved. One sentence covers both ("found or updated"), because splitting them meant a sentence with two numbers in it and nobody needs that in a notification bar.

Go and look

You cannot see this page without an account, and that is itself checkable:

$ curl -sI https://nakodo.app/campaigns | grep -iE "^HTTP|^location"
HTTP/2 307
location: /login?next=%2Fcampaigns

What is public is the explanation of what the table is showing: how Nakodo works walks through the brief, the search and the parts of the fit score, which are the score and stage columns the snapshot is holding steady. The pricing page has the row that makes the count interesting, "Creators shown per campaign: Best 20 on Free, All on the paid plans", because the free plan's hidden rows are counted by the same predicate the table filters on.

If you have a table that re-renders from the server while somebody is using it, the pattern is four lines: snapshot the fields the order depends on, render from the snapshot, count the difference, and let the person decide when to take it.

title: TIMERSI: Towards Self-Improved Agentic Deployment for Time-Series Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19725v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series foundation models provide strong zero-shot forecast, but deployment for real- world applications still requires task-specific designs for model inputs and outputs. Direct inference can leave domain knowledge and re- curring forecast errors unaddressed, while tai- lored pipelines require substantial human ex- pertise and effort. We introduce TIMERSI, a self-improving agentic deployment system around frozen forecasting models. A cod- ing agent translates task descriptions into ex- ecutable pipeline changes. It tests each re- vision on historical forecasting windows and uses observed errors to guide subsequent re- visions. During deployment, an adaptive se- lector chooses among the resulting pipelines using completed forecasts under similar con- ditions. Across 198 tasks on TIME and FEV- bench, TIMERSI outperforms all submissions on six point and probabilistic forecasting met- rics. Controlled comparisons support the value of feedback-guided revision over non-iterative pipeline search. Further experiments verify the generalization with different coding agents and forecasting models.

title: Fully sequential Gaussian process regression for preference learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19391v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study continuous global optimization problems in which the objective function cannot be directly evaluated; rather, we observe only which of two selected design points appears to perform better, subject to noise. Such comparisons complicate the use of Gaussian process regression because they yield non-Gaussian posteriors. We consider a fully sequential approximation, based on moment-matching, that yields a fast closed-form update of the metamodel's mean and covariance. We then propose DOVE, a fully sequential sampling policy that combines an information gain criterion with randomized sampling designed to control error accumulation. Under fairly standard regularity conditions, we prove convergence rates for both statistical error and expected simple regret that depend on kernel smoothness. To our knowledge, these are the first such rates for fully sequential approximate Bayesian inference in continuous global optimization.

title: Echo: Error-Compensated 4-Bit Tensor-Parallel Communication for LLM Training and Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.14277v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tensor parallelism ends every layer with an all-reduce that sits between two dependent matrix multiplications, so its cost cannot be hidden and grows as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth. Sending 4-bit instead of 16-bit values would cut this cost by nearly 4x, but the all-reduce must add the values it carries, and rounding the sum injects an error at every call. Model quality depends on how these errors accumulate over layers, yet existing methods treat each call on its own. We present Echo, a 4-bit all-reduce for training and inference that controls the accumulated error. Echo moves data in 4 bits and sums in high precision, so each value is quantized at most twice per call for any number of GPUs. The summation reveals each injected error, and Echo feeds it back into later calls, so old errors cancel instead of accumulating. We prove that the accumulated error stays bounded independently of depth. On A100 GPUs, Echo is 2.09x faster than the 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB messages. It speeds up the time to first token by up to 1.16x and the training step by up to 1.09x on an idle interconnect, and by up to 1.44x and 1.38x as background traffic grows. It keeps the average accuracy over seven benchmarks within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference on Qwen3-8B. In 10B-token pretraining, its final loss is less than 0.9% above that of 16-bit training. Echo needs no FP8 or FP4 hardware.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.19636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

java

graph.upsertDocument(docId, text);

How we proved parity

Most ports test final output. We tested ordered behavior.

* 33 scenarios vs Python RagLeap 0.13.0 (d210dab)
* Fake embedder, vector store, generator, memory, hooks
* Full ordered log must match — calls, hooks, memory writes
* Mutation test — change behavior → test fails

title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.15221v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.

title: PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
description:
arXiv:2610.14570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. We introduce PsyMemBehav, which maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning. To support this approach with comprehensive behavioral traces, we construct a dataset PsyMemBehav-bench from 5.57M observed behaviors of 5,862 real users (approximately 950 per user) across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter. Each recorded engagement is modeled as target selection followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation. PsyMemBehav combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO over complete reasoning-action trajectories. Experiments show that PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first in 11 of 12 reported individual-level metrics, improving average response quality over GPT-5.4 from 54.28 to 59.68 (9.95% relative), and obtains the lowest group-level MAE (0.081) and MSE (0.009) among simulated systems. These results support evidence-grounded user modeling for observed-thread continuation; the benchmark remains conditional on recorded engagement and does not model no-action decisions.

title: MCP Explained for Frontend Developers: The USB-C of AI Integrations
description:
AI is everywhere today. We have GitHub Copilot writing code, ChatGPT answering questions, and AI agents capable of performing complex workflows. But there is one problem: every AI application needs a different way to connect with tools, databases, APIs, and services.

Imagine buying a laptop that requires a different cable for charging, data transfer, and external displays. It would be frustrating.

That's exactly how AI integrations have looked for a long time.

Enter Model Context Protocol (MCP), a new standard designed to make AI systems communicate with external tools in a consistent way.

In simple terms, MCP is like USB-C for AI applications.

The Problem Before MCP

Let's say you're building a frontend application that allows users to interact with an AI assistant.

Your AI needs to:

Read customer data
Fetch project details
Query a database
Create tickets in Jira
Access GitHub repositories

Without MCP, every integration requires custom implementation.

Frontend App
|
├── Custom GitHub API Integration
├── Custom Jira API Integration
├── Custom Database Connector
└── Custom Internal Service Connector

Every tool has:

Different authentication methods
Different request formats
Different response structures

As the number of tools grows, maintenance becomes difficult.

What is MCP?

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that standardizes how AI models communicate with external systems.

Instead of building custom integrations for every tool, developers can expose functionality through an MCP server.

Frontend App
|
▼
AI Agent
|
▼
MCP Server
|
├── GitHub
├── Jira
├── Database
└── Internal APIs

The AI does not need to know how every system works internally.

It simply asks the MCP server for available tools and uses them when needed.

Why Should Frontend Developers Care?

Many frontend developers assume MCP is only for AI engineers.

That's not true.

If you're building:

AI-powered dashboards
Chat interfaces
Internal enterprise tools
Developer portals
Productivity applications

You'll likely interact with MCP-based systems sooner than you think.

For frontend developers, MCP offers three major benefits:

  1. Faster AI Integrations

You don't need to create separate integrations for every backend service.

The AI agent can discover available tools automatically.

  1. Cleaner Architecture

Instead of hardcoding API calls throughout the application, business actions can be exposed through MCP tools.

  1. Better Scalability

As new tools are added, the frontend often requires little or no changes.

The MCP server handles the complexity.

A Real-World Example

Imagine you're building a Project Management Assistant.

A user types:

Show all open bugs assigned to me and create a summary.

Without MCP:

Frontend calls Bug API
Frontend processes responses
Frontend calls AI API
Backend coordinates everything

With MCP:

User submits request
AI discovers available tools
AI calls Bug Tracker Tool
AI receives results
AI generates summary

The process becomes more intelligent and flexible.

MCP Components

There are three main components.

  1. MCP Host

The application where users interact with AI.

Examples:

AI chat applications
IDE extensions
Enterprise assistants

  1. MCP Client

Acts as the bridge between the host and the MCP server.

It sends requests and receives responses.

  1. MCP Server

Provides tools and resources that AI can use.

Examples:

GetUserDetails()
CreateJiraTicket()
FetchSalesReport()
SearchDocumentation()

The AI can discover and use these tools when needed.

Frontend Use Cases
Customer Support Portal

Users ask:

Show all unresolved support tickets from this week.

AI automatically retrieves data from connected systems.

Developer Dashboard

Users ask:

Show all failed deployments in production.

AI can fetch deployment logs through MCP tools.

Knowledge Management System

Users ask:

Summarize architecture documents related to authentication.

The AI retrieves documentation and generates insights.

A Simple Mental Model

Think of MCP as a restaurant.

User → Customer
AI → Waiter
MCP Server → Kitchen
Tools → Chefs

The customer doesn't walk into the kitchen.

The waiter knows which chef can prepare which dish.

Similarly, AI doesn't need direct knowledge of all systems.

It asks the MCP server for available tools and uses them when required.

Benefits of MCP
Reduced Development Effort

Build a tool once and expose it through MCP.

Multiple AI applications can reuse it.

Consistency

Every tool follows a common protocol.

Developers spend less time learning custom integrations.

Better User Experience

AI agents can accomplish tasks rather than just answer questions.

Future-Proof Architecture

As more organizations adopt AI agents, MCP provides a standardized integration layer.

Challenges to Consider

MCP is powerful, but it's not magic.

Security

Giving AI access to tools requires proper:

Authentication
Authorization
Audit logging
Tool Quality

Poorly designed tools lead to poor AI performance.

Monitoring

Track:

Tool usage
Failures
Response times

Just like any other API platform.

My Take

I believe MCP has the potential to become one of the most important standards in the AI ecosystem.

For frontend developers, the biggest shift is this:

We are moving from building applications that only display data to building applications that help users accomplish tasks through AI.

In the next few years, knowing how AI agents interact with tools may become just as important as understanding REST APIs or GraphQL today.

If you're a frontend developer exploring AI, now is a great time to learn MCP.

The earlier you understand it, the easier it will be to build the next generation of intelligent applications.

Final Thoughts

Frontend development has evolved from static pages to SPAs, then to cloud-connected applications, and now to AI-powered experiences.

MCP is another step in that evolution.

Instead of teaching AI about every system individually, we provide a standard way for systems to expose capabilities. The result is simpler integrations, smarter applications, and a better developer experience.

Think of MCP as USB-C for AI: one standard connection that makes everything work together. 🚀
