title: microservices
description:
question
Model Microservice

This repo is intended as a starter project for anyone intending to write a new microservice. It demonstrates the following key features:
A basic gradle spring-cloud project
Integration with the service directory
Implementing a REST service with tests
Calling microservices in DWS fabric using webclient and feign.
After cloning you should, at the very least, change the following things before you import it into your IDE.
Change the package name from modelmicroservice to something more appropriate.
Edit settings.gradle and change the rootProject.name property name to your service name.
Edit src/main/resources/application.yaml and change spring.application.name to the name of your project. Review the other properties in this file.
Edit gradle.properties and review all the properties commented with TODO.
Generate a keystore for local testing. More info: Guide
This repo will never be finished. As we evolve our capability and update recommended versions this repo will change and evolve accordingly.
Auto-generated documentation

Swagger
Code Quality: SonarQube

Follow these steps to run a SonarQube instance locally to measure your code quality.
docker-compose -f src/main/docker/sonar.yml up
./gradlew sonar
Visit SonarQube Dashboard
Spring Boot 3

The model-microservice is now (Aug 2023) built against spring boot 3.

i need to understand properly what this repo is for
And what all technical knowledge should i have to use this and understand everything properly
what skills do i need to learn

gemini response
Of course. Based on the documentation you provided, here is an explanation of the "Model Microservice" repository and the skills needed to use it effectively.
What is this Repository For?
This repository serves as a starter project or template for developers who need to create a new microservice. Its primary purpose is to provide a standardized, pre-configured foundation that includes best practices and essential integrations, saving developers time and effort during the initial setup phase.
Instead of starting from an empty project, you can clone this repository and have a functional service skeleton that already demonstrates key capabilities:

Foundation: It's a project built with Gradle and the Spring Cloud framework, which are standard for building distributed systems.
Service Discovery: It includes integration with a "service directory," allowing your new service to register itself and discover other services within the network.
API Implementation: It provides a template for creating a RESTful API, complete with example tests, which is the standard way microservices communicate.
Inter-Service Communication: It shows how to call other microservices using two popular methods: WebClient (a modern, reactive web client) and Feign (a declarative web service client).
Modern Framework: The project is updated to use Spring Boot 3, ensuring it leverages the latest features and performance improvements.

In short, this repository is a blueprint that helps you bootstrap a new microservice quickly while adhering to established architectural patterns and tooling.
Technical Knowledge and Skills Required
To fully understand and effectively use this starter project, you should have a solid grasp of the following technologies and concepts. They are listed in order of importance, from foundational to specific.

  1. Foundational Skills These are the core competencies you'll need before you can work with the specifics of the repository.

Java Programming:

Description: The project is written in Java. You need strong proficiency in the language, including object-oriented principles, data structures, and core libraries. Familiarity with features from Java 17 or later is beneficial, as Spring Boot 3 requires it.
Why it's needed: To write the business logic, controllers, services, and repository layers of your microservice.

RESTful APIs:

Description: Understanding the principles of Representational State Transfer (REST). This includes concepts like resources, URIs, HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), status codes, and data formats like JSON.
Why it's needed: Microservices primarily communicate via REST APIs. You will be building and consuming them.

Microservice Architecture:

Description: A conceptual understanding of why and how applications are broken down into smaller, independent services. This includes concepts like service discovery, configuration management, fault tolerance, and API gateways.
Why it's needed: This repository is a tool for implementing this architectural style. Knowing the "big picture" helps you understand the purpose of each feature (like service directory integration).

  1. Core Frameworks & Tools These are the specific technologies used directly in the repository.

Spring Framework / Spring Boot 3:

Description: This is the most critical framework. You should understand the core concepts of Spring, such as Dependency Injection (@Autowired), Inversion of Control (IoC), and aspect-oriented programming. For Spring Boot specifically, know how it simplifies configuration with auto-configuration, starters, and the application.yaml file.
Why it's needed: The entire application is built on Spring Boot. You'll use its annotations (@RestController, @Service, etc.) and configuration mechanisms daily.

Gradle:

Description: A build automation tool used to manage project dependencies, run tests, and build the application artifact. You should understand the structure of build.gradle and settings.gradle files and how to execute common tasks like gradlew build.
Why it's needed: You need to interact with Gradle to build the project, manage its libraries, and run tasks like the SonarQube analysis.

Spring Cloud:

Description: A sub-project of Spring that provides tools for building distributed systems. The repository mentions "service directory" integration, which is a core feature of Spring Cloud (often implemented with Netflix Eureka or Spring Cloud Consul).
Why it's needed: To make your service work correctly within a larger ecosystem of microservices.

  1. Specific Skills & Tooling These are skills for specific tasks mentioned in the repository's documentation.

Web Clients (WebClient and Feign):

Description: WebClient is a non-blocking, reactive client for making HTTP requests, part of the Spring WebFlux project. Feign is a declarative client that lets you define an API client by creating a simple Java interface.
Why it's needed: Your service will likely need to communicate with other services. The repository provides examples of both, and you should understand the trade-offs between them (e.g., reactive vs. blocking, verbosity vs. simplicity).

Docker and Docker Compose:

Description: Docker is a platform for creating, deploying, and running applications in containers. Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications.
Why it's needed: The repository uses Docker Compose to run a local instance of SonarQube for code quality analysis. Basic knowledge of docker-compose up is required to follow the instructions.

API Documentation (Swagger/OpenAPI):

Description: Swagger (now known as the OpenAPI Specification) is a standard for documenting REST APIs. Tools like Springdoc-openapi can automatically generate this documentation from your code.
Why it's needed: To provide clear, interactive documentation for the API your service exposes, making it easy for other developers to understand and use.

Code Quality (SonarQube):

Description: A platform for continuous inspection of code quality to perform automatic reviews with static analysis of code to detect bugs, code smells, and security vulnerabilities.
Why it's needed: To ensure your code meets quality standards. You'll need to know how to run the analysis and interpret the results on the SonarQube dashboard.

question 2
explain with a simple example of a microservice that can be build with this starter template
how would it be different when this template was not present

gemini response
Of course. Let's walk through a simple, practical example of a microservice you could build with this template and then compare the development process with and without it.
Simple Example: A "Currency Exchange Rate" Microservice
Let's imagine you need to build a microservice called exchange-rate-service. Its sole purpose is to provide the current exchange rate between two currencies (e.g., USD to EUR).
What the Microservice Does:

Exposes a REST API Endpoint: It will have an endpoint like GET /api/v1/rates. You can query it with parameters, for example: GET /api/v1/rates?from=USD&to=EUR.
Returns a JSON Response: A successful request would return a simple JSON object:
json{
"fromCurrency": "USD",
"toCurrency": "EUR",
"rate": 0.95,
"timestamp": "2026-10-15T10:00:00Z"
}

Gets Data from Another Service: This exchange-rate-service doesn't calculate rates itself. It fetches them from a central, authoritative source, let's call it the market-data-provider service.
Registers Itself: It announces its presence on the network so other services (e.g., a trade-booking-service) can find and use it.

How You Would Build This Using the "Model Microservice" Template
Following the instructions in the repository, the process would be streamlined:

Clone and Rename:

You clone the model-microservice repository.
You perform the initial setup:

Change the package name from modelmicroservice to com.db.trading.exchangerate.
Edit settings.gradle to set rootProject.name = 'exchange-rate-service'.
Edit application.yaml to set spring.application.name: exchange-rate-service.

Result: You now have a working, buildable Spring Boot project correctly named and configured.

Define the API Endpoint:

You would create a new Java class, ExchangeRateController.java.
Using Spring's annotations (which are already in the project's dependencies), you define the endpoint. The template already has an example controller you can adapt.

java@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/rates")
public class ExchangeRateController {
// ... inject your service here

@GetMapping
public Rate getRate(@RequestParam String from, @RequestParam String to) {
    return exchangeRateService.getExchangeRate(from, to);
}

}

Call the market-data-provider Service:

The template already includes WebClient and Feign as dependencies and provides examples of how to use them.
You could create a Feign client interface to declaratively define how to call the other service. The setup is already mostly done for you.

java@FeignClient(name = "market-data-provider")
public interface MarketDataProviderClient {
@GetMapping("/data/forex")
BigDecimal getRate(@RequestParam("pair") String currencyPair);
}

Your service logic would then simply call this Java interface, and Spring Cloud would handle the underlying HTTP request, service discovery, and response parsing.

Testing and Quality:

The template includes a testing framework (JUnit 5) and example tests for REST controllers. You can follow this pattern to write your own tests quickly.
To check your code quality, you just run the provided commands: docker-compose -f src/main/docker/sonar.yml up and ./gradlew sonar. The configuration is already done.

Run the Service:

You run the main application class. Because the template includes the Spring Cloud service discovery client, your service will automatically register itself with the service directory upon startup.

Key takeaway: The template provides the scaffolding. You don't spend time on setup, configuration, or figuring out which libraries to use. You focus almost immediately on writing the business logic for your specific service.

How It Would Be Different Without the Template (Starting from Scratch)
If this starter template did not exist, you would have to perform all of the following steps manually.

Project Initialization:

Go to a tool like start.spring.io or use your IDE's project wizard.
Manually select the project type (Gradle), language (Java), and Spring Boot version.
Dilemma: Which version of Spring Boot is standard? Is it compatible with the company's internal libraries? The template pre-answers this.
Manual Dependency Selection: You would need to manually add every single dependency:

Spring Web (for REST controllers)
Spring Boot Actuator (for health checks)
Spring Cloud Starter Netflix Eureka (or a similar client for service discovery)
Spring Cloud Starter OpenFeign (for the Feign client)
Spring Boot Starter Test (for testing)
Lombok (optional, for less boilerplate code)
Springdoc OpenAPI (for Swagger documentation)

Problem: You need to know exactly which dependencies are required and ensure their versions are compatible with each other. This is a common source of errors. The template provides a tested, known-good set of dependencies.

Configuration:

Create the application.yaml file from scratch.
Manually add configuration for the server port, application name, and the address of the service directory.
Manually configure logging patterns and levels.
The template provides a well-structured application.yaml with comments and placeholders for standard properties, which you would have to look up or guess.

Implementing Inter-Service Communication:

You would need to manually configure the Feign client or WebClient. This involves adding annotations like @EnableFeignClients to your main application class and potentially creating configuration beans for things like timeouts, retries, and error handling. The template would have this already set up.

Setting up Code Quality and Documentation:

SonarQube: You would need to find the correct SonarQube Docker image, write your own docker-compose.yml file, and configure the Gradle SonarQube plugin from scratch in your build.gradle file, connecting it to the Docker container.
Swagger: You would have to add the dependency and potentially write Java configuration beans to customize the generated API documentation (e.g., adding security definitions or metadata).

Build Logic:

You would write a build.gradle file from scratch. The template's gradle.properties and build.gradle files contain standardized version management, plugin configurations, and other best practices you would otherwise have to implement yourself.

In summary, without the template, a developer would spend a significant amount of time on boilerplate setup, configuration, and dependency management. This process is error-prone and leads to inconsistencies between microservices.
The template's value is that it encapsulates all of these initial decisions and configurations into a reusable, best-practice starting point, dramatically accelerating development and promoting standardization.

question 3
what things should i learn in proper sequence so that i completely understand each step of creation of a microservice with this template, so that i may understand the things used and also maybe later able to create a new microservice like this manually by my own

gemini response
Excellent question. Building a solid understanding requires a structured approach. Learning these concepts in the right order will ensure you grasp not just how to use the template, but why it is designed the way it is. This will empower you to use it effectively and eventually build a similar service from scratch.
Here is a recommended, sequential learning path, broken down into logical phases.

Phase 1: The Bedrock - Core Programming and Concepts
Start here. Without these fundamentals, the frameworks and tools in the later phases will be difficult to comprehend.

Java (Intermediate to Advanced):

What to Learn: Don't just learn the syntax. Focus on Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) principles (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism), interfaces, abstract classes, collections (Lists, Sets, Maps), and exception handling. Since Spring Boot 3 uses Java 17+, familiarize yourself with modern Java features like Records, var for local variables, and the Stream API for data manipulation.
Why: The entire application is written in Java. A deep understanding is non-negotiable for writing clean, efficient business logic.

HTTP and RESTful APIs:

What to Learn: Understand the client-server model of the web. Learn the core HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), what they semantically represent, and the importance of HTTP status codes (e.g., 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error). Grasp the core principles of REST: resources, statelessness, and using JSON as a data format.
Why: This is the universal language of microservices. You will be designing, building, and consuming REST APIs.

Phase 2: The Engine - The Spring Framework
This is the most critical framework in the template. Master it, and you're halfway there.

Spring Core Concepts:

What to Learn: Focus on the two pillars of Spring: Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI). Understand what the Spring "Application Context" or "IoC Container" is. Learn the most common annotations: @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Autowired.
Why: Spring manages the lifecycle of your objects (beans). Understanding DI is fundamental to how all the pieces of a Spring application are wired together.

Spring Boot:

What to Learn: Understand how Spring Boot simplifies Spring development. Focus on auto-configuration (how it automatically configures beans based on the JARs on your classpath), starter dependencies (e.g., spring-boot-starter-web), and externalized configuration using application.yaml or application.properties. Learn to build a simple REST controller using @RestController and @GetMapping/@PostMapping.
Why: The template is a Spring Boot project. This knowledge will allow you to understand how the service starts, how its configuration is managed, and how to add new API endpoints.

Gradle (Build Tool):

What to Learn: You don't need to be an expert, but you must understand the basics. Learn the purpose of build.gradle (declares dependencies and tasks) and settings.gradle (defines project structure). Know how to execute common tasks from the command line: ./gradlew build (compiles and packages the code), ./gradlew test (runs tests), and ./gradlew bootRun (runs the application).
Why: Gradle is the tool used to build, test, and manage all the libraries your project needs. You will interact with it constantly.

Phase 3: The Ecosystem - Connecting Microservices
Once you can build a standalone service, this phase teaches you how to make it part of a larger distributed system.

Microservice Architecture Concepts:

What to Learn: Before diving into the tools, understand the "why." Learn about key patterns like Service Discovery (how services find each other), Centralized Configuration (managing configuration for many services), and Fault Tolerance (e.g., circuit breakers).
Why: This provides the context for why tools like Spring Cloud are necessary.

Spring Cloud & Service Discovery:

What to Learn: Focus on the role of a "Service Directory" or "Discovery Server" (like Eureka, which is a common choice). Understand that when your service starts, it registers its name and address with this central server. When it needs to call another service, it asks the server for that service's address. Learn the annotations that enable this, like @EnableDiscoveryClient.
Why: In a microservice environment, you don't hardcode IP addresses. Service discovery allows services to find each other dynamically. The template is pre-configured for this.

Communicating Between Services (Feign & WebClient):

What to Learn:

Feign: Understand it as a "declarative" REST client. You create a Java interface, add annotations, and Spring Cloud automatically implements it for you. It's clean and easy to read.
WebClient: Learn this as the modern, more powerful way to make HTTP requests in Spring. It is non-blocking and reactive, which can be more efficient, but has a slightly steeper learning curve.

Why: Your microservice will inevitably need to call other microservices. The template provides examples of both, and you need to understand how to use them to fetch data.

Phase 4: The Polish - Professional Tooling & Practices
These tools ensure your microservice is maintainable, well-documented, and high-quality.

Testing in Spring:

What to Learn: Learn how to write unit tests for your services (@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)) and integration tests for your REST controllers (@SpringBootTest with @AutoConfigureMockMvc or WebTestClient). Understand the difference between mocking dependencies and running a test with a full application context.
Why: The template includes a testing setup. Writing automated tests is crucial for ensuring your service works correctly and doesn't break when you make changes.

API Documentation (Swagger/OpenAPI):

What to Learn: Understand that tools like Springdoc-openapi scan your @RestController code to automatically generate interactive API documentation (a Swagger UI page). Learn how to add annotations (@Operation, @ApiResponse) to make this documentation more descriptive.
Why: Good documentation makes your service easy to use for other developers and teams. The template automates the setup.

Docker & Docker Compose:

What to Learn: Understand what a Docker container is (a lightweight, portable package of an application and its dependencies). Learn the basics of Docker Compose for running multi-container applications from a single docker-compose.yml file. You only need to know how to run docker-compose up to start.
Why: The template uses this to run external dependencies locally, like the SonarQube database and server. This avoids complex local installations.

Code Quality (SonarQube):

What to Learn: Understand that SonarQube is a static analysis tool that scans your code for bugs, vulnerabilities, and "code smells" (bad practices). Learn how to run the Gradle task (./gradlew sonar) and how to interpret the dashboard to identify areas for improvement in your code.
Why: This helps you maintain high code quality and write more secure, robust applications.

By following this path, you will progressively build the knowledge required to not only use the template, but to understand its value and replicate its functionality on your own.

title: W-JEPA: Wavelet Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Wearable Activity Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.19411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A major challenge in wearable device activity recognition is the heterogeneity across datasets in sensor placement, channel count, sampling rate and subjects. Moreover, the motion patterns that distinguish activities often appear as subtle, scale-specific variations within otherwise similar waveforms. As a result, raw signals are often ambiguous, and models trained on them tend to rely on cues specific to a particular sensor setup or participant, which limits both cross-dataset transfer and generalization to unseen participants. Addressing this requires representations that preserve such activity-relevant, scale-specific variation. We introduce W-JEPA, a self-supervised framework that exploits the multiscale structure of inertial motion and leverages a joint-embedding predictive architecture, by organizing windows into a fixed grid of wavelet tokens indexed by scale, sensor axis, and time. These wavelet tokens help expose activity-specific detail within broadly similar raw signals, and serve as the units of masked latent prediction. W-JEPA predicts masked token representations supplied by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder. Because recovering a masked token requires relating motion at one scale and axis to motion at other scales and axes, the model learns the cross-scale, cross-axis structure of human movement. Across six wearable activity benchmarks, W-JEPA outperforms state-of-the-art methods under random-window splits and remains the strongest when subjects are held out, improving average macro-F1 by 8.7 percentage points over the strongest published baseline. These results indicate that physically grounded multiscale tokenization, combined together with latent predictive learning, provides a promising foundation for transferable representations of heterogeneous wearable inertial data.

title: Terraform Unleashed: Building Scalable Infra‑as‑Code Pipelines
description:
Terraform Unleashed: Building Scalable Infra‑as‑Code Pipelines

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) has transformed the way we think about cloud resources. Among the many tools in the IaC arena, Terraform stands out for its provider‑agnostic model, declarative language, and robust ecosystem. In this post we’ll walk through a practical, end‑to‑end workflow that takes you from a single resource definition to a production‑grade CI/CD pipeline. By the end, you’ll have a reusable Terraform module, a version‑controlled state backend, and a GitHub Actions workflow that automatically applies changes on merge.

TL;DR – Define resources in HCL, store state in a remote backend, modularize with reusable components, and automate with CI.

1. Why Terraform?

  • Provider‑agnostic – One language (HCL) works across AWS, Azure, GCP, and dozens of niche providers.
  • Immutable plans – terraform plan shows a precise diff before any change hits the cloud.
  • State handling – Remote backends keep a single source of truth, enabling collaboration.

These traits make Terraform a natural fit for teams that need repeatable, auditable infrastructure deployments.

2. Project Layout

A clean directory structure is the foundation of maintainable Terraform code. Here’s a minimal but production‑ready layout:

├── environments
│   ├── dev
│   │   ├── main.tf
│   │   └── backend.tf
│   └── prod
│       ├── main.tf
│       └── backend.tf
├── modules
│   └── vpc
│       ├── main.tf
│       ├── variables.tf
│       └── outputs.tf
└── .github
    └── workflows
        └── terraform.yml
  • modules/ – Reusable building blocks (e.g., VPC, IAM, RDS).
  • environments/ – Environment‑specific configurations that call modules.
  • .github/workflows/ – CI pipelines that run terraform fmt, plan, and apply.

3. A Simple VPC Module

Let’s start with a tiny VPC module for AWS. This example demonstrates variables, locals, and outputs.

# modules/vpc/variables.tf
variable "name" {
  description = "Name tag for the VPC"
  type        = string
}

variable "cidr" {
  description = "CIDR block for the VPC"
  type        = string
  default     = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

# modules/vpc/main.tf
resource "aws_vpc" "this" {
  cidr_block = var.cidr
  tags = {
    Name = var.name
  }
}

# modules/vpc/outputs.tf
output "vpc_id" {
  description = "The ID of the created VPC"
  value       = aws_vpc.this.id
}

You can now reference this module from any environment:

# environments/dev/main.tf
module "vpc" {
  source = "../../modules/vpc"
  name   = "dev-vpc"
  cidr   = "10.1.0.0/16"
}

4. Remote State Backend

Storing state locally works for single‑developer experiments, but teams need a remote backend. We’ll use Terraform Cloud (free tier) as an example.

# environments/dev/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "remote" {
    hostname = "app.terraform.io"
    organization = "my-org"

    workspaces {
      name = "dev"
    }
  }
}

Running terraform init now authenticates against Terraform Cloud, creates the workspace, and stores the state there. The same pattern applies to prod, just with a different workspace name.

5. Working with Workspaces

Terraform Cloud workspaces isolate state per environment. You can also use the built‑in CLI workspaces for quick experiments:

terraform workspace new staging
terraform workspace select staging

When you switch, Terraform automatically reads the corresponding state file, keeping your environments safely separated.

6. Linting, Formatting, and Validation

A clean codebase reduces friction in PR reviews.

# .github/workflows/terraform.yml
name: Terraform CI

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - '**/*.tf'

jobs:
  fmt-plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2

      - name: Terraform Format
        run: terraform fmt -check

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend=false

      - name: Terraform Validate
        run: terraform validate

      - name: Terraform Plan
        env:
          TF_VAR_aws_region: us-east-1
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.out

      - name: Upload Plan Artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: plan.out

The workflow runs on every PR, ensuring code is formatted, syntactically valid, and that a plan can be generated without side effects.

7. Automated Apply on Merge

Once a PR passes all checks, we can safely apply the changes to the target environment.

# continuation of .github/workflows/terraform.yml
  apply:
    needs: fmt-plan
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init

      - name: Download Plan Artifact
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: .

      - name: Terraform Apply
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve plan.out

Only pushes to main trigger an automatic apply, keeping production changes under version control.

8. Best Practices Checklist

✅ Practice Why it matters
1 Keep modules small and focused Easier to test and reuse.
2 Pin provider versions Prevents accidental breaking changes (required_providers).
3 Never commit state files Use remote backends to avoid drift and conflicts.
4 Use terraform fmt in CI Enforces a consistent style across the team.
5 Separate variables per environment Keeps dev, staging, prod isolated.
6 Enable Sentinel policies (if on Terraform Cloud) Adds policy‑as‑code guardrails.

9. Scaling Beyond a Single VPC

When you start managing dozens of resources—EKS clusters, RDS instances, IAM roles—consider these extensions:

  • Terragrunt – A thin wrapper that adds DRY capabilities (e.g., shared backend.tf across environments).
  • Terraform Cloud Sentinel – Enforce compliance policies (e.g., “no public S3 buckets”).
  • Modules Registry – Publish internal modules for organization‑wide reuse.

10. Debugging Tips

  • terraform console – Interactive HCL evaluation.
  • TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform apply – Verbose logs for provider communication.
  • terraform state list – Inspect current resources in state.

11. What’s Next?

  • Testing with Terratest – Write Go tests that spin up real infrastructure and assert expectations.
  • Policy as Code – Combine Sentinel with Open Policy Agent (OPA) for multi‑cloud guardrails.
  • Dynamic Secrets – Integrate with HashiCorp Vault to inject secrets at runtime, keeping them out of state.

Recommended Tools

If you’re ready to level up your Terraform workflow, check out these tools that have helped countless teams streamline their IaC pipelines:

  • Terraform Cloud – The official hosted backend that adds remote state, VCS integration, and policy enforcement. Sign up here and get a free tier that’s perfect for small teams.
  • Terragrunt – A lightweight wrapper that simplifies working with multiple environments and shared configurations. Grab the latest version from the official site here and start reducing duplication in seconds.

Happy provisioning!

title: Add S3 uploads to Vercel apps without storing long-lived AWS keys
description:
A Vercel app can accept a file upload and store the object in Amazon S3 without putting a long-lived AWS access key in source code or deployment variables. Vercel’s Amazon S3 Marketplace integration now connects an S3 resource to a Vercel project, supplies connection details as environment variables, and authenticates with short-lived OIDC credentials. The practical work remains yours: authorize the uploader, choose the object key, validate the file, and decide who can read it.

This guide walks through the setup boundary, the server-side upload path, and the security decisions that still matter after credentials are handled. It is for a team adding file uploads to a Vercel-hosted application, especially one that already uses AWS and wants its storage flow near the project configuration.

Choose the integration for the workflow you have

Amazon S3 and Vercel Blob solve overlapping but different setup problems. Vercel Blob is a storage service for files in a Vercel app, with Vercel-managed delivery features. The S3 Marketplace integration is a fit when the application already depends on AWS, when the team wants S3 resources visible beside its Vercel project, or when its storage workflow uses S3-specific services such as S3 Tables or S3 Vectors.

The Marketplace path keeps project setup together: create or connect the resource in the Vercel dashboard, then use the values made available to the project. A linked AWS account has an important constraint: the Vercel flow supports buckets created through Vercel, rather than attaching an arbitrary pre-existing bucket. If an application already writes to a bucket that was created elsewhere, check the current setup path before planning a migration. Do not assume “connect an AWS account” means every bucket in that account is selectable.

The integration also does not remove the need to understand AWS permissions. OIDC changes how the application obtains credentials; the IAM role still determines which AWS actions those credentials can perform. Treat the role policy, project environment, and upload route as separate controls.

Connect the S3 resource to the project

Start in the Vercel Marketplace from the project that will run the upload route. Create an S3 resource through the guided flow or link the AWS account you intend to use. Review the environment variables that Vercel adds and the project environments to which the connection applies. Keep production and preview behavior deliberate; a preview deployment should not automatically inherit broader access than it needs.

Vercel’s integration uses short-lived OIDC credentials instead of storing static AWS keys in the application. That means you do not paste an IAM user’s long-lived access key into an environment variable or commit it in a local file. The application still needs ordinary configuration such as the bucket name and region, and AWS still needs a role with a trust relationship for the intended Vercel project and environment.

For new integrations, inspect the connection details and the resulting IAM access before sending real user files. Confirm the role can write only to the bucket and key prefix the application requires. If a function only stores user uploads, it should not receive broad permissions to list every bucket or alter bucket policy. Keep any administrative bucket operations outside the request path.

Build a server-side upload route

The Vercel changelog’s example uses createS3 from @vercel/aws, then sends an AWS SDK PutObjectCommand from a route handler. The outline is small:

// lib/s3.ts
import { createS3 } from "@vercel/aws";

export const s3 = createS3();

// app/api/upload/route.ts
import { PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { s3 } from "@/lib/s3";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  // First authenticate the user and verify upload permission.
  const formData = await request.formData();
  const file = formData.get("file");

  if (!(file instanceof File)) {
    return Response.json({ error: "A file is required." }, { status: 400 });
  }

  // Apply application-specific size and content checks here.
  const objectKey = `uploads/${crypto.randomUUID()}`;

  await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: process.env.S3_BUCKET_NAME!,
    Key: objectKey,
    Body: Buffer.from(await file.arrayBuffer()),
    ContentType: file.type || "application/octet-stream",
  }));

  return Response.json({ key: objectKey });
}

An existing AWS account can be linked; buckets provisioned through the Vercel connection are new buckets. The older buckets shown remain untouched.

This is a route shape, not a complete production policy. The example deliberately leaves authentication and validation as explicit steps because they depend on the application. A successful AWS write does not prove that the requester is allowed to upload for the account identified by the URL or form.

The object key should be generated on the server. Do not accept a bucket name or unrestricted key from the browser: a user could otherwise choose another tenant’s path or overwrite an object the app treats as authoritative. Use an opaque identifier for the storage key and save the original filename as display metadata after normalizing it. Scope each upload to the authenticated user or tenant, and ensure the IAM policy and application checks agree about the allowed prefix.

Set upload limits before reading an entire file into memory. Check the declared MIME type, but do not trust it as proof of file contents; inspect or decode the bytes when the file type matters. Restrict accepted formats, cap size, and rate-limit requests. For larger uploads, design a multipart or direct-to-storage flow separately, including how a client receives narrowly scoped authorization and how unfinished uploads are cleaned up.

Decide who can read each object

Storage access is a product decision. A profile image meant to be public and an invoice or user export should not share the same read path. Keep private objects behind application authorization, and return a short-lived download mechanism only after checking the caller’s access. If a file is intentionally public, make that choice explicit and avoid placing sensitive content in that bucket or prefix.

The Marketplace S3 connection uses short-lived OIDC credentials rather than static AWS keys for the upload flow; the scene is conceptual, not a Vercel or OTF integration screen.

Do not rely on an unguessable object key as the authorization rule. Random identifiers reduce accidental discovery, but the app still needs to check ownership before returning a download URL or proxying bytes. Consider whether a user can replace a file, whether each replacement should create a new version, and how deletion requests propagate to S3 and the app’s metadata store.

Think through consistency as well. An upload can succeed in S3 while a database write fails, or the reverse if the application records an object before storage confirms it. Store the object key and upload state in a way that supports retries and cleanup. Make the route safe to retry where possible, and avoid returning a success response until the application has enough proof to show the file to the user.

Test the full path before opening it to users

Use a small, non-sensitive file in a development or preview environment. Verify the route rejects an unauthenticated request, a missing file, an oversized file, and a file type the product does not accept. Then upload an allowed file and confirm that the generated key uses the intended tenant prefix and that an authorized user can retrieve it.

Test the negative cases, too: a user from another tenant should not be able to overwrite or read the object; a preview project should not gain production access by accident; and a failed metadata write should not leave a misleading success state. Check the Vercel function logs and AWS-side audit trail without logging file bytes, user credentials, or temporary tokens.

Finally, test the deployment environments that matter. A route that works locally can still fail if the project is not connected to the S3 resource in Preview or Production, if the bucket region is wrong, or if the AWS role trust policy does not match the project and environment. Keep a short runbook with the resource owner, bucket and region, allowed prefixes, expected environment variables, and a safe way to rotate or narrow permissions.

Where an app template fits

Adding S3 is a storage integration task; it does not create the rest of the product around it. If the same team also needs an editable SaaS application shell, the OTF SaaS Dashboard template is an optional $99 starting point with a Vite and Hono app, sign-in, projects, teams, and sample analytics screens. It does not include Amazon S3 or configure this Marketplace integration. Keep the storage connection in the application’s own Vercel and AWS setup.

For an example of how a small Hono backend can be deployed on Vercel’s alternative serverless platform, see our guide to running a Hono backend on AWS Lambda. Use that as a separate deployment discussion; it is not a prerequisite for the Vercel Marketplace path described here.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 joins the Vercel Marketplace — October 14, 2026. Marketplace setup, environment variables, OIDC credentials, upload example, linked-account limits, and S3 versus Blob use cases.
  • SaaS Dashboard template and pricing — checked October 15, 2026. The kit is $99 and does not include this S3 integration.

title: Look Before You Restore: Learning to Predict Before Acting for Agentic Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2610.20384v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents for mixed-degradation image restoration typically learn what a tool does to an image only after running it: failed calls waste computation and harmful outputs go unnoticed until too late. We propose PreActIR, an agentic restoration framework that predicts tool consequences before execution. For each candidate tool, a tool-conditioned world model forecasts changes in residual degradation, image quality, and fidelity, together with the risk of harm and the uncertainty of the prediction. The agent executes the top-ranked candidate, and an independent verifier commits or rolls back its output before the agent replans from the observed state. PreActIR also audits whether performance is limited by the selector or by the candidate space, and studies targeted tool adaptation as a controlled way to expand that space. In a controlled evaluation that fixes the candidate pool, verifier, and budget and employs reference-annotated degradation states, PreActIR uses 42.5% fewer real tool calls and 63.4% fewer rejected calls than reactive, execute-then-evaluate trial and error, while improving Y-PSNR by 0.92 dB.

title: Building Inventory Applications That Don’t Lose Track Of Their Inventory
description:
Let’s imagine we have an inventory system. Two of its customers decide to order the last remaining unit of a given product at roughly the same time. Does our application allow both of these orders to go through?

This is just one example of a complex series of constraints and rules which go into making an inventory system.

Spreadsheets can be useful, but businesses that want centralized visibility, automation, and protection from mistakes need something more powerful.

Let’s look at some fundamentals of the inventory application development process and consider how engineers can build more robust, reliable tools.

1. Build Inventory Records With Audit Trails

Begin by creating or identifying the data model which our application will use. At the simplest possible level, this might consist of a product ID, product name, SKU, and stock quantity.

In practice, however, it will likely be necessary to track more information. Perhaps we will need to track where inventory is stored, or what products have been reserved for specific customers. Auditing and debugging issues later on will become significantly easier if we leave behind a paper trail of what events occurred and when.

Some examples of this information might include:

• What inventory adjustments have occurred? Has inventory been received from a supplier, sold to a customer, or returned? Has it been transferred from one warehouse to another?

• How did the application reach the state that it is currently in?

• What is the reason for this adjustment? Does it involve an order or reservation?

• What quantity of the given product has been physically affected by this transaction?

• What time did this occur, and what other contextual information might be relevant?

We may also want to associate inventory records with other values, such as an order ID or a customer reserving this product. In a multi-warehouse environment, a given inventory record might also have a location field.

Depending on specific business logic, the data model will take shape. It is important to track all of the relevant adjustments as transactions and build an auditable paper trail.

2. Avoid Overselling With Transactional Integrity

Let’s return to the example of two customers attempting to place an order for the last remaining unit of a product. We want to sell one unit of this product to one customer and prevent the other customer from getting the same item, but it is very difficult to do so if both processes read and write information concurrently.

Using a relational or NoSQL database engine, it might be possible to prevent this sort of issue through transactions and concurrency controls.

The above SQL statement, for instance, will reduce a product’s inventory by 1 if the quantity of this product is at least 1 and prevent any such changes from occurring otherwise.

An application making this request should then be able to determine whether one row was affected (in which case the update was successful) or zero rows (in which case the requested update has failed). This is useful, but there are also additional nuances and edge cases which need to be considered. This includes whether this is the right approach in the context of a reserve-inventory system, what happens if a similar request comes in again later, what occurs when transactions need to be applied concurrently, inventory location and availability, or how this will impact order cancellations.

The point is to ensure that the application itself prevents overselling rather than relying solely on application-layer controls.

3. Automate Inventory Updates With Caution

Inventory automation systems can be immensely helpful. By ensuring that inventory changes occur automatically when certain processes are followed, there is less of a need for manual records or adjustments to go wrong. An automated inventory application might automatically update quantity fields when a purchase is made or an order is processed.

There is a good reason to be cautious, however. The same automation that helps can also hurt if there is no appropriate protection in place. For instance, if the application tries to update inventory again after it has already done so successfully, it will lead to double-counting errors.

We can avoid such issues by including appropriate transaction constraints, such as idempotency keys. Inventory record validation is also important, particularly since we will be working with other systems such as payment processors, order management tools, and warehouses.

4. Barcode Reader And RFID Inventory System Software Requirements

Barcode scanners and RFID (radio-frequency identification) readers offer similar advantages. They allow products to be uniquely identified without requiring human intervention. They are valuable tools in warehouses, as they can help ensure that physical inventory changes are reflected in digital inventory records. They can work in tandem with inventory applications or be incorporated as part of an integrated system.

RFID readers operate differently than barcode scanners and can be further categorized into active and passive variants, depending on whether RFID tags are powered by their own batteries.

An RFID reader will generally operate within a working range (a distance of several centimeters to a few meters) and scan for RFID tags within this area. If RFID tags are affixed to products within this range, it will be possible to obtain unique RFID identifiers for these products.

As with barcode scanners, the specific details will vary depending on the specific use case. Some examples might involve scanning barcodes or QR codes, scanning multiple products at once, determining quantity, or performing inventory verification.

From a software standpoint, such systems should be able to translate a barcode or RFID tag into a given product. The application will also want to verify that the request is legitimate and actually allowed and perform the relevant inventory adjustments for the given RFID or barcode.

It is necessary to choose a method based on the specifics of the inventory environment. RFID systems tend to be more valuable at certain points and less valuable at others. They are generally much more expensive than traditional barcode scanners, for instance, but do not always need to be applied to individual products and can be read without being seen.

5. Inventory Application API: Exposing Product Catalog And Inventory

Inventory applications tend to integrate with a variety of other tools, ranging from e-commerce platforms to enterprise resource planning systems. An API will generally want to expose how inventory information is structured, how requests should be processed, and what error conditions can occur. There are also broader architectural decisions which need to be made as well.

Some important considerations include authorization, authentication, validating incoming requests (particularly IDs), rate limiting, transaction retries, error reporting, and product categorization.

Larger applications, in particular, should consider implementing an event-driven or asynchronous architecture, rather than making direct requests and receiving responses. In practice, asynchronous systems can be even more challenging to develop and are often more error-prone, unless there is a very compelling reason to adopt them. A database and transaction engine will likely suffice for the needs of most applications.

6. Build Inventory Management Reports And Insights To Support Decision Making

Inventory records can be analyzed to produce insights on inventory performance. The application can detect patterns and trends relating to inventory records, such as the most popular products, inventory turnover, or inventory shrinkage.

Historical sales and purchase records, when combined with current inventory records, can help in building forecasts and detecting demand fluctuations.

Reports produced by an inventory application should be focused on answering specific questions. What products are approaching their minimum threshold? What records need to be adjusted? Which products are consistently low-selling or high-selling? Where are the main bottlenecks and delays in operation?

Consistent metrics allow managers and executives to analyze the performance of this application and the state of the business in general, but only if the underlying records are accurate and trustworthy.

7. Test Edge Cases And Failure Scenarios In Inventory Applications

Applications should be tested not only against normal operations, but also against abnormal operations. It is important to have processes in place to manage unexpected problems, such as orders going through which should not have, inventory adjustments canceling each other, or inventory records becoming completely unusable. In the context of inventory applications, a few sample test scenarios might include the following:

• Attempt to reserve the same inventory item for two orders simultaneously.

• Submit the same request several times to an API endpoint.

• Cancel an order that had previously reserved some inventory.

• Return a product and increase its inventory.

• Cancel a warehouse transfer.

• Submit a request to an external API that times out.

• Adjust inventory quantity through an unauthorized or unexpected method.

• Ensure that failed transactions do not leave the system in an inconsistent state.

• Ensure that a few important inventory transactions are properly traceable in case of an incident.

It is important to test the integrity of the system under conditions simulating some of these problems. In practice, inventory errors tend to occur not during normal operation but at the interfaces between systems.

8. Inventory Platforms: Selecting The Best Option For Your Business

Inventory control and management systems vary widely in terms of scale, scope, and capabilities. The choice of one option over another will be informed by the specific needs of the business and its suppliers. Businesses considering this decision should examine its existing procedures and plan accordingly.

The Inventory Master web page offers a number of resources for engineers and managers interested in building or selecting an appropriate toolset. Businesses can use this resource to learn more about the available approaches and select a viable option. Documentation and requirements analysis can help set expectations and ensure that a given selection fits the needs of the business rather than the other way around.

title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.19758v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. Lumen follows a four-stage pipeline. First, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning jointly strengthen multilingual translation competence and the ability to follow translation-specific instructions, such as terminology, style, and format constraints. Second, we extend the originally offline M^{2}PO preference-optimization framework into an online preference-optimization stage: the current policy samples candidate translations, an LLM judge assigns continuous direct-assessment scores, and the resulting multi-pair preferences are used to update the model. Third, on-policy distillation transfers stronger translation-instruction-following behavior from a larger teacher model to the Qwen3-14B student, improving translation-instruction adherence while retaining a 14B primary translation backbone. Finally, structure-aware inference and postprocessing preserve required formats, while selective repair addresses clear structural or decoding failures before submission. We participate in 23 translation directions. Under an absolute 1--5 LLM-judge rubric that evaluates translation-instruction following and translation quality separately, Lumen reaches an overall mean score of 4.60. Despite using a 14B translation backbone, it achieves performance comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and translation-instruction following.

title: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
description:
arXiv:2610.19536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. Every request is sent in its original form and under 21 types of rewrite that keep its content, such as renaming the options or writing the table in another format. The decision models perform as well as the LLMs at a lower cost. Three of them are also far more robust to how the question is formulated. No model we test is robust to how the table is organized. For every model, at least a third of the row decisions change under some rewrite of the table or the question. The decisions to which a decision model gives low probability are the ones most likely to change. Decision models are a practical choice for tabular decisions, but their robustness remains an open problem.

title: Design a Template People Can Fill in Under 5 Minutes
description:
A template’s real product isn’t the dashboard. It’s the first successful entry by a tired human who has five minutes and zero patience for a scavenger hunt.

I’ve inherited “simple” spreadsheets that required a legend, three hidden tabs, and tribal knowledge about which columns were safe to touch. I’ve also shipped Notion templates where the empty properties looked like a job application. In both cases the failure mode was identical: time-to-first-valid-input was too high, so people bounced—or worse, half-filled rows that poisoned every summary downstream.

This post is a practical design guide for making templates fillable in under five minutes: input-zone layout, defaults, mobile friction, and onboarding notes that people actually read.

Define “five minutes” precisely

Five minutes means:

  1. Open the file / duplicate the template.
  2. Understand where to type without a tutorial video.
  3. Enter one complete, valid record (expense, task, lead, weekly log—whatever the atomic unit is).
  4. See some confirmation that the system registered it (a total updates, a status appears, a calendar populates).

If step 2 alone takes five minutes, the template is documentation cosplay.

Principle 1: One obvious input zone

Humans scan for “where am I allowed to touch?” Make the answer visual and boringly consistent.

In spreadsheets (Excel / Google Sheets)

  • Put entry cells in a contiguous block—top-left of the working tab, not scattered between charts.
  • Use a light fill (e.g., soft yellow or blue) only on editable cells. Leave calculated cells white or gray.
  • Freeze the header row. People should always see labels while scrolling.
  • Keep the first empty input row immediately under the last example—no decorative blank bands that look like the end of the sheet.

Optional but powerful: protect non-input ranges (Sheets/Excel both support this). Even if collaborators never notice the lock, you stop yourself from overwriting formulas at 11pm.

In Notion

  • Lead with a full-width callout: “Add a row in the database below. Only fill Properties A–D.”
  • Limit visible properties on the default view to the ones required for a valid entry. Park advanced fields in a secondary view (“Full detail”).
  • Use selects / statuses with presets so mobile users tap instead of inventing spellings.

Smell test: Hand the template to someone for sixty seconds. Watch their cursor. If it wanders, your input zone isn’t obvious.

Principle 2: Defaults do more than instructions

Blank fields feel like unpaid design work. Defaults shrink cognitive load.

Useful defaults

  • Today’s date prefilled (or a date picker that defaults to today).
  • Status = “Logged” / “Inbox” so a row is valid before refinement.
  • Category dropdown with a sensible short list—not thirty options and “Other” hidden at the bottom.
  • Example row that looks real (not “Sample Sample $0”). Users overwrite examples faster than they interpret empty schemas.
  • Units and currency in headers (Amount (USD), Hours) so nobody guesses.

Defaults to avoid

  • Fake precision (Tax rate 7.375% when users track whole dollars).
  • Overstuffed sample data that makes the template look already “done” and scary to clear.
  • Hidden default formulas that explode when someone deletes the example row—test deletion.

A good default answers a question the user shouldn’t have to ask on minute one.

Principle 3: Design for thumbs, not just desktops

Mobile friction kills five-minute entry more often than missing charts.

Spreadsheet mobile checklist

  • Avoid wide layouts that need horizontal scrolling to reach the Amount column. Put critical fields in the first 4–6 columns.
  • Don’t rely on hover comments as the only instructions—phones don’t hover.
  • Minimize merged cells; they behave poorly on mobile apps.
  • Test: add one row in the phone app, not just mobile Safari view-only.

Notion mobile checklist

  • Default view should be table or list with few properties, not a dense board that requires pinch-zoom.
  • Prefer select/status/date over long text for required fields.
  • Keep the “New” button path obvious; don’t bury the working database three pages deep behind a dashboard gallery.

If your template is “beautiful on desktop, hostile on phone,” it’s a poster—not a tool.

Principle 4: Onboarding notes people will actually read

Nobody wants a manifesto. They want three lines above the fold.

The three-line starter (paste at the top)

  1. Purpose: “Log each expense so monthly category totals stay honest.”
  2. How: “Add a row in the yellow cells. Pick a category. Amount is required.”
  3. Don’t: “Don’t edit gray cells—those are formulas.”

That’s it for minute zero. Longer docs can live on a README tab or a linked Notion page—but the first screen must stand alone.

Progressive disclosure

  • Minute 0: three lines.
  • Minute 5: a short “Edge cases” note (refunds, splits, multi-currency).
  • Week 1: a “Maintenance” note (how to archive months, how to add a category).

Dumping all three layers on first open guarantees none get read.

A five-minute entry walkthrough you can use as a test script

Use this as QA before you share any template:

Minute Action Pass if…
0:00–0:30 Open / duplicate No login maze, no empty workspace confusion
0:30–1:30 Find input zone Editable area obvious without scrolling past three dashboards
1:30–3:30 Enter one full record Required fields clear; dropdowns work; no #REF!
3:30–4:30 See feedback A total, count, or status updates
4:30–5:00 Know next step User can say “I’ll add the next one the same way”

Fail any row, and fix design—not the user’s “discipline.”

Field design: fewer columns beat clever columns

Every required field multiplies abandonment risk. Audit ruthlessly.

  • Must-have for a valid row: usually 3–6 fields (date, label, amount/status, category).
  • Nice-to-have: notes, tags, links, owner—default optional.
  • Analytics-only: derived fields that users never type.

If you’re tempted to require “Priority, Energy, Area of life, Linked goal, Mood…” for a habit log, you’re designing a journaling app, not a five-minute template. Split the deep reflection into a weekly page; keep daily entry thin.

Microcopy that reduces mistakes

Small words prevent big cleanup:

  • Placeholder text: e.g. Client kickoff deposit instead of empty.
  • Validation: reject blank amounts; constrain categories to the list.
  • Inline hint in header: Category (pick one).
  • Error-friendly formulas: show — or 0 instead of scary errors when inputs are empty—especially on newly duplicated templates.

Remember: the first broken experience trains people to distrust every future total.

Ship checklist before you share the link

  • [ ] Input zone colored / described.
  • [ ] Example row present and deletable without breaking formulas.
  • [ ] Required fields ≤ 6.
  • [ ] Phone entry tested once.
  • [ ] Three-line how-to above the fold.
  • [ ] One visible feedback number or status that updates on entry.
  • [ ] Non-input cells protected or clearly marked.
  • [ ] Duplicate-from-gallery / “Make a copy” path verified (permissions matter).

If you can’t check these boxes, you’re not ready to call it a template—you’re sharing a personal file that happens to be empty.

Closing

Under-five-minute entry is a design constraint, not a marketing slogan. Obvious input zones, sensible defaults, mobile-safe layouts, and three-line onboarding do more for adoption than another chart. Test with a stopwatch and a slightly impatient friend. Fix what makes them hesitate.

When I need a starting layout that’s already biased toward quick entry—for budgets, trackers, and lightweight workflows—I reach for templates on PlanoNest and then strip anything that doesn’t earn its place in the first five minutes. Borrow that habit even if you build your own: delete until entry feels obvious, then stop decorating.

A template people can fill quickly becomes a system. A template that demands a briefing becomes a screenshot in someone’s camera roll.

title: EffectCraft: The Open-Source Motion Graphics Powerhouse Built in Rust!
description:
Quick Summary: 📝

EffectCraft is an open-source motion graphics and compositing tool written in Rust, aiming to be a clean-room reimplementation of Adobe After Effects. It offers features like Lottie import/export, scriptability, and a readable project file format, making it suitable for creating animated titles, motion graphics, and visual effects.

Key Takeaways: 💡

  • ✅ EffectCraft is a free, open-source, Rust-based clean-room reimplementation of Adobe After Effects.

  • ✅ It offers a familiar UI with extensive features like 306 effects, 3D support, and cross-platform compatibility (including browser).

  • ✅ Developers benefit from built-in Lottie support for web/app animations and human-readable JSON project files for version control.

  • ✅ The entire application is scriptable, enabling powerful automation and custom workflow integrations.

  • ✅ Its pure Rust video/audio codecs ensure efficiency and minimal external dependencies.

Project Statistics: 📊

  • ⭐ Stars: 6363
  • 🍴 Forks: 3283
  • ❗ Open Issues: 298

Tech Stack: 💻

  • ✅ Rust

Hey fellow developers! Ever felt the pinch of proprietary software when diving into motion graphics or visual effects? Or wished for a more developer-friendly, open-source tool that lets you create stunning animations without breaking the bank or wrestling with opaque file formats? Well, prepare to get excited, because I just stumbled upon a GitHub project that's poised to revolutionize the game: EffectCraft!

Imagine having a tool that mirrors the power and flexibility of industry giants like Adobe After Effects, but is completely free, open-source, and built from the ground up in pure Rust. That's exactly what EffectCraft is aiming to be. It's a clean-room reimplementation, meaning it's not just a clone, but a fresh take on motion graphics, designed with modern development practices in mind. This isn't just a passion project; it's a rapidly evolving, already usable application for creating animated titles, complex compositions, and dazzling visual effects.

EffectCraft embraces the core concepts you'd expect: compositions, layers, keyframes for precise animation control, and a massive library of 306 effects. It even includes layer styles, expressions, and full 3D camera and light support, culminating in a robust render queue. What's truly impressive is its native availability across macOS, Windows, and Linux, and yes, even in the browser! This cross-platform versatility alone is a huge win for any developer or artist.

Now, let's talk about why EffectCraft is a game-changer for us developers. First off, it boasts built-in Lottie import and export. For anyone working on web or mobile applications, this is massive! No more clunky plugins or conversion headaches; your animations go straight from EffectCraft to your apps and websites seamlessly. This feature alone makes it incredibly appealing for front-end and UI/UX developers.

But wait, there's more! EffectCraft's project files are readable JSON (.ecproj). This is a huge deal for collaborative teams and version control. Imagine being able to git diff your animation projects! This level of transparency and integration with standard developer workflows is practically unheard of in this space. Furthermore, every single action within EffectCraft is scriptable. Whether you want to automate tasks via the command line, control it through a JSON channel, or integrate it with an agent-based system, the possibilities for automation and custom workflows are endless. And as a final cherry on top, it uses pure Rust for all video and audio decoding and encoding, ditching FFmpeg for a lean, efficient, and dependency-minimal approach.

EffectCraft is young and moving fast, but it's already incredibly powerful and brimming with potential. It offers a familiar interface for those coming from other tools, but with a foundational architecture that's built for the future. If you're into motion graphics, animation, or just curious about what's possible with Rust in the creative space, you absolutely need to check out EffectCraft. It's truly exciting to see such a robust and developer-friendly tool emerge in this domain. Go give it a star and join the community!

title: VisualWorldBench: A Fine-Grained Multi-Task Benchmark for Evaluating Visual World Knowledge in MLLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.20083v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual world knowledge is a core capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), underpinning knowledge-intensive visual question answering and fine-grained visual reasoning. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in two key respects. First, their category coverage is narrow: most benchmarks span only a small number of categories across a few domains, falling far short of the open-ended scale of real-world visual entities. Second, their task construction is often insufficiently rigorous: models can answer correctly using coarse-grained cues, vague associations, or elimination strategies without truly mastering precise concepts, making it difficult to accurately assess their knowledge of fine-grained entities. We introduce VisualWorldBench, a taxonomy-grounded multi-task benchmark built on a hierarchical taxonomy of 21,291 leaf-node classes across 8 visual domains, with 32,541 evaluation instances whose ground-truth labels cover 15,479 categories across four complementary tasks: closed-set recognition, contrastive selection, precise localization, and open-world naming, covering different directions of knowledge retrieval and varying degrees of answer openness to comprehensively evaluate visual world knowledge. Most questions are constructed from taxonomically proximate categories, forcing precise discrimination among fine-grained entities. Experiments reveal that the strongest closed-source model achieves only 80.4% average accuracy, exposing capability gaps hidden under conventional benchmarks. We further construct VisualWorldBench-50K, a training resource covering 50K+ categories. Fine-tuning on VisualWorldBench-50K yields over 21 percentage points improvement on VisualWorldBench, with consistent transfer to public fine-grained recognition and visual knowledge benchmarks.
