title: A share link should stop working when the person who made it loses access
description:
Most apps that let you share a record by link store the link as a random token plus the record ID. Someone opens the link, the server finds the token and shows the record. The app saves who created the link, but nothing checks that person again.

This breaks when the creator's own access changes. A contractor shares a project doc with a client, then the contract ends and an admin removes them from the workspace. The link they made still opens the doc. The same thing happens when someone moves to another team and loses a folder, or when a doc is moved into a restricted space after the link was made.

Treat the link as acting for its creator. When someone opens it, check that the creator can still read the record right now, and that the link's level (view, comment or edit) is no higher than what the creator has today. If either check fails, return the same error you'd return for an unknown token, so whoever holds the link can't tell the record still exists.

When you deactivate a user, list the links they created and show them to the admin doing it. Some are fine to keep, like a public pricing sheet, and the admin can hand those to someone who still has access.

To test it, create a link as a regular user, remove that user from the workspace, then open the link in a private window. If the record loads, your links don't check their creator.

title: Flask Unleashed: Building a Production‑Ready API in 30 Minutes
description:
Flask Unleashed: Building a Production‑Ready API in 30 Minutes

Flask has been the go‑to micro‑framework for Python developers who want to spin up a web service fast without the overhead of a full‑stack solution. In this post we’ll walk through the essential pieces you need to take a bare‑bones Flask app and turn it into a production‑ready, testable, and deployable API. By the end you’ll have a clean project layout, proper configuration handling, basic error handling, automated tests, and a deployment strategy using Gunicorn and Docker.

1. Project Skeleton

A well‑structured project makes scaling easier. Here’s a minimal layout:

my_flask_api/
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── routes.py
│   ├── errors.py
│   └── config.py
├── tests/
│   └── test_routes.py
├── Dockerfile
├── requirements.txt
└── run.py
  • app/__init__.py – creates the Flask instance.
  • app/routes.py – holds all endpoint definitions.
  • app/errors.py – centralised error handlers.
  • app/config.py – environment‑specific settings.

2. Bootstrapping the Application

app/init.py

from flask import Flask
from .config import config_by_name
from .routes import api_blueprint
from .errors import register_error_handlers

def create_app(env_name='development'):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config.from_object(config_by_name[env_name])

    # Register blueprints and error handlers
    app.register_blueprint(api_blueprint, url_prefix='/api')
    register_error_handlers(app)

    return app

app/config.py

import os

class BaseConfig:
    DEBUG = False
    TESTING = False
    SECRET_KEY = os.getenv('SECRET_KEY', 'fallback-secret')
    JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR = False

class DevelopmentConfig(BaseConfig):
    DEBUG = True

class ProductionConfig(BaseConfig):
    # In production you’ll probably pull secrets from a vault
    DEBUG = False

config_by_name = {
    'development': DevelopmentConfig,
    'production': ProductionConfig
}

run.py

import os
from app import create_app

environment = os.getenv('FLASK_ENV', 'development')
app = create_app(environment)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Flask’s built‑in server is fine for dev only
    app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000)

With this in place you can start the dev server:

$ export FLASK_ENV=development
$ python run.py

Visit http://localhost:5000/api/ping (we’ll add this route next) to see the API alive.

3. Defining Routes

app/routes.py

from flask import Blueprint, jsonify, request

api_blueprint = Blueprint('api', __name__)

@api_blueprint.route('/ping', methods=['GET'])
def ping():
    """Simple health‑check endpoint."""
    return jsonify(status='ok', message='pong'), 200

@api_blueprint.route('/echo', methods=['POST'])
def echo():
    """Echo back the JSON payload."""
    data = request.get_json(force=True)
    return jsonify(received=data), 200

Notice the use of a Blueprint. This isolates API routes under a common prefix and keeps __init__ tidy.

4. Centralised Error Handling

app/errors.py

from flask import jsonify

def register_error_handlers(app):
    @app.errorhandler(400)
    def bad_request(error):
        return jsonify(error='Bad request', message=str(error)), 400

    @app.errorhandler(404)
    def not_found(error):
        return jsonify(error='Not found', message=str(error)), 404

    @app.errorhandler(500)
    def internal_error(error):
        # In production you would log the stack trace
        return jsonify(error='Server error', message='An unexpected error occurred'), 500

Now every endpoint automatically returns JSON‑formatted error bodies, which is a best practice for APIs.

5. Adding a Simple Service Layer

For anything beyond trivial routes you’ll want to keep business logic out of the view functions.

app/services.py

def calculate_factorial(n: int) -> int:
    """Very small utility used by the demo endpoint."""
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError('Negative numbers are not allowed')
    result = 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        result *= i
    return result

app/routes.py (extend)

from .services import calculate_factorial

@api_blueprint.route('/factorial/<int:number>', methods=['GET'])
def factorial(number):
    try:
        result = calculate_factorial(number)
        return jsonify(number=number, factorial=result), 200
    except ValueError as exc:
        return jsonify(error='Invalid input', message=str(exc)), 400

The separation makes unit testing straightforward.

6. Unit Tests with pytest

tests/test_routes.py

import json
import pytest
from app import create_app

@pytest.fixture
def client():
    app = create_app('development')
    app.testing = True
    with app.test_client() as client:
        yield client

def test_ping(client):
    response = client.get('/api/ping')
    assert response.status_code == 200
    data = json.loads(response.data)
    assert data['status'] == 'ok'

def test_factorial_success(client):
    response = client.get('/api/factorial/5')
    assert response.status_code == 200
    data = json.loads(response.data)
    assert data['factorial'] == 120

def test_factorial_negative(client):
    response = client.get('/api/factorial/-3')
    assert response.status_code == 400
    data = json.loads(response.data)
    assert data['error'] == 'Invalid input'

Run the suite with:

$ pytest -q

All tests should pass, giving you confidence before you ship.

7. Dockerising the Service

Dockerfile

# Use the official lightweight Python image.
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Create a non‑root user.
RUN useradd -ms /bin/bash appuser
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy source code.
COPY . .

# Switch to non‑root user.
USER appuser

# Expose the port Flask will run on.
EXPOSE 5000

# Use Gunicorn for production WSGI serving.
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:5000", "run:app"]

requirements.txt

Flask==3.0.2
gunicorn==21.2.0
pytest==8.2.0

Build and run:

$ docker build -t my_flask_api .
$ docker run -d -p 5000:5000 my_flask_api

Your API is now behind a battle‑tested WSGI server, ready for traffic.

8. Environment Variables & Secrets

Never hard‑code secrets. Use a .env file locally (with python-dotenv if you like) and set real environment variables on your host or CI platform.

# .env (development only)
FLASK_ENV=development
SECRET_KEY=dev-secret-123

In production you might inject SECRET_KEY through your cloud provider’s secret manager or a Docker secret.

9. Basic CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions) 

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: |
          python -m pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install -r requirements.txt
      - name: Run tests
        run: pytest -q

Every push triggers the test suite, catching regressions before they reach production.

10. Performance Tweaks

  • Enable JSONIFY_MIMETYPE = "application/json" in config to avoid extra MIME negotiation.
  • Cache expensive results using Flask‑Caching or an external Redis layer.
  • Set worker_processes in Gunicorn to $(nproc) for optimal CPU utilisation.

11. Next Steps

  • Add Swagger/OpenAPI docs with flasgger or apispec.
  • Secure endpoints with Flask‑JWT‑Extended for token‑based auth.
  • Deploy to a managed platform like Render, Fly.io, or DigitalOcean App Platform for zero‑ops scaling.

Recommended Tools

If you’re looking for a fast, reliable VPS to host your Flask containers, DigitalOcean Droplets provide a developer‑friendly dashboard and straightforward pricing – perfect for small‑to‑medium APIs.

For a fully managed deployment experience, consider Render.com. Render can automatically build your Dockerfile, set up HTTPS, and scale your service without you touching any servers.

Both services offer generous free tiers and easy integration with GitHub, making the jump from local development to production seamless.

Enjoy building with Flask, and happy coding!

title: DigitalOcean costs 30-40% more than Hetzner for Node.js — is the premium worth it?
description:
After benchmarking Hetzner vs DigitalOcean for Node.js, I kept getting the same question: "but what about support and dashboard UX?" Here's what the premium actually buys you, beyond the spec sheet.

Pricing (2026)

Plan vCPU RAM Storage Price/month
Basic 1GB 1 1 GB 25 GB SSD $6
Basic 2GB 1 2 GB 50 GB SSD $12
Basic 4GB 2 4 GB 80 GB SSD $24
Basic 8GB 4 8 GB 160 GB SSD $48

Hetzner CX22 (2 vCPU, 4GB) runs ~€4.35/mo. DigitalOcean's equivalent Basic 4GB is $24/mo — roughly 5x. Premium AMD droplets (NVMe, dedicated thread) cost ~2x the Basic tier on top of that.

What the premium actually buys you

  • Live chat support that responds. This is the real differentiator — tickets get answered in minutes, not the 24-48h typical of budget providers.
  • A dashboard that doesn't fight you. Droplet creation, snapshots, firewalls — all obvious without reading docs.
  • A 1-Click Node.js Marketplace image that pre-installs Node, PM2, and Nginx — saves roughly 15 minutes on initial setup.
  • Managed databases, load balancers, and S3-compatible Spaces in the same dashboard if you need them later.

What it doesn't buy you

Basic plans use shared Intel CPUs with regular SSD, not NVMe — NVMe only comes on Premium droplets. Disk throughput on Basic was clearly the weak point:

Metric DigitalOcean Basic 4GB Hetzner CX22
Express API (light load, EU) 10–18ms 8–15ms
Disk read (sequential) ~500 MB/s ~2,000 MB/s
Price/month $24 ~€4.35

Premium AMD droplets close most of that gap, but then you're paying closer to 6-7x Hetzner's price for comparable performance.

Who this is actually for

  • ✅ You're new to VPS and don't want to debug SSH/firewall issues solo
  • ✅ Client work where "who do we call at 2am" needs a real answer
  • ✅ Short-lived environments — hourly billing is available
  • ✅ You'll actually use managed databases or load balancers later
  • ❌ Pure budget optimization — Hetzner or Contabo give more spec per dollar
  • ❌ Disk-heavy workloads on Basic plans specifically

Verdict

The premium is real, and for client work where support response time matters, I'd pay it again. If you're a solo dev optimizing your own side project's bill, it's genuinely hard to justify over Hetzner on specs alone — the thing you're paying for is the safety net, not the hardware.

Full benchmarks, regions, and Node.js setup steps at vpsfor.dev →

title: Evaluating Browser Storage Handoffs: React PUTs, Express Signing, Private Object Reads
description:
Short answer: use a private object storage bucket, have an Express server create a short-lived presigned PUT URL, and let React upload the bytes directly; issue another signed download URL when an authorized user needs the object. This keeps file transfer out of the application server, but it is not a good fit for permanent public links or a deployment that needs self-service bucket CORS rules.

The interesting part is the handoff. Express owns identity and the object key. React owns the byte transfer. Storage owns the bytes. That division is easy to describe and surprisingly easy to blur once a file becomes input to a RAG pipeline or an evaluation run.

My acceptance test is eval-driven: upload a fixture from the browser, verify the object, read it as the owning user, and confirm that a different user cannot obtain a signed download. Measure completion time by file-size bucket and count records that stay pending. Prompt-cost awareness belongs here too; a failed upload should not silently trigger a second document-ingestion run and double the tokens.

Keep the transfer boring.

How should React and Express handle a private object storage upload and signed download?

Create or check the bucket once during deployment. For each upload, the Express side authenticates the user, generates a server-owned key, records user_id and MIME type in the database, and asks storage for a presigned PUT URL. React sends the file to that returned URL with PUT. The platform credential stays on the server; it must never be sent with the browser's follow-up request.

After the upload, confirm the object before marking the database row ready. A successful browser request means the transfer request succeeded; it does not establish that the application has associated the intended key with the intended user. For a private read, the server checks ownership and returns a fresh signed download URL. There is no permanent public URL in this design.

Here is the control-plane part in Python. The HTTP shape is the same one a Node.js or Express handler would use. The body is kept empty because the current discovery response is the authority for the operation's request schema; do not copy an invented S3 field into production. The sample checks status, honors Retry-After, and backs off on 429.

import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


BASE_URL = os.environ["INFRAI_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")


def post_with_backoff(path, body):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(5):
        request = Request(
            BASE_URL + path,
            data=json.dumps(body).encode("utf-8"),
            method="POST",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
            },
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                payload = response.read()
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(
                        f"storage request returned {response.status}: {payload!r}"
                    )
                return json.loads(payload)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"storage request returned {error.code}: {detail}"
                ) from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("presign request exhausted its retries")


def create_private_upload(bucket, object_key):
    path_template = os.environ["INFRAI_STORAGE_PRESIGN_PATH"]
    path = path_template.format(
        bucket=quote(bucket, safe=""),
        key=quote(object_key, safe=""),
    )
    return post_with_backoff(path, {})


signed = create_private_upload("app-files", "users/42/eval-input.json")
print(signed)

The verified signing route is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. Its returned value is for the browser's upload step, not another API call with the platform credential. React should use the URL and the method or headers described by that response, then call your own confirmation endpoint. When the UI later needs the file, the server can use the same presign operation for a signed read according to the discovered request shape, or serve the file through an authorization-checked application endpoint. Never attach Authorization: Bearer ... to a returned presigned URL.

Use a fresh random component in a real key rather than letting the browser choose users/42/eval-input.json. There is no object versioning, no object lock, and no If-Match conditional write, so a reused key can make an accidental overwrite impossible to recover through storage history. A database or queue must coordinate strict replacement. The object key is for bytes; the application row is for ownership, MIME type, display name, and workflow state. It doesn't replace that application record.

What should you measure before copying this browser upload pattern?

The simple approach is a multipart Express endpoint: React posts the file to your app, and the app writes it onward. It is a useful prototype because it has one request to reason about. It is a poor default for large files, slow mobile connections, or a service that also runs ingestion and eval workers. The API process becomes the long-lived pipe, and its transfer load gets mixed with the short control-plane requests that authenticate users and start jobs.

Direct upload moves that pipe to object storage. The application still makes the important decisions, but it no longer buffers every byte. That helps a notebook-to-prod path: an AI builder can test the signer with a fixture, test the React transfer separately, and test the attachment state transition without pretending that a green API response proves the document is ready for retrieval.

Measure three things before standardizing it:

  • upload completion rate and duration by file-size range;
  • pending database rows that never reach verified;
  • duplicate ingestion or evaluation jobs after a browser retry.

The third metric is where prompt-cost awareness becomes operational. The storage URL should not be the event that starts a model call. Mark the object verified first, then enqueue one idempotent application job keyed by the attachment record. Your mileage may vary with mobile networks, so use production-like fixtures rather than a tiny local text file.

How do private buckets, CORS, and signed download URLs change the choice?

Private access changes the product contract. Uploaded objects should be read through short-lived signed URLs or an application-controlled download response. They should not be published as permanent links, and this storage shape is not suitable for static website hosting or a public image host.

React also needs the storage service to accept the deployed frontend origin, the PUT method, and the headers involved in the browser request. A server-generated signature cannot make a browser preflight succeed by itself. This matters because the storage capability has no exposed independent route for managing bucket CORS rules. If operators need to add origins without a provider change, choose a service that offers that control instead.

Lifecycle cleanup has a boundary as well: the shortest lifecycle is one day, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Do not use it as an hour-scale abandoned-upload janitor. Store application metadata in the database because server-side object metadata is not a searchable catalog; listing is prefix-based. There is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool either.

That is a lot of boundaries for one small upload feature. They are still easier to test when the browser and application own separate steps.

Which private object storage option fits this workflow?

The direct-upload pattern exists across the major choices. The decision is about the controls around it and how much integration surface the rest of the product needs.

Option Browser upload and private read Good fit Important trade-off
Amazon S3 Presigned PUT and signed download patterns Teams already operating in AWS More AWS-specific policy and service configuration
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible presigned requests Products centered on Cloudflare Confirm the required access and delivery controls in that platform
Google Cloud Storage Signed upload and download URLs Workloads already using Google Cloud identity The surrounding application still follows Google-specific operational conventions
Infrai storage Presigned object upload and signed access through REST A small AI product that wants storage and other backend capabilities behind one key and one bill Private-only access, no self-service CORS route, and no object history

Infrai's practical advantage here is the single control surface: one plain REST API and one credential can cover storage alongside other backend modules, so a Python service and a JavaScript frontend do not need a storage SDK just to agree on this boundary. That is a workflow advantage, not a claim about lowest price.

The catch is clear. Stick with S3, R2, or Google Cloud Storage when public delivery, version recovery, object lock, configurable CORS, cross-region replication, or bulk migration is a requirement you cannot move outside the application. Infrai is not suitable for those cases. It is a reasonable option when the files stay private and the team values a consistent backend contract more than provider-specific storage controls.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls

title: Filter in ASP.NET Core Web API
description:
Filters in ASP.NET Core Web API
What is a filter?
A filter is code that runs at a specific stage while ASP.NET Core processes a controller action. It can run before or after the action, check access, handle certain exceptions, or inspect the result. This helps you apply common behavior without repeating it in every action. learn.microsoft.com

Types of filters
Filter What it does Main methods
Authorization Checks whether the request can access the action. OnAuthorization
Resource Runs around most of the controller filter pipeline. OnResourceExecuting, OnResourceExecuted
Action Runs around the controller action. OnActionExecuting, OnActionExecuted
Exception Handles certain unhandled exceptions. OnException
Result Runs around execution of the action result. OnResultExecuting, OnResultExecuted
These are the five main controller filter types. ASP.NET Core also has endpoint filters, which run around endpoint handlers and can be used with API endpoints; they are separate from the five-stage controller sequence below. learn.microsoft.com

Order of execution
For a request that is authorized and completes successfully:

HTTP request
↓
Authorization filter
↓
OnResourceExecuting
↓
Model binding
↓
OnActionExecuting
↓
Controller action
↓
OnActionExecuted
↓
OnResultExecuting
↓
Result execution (for example, writing JSON)
↓
OnResultExecuted
↓
OnResourceExecuted
↓
HTTP response
The “Executing” methods run on the way toward the action or result. The “Executed” methods run as those stages finish. Model binding happens after the resource filter starts and before the action filter starts. learn.microsoft.com

Where does the exception filter fit? It is not a regular step in every request. It runs only when an applicable unhandled exception occurs; it does not catch exceptions from every stage of the pipeline. Also, a filter can stop the request early, so the full sequence above will not always run. learn.microsoft.com

Key point for interviews: Authorization → Resource → Action → Result, with the “after” methods running as their surrounding stages finish. Exception filtering is conditional.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Multilingual Abstractive Summarization: A Comprehensive Study of English and Bengali
description:
arXiv:2610.19003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.

title: Building a reading ruler that floats over every Android app: touch pass-through, Android 12's opacity cap, and masks
description:
I make ReadFocus+, a small Android app that floats a translucent strip (a "reading ruler") over the screen, mainly for people with dyslexia or ADHD who lose their place in long text. It has to work on top of any app: ebooks, PDFs, browsers, news apps. So it is built on a SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlay. These are the parts that took the most time.

Layout: one strip, two masks, one control panel

  • The strip: one window, MATCH_PARENT wide with adjustable height. TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY (TYPE_PHONE below API 26), PixelFormat.TRANSLUCENT.
  • Line highlight mode: a View inside the strip painted with a GradientDrawable in the theme colour; the View's alpha sets the strength. No custom onDraw.
  • Reading mask mode: two separate windows, a solid View pinned to Gravity.TOP and one to Gravity.BOTTOM, with the gap between them as the reading window. When you drag the strip, both masks follow.
  • Control panel: another window holding the mode switch and the lock button.

Letting touches through to the app underneath

(The code below is simplified for the article.)

A reading ruler is only useful if you can keep scrolling the app under it.

int flags = WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE
          | WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_TOUCH_MODAL
          | WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_LAYOUT_IN_SCREEN;
if (locked) flags |= WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE; // locked = touches pass through
  • The default is locked (touch pass-through). To move the strip you unlock it from the panel, then drag the strip itself with ACTION_DOWN/MOVE/UP and updateViewLayout on params.y.
  • When toggling FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE, I remove the window and add it again rather than only updating the flags.
  • y is clamped between the status bar and the navigation bar, using WindowInsets (statusBars, navigationBars, systemGestures, displayCutout).

Android 12: the opacity cap on pass-through windows

From Android 12 (API 31), an overlay that lets touches pass through to another app has a maximum opacity. Go above it and the system blocks the touches instead (the "untrusted touches" protection).

float maxAlpha = 1f;
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31) {
    InputManager im = getSystemService(InputManager.class);
    maxAlpha = (im != null) ? im.getMaximumObscuringOpacityForTouch() : 0.8f;
}
params.alpha = maxAlpha;

So the window alpha is pinned to that ceiling, and the visible strength comes from the inner View's alpha and the theme colour. This is also why the mask can never be fully black.

Display cutouts

On phones with a notch, the top mask must not leave a gap above it:

  • API 30+: LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_ALWAYS
  • API 28–29: LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_SHORT_EDGES

On rotation, onConfigurationChanged re-clamps the strip and redraws the masks. Every window also has FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON, so the screen doesn't go dark mid-page.

Staying alive and coming back after process death

  • A foreground service with foregroundServiceType="specialUse" (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE) and a low-importance, ongoing notification.
  • Besides START_STICKY, the overlay is restored on app launch, on process restart, and by a WorkManager watchdog every 15 minutes.
  • Users can revoke the overlay permission at any time, and adding a window after that throws BadTokenException, so Settings.canDrawOverlays() is checked before every addView.

The permission flow

ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION with a package: URI → retry without it → fall back to ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS. The guide screen checks canDrawOverlays() in onResume and returns as soon as it's true.

Wrapping up

Most of the work was in small details that let the overlay sit on top without getting in the way. If you're building an overlay of your own, I hope this saves you some time. The app is here (there's a Windows version too):

  • Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.codedac.readfocus
  • Website: https://codedac.com/apps/readfocus.html

title: Go Logistics Queue 2026: Publish Per Waiter Under Burst Recovery
description:
Short answer: send a small recipient-specific delta when a customer may see only their own queue position; send a whole-queue snapshot only to an authorized display that genuinely needs the entire ordered set. For a small SaaS, the least complex defensible design is usually a versioned delta plus a periodic or on-demand snapshot for repair. Every update carries a monotonically increasing queue version, clients reject older versions, and a detected gap triggers resynchronization.

The page says customer queue display stale, and the on-call sees an apparently healthy publisher beside a growing count of clients whose acknowledged version trails the current queue version. That is the useful symptom. A page based only on publish errors arrives too late, because a successful publish says nothing about whether the customer view converged.

The publisher was green.

This distinction drives the message-size comparison. A snapshot can repair state in one delivery but repeats data that most recipients neither need nor should receive; per-recipient deltas keep the hot path small but require explicit gap detection. Do the byte arithmetic with encoded messages, then choose the smallest disclosure boundary that still meets the recovery SLO.

Should a queue publish one message per waiter?

A logistics dispatch session is a state machine. A shipment request joins a queue, changes position, becomes ready, or leaves. The customer-facing display needs to converge on an authorized projection of that state. If one subscriber misses version 418, version 419 may still arrive, and a green publish counter can coexist with a wrong screen.

The signal that should fire earlier is version lag, measured at the receiving edge: current_queue_version - last_applied_version, grouped by session and bounded by the service-level objective. Transport acknowledgements help diagnose the path, but they do not prove that the UI applied the state. Define the SLO in terms of visible convergence, such as the proportion of active displays that apply the current authorized version within the chosen time window. The target and window must come from the product's tolerance for stale queue positions; there is no honest universal number.

Start with three counters: produced versions, applied versions, and resynchronizations. Add a histogram for convergence time and a gauge for connected displays by session. Do not put customer IDs into metric labels. High-cardinality identity belongs in sampled traces or structured logs with suitable access controls and retention.

One trap is paging on a single late client. A browser in the background, a device losing radio coverage, or a closed tab can all stop acknowledging progress without indicating a service-wide failure. Page on an SLO-burning cohort; retain per-connection lag for diagnosis. Otherwise the alarm measures client churn and trains the on-call to ignore it. The limitation of this cohort view is equally plain: aggregation can hide one customer who has been stale for a long time, so the dashboard still needs a longest-lag view even when that view does not page anyone.

Message size is multiplication, not a payload contest

Compare encoded bytes over the same observation window. Let S be encoded snapshot bytes, D encoded recipient-delta bytes, N connected recipients, C queue changes, and R snapshot repairs. Ignoring shared framing for a moment, whole-queue fan-out costs roughly C * N * S; recipient deltas cost roughly C * N * D + R * S. Add transport framing, authentication metadata, retries, and compression as measured terms rather than intuition.

For a capacity-planning example, suppose a test fixture has 80 waiting customers. Its encoded authorized snapshot is 6,400 bytes and its encoded per-recipient position update is 120 bytes. With 80 connected customers and 10 queue changes, the payload arithmetic is 5,120,000 bytes for repeated snapshots versus 96,000 bytes for deltas, before repairs and framing. These are illustrative inputs, not benchmarks. Serialize your actual schema because field names, identifiers, timestamps, and encoding choices change the result.

The ratio is informative; the absolute result decides capacity.

Eighty recipients matter.

Decision concern Recipient delta Authorized snapshot
Normal-path bytes Scales with the changed projection Scales with the full authorized projection
Recovery Needs gap detection and a snapshot fetch or push Replaces prior state when accepted
Ordering Version check is mandatory Version check is still mandatory
Privacy boundary Can disclose one customer's projection Must be filtered for the display's authorization
Server work More projections or routing keys Larger serialization and filtering work
Client work Apply a transition Replace and render state

Compression does not settle the architecture. It may reduce repeated fields in snapshots, but the sender still constructs the authorized payload and the receiver still handles it. Measure compressed and uncompressed sizes with representative data, then preserve hard limits for both. The trade-off is workload-dependent: a slowly changing, publicly visible depot board can make snapshots the simpler choice, while a private customer view with frequent position changes makes whole-queue publication inappropriate. Recipient deltas are not suitable when clients cannot preserve a version or request repair; snapshots are not suitable when their contents exceed the recipient's authorization boundary.

Instrument the version contract

The useful instrumentation sits beside the state transition. A message needs a session identifier, a queue version, a type, and the smallest authorized payload required for that recipient. This Go sketch shows application semantics, not a transport guarantee:

package queue

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type Update struct {
    SessionID string `json:"session_id"`
    Version   uint64 `json:"version"`
    Kind      string `json:"kind"`
    Position  int    `json:"position,omitempty"`
}

type View struct {
    SessionID string
    Version   uint64
    Position  int
}

var ErrVersionGap = errors.New("queue version gap")

func Apply(view View, update Update) (View, error) {
    if update.SessionID != view.SessionID {
        return view, errors.New("session mismatch")
    }
    if update.Version <= view.Version {
        return view, nil // Duplicate or reordered old delivery.
    }
    if update.Version != view.Version+1 {
        return view, fmt.Errorf("%w: have %d, received %d", ErrVersionGap, view.Version, update.Version)
    }
    if update.Kind != "position_changed" {
        return view, errors.New("unsupported update kind")
    }

    view.Version = update.Version
    view.Position = update.Position
    return view, nil
}

Old duplicates become harmless, while a forward gap becomes observable and recoverable. The resync path returns an authorized snapshot with a version; the client replaces local state only when that version is newer. A reconnect begins the same way. The end-to-end claim should remain modest: the display converges under the retry and repair policy you test.

No version, no guarantee.

Persisting the state transition and publishing its notification in unrelated operations creates an ambiguity: either the state commits without an event, or an event escapes before the state does. A durable change record processed asynchronously can close that gap, provided its retry behavior and retention meet the recovery objective. Test the crash points around commit, publication, acknowledgement, and client application.

Test disorder deliberately. Duplicate version 418, deliver 419 before 418, disconnect after receipt but before acknowledgement, expire retained events, and reconnect from an older snapshot. Also test authorization changes during a session. A whole-queue payload cached under yesterday's access decision is a data exposure, not a harmless stale view.

Delivery guarantees belong in the buy-versus-build review

A managed transport can remove socket operations from the on-call queue; a self-hosted path can offer tighter control over retention, placement, and protocol behavior. Neither choice removes the application version contract. Ask where acknowledgement occurs, how long replay remains possible, what ordering scope exists, what happens under subscriber backpressure, and which side owns reconnect storms.

Operating question Managed path Self-hosted path Decision evidence
Who pages for saturation? Service boundary may absorb part of it Platform team owns the full path Documented responsibility and drill results
Can retention meet repair time? Constrained by the offered contract Configurable within team capacity Tested maximum disconnect window
How is lock-in contained? Adapter and export paths matter Protocol and storage choices still create coupling Recovery exercise using the abstraction
What is the real cost? Usage plus integration and incident work Compute, storage, upgrades, and on-call load Same traffic model and staffing assumptions

WebRTC data channels are one standards-based option for peer-to-peer data exchange, and the W3C specification defines their behavior and API surface. That does not make a peer mesh the default for a customer queue: topology, authorization, discovery, and recovery remain system responsibilities. Apply the same encoded-byte and convergence tests to any transport.

The deployment gate should include a shadow calculation of both message shapes against production-like fixtures, a load test with synchronized reconnects, and a rollback rule tied to convergence rather than publisher throughput alone. Capacity must include headroom for repair traffic. If every client requests a snapshot after a brief network interruption, the recovery path can become the largest burst in the system.

Set the alert where action changes

Use recipient deltas for routine customer updates when authorization is narrow and changes are frequent. Use a versioned snapshot for initial load, verified gaps, and displays authorized to render the whole queue. If a client cannot implement version checks and repair, repeated snapshots may be simpler, but account for disclosure and fan-out before accepting that simplicity.

Then tune the page. An alert threshold below the normal tail of client behavior creates noise, interrupts sleep, and consumes the same engineering capacity needed to improve recovery. A threshold that waits until many displays are stale protects the pager while abandoning the SLO. Start from the error-budget burn that requires human action, validate it during disconnect and reconnect drills, and keep lower-severity signals on a dashboard for trend work.

False positives have a concrete cost: an engineer investigates transport health while the underlying event is a backgrounded browser or a session that has already ended. Filter inactive sessions, distinguish disconnected from connected-but-behind, and require enough affected traffic to justify a page. The final architecture is credible only when its alert points to an action the on-call can take.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

Further reading

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: NestJS vs Go: Lessons From Production Projects
description:
Four production systems, 18 user roles, around 460 candidates, deadline queues, and video lessons for up to 100 participants — what made NestJS a fit, and where Qtim introduced Go.

A student opens one lesson. The product checks their role, loads the schedule, shows the right assignments, accepts a file, and starts a video session.

For the student, this is one interface. For the backend, it is a set of different jobs: access control, state transitions, background processing, reports, integrations, and a live media path.

Qtim has used NestJS across several education systems because most of that work is shaped by business rules that keep changing after launch. Go entered the architecture in one specific subsystem: video, where WebRTC, an SFU, media routing, and latency created a different workload.

The takeaway from production is less dramatic than a “NestJS versus Go” debate. A stack decision starts with the part of the system that changes most often and the part that carries the heaviest load.

Eighteen roles made access control the product

Qtim joined the Online School №1 project after the client had struggled with previous contractors. The first release had to go live within three months without closing the door on later changes.

Students saw lessons, homework, materials, teacher chat, calendars, and progress. Behind that interface were more than ten subprojects and 18 user types, including teachers, curators, coordinators, and administrators. Each role needed its own view of groups, schedules, assignments, and project settings.

The team separated those rules with NestJS modules, services, guards, and policies. A guard checked whether a user could enter a scenario; a policy described what that user could do with a particular object. CASL supported the more detailed rules, such as giving a curator access to one student group while allowing a coordinator to manage schedules.

That structure made access changes predictable. A new permission could be configured in 15–20 minutes instead of being threaded through the entire backend. Assignments, attempts, calendars, and schedules later moved behind clearer service boundaries, with RabbitMQ carrying events away from the main user flow.

NestJS worked here because the difficult part was changeability. New roles and workflows had to fit without weakening the access model.

Around 460 candidates made every status transition consequential

The university attestation platform brought registration, document checks, exams, video evidence, assessment, protocols, reports, and federal-registry exports into one process.

A status error could break the chain. The candidate needed to move from registration to document verification, the exam, grading, and final records in the correct order. Administrators, examiners, and super administrators required different actions and different access to media.

Qtim kept status transitions in the service layer rather than controllers. The controller accepted an action; the service checked whether the application could move forward; guards blocked unauthorized media access before a request reached the handler.

Around 460 candidates passed through the platform. The value of the architecture was the ability to keep each status, document, recording, and permission inside one testable process. Raw request throughput was secondary to preserving the rules.

The deadline peak belonged in a queue

StudyCats needed a complete preparation system for Russian school exams: course pages, schedules, homework, mock tests, revision cards, statistics, and gamification. Qtim delivered it with NestJS and Nuxt.js in five months.

Education platforms have a predictable bad habit: many students submit work just before a deadline. File validation and audio conversion then compete with the learning interface at the exact moment that interface is busiest.

The heavy operations moved to BullMQ queues backed by Redis. A student submitted an assignment and returned to the lesson. A separate worker processed the files, ran the required checks, and updated the result status. Voice recordings followed the same path: conversion happened in the background, while the player received a consistent format across devices.

The queue protected the user journey without introducing another programming language. That distinction matters. A workload problem can often be isolated inside the current stack before a team adds a second runtime.

A 100-person video lesson created a second workload

The video-conferencing product for Online School №1 had a different profile. Lessons could include up to 100 participants while schedules, authorization, recordings, teacher controls, and the connection to the learning platform still had to work as one experience.

Qtim kept the API, administration tools, roles, and schedules in NestJS. The media subsystem used WebRTC and Go.

Node.js handles large volumes of concurrent I/O well. The media path brought CPU-heavy work: packet processing, SFU routing, fan-out to many participants, active connections, and latency control. That boundary justified a separate service with its own runtime.

The result was a mixed architecture with a clear division of responsibility. NestJS owned the product rules. Go handled the connection-heavy media path. Users still saw one lesson interface.

This case does not turn Go into the default choice for WebRTC. It shows the condition that made a second language reasonable: a bounded subsystem had a distinct workload and could be operated independently.

The second stack comes with a permanent bill

NestJS modules earn their keep in a large product with many roles and changing workflows. In a small service, the same structure can add ceremony where one handler would have been enough.

Microservices create independent boundaries and also introduce distributed debugging, message delivery, data consistency, and more operational surfaces. The online-school platform accepted that cost where assignments, attempts, calendars, and schedules needed more autonomy.

Go also adds a runtime, build process, deployment path, monitoring setup, and a boundary between product logic and the media subsystem. The performance gain has to cover those continuing costs. Otherwise, the team has created a second stack and kept the original problem.

Choose for the next production change

NestJS fits a product dominated by roles, workflows, documents, payments, reports, and integrations. Its value grows when the team expects those rules to change after launch.

A separate Go service becomes reasonable when production evidence points to a different workload, the hot path has a stable boundary, and the expected gain covers the cost of operating another stack.

The decision rule is straightforward: keep changing business logic in the application layer; isolate a second runtime only around a measured workload that can stand on its own.

If a product combines complex roles, background processing, integrations, or load-sensitive services, the Qtim team can map the boundaries and plan the next production architecture.

title: New Ubuntu 26.10 released with PDF signatures and Rust tools
description:
Ubuntu 26.10 arrives with Rust-based core utilities, passkey login support, Linux kernel 7.3, GNOME 51, and Mesa 26.2.

Explore the key technical updates, including improved window tiling, TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and a dedicated amd64v3 optimized installer image.

New features in apps and settings

On the apps side, the document viewer now allows users to add handwritten signatures to PDF files. Signatures can be made with a mouse, stylus, touchscreen, or via an imported photo. Taking screenshots has gained more precise control over options via the keyboard, while the sound heard during capture has also been changed.

The main app store has a separate section for additional hardware drivers and media files, while it aggregates details for different app formats. In the system settings, options have been added to automatically disable the touchpad when a mouse is connected, as well as control of auto-rotation on touchscreens. At the same time, the system remembers and restores brightness and color settings for each display separately even after rebooting, while old support for WEP-type wireless networks has been removed.

Hardware support and technical improvements

The new release is based on the GNOME 51 update series, Mesa 26.2 graphics drivers, and Linux kernel 7.3, with a planned nine-month support period. In disk management, full-disk encryption is now available on devices without built-in trusted hardware, requiring the use of a personal PIN or passphrase during installation.

READ ALSO

New Ubuntu 26.10 released with Snapdragon support and new GNOME

The system resource monitor can now display activity for specific AMD processor chips. A separate installation image optimized for the latest processors is available, and an official experimental version has been released for specific new board systems. Finally, the system package management tools offer more informative per-command help.

title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?
description:
arXiv:2610.19025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.

title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
description:
arXiv:2610.19520v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7-12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.

title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
description:
arXiv:2610.14118v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.

title: AWS Transfer Family console supports SVG logos and ICO favicons for web apps
description:
The AWS Transfer Family console now supports SVG files for logos and ICO files for favicons in web apps, with upload limits increased to 2 MB. This gives you more flexibility to use existing branding assets when customizing your web app.

Previously, the console accepted only JPG and PNG files and limited logo uploads to 50 KB and favicon uploads to 20 KB. The console automatically resizes images and converts them to JPG or PNG before saving them. Existing API upload limits and format requirements remain unchanged.

title: The Gap Is in the Geometry: A Convergent Meta-Analysis of Multi-Facet Aerial and Remote Sensing Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.19102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks

title: Load Balancing: The Matrix Reloaded
description:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")

Honestly, I was staring at our API gateway one Friday night, watching the metrics spike like a boss fight in Dark Souls. Every time a new feature rolled out, a handful of nodes would get hammered while the rest twiddled their thumbs. Our round‑robin balancer looked fine on paper, but in production it felt like we were sending all the Neo’s to the same agent while the others got bored. I kept asking myself: Is there a smarter way to spread the load without adding crazy complexity? That question sent me down a rabbit hole that ended with a simple, elegant trick that changed everything.

The Revelation (The Insight)

The “aha!” moment came when I read about the Power of Two Choices (sometimes called “random‑two‑choices load balancing”). The idea is ridiculous‑simple: for each incoming request, pick two servers at random, check their current load (e.g., active connection count), and send the request to the less loaded of the two.

Why does this work? Imagine you have n servers and you throw balls (requests) into bins (servers) uniformly at random. The max load grows like log n / log log n. If you instead always choose the lighter of two random bins, the max load drops to log log n—an exponential improvement! In plain English: a tiny bit of extra work (two random picks + a comparison) cuts the worst‑case hotspot dramatically.

The trade‑off? You need a lightweight way to query each server’s load. If you already expose a metric like current connection count or CPU usage via a sidecar or shared memory, the extra lookup is negligible. If you have to hit an external stats service for every request, the latency cost might outweigh the gain—so keep the load info local or cached for a few milliseconds.

Wielding the Power (Code & Examples)

The “before” – naïve round robin 

type RoundRobin struct {
    servers []*Server
    idx     int
}

func (rr *RoundRobin) Next() *Server {
    s := rr.servers[rr.idx]
    rr.idx = (rr.idx + 1) % len(rr.servers)
    return s
}

It’s clean, but when traffic is bursty, a few servers can end up with double the load while others stay idle. I spent three hours debugging why our latency spikes correlated with certain times of day—turns out it was just the luck of the draw.

The “after” – Power of Two Choices 

type PowerOfTwo struct {
    servers []*Server
    rand    *rand.Rand
}

func NewPowerOfTwo(servers []*Server) *PowerOfTwo {
    return &PowerOfTwo{
        servers: servers,
        rand:    rand.New(rand.NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano())),
    }
}

// pick two distinct servers at random
func (p *PowerOfTwo) chooseTwo() (*Server, *Server) {
    a := p.servers[p.rand.Intn(len(p.servers))]
    b := p.servers[p.rand.Intn(len(p.servers))]
    if a == b { // super rare, just retry
        return p.chooseTwo()
    }
    return a, b
}

func (p *PowerOfTwo) Next() *Server {
    a, b := p.chooseTwo()
    // assume Server.Load() returns current active connections (or CPU %)
    if a.Load() <= b.Load() {
        return a
    }
    return b
}

Traps to avoid:

  1. Stale load metrics – if Load() is updated only every few seconds, you might make decisions based on outdated info. Use a moving average or a lock‑free counter that increments/decrements on each request start/end.
  2. Repeatedly picking the same pair – the probability is low, but in a tiny cluster (2‑3 nodes) you could end up always comparing the same two. Adding a small retry loop (as shown) or shuffling the server list each request solves it.

Quick ASCII diagram of the decision flow 

+-------------------+
| Incoming Request  |
+----------+--------+
           |
   Pick two random servers
           |
   +------v------+   +------v------+
   |   Server A  |   |   Server B  |
   +------+------+   +------+------+
           \          /
            \        /
          Compare Load()
           /        \
   +------v------+   +------v------+
   |  Choose less|   |  (discard)  |
   +-------------+   +-------------+

Why This New Power Matters

Since we swapped in the Power of Two Choices, our 95th‑percentile latency dropped from ~120 ms to ~68 ms during peak bursts, and the standard deviation of per‑server request count shrunk by over 60 %. The best part? We didn’t need to rewrite our service mesh or add expensive centralized schedulers—just a few lines of code and a tiny metric expose.

It also plays nicely with existing patterns: sticky sessions, TLS termination, or circuit breakers all sit downstream of the load decision, so nothing else had to change.

If you’re still using plain round robin or even weighted round robin and you’re seeing hotspots, give this a spin. The insight is that a little randomness, applied twice, beats a lot of deterministic cleverness—kind of like how Neo’s “bullet‑time” dodge works better when he glances at two possible paths before choosing one.

Your Turn!

Grab a load balancer you maintain, instrument each backend with a simple active_conn counter (or use an existing exporter), and drop in the Power of Two Choices logic above. Run a benchmark with a tool like hey or wrk and watch the max‑per‑server load flatten.

Challenge: After you’ve tried it, tweet a before/after graph with the hashtag #PowerOfTwoLB and tag me—I’d love to see your results!

Now go forth and balance like a pro—your servers (and your users) will thank you. 🚀

title: Per-Core vs Named User: Choosing a Database Licensing Model
description:
• How vendors actually measure what you pay
  • Real-world cost and scalability trade-offs
  • Where audits bite: compliance traps and vendor perspectives
  • When per-core, named-user, or capacity-based licensing wins (practical case studies)
  • Negotiation levers that reduce audit risk and surprise bills
  • Practical decision checklist and break‑even calculator

Licensing is an architectural decision: it shapes your platform economics, your deployment patterns, and how auditors will read your telemetry. Choose the wrong model and you convert operational scale into steady, escalating license spend and audit exposure.

The signals most teams bring me are predictable: unexpectedly large license true-ups after cloud migrations, an exploding count of named users from service accounts and APIs, or a per-core bill that spikes as you move to larger VMs. Those symptoms hide two root problems — a mismatch between the license metric and the workload footprint, and weak evidence that proves your entitled scope during an audit — both of which drive cost and risk.

How vendors actually measure what you pay

Different vendors translate technical resources into commercial units in distinct ways; your choices are effectively how you convert compute and identity into dollars.

  • Per-core / Processor-based (per-core licensing): Charges map to CPU capacity — physical cores or virtual cores aggregated and adjusted by vendor-specific multipliers. Oracle uses a Processor metric with a published Processor Core Factor Table that converts physical cores (or OCPUs/vCPUs in cloud contexts) into license counts; the table is updated periodically and affects calculation and minimums.
    • Microsoft sells SQL Server in a core-based model (sold in two-core packs) and requires a minimum number of core licenses per physical processor when using physical licensing; virtualization rules differ if you license by VM.
  • Named-user / CAL-style (named user licensing): Licenses are counted per distinct user or device. Oracle’s Named User Plus (NUP) and Microsoft’s Client Access License (CAL) are the canonical examples; these models scale with headcount and require careful treatment of automated service accounts, shared devices, and multiplexing.
  • Capacity-based / subscription / cloud metrics (capacity-based licensing): Vendors or clouds sell capacity units (vCore, vCPU-hour, DTU, PVU) or fully-managed instances billed hourly/monthly. Azure’s vCore model and AWS RDS “license-included” vs BYOL are representative: you either pay a managed, capacity-priced SKU or bring existing licenses under specific rules.
  • Other capacity hybrids (PVU / RVU): IBM DB2 and other enterprise stacks use processor-value units or Authorized User units; PVU maps CPU families to a value table rather than a simple core count.

Table — Quick characteristic comparison

Model What you measure Typical cost driver Good fit Common vendor examples
per-core licensing Physical cores or vCPUs (adjusted by core factor) Core count, core factor, hyperthreading rules High-concurrency, unpredictable user counts, DW/analytics Oracle Processor, SQL Server core-based.
named user licensing Distinct users/devices (NUP/CAL) # of users / devices, service account counts Small fixed teams, known limited user lists Oracle NUP, Microsoft CAL.
capacity-based licensing vCore-hours, instance-hours, PVU Runtime hours, chosen instance class Cloud-native, bursty/ephemeral workloads Azure vCore, AWS RDS license-included, IBM PVU.

Real-world cost and scalability trade-offs

Cost math is rarely the only decision factor, but it’s the easiest place to misjudge long-term outcomes.

  • Predictability vs elasticity: per-core licensing commonly gives predictable capacity pricing for sustained, heavy workloads (big DW clusters, OLTP nodes). That predictability becomes a liability when you scale horizontally with many small VMs: core counts multiply and so do license obligations. The Oracle Processor Core Factor Table can materially change required license counts as CPU families change.
  • Headcount vs concurrency: named user licensing shines when the user population is small, stable, and well-controlled. Hidden costs appear when service accounts, APIs, contractors, and indirect access are counted as users — an easy audit trap. Microsoft’s Server+CAL model is only available for Standard edition and is intentionally intended for environments where counting users/devices is feasible.
  • Elastic cloud and short-lived workloads: capacity-based licensing (vCore, license-included hourly models) converts variable usage to variable cost and removes many inventory headaches — but it can be more expensive for steady-state heavy compute compared to a negotiated perpetual per-core deal or an optimized BYOL + Software Assurance strategy. Azure’s vCore model explicitly supports Licence included and Azure Hybrid Benefit (BYOL) choices that materially change economics.

Practical break-even approach (high level):

  1. Estimate steady-state compute (cores × hours/month) + growth projection.
  2. Estimate named-user population growth and service account count.
  3. Calculate per-month/per-year cost of: per-core, named user, and capacity-based with conservative growth.
  4. Model audit true-up scenarios — add an audit contingency (many teams use 10–30% of license budget as a conservative buffer per year when using aggressive virtualization). Flexera’s industry surveys show audit costs and unexpected fines remain a material line item for many organizations.

Where audits bite: compliance traps and vendor perspectives

Audits find the smallest ambiguities in your environment and convert them into license shortfalls.

  • Virtualization and partitioning: Oracle’s public Partitioning Policy and how LMS treats soft vs hard partitioning is the single biggest surprise for organizations that move to VMware, Hyper-V, or large virtual clusters; Oracle’s practical enforcement often treats a VM running Oracle as “contaminating” the host/cluster unless hard partitioning or explicit contractual carve-outs exist. That interpretation has led to large audit findings.
  • Multiplexing and named users: Multiplexing layers (web servers, API gateways, ETL services) do not reduce named-user counts for many vendors; the licensing rules require counting each distinct user/device or applying vendor-specific multiplexing guidance. Auditors expect proof (logs, identity lists, PoEs).
  • Minimums and rounding rules: Processor and NUP calculations often include minimums per CPU or per processor and explicit rounding rules; a fractional core result rounds up to whole licenses in Oracle’s Processor Core Factor calculation. Overlooking minimums increases license demand unexpectedly.
  • Audit mechanics and evidence: Vendors typically request Proof of Entitlement (PoE), license keys, support CSIs, and environment inventories. Modern audits increasingly correlate telemetry, virtualization metadata, and cloud billing records — poor telemetry equals poor outcomes. Flexera’s 2024 ITAM study reports rising audit fines and persistent visibility gaps that make audit defense harder.

Important: Legal language matters. Oracle’s Partitioning Policy is publicly available but often not contractually incorporated; your Master Agreement / Ordering Documents are the contract you’ll be judged by — don’t assume a vendor policy document protects you unless it’s explicitly part of the deal.

When per-core, named-user, or capacity-based licensing wins (practical case studies)

Below are concise, practitioner-rooted case studies built from patterns I’ve seen across enterprise accounts.

Case A — Small departmental application (ERP bolt-on for HR)

  • Footprint: one DB server, ~150 regular users, predictable daytime traffic, limited API access.
  • Recommendation pattern: named-user licensing (Server+CAL for SQL Server Standard or Oracle NUP) is usually cheaper because per-user count is small and stable; control service accounts and apply an access lifecycle to avoid user sprawl. Confirm minimums (Oracle NUP minimums per Processor apply).

Case B — Global analytics platform and data warehouse

  • Footprint: dozens of cores, heavy parallel queries, many concurrent users and unknown indirect access from BI tools.
  • Recommendation pattern: per-core licensing scales better — you avoid counting every BI user or extract process. Negotiate core counts, core-factor interpretation, and virtualization carve-outs before committing production. Expect to use core factor tables and to defend your virtual host mapping during audits.

Case C — Cloud-native microservices with autoscaling and short-lived DB instances

  • Footprint: transient DBs spun up by CI/CD, serverless/off-peak tiers, unpredictable bursts.
  • Recommendation pattern: capacity-based licensing (vCore/vCPU-hour, license-included DBaaS) typically reduces admin overhead and matches cost to usage. Evaluate BYOL options and hybrid benefits when you have existing on-prem licenses with active Software Assurance or support entitlements. Azure and AWS both publish clear license-inclusion and BYOL guidance.

Each case must be validated by a cost model based on your organization’s lifecycle: projected growth, VM sizing policy, failover topology, and the proportion of machine-to-human access.

Negotiation levers that reduce audit risk and surprise bills

When you negotiate, the right contract language buys you predictability and defensible boundaries.

  • Define the metric precisely in the contract: Processor vs vCPU vs OCPU vs Named User Plus — state the calculation method, rounding, and core-factor application. Reference the exact core-factor table version or freeze the factor for the contract term.
  • Virtualization carve-outs and permitted partitioning: Insist on explicit language that limits license counting to specific hosts or named resource pools, or that recognizes your chosen hard-partitioning technology (and the exact configuration you will run). Avoid relying on a vendor’s generic policy document unless it’s incorporated into the contract.
  • License mobility and cloud portability: Negotiate BYOL terms, movement windows (e.g., 90-day reassignment rules), and permitted cloud providers/regions. Microsoft documents license reassignment rules and Software Assurance benefits for mobility; secure similar language where possible.
  • Audit protocol and limits: Carve out audit timing, scope, notice periods, and frequency. Limit who can perform the audit, require a narrowly defined read-only data set to be delivered, and insist on a dispute-resolution process. Also negotiate an audit remediation cap or fixed schedule for true-ups to avoid open-ended demands.
  • Support uplift caps and price protection: Cap annual support increases, tie renewals to known indices, and get price hold guarantees for a defined period to avoid erosion of initial discounts.
  • Entitlement portability and affiliate coverage: If you operate multiple legal entities or expect M&A activity, put affiliate usage and transferability language into the agreement. Lack of territory/affiliate language is a common post‑audit exposure.

Concrete clause examples to ask for during negotiation (paraphrased, not legal advice):

  • “Processor definition: Processor license obligations shall be calculated using the Inventory listed in Appendix A and the Oracle Processor Core Factor Table dated [YYYY-MM-DD]; any change to core-factor will not apply retroactively during the term.”
  • “Virtualization carve‑out: Licensor confirms that for the customer’s named server cluster identifiers (Appendix B) only the physical processors shown therein are in‑scope for Processor calculations.”
  • “Audit scope: Vendor audit requires 60 days’ notice, limited to once per 24 months, and remediation is limited to an 18‑month look‑back.”

Practical decision checklist and break‑even calculator

Use this checklist as an operational protocol before you sign or renew any large database license.

Checklist — pre-purchase / renewal

  1. Inventory: authoritative list of servers, VMs, CPU families, vCPU → physical mapping, and PoE/support CSI records. collect: hostname, vCPU, physical host, CSI (keep immutable snapshots quarterly).
  2. Identity map: canonical user list, service accounts, API identities; mark service accounts and batch identities separately.
  3. Workload profile: steady-state cores, peak concurrency, duty cycle (hours/day), planned growth.
  4. Audit simulation: run a mock license calculation under each model and add a 10–30% audit contingency.
  5. Contract terms to negotiate: core factor freeze, partitioning carve-out, audit cadence, BYOL mobility, support cap, affiliate coverage.
  6. Evidence pack: PoE, entitlement spreadsheets, virtualization host mapping, change logs, and access logs for named users.

Break‑even calculator (example Python snippet)

# Simple break-even comparator (illustrative only)
def annual_cost_per_core(core_price, cores, support_pct=0.22):
    base = core_price * cores
    support = base * support_pct
    return base + support

def annual_cost_named_user(user_price, users, support_pct=0.22):
    base = user_price * users
    support = base * support_pct
    return base + support

# Example: compare per-core vs named-user
core_price = 10000   # $ per core per year (example)
users = 150
user_price = 500     # $ per named user per year (example)
cores = 4

cores_cost = annual_cost_per_core(core_price, cores)
users_cost = annual_cost_named_user(user_price, users)

print(f"Per-core annual cost: ${cores_cost:,}")
print(f"Named-user annual cost: ${users_cost:,}")

Audit‑readiness commands and sample evidence

  • Count distinct DB users (SQL Server example): 
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT name) AS distinct_logins
FROM sys.server_principals
WHERE type_desc IN ('SQL_LOGIN','WINDOWS_LOGIN','WINDOWS_GROUP');
  • Map VM to host and vCPU mapping (Linux example using lscpu and cloud metadata): 
lscpu | egrep 'CPU\\(s\\)|Model name'
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-type  # AWS instance type mapping

Final operational note: produce a short, signed Proof of Entitlement (PoE) index and store an immutable snapshot quarterly. During audits the difference between a well-documented entitlement and a fuzzy spreadsheet is the difference between a corrective purchase and a multi‑million dollar settlement.

The licensing model you pick will live on your balance sheet and in your audit record long after the architecture review is closed; choose the metric that maps cleanly to your workload, lock the rules into contract language, and make audit-grade evidence an operational output rather than a late-stage scramble.

Sources:

Microsoft — Server Virtualization Licensing Guidance - Guidance on license movement, Software Assurance benefits and license mobility across server farms.

Oracle — License Manager / Licensing Metrics - Oracle documentation showing licensing metrics available (Processors, Named User Plus) and how they appear in Oracle License Manager.

Oracle — Processor Core Factor Table (PDF) - The authoritative Oracle core factor table and notes on rounding, cloud mappings, and updates (effective for Processor calculations).

Scott & Scott LLP — How to Understand Oracle’s Use of its Partitioning Policy for Virtualization - Legal analysis of Oracle’s Partitioning Policy and how it is applied in audits.

Flexera — 2024 State of ITAM Report press release - Industry data on audit costs, visibility gaps, and the rising financial impact of software audits.
