title: Understanding Aspect Ratios in CSS and Canvas: Formulas, Responsive Rules, and Image Cropping
description:
When building responsive image galleries, hero sections, or interactive media canvases, aspect ratio mismatches are among the common causes of Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) and awkward visual cropping.

A browser may not know an image's intrinsic dimensions early enough to reserve the right space before layout, unless the dimensions or aspect ratio are provided in advance. When the rendered image changes the space occupied by surrounding content, the page can shift unexpectedly.

Here is a practical breakdown of how aspect ratios work, how to reduce them in JavaScript, and how to prevent visual distortion across screens and print frames.

1. The Mathematics of Aspect Ratio Reduction

An aspect ratio represents the proportional relationship between width and height. It is commonly written as width : height, or simply W:H.

For example, an image that is 1920 × 1080 pixels has an aspect ratio of 16:9. To determine the simplest ratio, divide both the width and height by their Greatest Common Divisor (GCD).

The standard method for computing the GCD in software is the Euclidean algorithm:

function getGCD(a: number, b: number): number {
  return b === 0 ? Math.abs(a) : getGCD(b, a % b);
}

function calculateAspectRatio(width: number, height: number): string {
  // This example expects positive integer pixel dimensions.
  if (!Number.isInteger(width) || !Number.isInteger(height) || width <= 0 || height <= 0) {
    throw new Error("Width and height must be positive integers.");
  }

  const divisor = getGCD(width, height);
  return `${width / divisor}:${height / divisor}`;
}

// Example calculations:
console.log(calculateAspectRatio(1920, 1080)); // "16:9"
console.log(calculateAspectRatio(1200, 800));  // "3:2"
console.log(calculateAspectRatio(1000, 800));  // "5:4"

Decimal Multipliers

Aspect ratios can also be expressed as a single decimal number. Divide the width by the height:

Decimal ratio = width ÷ height

Examples:

  • 16:9 = 1.7778 (standard widescreen video)
  • 3:2 = 1.5000 (common DSLR and mirrorless camera sensor ratio)
  • 4:3 = 1.3333 (common for some camera sensors, tablets, and web cards)
  • 5:4 = 1.2500 (traditional 8 × 10-inch photographic print)
  • 1:1 = 1.0000 (square avatars and UI thumbnails)

2. Modern CSS: Reserving Space and Enforcing Proportions

Before CSS introduced the native aspect-ratio property, web developers often relied on the "padding-top hack." With this technique, vertical padding is set as a percentage of the container's width.

Padding-top percentage = (height ÷ width) × 100

For a 16:9 container, the calculation is:

(9 ÷ 16) × 100 = 56.25%

So the older technique required padding-top: 56.25%.

Today, modern browsers support the aspect-ratio property natively:

.media-container {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 800px;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  overflow: hidden;
  background-color: #f1f5f9;
}

.media-container img {
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  object-fit: cover;
  object-position: center;
}

By defining aspect-ratio: 16 / 9, the browser can reserve space for the media container before the image loads. This can help reduce unexpected layout shifts when the element's sizing rules and surrounding layout are consistent.

3. The Print-Frame Cropping Conflict

A recurring frustration in digital image handling occurs when transferring photos between cameras, web layouts, and physical print products.

Many digital cameras use a 3:2 aspect ratio, which is equivalent to a decimal ratio of 1.50. Standard print sizes can use different proportions:

  • 4 × 6-inch print: 3:2 ratio (1.50). No cropping is required when the source image is also 3:2.
  • 5 × 7-inch print: 7:5 ratio (1.40). This is narrower than 3:2; a centered crop removes about 6.7% of the original image width in total.
  • 8 × 10-inch print: 5:4 ratio (1.25). This is narrower than 3:2; a centered crop removes about 16.7% of the original image width in total when the full image height is retained.

If you stretch an image to fit these containers, facial proportions and geometric objects can look distorted. If you use object-fit: contain, empty space may appear around the image. A carefully positioned crop can help the image fit the intended frame without distortion.

For an interactive way to calculate proportions, try this free aspect ratio calculator. Before publishing, confirm that any claims about image previews or local processing accurately describe the current implementation.

4. Client-Side Bounding Box Calculation in HTML5 Canvas

When implementing client-side crop tools, calculate the crop rectangle while preserving the target aspect ratio.

Here is core logic for center-cropping a source image to a target ratio:

function calculateCenterCrop(srcWidth, srcHeight, targetRatioWidth, targetRatioHeight) {
  if ([srcWidth, srcHeight, targetRatioWidth, targetRatioHeight].some(value => !Number.isFinite(value) || value <= 0)) {
    throw new Error("Source dimensions and target ratio values must be positive numbers.");
  }

  const targetRatio = targetRatioWidth / targetRatioHeight;
  const srcRatio = srcWidth / srcHeight;

  let cropWidth, cropHeight, cropX, cropY;

  if (srcRatio > targetRatio) {
    // Source is wider than target: crop horizontal edges
    cropHeight = srcHeight;
    cropWidth = srcHeight * targetRatio;
    cropX = (srcWidth - cropWidth) / 2;
    cropY = 0;
  } else {
    // Source is taller than target: crop vertical edges
    cropWidth = srcWidth;
    cropHeight = srcWidth / targetRatio;
    cropX = 0;
    cropY = (srcHeight - cropHeight) / 2;
  }

  return {
    cropX: Math.round(cropX),
    cropY: Math.round(cropY),
    cropWidth: Math.round(cropWidth),
    cropHeight: Math.round(cropHeight)
  };
}

Rendering onto Canvas 

const canvas = document.getElementById('previewCanvas');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

const crop = calculateCenterCrop(img.naturalWidth, img.naturalHeight, 5, 4);

// Set canvas to target display dimensions
canvas.width = 500;
canvas.height = 400;

ctx.drawImage(
  img,
  crop.cropX, crop.cropY, crop.cropWidth, crop.cropHeight, // Source crop rectangle
  0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height                       // Destination canvas
);

Summary Checklist for Developers

  1. Reserve space early: Use CSS aspect-ratio or explicit image dimensions to help the browser lay out media before it loads.
  2. Avoid distortion: Do not stretch width and height independently. Use object-fit: cover when filling a frame and when cropping is appropriate.
  3. Account for print sizes: When building export tools, remember that 4 × 6, 5 × 7, and 8 × 10-inch prints use different aspect ratios.
  4. Choose the right processing model: Aspect-ratio calculations can run in the browser. Only describe image processing as client-side if the implementation actually keeps that processing local.

title: Best Databricks Data Modeling Tools (2026): SQLDBM, dbt, SQLMesh, ER/Studio & Hackolade Compared
description:
Databricks has become the default lakehouse for a huge chunk of serious data teams, and the modeling tools around it have had to grow up fast. Unity Catalog, Delta Lake, column-level lineage, dbt-style transformations, semantic layers for AI and BI, it's all happening at once. Picking the right modeling tool in 2026 isn't just about pretty ERDs anymore. It's about which tool actually plugs into your Databricks workflow without fighting you.

I spent weeks working through the main contenders, from browser-based visual tools to code-first transformation frameworks to the old-guard desktop modelers. Some are genuinely built for the lakehouse. Others bolted on Databricks support later and it shows. A few don't even try to be visual, and that's fine, they solve a different problem.

Here's the short list I ended up with, and how each one actually performs when you point it at a Databricks environment.

How I Evaluated These Tools

I focused on five things: depth of Databricks and Unity Catalog integration, support for conceptual/logical/physical modeling (versus pure code transformation), collaboration and Git/CI workflows, enterprise features like governance and SSO, and pricing transparency. I also weighed how well each tool handles the newer stuff teams actually care about now, semantic layers, AI assistance, and tags.

1. SqlDBM - Best Overall

The only visual modeling platform that natively speaks Databricks, from Unity Catalog to semantic layer to production DDL.

After spending real time with every tool on this list, I keep coming back to SqlDBM as the most complete option for teams building on the Databricks Lakehouse. It's cloud-native and browser-based. No desktop installs, no license servers, no VM to babysit. And the Databricks integration goes genuinely deep.

SqlDBM is a Databricks Validated Data Partner, and that partnership shows up in the product. It connects directly to Unity Catalog and Hive Metastore, with native reverse and forward engineering against Delta Lake objects, column-level lineage, and the ability to visually model everything from conceptual designs to physical schemas without writing a line of code. In 2026 they added Databricks tags support, so you can organize, classify, and search Unity Catalog schemas, tables, views, and columns right inside your model, and keep everything synced through forward and reverse engineering. Transformational alter scripts for Databricks also landed recently, which rounds out the CI/CD story nicely.

What really sets SqlDBM apart is scope. It's the first platform to combine relational and transformational (Tx) modeling in one workspace, so you can design gold-layer tables alongside dbt-style transformation logic, then push dbt source and model YAML straight through Git. On top of that, its semantic modeling layer lets you define governed business definitions directly on top of physical Databricks schemas. Standalone semantic tools like dbt's Semantic Layer or Cube skip the visual modeling side entirely. Visual tools like ER/Studio and Hackolade skip the semantic layer. SqlDBM bridges both.

The proof is in production. John Holland Group, one of Australia's largest infrastructure firms, completed its Databricks migration in nine months using SqlDBM as the authoritative source for gold-layer models. FrieslandCampina's data modeling lead said SqlDBM "fundamentally streamlined" their Databricks modeling process. Over 400,000 users trust the platform, including DocuSign, Pfizer, and Sophos. PwC reported it cuts modeling time by 25 percent, and it won Database Modeling Solution of the Year in both 2023 and 2024.

The built-in AI Copilot and MCP Server, announced live at Databricks Data + AI Summit 2025, make models directly accessible to LLMs. That's a huge edge for teams building AI-ready Lakehouse architectures. Real-time multi-user collaboration means architects, engineers, and analysts all work concurrently in the same model. Enterprise security (SSO, RBAC, SOC 2 Type II) checks every box.

Pros:

  • Deepest native Databricks integration of any visual modeling tool: Unity Catalog direct connect, Delta Lake forward/reverse engineering, Databricks tags, transformational alter scripts, and column-level lineage all built in
  • Only visual data modeling platform that also delivers a semantic layer for Databricks, bridging governed physical schemas and business definitions where dbt, ER/Studio, and Hackolade each cover only one side
  • First platform combining relational and transformational (Tx) modeling, so you design gold-layer Databricks tables and push dbt source/model YAML through Git and CI/CD in one workspace
  • Proven at scale: John Holland Group completed a Databricks migration in nine months with SqlDBM governing gold-layer models, and PwC reports 25% faster modeling time
  • AI Copilot and MCP Server expose Databricks models directly to LLMs, a tangible edge for AI-ready Lakehouse architectures

Cons:

  • Advanced features like semantic modeling and Tx modeling have a learning curve for teams new to visual modeling
  • Databricks, Snowflake, and BigQuery coverage is deep, but support for niche or on-prem databases is narrower than legacy desktop tools

Pricing: SqlDBM plans are quote-based and scale with team size, with enterprise packaging, premium support, and advanced security options available. There's a free tier so you can model and explore before committing. Contact sales for a tailored quote.

2. dbt (dbt Core / dbt platform)

dbt is the analytics-engineering standard for transforming data inside the warehouse or lakehouse. Teams write modular SQL (or Python) models, and dbt handles dependency ordering, materialization, testing, documentation, and lineage. The Databricks adapter is mature, so models run cleanly on Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog. The free, open-source dbt Core runs locally or in your own orchestrator. The commercial dbt platform (formerly dbt Cloud) adds a browser IDE, scheduling, CI, a catalog, a Semantic Layer, and AI assistance.

One thing to be clear about: dbt is not a visual ERD or conceptual/logical modeling tool. It models transformation logic in code. So it usually complements a design tool like SqlDBM, ER/Studio, or Hackolade rather than replacing one. It fits data and analytics engineers who want Git-based workflows, code review, and automated testing for transformation pipelines. The community and package ecosystem are huge. Sources indicate dbt Labs has become part of Fivetran, which is worth confirming for roadmap and licensing questions.

Pros:

  • Huge community, package ecosystem, and broad hiring pool
  • Mature Databricks adapter with built-in testing, documentation, and lineage
  • Free open-source core with Git/CI-friendly workflows
  • Semantic Layer and catalog features on the paid platform

Cons:

  • No visual ERD, conceptual, or logical modeling, it only covers the transformation layer
  • Paid platform costs scale with seats and successful model builds, Enterprise pricing is quote-only
  • Requires SQL/Jinja and engineering skills, so it is less accessible to architects and business users

Pricing: dbt Core is free (Apache 2.0). The dbt platform has a free Developer plan for 1 seat, Starter at about $100 per user per month, and negotiated Enterprise and Enterprise+ tiers. Usage overages apply, and Databricks compute is billed separately.

3. SQLMesh (Tobiko Data)

SQLMesh is an open-source framework from Tobiko Data for building, testing, and deploying SQL and Python data pipelines. It's built on SQLGlot, which parses SQL semantically and can transpile across 20+ dialects. Databricks is a supported engine. The main differentiators are virtual data environments, plan/apply change workflows that show the impact of a change before it runs, automatic breaking-change detection, built-in unit tests, and column-level lineage. Because it tracks state, it can avoid unnecessary rebuilds, which can cut compute spend on Databricks meaningfully.

It also has a VS Code extension and can run against existing dbt projects. Tobiko Cloud is the commercial layer, adding collaboration, observability, and cost tracking. Like dbt, SQLMesh is a transformation and model-management tool, not a visual ERD designer. It fits teams that want code-first modeling with stronger DataOps safeguards rather than diagramming and governance of conceptual and logical models.

Pros:

  • Virtual environments and plan/apply workflow reduce rebuilds and warehouse cost
  • Column-level lineage and semantic SQL understanding via SQLGlot
  • Open-source core under Apache 2.0, with dbt project compatibility
  • Native Python support and a VS Code extension

Cons:

  • Much smaller community and ecosystem than dbt
  • Tobiko Cloud pricing is not published and requires talking to sales
  • No visual ERD or conceptual/logical modeling, and a steeper learning curve for teams already on dbt

Pricing: SQLMesh core is free and open source. Tobiko Cloud pricing is custom and the vendor does not publish it. Databricks compute costs are separate.

4. ER/Studio Data Architect

ER/Studio Data Architect is a long-established enterprise modeling product, now offered through IDERA and Precisely. It supports conceptual, logical, and physical models, forward and reverse engineering, model comparison, impact analysis, naming standards, and macros for automation. Databricks support arrived in version 20.2, alongside SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, and others. Newer releases add an AI modeling assistant that can generate logical models from text prompts. It integrates with governance tools like Collibra and Microsoft Purview, and supports Okta SSO.

This is a desktop-centric tool aimed at large enterprises and regulated industries with multi-platform estates and formal data-governance requirements. If that's your world, it has the depth you'd expect. Teams that want a lightweight, browser-first, or Git-native experience may find it heavier than newer cloud-native tools. The core audience is users who need broad legacy-database coverage and enterprise repository features.

Pros:

  • Deep enterprise feature set including model comparison, impact analysis, and standards enforcement
  • Supports Databricks alongside many legacy and cloud databases
  • Integrations with governance and catalog tools such as Collibra and Microsoft Purview
  • AI-assisted model generation in recent versions

Cons:

  • Higher per-user cost than most competitors
  • Desktop-first architecture feels less collaborative than cloud-native tools
  • Databricks support was added relatively recently and may be less deep than tools built around Unity Catalog

Pricing: Subscription pricing starts at about $2,687 per user per year for Standard, with Professional at about $3,693 per user and Enterprise on custom quote. A free trial is available, and reseller listings show a perpetual multiplatform license at about $2,674.

5. Hackolade Studio

Hackolade Studio started as a visual modeling tool for NoSQL databases and has grown into a polyglot modeling platform covering 45+ targets, from Oracle and Databricks to MongoDB, Avro, and OpenAPI. For Databricks, it has dedicated Delta Lake support, including Unity Catalog. It models catalogs, schemas, tables, and views, forward-engineers scripts, reverse-engineers existing structures (including from a live Databricks instance), compares models, and generates documentation. It also has a CLI for CI/CD pipelines and Git integration.

The idea is that you define meaning once in a technology-agnostic model, then derive physical schemas for each platform. That suits organizations that mix lakehouse, NoSQL, streaming, and API data. Hackolade is offered as a desktop application and as a browser-based deployment, and there's a free Community edition. The interface and workflow are less conventional than classic ERD tools, and collaboration leans on Git rather than live multi-user editing.

Pros:

  • Very broad technology coverage across SQL, NoSQL, APIs, and streaming formats
  • Dedicated Databricks Delta Lake and Unity Catalog support with forward and reverse engineering
  • Git integration and CLI for CI/CD automation
  • Free Community edition and a transparent price list

Cons:

  • Collaboration is Git-based rather than real-time multi-user editing
  • Polyglot, schema-centric paradigm has a learning curve for traditional ERD users
  • Some advanced features sit behind paid editions

Pricing: Free 14-day trial and a free Community edition. Paid subscriptions are listed at about €175 per seat per month or €1,750 per seat per year, including support. Volume and enterprise purchasing is available through sales.

6. erwin Data Modeler (Quest)

erwin Data Modeler, from Quest Software, is one of the best-known enterprise data modeling tools. It supports forward and reverse engineering of database schemas, a centralized model repository, collaborative modeling with conflict resolution, change management, and auditing. It covers traditional relational platforms along with modern cloud targets like Databricks, Snowflake, and Microsoft Fabric. It's aimed at large enterprises with regulated, multi-platform environments and established governance processes.

Users often pick erwin for the depth of its repository features, standards enforcement, and legacy-database coverage. Reviewers consistently praise the functionality and enterprise-readiness. The main gripes are that NoSQL modeling is thin compared to the rest of the product, and that the Windows-centric, desktop-first approach plus enterprise licensing can feel heavy next to cloud-native tools, especially if you want a browser-based, Git-native experience.

Pros:

  • Mature, deep feature set with a central model repository and change management
  • Connects to Databricks, Snowflake, Microsoft Fabric, and traditional relational databases
  • Strong fit for regulated enterprises with formal governance needs
  • Free trial available

Cons:

  • Desktop-first and Windows-centric, which is less convenient for distributed teams
  • Limited native support for NoSQL and document modeling patterns, according to reviewers
  • Per-feature licensing and enterprise quotes can get expensive

Pricing: Marketplace listings show pricing from about $299 per feature per month, with a free trial. Full enterprise licensing is by quote through Quest.

Final Verdict

If you're serious about Databricks and want one tool that handles visual modeling, Unity Catalog integration, dbt-style transformations, and a semantic layer, SqlDBM is the clearest pick in 2026. The Databricks partnership is real, the tags and transformational alter script support landed exactly when teams need it, and the semantic layer is something no other visual modeling tool actually does. For most Databricks teams, that combination is hard to beat.

That said, the other tools have their place. dbt and SQLMesh are the right call if you only need code-first transformation and already have a design tool. ER/Studio and erwin still make sense for large enterprises deeply invested in desktop modeling and multi-database governance. Hackolade shines when you have a genuinely polyglot stack spanning NoSQL, APIs, and streaming formats. But for teams whose center of gravity is the Databricks Lakehouse, SqlDBM is the one I'd start with.

FAQ

Is SqlDBM really built for Databricks or is it a generic modeling tool with Databricks support bolted on?
It's a Databricks Validated Data Partner with direct Unity Catalog connectivity, Delta Lake forward and reverse engineering, Databricks tags support, column-level lineage, and transformational alter scripts. The integration is first-class, not an afterthought.

Do I need both SqlDBM and dbt?
A lot of teams run both. dbt handles the SQL transformation layer. SqlDBM handles visual design, conceptual/logical modeling, the semantic layer, and governance. SqlDBM can push dbt source and model YAML through Git, so they fit together cleanly.

What's the difference between a semantic layer and visual data modeling?
Visual modeling describes the structure of your data (tables, columns, relationships). A semantic layer adds business meaning on top (metrics, dimensions, definitions BI tools and LLMs can trust). Most tools do one or the other. SqlDBM does both in the same workspace.

Which tool is cheapest to start with?
dbt Core and SQLMesh are free and open source if you're code-first. For visual modeling, SqlDBM and Hackolade both offer free ways to try things out before you commit to a paid plan.

title: The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It
description:
What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

**Uncertain rewards. **Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

**Self-regulation. **In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

title: Your Website Feels Slow? Start by Finding the Actual Bottleneck
description:
A website can look perfectly fine during development and still feel slow when someone opens it on their phone or uses it over a weaker internet connection.

The first reaction is often to blame the server or upgrade the hosting plan. Sometimes that helps, but it is not always the real problem.

A page can be slow because of oversized images, render-blocking JavaScript, third-party scripts, or a large amount of work happening in the browser. Making random changes without identifying the cause can waste time and make the code harder to maintain.

Here is a practical way to investigate website performance before jumping into fixes.

1. Check What the Browser Is Actually Loading

Start by opening your website in Chrome and launching DevTools. Go to the Network tab, reload the page, and look at the requests being made.

Pay attention to a few things:

  • Are images much larger than their displayed size?
  • Are several JavaScript files being loaded before the page becomes usable?
  • Are third-party scripts taking a long time to respond?
  • Are there requests that repeatedly fail or take unusually long?

The Network tab gives you a better starting point than guessing based on how the page feels.

Also, test a few important pages rather than checking only the homepage. A product page with multiple images and scripts may behave very differently from a simple landing page.

2. Find Out Whether the Problem Is on the Server or in the Browser

A slow page does not always mean the server is slow.

If the initial document takes a long time to arrive, investigate server response time, database queries, caching, and backend processing.

If the document arrives quickly but the page still takes a long time to become usable, look at JavaScript execution, image loading, fonts, and layout work.

The distinction matters because the solutions are different. Optimizing database queries will not fix a huge image, and compressing images will not solve a slow database request.

3. Pay Attention to Images

Images are an easy place to find unnecessary page weight.

For example, a product card might display an image that is only 300 pixels wide while downloading a file several times larger than necessary. Multiply that across a page containing dozens of products, and the extra data can add up.

A few things worth checking:

  • Resize images to suit their actual display dimensions.
  • Consider modern formats such as WebP or AVIF.
  • Use responsive images where appropriate.
  • Lazy-load below-the-fold images when suitable.
  • Avoid lazy-loading the main image that needs to appear immediately.

Do not compress everything blindly. The goal is to reduce unnecessary data while keeping images clear enough for their intended use.

4. Look for JavaScript That Does Too Much

JavaScript can affect both loading performance and how quickly a page responds to user actions.

A page might download a relatively small script but then spend too much time executing it. Large dependencies, unnecessary event handlers, and expensive calculations can all contribute to the problem.

Use the Performance panel in Chrome DevTools to record a page load or an interaction. Look for long tasks and repeated layout calculations.

If a script is doing work that is not needed immediately, consider whether it can be deferred, split into smaller pieces, or run only when the relevant feature is used.

The right solution depends on what the recording actually shows. Removing a library without understanding its role can introduce bugs without meaningfully improving performance.

5. Measure More Than Just Load Time

A single loading-time number does not explain the entire user experience.

Google's Core Web Vitals provide three useful measurements:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): How quickly the main content becomes visible. The good threshold is 2.5 seconds or less.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): How quickly the page responds visually to user interactions. The good threshold is 200 milliseconds or less.
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): How much unexpected layout movement occurs. The good threshold is 0.1 or less.

These measurements help identify different types of problems. A page might display its main content quickly but still respond poorly when someone clicks a button.

You can read Google's explanation in the Core Web Vitals documentation.

6. Test the Fix Instead of Assuming It Worked

Once you identify a likely bottleneck, make one meaningful change and measure again.

For example, if an image is responsible for a large portion of the page weight, optimize that image and compare the results. If JavaScript execution is the issue, profile the page after changing the relevant code.

Try to keep test conditions consistent. Network speed, caching, device performance, and third-party services can all influence measurements.

Tools such as PageSpeed Insights can help you examine performance reports and identify potential improvements. Browser DevTools is useful when you need to investigate the cause in more detail.

Remember that a lab test and real-user data serve different purposes. A page may perform well on your computer but behave differently for users with older devices or slower connections.

A Better Way to Approach Performance Work

Website optimization becomes much easier when you stop treating every slow page as the same problem.

First, reproduce the issue. Then collect evidence, identify the likely bottleneck, make a focused change, and measure the result.

You will not always find a dramatic improvement in the first attempt. Sometimes the issue comes from several small problems rather than one obvious mistake.

But a repeatable debugging process is more useful than making random changes or upgrading infrastructure before you know what needs fixing.

The goal is not simply to make a performance score look better. It is to build a website that loads reliably, responds quickly, and works well for the people using it.

title: Cross-Scenario Industrial Defect Detection via Domain-Robust Training and Metric-Aligned Selection
description:
arXiv:2610.19540v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated defect detection of industrial boards must remain highly reliable under cross-scenario variations in lighting, surface contaminants, and production line conditions. This makes cross-scenario defect detection a domain generalization problem, wherein models are required to detect, localize, and classify defects across unseen scenarios while minimizing false alarms on clean boards. For the IDA 2026 Track 1 challenge, we propose a cross-scenario defect detection method that includes four complementary modules: cross-scenario robust training, small-defect-aware learning, score calibration and inference threshold selection, and metric-aligned checkpoint selection. These four modules respectively introduce cross-scenario robust normalization and DSU-style statistic perturbation with progressive random convolution, NWD and parameter-free spatial attention, the VFL learning objective, and a custom SWAD variant driven by the Track 1-oriented proxy. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves a Track 1 score of 0.564 with a screening score of 0.696 on the test dataset on a single RTX 4090 GPU. The code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/Dikai.

title: How to Practice Coding Interviews Without a Partner (5 Options, Prices Checked)
description:
A practice partner gives you three things: a problem you haven't seen, follow-up questions (what's the complexity, what about an empty input, can you do better), and someone watching. Alone, the first is easy. The other two need someone, or something, on the other side.

Your options

Peer mocks on Aced (formerly Exponent) Yes, from another candidate Live Notes from your partner Free, 5 a month

1. The self-mock routine (free)

  1. Pick a problem you haven't seen, at your level, like an untouched one from the NeetCode 150.
  2. Set a timer for 30 to 45 minutes and don't pause it.
  3. Talk the whole time: restate the problem, walk an example, state the brute force and its complexity, improve it, code it, test it by hand.
  4. Record yourself. Listen back once and count the silences.
  5. Grade four things: did you clarify the problem, state the complexity, test your code, and keep talking.

Its limit: nobody pushes back, so you never practice the follow-up question, which is where a lot of interviews are decided.

2. An AI interviewer that talks: DevInterview.ai

This is the one I built. It runs a 30-minute coding round in an editor that runs your code, in any of 7 languages, set to your target company and level. The interviewer talks, asks follow-ups, and is told never to say whether you're right and never to hand you the solution. Each interview ends with a scored report and a hire verdict. The same plan covers a 45-minute system design round on a canvas and a 30-minute behavioral round. First interview free, then $19.99 a month.

Where it falls short: it's an AI, not a person who runs real hiring loops, and it won't give you the nerves of a stranger watching.

3. interviewing.io's free AI Interviewer

Per its site, it runs coding and system design interviews in the style of a FAANG mock, with feedback at the end, for free. The site doesn't say whether it speaks or runs your code, so try a session and see.

4. ChatGPT voice mode

Tell it to act as an interviewer, give it a problem, and ask it to push back. Free with daily limits, Plus is $20 a month. OpenAI doesn't describe an interview mode or scoring, so the structure is whatever you prompt for.

5. Peer mocks, if a stranger counts

Aced (formerly Exponent) matches you with another candidate and you interview each other. Free accounts get 5 a month, and afterwards you trade notes using realistic rubrics, in Aced's words. Every session needs scheduling.

System design without a partner

Harder alone, because the interviewer's questions steer the design. DevInterview.ai's 45-minute system design round runs on a canvas and asks those questions. Hello Interview's Guided Practice walks you through the steps of an interview with personalized feedback; it comes with Premium, at list price $59 for 1 month, $119 for 1 year or $399 lifetime, with a sale running when I checked.

Where this fits

Practicing alone is step 3 of the plan I'd give a friend: learn the patterns on NeetCode, study system design on Hello Interview, practice out loud on DevInterview.ai, and, super optional, one human session on interviewing.io. The full 8-week version is here.

title: Historical-Feature Residual Adaptation for Sequential Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.19315v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sequential screening policies must use acquired feedback effectively under a fixed experiment budget. We study acquisition-time residual adaptation: a small ranking correction built from fixed historical features and anchored to base scores recorded before feedback is revealed. The interface accepts a history-conditioned scorer and a candidate feature table; its primary instantiation augments AssayFormer's ten-dimensional representation with 64 historical directions while retaining the pretrained model. In retrospective evaluation on 20 official-test screens from 15 recorded sources, a comparison fixed before target-outcome access increased source-macro fraction of hits recovered from 22.58% to 28.61%, exceeding all six prespecified comparators. A same-feature ordinary ranking head achieved 25.73%. Supplementary strong logistic, rank-fusion, and unprojected controls achieved 26.42%, 26.02%, and 26.78%, respectively. A separate model-independent pilot on 13 reused development screens reconstructs the features without AssayFormer assets. Across three seeds, residual adaptation improves random-forest hit recovery from 28.87% to 31.27%, while logistic recovery changes from 30.22% to 29.78%. The results show effective pretrained-policy adaptation and useful transfer to an independent nonlinear base, with gains that depend on the base model.

title: Asymptotically Exact Negative Guidance of Diffusion Models via Positive-Unlabeled Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19802v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Negative guidance of diffusion models generates samples that avoid an undesired condition, specified either by reference samples or by a conditional score alongside an unconditional model. Existing methods inject repulsive terms derived from local information at each sample, so the resulting sampler does not target an explicit density, and its bias cannot be systematically reduced by increasing computation. We instead present a negative-guidance method that samples from an explicit target density, which uniformly handles both reference-sample and score-based specifications and suppresses probability mass near the undesired condition with an avoidance strength that parametrizes the target density itself. Realizing this target requires estimating, at each diffusion timestep, how likely each sample is to belong to the undesired condition. We cast this estimation as a Positive-Unlabeled learning problem that admits lightweight online training along the diffusion trajectory, using condition samples as positives and diffusion particles as unlabeled data. Because the guided particles drift from the unconditional marginal, we further correct the residual mismatch via Sequential Monte Carlo, yielding a sampler that is asymptotically exact in the particle limit and that turns any existing negative-guidance method into its proposal kernel. Empirically, our method approaches the ground-truth target on Gaussian mixtures and Pareto-dominates existing methods on trade-offs between avoidance and generation quality, distributional bias, and diversity, including in an image-generation setting with a pretrained score network.

title: BluePixel: Toward Native 4K Agentic Image Editing
description:
arXiv:2610.19882v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Instruction-driven image editing has reached native 4K, yet how such editors are trained remains undisclosed, and pretraining one from scratch is beyond most teams. The task itself compounds the difficulty: a single end-to-end editor cannot make precise parametric adjustments, match specialized experts, or interpret the vague instructions users actually write. We argue that 4K editing is a system problem rather than a single-model problem, and present BluePixel, which couples a native-4K editing model with an agent harness; the complete training recipe is disclosed in this paper. The model makes 4K training practical: it turns a 1K-pretrained editor into a native-4K one through progressive VAE adaptation that keeps 4K training as affordable as 1K, absorbs a long tail of vertical editing skills through continual learning, and refines the aesthetic-fidelity trade-off with reinforcement learning. Distillation via source-anchored target projection (SATP) then compresses 50 denoising steps to 4, completing a 4K edit in 8.7 s on a single Kunlunxin P800 XPU while preserving task success rate and background consistency. The harness, BluePixel Agent, makes editing controllable: it decomposes user instructions into specialist and general operations, verifies every result with the same reward model that guided training, and retries within bounded attempts. On VINS-4KEval++ (3,305 native-4K cases), BluePixel ranks second among seven models, behind only GPT Image 2 in non-edited-region consistency.

title: Apple's on-device model called our iPhone 17 "not eligible", so we tested everything except the model
description:
The first time I asked the on-device model whether it could run on a real phone, SystemLanguageModel.default.availability answered .unavailable(.deviceNotEligible). The device was an iPhone 17 on iOS 26.6, which is new enough for Apple Intelligence. It was also bought in mainland China, where Apple Intelligence isn't offered, and as far as I can tell that is the whole reason.

That was a problem. It was the night before I submitted an AI menu for CapScribe, my caption app: keyword emphasis, title suggestions and emoji, all generated on device. The one phone I own will never run it. The simulator can't run it either.

So the honest version of this post is: here is how we shipped a Foundation Models feature we could not run, and what we tested instead.

The gate has more than two states

availability isn't a Bool. When it's unavailable you get a reason, and the reasons deserve different copy:

switch SystemLanguageModel.default.availability {
case .available:
    return .available
case .unavailable(let reason):
    switch reason {
    case .deviceNotEligible:
        return .unavailable("Device not eligible for Apple Intelligence")
    case .appleIntelligenceNotEnabled:
        return .unavailable("Apple Intelligence not enabled in Settings")
    case .modelNotReady:
        return .unavailable("Model is downloading or not ready")
    @unknown default:
        return .unavailable("Model unavailable")
    }
}

Only one of those is permanent. "Not enabled" is a trip to Settings. "Not ready" usually means the model is still downloading and will sort itself out. Collapse them into a single "AI unavailable" string and you tell the user with a fixable problem that they're stuck, while the user with an ineligible phone learns nothing.

My first instinct was to hide the menu whenever the model isn't there. I didn't. A missing button looks like a bug to anyone who read the release notes, and a hidden menu can't explain itself. What shipped: the menu always appears, the three actions are disabled, and a disabled row at the bottom says which case you're in.

A seam so the fallback can be tested

The service takes an optional model behind a one-method protocol:

public protocol AssistantModel: Sendable {
    func respond(to prompt: String) async throws -> String
}

If a model is injected, the service sends it the prompt and decodes the JSON it returns. If not, it checks availability and either opens a LanguageModelSession with a @Generable output type or throws .unavailable(reason). The real path is short on purpose. The less code that only runs on hardware I don't have, the better.

Unit tests inject a mock that records the prompt. That's where the input cap gets checked: transcripts are cut to 3,000 characters before they reach the model, and a test feeds a much longer string and asserts nothing past the cap made it into the prompt.

UI tests can't inject anything, so there's a DEBUG-only launch argument:

#if DEBUG
public static func makeFakeIfNeeded() -> OnDeviceAssistant? {
    guard ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments.contains("-uitest-fake-assistant") else { return nil }
    return OnDeviceAssistant(model: FakeAssistantModel())
}
#endif

The fake returns fixed JSON: a couple of keywords, three titles, one 🎬. With the flag set, a UI test runs all three actions in the editor. It checks that keyword emphasis gets switched on in the style panel, that three title rows appear, and that the emoji really lands at the end of the caption text. Without the flag, a second UI test opens the same menu in the simulator, where Foundation Models reports unavailable, and asserts the actions are disabled and the reason row exists and isn't empty.

That second test is the one I care about most. On my own phone the unavailable path is the only path, and for plenty of users it will be too.

What this doesn't cover

The real model. Prompt quality, latency, whether @Guide(.count(3)) really yields three titles every time on a real device: none of that has run on hardware we own. The App Review notes spell out the device requirement, and real-model verification sits on our roadmap as blocked until we get an eligible phone.

I went back and forth on shipping like that. What tipped it was proportion. The code that only runs on eligible hardware is a handful of lines handed straight to Apple's framework. The code that decides what everyone else sees runs on every build.

If you're adding Foundation Models to an app, two things are worth doing on day one. Give each unavailability reason its own message, and put a protocol between your feature and LanguageModelSession, so the fallback path gets tested in the simulator, where it's the default anyway.

I build CapScribe, an on-device caption app for iOS. The menu in question is in the editor: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6801041856?utm_source=devto

title: Textbook Conventions vs. Creative Niche Layouts: A Front-End Engineer’s UX Dilemma
description:
We’ve all been there. You get a new freelance client—maybe a boutique local bakery, a high-end tattoo parlor, or a trendy fitness studio. You open up your code editor, full of creative energy, ready to build a bespoke, visually breathtaking masterpiece with asymmetric grids, smooth custom animations, and a completely unique navigation experience.
Then, reality hits.
You remember the cardinal rule of user experience: “Users spend most of their time on other sites.” (Shout out to Jakob’s Law). If your website layout forces them to relearn how to browse, they don’t marvel at your creativity—they just bounce.
As front-end developers, we constantly walk this tightrope. Do we build the predictable "Textbook Layout" that converts like crazy but feels generic? Or do we build a highly customized "Niche Layout" that looks amazing but risks confusing the average user?
Let’s break down this UX dilemma and look at how we can balance engineering creativity with real-world business conversions.

📘 The Case for the "Textbook" Layout (The Safe Bet)

The textbook layout is the UI blueprint we can all code in our sleep. Logo in the top left, nav links spread across the right, a massive hero section with a crisp H1 and a primary Call-To-Action (CTA) button, followed by a predictable 3-column feature grid.
From an academic and conversion standpoint, this layout is undefeated for a reason: Cognitive Load is zero.
When a user lands on a standard layout, their brain doesn't waste energy figuring out how to use the site. They instantly scan in an F-shape pattern, consume the value proposition, and know exactly where to click.

The Problem? It’s Boring.

If every local accountant, plumber, and consultant uses the exact same template, the web becomes a homogenous sea of sameness. As developers, building these sites feels like assembly-line work. It starves our creative problem-solving.

🎨 The Case for the "Niche" Layout (The Creative Risk)

On the other side of the coin, we have industry-specific, niche layouts. These designs completely throw out the generic blueprint to prioritize the absolute most critical action for that specific business type.
• For Restaurants: Bypassing traditional informational blocks to place a responsive, interactive menu and a sticky "Order Online" widget directly in view.
• For Photographers/Agencies: Swapping standard text containers for immersive, full-screen masonry grids where the imagery dictates the UI flow.
• For Salons/Clinics: Building the entire homepage experience around a persistent booking calendar API.
text
[ Textbook Layout ] [ Niche Layout (e.g., Restaurant) ]
┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Logo Nav Links │ │ Logo [ORDER NOW] │
├─────────────────────────┤ ├─────────────────────────┤
│ Hero Image │ │ [ TODAY'S SPECIALS ] │
│ [Learn More CTA] │ │ - Dish 1... $12 │
├─────────────────────────┤ │ - Dish 2... $15 │
│ Feature1 Feature2 Feat3 │ ├─────────────────────────┤
└─────────────────────────┘ │ 📅 [Book a Table Widget]│
└─────────────────────────┘
Use code with caution.
When done right, a niche layout feels incredibly premium. It creates an instant vibe that aligns with the business identity, drastically improving brand retention.

The Catch? Over-Engineering & Friction

If you make a layout too clever—like hiding the main menu behind an experimental, floating interactive particle bubble—you break the user's mental model. If a hungry customer can't find a restaurant's phone number or address within five seconds because it's buried in a parallax scrolling animation, they will leave and order from a competitor.

🤝 Resolving the Dilemma: The "Hybrid" Approach

So, how do we build something that looks fresh without killing our client’s conversion rates? We use a hybrid approach: Standard Architecture, Niche Execution.
Keep the structural skeleton predictable so the user never feels lost, but use your front-end skills to inject personality into the visual components, micro-interactions, and asset layouts.

A Quick Example: A Clean Tailwind Service Grid

Instead of a boring, static 3-column card section, you can keep the standard grid layout but make it feel incredibly intentional and polished using modern CSS and subtle transitions:
html

<h3>Our Niche Service</h3>
<p>Familiar layout structure, but the micro-interactions feel distinctly modern and premium.</p>
<a href="#book">
  Book Now <span>→</span>
</a>

Use code with caution.

🛠️ The Developer's Rule of Thumb

Before you start writing code for your next client project, ask yourself these two questions to choose your layout path:

  1. Is the user's intent informational or transactional? If they just need to find a phone number or a list of services (like a law firm), stick to a Textbook layout. If they are there to execute a highly specific task (like buying a shirt or booking a haircut), pivot to a specialized Niche layout designed around that action.
  2. Will this layout decision scale? Niche layouts often rely on third-party APIs and complex database states. If the small business owner doesn't have a developer on retainer, keeping the layout simple and standardized ensures they can maintain it long after you hand over the repository. What about you? Do you lean toward strict UI conventions for maximum conversions, or do you like to push the boundaries of layout design for your clients? Let’s talk in the comments! 👇 #ux #frontend #webdev #css

title: Sandbox persistence is now GA
description:
Vercel Sandboxes now automatically save and restore filesystem state between sessions. Persistence is on by default, meaning no snapshots to manage or state to track manually.

Each sandbox has a durable, customizable name that acts as a unique reference in your project. You can create, retrieve, or resume a sandbox by name. Vercel spins sessions up and down automatically, without interrupting your workflow.

Create a persistent sandbox

When you call Sandbox.create(), persistence is enabled by default:

Each automatic snapshot consumes snapshot storage, which is billed separately from compute. For ephemeral workloads, opt out of persistence to minimize storage costs:

To opt out of persistence with the CLI, pass --non-persistent to sandbox create. Non-persistent sandboxes discard their filesystem when the session ends.

Resume a persistent sandbox

Resuming is automatic. Any call on a stopped sandbox, like runCommand() or writeFiles(), starts a new session from the most recent snapshot.

Other improvements

  • Sandbox.fork(): Create a new sandbox from an existing one

  • Sandbox.getOrCreate(): Idempotent retrieve-or-create for long-lived sandboxes

  • Sandbox.delete(): Permanently delete a sandbox

  • Richer sandbox.stop(): Returns snapshot metadata plus active-CPU and network-transfer totals

  • Lifecycle hooks: onCreate and onResume hooks for create, get, and getOrCreate

  • Tags: Assign custom properties to sandboxes for multi-tenant tracking

Get started

Upgrade to the latest version to create persistent sandboxes by default:

  • pnpm install @vercel/sandbox@latest # SDK

  • pnpm install -g sandbox@latest # CLI

Learn more about persistent sandboxes in the documentation.

title: HyperLoop: Hyperspectral-Assisted Loop Closure Detection in 3D-SLAM for Planetary Exploration
description:
arXiv:2610.19742v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers is challenged by visually repetitive, featureless terrain. SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offer dense mapping but rely on RGB appearance descriptors that degrade under perceptual aliasing - a common failure mode in extraterrestrial environments where physically distinct locations appear visually identical. This paper presents HyperLoop, the first framework integrating hyperspectral imaging (HSI) into the loop closure module of a 3DGS-based SLAM system. Hyperspectral descriptors encode material-level spectral signatures complementing RGB features, providing robustness to illumination changes and visual repetitiveness. Two HSI descriptor families are introduced: Bag-of-Spectral-Words (BoSW), encoding spectral material distributions via TF-IDF weighted histograms, and PCA-K VLAD (PCAK-VLAD), capturing first-order residual statistics of PCA-compressed spectral signatures. Both are evaluated with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors under Strict-AND and Weighted fusion strategies on a custom dataset from the Moon-Mars Outdoor Test Site (MMOTS) at DLR, comprising synchronized RGB-D and hyperspectral sequences across four planetary analog traverses (65.5 m total). A key finding is that the sensor's Red-NIR range (600-860 nm) provides limited discriminability for rock terrain: the best HSI fusion (SIFT-VLAD + BoSW, Strict-AND) achieves 5.04 cm ATE RMSE, within 1.8% of SIFT-VLAD alone (4.95 cm). The gain over NetVLAD (8.81 cm) is attributable to SIFT-VLAD, not HSI fusion. This motivates future adoption of SWIR sensors capturing diagnostic mineral absorption features absent from the 600-860 nm range for planetary SLAM missions.

title: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
description:
arXiv:2610.19133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indirect prompt injection uses untrusted retrieved content, tool outputs, or agent messages to override an LLM's intended behavior. We show that defense robustness is channel-conditioned: the same attack succeeds 18% of the time as a follow-up message but 53% when placed in retrieved context. We propose TRACER (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping), a channel-aware adversarial training method that samples presentation wrappers and combines an answer-anchored, evidence-gated reward with ATRC, which aligns attacked reasoning with clean evidence when an injection is invalid. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, TRACER reduces RAG-framed ASR from 65.5% to 6.1% while preserving 78-82% clean accuracy. Joint RAG+tool training achieves 13.9% average ASR across framings at 3B scale, while a single epoch at 7B reaches 9.4%. These results demonstrate that robust defenses must explicitly train and evaluate across deployment channels.

title: How to Choose the Right Trading Indicator: A Beginner’s Guide to Smarter Trades
description:
Every trader, whether new or experienced, eventually asks the same question: “Which indicator should I use?” With hundreds of options available, picking the wrong one can lead to confusion, late entries and avoidable losses. This guide explains what trading indicators do, which types matter most, and how to pick ones that fit your strategy.

What Is a Trading Indicator?

A trading indicator is a mathematical tool applied to price and volume data. It shows up as lines, bars or signals on your chart and helps you:

Identify the direction of a trend
Spot possible entry and exit points
Measure momentum and volatility
Confirm whether a move is strong or weak

Indicators don’t predict the future. They help you read what the market is doing right now, so your decisions are based on data rather than emotion.

The Main Types of Trading Indicators

  1. Trend Indicators
    These show the market’s overall direction. Moving Averages (SMA, EMA) and MACD are the most popular. They work best in markets that are clearly moving up or down.

  2. Momentum Indicators
    RSI and Stochastic measure the speed of price movement. They help you spot overbought or oversold conditions and possible reversals.

  3. Volatility Indicators
    Bollinger Bands and ATR show how much the price is moving. They are useful for setting stop-loss levels and sizing positions.

  4. Volume Indicators
    OBV and Volume Profile show how many traders are behind a move. A breakout on high volume is generally more reliable than one on low volume.

5 Tips for Choosing the Right Indicator
Match it to your trading style. Scalpers, day traders and swing traders need different settings and timeframes.
Don’t overload your chart. Two to four indicators that complement each other are plenty.
Combine different types. Pair one trend indicator with one momentum indicator for better confirmation.
Backtest before using real money. Test any indicator on historical data first.
Use proper risk management. No indicator is 100% accurate, so always use a stop-loss.
Ready-Made Indicators vs. Free Indicators

Free indicators are fine for learning, but many traders prefer professionally built, tested and optimized indicators. These usually offer cleaner signals, custom alerts, better visuals and less lag, which saves time and helps you trade with more confidence.

If you’re looking for reliable trading indicators built for serious traders, you can explore the collection at [Bolts – Trading Indicators](https://bolts.xo.je/

  1. ). Check what’s available and find one that suits your strategy.

Final Thoughts

The best indicator is not the one with the most features. It is the one you understand, have tested, and can use consistently. Start simple, test carefully, manage your risk, and build your strategy step by step.

What Is a Trading Indicator?

A trading indicator is a mathematical tool applied to price and volume data. It shows up as lines, bars or signals on your chart and helps you:

Identify the direction of a trend
Spot possible entry and exit points
Measure momentum and volatility
Confirm whether a move is strong or weak

Indicators don’t predict the future. They help you read what the market is doing right now, so your decisions are based on data rather than emotion.

The Main Types of Trading Indicators

Match it to your trading style. Scalpers, day traders and swing traders need different settings and timeframes.
