title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19789v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-distillation in agentic reinforcement learning has produced a growing number of methods. However, existing evaluations often reuse published baseline scores under differing experimental conditions, provide few direct comparisons among contemporaneous methods, and give limited attention to training stability and computational cost. These limitations obscure the source of reported gains and the practical strengths and weaknesses of competing methods. Costly agent training further motivates a common basis for comparison. To address these gaps, we compare ten representative methods against GRPO on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop across three model sizes. Our study comprises 132 training runs totaling 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours, with repeated evaluations over eight rollout seeds for the pretrained backbones and all eleven trained methods. Beyond final task performance, we examine training progress, stability, and measured computational cost. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, gains over GRPO remain limited in scope, with no method consistently outperforming it across settings. Second, strong final performance can mask unstable training. Third, additional training cost does not consistently translate into better performance. We establish this benchmark to support fair, comprehensive comparison and guide future research toward reliable and cost-effective improvements in agent training. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/Self-Distillation-AgentRL/

title: Spectral-MoE: Heterogeneous Per-Layer Expert Utilization in Dense-to-MoE Conversion
description:
arXiv:2610.19232v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.

title: Architectural Breakdown: We Rendered a HQ Demo Video on a Free Farm Run by Strangers
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+We+Rendered+a+HQ+Demo+Video+on+round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# We Rendered a 4K Demo Video on a Free Farm Run by Strangers. Here's the Architecture That Stopped It from Melting Down at 3 AM

The ticket hit at 2:17 AM on a Tuesday. Client wanted a 90‑second 4K demo video. We had a GitHub repo, three unused API keys, and thirty‑seven stranger nodes with 8 GB RAM and zero SLA. I still see the stack trace when I close my eyes.

Here is what happens when you try to render a film on infrastructure you don’t own, don’t control, and absolutely should not trust, and how we patched the holes that nearly cost us the deliverable.

---

## The Night Everything Broke

By hour three, three catastrophes collided: OOM kills on edge nodes, event‑loop stalls hitting twelve seconds during synchronous disk writes, and a lock‑contention storm on the shared output file that dropped throughput to four frames per minute. The coordinator thought we were fine because the chunk tracker was counting optimistic ACKs that never touched durable storage.

Node 12 dropped mid‑chunk. We lost frames 1,847 through 2,103. No checkpoint. No retry. The dispatcher was measuring success flags, not actual bytes written.

That is when I learned the hard way: a distributed render farm without backpressure is just a more expensive way to crash your laptop.

---

## Root‑Cause Breakdown

| Symptom | Root Cause |
|---------|-----------|
| Random OOM kills on nodes | Unbounded per‑frame texture cache, no memory semaphore |
| Event‑loop stalls over 5 seconds | Synchronous I/O blocking the asyncio event loop |
| Lock contention on output files | Global threading.Lock serializing all worker writes |
| Missing frames after node dropout | No idempotent chunk tracking or resumable uploads |
| Rate‑limit errors from cloud storage | Unthrottled multipart uploads from dozens of parallel workers |
| CPU starvation on weak nodes | Hardcoded 4‑core assumption on 2‑core machines |

Every assumption about the free farm was a liability. We fixed them all.

---

## The Architecture: Back‑Pressure‑Driven, Not Hope‑Driven

+-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+
| Coordinator |<-------> | Dispatcher |<-------> | Worker Pool |
| (SQLite WAL) | HTTP | (RingBuffer) | HTTP | (FFmpeg/Blender) |
+-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+
^ ^ ^
| | |
Chunk bookkeeping Backpressure enforcement Memory semaphore gating
Checksum verification Rate limiter Multipart uploader
Watchdog timer Chunk reassignment Status reporting


### Coordinator: Single Source of Truth

SQLite with WAL mode. Every chunk gets a UUID, a status transition log, and a checksum. Nothing lives in memory that is not also on disk. If the coordinator dies, the next restart replays the WAL and picks up exactly where it left off.

The dispatcher pulls from a `collections.deque(maxlen=512)`. Queue fills → new chunks wait. No memory spikes. No queue explosions. This is the kind of boring, deterministic design that ShipMVP’s rapid development stack ships in production builds, no magic, just plumbing that works.

### Dispatcher: The Traffic Cop

Rate limiting via `asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS=12)`. Our S3 bucket started choking at ~15 simultaneous multipart uploads. Each dispatch triggers a checksum verification before handing off to a worker.

Workers heartbeat every 30 seconds. Three missed heartbeats → chunks marked `PENDING_RETRY` and re‑dispatched. Lost nothing.

---

## Production Code: The Critical Path


python
import asyncio
import hashlib
import os
import sqlite3
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional
import aiohttp

MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH = 512
HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT = 90
MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS = 12
CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES = 30
MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB = 256
NODE_RAM_MB = 8192

max_chunks_per_node = (NODE_RAM_MB * 0.7) // MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB # 22 max
MEMORY_SEMAPHORE = asyncio.Semaphore(max_chunks_per_node)

chunk_queue: deque = deque(maxlen=MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH)
worker_semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS)
active_workers: dict = {}
retry_backoff = 0.5

class ChunkTracker:
"""Idempotent chunk state with checksum verification and WAL durability."""

def _init_db(self):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, check_same_thread=False)
    conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
    conn.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS chunk_status (
            chunk_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            worker_id TEXT,
            status TEXT DEFAULT 'PENDING',
            frame_start INTEGER,
            frame_end INTEGER,
            checksum TEXT,
            started_at REAL,
            completed_at REAL,
            failed_at REAL,
            retry_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0
        )
    """)
    conn.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS heartbeats (
            worker_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            last_seen REAL
        )
    """)
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

async def _db_execute(self, sql: str, params: tuple = ()) -> list:
    async with self._lock:
        loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
        return await loop.run_in_executor(
            None,
            lambda: sqlite3.connect(self.db_path).execute(sql, params).fetchall()
        )

async def mark_started(self, chunk_id: str, worker_id: str) -> None:
    async with self._lock:
        await self._db_execute(
            "INSERT INTO chunk_status (chunk_id, worker_id, status, started_at, retry_count) "
            "VALUES (?, ?, 'IN_FLIGHT', strftime('%s','now'), "
            "COALESCE((SELECT retry_count FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?), 0)) "
            "ON CONFLICT(chunk_id) DO UPDATE SET status='IN_FLIGHT', worker_id=?, "
            "started_at=strftime('%s','now') WHERE chunk_id=?",
            (chunk_id, worker_id, chunk_id, worker_id, chunk_id)
        )

async def mark_completed(self, chunk_id: str, checksum: str) -> bool:
    async with self._lock:
        row = await self._db_execute(
            "SELECT status FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?", (chunk_id,)
        )
        if row and row[0][0] == "COMPLETED":
            return False
        await self._db_execute(
            "UPDATE chunk_status SET status='COMPLETED', checksum=?, "
            "completed_at=strftime('%s','now') WHERE chunk_id=?",
            (checksum, chunk_id)
        )
        return True

async def mark_failed(self, chunk_id: str) -> None:
    async with self._lock:
        await self._db_execute(
            "UPDATE chunk_status SET status='PENDING_RETRY', failed_at=strftime('%s','now'), "
            "retry_count=retry_count+1 WHERE chunk_id=? AND status='IN_FLIGHT'",
            (chunk_id,)
        )

async def get_pending_chunks(self, limit: int = 50) -> list:
    async with self._lock:
        return await self._db_execute(
            "SELECT chunk_id, frame_start, frame_end FROM chunk_status "
            "WHERE status IN ('PENDING','PENDING_RETRY') ORDER BY created_at LIMIT ?",
            (limit,)
        )

async def escalate_if_over_retry(self, chunk_id: str) -> bool:
    row = await self._db_execute(
        "SELECT retry_count FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?", (chunk_id,)
    )
    return row and row[0][0] >= 3


### Watchdog: Detecting Dead Nodes Before Data Loss


python
async def watchdog(task_queue: asyncio.Queue, tracker: ChunkTracker):
while True:
await asyncio.sleep(15)
now = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()
dead_workers = [
wid for wid, last in active_workers.items()
if now - last > HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT
]
for wid in dead_workers:
del active_workers[wid]
rows = await tracker._db_execute(
"SELECT chunk_id FROM chunk_status WHERE worker_id=? AND status='IN_FLIGHT'",
(wid,)
)
for (chunk_id,) in rows:
await tracker.mark_failed(chunk_id)
escaped = await tracker.escalate_if_over_retry(chunk_id)
if escaped:
print(f"[ALERT] Chunk {chunk_id} exceeded 3 retries")
task_queue.put_nowait(chunk_id)


### Worker: Bounded, Stateless, Idempotent


python
async def worker_task(worker_id: str, tracker: ChunkTracker, upload_queue: asyncio.Queue):
while True:
chunk_id = await asyncio.to_thread(upload_queue.get)

    async with MEMORY_SEMAPHORE:
        await tracker.mark_started(chunk_id, worker_id)
        active_workers[worker_id] = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()

        env = os.environ.copy()
        env["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "2"
        cmd = [
            "ffmpeg", "-y", "-i", f"frames_{chunk_id}.txt",
            "-frames:v", str(CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES),
            "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", "-c:v", "libx264",
            "-preset", "fast", "-threads", "2",
            "-movflags", "+faststart", f"chunk_{chunk_id}.mp4"
        ]

        proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
            *cmd, env=env,
            stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE
        )
        stdout, stderr = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=120)

        if proc.returncode != 0:
            await tracker.mark_failed(chunk_id)
            continue

        with open(f"chunk_{chunk_id}.mp4", "rb") as f:
            checksum = hashlib.md5(f.read()).hexdigest()

        completed = await tracker.mark_completed(chunk_id, checksum)
        if completed:
            print(f"[OK] {chunk_id} checksum={checksum}")
        else:
            print(f"[SKIP] {chunk_id} already completed (idempotent)")


---

## Hardware Profiling: What 8 GB RAM Actually Gives You

| Node Type | vCPUs | RAM | Measured FPS | Peak Memory | Stall Events |
|-----------|-------|-----|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| t2.micro clone | 1 | 4 GB | 2.1 | 3.8 GB | 47 |
| t3.small clone | 2 | 8 GB | 4.3 | 6.1 GB | 12 |
| c5.large clone | 2 | 4 GB | 3.8 | 3.9 GB | 31 |
| n1‑standard‑2 | 2 | 7.5 GB | 5.1 | 6.8 GB | 8 |
| Custom 4‑core | 4 | 8 GB | 6.2 | 7.4 GB | 3 |

The 2‑core 8 GB nodes were the sweet spot. More cores did not help; FFmpeg’s CPU‑bound rendering hit diminishing returns past 2 threads per chunk, and extra context switching killed tail latency. The 4‑core nodes looked great on paper but aggressive CPU sharing with other tenants caused unpredictable pauses that wrecked frame‑timing consistency.

We locked in `CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES=30` with `MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB=256`. Stayed under 6 GB peak on the worst node. Render times between 8 and 14 seconds per chunk.

---

## The Multipart Upload That Saved Us

Resumable multipart uploads with per‑part checksums. Every worker streams directly to cloud storage in 5 MB parts. Each part gets an MD5 before upload. If a worker drops mid‑upload, the next one picks up from the last successful part boundary. No re‑rendering. No wasted cycles.

When Node 28 vanished during a 47‑minute upload window, we resumed from part 94 of 127. The client saw a green dot because we reported partial completion percentages, not binary success or failure.

---

## What We Learned the Hard Way

Three uncomfortable truths: the free farm would betray you, your monitoring would always be incomplete, and the first design would fail. We learned to measure actual bytes transferred instead of trusting optimistic progress bars. We learned to treat every node as temporary and stateless. We learned that backpressure is not a performance feature; it is the difference between graceful degradation and silent corruption.

The video rendered. 94 seconds of 4K. Zero missing frames. Two nodes died mid‑job and neither loss showed up. Total cost: $0.00. Engineering effort: ~180 person‑hours.

Worth it.

---

**Question for the comments:** What is the most painful distributed system failure you have debugged at 3 AM, and did you solve it by adding more observability or by removing entire components from the critical path?

title: Vocab deck
description:
Vocab Deck

I've been revisiting my existing projects to improve them by adding features, refining the UI/UX, and making them more reliable. Vocab Deck is one of them.

It's a vocabulary practice app that helps users learn words through different study modes and track their progress.

Vocab Deck lets users choose a built-in or custom vocabulary deck and practice through flashcards, quizzes, typing exercises, or a matching game. The frontend validates vocabulary data and uses a pure-function game engine to generate randomized sessions, with features like answer checking, distractor generation, and real-time feedback. Built-in decks are served by the FastAPI backend, while custom decks and theme preferences are stored in the browser. Study progress stays in memory and resets when the page reloads.

FEATURES -

Four Study Modes
• 3D Flashcards - Review words and meanings.
• Multiple-Choice Quizzes - Test your understanding.
• Typing Practice - Practice active recall with accent-insensitive answer checking.
• Matching Game - Match words with their meanings

Built-in Language Decks:
• English → French
• English → German
• English → Japanese

Custom Decks:
Create and edit decks, with JSON and CSV import/export to manage and reuse vocabulary lists.

Progress Tracking:
Track study statistics, streaks, and time spent across different study modes.

TECH STACK
Backend -
Python 3.11
FastAPI 0.110+
Uvicorn
Pydantic 2

Frontend -
Node.js 18+
React 18 + TypeScript
Vite

Testing -
Vitest + Testing Library
Playwright

The project is live, and contributions are welcome! You can contribute to the codebase or open an issue to report bugs, suggest improvements, or propose new features.

Live Demo: https://vocab-deck.vercel.app/

PIYUSH-NEXTGEN / Vocab-Deck

Vocab Deck

Vocab Deck is a vocabulary practice application that helps language learners memorize words through four interactive study modes. It provides a modern React frontend backed by a FastAPI vocabulary service. Built-in decks cover English→French, English→German, and English→Japanese; users can also create, edit, import, and export custom decks entirely in the browser.

Features

  • Four study modes: Flashcards (with 3D flip), Multiple-choice Quiz, Typing (accent-insensitive option), Matching
  • Three built-in language pairs: English→French, English→German, English→Japanese (50 entries each, directly comparable)
  • Custom decks: Create, edit, import (JSON/CSV), export; validated client-side with same rules as built-in decks
  • Session tracking: Per-mode stats (correct/incorrect, streaks, time) preserved across mode switches; reset on demand
  • Theme support: Light/dark with prefers-color-scheme detection and localStorage persistence, no flash on load
  • Accessibility: prefers-reduced-motion swaps flip for instant face swap; focus-visible outlines; semantic HTML
  • Offline-capable custom decks: Stored in localStorage, portable via JSON/CSV…

title: RepForcing: Representation-Space Initialization for Autoregressive Video Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.20111v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distilling pretrained video diffusion models into few-step autoregressive (AR) generators typically combines student initialization with distribution matching distillation (DMD). An intermediate AR teacher can provide causally compatible targets for ODE initialization. However, causally compatible targets alone do not ensure high-quality generation under a short sampling schedule. We analyze the posterior-mean predictions favored by direct latent regression and empirically find that causal ODE initialization alleviates blur but still leaves fine detail unresolved. To address this limitation, we propose Representation Forcing, which learns few-step causal initialization through representation-space supervision rather than intermediate-teacher trajectory regression. The student is trained with teacher forcing by comparing clean predictions and training targets through normalized features of a frozen video diffusion transformer. This phase reuses the synthetic videos generated by a bidirectional model for AR teacher training and replaces both teacher training and causal ODE distillation, without generating additional causal ODE trajectories. The subsequent asymmetric DMD procedure remains unchanged. Empirical results show that, at four sampling steps, RepForcing better preserves generation quality than intermediate-teacher-based initialization before DMD. After DMD, our four-step chunk-wise model improves VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.66 (+0.62 points) and VisionReward from 6.326 to 10.074 (+59.25%) over the reported causal-ODE-based baseline.

title: Vercel Sandbox firewall now supports request proxying and filtering
description:
The Vercel Sandbox firewall now supports forwarding specific HTTP requests to a proxy you control. You can also use matchers to filter forwarding and credentials brokering to only the requests that need it.

Requests proxying

You can now route outbound sandbox traffic through your own proxy for logging, debugging, or transforming requests and responses. Set a forwardURL on any allowed domain, and the firewall will forward matching HTTPS requests to your server.

The proxy receives the original request along with additional headers to identify the source:

  • vercel-forwarded-host: The original request's SNI

  • vercel-forwarded-scheme: The original request's scheme

  • vercel-forwarded-port: The original request's port

  • vercel-sandbox-oidc-token: A Vercel-issued OIDC token that the proxy can use to authenticate the request and identity the source team / project / sandbox. Learn more about it in the docs

Filtering

Additionally, you can now use matchers to filter request forwarding or credentials brokering to requests matching a specific path, method, query string, or headers. This gives you fine-grained control over which requests get transformed; for example, only forwarding POST requests to a specific API path while allowing all other traffic through untouched.

These features are available in beta for Pro and Enterprise plans. Get started by installing the @vercel/sandbox@beta SDK, and learn more in the docs about requests proxying and matchers.

title: Kandinsky S2V 1.0: Audio-Driven Avatar Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19290v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Kandinsky S2V 1.0, an open family of speech-to-video models for controllable audio-driven human animation, comprising Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite (2B parameters) and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro (21B parameters). From a single reference image, a speech waveform, and a text prompt, the models generate long-form 25 FPS video in which lip motion, expression, pose, and gesture follow the speech. The architecture draws text and audio conditioning from one Qwen2.5-Omni model and adds a reference-aware three-scale visual memory. Training starts from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video foundation models [1] and combines mixed reference-memory layouts with an area-adaptive face loss. The training corpus contains 1.17M single-speaker clips selected by active-speaker detection, with captions generated directly in English and Russian. A side-by-side human evaluation against the strongest open-source baseline and two proprietary commercial models shows that Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro performs comparably to or better than these models on average and is also preferred for lip synchronization. On common speech to video benchmarks, Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro rank among the top performing models according to mean rank over five reported metrics. Beyond the base models, we provide {\pi}-Flow distilled variants of both Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro. The distilled Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro model generates video in 16 sampling steps without classifier-free guidance, achieving a 5.4 times end-to-end speedup over the base model, while matching or exceeding it on nearly all reported benchmark metrics. To accelerate open research and deployment in speech-to-video generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.

title: Load Testing: Read the Queue Behind Successful Bookings
description:
A booking endpoint can keep returning success while concurrent users wait much longer. Lab 15 makes that behavior visible with a local HTTP server, a constrained work pool, and a small Go load generator.

Load testing reveals how latency changes when demand competes for limited resources.

Fast bookings can queue under load

One successful booking does not explain concurrent behavior. Lab 15 sends POST /booking to a local HTTP server, comparing low and high concurrency to expose queueing and latency distributions. It models bounded work slots, not a production database.

Two scenarios share one server

The demo uses five simulated database slots and a 20 ms base query. Smoke runs two VUs; stress runs 50. Both run for two seconds, sequentially, with the same endpoint and booking body. These are demonstration settings, not production capacity targets.

Each VU waits before sending again

Each VU has one goroutine and sends its next request after the previous attempt finishes. There is no think time, ramp-up, or arrival-rate scheduler. This is a closed loop: slower responses reduce each VU's request rate.

A buffered channel bounds simulated work

A buffered channel acts as a semaphore. Handlers acquire a token before simulated query work and release it with defer. Full capacity makes additional handlers wait; there is no explicit bounded waiting queue or overload rejection policy.

select {
case s.semaphore <- struct{}{}:
case <-r.Context().Done():
    return
}
defer func() { <-s.semaphore }()

The database pool is simulated

There is no SQL driver, real query, booking table, or database transaction. A timer simulates work. ActiveConnections returns len(semaphore): acquired slots, not waiting handlers, TCP connections, or real database telemetry.

Random slow work amplifies queueing

activeReq includes waiting and working POST handlers. After admission, when activeReq exceeds capacity, a 10% random branch multiplies query duration by 25. The demo's 20 ms becomes 500 ms. Stress results therefore combine queueing with deliberately injected slow work.

if atomic.LoadInt64(&s.activeReq) >
    int64(s.cfg.MaxDBConnections) {
    if rand.Float32() < 0.10 {
        dur = s.cfg.DBQueryDuration * 25
    }
}

Context bounds the test lifetime

Run uses context.WithTimeout for the configured duration and passes that context to each HTTP request. A five-second client timeout also applies. The server checks cancellation while acquiring a slot and waiting for simulated work; it does not return a dedicated overload response.

Canceled attempts are not all counted

Request-construction and client.Do errors are counted only while ctx.Err() is nil. End-of-test canceled attempts can be omitted. TotalRequests is recorded success samples plus counted errors, not every attempt started.

if err != nil {
    if ctx.Err() == nil {
        errs++
    }
    continue
}

Success follows an HTTP status rule

The runner drains and closes response bodies. Status >=400 increments errors; status <400 records success latency, which is broader than a 2xx-only rule. JSON business fields are not validated, and body-read errors are ignored.

Latency includes reading the body

Timing starts before client.Do and ends after the successful response body is drained and closed. It is not query-only time. DNS, dialing, TLS, first-byte wait, pool wait, and body transfer are not separately measured.

Percentiles use successful samples only

Failed responses and transport errors have no latency samples. Percentiles, average, min, and max use successful samples only. With no successes, latency fields remain zero; that does not mean the service responded instantly.

RPS includes counted errors

Total is len(latencies)+errors. RPS divides that total by Run's actual elapsed duration after goroutines finish, so it is not success-only throughput. With no total requests, an empty Result is returned, including zero Duration.

total := len(latencies) + errors
res.RPS = float64(total) /
    totalDuration.Seconds()

Percentiles select a floored index

The calculator copies and sorts samples, then selects int((n-1)*p/100) without interpolation. For the test fixture 1–100 ms, P50=50 ms, P95=95 ms, and P99=99 ms. Other tools may use different percentile conventions.

idx := int(float64(len(sorted)-1) *
    (pct / 100.0))
return sorted[idx]

A fixture makes the calculation explicit

The 1–100 ms fixture has min 1 ms, max 100 ms, and average 50.5 ms. time.Duration retains nanosecond units, so division does not force whole-millisecond rounding. These are calculated fixture values, not HTTP performance measurements.

Small samples make the tail coarse

With one 42 ms sample, every percentile is 42 ms. Small datasets can map several tail percentiles to the same sample and may exclude the maximum under this formula. Sample count and method matter when interpreting precision.

Average and tail answer different questions

Average summarizes all successful samples; P95 selects a high-ranked sample. Unit tests verify ordered percentile invariants. The integration test separately checks stress P95 exceeds stress average; that relationship is not guaranteed for every possible distribution.

Demo numbers are recorded examples

The repository records a sample smoke P95 of about 21.37 ms and stress P95 of about 1.357 s, with zero counted errors. These are historical example results, not a fresh measurement. Random spikes and scheduling vary; omitted canceled attempts also qualify the zero-error interpretation.

Transport settings are not a full generator audit

MaxIdleConns and MaxIdleConnsPerHost are both 1000; these are idle-connection retention settings, not proof that every client bottleneck is eliminated. All successful latencies are retained per VU, merged, copied, and sorted, so memory grows with collected samples.

A booking response is not a real transaction

Non-POST methods receive 405. Completed POST requests return 201, confirmed, and the fixed ID BK-1001. Request JSON is not decoded or validated, and there is no persistence, authentication, idempotency, or unique booking creation.

Tests establish specific behaviors

Five metric tests cover fixtures, empty input, one sample, RPS, and ordering. Seven integration tests cover load comparison, HTTP 500, method rejection, dial errors, cancellation, slot limits, and total-count invariants. They do not prove queue fairness or maximum capacity.

The lab bottleneck is known by design

The slot bottleneck is deliberately constructed. In production, rising P95 alone does not isolate application queues, database work, network, or external dependencies. The runtime has no exporter, tracing, or automated SLA threshold; the demo prints summaries.

Rerun and interpret in context

The module declares Go 1.22 and uses the standard library. Go is unavailable in this authoring environment, so source and assertions were inspected without rerunning tests. Recorded repository results are prior-run evidence. Load testing reveals how latency changes when demand competes for limited resources.

cd labs/15-load-testing
go test -v ./...
go test -race ./...
go run ./cmd/demo

Source

Software Engineering Lab 15, snapshot commit 82af988b89439fa92b1200406c5afbd59ce72a56. Source: README, runner, metric calculator and tests, server, integration tests, demo, execution record, and go.mod. Code excerpts belong in their original package context.

title: You Cannot Stop What Arrives
description:
What I notice

I cannot stop my thoughts. Try it yourself. Set a timer for thirty seconds and think of nothing. A thought will arrive before you pick it. This is my own observation. I have not checked the research on it.

Some thoughts arrive with weight. One kind is a standard I did not choose. It asks me to be someone before I have done anything. I cannot meet that kind by working, because it never says what finished looks like.

This piece started from a line in the Marvel series VisionQuest, about holding someone's memories without their feelings. I have not tried to explain the show. I took the line as a place to start thinking.

Three answers to an arrival

I see three ways to answer a thought that weighs too much.

  1. Act on it at once, as if it were an order.
  2. Shrink so the test never comes. If I never try, I cannot fall short.
  3. Record what is true, decide what I can, and leave the rest marked as unknown.

The second answer is the one I want to look at. It feels like relief. It also removes the one thing that would tell me whether the weight was real.

The same shape in a settlement engine

My settlement engine cannot choose what arrives either. A payment gateway times out. Postgres deadlocks two transactions against each other. Neither event waits for permission. What I control is the state the engine writes next.

Here is the first decision, trimmed from SettlementService.createSettlement:

try {
    gatewayResult = externalSettlementGateway.execute(executionRequest);
} catch (Exception gatewayFailure) {
    gatewayResult = new GatewayResult(SettlementOutcome.UNKNOWN, null);
}
return finalizeWithRetry(executionRequest.settlementId(), gatewayResult);

A timeout means the engine does not know whether the gateway processed the payment. The code says so. It writes UNKNOWN, not CONFIRMED and not FAILED. The comment in the file gives the reason: leaving the settlement PENDING would leave its idempotency key IN_PROGRESS, and every retry with that key would get a 409 with no way to resolve it.

Here is the second decision, trimmed from finalizeWithRetry:

for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_FINALIZE_ATTEMPTS; attempt++) {
    try {
        return settlementTransactions.finalizeSettlement(settlementId, gatewayResult);
    } catch (TransientDataAccessException transientFailure) {
        if (attempt == MAX_FINALIZE_ATTEMPTS) {
            return finalizeAsUnknownAfterExhaustingRetries(settlementId, transientFailure);
        }
        meterRegistry.counter("settlement.finalize.retries").increment();
        sleepBriefly(attempt);
    }
}

The last branch is the part that matters. A comment above it says the Phase 9 load test found a bug. When the five attempts ran out with no fallback, the settlement stayed PENDING and its key stayed IN_PROGRESS forever. The failure was not the deadlock. Deadlocks were expected and retried. The failure was that the engine reached a point where it made no decision, and a state with no decision never ends.

The fix gave the engine a second budget of five attempts that writes UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is a smaller claim than CONFIRMED. It is also true, and a later reconciliation can resolve it.

What I take from the comparison

I do not need to claim greatness, and I do not need to claim failure. Both are large claims, and the evidence for either does not exist yet. The smaller true claim is available: here is what I made today. For anything bigger I can write unknown, and let the record settle it later. My journal does the job that reconciliation does for the engine.

The stall is the bug. Shrinking so the test never comes is the PENDING state with the key stuck. It looks like safety. It blocks every later attempt.

Where the comparison stops

A person is not a service. Three differences matter.

The engine stops after ten attempts. A person should not cap attempts at ten.

The engine's UNKNOWN resolves against an outside system that holds the answer. A record of my own work does not hold the answer to my worth. It only holds what I did.

The engine decides in milliseconds. This decision takes years, and I may get it wrong in both directions. The feeling that I could do great things is a feeling, not evidence. It may be potential. It may be the weight of an expectation. I cannot tell which from inside.

What I do not know

I do not know how common the shrinking answer is. I am drawing on my own experience, not on data.

I read only createSettlement and finalizeWithRetry for this piece. I am still restudying the rest of the retry path, so I make no claim about how it behaves under load beyond what the code comments say.

What I took from it

  1. I cannot stop what arrives. I can choose the state I write next.
  2. A state that never ends is worse than an honest "unknown".
  3. Make the next claim small enough to be true: what I made today.
  4. Keep the record. It settles questions that a feeling at 4 in the morning cannot.

Originally published on my site.

title: The first stable version 1.0 of Strata for Linux has been released
description:
Strata 1.0 is now available, marking the first stable release of the Rust-based, GTK4 file manager.

Designed for Linux environments like Omarchy, version 1.0 introduces session-restoring tabs, large directory optimizations, and sandboxed file previews using Bubblewrap.

Three display modes and keyboard control

Strata supports three different layouts for browsing files: icon view, traditional list view, and columns that allow for easy navigation into deeper folders.

For those who prefer not to use the mouse, navigation includes shortcuts inspired by the well-known Vim text editor, customizable shortcuts, and quick file search based on the letters of their name.

File previews and security

The program has a preview system that supports images, RAW photos, PDF files, text documents, source code, as well as audio and video files. For greater security, previews based on internal analysis tools are isolated using special containment mechanisms.

READ ALSO

New version of Fastfetch released with improvements for Linux and Android

Additionally, the application supports common file operations, browsing and extracting from compressed archives, managing removable disks, and connecting to remote network locations via standard Linux protocols.

What version 1.0 brings and system requirements

This first stable release includes tabs with the ability to restore a previous session, improved mouse-based file transfer handling, and optimizations for folders with a large amount of content.

The developers' published metrics show satisfactory memory usage compared to other programs, although competitors are often faster at generating common preview images, and independent testing is needed. Strata 1.0 is available for Linux systems with x86_64 and AArch64 architectures. Out-of-the-box programs require newer versions of the core system libraries, while source code and installation instructions are available on the project's GitHub page.

title: I Turned 44 Blog Posts Into a Frontend Roadmap You Have to Pass
description:
It's Sunday night, the interview is on Thursday, and the frontend roadmap in your other tab has more topics than you have evenings. You're sure about half of them and fairly sure about the rest.

The roadmap can't tell you which "fairly sure" is real. It only knows what you ticked.

So test the topics before you read them. Here's what that looks like for HTML: ten questions drawn at random, seven right to pass, and the whole stage counts as cleared.

No account and no reading, just ten questions. Here's why that beats a checkbox, and how it works.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself overstates what you know, using a 2006 study of re-reading versus testing
  • Compare seven well-known frontend roadmaps and courses on price, sign-up, checks, skipping and certificates
  • Use checkpoints to skip the stages you already know and find the gaps you don't
  • Compute learning progress from quiz attempts instead of storing it
  • Tell when this path is the wrong tool, and what to use instead

Who this is for

You've shipped frontend code for a year or more, in Vue or React, and you want to find out quickly what you actually know: for an interview, a promotion or your own peace of mind. If you build learning tools, read "Under the hood". If you're starting from zero, read "When not to use it" first.

Table of contents

  • Why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself stops working
  • What people do today: seven frontend roadmaps and courses
  • Where today's options break
  • The mental model
  • Enter the Frontend Developer path
  • How the frontend roadmap works, in four steps
  • Under the hood: progress computed from quiz attempts
  • When not to use it
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet: the path at a glance

Why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself stops working

Strip a self-marked roadmap down to its data, and this is all of it:

type Status = "done" | "learning" | "skipped" | "pending";

const progress: Record<string, Status> = {
  "semantic-html": "done",  // ticked two years ago
  "event-loop": "done",     // read the article, felt fine
  promises: "skipped",      // "I use them every day"
  specificity: "pending",
};

Every value in that object is an opinion, typed in by the person it describes. Nothing can make it wrong, and that is the bug.

It fails in three ways:

  1. "done" records reading, not knowing. Reaching the end of an article and answering a question about it are different events. The tick records the first one.
  2. "skipped" is a guess, in both directions. You skip HTML because you've written it for years. Whether you know what inert does, or what showModal() gives you that show() doesn't, the tick can't say. Some of what you skip, you don't know; some of what you re-read, you did.
  3. Nobody else can read it. A lead, a mentor or an interviewer can't tell your "done" from anyone else's.

The fix isn't a better checkbox. It's taking the checkbox away from the person being measured.

What people do today: seven frontend roadmaps and courses

Here's how the best-known options handle it, checked on their own pages on 14 October 2026:

Free? Account How your learning is checked Skip what you know Certificate
roadmap.sh frontend roadmap Yes; AI quizzes: 2 on the free plan, unlimited on Pro ($10/month) To save progress You mark topics done; AI quizzes and self-graded flashcards sit alongside Mark a topic "skipped" yourself None found
freeCodeCamp v9 certifications Yes To save progress Questions after every lesson, 20-question module quizzes, 5 projects, then a 50-question closed-book exam No placement test found Yes, free
The Odin Project Yes Optional, to check off lessons Projects, compared with other students' solutions Cherry-pick lessons and projects "We don't provide a certificate"
MDN Curriculum Yes No Not graded: a syllabus with recommended resources, plus "Test your skills" self-checks in MDN's Learn modules A self-paced reading list None
Codecademy Front-End Engineer No: Pro, from $15.99/month billed annually Yes 103 quizzes, 77 projects, certification exams "Skip ahead to the exam" Professional certification (Pro)
Scrimba Frontend Developer path No: subscription Yes Coding challenges inside the screencasts, solo projects, some quizzes None found Certificate of completion
Frontend Mentor learning paths Mostly To submit (GitHub login) Feedback on what you build: the community, plus AI review (1 a month free, every solution on Pro) Pick any challenge None found

Three of these deserve more than a row.

roadmap.sh is the best map of what to learn. Its roadmaps are free, the project has 369K GitHub stars, and the site counts more than 3.2 million registered users. If you want to know what exists, look there first; nothing here argues against it.

freeCodeCamp's v9 certifications are the most rigorous free credential in that table, and more rigorous than the quizzes in this article. The new Responsive Web Design certification ends each lesson with three comprehension questions and each module with a 20-question quiz (18 right to pass). Then it asks for five certification projects before a 50-question, closed-book exam: one attempt a week, reviewed by staff before the result is released.

The Odin Project is right about proof. It gives no certificate because, in its FAQ's words, "Employers will be much more impressed with your amazing personal portfolio of projects." Projects are the strongest evidence anywhere in that table.

Where today's options break

None of these is broken. The gap only shows when you want four things at once: free, no sign-up to start, a check on every step, and a skip you have to earn.

On roadmap.sh you mark a topic done. Its AI-generated quizzes sit beside the roadmap rather than gating it: two on the free plan ("These don't reset"), unlimited on Pro at $10 a month. freeCodeCamp checks properly, but it is built to take you from the start: its own figure is 300 hours per certification, and the exam waits for five projects. Right for learning, heavy for finding out what you already know.

Codecademy built exactly the skip I wanted ("Don't waste time learning what you already know") and put it behind Pro, from $15.99 a month billed annually. The Odin Project and MDN Curriculum have nothing to pass, Scrimba is paid, and Frontend Mentor checks what you build rather than what you know.

No single piece of what I built is new; quizzes, skipping, forks and certificates all exist in that table. What I couldn't find among those seven was all four together.

The mental model

The mental model: reading is input, answering is evidence, and progress should be computed from the evidence, never typed in by the person being measured.

The evidence isn't only for other people. Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study, Test-Enhanced Learning (Psychological Science 17(3), 249–255), compared re-reading with testing. On a test five minutes later, re-reading came out ahead. Two days later, and again a week later, testing did, even though re-reading had left students more confident. No feedback was given in that study: nobody told the tested students what they had missed.

Three things follow:

  • Skipping is evidence arriving early. If you can pass the check without reading, the reading would have been re-reading, the strategy that lost at two days and at a week.
  • A check can be open-book and still be a check. Its job is to make you answer, and to show you exactly where you couldn't.
  • Failing is the useful part. A wrong answer that arrives with an explanation is a reading list. A tick never told you anything.

Enter the Frontend Developer path

I'd already written the articles. Between July and October, 44 of my posts each taught one piece of frontend, from the native <dialog> to the back/forward cache, and every one has a quiz. What they lacked was an order, and a reason to take the quiz.

So I put them on a map: a free frontend developer roadmap on bestpractic.org, where every step is an article and a quiz you have to pass. Read it. Pass it. Unlock the next stage.

Honestly, in one sentence: 44 existing articles and their 336 quiz questions, in 7 stages that each close with a checkpoint, free, with no account needed to start, about 16 hours by the site's own estimate, and 7 more levels still being written.

  • 🗺️ The map: https://bestpractic.org/paths/frontend-developer
  • ⏭️ The HTML checkpoint: https://bestpractic.org/paths/frontend-developer/checkpoint/html
  • 1️⃣ Level 1, the native <dialog>: https://bestpractic.org/blog/dialog-element-native-modal?path=frontend-developer
  • 📚 All learning paths: https://bestpractic.org/paths

How the frontend roadmap works, in four steps

Step 1: the map

The route has seven stages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Vue or React, Nuxt or Next.js, TypeScript, and Ship it, the production stage. The two forks make nine stage cards, each pair sharing one tier of the map: Nuxt follows Vue, Next.js follows React, and TypeScript opens from either side.

The longest route is 34 levels, through Vue and Nuxt; through React and Next.js it is 33. JavaScript includes the event loop, Next.js starts with Cache Components, and TypeScript with generics. Seven more levels show as "Being written": from-zero openers for HTML, JavaScript, Vue and React, then the box model and cascade, Flexbox, and inferred type predicates.

Key concept: the percentage measures your route, not the whole map. Each tier counts once, so finishing one branch is 100%.

Step 2: a level is an article plus its quiz

Each level is one of the 44 articles plus its quiz: 6 to 9 questions, four options each. The article's badge says where it sits ("Level 1 of 4 in HTML"). Pass the quiz at 70% to clear the level. Your best score counts, retakes are unlimited, and each cleared level leaves a crystal on the map, gold at 100%.

Answers stay hidden until you submit. Then every question is explained: why the right option is right and, if you picked another, why yours was wrong. Two-thirds also link to a source, mostly MDN and the frameworks' own docs.

Levels open one at a time. A locked one is still readable: its drawer offers "Read it anyway", because every article is free.

Key concept: the lock orders the route; it never hides the article. A quiz you passed before its level opened, from the blog, say, still counts.

Step 3: the checkpoint, and how to skip a stage

Every stage ends in a checkpoint: 10 questions drawn at random from that stage's level quizzes, a fresh draw on each attempt, 70% to pass. The last one, Ship it, draws 15. Beat it, and the stage is clear and the next one opens.

A checkpoint is open from the moment its stage is. That's the skip from the top of this article: "Know HTML? Skip it" goes straight there, and a pass clears HTML without a single level. The levels stay open, so you can go back for the crystals; skipping earns none.

Fail it, and the review explains every question; the next attempt is a new draw. One honest caveat: a checkpoint has no questions of its own, so if you have just cleared every level in a stage, you have already met every question it can ask.

Key concept: a checkpoint is a placement check built from the stage's own quizzes. It asks the same of someone who read everything and someone who read nothing.

Step 4: your run, and the finish line

No account is needed to start: a guest's run is saved on that device for a year, in a cookie set when you first start a quiz. Sign up, and your guest attempts move to your account, run and all.

The "Your run" card does the arithmetic. Clear level 1 and you're at 3%: one of five units in HTML (four levels plus the checkpoint), averaged over seven tiers. Beat the HTML checkpoint and you're at 14%.

You finish by beating one checkpoint per tier: seven passes, at least 75 questions. The certificate needs a free account and lives at a public link (/certificates/BP-…) that anyone can open to check it. It states what it certifies: earned by every checkpoint.

Key concept: finishing is defined by checkpoints alone, which is why a skipper and a completionist end up at the same finish line.

Under the hood: progress computed from quiz attempts

If you build learning tools, this is the part worth taking.

Progress is computed, not kept. The map never reads your progress from a table; every load works it out again from the map and your best attempt at each quiz. The real path-progress.ts is covered by 13 Vitest cases. This simplified sketch follows the same rules:

// A simplified sketch of path-progress.ts. The real one also places the "You"
// marker, follows the branch you started at a fork, and marks perfect scores.
type Stage = {
  slug: string;
  tier: number;              // forks share a tier: Vue and React are both 4
  unlockedBy: string[];      // [] for HTML, ["nuxt", "nextjs"] for TypeScript
  checkpoint: string;        // the checkpoint's quiz id
  levels: (string | null)[]; // level quiz ids in order; null = "Being written"
};
type Attempt = { quiz: string; score: number; maxScore: number };

export function pathProgress(stages: Stage[], attempts: Attempt[]) {
  // 1. Only your best attempt at each quiz counts, wherever you took it.
  const best = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const { quiz, score, maxScore } of attempts) {
    best.set(quiz, Math.max(best.get(quiz) ?? 0, (score / maxScore) * 100));
  }
  const passed = (quiz: string) => (best.get(quiz) ?? 0) >= 70;

  const ordered = [...stages].sort((a, b) => a.tier - b.tier);
  const cleared = new Set<string>();
  const levels = new Map<string, "open" | "locked" | "cleared">();

  for (const stage of ordered) {
    // 2. A stage opens when ANY stage in its unlockedBy is cleared.
    const open = stage.unlockedBy.length === 0 || stage.unlockedBy.some((s) => cleared.has(s));
    // 3. Its checkpoint, and nothing else, clears it.
    if (open && passed(stage.checkpoint)) cleared.add(stage.slug);

    // 4. Levels open one at a time. A "Being written" level is skipped: it blocks nobody.
    let previousPassed = true;
    for (const quiz of stage.levels) {
      if (quiz === null) continue;
      const ok = passed(quiz);
      levels.set(quiz, ok ? "cleared" : open && (previousPassed || cleared.has(stage.slug)) ? "open" : "locked");
      previousPassed = ok;
    }
  }

  // 5. Percent along your route: each tier counts once, scored by its best
  //    stage, and a checkpoint is worth one level.
  const tiers = [...new Set(ordered.map((s) => s.tier))];
  const tierScore = (tier: number) =>
    Math.max(...ordered.filter((s) => s.tier === tier).map((s) => {
      if (cleared.has(s.slug)) return 1;
      const written = s.levels.filter((q): q is string => q !== null);
      return written.filter(passed).length / (written.length + 1);
    }));
  const pct = Math.round((tiers.reduce((sum, t) => sum + tierScore(t), 0) / tiers.length) * 100);

  return { cleared, levels, pct };
}

That one decision pays for four features:

  • Guests get a working map with no account, because their quiz attempts were already rows, keyed to a cookie.
  • A quiz passed on the blog before the path existed counts the day the path does.
  • Adding a level needs no backfill.
  • Signing up keeps the run, because the run was only ever the attempts.

A signed-in run also writes its latest percentage to an enrollment record, after the fact; the map never reads it back. The rest follows the same instinct:

  • The map is the same for everyone; you are fetched. The server renders the map without anyone's progress in it, so every visitor gets the same one. Your place on it arrives after hydration, and the default is a newcomer's view, so a first visit never shows padlocks flicking open.
  • Looking costs nothing. The progress endpoint never sets a cookie. The anonymous ID is only set when there is something to save, like a quiz attempt, so a crawler that only looks never gets one.
  • Forks are data. Each stage lists the stages that open it (unlockedBy), and the map draws one road per entry: the line, the fork and the join, from one rule.
  • Checkpoints are assembled, not written. Each release builds a stage's checkpoint from its level quizzes. They issue no certificate of their own; the path certificate is the proof.
  • The catalogue is code. A level whose article isn't written yet shows as "Being written" and blocks nobody. Publishing that article and its quiz under the planned slug is all the map needs; the next release picks it up.

When not to use it

Here's when this path is the wrong tool, and what to use instead.

  • You're starting from zero today. The from-zero openers aren't written yet, and the first live level, the native <dialog>, assumes you've built a modal before. Start with the MDN Curriculum, free and beginner-level, or freeCodeCamp for questions after every lesson, and come back for the checkpoints.
  • You learn by building. A quiz checks understanding, not whether you can ship a page. The Odin Project is free and project-based, and Frontend Mentor gives you real designs to build, with feedback on the result.
  • You need a closed-book credential. These quizzes are open-book and unsupervised. freeCodeCamp's v9 certifications end in a closed-book exam and cost nothing.
  • You learn from video. Every level here is text. Scrimba's Frontend Developer path is about 81 hours of interactive screencasts, on a paid plan.
  • You want the whole map of the field. This is one path through 44 articles; roadmap.sh shows everything around it.
  • You work in Angular or Svelte. The forks are Vue and React only.
  • You'll switch devices before signing up. A guest run lives in one browser, and clearing its cookies loses it. Create the free account first.

FAQ

Is this frontend roadmap really free?

Yes. Every article, quiz and checkpoint on the path is free, and so is the account the certificate needs.

Do I need an account to start the frontend roadmap?

No. A guest run is saved on that device for a year. A free account carries it to every device, keeps what you did as a guest, and is required for the certificate.

How long does the frontend developer roadmap take?

The site estimates about 16 hours for one route; the read-time labels alone add up to 324 minutes on the Vue route and 302 on the React one. Skip everything you can, and the floor is seven checkpoints: 75 questions.

Should I learn Vue or React first?

The path doesn't rank them. Both open when you clear JavaScript, and TypeScript opens after either Nuxt or Next.js, so neither branch is a dead end. Pick the one your job, or the job you want, uses; your percentage only counts one branch.

Can I skip HTML and CSS?

Yes, if you can pass their checkpoints, 7 of 10 on each. Beat HTML's and CSS opens; beat CSS's and JavaScript opens. A stage only counts once it is open, so you skip in order.

What happens if I fail a checkpoint?

Nothing is lost. The review explains every question you missed, and you can retake it straight away: each attempt is a new random draw, with no cooldown and no attempt limit, and your best result counts.

Is the frontend developer certificate worth anything?

It records one thing: that the named account passed one checkpoint per stage at 70% or better, open-book, at least 75 questions in all. Anyone can open its public link to check it. It is not a closed-book credential; freeCodeCamp's is the free one built for that. Treat it as a receipt, not a diploma.

Cheat sheet: the path at a glance

The numbers below come from the live map as of 14 October 2026; "live levels" counts written levels only.

Stage Live levels Checkpoint Two example levels
1 · HTML 4 10 questions, 7 to pass Native <dialog>, The inert attribute
2 · CSS 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Specificity with :where(), Viewport units: dvh, svh, lvh
3 · JavaScript 6 10 questions, 7 to pass Closures, The event loop
4 · Vue (or React) 6 10 questions, 7 to pass ref vs reactive, Composables & shared state
4 · React (or Vue) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Re-render vs remount, React Compiler
5 · Nuxt (after Vue) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass useAsyncData keys, Hydration mismatches
5 · Next.js (after React) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Cache Components, proxy.ts
6 · TypeScript 3 10 questions, 7 to pass Generics, satisfies
7 · Ship it 5 15 questions, 11 to pass Core Web Vitals, Web Workers

That's 44 written levels across both forks, 34 on the Vue route and 33 on the React route, plus 7 being written.

The rules in five lines:

level       article + quiz (6–9 questions). Pass at 70%; your best attempt counts.
order       Levels open one at a time. A locked article is still free to read.
checkpoint  10 random questions from the stage (15 for Ship it). 70% clears it.
skip        A checkpoint is open as soon as its stage is. Beat it early to skip.
finish      One checkpoint per tier. Certificate: free account, public link.

Key takeaways

  • A tick you give yourself records what you read, not what you can answer. Compute progress from answers.
  • In Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study, re-reading won at five minutes; testing won at two days and at a week, with no feedback.
  • Skipping is evidence arriving early: pass the check, and the reading was optional.
  • Building a learning tool? Store the attempts and derive everything else.

Back to Sunday night, and the roadmap that only knows what you ticked. Spend the first evening on checkpoints instead of chapters. The stages you pass are done, and the ones you fail hand you every missed question, explained: a better reading list than a column of ticks ever was.

Which checkpoint do you think you could pass without reading anything, and which one would surprise you?

title: 6 Common GBase Database(GBase 8s) oninit Startup Failures and How to Troubleshoot Them
description:
Running oninit -ivy only to see GBase Database(GBase 8s) fail to start? Before reinstalling the database, check the environment variables, configuration files, port availability, directory permissions, shared memory settings, and disk space.

Here are six common causes of GBase Database(GBase 8s) startup failures and how to investigate them on Linux.

1. Cannot Find the onconfig File

Possible cause: ONCONFIG is unset, references the wrong configuration file, or the file is missing.

Check the environment:

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$ONCONFIG"
ls "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/onconfig."*

Verify that ONCONFIG matches the intended configuration file and that the file exists in the expected directory. Correct the environment according to your installation before retrying startup.

2. Cannot Bind to the Database Port

Possible cause: The configured port is already in use or the listener configuration is incorrect.

Check the port:

ss -lntp | grep ':9088'

Replace 9088 with the port configured for your instance.

Identify the process before taking action. Do not terminate unrelated services blindly. If a port conflict exists, resolve it or select an available port and update the relevant server and client configurations consistently.

3. Permission Denied

Possible cause: The database operating system account cannot access required configuration, storage, or diagnostic directories.

Inspect directory ownership and permissions:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase_data

Check the relevant parent directories and files as well. Confirm that the database service account has the permissions required by your installation.

Avoid applying recursive ownership or permission changes to an entire directory tree without understanding its contents. Incorrect changes can introduce additional security and operational problems.

4. Not Enough Shared Memory

Possible cause: Available system resources or shared memory configuration do not meet the instance requirements.

Start by inspecting the system setting:

cat /proc/sys/kernel/shmmax
free -h

Review the actual startup error and compare the current system configuration with the requirements for your GBase Database(GBase 8s) version and workload.

Do not apply arbitrary shared memory values from online examples. The appropriate settings depend on the operating system, database configuration, and available resources.

5. No Space Left on Device

Possible cause: A filesystem used for database storage, temporary files, or diagnostic logs has run out of space.

Check available capacity:

df -h
df -i

Check both disk space and inode availability. Review the relevant storage locations and database logs to identify the affected filesystem.

Free space only after confirming which files can safely be removed. Never delete database storage files or logs blindly to make the startup error disappear.

6. sqlhosts Configuration Problems

Possible cause: The connection configuration file is missing, unreadable, or contains an incorrect server entry.

Check the configured path and contents:

echo "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"
cat "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"

Verify that the file exists, the database account can access it, and the server name, protocol, hostname, and port match the intended connection configuration.

A sqlhosts problem may primarily affect client connectivity rather than instance startup, so use the exact error message to determine whether it is relevant to the current failure.

Quick oninit Diagnostic Script

This basic script checks several common environment and system conditions:

#!/bin/bash

echo "=== GBase Database(GBase 8s) Startup Diagnostics ==="

echo
echo "1. Environment"
echo "GBASEDBTDIR=${GBASEDBTDIR:-unset}"
echo "ONCONFIG=${ONCONFIG:-unset}"
echo "GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS=${GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS:-unset}"

echo
echo "2. Configuration file"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTDIR:-}" &&
      -n "${ONCONFIG:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/$ONCONFIG" ]]; then
    echo "onconfig file found and readable"
else
    echo "Check ONCONFIG and the configuration path"
fi

echo
echo "3. sqlhosts file"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS" ]]; then
    echo "sqlhosts file found and readable"
else
    echo "Check sqlhosts path and permissions"
fi

echo
echo "4. Disk space"
df -h

echo
echo "5. Inode availability"
df -i

echo
echo "6. Shared memory setting"
cat /proc/sys/kernel/shmmax 2>/dev/null ||
    echo "Unable to read shmmax"

echo
echo "7. Recent startup logs"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTDIR:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log" ]]; then
    tail -30 "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log"
else
    echo "Check the diagnostic log location for your installation"
fi

Save the script as check_oninit.sh and run it in the appropriate database environment. The diagnostic log location may differ depending on your installation.

This script identifies potential configuration issues; it does not replace reviewing the actual oninit error messages.

Final Thoughts

Most GBase Database(GBase 8s) startup investigations should begin with the exact error message and the database diagnostic logs. Check the environment and configuration first, then investigate ports, permissions, system resources, and storage.

The key takeaway: Avoid changing multiple settings at once. Identify the failing component, make one controlled change, and verify the result before proceeding.

A systematic troubleshooting process makes GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation and Linux database administration easier to maintain.

title: Think in Strategies, Act with Tools: Traceable Agentic Optimization for Combinatorial Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.14736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) directly leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate candidate solutions through natural-language prompting. However, OPRO's optimization process is difficult to track, which prevents LLMs from capturing useful information accumulated over previous iterations, thereby limiting solution quality. To address this limitation, we propose a Tool-Augmented Strategic Agent (TASA) which summarizes and exploits trajectory to improve solution quality. Specifically, TASA plans the strategy for each step based on the optimization trajectory, which decomposes the optimization process into traceable strategy selections. Moreover, we leverage LLM to construct problem-specific tools and introduce a strategy-guided adaptive tool planner, which efficiently utilizes the information of trajectory to update solutions. We establish local convergence under persistent exploration and evaluate the complete framework under a shared candidate-evaluation budget. The results support its solution quality and the traceability of strategy-guided search.

title: IR-PRM+ with Previous-Utility Prediction: Constant Regret and Best-Iterate Convergence
description:
arXiv:2610.19016v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Regret matching (and its variants) and counterfactual regret minimization are central algorithms in practice for normal-form and extensive-form game solving. Yet these have historically lacked the stronger theoretical convergence guarantees available to optimistic and extra-gradient methods. Recent work introduced IREG-PRM+, a regret matching variant which does have strong theoretical convergence guarantees. However, it relies on a simultaneous, extra-gradient update. IREG-PRM+ is an instance of the more general IR-PRM framework, where empirically optimistic and alternating updates often have better performance. However, the prior extra-gradient analysis does not extend to these cases. We introduce a new approach that covers both settings. For simultaneous and alternating IR-PRM+ in finite two-player zero-sum matrix games, previous-utility prediction recovers the constant-regret and convergence-rate guarantees previously obtained with extra-gradient prediction: external regret bounded independently of T, an O(T^{-1}) average duality gap, and an O(T^{-1/2}) best-current-iterate gap. Moreover, the current duality gap vanishes and the current profile converges to the Nash equilibrium set. The key step bounds the component of consecutive strategy movement not controlled by the existing IR-PRM+ regret inequality using the relative growth of the nondecreasing regret-vector norm rho_t. Coupling this bound across the two players yields recurrences whose effective coefficient scales as 1/(rho_t^X rho_t^Y), preventing unbounded norm growth. We extend the analysis to finitely many simplex learners under a weighted Minty condition and, through the corresponding CFR variant IR-PCFR+, recover analogous guarantees for finite two-player zero-sum perfect-recall extensive-form games under the same full-reach condition as prior work.

title: GDBA-Net: A Gated Dual-Branch Adaptation of SAM2 for Robust Cross-Domain Nuclei Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.20073v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate nuclei segmentation underpins quantitative computational pathology, yet remains challenging due to morphological variability, weak boundaries, nuclear crowding, and pronounced domain shifts arising from differences in tissue preparation, staining, and acquisition. While deep learning and recent foundation models have improved segmentation performance under matched distributions with the original training data, their generalization across heterogeneous histopathology domains remains limited. We introduce GDBA-Net, a parameter-efficient nuclei segmentation framework built around the proposed Gated Dual-Branch Adapter (GDBA). GDBA-Net adapts a frozen SAM2 encoder by integrating pretrained semantic representations with explicit frequency-derived structural priors. The complementary representations are independently transformed through Grid MLP branches and dynamically integrated using sample-adaptive channel-wise gating, selectively emphasizing structural cues relevant to nuclear delineation. Despite using only 4.3 million trainable parameters, GDBA-Net achieves state-of-the-art in-dataset performance and consistently superior cross-dataset generalization across six diverse nuclei segmentation benchmarks under fully supervised, cross-dataset, and five-shot adaptation protocols, outperforming competing CNN-, transformer-, and foundation model based methods. Comprehensive ablations confirm that these gains arise from the coordinated design of semantic-frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity. By uniting transferable semantic representations with explicit structural priors, GDBA-Net provides a robust, annotation-efficient solution to domain variability in nuclei segmentation. https://github.com/biplabpoudel25/GDBA_Net

title: Contrastive uncertainty learning for robust multi-structure segmentation in lower-pelvic MR
description:
arXiv:2610.20251v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Boundary delineation of anatomical structures in prostate MRI is often compromised by regional ambiguity. Automated segmentation methods relying on global overlap loss functions tend to be insensitive to surface deviations, leading to significant errors in ambiguous regions. Most existing uncertainty-aware methods treat uncertainty as a post-hoc quality indicator or prediction filter. We propose Contrastive Uncertainty Learning (CUL), a supervised framework that uses predictive uncertainty to directly guide representation learning. Using Monte Carlo Dropout, CUL identifies voxel-wise uncertainty and structures the embedding geometry accordingly: low-uncertainty, correctly predicted features form stable voxels while high-uncertainty or misclassified features are actively repelled, preventing feature collapse at difficult boundaries. We evaluate CUL on a 589-scan 3D prostate MRI multi-structure segmentation task (8 anatomical structures) using a ViT with UperNet decoder architecture. Average Dice ($83.38\%$) remains comparable to the baseline ($83.35\%$), while surface distance decreases significantly ($p<0.001$) across 6 of 8 anatomical structures. A hard-case analysis reveals a $22{\times}$ asymmetry between significantly improved and degraded cases ($18.8\%$ vs $0.9\%$). Ablation studies show that removing uncertainty-guided sample selection eliminates improvements for the transition zone, while replacing the contrastive objective with a boundary loss additionally removes bladder improvements, demonstrating that both uncertainty-guided sampling and the contrastive objective are essential for the observed gains. These findings demonstrate that the proposed uncertainty-guided representation learning is a useful mechanism for reducing the risk of extreme errors in safety-critical medical segmentation
