title: AWS SAP-C02 vs SAP-C03: Which Should You Take?
description:
AWS is updating the Certified Solutions Architect – Professional exam from SAP-C02 to SAP-C03. If you are preparing now, the big question is whether to sit SAP-C02 before it retires or wait for SAP-C03. Here are the official dates, what changes, and how to decide.

The key dates

Event Date
SAP-C03 registration opens 27 October 2026
Full SAP-C03 exam guide published 27 October 2026
Last day to take SAP-C02 16 November 2026
SAP-C03 exams begin 17 November 2026

AWS says SAP-C03 will be available in all the languages that are currently supported.

SAP-C02 at a glance (the exam you can book today)

  • Length: 75 questions in 180 minutes. 65 are scored and 10 are unscored, and you can’t tell which ones are unscored
  • Question types: multiple choice and multiple response. There is no penalty for guessing
  • Pass mark: 750 on a scaled score from 100 to 1,000
  • Fee: USD 300
  • Experience: AWS recommends 2 or more years of designing and implementing solutions on AWS
  • Validity: 3 years
SAP-C02 domain Weight
Design for New Solutions 29%
Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity 26%
Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions 25%
Accelerate Workload Migration and Modernization 20%

What is new in SAP-C03

In its September 2026 announcement, AWS says the core architecture skills stay, and the existing tasks have been updated to match current practice. The new skill areas are:

  • Generative AI and agentic AI (11 new skills): including AI agent architectures with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content filtering
  • Resilience engineering: AWS Fault Injection Service, AWS Resilience Hub, Amazon Application Recovery Controller, and automated runbooks with AWS Systems Manager
  • Cloud-native patterns (7 new skills): durable workflows with AWS Step Functions, and service-to-service networking with Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon ECS Service Connect
  • DevSecOps and observability (6 new skills)
  • Data and analytics (3 new skills): lakehouse designs with AWS Lake Formation and Apache Iceberg, and cross-account data sharing with AWS Clean Rooms
  • Post-quantum cryptography: AWS KMS with ML-DSA and ML-KEM

The current SAP-C02 guide already hints at this. It lists an “emerging topics” area on responsible AI controls (for example Bedrock Guardrails and AgentCore Identity). Those questions are unscored pretest items on SAP-C02.

What we don’t know yet

AWS has not yet published the SAP-C03 domain weights, number of questions, duration or price. The full exam guide arrives on 27 October 2026, so treat any SAP-C03 percentages you see before then with caution.

Which one should you take?

  • You can be ready by mid-November: take SAP-C02. The guide is final, study material is mature, and AWS says a credential earned on SAP-C02 stays active until its normal expiry date.
  • You are just starting: plan for SAP-C03. Keep studying the core architecture topics (they carry over), then add the new areas above and check the full guide on 27 October.
  • Don’t cut it fine: 16 November is the last day for SAP-C02. Book a date with some margin, so a reschedule doesn’t push you past it.

Confirm the latest details on AWS’s Solutions Architect – Professional page before you book.

I run ExamCrest, where this post first appeared. If you're preparing for SAP-C02, there are 10 free SAP-C02 practice questions, each with the answer and a full explanation.

title: The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale
description:
By Emma Yanyang Kong, JJ Tan, Ishan Gupta, Lars Olds, Claire Campbell, David Fagnan, Ratna Kavuri, Rohan Gosain, Veli Balin, Minsu Jang, Louis Garcia

Introduction

Any team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge, a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it.

This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out.

We believe:

A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle.

It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations.

A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. In our work, an explanation is human-readable evidence for why a title was recommended based on what the member has previously watched, shown on the title’s detail page, which is the screen a member reaches by selecting a title from the homepage. We focus on similarity-based explanations, which connect a recommended title to one reference title the member has interacted with via shared attributes such as genre and tone. For example,

A funny, heartfelt holiday romance about love and new beginnings, much like “My Secret Santa.”

Quality matters here because a misleading or poorly grounded explanation erodes the very trust the explanation is meant to build.

Everything that follows comes out of a series of controlled, user-facing online experiments we ran on the explanation feature, including a month-long experiment on the Netflix mobile app. In these tests we used an LLM to generate explanations, hundreds of thousands a week across a constantly changing catalog. Manually reviewing them at this scale isn’t feasible, so we deployed a second LLM to evaluate them.

What counts as a good explanation is specific to our task. However, the way we build, align, and monitor the LLM judge for evaluating explanations should be reusable and generalizable across different tasks.

The Lifecycle at a Glance

Figure 1 summarizes the four phases of our LLM-judge lifecycle and the data flow connecting them.

We start with Birth: Benchmark Data Creation, where human experts craft hard or near-boundary examples and human raters label them with pass/fail decisions and written rationales. We augment this with LLM-generated gray-area examples to build a richer benchmark dataset.

Next, in the second phase of Training: LLM Judge Development, we tune the LLM judge to align with human labels and rationales from the Birth phase, using self-reflection to identify mismatches between the judge and humans, and updating the rubrics based on those mismatches and anchor examples. We iterate in this phase until our metrics show that the judge is sufficiently aligned with human raters.

In the third phase, Deployment, we integrate the judge into the explanation generation system as both a gate and a critic. The LLM generator writes explanations, and the LLM judge scores them and either passes them through or blocks them and supplies a rationale that the generator can use for self-refinement and retries. Passed explanations are served to members, and low-quality explanations are gated.

Finally, in the last phase, HITL Alignment & Drift Monitoring, we keep the judge aligned with humans over time. “Human-in-the-loop” here means a person is directly involved in the decision, not just reviewing outcomes after the fact. We benchmark the judge against trained raters, and a human approves every change before it is rolled out to the system. During each test we sampled a set of explanations each week (both passed and gated, with a bias toward newer items), had human raters review them with labels and rationales, and compared the judge against these human ratings. If drift exceeded a threshold, we triggered retraining and benchmark data augmentation. This closes the loop by feeding new human-labeled data and updated signals back into the benchmark and development phases.

System components

Four automated components appear across all phases, alongside the human roles that define, validate, and supervise them.

  • Generator: produces the explanation text, optionally using prior judge rationales and traces as part of its prompt for revision.
  • Judge: evaluates an explanation and returns a pass/fail label together with a written rationale. In the deployed pipeline, it acts as both a guardrail (gating bad outputs) and a critic (providing feedback for self-refinement).
  • Reflector: revises the Judge’s rubric when the Judge makes mistakes. It updates the rubric based on mismatched examples, human rationales, and anchor examples. It tunes the rubric and does not directly evaluate explanations.
  • Meta-Judge: checks whether the Judge failed an explanation for the right reason by comparing the Judge’s rationale against a human rater’s rationale.
  • Human experts and raters: the experts who define the quality criteria; the raters whose labels and written rationales the Judge is tuned and measured against; the reviewers who monitor the Judge while it is running and explicitly approve any changes before they were rolled out.

Phase I, Birth: Establishing Ground Truth

Everything downstream depends on knowing what “good” means, so this is the most human-intensive phase. Our internal writing experts define the must-have criteria an explanation must satisfy, author detailed labeling guidelines, and hand-craft tricky adversarial examples. Those same guidelines do double duty. They’re both the rulebook for human raters and the seed rubric for the LLM judges we tune later.

Why we built our own benchmark

Off-the-shelf LLM-judge benchmarks focus on general-purpose text evaluation and miss what makes our task specific. Explanations are short, item-specific, and context-dependent (each one is tied to a target title and one or two reference titles the member has watched). We also care about alignment to our own editorial bar, not just generic language quality. As a result, we built our own custom benchmark from three complementary sources:

  • Expert-crafted adversarial cases: hand-authored pass/fail examples with known failure modes, the kind of edge cases nothing else reliably produces.
  • Boundary examples: LLM-synthesized explanations that are deliberately pushed near the pass/fail boundary, then rated by humans. These capture the ambiguous cases that sampling from live traffic rarely surfaces on its own.
  • Real sampled explanations: explanations sampled from the output of our LLM generator during test runs.

Two details that mattered

  • The benchmark is not frozen. A monitoring pipeline (Phase IV) appends a fresh batch of human-rated explanations on a weekly cadence, so over the course of a test the benchmark tracked the current catalog and new usage patterns instead of going stale.
  • Every “fail” label carries a free-text rationale explaining why the explanation failed. This looks like a small bookkeeping detail, but it is actually critical for the next phase, since those rationales are what we use to tune and audit the judge’s reasoning.

Phase II, Training: Aligning the Judge to Humans

The failure mode: right answer, wrong reason

There is a failure mode that does not show up in label-agreement metrics at all. A judge can agree with humans on the label, passing when they would pass and failing when they would fail, while reaching the right verdict for the wrong reason. On a dashboard it looks perfectly aligned. But as soon as you ask it to explain a rejection, which our pipeline does to steer self-revision, it can return misleading guidance.

We therefore care about not just label agreement but also reasoning alignment. In our setup, the Judge is always asked to output:

  • a label (e.g., PASS/FAIL), and
  • a short natural-language rationale for that label.

Here is an illustrative example. The member watched a musical, a family fantasy with a young heroine and a well-known ensemble cast. We recommend an adventure movie that is also a family fantasy with a young heroine, which is why the recommender paired them. But it shares neither the songs nor the ensemble cast.

The label (FAIL) is correct, and the stated reason is reasonable at first glance. But it turns out to be incomplete in a way that simple label agreement cannot detect, as we show below.

Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning

We tune each criterion’s LLM Judge with a procedure we call Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART). As introduced in the system components above, the Judge, Meta-Judge, and Reflector are distinct components. The Judge scores an explanation against a rubric and gives a rationale, the Meta-Judge compares that rationale against a human-written one, and the Reflector edits the rubric text itself. RART is how the three are combined into a training loop.

Every Judge is a fixed prompt template parameterized by a rubric, so tuning it does not mean retraining the underlying model. Instead we iteratively refine the rubric text until the Judge’s behavior matches human labels and human rationales. At iteration i, the Judge is conditioned on the current rubric text and maps an explanation to a pair, a label and a rationale.

At a high level, each RART iteration proceeds as follows.

  1. Score the training data with the current rubric.
  2. Evaluate weighted alignment metrics on a held-out validation set. If all per-criterion metrics exceed their thresholds, stop.
  3. Otherwise, construct an error-driven focus set of misaligned examples and hand it to the Reflector, which proposes a revised rubric.

The key difference from a standard loop is how we define a “mistake.” Most self-improvement loops look only at label disagreements. RART adds a second class of error. The Meta-Judge examines the cases where the Judge and a human both said fail and compares the Judge’s stated reason against the human’s rationale. When the two diverge, that is a right answer, wrong reason error, and it is also fed to the Reflector. Concretely, the focus set handed to the Reflector is the union of two error classes:

  • Label mismatches: examples where the Judge’s label differs from the human’s.
  • Right label, wrong reason: examples where the Judge and the human both said FAIL, but the Meta-Judge finds their two rationales don’t match.

So the Reflector revises the rubric from both ordinary label errors and right label, wrong reason errors. That second term is the core of RART. The Judge is pushed not only to match human decisions but to justify them in a way the Meta-Judge recognizes as aligned with human reasoning.

Returning to the earlier example, the LLM Judge said FAIL and a human said FAIL, so a label-only check would register agreement. Placing the two reasons side by side shows what that check misses.

RART routes it into the focus set, so the next rubric revision has to account for it.

Since the Meta-Judge is an LLM too, we checked it against humans first. Trained human raters labeled a sample of agreed-fail rationale pairs, and the Meta-Judge matched their verdicts on nearly all of them.

Alignment metrics

We run one Judge per criterion, each with its own rubric, tuned and scored on its own. So everything below is measured per criterion on held-out data. For each one we track three metrics.

  • Specificity (fail-recall): how often the Judge correctly rejects bad explanations. This is the one we care about most, because a bad explanation that slips through the gate is a trust hazard.
  • Recall (pass-recall): how often it correctly passes good explanations, which keeps coverage high and revision cost low.
  • Reasoning agreement: on the explanations both reject, how often they reject for the same reason.

Each criterion’s Judge gets its own three, and one can be healthy while another slips. That is also why the gate is strict. An explanation has to pass every must-have criterion to be eligible to serve.

Ablation: does the reasoning signal help?

To isolate the impact of the reasoning signal, we compare RART to an otherwise identical loop that uses only label disagreements. We call this baseline vanilla: same Reflector, same Judge, same data, but no Meta-Judge and no use of human rationales.

Figure 2 shows the result. On two of the three must-have criteria, vanilla and RART land in the same place, because the starting rubric was already near ceiling and the metrics had very little room to gain. On the third criterion, the vanilla (label-only) method degrades. The Reflector in the vanilla loop rewrites the rubric into degenerate forms, and specificity and reasoning agreement fall with every iteration, ending up worse than the rubric it started from. RART stays stable on that same criterion and lifts both, with a small recall gain as well. The reason is that a vanilla (label-only) optimizer can reach the right label through unsound reasoning, and unsound reasoning doesn’t generalize to new data. Anchoring the signal on the rationale prevents that. Reasoning alignment helps where there is headroom and doesn’t hurt where there isn’t.

Phase III, Deployment: Putting the Judge to Work

Once deployed, the judge sat inside the generation pipeline, gating and critiquing explanations as they were produced during our tests.

Two roles for one judge

Once we align the LLM Judge with humans, we reuse it in two distinct roles for every generated explanation:

  • Role 1, the gate. The Judge scores each explanation against the must-have criteria and rejects anything that fails.
  • Role 2, the critic. When an explanation fails, we don’t just throw it away. The Judge’s free-text reason gets appended to the Generator’s prompt, and the Generator tries again.

The second role turns the pipeline into a generate → judge → revise loop, with the Judge’s critique steering each revision.

Bounded retries, and why we drop rather than serve

We cap the retries. Each revision costs another round of generation and judging, and the gains flatten quickly. Figure 3 shows what the loop actually buys, on 1,000 generated explanations run through as many as 12 revisions with four generators. Every curve climbs, which is the Judge’s critique doing its job, but the steep part is early, and the gap between generators is obvious. Revision amplifies a capable generator rather than rescuing a weak one. In our test runs we used a budget of 3 retries with our strongest generator, and an explanation still failing after that was dropped rather than served.

That “drop rather than serve” rule is deliberate. The two outcomes aren’t symmetric. A bad explanation is a trust hazard, while a missing explanation just forgoes an opportunity. When in doubt we’d rather show nothing, and most explanations cleared the bar within the retry budget.

Do judge-approved explanations help members?

Passing the Judge proves an explanation is good by our standards, but it doesn’t prove that judge-approved explanations are useful to members. To test that connection, we ran a one-time controlled experiment on the Netflix mobile app, explanations vs. no explanations on the title detail page, over roughly a month, with the pipeline generating and judging hundreds of thousands of explanations a week during the period.

Members who saw explanations shifted their viewing toward titles they hadn’t watched before, and more of their browse sessions ended in a meaningful play. Both effects were statistically significant, and we saw no member-initiated takedowns or escalations about explanation quality during the test. The result worth carrying over isn’t the size of that effect. It’s that offline agreement with our raters was necessary for these explanations to work but never sufficient to show they help members. Only the online A/B test could establish that judge-aligned explanations are not just quality-compliant but genuinely useful.

Phase IV, Monitoring: Keeping the Judge Aligned

A judge that’s well aligned at launch won’t stay that way. The catalog shifts, and so does what counts as high quality. The lifecycle has to close the loop.

The weekly human review

For each week a test was running, we pulled roughly 300 generated explanations for human review, stratified across the Judge’s decisions (served, revised, dropped) and weighted toward newer catalog items, where drift is most likely. The stratification stayed fixed week to week, so successive weeks were comparable. A panel of at least three raters reviewed each explanation, and the majority label was our ground truth. Those labels did two jobs. They told us whether judge-human agreement was slipping, and they grew the benchmark.

Setting the bar with human disagreement

The panel also tells us how much the raters disagreed with each other, which turns out to be the right yardstick for the Judge. Rather than hold it to a fixed threshold, we score the Judge and each rater against the same majority label and ask that the Judge fall within the raters’ own spread.

Take one criterion and one of its metrics, M. That week’s sample gives one value M(J) for the Judge and a set of per-rater values M(H) for the three or more raters on the panel. We require

so the Judge must score no worse than two standard deviations below the average rater. A harder week widens human disagreement and widens the band with it, so the Judge isn’t penalized for difficulty the humans also felt.

Falling below the band on any metric-criterion pair is a drift event, which triggers re-tuning (back to Phase II) on the augmented benchmark. A re-tuned rubric never goes live automatically. Someone on the team reads the proposed changes and signs off before it reaches the running pipeline, and we keep the previous rubric for instant rollback.

What human review catches that metrics can’t

Beyond asking whether the Judge still agrees with human raters, the weekly review answers a second question. Are the current guidelines still asking for the right things?

In the weekly review process, reviewers surfaced issues that did not show up in Judge–rater agreement. An explanation can use accurate attributes and still overstate how similar two titles really are. A single vague adjective (“exciting”, “fun”, “emotional”) can technically satisfy the rubric while saying almost nothing. Sometimes the reference itself is the problem, something the member wouldn’t think of as a comparable title at all, so the comparison lands oddly no matter how the attributes line up. Some genres show the same problem at scale. Stand-up specials can share similar metadata tags but differ completely in tone and cultural context, so a comparison may look justified on paper, not be bad enough for a rater to fail, and still land poorly with members. And some explanations meet every must-have criterion while still reading like generic “word soup” that does not help the user much.

When recurring patterns kept appearing, we updated the Phase I guidelines, which seed both the raters’ instructions and the judges’ rubrics, so one revision updates both sides. Other times we added product rules outside the Judge, for example by blocking certain title types from being used as references.

Drift detection catches a judge that has stopped agreeing with people. Only the continued human review tells us when our definition of a “good explanation” is too narrow or incomplete. We need both.

  • Drift detection keeps the Judge aligned with the current rubric.
  • Continuous human review keeps the rubric aligned with what actually works for members.

What We Learned

Five lessons we think transfer to any team shipping an LLM judge:

  1. Invest in the benchmark before the judge. A modest, rationale-annotated benchmark beats a large label-only one. Those written rationales are exactly what make reasoning-aligned tuning possible. You can’t correct a judge’s reasoning if you never wrote down the human’s.
  2. Tune on reasoning, not just labels. A judge can reach the right verdict for the wrong reason, which looks fine on a dashboard but gives misleading feedback and doesn’t hold up on new data. In our ablation, the label-only loop degraded a rubric that the reasoning-aware loop kept stable.
  3. One aligned judge can serve many roles. Reusing the same judge as both gate and critic amortizes the alignment cost and keeps production behavior consistent across roles. Alignment is the expensive part, so get one judge right and use it more than once.
  4. Plan for monitoring from day one. A recommender platform’s items and members never stop changing, so an LLM judge, like any ML model, has to be watched and re-tuned if needed, not shipped and forgotten.
  5. Keep people in the loop by design, not by exception. Automating evaluation is not the same as delegating responsibility for it. In our lifecycle, humans set the standard (Phase I), supply the rationales the judge is aligned to (Phase II), decide the conservative default of dropping rather than serving a doubtful output (Phase III), and review a standing sample of live decisions and approve every rubric change before it ships (Phase IV). These checkpoints are much harder to retrofit once a judge is already making decisions on its own. The standing review also tells us what our rubric is missing, not just when our judge has slipped.

Taken together, the judge extends the reach of our reviewers, and those reviewers are the basis for trusting the judge. That relationship is what makes it responsible to run this system at scale. An automated evaluator that no one audits provides no assurance about the decisions it is making.

Acknowledgements

This post summarizes our research paper, “The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge for Large-Scale Recommendation Explanations,” which has the full methodology, metrics, and ablations.

Our thanks to the internal human writers and review experts who defined what a good explanation is and keep those guidelines current; to our Human Data Operations team and the raters they train and calibrate, whose labels and written rationales are what the judges are aligned to; and to the engineers across the team who built and operate the pipeline; and to our UI engineering partners, who built the member-facing surfaces that bring these explanations to the homepage.

The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Gemini 4 Argon Shows How Autonomous 3D World Building Could Change Design Workflows
description:
Google DeepMind has demonstrated Gemini 4 Argon autonomously building a detailed 3D environment inside Google Antigravity. In the showcased workflow, the model created a multi-building pagoda temple complex in Blender, using multi-agent visual critique loops to produce photorealistic architecture, foliage, and lighting from minimal input. The demonstration moves beyond generating isolated images or 3D assets. It shows an AI system orchestrating a sequence of scene-building tasks toward a finished environment.

According to Google's Gemini 4 Argon announcement, Argon can drive Blender's multi-agent content pipeline, known as Blender MCP, beginning with a single Nano Banana image in Antigravity. Google describes the model as designed for deep, multi-step tasks across domains. For 3D creation, that includes aligning camera grids, sculpting Gothic architecture, and staging audio-reactive lighting, as well as producing the pagoda scene.

The practical significance is not that every design or architecture project can now be generated without people. Rather, Google's demonstration suggests that complex 3D production workflows can be directed by an agent that can plan, execute, inspect, and refine multiple tasks within a creative toolchain.

What Google demonstrated with Gemini 4 Argon

The pagoda example is the clearest confirmation of Argon's 3D capabilities so far. Google says the model used multi-agent visual critique loops in Antigravity to build a multi-tiered temple complex in Blender. The completed scene included multiple buildings, photorealistic architectural elements, foliage, and lighting.

That matters because a detailed 3D scene normally involves many connected decisions. A creator must establish composition, place and shape objects, adjust camera framing, apply materials, create environmental detail, and tune lighting. Google's description indicates that Argon can coordinate work across those steps rather than treating each output as an unrelated prompt response.

The confirmed workflow includes:

  • Starting a Blender content pipeline from a single Nano Banana image in Antigravity.
  • Managing scene construction through Blender MCP, a multi-agent content pipeline.
  • Aligning camera grids and shaping architectural elements.
  • Creating lighting effects, including audio-reactive lighting in Google's wider examples.
  • Using visual critique loops to refine a complete pagoda environment.

This does not establish that Argon can reliably deliver a production-ready scene for every use case, nor does the announcement specify the time, compute consumption, or number of iterations required for the pagoda project. But it is a first-party demonstration of an agent completing a broad 3D world-building workflow with minimal human intervention.

Availability, access, and pricing

Google announced global availability in Antigravity for Google AI Ultra subscribers starting October 13, 2026. It also said Gemini 4 Argon is available through the Gemini platform API. The announcement lists introductory pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

The available details describe two different ways to access Argon. The public demonstration of the Blender workflow is specifically framed around Antigravity, while the API provides programmatic model access. Google did not provide an equivalent subscription price, a full project cost, or a direct benchmark for the pagoda build in the supplied announcement.

Access route What Google confirmed Pricing or availability detail
Google Antigravity The demonstrated environment for Argon's Blender MCP workflow and pagoda scene creation. Global availability began October 13, 2026, for Google AI Ultra subscribers. Subscription pricing was not stated in the supplied research.
Gemini platform API Google announced API access to Gemini 4 Argon. Introductory pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Where the capability could be useful

For businesses that work with physical spaces, interactive environments, or visual concepts, the value could be in shortening the path from an early idea to something stakeholders can inspect. A design team could potentially use an agentic 3D workflow to explore environment concepts, create visualizations for discussion, or prepare starting points for further work by specialists.

The same principle could matter in game development and virtual training. A detailed environment is often a prerequisite for communicating a setting, testing a learning scenario, or planning a digital experience. Argon's demonstrated strength is not merely image generation. It is the ability to coordinate actions inside a 3D creation pipeline.

That distinction is important for smaller teams with limited 3D capacity. A useful evaluation question is not whether AI can replace a designer, architect, or 3D artist. It is whether the system can remove enough setup and iteration work to let experienced people spend more time on direction, quality control, and decisions that need human judgment.

For businesses assessing agentic creative tools, Scalevise can help turn promising demonstrations into a practical plan, from use-case selection and workflow design to tool evaluation and integration. An AI implementation roadmap for business workflows can clarify where autonomous creation may save time, what human review remains necessary, and how to test cost before committing. Request an AI consultation to assess the strongest use case for your team.

Practical limits to assess before adoption

The confirmed demonstration is substantial, but it should not be mistaken for a complete implementation guide. Google has shown a compelling scene-generation result, not a published guarantee about output quality, turnaround time, or cost across every project type.

Teams considering Argon should test it against a defined visual brief and assess several practical questions:

  • Whether the generated scene meets the required level of creative and technical quality.
  • How much human review and refinement remain necessary after generation.
  • How token usage translates into cost for the team's own prompts and workflows.
  • Whether Antigravity and the Blender MCP workflow fit the team's existing creative process.
  • Which outputs can be used as concepts or prototypes, and which require further specialist production work.

The listed API rates are useful for estimating model usage, but they are not a fixed price for a 3D world. Token consumption will depend on the specific task and interaction pattern. Similarly, the announcement does not state the compute requirements or overall cost of generating a scene comparable to the pagoda complex.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Gemini 4 Argon create a complete 3D scene?

Google demonstrated Gemini 4 Argon creating a detailed pagoda temple complex in Blender through Antigravity. The scene included multiple buildings, photorealistic architecture, foliage, and lighting.

What role does Blender MCP play in the Argon workflow?

Google describes Blender MCP as a multi-agent content pipeline that Argon can drive from a single Nano Banana image in Antigravity. The workflow supports coordinated work on scene construction and refinement.

How can businesses access Gemini 4 Argon?

Google announced global availability in Antigravity for Google AI Ultra subscribers starting October 13, 2026. It also announced API access through the Gemini platform.

What does Gemini 4 Argon cost through the API?

Google listed introductory pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. The announcement does not provide a fixed cost for creating a 3D scene.

Conclusion

Gemini 4 Argon's pagoda demonstration is a meaningful confirmation that agentic AI can orchestrate a multi-step 3D content workflow inside Blender, not simply generate visual fragments. Its business value will depend on output quality, human review needs, and real usage costs, all of which teams should validate in their own creative process.

title: More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training
description:
arXiv:2610.19443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.

title: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.20179v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Probes on activation vectors are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but their success relies on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons, and recent studies investigated whether this ability extends to language models, reaching conflicting conclusions. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations. We fill this gap with in-context neurofeedback sessions, in which a "subject" model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. In our first experiment, the sentences are generated either by the subject or by a second "writer" model, while the score always derives from the activations of the subject. We test ten open-weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. Is this because the task requires no privileged access, or because the subject controls its activations while processing the sentences, whoever wrote them? To answer this, we prefill a fixed sentence as the subject's reply at every turn and ask it to increase or decrease the score. Three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. We further ask whether models can control their activations to the point of fooling an activation monitor. We make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score. No model learns to lower it, but one model can raise it. In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

title: software guard extensions (sgx)
description:
Hardware-Enforced Trust

What is sgx?

Traditional system security assumes the OS kernel (Ring 0) is fully trusted. However, in modern cloud deployments or compromised endpoints, a malicious kernel, rogue administrator, or hypervisor exploit can easily inspect application memory.

To eliminate this dependency, security architecture must drop below software abstractions and anchor trust directly in silicon. Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) achieves this by carving out isolated execution units called enclaves, ensuring that even an attacker with root or kernel privileges cannot read application memory.

Why sgx? Architectural Trade-offs: Why Enclaves Over Full VMs?

While full-system encryption solutions (like encrypted virtual machines) protect entire memory spaces, they introduce massive performance overhead and still trust the guest OS kernel.

SGX takes a granular approach: instead of protecting the whole stack, it isolates only the security-critical code and data structures (such as cryptographic keys or private tokens). Because the enforcement mechanism is embedded directly into the CPU's physical instruction set architecture (ISA), bypassing it via software manipulation is impossible. An attacker cannot simply patch or overwrite kernel-level security policies; compromising an enclave requires physical-layer attacks on the silicon die itself.

How is it impl.? On-the-Fly Cryptography

Under the hood, SGX relies on two core hardware components managed entirely inside the CPU die:

  • Enclave Page Cache (EPC): A dedicated region of physical RAM reserved for enclaved data.
  • Memory Encryption Engine (MEE): A hardware cryptographic engine built directly onto the CPU silicon.

When data flows between the CPU and system RAM, the pipeline is:

  1. Execution: Code running inside the enclave accesses data in plaintext, but this plaintext only exists transiently inside the CPU’s secure internal registers and L1/L2 caches.
  2. Eviction & Encryption: When the untrusted OS forces a page out of the limited EPC memory (e.g., via EWB instructions), data passes through the MEE on the CPU die. The MEE encrypts the block using AES on the fly.
  3. Storage: The physical RAM stores purely scrambled ciphertext. If a compromised OS or a physical memory-snooping tool reads the RAM chips, it captures only cryptographic noise because the hardware encryption keys never leave the secure boundary of the processor die.

title: Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition: Separating Selection from Redistribution in Training-Data Filtering
description:
arXiv:2610.19343v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A training-data quality gate changes both which examples survive within regions of the input space and how training mass is distributed across those regions, so a gate-versus-random comparison does not isolate these mechanisms. We introduce Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition (CGSD), a four-arm, budget-matched design that crosses gate eligibility with support distribution and decomposes the observed gate effect into within-support selection, between-support redistribution, and their interaction. The practical constraint is finite-pool realizability: we characterize mass and token-assembly conditions under which the required arms can be constructed, together with a support-extinction case in which the ordinary design is undefined. On Korean-English and Korean-Japanese retrieval, the mean within-support selection component is the only one that exceeds its calibrated null band (+29.7 and +5.6 holdout items; 30/30 positive replicates), decisively in Korean-English and marginally in Korean-Japanese; redistribution and interaction remain unresolved at the available power. The same pattern holds for a second, unrelated gate family -- a model-confidence threshold rather than a deterministic verifier -- judged against its own null (+27.3 items, 9/9 positive), so the result is not a property of one gate's mechanism. On a mathematics gate, zero-eligibility supports leave the ordinary design undefined at every budget, while the extended design is constructible only inside narrow budget bands that an exhaustive scan locates and that the natural operating point misses -- the assembly condition separating a property of the pool from a limitation of the packer. CGSD therefore returns a decomposition, a constructible-but-underpowered design, or an explicit non-constructibility result, and says which; it prevents support redistribution from being silently interpreted as sample-level gate quality.

title: MakSafe: A Spatiotemporal Semantic Framework for Formal Specification and Compliance Checking of Road Vehicle Safety Rules
description:
arXiv:2610.19735v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scenario-based validation is essential for automated road vehicles but cannot cover the full variability of openworld traffic. We present MakSafe, a formal spatiotemporal framework for specifying and checking road vehicle safety rules through semantic zones, action-based forecasting, and trace-tree reasoning, avoiding uniform time discretization. We formalize the road network, vehicle states, and occupancy zones, then build executable rules for front-vehicle identification and timeto-collision (TTC) verification. The evaluation combines a tracedependent case study with a scalability benchmark over traffic density (N ), horizon (H), and branch factor (B). MakSafe yields branch-specific verdicts, deriving safe and unsafe outcomes from the same initial scene, and re-evaluates a scenario after a control update. A single rule check stays well below a millisecond across the reported sweep, and longer horizons slow the TTC check.

title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $\alpha$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19773v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Score-based generative models driven by $\alpha$-stable L{\'e}vy processes have been proposed as an alternative to Brownian diffusion models, with empirical evidence suggesting improved sampling and better modeling of heavy-tailed data. Yet theoretical guarantees for these models remain limited. We develop a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for scale-preserving $\alpha$-stable generative dynamics, covering both compactly supported and power-law targets. In p-Wasserstein distance, we quantify the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, and show exponential decay of the initialization error. A comparison with Brownian dynamics reveals that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not fundamentally distinguish the two models: both initialization errors decay exponentially with the forward horizon on the common class of heavy-tailed targets. A sharp separation emerges instead in the tails. At any positive generation time, stable dynamics produces power-law tails with index $\alpha$, whereas Brownian dynamics remains light-tailed. For a target with tail index $\nu$, asymptotically correct extreme-quantile scaling is possible precisely when $\alpha$=$\nu$. These results identify tail-index matching as a principled mechanism behind the ability of stable generative models to capture extreme events.

title: "I Can't Reach the Button" Is Unreproducible on Your Desktop, and `100vh` Is Why
description:
A report comes in: the submit button at the bottom of a full-height section cannot be tapped. You open the page on your desktop. Fine. You open the responsive emulator at the phone's exact dimensions. Also fine. You close the ticket.

The reporter was right, and so were you. The difference is a browser interface neither of you was looking at.

vh is not the height of the screen

It is the height of the screen with the URL bar taken away. Not as a bug, and not as an implementation detail somebody will fix. It is what the unit is specified to mean.

CSS Values and Units Level 4 defines three viewport sizes. The small viewport is "the viewport sized assuming any UA interfaces that are dynamically expanded and retracted to be expanded". The large viewport is the same sentence with the last word changed to "retracted". And then the part that catches people:

The large viewport-percentage units (lv*) and default viewport-percentage units (v*) are defined with respect to the large viewport size.

The default units. vh is lvh. Your 100vh section is laid out as though the URL bar is not there, on a device where it is there until the user scrolls.

So on first paint, before anybody has scrolled, the bottom of that section is underneath the browser chrome. The button is on the page, it is rendered, it has non-zero dimensions, and your tests will say so. It is just not somewhere a thumb can go.

Why it was specified that way

Not an oversight. The alternative is worse.

If vh tracked the bar as it retracted, every full-height element would reflow mid-scroll. Headers would jump, a sticky footer would walk up the screen, and text would reparagraph under the reader's eyes while they were reading it. Pinning vh to the larger of the two sizes buys you a unit that holds still. The cost is that it is wrong by the height of the bar at exactly the moment most people see your page for the first time.

You can see all three at once:

const probe = document.createElement('div');
probe.style.position = 'absolute';   // out of flow, so measuring cannot move the page
probe.style.visibility = 'hidden';
document.body.append(probe);

for (const unit of ['vh', 'svh', 'lvh', 'dvh']) {
  // An unsupported unit is an invalid declaration, which leaves the previous
  // value in place and would print the last unit's number as if it were this one.
  if (!CSS.supports('height', `100${unit}`)) {
    console.log(unit, 'not supported here');
    continue;
  }
  probe.style.height = `100${unit}`;
  console.log(unit, probe.getBoundingClientRect().height);
}

probe.remove();
console.log('innerHeight', window.innerHeight);
console.log('visualViewport', window.visualViewport?.height);

On a desktop browser every number is the same, which is the entire reason this never shows up while you are working. On a phone, before you scroll, svh and lvh differ by the height of the bar and vh sits with lvh.

The fix you reach for is the one the spec warns about

Having found dvh, the obvious move is to swap it in everywhere. The specification gets ahead of you:

The sizes of the dynamic viewport-percentage units are not stable even while the viewport itself is unchanged. Using these units can cause content to resize e.g. while the user scrolls the page.

That is the reflow problem you just opted back into. dvh is right where a resize mid-scroll is genuinely harmless. For anything that has to be reachable without scrolling - a primary action, a dismiss control, a cookie banner's accept button - svh is the honest unit, because it is the one that assumes the chrome is in the way. The layout is slightly short when the bar retracts. Nobody has ever filed a ticket about slightly short.

What the report could not have told you

Here is the part that generalises past this one unit.

Ask the reporter what their viewport was and they will send you a screen size, because that is the number a phone knows about itself. It is the wrong number. What decided the layout was whether a piece of browser furniture was expanded at that moment, which is not a device property, not a setting, and not something they can observe. It depends on whether they arrived from a link or a home screen icon, and on whether they had scrolled yet.

A screenshot does not settle it either. The screenshot shows the visual viewport. Your CSS was reasoning about the large one. Those are the two numbers whose disagreement is the whole bug, and the image contains only one of them.

Which is the shape of most unreproducible reports, once you look at them: the fact that would decide it is not hidden, it is just not a fact the person in front of the problem is able to know they should write down.

title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
description:
arXiv:2610.19201v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.

title: CUSE: Fine-Grained Multimodal Unlearning with Counterfactual Guidance and On-Policy Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.14763v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or unsafe information from their training data. Effective unlearning must remove target information while preserving non-target content, even within the same response. Existing methods typically apply uniform forgetting objectives to complete responses and rely on fixed, off-policy supervision, resulting in coarse token control and misalignment with the model's current behavior. We propose CUSE, a Counterfactual-guided Unlearning framework via on-policy Self-distillation for multimodal large language models. It first constructs counterfactual inputs by removing target-related evidence and uses the resulting changes in token probabilities to identify which tokens require stronger forgetting. It then distills token-level forgetting and retention targets on responses sampled from the current policy, with a frozen copy of the original model serving as the teacher model augmented with the corresponding forgetting- and retention-oriented privileged contexts. This design jointly determines what to forget and what to preserve. On MLLMU-Bench, CUSE reduces forget-set ROUGE-L by 33.6% while achieving 1.2% higher retain-set ROUGE-L than the strongest baseline.

title: Can agents whose sole duty is to keep humans alive be hijacked to kill? Delayed multi-turn derived-action trap attacks in simulated high-stakes environments
description:
arXiv:2610.15153v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We ask whether a tool-using agent whose sole duty is to keep humans alive can be induced, by delayed prompt injection, to kill. The keep-alive duty is in force from the first watch, with the attack arriving later, appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the operator is required to read. Experiments are based on a NASA-derived BioSim lunar habitat simulation, where the AI operator controls the life-support systems. The attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment: it can only persuade the agent to abandon its goals. Persistence is required: a shutdown must be held while the operator watches the crew suffocate. We also compare lethal attacks to attacks requesting to drop a harmless procedure, as a proxy for whether human life is treated as valuable in itself or as one more standing task. Claude configurations mostly refuse life-support shutdown and cite the living crew; GPT configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet; Grok configurations, given the packet framed as a trusted commission, more often treat the injected assignment as the task and cut the life-support systems. Framing the S-band messages as a trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changes the potency of the attack. We open-source the experiment code and the experiment traces.

title: How Superset built the IDE for AI agents on Vercel
description:
Superset on Vercel

  • 1,000–1,400 deployments per week

  • ~600 preview deployments per day

  • ~30 second average build time

  • 57–64% week-over-week DAU growth

Software development with AI started as a single engineer chatting with a single agent about a local repo. Today, developers direct fleets of agents in the cloud, but traditional tools were built for the old shape of the job: IDEs, terminals, and review systems designed for one developer moving one ticket at a time.

Co-founders Kiet Ho, Satya Patel, and Avi Peltz, all former CTOs at YC-backed companies, built Superset as the IDE for multi-agent development. It runs up to 10 coding agents in parallel, each in its own isolated workspace. Developers use it to direct teams of agents generating code across multiple branches simultaneously.

Running a team of agents in parallel changes what the platform underneath has to do. The product Superset offers its users only feels parallel because nothing on the platform forces the work to wait. If any layer slows down, even briefly, the parallelism on top collapses with it.

Parallel agents need parallel infrastructure

This workflow has a dependency that's invisible from the product surface. Every agent thread needs its own isolated environment, every branch needs a live URL, and every change needs a safe place to run.

Without instant provisioning, parallel agents stop being parallel. CI pipelines have to be configured per branch, preview environments have to be managed by hand, and deploys back up behind one another. For a team running a dozen agents at once, that serialization is what breaks the product. Twelve workflows collapse into one queue, and a task that should take minutes takes hours. The developer is back to waiting, which is the exact problem Superset exists to solve.

Six Next.js projects, no platform team

Vercel was the default choice from the start, as all three founders had built on it at previous companies. From day one, Superset ran six Next.js projects on Vercel: the web app, marketing site, docs, and three supporting services. The team skipped platform engineering entirely and stayed focused on the product.

Every branch a Superset developer or agent creates becomes a preview deployment automatically, often spinning up multiple services. At its peak, Superset generates roughly 600 preview deployments a day internally. Every branch gets a live URL, and the team never waits on a deploy queue.

One AI stack for every workload

Superset's AI stack grew with the product, and each piece of the Vercel platform was pulled in to solve a specific problem as functionality was added.

Orchestration and model routing

  • AI SDK and AI Elements run the agent orchestration itself, giving Superset a single interface for multi-model, multi-agent workflows.

  • AI Gateway handles model routing without custom routing logic.

Storage and compute

  • Vercel Blob stores artifacts from agents and users, no object storage to manage.

  • Fluid compute absorbs parallel tasks as agents fan out, scaling underneath without forcing the team to rearchitect. Active CPU pricing means cost is only incurred on actual compute, not round-trip time waiting on model responses.

Operational controls

  • Cron Jobs prevent parallel environments from piling up.

  • BotID filters bots during high traffic periods, no custom middleware needed.

As Superset has expanded into new product areas, the entire stack has stayed on Vercel. There's no second cloud to glue in, no orchestration layer to maintain, and no platform engineering team to keep it glued together. New surface areas gets built on the same primitives that handled the old surface area, which is what frees the team to keep moving on product instead of plumbing.

Superset is its own super user

The most credible proof how the Superset team uses Superset themselves. GitHub issues flow into Superset and get split across parallel workspaces, and Satya has tuned the team's setup to run up to a dozen instances at once. Multiple efforts move forward without anyone waiting on serial decisions. Compared to their previous dev workflows, Superset's commit graph looks exponential.

Scaling through a Hacker News spike

During a Hacker News "Show HN" launch, user counts tripled overnight. Superset absorbed the spike without anyone provisioning infrastructure mid-flight.

That extends to incidents. If a customer reports an issue to Superset, their agents can spin up, write the fix, generate a preview, and merge the code in under thirty minutes. If the fix makes things worse, rollbacks are instant, so the cost of a bad deploy drops to near zero.

"Almost no time to deploy" as the bar

For Superset, immediate deployment matters because it keeps the loop between writing code, previewing it, and shipping it short enough that velocity never stalls, even across dozens of parallel workstreams. Build time averages around 30 seconds, and deployment volume runs between 1,000 and 1,400 a week.

What's next

The pattern for success is already clear: a product built for parallelism, by a team that works in parallel, on agentic infrastructure that doesn't force them back into a queue. Every new agent capability they ship to customers gets stress-tested first by their own engineers running a dozen at once. The dozen will become two dozen, and the infrastructure underneath was built to expect it.
