title: SEO AI Engineering
description:
Why the Future of SEO Looks More Like Software Engineering

SEO is quietly becoming an engineering discipline.

For years, SEO revolved around familiar activities:

  • Keyword research
  • Content optimisation
  • Internal linking
  • Backlinks
  • Technical audits
  • Rank tracking

These things are not disappearing.

But the environment around them is changing.

Search is becoming multi-engine.

Users increasingly discover information through Google, ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, AI Overviews, recommendation systems, and AI-powered assistants.

At the same time, SEO teams are dealing with increasingly large websites, complex JavaScript applications, thousands of URLs, structured data, log files, APIs, automated publishing systems, and enormous datasets.

The result is the emergence of a discipline I call SEO AI Engineering.

It sits at the intersection of:

SEO + Software Engineering + Data Engineering + AI Engineering

And I believe it represents one of the most important evolutions of technical SEO.

1. SEO Is Moving From Pages to Systems

Traditional SEO often asks:

How do we optimise this page?

SEO engineering asks a different question:

How do we design a system that continuously detects, prioritises, and fixes search visibility problems?

Imagine a website with 500,000 URLs.

Manually checking canonical tags, internal links, indexability, schema markup, and page performance at that scale is impractical.

Instead, an SEO engineer might build a pipeline:

Crawler
   ↓
Data extraction
   ↓
Validation rules
   ↓
Issue classification
   ↓
Priority scoring
   ↓
AI-assisted analysis
   ↓
Recommended fix
   ↓
Automated test
   ↓
Deployment
   ↓
Monitoring

That changes SEO completely.

An audit is no longer necessarily a PDF produced once every six months.

It can become a continuously running quality-control system.

2. Python Will Become Increasingly Useful in SEO

SEO professionals do not need to become full-time software engineers.

But basic programming creates enormous leverage.

Python can automate tasks such as:

  • Checking HTTP status codes
  • Validating canonical tags
  • Analysing internal links
  • Detecting orphan pages
  • Comparing XML sitemaps
  • Extracting structured data
  • Analysing server log files
  • Clustering keywords
  • Monitoring SERP changes

Instead of manually inspecting spreadsheets containing hundreds of thousands of rows, an SEO engineer can build reproducible pipelines.

Here is a simplified example using Python and requests:

import requests

urls = [
    "https://example.com/",
    "https://example.com/products/",
    "https://example.com/blog/",
]

for url in urls:
    try:
        response = requests.get(
            url,
            timeout=10,
            allow_redirects=True
        )

        if response.status_code != 200:
            print(
                f"ISSUE: {url} "
                f"returned {response.status_code}"
            )

    except requests.RequestException as error:
        print(f"ERROR: {url} - {error}")

This is a basic example, not a production crawler.

But the principle is powerful.

A repeatable script can execute checks that would otherwise require substantial manual work.

Simple automation. Massive operational difference.

3. AI Changes the Equation Again

Now add large language models.

Traditional SEO automation is largely deterministic.

For example:

If HTTP status code = 404, flag the URL.

AI systems can assist with tasks that require more contextual interpretation.

Examples include:

  • Analysing page intent
  • Evaluating content similarity
  • Classifying search intent
  • Generating remediation suggestions
  • Detecting unusual content patterns
  • Analysing entity coverage
  • Summarising crawl anomalies
  • Evaluating internal linking opportunities
  • Comparing competitor information architecture

Consider internal linking.

Instead of simply finding pages containing the same keyword, an AI-assisted system could evaluate multiple signals:

Semantic similarity
        +
Topical relationship
        +
Page importance
        +
Anchor-text suitability
        +
Crawl depth
        +
Business priority
        ↓
Suggested internal links

An engineer could combine embeddings, graph analysis, deterministic rules, and LLM-assisted evaluation.

The system could propose links for review rather than automatically inserting them into production pages.

The SEO professional becomes the person designing and validating the system instead of manually discovering every opportunity.

4. The Modern SEO Engineering Stack

A modern SEO engineering environment might include:

Layer Technologies
Data collection Search Console API, GA4, crawlers, server logs
Programming Python, JavaScript, SQL
Data processing Pandas, DuckDB, PostgreSQL
AI LLM APIs, embeddings, vector search
Automation GitHub Actions, scheduled jobs
Testing Pytest, Playwright, custom validators
Monitoring Dashboards, alerts, anomaly detection
Deployment Git, CI/CD, cloud infrastructure

This is where SEO starts to resemble a software engineering workflow.

For example:

SEO specification
      ↓
Git commit
      ↓
Automated SEO tests
      ↓
Build
      ↓
Deployment
      ↓
Production validation
      ↓
Search performance monitoring

Which leads to another concept I believe deserves more attention.

5. Spec-Driven Development for SEO

Software engineers use explicit specifications to define expected system behaviour.

SEO can adopt the same approach.

Instead of writing:

Make sure canonical tags are correct.

Define the expected behaviour in a machine-readable specification.

For example:

page_type: article

canonical:
  required: true
  strategy: self_referencing
  allow_cross_domain: false

indexability:
  expected_status: 200
  robots: index,follow

structured_data:
  required_types:
    - Article
    - BreadcrumbList

These are project-specific rules, not a universal SEO standard.

But once requirements become machine-readable, they can drive automated tests.

For example:

def test_article_seo(page):
    assert page.status_code == 200
    assert page.canonical == page.url
    assert page.is_indexable is True

    assert "Article" in page.schema_types
    assert "BreadcrumbList" in page.schema_types

Here, page represents a parsed page object supplied by a testing framework.

This approach changes the relationship between SEO and development teams.

SEO requirements no longer need to exist exclusively in documents, tickets, and Slack conversations.

They can become part of the engineering workflow.

SEO specifications → automated tests → deployment validation.

And that means fewer regressions reaching production.

6. AI Search Creates an Entirely New Measurement Problem

SEO is expanding beyond traditional rankings.

Brands increasingly want answers to questions such as:

Does ChatGPT mention our company?

Does Gemini recommend our product?

Which sources does Perplexity cite when discussing our brand?

Does changing the prompt change how AI describes us?

These questions require a different measurement infrastructure.

Imagine evaluating a brand across multiple AI systems.

A simplified experimental workflow might look like this:

prompts = [
    "What are the best tools for technical SEO?",
    "Which technical SEO platforms are recommended?",
    "What software helps identify technical SEO issues?"
]

for prompt in prompts:
    for run in range(10):
        response = query_model(prompt)
        save_result(
            prompt=prompt,
            run=run,
            response=response
        )

In this pseudocode, query_model() and save_result() represent functions implemented by the researcher.

The resulting dataset can be analysed for:

  • Brand mention frequency
  • Citation frequency
  • Recommendation frequency
  • Sentiment and framing
  • Claim consistency
  • Source concentration
  • Response volatility

The important point is reproducibility.

AI responses may vary between repeated runs, prompt formulations, model versions, and retrieval conditions.

A single answer is not a reliable measure of overall brand visibility.

AI visibility measurement is not just prompt engineering. It is experimental design, data collection, and statistical analysis.

That makes it an engineering problem.

7. AI Agents Will Transform SEO Investigations

Another major shift will come from AI agents.

Imagine an SEO agent receiving the following task:

Investigate the organic traffic decline affecting /products/.

With appropriate permissions and integrations, the agent could:

  1. Query Google Search Console.
  2. Identify when the decline began.
  3. Detect affected pages and queries.
  4. Crawl the affected URLs.
  5. Inspect canonical and robots directives.
  6. Compare internal linking patterns.
  7. Check recent deployments.
  8. Examine server-side rendering.
  9. Formulate possible explanations.
  10. Produce an evidence-based investigation report.

The agent would not know the true cause automatically.

It would generate hypotheses supported by collected evidence.

A human specialist would still validate the findings and approve changes.

But the workflow becomes significantly more efficient.

Instead of spending hours collecting data, the specialist can focus on interpreting results and making decisions.

This is the difference between using AI to write SEO content and using AI to operate SEO engineering workflows.

8. SEO Professionals Will Become Workflow Designers

This is probably the biggest change.

The valuable skill will not simply be knowing which SEO tools to click.

It will be knowing how to design a reliable process.

Problem
   ↓
Data
   ↓
Specification
   ↓
Automation
   ↓
Validation
   ↓
Decision
   ↓
Monitoring

That mindset scales.

A good SEO AI engineer asks:

  • Can this task be automated?
  • Can this rule be expressed as a specification?
  • Can the result be tested automatically?
  • Can the data be collected through an API?
  • Can AI assist with classification or analysis?
  • Can the recommendation be validated?
  • Can the impact be measured after deployment?

These are engineering questions applied to search visibility.

And they are very different from simply producing another SEO checklist.

9. Will AI Replace SEO Specialists?

I don't think that is the most useful question.

AI will automate many tasks currently performed manually.

But automation creates new responsibilities.

Someone still needs to define:

  • What should be measured
  • Which signals matter
  • What counts as an error
  • How systems should behave
  • How experiments should be designed
  • Whether AI output is trustworthy
  • When automation should stop
  • How SEO requirements interact with product and engineering constraints

The SEO professional of the future may spend less time manually producing recommendations and more time designing systems that generate, test, and monitor those recommendations.

The competitive advantage moves from executing individual tasks to designing reliable systems.

10. What Will the Future SEO Team Look Like?

I can imagine SEO responsibilities evolving into several increasingly specialised disciplines.

SEO Strategist

Search demand, market analysis, competitive positioning, and business prioritisation.

Technical SEO Engineer

Rendering, crawling, indexing, architecture, structured data, and web performance.

SEO Data Analyst

Search Console analysis, server logs, experimentation, forecasting, and statistical evaluation.

SEO AI Engineer

LLM workflows, AI agents, AI visibility measurement, evaluation pipelines, and automation.

SEO Content Engineer

Structured content systems, entity architecture, knowledge organisation, and content operations at scale.

Not every organisation will use these titles.

And smaller teams will combine many of these responsibilities.

But the technical capabilities required for SEO are expanding.

11. The Most Interesting Part? We're Still Early.

Many organisations still operate SEO through spreadsheets, manual audits, isolated recommendations, and disconnected tools.

That leaves enormous room for experimentation.

You can start today:

  1. Learn Python. Automate a repetitive SEO task.
  2. Explore APIs. Connect Google Search Console to your own scripts.
  3. Learn SQL. Analyse SEO data without depending entirely on spreadsheets.
  4. Experiment with embeddings. Explore semantic similarity and topic relationships.
  5. Build SEO tests. Validate technical requirements automatically.
  6. Learn Git and CI/CD. Integrate SEO checks into development workflows.
  7. Study LLM evaluation. Measure AI responses systematically.
  8. Experiment with AI agents. Automate investigations with human review.
  9. Create machine-readable SEO specifications. Turn requirements into executable tests.
  10. Publish your experiments. Share code, datasets, methods, and findings.

You do not need to master all these technologies at once.

Choose one SEO problem.

Build a small engineering solution.

Document it.

Test it.

Improve it.

Then move to the next problem.

Final Thoughts

The future of SEO is not simply about generating more content with AI.

And it is not just about getting mentioned in ChatGPT.

It is about building reliable systems that collect data, understand search visibility problems, test technical requirements, evaluate AI responses, and support better decisions.

Traditional SEO knowledge will remain essential.

But its implementation will increasingly involve code, data pipelines, AI models, automation, and software engineering practices.

The future of SEO is not just optimisation. It is engineering.

And that is why I believe SEO AI Engineering is a discipline worth exploring.

What Do You Think?

If you're a developer, technical SEO specialist, data engineer, or AI practitioner:

What technologies would you include in an SEO AI Engineering stack?

Python? SQL? LLM APIs? Vector databases? CI/CD? Search Console?

And which SEO tasks do you think should become automated first?

I'd love to hear how others see software engineering and search visibility converging.

title: At-Least-Once Queue Retries Explained (and 1 Idempotency Key That Stops Duplicate Digests)
description:
If you just want the weekly digest to stop landing twice in the same inbox, don't go shopping for a better broker. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so a duplicate reminder is ordinary traffic rather than an incident — every broker worth running will replay a message when a worker dies mid-job. What stops the second copy is a send ledger: one uniquely-keyed row per user, per reminder, per scheduled run, written by the consumer before the email leaves the building.

That's it. One row.

The rest of this is the stuff that bites afterwards — how to pick the queue, how to write the worker in Node.js, and which three counters tell you the dedupe is doing anything at all.

Where the second copy of a fintech digest comes from

Picture the Friday 06:00 job at a payments company. A cron trigger fans out one message per active customer — call it 40,000 of them — and a pool of Node.js workers drains the queue, renders the week's balance and transaction summary, and hands it to the mail API. Ten messages per batch, roughly sixty seconds of work each. Nothing exotic.

Now kill one worker between "mail accepted" and "ack sent".

The broker has no idea the mail went out. Its visibility timeout expires, the message becomes visible again, a second worker claims it, and a customer receives their account summary twice. At a fintech that lands differently than a duplicate newsletter: support has to establish that the customer got two copies of one statement and not one copy of two settlement runs, and that conversation costs more than the send ever did.

Deploys do the same thing, quietly. Roll the worker pool during the run and every message in flight goes back on the queue — correct behaviour, duplicate processing, same outcome.

FIFO queues help less than the marketing suggests. Content-based or explicit deduplication ids are real, but they cover a window of about five minutes, and the retry that hurts is the one that arrives after a crash loop, a redeploy, or a mail provider that took ninety seconds to answer. Past the window, the broker has forgotten. Your consumer has not, if you gave it somewhere to remember.

There's a cost axis hiding in here too. You can shrink the duplicate window by acking earlier, which trades a risk of losing a digest entirely for lower latency, or you can run fatter batches with fewer workers, which trades wall-clock time for a smaller bill. Both dials move duplicates around. Neither removes them.

Which queue setup should I use if the same reminder message gets sent twice to users?

Pick on two questions: does the platform remember completed work for you, and do you already run the infrastructure it needs. Nothing in the table below makes consumer idempotency optional — it changes how much of the ledger you write yourself.

Option Delivery model Dedupe you get for free Where the send ledger goes
BullMQ on Redis at-least-once, in-process workers job ids are unique while the job is retained your Postgres, or a Redis key with a TTL
Inngest at-least-once with step memoisation completed steps are not re-run on retry the platform, for step results
Temporal at-least-once activity execution none — activities must be idempotent by contract your own activity guard
Upstash QStash at-least-once HTTP delivery optional deduplication id per publish your own store
Infrai queues at-least-once, FIFO dedupe over a 5-minute window an Idempotency-Key convention on writes your own store, behind one REST API and one key

BullMQ is the default pick when Redis is already in the stack and you want the worker to be a Node.js process you can attach a debugger to. The catch is that Redis persistence becomes part of your delivery guarantee, which is a conversation with whoever owns the Redis budget.

Inngest earns its keep when the digest is a flow rather than a send — fetch balances, wait for a reconciliation event, then mail — because step memoisation means a retry resumes instead of restarting. Temporal is the heavier version of that answer, and it's the right one when the workflow spans days and you can staff a cluster. Neither is a good fit if all you have is one queue and one worker.

QStash suits serverless deployments with no long-lived process to drain a queue; it pushes to your HTTP endpoint instead.

Infrai fits the narrower, very common shape of this job: a cron trigger, a queue, and an email send that all belong to the same weekly run and would otherwise mean three signups, three keys, and three invoices to reconcile at month end. One REST API covers the lot, which is mostly a procurement and on-call convenience rather than a technical one — but on a two-person platform team, it's the difference between one runbook and three. It doesn't support DAG-style orchestration or fan-in joins, so if the digest needs a real workflow graph, stick with Temporal or Inngest.

A Node.js worker that claims the reminder before it sends

The ordering matters more than the storage engine. Claim, send, ack — and if any step throws, don't ack, because the message coming back is the behaviour you want.

import { Pool } from "pg";
import { sendDigest } from "./mail.ts";

const BASE = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE!;   // API root for your queue provider
const KEY = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY!;
const QUEUE = "weekly-digest";

const db = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

type DigestJob = { user_id: string; reminder_id: string; scheduled_at: string };
type QueueMessage = { message_id: string; receipt: string; body: DigestJob };

async function call(path: string, payload: unknown, idempotencyKey?: string): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(`${BASE}${path}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}`,
        "content-type": "application/json",
        ...(idempotencyKey ? { "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey } : {}),
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });
    if (res.status !== 429) return res;
    const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get("retry-after") ?? 0);
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250));
  }
  throw new Error("rate limited five times in a row; leaving the batch for the next tick");
}

function sendKey(job: DigestJob): string {
  return `${job.user_id}:${job.reminder_id}:${job.scheduled_at}`;
}

// One row per (user, reminder, scheduled run). The unique index is the idempotency.
async function claim(job: DigestJob): Promise<boolean> {
  const { rowCount } = await db.query(
    "insert into digest_sends (send_key, claimed_at) values ($1, now()) on conflict (send_key) do nothing",
    [sendKey(job)],
  );
  return rowCount === 1;
}

export async function drainOnce(): Promise<number> {
  const res = await call("/v1/queue/consume", { queue: QUEUE, max_messages: 10, visibility_timeout: 120 });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`consume returned ${res.status}: ${await res.text()}`);

  const { data } = (await res.json()) as { data: { messages: QueueMessage[] } };
  let suppressed = 0;

  for (const msg of data.messages) {
    const first = await claim(msg.body);
    if (first) await sendDigest(msg.body, sendKey(msg.body));
    else suppressed++;

    const ack = await call("/v1/queue/ack", { queue: QUEUE, receipt: msg.receipt });
    if (!ack.ok) console.error("ack rejected", ack.status, await ack.text());
  }
  return suppressed;
}

Three details carry the whole thing. The claim happens before the send, so a crash after the insert leaves a row that suppresses the retry rather than a customer with two statements. The same sendKey is passed to the mail call as its idempotency key, so the provider gets a second chance to catch what your database missed. And the ack only runs after the send returns, which is the part people invert when they're chasing throughput.

rowCount === 1 is doing a lot of work in that function, so give the table a unique index on send_key and a claimed_at column you can prune on. Thirty-five days of retention is plenty for a weekly job.

If storing raw account identifiers in a send table is awkward for your data classification, hash the tuple with HMAC (RFC 2104) and store the hex output. Uniqueness survives; the identifiers don't leak into a second table.

Three counters that prove the dedupe is doing something

I teach this as a before/after, because the ledger is invisible until you count it.

Count suppressed claims — the else branch above. A healthy weekly run shows a small non-zero number, usually a handful out of tens of thousands. Zero across several runs means either your workers never crash (possible) or the ledger isn't actually on the send path (more likely, and worth a lunchtime investigation). A number climbing past one percent of the run says the visibility timeout is shorter than your real handler latency, and the fix is the timeout, not the ledger.

Second, track age of the oldest unacked message during the run. That's your real duplicate exposure window: everything older than the visibility timeout is a candidate for redelivery. It's also the honest latency metric for a digest — not how fast one send is, but how long the tail takes to clear.

Third, count sends per send_key from the mail provider's own logs, not yours. Your ledger says the worker behaved. The provider's log says the customer's inbox agrees. Those two disagreeing is the only evidence worth paging someone about, and I'd wire that one to an alert rather than a dashboard nobody opens on a Friday.

What this design doesn't cover

The ledger is now a dependency of sending. If the database is unreachable, the correct move is to let the worker throw and the message return on its visibility timeout — sending blind is how you get the duplicates back.

Two platform limits are worth checking before you commit. Ack usually deletes the message, and retention caps out well short of a log-structured broker, so if replaying last month's digest run is a requirement, stick with Kafka or a stream you control rather than a work queue. Delayed delivery is also bounded — seven days on hosted queues is a common ceiling, which is fine for a weekly cadence and useless for an annual renewal reminder.

Long fan-outs need the same care. A scheduled trigger that runs a single HTTP handler will hit a hard execution ceiling — 900 seconds on some platforms — so the trigger should enqueue and return, and the workers should do the sending. Forty thousand renders inside one cron invocation is a timeout waiting to happen, and a timeout mid-run is exactly the retry that duplicates.

I'm not certain the HMAC step is worth it for every team; if your send table already lives inside the same compliance boundary as the customer record, it's ceremony. The claim row, though, is not optional. At-least-once is a promise the broker keeps by sending twice — idempotency is how your consumer keeps it once.

References

  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview (at-least-once delivery semantics): https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview
  • Amazon SQS FIFO queues, deduplication ids and the 5-minute interval: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues.html
  • Stripe API: idempotent requests and idempotency keys: https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
  • BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • Temporal documentation on activity idempotency: https://docs.temporal.io/activities
  • Inngest step memoisation and retries: https://www.inngest.com/docs/learn/inngest-steps
  • Upstash QStash deduplication: https://upstash.com/docs/qstash/features/deduplication
  • RFC 2104, HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

title: A Strong Harness Narrows the Model Gap: A Comparative Evaluation for Legislative Document-to-XML Conversion
description:
arXiv:2610.19999v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Legal-content reproduction requires matching the source exactly in section hierarchy, verbatim text, citations, and amendment spans; a dropped citation or mislabeled amendment carries into the products lawyers rely on. We report an industrial pipeline converting U.S. state legislation into strict, schema-constrained XML, and hypothesize that its accuracy comes from harness engineering, the deterministic tooling built around a model, more than the model itself. Our controlled ablation crosses three harnesses (zero-shot, a single tool-using agent, and a decomposed multi-agent pipeline) with three Claude models on 153 gold bills from two jurisdictions. The harness narrows the model gap: the weakest model in the full pipeline beats the strongest model alone (0.948 versus 0.806, paired bootstrap p less than 0.001). Because the two agentic harnesses share identical tools, their gap comes from orchestration: decomposition plus the persisted state and per-agent context it brings. Across four scored dimensions, the model spread at zero-shot (0.68 to 0.81) narrows to 0.95 at the full pipeline; the residual sits almost entirely in citation normalization, where the canonical identifier is retrieved from an external authority rather than generated from the weights, so a deterministic lookup tool supplies the exactness that a larger model does not.

title: Reasoning Models Aren't Smarter — They're Just Slower
description:
Test-time compute is real — and expensive. A practitioner's routing guide for when to use reasoning models vs. fast models.

#reasoning#models#research

Sarah's team swapped in a reasoning model for their code review pipeline expecting smarter results. They got slower responses, a $3,700 monthly bill increase, and answers that were still wrong — just wrong with more steps and more confidence. Reasoning models aren't smarter — they just spend more compute being wrong in a more convincing way.

I've been routing production workloads through both fast models (qwen2.5-coder:14b, llama3.1:8b) and reasoning models (deepseek-r1:14b, o1-style models) for six months. Here's the routing guide I wish I had when I started.

3–10×typical latency multiplier for reasoning-mode vs. single-pass generation on comparable hardwareIllustrative — workload-dependent~15%of enterprise prompts actually benefit from extended reasoning in our routing auditsInternal pattern — your mix will differ

What reasoning actually buys

Multi-step logic with verifiable intermediate states. Math, constraint puzzles, code that must compile, policy interpretation where one wrong clause cascades. The model earns accuracy by spending tokens on scratch work — visible or hidden — instead of gambling on a single shot.

What it doesn't buy: speed, cheapness, or immunity to hallucination. A reasoning trace can be confidently wrong in twelve meticulous steps. Observability matters more, not less, when the model "shows its work."

Reasoning models draining tokens on a slow dial.

Test-Time Compute: The Cost Equation

Model Latency Tokens/Answer Cost/1M Answers
qwen2.5-coder:14b (fast) ~2s ~500 ~$5
deepseek-r1:14b (thinking) ~15s ~3,000 ~$30
o1-style (reasoning) ~45s ~15,000 ~$150

RoutingWhere reasoning tax pays offIllustrativeAmbiguous policy / legalHighMulti-file code changesHighEmail tone rewriteLowClassification / taggingLowIllustrative ROI of reasoning-mode by task type — use your own eval set.

Fast models for the bulk. Reasoning models for the escalations. Same waterfall you've always run — new lane.

Design patterns that work

Escalation, not default. Classify intent cheaply; invoke reasoning only when confidence is low or stakes are high. Users waiting eight seconds for a hashtag suggestion will not become fans.

Budget the thinking. Cap reasoning tokens, steps, and wall time. An agent that can think forever will — and charge you for the privilege.

Cache conclusions, not chains. Store verified outputs. Don't replay full reasoning traces on every similar ticket.

Routing Rules That Work

Task Type Route To Why
Code completion, simple edits, formatting Fast (qwen2.5-coder:14b) Speed matters, single-step
Debugging, refactoring, multi-file changes Think (deepseek-r1:14b) Multi-step, self-correction helps
Architecture decisions, math proofs, novel algorithms Reason (o1-style) Correctness > latency
Summarization, extraction, classification Fast Single pass, no reasoning needed

What this means for you

Map your request types before you map models. Tag traffic by stakes, reversibility, and user patience. Password resets and invoice approvals live in different latency universes than brainstorming subject lines. Reasoning belongs where wrong answers are expensive and users expect to wait — not where speed is the product.

  • Interactive UI — keep under 2s perceived; reasoning rarely belongs here
  • Async jobs — batch reasoning overnight; users get email when done
  • Human-in-the-loop — reasoning while someone watches is fine; alone in chat is not
  • Agent loops — cap iterations; reasoning agents love infinite "let me reconsider"

The latency bill nobody budgets

Reasoning models don't just cost more per token — they cost more wall-clock time. An eight-second response in a support widget isn't "thinking harder"; it's a user opening another tab and filing the ticket manually. Your SLA doesn't care that the model was philosophically thorough.

The latency bill reasoning models hide.

Here's the thing: every millisecond of reasoning compute is a tradeoff against user patience. Model providers sell "thinking" as a feature. What they don't put in the marketing copy is that each thought token is paid for twice — once in compute, once in user experience. The faster your alternative, the more expensive the reasoning tax actually is.

A reasoning trace you can't afford to run twice is a reasoning trace you can't afford to run in production.

Measuring whether reasoning earns its keep

Run A/B on your eval set: fast model vs. reasoning model on the same prompts. Measure accuracy delta, latency p95, and cost per correct answer — not cost per request. You'll often find reasoning wins on 12% of tasks and loses on economics for the other 88%. That's not failure; that's a routing table.

Add a feature flag for reasoning escalation and log every trigger reason. After two weeks you'll have real data on whether "low confidence" actually correlates with needing a bigger brain — or whether your classifier is just nervous. Tune thresholds weekly; this is product work, not a one-time architecture decision.

EconomicsWhen reasoning pays for itself

Signal Escalate?
Financial/legal commitment Yes
Multi-step dependency chain Yes
Style or tone adjustment No
User already waiting >5s Defer or async

Product copy matters

Don't tell users the system is "thinking" for eight seconds without setting expectations. Progress UI, async handoff, or honest latency labels beat a spinning dot that feels broken. Reasoning models trained users to expect depth — your UX must match or they'll abandon before the answer arrives.

A/B test copy on slow paths. "Analyzing policy" outperforms "Loading" for legal workflows. Measure completion rate, not just accuracy — a correct answer nobody waited for is a failed request.

If your architecture treats "reasoning model" as the new default LLM, you're about to learn what API bills and SLA breaches have in common. Treat reasoning as a premium tier with explicit admission criteria. Your CFO and your users will both thank you.

Stay with us · dig next

How Do You Determine When to Use Reasoning Models?

In your experience, what criteria do you use to decide whether a task requires a reasoning model or can be handled by a fast model?

No account needed — pick a take, then keep reading. We rotate these prompts so each piece feels like a conversation, not a clone.

Ayraix.com publisher analysis

What we're really seeing

The article highlights a crucial distinction between fast models and reasoning models, emphasizing that the latter are not inherently smarter but simply more computationally expensive and slower. This nuanced understanding is vital for businesses looking to optimize their AI investments. While reasoning models can be beneficial for complex tasks requiring multi-step logic and verifiable intermediate states, they come with higher latency and costs. The key takeaway is to carefully evaluate which tasks require the added accuracy of reasoning models and where fast models suffice.

Organizations must weigh the need for precision against the trade-offs in speed and cost. A strategic approach to routing workloads through appropriate models can lead to more efficient AI deployments, avoiding unnecessary expenses and maintaining productivity. This analysis underscores the importance of observability and transparent reasoning processes in modern AI systems, ensuring that decisions are based on accurate and reliable data.

title: Guarding Your Code: A Pragmatic Guide to Modern Application Security
description:
Introduction

Security isn’t a one‑time checklist; it’s a mindset that must be woven into every line of code, every CI/CD pipeline, and every deployment. In this post we’ll walk through practical techniques you can start using today to harden your applications-whether you’re building a simple Flask API or a full‑blown microservices ecosystem. We’ll cover threat modeling, secure defaults, runtime defenses, and automated testing, all backed by concrete code snippets you can drop into your projects.

TL;DR: Adopt a “shift‑left” approach, validate everything, use modern libraries, and let automation enforce the rules.

1. Threat Modeling Made Simple

Before you write a single line of code, ask yourself: what can go wrong? The classic OWASP Top 10 is a great starting point, but a lightweight threat model helps you prioritize.

graph LR
    A[User Input] --> B[API Endpoint]
    B --> C{Validation}
    C -->|Pass| D[Business Logic]
    C -->|Fail| E[Reject Request]
    D --> F[Data Store]
    F --> G[Response]
  • Identify assets - e.g., user credentials, financial data.
  • Identify entry points - public APIs, file uploads, third‑party callbacks.
  • Identify threats - injection, broken authentication, data leakage.

Document this in a markdown table:

Asset Entry Point Threat Mitigation
JWT token Authorization header Token replay Short expiry + rotating secret
User avatar File upload Malicious script Content‑type whitelist, scanning
Payment info POST /pay SQL injection Parameterized queries

2. Secure Defaults in Code

2.1. Use Safe Libraries

Never roll your own cryptography. In Python, stick with cryptography or hashlib for hashing.

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.pbkdf2 import PBKDF2HMAC
import os, base64

def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    salt = os.urandom(16)
    kdf = PBKDF2HMAC(
        algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
        length=32,
        salt=salt,
        iterations=100_000,
    )
    key = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(kdf.derive(password.encode()))
    return f"{base64.b64encode(salt).decode()}${key.decode()}"

Why it matters: Using a well‑vetted KDF (Key Derivation Function) protects against brute‑force attacks and eliminates common pitfalls like low‑entropy salts.

2.2. Enforce HTTPS Everywhere

Never serve mixed content. In Flask, you can force HTTPS with a simple middleware:

from flask import Flask, request, redirect

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.before_request
def enforce_https():
    if request.headers.get('X-Forwarded-Proto', 'http') != 'https':
        url = request.url.replace('http://', 'https://')
        return redirect(url, code=301)

Deploy behind a reverse proxy (NGINX, Traefik) that terminates TLS, and set Strict-Transport-Security headers:

add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;

3. Input Validation & Output Encoding

3.1. Validate All Inputs

Never trust client data. Use schema validation libraries like pydantic:

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, constr

class RegisterPayload(BaseModel):
    username: constr(min_length=3, max_length=30, regex=r'^\w+$')
    email: EmailStr
    password: constr(min_length=8)

FastAPI automatically validates the request body against this model and returns a 422 response if anything is off.

3.2. Encode on Output

Cross‑site scripting (XSS) is mitigated by escaping data when rendering HTML. In Jinja2, enable autoescaping:

from flask import Flask, render_template
app = Flask(__name__)
app.jinja_env.autoescape = True

If you must embed user‑generated data into JavaScript, JSON‑encode it:

<script>
    const user = {{ user|tojson|safe }};
</script>

4. Authentication & Authorization

4.1. JWT Best Practices

  • Use asymmetric keys (RS256) for signing.
  • Keep the token lifetime short (5‑15 minutes) and rotate refresh tokens.
  • Store tokens in httpOnly, secure cookies to mitigate XSS. 
import jwt
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def create_access_token(user_id: str, private_key: str) -> str:
    payload = {
        "sub": user_id,
        "iat": datetime.utcnow(),
        "exp": datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(minutes=10),
        "iss": "myapp"
    }
    return jwt.encode(payload, private_key, algorithm="RS256")

4.2. Role‑Based Access Control (RBAC)

Define a central permission map:

PERMISSIONS = {
    "admin": {"read:any", "write:any", "delete:any"},
    "editor": {"read:any", "write:own"},
    "viewer": {"read:any"},
}

Middleware checks the claim against the required permission:

def require_permission(permission):
    def decorator(fn):
        @wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            token = get_jwt_from_request()
            user_perms = PERMISSIONS.get(token["role"], set())
            if permission not in user_perms:
                abort(403, "Insufficient privileges")
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapper
    return decorator

5. Runtime Defenses

5.1. Security Headers

Add the following headers to every response:

Header Value
Content-Security-Policy default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'
X-Content-Type-Options nosniff
X-Frame-Options DENY
Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin

In Flask:

@app.after_request
def set_security_headers(response):
    response.headers["Content-Security-Policy"] = "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'"
    response.headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff"
    response.headers["X-Frame-Options"] = "DENY"
    response.headers["Referrer-Policy"] = "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
    return response

5.2. Rate Limiting

Prevent brute‑force attacks with token bucket algorithms. Flask-Limiter makes it painless:

from flask_limiter import Limiter
from flask_limiter.util import get_remote_address

limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address, default_limits=["200 per day", "50 per hour"])
limiter.init_app(app)

@app.route("/login", methods=["POST"])
@limiter.limit("5 per minute")
def login():
    # authentication logic
    pass

6. Automated Security Testing

6.1. Static Analysis

Integrate tools like Bandit (Python) into your CI pipeline:

# .github/workflows/security.yml
name: Security Scan
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  bandit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Install Bandit
        run: pip install bandit
      - name: Run Bandit
        run: bandit -r . -lll

6.2. Dependency Scanning

Leverage Dependabot (built‑in on GitHub) or Snyk for continuous vulnerability alerts.

6.3. Dynamic Scanning

Run a lightweight OWASP ZAP scan against a staging environment after deployment:

docker run -t owasp/zap2docker-stable zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.myapp.com -r zap_report.html

Fail the pipeline if the report contains high severity findings.

7. Incident Response Basics

Even with best practices, breaches happen. Prepare a concise run‑book:

  1. Identify - Pull logs from CloudWatch / ELK, look for anomalies.
  2. Contain - Disable compromised credentials, rotate secrets.
  3. Eradicate - Patch vulnerable code, run a fresh scan.
  4. Recover - Redeploy from a known‑good image, verify integrity.
  5. Post‑mortem - Document lessons, adjust policies.

Automation can speed up steps 2‑3. For example, a Lambda function that revokes all JWT refresh tokens for a user when a suspicious login is detected.

Conclusion

Security is a continuous journey, not a destination. By embedding threat modeling, secure defaults, rigorous validation, strong auth, runtime hardening, and automated testing into your development lifecycle, you dramatically reduce risk while keeping velocity high. Remember: shift left, automate, and never assume the client is trustworthy.

Recommended Tools

If you’re looking for a hassle‑free way to keep your codebase secure, I’ve been using Snyk’s Developer Security Platform for automated dependency scanning and container hardening. Their free tier is generous, and the paid plans integrate seamlessly with GitHub Actions and GitLab CI.

For runtime protection, especially around API gateways, I recommend the Imperva Cloud WAF. It offers out‑of‑the‑box OWASP Top 10 rule sets, bot mitigation, and real‑time analytics-perfect for teams that want enterprise‑grade security without managing infrastructure.

Happy coding, and stay secure!

title: Structure-Preserving Document-Level Data Augmentation via Discourse Parsing
description:
arXiv:2610.19497v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data augmentation (DA) plays a vital role in improving model performance in low-resource or limited-supervision scenarios within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Existing DA methods, such as synonym replacement and back-translation, have demonstrated effectiveness on the word or sentence level; however, they frequently neglect discourse-level coherence and logical flow, which are essential for complex tasks dependent on inter-sentential relationships. In this paper, we propose a structure-preserving document-level data augmentation framework based on large language models (LLMs) and document-level discourse structure parsing. Our approach identifies rhetorical relations between sentence pairs and extracts key phrases, which are then replaced with semantically coherent but topically shifted content while preserving the original discourse structure. Experimental results on text summarization and question answering show that the proposed augmented data provides complementary supervision and improves combined-data training across the evaluated tasks. Comparisons with a standard RST parser and controlled ablations further support the proposed discourse representation.

title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone
description:
arXiv:2610.19568v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. The encoder iteratively maps the backbone's hidden states to new latent blocks, constructing a latent reasoning prefix, after which the frozen model writes its remaining reasoning and its answer as text. Our method, INTACT, trains this encoder through distillation to reproduce the effect of written reasoning steps while keeping the model's behavior close to that of the frozen backbone, and then reinforces it on answer correctness. Across four frozen backbones from 1B to 8B, INTACT improves both GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy, including GSM8K gains from 75.8% to 79.3% on Llama-3.2-3B and from 77.6% to 79.7% on Qwen2.5-3B. It also reduces end-to-end latency per problem by 19% on Llama-3.2-3B and outperforms the evaluated latent-reasoning baselines at the 3B and 8B scales. Beyond the mathematics setting, the same recipe trained on a multi-domain corpus improves the frozen backbone on twelve evaluation benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and commonsense, without task-specific adaptation.

title: Where to Start, How to Move: Analyzing Curricula under GRPO for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.19349v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) provides no reward-relative learning signal when all rollouts receive identical rewards. In long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions, rewards are given only upon successful task completion, making all-fail groups common early in training and limiting opportunities to practice later steps. Guide Assisted GRPO replays a successful reference prefix before the learner continues. We study how initial positions, handoff units, and movement rules affect unassisted task completion. Across three model sizes on BFCL, starting near completion is more effective under a fixed turn-level threshold rule. Finer handoffs alone do not consistently help, but outcome-informed tool-call selection outperforms GRPO on trained and untrained task categories. Guided starts also improve AppWorld success on both evaluation splits. These findings highlight where learning starts and how starting positions move as key curriculum choices.

title: Does Machine Translation Retain Media Bias?
description:
arXiv:2610.19945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Within the most recent two decades, machine translation (MT) has been advanced from a research area to a mature, deployed technology for prose text and most language pairs. However, language has different dimensions of meaning, and the alluded progress has primarily been demonstrated for propositional meaning.
  In this small exploratory study, we investigate whether one type of affective meaning, namely different types of linguistically expressed media bias, are retained under automatic translation for two language pairs, English and German as the source languages, and Bulgarian as the target language. We evaluate four state-of-the-art translation methods to answer the question whether and to what degree a loss of non-neutral language (specifically, 27 types of media bias) can occur as a result of applying MT.
  Our empirical findings are consistent with the claim that MT does not fully retain existing news bias of its input source text, but also may add extra bias of its own. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental study of MT media bias retention.

title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
description:
arXiv:2610.19367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.
