title: Where Should the Gaussians Go? Reusable Label-Aware Allocation for Budget-Constrained Gaussian Splatting of Cinematic CT
description:
arXiv:2610.20397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Anatomical labels help 3D Gaussian splatting preserve vessels in cinematic renderings of CT, but the representation is still found by optimising each patient's scene, where densification decides where Gaussians go, while real-time displays cap their number. We address one part of this process: deciding where a fixed budget of B Gaussians should be placed. We propose a reusable, labelaware allocation front end that maps a patient's CT, labels and transfer function to a density over 2mm cells and draws exactly B positions from it without per-patient optimisation; the other Gaussian attributes are still fitted per patient. The front end is learned once from per-patient optimised scenes and implemented as a population-trained neural prior and an interpretable seven-parameter visibility-aware closed form (VACF). With identical attribute fitting on 20 held-out patients at 10K-100K Gaussians, both raise vessel-masked PSNR over uniform allocation by 4.5-7.1dB and over pruning a dense voxel-aligned model by 1.6-3.3dB. The neural prior does not differ significantly from per-patient optimised allocation at any budget, and VACF is within 0.6dB of it on vessels; on 19 external patients the neural prior again matches it on vessels and VACF is within 0.7dB. As an initialisation for position optimisation, VACF allocation beats per-patient densification on vessels at 10K Gaussians and, at 25K, reaches a higher vessel PSNR after 118s of optimisation than densification after 248s. Under altered rendering presets, VACF transfers to new colours and lighting but not to a label-free transfer function, whereas the neural prior shows the opposite pattern.

title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.14190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.

title: Engineering a Frictionless Location-Based Vehicle Rental Discovery Platform for China
description:
Introduction

When product teams and software engineers set out to build a modern discovery platform for physical assets, the complexity often exceeds basic CRUD operations and simple map integrations. Building a marketplace for mobility—where users need to find, compare, and reserve vehicles across complex geographic and regulatory landscapes—demands meticulous attention to structured data, location accuracy, and user trust. Whether designing for short urban commutes or extended regional tours, creating a reliable discovery experience involves far more than simply displaying a flat list of available assets.

A robust discovery experience must help users navigate multiple variables: understanding what vehicle types are available, confirming exact pickup points, validating documentation requirements, and ensuring pricing transparency. For developers and product designers tackling mobility marketplaces in complex markets like China, solving these discovery hurdles requires treating location, inventory, and user intent as first-class citizens in the architecture.

Model the User's Actual Transportation Need

Vehicle search should never begin with an unfiltered database dump. Instead, the discovery flow must start by capturing the user's authentic transportation intent. Different journeys dictate entirely different vehicle categories, durations, and supporting information requirements.

For instance, urban commuters navigating dense metropolitan centers may look for agile options such as a bike rental China solution for short trips, or a scooter rental China listing for efficient daily transit. Conversely, travelers planning longer journeys or regional excursions often require a dependable motorcycle rental China option to navigate diverse terrain efficiently.

To make discovery effective, the search interface should prompt users to specify critical parameters upfront:

  • Pickup and drop-off locations or regions
  • Intended rental duration and dates
  • Vehicle category and engine displacement where relevant
  • Passenger capacity and luggage or storage requirements
  • Applicable licensing and eligibility parameters

By capturing these parameters early, the platform can filter out irrelevant inventory and present options that genuinely match the user's journey constraints. It is equally important to design interfaces that do not imply universal availability; vehicle categories vary significantly by provider and region.

Treat Location as Structured Product Data

Geographic discovery in a regional marketplace fails when locations are treated as unstructured strings rather than hierarchical, structured entities. Relying on broad regional tags often leaves users uncertain about where they actually need to pick up or return a vehicle.

Product teams should model locations using clear, consistent hierarchies—distinguishing between administrative provinces, major metropolitan hubs, specific districts, and individual provider storefronts. For example, search and filter components should cleanly separate listings situated in a bustling capital district from those located in regional hubs. When users search within major centers like motorcycle rental Beijing or explore coastal options like motorcycle rental Shanghai, the underlying system must tie coordinates and localized zoning data directly to the inventory items.

Effective location design involves several practical patterns:

  • Standardizing city and district naming conventions across all provider inputs.
  • Providing explicit storefront addresses, landmarks, and operational hours for pickups.
  • Ensuring that filters dynamically adapt to show only active inventory within the selected geographic boundary.
  • Preventing destination-level pages from displaying generic inventory when no verified local providers are active.

Make Inventory Information Trustworthy

Inconsistent listing data erodes user trust faster than almost any other marketplace friction point. When a traveler browses options—whether looking for a standard urban vehicle or a comprehensive car rental China package—every listing must maintain a uniform schema of essential attributes.

A trustworthy listing card or detail view should consistently expose:

  • Exact vehicle make, model, and year (such as configurations from prominent manufacturers like CFMOTO or Benelli)
  • Verified vehicle category and technical specifications
  • Precise pickup location and return flexibility
  • Clear pricing structures, itemizing base rates, daily fees, and included mileage
  • Availability calendar matching real-time provider schedules
  • Security deposit terms, cancellation policies, and required identification documents

When listings omit critical details or present conflicting pricing, users experience cognitive overload and hesitation, leading to abandoned booking flows.

Design for International Visitors

Supporting international travelers introduces distinct UX and compliance hurdles that go beyond standard multi-language localization. Visitors navigating unfamiliar transportation ecosystems require explicit guidance across documentation, legal eligibility, and operational procedures.

For those exploring options such as car rental China for foreigners or independent self drive car rental China arrangements, the platform must clearly surface prerequisites before the final checkout step. Key information areas include:

  • Transparent breakdowns of payment terms and accepted international payment methods.
  • Clear instructions regarding driving-licence eligibility, temporary driving permits, and necessary notarization or translation steps.
  • Explicit details regarding insurance coverage, deductibles, and roadside assistance protocols.
  • Step-by-step guidance for vehicle handover, inspection protocols, and return instructions.

Note: Driving and vehicle operation regulations in mainland China are subject to specific national and local laws. Product teams must encourage users to verify official regulatory requirements directly with local authorities rather than relying solely on platform-generated summaries.

Build Useful Discovery Paths for Different Journeys

Different travel scenarios demand tailored discovery paths. A user planning a weekend getaway requires a very different set of informational cues compared to someone booking a multi-week expedition.

For specialized itineraries—such as an adventure motorcycle rental China arrangement for remote mountain passes or planning a multi-stop motorcycle road trip China expedition—the interface should highlight journey-specific attributes. These may include permitted travel zones, provider-approved maintenance support networks, luggage mounting accessories, and long-term rental tier pricing. Structuring search facets around journey types helps users evaluate whether a selected vehicle can safely and legally support their intended route.

Localize the Marketplace, Not Just the Keywords

True localization extends far beyond swapping out country names in a template. When developing a discovery platform tailored to a specific region, product and engineering teams must audit the entire interface for mismatched regional templates, legacy terminology, and incorrect currency or regulatory references.

Common localization debt to eliminate during content and code audits includes:

  • Accidental retention of regional identification terminology or local regulatory codes from unrelated jurisdictions.
  • Mismatched currency symbols or pricing models that do not reflect local financial structures.
  • Outdated support contact information or registration language.
  • Generic city pages that lack verified local inventory or feature mismatched geographic descriptions.

Conducting rigorous content and data audits ensures that every touchpoint respects the operational reality of the target market.

A Practical Marketplace Quality Checklist

To help product teams evaluate their mobility discovery workflows, consider this foundational quality framework:

  • [ ] Search filters correspond accurately to available vehicle categories and regional inventories.
  • [ ] Listing locations use structured, hierarchical data rather than ambiguous text strings.
  • [ ] Pricing disclosures clearly separate base rental fees from deposits and optional charges.
  • [ ] Documentation and licensing requirements are prominently displayed prior to booking initiation.
  • [ ] Provider metadata, including operational hours and pickup instructions, is updated consistently.
  • [ ] Mobile layouts prioritize essential booking attributes and map-based pickup details.
  • [ ] Legal, insurance, and safety disclaimers are verified against current local regulations.

Where MotoShare.com.cn Fits

Platforms like MotoShare.com.cn illustrate these marketplace principles in practice by operating as a specialized discovery and booking ecosystem connecting international travelers, local commuters, and road-trip enthusiasts with independent rental providers across China. By focusing on direct vehicle discovery, transparent pricing structures, flexible rental durations—spanning hourly options to extended weekly bookings—and zero additional platform booking fees, such platforms highlight how structured inventory and clear location data streamline the transition from a broad travel aspiration to a confident reservation.

Conclusion

Building a dependable vehicle-rental discovery experience requires treating location, inventory consistency, and eligibility requirements as core architectural components. By modeling user intent accurately, structuring geographic data, maintaining transparent listing schemas, and avoiding generic localization shortcuts, engineering and product teams can construct marketplaces that turn complex travel logistics into a seamless, trustworthy user experience.

title: Why Java Developers Use Maven (and Not javac by Hand)
description:
When I wrote my first real Java project, I had a folder of .java files, a folder of JAR files I had downloaded by hand and a very long javac command that I kept in a text file. When a teammate cloned the project, it didn't compile on their machine. Their JAR versions were different, their folders were different and the command had to be changed.

That's the problem Maven solves. You describe your project in one file, and one short command builds it the same way on every machine: it downloads the libraries, compiles the code, runs the tests and packages everything into a JAR or WAR.

In this post, we'll cover what build tools are, why we need them, how Maven works, what pom.xml is, the full archetype:generate command, Maven's terms (group id, artifact id, version, packaging), dependencies, goals, repositories and the three build lifecycles. I've drawn the important pictures in text so you can see how the pieces fit.

A note about versions: I'm using Maven 3.9.x, the stable line at the time of writing. Everything here works the same in newer versions.

Part 1: Build tools and why we need them

What is a build tool?

A build tool is a program that automates the steps between your source code and a finished, runnable application. Instead of running those steps by hand, you describe them once, and the tool repeats them exactly the same way every time.

The journey of your code

Every Java project goes through the same steps:

   source code        byte code          unit tests          package            build output
    (.java)    -->    (.class)    -->    (JUnit)     -->    (zip it up)  -->   .jar or .war
       |                  |                  |                   |
    you write          javac             check that         deployable
                       compiles          the code works     format
  • Compile: javac turns .java files into .class bytecode.
  • Test: unit tests check that your code behaves correctly.
  • Package: the .class files and resources are bundled into one file. A JAR (Java ARchive) is for libraries and normal applications. A WAR (Web ARchive) is for web applications that run on a server like Tomcat.

Doing it by hand

Without a build tool, here's what a tiny project with one library needs:

javac -cp lib/gson-2.11.0.jar -d out src/com/example/App.java
java  -cp out:lib/gson-2.11.0.jar com.example.App
jar cf app.jar -C out .

(On Windows, the classpath separator is ; instead of :.)

That's already awkward for one library and one file. Now imagine 200 files, 30 libraries, tests and three developers. The real problems are:

  • Downloading libraries by hand. You have to find each JAR, pick a version and put it in a folder.
  • Libraries need other libraries. Library A needs B, which needs C. You'd have to find all of them yourself.
  • Version clashes. Two libraries need different versions of the same one. This is nicknamed "JAR hell."
  • "Works on my machine." Everyone's folders and versions are slightly different.
  • Long manual steps. Compile, test and package in the right order, every time.

Dependency management

A dependency is a library your project needs. Dependency management means the tool finds, downloads and organizes those libraries for you. You just say what you need, with a name and a version, and the tool does the rest, including the libraries that your libraries need.

   WITHOUT a build tool                        WITH Maven

   you --> search the web for gson.jar         you --> write 5 lines in pom.xml
   you --> download it, copy to lib/                    |
   you --> find the jars gson needs                     v
   you --> fix the classpath by hand           Maven --> downloads gson + what it needs
   you --> repeat for every library                     and puts them on the classpath

The popular build tools

  • Ant: an early tool. You write every step yourself in build.xml. Flexible, but a lot of manual work.
  • Maven: you follow standard conventions and describe the project in pom.xml. Dependencies are built in. This is what we're learning.
  • Gradle: similar goals to Maven, but build files are written in Groovy or Kotlin code instead of XML, and it's known for fast, incremental builds.

All three are used in real projects. Maven is the most common starting point, and its ideas (repositories, coordinates, lifecycles) show up everywhere.

Part 2: What is Apache Maven?

Apache Maven is a build automation and dependency management tool, mostly used for Java. Its name comes from a word meaning "accumulator of knowledge." The key idea is the POM (Project Object Model): a file called pom.xml that describes your project.

What does Maven do?

  1. Project structure. It gives every project the same standard folder layout.
  2. Dependencies. It downloads the libraries you list, and the ones they need.
  3. Unit tests. It runs your tests (for example, with JUnit) automatically.
  4. Compile. It compiles your code with the right Java settings.
  5. Package. It builds a deployable file (JAR or WAR).

And a few more: it can install the result into your local library folder, deploy it to a shared server, and generate project reports and documentation.

How does Maven do it?

Maven works on two simple ideas:

1. Convention over configuration. If you put files in the standard places and follow the standard naming, you don't have to configure anything. Maven already knows where your code and tests are, and where to put the output.

2. Plugins do the real work. Maven itself is a small "coordinator." It reads your pom.xml, decides which steps to run in which order, and hands each step to a plugin. The compiler plugin compiles, the surefire plugin runs tests, the jar plugin builds the JAR.

Here is what happens when you type one command:

   mvn package
      |
      v
   1. Maven reads pom.xml
      |
      v
   2. Works out the lifecycle: validate -> compile -> test -> package
      |
      v
   3. For each step, runs the plugin goal attached to it
        compile  ->  compiler plugin   (javac)
        test     ->  surefire plugin   (runs JUnit tests)
        package  ->  jar plugin        (builds the .jar)
      |
      v
   4. Needs a library or plugin? Looks in the local repository,
      and downloads it from the internet if it's missing
      |
      v
   5. Puts all results in the "target" folder

Install and check

Maven needs a JDK, and the JAVA_HOME environment variable should point to it. After installing Maven, check it:

mvn -v

You'll see something like this (your numbers will differ):

Apache Maven 3.9.x
Maven home: /opt/maven
Java version: 17.0.x, vendor: ...

Look at the Java version line. Maven uses whichever JDK it finds, so make sure it's the one you intend.

The standard project structure

Every Maven project looks like this:

   my-app/
   |-- pom.xml                      <- the project description
   |-- src/
   |    |-- main/
   |    |    |-- java/              <- your application code (.java)
   |    |    +-- resources/         <- config files, images, etc.
   |    +-- test/
   |         |-- java/              <- your unit tests
   |         +-- resources/         <- files used only by tests
   +-- target/                      <- created by Maven: all build output
  • src/main is code that goes into your finished application.
  • src/test is code that only checks it. It's never packaged.
  • target is created by Maven. It holds the compiled classes, test reports and the JAR. You can delete it any time and nothing is lost.

Because everyone uses this layout, you can open any Maven project in the world and find your way around.

pom.xml

The POM (Project Object Model) is the heart of a Maven project. Here's a small but complete example:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
                             http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">

  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>my-app</artifactId>
  <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>

  <name>my-app</name>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
      <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
      <version>5.11.0</version>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
        <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>3.5.0</version>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>

What each part means:

  • modelVersion: the version of the POM format. It's always 4.0.0.
  • groupId, artifactId, version: the project's identity (we'll explain them in a moment).
  • packaging: what kind of file to build (jar is the default).
  • name: a friendly name for humans.
  • properties: settings and variables. maven.compiler.release is the Java version to compile for (set it to your JDK version, like 17 or 21), and the encoding avoids platform surprises.
  • dependencies: the libraries you need.
  • build / plugins: extra configuration for the build. Here we pin the test plugin version, which also makes sure JUnit 5 tests are found. Pinning plugin versions makes builds repeatable.

Behind the scenes: your POM is tiny

Your pom.xml looks short because it inherits from a hidden built-in file called the Super POM. It holds all the defaults: the folder layout, the repository address and the default plugins. Maven merges the Super POM and your POM into one effective POM. You can see the full result:

mvn help:effective-pom

It's long, but it shows you everything Maven is actually using.

Creating a project: mvn archetype:generate

You can create the folders and pom.xml by hand, but Maven can generate a ready-made project from a template. That's what archetype:generate does. Here's the full command:

mvn archetype:generate \
  -DgroupId=com.example \
  -DartifactId=my-app \
  -DarchetypeArtifactId=maven-archetype-quickstart \
  -DarchetypeVersion=1.5 \
  -DinteractiveMode=false

(On Windows Command Prompt, write it on one line without the \ characters.)

Let's break it down piece by piece:

  • mvn: runs Maven.
  • archetype:generate: this is plugin:goal. It means "use the archetype plugin and run its generate goal."
  • -D: sets a property. Each option is written as -Dname=value.
  • -DgroupId=com.example: the group id of your new project (usually your reversed domain or company).
  • -DartifactId=my-app: the name of your project. Maven also creates a folder with this name.
  • -DarchetypeArtifactId=maven-archetype-quickstart: which template to use. The quickstart template makes a simple Java project with a sample class and a sample test.
  • -DarchetypeVersion=1.5: the version of that template. Version 1.5 generates a project that uses JUnit 5. (If your Maven can't find it, remove this option, and Maven will pick a version for you.)
  • -DinteractiveMode=false: don't ask questions. Without it, Maven asks you for the template version, the package name and a final confirmation.

Two extra options you may see:

  • -Dversion=1.0-SNAPSHOT: the starting version (this is already the default).
  • -Dpackage=com.example.app: the Java package for the sample classes. If you skip it, it defaults to the group id.

The first run downloads the archetype and some plugins from the internet, so it takes a little while. When it finishes, you'll see BUILD SUCCESS, and this project:

   my-app/
   |-- pom.xml
   +-- src/
        |-- main/java/com/example/App.java
        +-- test/java/com/example/AppTest.java

The generated App.java is a simple "Hello World" with a main method. Open the generated pom.xml and check the Java version property. If it's older than your JDK, change maven.compiler.release to your Java version (for example 17 or 21).

Maven terminology

Archetype

An archetype is a project template. It's a pattern for creating new projects, like a "starter kit." Besides maven-archetype-quickstart, there are archetypes for web applications and more.

Maven coordinates: groupId, artifactId, version

Every project and library in the Maven world is identified by three values, called its coordinates (or GAV):

  • groupId: who it belongs to. Usually a reversed domain, like Java packages: com.example, org.junit.jupiter.
  • artifactId: the name of the project or library: my-app, gson.
  • version: which version: 1.0-SNAPSHOT, 2.11.0.

Together they point to exactly one thing, anywhere in the world:

   com.google.code.gson : gson : 2.11.0
        groupId          artifactId   version

The coordinates also decide where the file lives in a repository, which is just a folder path:

   com.example : my-app : 1.0-SNAPSHOT
         |
         v   dots in groupId become folders
   com/example/my-app/1.0-SNAPSHOT/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

Version: SNAPSHOT vs release

  • A version that ends in -SNAPSHOT (like 1.0-SNAPSHOT) means work in progress. It can change as you keep developing. Maven treats it as "may have a newer build," and can check for updates.
  • A version without -SNAPSHOT (like 1.0.0) is a release. It's a fixed, finished version. Once a release is published to a public repository such as Maven Central, it can never be changed or replaced.

A typical life of a version: 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT while you build it, then you publish 1.0.0 (the release), then you start 1.1.0-SNAPSHOT for the next work. A good tip is to follow a clear numbering scheme, such as major.minor.patch.

Packaging type

packaging tells Maven what to build from your project. It also decides which plugin goals run at each step of the lifecycle.

  • jar (the default): a library or a normal application.
  • war: a web application for a server like Tomcat.
  • pom: no code of its own. Used for parent projects that group other projects.
  • ear: an enterprise application (less common today).

Maven dependencies

A dependency is declared with its coordinates:

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.google.code.gson</groupId>
    <artifactId>gson</artifactId>
    <version>2.11.0</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
</xml>

Save the file, and Maven downloads the library the next time you build. Now you can use it in your code right away:

import com.google.gson.Gson;
import java.util.Map;

public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Gson gson = new Gson();
        System.out.println(gson.toJson(Map.of("name", "Asha")));
    }
}

Output:

{"name":"Asha"}

No JAR downloads and no classpath editing.

Scope: when is the dependency needed?

The <scope> tag says when a library is needed:

  • compile (default): needed to compile and run. It's packaged with your app.
  • test: only for compiling and running tests, like JUnit. Not packaged.
  • provided: needed to compile, but the server provides it when running (for example, the servlet API on Tomcat). Not packaged.
  • runtime: not needed to compile, but needed when running (for example, a database driver).

Using the right scope keeps your final package small and clean.

Transitive dependencies

Libraries often depend on other libraries. If you add library A, and A needs B, Maven fetches B too. These are called transitive dependencies. You can see the whole tree:

mvn dependency:tree

[INFO] com.example:my-app:jar:1.0-SNAPSHOT
[INFO] +- com.google.code.gson:gson:jar:2.11.0:compile
[INFO] \- org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:jar:5.11.0:test
[INFO]    +- org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter-api:jar:5.11.0:test
[INFO]    ...

(The list is trimmed here. Maven also shows the libraries that each one needs, indented underneath.)

What if two libraries need different versions of the same third library? Maven uses a simple rule: the version nearest to your project wins. If they're equally near, the first one declared wins.

   my-app
     |-- lib-a 1.0
     |      +-- lib-b 2.0      (two steps away)
     +-- lib-c 1.0
            +-- lib-b 1.5      (two steps away: a tie, so the first one, 2.0, wins)

   To take control, declare lib-b yourself in your pom.xml. A direct dependency is nearest.

Maven goals and phases

Here's an important distinction:

  • A goal is one specific task done by a plugin. It's written as plugin:goal, like compiler:compile or surefire:test.
  • A phase is a named step in a lifecycle, like compile or test. Each phase has goals attached to it.

When you run a phase, Maven runs every earlier phase first, then the goals attached to that one. You can also run a goal directly, like mvn archetype:generate.

The commands you'll use most:

  • mvn clean: deletes the target folder, so you start fresh.
  • mvn compile: compiles the main code.
  • mvn test: compiles, then runs the unit tests.
  • mvn package: runs the tests, then builds the JAR (or WAR).
  • mvn install: packages, then copies the result into your local repository, so other projects on your machine can use it.
  • mvn deploy: uploads the package to a remote repository for others to use.

Here is what a run looks like. This is a trimmed mvn package:

[INFO] --- resources:3.x:resources (default-resources) @ my-app ---
[INFO] --- compiler:3.x:compile (default-compile) @ my-app ---
[INFO] Compiling 1 source file with javac [debug release 17] to target/classes
[INFO] --- surefire:3.5.0:test (default-test) @ my-app ---
[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] --- jar:3.x:jar (default-jar) @ my-app ---
[INFO] Building jar: /.../my-app/target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

(Version numbers on your screen will differ.) Each --- plugin:version:goal --- line is one goal running. You can see Maven working through the lifecycle: resources, compile, test, jar.

Testing with JUnit

Let's write a real class and test. Create src/main/java/com/example/Calculator.java:

package com.example;

public class Calculator {
    public int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

And the test, src/test/java/com/example/CalculatorTest.java:

package com.example;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class CalculatorTest {
    @Test
    void addsTwoNumbers() {
        assertEquals(5, new Calculator().add(2, 3));
    }
}

mvn test

[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

Now break the test on purpose, by changing 5 to 6, and run mvn package:

[ERROR] Tests run: 1, Failures: 1, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD FAILURE

Look what didn't happen: no JAR was created. The test phase failed, so Maven stopped before the package phase. That's the value of the lifecycle: broken code can't become a package by accident.

Maven's test plugin finds tests by name. By default it looks for classes named *Test, Test*, *Tests or *TestCase, in src/test/java.

Running your JAR

After mvn package, your JAR is in target/. If you try to run it like a normal application:

java -jar target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

no main manifest attribute, in target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

The JAR doesn't say which class has main. You can run it by naming the class:

java -cp target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.example.App

Or make the JAR runnable by telling the jar plugin about your main class, in pom.xml:

<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-jar-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.4.2</version>
      <configuration>
        <archive>
          <manifest>
            <mainClass>com.example.App</mainClass>
          </manifest>
        </archive>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

(If your app uses outside libraries, you'd need another plugin, such as the shade or assembly plugin, to bundle them into one "fat" JAR.)

Maven repositories

A repository is a storage place for libraries and plugins, organized by their coordinates. Maven uses three kinds:

  • Local repository: a folder on your own computer, by default ~/.m2/repository. It's a cache of everything you've downloaded, plus anything you install.
  • Central repository: Maven Central, the huge public repository on the internet. It's where most open-source libraries live, and Maven uses it by default.
  • Remote repository: any other server. Companies often run their own (with tools such as Nexus or Artifactory) for private libraries, and to cache Central.

When Maven needs a library, it follows this search:

   Need gson 2.11.0
        |
        v
   1. Local repository  (~/.m2/repository)  --- found? ---> use it (no internet needed)
        | not found
        v
   2. Remote repositories you configured (company server)  --- found? ---+
        | not found                                                      |
        v                                                                v
   3. Maven Central (internet)  --- found? ---> download ---------> save a copy in
                                                                      the local repository

Because of that last step, each library is downloaded only once. Later builds use the local copy, and you can even work offline with mvn -o.

How the lifecycle phases connect to repositories:

  • install copies your JAR into the local repository.
  • deploy uploads it to a remote repository (you must configure the server address and your login).

You can configure repositories, mirrors and passwords in a settings.xml file in your .m2 folder.

The Maven build lifecycle

A build lifecycle is a fixed sequence of phases. Maven has three built-in lifecycles: default, clean and site.

1. The default lifecycle (building your project)

These are the main phases, in order:

   validate --> compile --> test --> package --> verify --> install --> deploy
  • validate: checks that the project is correct and the needed information is there.
  • compile: compiles the source code in src/main/java.
  • test: runs unit tests, using the compiled code. The tests don't need to be packaged.
  • package: bundles the compiled code into the packaging type (JAR, WAR).
  • verify: runs any extra checks on the package, like integration tests and quality rules.
  • install: copies the package into the local repository.
  • deploy: copies the final package to a remote repository for sharing.

(The real lifecycle has more phases in between, such as generate-sources, process-resources and test-compile. The ones above are the ones you'll use directly.)

The key rule: when you run a phase, Maven runs all the phases before it, in order.

   mvn compile   runs:  validate, compile
   mvn test      runs:  validate, compile, test
   mvn package   runs:  validate, compile, test, package
   mvn install   runs:  validate, compile, test, package, verify, install

You never need to run mvn compile and then mvn test separately. Just run the last phase you want.

What runs in each phase?

Each phase has plugin goals attached, and which ones depend on your packaging type. For a normal jar project:

   PHASE        GOAL THAT RUNS               WHAT IT DOES
   compile      compiler:compile             javac on src/main/java
   test         surefire:test                runs the unit tests
   package      jar:jar                      builds the .jar
   install      install:install              copies it to ~/.m2
   deploy       deploy:deploy                uploads to a remote repository

   For packaging "war":   package runs  war:war  instead of  jar:jar

This answers the question "how does Maven know what to do?" The packaging type chooses which goals are attached to which phases. That's why <packaging> matters.

2. The clean lifecycle

This one cleans up. It has three phases: pre-clean, clean and post-clean. In practice you use only clean, which deletes the target folder.

mvn clean

It's the way to get rid of old compiled files, so nothing stale is left behind. You'll often combine it with the default lifecycle:

mvn clean package

Maven runs clean (the clean lifecycle) first, then the default lifecycle up to package.

3. The site lifecycle

This one creates project documentation and reports. Its phases are pre-site, site, post-site and site-deploy.

mvn site

It generates a website describing your project (test reports, dependency lists, and so on) in target/site. It's optional, and less common in day-to-day work than the other two.

What's inside target/ after a build? 

   target/
   |-- classes/                      <- compiled main code (.class)
   |-- test-classes/                 <- compiled test code
   |-- surefire-reports/             <- test result reports
   +-- my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar       <- the packaged result

A few tips and commands

  • Skip tests when you must (for example, to package quickly): mvn package -DskipTests. This still compiles the tests. -Dmaven.test.skip=true skips compiling them too. Don't make this a habit, since tests are your safety net.
  • Run one test class: mvn test -Dtest=CalculatorTest
  • Force re-download of snapshots and failed items: mvn package -U
  • Work offline: mvn -o package
  • See the dependency tree: mvn dependency:tree
  • See the full merged POM: mvn help:effective-pom

Which one should I use?

  • mvn package, verify or install? Use package to build the JAR. Use verify when you also want the extra checks. Use install when another project on your machine needs this one as a dependency.
  • mvn clean package or just package? Use clean when you want a guaranteed fresh build, for example after renaming or deleting files, so old .class files don't linger.
  • JAR or WAR? A JAR for libraries and normal applications. A WAR for web apps that go on a server like Tomcat. (Frameworks such as Spring Boot also build runnable JARs with an embedded server.)
  • SNAPSHOT or release? Use -SNAPSHOT while developing. Publish a release version when something is finished and tagged, because releases never change.
  • Which scope? test for testing libraries, provided for things the server gives you, runtime for things only needed when running, and compile for everything else.
  • Archetype or generator website? For plain Java, an archetype is great. For Spring Boot projects, most people use the Spring Initializr website, which creates a ready Maven project.
  • Maven or Gradle? Both work well. Maven is more standard and predictable. Gradle is more flexible and often faster on big builds. Learning Maven first gives you the concepts that both share.

Common mistakes

  1. JAVA_HOME or Java version problems. If mvn -v shows the wrong Java, or fails, fix JAVA_HOME. Also set maven.compiler.release in pom.xml to match your JDK.
  2. Running java -jar on a JAR with no main class. You get "no main manifest attribute." Set the main class in the jar plugin, or run it with -cp and the class name.
  3. Wrong folders or test names. Code outside src/main/java, or tests outside src/test/java or not named like *Test, are silently ignored. "No tests to run" usually means this.
  4. Skipping tests all the time. -DskipTests hides real problems. Use it rarely.
  5. Version surprises. Using SNAPSHOT dependencies in something you release, or two libraries needing different versions of a third. Check with mvn dependency:tree, and declare the version you want directly.
  6. Stale or broken builds. Old classes in target/ or a half-downloaded file in ~/.m2 can cause strange errors. Run mvn clean, and use -U to force a fresh download.

Quick recap

  • A build tool automates compile, test, package and dependency handling, so builds are repeatable on every machine.
  • Dependency management means you declare what you need, and the tool downloads it, including what your libraries need.
  • The code journey: .java → .class → unit tests → package → .jar / .war.
  • Maven follows convention over configuration. It reads pom.xml, runs the lifecycle, and uses plugins to do each step.
  • The standard layout: src/main/java, src/main/resources, src/test/java, and output in target/.
  • pom.xml holds the project's identity (groupId, artifactId, version, packaging), properties, dependencies and plugins. It inherits defaults from the Super POM.
  • mvn archetype:generate creates a project from a template. -D options set properties.
  • Coordinates (groupId:artifactId:version) identify anything uniquely. -SNAPSHOT means in development, and a release never changes.
  • Packaging (jar, war, pom) decides what is built.
  • Goals are plugin tasks (plugin:goal). Phases are lifecycle steps. Running a phase runs all earlier ones.
  • Repositories: local (~/.m2), central (Maven Central) and remote (company servers). install goes to local, deploy goes to remote.
  • Lifecycles: default (validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy), clean (deletes target) and site (generates documentation).

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: generate a project with the archetype:generate command from this post. Add the Calculator class and CalculatorTest, run mvn test, and then break the test on purpose and run mvn package to see that no JAR gets built. Fix it, run mvn clean package, and find your JAR in target/. Finally, run mvn dependency:tree and mvn help:effective-pom and see how much Maven was doing for you.

For a bonus experiment, add the Gson dependency, print some JSON from your App, and then look inside ~/.m2/repository/com/google/code/gson to see the exact folder path your coordinates turned into.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Trace Evolution Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Improve from Their Own Environment Traces
description:
arXiv:2610.15055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after an update minus success before. That difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. We introduce Trace Evolution Bench (TEB), a protocol that separates that rescore from a context or weight update, together with three frozen 80/20/40 packs. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out identifiers never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The primary scoreboard is coding, graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace. On that pack (40 held-out tasks, one family), DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds. Of nine text-update cells inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, seven have positive excess above that seed's own band, and one gepa_llm seed moves down by the width of its band (-12.5, regression 0.48). GLM and MiniMax do not reproduce that seven-of-nine pattern. No method stays above its own band on every seed of all three models: GLM has two paired cells above their own bands, and MiniMax expel_llm seed 44 is a third (regression 0.30). The methods were fixed on a validation screen before held-out was read. Office, graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA are separate packs: office DeepSeek does not exceed its own bands (widest 17.5 points), and manufacturing has no paired positive excess beyond its seed band.

title: Your Swap Screen Is Showing the Wrong Number
description:
A month ago I wrote about what a crypto app should do before you press "Send". There's one more thing that happens before that button, and most swap interfaces still get it wrong: the number they put in the biggest font.

Usually it's the exchange rate. 1 XMR = 0.12 ETH. Clean, comparable, easy to sort.

It's also the least useful figure on the screen.

What lands in the user's wallet is an amount. Between the rate and that amount sit several costs the rate doesn't show.

One quote, four costs

Cross-chain swaps make this easy to see, because each leg has its own costs. Take Monero to Ethereum. CoinMarketCal recently published a breakdown of XMR to ETH exchange fees and counted four separate costs behind a single quote:

XMR network fee   → paid by the user, from their own wallet
Provider fees     → trading fees charged by liquidity sources
Spread            → gap between the market price and the offered rate
ETH payout fee    → gas to send ETH to the user's address

Only the first one is under the user's control. The Monero fee depends on network load and transaction size, not on the amount sent, and wallets let you choose from four priority levels. Everything else is decided by the provider.

The Ethereum side has its own formula. According to ethereum.org, a transaction costs gas units multiplied by the base fee plus a priority fee. A plain ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. The base fee can move by up to 12.5% per block with demand, so the same payout can cost noticeably more at a busy moment.

None of this shows up in "1 XMR = 0.12 ETH".

Better rate, worse result

Here's a simple case. Two quotes for a 2 XMR swap (the numbers are illustrative):

  • Quote A shows a rate of 0.12000 ETH, charges a 0.1% trading fee, and takes a 0.002 ETH withdrawal fee afterwards.
  • Quote B shows 0.11925 ETH, with every cost after the deposit already included.

Sort by rate and A wins. Now compute what actually arrives:

function rankByReceived(quotes) {
  return quotes
    .map((q) => ({
      name: q.name,
      received: Number(
        (q.amountIn * q.rate * (1 - q.tradingFee) - q.fixedFees).toFixed(6)
      ),
    }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.received - a.received);
}

rankByReceived([
  { name: "A", amountIn: 2, rate: 0.12, tradingFee: 0.001, fixedFees: 0.002 },
  { name: "B", amountIn: 2, rate: 0.11925, tradingFee: 0, fixedFees: 0 },
]);
// [ { name: "B", received: 0.2385 }, { name: "A", received: 0.23776 } ]

B pays out more. The gap is small here, but a UI that ranks by rate picks the wrong option every time this pattern appears. And it appears a lot, because "no fees" usually means the fees moved into the spread or into a step that comes later.

The rate wasn't lying. It answered a question the user didn't ask.

Small swaps hurt the most

Network fees are roughly fixed per transaction. They don't scale with the amount, so their share grows as the swap gets smaller.

const feeShare = (receivedEth, fixedFeesEth) => fixedFeesEth / receivedEth;

feeShare(0.24, 0.002); // ≈ 0.0083 → 0.8%
feeShare(0.03, 0.002); // ≈ 0.0667 → 6.7%

Same fees, eight times the impact. This is also why providers set minimum amounts: below a certain point, fees eat most of the order. A screen that shows only the rate hides this completely. A screen that shows the received amount makes it visible the moment someone types a small number.

What the quote object should carry

If I were designing the API behind a swap screen, the response would put the received amount first and say what's inside it:

{
  "amountIn": { "value": "2.0", "asset": "XMR" },
  "amountOut": { "value": "0.2385", "asset": "ETH" },
  "rateMode": "floating",
  "includedInQuote": ["spread", "provider fees", "ETH payout fee"],
  "paidSeparately": ["XMR network fee"],
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-15T12:00:00Z"
}

amountOut is the headline. Anyone who wants the rate can derive it.

includedInQuote and paidSeparately matter more than they look. Two quotes are only comparable if they cover the same costs. Without these fields, the frontend has no way to tell whether it's comparing like with like.

rateMode tells the user what kind of promise they're getting. A floating quote follows the market until execution and can land slightly above or below the estimate. A fixed quote locks the amount for a limited window, usually with a small buffer priced in for volatility. Both are fine. Hiding which one it is isn't.

expiresAt is there for fixed quotes. A locked amount with no visible deadline is a support ticket waiting to happen.

Thin liquidity widens the gap

For pairs with deep markets, the difference between the rate and the received amount stays small. For thinner pairs it grows, and Monero is a good example. Kraken stopped XMR trading and deposits for clients in the European Economic Area from October 31, 2024. Fewer venues usually means wider spreads, and the spread is exactly the cost a rate-first screen never shows.

So the less liquid the asset, the more misleading the headline rate gets. That's the opposite of what users need.

A short checklist for swap screens

  • Lead with the amount the user will receive.
  • Say whether that number is an estimate or a guaranteed amount, and for how long.
  • List what's already included and what the user still pays.
  • Flag amounts close to the minimum, where fixed fees dominate.
  • Compare quotes by received amount, never by rate.

None of this needs new infrastructure. The provider already calculates every one of these numbers to build the quote. The only question is whether the interface passes them on.

People spend what arrives in their wallet. The screen should start there.

title: PII Redaction for Web Scraping: A Practical Python Pipeline
description:
TL;DR:

  • Remove unnecessary personal fields before storing scraped records.
  • Detection and redaction are separate operations with different failure modes.
  • A redaction middleware reduces data exposure; it does not establish GDPR compliance by itself.

A scraping pipeline can collect contact details even when its business task only needs organization names or product descriptions. Those details may enter logs, storage, embeddings, and model prompts before anyone notices them. The useful place to reduce exposure is immediately after extraction and before those downstream systems receive the record.

This tutorial implements a small middleware with Presidio. It uses synthetic contact information, a narrow pattern-based detector, and an explicit storage allowlist. The example is intentionally limited so you can see which entities it recognizes and which responsibilities remain outside the code.

Pipeline at a Glance

The pipeline runs acquisition, extraction, detection, redaction, validation, and storage in that order. Acquisition returns page content. Extraction selects business fields. The privacy stage then examines the selected text and removes recognized contact details before the storage stage receives anything.

Keep this boundary close to extraction. If raw HTML is logged upstream, a later redaction function cannot remove the copy already written to your logs. Treat raw captures as restricted diagnostic material when they may contain personal data, and give them a separate retention policy.

The Scrapeless Web Unlocker guide describes a URL acquisition path. Your middleware remains responsible for the field-level decisions after acquisition.

Identify Fields You Need to Keep

Define the allowed business fields before selecting a detector. If your task needs an organization name, category, and public description, do not persist contact emails merely because the page includes them. An allowlist makes that decision visible in code.

Also distinguish redaction from pseudonymization and anonymization. Removing a matched substring is a text transformation. Replacing a value with a stable token may still let records be linked. An anonymous result requires a broader assessment of whether a person can be identified from the remaining data and available context.

The pseudonymization discussion in the EDPB consultation guidelines explains why replacing an identifier alone does not settle whether a record can be attributed to a person. Whether a particular workflow has an appropriate legal basis, notice, retention policy, or transfer arrangement depends on its circumstances. The middleware below does not answer those questions.

Detect PII with Presidio

Presidio separates recognition from text transformation. Its regular-expression tutorial shows how PatternRecognizer accepts patterns with entity types and scores.

Install the analyzer and anonymizer:

python -m pip install presidio-analyzer presidio-anonymizer

This starter uses pattern recognizers directly. It does not load a language model or claim to identify names, addresses, or all phone formats. Add suitable recognizers and evaluate them against your actual language and data distribution before expanding the scope.

Redact, Tokenize, or Quarantine Records

The following program processes synthetic data, redacts two supported patterns, and writes only approved fields. The example.com email address and phone format are demonstration inputs, not scraped personal information.

import json
from pathlib import Path

from presidio_analyzer import Pattern, PatternRecognizer
from presidio_anonymizer import AnonymizerEngine
from presidio_anonymizer.entities import OperatorConfig

recognizers = [
    PatternRecognizer(
        supported_entity="EMAIL_ADDRESS",
        patterns=[Pattern(
            name="email",
            regex=r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}",
            score=0.8,
        )],
    ),
    PatternRecognizer(
        supported_entity="PHONE_NUMBER",
        patterns=[Pattern(
            name="demo_us_phone",
            regex=r"\b\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}\b",
            score=0.7,
        )],
    ),
]
engine = AnonymizerEngine()
allowed_fields = {"organization", "description", "source_url"}


def detect(text):
    found = []
    for recognizer in recognizers:
        found.extend(recognizer.analyze(
            text=text, entities=recognizer.supported_entities
        ))
    return found


def clean_record(record):
    cleaned = {}
    for key, value in record.items():
        if key not in allowed_fields:
            continue
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("This schema permits string fields only")
        cleaned[key] = engine.anonymize(
            text=value,
            analyzer_results=detect(value),
            operators={"DEFAULT": OperatorConfig("replace", {
                "new_value": "<REDACTED>"
            })},
        ).text
    if any(detect(value) for value in cleaned.values()):
        raise ValueError("Recognized contact data remains")
    return cleaned


synthetic = {
    "organization": "Example Research Lab",
    "description": "Contact sample.person@example.com or 202-555-0143.",
    "source_url": "https://example.com/",
    "raw_contact": "sample.person@example.com",
}
result = clean_record(synthetic)
assert "raw_contact" not in result
assert "sample.person@example.com" not in result["description"]
assert "202-555-0143" not in result["description"]
Path("clean-record.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(result, indent=2), encoding="utf-8"
)
print(result["description"])

The synthetic demonstration prints:

Contact <REDACTED> or <REDACTED>.

The Presidio anonymizer supports different transformations. Choose them deliberately. A reversible transformation needs key management and access rules; a stable replacement can preserve relationships that you may not want to retain.

If a required business field becomes unusable after redaction, quarantine the record for review instead of restoring the removed personal value automatically. Store a reason code without copying the sensitive substring into that reason.

Apply the Middleware to Scrapeless Output

Run the middleware after your parser maps the acquisition response into the declared record schema. Pass only the extracted fields to clean_record, rather than treating every HTML attribute as an approved business field.

For a page fetched through Scrapeless Web Unlocker, the sequence is: check the API envelope, verify page identity, parse the selected content, clean each record, and then export accepted records. A browser session follows the same storage boundary after its extraction step.

Some personal information lives outside body text. Query parameters, document names, images, and free-form metadata need their own treatment. If a URL can identify a person, do not assume it is safe merely because your current contact regex does not match it.

Validate Missed Entities and Retention Rules

A detector needs both positive and negative test cases. Positive cases check that supported personal values are removed. Negative cases check that normal product identifiers, dates, and technical strings are preserved. Include nonstandard formatting and the languages present in your real data.

The final detector call in the code confirms that its own recognized patterns are absent. It cannot detect an entity type the recognizer never supported. Document that scope so the check is not presented as a complete privacy assessment.

Keep raw captures out of routine logs. Record counts, entity types, reason codes, and schema outcomes instead of raw snippets. Define who can review quarantined records and when diagnostic captures are deleted. Apply the same controls to embeddings and model inputs, because those are additional downstream copies.

Conclusion

A practical privacy boundary starts with collecting and storing fewer fields. Add detection and redaction for the fields you still need, test the recognizers on realistic examples, and keep raw diagnostics separate. The software can enforce those decisions consistently once the decisions have been made.

FAQ

Does replacing matched emails make a dataset anonymous?

No. Other fields and contextual information may still identify a person. Anonymity depends on the complete dataset and use context.

Does this code recognize names and addresses?

No. It recognizes its configured email pattern and one demonstration phone format. Additional entity types need their own recognizers and evaluation.

Why use an allowlist as well as a detector?

An allowlist prevents unnecessary fields from reaching storage. Detection handles supported personal values inside fields that remain allowed.

Is a privacy middleware enough for GDPR compliance?

No. The workflow also needs decisions about its purpose, legal basis, transparency, retention, security, and other applicable obligations.

Only collect data you are authorized to access, and review applicable terms and privacy requirements. This article provides technical information, not legal advice.

title: Mycelium’s useful next step: make the liquidity map easier to act on
description:
For developers building Solana dashboards or agent tools, Mycelium Finance offers something concrete to inspect: a map of liquidity connecting its own tokens with partner projects. $MYC is the core token; $ESF is the staking token. The Mycelium Strategy places liquidity across those partner pools. Its free MCP tools expose the allocation, token distribution, pool addresses and selected market data, giving a builder a starting point for checking the project’s claims.

My free tool calls on 15 October 2026 returned a Strategy allocation of $31,984.17 across ten projects. KNOTS accounted for 20.33%, PRCL 14.98%, and KINS 11.78%. Together, those three represented 47.09%, calculated from the reported shares. The remaining allocation included SOL, GABLE, STREAM, GUAC, DREAMS, JUBJUB and USDC. This is a spread across several projects, with a substantial concentration in its largest positions.

There is also a useful distinction inside that allocation. The tool reports both $MYC and $ESF partner pairs, explaining that pools are being migrated from $ESF to $MYC. KNOTS and SOL have both kinds of pair in this snapshot; PRCL is shown through an $ESF pair, while KINS and DREAMS are shown through $MYC pairs. A developer can therefore show the actual pool structure rather than treating every connection as an identical $MYC relationship. The reported pool addresses make that view traceable.

The supply picture adds context. Against one billion minted $MYC, the distribution tool assigns 55.10% to time-locked supply, 23.34% to unlocked LP liquidity, 14.51% to locked LP liquidity, 6.90% to the category called “trading liquidity,” and 0.14% to burned tokens. Percentages are rounded. That “trading” category includes holder wallets and other pools; it is not a measurement of trading volume.

The tool separately defines 447.56 million $MYC as tradable, with 84.58% of that amount in the identified liquidity pools. This is the important denominator: the figure describes token placement within tradable supply, not the share of all minted tokens. It also does not establish executable trade depth, active demand or fee income. Those need different measurements. Locked liquidity positions and time-locked token supply likewise describe different constraints and should stay separate in an interface.

The performers tool provides another check against overinterpreting the allocation. In this snapshot, pinned partner STREAM showed a −0.25% seven-day price change, PRCL −0.87%, and KNOTS −11.84%. These are individual token price changes, not returns earned by the Strategy’s LP positions. The data can support a comparison screen; it cannot, by itself, show that the Strategy outperformed an alternative.

My concrete suggestion is a pool-level connection dashboard: show each partner’s $MYC/$ESF split, its source timestamp, lock status where verifiable, and links to the underlying pools. Add executable quote depth and realized fees when those data are available, with explicit gaps otherwise. That would build on the useful allocation feed while helping partners and agents distinguish liquidity placement from liquidity performance.

Snapshot sources: free get_mycelium_allocation and get_solana_top_performers outputs updated around 04:30:43 UTC; get_mycelium_distribution updated 04:30:12 UTC; get_myc_token_info identifies token roles. All figures come from the saved tool responses or labeled calculations. This is a snapshot analysis, not a forecast.

title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
description:
arXiv:2610.14539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle to articulate rules they know from experience. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance criteria. Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks. We introduce FDE-Bench, the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery tasks that require interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case-specific evaluators assess final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference, is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE-level end-to-end delivery remains out of reach for the evaluated agents on underspecified real-world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at https://baidubce.github.io/FM-Agent/FDE-Bench/.

title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
description:
arXiv:2610.19644v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.

title: AI Mobile Testing: A Complete Guide for QA Teams in 2026
description:
Mobile test automation becomes harder to maintain as applications evolve. A minor UI change can break an automated test even when the app works as expected, while genuine defects can produce similar failures.
AI is changing how QA teams approach these problems, helping them generate tests, adapt automation to supported UI changes, and analyze failures with less manual effort. However, generated tests can still miss requirements, and self-healing test can introduce incorrect steps.
This guide explores how AI is used in mobile testing, practical examples of its capabilities, the tools available, and what QA teams should consider before adopting it.

What is AI mobile testing?

AI mobile testing uses artificial intelligence to interpret natural-language test instructions, identify UI elements, and generate test steps. Unlike traditional automation, which relies on predefined steps and locators that often require manual updates when the UI changes, AI can use the application's current state to adapt tests to supported UI changes.
AI mobile testing can support several parts of the testing process:
Write tests in plain language: Testers describe a test scenario in natural language, and AI interprets it to create a step-by-step user journey.
Understand the app as it runs: AI uses the application's live UI DOM/XML to understand the elements available during test execution and determine how the journey should proceed.
Generate executable automation: The generated journey can be converted into executable automation for established frameworks such as Appium and Selenium.
Validate each step: The system checks each step during execution before moving to the next, helping verify that the journey is progressing as expected.
Adapt to UI changes: When supported UI elements change, AI can use the current application state to identify the corresponding element and adapt the test instead of requiring the automation to be manually rewritten.

Why mobile testing needs AI

Mobile test automation becomes harder to maintain as apps evolve and device coverage expands. UI changes can break tests that rely on predefined locators, while large regression suites make it difficult to distinguish application defects from test failures.
AI can help address these challenges by adapting tests to supported UI changes, prioritizing relevant test coverage, and analyzing failures. However, device and OS fragmentation still requires careful test selection, and physical devices remain important for validating hardware-dependent behavior and network conditions.

1. Device coverage
Teams cannot test every device and OS combination. They need to select the combinations that matter most based on user data and application requirements.

2. Test maintenance
Automated tests depend on locators to identify UI elements. When an element is renamed, moved, or otherwise changed, the test can fail even when the app still works as expected.

3. Failure analysis
Large regression suites can produce many failures. Some may come from application defects, while others result from test instability, changed UI elements, test data, or the test environment. Determining which failures require investigation takes time.

How AI is used across the mobile testing workflow

AI can support several stages of mobile test automation, from creating tests to executing them, adapting them to UI changes, and analyzing the results.

1. Creating tests
AI reduces the manual effort involved in turning a test scenario into automation.

  • Natural-language authoring: A tester describes a test scenario in plain language. The system interprets the intent and converts it into executable test steps.
  • UI-aware test generation: The application's current UI structure, including live DOM or XML information, provides the context needed to identify elements and determine how each step should be performed.
  • Automation generation: Generated steps can be converted into automation that works with frameworks such as Appium and Selenium.
  • Goal-based testing: A tester provides a goal, such as completing a checkout flow. An AI agent determines the required actions, navigates the application, and reports the path it took.

Generated tests still require review. The system may misunderstand the intended behavior or generate an incorrect assertion.

2. Executing tests
Once a test has been generated, AI adds context to its execution and validation.

  • Context-aware execution: The application's current state is used to identify which UI element corresponds to each test step.
  • Step validation: Each action can be checked against the resulting application state before the test moves to the next step.
  • Execution across devices: The same test journey can run across different physical devices and operating system versions to validate behavior across supported device coverage.

3. Maintaining tests
UI changes are a common source of failures in mobile automation. AI reduces the manual effort required to adapt tests to those changes.

  • Element identification: When a UI element's identifier changes, other attributes and the current UI structure can be used to identify the corresponding element.
  • Self-healing: A changed element can be mapped to its updated counterpart instead of requiring the locator to be manually rewritten.
  • Change validation: The updated step can be checked against the application's current state before the test continues.

Self-healing does not determine whether a UI change is correct. A test can still pass after being adapted to the wrong element. Healed steps therefore need review, particularly when the application has undergone significant UI changes.

4. Analyzing results
AI also adds context to the data produced during test execution.

  • Failure analysis: Failed steps can be grouped by patterns and examined in the context of the test, application, and execution environment.
  • Visual analysis: Application screens can be compared to identify meaningful changes, such as an element appearing in the wrong location or overlapping another element.
  • Performance analysis: Performance data can be analyzed across builds, devices, and network conditions to identify regressions and performance issues.
  • Issue prioritization: Detected issues can be surfaced based on their observed impact, helping teams focus investigation on the problems that require attention.

Across these stages, AI does not replace the underlying automation framework or the need for testers to define expected behavior. It adds intelligence to test creation, execution, maintenance, and analysis.

AI mobile testing examples

These examples show how the capabilities above appear in everyday QA work. Each one describes a general scenario, not a specific customer result.

1. A renamed button no longer breaks the test
A release changes the internal identifier of the Login button. A script that relies on that identifier fails, even though the button looks and works the same for users. A self-healing system uses the current UI context and other available attributes to identify the corresponding button, completes the test, and flags the change for review. The test does not need to be manually rewritten just because the identifier changed.

2. A tester writes a test in plain English
A tester enters the instruction, "Search for running shoes, filter by size 10, add the first result to the cart, and confirm the cart shows one item." The system interprets the intent, identifies the relevant UI elements, and converts the instruction into executable test steps. The tester reviews the generated steps and assertions before using the test.

3. An agent explores a checkout flow from a goal
A tester gives an AI agent the goal of buying a product as a guest. The agent opens the app, moves through the screens, fills in generated data, and reports the steps it took and where it got stuck. The tester can turn a successful path into a repeatable test and investigate steps where the agent struggled, which may indicate an unexpected application state or a usability issue.

4. A slowdown shows up on one device
A screen loads in a similar time on a recent flagship phone but takes noticeably longer on an older mid-range device. Regression analysis compares performance across builds and identifies the slowdown along with the device and network conditions where it appears. Testing on physical devices adds hardware and network conditions that emulators cannot fully reproduce, helping teams identify device-specific performance issues.

AI mobile app testing across test types

AI helps different test types in different ways, and none of them removes the need for people or physical devices. The table shows where AI helps most:

AI-Powered Mobile Test Automation with ACE by HeadSpin

What if QA teams could move from describing a test to executing it without writing automation scripts from scratch? ACE by HeadSpin makes this possible, turning plain-English instructions into executable mobile and web test journeys.
ACE captures the application's live DOM/XML to understand its UI, generates automation scripts, and validates each step during execution. Teams can run these tests across real devices and browsers, then use HeadSpin's performance analytics to investigate application behavior and identify issues.

Describe → Generate → Execute → Analyze.

When supported UI elements change, ACE can also use self-healing to reduce the manual effort required to maintain automation.
ACE brings test generation, execution, and performance analysis into one workflow, helping QA teams spend less time writing and maintaining scripts and more time validating application quality.

How to start with AI mobile testing

1. Start with one measurable problem
Choose the part of your testing process that consumes the most time, such as locator maintenance, slow regression cycles, or investigating noisy failures. Starting with one clear problem gives you a baseline for measuring whether AI actually improves the process.

2. Pilot one critical flow
Pick a user journey that matters to the application and changes frequently, such as login, search, or checkout. Keep the initial scope small enough for the team to review generated tests, assertions, and execution results closely.

3. Establish a baseline
Measure the current process before introducing AI. Track metrics such as time spent maintaining tests, false or non-actionable failures, regression execution time, and test coverage. Use the same measures during the pilot to compare the results.

4. Keep human review in the loop
Treat generated tests and self-healed steps as automation that needs validation, not as automatically correct output. Review generated assertions and healed interactions to ensure they still reflect the intended application behavior.

5. Test on representative devices
Run the pilot on the physical devices and OS versions that matter to your users. Device analytics can help prioritize coverage, while physical devices are important for scenarios affected by hardware, sensors, battery, or network conditions.

6. Integrate and expand gradually
Once the pilot produces reliable results, connect the tests to your CI/CD pipeline and run them as part of the regular release process. Expand coverage one flow at a time, using the same measures to determine whether the approach continues to deliver value.

Conclusion

AI mobile testing does not change what mobile QA is for. It changes where the effort goes. Writing tests, keeping them working as the app changes, choosing what to run, and sorting through failures all take less manual work when the right AI capabilities are in place. Deciding what correct behavior is, testing on the devices users actually own, and judging the experience remain human work.

Teams get the most from it by starting with one specific problem, keeping people in the review loop, and choosing tools that show their decisions and export tests in standard formats. Used that way, AI reduces the maintenance and triage work that slows down mobile QA without hiding the defects that QA exists to find.
