title: MontageFlow: Physically Valid High Fidelity EEG Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.14507v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative modeling offers a promising solution to the scarcity of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under strict privacy constraints. Although recent generative models report substantial improvements in generation fidelity, we show that these gains conceal a categorical failure. EEG is not an arbitrary multichannel signal: each channel records the voltage difference between two scalp electrodes. So, real recordings satisfy exact linear identities among their channels. Current generators invariably violate these identities, yet this has gone unnoticed. We therefore propose MontageFlow, a flow-matching model that enforces these identities by restricting its output to signals that satisfy them. We find that ensuring validity improves fidelity too. Furthermore, to retain the EEG characteristics that oversmoothing washes out, we also condition the model on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window. For generation, this vector is drawn from a prior fitted in latent space. Across 3 large-scale benchmarks, our model improves TS-FID by 1.6-3.6$\times$ over the closest rival while ensuring validity.

title: EyeZen v1.2.0: Bringing Local-First Workspace Customization to the Browser
description:
EyeZen v1.2.0: Bringing Local-First Workspace Customization to the Browser

EyeZen v1.2.0 is officially available!

After building the desktop foundation of EyeZen with Rust, Tauri 2, React and TypeScript, I've reached a new milestone: a functional browser edition with local settings persistence and a dedicated documentation website.

Why a web edition?

EyeZen started as a desktop application focused on workspace personalization, comfort preferences, profiles and break routines.

However, many features—such as changing themes, creating profiles and organizing break reminders—don't require access to native operating-system APIs.

Version 1.2.0 makes these capabilities accessible directly from a browser.

What's new in v1.2.0?

1. EyeZen Web

The browser edition includes ten appearance themes, nine starter workspace profiles, customizable profiles, scheduled routines, break reminders and accessibility preferences.

Users can personalize their environment without installing the desktop application.

2. Persistent local browser settings

A major part of this release involved implementing reliable browser persistence.

EyeZen stores settings locally, validates saved data and handles malformed records rather than silently overwriting them.

Settings can also be exported and imported as JSON.

The web and desktop editions use compatible settings schemas, although synchronization is manual rather than automatic.

3. Permission-aware reminders

EyeZen supports optional in-app break reminders and notification functionality.

Browser notification permission is requested through an explicit user interaction.

Reminders depend on the active application or browser tab and remain subject to browser and operating-system restrictions.

4. A new documentation website

Version 1.2.0 also introduces comprehensive public documentation.

It covers:

  • Application features and configuration
  • Web versus desktop compatibility
  • Installation and setup
  • Privacy and local storage
  • Architecture and accessibility
  • Troubleshooting and frequently asked questions

5. Maintaining honest platform boundaries

The browser edition cannot tint unrelated desktop windows, enumerate physical monitors or change hardware brightness.

The installed desktop application retains optional software-based visual tint overlays on supported environments.

Neither edition claims medical benefits or hardware-level display calibration.

Communicating these differences clearly is important when building trustworthy cross-platform software.

Built with open technologies

The project uses:

  • Rust and Tauri 2 for native desktop functionality
  • React and TypeScript for the interface
  • Vite for web builds
  • GitHub Actions for automated builds and deployment
  • GitHub Pages for the static browser application and documentation

EyeZen is open source under the Mozilla Public License 2.0.

Try EyeZen

Web edition: https://sanskarin.github.io/EyeZen/

Documentation: https://sanskarin.github.io/EyeZen/docs/

GitHub release: https://github.com/sanskarIN/EyeZen/releases/tag/v1.2.0

Source code: https://github.com/sanskarIN/EyeZen

What's next?

EyeZen will continue evolving through better workspace customization, platform compatibility, accessibility improvements and stronger real-device testing.

If you use EyeZen or work with Rust, Tauri, TypeScript or cross-platform applications, I'd welcome your feedback and contributions.

What would you prioritize next for EyeZen?

title: PEAM: On-device Communication Agent for Personalized, Efficient and Autonomous Mobile Network Configuration
description:
arXiv:2610.14855v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing deployment of compact large language models on smartphones is enabling autonomous on-device decision-making, such as emerging mobile GUI agents. However, many mobile decisions, such as network configuration when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, must satisfy stringent latency constraints to preserve user experience. In this paper, we propose PEAM, an on-device LLM-based communication agent that autonomously generates personalized network-configuration rules executable within milliseconds. Specifically, PEAM first fine-tune the on-device LLM with a dataset constructed from manually annotated real-user data to integrate the communication knowledge into the local model. PEAM then operates in two phases. In the rule-generation phase, which is performed when the device is idle, such as overnight, PEAM analyzes historical network-configuration records in batches and reflects across batches to consolidate consistent evidence, reduce local bias, and derive robust configuration rules. To enable more accurate and stable rule generation over time, PEAM further constructs a user profile from high-confidence rules to capture the user's network preferences and incorporates this profile into each rule-generation cycle. In the rule-execution phase, PEAM is invoked when the communication context changes, such as when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, and searches the rule library to identify and execute the appropriate rule. Experiments demonstrate that PEAM, based on a fine-tuned 4B model, achieves 99.13% correct network configuration decisions, while 92.50% of the rules generated by PEAM are valid, outperforming the traditional expert-rule based method by 4.41% and 84.50%, respectively.

title: LAMP: 3D Source-Aware Lighting Estimation at Multiple Points
description:
arXiv:2610.19266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing illumination estimation methods primarily recover lighting distributions for rendering, but typically leave the contributions of individual physical light sources at specific scene locations implicit. We address this gap by leveraging the scene understanding capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to connect local illumination with its physical sources. We introduce LAMP, a framework for point-conditioned, source-aware illumination reasoning from a single RGB image with marked query points. LAMP constructs a shared inventory of active light sources, ranks contributing sources for each query, and predicts their 3D query-to-source directions. We supervise these relationships using procedurally controlled indoor scenes, reusing independently rendered source responses to derive contribution targets across lighting configurations and obtaining exact directions from source and query positions. On the Infinigen test set, fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B increases dominant-source 3D PCK@0.5m from 0% to 70.6%, with 94.5% of directions within 12.5 degrees of ground truth among correctly localized sources. Combined with a lightweight network predicting dense RGB irradiance, LAMP achieves probe-rendering quality comparable to prior lighting-estimation methods while additionally localizing individual physical sources in 3D and explicitly attributing local illumination to them.

title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.19013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current scaling law formulations suggest that increasing the number of unique samples in a dataset improves model performance, while repeated exposure to the same samples provides diminishing value. In this work, we examine this assumption for image self-distillation models. Through systematic experiments across diverse datasets, namely Maxar, SATLAS, Waymo, nuPlan, Ego4D, ImageNet, and YFCC15M, we demonstrate that the effects of sample repetition on downstream performance are non-trivial and dataset-dependent. We identify settings where repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on a larger set of unique samples. This finding highlights a limitation of existing scaling laws. To address this gap, we propose a modified version of a Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly accounts for two factors: the number of unique samples and repetition per sample. This formulation provides a framework for understanding data-compute trade-offs and improves prediction in some regimes where repetition plays a central role, although its benefits are not consistent across datasets. Finally, we examine how subset selection and augmentation affect downstream performance.

title: Feasibility of a Patient-Specific Digital Twin for Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Trajectory Planning
description:
arXiv:2610.20074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Catheter obstruction is the commonest cause of shunt failure; freehand insertion at Keen's point leaves the tip free in cerebrospinal fluid in only one case in ten. We built a digital twin that reconstructs skull, scalp, ear and ventricles from preoperative CT by deterministic geometry, searches every entry around Keen's point for the perpendicular trajectory with the longest intraventricular length under safety constraints, and returns the plan as two ruler measurements from the ear and two depths. Executed freehand in 11 consecutive adults (IDEAL Stage 2a), it achieved Hayhurst Grade 1 placement in 10 of 11 against 22 of 213 historically (p = 9 x 10^-9), median entry and angular deviations 2.5 mm and 5.9 degrees, 1.4 cm more intraventricular catheter than Keen's point, and no intraoperative complication. The technique was unchanged; the gain came from choosing entry and depth per patient. Whether it lowers revision is the next stage's hypothesis.

title: Shopify Payments for Mainland China How to Decide Whether to Switch
description:
Mainland Chinese businesses now have an official route to Shopify Payments. As of October 15, 2026, Shopify describes its China offering as early access, available by invitation only, for eligible mainland businesses making cross-border sales. Availability still depends on the individual merchant's invitation and verification outcome. Shopify Payments for China

For a team already operating a store, the useful question is how this option compares with its current payment arrangements. Identify the problem first, then establish how much the new service could address and what a change would require.

Invitation-only access for eligible mainland Chinese businesses making cross-border sales. The accompanying illustration uses Chinese labels.

Match the business entity and the sales activity

The China offering requires a business registered in mainland China, cross-border sales, and a connected and verified WorldFirst account. It does not support domestic sales to customers in mainland China. Hong Kong-registered businesses follow the separate Hong Kong requirements. China requirements

A mainland business selling homeware to overseas consumers can assess this route after receiving an invitation. A store primarily selling to mainland consumers cannot treat a mainland business registration alone as sufficient for domestic payment collection. Teams serving several markets should check the customer location and available payment methods for each relevant scenario.

If payment access was the only reason for considering an overseas entity, the mainland option can now enter the comparison. A business with an existing overseas operation should assess its contracts, bank accounts and day-to-day operations together. The arrival of another payment option alone does not justify restructuring a company.

Evaluate the payment experience in the markets you serve

The China documentation currently lists Visa and Mastercard, plus Shop Pay, Apple Pay and Google Pay. A wallet's visibility also depends on merchant eligibility, account configuration, and the customer's location, device, browser and other requirements. Supported payment methods

Build the comparison around customers' actual circumstances. Which markets generate orders? Do people mostly buy on phones or computers? Which methods do existing customers use? At which stage do payment-failure complaints occur? Those observations provide a better basis for evaluating a switch than adding payment logos to the homepage.

If mobile checkout is the priority, inspect eligible iPhone, Android and desktop-browser scenarios separately. Storefront payment claims should match the methods actually enabled and available. An activated account alone cannot establish that customers have a better purchase experience.

Separate customer currency from payout currency and available funds

The China service sends payouts to a verified WorldFirst account. Accounts without Multi-Currency Payouts settle in HKD; accounts with that capability support HKD and USD payouts. Merchants cannot freely select or change the payout currency in the Shopify admin. China payout rules

Three currencies may matter to the business: the currency the customer pays, the currency the payment service pays out, and the currency the business ultimately needs. A merchant paying suppliers in USD should confirm whether its account supports USD payouts before calculating how to use the proceeds. Pricing a product in dollars does not prove that the payout will arrive in dollars.

Shopify specifies a minimum settlement time of four business days, with an initial settlement potentially taking longer. This is the time from payment capture until funds become available to send to WorldFirst. Further processing can add time. It is not a promise that money will be available in the receiving account on the fourth day. Settlement timing

Plan inventory purchases, supplier payments and advertising budgets against funds actually available. Order revenue, pending payouts and credited balances represent different stages of the same cash flow.

Minimum settlement and actual arrival are separate milestones. USD payouts depend on account capability. The accompanying illustration uses Chinese labels.

Compare the whole transaction before comparing the rate

Official guidance says rates depend on the subscription plan. After activation, the store's applicable rates can be viewed at Settings → Payments → Shopify Payments → Manage. Do not apply a US or Hong Kong rate, or an unattributed figure circulating online, to a mainland invitation account. Where to check rates

Use a set of actual existing business statements as the baseline. Keep the sales market, order values and reporting period comparable, then record:

  • The amount and currency paid by the customer, and how payment-processing fees are calculated.
  • The amount and currency paid to the receiving account, including any currency conversion or other disclosed charges.
  • The observed time until funds arrive, and the effect of refunds, disputes or adjustments on the balance.
  • The work required to issue refunds, investigate exceptions and reconcile accounts.

Where the new option has no actual statement yet, use the merchant's formal quote or account terms and mark the item for later verification. Missing price information should not become a zero-cost assumption. An invented percentage makes the comparison look complete while making the decision less reliable.

Some stores need fewer payment failures. Others need simpler reconciliation or a more suitable payout currency. Define the present problem before judging whether a switch justifies verification, integration checks and staff training.

Choose the next action according to the store's position

An invited merchant can check its entity and business eligibility, obtain its applicable fees, payout conditions and verification requirements, and prepare a testing and transition plan. Eligibility, actual available capabilities and business value are separate decisions.

A merchant without an invitation should plan its launch around payment options it can actually apply for and that suit its business. Preparing accurate information and following official updates are reasonable steps; committing a launch to access it has not received is not.

A store with a stable existing provider should first collect evidence of the problems it wants to solve. A transition plan also needs owners for the old provider's balance, historical refunds and disputes. Routing new orders through another service does not settle those earlier obligations.

During WorldFirst verification, Shopify's setup guidance allows the existing provider to remain in place so that checkout can keep working. Keep that continuity in the transition plan. Switching guidance

Assess eligibility, actual costs and the funding cycle before changing providers. The accompanying illustration uses Chinese labels.

What the Shopify design and development work should cover

Payment setup affects several parts of a store. In WESWOO's Shopify design and development work, product-page payment information, cart entry points, available checkout methods and order processing belong in the same acceptance review. Customers should see payment claims consistent with the store's actual configuration.

The practical work includes checking mobile payment entry points and errors, reviewing the path back after a cancellation or failure, and verifying that custom features and business systems handle orders according to the correct payment state. Operations and finance should also be able to locate the corresponding transaction records. These checks support a clearer handover and faster troubleshooting; invitations and merchant approval remain decisions for the platform and relevant service providers.

A useful first deliverable is a one-page payment comparison: the current problem, existing costs and observed funding times, confirmed conditions for the new account, and the items still awaiting verification. That record gives the business a concrete basis for deciding whether to switch.

Full English source: https://www.weswoo.com/shopify-payments-mainland-china-eligibility-costs-switching/

title: Half-open delivery zones: the shared street belongs to exactly one
description:
Draw two delivery zones against the same street and you get a line of addresses sitting exactly on the boundary, and a containment test that is inclusive on both sides hands those doorsteps to two stores at once. Make it exclusive on both sides and nobody gets them. The seam between two zones is not a business question, so a business rule should not be the thing that answers it: the crossing test itself can be half-open, and then a shared edge belongs to exactly one zone by construction.

An overlap is deliberate; a seam is arithmetic

Overlapping coverage is normal, and we design for it. A city-wide hub ring and one store's own ring routinely cover the same district, and which of them serves an address is a rule the business owns: priority, smallest area, nearest store. Our delivery-zones library (https://github.com/shipmindlabs/delivery-zones) keeps that separation. zones_containing collects every match in the order the zones were declared and hands the list to a policy, and the default policy keeps all of them, because picking a winner belongs to the caller rather than to the index.

A seam looks like the same problem and isn't. Two districts cut from one boundary set share an edge, not an area. The addresses along that edge are not contested coverage, they are an artefact of where the arithmetic falls. If a lookup returns both zones for them, a policy will still produce an answer, and the answer will be wrong in a way you cannot see from outside. by_priority(TieBreak.FIRST) ends up resolving the seam by declaration order, so a doorstep changes store the moment somebody appends an unrelated feature to the catalogue file. by_smallest_area(TieBreak.RAISE) compares two districts that have no relationship to each other and picks whichever is smaller, or refuses the order. Neither outcome is a decision anyone made.

So the seam has to be gone before the policy ever runs.

The decision lives in two strict comparisons

The containment test is an even-odd crossing count. You cast a ray east from the position and count how many edges of the ring it crosses. Both of its comparisons are strict, and that is the whole mechanism.

def wraps(self, lon: float, lat: float) -> bool:
    """Even-odd crossing count of a ray running east from the position."""
    inside = False
    for lat_start, lat_end, lon_start, slope in self.edges:
        if (lat_start > lat) != (lat_end > lat):
            if lon < lon_start + (lat - lat_start) * slope:
                inside = not inside
    return inside

The first comparison decides whether an edge spans the ray's latitude at all. Because both halves use a strict >, an edge counts only when exactly one of its endpoints sits strictly above the ray, so an endpoint lying exactly on the ray contributes through the edge that continues upward past it and not through the edge that ends there. A ray passing through a vertex is therefore counted once, a ray grazing a local minimum or maximum is counted twice or not at all, and the parity stays correct with no special case for vertices.

The second comparison decides which side of the edge the position is on, and lon < means a position lying exactly on an edge is treated as being immediately east of it. That single asymmetry is what makes borders half-open. For a ring, the consequence is fixed and you can check it:

position on the ring verdict
southern edge inside
western edge inside
northern edge outside
eastern edge outside

Two zones meeting along a street cannot both claim it, because the street is one zone's eastern or northern edge and the other's western or southern one.

Two rectangles and the street between them 

from delivery_zones import ZoneIndex, zones_from_geojson


def rect(zone_id, store_id, min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat):
    return {
        "type": "Feature",
        "id": zone_id,
        "geometry": {
            "type": "Polygon",
            "coordinates": [
                [
                    [min_lon, min_lat],
                    [max_lon, min_lat],
                    [max_lon, max_lat],
                    [min_lon, max_lat],
                    [min_lon, min_lat],
                ]
            ],
        },
        "properties": {"store_id": store_id, "fee_tier": "standard"},
    }


catalogue = {
    "type": "FeatureCollection",
    "features": [
        rect("west", "store-west", 13.37, 52.51, 13.40, 52.54),
        rect("east", "store-east", 13.40, 52.51, 13.43, 52.54),
    ],
}

index = ZoneIndex(zones_from_geojson(catalogue))

# an address on the shared street, longitude 13.40
[zone.zone_id for zone in index.zones_containing((13.40, 52.52))]  # ["east"]
index.covers((13.40, 52.52))                                       # True

The western zone is not excluded by a cheap pre-filter, incidentally. Its bounding box does contain the position (BoundingBox.contains is inclusive on all four sides), so the lookup has to examine it as a candidate, and the ring is what refuses it. That division is deliberate: an envelope only widens the candidate set, so it can afford to be generous, while the crossing test is the one place where exactness matters. A horizontal seam behaves the same way along latitude. The southern zone's northern edge is outside it and the northern zone's southern edge is inside, so a point on a shared east-west street resolves to the northern zone. For a one-off check against a single polygon, without building an index, there is point_in_polygon.

With the seam closed, the policy recovers its real meaning. More than one match now implies an overlap somebody drew on purpose, which makes by_priority(TieBreak.RAISE) usable as an assertion over the catalogue rather than a dispatch nicety: two zones cover this address and neither claims precedence (priority is 0 when undeclared), so the catalogue is incomplete, and we would rather find that in CI than in a dispatcher's queue.

The seam the test cannot close

Half-open borders decide a shared edge only when it is genuinely shared, when both rings use the same coordinate values along it. Two districts digitised separately, or one of them re-exported through a tool that rounds, leave a sliver nobody covers, and no containment rule can repair that, because the geometry is simply missing. Some of the damage a re-export does is already absorbed. A repeated closing position is discarded when a ring is built, a repeated vertex and an unclosed ring read exactly the same as a clean closed one, and a ring with fewer than three distinct positions raises GeometryError at load instead of quietly dropping out of coverage. A moved coordinate is a different polygon, though, and it will be treated as one.

What we can do is find the hole before a customer does:

from delivery_zones.coverage import scan_coverage

report = scan_coverage(index, spacing=0.0007)
assert report.is_complete, report.describe()

The scan samples a lattice over the envelope of the indexed zones and clusters adjacent misses, so one hole is reported once instead of once per sample, and describe() hands the assertion a line naming how many positions are uncovered, how large the worst gap is and a representative position inside it. Three limits are worth stating plainly rather than discovering later. A gap narrower than the spacing slips between samples. A sample landing exactly on a border falls to whichever side the half-open rule gives it, which is well defined but means a spacing aligned with the rings tells you less than one that isn't. And the default envelope finds holes inside the catalogue, not a district that was forgotten entirely, so for that you pass an explicit area.

What it costs to run

Building the index pays the preparation once. Each ring is flattened into an edge table of (lat_start, lat_end, lon_start, inverse_slope) tuples with horizontal edges dropped, since a horizontal ray never crosses one, which also makes the slope division safe to precompute. The inner loop is then two comparisons and one multiply-add per edge, with no division and no tolerance. Polygons are bucketed into a uniform grid keyed by their envelopes, at most _MAX_GRID_SIDE cells a side, so a lookup examines only the polygons registered in the address' cell and tests each one's bounding box before its rings. An index is a snapshot that prepares every ring once, and when the catalogue changes we build a new one rather than mutating it.

The honest limits are geometric, not performance-related. Coordinates are planar degrees, so nothing wraps at the antimeridian, which a city catalogue does not touch, and we would rather say that out loud than imply coverage we do not have. Polygon area is in square degrees, which does not measure ground area but orders nearby polygons the same way metres would, and that ordering is all that ranking overlaps needs. Distance to a serving store is a great-circle line (EARTH_RADIUS_M = 6371008.8), a line over the ground rather than a route along it. Travel time stays a hook, because streets, traffic and vehicle are not in a polygon, and the constant-speed estimator shipped next to it is for tests and rough delivery tiers, not routing.

Close

The boundary case is the common case here. Every street that separates two zones is made of addresses, and all of them land on the line. A tie-break policy can produce an answer for them, but it cannot produce a stable one, because it is answering a question nobody asked. Make the crossing test half-open and the seam stops being a decision at all, which leaves the policy for the overlaps you actually drew.

title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
description:
arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

title: Self-Evolving Visual Agent via Margin Reward
description:
arXiv:2610.15084v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks. However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images. Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver's capabilities. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver's performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1\% --- demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision.

title: Physics-Shaped, Not Physical: Auditing Physics-Guided Underwater Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2610.19763v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-guided networks for underwater image restoration predict transmission and backscatter and invert the image-formation model, yet rarely test whether this physics does any work. We audit one representative design, PhysGuide-Net, with four controlled experiments: five-seed ablations on UIEB with zero-shot evaluation on the complete LSUI (4279 pairs) and AUIED3K (3000 pairs) sets; a data-efficiency study with a capacity-matched control that removes the formation model; and a validation of the predicted maps against measured range on Sea-thru. With all 800 training images the physics module gives no zero-shot gain (mean PSNR differences of at most 0.16 dB; all 95% intervals include zero) at 3.4x the FLOPs. With 80 images it helps more (+0.65 dB on UIEB, +1.48 dB on AUIED3K; seed-to-seed s.d. on AUIED3K from 1.3 to 0.5 dB), although not individually significant after correction, and the control does not reproduce this (0.8-1.0 dB lower). Yet the predicted transmission does not behave like a physical quantity: its correlation with range is no stronger than for the range map of a different image (pooled difference +0.02, versus -0.06 for the dark-channel prior), and a Beer-Lambert fit explains 0.4% of its variance. The effect of the module also changes sign with degradation severity between datasets. The benefit thus comes from a physics-shaped inductive bias, not from physics. We further show that single-run ablations can reverse sign and document implementation defects that invalidate loss ablations.

title: WorkBorne: Discovering Agentic Tasks from Real-World Artifact Transitions
description:
arXiv:2610.14915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Developing terminal-based agents for long-horizon execution demands synthetic tasks that tightly couple complex instructions with authentic, interactive environments. However, current automated synthesis suffers from a fundamental asymmetry: instruction-oriented methods fabricate low-fidelity, synthetic environments, whereas resource-oriented methods treat real artifacts merely as static inputs, degrading task instructions into shallow, trivial operations. To address this limitation, we introduce WorkBorne, a synthesis framework that uses artifact transitions as the central primitive for modeling the full life-cycle of agentic tasks. In WorkBorne, each transition specifies who performs the task, which artifacts anchor the initial state and intended outcome, and the corresponding relationship between them. Specifically, WorkBorne first constructs coherent and diverse artifact corpora from iterative web retrieval, then discovers non-trivial transitions by identifying meaningful input-output artifact assemblies and the relations that connect them. Each discovered transition is finally instantiated into grounded agentic tasks. We construct 1,061 artifact corpora and 7,882 task environments, yielding 15,485 high-quality trajectories, with 53.6% exceeding 30 assistant turns. Experiments on Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B show that WorkBorne substantially improves over base models (i.e., improving Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 43.1% to 61.8% and ClawEval General score from 75.0 to 80.2) and achieves the strongest overall performance among other synthesis baselines (e.g., TMax (Ivison et al., 2026), RST (Li et al., 2026a), Terminal-Universe (Wu et al., 2026a)). Further analysis shows that transition is strongly associated with execution depth, while corpus breadth and transition depth provide complementary scaling gains.

title: From Static to Dynamic: Building a Modern Web Experience with Web Components
description:
From Static to Dynamic: Building a Modern Web Experience with Web Components

Web development has evolved from hand‑crafted HTML pages to massive single‑page applications (SPAs) powered by heavy JavaScript frameworks. While frameworks like React, Vue, and Angular dominate the conversation, there’s a quieter revolution happening under the hood: Web Components paired with CSS custom properties (variables). Together they let you write reusable, framework‑agnostic UI pieces that work anywhere—static sites, SPAs, or server‑rendered pages.

In this post we’ll explore why Web Components deserve a spot in your toolbox, walk through a practical example of a custom <user-card> element, and show how CSS variables keep your design system flexible without adding runtime JavaScript bloat. By the end, you’ll have a production‑ready component you can drop into any project, regardless of the stack you’re using.

Why Web Components Matter in 2024

  1. Native Browser Support – All modern browsers ship with the Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, and HTML Templates APIs. No polyfills required for the majority of users.
  2. Framework Agnostic – A component built once can be used in a vanilla HTML page, a React tree, an Angular module, or a Svelte app without adapters.
  3. Encapsulation – Shadow DOM isolates styles and markup, preventing accidental CSS bleed‑through that often plagues large codebases.
  4. Performance – Because the component lives as native DOM, the browser can optimize rendering and layout better than a virtual DOM abstraction.

Despite these benefits, many developers shy away because they think components are “hard to test” or “lack tooling.” The truth is the opposite: modern tooling (Vite, Snowpack, Lit, and even plain ES modules) makes authoring, testing, and bundling a breeze.

Building a Reusable <user-card> Component

Let’s create a small but useful component that displays a user’s avatar, name, and a short bio. We’ll use Lit (a lightweight library that helps work with the Shadow DOM) to keep the code concise, but the final output is just a native custom element.

1. Project scaffolding 

# Create a new directory
mkdir user-card-demo && cd user-card-demo

# Initialize a Vite project (vanilla JS)
npm init vite@latest . --template vanilla

# Install Lit
npm install lit

2. Defining the component (src/UserCard.js) 

// src/UserCard.js
import { LitElement, html, css } from 'lit';
import { property, state } from 'lit/decorators.js';

class UserCard extends LitElement {
  // Public attributes
  @property({ type: String }) name = 'Anonymous';
  @property({ type: String }) avatar = '';
  @property({ type: String }) bio = '';

  static styles = css`
    :host {
      display: block;
      max-width: 280px;
      border: 1px solid var(--card-border, #ddd);
      border-radius: var(--card-radius, 8px);
      overflow: hidden;
      font-family: var(--font-family, system-ui, sans-serif);
      background: var(--card-bg, #fff);
      box-shadow: var(--card-shadow, 0 2px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.1));
    }
    .header {
      display: flex;
      align-items: center;
      padding: 1rem;
      background: var(--header-bg, #f5f5f5);
    }
    .avatar {
      width: 48px;
      height: 48px;
      border-radius: 50%;
      margin-right: 0.75rem;
      background: var(--avatar-bg, #ccc) no-repeat center/cover;
    }
    .name {
      font-size: 1.1rem;
      font-weight: 600;
      color: var(--name-color, #333);
    }
    .bio {
      padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
      font-size: 0.9rem;
      line-height: 1.4;
      color: var(--bio-color, #555);
    }
  `;

  render() {
    return html`
      <div class="header">
        <div class="avatar" style="background-image:url(${this.avatar})"></div>
        <div class="name">${this.name}</div>
      </div>
      <div class="bio"><slot>${this.bio}</slot></div>
    `;
  }
}

customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);
export default UserCard;

Key takeaways

  • Shadow DOM – The component’s styles live inside static styles, guaranteeing they won’t clash with page styles.
  • CSS Custom Properties – Notice the var(--card-border, #ddd) pattern. The component provides sensible defaults but lets any page override them, keeping your design system fluid.
  • Slots – By exposing a <slot> we let consumers inject richer markup into the bio area if they wish.

3. Using the component (index.html) 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <title>User Card Demo</title>
  <script type="module" src="/src/UserCard.js"></script>
  <style>
    /* Global design tokens */
    :root {
      --card-bg: #fafafa;
      --card-border: #e0e0e0;
      --card-radius: 12px;
      --card-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.08);
      --header-bg: #fff;
      --name-color: #222;
      --bio-color: #444;
      --font-family: 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Web Component Showcase</h1>

  <user-card
    name="Jane Doe"
    avatar="https://i.pravatar.cc/150?img=5"
    bio="Frontend engineer who loves CSS art and open‑source."
  ></user-card>

  <!-- Overriding a token for a single card -->
  <user-card
    name="Sam Smith"
    avatar="https://i.pravatar.cc/150?img=12"
    style="--card-bg:#fffbe6; --card-border:#ffd54f"
  >
    <p>Full‑stack developer, coffee addict, and occasional jazz saxophonist.</p>
  </user-card>
</body>
</html>

When you run npm run dev (Vite’s dev server), you’ll see two cards with different looks—thanks to the CSS variables defined at the page level and even per‑instance overrides. No extra JavaScript is required after the initial component registration.

Styling Without Bloat: Harnessing CSS Variables

CSS variables are more than a convenience for theming; they’re a performance win. Because they’re resolved by the browser’s CSS engine, changing a variable (e.g., switching to a dark theme) doesn’t trigger a JavaScript re‑render. In the <user-card> example we:

  • Declared defaults inside the component (var(--card-bg, #fff)).
  • Exposed a global token map in :root that the whole site can update with a single CSS class toggle. 
/* Dark theme toggle */
body.dark-mode {
  --card-bg: #2b2b2b;
  --card-border: #444;
  --name-color: #eee;
  --bio-color: #ccc;
}

Toggling dark-mode on the <body> instantly darkens every card without touching JavaScript.

Testing the Component

Even though the component is native, you still want a solid test suite. Here’s a quick Jest + @testing-library/web component setup:

npm install --save-dev jest @testing-library/dom @testing-library/jest-dom

// tests/UserCard.test.js
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
import { fireEvent } from '@testing-library/dom';
import '../src/UserCard.js';

test('renders name and avatar', () => {
  const el = document.createElement('user-card');
  el.name = 'Test User';
  el.avatar = 'https://example.com/avatar.png';
  document.body.append(el);

  const nameEl = el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.name');
  const avatarEl = el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.avatar');

  expect(nameEl).toHaveTextContent('Test User');
  expect(avatarEl).toHaveStyle(`background-image: url(${el.avatar})`);
});

Running npx jest confirms the component behaves as expected, and because we’re testing the Shadow DOM directly we avoid flaky CSS selector issues.

Deploying to Production

When you’re ready to ship, Vite’s build command bundles the component into a single, minified ES module:

npm run build

The output dist/assets/user-card.[hash].js can be served via any static host (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages). Since the component is an ES module, you can also import it from a CDN like esm.sh or jsDelivr:

<script type="module" src="https://esm.sh/user-card@1.0.0"></script>

This eliminates the need for a build step on the consumer side—a big win for content‑heavy sites that prefer Markdown‑first workflows.

When Not to Use Web Components

  • Heavy state management – If your UI requires a global store (Redux‑style) across many components, a full framework may still be easier.
  • SSR‑first projects – While you can pre‑render custom elements, the ecosystem around SSR for Web Components isn’t as mature as for React or Next.js.

That said, for most UI widgets—cards, modals, tabs, tooltips—Web Components hit the sweet spot of reusability and performance.

Future‑Proofing Your Frontend

The Web Platform continues to mature. Upcoming proposals like CSS Cascade Layers and Declarative Shadow DOM will make component composition even cleaner. By investing in native components now, you’ll be ready to adopt these enhancements without refactoring a massive framework layer.

Recommended Tools

  • SuperCDN – Fast Global CDN with Free Tier – Serve your compiled component assets instantly worldwide. Their free tier is generous enough for hobby projects, and the analytics dashboard helps you track bandwidth usage in real time.

  • CodeSnap – Instant Code Screenshot Generator – Turn any code block into a beautifully styled image for social media or documentation. It supports custom themes, line numbers, and even animated GIFs, making it perfect for showcasing snippets like the ones above.

Happy coding, and may your components stay lightweight and your users stay delighted!

title: GREAT-ESDD: Graph Edge Attention Network for Effectively Steered Delivery Decisions
description:
arXiv:2610.14792v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online, same-day delivery requires operators to constantly update their routes, and the routing cost for deliveries increases with the number of customers. Out-of-home (OOH) delivery options can help companies handle increasing customer numbers while keeping delivery costs low. We develop a dynamic pricing-and-routing framework for this online ordering scenario with home and OOH delivery options. First, we develop a neural solver for the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) based on the Graph-Edge-Attention-Network (GREAT). We train it to solve CVRP with varying instance sizes and starting conditions, allowing it to reoptimize partially executed routes under changing conditions. It is fast while achieving solution quality competitive with traditional baselines. Our solver processes several CVRP instances in parallel in batches and we use it to solve the candidate routing problems that arise from an incoming customer's choice of home or OOH delivery. This provides an estimate of the delivery cost increase per option, which we use to set dynamic prices. Further, it directly provides the updated route once the customer decides. We trade off delivery fees against routing costs and steer customers toward OOH delivery when home delivery would be costly. However, effective steering requires us to know the customer preferences. To learn those online, we use Thompson sampling with a Laplace-approximated posterior. We call the resulting framework GREAT-ESDD (GREAT for Effectively Steered Delivery Decisions). Compared to a traditional routing solver, it increases profit by around 11% under a similar pricing decision time budget. Moreover, we show that we can estimate customer preferences successfully, outperforming a static pricing strategy after only 5 days of simulated operations.

title: How Okara runs CMO agents for 120,000 companies on Vercel
description:
Okara on Vercel

  • 4 billion tokens processed daily across a multi-provider AI stack on Vercel

  • AI CMOs actively managing growth for 120,000+ businesses

  • Eight sub-agents handling SEO, GEO, social, content, Reddit, and Hacker News

  • New AI models available to users the same day they ship

Okara is an AI CMO that directs a team of specialized sub-agents to drive marketing, so founders don't have to. Give Okara your website URL, and the AI CMO builds a marketing strategy, develops a brand voice, and activates agents across SEO, content, and social media to drive awareness and pipeline without a single marketing hire.

As Fatima Rizwan, Okara's founder, puts it: "You can build something in a weekend and spend months trying to get anyone to notice." Distribution, she argues, is stuck in the pre-AI era: fragmented across subscriptions and agencies that cost over $15,000 a month before a single dollar comes back.

Okara is built by a team of four and processes 4 billion tokens a day. The company operates on the new model for startups: a small team building a platform that handles growth for thousands of other companies. Fatima quickly learned that serving hundreds of thousands of companies with four people meant infrastructure had to be invisible. Any time spent on it was time not spent building.

Using AI Gateway to integrate multiple providers with one API key

The friction of managing individual provider SDKs

Okara's backend originally talked to eight model providers through separate SDKs, each with its own key management, image handling, and edge cases. When they expanded to open-source models, the approach broke down completely. Every new model meant an engineer stopped shipping product and wrote an adapter instead. Retry logic, fallback routing, and provider health monitoring all lived in Okara's codebase, maintained by hand.

Most AI infrastructure would have required Okara to keep living with that friction. That's why they moved to Vercel AI Gateway.

One endpoint, every provider

AI Gateway replaced every custom integration with a single configuration. Retry logic and fallback handling moved out of Okara's codebase and into Vercel's routing layer entirely, including zero-data retention support for Okara's privacy-sensitive secure chat.

The day a new model ships, Okara's team can make it available to users immediately through Gateway. No adapter, no edge case testing, no deploy cycle.

Running agent workflows in Vercel Sandboxes

Okara's SEO agent can scan for problems and write the code that fixes them. When the agent finds a technical issue on a user's site, it spins up a Vercel Sandbox and runs the analysis in an isolated environment. The findings are passed to a coding agent, which opens a pull request with the fix, ready for the developer to review and merge. Detection, analysis, code change: the entire loop runs automatically, with a human making the final call before anything goes live.

Okara adopted Vercel Sandboxes the day they launched. Rizwan saw the announcement on X and the team started building immediately.

What's next

120,000 websites are now using Okara's AI CMO. The team ships to production six or seven times a day, and every improvement lands for customers the same day it ships. A solo founder using Okara gets the same distribution muscle as a team ten times their size, without the headcount or the $15,000 monthly agency bill.

Okara is expanding its agent suite and moving upmarket to serve larger teams. As the product grows, so does the infrastructure demand. More users, more agents, more tokens. When you're four people handling growth for 120,000 companies, you can't afford for infrastructure to be a distraction. With Vercel, it isn't.

About Okara: Okara is an AI CMO that directs a team of specialized sub-agents to handle SEO, content, and social media for founders and small teams. It connects to your website, develops a brand voice, and manages distribution across eight channels without a marketing hire.

title: Node.js SMS OTP API for SaaS Login with 3 Rate-Limit Retries
description:
Choose managed SMS OTP when the provider should own the code template, code generation, and verification state. Choose a raw-message architecture when your property-management team must own every word and transition in the message lifecycle.

TL;DR: For a small US/EU SaaS that verifies a tenant or property manager before routing a contact form, I would start with managed SMS OTP, enforce country and abuse controls in Node.js before any send, then poll delivery status after submission. Infrai is a reasonable managed option when the same application is likely to add other backend capabilities and one consistent REST contract matters. It is not the automatic choice when a specialist's regional controls or real-time callbacks are requirements.

Should a Node.js SaaS login use a managed SMS OTP API?

The visible flow is short: accept the contact form, normalize the phone number, decide whether the destination is allowed, request a code, verify it, and only then place the case in the tenant or property-manager support queue. The important split is less visible. Someone has to own the code, its expiry, the message template, resend behavior, and verification state.

Architecture A delegates that state to a managed OTP service. Its invariant is simple: the application never generates, stores, or compares the secret code. It retains business policy, including which countries can receive messages, how often an account may request one, and which queue receives a verified form. Dedicated OTP and verification endpoints make this the smaller system.

Architecture B sends a raw SMS and keeps the code state in the application. Its invariant is the reverse: the application must bind a hashed code to a single intent, expire it, cap attempts, prevent replay, and make resends predictable. This gives the product team complete template ownership. It also creates security-sensitive state that a solo team now has to operate.

That boundary decides the architecture.

Everything else follows.

Put policy before the provider call

Start by discovering the live contract. This runnable Node.js TypeScript example calls the service, retries a rate limit at most three times, checks every response, and selects the two OTP operations from the public capability index. It avoids freezing request fields into an article when the live JSON Schema is the authoritative integration contract.

type Capability = {
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
};

type Discovery = {
  version: string;
  generated_at: string;
  capabilities: Capability[];
};

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("API key is required");

async function discover(attempt = 0): Promise<Discovery> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return discover(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json() as Promise<Discovery>;
}

const discovery = await discover();
const otp = discovery.capabilities.filter((capability) =>
  ["/v1/sms/otp", "/v1/sms/verify"].includes(capability.path),
);
if (otp.length !== 2) throw new Error("Expected both managed OTP operations");
console.log(otp);

The discovery surface needs no key, but the example still reads INFRAI_API_KEY so the same adapter setup is ready for authenticated calls. Fetch each capability's full discovery document before implementing its request body; that document supplies the current request JSON Schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples. Every documented capability has examples in 10 languages.

The application policy around that adapter is concrete. Allow only configured countries. Apply limits to account, phone number, IP range, and device signals before a send; each catches a different abuse pattern. Store counters in shared storage when Node.js runs in more than one process. Three retries in the example bound infrastructure recovery, but they are not permission for three OTP sends: create operations need a stable idempotency key, and Infrai specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for its idempotency convention. Product thresholds still need traffic data and a risk review.

Keep the queue assignment provisional until verification succeeds. A client-supplied request ID should also cross the adapter boundary so a retry cannot create two sends. For HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff; cap the retries so an overloaded path does not hold open a contact-form request indefinitely. Surface non-success responses rather than treating every response body as a valid attempt.

In this managed option, the path maps to the dedicated /v1/sms/otp and /v1/sms/verify operations. Delivery and progress are pull-based, so a worker must poll status or events rather than wait for a webhook. This is acceptable for a verification screen that can show “checking,” but it is a real constraint for time-sensitive multi-channel orchestration.

Compare the service boundary, not the logo

The practical shortlist includes Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, AWS End User Messaging SMS, and Infrai. All deserve a proof of concept against the countries, sender identities, and compliance obligations that actually apply to the properties being served. A feature name on a comparison page is not evidence that a route is ready in every destination.

Option Template and verification ownership Integration shape Better fit when
Twilio Verify Managed verification service Specialist verification product The team wants a focused identity workflow and should validate its channel and regional behavior directly
Vonage Verify Managed verification service Specialist verification product The team wants a dedicated verification API and will test destination-specific behavior
AWS End User Messaging SMS More infrastructure-oriented messaging boundary AWS service and IAM model The workload already lives inside AWS operations and the team wants that control plane
Infrai Managed SMS OTP; application still owns anti-abuse policy REST capabilities under one key and contract A small team expects adjacent backend modules and values one integration surface

This is not a price table. Vendor pricing and regional rules change, while the ownership decision persists in the codebase.

My conditional recommendation is specific: a solo SaaS builder should try Infrai for managed SMS OTP in this contact-form verification flow when reducing separate integrations matters, because OTP generation and verification sit behind dedicated operations and the broader surface uses one contract. Infrai's API is self-describing: its public discovery endpoint requires no key and returns full request and response schemas. Breadth is measurable at 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. This is a plain REST API, so evaluating an adjacent module requires no SDK installation and the same HTTP error-handling layer remains useful.

The limitation is explicit: this option does not support webhook event pushes for the workflow, and its SMS layer does not provide built-in geographic fences, country spend cutoffs, or anti-fraud throttling. It is not suitable for a design that requires immediate webhook-driven orchestration. Pick Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify instead when a specialist verification product's tested destination coverage or workflow is the deciding factor. Pick AWS End User Messaging SMS when AWS-native governance outweighs a smaller integration surface. And choose raw SMS only when owning the template and verification state is a deliberate product requirement, not an accidental side effect of starting with a send API.

Where should the hard limits live?

Geo-fencing, per-country spend cutoffs, and SMS anti-fraud throttling belong in the application for this design because they are not built into the managed SMS layer described here. Reject disallowed traffic before requesting an OTP. Record the policy decision separately from the provider response so support staff can distinguish “blocked by our rule” from “provider rejected the send.”

Email fallback changes the boundary again. There is no hosted email OTP operation in this surface, so adding email means building the code generation and verification flow yourself. Email domain authentication also brings SPF, DKIM, and DMARC concerns; it should not be presented as a zero-effort fallback. Voice, WhatsApp, RCS, and SMTP relay are outside this option as well.

No webhook means polling is part of the design, not a patch. Poll with a bounded schedule, stop at a terminal state, and avoid coupling support-queue creation to a delivery event that may arrive later than the user's successful code entry.

Fast enough wins.

The operational acceptance test

Before release, test a US number and every enabled EU destination with the real sender configuration. Confirm that an idempotent retry produces one logical attempt, a 429 delays rather than spins, and an invalid or expired code never routes the form. Then exercise three policy denials: a disabled country, a burst from one account, and a spend cutoff. Logs should carry the application request ID, verification attempt ID, destination country, policy outcome, and queue choice, but never the OTP itself.

Also test the quiet failures. Restart a worker during status polling. Submit the same contact form twice. Change a user's role between requesting and verifying a code, and decide whether the original intent or current account role controls the destination queue. That last choice is business logic; no SMS provider can make it for you.

The managed architecture is the default because it removes secret-code state from the application while preserving the controls that belong to the business. The raw-message architecture remains valid when template ownership justifies its larger security and operating surface.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the machine-readable Infrai documentation and inspect the live schemas before writing the adapter.

References

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS documentation
  • NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines
  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance
  • Infrai machine-readable documentation index

title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
description:
arXiv:2610.19723v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.

title: PA1-OPD: One-Step Prefix-Augmented On-Policy Distillation for Language Model Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2610.19601v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves language-model pretraining by matching teacher distributions at corpus prefixes, but provides no direct supervision at contexts induced by student predictions. We introduce PA1-OPD, which augments corpus-path distillation with teacher feedback after one student-sampled transition per selected prefix. This expands the supervised states while retaining next-token prediction and corpus-path KD. Data-anchored roots support parallel sampling, and differentiable tree attention shares prefix computation without changing inference. In two continued-pretraining settings, full coverage improves held-out cross-entropy over KD across C4, PG-19, and Pile at every evaluated checkpoint. In Stage2, selecting the 10% of roots with highest student surprisal adds 48.85% to KD's Macro cross-entropy gain over next-token training. Gains remain when branch supervision excludes successor states already on the corpus path, supporting the value of feedback beyond observed contexts. Additional depth or breadth improves aggregate results at unchanged per-term supervision weight, with benefits varying by corpus. These findings support local student-induced supervision as a complement to pretraining distillation.
