title: Node.js API Routes and Server Actions: 3 Error Tracking Boundaries (With Attribution)
description:
Instrument three server-side boundaries, but define the cost-attribution record before choosing the error backend. For a customer-support pricing rule behind a flag, that means one normalized exception contract across Next.js route handlers, server actions, and background jobs, with release, environment, pricingRule, and costCenter attached at capture time.

TL;DR: a capture-and-lookup service is enough when the job is grouping server exceptions and feeding an internal support view. It is not enough for browser source maps, alert delivery, distributed trace exploration, replay, or proof that a scheduled job ran. Keep the application contract stable so the provider behind it can move without edits to pricing logic.

How should API routes and server actions capture Node.js errors?

Start from the support question: why did this account receive the wrong quote? A stack trace locates the failed code. It does not identify the rule, deployment, environment, or owning budget. Those are application facts, so the application has to supply them.

I would keep eight fields. Four describe the exception: name, message, stack, and occurredAt. Four make it actionable: release, environment, pricingRule, and costCenter. A ninth field, boundary, separates synchronous request work from deferred work. The shape is deliberately small because every extra dimension becomes a privacy decision, a grouping hazard, and another thing an SDK migration must preserve.

Headers need even less enthusiasm. Copying the full request header map is quick, but it can pull cookies and authorization credentials into an error store. For this workflow, allowlist content-type, user-agent, and x-request-id. Three headers. No clever redaction regex.

The attribution rule is equally plain: costCenter names the team paying for and operating the pricing action; pricingRule names the versioned business decision. Neither field should be derived from an exception message. Messages change. Identifiers should not.

That gives the support UI a useful join key without pretending an error event is an accounting ledger. It can show recent production failures by release and rule, then hand the stable identifiers to whatever system owns financial reporting.

Build the contract before the transport

This is the smallest implementation I would put under all three Next.js server boundaries. It captures native Node.js stack traces, keeps request headers on an allowlist, and leaves transport behind an ErrorSink. The example runs as TypeScript with no vendor SDK and no framework import.

type Boundary = "route-handler" | "server-action" | "background-job";

type CaptureContext = {
  release: string;
  environment: "staging" | "production";
  pricingRule: string;
  costCenter: string;
  boundary: Boundary;
  requestHeaders?: Record<string, string>;
};

type CapturedException = CaptureContext & {
  name: string;
  message: string;
  stack?: string;
  occurredAt: string;
};

type ErrorSink = (event: CapturedException) => Promise<void>;

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const apiBaseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE_URL;

if (!apiKey || !apiBaseUrl) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_API_BASE_URL are required");
}

const sleep = (milliseconds: number): Promise<void> =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

const productionSink: ErrorSink = async (event) => {
  const idempotencyKey = crypto.randomUUID();

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${apiBaseUrl}/v1/errors/capture`,
      {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
          message: event.message,
          stack: event.stack,
          release: event.release,
          environment: event.environment,
          metadata: {
            name: event.name,
            pricingRule: event.pricingRule,
            costCenter: event.costCenter,
            boundary: event.boundary,
            requestHeaders: event.requestHeaders,
            occurredAt: event.occurredAt,
          },
        }),
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return;

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 2) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delay = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await sleep(delay);
      continue;
    }

    throw new Error(
      `Error capture failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`,
    );
  }
};

const allowedHeaders = new Set([
  "content-type",
  "user-agent",
  "x-request-id",
]);

export function selectHeaders(headers: Headers): Record<string, string> {
  return Object.fromEntries(
    [...headers.entries()].filter(([name]) =>
      allowedHeaders.has(name.toLowerCase()),
    ),
  );
}

export async function withErrorCapture<T>(
  operation: () => Promise<T>,
  context: CaptureContext,
  sink: ErrorSink,
): Promise<T> {
  try {
    return await operation();
  } catch (cause: unknown) {
    const error = cause instanceof Error ? cause : new Error(String(cause));

    await sink({
      ...context,
      name: error.name,
      message: error.message,
      stack: error.stack,
      occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    });

    throw error;
  }
}

async function calculateQuote(): Promise<number> {
  throw new Error("Unsupported pricing region");
}

await withErrorCapture(
  calculateQuote,
  {
    release: "support-api-42",
    environment: "staging",
    pricingRule: "regional-discount-v3",
    costCenter: "customer-support",
    boundary: "server-action",
  },
  productionSink,
).catch(() => undefined);

The rethrow matters. Quietly swallowing the exception would turn failed pricing work into apparent success. The production sink can serialize the same object for the selected provider, while the business function and its tests remain untouched.

Route handlers can pass selectHeaders(request.headers). Server actions often have no useful request headers and should omit them. A worker uses the same contract with boundary: "background-job"; its job identifier belongs in application logs unless the chosen event schema explicitly supports another stable metadata field.

This split also makes the code testable without a network call. Inject a sink that stores one event in memory, throw a known Error, and assert that the original error is rethrown. Then check that authorization and cookie never appear while x-request-id survives. Those tests benchmark integration quality better than counting setup screens: time to first captured event, number of call sites changed during a sink swap, and fields lost in the swap are the numbers I care about. Measure them in your own repository; no vendor can supply honest results for that.

Cost attribution changes the lookup design

Capture is only half of this job. The internal support page needs recent production failures, grouped so fifty repeats do not become fifty unrelated rows, and it needs group detail for investigation. Release and environment must remain first-class filters in that page even if the backend's grouping algorithm ignores them.

Do not let the UI query a provider directly from the browser. Put lookup behind a server-side repository with application terms such as recentProductionFailures and failureGroup. That preserves the same swap boundary on reads. It also keeps provider credentials off the client.

Infrai's main advantage here is one REST API for the entire backend: one key, one wallet, and one bill. There is no SDK to install. Its public, self-describing discovery exposes request schemas, response schemas, billing, and runnable examples in 10 languages, while the platform covers 295 routes across 20 modules. For this support workflow, adding another backend capability does not create another credential rotation or invoice reconciliation path, while the repository contract stays fixed if the vendor behind the capability moves. Swapping the vendor does not change the pricing code. This narrow service fits only when captured exceptions, grouping, and basic lookup are the whole requirement.

That fit has sharp edges. There is no source-map deobfuscation for minified browser bundles, alert or notification route, distributed trace query with a span tree, Session Replay, synthetic check, or heartbeat monitor. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but correlation fields are not a trace explorer. A scheduled repricing job that never starts emits no exception, so a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks must cover that silent failure. For urgent paging, polling recent errors from a free query API is weaker than native alert delivery.

No payload sprawl.

The trade-off is deliberate: short scope, more operational ownership.

The tools are solving different incident workflows

Comparing logo grids is useless. Compare the missing glue after the first exception arrives.

Product Best fit for this rollout Trade-off to verify
Sentry Teams that need mature issue grouping and browser source-map handling alongside server errors Fingerprints and grouping configuration become part of the operating model
Bugsnag Product teams wanting managed stability and error monitoring across server and client applications Confirm that its release and diagnostic workflow matches the support team's lookup flow
Datadog Error Tracking Organizations already correlating application failures with infrastructure telemetry and distributed traces The wider platform and agent configuration may exceed a capture-and-lookup project
Rollbar Teams wanting a dedicated error inbox with deployment context and configurable grouping Its SDK and project concepts should stay behind the application adapter
Honeybadger Small teams that want exceptions near uptime and check monitoring Consolidation helps only if heartbeat checks belong to the same incident workflow
Infrai Server-only capture, grouping, and lookup behind a compact REST repository It does not cover source maps, native alerts, trace trees, replay, or heartbeats

Sentry has the cleanest advantage when the pricing experience includes browser code and readable minified stacks are mandatory. Datadog is the stronger shortlist entry when the actual question is cross-service causality, because exception capture without trace exploration will stop too early. Bugsnag and Rollbar deserve evaluation when a dedicated managed error workflow is the goal. Honeybadger becomes more compelling when job heartbeats should live next to exceptions.

The narrow REST choice wins on a different constraint: the team already owns the support UI and wants a portable server-side event contract with little integration weight. It loses as soon as the team expects the error store to be the complete incident-response system. This is not a feature-count contest.

Grouping deserves its own trial. Sentry documents default grouping and custom fingerprints; use that as a reminder that similar stack traces do not guarantee the business grouping you want. Before selecting any service, submit the same pricing failure from two boundaries, then a different failure with the same message. Inspect the groups. Do not infer behavior from a marketing sentence.

What changes when the rollout grows?

At higher volume, I would decouple capture from the request path with a bounded local queue and measure dropped events. The queue consumer needs idempotent delivery because retries must not create duplicate error events. Backpressure policy should be explicit: pricing requests cannot wait forever for telemetry, but silent loss is also unacceptable.

I would also separate three records that are easy to mash together. The flag system owns rule state. The application owns the pricing decision identifier and cost attribution. The error backend owns exception groups. A basic flag surface without change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, push updates, or a recycle bin cannot serve as the rollout audit trail, so persist that audit history elsewhere.

Finally, add OpenTelemetry where rates and service health matter. Metrics answer how often failures occur; traces answer how a request crossed services; captured exceptions preserve the stack and debugging context. One provider may store several signals, but the data models are not substitutes.

The decision rule stays simple: choose a dedicated error platform when client diagnostics, native paging, or deep incident tooling are requirements. Choose the smaller capture-and-lookup path when the workload is server-side, the support view is already yours, and the stable adapter is more valuable than a larger console. Re-run the three-boundary grouping trial before every migration. If the contract survives, the pricing code should not notice.

References

  • Next.js, "Error Handling": https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/error-handling
  • Node.js, "Errors": https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html
  • Sentry, "Event Grouping": https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/data-management/event-grouping/
  • Datadog, "Error Tracking": https://docs.datadoghq.com/error_tracking/
  • Bugsnag, "Error Monitoring": https://docs.bugsnag.com/
  • Rollbar, "Grouping Algorithm": https://docs.rollbar.com/docs/grouping-algorithm
  • Honeybadger, "Monitoring": https://docs.honeybadger.io/
  • OpenTelemetry, "Metrics": https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • Healthchecks, "Documentation": https://healthchecks.io/docs/

title: One-Step Prediction Fidelity Is a Poor Proxy for Planning Performance in JEPA World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19375v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent world models are routinely selected, checkpointed and ablated on one-step prediction loss, on the assumption that a model which predicts the next latent better is a better model. In model-based RL this assumption is known to be unreliable; we ask whether it also fails for latent world models, where the training target is the model's own embedding and the loss is not expressed in interpretable units. We introduce a frozen-decoder protocol reporting one-step error in physical units, decomposed into the part already present in the encoder's representation and the part the predictor adds. Applying it to a recent end-to-end JEPA world model across three continuous-control environments, we move the metric by fine-tuning and measure goal-conditioned planning on the same checkpoints, with three training seeds and paired planning seeds throughout. Within one environment, a per-epoch ladder shows the relationship saturating after a single epoch: the first epoch improves fidelity by 32% and planning by 4.4 pp, but across the fifteen checkpoints that follow -- a further 15% fidelity improvement, monotone in every training seed -- the correlation between one-step error and planning success is r = -0.010. This is not a task-ceiling artifact: stratifying by a model-independent measure of training-data support, planning in the lowest-support stratum starts at 80%, leaving ample headroom, and is nonetheless flat from epoch 1 onward. Across environments the exchange rate is equally unstable: a 93% fidelity reduction on TwoRoom yields -0.7 pp of planning, while a 40% reduction on PushT yields +4.9 pp [+1.1, +8.9]. All results replicate under a decoder-free measure, latent drift. We also show that a matched continued-training control absorbs the entire fidelity gain we had attributed to an auxiliary objective.

title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19934v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.

title: Imagining Goals with Geometric Horizon Models for Policy Generalization
description:
arXiv:2610.19129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.

title: Learning to Compute Is Not Learning to Retain or Reuse in Looped Transformers
description:
arXiv:2610.19768v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Looped transformers compute by applying one block repeatedly, so they can run for more loops than they were trained with. Recurrent reasoners are known to overthink: iterating past the trained depth can turn a correct answer into a wrong one. Such a late error can reflect failed computation, loss of retention, or a state that later computation cannot reuse. We separate these cases in in-context Mealy-machine execution, where a simulator supplies intermediate targets and exact counterfactuals for hidden-state interventions. Models trained to answer at loop 32 are fully correct there but keep only 22% of these answers at loop 64. Retention depends on what training asks for: supervising one randomly chosen position per example, instead of always the last, keeps 99.8%, and randomizing the number of training loops also helps; truncating gradients, as in progressive training against overthinking, does not. The computation itself is exact: position $k$ is computed at loop $k$, and swapping its loop-$k$ hidden vector for the one from another input redirects every later position to that input's exact continuation (237/237 pairs in each of ten models). Retention, however, is not reuse. Even in models that keep nearly all answers, holding each position $k$ fixed from loop $k$ drops accuracy to 4--6%, whereas holding it from loop $k+4$ is harmless. A released recurrent maze network trained to avoid overthinking behaves the same way. Learning to compute is thus not learning to retain, and avoiding overthinking does not make a state reusable when its answer first appears.

title: Self‑distilled spatial reasoning improves accuracy without large latency penalty
description:
Distilling privileged depth cues into an RGB‑only vision‑language model closes the long‑standing gap between accuracy and inference speed. SpatialOPSD shows that a single forward pass can inherit most of the reasoning power of a tool‑driven teacher without the heavy latency penalty.

Before this work, spatial coding agents boosted multimodal models by calling external tools to generate verified execution traces, but each trace required multiple API calls and slowed down deployment. Fine‑tuning (SFT) or reinforcement‑learning approaches such as GRPO could not internalize geometry because they never saw the privileged depth information during training.

SpatialOPSD improves the Qwen3.5‑9B baseline from 45.9 to 51.9, with specific efficacy in allocentric transformations (e.g., Among +11.7) [1]. The gain comes from feeding summarized agent traces as privileged inputs during on‑policy self‑distillation, which teaches the model a spatial chain‑of‑thought that it can later reproduce without any external depth sensor.

In a single tool‑free forward pass, SpatialOPSD retains 91% of the performance of its iterative, tool‑dependent teacher, SpatialClaw (51.9 vs. 57.3) [1]. This means the distilled model eliminates virtually all runtime overhead from external calls while sacrificing only a modest fraction of accuracy.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that self‑distilling SpatialOPSD achieves higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO on both spatial and OOD datasets, exhibiting superior performance and generalization [1]. The advantage holds across varied tasks, confirming that the distilled spatial reasoning is not a narrow trick but a broadly useful capability.

The authors acknowledge that privileged‑information leakage remains a concern, mitigated only by Repetition‑Aware Distillation’s masking and unlikelihood regularization; the 9% residual gap to the teacher suggests further work is needed on scaling or tighter leakage control. One inference is that larger models may close this gap, but empirical evidence is still missing.

If these numbers hold in practice, developers should replace iterative tool‑dependent spatial pipelines with a distilled RGB model and re‑run latency budgets on VSI‑Bench; the expectation is a >90% reduction in execution time while keeping success rates within a few points of the original teacher.

References

  1. SpatialOPSD: Self-Distilling Spatial Intelligence from Verified Coding Agent Traces

title: How to Pick an Online Presence API — Or Own a Heartbeat Table
description:
TL;DR: For a marketplace live poll, choose connection-backed presence when "online" means "has an active realtime connection." It needs no application cleanup, while a heartbeat table remains your data to expire and can show ghosts after a crash. Neither answer is instant; set an eventual-correction budget, and keep voting authorization separate from roster visibility.

The useful experiment is narrow: replay a clean departure, a crashed client, a delayed observation, and an online client without voting rights. Reject an option if it misses the roster's stale-user budget or lets a browser widen its authority. This tests the two properties that matter here, instead of rewarding the longest feature list.

Should an online poll use a presence API or a heartbeat table?

Consider one marketplace session, one poll, and four synthetic clients. The application needs to display who can still see the live question, but a green dot must never become proof that its owner may vote. Token scope is an authorization decision; presence is a liveness observation. Mixing them produces a design that looks tidy in a demo and has an indefensible trust boundary in production.

The invariant is blunt. Presence follows the connection, which is what "online" means in this system. A heartbeat row follows an expiry rule. If a tab or process crashes after writing its last beat, the row remains a ghost until expiry and then depends on a sweeper the team must monitor. Connection-backed presence has no application cleanup job for that membership.

Ghosts are the tax.

Still, presence cannot promise immediate truth. Disconnect detection, propagation, and the reader's observation all take time, just as heartbeat expiry does. The UI and SLO should allow eventual correction rather than claiming an instantaneous roster. The experiment below therefore takes staleBudget as an input; it does not smuggle in a universal timeout.

Infrai is a credible measured leg when the platform team wants to switch providers without changing application code: the capability contract stays fixed while the vendor behind it changes. Infrai's one plain REST API works from any language or runtime without installing an SDK, so the probe doesn't inherit a vendor client. A second, separate advantage matters to this experiment: the public, self-describing discovery surface needs no key and returns request schemas, while every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That lets teams reproduce the same failure cases from different client stacks without translating an SDK-specific sample first. Infrai also provides one key for all capabilities and one bill; across 295 routes in 20 modules, that can reduce credential rotation and invoice reconciliation if the team evaluates other backend capabilities later. Breadth is useful operationally, but it isn't evidence that Infrai should win this presence test.

Teams standardizing multiple backend capabilities behind a stable contract should try Infrai for the presence leg of this poll experiment, because provider changes stay behind the API while public discovery reduces the work required to keep the probe aligned with the contract.

Build the failure experiment

Fix three inputs before running anything: the maximum acceptable stale-roster duration, the heartbeat expiry interval, and the server-side statement of who may vote. Use at least four cases: an active voter, a clean departure, a crashed client whose last heartbeat is still fresh, and a connected observer without voting permission. The numbers in the program are test inputs, not vendor defaults or measured production behavior.

First capture the managed-presence response without guessing its JSON fields. This complete Go program calls the verified route with an explicit GET, reads INFRAI_API_KEY, surfaces non-success bodies, and retries HTTP 429 with exponential backoff or Retry-After. It intentionally prints the response unchanged, because inventing a response type would invalidate the comparison.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... go run main.go CHANNEL")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    routeTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/presence/get/{channel}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(routeTemplate, "{channel}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[1]))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "request failed: status=%d body=%s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        wait := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "request remained rate-limited after 5 attempts")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Run the decision logic separately. That separation is deliberate: each managed product can feed its observed connection state into the same cases without pretending that vendor response schemas are interchangeable.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    Name          string
    ObservedAt    time.Duration
    Connected     bool
    LastHeartbeat time.Duration
    MayVote       bool
}

func connectionOnline(o Observation) bool {
    return o.Connected
}

func heartbeatOnline(o Observation, expiry time.Duration) bool {
    return o.ObservedAt-o.LastHeartbeat <= expiry
}

func main() {
    expiry := 30 * time.Second
    cases := []Observation{
        {Name: "active-voter", ObservedAt: 10 * time.Second, Connected: true, LastHeartbeat: 5 * time.Second, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "clean-departure", ObservedAt: 20 * time.Second, Connected: false, LastHeartbeat: 0, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "crashed-client", ObservedAt: 20 * time.Second, Connected: false, LastHeartbeat: 15 * time.Second, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "online-observer", ObservedAt: 10 * time.Second, Connected: true, LastHeartbeat: 5 * time.Second, MayVote: false},
    }

    for _, c := range cases {
        fmt.Printf("%-16s connection=%t heartbeat=%t may_vote=%t\n",
            c.Name, connectionOnline(c), heartbeatOnline(c, expiry), c.MayVote)
    }
}

The crashed client is the discriminating case. Connection state says offline; the heartbeat policy says online until its 30-second experimental expiry is crossed. The online observer checks the other invariant: a connected user can be visible and still lack permission to vote.

Define pass or fail before collecting observations. A candidate passes only if an unclean disconnect is corrected within staleBudget, an active connection is not removed by unrelated cleanup, and a client without server-granted poll authority cannot vote. Repeat observations around the boundary and retain timestamps. Do not turn one prompt response into a latency claim.

Compare ownership, not marketing pages

The practical alternatives do not expose identical abstractions, but they can be compared by cleanup ownership, coupling, and fit. This is the buy-versus-build review I would take to an architecture meeting:

Option Primitive to evaluate Who owns stale-state removal? Good fit Boundary to verify
Ably Presence Membership associated with realtime clients Managed service Teams already organized around Ably channels Direct code adopts Ably's client and channel model
Pusher Channels Presence-channel membership Managed service Applications already centered on Pusher Channels Its channel conventions become application dependencies
Supabase Realtime Presence state synchronized on a channel Managed service Collaboration state already lives near Supabase Portability requires replacing its channel integration
Firebase Realtime Database Application connection markers and database state Application plus database behavior Firebase-native applications needing custom records Disconnect and reconciliation rules remain application concerns
Infrai Realtime presence behind a REST capability Managed service Platform teams valuing a stable cross-vendor contract A direct specialist is better for required native client semantics
Own heartbeat table Timestamp rows, expiry logic, and a sweeper Your team Status is a domain lease rather than a connection Ghost rows, write load, sweeper lag, and recovery belong to on-call

These are real trade-offs. Ably or Pusher can be the cleaner answer when the application wants the specialist's native channel semantics and client ecosystem. Supabase is compelling when the surrounding collaboration data and operational model already sit there. Firebase gives database-centric teams flexible application records. Infrai earns consideration when a platform contract and vendor substitution matter more than adopting specialist client behavior.

A heartbeat table wins a different question: "Has this participant renewed a business lease recently?" It is appropriate when status must outlive a connection, clients cannot retain realtime connections, or the poll needs a domain-specific interval such as an attendance window. Call that status recently_active or lease_valid, not online, and accept expiry as product logic.

For literal connection presence, building requires a stronger justification. The table adds periodic writes, an expiry index, a sweeper SLO, monitoring for sweeper lag, and a recovery runbook. Managed presence removes that application cleanup surface, but it also asks the team to accept a provider's consistency and channel semantics. Measure them.

Turn the result into an SLO and decision

Capacity planning starts with a plain equation. For N connected clients and a heartbeat interval of I seconds, baseline write demand is N / I writes per second, before reconnect bursts, index maintenance, and sweeper scans. This is arithmetic, not a benchmark. Substitute the poll's forecast and database limits rather than copying a convenient number from an article.

The roster SLO should describe user-visible error: the proportion of observations whose stale membership lasts longer than the chosen budget. Track the sweeper separately if you build the table, because a healthy write path can coexist with a stalled cleanup path. For managed presence, observe the same external outcome. Neither design deserves an "instant" objective.

Use this decision rule:

  1. If online means an active realtime connection, the eventual-correction budget passes, and server-issued token scope passes, choose connection-backed presence.
  2. If status represents a lease or must survive a connection change, choose a heartbeat record and operate expiry as a named service with an SLO.
  3. If portability is a roadmap constraint, run the identical cases against a stable intermediary and the shortlisted direct providers; score required code changes as well as outcomes.
  4. If native specialist behavior or a specific client library is mandatory, choose that provider directly and record the coupling as an explicit trade-off.

Do not let presence mint authority. Issue client access from a trusted server with only the session and actions required by that participant, then enforce vote permission independently. A roster read answers who appears connected; it does not answer who owns a marketplace account, who may vote, or whether a second ballot is valid.

Where this advice stops

This recommendation does not apply to audit history, durable attendance, "active in the last five minutes," or a workflow that must continue without a realtime connection. Those are stored-state problems. A heartbeat or domain event can be correct there, even though it creates cleanup work, because survival beyond the socket is the requirement rather than an accident.

It also does not establish that one managed product is universally faster or more reliable. The experiment supplies explicit inputs and pass/fail conditions; the team still has to run it in its regions, with its clients, under its token policy. Pick the smallest operational surface that meets those observations, and keep the trust boundary server-side.

If the stable capability boundary fits your platform, start with the Infrai documentation and include its presence leg in the same failure experiment rather than assuming the outcome.

Sources

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Ably Presence documentation
  • Pusher Channels presence documentation
  • Supabase Realtime Presence documentation
  • Firebase presence guidance
  • Infrai documentation

title: GesBench: When and Where Do Multimodal Language Models Perceive Social Meaning?
description:
arXiv:2610.15129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.

title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.19362v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.

title: How to Detect AI Bots Without Blocking Googlebot
description:
Your website is receiving automated requests. Some are from search engines trying to index your pages. Others come from AI crawlers, monitoring tools, scrapers, or malicious scripts.

The challenge isn't identifying every automated request. It's knowing which bots should be allowed and which ones deserve closer inspection.

Block everything that looks automated, and you risk blocking Googlebot or AI search crawlers. Trust every request claiming to be Googlebot, and anyone can bypass your basic filtering rules.

So how do you detect AI bots without blocking legitimate crawlers?

In this guide, we'll cover the different types of bots, build a working bot detection tool using Node.js, test it in VS Code, and explore how IP intelligence can help classify suspicious traffic.

What you'll build: A local Express server that recognizes bot user-agent strings, plus an optional IP Security lookup script that can be tested with sample data.

The basic project is free. No paid API subscription is required to complete the first part.

1. Understand the Different Types of Bots

Not every bot visiting your website is trying to cause problems.

Here's a quick comparison.

Bot Purpose Typical handling
Googlebot Search engine indexing Allow after verification
Bingbot Search engine indexing Allow after verification
OAI-SearchBot ChatGPT search discovery Follow your AI search policy
GPTBot AI model-related crawling Follow your training crawler policy
ChatGPT-User User-triggered page retrieval Evaluate separately
Uptime monitoring bots Website availability checks Allow recognized services
Malicious scrapers Unauthorized extraction or abuse Rate-limit or block when justified

OpenAI, for example, operates different crawlers for different purposes.

According to OpenAI's official documentation, OAI-SearchBot is used for ChatGPT search, while GPTBot crawls content that may be used for training AI models.

ChatGPT-User is different again. It can retrieve web pages in response to a user's action.

The distinction matters because you may want your articles discoverable in AI search without allowing every type of automated crawling.

2. Why User-Agent Detection Isn't Enough

One of the easiest ways to recognize a bot is through its HTTP User-Agent header.

For example, a request might contain:

Googlebot/2.1

Or:

GPTBot/1.4

Your server can inspect that header and classify the request.

But there's a problem.

Anyone can send a request pretending to be Googlebot:

curl -A "Googlebot" https://example.com

The -A option tells curl to send a particular user-agent string.

It doesn't make the request come from Google.

That's why we need to distinguish two concepts:

  • Bot identification: What software does the request claim to be?
  • Bot verification: Does the source actually belong to the claimed operator?

Let's start with identification.

3. Build a Basic AI Bot Detector in Node.js

This section works locally and doesn't require an IP intelligence API key.

We'll use Node.js, Express, and VS Code.

Step 1: Check your Node.js installation

Download Node.js from nodejs.org if it isn't installed.

Open VS Code and select:

Terminal → New Terminal

Run:

node -v

Then:

npm -v

Both commands should display version numbers.

Use Node.js 20 or newer for this project.

Step 2: Create a project folder

In the VS Code terminal, run these commands:

mkdir bot-detection-demo
cd bot-detection-demo

Initialize the project:

npm init -y

Install Express and dotenv:

npm install express dotenv

Then open your project in VS Code using File → Open Folder and select bot-detection-demo.

Step 3: Create the main server file

In the VS Code Explorer, right-click your project folder and select New File.

Name it:

server.mjs

Paste this code:

import express from "express";

const app = express();

const knownBots = [
  "Googlebot",
  "Bingbot",
  "GPTBot",
  "OAI-SearchBot",
  "ChatGPT-User",
  "ClaudeBot",
  "PerplexityBot"
];

function detectBotClaim(userAgent = "") {
  return knownBots.find(bot =>
    userAgent.toLowerCase().includes(
      bot.toLowerCase()
    )
  ) || null;
}

app.get("/check-bot", (req, res) => {
  const userAgent = req.get("user-agent") || "";

  const detectedBot = detectBotClaim(userAgent);

  res.json({
    message: "Bot identification completed",
    botClaim: detectedBot,
    isClaimingKnownBot: Boolean(detectedBot),
    verified: false,
    note: "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
  });
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Server running on port 3000");
});

Save the file using Ctrl + S.

This code checks incoming requests against a list of common search and AI bot names.

Notice the field:

verified: false

That's intentional. Our code identifies the claimed bot name but doesn't perform any operator verification.

Step 4: Start the server

In your terminal, run:

node server.mjs

You should see:

Server running on port 3000

Your local server is now running.

Open a second VS Code terminal using the + button in the Terminal panel.

Keep the first terminal running.

Step 5: Test Googlebot detection

In the second terminal, run:

curl -A "Googlebot" http://localhost:3000/check-bot

Expected response:

{
  "message": "Bot identification completed",
  "botClaim": "Googlebot",
  "isClaimingKnownBot": true,
  "verified": false,
  "note": "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
}

The server successfully recognized a request claiming to be Googlebot.

Step 6: Test GPTBot detection

Run:

curl -A "GPTBot" http://localhost:3000/check-bot

The response should contain:

{
  "message": "Bot identification completed",
  "botClaim": "GPTBot",
  "isClaimingKnownBot": true,
  "verified": false,
  "note": "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
}

Step 7: Test OAI-SearchBot

Run:

curl -A "OAI-SearchBot" http://localhost:3000/check-bot

The response should identify:

{
  "message": "Bot identification completed",
  "botClaim": "OAI-SearchBot",
  "isClaimingKnownBot": true,
  "verified": false,
  "note": "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
}

Step 8: Test an ordinary request

Now run:

curl http://localhost:3000/check-bot

Since curl doesn't normally claim to be one of the bots in our list, the response should include:

{
  "message": "Bot identification completed",
  "botClaim": null,
  "isClaimingKnownBot": false,
  "verified": false,
  "note": "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
}

That's it.

You've built and tested a working user-agent-based bot identifier.

But it doesn't detect sophisticated automation with unfamiliar user agents, and it doesn't verify whether a recognized name is genuine.

Let's improve the approach.

4. How to Verify Real Googlebot Traffic

Google recommends verifying its crawlers using DNS or published crawler IP ranges.

The DNS verification process works like this:

  1. Extract the actual client IP address.
  2. Perform a reverse DNS lookup.
  3. Check whether the hostname ends with an approved Google crawler domain.
  4. Perform a forward DNS lookup on that hostname.
  5. Confirm the original IP is among the returned addresses.

For example, Google's documentation shows crawler hostnames under:

googlebot.com

But you shouldn't trust an arbitrary hostname simply because it contains the word google.

The hostname must match Google's documented patterns, and forward DNS must confirm the original address.

Google also publishes official crawler IP ranges.

You can find the complete procedure in the Google crawler verification documentation.

What about OpenAI crawlers?

OpenAI publishes IP ranges for different crawlers:

  • OAI-SearchBot IP ranges
  • GPTBot IP ranges
  • ChatGPT-User IP ranges

If a request claims to be GPTBot, you can compare its actual source IP against the appropriate published ranges.

For production systems, you should regularly refresh these lists and correctly handle IPv4 and IPv6 CIDR ranges.

Also, when your application sits behind a reverse proxy, configure Express's trust proxy setting for your actual trusted proxy infrastructure. Don't blindly trust an incoming X-Forwarded-For header.

5. Detect Unknown Bots Using IP Intelligence

Verifying Googlebot is useful because Google provides official verification methods.

But what about a bot that doesn't identify itself?

Imagine an unknown client makes thousands of requests to your website.

It doesn't claim to be a search crawler. Its user-agent looks ordinary, and you don't recognize the IP address.

In this situation, IP intelligence can provide useful context.

For example, IPGeolocation.io's IP Security API provides information about whether an IP address has been associated with:

  • Automated bot activity
  • Known legitimate bots
  • Brute-force attacks
  • VPNs and proxy networks
  • Tor exit nodes
  • Cloud hosting providers
  • Other security risks

The API can return fields such as:

Field Purpose
is_bot Identifies bot activity associated with the IP
bot_type Describes the bot activity category
bot_operator_name Identifies a known operator when available
is_known_good_bot Indicates a recognized legitimate bot
bot_confidence_score Confidence score for bot activity
threat_score Overall IP risk score
is_known_attacker Indicates known attacker activity

These signals help distinguish a recognized crawler from suspicious automation.

An important limitation is that IP intelligence classifies an address based on available intelligence. It doesn't prove that every individual request from that address came from the same software.

Is the IP Security API free?

The IP Security Lookup feature requires a paid subscription.

According to the current documentation, each successful security lookup costs two API credits. The provider also describes an option to request trial access through customer support.

You can still follow the next example without paid access by using mock security data.

6. Test IP Bot Classification in VS Code

Now we'll create a separate script to inspect security information.

We'll support two testing methods:

  • Mock mode: Uses example data locally and requires no paid subscription.
  • Live mode: Calls the actual IP Security API when your subscription permits it.

Step 1: Create the test file

Inside the same project, create:

test-ip.mjs

Paste:

import "dotenv/config";
import net from "node:net";

const API_KEY = process.env.IPGEOLOCATION_API_KEY;
const mode = process.argv[2] || "mock";
const ip = process.argv[3] || "4.227.36.0";

function classifySecurity(security) {
  if (security.is_known_attacker) {
    return "Review and consider blocking";
  }

  if (security.is_known_good_bot) {
    return "Verify operator before allowing";
  }

  if (security.is_bot) {
    return "Monitor or challenge";
  }

  return "Allow and monitor";
}

const mockSecurity = {
  is_bot: true,
  bot_type: "ai_crawler",
  bot_operator_name: "Example AI Operator",
  is_known_good_bot: true,
  bot_confidence_score: 95,
  threat_score: 10,
  is_known_attacker: false
};

async function getSecurityData() {
  if (mode === "mock") {
    return mockSecurity;
  }

  if (mode !== "live") {
    throw new Error("Use mock or live mode");
  }

  if (!API_KEY) {
    throw new Error(
      "Add IPGEOLOCATION_API_KEY to your .env file"
    );
  }

  if (!net.isIP(ip)) {
    throw new Error("Invalid IP address");
  }

  const url = new URL(
    "https://api.ipgeolocation.io/v3/security"
  );

  url.searchParams.set("apiKey", API_KEY);
  url.searchParams.set("ip", ip);

  const response = await fetch(url, {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000)
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const error = await response.text();

    throw new Error(
      `API returned ${response.status}: ${error}`
    );
  }

  const data = await response.json();

  if (!data.security) {
    throw new Error("Security object missing");
  }

  return data.security;
}

async function main() {
  try {
    const security = await getSecurityData();

    console.log("\nMode:", mode);

    if (mode === "mock") {
      console.log("Using simulated security data");
    } else {
      console.log("Checked IP:", ip);
    }

    console.log("\nSecurity information:");
    console.log(JSON.stringify(security, null, 2));

    console.log(
      "\nSuggested action:",
      classifySecurity(security)
    );

  } catch (error) {
    console.error("\nTest failed:", error.message);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
}

main();

Save the file.

Step 2: Run the free mock test

Open your VS Code terminal and run:

node test-ip.mjs mock

The script should display:

Mode: mock
Using simulated security data

Followed by the sample security information and:

Suggested action: Verify operator before allowing

This verifies your classification logic without making an external API request.

The data is simulated. Don't present this output as real IP intelligence.

Step 3: Configure live API access

If you have access to the paid Security API or an enabled trial, create a file named:

.env

Add:

IPGEOLOCATION_API_KEY=your_actual_api_key

Replace the placeholder with your API key.

Also create .gitignore:

.env
node_modules/

Never publish your real API key in screenshots, code examples, or a GitHub repository.

Step 4: Run a live lookup

Once your account has Security API access, execute:

node test-ip.mjs live 4.227.36.0

This IP appears in IPGeolocation's documentation as an example associated with a recognized AI crawler.

If the request succeeds, you'll receive real security fields and the script's suggested action.

The current classification may differ from the documentation example because IP intelligence changes over time.

Step 5: Understand API access errors

If your account doesn't support the Security API, you may receive an error similar to:

API returned 401:
IP Security Lookup is not supported
on your current subscription.

This doesn't mean your Node.js code is broken.

It means the API received your request but the subscription doesn't permit this feature.

To continue learning, run:

node test-ip.mjs mock

Or check the IP Security API documentation for subscription and trial information.

7. How to Decide Which Bots to Allow or Block

Once you have identification and risk signals, you need a policy.

A sensible starting point looks like this:

Traffic Suggested response
Verified Googlebot Allow indexing of public pages
Verified OAI-SearchBot Follow your AI search visibility policy
Verified GPTBot Follow your AI training access policy
Known monitoring service Allow expected monitoring traffic
Unrecognized automated traffic Monitor or rate-limit
Known malicious activity Investigate or block
Uncertain classification Collect more signals

Don't automatically block every datacenter IP.

Many legitimate crawlers operate from cloud infrastructure.

Similarly, don't automatically trust a bot simply because its IP reputation looks good.

For sensitive endpoints such as login forms, combine IP intelligence with request frequency, failed-login patterns, rate limits, and other behavioral signals.

The examples in this article return suggested actions. They don't implement firewall rules or automatically block requests.

That's intentional because a production blocking decision requires stronger verification and a tested false-positive policy.

8. Use robots.txt to Manage AI Crawlers

Some crawler operators support separate instructions for different purposes.

For example, you might allow Googlebot and OAI-SearchBot while asking GPTBot not to crawl your website.

Your robots.txt file could include:

User-agent: Googlebot
Allow: /

User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Allow: /

User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

This tells compliant crawlers that:

  • Googlebot may crawl public content.
  • OAI-SearchBot may crawl public content.
  • GPTBot should not crawl the site.

Remember that robots.txt is not a security mechanism.

Malicious bots can ignore it.

OpenAI also notes that user-triggered ChatGPT-User requests are different from its automatic crawlers, and ordinary robots.txt rules may not apply in the same way.

When you need actual enforcement, use verified network identity and appropriate server-side access controls.

9. Common Bot Detection Mistakes

Trusting user-agent strings

Anyone can claim to be Googlebot.

A matching string isn't proof of identity.

Blocking every cloud IP

Legitimate crawlers, monitoring tools, and real users may access your website from cloud infrastructure.

Treating all AI bots identically

AI search crawlers, training crawlers, and assistant-triggered fetchers serve different purposes.

Making an IP lookup for every request

External API calls introduce latency and cost.

Cache appropriate results and avoid unnecessary repeated lookups.

Blocking based on a single risk indicator

A flagged IP address doesn't necessarily prove malicious intent for every request.

Use additional signals and provide a way to investigate false positives.

Ignoring API failures

Your website shouldn't become unavailable just because a security intelligence API temporarily fails or your account reaches its limits.

Choose an explicit failure policy. For public informational pages, continuing with monitoring may be reasonable. Sensitive endpoints may require stricter controls.

10. Frequently Asked Questions

How do I detect AI bots on my website?

Start by examining user-agent strings and request logs. Verify recognized crawlers using their operators' published IP ranges or DNS verification methods. For unknown traffic, combine behavioral analysis with IP intelligence.

Can someone fake Googlebot?

Yes. User-agent headers can be changed freely. Google recommends verifying crawler requests using its documented DNS procedure or official IP ranges.

Can I test bot detection without paying for an API?

Yes. The basic Node.js user-agent detector in this article runs locally without an API key. You can also test the classification logic using simulated security data. Real IP Security lookup results require the appropriate API subscription or trial access.

Will blocking AI training crawlers affect Google rankings?

Blocking GPTBot through its specific robots.txt rule doesn't directly block Googlebot. However, broad server or firewall restrictions could accidentally affect search engine access.

Is IP intelligence enough to identify malicious bots?

No. It's one useful layer. Combine it with identity verification, request rates, behavioral patterns, and your website's own access policy.

Final Thoughts

Detecting AI bots isn't simply about checking whether a request contains the word bot.

You need to understand the traffic, identify known crawlers, verify their identities when necessary, and make decisions based on both reputation and behavior.

In this guide, we built a basic bot identifier, tested Googlebot and AI crawler user-agent strings, and added an optional IP Security classification example.

The most important lesson is simple:

Don't block a request just because it looks automated, and don't trust a request just because it claims to be legitimate.

Verify what you can, monitor what you can't, and apply policies that protect your website without unnecessarily restricting search engine access.

How are you handling AI crawlers on your own websites? Are you allowing them, blocking certain types, or monitoring everything first?

title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
description:
arXiv:2610.19674v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.

title: Energy Ring: Stabilizing Feature Energy for Reliable Test-Time Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.14525v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones while the model is already deployed, operating directly on a continual unlabeled test-time stream. Existing TTD methods are overly conservative, making known and unknown features collapse together and difficult to separate during test-time adaptation. In this paper, we revisit TTD from an energy perspective and find that the natural energy gap between known and unknown classes is unstable and easily collapses. We therefore propose Energy Ring to stabilize this gap by anchoring the two types of classes on separate energy rings. A lightweight adapter enlarges the norm-based gap while preserving known-class directions, and a perturbation consistency module forms compact clusters for unknown classes. During testing, energy-guided confidence weighting improves prediction, and a stability-based rectification mechanism corrects unreliable updates. Experimental results show that Energy Ring significantly improves TTD performance against existing TTD methods.

title: FPV-CRASH: A Dataset for Offline Crash Moment Localization in Drone First-Person-View Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.19785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Crash Moment Localization aims to localize the major physical impact that interrupts controlled flight in an onboard first-person-view (FPV) video recorded by a drone, thereby providing a temporal reference for retrospective crash analysis in aerial robotics. However, existing crash-video datasets predominantly target surveillance or dash-camera footage, and their annotation schemes and task formulations are not designed for temporal localization of the major physical impact in UAV onboard FPV videos. To address this gap, we present FPV-CRASH, a dataset and fixed-protocol reference evaluation for offline Crash Moment Localization in drone FPV videos. FPV-CRASH contains 1,052 drone FPV clips (526 Crash and 526 Normal); each Crash clip has a single-frame reference annotation for the Crash Moment, and every clip is paired with four English captions automatically generated from sampled frames and the known Crash/Normal label. Normal clips carry no timestamp target and provide training-time background supervision. The captions support an auxiliary Text-to-Video Retrieval task, whereas localization inference remains video-only. We further provide a heatmap-based reference model that estimates a continuous Crash Moment timestamp from sparsely sampled frames. Under the fixed, non-source-disjoint clip-level protocol, the reference model reduces MAE from 1.12 s for the strongest fixed timing-prior baseline to 0.56 s (a 50% relative reduction) and achieves a median absolute error (MedAE) of 0.33 s; the fraction of clips localized within 0.5 s rises from 37.14% to 65.71%. The release includes annotations, available source video identifiers and URLs, clipping metadata, fixed split lists, and preprocessing code so that the reportable portion can be reconstructed without redistributing source footage. At submission time, all source-compilation URLs remained accessible.

title: SkillHorizon: Constructing Long-Horizon Agent Tasks through Skill Composition
description:
arXiv:2610.14966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon agents must complete workflows in which later activities depend on earlier outputs and changes to shared state. A key challenge for evaluation is to expand task requirements and their dependencies while keeping tasks executable and outcomes verifiable. We introduce SkillHorizon, a benchmark that constructs long-horizon tasks through skill composition in seven business environments. Its generators use domain-specific rules to turn reusable skill procedures into concrete business activities. These activities are connected through input-output dependencies, shared resources, and state updates, allowing workload and coordination demands to grow together. Successful reference executions validate task feasibility and measure interaction workload, while programmatic evaluators assess local completion and whole-task success. We evaluate five language models on 1,050 tasks with reference interaction workloads ranging from 64K to 1M tokens. Across these scales, mean local-goal completion falls from 90.4% to 46.8%, as completed work fails to keep pace with growing requirements. At larger workloads, agents more often submit unsuccessful final answers with substantial work unfinished and tool-call allowance remaining. Trace analysis also identifies cases where scripts execute successfully but their outputs fail downstream business checks. SkillHorizon provides a configurable testbed for studying sustained progress, dependency coordination, and complete task delivery in growing workflows. Our code is available at https://github.com/KnowComp/SkillHorizon.

title: Beyond Static Cues: Unified Dynamic Detection of MLLM Backdoors via Dual-Flow Trajectory Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.20319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, yet their susceptibility to backdoor attacks remains a formidable challenge. While existing defenses have evolved from visual-centric patch cues to unsupervised internal attention statistics, they are fundamentally constrained by a reliance on static snapshots and attack-specific heuristics. Given the intricate interplay between dual modalities, the vast design space for multimodal triggers allows diverse threats, such as textual injections, sub-perceptual noises, and coordinated cross-modal triggers, to easily circumvent such rigid priors, particularly when attack types are unknown in real-world applications. In this paper, we rethink backdoor detection by shifting the diagnostic paradigm from static observations to dynamic output evolution. We observe that a successful attack inevitably hijacks the model's decoding trajectory, skewing internal modal contributions during generation while maintaining an abnormal output invariance despite input perturbations. To capture this behavior, we propose EVO-Detect, a unified detection framework that monitors the dynamic evolution of internal signals during early decoding steps through two complementary channels: Attention Flow and Logits Flow. The attention branch measures how image-text attention allocation evolves during early generation, whereas the logits branch quantifies the sensitivity of the output distribution to modal perturbations through interventional ablations. We then convert these trajectories into compact sample-level metrics and normalize them against negative-control signatures so that natural perturbations are less likely to be mistaken for backdoor evidence. Extensive evaluations show that our approach substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines such as BYE and TCAP across diverse attack families.
