title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
description:
arXiv:2610.19528v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.

title: Single-step Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback
description:
arXiv:2610.15141v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Single-step retrosynthesis is a one-to-many inverse problem, yet most models are trained and evaluated against a single recorded reactant set. Reference-based training gives no explicit positive signal for unrecorded alternatives, and exact-match evaluation rejects non-matching predictions regardless of chemical plausibility. We propose Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback (RetroRLFF), which optimizes reactant generation using both reference agreement and forward consistency with the target product. Starting from a supervised decoder-only Transformer, RetroRLFF generates complete reactant candidates and uses a frozen forward reaction model to predict products. A sequence-level reward combines reference agreement and forward consistency while penalizing invalid outputs. Direct Advantage-Based Policy Optimization updates the policy without human preference annotations or a preference-trained reward model. On USPTO-50K, RetroRLFF outperforms all 14 baselines in candidate-level round-trip accuracy at k = 1, 3, 5, and 10. With approximately 50 million parameters, it achieves 90.1% top-1 round-trip accuracy, exceeding R-SMILES, the strongest competing baseline on this metric, by 8.5 percentage points. Compared with its supervised policy, round-trip accuracy increases from 83.1% to 90.1%, while exact-match accuracy is maintained at 57.9% versus 57.5%. In an anonymized expert assessment of 131 randomly selected test cases, organic synthesis experts prefer RetroRLFF over EditRetro in 67.9% of comparisons. These results support forward feedback as a training signal for improving forward consistency while retaining top-1 reference recovery. Expert assessment provides complementary evidence of synthetic feasibility on the selected cases, although neither forward consistency nor expert preference establishes experimental feasibility.

title: Your voice agent sounds right. Did it place the right order?
description:
Here is a Hinglish call to a restaurant voice agent:

caller:  Do paneer wrap... actually ek hi karo. Bina pyaaz. Aur ek mango lassi.
agent:   2 Paneer Wrap add kar diya. Paneer Wrap 1 kar diya. Paneer Wrap No onion kar diya.
         1 Mango Lassi add kar diya. Aur kuch?
caller:  Bas itna hi, thanks.
agent:   Aapka order: 1 Paneer Wrap, No onion; 1 Mango Lassi. Order place ho gaya, shukriya!

The agent read back one wrap without onion. This is what it committed:

Field Expected Actual Result
Submitted orders 1 1 Pass
Paneer Wrap quantity 1 2 Fail
Paneer Wrap · Onion No onion With onion Fail
Mango Lassi quantity 1 1 Pass

A transcript-based test, or an LLM judge reading the conversation, passes this call. The customer gets two wraps with onion.

What I built

IndicOrderBench is an open-source benchmark and CI gate for voice ordering agents. It compares the committed backend state against each scenario's acceptable end states, in English and Hinglish, instead of grading the words the agent said.

The single-file HTML report from the fixed reference agent. The failing run of the same scenario is the one that catches the wrong order.

The hard failures it targets aren't accent or latency. They're mid-sentence corrections ("two... actually one"), modifiers ("no onion"), cancellations and duplicate submissions, especially in code-mixed speech where number words and negations don't look like English.

pip install indicorderbench

iob demo --out demo-out     # buggy vs fixed reference agent, no network, no keys
iob run starter --agent builtin:correct --tag smoke --trials 3

A run writes results.json (every transcript, tool call and backend snapshot), junit.xml for any CI system, and a single-file report.html that opens from file://. The exit code is non-zero when an agent change starts placing wrong orders, so the build fails before a customer sees it.

You can connect your agent in-process from Python, or over an HTTP adapter. The sandbox backend hands you JSON-schema tool definitions to give your LLM.

Scope

It's small and deterministic on purpose: reproducible runs, no API keys for the demo. It's an early benchmark, not a leaderboard of production systems.

Repo (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Lingikaushikreddy/indicorderbench
PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/indicorderbench/

If you've seen a voice agent fail in a way this doesn't cover, open an issue with the transcript. Scenarios are easy to add.

title: Data-free Multistep Diffusion Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.19305v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-step diffusion distillation achieves strong performance on small datasets but remains insufficient for high-resolution or complex text-to-image settings. Extending to multistep distillation often requires training data, suffers from early-step degradation, inconsistent outputs across sampling budgets, and incurs high computational cost. We identify that these limitations stem from simultaneous training, where a single adapted network approximates multiple score functions of different student distributions at once, causing biased distribution matching and unstable optimization. Therefore, we propose Progressive Multistep Data-free Distillation (PMDD), which assigns a dedicated adapted network per student distribution while avoiding the memory overhead of maintaining multiple adapted networks. Combined with a stage-wise unforget loss to preserve earlier-step generations, PMDD reduces optimization bias in the student, provides faster convergence, and a single unified model that supports multiple inference budgets. Extensive experiments show that PMDD matches or outperforms data-free few-step baselines at every multistep budget, reaches FID 1.99 on ImageNet 64x64 in two steps, below its 512-NFE teacher (2.32), and achieves FID 7.76 on zero-shot COCO 512x512, while requiring 4-5x less training compute than data-free DMDv2 to support three inference budgets.

title: PCAD-31-02 in Code: Validation Checks and Safe sqlite3 Queries Behind 30 of the 48 Items
description:
The Python Institute PCAD-31-02 exam has 48 items, and 30 of them come from two syllabus blocks: Data Acquisition and Pre-Processing (14) and Programming and Database Skills (16). If you can clean a messy file, validate it, move it into a database with safe queries and read the result back into pandas, you have practised the skills behind 62.5% of the exam.

This post does all of that in one small script you can run. Every output shown below was produced by running it with Python 3.12 and pandas 3.0.6, using only sqlite3 from the standard library for the database part.

What does the PCAD-31-02 exam look like?

PCAD (Certified Associate Data Analyst with Python) is the associate-level data exam of the OpenEDG Python Institute. The figures below come from the official PCAD certification page, read on 15 October 2026.

Item Value
Exam code PCAD-31-02, active since July 15, 2025 (PCAD-31-01 retired July 14, 2025)
Questions 48 single-select and multiple-select items, some scenario-based
Time 60 minutes, plus the NDA screen
Passing score 75%
Price Exam from $195; exam with retake from $225; practice test $49
Delivery Online through OpenEDG Testing Service (TestNow)
Prerequisites None formal; PCAP and PCED (or equivalent) recommended
Validity 6 years

How are the 48 items split across the five blocks?

The Python Institute publishes the split in the PCAD-31-02 exam syllabus, last updated July 15, 2025. Each item is worth up to one point, and the raw score is normalized to a percentage.

Block Items Weight
1. Data Acquisition and Pre-Processing 14 29.2%
2. Programming and Database Skills 16 33.3%
3. Statistical Analysis 4 8.3%
4. Data Analysis and Modeling 9 18.8%
5. Data Communication and Visualization 5 10.4%

Note what that means for your study plan. Blocks 1 and 2 are the bulk, but 30 of 48 is still below the 75% pass mark, so the statistics, pandas and charting blocks cannot be skipped. The script below covers the large blocks; it also touches objective 4.1.1 (cleaning with pandas) on the way.

Why load every column as text first?

Objective 1.2.2 asks you to identify erroneous data before you fix it. If pandas guesses types on load, a bad value can silently change a whole column's type, and you lose the chance to see which rows were wrong. Loading with dtype=str keeps the raw values so the cleaning step decides what each one means.

Here is a small order file with the problems the syllabus lists by name: stray spaces, mixed case, a thousands separator, a missing value written as text, a negative amount, a duplicate row, a date in the wrong format and five spellings of yes and no.

import io
import sqlite3

import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.width", 120, "display.max_columns", 10)   # print tables in full

RAW = """order_id,customer,country,amount,paid,order_date,ship_date
1001,  Ana Lima ,BR,120.50,yes,2026-09-01,2026-09-03
1002,ben okafor,NG,"1,080.00",Y,2026-09-02,2026-09-01
1003,Chen Wei,CN,n/a,no,2026-09-02,2026-09-05
1004,Ana Lima,br,-15,TRUE,2026-09-03,2026-09-04
1004,Ana Lima,br,-15,TRUE,2026-09-03,2026-09-04
1005,Dara Singh,IN,64.00,0,03/09/2026,2026-09-06
1006,Ben Okafor,NG,310.00,1,2026-09-04,2026-09-07
1007,Chen Wei,cn,89.90,yes,2026-09-05,2026-09-05
1008,Dara Singh,IN,455.00,N,2026-09-06,2026-09-09
1009,ana lima,BR,72.25,y,2026-09-07,2026-09-08
"""
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(RAW), dtype=str)
print(len(df), "rows")   # 10 rows

Which cleaning steps does Block 1 name, and what do they look like?

Objective 1.2.4 lists them in one sentence: string manipulation, format standardization, boolean normalization, case normalization and string-to-number conversion. Each one is a single line in pandas.

BOOL = {"yes": True, "y": True, "true": True, "1": True,
        "no": False, "n": False, "false": False, "0": False}

df = df.drop_duplicates()
df["customer"] = df["customer"].str.strip().str.title()
df["country"] = df["country"].str.strip().str.upper()
df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount"].str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")
df["paid"] = df["paid"].str.strip().str.lower().map(BOOL)
for col in ("order_date", "ship_date"):
    df[col] = pd.to_datetime(df[col], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
df["order_id"] = df["order_id"].astype(int)
print(df.dtypes)

order_id               int64
customer                 str
country                  str
amount               float64
paid                    bool
order_date    datetime64[us]
ship_date     datetime64[us]
dtype: object

The key argument is errors="coerce". As the pandas.to_numeric reference explains, it turns a value that cannot be parsed into NaN instead of raising an exception. That is what you want during cleaning: the bad value becomes a marker you can count and report, not a crash halfway through a file.

The same idea applies to dates. Passing an explicit format means 03/09/2026 becomes NaT rather than being guessed as March 9 or September 3. Whether that date was day-first or month-first is a question for the data owner, not for the parser.

What do type, range and cross-field checks look like in pandas?

Objective 1.3.1 names three kinds of validation: type, range and cross-field. Build each check as a boolean column, then keep the rows where no check fired. A table of named checks is easier to report to a stakeholder than a chain of filters.

checks = pd.DataFrame({
    "amount_not_numeric": df["amount"].isna(),            # type
    "order_date_unparsed": df["order_date"].isna(),       # type
    "amount_not_positive": df["amount"] <= 0,             # range
    "shipped_before_order": df["ship_date"] < df["order_date"],  # cross-field
})
bad = checks.any(axis=1)
print(checks[bad].set_axis(df.loc[bad, "order_id"]))
clean = df[~bad]
print(len(clean), "rows pass")

          amount_not_numeric  order_date_unparsed  amount_not_positive  shipped_before_order
order_id
1002                   False                False                False                  True
1003                    True                False                False                 False
1004                   False                False                 True                 False
1005                   False                 True                False                 False
5 rows pass

Two details are worth knowing for the exam. First, a comparison with NaN or NaT is always False, so a missing amount does not trip the range check; that is why the type check exists separately. Second, the duplicate of order 1004 was already gone, because drop_duplicates() ran before validation. Removing or imputing a row is a decision with consequences, and objective 1.2.4 asks you to discuss imputation against exclusion. Here exclusion is the honest choice: there is no sensible value to invent for a missing order amount.

How do Python types map to SQLite columns?

Objective 2.4.5 is about converting data types between SQL and Python. The sqlite3 module documentation lists exactly five Python types that go into SQLite without help: None, int, float, str and bytes.

Python value SQLite storage What to do
None NULL Nothing
int INTEGER Nothing
float REAL Nothing
str TEXT Nothing
bool INTEGER (0 or 1) Store as int(value)
datetime or pandas Timestamp No date type Store as ISO 8601 text

SQLite has no boolean and no date storage class. The SQLite page on datatypes and type affinity says booleans are stored as the integers 0 and 1, and dates as ISO 8601 text, a real number or an integer. Here is what happens if you skip the conversion:

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("""
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer   TEXT    NOT NULL,
    country    TEXT    NOT NULL,
    amount     REAL    CHECK (amount > 0),
    paid       INTEGER NOT NULL,
    order_date TEXT    NOT NULL
)""")
first = clean.iloc[0]
try:
    con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                (first["order_id"], first["customer"], first["country"],
                 first["amount"], first["paid"], first["order_date"]))
except sqlite3.ProgrammingError as e:
    print("ProgrammingError:", e)

ProgrammingError: Error binding parameter 6: type 'Timestamp' is not supported

So convert each row explicitly and insert the batch with executemany. The with con: block commits on success and rolls back on an exception, and the CHECK constraint in the table is a second line of defence for the range rule:

rows = [
    (int(r.order_id), r.customer, r.country, float(r.amount),
     int(r.paid), r.order_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
    for r in clean.itertuples(index=False)
]
with con:
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders").fetchone())   # (5,)

try:
    with con:
        con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                    (1010, "Eve Park", "KR", -5.0, 1, "2026-09-08"))
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("IntegrityError:", e)   # CHECK constraint failed: amount > 0

Why does the exam keep asking about parameterized queries?

Two Block 2 objectives, 2.4.4 and 2.4.6, come back to the same point: never build SQL by pasting values into a string. The demonstration takes four lines.

name = "x' OR '1'='1"
unsafe = f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = '{name}'"
print(con.execute(unsafe).fetchone())        # (5,)  every row matched
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = ?", (name,)).fetchone())   # (0,)
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = :who",
                  {"who": "Ana Lima"}).fetchone())   # (2,)

The f-string version closes the quote early and turns the filter into a condition that is always true. With a ? placeholder the driver sends the value separately from the SQL text, so the quote characters are just part of a name that matches nobody. The third line shows the named style, :who with a dictionary, which reads better once a query has several parameters.

How do you get query results back into pandas?

Objective 2.4.1 lists the clauses the exam expects you to combine: SELECT, FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY and LIMIT. The query below uses all of them, with a LEFT JOIN so that an order from a country missing in the lookup table is kept and labelled rather than dropped.

con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE countries (code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO countries VALUES ('BR', 'Americas'), ('NG', 'Africa'), ('IN', 'Asia');
""")
QUERY = """
SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unmapped') AS region,
       COUNT(*)                       AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(o.amount), 2)        AS revenue,
       MIN(o.order_date)              AS first_order
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN countries AS c ON c.code = o.country
WHERE o.paid = :paid
GROUP BY region
HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_orders
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5
"""
summary = pd.read_sql_query(QUERY, con, params={"paid": 1, "min_orders": 1})
print(summary)
print(summary.dtypes)

     region  orders  revenue first_order
0    Africa       1   310.00  2026-09-04
1  Americas       2   192.75  2026-09-01
2  Unmapped       1    89.90  2026-09-05
region             str
orders           int64
revenue        float64
first_order        str
dtype: object

The params argument of pandas.read_sql_query passes values to the driver, so the placeholder rule still holds. Look at the last dtype, though: first_order came back as text, because that is how SQLite stored it. Add parse_dates=["first_order"] to the call and the column comes back as datetime64. The round trip from Timestamp to text and back is exactly the kind of conversion objective 2.4.5 has in mind.

The Chen Wei order lands in "Unmapped" because CN is not in the lookup table. With an INNER JOIN that paid order would vanish from the revenue total without any warning, which is a classic scenario question.

Is there a short video on preparing for PCAD?

This three-minute video from the EduSum channel gives preparation tips for the PCAD exam. It is about study habits rather than code, so it pairs well with the hands-on script above.

What should you practise after this script?

Run the script, then break it on purpose. Add a row whose paid value is maybe and see what map() produces; it gives NaN, and the column is no longer boolean. Then write a validation check for it. That loop of breaking the data and then catching the break is a fast way to learn Blocks 1 and 2.

To track the rest of the syllabus objective by objective, this PCAD-31-02 syllabus breakdown with exam details lists every block and topic on one page.

For Blocks 3 to 5, write small scripts of the same kind: a bootstrap of the mean with NumPy, a linear and a logistic regression with a train and test split, and one Matplotlib chart with labelled axes, a title and a legend.

When you want to see how the scenario items are phrased, work through these PCAD sample questions with answers and note which block each one belongs to.

Frequently asked questions

1. How many questions are on the PCAD-31-02 exam, and what score do I need to pass?

The exam has 48 single-select and multiple-select items, and you have 60 minutes plus the NDA screen. You pass with a cumulative score of at least 75%.

2. How much does the PCAD exam cost?

The Python Institute lists the exam from $195, the exam with a retake from $225, the exam with a practice test from $215 and all three from $245. The practice test alone is $49.

3. Is PCAD-31-01 still available?

No. PCAD-31-01 was retired on July 14, 2025, and PCAD-31-02 has been the active version since July 15, 2025. Use the PCAD-31-02 syllabus when you study.

4. Do I need PCAP or PCED before taking PCAD?

There are no formal prerequisites. The Python Institute recommends PCAP and PCED, or equivalent knowledge, plus field-specific skills.

5. How long is the PCAD certification valid, and when can I retake a failed exam?

The certification is valid for 6 years. After a failed attempt you must wait 15 days before you can take the exam again.

title: A Guide to 4 Sequence Guarantees for Accepted High Bid Broadcasts
description:
The page says students in a live classroom auction have seen different winning bids after reconnecting. An instructor's screen shows the latest accepted bid, while a student's chat still shows the previous one. Short answer: commit the accepted bid and its room-local sequence number in one authoritative transaction, then broadcast that committed event; on reconnect, fetch the missing sequence range before showing the room as caught up. An Express handler can accept the request, but an HTTP 200 or a successful socket write cannot establish that every student received it.

This is a delivery problem, not a faster-socket problem. A WebSocket connection gives a channel for messages, while application-level recovery still needs an event identifier and a way to read events missed while disconnected. The WebSocket protocol defines framing and connection behavior, not durable room history or exactly-once application processing. See RFC 6455 in Further reading.

No receipt, no certainty.

What should have paged before the classroom diverged?

An alert on disconnected sockets comes late and can miss the actual failure: a connected client may also skip an event after a server restart or a failed fan-out. Measure the age of the oldest committed room event that has not reached the delivery worker, and count detected sequence gaps during client catch-up. Page on sustained backlog age against the room's delivery SLO; use a separate, lower-severity signal for a rising gap-recovery rate. The SLO and alert window need to come from measured classroom requirements, not a copied threshold.

First distinguish three positions: the room's committed sequence, the last sequence a fan-out worker has attempted, and the last contiguous sequence each client has applied. Those counters answer different questions. A broadcast counter that increments before the database transaction commits can advance even when the bid is rejected, leaving a gap that no reconnect can fill. Conversely, a committed event with no delivery attempt is a useful early warning while clients may still appear healthy.

For a live auction inside a course room, a bid request should carry an idempotency key, room ID, bidder identity, and offered amount. The server checks authorization and the current high bid inside the transaction, assigns the next room-local sequence only to an accepted bid, and persists an event with that accepted amount. The acceptance response returns the committed sequence. Other bidders learn the result from the room stream, not from trusting their own submitted amount. Two concurrent requests must serialize around the room's authoritative bid state; otherwise both can claim the same predecessor.

How should an accepted high bid broadcast carry its sequence number?

At the commit boundary. Publishing before commit lets students see a winning bid that later rolls back. Publishing only from the request handler after commit creates the opposite hole: the handler can die between commit and broadcast. A transactional outbox closes that hole by storing the accepted-bid event and the state update in the same transaction; a worker retries delivery afterward. The outbox does not make client delivery exactly once. A worker may send and then crash before recording progress, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. The transactional outbox pattern and its duplicate-delivery consequence are documented in Further reading.

For an Express implementation, keep the route thin: authenticate, pass the command and idempotency key to the transactional bid service, and return the committed sequence; a separate broadcaster drains the outbox. Here is the smaller, transport-independent piece of client-side recovery logic in Go. It never assumes a WebSocket callback represents a durable acknowledgment:

package room

import "errors"

var ErrGap = errors.New("fetch missing room events")

type Event struct {
    RoomID   string
    Sequence uint64
    Kind     string
    Amount   int64 // Minor currency units, as stored by the server.
}

type Cursor struct {
    RoomID   string
    Sequence uint64
}

func Apply(cursor *Cursor, event Event) error {
    if event.RoomID != cursor.RoomID {
        return errors.New("event belongs to another room")
    }
    if event.Sequence <= cursor.Sequence {
        return nil // Retried delivery or replay overlap.
    }
    if event.Sequence != cursor.Sequence+1 {
        return ErrGap
    }
    cursor.Sequence = event.Sequence
    return nil
}

Persist the cursor only after applying the corresponding event to the local view. If the client sees a gap, pause live application, request events after its last contiguous sequence, and replay them in order before resuming the stream. During that handoff, buffer later live events or open the stream first and deduplicate replay overlap by sequence; otherwise an event committed between the history query and subscription can disappear from the view. Consider a student whose cursor is 41 while the worker has committed 42 and 43: if the client queries history through 42, then subscribes after 43 was broadcast, neither the replay nor the live stream contains 43. Opening the stream first and holding its events during replay removes that specific handoff window, provided duplicates are collapsed by sequence. Reconnection needs a bounded retention policy too: if the cursor predates available history, return an authoritative snapshot plus its sequence, then resume from there. A snapshot without its sequence cannot establish a clean handoff.

Replay can get expensive.

Which guarantee is worth carrying on call?

The table is a capacity-planning question as much as a correctness question. A larger room multiplies simultaneous connections and replay demand, while a slow client can retain an unbounded send queue unless the server caps it and forces a clean reconnect.

Choice What it establishes Operational cost
Fire-and-forget fan-out Best-effort live display Small state footprint; disconnected learners miss events.
Persisted room log with replay At-least-once delivery opportunity while events remain retained Storage, replay reads, retention policy, and duplicate handling.
Client acknowledgment of contiguous sequence Evidence of application progress per client Ack storage and extra traffic; acks can also be lost.
Exactly-once display effect One visible application of each room sequence Requires idempotent client state transitions; transport alone cannot provide it.

I would choose a retained log and idempotent application for accepted bids because a duplicated chat bubble is repairable, but a missing high bid changes the apparent outcome. Ordinary typing indicators warrant a different choice: replaying stale presence is more misleading than dropping it. Keep these message classes separate even if they share a connection.

The limitation of a retained log is that it cannot replay forever without a retention and storage budget, and it cannot establish what a client actually displayed unless that client acknowledges application. For a course that does not need recoverable bid history, best-effort broadcasts avoid much of that persistent-state burden; for an auction where the displayed winner matters, that trade-off is unacceptable. Choose the guarantee by event class, not by transport branding.

The buy-versus-build decision follows the same boundary. A managed transport can reduce connection operations, but the team still owns acceptance rules, sequence assignment, retention requirements, and the definition of a caught-up room; self-hosting the transport adds capacity limits, deployment drains, and on-call work. Neither option turns an acknowledgment of network delivery into proof that a student rendered the accepted bid. Test both with a forced disconnect after commit, a duplicate outbox dispatch, two concurrent higher bids, and a reconnect during replay. Track rejected bids separately from accepted-event delivery latency so a legitimate rejection does not appear as lost fan-out.

When does the alert do more harm than good?

Do not page on every reconnect or each transient replay gap. Wireless classroom networks make both common, and a gap that closes within the delivery SLO has not yet violated the user-facing objective. Alert on sustained oldest-undelivered age and on rooms that remain behind after recovery; annotate those signals with room size, replay rate, and outbox backlog so on-call can distinguish a single slow client from a worker-wide stall.

The cost of an aggressive threshold is real: noisy pages train the team to disregard the one backlog that will leave an instructor and students looking at different accepted bids. The cost of a permissive one is a silent, durable disagreement. Set the threshold from observed delivery latency and the classroom's recovery target, then exercise it during controlled worker restarts and client disconnects. The alert should tell on-call which committed sequence is waiting, not merely that a socket closed.

Further reading

  • WebSocket Protocol, RFC 6455: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • Transactional Outbox pattern and duplicate delivery: https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • WebRTC 1.0 specification, for the separate peer-connection transport boundary: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Likelihood Is Not Authorship: Can We Reliably Measure Human Contribution in AI-Assisted Writing?
description:
arXiv:2610.19767v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI-text detection generally asks whether a machine wrote a text. As AI becomes an increasingly integral and accepted part of writing, the more relevant question is no longer whether AI was used, but how much of the text reflects human contribution. A prominent line of work estimates this by measuring how predictive a person's prompt is of the final text. We show that this measure can be easily manipulated. We introduce SPECIFICITY PADDING that simply asks the model to copy a few random IDs from the prompt, and that alone makes a title-only request look more human than one that supplies the article's key ideas. A context-swap audit then holds each document fixed, and only shows or hides the IDs to the evaluator. The score of the unchanged text swings by a third to half of its scale, and it rises for every document we test, on news and scientific abstracts, across varied LLMs from 3.8B to 753B parameters. The same articles can average 85\% human or 15\% human depending only on which prompt is on record, and even with no prompt at all, the output-only variant rewards the random strings themselves. An exact identity, the credit ledger, explains why. The score is a surprisal-weighted average over the text, so rare strings that the context makes copyable collect the credit, whatever they mean. A two-point bound marks a deeper limit. If the prompt could have been machine-written, every transcript-only method must, in the worst case, miss by half the contribution at stake. Likelihood-based scores alone cannot reliably establish human contribution without evidence of what the person added and how the text was produced.

title: ScienceBuddy-PV: A Verifier-Governed Recursive Improvement Protocol for Panvascular Intervention Research
description:
arXiv:2610.14523v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: ScienceBuddy-PV adapts the ScienceBuddy recursive-in-recursive design to panvascular intervention research through a structured evidence ledger, device-vessel ontology, abstention contract and retained failure bank. Recursive harness optimization and outer-loop model learning, including reinforcement learning, are specified but not executed. We audit a fixed component, rather than the complete agent system, using separate ARCADE syntax and stenosis tasks (1,000 training, 200 validation and 300 test images per task). A shared task-masked convolutional model was trained once per representation setting; its parameters and the heuristic support gate were then held fixed, with the stenosis threshold selected on validation data. On the locked test sets, syntax Dice was 0.475 (95% CI 0.459-0.490) and stenosis Dice was 0.231 (95% CI 0.214-0.249). Stenosis pixel AUROC was 0.957 and AUPRC was 0.180 at prevalence 0.00975. The gate accepted 76.7% of stenosis-frame outputs versus 100% for a score-only comparator. In a constructed mask audit, it accepted 44.3% of reference candidates and rejected 55.7%, exposing the cost of abstention. Acceptance does not establish correctness or clinical safety. This public-data component audit makes support and abstention measurable and provides a reproducible protocol for future collaborative agent studies. It does not demonstrate recursive improvement, patient-level validity or clinical device recommendations.

title: Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Equivariant structure-prediction pipelines alternate coordinate updates with the construction of a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph whose membership is a discrete, piecewise-constant function of the coordinates. Rebuilding that graph at every block boundary (PB) is the expensive part of an epoch, whereas reusing one frozen graph (F) is fast but leaves a topology gap. We study a two-pass design in which the cheap pass records a small amount of state (margins, kNN radii, measured per-boundary displacements) and a second pass compensates conservatively. We formulate the choice of the graph-construction basis as a damped fixed-point iteration whose unique fixed point is exactly PB, and derive (i) exact non-flip certificates with the two-sided constant $m_i/4$ and one-sided constant $m_i/2$, (ii) the minimum-variance (BLUE) replay gain $\gamma^*$ and the resulting feasibility crossover, (iii) an $\ell_\infty$ trust-region projection that preserves convergence, and (iv) an analytic near-tie spacing law $E[m] \approx r_k/(3k)$ that matches measurements to 1\%. Three compensation levels are implemented in C++ (L1: frozen set with live geometry; L2: margin-gated local repair; L3: damped, projected basis) and validated under a matched-conditions protocol (identical seed, MSA depth and trajectory family, only the topology mode differs). L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly ($D = 0.0000$ at every boundary), L1 stays within 0.6% and L3 interpolates monotonically: L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly when the trust region is removed, and L3 interpolates between the frozen and the PB topology. The recorded trajectory itself yields a measured $1.5\times$ Pass-1 and $1.76\times$ epoch speed-up with no measurable loss gap. An open-source implementation of the runtime and of all the experiments reported here is available at https://github.com/AlbertHuang96/ProteinPredictMachineLearning.

title: CSAT, NPS or CES: which metric should customer service use?
description:
Short answer: Customer service should primarily measure per ticket, with CSAT for how satisfied the customer was and CES for how much effort it took. NPS and customer satisfaction indexes measure the relationship with the company as a whole, are asked rarely and suit management's annual review, not the daily work. The metric is chosen by the decision it should drive, and the number means nothing without response rate and comments.

Anyone who runs customer service sooner or later gets the question from management: what is our NPS? At the same time the customer service tool shows a CSAT number, someone has read that CES is the metric that predicts loyalty, and an industry benchmark from the Swedish Quality Index talks about a customer satisfaction index. This article sorts out what they measure, what the research says about them and how a customer service team with a few hundred tickets a week should choose.

What do CSAT, NPS, CES and satisfaction indexes actually measure?

The four metrics measure different things at different moments, and that difference decides which one you should use. This is how they differ:

Metric The question the customer gets Scale When it is asked What the answer says
CSAT, customer satisfaction score How satisfied were you with the help you received? Often 1â€“5 or satisfied/dissatisfied Right after a closed ticket How that particular ticket went
CES, customer effort score Did the company make it easy for you to resolve your issue? 1â€“7 in Gartner's version Right after a closed ticket How much effort the customer had to put in
NPS, net promoter score How likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague? 0â€“10 At regular intervals, independent of tickets The customer's attitude to the company as a whole
Customer satisfaction index (NKI in Sweden) Several questions on expectations, quality and satisfaction Index 0â€“100 Annually, often via an external survey The relationship with the company compared with others in the industry

NPS is calculated as the share answering 9 or 10 minus the share answering 0 to 6, and can therefore range from minus 100 to plus 100. NKI is the Swedish variant of a customer satisfaction index; the Swedish Quality Index measures it with a statistical model that combines several questions into one index, and reports NPS alongside it.

Why is NPS not enough for customer service?

NPS measures the customer's relationship with the company and was designed to predict growth, not to run a customer service department. The metric was introduced by Fred Reichheld in Harvard Business Review in 2003, where he showed that the share of customers willing to recommend the company correlated with growth in most of the industries studied. The question therefore concerns the company as a whole, and the answer is affected by price, product, delivery and brand as much as by customer service.

For customer service that creates three problems:

  1. The answer cannot be tied to an action. A customer who gives a 6 may be unhappy with the shipping cost. Customer service can do nothing about that, and does not even know it was the reason.
  2. The frequency is too low. NPS is typically asked a few times a year to a sample, while customer service needs signals per week and per ticket type.
  3. The scale is blunt at low volumes. A team with 300 tickets a week and a 20 percent response rate gets 60 answers. With the NPS formula a single customer moves the metric several points.

That does not make NPS wrong. It is the right metric at management level, ideally compared with the industry through a satisfaction index. Customer service contributes to the number, but does not steer by it.

What does the research say about customer effort?

How easy the customer had it weighs more for loyalty than how delighted the customer became. That conclusion comes from a study of more than 75,000 customers who contacted customer service or used self-service, published by Matthew Dixon, Karen Freeman and Nicholas Toman in Harvard Business Review in 2010. The researchers found that going above and beyond made little difference: customers wanted a simple and quick solution to their problem. They introduced the customer effort score and showed that it predicted loyalty better than both customer satisfaction measures and NPS.

Gartner, which manages the research today, describes customer effort as a good indicator of whether the customer buys again and buys more, and phrases the question as a statement to rate on a seven-point scale: the company made it easy for me to resolve my issue. What drives effort is what customer service actually controls: having to contact the company again, switching channels, repeating your story, being passed around.

The customer who emailed about a return, got a reply with a question back, answered, waited and finally called may well answer "satisfied" on CSAT because the return went through. On CES the same customer scores low, and that is the answer that predicts whether the customer shops again.

How do you measure CSAT and CES per ticket without wearing customers out?

With one question, asked once per ticket, shortly after the ticket is resolved, and with a free-text field. Zendesk by default sends its CSAT survey a day after the ticket is marked as solved, asks for a positive or negative rating and an optional comment, and lets the customer respond within 28 days.

A few rules that keep the response rate up and the answers useful:

  • One survey per ticket, not per message. A customer with three tickets in a month gets three surveys; a customer with ten messages in one ticket gets one.
  • Ask about the ticket, not the agent. "How satisfied are you with the help?" rather than "How satisfied are you with Anna?". The customer often rates the decision anyway, and that should show in the comment, not in the agent's pay review.
  • Put CES in the same survey if you want both. Two questions and a free-text field is the limit. More questions lower the response rate more than they add.
  • Report the response rate next to the number. A CSAT of 90 percent from 8 percent of customers is a different thing from 35 percent.

Which metric fits which decision?

The metric is chosen by the decision it should drive, not by what the tool happens to show on its dashboard. This is how they fit together:

Decision you need to make Metric to look at Why
Is the chatbot or the new AI draft working? CSAT and CES per channel, before and after The customer judges exactly those tickets; a CSAT that drops after automation is a clear signal, as we describe in the article on grounded chatbots
Which ticket types should we write better answers for? CES per ticket type, plus the comments High effort points to answers that require follow-up questions or channel switches
Does the help centre need new articles? The comments in CSAT and CES The free text reveals questions you could not answer, the same method as in the article on knowledge gaps
How do we compare with the industry? Satisfaction index and NPS, annually Comparable metrics at company level
Should we staff differently? No satisfaction metric; response time and queue Satisfaction is an outcome, not a planning input

The satisfaction metrics say how it went, not why, and should be read together with the operational metrics such as response time and resolution rate, described in the article on customer service metrics.

How do you read the result without fooling yourselves?

By always looking at three things at once: the number, the response rate and the comments. The number alone misleads in predictable ways.

  • Non-response is not random. Those who respond are more often very satisfied or very dissatisfied. If CSAT rises while the response rate falls, you have probably not improved, just lost the middle.
  • Channels cannot be compared directly. The chat gets answers from customers still in the window, email from those who bothered to open one more email. Compare each channel with its own history.
  • The rating is often about the decision. A rejected complaint gives a low CSAT even when the handling was correct. Sort the negative answers into wrong answer, slow answer and bad decision. The action is different for each pile.

The comments are the part of the measurement that gives the most. The free text shows which answers are missing, which articles are unclear and where customers switch channels. Read systematically, they give the same picture as an analysis of the inbox does, but from the customer's side.

What to do

  1. Turn on one question per ticket. CSAT with satisfied or dissatisfied and a free-text field, sent a day after the ticket is resolved. Most tools have it built in.
  2. Add CES if you have the volume. The statement "it was easy to get help" on a seven-point scale, in the same survey. Start with CSAT alone if you have fewer than a hundred tickets a week.
  3. Report three numbers every week: share positive, response rate and number of answers. Per channel and per ticket type when volume allows.
  4. Read every negative comment and sort them into wrong answer, slow answer and bad decision. Decide one action per pile.
  5. Measure before and after every change in how you answer: new article, new template, chatbot or AI draft. In Supportifier you follow the customer's rating per channel and per article, so a drop can be traced to the answer that caused it.
  6. Leave NPS and the satisfaction index to management, once a year, and contribute what customer service's numbers say about why.

Common questions

Should customer service measure NPS?

Not as a steering metric. NPS concerns the customer's relationship with the whole company and is affected by price, product and delivery as much as by customer service, so the answer can rarely be tied to something customer service can change. Measure it at company level a few times a year, and let customer service measure CSAT and CES per ticket. Customer service's numbers often explain why NPS moves.

How many answers do you need to trust CSAT?

Enough that a single customer does not move the metric. With 30 answers a week one customer is worth just over 3 percentage points, so look at four weeks at a time or per month. More important than the count is the response rate: report it next to the number, and only compare periods with roughly the same response rate. The comments are useful from the first answer.

Can we measure CSAT on the chatbot?

Yes, and you should do it separately from the tickets a person handled. Ask the same question in the chat when the bot closes a ticket, and follow the share of positive answers per question or article the bot answered from. If CSAT drops or CES rises for a certain ticket type, the source material is missing or wrong, and the handover to a person should then come earlier for that type.

What is a good CES?

There is no industry figure to compare with, because scales and wording differ between tools. Use the metric relatively: per ticket type, per channel and over time. The ticket types that score worst are where customers have to come back, switch channels or repeat themselves, and they should be fixed first. An improvement that holds over several weeks is what counts, not the level itself.

Sources

  • The One Number You Need to Grow â€” Harvard Business Review, 2003
  • Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers â€” Harvard Business Review, 2010
  • Improve Customer Experience to Gain Loyalty: Effortless Experience â€” Gartner, read 2026
  • About the CSAT (Customer Satisfaction) user experience for email and messaging â€” Zendesk, read 2026
  • Svenskt Kvalitetsindex modell â€” Swedish Quality Index, read 2026

title: Validando CPF dentro do PostgreSQL: função, CHECK constraint e domínio
description:
Transparência: sou fundador da CPFHub, citada no final. O conteúdo é puramente SQL e não depende de nenhum serviço.

Validar CPF só na aplicação deixa uma porta aberta: scripts de importação, outro microsserviço, um UPDATE manual feito às pressas. Se o banco é a fonte da verdade, faz sentido que ele recuse CPFs malformados. Vamos implementar isso no PostgreSQL.

1. Função de validação 

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION cpf_valido(p text)
RETURNS boolean
LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE STRICT PARALLEL SAFE AS $$
DECLARE
  d text := regexp_replace(p, '\D', '', 'g');
  soma int;
  dv int;
BEGIN
  IF length(d) <> 11 OR d ~ '^(\d)\1{10}$' THEN
    RETURN false;
  END IF;
  FOR t IN 9..10 LOOP
    soma := 0;
    FOR i IN 1..t LOOP
      soma := soma + substr(d, i, 1)::int * (t + 2 - i);
    END LOOP;
    dv := (soma * 10) % 11 % 10;
    IF dv <> substr(d, t + 1, 1)::int THEN
      RETURN false;
    END IF;
  END LOOP;
  RETURN true;
END $$;

Atenção ao índice: em SQL, substr começa em 1. Para o primeiro DV (t = 9), o peso do primeiro dígito é 10 (9 + 2 - 1); para o segundo (t = 10), é 11.

Marcar como IMMUTABLE permite usá-la em índices e constraints. STRICT faz cpf_valido(NULL) devolver NULL, o que em um CHECK significa "passa", então a obrigatoriedade fica com o NOT NULL.

SELECT cpf_valido('529.982.247-25'),  -- t
       cpf_valido('111.111.111-11'),  -- f
       cpf_valido('529.982.247-24');  -- f

2. Domínio

Um domínio deixa a regra reutilizável em várias tabelas:

CREATE DOMAIN cpf AS char(11)
  CHECK (VALUE ~ '^\d{11}$' AND cpf_valido(VALUE));

CREATE TABLE clientes (
  id    bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  nome  text NOT NULL,
  cpf   cpf  NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  criado_em timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

O ^\d{11}$ dentro do domínio impede gravar com máscara. A aplicação normaliza; o banco garante.

3. Adicionando a uma tabela existente

Em uma tabela antiga, cheia de lixo, não dá para simplesmente criar a constraint. Use NOT VALID:

ALTER TABLE clientes_legado
  ADD CONSTRAINT cpf_ok CHECK (cpf_valido(cpf)) NOT VALID;

Novas linhas e updates passam a ser checados imediatamente. As antigas ficam como estão até você limpá-las:

SELECT id, cpf FROM clientes_legado WHERE NOT cpf_valido(cpf);
-- corrija ou mova para quarentena, depois:
ALTER TABLE clientes_legado VALIDATE CONSTRAINT cpf_ok;

VALIDATE CONSTRAINT usa um lock mais leve que a criação direta, o que importa em tabelas grandes.

4. Normalizando o legado 

UPDATE clientes_legado
SET cpf = lpad(regexp_replace(cpf, '\D', '', 'g'), 11, '0')
WHERE cpf ~ '\D' OR length(cpf) BETWEEN 9 AND 10;

O lpad recupera zeros à esquerda perdidos em exportações para Excel. Antes de rodar, conte quantas linhas serão afetadas e faça em transação.

5. Duplicados disfarçados 

SELECT regexp_replace(cpf, '\D', '', 'g') AS d, count(*)
FROM clientes_legado
GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1;

6. Performance

A função é chamada a cada INSERT/UPDATE da coluna. Em PL/pgSQL ela custa microssegundos; não vai ser o seu gargalo. Se você importa dezenas de milhões de linhas, desabilite a constraint na carga e valide no final.

7. SQLite e MySQL

No MySQL 8, CHECK constraints funcionam, mas não aceitam funções armazenadas. A alternativa é um trigger BEFORE INSERT. No SQLite, registre a função a partir da aplicação (por exemplo, create_function no Python) ou valide na camada de app.

8. E a existência do CPF?

O banco garante que o número é bem formado. Saber se ele existe e a quem pertence depende de uma fonte externa, e isso deve acontecer na aplicação, não em um trigger: uma chamada HTTP dentro de transação segura locks e transforma latência de rede em latência de banco. Um padrão melhor é gravar com status_verificacao = 'pendente' e ter um worker que consulta a API e atualiza a linha.

Sobre a CPFHub

Para esse worker, a API de consulta de CPF oferece consulta individual (GET /cpf/{cpf}) e em lote (POST /cpf/bulk, até 10.000 CPFs por envio, assíncrono), com 50 créditos grátis por mês.

title: VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting
description:
arXiv:2610.19847v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We address inverse rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing explicit visibility modeling for relighting as well as material and light decomposition. Our approach augments the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline with a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion for Gaussian primitives from sampled lighting directions. This oracle is implemented using a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) and queried sparsely within the inverse-rendering objectives, while the original 3DGS loop is retained for training efficiency, interactive visualization, and tooling compatibility. Shading follows a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation with a principled microfacet bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) and low-resolution high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps. We evaluate our method on the TensoIR synthetic dataset against baselines based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), tensor representations, and 3DGS. The results show competitive performance and improvements over several earlier baselines for novel-view synthesis (NVS), albedo reconstruction, and relighting. Ablations indicate that explicit visibility modeling is an important contributor to relighting and material-illumination disentanglement, while pure PBR supervision can favor appearance fitting in NVS. Overall, the findings suggest that sparse, point-based visibility queries effectively complement rasterized splatting for inverse rendering while preserving the practical advantages of the 3DGS ecosystem.

title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.19613v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

title: I Used to Think Software Testing Was Unnecessary. Then I Started Building My Own Project.
description:
I used to think writing unit tests, E2E tests, and maintaining a proper testing suite was unnecessary for most projects.

If developers write the code, can't they just test it themselves?

For a long time, that made sense to me.

Until I started building something of my own.

How It Started

At the end of June, I started building The Last Deploy — an open-source platform where people can learn DevOps and Platform Engineering through hands-on labs.

In the beginning, I made a lot of decisions based on one thing:

If it works, ship it. I'll fix it if something breaks.

I even coded directly on the production server for a while.

Not because it was a good engineering practice, but because it felt faster. There were no users back then, and if I broke something, the consequences didn't feel that serious.

Eventually, I separated development and production environments. That helped, and things worked reasonably well for a while.

But the project kept growing.

And then, people started using it.

The Problem With "I'll Just Test It Manually"

When you're building a small project alone, manually checking whether a feature works can feel sufficient.

You make a change, run the application, try the feature, and if everything looks fine, you move on.

The problem is that your change doesn't exist in isolation.

A change to one part of the codebase can affect something you haven't touched in weeks.

For TLD, that could mean:

  • A lab that worked yesterday suddenly fails to start.
  • An update to the curriculum breaks existing modules.
  • A Docker container fails, but the cleanup process doesn't run correctly.
  • The CLI and backend stop handling an error the way they used to.
  • Something appears to work locally but fails in another environment.

And you might not notice any of it until someone else runs into the problem.

The more a project grows, the harder it becomes to confidently verify everything manually after every change.

That's where I started reconsidering my approach.

Testing One Feature Isn't the Same as Testing Your Application

Suppose I'm updating TLD's lab execution system.

I test the new feature. It works. Great.

But what about everything around it?

What I changed What I still need to verify
Lab execution Do existing labs still run?
Docker environment setup What happens if the container fails to start?
Curriculum sync Are existing modules and labs handled correctly?
Error handling Does the user get a useful error instead of a crash?
CLI/backend interaction Are both sides still communicating correctly?

Manually checking every possible interaction gets harder as the codebase grows.

And relying on memory to remember everything I need to test isn't exactly a reliable strategy either.

That's the difference between checking whether my latest change works and having a system that helps verify whether the application still works.

So, What Am I Learning About Testing?

I've been learning more about different types of tests and how they fit into a software project.

1. Unit tests

Test a small, isolated piece of logic.

For example, checking whether a function correctly validates lab configuration without needing to start an actual lab.

2. Integration tests

Check whether multiple components work together correctly.

For example, verifying that the backend handles a lab execution request and responds appropriately when something fails.

3. End-to-end (E2E) tests

Test a complete flow from the user's perspective.

For example, checking whether a user can initiate a lab and receive the expected result through the application.

4. Regression tests

Verify that functionality that worked previously still works after a change.

This is particularly important for a project like TLD, where a change to shared execution logic could affect multiple existing labs.

How I think about the difference

  • Unit: Does this piece of logic work?
  • Integration: Do these components work together?
  • E2E: Does the complete user flow work?
  • Regression: Did my changes break something that already worked?

Of course, these tests don't guarantee that an application is bug-free. They help catch specific classes of problems before those problems reach users.

And that's already valuable.

What I Want to Do With TLD

I'm not trying to introduce a massive testing framework overnight or chase a particular code coverage percentage.

I want to start with the parts where a regression could have the biggest impact.

My initial focus is on:

  1. Lab execution and cleanup
  2. Curriculum synchronization and local file handling
  3. Error handling and failure scenarios
  4. CLI and backend interactions
  5. Existing functionality that could break when shared code changes

The goal is to gradually build a testing suite that gives me more confidence when making changes.

Something that lets me spend less time worrying about what I might have accidentally broken and more time building what comes next.

What Changed My Mind?

I still believe developers should test their own code. That's an important part of writing software.

But I've started to understand why that alone isn't always enough.

When a project is small, you can often keep most of it in your head. As it grows, that becomes increasingly difficult.

And when real people start depending on what you're building, "it worked on my machine" stops being a satisfying answer.

I don't want TLD to be a project where users have to hope that the latest update didn't break something they were using.

I want to build something that I can keep improving without being afraid of every change.

Because, at the end of the day:

Writing code that works is one thing. Being confident that it keeps working as your project evolves is another.

I'm still figuring out the right testing strategy for TLD, and this is just the beginning.

Follow the project: The Last Deploy on GitHub

I'd love to hear from other developers: At what point did testing stop feeling like overhead and start feeling like a necessity?

title: Holi-Spatial 360: Generative Reconstruction from Sparse Panoramas for Spatial Rendering and Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2610.19502v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial intelligence requires scalable 3D environments that are both photorealistic and semantically grounded, yet existing indoor datasets are dominated by room-scale captures and costly LiDAR acquisition. Online real-estate platforms offer abundant panoramas of diverse multi-room homes, but sparse viewpoints and texture-poor regions make reconstruction severely under-constrained. We introduce Holi-Spatial 360, a generative reconstruction and data curation framework for converting these panoramas into annotated multi-room 3D environments. Because reconstruction quality bounds subsequent generation, our Correspondence-Guided Geometric Optimization converts feed-forward reconstruction priors into reliable cross-view constraints and builds a coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting representation as 3D spatial memory. Adapted single-image and video priors then restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content. The reconstructed scenes support arbitrary RGB-D rendering and an automated curation pipeline that combines end-to-end 3D grounding with VLM-based verification. Holi360 contains over 1K multi-room 3DGS scenes, more than 100K instance annotations, and 2M spatial question-answer pairs. We also introduce the Holi360 benchmark to evaluate the spatial understanding of VLMs in real-world, multi-room indoor environments. Experiments demonstrate superior reconstruction and curation quality under sparse panoramic inputs, while fine-tuning VLMs on Holi360 substantially improves spatial reasoning capabilities.

title: GLoD-LVSM: Learning Geometry-Grounded Continuous-LoD Scene Representations for Large View Synthesis Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) reconstruct scenes from sparse views and render novel views quickly, but they incur unnecessary storage and rendering costs due to token redundancy. We present GLoD-LVSM, a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation for LVSMs with continuous levels of detail. First, instead of learning a fixed set of scene anchor initializations, GLoD-LVSM learns a continuous field that initializes a flexible number of anchors to match the desired budget. A condenser then aggregates scene information into these anchors, with both the field and condenser trained end-to-end. Second, the condenser infers reference-token and anchor geometry to guide compression through geometry-grounded attention, improving rendering quality and enabling frustum culling during decoding. Compared with existing LVSM scene-compression baselines, GLoD-LVSM achieves the best trade-off between rendering quality and scene token count. Compared with the uncompressed base model, GLoD-LVSM reduces the scene-token count by 33.4% and accelerates rendering by $1.23\times$ with no quality loss. Under a relaxed quality-loss budget, the reduction increases to 85.5%, with $3.00\times$ rendering speedup. Further analysis reveals that view-synthesis supervision yields emergent scene depth and self-organized anchors that align with surfaces and adapt their density to local texture complexity. Beyond rendering, we further show that our scene representation also supports scene-semantic understanding, highlighting its potential for broader downstream tasks.

title: Node.js Media Digest Recovery — 2-Stage Cron and Queue Boundaries for SaaS Email
description:
Short answer: for a media SaaS sending a daily report email, let cron start the day and let a queue worker do the delivery. That split keeps the scheduled HTTP task short, gives each report a retry boundary, and makes a partial morning failure recoverable without rerunning every tenant.

The decision is operational recovery, not whether a cron expression looks simpler. A cron execution is capped at 900 seconds. A report batch can spend that window waiting on an email provider, rendering a large tenant, or backing off after a rate limit. The trigger should select work and enqueue it; the worker should own the slow and failure-prone part.

I build the example around a media publisher's daily digest: active customers receive the previous day's article and subscription metrics. The useful unit of recovery is one tenant, one report date, and one delivery attempt. Short rule. Keep that identity durable.

Infrai fits this narrow handoff when integration friction is the main constraint. Infrai exposes one REST API, so a Node.js service can call it over HTTP with no SDK to install; Infrai uses the same key for the scheduling and queue capabilities. That is a concrete way to keep a contract stable while the service behind it changes, not a reason to turn a two-stage job into a workflow platform.

What should a Node.js SaaS use for daily report email recovery?

A cron-only handler is acceptable when the job is tiny, bounded, and safe to repeat. It is a poor boundary once the recipient set is bursty. If tenant 8,401 is rate-limited after 8,400 successful sends, the handler has no clean answer to “what should I run again?” A second run can resend the first 8,400 messages; an in-process counter disappears with the process.

Consider a Monday after a holiday weekend. The publisher has 12,000 active customers, three tenants have unusually large article archives, and the mail provider returns 429 for a few minutes. A cron-only process now mixes pagination, template rendering, provider backoff, and progress tracking in one request. If it dies at customer 8,401, its last log line is not a recovery plan. With a queue, the trigger can finish after publishing stable references, while workers drain at a known rate; a failed tenant is one visible job, not an ambiguous suffix of a batch. The ledger can distinguish “not published,” “published but not acknowledged,” and “sent,” which lets an operator replay exactly the missing identity instead of guessing from timestamps.

With cron plus a queue, the scheduled endpoint records the report date, derives deterministic job IDs, and publishes one compact message per tenant. Workers consume at a controlled rate, retry transient failures, and acknowledge only after the send result is durable. Standard queues are at-least-once, so duplicate delivery is expected input. The email side effect must be idempotent.

The trigger target must be a public HTTP URL; the scheduling service does not host application code. For a push subscription, use public HTTPS. Put report data in the database or object store and send references in the message because queue bodies are limited to 256KB. Acknowledged messages are removed, so the queue is transport, not an audit log.

The boundary also keeps the recovery questions concrete: was the date scheduled, were all intended tenant jobs published, and did each job reach a terminal send state? A cron run marked successful proves only that the trigger returned. Run-history output is retained only for the first 4KB, so it cannot be the report ledger.

How do cron, queues, and SaaS alternatives divide the work?

The candidates below can all be sensible. Their difference is who owns credentials, broker operations, and the evidence needed after a partial send.

Option Good fit for the daily digest Recovery trade-off
Infrai cron plus queue A small service that wants one REST contract for scheduling and delivery handoff No DAG or fan-out/join primitive; the application still owns idempotent sending
AWS EventBridge Scheduler plus SQS A team already operating identity, alerts, and workers in AWS Strong cloud integration, but AWS-specific accounts and controls remain part of the design
Google Cloud Scheduler plus Pub/Sub A service already standardized on Google Cloud Useful native tooling, with another cloud-specific integration surface
BullMQ A Node.js team that deliberately owns Redis-backed jobs Familiar application code, but Redis, retention, and worker operations stay with the team
RabbitMQ A team needing direct broker and acknowledgement control More broker administration and recovery procedure to carry
Temporal or Airflow A report that has several dependent stages and long-lived state Better workflow semantics, but more machinery than schedule → enqueue → consume

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the first row when the friction is integration rather than workflow design. Its public discovery surface describes a capability's method, path, request schema, response schema, and runnable examples, and one key covers the scheduling and queue calls. I would try it for the handoff in a small media SaaS that wants this narrow boundary and already keeps report state in its own database.

The catch is important. This is not a workflow engine. There is no DAG orchestration, fan-out/join primitive, native debounce, or topic-style one-to-many delivery. Stick with Temporal or Airflow when the digest becomes a branching pipeline with compensation and joins; use a specialist broker when replay across multiple consumer groups is a hard requirement.

A minimal critical path with explicit retry behavior

The safest implementation starts with discovery rather than guessing a REST path. The following Python sample checks the documented cron capability, honors Retry-After on 429, and prints the verified method and path. The live discovery response supplies the current request schema, so the creation payload is not invented here.

import os
import random
import time
import requests


def get_capability(capability: str) -> dict:
    url = f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/{capability}"
    headers = {}
    key = os.getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key:
        headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {key}"

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.get("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/cron.create", headers=headers, timeout=15)
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay + random.random() / 4)
            continue
        if not 200 <= response.status_code < 300:
            raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: {response.status_code} {response.text[:4000]}")
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("discovery rate limit persisted after five attempts")


for name in ("cron.create", "queue.create", "queue.publish"):
    capability = get_capability(name)
    print(name, capability["method"], capability["path"])

The production flow is small. The scheduler points at a public endpoint that computes the report date and publishes jobs to a queue. Set the cron timeout no higher than 900 seconds. Keep queue delay at or below seven days and retention at or below 30 days. A client-supplied idempotency key should cover each create or publish retry.

The worker claims (tenant_id, report_date, report_kind) in durable state, renders the digest, sends it, records the provider result, and only then acknowledges. On a 429, honor Retry-After when supplied and back off with jitter. Never tight-loop. If a worker dies after sending but before acknowledgement, the same deterministic identity prevents a second side effect.

One detail catches teams late: cron does not backfill triggers missed while paused, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. A recovery runbook must explicitly enqueue a missed date once. Queue retention is at most 30 days and there is no Kafka-style replay or multi-consumer-group history, so retain the job ledger and report inputs outside the queue.

Where the simple architecture stops fitting

Cron plus a queue is not a universal answer. It is unsuitable when the report requires a multi-stage dependency graph, a join over several data products, or replay for independent consumers. In those cases, Temporal, Airflow, or a deliberately operated broker is the better choice even if setup takes longer.

I'm not sure how bursty a particular publisher's tenant set will be; time zones, report size, and the provider quota decide that. Your mileage may vary. Measure queue age and worker throughput with non-production recipients before choosing concurrency, then keep the schedule contract unchanged while tuning workers.

The rollout test should be intentionally boring: publish the same test identity twice and verify one email side effect, inject a synthetic 429 and verify delayed retry, then stop a worker after send but before acknowledgement and confirm the identity check suppresses a duplicate. In one media tenant I would also hold a deliberately oversized report, let the worker hit its provider quota, and compare the ledger after recovery; that single exercise catches duplicate sends, an under-sized message reference, and a retry loop that ignores Retry-After in the same morning. Alert on oldest unacknowledged age and on a mismatch between intended, published, acknowledged, and terminal-send counts.

Keep the ledger.
