title: MedScribe AI — An Agentic Radiologist's Assistant
description:
---
title: "MedScribe AI — An Agentic Radiologist's Assistant Built with Open-Source AI"
published: true

tags: devchallenge, hf26challenge, ai, healthcare

The Problem

Radiology reporting is slow, expensive, and inaccessible — especially in
low-resource settings like Pakistan where radiologists are scarce. Most
diagnostic AI tools stop at a raw prediction, leaving clinicians unable
to act efficiently.

MedScribe AI changes that.

What We Built

MedScribe AI is an agentic assistant that supports radiologists by
combining computer vision with generative AI to produce full clinical
reports from chest X-ray images — in seconds.

🔗 Live Demo:


How It Works

The system runs in three stages:

1. Computer Vision Model

  • ResNet18 trained on pediatric chest X-rays (Kaggle dataset)
  • 90.5% accuracy, 98.4% precision, 93.2% F1-score
  • Grad-CAM explainability — highlights exactly which regions influenced the prediction

2. AI Agent Pipeline (LangGraph + Groq)

Four agents run in sequence:

Agent What it does
Vision Runs CV model, returns findings + confidence
Reasoning LLM decides which tools to call (ReAct loop)
Reporting Generates structured clinical report
Escalation Flags critical cases for immediate attention

3. Application Interface (Streamlit)

  • Upload chest X-ray → get full clinical report in seconds
  • Doctor-facing report + patient-facing plain language summary
  • Bilingual output: English + Urdu 🇵🇰
  • Downloadable PDF with original X-ray + Grad-CAM heatmap

Why Open Source AI?

  • openai/gpt-oss-120b via Groq — fast, free inference with no data sent to proprietary servers
  • TorchXRayVision — open-source medical imaging foundation model
  • LangGraph — open-source agent framework, fully customizable
  • PyTorch + torchvision — open weights, reproducible training

Running on open models means patient X-rays never leave the
user's control — critical for healthcare privacy.

Who Would Pay For This?

  • Private clinics in Pakistan and South Asia with no on-site radiologist
  • Telehealth platforms needing automated preliminary reports
  • Hospital chains processing high volumes of routine chest X-rays

A clinic paying $50/month for preliminary AI triage is far cheaper
than hiring a part-time radiologist.

Tech Stack

CV Model: PyTorch · ResNet18 · TorchXRayVision · Grad-CAM
AI Agents: LangGraph · Groq (gpt-oss-120b) · ReAct
App: Streamlit · Python

Team

Built in 48 hours at Pak Angels Generative & Agentic AI Hackathon
(Cohort 11) by a team of 6 from Pakistan 🇵🇰

Open source AI isn't just a technical choice — for healthcare in
underserved regions, it's the only choice that makes the economics work.

title: Reply Desk: a review-reply assistant for small shops, where customers' words never leave the counter
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 2 — Side Hustle.

What I Built

Reply Desk is a review-reply assistant for small businesses: the chai stall, the salon, the neighbourhood clinic, the coaching centre, the home baker.

These businesses live and die on Google and Zomato reviews. Replying to every review helps, and nobody behind the counter has time to do it. Worse, the reviews that actually matter ("found a hair in my food", "the staff was rude") get buried under twenty "nice chai!" ones.

Reply Desk does three things:

  1. It puts urgent reviews first. Food-safety, health, money and staff-behaviour complaints are flagged "Today" and moved to the top, the moment you paste them.
  2. It reads the mood of each review: positive, mixed or negative.
  3. It drafts a reply in the owner's voice, signed with their name. Unhappy customers are pointed to the owner's own contact, like a WhatsApp number, instead of an argument in public.

You read it, tweak it, copy it, post it. If the mood is wrong, tap the right one and it redrafts.

All of this runs on an open-weight model, Gemma 3 1B, inside the browser tab. No account, no API key, no server, no upload.

Who would pay for it

A café owner who would never pay for "AI". They would pay ₹199–299 a month for "every review answered in two minutes, and you'll never miss a complaint again". The same goes for a small agency that manages listings for ten local shops.

The pricing only works because of the open model, which is a later section.

Demo

It's a static web app with no backend, so you run it on your own machine:

git clone https://github.com/Yash11778/reply-desk
cd reply-desk
npm install
npm run dev

Open the local URL, click "Fill in an example", then "Draft replies". With WebGPU it's quick. Without it, it falls back to the CPU and takes roughly 10–20 seconds a reply, but it works. The first run downloads the model once (~0.8–1 GB), and after that it's cached.

This is real, unedited output from a test run on a laptop with no GPU at all (CPU only, inside the browser), for a made-up café called "Chai Point Corner" run by "Priya":

Review: Found a hair in my poha. Disgusting. Want my money back.
Flag: Today: Something found in the food · Mood: negative
Reply: I sincerely apologize for the unpleasant experience you had with our poha. I'm truly sorry that your experience was so disappointing. Please contact me directly at 98765 43210 so we can discuss this further and make things right. I value your feedback and want to ensure you're satisfied.
Priya

Review: Waited 25 minutes for two sandwiches and the guy at the counter was rude when I asked.
Flag: Today: Staff behaviour · Mood: negative
Reply: Thank you for your feedback. I sincerely apologize for the delay and the experience you had with our staff. I want to assure you that I'll investigate this matter immediately. Please contact me directly at 98765 43210 so we can discuss this further.
Priya

Review: Nice ambience, friendly owner aunty. Sandwich was soggy though.
Mood: mixed
Reply: I'm sorry to hear you had a disappointing experience. Thank you for your feedback. I'll certainly take your comments about the sandwich and will investigate further to understand what went wrong.
Priya

They aren't Shakespeare, and they don't need to be. They're polite, specific, signed, and they never invent a discount or a fake phone number. That last part took work (see below). The third one is also a fair example of why the owner reads before posting: it skipped thanking her for the "friendly owner aunty" bit, and a human would add that back in five seconds.

Code

Yash11778 / reply-desk

Draft replies to customer reviews with an open-weigh model (Gemma) that runs in your browser. Nothing isuploaded.

Reply Desk

Paste your Google or Zomato reviews. An open-weight model running in your browser tab sorts them, flags the ones you must deal with today, and drafts a reply to each one in your own voice. Your customers' words never leave your computer.

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2: Side Hustle.

Who it's for

Small businesses that live on reviews: cafés, salons, clinics, coaching centres, home bakers. Replying to every review is good for them and nobody has time for it. The ones that matter most, like "found a hair in my food" or "staff was rude", get buried under "nice chai!".

How it works

  1. Set up once: business name, what it is, your name, and where unhappy customers should reach you. It's saved in your browser.
  2. Paste reviews, with a blank line between each.
  3. Urgent first: a plain keyword check flags food-safety, health, money…
View on GitHub

MIT licensed. TypeScript and Vite, no framework, about 9 kB of app code plus the model runtime.

How It Works 

paste reviews ──► split on blank lines
              ──► keyword check: urgent?  (instant, no model)
              ──► complaint words?  no ──► positive (no model)
                                    yes ─► Gemma: mixed or negative?
              ──► Gemma: draft a reply with the prompt for that mood
              ──► clean-up: strip chatter, placeholders, double sign-offs

The model runs in a Web Worker through Transformers.js, using onnx-community/gemma-3-1b-it-ONNX. That's 4-bit weights on WebGPU, and 8-bit on CPU.

Lesson 1: give a 1B model one job, not three

My first prompt asked Gemma to classify the mood, flag urgency and write the reply, in a fixed format. It ignored the format and wrote things like **First line: POSITIVE**. It also wrote this, for a real-looking complaint:

Please contact Priya directly at [Priya's Phone Number or Email]

Two changes fixed it:

  • One prompt per job. Classification is its own short prompt, and the reply is another.
  • One prompt per mood. "If the review is bad, apologise" made it apologise to happy customers. So the code picks the mood first, and each mood gets its own one-line instruction: 
const TASK: Record<Mood, (b: Business) => string> = {
  positive: () => 'Thank them for their review.',
  mixed: () => "Thank them for the good part, and say plainly that you'll look at the thing they didn't like.",
  negative: (b) => `Apologise once, without excuses, and ask them to contact you on ${b.contact} so you can make it right.`,
};

The owner's real contact detail is passed in, and the prompt says "Do not invent phone numbers, emails, discounts or promises." A small clean-up pass then strips anything in [square brackets], "Okay, here's a reply:" preambles, markdown, and a doubled sign-off.

Lesson 2: don't use the model where a word list is better

Missing a food-safety complaint is the one mistake that really matters, so urgency is a plain keyword list, not the model: hair, cockroach, sick, food poisoning, stale, refund, rude, and so on. It's predictable and instant, and it lets the urgent cards appear at the top before the model has even loaded.

The same goes for clearly happy reviews. The CPU (8-bit) build liked to hedge and call "Best masala chai in the area!!" "mixed". Now a review with no complaint words at all (but, though, cold, slow, rude, not…) is positive without asking the model. Gemma only decides the hard case: mixed or negative.

Lesson 3: "runs in the browser" has fine print

Getting the no-GPU path working took three fixes, all found by running it rather than reading docs:

  1. The 4-bit build crashed on CPU: Could not find an implementation for GatherBlockQuantized. onnxruntime-web's WASM backend doesn't have that kernel, so the CPU path loads the 8-bit build instead.
  2. The 8-bit build then 404'd on model_int8.onnx_data. The model repo's config says its weights live in an external data file, which is true for the other builds but not for int8, which is one self-contained file. Passing use_external_data_format: { 'model_int8.onnx': 0, … } fixed it.
  3. It ran on one CPU core. WASM threads need SharedArrayBuffer, which needs the page to be cross-origin isolated. Two headers in vite.config.ts (Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless) let it use every core. credentialless matters here, because it keeps the Hugging Face CDN download working without that server sending extra headers.

Why Open Matters Here

It's what makes the business work.

  • Privacy is the product. Reviews carry customers' names, phone numbers, and complaints about named staff. "Your customers' words never leave this computer" is a promise I can actually keep, because there's no server to leave to.
  • Zero cost per reply. A hosted model charges per token, forever. Here the shop's own laptop does the work, so a ₹199/month price has no API bill eating it. A hosted model would also force me to meter usage, and "unlimited replies" is a much easier sell to a shop owner.
  • No lock-in. No API key to leak, no provider changing prices or deprecating the model under me. If a better small open model comes out, swapping it is one line (MODEL in worker.ts).
  • It still works offline once the model is cached, for example in a shop with patchy internet.

What's Next

  • Hindi, Marathi and Hinglish replies, since many reviews here are written that way. That needs a bigger or fine-tuned model.
  • Per-business tone examples: paste three replies you've written, and it matches them.
  • A weekly summary: "4 people mentioned slow service this week".

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 3 1B is the only model in the app. It runs on-device through Transformers.js and does both the mood reading and every reply.

Built with AI assistance (Claude Code) for scaffolding, testing and debugging. All sample reviews are invented for the demo.

title: Building a Multi-Tenant RAG in 8GB RAM: Why I Ditched Qdrant and Kafka (Phase 0)
description:
I have 8 GB of RAM and 6 vCPUs. With those specs, I'm building and running a full production-ready RAG system.

I’m not self-hosting the LLM. I’m not spinning up Qdrant. I’m not adding Kafka.
Those aren't my personal preferences—they are constraints strictly dictated by the hardware. When you run a JVM alongside a Python AI worker on an 8 GB machine, every megabyte counts.

Today, I’m starting to build Corpus in public: a document chat platform where every answer strictly cites its sources, and each organization's data remains completely isolated from the rest (strict multi-tenancy).

The Stack (100% Dockerized)

  • Backend API: Java 21 + Spring Boot 4
  • AI & Embeddings Service: Python + FastAPI
  • Storage & Vector DB: PostgreSQL (pgvector) + Redis
  • Frontend: React

Why this architecture?

  • PostgreSQL + pgvector over Qdrant/Milvus: Maintaining a dedicated vector database alongside a relational DB in 8 GB of RAM is overkill. Keeping relational metadata and vector embeddings in the same engine simplifies transactions and saves precious memory.
  • Redis over Kafka: I need asynchronous processing for document ingestion, not a massive distributed event-streaming cluster eating up heap memory.

Current Status: Phase 0

All 5 services spin up cleanly with a single docker compose up, and the core system design is locked in the repository. There is no live demo yet.

Next step: The ingestion pipeline—turning raw PDFs into queryable vector chunks without triggering the Linux OOM killer.

I’ll be documenting every architectural trade-off and every failure along the way.

🔗 GitHub Repository: aletgdev/corpus-rag

Looking for advice from the community 👇

For those of you who have built something similar under tight resource constraints: How would you handle local embedding generation within an 8 GB RAM budget while guaranteeing strict multi-tenant isolation in pgvector? (e.g., Row-Level Security vs. schema-per-tenant vs. metadata filtering).

Any war stories or tips are more than welcome in the comments!

title: ARC Region switch adds four new capabilities
description:
Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region switch helps you orchestrate the failover of multi-Region applications to achieve a bounded recovery time during a Regional impairment. Today, Region switch adds four new capabilities: AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block, payloads for custom action Lambda execution block, service quota parity checks, and wait for target group health feature for compute scaling actions.

AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block. During failover, you often need to run commands on managed instances and VMs. This execution block lets you invoke Run Command actions on managed instances during failover, with plan evaluation verifying that command documents target valid instances and that IAM permissions are correctly configured.

Payloads for custom action Lambda execution block. ARC Region switch now lets you pass payloads to your custom action Lambda execution block, allowing reusability of your Lambda functions across recovery plans.

Service quota checks. Service quota limits are a common failure mode during recovery. Region switch now verifies quota parity between your primary and standby Region, and automatically submits quota limit increases, reducing the risk of insufficient service quotas during recovery.

Wait for target group health. Amazon ECS service scaling and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution blocks help you provision compute capacity during recovery, but provisioned capacity may not be ready to serve traffic. The optional wait for target group health feature verifies that your provisioned capacity is ready to serve traffic.

To get started, see the documentation for AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block , custom action Lambda execution block , Service quota checks  and the Wait for target group health for Amazon ECS service scaling execution block  and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution block .

Create a controller inside a workflow, pass its signal into one or more steps, and cancel in-flight operations using the same API fetch already uses.

Use it to stop a slow step when a durable timeout wins a race, cancel the remaining requests after the first successful response, thread one signal through a multi-step pipeline, or cancel parallel work when an external condition changes.

title: How to Build a Benchmark That Actually Measures Taste
description:
arXiv:2610.14707v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Expert-aligned "taste" benchmarks should reward craft judgment, not the ability to game the test. We introduce TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark across visual, brand, book, and tech items under a frozen rubric with expert-only gold (panel n>=3; percent agreement >=0.60 primary gate; weak engagement labels train/analysis-only), together with a control protocol that separates craft judgment from test-gaming. Applying the protocol to a Round-1 pilot (primary_human_expert; three biological human experts; n=250 pairs) surfaces and quantifies three validity threats: two construction artifacts that inflate the trivial-baseline layer, and a difficulty ceiling that inflates every score. (1) Position: the preferred item is slot A with probability 0.956, so an always_item_a policy scores 0.956 (fair chance 0.5). (2) Lexical leakage: a filename token cue scores 0.912. (3) Difficulty ceiling: craft domains show near-ceiling human agreement (book/brand/tech 1.0), and even under A/B randomization (eval_assignment_seed7; gold_side_A ~0.47) all five VLM cards reach 1.0 on craft, with only visual separating (~0.84-0.91; a post-hoc hard subset, n=107, leaves craft at 1.0). The protocol (expert-only gold, a weak-label firewall, side randomization at construction, filename scrubbing, and hard filters) makes each artifact measurable and, for the two construction artifacts, correctable; we release a reference eval harness and a side-randomization tool, and show the tool removes the position skew (0.916 to 0.495/0.505). The result is a calibrated view of what the benchmark does and does not yet measure: position and leakage are fixable, whereas the craft-domain ceiling is a pair-difficulty limit that Round-2 must address. We do not evaluate engagement, era/circle conditioning, or calibration here, and we claim no general taste SOTA.

title: EGCForest: Structured Agent Memory Organization for Enterprise Group Chats
description:
arXiv:2610.19836v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise group chats record project progress, decisions, task ownership, and other organizational information valuable to enterprise agents. Reliable retrieval is challenging because evidence spans interleaved threads, channels, and time, with meaning and authority conditioned on the speaker. Neither RAG's independent chunk retrieval nor memory systems' summary-based consolidation can reliably recover such distributed evidence. We present EGCForest, a novel multi-view hierarchical memory framework for enterprise group chats. EGCForest organizes an immutable message log into three complementary forests: a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles. Cross-view connections are enabled by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Built on this memory backbone, EGCForest retrieves and assembles evidence by jointly leveraging message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links, recovering distributed evidence. Experiments on three enterprise-chat benchmarks show that EGCForest consistently outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over MemOS while supporting efficient online retrieval.

title: On the Complexity Gap Between POMDPs and Multi-Environment POMDPs
description:
arXiv:2610.15010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-environment POMDPs (ME-POMDPs) generalize POMDPs by encoding a finite set of possible environments, capturing model uncertainty. The finite-horizon robust reward maximization problem for a ME-POMDP asks for a policy that maximizes reward in the worst environment, and recent work has shown this problem to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete. We expand the complexity landscape of ME-POMDPs by identifying which subclasses retain this $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness. In particular, we take subclasses of POMDPs that are tractable in the single-environment case, and investigate the computational complexity of these classes when extended to the multi-environment setting. We first prove the $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of multi-environment blind MDPs and deterministic POMDPs using a certain closure-under-mixture condition. We then prove $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness for a range of subclasses that do not satisfy that closure condition, yielding new complexity results for multi-observation POMDPs. Finally, we show existential theory of the reals ($\exists \mathbb{R}$)-completeness for numerous ME-POMDP problems under time-dependent Markovian policies or finite-state controllers that are $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for standard POMDPs. These results reveal a subtle relationship between POMDP and ME-POMDP complexity that depends heavily on the subclasses involved.

title: FACES: Fine-grained Gated Semantic Alignment for Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation
description:
arXiv:2610.20051v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, with advances in multimodal interaction technologies and the growing demand for intelligent emotional support, Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation (MESC) has emerged as an important task. However, existing systems still suffer from shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies due to weak semantic feedback, cross-dimension reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision. To address these challenges, we propose FACES, a fine-grained gated semantic alignment framework for MESC. Specifically, FACES integrates multi-source rewards to construct multidimensional semantic and functional alignment signals, employs a non-compensatory gated fusion mechanism to reduce cross-dimension reward offset, and leverages structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) anchors to perform token-level credit assignment. Under a controlled response-length protocol, FACES improves the average MLLM-based evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04 and achieves an 80.22% pairwise win rate over SOTA. Human evaluation under the same protocol yields a 75.3% preference rate. Results on three external datasets further support transferability. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/OCT-ARR/arr.

title: What Is a Clarification? Estimating Model-Dependent Input Ambiguity
description:
arXiv:2610.20052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ambiguous inputs can admit multiple interpretations, each potentially yielding a different answer. Existing work largely treats this ambiguity as a property of the input, yet for a particular language model, only some alternatives may be known and answerable. We therefore distinguish world ambiguity, capturing all alternatives admitted by an input, from model ambiguity, capturing those accessible to the responding model. To characterize these alternatives, we formalize natural-language clarifications through three desiderata: \emph{uniqueness}, \emph{faithfulness}, and \emph{answer equivalence}. We show that these desiderata induce a one-to-one correspondence between valid answers and equivalence classes of clarifications, implying that any interpretation can be represented either by its answer or by the clarifications that uniquely express it. We leverage this correspondence to introduce \circleclar{}, a black-box method that estimates the set of answers available to a model by checking consistency along an answer--clarification--answer cycle. Across open-domain QA and executable Text-to-SQL, \circleclar{} achieves strong recovery of these answer sets. In QA, the recovered support yields the strongest overall performance in model-dependent ambiguity detection and enables effective selection among answering, clarifying, and abstaining. Together, these results demonstrate the practical value of a model-dependent view of ambiguity and its characterization through an answer-clarification correspondence.

title: Object Pose from 2-D to 3-D Point and Line Correspondences
description:
arXiv:2610.19734v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper we present a method for optimally estimating the rotation and translation between a camera and a 3-D object from point and/or line correspondences. First we devise an error function and second we show how to minimize this error function. The quadratic nature of this function is made possible by representing rotation and translation with a dual number quaternion. We provide a detailed account of the computational aspects of a trust-region optimization method. This method compares favourably with Newton's method which has extensively been used to solve the problem at hand, with Faugeras-Toscani linear method [6] for calibrating a camera, and with the Levenberg-Marquardt non-linear optimization method. Finally we present some experimental results which demonstrate the robustness of our method with respect to image noise and matching errors.

title: Make text show up instantly: one CSS line most small-business sites miss
description:
When your site loads custom fonts, Chrome often hides all text until the font file arrives. Visitors stare at a blank page for a second or two — and bounce.

Fix it with one line on your @font-face rule or Google Fonts link:

font-display: swap;

Or on a Google Fonts URL, add &display=swap.

Text shows immediately in a system font, then swaps to your brand font when ready. Pair it with a similar fallback (system-ui, Arial, sans-serif) so the swap is barely noticeable.

This is a five-minute change that improves perceived speed on almost every small-business site we audit.

title: Which Metadata Matters for LLM Tool Selection in MCP? Evidence from Controlled Factor-Level Interventions
description:
arXiv:2610.14334v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In Model Context Protocol (MCP) systems, LLMs select tools from metadata rather than from their implementations. Names and descriptions summarize what a tool does, while the parameter schema specifies the fields a tool accepts and how they are organized. Our analysis of metadata for 367,174 MCP tools reveals substantial schema variation among functionally similar tools. Many of these tools share names and similar descriptions but expose different parameter schemas. This raises a key question: can parameter-schema differences influence tool selection before any call is made? We study this question through controlled metadata interventions across five LLMs and five tasks. Each comparison changes exactly one metadata factor (server name, tool name, description, or parameter schema) while keeping the others fixed. We balance tool positions and use conditional logistic regression to estimate position-adjusted effects. We find that: (1) parameter-schema changes produce the largest and most consistent selection shifts among the tested interventions. Models tend to favor separate top-level parameters over grouped or composite forms. (2) Descriptions that explain parameters also tend to increase selection, while name effects are weaker and less consistent. (3) Targeted comparisons show that schema effects depend on the specific parameter names and on how the request represents the same information. When only one schema satisfies an explicit request requirement, all five models select the compatible tool despite position preferences. These results show that parameter schemas influence not only how tools are called, but also whether they are selected. For MCP developers and evaluators, schema design and tool ordering can therefore affect which implementation is invoked even when functionality is unchanged.

title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
description:
arXiv:2610.19121v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.

title: Why Is Molecular Dynamics Research Moving to Cloud GPUs?
description:
Molecular dynamics research is moving to cloud GPUs because the hardware available on-premises has stopped keeping pace with the simulations researchers need to run. Molecular dynamics is the computational method used to simulate how atoms and molecules move over time, and it is one of the most GPU-intensive workloads in scientific computing. Labs that built clusters five years ago are still running them today, on the same GPUs, with the same memory limits. The simulations have grown larger. The GPU generations that handle them have moved two cycles ahead. The gap between what the institution owns and what the work needs is widening every year.

Cloud GPUs give research groups access to current GPU generations without capital investment, remove shared-cluster queue time, bill only for compute used, and provide consistent software environments across every team member. These four changes together explain why molecular dynamics labs are shifting from on-premises clusters to cloud infrastructure. Capital budget cycles narrow that gap over eighteen months from approval to installation. Cloud GPUs close that gap in minutes. This is why Yobitel has built a GPU-optimized GROMACS HPC environment on AWS.

What Slows Molecular Dynamics Research Down?

Three infrastructure problems slow molecular dynamics research down before the science even begins: ageing hardware, hidden queue costs, and environment drift across the team.

1. Hardware Generation Gap

On-premises clusters are bought once and run until they are replaced. A cluster purchased in 2021 with NVIDIA V100 GPUs still runs V100s in 2026, while A100, H100, and L4 GPUs have moved through release, widespread deployment, and into standard research use. The institution pays for the cluster regardless of whether it matches the work. Researchers accept the throughput ceiling of hardware that was already ageing when the procurement paperwork cleared.

The memory limit is the harder problem. Older GPU generations carry less memory per card, and molecular dynamics system size is directly constrained by how much GPU memory is available. Three situations push a simulation past what the on-premises hardware can hold:

  • Large membrane-protein complexes that exceed GPU memory per card.
  • Fully solvated biomolecular assemblies that require the workload to split across nodes.
  • Systems that need the memory of a newer GPU generation to avoid communication overhead.

When the workload splits across nodes, communication overhead adds to every step. That overhead increases setup complexity and reduces throughput at the same time.

2. Queue Time as a Hidden Cost

A shared cluster runs on a job scheduler. A researcher submits a job; the scheduler waits for an opening in the queue, and the job starts when resources open. On a busy cluster, that wait lasts hours to days. There is no way to accelerate it without reducing the job, which changes the simulation rather than just the timeline.

The queue does not appear in hardware benchmarks. A cluster rated for high throughput delivers that throughput only to the job that is running. Every job behind it waits, and the researcher who submitted it waits with it. The table below shows the actual time cost of queue delays across common research patterns:

Scenario Clock Time Queue Time Effective Turnaround
Single simulation run 6 hours 48 hours 54 hours
Ten iterative rounds 60 hours 480 hours 540 hours
Grant deadline cycle 2 weeks of compute 4 weeks of waiting 6 weeks total

Queue delay does not appear in any hardware benchmark. It is also the first cost cloud compute eliminates.

3. Environment Consistency Across a Team

On-premises clusters accumulate drift over their operational lifetime. A software update one group installs affects the environment for groups sharing the same nodes. A driver update applied for one application changes the behaviour of another.

GROMACS is sensitive to three configuration variables simultaneously:

  • GPU driver version.
  • CUDA version.
  • Compile flags used to build the binary.

Small differences in any of these produce results that are numerically different even when the scientific inputs are identical. Two researchers with the same input files can get different results for no scientific reason, only because one machine carries a different library version. Reviewers then ask questions the authors cannot answer.

Cloud instances start from a defined image. Every researcher who launches the same AMI gets the same driver, the same CUDA version, and the same GROMACS build. Groups that need to reproduce a result launch the same image rather than reconstructing a software environment from documentation that is often incomplete.

What Does a Cloud GPU Actually Change?

A cloud GPU removes queue time, provides access to current hardware generations, and keeps costs proportional to actual compute used. There is no queue in the shared-cluster sense because the researcher is not competing with other groups for a fixed pool of hardware. The instance terminates when the simulation finishes, and the cost is proportional to the compute used, not to an annual allocation paid regardless of utilisation.

Factor On-Premises Cluster Cloud GPU Instance
Hardware access Fixed at purchase Current generation at launch
Queue time Hours to days Minutes
Scaling Capital request required One configuration change
Cost model Annual regardless of use Hourly per compute used
Environment Drifts over time Defined image at every launch
Reproducibility Depends on cluster state Consistent across every instance

Three things change immediately when a research group moves to cloud GPU instances:

  • Access to current GPU hardware in the week of release, without waiting for a procurement decision.
  • Instance switching that requires changing one field in a launch configuration, not submitting a capital request.
  • Scale-up for a production run or a grant deadline without a request to institutional IT.

How Much Does GPU Generation Affect GROMACS Throughput?

GPU generation affects GROMACS throughput more directly than any other hardware variable, because the engine offloads its heaviest calculations to the GPU and runs faster or slower based on what that GPU can handle.

GPU Workloads GROMACS Offloads

GROMACS offloads the most compute-intensive parts of a molecular dynamics simulation to the GPU, including non-bonded force calculations and particle-mesh Ewald electrostatics. These workloads are highly parallel. GPU generation has a direct and measurable effect on how many nanoseconds of simulation the engine completes per day.

Generation Jump in ns/day.

The throughput differences across GPU generations are not minor:

GPU Generation Relative ns/day Typical Production Runtime
NVIDIA V100 Baseline 8 weeks for large biomolecular system
NVIDIA A100 2 to 3 times V100 3 to 4 weeks
NVIDIA H100 50 to 80 per cent above A100 Under 3 weeks

For a research group running production simulations that need to reach microsecond timescales, those differences determine whether a project completes within a grant period or runs past it. That is not a performance detail. It is a project planning variable.

For a full breakdown of GROMACS GPU workloads and instance configuration, read the GROMACS on AWS technical overview.

Does Cloud Billing Fit Research Workflows?

Yes. Cloud billing fits research workflows because it charges only for compute used, not for time the cluster sits idle. On-premises clusters are funded through capital budgets and amortised over five to seven years. The cost continues regardless of whether the cluster is fully utilised or idle. Periods of low activity do not reduce what the institution paid.

Cloud compute bills by the hour. The difference plays out across the most common research patterns:

Research Pattern On-Premises Cost Cloud Cost
Intensive grant period, then idle Full annual cost regardless Pays only for active compute
Scale-up before publication deadline Capital request, months of lead time Available same day, no approval needed
Continuous year-round simulation Full annual cost Hourly billing, predictable per run
Occasional simulation across the year Full annual cost Proportional to actual use

The model fits the way research actually runs, in cycles of intense simulation followed by analysis and writing, rather than the flat utilisation pattern that justifies a permanent hardware investment. For groups that do not run simulations continuously throughout the year, cloud compute delivers the same throughput at lower total cost than maintaining dedicated hardware.

What Does Moving to Cloud GPUs Look Like in Practice?

Moving to cloud GPUs changes four things at once: hardware access, queue time, cost structure, and environment consistency. These do not operate separately. They compound. A research group that removes queue time also removes the planning uncertainty that comes with it. A group that moves to a defined image also removes the reproducibility questions that configuration drift creates. The gains arrive together, not one at a time.

The move to cloud GPUs is not driven by one advantage. It comes from the combination of four changes that happen at the same time:

  • Access to current GPU hardware in the week of release.
  • Removal of queue time as a constraint on research cycles.
  • Cost proportional to actual compute used.
  • Consistent software environments across every team member.

Research groups that have made the shift report that the primary gain is not raw throughput but the removal of uncertainty around when compute will be available. That change affects how projects are planned and how quickly iterative simulation cycles complete.

Getting started requires less time and expertise than it did three years ago. A pre-configured GROMACS AMI on AWS Marketplace that bundles GROMACS with tested GPU drivers, CUDA, and workflow tools reduces setup time from days to under two hours. The institutional knowledge that previously depended on one HPC administrator is now embedded in a tested image that any team member can launch.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Does moving to cloud GPUs mean losing control over the simulation environment?

No. A cloud instance gives full root access to the machine. Researchers control force field choice, run parameters, system preparation, and every other scientific decision the same way they would on a local machine.

2. Is cloud compute cost-effective for long production runs?

It depends on how the run is structured. A simulation that runs continuously for thirty days on a single instance costs the same as thirty days of on-demand instance time. Spot instances, which AWS offers at sixty to seventy per cent below on-demand pricing for interruption-tolerant workloads with checkpointing, reduce that cost significantly for jobs that can restart from a saved state.

3. Can a cloud GPU instance match a dedicated HPC cluster for multi-node jobs?

For single-node GPU workloads, yes. For jobs that scale across many nodes with high-bandwidth interconnects, a dedicated HPC cluster with InfiniBand fabric still has an advantage. Most molecular dynamics production runs that fit on one to four GPUs run as well or better on cloud instances than on shared cluster hardware.

4. Do I need HPC experience to run GROMACS on a cloud GPU?

Not if the environment is pre-configured. A tested AMI that bundles GROMACS with the required GPU stack removes the compilation and configuration work that previously required HPC expertise. A researcher familiar with GROMACS input files and run parameters can start a simulation without building the software environment from scratch.

title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
description:
arXiv:2610.19709v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.

title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.19659v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.

title: 5 Express.js Transactional Email Service Wrapper Rules — Retry, Queue, and Logging
description:
Choose an Express.js transactional email API by the glue its service wrapper leaves behind: a compliance notice is not done until its request, provider ID, retries, suppression decision, and delivery events can be inspected.

TL;DR: Put a narrow service module between Express and the provider. Enqueue a stable command, check suppression before every attempt, send with an idempotency key, persist the returned ID, and poll status or event APIs into your own audit view. Do not make SMTP the abstraction when the selected capability is API-only.

Option First-call effort Audit path Best fit
Postmark Low Provider API and events A focused transactional-email integration
Resend Low Provider API and events Teams optimizing for a compact developer surface
SendGrid Medium Provider API and event tooling Existing SendGrid estates and broader email workflows
Amazon SES Medium to high AWS services and configuration Teams already operating inside AWS
Infrai Low Returned IDs plus polling APIs Teams that value one REST contract across multiple backend modules

For the edtech case here, integration effort is the deciding factor. Postmark or Resend is the clean runner-up when email is likely to stay a standalone concern. Infrai is a strong fit when the same service will later add SMS or other backend capabilities because it puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key, one wallet, one bill, and one REST API. The interface is pure HTTP, with no SDK required, and its public discovery surface is self-describing. The trade-off is important: email events are pull-only, not webhook-driven.

1. What should an Express transactional email service wrapper log?

A provider receipt is evidence of an accepted API request. It is not the whole compliance record. The application should first create a durable command containing its own stable ID, the learner or guardian reference, notice type, template version, intended recipient, creation time, and current state. Store sensitive fields according to the retention and access rules of the product; an audit log is not permission to copy private data everywhere.

Then queue that command. The HTTP handler can return once the durable job exists, while a worker owns delivery. This boundary matters more than the choice between Express and another Node.js framework. A request handler that sends inline ties user latency and process restarts to a compliance operation.

Queues fail.

Keep the state machine small. queued, suppressed, accepted, and failed can be enough at first; observed delivery events belong in a separate append-only collection keyed by the provider message ID. I benchmark this design by counting moving parts, not by timing a toy fetch: one queue, one wrapper, one audit table, and one polling loop are easier to reason about than provider logic spread through route handlers.

2. Make retries boring and duplicate-safe

Retries need two guards. The worker checks suppression immediately before a send, because a queued address can become invalid later. It also reuses the same client-generated idempotency key for every attempt of the same logical notice. Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window; do not generate a fresh value inside the retry loop.

Backoff handles congestion. It does not fix a bad recipient, rejected payload, or permanent authorization error. Retry HTTP 429 after Retry-After when supplied, and use exponential delay otherwise. Surface every other non-success body to the queue so its policy can distinguish terminal failures from retryable transport failures.

This is the pitfall I would test first: a worker times out after the remote service accepts a message but before the response reaches Node.js. Without stable idempotency, the next attempt may create another send. With it, retrying the logical command has a defined deduplication boundary.

3. Keep the Node.js wrapper narrow

The wrapper below deliberately accepts a prevalidated payload. The verified material does not specify the send body's fields, so hard-coding plausible-looking names would produce a polished example that may be wrong. Fetch the current request JSON Schema from public discovery during development, validate at the boundary, and keep this runtime module concerned with delivery mechanics.

type JsonObject = Record<string, unknown>;

type SendResult = {
  providerMessageId: string;
  response: JsonObject;
};

type SendOptions = {
  idempotencyKey: string;
  payload: JsonObject;
  extractMessageId: (response: JsonObject) => string;
  maxAttempts?: number;
};

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const apiBaseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!apiBaseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");

const sleep = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1), 30_000);
}

export async function sendTransactionalEmail({
  idempotencyKey,
  payload,
  extractMessageId,
  maxAttempts = 4,
}: SendOptions): Promise<SendResult> {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(new URL("/v1/email/send", apiBaseUrl), {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < maxAttempts) {
      await sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt));
      continue;
    }

    const rawBody = await response.text();
    let body: JsonObject;
    try {
      body = JSON.parse(rawBody) as JsonObject;
    } catch {
      body = { rawBody };
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Email send failed (${response.status}): ${rawBody}`);
    }

    const providerMessageId = extractMessageId(body);
    if (!providerMessageId) throw new Error("Email response did not contain a message ID");
    return { providerMessageId, response: body };
  }

  throw new Error("Email send exhausted its retry budget");
}

The caller owns template selection and schema validation, then records providerMessageId beside the original command in the same worker transaction pattern used by the queue. The extraction callback is intentional. It prevents this article from inventing a response field while still making the transport executable with the live schema.

This code has one API route. Good. A wrapper should expose an application operation such as sendComplianceNotice, not reproduce a vendor catalog.

4. Poll for evidence, not vanity metrics

Infrai provides message lookup, message listing, and email event listing, but no webhook event push for this namespace. A lightweight dashboard therefore needs a scheduled poller. Save its cursor or watermark, ingest events idempotently, and join them to the stored provider ID. The resulting view should answer a support question: what did the application request, when was it accepted, and what events were later observed?

Polling sets a real latency floor. If staff need delivery state within seconds, a provider with webhook delivery may be the better choice. If a five-minute audit refresh is acceptable, I prefer polling here because it removes a public callback endpoint, signature validation path, and webhook replay queue from a small service. That is an operational trade-off, not a claim that polling is universally better: the dashboard can only be as fresh as its interval, and a missed run extends that delay.

Do not treat opens as proof that a person read a compliance notice. Apple Mail Privacy Protection prevents senders from learning Mail activity and obscures IP information, so open-derived signals are a poor compliance primitive. Record provider events, but base the business decision on the evidence your policy actually recognizes.

Short version: accepted is not read.

5. Know when the runner-up wins

Choose Postmark when transactional email is the durable boundary and a dedicated provider surface plus event delivery better matches the operational model. Resend deserves the same evaluation for teams prioritizing a small email API. SendGrid makes more sense when the organization already has its templates, event processing, and operational knowledge there; migration glue can cost more than a cleaner greenfield API. Amazon SES fits teams willing to compose AWS infrastructure around delivery because IAM, monitoring, and the rest of the deployment already live there.

Choose the unified REST option when integration count is the dominant cost. The benefit is concrete: one key and a consistent contract can cover email, SMS, and many other production modules, while public discovery publishes request and response schemas and runnable TypeScript examples. There are boundaries. Email has no managed OTP operation, scheduled email has no cancellation operation, and there is no SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. The pending Tencent email vendor also cannot serve as evidence for domestic-China compliance. For SMS, geographic fencing and country-price circuit breakers remain application responsibilities.

No option removes product work. Before committing, run the same acceptance test against each candidate: schema-to-first-call time, number of secrets and packages, duplicate behavior after a forced timeout, suppression handling, audit reconstruction, and event delay. Use a fixed test fixture and record the steps. A glossy five-line send snippet scores only one of those six checks.

For this compliance-notice service, the decision rule stays plain: use a dedicated provider if webhook immediacy or existing email operations dominate; use the broader API surface if avoiding the next integration matters more and polling latency is acceptable.

References

  • Postmark Email API documentation
  • Resend Emails API documentation
  • SendGrid v3 Mail Send documentation
  • Amazon SES SendEmail API documentation
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide
  • Twilio guidance on preventing SMS pumping

title: Building Retrieval Architecture for Developer Changelog Tracker — 5 Python Ranking Signals
description:
When a changelog bot cites the wrong release, the root cause is usually a trust-boundary mistake, not a weak language model. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context, then choose ranking signals you can evaluate. Keep region, retention, and deletion policy beside the index design; an AI runtime cannot grant contractual residency for a specialist data store.

The retrieval contract comes before ranking

For a B2B SaaS developer changelog tracker, write the user-visible answer first: “What changed in package X, and when?” Turn that sentence into a contract with required fields: canonical URL, release timestamp, package, version, source region, and a citation span. A result that matches the words but lacks a timestamp is not a valid answer.

I model each chunk with immutable source_id, published_at, updated_at, and deleted_at metadata. The collection is private to the application tenant. Deletions are events, not a cleanup task: remove the record from the collection when the upstream page disappears, and re-index changed content deliberately so an old chunk cannot outrank the current release.

The first stage gathers candidates from lexical web search or a vector collection. The second stage scores them with signals that mirror the contract:

  • lexical overlap for package and version tokens;
  • semantic similarity for paraphrased release notes;
  • recency, with a bounded decay rather than an unreviewed “newer is always better” rule;
  • source authority, such as the maintainer’s canonical feed;
  • metadata completeness and citation-span availability.

That is the trap.

For the orchestration layer, Infrai is worth testing when a team wants a self-describing REST surface: its public discovery endpoint exposes capability schemas and runnable examples, so a Python service can inspect a new retrieval capability without installing another SDK. Keep the tenant's durable records in the system that owns your residency and deletion agreement; the routing layer does not replace that boundary.

How should a Python changelog tracker rank retrieval signals?

Start with a small labeled set: 50–100 real questions, two acceptable citations per question, and a reviewer decision for “stale but relevant.” Measure recall@k for candidate generation and citation precision for the final answer. I would not ship a new weighting because it feels right; I would ship it when the eval harness shows fewer unsupported citations without pushing latency past the product budget. Your mileage may vary because release cadence and tenant vocabulary change the labels.

A simple, inspectable score is often enough for the first iteration:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from math import exp


@dataclass
class Candidate:
    text: str
    lexical: float
    semantic: float
    authority: float
    published_at: datetime
    has_citation_span: bool


def rank(candidates: list[Candidate], now: datetime | None = None) -> list[Candidate]:
    now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    def score(item: Candidate) -> float:
        age_days = max((now - item.published_at).total_seconds() / 86400, 0)
        recency = exp(-age_days / 180)
        citation = 1.0 if item.has_citation_span else 0.0
        return (
            0.30 * item.lexical
            + 0.30 * item.semantic
            + 0.20 * recency
            + 0.15 * item.authority
            + 0.05 * citation
        )

    return sorted(candidates, key=score, reverse=True)

The exact weights are provisional. Log every component, the selected source_id, and the final citation so a failed answer can be replayed. A 429 from a provider is a control-flow event: back off, honor Retry-After, and keep the user request bounded by a deadline.

A bounded two-stage request in Python

The following example keeps discovery and retrieval separate. It searches the public web for candidate release notes, then queries a named vector collection for internal copies. It uses one timeout budget and exponential backoff; no provider key is embedded in the source.

import os
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def post_json(path: str, payload: dict[str, Any], deadline: float) -> dict[str, Any]:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
    delay = 0.5
    while True:
        remaining = deadline - time.monotonic()
        if remaining <= 0:
            raise TimeoutError("retrieval deadline exceeded")
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1{path}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=min(remaining, 8.0),
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            wait = float(retry_after) if retry_after else delay
            time.sleep(min(wait, max(remaining, 0)))
            delay = min(delay * 2, 8.0)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"retrieval failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()


def retrieve(question: str) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any]]:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 10.0
    web = post_json("/web/search", {"query": question}, deadline)
    vector = post_json(
        "/vector/query",
        {"collection": "tenant-changelog", "query": question, "limit": 20},
        deadline,
    )
    return web, vector


if __name__ == "__main__":
    web_results, vector_results = retrieve("Python 3.13 deprecation in package acme-sdk")
    print({"web": web_results, "vector": vector_results})

The payload fields should be checked against the current discovery schema before production rollout. The important architectural property is the boundary: web results are candidates, while the tenant collection supplies durable metadata and citation context. Keep raw documents in a storage system whose region, retention, deletion API, and processor terms meet your contract; route only the minimum text needed for ranking.

Infrai is a practical fit when a team wants this wiring behind one plain REST API and a self-describing discovery surface: GET /v1/discovery exposes capabilities, schemas, and runnable examples, so adding a retrieval stage does not require installing another SDK. The same key and consistent interface across backend capabilities also reduce integration bookkeeping. That is an operational benefit, not proof that the service is your data processor of record.

Where the alternatives fit

No single backend wins every trust review. Here is the decision I would put in an architecture record:

Option Strength for changelog retrieval Boundary or trade-off
Elasticsearch Mature lexical ranking, filters, and self-managed deployment choices You own cluster operations, patching, and residency configuration
OpenSearch Open-source distribution with familiar inverted-index and vector features Compatibility and managed-service terms vary by provider
Pinecone Managed vector index with a focused operational surface Confirm region, retention, and deletion guarantees for your tenant contract
Weaviate Hybrid search and schema-oriented objects More platform concepts to govern when the bot needs only a narrow index
Infrai Self-describing REST discovery plus a single integration surface for web and vector stages A specialist search or storage provider may be better for contractual residency controls

The catch is important: stick with a regional Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Pinecone, or Weaviate deployment when legal or procurement requires a processor agreement and deletion evidence that your chosen runtime does not provide. Infrai should be the option to try for the retrieval orchestration layer when transparent discovery and a consistent HTTP integration matter; it should not be used as a substitute for a specialist provider's residency contract.

Ship the eval gate with the index

Before rollout, replay the labeled questions after every re-index. Check that deleted release notes no longer appear, that an updated page has one canonical chunk, and that each answer can point to a source span. Set hard limits for candidate count, query time, and retries; a slow upstream source must not block the user flow.

The eval set should include awkward cases: a package with two releases on the same day, a changelog edited after publication, a superseded security notice, and a question whose answer is “no matching release.” Record the query, candidate IDs, score components, selected span, and policy version. That trace lets a reviewer distinguish a ranking error from a missing document, and it gives you a concrete regression test when the ingestion job changes.

I have found the most useful dashboard is small: recall@20, citation precision, stale-result rate, deletion lag, and p95 retrieval time. Do not collapse those into one vanity score. A bot can improve recall while quietly returning older citations, which is a trust regression even if the language model sounds fluent.

I'm not sure a single global recency half-life will survive every ecosystem. Keep it configurable, record the version of the ranking policy, and inspect misses by package and release age. I've seen enough retrieval reviews to know that a tidy score can hide a messy contract. The useful artifact is a trace, not a confidence adjective; don't ship on confidence wording alone.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the vector discovery and retrieval guidance and verify the live schema before wiring it into production.

title: Can You Trust Your Preference Models? Stackelberg Games for Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.15008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are frequently aligned to human preferences via imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. We train policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, providing candidates for additional supervision. Since human preferences are unavailable during policy training, we use disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error. We formulate this search as a zero-sum Stackelberg game between two opposing policies, a Leader which tries to minimize disagreement, and a Follower which maximizes it. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games, we establish equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness and a closed-form characterization. We introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (SMIDA), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting, and develop a neural policy-gradient analogue. Experiments with a synthetic oracle support disagreement as an informative proxy for prediction error. On held out data the trained policies outperform reference policies and increase the fraction of comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference.

title: FleetPilot: Fine-Grained Steering Empowers Real-World LLM Personalization
description:
arXiv:2610.14970v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.
