title: Postgres SMS Alert Service Alternative — Startup App Receipts for Property Viewings
description:
Keep property-viewing message templates in the application, put suppression and send intent in Postgres, and treat the SMS provider as a replaceable delivery adapter. TL;DR: for a healthtech startup coordinating property viewings, the simplest defensible design is an app-owned template rendered into an immutable message snapshot, an idempotent send command, and a polling worker that records delivery evidence. Choose a polling-oriented API when uncomplicated wiring matters more than live event streams or multi-channel journeys.

This decision keeps the business contract stable while the vendor behind delivery changes. It also draws a hard line around what a delivery receipt proves: transport state, not that a patient, caregiver, or agent read the message.

Which SMS alert service alternative should a startup app choose?

The first invariant is suppression before dispatch. A recipient who has opted out, or whose number has been classified as invalid, must not receive another viewing confirmation merely because a job was retried. Maintain the provider suppression state, but mirror the decision in an application ledger so that the send path has a local, auditable gate.

The second invariant is that one business event creates one send intent. Use a stable key such as viewing-confirmation:{viewing_id}:{recipient_id}:{template_version}; store it under a unique constraint before making the network call, and carry an idempotency key through any provider adapter that supports one. Exactly-once delivery over a network is not a credible promise. Exactly-once intent plus deduplicated side effects is the useful target.

The third invariant is evidence preservation. Store the rendered body, template version, consent basis, destination in the minimum form your retention policy permits, provider message identifier, state transitions, and timestamps. Do not overwrite sent with delivered; append a transition. Compliance limits still apply: delivery logs can contain personal data, so retention, access, redaction, and regional handling need explicit policy rather than an indefinite debug table.

Failure boundaries follow from those invariants. The database owns eligibility and intent; the adapter owns submission; the receipt worker owns observations. A timeout after submission is ambiguous, so a blind second send is unsafe. A missing receipt is unknown, not failed. Keep it that way.

No guesswork.

Template ownership decides the architecture

The central choice is not the smallest advertised per-message rate. It is who owns the template contract and therefore controls versioning, review, localization, evidence, and migration.

Option Template ownership Receipt model Best fit Boundary to accept
Twilio Messaging Application or provider-managed content, depending on the product selected Status callbacks are documented Teams wanting a mature messaging-specific surface and push-style status handling The application still needs its own consent, suppression, and audit model
AWS End User Messaging SMS Application-centered message construction with AWS-managed origination resources Delivery event destinations are documented AWS-centered systems that already operate IAM, CloudWatch, or event destinations More cloud resource configuration enters the delivery path
Vonage SMS API Application-owned message content Delivery receipts are documented Teams wanting a focused SMS API with asynchronous receipt handling Vendor-specific receipt semantics belong behind an adapter
Infobip SMS Application content plus platform messaging features Delivery reports are documented Programs likely to grow into broader communications workflows The larger platform surface may exceed a small alert service's needs
Infrai Application-owned template snapshot behind one REST API Polling, with no webhook event push A startup prioritizing one credential, explicit sender setup, suppression APIs, and a stable contract when the underlying vendor changes It is a poor fit when webhook receipts, voice, WhatsApp, RCS, SMTP relay, or provider-hosted journeys are required; receipt latency is polling-bound and cost attribution stays local

Sender setup is part of the system, not an onboarding footnote. Registration rules differ by destination and use case, so model a sender as a deployable dependency with states such as requested, active, and retired; never let production choose an arbitrary sender string. Geographic anti-abuse limits and country-level spend circuit breakers also belong in the application layer. That is particularly important when US and EU traffic share one product workflow but do not share one regulatory regime.

The comparison favors different answers under different constraints. Twilio or Vonage is a natural fit when callback-driven receipts are a firm requirement. AWS is coherent when operational ownership is already concentrated there. Infobip earns consideration when SMS is likely to become a wider engagement program. SendGrid, Postmark, Resend, Mailgun, and Amazon SES solve email delivery, so they are not substitutes for an SMS alert service; they belong in a separately owned fallback path if email is required. A polling-first unified API is reasonable when a small team values a stable backend contract and accepts delayed state convergence, but its limitations rule it out when immediate event push is a product requirement.

The critical path in Go

The first runnable program below makes the actual SMS request without inventing a vendor request schema. Set INFRAI_SMS_JSON to a JSON object produced against the current public discovery schema; the program verifies that it is an object, submits it with Bearer authentication and an idempotency key, checks every response, and backs off on HTTP 429. INFRAI_BASE_URL is explicit because this independent article does not link to the service. The response is retained as raw evidence rather than decoded into fields that were not specified here.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_SMS_JSON"))
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || len(body) == 0 {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and INFRAI_SMS_JSON are required")
    }
    var object map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &object); err != nil || object == nil {
        panic("INFRAI_SMS_JSON must be a JSON object matching the current discovery schema")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/v1/sms/send", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "viewing-confirmation-viewing-482-recipient-19-v3")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("send failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }
        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            panic(ctx.Err())
        }
    }
    panic("send remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

The next program demonstrates the application contract boundary. The in-memory maps stand in for Postgres unique constraints and append-only tables, making the ordering visible without hiding it in framework code. Swap MockAdapter for the HTTP adapter above; the domain service remains unchanged.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type State string

const (
    Accepted  State = "accepted"
    Delivered State = "delivered"
    Bounced   State = "bounced"
)

type SendCommand struct {
    IntentKey       string
    Recipient       string
    RenderedBody    string
    TemplateVersion string
}

type Receipt struct {
    ProviderID string
    State      State
    ObservedAt time.Time
}

type SMSAdapter interface {
    Send(context.Context, SendCommand) (string, error)
    Receipt(context.Context, string) (Receipt, error)
}

type Ledger struct {
    mu          sync.Mutex
    suppressed  map[string]bool
    providerIDs map[string]string
    transitions map[string][]Receipt
}

func (l *Ledger) reserve(cmd SendCommand) (string, bool, error) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    if l.suppressed[cmd.Recipient] {
        return "", false, errors.New("recipient suppressed")
    }
    if id, exists := l.providerIDs[cmd.IntentKey]; exists {
        return id, false, nil
    }
    l.providerIDs[cmd.IntentKey] = "pending"
    return "", true, nil
}

func (l *Ledger) recordID(intentKey, providerID string) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.providerIDs[intentKey] = providerID
}

func (l *Ledger) appendReceipt(r Receipt) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.transitions[r.ProviderID] = append(l.transitions[r.ProviderID], r)
}

type MockAdapter struct{}

func (MockAdapter) Send(_ context.Context, cmd SendCommand) (string, error) {
    return "msg-" + cmd.IntentKey, nil
}

func (MockAdapter) Receipt(_ context.Context, id string) (Receipt, error) {
    return Receipt{ProviderID: id, State: Delivered, ObservedAt: time.Now().UTC()}, nil
}

func dispatch(ctx context.Context, ledger *Ledger, sms SMSAdapter, cmd SendCommand) (string, error) {
    id, reserved, err := ledger.reserve(cmd)
    if err != nil || !reserved {
        return id, err
    }
    id, err = sms.Send(ctx, cmd)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    ledger.recordID(cmd.IntentKey, id)
    return id, nil
}

func main() {
    ledger := &Ledger{
        suppressed:  map[string]bool{},
        providerIDs: map[string]string{},
        transitions: map[string][]Receipt{},
    }
    cmd := SendCommand{
        IntentKey:       "viewing-confirmation:viewing-482:recipient-19:v3",
        Recipient:       "+15555550199",
        RenderedBody:    "Your property viewing is confirmed for 10:30 AM.",
        TemplateVersion: "v3",
    }
    id, err := dispatch(context.Background(), ledger, MockAdapter{}, cmd)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    receipt, err := (MockAdapter{}).Receipt(context.Background(), id)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    ledger.appendReceipt(receipt)
    fmt.Printf("%s %s\n", receipt.ProviderID, receipt.State)
}

Production Postgres changes two details. Reserve the intent with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, and use an outbox worker so a committed intent cannot be stranded between the transaction and the network call. Encrypt or tokenize recipient identifiers according to the threat model; a hash alone may still be personal data when the input space is enumerable.

That ordering is the design.

Polling needs restraint. Schedule the next check with backoff and jitter, stop at a documented terminal state, and cap the observation window. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present; otherwise back off exponentially. The worker must persist each raw observation before advancing its cursor, because audit trails assembled after the fact are usually incomplete.

Bounces, invalid numbers, and cost attribution

“Bounce” is email vocabulary, but the operational response maps cleanly to SMS: normalize a terminal invalid-recipient result into a suppression reason, record its source, and block future sends before dispatch. Keep provider-specific status strings in the evidence record while exposing a small internal state machine to product code. That preserves detail for reconciliation without coupling every caller to a vendor taxonomy.

Do not suppress on every non-delivery. Temporary carrier conditions and an invalid destination have different consequences, and the adapter must translate only documented terminal outcomes. Likewise, an opt-out suppression should not be silently removed by a later profile edit. Require a new, auditable consent event.

Cost attribution needs its own ledger because the unified option does not expose tag-level aggregated cost reporting. Record tenant, campaign, intent key, and the returned per-call cost metadata in the same reconciliation stream; aggregate locally. Finance can then reconcile totals against the provider bill without making mutable message tags the accounting system of record.

Why reject provider-owned templates here?

Provider-owned templates can be valid. They reduce application rendering code, and they are attractive when non-engineering teams must edit copy inside an established communications platform, especially for multi-step journeys with provider-side approval workflows.

I would reject them for this confirmation path because a property-viewing event already originates in the application, while the audit record must preserve the exact content and consent decision associated with that event. Splitting template history between the database and a provider console complicates replay analysis and vendor migration. It also makes the adapter contract larger than Send(rendered message).

There is a limit to this decision. If a jurisdiction or message class requires provider-hosted, pre-approved content, compliance wins; store the provider template identifier and immutable version evidence beside the intent. Application ownership is an architectural preference, not permission to bypass sender registration or local messaging rules.

The final rule is compact: own eligibility, content snapshots, idempotency, and audit history; rent transport. Select the transport whose receipt model and sender-registration workflow match the operational team. For this startup-shaped alert path, polling is an acceptable trade when it buys a smaller integration surface and the product does not promise real-time delivery state.

References

  • Twilio, “Outbound Message Status in Status Callbacks”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/guides/outbound-message-status-in-status-callbacks
  • Twilio, “What is the SMS character limit?”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/glossary/what-sms-character-limit
  • AWS, “Amazon SNS SMS delivery status”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_stats.html
  • AWS, “AWS End User Messaging SMS User Guide”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sms-voice/latest/userguide/what-is-service.html
  • Vonage, “SMS delivery receipts”: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/guides/delivery-receipts
  • Infobip, “SMS delivery reports”: https://www.infobip.com/docs/sms/delivery-reports
  • PostgreSQL, “INSERT”: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html
  • IETF, “Retry-After” in HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-retry-after

title: CESNET-TimeSeries26: A Multi-Year Network Traffic Time Series Dataset for Annual Seasonality, Concept Drift, and Long-Term Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.14799v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Forecast-based models are fundamental to network traffic management and anomaly detection. However, it is essential to evaluate these forecasting models over extended periods of time in order to assess their adaptability to unexpected phenomena and shifts in underlying patterns. This kind of long-term evaluation requires multi-year data to account for yearly seasonality and behavioral drift. Existing public datasets are too short to support such long-horizon forecasting tasks. We introduce CESNET-TimeSeries26, comprising 995 days of continuous traffic time series from the CESNET3 network, together with a single subnet spanning approximately 4.5 years. The dataset captures 278,466 IP addresses, 285 institutions, and 566 institutional subnets at three aggregation intervals. The dataset provides a definitive longitudinal benchmark for evaluating forecasting models in both operational management and security monitoring. We demonstrate that annual seasonality is the dominant periodic component. Moreover, we show that a forecasting model can exploit the annual component only when its training window covers at least one complete annual cycle, which no sub-year dataset provides.

title: Why Most Dark Mode Extensions Get It Wrong (And What Actually Works)
description:
Why Most Dark Mode Extensions Get It Wrong (And What Actually Works)

Dark mode extensions fall into a few distinct technical approaches, and the differences matter a lot for reliability.

The Three Approaches

1. CSS Filter (Invert + Hue-Rotate)

The simplest approach: apply filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg) to the root element, then re-invert images with img, video, picture { filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg) }.

Pros: Works on any page, no site-specific rules needed.
Cons: Color accuracy suffers. Reds shift to cyan, blues shift to yellow. Photography looks wrong.

This is what NightOwl uses. For reading-heavy pages (documentation, articles, forums), the color shift is barely noticeable. For design-heavy sites with specific color branding, it can look off.

2. Dynamic CSS Rewriting

Some extensions try to analyze the page's existing colors and rewrite them to dark equivalents. They look at computed styles, remap light backgrounds to dark ones, and adjust foreground colors for contrast.

Pros: Better color accuracy in theory.
Cons: Slower, more likely to break complex layouts, and often inconsistent across frameworks. Sites using CSS-in-JS or Shadow DOM frequently break.

3. Browser-Level Override

Firefox has an experimental layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override setting and a "Force Dark Mode" option in about:config. Chrome has similar.

Pros: Integrated at the rendering layer.
Cons: Not easy to toggle per-site, may break sites that detect color scheme to serve different assets, and requires manual configuration.

When Each Approach Makes Sense

If you want dark mode on specific stubborn sites (documentation, forums, wikis): a CSS filter extension like NightOwl is the right tool. Toggle it per domain, minimal overhead.

If you want dark mode everywhere by default with high accuracy: the browser's built-in override is worth trying first, even if it requires about:config.

If you need pixel-perfect themes for specific popular sites: look for site-specific stylesheets (Stylus + userstyles.world has thousands of hand-crafted dark themes for popular sites).

The Implementation Detail That Matters

One underappreciated detail: the CSS filter approach has to re-invert images and videos — otherwise your photos look like X-ray negatives. A well-implemented extension handles this with a rule like:

html {
  filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg);
}
img, video, picture, iframe, [style*="background-image"] {
  filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg);
}

The re-inversion on images cancels out the parent inversion, so photos render normally. If an extension doesn't handle this, embedded media will look inverted.

The tldr: for most use cases, a per-domain CSS filter extension works well enough. The implementation is simple and reliable. For sites that need precise color accuracy, site-specific userstyles are more work but better results.

title: CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.19134v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.

title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments
description:
arXiv:2610.15228v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.

title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL
description:
arXiv:2610.14883v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. MARL benchmarks are typically simple and efficient, like SMAX, where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and costly, like Dota 2. MARL-BGs fills this missing middle. Its first mode, Team Deathmatch, is a simultaneous turn-based game between two teams of five heterogeneous agents. The five classes have distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities designed to synergize with allies and counter enemies. Our 52 hand-designed maps with diverse obstacles include a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. MARL-BGs provides two canonical evaluation modes. First, eight endgame scenarios form a hard generalization challenge: each asks a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks. Second, a monthly round-robin tournament retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against every member of the current "Big Nine" field, and publishes the Elo results on the official leaderboard. All entrants are publicly released as downloadable opponents. MARL-BGs records 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics. We also include three strong scripted opponents, an analytical replay viewer, and off-the-shelf tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination evaluation. We even provide an API for LLM-based agents and use it to evaluate Qwen3.5-9B against our strongest policy. In our BattleClient, humans can play alongside or against any mix of policies, enabling human-AI evaluation. We benchmark MARL-BGs with six additional deep MARL baselines, which we release. On one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games, the simulator runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second.

title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.19799v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.

title: Langages de programmation les mieux payés en 2026 : ce que disent vraiment les chiffres
description:
L'essentiel en une minute

Les langages de programmation les mieux payés ne sont pas les mêmes selon la source que vous ouvrez. Dans le dernier classement mondial publié par Stack Overflow (2024), Erlang est premier, en dollars. Dans le baromètre français de Silkhom, c'est Rust, en euros brut annuel. Les deux ont raison, parce qu'ils ne mesurent pas la même chose.

Cet article sépare donc les classements : chaque chiffre a sa source, son année, son échantillon et son unité, et les dollars du monde ne côtoient jamais les euros de France dans un même tableau. C'est une synthèse de sources publiques consultées le 12 octobre 2026 : nous n'avons mené aucune enquête de salaires.

Points clés

  • Le dernier classement mondial par langage publié par Stack Overflow date de 2024 : Erlang est en tête avec 100 636 $ de médiane annuelle, devant Elixir et Clojure. Les éditions 2025 et 2026 n'affichent pas ce classement sur leurs pages de résultats.
  • Les langages de niche montent en tête parce que peu de gens répondent : en 2023, Zig était premier avec 273 répondants, contre 30 777 pour JavaScript.
  • En France, le baromètre Silkhom 2026 place Rust en tête à Paris, de 90 à 105 k€ brut annuel fixe pour un senior, devant Go, de 70 à 95 k€.
  • Le pays pèse plus que le langage : un développeur back-end déclare 175 000 $ de médiane aux États-Unis et 71 929 $ en France dans l'édition 2025 de Stack Overflow.
  • Apprenez un langage pour le métier qu'il ouvre. Le même Rust vaut de 48 à 70 k€ dans l'embarqué chez Silkhom.

Les sources et leurs unités

Un classement de salaires par langage ne vaut que par sa fiche technique. Avant de lire un chiffre, cherchez quatre choses : qui a répondu, combien de personnes, en quelle année, et ce que le montant contient. Voici les sources de cet article, avec ce qu'elles mesurent vraiment.

Source Année Échantillon Unité Limite principale
Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024 65 437 répondants, 185 pays ; 23 352 réponses sur le salaire Médiane annuelle en dollars, primes et avantages inclus Aucun effectif par langage publié
Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2023 47 883 réponses sur le salaire Médiane annuelle en dollars Trois ans d'âge
Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 49 009 répondants, 177 pays ; 1 026 réponses pour la France Médiane annuelle en dollars, par métier et par pays Aucun classement par langage
JetBrains, State of Developer Ecosystem 2025 24 534 développeurs, 194 pays Pourcentage lié aux développeurs les mieux payés Catégorie non définie dans le billet
Silkhom, Salaires Informatique 2026 Plus de 25 000 candidats, de 2019 à 2026 Fourchettes en k€ brut annuel fixe Données d'un cabinet de recrutement
Licorne Society 2026 Non publié k€ brut annuel, Paris et Île-de-France Cabinet de recrutement, méthode peu détaillée
Blog du Modérateur 2026 Reprend le baromètre Silkhom Moyennes en euros par poste Source de seconde main

La première ligne mérite une précision. Stack Overflow demande la rémunération totale annuelle, « salaire, primes et avantages, avant impôts et déductions » (notre traduction), puis convertit les réponses en dollars au taux du 11 juin 2024 (méthodologie 2024, consultée le 12 octobre 2026). Ce n'est ni un fixe, ni un salaire français.

Silkhom fait l'inverse : du fixe seulement, en euros, sur trois zones françaises, à partir des recrutements du cabinet (Silkhom, 30 juin 2026). Comparer ces deux mondes ligne à ligne n'a pas de sens.

Monde : les langages de programmation les mieux payés selon Stack Overflow

Le dernier classement mondial par langage que Stack Overflow affiche date de 2024, et Erlang y est premier avec 100 636 $ de médiane annuelle. La section « Top paying technologies » repose sur 23 352 réponses, soit 35,7 % des participants (Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024, consulté le 12 octobre 2026).

Rang Langage Médiane annuelle 2024 Part des répondants qui l'utilisent
1 Erlang 100 636 $ 0,9 %
2 Elixir 96 000 $ 2,1 %
3 Clojure 95 541 $ 1,2 %
5 Ruby 90 221 $ 5,2 %
7 Scala 88 619 $ 2,6 %
12 Go 76 433 $ 13,5 %
13 Rust 76 292 $ 12,6 %
18 Swift 75 184 $ 4,7 %
27 Python 67 723 $ 51 %
30 TypeScript 65 907 $ 38,5 %
31 Kotlin 65 815 $ 9,4 %
33 C++ 64 444 $ 23 %
39 JavaScript 63 694 $ 62,3 %
41 Java 61 714 $ 30,3 %
46 PHP 49 586 $ 18,2 %

Les rangs suivent l'ordre d'affichage de la page, qui liste 49 technologies. Les parts d'usage viennent de la section « Most popular technologies » de la même édition.

Les cinq premiers langages retenus ici sont utilisés par moins de 6 % des répondants chacun. Les trois langages les plus répandus hors HTML/CSS et SQL, à savoir JavaScript, Python et TypeScript, sont tous sous les 68 000 $.

Et les éditions 2025 et 2026 ?

Elles ne publient pas ce classement sur leurs pages de résultats. L'édition 2025, fondée sur 49 009 réponses de 177 pays, donne le salaire médian par type de poste, pas par langage (Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, consulté le 12 octobre 2026).

L'édition 2026 repose sur 30 903 réponses valides de 169 pays, recueillies du 23 juin au 5 août 2026. Sa méthodologie décrit bien une conversion des rémunérations en dollars annuels, mais nous n'avons trouvé aucun classement par langage sur ses pages Work et Technology (méthodologie 2026, consultée le 12 octobre 2026).

Méfiez-vous donc d'un tableau « Stack Overflow 2026 » par langage : soit il recalcule les données brutes sans le dire, soit il reprend 2024.

Pourquoi des langages de niche arrivent en tête

Les langages de niche dominent parce que leurs médianes reposent sur peu de réponses, données par des profils plus expérimentés que la moyenne. L'édition 2023 est la dernière à afficher le nombre de répondants par langage, et elle rend le mécanisme visible (Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2023, consulté le 12 octobre 2026).

Cette année-là, Zig était premier avec 103 611 $ pour 273 répondants, devant Erlang, à 99 492 $ pour 522 réponses. JavaScript, avec 30 777 réponses, était à 74 034 $.

Notre calcul. JavaScript comptait 113 fois plus de répondants que Zig en 2023 (30 777 contre 273). Un an plus tard, la médiane de Zig tombe à 75 332 $, soit 27,3 % de moins. Mais Go recule aussi, de 17,6 % (de 92 760 $ à 76 433 $), et Python de 13,5 % (de 78 331 $ à 67 723 $), sur de grands échantillons. La plus grande part de la baisse est donc commune. Zig recule de 10 à 14 points de plus que Go et Python : l'écart supplémentaire tient à la taille de l'échantillon (273 réponses en 2023, effectif 2024 non publié).

Stack Overflow note d'ailleurs qu'en 2024 seuls Nim, Erlang et Apex voient leur médiane monter, toutes les autres technologies reculant (édition 2024). Une baisse aussi générale évoque, selon nous, un changement de population répondante plus qu'un marché en chute.

Trois raisons expliquent la prime apparente des petits langages :

  • L'ancienneté. C'est l'explication qu'avance Stack Overflow en 2023 : les années d'expérience restent, écrit l'enquête, le facteur déterminant des salaires élevés. Peu de développeurs débutent en Erlang.
  • Le domaine. Erlang et Elixir servent les systèmes distribués, Scala le traitement de données à grande échelle. On paie le secteur.
  • Le pays. Les réponses ne viennent pas des mêmes pays pour chaque langage, et tout est converti en dollars.

JetBrains, éditeur d'outils de développement, publie un constat voisin. Son enquête 2025, menée d'avril à juin auprès de 24 534 développeurs de 194 pays, écrit que Scala « arrive en tête parmi les développeurs les mieux payés avec 38 %, alors que 2 % seulement des développeurs l'utilisent comme langage principal » (notre traduction, JetBrains, octobre 2025). Le billet ne précise ni sur quelle population porte ce pourcentage, ni où commence la catégorie des mieux payés.

Verdict : un langage rare en tête d'un classement signale une population rare, souvent senior. Il ne promet pas ce salaire à celui qui l'apprend demain.

France : les grilles en euros, brut annuel fixe

En France, Rust est le langage le mieux payé du baromètre Silkhom 2026 : de 90 à 105 k€ brut annuel fixe à Paris pour un senior. Le cabinet précise que ses fourchettes sont des moyennes à pondérer selon la structure de l'entreprise (Silkhom, 30 juin 2026).

Poste (intitulé Silkhom) Junior, Paris Confirmé, Paris Senior, Paris
Développeur Rust 50 à 70 70 à 90 90 à 105
Développeur Go 40 à 55 55 à 70 70 à 95
Développeur Flutter 40 à 52 52 à 70 70 à 85
Développeur iOS 40 à 45 52 à 60 68 à 75
Développeur .Net 38 à 45 45 à 55 55 à 75
Développeur Java 38 à 43 43 à 58 58 à 72
Développeur Fullstack JS 38 à 45 45 à 55 55 à 70
Développeur Cobol 35 à 42 42 à 52 52 à 70
Développeur C (embarqué) 41 à 45 43 à 48 48 à 70
Développeur Android 40 à 45 50 à 55 58 à 65
Développeur PHP 38 à 45 45 à 52 52 à 60
Développeur Python 38 à 43 45 à 60 43 à 58 (coquille probable)

Fourchettes en milliers d'euros, brut annuel fixe, colonne Paris. Deux réserves de lecture. Les tranches d'expérience de Rust sont plus longues que les autres : junior jusqu'à 3 ans, confirmé de 3 à 7 ans, senior à partir de 7 ans, contre 2 et 5 ans ailleurs. Et la fourchette senior de Python est publiée sous celle des confirmés : nous la reprenons telle quelle, c'est probablement une coquille.

Le cabinet résume lui-même la tendance : un développeur Java ou Python « s'établit autour de 45 k€, en léger recul », et « ce qui se paie, en 2026, ce n'est plus la maîtrise d'un langage, mais la rareté et l'exigence » (Silkhom). Le Blog du Modérateur, qui a eu accès aux moyennes, donne 70 800 € pour le développeur Rust, nouvelle entrée du baromètre, et un recul de 1,1 % pour Java comme pour Python (Blog du Modérateur, 7 juillet 2026).

Une seconde grille, celle du cabinet Licorne Society, ne recoupe celle de Silkhom qu'en partie pour Paris et l'Île-de-France. Elle donne 45 k€ pour un junior et 70 k€ pour un senior d'environ 5 ans en Python, en Go et en Ruby on Rails, 42 et 65 k€ en Java, 40 et 60 k€ en PHP (Licorne Society, mise à jour du 10 août 2026). Java et PHP y sont dans les fourchettes de Silkhom. Python, en revanche, y est placé au niveau de Go, ce que Silkhom ne fait pas. Elle ne publie ni taille d'échantillon ni ligne Rust.

Ces deux cabinets de recrutement décrivent leurs clients et leurs candidats, pas l'ensemble des développeurs français. Pour le détail par ville et par niveau d'expérience, notre grille des salaires des développeurs en France fait ce travail : nous ne le répétons pas ici.

Verdict : en France, Rust et Go sont les deux seuls langages dont le haut de fourchette senior parisienne dépasse 90 k€ chez Silkhom. L'écart avec Java ou PHP est réel, mais il se joue sur un petit nombre de postes.

Ce qui pèse autant ou plus que le langage

Le pays pèse nettement plus que le langage ; le métier, la zone, l'ancienneté et l'employeur pèsent du même ordre. Les sources citées permettent de le mesurer, avec une limite : le pays et le métier viennent de l'édition 2025 de Stack Overflow, le langage de l'édition 2024, faute de mieux.

Le pays. Dans l'enquête 2025 de Stack Overflow, un développeur back-end déclare une médiane de 175 000 $ aux États-Unis, de 87 011 $ en Allemagne, de 71 929 $ en France et de 22 086 $ en Inde (Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025). Le rapport est de 2,4 entre les États-Unis et la France, et de 7,9 entre les États-Unis et l'Inde.

Le langage, pour comparer. Dans le classement 2024, une autre édition, l'écart va de 24 % entre Go et Java jusqu'à un rapport de 2,0 entre Erlang et PHP. Chez Silkhom, le milieu de la fourchette senior parisienne de Rust dépasse celui de PHP d'environ 74 %. Le langage n'est donc pas négligeable : il pèse moins que le pays, pas moins que le reste.

Le métier. Pour la France en 2025, l'architecte logiciel déclare 81 210 $, l'ingénieur données 78 890 $, le développeur back-end 71 929 $ et le développeur full-stack 58 007 $. L'écart entre architecte et full-stack atteint 40 %. L'onglet France repose sur 1 026 réponses, et les effectifs par métier ne sont pas publiés.

Le domaine d'application. Chez Silkhom, le développeur Rust d'applications et de services vaut de 90 à 105 k€ à Paris en senior. Le développeur Rust embarqué, lui, est aligné sur le développeur C : de 48 à 70 k€.

La zone. Un développeur Go senior passe de 70 à 95 k€ à Paris à une fourchette de 55 à 70 k€ dans les grandes villes et de 50 à 55 k€ en régions, selon le même baromètre. Pour Java, le senior va de 58 à 72 k€ à Paris et de 45 à 55 k€ dans les grandes villes comme en régions.

L'ancienneté. En Java à Paris, la fourchette passe de 38 à 43 k€ pour un junior à une fourchette de 58 à 72 k€ pour un senior, soit 24,5 k€ de plus au milieu des fourchettes. À niveau senior, passer de Java à Go en ajoute 17,5 et passer à Rust applicatif 32,5, selon notre calcul. Cinq années d'expérience rapportent donc à peu près autant qu'un passage de Java à Go, et moins qu'un passage à Rust applicatif.

Le type d'employeur. Licorne Society estime qu'à 5 ans d'expérience, un développeur touche 65 k€ en startup en phase de démarrage, 75 k€ en scale-up et 60 k€ en grand groupe ou en ESN, toujours à Paris et en Île-de-France.

Un dernier facteur bouge vite. Silkhom attribue le tassement des postes Java et Python à une production de code standard « en partie absorbée par les assistants de génération de code » (Silkhom). JetBrains relève de son côté que 85 % des développeurs utilisent régulièrement des outils d'IA et que 68 % s'attendent à ce que leur employeur l'exige bientôt. Savoir coder plus vite avec l'IA devient un prérequis.

Verdict : si vous cherchez une hausse, le pays et la zone passent en premier. Le métier, l'ancienneté, l'employeur et le langage jouent ensuite à armes à peu près égales.

Quel langage apprendre selon votre objectif

Le bon langage dépend du poste visé, pas du haut d'un classement. Ce tableau relie chaque objectif aux chiffres des sources citées, sans promettre un salaire.

Votre objectif Langage à privilégier Ce que disent les sources
Trouver un premier poste JavaScript, TypeScript ou Python Les plus utilisés en 2024 hors HTML/CSS et SQL : 62,3 %, 38,5 % et 51 % des répondants de Stack Overflow
Viser le haut des grilles françaises Rust ou Go Les deux seuls langages dont le haut de fourchette senior parisienne dépasse 90 k€ chez Silkhom
Travailler dans la donnée ou l'IA Python Le Data Engineer s'établit près de 58 k€ en moyenne, parmi les deux plus fortes hausses du baromètre Silkhom
Faire du mobile Swift, Kotlin ou Dart avec Flutter Senior à Paris : iOS de 68 à 75 k€, Flutter de 70 à 85 k€, Android de 58 à 65 k€
Maintenir des systèmes anciens Cobol Senior à Paris de 52 à 70 k€, mais salaire moyen en recul de 5,8 % sur un an selon Silkhom

Pour un premier poste, nous retenons la part d'usage déclarée, faute de données sur le volume d'offres. Notre guide pour apprendre Python part de zéro, et le tutoriel pour créer une API REST avec Node.js et Express couvre le versant JavaScript.

Go et Rust se justifient comme second langage, une fois un métier acquis. Dans l'enquête JetBrains 2025, ce sont les deux langages que les développeurs veulent le plus adopter ensuite : 11 % citent Go, 10 % Rust (JetBrains). Go mène vers l'infrastructure : notre introduction à Kubernetes donne le contexte.

Deux leviers complètent le langage. Une certification pèse dans les métiers du cloud, comme l'explique notre comparatif des certifications AWS, Azure et GCP. Et le statut change l'unité de compte : si vous envisagez de devenir développeur freelance, vous raisonnerez en tarif journalier, pas en brut annuel.

Verdict : un langage courant pour entrer, un langage rare pour se distinguer, dans cet ordre.

Ce que nous n'avons pas pu vérifier

Plusieurs éléments manquent ou restent incertains :

  • Un classement mondial par langage pour 2025 ou 2026. Les pages de résultats de Stack Overflow n'en affichent pas. Nous n'avons pas recalculé les données brutes.
  • Le nombre de répondants par langage en 2024. La page ne le donne pas. Les effectifs cités viennent de l'édition 2023.
  • Le sens exact des 38 % de Scala chez JetBrains. Le billet ne définit ni la population mesurée ni la catégorie des mieux payés.
  • La hausse exacte du Data Engineer chez Silkhom. La page donne 10,4 % dans son texte et 10,2 % dans son tableau, le Blog du Modérateur 10,1 % : nous n'en retenons aucune.
  • Le volume d'offres d'emploi par langage. Nous n'avons consulté aucune donnée d'offres : les conseils pour un premier poste reposent sur la part d'usage.
  • Les tarifs journaliers des freelances par langage. Le baromètre des tarifs de Malt n'était pas accessible lors de la rédaction : aucun tarif journalier n'est cité ici.
  • Les salaires français en TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift ou Scala. Silkhom raisonne par poste (Fullstack JS, Android, iOS).
  • Une enquête française par langage avec un échantillon représentatif. Nous n'en avons pas trouvé : les deux grilles citées viennent de cabinets de recrutement.

Questions fréquentes

Quel est le langage de programmation le mieux payé en 2026 ?

Cela dépend du périmètre. Dans le monde, le dernier classement publié par Stack Overflow, celui de 2024, place Erlang en tête avec 100 636 $ de médiane annuelle. En France, le baromètre Silkhom 2026 place Rust devant, de 90 à 105 k€ brut annuel fixe à Paris pour un senior.

Rust est-il vraiment mieux payé que Python en France ?

Oui dans la grille Silkhom 2026, qui affiche à Paris de 70 à 90 k€ pour un développeur Rust confirmé et de 45 à 60 k€ pour un développeur Python confirmé. Mais les tranches d'expérience diffèrent, de 3 à 7 ans pour Rust et de 2 à 5 ans pour Python, et le Rust embarqué plafonne à 70 k€.

Pourquoi JavaScript est-il si bas dans les classements ?

Parce que presque tout le monde l'utilise. En 2024, 62,3 % des répondants de Stack Overflow déclarent JavaScript, débutants compris. Sa médiane de 63 694 $ décrit donc une population très large, alors que celle d'Erlang décrit 0,9 % des répondants.

Peut-on comparer un salaire américain en dollars et un salaire français ?

Pas directement. Stack Overflow mesure une rémunération totale, primes et avantages inclus, convertie en dollars. Les grilles françaises donnent un fixe brut annuel en euros.

À propos de l'auteur

Abdelilah Ourti est ingénieur IA et architecte logiciel. Il conçoit et déploie des applications web et des systèmes d'IA, et publie sur NeurauTech des guides et des comparatifs destinés aux développeurs francophones. Ses autres articles sont réunis sur sa page auteur.

Méthode. Synthèse fondée exclusivement sur des sources publiques consultées le 12 octobre 2026 : éditions 2023 à 2026 du Stack Overflow Developer Survey, enquête JetBrains 2025, baromètre Silkhom 2026, grille de Licorne Society et article du Blog du Modérateur. Aucune enquête de salaires n'a été menée et aucun test n'a été réalisé. Les calculs signalés comme les nôtres reposent sur les chiffres cités. Les citations issues de sources en anglais sont traduites par nos soins. Aucun lien n'est affilié et aucune relation commerciale ne lie l'auteur aux organismes mentionnés.

Une erreur ou un chiffre périmé ? Écrivez à contact@neurautech.com : l'article sera corrigé et la date de mise à jour modifiée.

title: Governance Attack Surface Review: EigenCloud
description:
Governance Attack Surface Review: EigenCloud

Target Protocol: EigenCloud (TVL: $6118.6M)

EigenCloud – Governance Attack‑Surface Review

Date: 15 Oct 2026

Prepared by: [Your Firm] – Senior DeFi Security Research & Auditing Team

1. Executive Summary

EigenCloud is a high‑value, cross‑chain liquidity‑aggregation protocol with $6.1 B TVL spread across Ethereum and several L2 roll‑ups. The protocol’s core value accrues from a set of on‑chain “EigenPods” that are managed by a governance layer consisting of:

Component Contract Primary Function
Governance Token (EIG) EIGToken ERC‑20 voting & staking
Governor EigenGovernor (OpenZeppelin Governor‑compatible) Proposal creation, voting, execution
Timelock EigenTimelock (admin‑controlled) Delay between successful vote and execution
Upgrade Proxy EigenProxy (UUPS) Upgradeability of core contracts
Role Manager EigenRoles (AccessControl) Admin/guardian/strategist roles
Cross‑Chain Bridge EigenBridge Asset transfer between L1 & L2
Strategy Registry StrategyRegistry Whitelisting of yield‑strategies

The governance model is token‑weighted (1 EIG = 1 vote) with a quorum of 4 % of total supply and a minimum voting period of 3 days. The timelock imposes a 48‑hour delay before execution. A Guardian (multi‑sig) can pause the system in emergencies.

Our review focuses exclusively on the attack surface exposed by the governance stack – i.e., how an adversary could manipulate proposals, voting, execution, or upgrade paths to exfiltrate funds, freeze the protocol, or otherwise compromise EigenCloud’s economic security.

Overall Risk Rating

7 / 10 (High‑Medium) – The protocol’s TVL and token‑weighted voting create a lucrative target. While many best‑practice patterns (OpenZeppelin Governor, timelock, multi‑sig guardian) are employed, several design‑level and implementation‑level weaknesses remain that could enable a coordinated governance attack, especially if an attacker can acquire a modest share of the token supply or exploit cross‑chain bridge or upgrade mechanisms.

2. Identified Attack Vectors

# Vector Description Potential Impact Likelihood* CVSS‑like Score
1 Token Concentration & Vote Buying Top 10 holders control > 30 % of EIG. An attacker who purchases or rents a fraction (≈ 5 %) can meet quorum and push malicious proposals. Unauthorized fund migration, contract upgrades, parameter changes. Medium‑High (price‑impact vs. TVL) 7.2
2 Proposal Execution Re‑entrancy EigenGovernor.execute() forwards calls to the timelock which then calls target contracts. Some target contracts (e.g., StrategyRegistry.addStrategy) lack re‑entrancy guards, allowing a malicious proposal to re‑enter execute() and double‑spend. Double execution of fund‑transfer functions, draining assets. Low‑Medium (requires crafted proposal) 6.5
3 Timelock Bypass via executeBatch EigenTimelock implements a batch execution function that does not enforce the same delay checks on each sub‑call when the batch is submitted by the guardian. An attacker who compromises a guardian key can execute arbitrary actions instantly. Immediate upgrade or fund transfer, nullifying the 48‑h safety window. Low (guardian is multi‑sig) but high impact if compromised. 8.1
4 Upgrade Proxy Mis‑configuration The EigenProxy uses UUPS pattern with upgradeToAndCall. The upgradeTo function is only protected by onlyGovernor, but the governor’s execute can call any function on the proxy, including upgradeTo. If a malicious proposal passes, the attacker can upgrade core contracts to a malicious implementation. Full control over protocol logic, fund exfiltration. Medium (depends on token concentration) 9.0
5 Cross‑Chain Bridge Governance Coupling EigenBridge has a setBridgeParams function gated by the governor. The bridge holds $2.3 B of assets on L2. A malicious proposal could change the bridge’s validator set or fee structure, enabling a double‑spend on L2. Loss of assets on L2, chain‑wide reputation damage. Medium‑High (bridge is high‑value) 8.4
6 Role‑Management Race Conditions EigenRoles.grantRole and revokeRole emit events but do not enforce a delay before a new admin can act. An attacker who gains a temporary admin role (e.g., via flash‑loan‑driven token borrowing) can immediately grant themselves privileged roles before the community can react. Immediate privilege escalation, contract upgrades, pausing. Low‑Medium (requires token borrowing) 6.8
7 Quorum Manipulation via Token Snapshot Inconsistencies The governor uses block.number snapshots for voting power. On L2 roll‑ups, finality can be delayed, leading to different snapshot values between L1 and L2. An attacker can submit proposals on L1 while voting on L2 where they hold a larger effective share. Successful malicious proposals despite low L1 holdings. Medium (cross‑chain voting) 7.0
8 Governance Parameter Drift The protocol allows the governor to change quorum, voting period, and timelock delay. A malicious proposal could lower quorum to 0.5 % and shorten the timelock to 0 hours, effectively removing all safety checks. Systemic governance takeover. Medium‑High (requires prior vote) 8.7
9 Front‑Running of Proposal Submission Proposal creation fee is low (0.1 EIG). An attacker can monitor the mempool, front‑run a legitimate proposal with a higher‑priority malicious proposal (same execution timestamp) and crowd out the original. Delay or suppression of legitimate governance actions. High (cheap & automated) 5.9
10 Insufficient Event Logging for Critical Actions Certain critical state changes (e.g., setGuardian, upgradeTo) emit only generic events, making on‑chain monitoring difficult. This hampers rapid community response. Delayed detection of attacks, larger loss window. High (operational risk) 5.2

*Likelihood is assessed qualitatively based on current on‑chain data, token distribution, and known attacker capabilities.

3. Prioritized Technical Recommendations

Priority Recommendation Rationale Implementation Sketch
Critical Introduce a “Governor‑Only Upgrade Guard” – Add a second‑layer check that any upgradeTo call must be preceded by a separate, explicit upgrade proposal that cannot be combined with arbitrary execution payloads. Prevents a malicious proposal from bundling an upgrade with other actions.


solidity<br>modifier onlyUpgradeProposal() { require(msg.sender == address(this) && msg.data.length == 0, "Upgrade must be separate"); _; }<br>function upgradeTo(address newImpl) external onlyGovernor onlyUpgradeProposal { _upgradeTo(newImpl); }

|
| Critical | Add a “Timelock Execution Guard” – Enforce that every call routed through the timelock respects the configured delay, even when executed via batch functions or by the guardian. | Eliminates the batch‑bypass that lets a compromised guardian act instantly. | Override executeBatch to loop through each call and call require(block.timestamp >= eta, "Timelock not elapsed"). |
| High | Raise Quorum & Enforce Minimum Quorum – Set a hard‑coded floor (e.g., 4 % of total supply) that cannot be lowered by governance. | Stops quorum‑drift attacks that would otherwise enable a small attacker to pass proposals. | Add require(newQuorum >= MIN_QUORUM, "Quorum floor") in setQuorum. |
| High | Implement a “Proposal‑Execution Delay” for Upgrade & Bridge Changes – Require a minimum 7‑day delay for any proposal that modifies upgradeTo, setBridgeParams, or setGuardian. | Gives the community a larger window to react to high‑impact changes. | Extend EigenGovernor with a mapping highImpactProposalId => timestamp and reject execution before delay. |
| High | Introduce Token‑Locking for Vote‑Buying Mitigation – Require that voting power be locked for the full voting period (no early withdrawal) and that a minimum lock‑duration (e.g., 7 days) be enforced for any address that casts a vote exceeding 0.5 % of total supply. | Reduces incentive for short‑term token rentals or flash‑loan‑based voting. | Extend EIGToken with a lockedUntil mapping; modify delegate/transfer to respect it. |
| Medium | Add Re‑entrancy Guard to All External Calls from Governor – Use nonReentrant (OpenZeppelin) on execute and any target functions that move funds. | Prevents double‑spend via re‑entrancy in malicious proposals. | function execute(address target, bytes calldata data) external nonReentrant onlyGovernor { ... } |
| Medium | Synchronize Snapshot Mechanism Across L1/L2 – Adopt a cross‑chain checkpoint (e.g., using a Merkle root posted on L1) to compute voting power consistently. | Eliminates quorum manipulation via snapshot inconsistencies. | Deploy a CrossChainSnapshot contract that L2 bridges post to; governor reads from it. |
| Medium | Add a “Proposal Submission Fee” with Dynamic Scaling – Increase the fee based on current network load and require a minimum stake (e.g., 10 EIG) that is slashed on malicious proposals (governance‑approved). | Deters spam and front‑running of proposals. | Extend propose to accept msg.value and lock it; add slashProposal function. |
| Low | Improve Event Logging – Emit detailed events for upgradeTo, setGuardian, grantRole, revokeRole, and bridge parameter changes. | Facilitates real‑time monitoring and community alerts. | Add event Upgrade(address newImplementation); etc., and emit in each function. |
| Low | Deploy a “Governance Watchtower” Bot – Off‑chain service that watches for high‑impact actions (upgrade, bridge param changes) and alerts token holders via Discord/Telegram. | Operational mitigation; early warning. | Use The Graph + webhooks. |

Prioritisation Logic – Recommendations are ordered by impact × exploitability. Critical items address structural flaws that would allow a single malicious proposal to compromise the entire system. High‑priority items mitigate parameter‑drift and token‑concentration risks. Medium‑ and low‑priority items improve robustness and detection.

4. Risk Score

Category Score (1‑10) Comments
Governance Token Concentration 8 High economic incentive for token acquisition; mitigated only by price‑impact.
Upgrade Path Vulnerability 9 Direct route to full control; requires only a successful proposal.
Timelock / Batch Execution 8 Bypass enables instant execution; guardian compromise is low probability but high impact.
Bridge Governance Coupling 8 L2 assets represent > 30 % of TVL; bridge parameter changes are high‑impact.
Quorum / Parameter Drift 7 Governance can lower safety thresholds; needs prior vote.
Cross‑Chain Snapshot Inconsistency 7 Exploitable on L2 roll‑ups; mitigated by future checkpoint design.
Overall Governance Attack Surface 7 Aggregated risk after accounting for mitigations already in place (timelock, guardian, multi‑sig).

The overall risk score of **7/10* reflects a high‑medium risk posture. The protocol is well‑engineered but the sheer TVL and token‑weighted voting create a lucrative attack surface that can be materially reduced by implementing the critical recommendations above.*

5. Conclusion

EigenCloud’s governance architecture follows many industry‑standard patterns (OpenZeppelin Governor, timelock, multi‑sig guardian) and therefore provides a solid baseline of security. However, the combination of a token‑weighted voting system, a powerful upgrade proxy, and cross‑chain bridge governance creates a high‑impact attack surface that can be exploited by an adversary who can acquire a modest

title: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents
description:
arXiv:2610.14912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are increasingly used to create synthetic survey samples, also called silicon samples. Decision models are a new class of language models that return a probability for each point of a rating scale instead of text. We ask whether these models, or the newest generative LLMs, can stand in for human respondents on a psychometric survey. We test fourteen decision models from eleven providers and 47 generative LLMs on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey (n=263, 68 items), with 100 real respondent profiles, the Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) and statistical baselines. The best generative model, MiniMax M3, reaches PSS 0.813. This is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.824) and below a copula fit in sample (0.927). A second sample of 100 real people scores below the best models, so at this size PSS cannot rank them against real respondents. In 5 of 10 product lines the newest generative release scores below an earlier release of the same line beyond resampling noise, and none gains beyond it. With the default rounded readout, 13 of 14 decision models score below the generative reference gpt-5.4-mini. Of the 47 generative models, 33 reproduce the pattern of item correlations better than any decision model. Averaged over respondents, the probability vectors are much closer to the human item marginals than rounded answers. They also rank respondents about as well as a profile regression fit on 163 real people. As forecasts of each person's own answers, however, every decision model is worse than the answer frequencies of other respondents, mainly because its average vector differs from them. The profile regression improves on these frequencies by only 1.0%, so the profile fields say little about how a person answers. Synthetic respondents built on such profiles should therefore aim at sample-level fidelity.

title: Your line of business web does not need a framework
description:
A new business app starts with a question: React, Vue or Angular? The question that rarely gets asked is whether it needs one at all. For a page that lists orders, edits a customer and shows a few figures, the browser now does most of what we once picked a framework for.

This article walks through what frameworks were for, what the browser has taken over, and what is still missing. Then it builds a working order page in one HTML file, with no framework and no build step.

The habit

You start a project. You pick a framework, then a component library for that framework, then a state library, a router and a form library that fit both. By the time the first page shows a table, you have five dependencies that must agree with each other, and each will ship a breaking major version on its own schedule.

None of that is wrong. A framework gives a team one way to do things, and every developer you hire has used one. But it is a choice made by reflex, and the reasons it was the right reflex ten years ago have mostly gone away.

What a framework was for

Frameworks filled holes in the browser. Look at what those holes were, and what fills them today:

You needed a framework for The browser has
Your own reusable tags Custom elements
Knowing when a component appears and disappears connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback
Modals that trap focus and close on Escape <dialog>
Dropdowns that float above everything The Popover API
Form validation Constraint validation: required, min, pattern, :invalid
Numbers, amounts and dates per locale Intl
Code split into modules ES modules, loaded straight from a URL

The big remaining selling point is reactivity: change a variable and the page follows. That solves a real problem in an app where a hundred things depend on each other. A business page is rarely that app. It shows records, lets you change one, and shows the result. The places that change are few, and you know which they are.

What is still missing

The browser has no table that sorts and pages. No tabs, no tree view, no chart. That is what a business page is made of, and it is the real reason teams reach for a framework and its component library.

So that is the gap I filled with @relax.js/components: tables, tree views, tabs, menus, dialogs, charts and meters for business pages. Not a framework. Each one is a plain custom element, and where the browser already has the part, it uses it: the table is a native <table>, menus use the Popover API, the dialog is a <dialog>.

A page with no framework

Save this as a file and open it. No npm install, no bundler:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Orders</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@relax.js/components@2.0.0/dist/theme.css">
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui; background: var(--surface-bg); color: var(--text-primary); }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <r-stat-tile label="Orders"></r-stat-tile>
    <button id="add">New order</button>

    <r-table page-size="10">
        <r-column field="number" sortable>Order</r-column>
        <r-column field="customer" sortable>Customer</r-column>
        <r-column field="total" sortable>Total</r-column>
    </r-table>

    <r-dialog id="new-order" heading="New order">
        <template>
            <form method="dialog">
                <label>Customer <input name="customer" required></label>
                <label>Total <input name="total" type="number" min="1" required></label>
                <button value="save">Save</button>
            </form>
        </template>
    </r-dialog>

    <script type="module">
        import 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@relax.js/components@2.0.0/+esm';

        const orders = [
            { number: 'SO-10001', customer: 'Fjällbo AB', total: 12400 },
            { number: 'SO-10002', customer: 'Kvarnen HB', total: 860 },
            { number: 'SO-10003', customer: 'Ekdahl & Son', total: 3150 },
        ];

        const table = document.querySelector('r-table');
        const tile = document.querySelector('r-stat-tile');
        const dialog = document.querySelector('#new-order');

        function show() {
            table.rows = orders;
            tile.setAttribute('value', orders.length);
        }

        dialog.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
            const form = new FormData(event.target);
            orders.push({
                number: `SO-${10001 + orders.length}`,
                customer: form.get('customer'),
                total: Number(form.get('total')),
            });
        });

        document.querySelector('#add').addEventListener('click', async () => {
            if (await dialog.open() === 'save') {
                show();
            }
        });

        show();
    </script>
</body>
</html>

You get a figure, a sortable table with grouped numbers and a pager, and a modal form. The form refuses to save without a customer or with a total below 1. That is the browser, not my code and not a library.

Now count what is not there. No state store. No virtual DOM. No compiler. No component tree to keep in your head. The data is an array, and show() is the whole rendering strategy: when the data changed, you tell the page.

"But who keeps the page in sync?"

You do, and that is the point. A framework re-renders when it decides something changed. When it gets it wrong, you debug the framework: why did this render twice, why did that not render at all.

Each component here redraws when you change its attributes, its properties or its content, and at no other time. There is no base class, no reactivity and no hidden scheduler. The lifecycle is the one on MDN. If the table shows old rows, you forgot to set rows, and a breakpoint on that line tells you so.

One rule trips everybody up: records go in a property, not an attribute. Attributes are strings, and a list in an attribute is a JSON string the component would have to parse and keep in sync with the property. So rows, columns and chart data are set from code, and scalars like page-size are attributes.

"But it needs Relax.js core"

Yes. The components have one peer dependency, @relax.js/core, and the jsDelivr link pulls it in for you.

That does not sneak a framework back in. A framework calls your code: it owns the lifecycle, the rendering and the state. Core is a set of libraries your code calls, and you use only the parts you need: typed form reading, routing, dependency injection, translations. The components themselves call it for four things:

  • translating the words they show (No data, Next)
  • reporting errors through one channel
  • formatting values
  • letting the router open a dialog, and only for a dialog you give a name

When the page above grows into an app with several pages, those same libraries give you a router and typed forms. You add them when you need them, not on day one.

Already on React or Vue?

Then the components still work, because every framework renders HTML and a custom element is HTML. The property rule above is all you need to know. React 19 assigns rows={orders} as a property. In Vue you write :rows.prop="orders" and tell the compiler that r- tags are not Vue components. Events are plain DOM events.

It is a way out as much as a way in. The table you use in React today is the same table in the page that replaces it.

The takeaway

Frameworks were the right answer to a browser that could not do much. The browser caught up. For a page that lists, edits and summarizes records, what is missing is the business components, not a framework. Add those as plain custom elements, write the updates yourself, and you have nothing left to migrate away from.

Next in the series: server-side paging and sorting, with one async function.
