title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19103v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.

title: InstructPro2: Natural Language and Biological Grounding Guided De Novo Protein Design
description:
arXiv:2610.19592v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The ability to generate proteins with desired functions is a central goal of computational biology. Although natural language can express diverse design objectives, existing protein generation methods often support only narrow tasks or make limited use of biological constraints. We develop InstructPro2 to translate natural-language design objectives into protein sequences while incorporating task-specific biological context. A text encoder captures the design instructions, while dedicated ligand and antigen encoders provide biological context to the sequence-generating decoder. For pretraining, we assemble InstructPro2Bench, comprising 205.7 million  pairs from UniProtKB. We subsequently adapt the model to ligand-binding protein and antibody design. On functional protein generation benchmarks, InstructPro2 outperforms Pinal, the strongest baseline, achieving a functional recovery F1 of 74.8 versus 62.2 and lowering global RMSD from 5.33A to 3.04A. For antibody design, the model obtains a DockQ score of 0.39, while ligand-binding protein design reaches a docking success rate of 72.6%. These findings highlight how integrating language-based instructions with biological conditioning can extend protein generation to distinct design settings.

title: Gray-Box Hallucination Detection in LLMs with Token Identities
description:
arXiv:2610.19996v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models often produce fluent but factually incorrect output. Gray-box detectors identify such hallucinations from the token-probability statistics emitted during generation, avoiding the need for white-box access to hidden states that frontier models do not provide. These detectors, however, typically rely only on probability-derived representations and ignore the identities of the candidate tokens. They can therefore observe how uncertain the model is, but not what it is uncertain about. Consequently, they cannot distinguish between a model that is torn between "big" and "small" and one that is torn between "big" and "huge" when the two pairs receive the same probability distribution.
  We introduce GURI (Gray-box Uncertainty Representations with Identity), a lightweight gray-box hallucination detector that combines candidate-token probabilities with per-token vector identifiers. This exposes which alternatives the model considered while preserving the accessibility and transferability of the gray-box setting. Across three open-weight models and three question-answering benchmarks, GURI increases mean test ROC-AUC from 72.09% to 79.09% over a probability-only baseline. On the closed-source GPT-4.1 model, mean ROC-AUC increases from 67.39% to 71.84%. Among the three open-weight models, GURI outperforms transferred probability-only baseline in 17 of 18 directed cross-model transfers without fine-tuning. For the three open-weight models, cross-dataset transfer between HotpotQA and TriviaQA with the model held fixed improves mean ROC-AUC over transferred LOS-Net by 3.76 points.

title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
description:
arXiv:2610.19021v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

title: Comprehensive Comparisons of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms in Autonomous Driving
description:
arXiv:2610.19429v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative reinforcement learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including: Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). The four methods are applied to the same AV decision-making problem at an unsignalized intersection and are compared in terms of optimality and safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. RCPI is the closest to a reference solution and has the most stable training process. However, it is the least data-efficient. D-DDPG reaches the second-smallest gap to a reference solution with the highest data efficiency, but has the least training stability. DQN is the most stable model-free method but has the highest collision rate. FVI achieves a lower collision rate than DQN, but is less data-efficient and less stable. Based on these results, we provide suggestions for selecting a method according to whether a model is available, the budget for training, and whether stable training is required.

title: ScopeShield: A Local AI Scope-Creep Detector for Freelancers
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

ScopeShield is a local AI assistant that helps freelancers identify scope creep before agreeing to additional client work.

Every freelancer knows the situation: a project starts with a clear brief, but new requests gradually appear. A client asks for another feature, extra revisions, content migration, or work that was never included in the original agreement.

Freelancers must decide whether the request is already covered, needs clarification, or should be discussed as additional work. Handling this repeatedly takes time and can create uncomfortable client conversations.

ScopeShield compares the original project brief with the client's new request and classifies it as:

Included — the request appears to fit the original scope.
Needs clarification — the brief or request is ambiguous.
Likely out of scope — the request appears to involve additional work.

It also provides supporting evidence, clarifying questions, recommended next steps, a change-request checklist, and a professional response the freelancer can adapt and send to the client.

The intended users are freelancers, independent consultants, designers, developers, and small agencies. A potential business model could be a paid desktop tool or a subscription for professionals who manage multiple client projects. I have not yet validated willingness to pay.

Demo

Demo

Code

https://github.com/Veerhan-glitch/ScopeShield

How I Built It

I built ScopeShield around Gemma 4 E2B, an open-weight model that runs locally through Ollama.

The application has three main parts:

Frontend: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript provide fields for the original brief, the new client request, and optional context.

Backend: A Python HTTP server validates the input and sends the comparison task to the local Ollama API.

AI analysis: Gemma evaluates the relationship between the original scope and the new request and returns structured JSON for the interface to display.

The prompt instructs the model to be fair to both parties, avoid inventing contract terms, and ask for clarification when the brief is ambiguous. It also tells the model not to provide legal advice or invent prices and timelines.

I tested the application locally and worked through issues involving JSON response encoding, model request handling, and structured-output parsing.

The goal is not to replace a freelancer's judgment. It is to make scope discussions easier to start and more consistent to handle.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation made it possible to build and experiment with an AI-powered tool without making a hosted AI API the centre of the application.

By using an open-weight model with local inference, I can develop and test ScopeShield on my own machine, inspect the application code, change the prompts, and control how client text is processed.

This is especially relevant because project briefs and client communications can contain confidential business information. With the local setup, text is sent to the Ollama service on the same machine rather than intentionally transmitted to a third-party hosted AI API. Users should still verify their configuration and avoid entering confidential information without authorization.

Open-weight models also make experimentation more accessible to independent developers who want to build practical products without depending entirely on a proprietary AI service.

For me, open innovation is about more than access to a model. It is the ability to adapt the technology to a specific problem, understand the complete workflow, and build a useful tool around it.

title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress
description:
arXiv:2610.14146v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon terminal benchmarks measure whether an agent can sustain progress through extended workflows with process rewards, not only whether its final state passes a binary check. We present Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0 (LHTB 2.0), an extension of Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench that preserves its 46 original tasks while correcting task and evaluation-infrastructure defects and extending 31 tasks. LHTB 2.0 contains 77 tasks across 13 domains and eight task types. The extended tasks are produced through a systematic reconstruction-task pipeline. We start from a working scientific or engineering artifact, then use a parameterized reference implementation to generate multiple scenarios, reveal six as behavioral evidence, hold out three for evaluation, and use dense progress ladders to reward partial progress while preventing memorization of public outputs. We also extend the evaluation horizon from 90 minutes to three hours and record verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes, enabling direct measurement of sustained progress within a run. Across 1,145 scored model-task runs from 15 frontier models, GPT-6-astra leads with dense mean reward 0.69 and 37 tasks at R at least 0.95, followed by GPT-5.6-sol with dense mean reward 0.67 and 32 tasks at the same threshold. On the 30 reconstruction tasks, binary verifier scores average 0.221, whereas dense ladder scores average 0.653, showing that outcome-only evaluation discards substantial intermediate progress. LHTB 2.0 provides a broader, hardened, and process-aware testbed for studying reliable agent execution over hours.

title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
description:
arXiv:2610.19762v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.

title: OmniPoser: Flexible Human Motion Recovery in the Wild with Masked Flow Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.19857v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recovering 3D human motion from sparse wearable sensors is challenging due to the inherent noise, occlusion, and instability of real-world tracking signals. Existing approaches are restricted to fixed sensor configurations and, when built on diffusion models, are computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment. We propose OmniPoser, a universal framework that recovers full-body SMPL motion from a flexible combination of heterogeneous inputs, such as 3D keypoints, sparse IMU rotations, head-mounted 6-DoF poses, or any subset thereof, within a single model. OmniPoser introduces a cross-modal masking mechanism paired with a Masked Conditioning Encoder, enabling one architecture to incorporate diverse sensor configurations through a masked design. A decoupled dual-stream generative backbone generates complete motion via Conditional Flow Matching, requiring only a single ODE integration step at inference. Across three settings and seven benchmarks, including in-the-wild Nymeria and Ego-Exo4D datasets, OmniPoser performs on par with state-of-the-art methods while running at over 700 FPS. The project page is available at https://jamesbridgewater51.github.io/omniposer-eccv/.

title: Why your Puppeteer PDF shows empty boxes for Arabic, Chinese and Hindi (and how to fix it)
description:
You generate an invoice PDF from HTML. On your laptop it looks perfect. In production, every Arabic, Chinese or Hindi character is an empty box (□□□). No error, no warning, a perfectly valid PDF. Usually a customer is the first to notice.

I ran into this enough times that I wrote down what is going on. Nothing is wrong with your code or with Puppeteer.

The problem

Here is a script that reproduces it. On a machine with suitable fonts the output looks fine. In a slim container you get boxes:

const puppeteer = require("puppeteer");

(async () => {
  const browser = await puppeteer.launch({ args: ["--no-sandbox"] });
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.setContent(
    '<html lang="ar" dir="rtl"><body>' +
    "<h1>فاتورة</h1><p>你好，世界 · नमस्ते</p>" +
    "</body></html>"
  );
  await page.pdf({ path: "invoice.pdf", format: "A4" });
  await browser.close();
})();

Why it happens

Chrome draws text with the fonts installed on the machine that runs it. Your laptop has hundreds. A minimal Docker image, a CI runner or a serverless function usually has a handful of Latin fonts and nothing else.

When no installed font contains a character, Chrome draws the "missing glyph" box and moves on. It does not throw. That is why the classic symptom is "works on my machine, broken in production".

The same is true for Playwright, Selenium or anything else that prints through headless Chrome: the fonts come from the machine, not from the library.

The fix: install Noto fonts in the image

Noto covers Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari (Hindi) and most other scripts. Chinese, Japanese and Korean live in a separate package. On a Debian-based image:

FROM node:20-bookworm-slim

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      fontconfig fonts-noto-core fonts-noto-cjk fonts-noto-color-emoji \
    && fc-cache -f \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Rebuild, then check that the system can see a font for each language:

fc-list :lang=ar family | head -3
fc-list :lang=zh-cn family | head -3
fc-list :lang=hi family | head -3

If one of these prints nothing, that language still has no font. Be aware that the CJK package makes the image noticeably bigger, so if size matters, install it only in the image that renders PDFs.

Fonts are not enough: set lang and dir

Two more details decide whether the result looks right, not just not-broken.

Right-to-left text. For Arabic and Hebrew, put dir="rtl" on the <html> tag (or the container) together with a matching lang. Chrome handles letter joining and mixed-direction text once a font exists, but without dir="rtl" alignment, punctuation and numbers can land in the wrong place.

Chinese vs Japanese. The same Han character can be drawn with a different regional shape depending on the language. Characters like 直 and 骨 are good examples. If the page has no lang, Chrome may pick a font you did not intend, and Chinese text can show up with Japanese shapes. Set lang="zh-CN", lang="zh-TW" or lang="ja", and for mixed documents put lang on the element that holds each piece.

:lang(zh-CN) { font-family: "Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif; }
:lang(zh-TW) { font-family: "Noto Sans CJK TC", sans-serif; }
:lang(ja)    { font-family: "Noto Sans CJK JP", sans-serif; }

Turkish has its own trap: the dotted and dotless İ / ı pair is only upper- and lower-cased correctly when the page declares lang="tr".

Test with a real document

A one-line test hides most problems. Real invoices mix scripts, digits, currency symbols and punctuation. Render one realistic PDF per language in your CI and actually look at it. That is the only way to catch this before a customer does.

If you would rather not maintain this

I built a small hosted API around exactly this problem, because I did not want to maintain Chromium and font packages in every project. You POST HTML and get a PDF back, with Noto fonts for 11 languages already installed (en, tr, es, fr, de, ru, ar, he, zh, ja, hi):

curl -X POST https://getprintoza.com/v1/convert \
  -H "x-api-key: YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"language": "ar", "html": "<h1>مرحبا</h1><p>فاتورة مبيعات</p>"}' \
  --output arabic.pdf

If your HTML contains characters that none of the fonts can draw, the PDF is still created and the response carries an X-Getprintoza-Warnings header listing them. It is a best-effort check, so still look at a few real documents. The free plan is 50 PDFs a month. It is new and run by one person, so I would genuinely like to hear which languages or edge cases still break for you.

The guides behind this article work with plain Puppeteer and Docker, no API needed:

  • Empty boxes in Puppeteer PDFs (Arabic, Chinese, Hindi)
  • Right-to-left layout for Arabic and Hebrew
  • Chinese and Japanese fonts and lang
  • Turkish characters ğ ş ı İ

title: Migrating On-Prem SQL Server to Azure SQL PaaS: How We Cut Infrastructure Costs by 25%
description:
At S&P Global Market Intelligence I helped migrate on-premise SQL Server databases to Azure SQL PaaS. Our team moved between 10 and 50 databases to Azure SQL Managed Instance. The headline result was a reduction in infrastructure costs of about 25%. The more important result was that the people using those databases barely noticed it happened.

Here's what I learned about doing a migration like that well.

1. Inventory before you plan

Before choosing a target, list everything that touches the database: ETL jobs, reports, linked servers, SQL Agent jobs, cross-database queries, CLR assemblies. PaaS options don't support every on-prem feature in the same way, and you want to find the gaps on a spreadsheet, not in production.

Microsoft's Data Migration Assistant and Azure Migrate help here, but they don't know about the Excel workbook someone in finance refreshes every Monday. Talk to users.

2. Pick the right PaaS flavour

Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance trade compatibility against simplicity. Managed Instance keeps more instance-level features (Agent jobs, cross-database queries), so it suits lift-and-shift. Single databases are simpler and can be cheaper, but may need refactoring. Decide per workload, not per estate. We went with Managed Instance, which kept most instance-level features in place and meant fewer changes to existing code.

3. Right-size, don't copy

Most of the savings came from not paying for capacity we didn't use. On-prem servers are sized for peak load plus growth plus fear. In the cloud you can measure actual usage and scale. Look at real CPU, memory and IO over several weeks before choosing service tiers.

4. Migrate in waves

Start with low-risk databases: development, reporting copies, internal tools. Each wave teaches you something about networking, permissions or performance that makes the next wave smoother.

5. Test the boring things

Performance gets attention. In our migration, the real problems came from elsewhere:

  • Connection strings hard-coded in old applications and reports
  • SSIS packages and SQL Agent jobs that needed reworking to run against Azure
  • Jobs that relied on local file paths on the old servers

Also worth checking: time zone and collation differences, firewall rules and private endpoints.

6. Define "done" with the users

A migration isn't finished when the data moves. It's finished when every report, job and application works as before and the old servers are switched off. Agree that checklist with stakeholders up front.

The takeaway

Cloud migration savings come mostly from right-sizing and retiring infrastructure. Keeping users happy comes from inventory, testing and communication. Neither is glamorous, and both matter more than the migration tooling.

title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
description:
arXiv:2610.19704v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.

title: Ito: Build Terminal UIs in Lua!
description:
Architecture of Ito: Bridging Lua and Terminal Graphics

The landscape of terminal user interface (TUI) development has been dominated by abstractions that favor either high-level runtime environments (Node.js) or systems-level paradigms (Rust/C++). While Ratatui provides a robust immediate-mode rendering loop for Rust developers, the barrier to entry for rapid prototyping often remains high due to the necessity of compilation steps and strict type safety. Ito represents a departure from this pattern, shifting the TUI development lifecycle into the Lua runtime while maintaining high-performance rendering via a Rust-based core.

The Problem of Execution Contexts

In typical TUI libraries, the state management and rendering logic are bound to the host language’s threading model and memory management. To build a library that feels like a natural extension of a Neovim-centric workflow, one must address the impedance mismatch between a high-level scripting language and the raw byte-stream manipulation required for terminal escape sequences.

Ito addresses this by utilizing a "Core-Provider" architecture. The core is an engine written in Rust, which acts as the terminal driver, managing the virtual buffer, input event polling, and ANSI sequence serialization. Lua serves as the domain-specific language (DSL) for component orchestration, layout calculation, and style definition.

The Core Rendering Pipeline

At the heart of Ito is a custom canvas implementation. Unlike traditional terminal libraries that rely on existing wrappers (like ncurses or termion), Ito implements a double-buffered grid system. This allows for differential updates: rather than redrawing the entire screen on every frame, the engine calculates the diff between the back buffer and the front buffer, emitting only the minimal set of ANSI escape codes required to reconcile the state.

// Simplified representation of the Ito buffer reconcile logic
impl Buffer {
    pub fn diff(&self, previous: &Buffer) -> Vec<Operation> {
        let mut ops = Vec::new();
        for (y, row) in self.cells.iter().enumerate() {
            for (x, cell) in row.iter().enumerate() {
                if cell != &previous.cells[y][x] {
                    ops.push(Operation::MoveCursor(x as u16, y as u16));
                    ops.push(Operation::Write(cell.content.clone()));
                }
            }
        }
        ops
    }
}

By offloading this logic to Rust, Ito maintains a sub-millisecond frame time, which is critical for smooth animations and high-frequency UI updates. The Lua runtime interacts with this system through a strictly defined foreign function interface (FFI), ensuring that overhead remains negligible.

The Lua Integration Layer

The design philosophy of Ito is to provide minimal, composable primitives. In Lua, this manifests as a declarative tree structure. Every element in Ito is a node, and layouts are handled by hierarchical constraints.

Consider the implementation of a basic panel structure in Lua:

local ito = require("ito")

local root = ito.container({
    layout = "vertical",
    children = {
        ito.text("System Monitor", { color = "blue", bold = true }),
        ito.progress({ value = 0.75, width = "100%" }),
        ito.button("Restart", { on_click = function() print("clicked") end })
    }
})

ito.render(root)

The underlying bridge translates these Lua tables into the Rust internal component tree. By utilizing LuaJIT, the performance penalty is essentially non-existent for the majority of UI tasks, as the heavy lifting of terminal output is performed in the compiled binary.

Decoupling Logic from Display: The Canvas Abstraction

One of the more unique engineering choices in Ito is the separation of the TUI library from the physical terminal adaptor. During development, it became evident that testing UI layouts required a more robust debugging mechanism than standard terminal output.

We developed a custom canvas implementation that renders the TUI logic into an HTML5 Canvas via WebAssembly. This was achieved by abstracting the output layer:

  1. Terminal Adaptor: Standard ANSI escape sequence emission.
  2. Canvas Adaptor: Converts the internal grid buffer into WebGL-accelerated drawing commands for a browser context.

This allows developers to experiment with complex layouts in the browser at uji.sh/ito before deploying them to the local terminal environment. This portability ensures that "ricing" a UI becomes a visual, iterative process rather than a cycle of recompilation and terminal toggling.

Handling Input Events

Input management in TUIs is notoriously difficult due to terminal signal handling (SIGINT, SIGWINCH). Ito uses a non-blocking poll loop in Rust that captures input events and pushes them into a thread-safe MPSC (multi-producer, single-consumer) channel.

The Lua runtime monitors this channel periodically. When an input event (e.g., Key(Enter)) is received, Ito invokes the registered callback within the Lua VM context:

ito.on_event("key", function(key)
    if key == "q" then
        ito.quit()
    end
end)

This event-driven model keeps the main UI thread responsive, even when the Lua script is performing heavy data processing or waiting on external IO.

Memory Safety and GC Interaction

Interfacing Lua with Rust presents specific challenges regarding garbage collection. If a Lua object is passed to Rust, there is a risk that the Lua GC might collect it while the Rust side still maintains a pointer to it.

To mitigate this, Ito employs a handle-based system. When a component is created in Lua, Rust returns an integer identifier (handle). The Rust core manages the actual component lifecycle in a stable memory segment, while Lua only maintains the identifier. When the component is garbage collected in Lua, it sends a finalizer event to the Rust side to safely deallocate the associated memory.

Optimization and Future Trajectories

The current version of Ito is optimized for low-latency feedback. Future development is focused on three areas:

  1. Reactive State Binding: Implementing a Lua-side observable pattern that automatically triggers re-renders when data structures change, reducing the boilerplate required for state management.
  2. Extended ANSI Support: Moving beyond basic 16-color support toward full TrueColor (24-bit) implementation and under-the-hood optimization for terminal multiplexers like tmux.
  3. WebAssembly Tooling: Enhancing the llms.txt integration to ensure that AI coding assistants can generate valid Ito layouts by understanding the hierarchical constraints and component API of the library.

Conclusion

The creation of Ito was born from the realization that existing TUI frameworks often impose too much structure at the expense of flexibility. By decoupling the performance-critical rendering engine from the stylistic configuration layer, we have enabled a development loop that feels as fluid as configuring a Neovim plugin. Whether you are building a dashboard, a terminal-based system monitoring tool, or an experimental interface, the ability to control the terminal environment with pure Lua offers a degree of customization previously reserved for lower-level languages.

For those interested in leveraging professional engineering support to integrate these high-performance interface patterns into your own infrastructure, please visit https://www.mgatc.com for consulting services.

Originally published in Spanish at www.mgatc.com/blog/ito-build-terminal-uis-in-lua/

title: Sentry or Error Tracking API — Node.js SaaS Checkout Evidence
description:
A small Node.js commerce SaaS does not automatically need Sentry-sized machinery. Start with a simple error-tracking API when the job is narrow: capture exceptions, inspect grouped issues and their event payloads, search the evidence, then resolve a group after the fix ships. Choose Sentry when notification routing, distributed trace exploration, source maps, Session Replay, or polished frontend debugging are actual acceptance criteria.

TL;DR: For one checkout API, optimize for evidence you can reconstruct, not the largest feature list. Infrai is a reasonable lightweight choice when a plain REST boundary and fast capability discovery matter more than built-in alert delivery. It is not a substitute for a full observability suite.

The useful question is not "which tool records errors?" It is "after a customer says payment failed, can we find the right failure, inspect its payload, connect it to the request, and close the group without drowning in repeats?"

Noise wins otherwise.

Should a Node.js SaaS use Sentry or a simple error-tracking API?

The concrete constraint is signal quality versus noise. A raw stream of exceptions is noisy. A count without event detail is quiet but nearly useless. For an MVP, the productive middle is grouped issues plus the underlying event payload: the group shows recurrence, while the event preserves the evidence needed to understand one customer's failure. Search narrows the set. Resolve records that a shipped fix has dealt with the group.

I use a four-part acceptance test:

  1. Can the app capture the exception at the server boundary?
  2. Can an operator inspect grouped issues and individual event payloads?
  3. Can the operator search for the relevant failure without exporting everything?
  4. Can the group be resolved after the fix ships?

This is deliberately small. It matches the incident, not an imagined platform team. It also exposes a dangerous gap: a captured event is not an alert. If nobody is looking, perfect evidence can still produce a late response.

For this loop, I recommend that a small team try Infrai for exception capture and triage when it wants a self-describing REST API instead of another product SDK. Its public discovery surface returns request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples without an API key. That removes a specific integration cost: the client can read one capability contract before adding dependencies or guessing payload fields. A second benefit is consolidation; its broader surface spans 295 routes in 20 modules behind one key, so a team already using that boundary avoids another credential and SDK surface.

Keep the recommendation in its lane. These are real limitations and a deliberate trade-off: Infrai has no built-in notification routing, threshold rules, phone or SMS escalation, or webhook delivery for errors. On-call needs a custom poller over error list or search results. There is no distributed trace query view or span tree either; trace and span identifiers can correlate records, but they do not create a root-cause workflow across services. Choose a specialist instead when those workflows are requirements.

The smallest integration starts with discovery

I dislike configuration that exists only because documentation and runtime drift apart. Before sending production evidence, inspect the live capability contract. This TypeScript script needs Node.js 20 or later, makes one unauthenticated request, checks the status, and prints the schema and supplied examples for error capture.

type DiscoveryCapability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: unknown;
  [key: string]: unknown;
};

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/errors.capture",
    { method: "GET" },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  const capability = (await response.json()) as DiscoveryCapability;
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    id: capability.id,
    method: capability.method,
    path: capability.path,
    available: capability.available,
    params: capability.params,
    examples: capability.examples,
  }, null, 2));
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Run it before writing the capture call. The returned path is authoritative, and the request schema prevents a subtle kind of glue-code debt: locally invented fields that happen to compile. Every documented capability has runnable examples across 10 languages, including TypeScript. Use the returned example, supply Authorization: Bearer from process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY, preserve its explicit HTTP method, and surface non-2xx bodies. Never hardcode an ifr_... key.

This is time-to-first-useful-result in a form that needs no invented latency benchmark: one public read reveals the live contract. No package selection. No SDK initialization.

That is enough.

The production capture path is /v1/errors/capture. I am not reproducing a request body because the live discovery schema is the contract, and hand-copying fields into an article makes the article another stale SDK.

Where do the specialist tools win?

Sentry is the stronger choice when Sentry-level alerting and frontend ergonomics are requirements. It is also the sensible direction when source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or Session Replay must sit beside exception triage. A simple capture-and-query API does not supply those experiences.

Rollbar and Bugsnag belong in the specialist shortlist: evaluate them when the purchase is an error-tracking workflow rather than a small REST primitive. Require each candidate to demonstrate the same checkout reconstruction with grouping, search, event detail, resolution, notification delivery, and the frontend evidence your stack needs. Do not award points for a dashboard that cannot answer the incident question. Their current product behavior should be verified directly during the trial; this comparison does not assume unverified parity.

Datadog, Grafana, and Better Stack are also real alternatives when the decision expands beyond exception triage into a broader observability operating surface. That is a different buy. Test them against the same evidence checklist, then account for the extra setup, credentials, and product surface instead of assuming more coverage always creates a better MVP signal.

OpenTelemetry solves a different layer. Its logs model explains how trace and span identifiers can correlate log records, useful when evidence already moves through an instrumentation pipeline. It does not turn stored identifiers into a distributed trace query interface. Collection and investigation are separate jobs.

Healthchecks addresses silence. Error capture sees code that ran and failed. It cannot report that a scheduled order-reconciliation task never ran. There is no synthetic check or heartbeat monitor here, so pair the tracker with a Healthchecks-style tool when "the job did not execute" is an incident you must catch.

Option Choose it when Boundary to test
Infrai One API needs capture, grouping, event inspection, search, and resolve through REST Alerts require polling; no trace tree, source maps, replay, or heartbeats
Sentry Alerting and frontend debugging ergonomics are required More workflow than a narrow backend MVP may need
Rollbar A specialist error-tracking product is the intended operating surface Prove checkout reconstruction and notifications in a trial
Bugsnag A specialist workflow is preferable to a generic REST boundary Verify required grouping, evidence, and frontend behavior directly
Datadog The evaluation covers a broader observability operating surface Measure the setup and product surface against the narrow incident job
Grafana The team is evaluating a broader observability stack Confirm that the chosen components deliver the required triage loop
Better Stack A broader hosted operations workflow is under evaluation Prove the same evidence and notification requirements in a trial
OpenTelemetry Existing telemetry needs portable correlation concepts Instrumentation is not a hosted triage workflow
Healthchecks Missing scheduled work must raise a signal Complements exception capture rather than replacing it

The table is not a scorecard. It is a routing rule. A team that needs three absent workflows should stop building glue and pick the specialist.

What I would change at scale

First, assign alert ownership. A poller can query errors and forward a notification, but the team then owns cadence, deduplication, delivery retries, and escalation. That is acceptable for a low-volume MVP only when someone explicitly owns it. Once missed alerts carry material customer impact, built-in routing belongs in the product requirement.

Second, separate debugging data from sensitive customer data. Checkout payloads tempt developers to capture everything. Don't. OWASP's logging guidance is the useful constraint: exclude or mask sensitive material, protect logs against tampering and unauthorized access, and decide retention intentionally. Infrai logs have no per-user deletion API, bulk export, or subscription interface; retention and cold storage have no configuration entry point. Those boundaries matter for deletion and portability obligations.

Third, reassess topology. One small Node.js service can often reconstruct an incident from grouped errors and event detail. Several services introduce causal gaps. Trace and span IDs help correlate records, but without distributed trace queries and a span tree, the operator still assembles the path manually. At that point a full observability suite earns its complexity.

There are smaller edges too. Feature flags have no change audit log, evaluation statistics, or parent-child dependencies; deletion has no recycle bin, and clients poll. Those facts do not disqualify a narrow error tracker. They do disqualify treating one API as an unlimited operations platform.

My cutoff is simple: use the lightweight route while incident reconstruction is a capture-search-inspect-resolve loop for one service. Move to a specialist when notification delivery, browser evidence, scheduled-job silence, compliance operations, or cross-service causality becomes part of the incident definition.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai error grouping, search, and resolve guide and verify the live schema before integrating.

References

  • OpenTelemetry logs signal concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • Sentry Node.js documentation: https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/guides/node/
  • Datadog Error Tracking documentation: https://docs.datadoghq.com/error_tracking/
  • Grafana application observability documentation: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/monitor-applications/application-observability/
  • Better Stack errors documentation: https://betterstack.com/docs/errors/

title: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports the Cyber Risk Institute profile version 2.2
description:
AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports automated security checks that align with the Cyber Risk Institute (CRI) profile. The CRI Profile is a cybersecurity framework developed by the Cyber Risk Institute, a non-profit coalition of financial institutions and trade associations. The framework harmonizes cybersecurity and regulatory expectations that apply to the financial services sector into a common set of requirements, so that an organization can assess itself once and report against multiple regulations. AWS Security Hub CSPM provides 404 controls that support a subset of CRI Profile v2.2 requirements; the controls don't support requirements that require manual checks.

The new standard is now available in all AWS Regions where Security Hub CSPM is currently available, including the AWS GovCloud (US) and the China Regions. To quickly enable the standard across your AWS environment, we recommend that you use Security Hub central configuration. With this approach, you can enable the standard in all or only some of your organization's accounts and across all AWS Regions that are linked to Security Hub with a single action.

To learn more, see CRI Profile v2.2 in the AWS Security Hub CSPM user guide. To receive notifications about new Security Hub CSPM features and controls subscribe to the Security Hub SNS topic. You can also try Security Hub CSPM at no cost for 30 days with the AWS Free Tier offering.

title: Beyond Time Induction: Structured Conditional Neural Solvers for Parametric Stochastic-Volatility Pricing
description:
arXiv:2610.19254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks provide a flexible framework for learning parametric PDE solution families without labeled data, yet preserving accurate derivatives across heterogeneous regimes remains challenging. Structured neural solvers offer compact representations, but restrictive conditional parameterizations can limit adaptation across the solution family. We introduce BeTINN, a structured conditional architecture extending time-induced modulation through multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a joint residual pathway. We evaluate BeTINN on the Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, a demanding parametric problem with mixed derivatives and economically relevant first- and second-order sensitivities. BeTINN improves joint accuracy across normalized option value and key sensitivity metrics relative to our baselines. Controlled ablations characterize the roles of its architectural components. We further find that validation physics loss is informative but does not fully determine differential fidelity, and that accurate solution values can coexist with localized derivative errors. These results support structured conditional adaptation and motivate derivative-aware evaluation when sensitivities are downstream quantities of interest.

title: Your Test Suite Is Growing. But Is It Getting Better?
description:
When a project starts, maintaining automated tests usually feels manageable.

There are a few test cases, execution is quick, and when something fails, finding the reason isn't too difficult.

But as the application grows, things start to change.

More features mean more tests. More tests mean longer execution times. And as the UI and application behaviour change, some existing tests need regular maintenance.

Before long, the team might be dealing with hundreds of tests, repeated failures, and a test suite that takes much longer to run than it used to.

The problem isn't that the test suite is growing. It's whether the team can still trust it.

Imagine running 600 tests and getting 30 failures.

Some might be real bugs. Others could be broken locators, outdated test data, environment issues, or flaky tests.

Now the team has another problem: figuring out which failures actually need attention.

This is something I've been exploring at X360 AI Tech.

Instead of looking at test results as just pass or fail, we're interested in how execution details can help make failures easier to investigate. Test steps, assertions, browser actions, network activity, logs, screenshots, and execution videos can provide useful context about what happened.

The goal isn't simply to add more tests or make every failure disappear.

It's to help the team understand what happened during execution and decide what needs attention.

I also think growing test suites need regular review.

Some tests protect critical business flows and should remain part of the regression suite. Others may be redundant, unstable, or no longer relevant after application changes.

More tests don't automatically mean better coverage. And better coverage doesn't automatically mean better feedback.

For me, a healthy test suite is one that covers important behaviour, runs reliably, and helps developers understand problems without spending hours investigating every failure.

As a test suite grows, maintaining trust in the results becomes just as important as adding new tests.

I'm curious how other teams handle this.

When your test suite starts getting bigger and slower, what do you focus on first: reducing execution time, fixing flaky tests, or removing tests that no longer add much value?

title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
description:
arXiv:2610.14115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.

title: OneLA: Learning Many Worlds from Latent Actions
description:
arXiv:2610.20160v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning world models across diverse domains calls for a unified control space, yet ac- tion interfaces vary across domains and action annotations are often scarce. Latent ac- tions learned directly from videos offer a promising way to establish such a space without explicit action supervision. However, learning shared latent actions across domains re- mains challenging, as variations in appearance, embodiment, and dynamics can entangle domain-specific visual cues with transferable transition structure. To this end, we intro- duce OneLA, a simple framework that learns continuous latent actions through a shared orthogonal dictionary and a common predictive objective, without task-specific designs or cross-domain alignment losses during latent action pretraining. These latent actions pro- vide a shared conditioning interface for world models, with lightweight adapters mapping native control commands into the same space. Conditioned on latent actions and the cur- rent visual state, the world model predicts context-dependent transitions for controllable rollout. OneLA improves action readout across domains and reduces action cycle-transfer rotation error by 24.8% over the strongest evaluated baseline. A joint-training comparison further shows a 20.5% improvement in Human Preference Score v3 (HPSv3) for real- scene generation. These results suggest a path toward general-purpose world models that learn from diverse videos and support flexible control through latent action space.

title: Using Evidence-Centered Design to Guide Prompt Engineering in Measurement: An Illustration with Automated Essay Scoring
description:
arXiv:2610.15231v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used in educational settings for tasks such as item generation, automated scoring, and feedback delivery. The quality of these outputs depends not only on the AI model but also on how users construct the prompts that guide model behaviors. Current prompt engineering practices are largely ad hoc, relying on trial and error rather than principled design. This lack of structure introduces validity threats including construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and limited reproducibility. We propose that Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), a framework in educational measurement for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, can serve as a principled foundation for prompt engineering in educational applications. We map the three core ECD models, the student model, the evidence model, and the task model, onto the components of educational prompt design, and describe a workflow for ECD-based prompt engineering. We derive five design principles from this mapping and present an empirical study contrasting ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines on an automated scoring task. Our empirical study demonstrates the usefulness of this framework on automated scoring. Results suggest that treating prompting as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.

title: Does the Linguistic Register of Thinking Matter? Wenyan as a Compact Reasoning Register for Chinese LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.19741v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visible reasoning traces of Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are typically written in modern vernacular Chinese, which may be verbose under limited decoding budgets. We ask whether the linguistic register of reasoning can be used to improve efficiency. We propose Wenyan Thinking, which emits intermediate reasoning in Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while retaining a short direct-answer output. Starting from modern-Chinese reasoning traces, we rewrite only the reasoning field into wenyan and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on the rewritten supervision. To distinguish register shift from generic compression, we construct a compact modern-Chinese control using the same source data, teacher family, base model, and SFT recipe. Across budget-sensitive evaluations on MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH, CEVAL, and AGIEval-CN, Wenyan Thinking substantially reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding. Compact rewriting explains much of the efficiency gain, while wenyan consistently outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive across the additional benchmarks. These results identify linguistic register as a practical design axis for efficient visible reasoning in Chinese LLMs.

title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.19623v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.

title: Ledger errors should name the invariant they protect
description:
A payout worker catches an exception from the ledger and has to decide, with no human in the loop, whether to retry the request, park it, or escalate. If the refusal says "invalid entry", it cannot decide any of those, so the request goes to a dead-letter queue and the string goes to the logs, where a person reads it an hour later and learns exactly as little. A refusal is part of a ledger's interface, and in most systems it is the one part nobody designed.

I have been building payment and custodial systems since 2018, and the error taxonomy is reliably the piece written last and read most. The balance code gets reviewed twice. The exception that stops a write from happening gets a string literal and a shrug. That is backwards: the write that succeeds is self-documenting, since there is an entry you can read. The write that was refused leaves nothing behind except whatever the message said.

Two readers, one string

The message has two audiences with incompatible requirements. The machine wants something narrow and stable: a key it can branch on, which does not move when someone improves the wording. The human wants the opposite, enough context to know whether money is at risk, and whether refusing was the right call.

"Insufficient funds" serves the machine and leaves the human guessing what the ledger was protecting. "The customer's available balance would have gone below zero, so the write was refused" serves the human and is a terrible thing to pattern-match. The usual compromise is a short code plus a wiki page that explains it, and the wiki page is stale within two quarters because nothing fails when it drifts.

In ledger-core (https://github.com/polycratia/ledger-core) I split it differently. The exception class is the branch key. The promise it protects is a class attribute on that class. The message is the two of them joined at raise time, and the bare reason stays reachable on its own.

class InvariantViolated(ValueError):
    """A refused write, carrying the promise that refused it."""

    protects: ClassVar[str] = "a rule of the ledger"

    def __init__(self, detail: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"{detail} \u2014 protects: {self.protects}")
        self.detail = detail


class InsufficientFunds(InvariantViolated):
    """Raised when a reservation or a movement takes more than is available."""

    protects: ClassVar[str] = (
        "available balances stay at or above zero, so the same funds are never spent twice"
    )

There are three of these: UnbalancedEntry, InsufficientFunds, ClosedAccount. Each overrides protects with one sentence written from the ledger's point of view, not the caller's. What reaches a log line is the specific reason and the general promise, separated by an em dash so the two halves stay legible as two halves. What reaches code is the class, plus .detail holding the reason without the promise appended.

That last part matters more than it looks. The promise sentence is editorial copy. Someone will reword it, because it is the sort of thing that gets reworded in review. If callers are storing the full message as a rejection reason on a request row, every rewording changes historical data and any accumulated string matching. .detail is the half that does not carry the editorial text, so it is the half you persist and forward.

Enforced at the one place it can be broken

A promise is only worth printing if it holds where the caller forgot to check. So each of the three is enforced at the single point where it could be violated, and nowhere else pretends to cover it.

Journal.append asks only whether an entry balances. It is not a funds check and does not imply one. The funds check lives in Holds.spend, which computes -effect_on(entry, account), compares that against available(), raises InsufficientFunds if it exceeds it, and only then appends. Closure is enforced where a closed account can actually be touched: in Account._posting, and in Hold.__post_init__.

    def _posting(self, amount: MoneyLike, side: Side) -> Posting:
        if self.closed_at is not None:
            raise ClosedAccount(
                f"account {self.account_id} was closed at {self.closed_at}, "
                f"{side.value} of {amount} is refused"
            )

Putting it there has a consequence worth stating plainly: an Entry.transfer against a closed account raises before the journal appears anywhere in the call stack. The refusal happens while the write is still a value. Same for a one-sided movement: an unbalanced entry never becomes an object, so it cannot be discovered later by something reading the journal. And closing an account refuses new movement without erasing anything, since a closed account's balance still folds from the entries it already has.

Branch on the class, store the detail

With the taxonomy on the classes, the worker's decision is a try block and nothing else:

from ledger_core import ClosedAccount, InsufficientFunds


def settle(holds, entry, account, requests):
    try:
        holds.spend(entry, account=account)
    except InsufficientFunds as refused:
        requests.park(entry.entry_id, reason=refused.detail)
        return "retry_after_funding"
    except ClosedAccount as refused:
        requests.escalate(entry.entry_id, reason=refused.detail, alert=str(refused))
        return "manual"
    return "settled"

The two branches differ because the underlying facts differ. InsufficientFunds is a statement about a quantity that changes: a deposit lands and the same instruction succeeds, so retrying is meaningful. ClosedAccount is a statement about a terminal state, so retrying is guaranteed waste and a human needs to look. The alert carries str(refused), which includes the promise, because the person being woken up has not read this module. The parked row carries refused.detail, because repeating the same promise sentence across ten thousand rows is noise.

Not every refusal is an invariant

The holds module also raises CaptureMismatch, DuplicateHold, HoldNotOpen and UnknownHold. None of them subclass InvariantViolated, and that is deliberate.

Holds.capture skips the funds check entirely: the funds were reserved when the hold was placed, and the reservation is what the balance has been standing behind since. What capture checks is that the amount taken equals hold.amount.amount, raising CaptureMismatch if it does not. That is not a money problem. It is the caller's instruction disagreeing with the caller's own reservation, and collapsing it into InsufficientFunds would make the retry decision wrong: one is worth re-reading a balance for, the other will fail identically forever.

So the dividing question is this: does this refusal protect a promise the ledger makes to everyone, or does it report that the instruction disagrees with state the caller named? The first gets a protects sentence. The second gets a precise message and a plain exception type. That is the only taxonomy rule I have found that keeps working when a new error case shows up six months later.

The test that keeps it honest

Because protects has a default, a subclass that forgets to override it inherits "a rule of the ledger", which is worse than silence, since it looks like a promise and says nothing. One parametrised test closes that:

@pytest.mark.parametrize("violation", [UnbalancedEntry, InsufficientFunds, ClosedAccount])
def test_every_violation_names_what_it_protects(violation: type[InvariantViolated]) -> None:
    assert issubclass(violation, InvariantViolated)
    assert violation.protects != InvariantViolated.protects
    assert violation.protects in str(violation("refused"))

It asserts the override exists and that the sentence actually reaches the message. Since protects is a class attribute, it is readable without raising anything, which means documentation can be generated from the classes rather than maintained beside them.

What I would do differently

First, the default. A ClassVar default makes the base class convenient and makes forgetting silent, and a test is a weaker guard than a definition-time failure. I would check the override in __init_subclass__ so a new invariant without a promise fails at import rather than in CI.

Second, I would write down, in the base class docstring, that the message is for humans and the class is for code. Without that sentence, someone eventually matches on the full string, and then the promise sentence is load-bearing text that cannot be edited.

Third, the gap a refusal cannot close. Holds.place and Holds.spend read available() and then write, as two steps, and the Storage protocol has no transaction, so the atomic pair is left to the backend. InsufficientFunds is then a true statement about what available() was a moment before the append, not a guarantee about what it was during it. Where more than one writer posts to one account, making that pair a single step belongs to the store underneath. A message that names its invariant is honest about the rule, and it cannot be honest about a race the layer below allows. That belongs in the exception's own docstring, next to the promise, so nobody reads the promise as stronger than it is.

A ledger earns trust by what it refuses, and a refusal nobody can act on is barely better than a write nobody checked. Making the promise a class attribute and putting it in the message costs about four lines in one module. What you get for that is that the retry logic and the person on call are reading the same refusal and reaching the same conclusion about it.

Originally published on polycratia.com — where I write about payment systems, crypto rails and marketplace backends.

title: Verifier-Grounded Agentic RL for Provably Correct Code
description:
arXiv:2610.19298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.

title: Unlocking Go: A Deep Dive into the Language that Powers Modern Cloud Apps
description:
Introduction

If you’ve been watching the cloud-native wave for the past few years, you’ve probably heard the name Go (or Golang) tossed around a lot. From Docker and Kubernetes to HashiCorp’s suite of tools, Go has become the lingua franca of infrastructure software. But what makes Go so compelling for developers building high‑performance, maintainable services? In this post we’ll explore Go’s core philosophy, walk through practical code examples, and highlight best‑practices that will help you write production‑grade Go code.

Why Go?

Go was created at Google in 2007 by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson. Their goal was simple: a language that feels like a scripting language but compiles to fast, native binaries. The design principles are:

  • Simplicity – a small standard library, minimal syntax, and a single, opinionated way to do things.
  • Concurrency as a first‑class citizen – goroutines and channels provide lightweight parallelism.
  • Fast compilation – sub‑second build times keep the feedback loop tight.
  • Static typing with type inference – catch bugs early while keeping code readable.

These goals translate into tangible benefits for cloud‑native development: quick iteration, low overhead binaries, and reliable concurrency.

Getting Started: Hello, World! 

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, World!")
}

Compile with go build -o hello . and run ./hello. The binary is self‑contained – no runtime dependencies needed.

Structuring a Go Project

A typical Go module looks like this:

myapp/
├─ go.mod          # module definition
├─ cmd/            # entry points (main packages)
│   └─ server/main.go
├─ internal/       # private packages
│   └─ handler/
│       └─ handler.go
└─ pkg/            # reusable libraries (optional)
    └─ config/
        └─ config.go
  • go.mod declares the module path and dependencies. Run go mod init github.com/yourname/myapp to create it.
  • Keep business logic inside internal/ – this prevents other modules from importing it unintentionally.
  • Use cmd/ for the executable(s) that wire everything together.

Concurrency Made Easy: Goroutines & Channels

Go’s concurrency model is built around goroutines (lightweight threads) and channels (typed pipes). Here’s a classic example that fetches URLs concurrently:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io/ioutil"
    "net/http"
    "sync"
)

func fetch(url string, wg *sync.WaitGroup, ch chan<- string) {
    defer wg.Done()
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        ch <- fmt.Sprintf("%s: error %v", url, err)
        return
    }
    body, _ := ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    ch <- fmt.Sprintf("%s: %d bytes", url, len(body))
}

func main() {
    urls := []string{"https://golang.org", "https://dev.to", "https://github.com"}
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    ch := make(chan string, len(urls))

    for _, u := range urls {
        wg.Add(1)
        go fetch(u, &wg, ch)
    }
    wg.Wait()
    close(ch)

    for result := range ch {
        fmt.Println(result)
    }
}

Key takeaways:

  • go fetch(...) launches a goroutine instantly.
  • sync.WaitGroup ensures the main routine waits for all workers.
  • The buffered channel collects results without blocking the workers.

Error Handling – The Go Way

Go eschews exceptions; errors are explicit values. This makes failure paths clear and testable.

func readFile(path string) ([]byte, error) {
    data, err := os.ReadFile(path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("read %s: %w", path, err)
    }
    return data, nil
}

func main() {
    if _, err := readFile("/nonexistent"); err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Fatal error: %v", err)
    }
}
  • Wrap errors with %w to retain the original cause – errors.Is and errors.As can later inspect it.
  • Use log.Fatalf for unrecoverable errors in simple tools; in libraries, return the error up the stack.

Testing & Benchmarking

Go ships with a built‑in testing framework. A typical test file ends with _test.go:

package math

import "testing"

func Add(a, b int) int { return a + b }

func TestAdd(t *testing.T) {
    got := Add(2, 3)
    if got != 5 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 5, got %d", got)
    }
}

func BenchmarkAdd(b *testing.B) {
    for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
        Add(i, i)
    }
}

Run go test -v ./... for verbose output, and go test -bench=. ./... to execute benchmarks. The testing package also supports table‑driven tests, subtests, and coverage reporting (go test -cover).

Dependency Management with Modules

Since Go 1.11, modules are the default. Add a third‑party library with:

go get github.com/spf13/viper@v1.15.0

The go.mod file will now contain:

module github.com/yourname/myapp

go 1.22

require (
    github.com/spf13/viper v1.15.0 // indirect
)

Run go mod tidy to prune unused dependencies and ensure reproducible builds.

Deploying Go Binaries – From Docker to Serverless

Because Go produces static binaries, containerization is straightforward:

FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o server ./cmd/server

FROM alpine:latest
COPY --from=builder /app/server /usr/local/bin/server
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["server"]

The final image is only ~15 MB. For serverless platforms like AWS Lambda, use the aws-lambda-go library and compile with GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64.

Best Practices Checklist

✅ Practice
✅ Keep functions small (ideally < 30 lines)
✅ Prefer composition over inheritance – use interfaces
✅ Use context for cancellation & deadlines
✅ Run go vet, staticcheck, and golint in CI
✅ Document exported symbols with GoDoc comments
✅ Avoid global variables – inject dependencies
✅ Write table‑driven tests for edge cases

Conclusion

Go’s blend of simplicity, performance, and first‑class concurrency makes it a natural fit for modern cloud‑native services. By embracing Go’s idioms – explicit error handling, lightweight goroutines, and a strong standard library – you can ship reliable binaries fast and keep your codebase maintainable.

Ready to give Go a spin? Clone the starter repo, run go test ./..., and watch your first binary fire up in seconds. Happy coding!
