title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
description:
arXiv:2610.14180v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges. Our main finding is that an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it is given enough turns. The benchmark's published limit on agent messages is a confound: a task that exhausts the limit scores zero on every checkpoint, including those it had already passed, so results at that limit partly measure which models finish in time. At the published limit the leading open-weight and closed models cannot be distinguished. With the limit relaxed, the models it was truncating recover, and the highest rewards belong to open-weight models. Among the leading models, price is a poor guide to capability: models with similar rewards differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. Because the benchmark's checkpoint scores largely record what an agent did or mentioned, we also introduce stage-level metrics that score what the agent submits, by executing its detection queries in the telemetry store and judging its outputs against the answer key. Rather than combining them into one more overall reward, we show that different models lead different stages, which suggests routing each stage of the workflow to the model that performs it best rather than choosing a single model by its overall score. We also report how many tokens each model generates, and find that the share of output spent on thinking does not track the reward.

title: Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
description:
By Prashanth Gedde Narayanaswamy

As one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile.

A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result.

That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way.

The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale Bugs

Standard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks.

While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. A standard 1% sample misses these extreme long-tail sessions entirely.

To catch the real bugs, every test run had to execute against a full hour of unsampled production data, along with all the deployment overhead that came with it.

The Strategy: Branch-Driven Isolation

The biggest win came from a feature in Dataflow, Netflix’s command-line tool for building, testing, and deploying data pipelines. It supports branch-driven development: our workflows run on Maestro (Netflix’s workflow orchestrator), which schedules and executes the jobs, and they already use a sanitized branch name (the ${dataflow.sanitizedbranch} placeholder). So if I push a branch like pgn/cap-experiment, then the deployed workflow, its tables, and its run namespace all get tagged with that branch name. This eliminates collisions with team members or between my own concurrent runs.

With that isolation in place, the model was simple: one branch is one independent experiment. I parameterized the scheduler (cap size, shuffle partitions, heavy-device threshold, feature flags) and gave each variant its own branch and output table. Instead of queuing five sequential tests over 10 hours, I fired off five variants simultaneously against the same time window. Total execution time dropped from the sum of all runs to just the length of the single slowest job.

Managing per-branch tables added zero overhead. Dataflow provisions and updates tables automatically from declared schemas without manual DDL. Whenever I modified the event bag structure between experiments, the table schema updated seamlessly, no CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE required.

The only real constraint was cluster contention. Because these heavy Spark jobs shared resources with the rest of the company, peak hours sometimes limited me to two concurrent runs instead of five. But even running two or three jobs in parallel was a massive improvement over single-threaded debugging.

The key takeaway: don’t focus on making a single multi-hour run faster, build a setup where you can run many experiments simultaneously without them stepping on each other.

While the previous chart shows the time savings, the architecture that enables this isolation looks like below:

How an AI Agent Helped

Running five parallel experiments gets messy fast. Tracking instance IDs, configs, memory spills, and stage failures across variants makes it easy to lose track.

This is where an AI agent stepped in, not to write clever code, but to handle operational grunt work. I described variants in plain English, and the agent updated scheduler configs, deployed to the branch, triggered jobs, and polled metrics. Once complete, it compared spill and failure counts across variants in a summary table, allowing me to ask, “Which run is closest to OOM-free at peak load?” and get an immediate answer.

The value wasn’t deep Spark expertise, but operational memory. It turned tedious Spark UI cross-checks into a single prompt.

Eventually, I packaged this workflow into a reusable agent skill (.agents/skills/sandbox-deploy-and-run/) run via /sandbox-deploy-and-run <module> <scheduler-file> [PARAM=value]. It handles the full lifecycle—preflight, deploy, background polling, auto-diagnostics, and re-entrant resume <instance_id> support—turning multi-hour experiments into a single command.

Why tmux Mattered

All of this ran on Workbench, Netflix’s cloud dev environment, using my laptop as a thin terminal. Without session persistence, an SSH drop or sleeping laptop would kill multi-hour Spark runs mid-flight.

tmux running directly on Workbench solved this. Every experiment lived in a named cloud session: I could close my laptop, reattach hours later, and pick up where I left off. Combined with branch isolation, this made "start five and walk away" possible.

This is now my default setup: a local terminal (Ghostty), dedicated git worktrees per branch, and persistent tmux sessions on Workbench. The local laptop is disposable—closing it or losing network never interrupts the jobs.

That setup turned a long travel day into active iteration time. I kicked off batches at the gate, checked results via AI agent over spotty inflight Wi-Fi, and squeezed 4–5 full experiment cycles into a single 24-hour flight.

What All Experiments Uncovered

The root cause came down to a single operator: collect_list. Because Spark buffers each full event bag in memory, long-session OOMs were driven by individual bag size, not total dataset volume. The legacy pipeline handled identical row counts without crashing, proving that each event in the new bag had grown significantly heavier.

Two factors inflated event weight:

  • Field types and Option boxing: The session ID changed from an 8-byte Long to a UUID string. Worse, wrapping fields in Scala Option forced Spark to deserialize typed Datasets into JVM objects (Some wrappers), driving up object allocation and GC pressure across tens of thousands of events per session.
  • Bloated string attributes: Low-value fields (e.g., referrer URLs, test allocations) added several hundred bytes per event. Multiplying these strings across collect_list wasted terabytes per hour, even though downstream tasks rarely used them.

The Fixes:

  1. Unboxed primitives: Removing Option wrappers from non-nullable fields dropped peak executor memory from 112% to 58% of the slot with zero disk spill.
  2. Slimmed event bags: Dropped unused per-event attributes and hoisted session-invariant metadata (app version, country) up to the session header.

Takeaway: Reducing individual event weight delivered far better stability than throwing more cluster memory at the problem.

Two Experiments That Changed My Mind

Out of dozens of runs, two findings completely overturned my assumptions about Spark memory management:

  • Finding 1: Narrowing rows can trigger faster OOMs. Slimming our table dropped its size below Spark’s auto-broadcast threshold, prompting the query planner to switch from shuffle joins to broadcast joins. Because broadcast joins pin build-side tables directly into executor memory, narrower rows actually increased total memory pressure.
  • Finding 2: Broadcast hash joins were silently draining memory. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) rewrote nine sort-merge joins into broadcast hash joins at runtime. While each join stayed under our 400 MB broadcast limit individually, AQE pinned ~3.1 GB of cumulative data simultaneously in a single executor, pushing containers over the edge.

The Surgical Fix: Instead of disabling broadcast joins globally, I lowered only AQE’s runtime threshold (spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) to 10 MB while leaving the compile-time threshold untouched. That single change freed up ~3.1 GB of executor memory without impacting initial query planning.

Takeaway: Broadcast joins speed up queries, but pinned memory isn’t free. Watch accumulated broadcasts in your execution plan, not just dataset sizes.

Keeping a Single Experiment Log

When running dozens of parallel tests, the biggest risk isn’t job failure, it’s losing track of what you’ve already tried or confusing which JAR and config produced a result.

To solve this, I scaffolded the AI agent to append a row to a repository Markdown table after every run:

  • Run # | Jar ver | Change vs. Previous Run | Config | Key Metrics (Spill, Failed Tasks, Peak Memory, Duration)

If a run yielded a key finding, the agent added a short note explaining what the result proved or disproved.

Key Takeaways:

  • Single source of truth: It created an auditable history for the entire investigation.
  • Forced discipline: Requiring “Change vs. Previous Run” forced me to isolate variables. Whenever I bundled multiple changes, I couldn’t isolate the root cause and had to rerun the test — a mistake the log format immediately exposed.

A secondary doc (events-join-spark-tuning.md) captured the distilled findings as a quick "symptom-to-knob" lookup, so teammates didn't have to wade through the full chronological history.

A Mistake I Learned From: The Fix That Only Worked Off-Peak.

To cap session size, I added row_number().over(Window...) and filtered for the first N events. It passed off-peak tests cleanly, but crashed with OOMs at peak load.

The issue was structural: Spark’s Window operator buffers an entire session in memory before evaluating row numbers and filtering. The cap trimmed output downstream, but it didn't limit memory usage during buffering, so a single skewed session overwhelmed executor memory.

The Fix & Lesson: We moved truncation ahead of the Window stage to cap events before buffering occurs.

Takeaway: Test fixes against worst-case input skew. Off-peak runs hide structural bottlenecks that peak scale will immediately trigger.

The final fix

Pulling it together, four changes shipped, each isolated to a single experiment before it landed:

  • Unboxed the never-null fields from Option to plain primitives. Peak executor memory dropped from about 112% of the slot to about 58%, with zero spill.
  • Slimmed the event bag. Dropped per-event fields nobody used, and hoisted session-invariant fields (versions, country, connection type) to the session level so they are stored once per session, not once per event.
  • Capped session size before the Window stage. Dropped oversized sessions ahead of the buffering, and truncated the bag to the cap rather than dropping whole sessions.
  • Lowered AQE’s runtime broadcast threshold. Set spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 10 MB, leaving the compile-time threshold untouched.

The Unresolved Bottleneck

While these fixes made the pipeline run cleanly, they didn’t solve the underlying scaling issue: aggregating an entire session’s event bag into a single row has a hard ceiling. As our upstream telemetry source evolves and adds new attributes, each event in the bag becomes heavier, meaning this memory pressure will eventually return without a single line of code changing on our end.

Slimming and unboxing bought us headroom, but they didn’t change the fundamental data shape. The biggest takeaway from this effort is that tuning buys time, not infinite scale. If your underlying data model allows unbounded row growth, tuning alone won’t save you , eventually, the architecture itself has to change.

Summary

  • If the bug only appears at scale, stop trying to sample. Build a way to run many full-scale runs in parallel instead.
  • If your scheduler can use the branch name, then one branch becomes one isolated experiment, and running many at once becomes easy.
  • Use an AI agent to run the operation, not only to write code. Deploy, poll, pull metrics, compare variants: this is where most of the time goes.
  • Once a loop repeats, package it as a skill. The deploy-run-watch-diagnose cycle becomes one command.
  • Use tmux for long runs. The run must survive you closing the laptop.
  • Keep one single experiment log, and make every entry state the one change from the previous run. The format itself forces you to change one variable at a time.
  • For memory problems, look at the per-row width first, not only at the total data volume. Bigger field types, Option boxing, and fat unused strings all add up inside a collect_list bag.
  • Tuning buys headroom, not a new ceiling. If the data shape can grow without a bound, the design has to change eventually, tuning alone will not save you.

Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane) was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Oracle GoldenGate 23ai: Real-Time Replication to the Cloud Without a Downtime Window
description:
Last quarter I migrated a 4TB on-prem Oracle order-management database to OCI Autonomous Database with a change window of exactly zero minutes. No maintenance page, no "please don't place orders between 2 and 4 AM." The tool that made that possible was Oracle GoldenGate 23ai, and if you're still running the classic architecture from a few years ago, the upgrade path itself is worth knowing about before you touch a single extract.

Here's what actually changed, why it matters for cloud migrations specifically, and where I got bitten during setup.

What GoldenGate 23ai actually is

GoldenGate has always done one thing: capture committed changes from a source database's redo/transaction logs and apply them to a target, in near real time, without touching the source workload. 23ai (GA since April 2024, still shipping incremental releases under that name) adds a few things that matter if your target is a cloud database:

  • Microservices architecture is now the only architecture. Classic GGSCI-only deployments are on their way out. Everything runs as a set of REST-managed services (Administration Server, Distribution Server, Receiver Server) fronted by a browser console, managed through adminclient instead of the old ggsci shell alone.
  • AI vector data type support. GoldenGate can now replicate Oracle 23ai VECTOR columns in real time, including to non-Oracle vector stores like pgvector, MySQL HeatWave, and OpenSearch, as long as the embedding algorithm and dimensions match on both sides.
  • Data Streams. DDL and DML changes can be exposed as JSON CloudEvents over AsyncAPI, so a downstream microservice can subscribe to a table's changes without you writing a Kafka Connect pipeline for it.
  • OCI GoldenGate as a managed service. Fully managed deployments across 45+ OCI regions with elastic autoscaling, so you're not babysitting a VM running the hub.

For a straight database migration, the piece that matters most is still the boring one: extract, trail, replicat. Let's build it.

Setting up real-time replication to the cloud

Assume an on-prem Oracle 19c/23ai source and an OCI Autonomous Database (or Oracle on RDS, the pattern is nearly identical) as target. First, enable supplemental logging on the source. Do this at the PDB level, not the CDB root, unless you're specifically doing downstream mining, Oracle explicitly does not recommend root-level capture with a common user for normal replication.

-- Run inside the source PDB, connected as the GoldenGate admin user
ALTER SYSTEM SET ENABLE_GOLDENGATE_REPLICATION=TRUE SCOPE=BOTH;

ALTER TABLE ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER ADD SUPPLEMENTAL LOG DATA (ALL) COLUMNS;

Then, from the admin client (or GGSCI if you're still mid-upgrade), enable trandata and add the extract:

GGSCI> DBLOGIN USERID ggadmin@ORCLPDB1, PASSWORD ******
GGSCI> ADD TRANDATA ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER
GGSCI> ADD EXTRACT EXTORD, TRANLOG, INTEGRATED TRANLOG, BEGIN NOW
GGSCI> ADD EXTTRAIL /u01/ogg/dirdat/ab, EXTRACT EXTORD, MEGABYTES 200

The extract's parameter file is where you actually tell it what to capture:

EXTRACT EXTORD
USERID ggadmin@ORCLPDB1, PASSWORD ******
EXTTRAIL /u01/ogg/dirdat/ab
TRANLOGOPTIONS EXCLUDEUSER GGADMIN
TABLE ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER;
TABLE ORDERS.ORDER_LINES;

On the target side (Autonomous Database, connecting over the wallet TNS alias), add the replicat against a checkpoint table:

GGSCI> DBLOGIN USERID ggadmin@ORCLADB_HIGH, PASSWORD ******
GGSCI> ADD CHECKPOINTTABLE ggadmin.ggchkpt
GGSCI> ADD REPLICAT REPORD, EXTTRAIL /u01/ogg/dirdat/ab, CHECKPOINTTABLE ggadmin.ggchkpt

And its parameter file:

REPLICAT REPORD
USERID ggadmin@ORCLADB_HIGH, PASSWORD ******
ASSUMETARGETDEFS
MAP ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER, TARGET ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER;
MAP ORDERS.ORDER_LINES, TARGET ORDERS.ORDER_LINES;

Start both, watch the lag, and once REPORD reports zero lag against a quiet source, you cut over the application's connection string. That's the whole trick to a zero-downtime migration: the cutover is a DNS/connection-string change, not a data-loading exercise.

GGSCI> START EXTRACT EXTORD
GGSCI> START REPLICAT REPORD
GGSCI> INFO REPLICAT REPORD, DETAIL

Where this requires care

A few things cost me real time on that migration, and I'd rather you skip them:

The classic-to-microservices jump isn't optional anymore. If you're on an older GoldenGate install, plan a separate upgrade step before the migration project, not during it. Trying to learn adminclient REST semantics on the same day you're cutting a production database over is a bad combination.

Autonomous Database needs the wallet, and the wallet needs network ACLs. GoldenGate connects to Autonomous Database over TLS using the downloaded wallet's TNS entry. If your GoldenGate host can't reach the ADB's public or private endpoint, or the ACL on the ADB instance hasn't been opened for that host, you'll get a connection failure that looks like a credentials problem and isn't.

Trail files will eat your disk if replicat lags. On a large initial sync, extract runs ahead of replicat easily. Watch trail directory growth, not just lag in seconds, especially if the target is on a slower network path like a cross-region OCI link.

Vector column replication has real constraints. It's not a magic heterogeneous conversion. Source and target vector dimensions and distance metric need to line up, or you're replicating garbage embeddings that happen to be the right data type.

Root-level capture with a common user works but isn't the recommended path. If you inherited a GoldenGate config that captures from the CDB root, budget time to migrate it to per-PDB extracts before you lean on it for a cloud migration you actually care about.

My take

GoldenGate 23ai's headline features (vector replication, Data Streams, the AI service integrations) are the interesting demo material, but the reason it's worth learning right now is much less flashy: it's the most reliable way I've found to move a live Oracle database to the cloud without asking the business for a maintenance window. The microservices architecture switch is a real cost if you're upgrading from an old classic install, but once it's running, the extract-trail-replicat pattern is the same discipline it's always been, just pointed at a cloud endpoint instead of a second on-prem box.

Further reading

  • Oracle GoldenGate 23ai: What's New
  • Announcing GoldenGate 23ai General Availability
  • Add a Replicat for Autonomous AI Database (OCI GoldenGate)
  • Working with the EXTRACT and REPLICAT utilities of Oracle GoldenGate (AWS RDS docs)

title: Verify authentication recovery before treating Configuration as the root cause
description:
A return URL containing error=Configuration suggests a configuration mistake. Yet the inspected Auth.js version also produces that destination when a PKCE cookie is missing. The user-facing classification does not identify the cause by itself.

This investigation read SquadNote's recovery implementation and reran tests against its actual Auth.js dependency. It examines rejection, retry navigation, and diagnostic evidence before drawing a causal conclusion.

The source is circle-hub at d116e8a, checked on September 11, 2026. No production authentication logs or user histories were collected. This is an account of recovery code and rerun verification, not proof of a production incident's cause or resolution.

Distinguish the internal error from Configuration

Auth.js's InvalidCheck reference covers PKCE, state, or nonce checks that cannot be performed. Unavailable cookies can produce it, as can configuration issues.

The repository regression test resolves @auth/core through the application's next-auth dependency. It does not substitute a separately installed latest release.

A synthetic callback without its PKCE cookie produced:

Observation Result
HTTP status 302
Redirect destination /sign-in/error?error=Configuration
Internal type passed to the logger InvalidCheck

The fixture deliberately omitted the cookie, so its cause is known. Seeing the same internal type in production would still require investigating why the cookie did not arrive. Expiration, another initiation, and browser behavior cannot be distinguished from that display alone.

First restore a path from failure to a fresh start

The recovery design record and history show the recovery screen in 061a5f2, repeated-submission protection in 2b88c31, and diagnostics in 7f180ad.

The recovery screen presents sign-in and public help without depending on auth() or the database. Displaying an authentication failure does not require successfully repeating the same authentication dependency.

Return destinations are restricted to safe paths on the same origin. Tests preserve invitation-page returns while rejecting external redirection and authentication-page loops. The original callback URL is not reused unconditionally.

Two new initiation requests sent to the actual Auth.js implementation produced different PKCE challenges, S256, and fresh PKCE cookies. However, the initiation fixture uses the internal CSRF-skip option. It does not verify browser CSRF protection or a round trip through the OAuth provider, and no production setting was changed to disable CSRF checks.

Reject a second start before React rerenders

Disabling a button visually can leave a window before React rerenders in which another button can be pressed. The implementation uses a synchronous guard shared by Google and Apple initiation on the same screen:

export function createSubmissionGuard() {
  let submitting = false;
  return {
    acquire() {
      if (submitting) return false;
      submitting = true;
      return true;
    },
    reset() { submitting = false; },
  };
}

Tests against the actual guard reject immediate reacquisition, allow acquisition after the reset used for failure or history restoration, and keep separate instances independent.

Its scope is repeated submission from one screen. It does not serialize initiation across tabs or browsers, nor remove every possible cause of missing cookies.

Correlate how far the flow progressed

The diagnostics investigate initiation and callback boundaries without storing authentication values. The principal events mean:

Event What it establishes
auth.sign_in_started A start request occurred
auth.authorization_redirect Initiation generated a destination
auth.callback_received A callback arrived
auth.sign_in_succeeded Auth.js emitted its signIn event
auth.server_error Failure and diagnostic information were recorded

Initiation and destination generation do not mean authentication succeeded. In particular, the server action's cookiesAfterStart observes the cookie jar at that time. Existing cookies can be present, so presence alone does not establish fresh issuance.

requestId identifies a failing request; attemptId supports correlation with initiation. The latter marker is client-originated diagnostic information and does not authorize authentication. It represents the browser's most recent initiation, so it does not prove the same OAuth transaction across multiple tabs.

Absent, expired, or provider-mismatched markers can prevent correlation. Record why correlation failed instead of rephrasing that as “no initiation happened.”

Add diagnostics without weakening authentication checks

Diagnostic tests verify that synthetic sensitive values, including cookie values, authorization codes, tokens, raw User-Agent strings, and IPs, do not appear in logs. Cookie observations retain only presence for specific names, and paths are restricted to authentication routes.

Tests also check isolation between concurrent requests, preservation of authentication responses when diagnostics or notifications fail, and preservation of the original Auth.js response cookies. The change does not obtain successful logins by relaxing PKCE, state, or nonce requirements.

Alert suppression operates within a Worker instance; it is not a delivery guarantee across all distributed instances. The diagnostic cookie is not a session replacement either. Neither mechanism belongs in the decision that authentication has succeeded.

The 47 tests and the remaining environment checks

The run passed 47 tests across 8 files copied from the fixed commit. It used Node.js v24.15.0, Vitest 4.1.4, Next.js 15.5.15, next-auth 5.0.0-beta.25, and its Auth.js core dependency 0.37.2. The runner and results are preserved.

Some tests invoke the actual Auth.js implementation; others mock route or notification dependencies. Real Google or Apple accounts, Safari or embedded browsers, multiple tabs, and manual browser-cookie deletion were not tested in this run. Historical UI verification documented in the repository is also separate from these rerun results.

Verify the failure classification, fresh initiation, safe return destination, same-screen repeat protection, and the limits of log correlation in order. While the cause remains uncertain, record the conditions for retry and the questions requiring further investigation.

title: Pre-Registered Genesis Accounting for Recursive Self-Improvement: First Audited Operator-Genesis Events in a Physics-Discovery Runtime
description:
arXiv:2610.14843v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Claims of recursive self-improvement are easy to make and hard to falsify: did improvement come from re-using designer-provided mechanisms, or from mechanisms the system authored itself? We introduce a pre-registered, two-tier accounting: M1 counts machine-generated content instances within a designer-provided vocabulary, while M2 counts machine-authored mechanism types (new operators registered into the runtime's own vocabulary, with a held-out-validation certificate). We report the first audited M2 genesis events. In the primary event, depth-limited compositional search over elementary operators, judged by held-out R^2 on real NIST hydrogen Balmer measurements, produced the operator sq(inv(n)) = 1/n^2 -- the Rydberg-level form -- which no standard-library transform could express (held-out R^2: -0.546 best standard transform vs. 1.0000000 composed). A protocol flaw (independent variable built by inverting the very law under test) was caught in audit and repaired via an independent-label protocol; extrapolation to unseen levels (n=8,9 trained on n<=7) attains relative error ~10^-6, four to six orders beyond the best standard operator. A second event independently recovered sqrt(inv(a)) -- Kepler's velocity law -- from JPL ephemeris vectors. Also incorporated: an audited compounding channel (first domain-level measurement: 1.109x accuracy ratio on a real held-out domain) and blind, decurated genesis exams whose honest tally is zero. The Kepler event passes line audit; the hydrogen gap reproduces on He II; the certificate is threshold-stable. Against eleven prior systems, the contribution is the measurement and governance of machine-authored mechanisms, not the search algorithm or rediscovered physics. Limitations: exams were curated by agents who knew the textbook answer, triggers manual, grammar observer-injected; both events demonstrate capability to author, not yet autonomous genesis.

title: How to choose the right hosting for your website
description:
When selecting a hosting environment, the choice between shared, VPS, dedicated, or cloud hosting impacts your resource isolation, scalability, and maintenance requirements.

Understanding the trade-offs between managed and unmanaged services is crucial for balancing operational overhead with infrastructure control.

This guide breaks down the essential factors for choosing a provider, from uptime reliability and SSL requirements to the specific needs of Linux vs.

Windows-based environments.

The main types of hospitality

Your choice depends on the needs of your project and the available cost:

  • Shared hosting: The most economical solution, ideal for starting out. Many websites share the same computer. However, if another page hosted on the same computer receives a lot of traffic, the speed of yours may be affected.
  • Virtual Private Server (VPS): You share the main computer with others, but you have your own isolated space and exclusive resources. It's like having your own apartment in an apartment building.
  • Exclusive hospitality: The entire computer belongs exclusively to you. It is the most powerful but also the most expensive option.
  • Cloud Hosting: Your website is hosted on an entire network of computers. It is a very flexible option, as if a problem occurs on one of them, your website can continue to operate using the others.

What to consider before choosing

Before you settle on a company, consider the following points:

  • Availability: It is the most important indicator of whether the provider is reliable. You want your page to remain open for visitors 24 hours a day.
  • Management: In managed hosting, the company takes care of the maintenance and security of the system for you. In unmanaged hosting, you are responsible for all the settings yourself.
  • Specialized packages: Many companies offer WordPress-specific packages that automatically handle tasks like updates and backups.
  • Security: If you are going to have an online store, it is necessary to use a security certificate so that your customer data is encrypted.
  • Additional services: Some companies, such as WP Engine, do not provide email services, so you will have to use another provider for your email.

Switching from one provider to another can be a complex process, so if you're starting out, a good approach is to choose a solution that meets your current needs, knowing that you can upgrade your package later.

title: WinARDet: Compressed Window Auto-Regression for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Grounding
description:
arXiv:2610.19419v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. % To break this loop, in this paper, we propose \textbf{Compressed Window Auto-Regression} (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.

title: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources
description:
arXiv:2610.19268v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarks shape how model capabilities are measured and interpreted, yet their scores can obscure whose conventions, contexts, and judgments define successful performance. We introduce a user-centric audit framework that distinguishes users who contribute benchmark content from those whose needs evaluation results are intended to represent. The framework operationalizes seven dimensions across benchmark content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Across 16 resources, we find that American-centered conventions account for 62.4-94.4% of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, while geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly associated with national GDP share (mean Pearson r = 0.780; Spearman p = 0.778). Documentation reveals a systematic source-target gap: all 16 resources operationalize source-user context, but none operationalize target-user context. Paired scoring experiments further show that meaning-preserving answer variants reduce DROP exact-match accuracy from 100.0% to 33.3%, while TruthfulQA exhibits metric-dependent reductions in reference similarity. Our framework and documentation checklist make user assumptions auditable, clarifying what benchmark scores represent and where evaluation claims are supported.

title: 371 translations crash their Android apps: a census of 1.26 million strings on F-Droid
description:
Made with AI agents by MV2 of Munim, Inc. Every number below comes from code and data you can rerun: android-translation-crash-census (code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0).

When an Android app calls getString(R.string.files_left, n), the translation for the user's language goes to java.util.Formatter. If a translator typed %1$ where the English says %1$s, or wrote 50% without escaping it, the call throws. English never breaks, so the developer never sees it. Only people using that language do.

How often does that happen in practice? Searches of GitHub, arXiv and the web turned up single-project fixes (Commons, Firefox for Android, ConnectBot, OsmAnd) but no measurement across apps. The census makes one.

What was checked

  • Every source repository behind F-Droid's index: 4,476 repositories for 4,667 apps, latest commit, read in 11 minutes on 4 cores.
  • 3,755 have Android string resources. 1,703 have translations of strings with printf placeholders.
  • That is 1,262,958 translations. Each one, and its English source, was formatted with OpenJDK 21's real java.util.Formatter, using arguments of the types the English string expects.
  • For repositories with a failing translation, the census also reads the Kotlin and Java code to see whether anything formats that string with arguments. A broken string nobody formats can't crash.

What it found

  • 371 translations in 98 repositories throw with the arguments the English string expects.
  • 238 of them, in 66 repositories, are strings the app's own code formats. Those are the crashes users can actually hit. That count is after two corrections made by reading rows by hand (below).
  • About 1 in 3,400 formatted translations crashes. It's concentrated: ownCloud's Uyghur file alone has 47 reachable crashes (% 1 $ s instead of %1$s), and Cashiro and Wikimedia Commons follow. Most affected apps have one to four.
  • The exceptions are UnknownFormatConversionException 251, MissingFormatArgumentException 48, FormatFlagsConversionMismatchException 48, IllegalFormatConversionException 20 and IllegalFormatFlagsException 4.

Two false positives the census found in itself

The first run reported 382 crashes, 250 of them reachable. Reading the rows against each app's code took 12 out of the reachable 250, and 11 out of the 382:

  • %t and Long. Four Cashiro strings use %t where the English has %d. %t rejects the Integer the census passed but accepts the Long the app passes, so they print the wrong text instead of crashing.
  • Markup that is text. Wikipedia writes some English strings in CDATA: <![CDATA[... attributed to %1$s. <a href="%2$s">Learn more</a>.]]>. To Android that link is plain text, so the app formats it with two arguments and passes it to Html.fromHtml. The checker removed every <...> before reading placeholders, so the %2$s in the href disappeared from the English. Translations whose link markup was itself broken kept their %2$s, and looked like they read an argument the app never passes. They show a broken link, but they don't throw. That is six rows in Danish, Indonesian, Portuguese, Romanian and Russian. Five more were in values-qq, translatewiki.net's notes for translators, which no device loads. All 11 are gone from the totals above, and 8 of them were in strings the code formats.

The real JVM agreed with the static check on all of these, because both read the same extracted text. Checking the checker against a JVM doesn't catch a mistake in what you feed them both. Census 0.3.1 fixes the extraction (only real XML elements lose their markup), and a full re-run will list every row that changes.

The mistakes, by kind

A small rule-based classifier names the mistake behind the first placeholder Formatter can't use. For the 242 reachable rows left after the Wikipedia correction (238 after %t):

Kind Example Rows Repos
malformed index % 1 $ s, %$1s 50 5
stray percent (%1$d%), 电量 %1$d % 45 26
conversion missing %1$ musikspelare, Wideo (%1) 43 18
flag mismatch Mesaj:% s 34 14
argument not passed a Russian few form reading %2$d 27 14
conversion letter in another script %1$с, %1$دم, %1$δδ 26 6
wrong type %g or %t for %d 10 5
unknown Latin conversion %1$DH, %2$vs 7 4

A stray % is the most widespread mistake (26 repositories). The malformed index is the biggest cluster, but it is almost all one Uyghur file. Turkish % s makes up 22 of the 34 flag mismatches: the space between % and s is read as a flag.

The kind I didn't expect: the placeholder letter itself gets translated. Russian %1$с (a Cyrillic es, not an s), Bulgarian %1$дмлн. for %1$dM, Arabic %1$دم (dal for d), Greek %1$δδ. To a reader each looks fine. To Formatter, с is an unknown conversion. It's narrower than I expected: 26 reachable rows in 6 apps, and in 14 of them the letter looks like or transliterates the Latin one.

Every route shipped one

The hand-checked cases came through Crowdin, Transifex, translatewiki.net, Lokalise, Weblate, and files edited straight in the repository. All of those platforms have placeholder checks of some kind. A check that warns but doesn't block isn't enough once a release script pulls translations in automatically. (A per-platform crash rate is the next thing the census measures.)

A static check you can run in CI

The census compares the real JVM with a static check, the java-format rule in l10n-guard (Python, standard library only, Apache-2.0). Of the 371 JVM crashes it called 364 errors and the other 7 warnings, and it called nothing an error that the JVM accepted. Both share the text-extraction mistake above, which the next l10n-guard release fixes.

python l10n_guard.py android app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml app/src/main/res/values-ru/strings.xml

It exits non-zero on an error, so it can gate a pull request that brings in translations.

Android Lint's StringFormatInvalid catches many of these too, but only in builds that run lint after the translations land.

Reporting them

The census files nothing by itself. Each case was checked by hand against the project's current code before anything was reported, and only to projects whose rules allow AI-assisted reports. Mastodon and AnkiDroid don't, so they weren't reported; their rows are in the data for their translators.

So far:

  • Tallybook merged the fix for 9 Turkish strings (#397). The maintainer reproduced the crash on an emulator and found a path I had missed: one of the strings crashes the Utility settings screen as soon as it opens, and has since 2019.
  • ownCloud acknowledged the 55 broken Uyghur strings (#5018).
  • Open: Homer Audio Player 2 #26 (Chinese battery indicator), Shader Editor #294 (a Russian plural reading an argument it never gets), FadCam #360 (Italian and Greek strings in video deletion and export).

Limits

  • Only the latest commit of each default branch was read, so a translation may already be fixed on its platform.
  • Code use is pattern-matched. Strings looked up by name at runtime count as unused, so the reachable count is a floor in that sense. So is leaving out the 190 translations that throw only if the app passes text: reading code shows some of those do crash.
  • It can also overcount, as the two corrections above show. Both were found by reading rows by hand, and more may exist.
  • Verdicts come from OpenJDK 21. Android's Formatter is the same code for these cases, but edge cases can differ by API level.
  • I reproduced nothing on a device. One maintainer did, on an emulator.

If you maintain an app in the data, findings.csv links every row to the exact line at the commit read.

This article and the census were made with AI agents working for MV2 of Munim, Inc. The numbers were checked against the published data.

title: WorldMemBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Memory of Video World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19063v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As video models enable longer and more realistic interactive experiences, maintaining a world consistent with its history becomes essential. This requires both preserving previously observed content and ensuring coherent world evolution over time. World memory is a critical capability to evaluate alongside visual fidelity and video duration. We introduce WorldMemBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating world memory in video world models. Across 260 test cases, it assesses static memory through the retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry, and dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence. Using controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories, the benchmark evaluates static content against fixed initial references and dynamic events against expected state transitions. It combines appearance and geometry metrics with event-specific assessments, and reports video quality and camera-following accuracy as complementary diagnostics. Evaluation of nine representative models shows that strong static retention does not imply reliable dynamic state evolution, while repeated revisits reveal memory degradation beyond the first return. Human studies support the alignment between our automatic evaluations and human judgments. WorldMemBench provides a systematic testbed for diagnosing memory failures and guiding the development of persistent, temporally coherent video worlds.

title: Escape Analysis: How Can a Compiler Eliminate a Heap Allocation Without Changing Your Code?
description:
Consider this Java method:

double distanceBetween(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
    Point b = new Point(x2, y2);
    return Math.sqrt(
        Math.pow(b.x - a.x, 2) + Math.pow(b.y - a.y, 2)
    );
}

Two Point objects are created, used in a calculation, and then discarded. The source code calls new, which in Java means heap allocation, object initialization, and eventually garbage collection. But if you look at this from a different angle: both objects are born at the start of the method, used for arithmetic, and are completely useless after the return statement. Nothing outside the method ever sees them. No other thread can observe them. They exist solely to hold two doubles each.

Does the runtime actually need to allocate heap memory for them? That question is what escape analysis is designed to answer.

What It Means for an Object to Escape

Before a compiler can eliminate an allocation, it needs to prove that the allocation can be eliminated. The key concept is whether an object escapes its local scope.

An object escapes when a reference to it can be observed from outside the context in which it was created. There are several ways this happens:

Return. A method that returns a reference to a locally created object immediately causes it to escape. The caller now holds a live reference, so the object must exist somewhere accessible after the method returns. Stack frames are discarded on return, which means the object cannot safely live in one.

Shared state. Storing a reference in a field of an object that outlives the current scope, or in a static field, allows code anywhere in the program to observe the object. The compiler must assume the object could be read at any time.

Opaque callees. When a method passes an object to another function and the compiler cannot fully analyze what that function does with the reference, it must conservatively assume the object might escape. If the callee stores the reference in a field or returns it to its own callers, the assumption would be violated.

Non-escaping objects are those where the compiler can prove that every reference to the object stays within a bounded scope. It is created, used, and the last reference to it disappears, all within a region the compiler can reason about.

The Point objects in the opening example are non-escaping. The references a and b are local variables. They are never returned, never stored in any field, never passed to an opaque method. The compiler can trace every use of them.

How the Compiler Reasons About References

Escape analysis is not a single yes-or-no check. It is a data flow analysis that the compiler runs over the program's intermediate representation, tracking how references to each object propagate through the code.

The classic formulation, and the one underlying HotSpot's C2 compiler, builds a connection graph: a representation of the relationships between object references, the fields through which they flow, and the boundaries across which they might cross. Each object in the graph carries an escape state. HotSpot's C2 uses three states: NoEscape, for objects whose references are entirely contained within the method; ArgEscape, for objects passed as arguments but not observed to escape further; and GlobalEscape, for objects accessible from outside the method or thread.

The analysis is conservative. If the compiler cannot prove that a reference stays local, it assumes it might escape. Conservative analysis is safe: it never eliminates a necessary allocation. But it also means some allocations that a human could see are unnecessary will be retained because the compiler's model of the code is not complete. Inlining is one of the most important enablers of escape analysis. When a callee is inlined into the caller, the compiler gains full visibility into what the callee does with every argument, which allows escape states to be refined. HotSpot's C2 requires inlining to occur before scalar replacement can work. If a method is not inlined because it is too large or was not compiled at the right optimization tier, the analysis may classify its arguments as escaping, even if they do not.

The Optimization: Scalar Replacement

The natural first guess is that escape analysis moves objects from the heap to the stack. For some compilers and runtimes, that is exactly what happens. The Go compiler does this: if it proves that a value will not outlive the current function, it allocates the value in the goroutine's stack frame rather than on the heap. You can observe this directly with go build -gcflags="-m", which annotates each allocation decision.

HotSpot's C2 JIT takes a different path. According to the OpenJDK wiki: "C2 does NOT replace a heap allocation with a stack allocation for non globally escaping objects." Instead, C2 performs scalar replacement.

Scalar replacement decomposes an object into its constituent fields and eliminates the object itself. Rather than allocating a block of memory and storing field values in it, the compiler treats each field as an independent local variable. The object never materializes as a contiguous region of memory. No allocation happens. No garbage collector ever needs to reclaim it.

The transformation for the Point example looks conceptually like this. Before scalar replacement:

// What you wrote
Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
double ax = a.x;
double ay = a.y;

After scalar replacement, the compiler replaces all field accesses with synthetic local values:

// What the compiler works with internally
double a_x = x1;  // scalar substitute for a.x
double a_y = y1;  // scalar substitute for a.y

The Point object never exists. The field reads (a.x, a.y) become references to local values that can be kept in registers. Aleksey Shipilëv's JVM Anatomy Quarks describes this precisely: HotSpot "does not do stack allocations per se, but it does approximate that with Scalar Replacement."

From there, register allocation can place those scalar values in CPU registers for the duration of the computation. The two doubles that would have been heap-allocated objects end up as register values, with no allocation, no initialization overhead, and no GC involvement.

A Concrete Walk-Through

Take the full distance method from the opening:

double distanceBetween(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
    Point b = new Point(x2, y2);
    return Math.sqrt(
        Math.pow(b.x - a.x, 2) + Math.pow(b.y - a.y, 2)
    );
}

For scalar replacement to apply, C2 needs to:

  1. Inline the Point constructor so it can see that no reference to the new object leaks out of the construction.
  2. Determine that a and b have escape state NoEscape: no return of the references, no field stores into external objects, no passing to opaque methods.
  3. Replace new Point(x1, y1) with two scalar variables a_x = x1, a_y = y1.
  4. Rewrite every a.x and a.y access to use those scalars.
  5. Eliminate the allocation instruction entirely. After this transformation, the method compiles to arithmetic on four double values, none of which requires heap memory. The behavior observed by any caller is identical: they receive the same double result. The only change is internal to the representation of the computation.

Lock elimination is a related optimization that escape analysis enables. If an object is non-escaping, no other thread can hold a reference to it, so any synchronized blocks on that object are unnecessary. The compiler can remove them.

Where the Analysis Fails

Escape analysis has hard limits, and understanding them is as important as understanding what it can do.

The most common barrier is an opaque method call. If distanceBetween passed a to any method that C2 has not inlined, the compiler would have to assume the reference might escape. The Point would remain heap-allocated. This is why HotSpot's OpenJDK scalar replacement documentation explicitly lists non-inlined methods as a case where scalar replacement is prevented.

Interface dispatch is a related problem. When a method is called through an interface, the compiler cannot always determine which concrete implementation will run, which makes it impossible to inline the callee. Without inlining, the escape state of the argument is unknown.

Some operations are identity-sensitive. Java's == operator on objects tests reference identity. If the compiler replaces an object with scalars, two allocations that previously produced distinct references might appear identical or might behave incorrectly if the program depends on them being different objects. The compiler must verify that no code in scope depends on the object's identity before it can safely decompose it.

Synchronization presents a harder constraint. If code synchronizes on an object that the compiler is considering for scalar replacement, the semantics of Java's memory model require that the lock be observable. Lock elimination is sound only when the object is genuinely non-escaping, so the compiler must be certain before removing it.

Conservative analysis also means that HotSpot will retain an allocation if any uncertainty exists. The analysis can handle many cases that appear complex in source code, but it cannot analyze beyond what it can observe. Dynamic loading of classes, reflection, and native code are all effectively opaque.

The Performance Picture

Removing allocations reduces pressure on the garbage collector by producing fewer objects that need to be tracked and collected. In throughput-sensitive code that creates many short-lived objects in tight loops, this can meaningfully reduce GC pause frequency and time spent in allocation paths. Keeping data in registers rather than memory also reduces memory traffic.

That said, allocation in modern JVMs is fast. HotSpot's thread-local allocation buffers (TLABs) allow most allocations to complete with a simple pointer bump. The cost of a single allocation is small. The benefit of elimination comes from the aggregate effect over many allocations, particularly in hot loops, and from the downstream reduction in GC work.

Whether scalar replacement improves a specific workload depends on the compiler's ability to apply it, the allocation rate of the relevant code, and the GC configuration. Profiling with allocation-aware tools is the right way to measure this, not inference from source code alone.

The Developer's Relationship With This Optimization

The existence of escape analysis and scalar replacement changes what source-level object creation actually means. Writing new Point(x, y) in Java does not guarantee that a heap allocation will occur at runtime. Whether one does depends on the JIT compiler's escape analysis, whether the relevant methods were inlined, and the escape state the analysis assigned to the object.

This is intentional. The language specification defines what the program must compute and what observable side effects it must produce. It says nothing about whether intermediate objects need physical representation. The JIT compiler is free to choose any implementation that preserves observable behavior.

Several practical points follow from this:

Write code that is clear and correct. Avoiding allocation for its own sake by using awkward data structures or manual field decomposition will not necessarily produce faster code and will make the compiler's job harder if it disrupts inlining.

Measure before concluding. Allocation sampling profilers can show which allocations actually reach the heap at runtime. An allocation that appears in source code may not appear in profiles if scalar replacement has already eliminated it.

Do not assume Java and Go behave identically. Go's escape analysis operates at compile time and makes stack-allocation decisions that are baked into the generated machine code. HotSpot's analysis operates in the JIT compiler and uses scalar replacement rather than stack allocation. The mechanisms, the triggering conditions, and the diagnostics are different.

Check compiler output when it matters. Go's -gcflags="-m" flag reports escape decisions. HotSpot's -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations flag reports scalar replacement. These are the ground truth; source code is not.

The Deeper Insight

Escape analysis reflects a broader principle in compiler design: a language's specification describes the required observable behavior of a program, not its required internal representation. The compiler is free to transform how data is stored, how operations are sequenced, and how objects are physically represented, as long as anything the program is permitted to observe remains consistent with the specification.

A heap allocation is a mechanism for giving data a lifetime that outlives a function call. When the compiler can prove that a particular datum does not need that extended lifetime, the allocation is unnecessary. The datum can be represented as local values, stored in registers, and discarded the moment the function returns. The program computes the same result. The method's caller observes the same returned value. Nothing that any correct program could observe has changed.

What the compiler has changed is what never needed to exist in the first place.

Sources

  • OpenJDK HotSpot Escape Analysis Wiki — authoritative description of C2's escape analysis algorithm and its explicit statement that C2 does not perform stack allocation.
  • Aleksey Shipilëv: JVM Anatomy Quarks #18 — Scalar Replacement — detailed technical explanation of scalar replacement in HotSpot C2.
  • HotSpot Escape Analysis and Scalar Replacement Status (OpenJDK) — analysis of escape analysis coverage and limitations in C2.
  • Oracle Java Magazine: Escape Analysis in the HotSpot JIT Compiler — accessible explanation with GC log evidence.
  • Segment Engineering: Allocation Efficiency in High-Performance Go Services — practical explanation of Go's stack-allocation-first approach and escape analysis flags.
  • Go compiler escape analysis flags — go build -gcflags="-m" documentation.

title: Not All Criteria Matter: Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting for Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.19915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rubric-based evaluation assesses the responses of large language models (LLMs) by aggregating the verification results of explicit criteria, yet not all criteria matter equally. However, existing methods commonly aggregate the verification results with uniform weighting, which assigns minor and overlapping criteria the same weight as essential ones and thus produces misleading evaluation scores. Although some methods prompt an LLM to directly assign weights, direct weighting requires a holistic judgment over all criteria that LLMs struggle to make reliably. To address these limitations, we propose Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting (ICW), which derives the weights of criteria from pairwise importance comparisons made by an LLM. Specifically, ICW transforms the holistic judgment over all criteria into a series of pairwise importance comparisons, checks and revises inconsistent comparisons, and derives the weights from the principal eigenvector of the comparison matrix. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ICW consistently outperforms uniform weighting and competitive weighting methods, and translates into better policy models in downstream reinforcement learning.

title: What Breaks in Multi-Image Schema Application? Factorial Oracle Interventions Reveal an Instance-Information Bottleneck
description:
arXiv:2610.19611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). An auxiliary retrieval diagnostic reached only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy even after removing code-name generation. Providing both Oracle sources yielded 100% accuracy across all models. These results localize the dominant recoverable deficit to upstream ordered instance recovery rather than primarily to downstream schema use and composition.

title: React state has no type of its own. I gave it one, and it compiles away
description:
In Vue, Solid, and Angular, state has a type of its own: Ref<T>, Accessor<T>, Signal<T>.

In React, the count from useState is just a number. Nothing in the type tells you:

  • that it re-renders the component,
  • that it belongs in the dependency array of an effect,
  • that a closure may be holding an old copy of it.

Those questions are left to you and to lint rules. I wanted the type to answer them, so I built
react-preprocessor.

Status: experimental. The API is still changing. I am posting this to get feedback.

What it looks like

State is Reactive<T>. What is computed from it is Derived<T>.

import { $, reactive } from "react-preprocessor";

type Todo = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean };

export const Todos = ({ owner }: { owner: string }) => {
  const todos = reactive.new<Todo[]>([]); // Reactive<Todo[]>
  const left = todos.derive((list) => list.filter((t) => !t.done).length); // Derived<number>

  reactive.effect(() => {
    document.title = `${owner}: ${$(left)} left`;
  });

  return (
    <ul>
      {todos.each(
        (todo) => todo.id,
        (todo) => (
          <li onClick={() => todo.focus("done").update((done) => !done)}>
            {todo.derive((t) => t.title)}
          </li>
        ),
      )}
    </ul>
  );
};

At build time, this is rewritten into plain React:

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

type Todo = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean };

export const Todos = ({ owner }: { owner: string }) => {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState<Todo[]>([]);
  const left = todos.filter((t) => !t.done).length;
  useEffect(() => {
    document.title = `${owner}: ${left} left`;
  }, [owner, left]);
  return (
    <ul>
      {todos.map((todo) => (
        <li
          onClick={() =>
            setTodos((prev) =>
              prev.map((item) => (item.id === todo.id ? { ...item, done: !item.done } : item)),
            )
          }
          key={todo.id}
        >
          {todo.title}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

What the preprocessor wrote for you:

  1. The dependency array [owner, left], from what the effect reads.
  2. The nested immutable update, from todo.focus("done").update(...). The item is found by key, not by index, so the update hits the right item even if the list was reordered in the same batch.
  3. The key, from the first argument of todos.each.

The rules

  • There is no get. You cannot pull the value out of a Reactive<T>. You derive from it, or put it in JSX.
  • Using a reactive value as a plain value (`${count}`, if (count)) is a build error with a code frame.
  • Updates are pure functions: update(old => next). set(next) is the shortcut for a constant.
  • Nested state is updated through lenses (focus, each). Unions are narrowed with when and match, and the narrowed value is still writable.

The source is valid TypeScript, so your editor, type checker, and formatter work unchanged.

What it is not

  • Not a runtime library. Reactive<T> exists only at compile time. The output imports only React.
  • Not a performance tool. Memoization is left to the React Compiler, which runs after the preprocessor: 
React + sugar (.tsx)
  ↓ react-preprocessor
plain React (.tsx)
  ↓ React Compiler
optimized React

Low commitment

  • Adopt per file. Files without the sugar are left as they are.
  • See the output. react-preprocessor print src/Todos.tsx prints the plain React a file becomes.
  • Leave any time. react-preprocessor eject src --write rewrites the project to the plain React it compiles to.

It works with Vite, Next.js (Turbopack or webpack), and Babel. It also has a Jotai adapter and an oxlint/ESLint rule.

Try it

  • In the browser: the website lets you edit the examples and see the plain React they become.
  • In a project: pnpm add -D react-preprocessor, then follow the setup in the README.

Feedback wanted

I would like to hear:

  1. Does the Reactive<T> / Derived<T> split make the code easier to read for you, or harder?
  2. Which part of the API feels wrong?

Issues and comments are welcome on GitHub. A star helps other people find it.

title: Do You Want Your Web App to Feel Like a Native App?
description:
You can give your Codename One web app the same desktop theme family as your users' operating system: Aqua on macOS, Fluent on Windows, or Adwaita on Linux. Menus can sit above the app in HTML, with commands such as File and View visible instead of tucked into a mobile overflow menu.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

That gives you a browser version of your app that fits more comfortably on a desktop. The JavaScript port now supports both choices, and the same theme work reaches the Certificate Wizard you use to sign your apps.

Follow the operating system, or choose a theme

Set these in the Settings app's Build Hints:

nativeTheme=native
javascript.titleBar=html

In codenameone_settings.properties, use codename1.arg.nativeTheme and codename1.arg.javascript.titleBar instead. Desktop browsers select Fluent for Windows, Aqua for macOS, and Adwaita for Linux and the remaining desktop systems. Phones and tablets keep the mobile theme selection. The browser detection treats an iPad as a tablet even when it reports a Mac browser.

These are Codename One themes drawing the controls. They are not the operating system's native widget toolkit embedded in the page.

The Settings app demonstrates the three desktop theme families now available to browser apps. Click to compare the controls at full size.

You can pin a desktop theme when the application's design calls for it:

javascript.desktopTheme=fluent

The other explicit choices are aqua, adwaita and none. none keeps mobile themes on desktop browsers. Leave the value at auto to follow the operating system. The broader nativeTheme=modern setting has different behavior: it selects the modern mobile families, including on desktop browsers. Use native when desktop family selection is what you want.

Put commands above the app

The default javascript.titleBar=toolbar keeps the themed Toolbar inside the app. With html, the page supplies title and menu bars instead. The title follows the current form; commands group into menus using the same Command.setDesktopMenu() hint used on the desktop ports.

For example, inside an initialized app:

com.codename1.ui.Form form = new com.codename1.ui.Form("Notes");
com.codename1.ui.Command refresh = new com.codename1.ui.Command("Refresh") {
    public void actionPerformed(com.codename1.ui.events.ActionEvent event) {
        form.setTitle("Notes refreshed");
    }
};
refresh.setDesktopMenu("View");
form.getToolbar().addCommandToOverflowMenu(refresh);
form.show();

Commands without a menu hint go into a Commands menu. The HTML bars follow the selected appearance and the browser's light or dark preference. They do not have fake minimize, maximize or close buttons: the page does not own the browser window. The browser tab title remains the application's display name.

The source is in JavaScriptDesktopChrome, with build-hint and page behavior documented in the JavaScript guide.

Keep navigation inside your browser app

We do not support additional native Window surfaces in the JavaScript port. Popup blockers and the browser's window ownership make that a different promise from drawing a menu inside the current page. Windows browsers are supported; extra OS windows are the unsupported feature. Dialogs and navigation within the app remain the appropriate model.

There are renderer limits too. For example, the full lifted-lens optics from Sunday's iOS article are not implemented in the browser. Try the actual controls and effects your app uses rather than assuming a theme name proves complete renderer parity.

The build prunes theme resources it can prove the app will not reach. If your code constructs resource names dynamically, set javascript.pruneThemes=false; otherwise a theme loaded only through that constructed name may be missing.

Use the same desktop styling when you sign your app

A gallery of buttons cannot tell us whether an application works comfortably with a desktop theme. The Certificate Wizard has longer forms, tables, dialogs and instructions that people must actually read to finish a task.

PR #5916 adopts the native desktop themes there, continuing the work we did in Settings. Its current source uses @DesktopBuild(themeMode = "native", titleBar = DesktopTitleBar.NATIVE, ...), with interactive scrollbars. Fluent, Aqua and Adwaita now provide the surrounding control styles instead of a separate wizard-specific desktop imitation.

The same change fixes handling of an App ID's team prefix. That is a separate functional repair, not a consequence of adopting a theme. The wizard's current source keeps both changes visible.

Try the browser theme with a form that has real commands and enough content to scroll. Switch appearances, open its menus and check keyboard navigation. That will teach you more than another screenshot of an isolated button.

The weekly overview links the rest of the release. It also includes this week's smaller map-label improvement.

title: CedarDB brings its new online data management service
description:
CedarDB, a startup born from the Umbra research project at the Technical University of Munich, is bringing its PostgreSQL-compatible database to the cloud.

The platform is optimized for running high-speed analytical queries alongside daily transaction processing without additional memory overhead.

The move into the cloud marks a new phase for the team as they look to help enterprises query long-term transaction data using natural language.

According to Sichert, large companies have systems with many years of transaction data, but these cannot always quickly answer analytical questions formulated in everyday language.

CedarDB has been in development for about ten years and began as a research project at the Technical University of Munich, called Umbra. It was designed to run quickly without requiring more processors, more computing power, or more memory.

It is also compatible with PostgreSQL, which means customers don't have to rebuild their applications to use it, which reduces the cost of migration, according to Sichert.

READ ALSO

Eight US states take legal action against OpenAI over minors' safety

In May 2025, the company announced the free CedarDB Community Edition and CedarDB Enterprise, which is installed on customer premises. At the same time, it announced initial funding of 5,3 million euros, approximately $6 million.

CedarDB had been testing its online service with users on a waitlist. On October 14, 2026, it announced on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt that CedarDB Cloud is available to a limited number of users. The fully managed online version is expected to help the company reach more users beyond large enterprises.

In June, Databricks introduced LTAP, an architecture that aims to combine transactional, analytics, dataflow, and day-to-day operations data using a common data copy. Sichert sees the move as a sign that there is demand for CedarDB’s approach. However, it’s not yet clear how much of an impact it will have on the market.

CedarDB currently has 14 employees and plans to serve the first users of the online service with these. Sichert estimates that the company will need a larger team if it gains more traction. In that case, it will seek a new round of funding.
