title: Designing Tools Your AI Agent Will Actually Use Correctly
description:
The previous article showed how to wire tools into a Spring AI agent. The mechanics are straightforward — annotate a method, pass it to the ChatClient, done. What's less obvious is that the quality of your tools determines whether the agent works correctly.

A poorly described tool gets called at the wrong time, with the wrong arguments, or not at all. A well-designed tool gets called exactly when it should, with exactly the right input.

The description is an instruction to the model

When you write @Tool(description = "..."), that string isn't documentation for your team. It's a runtime instruction that the model reads before every single request.

The model's decision process looks like this:

  1. What did the user ask?
  2. What tools do I have available? (reads each description)
  3. Do I need a tool to answer this? Which one?
  4. What arguments should I pass? (reads each @ToolParam description)

If your description is vague, the model makes a guess. Sometimes the guess is right. Often it isn't — and because it's a language model, it won't tell you it was guessing. It will just proceed with what seemed most reasonable.

Vague description:

@Tool(description = "Get weather")
public String getWeather(String city) { ... }

The model doesn't know: Is this current weather or a forecast? What does it return — temperature? conditions? Both? What format is the city name expected in?

Clear description:

@Tool(description = "Get the current weather for a city in India. " +
    "Returns temperature in Celsius and sky conditions (sunny, cloudy, rainy). " +
    "Use this when the user asks about current weather or whether to carry an umbrella.")
public String getWeather(
        @ToolParam(description = "City name in English, e.g. Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru") 
        String city) { ... }

Now the model knows exactly when to call it, what it returns, and how to pass the city name. Same method, entirely different instruction.

What to include in a tool description

A useful tool description answers four questions:

What does it do? State the action clearly. "Fetches", "returns", "calculates", "queries" — be specific about the operation.

When should the model use it? This is the most commonly missed part. Add a "use this when..." clause. Without it, the model may skip the tool in cases where it should call it, because it isn't sure the tool applies.

What does it return? Describe the shape of the output. If it returns a price, say what currency. If it returns a date, say what format. If it returns a list, say roughly how many items.

What are the constraints? If the tool only works for certain inputs — cities in India, dates in the future, IDs that exist in the database — say that. The model will avoid calling it in unsupported cases, which prevents unnecessary tool failures.

Example applying all four:

@Tool(description = "Get the cheapest available bus or train ticket price between two cities in India. " +
    "Returns the price in INR and the transport type (bus or train). " +
    "Use this when the user asks about travel cost, ticket price, or how to get between cities. " +
    "Only works for cities with bus or rail connections — does not cover flights.")
public String getTicketPrice(
        @ToolParam(description = "Departure city name in English, e.g. Bengaluru") String from,
        @ToolParam(description = "Destination city name in English, e.g. Mysore") String to) {
    // ...
}

Writing good parameter descriptions

Parameter descriptions are just as important as the tool description. The model constructs arguments from them.

Be specific about format:

// Bad — model doesn't know what format to use
@ToolParam(description = "Date") String date

// Good — model knows exactly what to pass
@ToolParam(description = "Travel date in YYYY-MM-DD format, e.g. 2026-10-15") String date

Specify units:

// Bad
@ToolParam(description = "Budget") int amount

// Good
@ToolParam(description = "Maximum budget in INR, e.g. 5000") int amountInr

Clarify expected values for enums or limited options:

@ToolParam(description = "Seat class: SLEEPER, AC_3_TIER, or AC_2_TIER") String seatClass

When the model knows the exact expected values, it passes valid ones instead of guessing.

Returning results the model can reason about

Your tool's return value is what the model reads next. It uses that text to decide what to do — call another tool, ask a clarifying question, or produce the final answer.

Don't return raw JSON:

// Bad — the model has to parse this in its head
return "{\"temp\":28,\"condition\":\"PC\",\"humidity\":85}";

The model can handle JSON, but it has to mentally parse it first. That's cognitive overhead that introduces errors. Write the return value as natural language.

Return readable sentences:

// Good — the model reads this like a human would
return "Current weather in Mumbai: 28°C, partly cloudy, humidity 85%.";

Include context in the result:

If a tool fetches a price, include what the price is for. The model may call multiple tools and combine results — it needs context in each result to do that correctly.

// Without context — confusing when combined with other results
return "₹3,240";

// With context — clear when combined
return "Flight from Bengaluru to Goa on 2026-11-15: ₹3,240 (economy, non-stop, IndiGo 6E-502).";

Common failure modes

The model answers without calling the tool

This happens when the description doesn't say when to use the tool, and the model happens to know something relevant from training data. It answers directly, skipping the tool entirely.

Fix: add "Use this when..." to the description. Add to the system prompt: "Always use available tools to get current information — do not answer from memory."

The model calls the tool with the wrong argument format

A date tool receiving "15th October 2026" instead of "2026-10-15". A city tool receiving "Blr" instead of "Bengaluru".

Fix: specify the exact format in @ToolParam. Add examples: "e.g. 2026-10-15", "e.g. Bengaluru".

The model calls the wrong tool

Two tools with similar descriptions cause the model to mix them up. A getWeather and a getForecast tool with overlapping descriptions leads to unpredictable choices.

Fix: make descriptions explicitly distinct. State what each tool does NOT do: "Returns current conditions — for forecasts, use getForecast."

The tool returns an error and the model hallucinates a result

The tool throws an exception, returns an empty string, or returns an error message the model didn't expect. The model sees this as an unhelpful result and fabricates what the result probably would have been.

Fix: return meaningful error strings, not exceptions. "Unable to fetch weather for this city — city not found." is something the model can relay honestly to the user. An uncaught exception that surfaces as an empty result is something the model will try to paper over.

How many tools is too many?

There's no hard rule, but there's a practical limit. A model given 20 tools spends more time deciding which one to use. The chance of picking the wrong tool increases. The context window fills with tool definitions.

Keep tools focused. One tool should do one thing. A tool that fetches weather AND attractions AND ticket prices is three tools masquerading as one — split it.

Name tools clearly. The tool name is part of what the model reads. getWeather, getAttractions, getTicketPrice are clear. getData, fetch, process are not.

Remove tools the agent doesn't need. If a tool exists but the current use case will never need it, don't register it. Fewer tools mean faster, more accurate decisions.

Testing your tools

Tool quality is easy to verify. Ask questions that should and shouldn't trigger each tool, then inspect whether the right tools were called with the right arguments.

Three test cases every tool should pass:

Positive case — ask something that clearly requires this tool. Verify it was called and returned a sensible result.

Negative case — ask something unrelated. Verify the tool was NOT called.

Edge case — ask something ambiguous or with unusual input. Verify the arguments the model constructed are valid.

Add logging to each tool method during development:

@Tool(description = "...")
public String getWeather(@ToolParam(description = "City name") String city) {
    log.info("getWeather called with city={}", city);
    // ...
}

The log shows you exactly what the model passed. Wrong argument format? Fix the @ToolParam description. Tool not called at all? Fix the tool description or the system prompt.

What's next

Tools are methods. The agent loop runs them in sequence or parallel. But there's a limit to what single tool calls can do — some problems require a model to plan across many steps, remember intermediate results, and course-correct when something goes wrong. That's where more structured agent patterns come in.

The next article covers memory in agents — how to give your agent context from previous turns so it can handle multi-turn conversations, remember what it learned from earlier tool calls, and build on its own previous answers.

Sham Prakash K — Backend Engineer, 4+ years in Java, Spring Boot, and distributed systems. Building AI backend infrastructure. Writing about what I actually learned, mistakes included.

title: Designing an Audit Trail for Attendance Edits Without Overwriting Source Events
description:
An attendance correction looks like a simple update:

UPDATE attendance_records
SET clock_out_at = '2026-10-15T18:04:00+09:00'
WHERE id = 8412;

That query fixes the current row, but it also destroys the answer to several questions: What was recorded first? Who requested the correction? What evidence supported it? Who approved it? Which value was used for payroll before the change?

For systems that affect pay, deleting that context is a design problem. A safer model treats the original clock event as immutable and records corrections as a separate, reviewable trail.

Start with two different kinds of truth

Attendance software usually contains at least two truths:

  1. Observed truth: the raw event produced by a device, browser, QR scan, or administrator import.
  2. Operational truth: the approved interpretation used for schedules, overtime, and payroll.

Those values can disagree without either being useless. A raw 18:47 clock-out may be genuine, while an approved 18:00 work end may reflect an employee who forgot to clock out after changing clothes. The system should preserve both facts instead of rewriting one into the other.

In Korean workplaces, teams often search for these tools as 출퇴근기록기 (clock-in recorder) or 근태관리기 (attendance management tool). Whatever label the product uses, the important architectural question is the same: does a correction replace evidence, or does it add a decision to the evidence?

Model source events as append-only data

A source event should identify where it came from and when the server received it. Device time alone is not enough because a phone clock can be wrong or an offline client may synchronize later.

CREATE TABLE attendance_events (
  id                BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  event_type        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (event_type IN ('clock_in', 'clock_out')),
  occurred_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  received_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  source_type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  source_reference  TEXT,
  payload_hash      TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The application role that inserts these rows should not have permission to update or delete them. Retention and privacy rules may eventually require controlled deletion, but that should be a separate administrative process rather than an ordinary edit endpoint.

Put corrections in their own workflow

A correction request is not another clock event. It is a proposal to interpret one or more source events differently.

CREATE TABLE attendance_corrections (
  id                  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
  work_date           DATE NOT NULL,
  requested_clock_in  TIMESTAMPTZ,
  requested_clock_out TIMESTAMPTZ,
  reason_code         TEXT NOT NULL,
  reason_detail       TEXT,
  requested_by        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  requested_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  status              TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'approved', 'rejected', 'cancelled')),
  decided_by          BIGINT,
  decided_at          TIMESTAMPTZ,
  decision_note       TEXT
);

The correction should reference the affected source events through a join table. This matters when one workday has duplicate scans, a missing clock-out, or a shift that crosses midnight.

Build the effective record instead of mutating it

Read models can combine raw events with the latest approved correction. The calculation can live in a database view, a materialized projection, or an application service.

effective attendance
  = original source events
  + latest approved correction
  + policy version used for interpretation

Keeping the policy version is important. A record calculated under a 30-minute break rule should not silently change when the company later adopts a 45-minute rule.

For a practical example of the employee-facing recording flow, this attendance record management guide is useful context. The implementation detail to preserve is the boundary between captured events and later administrative decisions.

Make state transitions explicit

Do not let clients set any status they want. Define legal transitions in one domain function:

type Status = "pending" | "approved" | "rejected" | "cancelled";

const allowed: Record<Status, Status[]> = {
  pending: ["approved", "rejected", "cancelled"],
  approved: [],
  rejected: [],
  cancelled: [],
};

export function canTransition(from: Status, to: Status): boolean {
  return allowed[from].includes(to);
}

If an approved correction is wrong, create a new correction that supersedes it. Reopening and editing the old decision makes the audit trail ambiguous.

Protect the workflow from concurrency bugs

Two managers can open the same pending request and approve different values. Use optimistic locking or a conditional update:

UPDATE attendance_corrections
SET status = 'approved',
    decided_by = $1,
    decided_at = now()
WHERE id = $2
  AND status = 'pending';

The update must affect exactly one row. A zero-row result means the request was already handled and the client should refresh instead of pretending the approval succeeded.

For payroll export, store a snapshot identifier or cutoff time. Otherwise, an approval that arrives during export can create a file that cannot be reproduced later.

Log business meaning, not just HTTP requests

An infrastructure log saying PATCH /attendance/8412 200 is not enough. Emit a domain event with the decision context:

{
  "event": "attendance_correction_approved",
  "correction_id": 392,
  "employee_id": 117,
  "work_date": "2026-10-15",
  "previous_effective_clock_out": "2026-10-15T18:47:12+09:00",
  "new_effective_clock_out": "2026-10-15T18:00:00+09:00",
  "reason_code": "forgot_to_clock_out",
  "decided_by": 42,
  "policy_version": "attendance-policy-2026-09"
}

Avoid copying free-form notes, precise location data, or device identifiers into every analytics system. The audit store can retain necessary evidence with stricter access controls, while downstream events carry only the fields needed for operations.

Test invariants, not only endpoints

The most valuable tests assert properties that must remain true across refactors:

  • A source event cannot be updated through the normal application role.
  • A pending correction can be decided only once.
  • A rejected correction never changes the effective attendance record.
  • An approved correction does not erase the referenced source events.
  • Payroll export can be reproduced from a recorded cutoff and policy version.
  • A manager cannot approve a correction outside the manager's authorized team.

Property-based tests are particularly useful around overnight shifts, duplicate events, daylight-saving transitions, and late offline synchronization.

A small implementation checklist

Before shipping an attendance correction feature, verify that the system can answer these questions without reading application logs by hand:

  1. What did the employee or device originally submit?
  2. When did the server receive it?
  3. What replacement value was requested, and why?
  4. Who approved or rejected the request?
  5. Which policy version produced the payable result?
  6. Which version was included in a specific payroll export?

If any answer disappears after an edit, the design is still overwriting history.

The goal is not to implement event sourcing everywhere. It is to preserve the few boundaries that matter: observations remain observations, decisions remain decisions, and payroll results remain reproducible. That separation makes corrections easier to explain, safer to authorize, and much less painful to debug.

title: Frame Evidence:A Benchmark for Reference Frames and Visual Evidence in Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.19564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.

title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19475v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.

title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
description:
arXiv:2610.19206v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

title: 1Z0-078 Lists RAC First, but Your Cluster Is Built from the Bottom Up
description:
If you run Oracle databases on more than one server, you already know the order things happen in on a real cluster. Someone prepares the operating system, the shared disks and the networks. Then Grid Infrastructure goes on, which brings Oracle Clusterware and Oracle Automatic Storage Management with it. Only after that does anyone install the database software, and only after that does a RAC database exist to tune, patch and connect to.

Oracle's exam page for 1Z0-078 lists the same material in the opposite order. It starts with RAC databases and architecture, moves on to Grid Infrastructure in the middle, and ends with ASM disk groups, files and the ASM Cluster File System. That is a fine way to describe a job. It is a poor way to learn one, because almost every RAC objective assumes you understand the layers underneath it.

This article follows the build order instead. It is written for the DBA or systems administrator who already looks after clustered databases and wants to know whether 1Z0-078 matches the work on their desk. Every number in it comes from Oracle's own exam page and Oracle's 19c documentation, both checked on 15 October 2026.

What Is the Oracle 1Z0-078 RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Exam?

1Z0-078 is the exam behind the Oracle Certified Professional, Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administrator credential. Its full title on Oracle MyLearn is "Exam 1Z0-078: Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administration", and the official 1Z0-078 exam page on Oracle MyLearn is where the topic list, the format and the session rules live.

Oracle describes the audience plainly. The certification is for database production systems administrators and database administrators with 12 to 18 months of experience using RAC, ASM and Grid Infrastructure. The exam measures installation, configuration, backup and recovery, monitoring and tuning of those components. Read that as a description of who does well, not as an entry rule: the page states an experience profile, and it is worth being honest with yourself about whether you match it.

The three names in the title are three layers of one stack, and it helps to be precise about how they relate, because the exam is.

Grid Infrastructure: the base layer

Oracle's Introduction to Oracle Clusterware in the 19c Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide explains that Clusterware lets separate servers communicate so they appear to applications and users as one system. Since Oracle Clusterware 12c, the Clusterware and ASM binaries are installed as a single binary called Oracle Grid Infrastructure. The same guide notes that Clusterware 19c supports only ASM 19c, because ASM sits in the Grid Infrastructure home that also holds Clusterware.

Clusterware keeps two stored components besides its binaries. Voting files record node membership. The Oracle Cluster Registry, or OCR, records cluster configuration: databases, listeners, virtual IP addresses, services and any applications Clusterware manages. Both must sit on shared storage that every cluster node can reach.

ASM: the storage layer

ASM is Oracle's volume manager and file system for database files. Oracle's overview chapter of the 19c ASM Administrator's Guide describes disk groups made of disks, files and allocation units, with normal redundancy giving two-way mirroring, high redundancy three-way mirroring, and external redundancy leaving the mirroring to a RAID subsystem.

RAC: the database layer

Oracle RAC lets several instances open one database. The RAC guide says that having multiple instances access a single database prevents the server from being a single point of failure, and that applications deployed on RAC databases can operate without code changes. RAC depends on Clusterware; the guide calls Clusterware a required component that provides the infrastructure RAC runs on.

So the order on the exam page is top-down, while the order on a real system is bottom-up. Hold on to that idea. It shapes the study plan later in this article.

1Z0-078 Exam Overview and Details

The format is short to state. Everything below is from Oracle's exam page unless marked otherwise.

  • Exam code: 1Z0-078
  • Exam name: Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administration
  • Credential: Oracle Certified Professional, Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administrator
  • Delivery: Proctored Online
  • Format: Multiple Choice
  • Duration: 120 minutes
  • Number of questions: 77
  • Passing score: 65%
  • Price: Oracle's page shows no price to a signed-out visitor. The DBExam syllabus page lists USD $245 and notes that pricing may vary by country or local currency; confirm the figure in your Oracle account at checkout.

What 77 questions in 120 minutes means at the desk

120 minutes across 77 questions is about 93 seconds a question. That is generous for a question that asks you to recognise a view name and tight for one that describes a failed node, a set of services and a client configuration, then asks what the client sees. Plan to move quickly through recall questions so the scenario questions get the time they need.

A 65% passing score on 77 questions works out to just over 50 correct answers, if every question counts the same. Oracle does not publish how it weights individual questions, so treat 51 as a planning number rather than a rule, and aim well above it.

Session rules worth knowing in advance

  • A government-issued identification is required to take the exam.
  • Check-in time is 30 minutes before the exam time.
  • Your computer must meet Oracle's minimum system requirements for online proctoring.
  • Results are shown on screen at the close of the exam, and the detailed score report is in Oracle CertView.
  • To reschedule, you must do it at least 24 hours before your appointment time.

None of these is unusual, but the 30-minute check-in catches people who block exactly two hours in their calendar. Block three.

Key Topics and Syllabus for 1Z0-078

Oracle's exam page lists 30 topics and 115 objective lines under three groupings. The first grouping has no heading of its own on the page; it is the RAC material. Then come the headings "Grid Infrastructure Administration" and "Automatic Storage Management (ASM) Administration". Counted line by line:

  • RAC administration: 12 topics, 49 objective lines
  • Grid Infrastructure administration: 11 topics, 41 objective lines
  • ASM administration: 7 topics, 25 objective lines

One caution before you use those counts: Oracle publishes no percentage weights for 1Z0-078. A line count shows where the page spends its words, not how many questions each area gets. The 1Z0-078 syllabus on DBExam sets the same topics out on one page with the exam facts beside them, which is handy as a checklist.

Here is the syllabus in the order you would build the system, bottom layer first.

Layer 1: Grid Infrastructure and Clusterware (11 topics)

The Grid Infrastructure grouping covers the life of the cluster itself:

  • Introduction to Clusterware and Oracle Clusterware architecture, including startup details and how Grid Plug and Play affects Clusterware
  • Flex Clusters and the effect of node failure in one
  • Installation planning and pre-tasks: system and network requirements, groups, users and directories
  • Grid Infrastructure installation, verifying it, configuring ASM disk groups, and the optional Grid Infrastructure Management Repository
  • Managing cluster nodes: extending a cluster, deleting a node, and adding nodes with DBCA
  • Traditional Clusterware management: day-to-day tasks, OCR backup and recovery, network settings, what-if command evaluation and secure cluster communication
  • Policy-based cluster management: server categorization, policy sets and activating a policy
  • Upgrading and patching Grid Infrastructure, including rolling patches and zero-downtime Grid Infrastructure patching
  • Troubleshooting Clusterware: log files, diagcollection.pl, resource and component debugging, and OCR problems
  • Making applications highly available with Clusterware: policy-managed and administrator-managed databases, application VIPs and application resources

Two documented facts from this layer tend to matter. First, Oracle recommends no more than five voting files, although Clusterware supports up to 15. Second, you can have up to five OCR locations, and you can replace a failed OCR location online as long as it is not the only one. Small numbers like these make good exam distractors, so learn them exactly.

Flex Clusters have their own rules in the Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide: a Flex Cluster can have as many as 64 Hub Nodes, Hub Nodes have direct access to shared storage and host read-write instances, other nodes request data through Hub Nodes and host read-only instances, Flex Clusters require Grid Naming Service, and you can convert a standard cluster to a Flex Cluster but not the reverse.

Layer 2: ASM, ACFS and ADVM (7 topics)

The ASM grouping is the shortest, but it sits under everything else:

  • ASM architecture and components
  • ASM instances: initialization parameters, processes, and monitoring with the V$ASM dynamic performance views
  • Flex ASM: architecture, installation, configuration and management
  • Disk groups: creating, dropping, setting attributes, maintenance, and performance and scalability considerations
  • Files, directories and templates, including the format of a fully qualified ASM file name
  • Oracle CloudFS: the ASM Dynamic Volume Manager, ASM volumes, ACFS and ACFS snapshots
  • CloudFS advanced topics: ACFS auditing, encryption, replication and tagging, and High Availability NFS

The file name objective is a good example of how literal the exam can be. Oracle's chapter on ASM files, directories and templates gives the form as +diskgroup/dbname/filetype/filetypetag.file.incarnation in a non-multitenant database, and +diskgroup/cdb/pdb_guid/filetype/filetypetag.file.incarnation with multitenant. Alias names are told apart because they do not end in a dotted pair of numbers. If you can read +DATA/ORCL/DATAFILE/system.257.967544915 and name every field, that objective is done.

Flex ASM gets three objective lines. The key documented behaviour is in Oracle's Managing Oracle Flex ASM chapter: a small set of ASM instances serves the whole cluster, the number is set with a cardinality setting, and the default is three instances. The ASM overview adds why it matters: in a standard ASM cluster, if the ASM instance on a node fails, the database instances on that node fail too, while with Flex ASM a database instance can reach another ASM instance on another node.

Layer 3: The RAC database (12 topics)

RAC gets the most objective lines, and it is where most candidates already feel at home:

  • RAC architecture: the benefits of RAC, why global resources are needed, and global cache coordination
  • Installing and configuring RAC, creating a cluster database, and converting a single-instance database to RAC
  • Administering RAC: redo log files, undo tablespaces, starting and stopping, and initialization parameters
  • Backup and recovery: ARCHIVELOG mode, the fast recovery area, and RMAN in a RAC environment
  • Global resources: the Global Resource Directory, global enqueue and instance locks, global buffer cache management, and affinity
  • Monitoring and tuning: RAC wait events, AWR and ADDM in RAC, the Cluster Database Performance pages, and SGA runtime management
  • High availability of services, and high availability for connections and applications: load balancing, the Load Balancing Advisory, FAN, TAF, Transparent Application Continuity and Dynamic Services Fallback
  • Upgrading and patching RAC with OUI and opatch
  • RAC One Node conversions in both directions
  • Quality of Service Management
  • Multitenant in RAC: CDBs, PDBs, PDB services and server pools, and automated PDB patching and relocation

The connections topic is the largest single topic on the page, with eight objective lines. That fits what happens on the job: users rarely notice a cluster until a node goes away and their session either survives or does not.

1Z0-078 Preparation Guide

The practitioner's advantage on this exam is that you can study it the way you would build it. A bottom-up plan means every new topic rests on one you have already worked through, and it keeps you from memorising RAC behaviour that you cannot explain.

Step 1: Build or borrow a lab you can break

Reading alone will not carry you through 77 questions on clustered systems. You need a two-node lab, or access to one, where you can stop Clusterware, pull a node, fill a disk group and watch what happens. Keep a log of each test. When a question later describes a symptom, you will have seen it.

Step 2: Start with Grid Infrastructure

Begin with the installation planning topics, because the exam asks about them directly and because they force you to understand the networks a cluster needs. Then install Grid Infrastructure and walk the startup sequence until you can explain what starts before what.

Spend real time on the OCR and voting files. Oracle's 19c documentation has a detail worth noticing here. The Clusterware guide says Clusterware files must be stored on ASM, yet the 19c changes page of the RAC Administration and Deployment Guide records that, starting with Grid Infrastructure 19c, the desupport of direct placement of OCR and voting files on shared file systems is rescinded for Oracle Standalone Clusters. Know both statements and which cluster type each applies to; that is exactly the kind of distinction a question can turn on.

Finish the layer with OCR backup and recovery, node addition and deletion, and policy-based management. Server pools come back later in the RAC topics, so understanding them here saves time.

Step 3: Move to ASM

Create disk groups at each redundancy level and look at the result. Oracle's ASM overview gives you rules you can test in a lab:

  • Normal redundancy disk groups require at least two failure groups, and high redundancy disk groups at least three.
  • If you omit the failure group specification, ASM places each disk in its own failure group (Exadata cells excepted).
  • You cannot alter the redundancy level of a disk group after it is created.
  • Allocation unit sizes can be 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 MB, depending on the disk group compatibility level.
  • ASM starts a rebalance automatically after you add, drop or resize disks, the power setting controls its speed, and databases can stay operational while it runs.

Then set up Flex ASM, change its cardinality, and work through ACFS: a volume, a file system on it, a snapshot, and at least one of the advanced features. The CloudFS topics hold nine objective lines between them, which is more than many candidates expect from the storage side.

Step 4: Finish with RAC

Now the RAC topics read as consequences of what sits underneath. Oracle's Introduction to Oracle RAC in the 19c RAC guide covers the ideas the exam builds on:

  • Cache Fusion uses the private interconnect for communication between instances, which is why the guide tells you not to use the interconnect for user traffic.
  • The Global Cache Service and the Global Enqueue Service coordinate buffer cache blocks and enqueues in the Global Resource Directory.
  • SCAN is a single network name, in DNS or Grid Naming Service, that round-robins to three IP addresses, and Oracle recommends that all client connections use it.
  • DBCA creates one default database service, which Oracle says should be reserved for maintenance; you create dynamic services for application connections.
  • RAC One Node runs a single instance of a RAC-enabled database on one node under normal operations, can relocate online with no downtime for users, and needs at least one dynamic database service.

Work the connection topics in the lab with a real client. Configure services, kill an instance, and watch what FAN, TAF and Application Continuity do. Then cover backup and recovery, tuning with AWR and ADDM, patching, and the multitenant topics.

Step 5: Read the objectives back as questions

In the last week, go through all 115 objective lines and turn each into a question you could answer out loud. "Explain the scope and capabilities of what-if command evaluation" becomes "what does SRVCTL evaluate mode report, and when would I run it?" Any line you cannot answer goes back to the lab.

Benefits and Career Scope of the 1Z0-078 Certification

The honest benefit of 1Z0-078 is that it names, in an employer's language, work that is otherwise hard to show on paper. A résumé line that says "supported RAC" can mean anything from running one SRVCTL command to rebuilding a cluster after a failed patch. An Oracle Certified Professional credential for RAC, ASM and Grid Infrastructure tells a reader that you were tested on the whole stack, including the storage and cluster layers that many database administrators never touch directly.

It also changes the work you get asked to do. Teams that run clustered Oracle databases need people who can plan an installation, patch Grid Infrastructure with minimal downtime, recover the OCR, and explain to an application team why their sessions dropped during a node failure. Those tasks map directly onto the exam topics, so preparing for the exam and becoming the person who handles those tickets are the same project.

There are limits worth stating. The credential is tied to Oracle Database 19c, and this article quotes no salary figures, because none comes from an official source. Oracle's exam page carried no retirement notice on 15 October 2026; check it again before you book, because Oracle updates its catalog.

The study itself has value even if you never sit the exam. Working through every objective line usually turns up at least one area, often ACFS, QoS Management or policy-based cluster management, that your current environment does not use and that you would otherwise meet for the first time during an incident.

Practice Test and Preparation Resources for 1Z0-078

Oracle's exam page links its recommended training. Three Oracle University courses on MyLearn line up with the three groupings of the syllabus, and their course pages show the module count and running time:

  • Oracle Database 19c: Clusterware Administration Workshop: 13 modules, 12 h 18 min, covering Clusterware architecture, cluster configuration options, preinstallation and installation, node management, policy-based management, patching, troubleshooting and application high availability.
  • Oracle Database 19c: ASM Administration Workshop: 13 modules, 8 h 7 min, covering ASM instances, Flex ASM, disk groups, files and templates, and ACFS with ADVM.
  • Oracle Database 19c: RAC Administration Workshop: 14 modules, 20 h 11 min, covering installation, administration, patching, backup and recovery, tuning, services, connection high availability, RAC One Node, multitenant and QoS in RAC.

Together that is about 40 hours of video before any lab time. Taken in the order listed, Clusterware first and RAC last, the courses follow the same bottom-up path as this article.

Oracle's documentation

The 19c guides are free and they are the source the exam objectives are written against. Keep three open while you study: the Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide, the Automatic Storage Management Administrator's Guide, and the Real Application Clusters Administration and Deployment Guide. When a course and a guide seem to disagree, the guide for your exact release wins.

Practice questions

Once each layer is done, test it. The free 1Z0-078 sample questions on DBExam show the multiple-choice style and make a quick check after a study block. A full timed practice exam is the better rehearsal for the 93-second pace, and DBExam offers one for 1Z0-078 alongside the free set. Use the score report to send you back to specific topics rather than retaking until the number looks good.

A short video on working through answer options

The DBExam YouTube channel has no 1Z0-078 video yet. The walk-through below is about a different Oracle exam, 1Z0-149 on PL/SQL programming, but its method carries over: read every option, rule out the ones that contradict a documented fact, and only then choose.

Conclusion

1Z0-078 lists its 30 topics with RAC first, Grid Infrastructure second and ASM last. A working cluster is built the other way round, and the most reliable way to prepare is to follow the build: Clusterware and the OCR and voting files, then ASM disk groups, Flex ASM and ACFS, then the RAC database, its services and its clients.

The format is fixed and published: 77 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes, a 65% passing score, delivered online with a proctor. The topic list is long but concrete, and almost every line can be practised in a two-node lab. If the work it describes is the work on your desk, the exam mostly asks you to prove you understand why that work is done the way it is.

FAQs

How many questions are on the 1Z0-078 exam, and how long do I get?

Oracle's exam page lists 77 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes and a 65% passing score. That is about 93 seconds a question. The exam is delivered as Proctored Online.

Does Oracle publish topic weights for 1Z0-078?

No. The exam page lists 30 topics with 115 objective lines: 49 for RAC, 41 for Grid Infrastructure and 25 for ASM. Those are line counts, not percentages, so use them to judge coverage, not to predict how many questions each area will get.

Where can the OCR and voting files live in Grid Infrastructure 19c?

Oracle's Clusterware guide says both must sit on shared storage reachable by every node, and that Clusterware files must be stored on ASM. The 19c changes page of the RAC guide adds that, from Grid Infrastructure 19c, the desupport of placing OCR and voting files directly on shared file systems is rescinded for Oracle Standalone Clusters. Learn both statements and the cluster type each one covers.

What is the default number of ASM instances in Flex ASM?

Three. Oracle's Managing Oracle Flex ASM chapter says the number of ASM instances is set with a cardinality setting and that the default is three instances. You can change it with SRVCTL.

Do I have to take Oracle's training before I book 1Z0-078?

The exam page offers recommended training: the Clusterware, ASM and RAC administration workshops on MyLearn, about 40 hours combined. The page does not state a course requirement. Check Oracle's Certification Program Guidelines for the credential before you book.

What should I bring to the online 1Z0-078 session?

A government-issued identification, a computer that meets Oracle's minimum system requirements, and a testing space that meets Oracle's rules. Check in 30 minutes before the exam time. Your result appears on screen at the end, and the detailed score report is in Oracle CertView. If you need to reschedule, do it at least 24 hours before your appointment.

title: Java Data Types in AI Applications
description:
Introduction

Java data types define the kind of data a variable can store.

They help developers organize and process information correctly.

In AI applications, data types manage user prompts, AI responses, scores, and processing results.

Choosing the correct data type makes code easier to understand and maintain.

What Are Java Data Types?

Java data types specify the type of value a variable can hold, such as text, numbers, or Boolean values.

Syntax / Example 

String prompt = "Explain Artificial Intelligence";
int tokenCount = 100;
double confidenceScore = 0.95;
boolean responseGenerated = true;

System.out.println(prompt);
System.out.println(tokenCount);
System.out.println(confidenceScore);
System.out.println(responseGenerated);

Practical Example

In an AI chatbot, String stores the user's prompt, int stores a token count, double stores a numerical score, and boolean indicates whether a response was generated.

Key Takeaways

  • String stores text.
  • int stores whole numbers.
  • double stores decimal numbers.
  • boolean stores true or false.
  • Choosing suitable data types improves code clarity.

Conclusion

Java data types are the foundation of data handling in AI applications. They help developers manage different kinds of information efficiently. Understanding them is an important step toward building Java-based GenAI projects.

Question: Which Java data type would you use to store an AI-generated response?

Thanks for reading! 🚀

Follow me on DEV Community for more Java, GenAI, and software development tutorials.

Follow me: @manikandan4411

title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
description:
arXiv:2610.19731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.
