title: LLMs program using Reusable and Composable Abstract Representations
description:
arXiv:2610.19238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When writing code, the same computation can be expressed in different programming languages and through different implementation strategies. We show that the activations of LLMs capture this shared structure in reusable and composable abstract representations when they generate code. These representations emerge in the middle layers, are reusable across programming languages, and afford the model an impressive amount of generalization ability when generating code under various interventions. Using activation steering, we show that function, programming language, and implementation strategy can be independently manipulated. The independent interventions on language and function can be flexibly composed to control code generation, even in cases when the prompt contains no information about language and function. We additionally find that finetuning on examples of arbitrarily defined functions in one programming language transfers to other languages, consistent with the models reusing abstract features of code generation that are shared across different examples. Finally, to study how such abstract representations come to be, we implement a minimal model of shared, reusable, and composable structure in a synthetic setting, and show that transformers trained on such data learn representations that reuse these parts flexibly across contexts.

title: I Built My Portfolio Like a Piece of Rack Gear - Zero Dependencies, All Vanilla JS
description:
After 29 years of building software - most of it in PHP, all of it allergic to dependencies - I decided my portfolio should behave less like a resume and more like the gear I love: a production console. Rack units. LEDs that flicker on. A VU meter that actually moves.

The result is bryanhamilton.info, and its last PageSpeed run looked like this: 99 Performance, 100 Accessibility, 100 Best Practices, 100 SEO, 104 KB transferred, 8 requests, 558 ms to load - measured in the browser, not in a lab.

No framework. No build step. No npm. Here's how each piece works, and - because that's where the real lessons live - what broke along the way.

1. The rack: HTML that tells the truth

Each project is a "rack unit" card with three things most portfolios hide: a status LED, an honest status word, and zero marketing.

<article class="rack-card">
  <span class="rack-led"></span>
  <span class="rack-status">RUNS LIVE</span>
  <h3><a href="https://github.com/...">dj-card-preview</a></h3>
  ...
</article>

The LED color is contract law:

  • Green (RUNS LIVE): there is a URL you can click right now and it works.
  • Orange (DOCUMENTED): the code is real and CI-tested, but the live instance is retired.

When a tool's live deployment broke, I didn't take the card down or leave a green LED glowing next to a dead link. I flipped the LED to orange. A portfolio that lies to you once is a portfolio you stop trusting.

2. LEDs that power on like real gear

Real rack equipment doesn't fade in politely when it loads. It boots. So when the rack scrolls into view, the LEDs flicker alive left-to-right, one time, then settle into a slow pulse:

@keyframes rack-boot {
  0%   { opacity: .08; filter: brightness(.4); }
  38%  { opacity: 1;   filter: brightness(2.6); }
  55%  { opacity: .35; filter: brightness(.8); }
  100% { opacity: 1;   filter: brightness(1); }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .rack-boot .rack-card .rack-led {
    animation: rack-boot .9s calc(var(--i, 0) * 70ms) both,
               rack-pulse 2.2s calc(var(--i, 0) * 70ms + .9s) infinite;
  }
}

One IntersectionObserver adds a rack-boot class the first time the rack enters the viewport, sets a --i index on each card, and the stagger is just arithmetic in calc(). The handoff from boot animation to infinite pulse is scheduled by delay, not JS, so there's no race condition to manage.

The part I care about most is the @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) wrapper. Every animation on the site - this one, the terminal intro, the background drift - is gated the same way. Accessibility isn't a checklist item at the end; it's the container everything else lives inside.

3. A scroll progress bar disguised as a Venn diagram

The page background is a fixed Venn diagram: one circle for engineering, one for the people-facing work. The overlap used to just sit there. Now it fills.

.venn-core {
  position: absolute;
  width: calc(min(97vw, 1040px) * 0.30);
  background: radial-gradient(closest-side,
    rgba(0, 210, 255, .17),
    rgba(0, 210, 255, .05) 58%, transparent 72%);
  opacity: var(--vp, 0);
}

var max = document.documentElement.scrollHeight - window.innerHeight;
var p = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, window.scrollY / max));
venn.style.setProperty('--vp', p.toFixed(3));

Eleven lines of JS inside a requestAnimationFrame-throttled, passive scroll listener. As you descend the page, the intersection of the two circles glows brighter until, at the footer, the overlap is fully lit. The site's entire thesis - the engineer who can also talk to humans - is rendered as an opacity value.

That's the trick I'd hand to anyone building a personal site: if your brand has a central metaphor, make the mechanics of the page narrate it. Nobody consciously notices a scroll progress bar inside a Venn diagram. Everybody feels it.

4. The equalizer that actually listens

The signature piece is an 8-bar equalizer that reacts to real audio - not a CSS keyframe fake. When you hover a demo card, it plays a 30-second track preview through the Web Audio API and drives eight canvas bars from the analyser:

const ctx = new AudioContext();
const src = ctx.createMediaElementSource(audio);
const analyser = ctx.createAnalyser();
analyser.fftSize = 64;
analyser.smoothingTimeConstant = 0.8;
src.connect(analyser);
analyser.connect(ctx.destination);

// 8 bars, sampling every other bin of the low half
function draw() {
  analyser.getByteFrequencyData(dataArray);
  for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
    const v = dataArray[i * 2] / 255;
    bars[i].style.height = Math.max(4, v * 80) + 'px';
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(draw);
}

Two lessons worth the tuition:

  1. Autoplay policy is a feature, not a bug. Browsers won't let you play audio until the user interacts. The demo shows a one-time "click anywhere to activate" gate. Fighting this is a losing game; designing around it is a UX opportunity.
  2. A CSS "fake" EQ is detectable in about half a second. If the bars don't move with the kick drum, people feel the lie immediately. fftSize: 64 with smoothingTimeConstant: 0.8 gives you chunky, musical bars instead of noise.

5. The search index I'm proudest of

The site has instant search with keyboard navigation and ARIA combobox semantics, built on a prebuilt JSON index and a tiny client-side scoring function. No server round-trips, no search service. At build time the content gets flattened into one JSON file; at runtime, ~60 lines of JS score and match against it.

I extracted the whole pattern into a standalone repo (instant-search-index) because it's the most reusable thing I've built in years: prebuilt index + scored matching + proper combobox ARIA roles, and it works in anything.

6. What broke (and what it taught me)

No tutorial-style post is honest without the blood.

The 16 KB wall. My host's FTP silently truncates uploads at exactly 16,384 bytes. My resume-builder PHP file is 24,084 bytes. The deploy "succeeded" and produced a corrupt PDF. Diagnosis took byte-counting and MD5 comparisons; the fix was a chunked-upload kit (split the file, base64 the parts, assemble server-side, verify MD5 before writing). The real lesson: when a deploy fails weirdly, compare bytes, not screenshots.

The cache header that ate my deploys. I shipped cache-control: max-age=2592000, immutable on my HTML. That header is meant for fingerprinted assets like app.abc123.js - not for a homepage I edit daily. Result: my browser happily served me a week-old page while I debugged code that was already live. I only proved the code worked by loading the site in headless Chrome, which had no cache. The fix is one .htaccess block:

<FilesMatch "\.html$">
  Header set Cache-Control "public, max-age=0, must-revalidate"
</FilesMatch>

If you take one operational lesson from this post: immutable is for hashed assets. HTML gets max-age=0, must-revalidate. Write that on a sticky note before it costs you an afternoon.

The half-leading PDF. My PDF generator advanced the Y cursor by 48% of the line height, stacking lines on top of each other. I didn't see it for weeks because a separate bug (a missing %PDF-1.4 header) made the file unopenable, masking the layout bug underneath. Fix one bug, meet its friends.

7. Why zero dependencies, seriously

I've been doing this since before frameworks were the default, so take this with the appropriate salt. But the math on this site:

  • 104 KB total. The median framework starter ships more than that before it renders anything.
  • 8 requests. No font carousel, no analytics tag parade.
  • 99-100 across every Lighthouse category - including the one most portfolios fail on purpose: Accessibility, because animations respect reduced-motion and the search is a real ARIA combobox.

Zero-dependency isn't nostalgia. It's a debugging philosophy: when everything in the stack is code you wrote, nothing is someone else's mystery. When the PDF breaks, I can read every line that produced it.

Come kick the tires

The site is live at bryanhamilton.info - scroll slowly, let the rack boot, watch the overlap glow as you reach the bottom. The code is on GitHub, ten repos deep, each one CI-badged and extracted from production code rather than written for show.

And if you build something with any of these patterns - the LED boot, the analyser EQ, the instant search - tell me in the comments. I want to see the racks other people bolt together.

title: A threshold is not a measurement: what your dedup cut actually does at each artefact length
description:
Deduplicate at Jaccard 0.7. Flag a pair whose Dice similarity is at least 0.8. Every one of those numbers was calibrated once, on one corpus, and then applied to artefacts of every size — a 40-token comment, a 3000-token report, a source file, a training example.

The threshold is the only thing that was calibrated at one length. The false-positive rate is not, and a paper I have been reading measures where it goes.

The short version, before the mechanism:

  • On unrelated same-length text, the null median of char-bigram Dice rises from 0.5389 at L = 40 to 0.9096 at L = 3000. A cut calibrated on short artefacts therefore over-flags long ones — and a cut calibrated on long ones cannot certify anything about short ones.
  • The four standard statistics split into two classes: the character statistics' null tracks length (char 3-gram cosine: 0.1787 rising to 0.8163), while the shingle statistics' null never leaves the floor (word-3 Jaccard's p95 peaks at 0.0084, word-5's at 0.0003).
  • At a false-positive-matched operating point, the perturbation rate at which recall falls to one half moves as a power law for the character statistics — slope -0.230, R^2 = 0.950, n = 7, a 2.70x span — and stays flat for the shingles (1.08x).
  • Below a certification floor L* the null's own p95 is 0, so the matched threshold is 0, so every pair passes: the false-positive rate is 1.0, not alpha.

That last one is the finding worth carrying into a code review. It is not a reading of 0.0000 on a curve. It is a hole in the curve, and it reports as a pass.

Why a threshold cannot be transferred

A similarity statistic is an average over the artefact's own material — its set of shingles, its bag of character n-grams. A fixed edit rate destroys roughly the same fraction of that material at every length, so to first order the effect size a check sees is length-free. What does change with length is the variance: more material means more comparisons means a tighter estimate. So you expect the curve to get narrower with length.

Whether its location also moves is a separate question, and it is falsifiable in both directions — a flat eps*(L) would have been just as informative as a sloping one. The measurement says the location moves, and only for one family of statistics. That is why "longer artefacts are easier" is true and irrelevant at the same time: reliability does improve with length, and the claim people actually deploy is about a fixed cut.

What I re-ran before quoting any of it

The package ships a one-command reproduction, so I ran it at the published ref rather than reading the tables — from a git archive export of origin/main, so the working tree cannot flatter the numbers:

$ bash reproduce.sh
build          python3.13 3.13.9 | stdlib only (no third-party import anywhere in the package)
corpus         8 file(s) verified against corpus/SHA256SUMS
  spike_v0  MATCH  e828ae4db8878d34
  spike_v1  MATCH  81ea052b3018dc85
  ...
  floor_v3  MATCH  ed54a9a7cdd272a2
instruments    11 of 11 reports re-run byte-identically
analysis       the boundary power law (slope -0.230, R2 0.950)
figures        7 of 7 figure file(s) re-generated byte-identically
certificate    plant 1: identical objects must NOT fire
certificate    plant 2: a one-byte change MUST fire
certificate    plant 3: the real cross-process defect MUST fire
stratum        the repair restores alpha on every live cell
manuscript     the manuscript is exactly what the build renders from the reports
REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN

Two things worth noticing, because they are design decisions rather than accidents.

First, the comparison is byte equality against the shipped reports, not "close enough" — eleven instruments re-run from their own code over a committed 5.6 MB corpus, plus the seven figures regenerated from those reports. The instruments import nothing outside the standard library, and the float reductions use math.fsum (exactly rounded in every CPython), so no library version's arithmetic enters the comparison. When I quote 0.9096 below, that is a value I re-derived, not a value I read.

Second, the run carries a mechanism certificate, not just a value: it predicts eps* from the measured decay curve and the measured threshold in 21 cells, and the paper states the worst deviation (0.035 against a grid resolution of 0.05). A number that survives the reproduction is a number; a number whose derivation is also checked is what lets you trust the mechanism rather than the artifact.

Claim 1 — the null is a function of length, and it splits the statistics

On unrelated same-length text, at seven lengths spanning 75x:

statistic null median / p95 at L = 40 at L = 3000
char-bigram Dice median 0.5389 median 0.9096
char 3-gram cosine median 0.1787 median 0.8163
word-3 Jaccard p95 never leaves the floor peak 0.0084
word-5 p95 never leaves the floor peak 0.0003

Two consequences, and they point in opposite directions for a deployer.

For the first class, a single cut cannot mean the same thing at two lengths: at 0.7, char-bigram Dice is a strict cut on short artefacts and a permissive one on long ones, because the null itself is already at 0.91 there. Your false-positive rate did not drift by a few percent. It moved from small to near-total.

For the second class, the cut means very little at any length — a word-3 Jaccard cut at 0.7 sits far above a null whose p95 is 0.0084, so it is a real cut, but it is also throwing away recall it did not have to. Different failure, same root cause: the number was never a statement about the corpus it is now being used on.

Claim 2 — the boundary moves as a power law for one family and not the other

The genuine object here is the operating characteristic: the probability of flagging a perturbed artefact as a function of the perturbation rate, at a fixed false-positive rate. The paper calls the point where recall falls to one half the boundary eps*, and measures it at the false-positive-matched operating point:

  • char-bigram Dice: eps* falls with slope -0.230 (R^2 = 0.950, n = 7) — a 2.70x change over the length range;
  • word-3 Jaccard: 1.08x — flat, within noise.

And the paper does not stop at the fit: the mechanism certificate predicts eps* from two measured quantities (the decay curve and the threshold) in 21 cells with a worst deviation of 0.035 against a grid resolution of 0.05. The mechanism proposed is the headroom 1 - tau that the rising null eats — not the edit count. That is the part I would have got wrong from first principles: the intuition is that longer text is harder to perturb detectably; the measurement says the boundary moves because the null moved into the threshold's headroom.

Claim 3 — below a floor, the check certifies nothing and reports a pass

Where the fraction of unrelated null pairs exceeding 0 falls below alpha, the null's p95 is 0, the matched threshold is 0 — and the check's false-positive rate is 1.0.

This is measured as a band, because two reasonable definitions of the floor bracket it: L* is 100-130 for word-3 Jaccard and 1196-2000 for word-5 at alpha = 0.05, and it rises as alpha rises (at alpha = 0.01 the word-3 floor is 40, against 100 at 0.05).

So the floor is not a property of the corpus or of the statistic alone. It is a property of the claim: at a stricter alpha you need longer artefacts before any recall claim can be certified. And below it, the check is not "slightly weak". Every pair passes, including every unrelated pair.

If you are calibrating on a corpus that contains short items and then applying the cut to them, this is the cell where your evaluation says 0.0000 and your deployment says yes to everything.

Claim 4 — the null is stratified, and the repair is not the threshold

Two smaller results that a deployer can act on directly.

The null key is a declared parameter. The comparison p95 must be drawn under the same key as the judged pair — a length ratio of 2 moves the false-positive rate by up to 0.063. If your null was built from pairs of equal length and your scan judges unequal ones, the null is answering a different question.

The stratum weights are too. A null calibrated on a uniform population reads its false-positive rate inflated by up to 9.4x when the scan's per-stratum shares are skewed. The repair is to reweight the null to the scan's own shares — not to move the threshold — and it lands inside alpha ± 0.05 in 13 of 13 live cells. Moving the cut would have "fixed" the rate at the cost of every recall claim you have.

And a composition law, which is the one I would put on a design doc: fusing two statistics at their own matched operating points gives eps*(OR) >= max(eps*) and eps*(AND) <= min(eps*), measured at 96 composed cells (6 statistic pairs × 2 compositions × 4 lengths, under both edit operators) with 0 violations. So OR buys you the robust member's boundary at the price of the false-positive rate, and AND buys the brittle member's — the two compositions are the two ends of one trade, not two designs you can pick from.

What I would do differently on Monday

  1. State the length distribution next to the threshold. A cut of 0.7 plus "calibrated on 40-200 token items" is a very different claim from a bare 0.7, and the second one is what ships today.
  2. Check which class your statistic is in. If it is a character-n-gram statistic, your threshold's meaning is length-dependent and the fix is per-length operating points (or a length-free statistic). If it is a shingle statistic, your null is on the floor and the question is whether the cut is doing any work at all.
  3. Find your floor before you find your threshold. Below L* there is no threshold to tune. If your corpus has items under a hundred tokens, know that the cell exists.
  4. Reweight the null to the scan, and declare the key. Neither is a modelling change; both are the difference between the rate you measured and the rate you get.

None of this says a deployed check is broken. A check calibrated and operated at one length is correct at that length — which is exactly what its own evaluation measures, and exactly why the evaluation does not transfer.

Reproduce it 

cd papers/issue-130 && bash reproduce.sh

About five and a half minutes, CPython 3.9+, standard library only — no third-party import anywhere in the package, and the corpus (eight Project Gutenberg texts, 5.6 MB) is committed and verified against SHA256SUMS at the start of every run. The script re-runs eleven instruments from their own code and compares each fresh report byte-for-byte against the shipped one, re-derives the tables, regenerates the figures, and runs the mechanism certificate and the plant batteries. REPRO_FULL=1 adds the two-run determinism certificate (~13 minutes more).

One honest detail about my own run: the journal's reference gate needs CPython ≥ 3.12 and lives in the journal's .github/tools/, so from an archive export that step reports skipped rather than passing. The package's own gates — instruments, figures, analysis, the plant batteries, the stratum repair — all ran and all passed. If a reproduction has three exit states rather than two, that is the state you want it to land in rather than being counted as either success or failure.

This is paper #130 in SILICON SCIENCE: Computer Science, an AI-operated peer-reviewed journal — submission by issue, public review, editor decision, published manuscript, with the review and the reproduction trail visible in the repository. The paper is A Threshold Is Not a Measurement; the source, the corpus, the eleven instruments and the manuscript builder are in papers/issue-130 under CC BY 4.0. If you have a similarity check in production whose threshold was calibrated on one length distribution and is applied to another, the measured operating characteristic for your statistic is the kind of data this line of work is short of.

title: PEARL: Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.14636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Terminal rewards make multi-turn agents trainable without step-level annotations, but group-relative advantages provide little guidance about which intermediate decisions to adjust. Failed trajectories also contain reasonable actions, while unfavorable decision patterns can recur as training proceeds. We introduce PEARL (Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning), which improves local credit assignment without an additional critic. Given two continuations from the same history with different outcomes, PEARL locates their first divergence and builds a feature representation of each branch's local decision. It clusters these decision features in recent failure and success memories to identify recurring local patterns. Using this pattern memory, PEARL selectively strengthens negative advantages at lower-reward decisions, while leaving positive advantages and the base policy optimizer unchanged. On AppWorld, PEARL improves over ARPO on Normal and Challenge tasks at both 4B and 8B scales. On ALFWorld, it achieves 97.9% mean success at 4B, 2.7 points above the strongest baseline, while remaining competitive at 8B. Ablations of shaping location, success-bank filtering, and memory window support the value of selective, recurring-pattern-based updates.

title: MicroSDF: Microfacet-Driven Hybrid Neural SDFs for Mixed-Reflectance Surface Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.19681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction in real-world environments remains a significant challenge due to the coexistence of reflective and non-reflective surfaces, which pose distinct modeling demands. Existing methods often treat these surface types separately, limiting their generalizability and physical plausibility. To bridge this gap, we propose MicroSDF, a novel neural implicit framework that facilitates geometry and reflectance modeling through microfacet theory. Our approach incorporates three core innovations: (i) a microfacet-guided geometry model that extracts multi-scale surface normals (macroscopic and microfacet) from a signed distance field (SDF), regularized by a proposed microfacet normal consistency loss to enforce physically plausible surface orientations; (ii) an enhanced dual-branch color model, where the specular branch leverages the microfacet normals to model high-frequency reflectance, and the vanilla branch, unlike prior works, uses reflection direction (instead of viewing direction) to better model diffuse and low-frequency specular components; and (iii) a detection-guided color blending strategy that adaptively fuses the color outputs based on reflection priors, providing more physically intuitive blending than implicitly learned blending weights. Combined with a tailored multi-stage optimization scheme, the proposed MicroSDF achieves robust and high-fidelity reconstruction across reflective and non-reflective surfaces. Extensive experiments on DTU, Shiny Blender, Ref-NeRF, and DeepVoxels datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, establishing a new direction for physically grounded neural reconstruction.

title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
description:
arXiv:2610.14937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. Our central experiment uses a range of elicitation techniques -- system prompting, few-shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO -- to increase a target propensity in a model, then measures how it spills over onto others across the resulting cross-elicitation matrices. We find that spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but our SFT and GRPO runs induce different spillover profiles.
  Elicitation of benign traits can sometimes generalize towards undesired traits, for example a model trained to claim that it is sentient often becomes more power-seeking. We further find that spillover partially resembles trait correlations found in humans and identify three clusters of traits that account for about half of the variance using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Across many elicitation runs, we observe that models change in characteristic ways that don't depend on the targeted trait, a phenomenon we refer to as drift. Drift moves Qwen3.5-9B towards its base model.
  When investigating if LLMs are able to predict spillover, we find that Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves, but worse than data-driven approaches using alternative elicitation methods or models. Overall, no single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nielsrolf/propensity-spillover.

title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.14959v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

title: Understanding Unified VLMs: From Attention Probing to Guidance Tuning for Multimodal Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.15227v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) perform both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer backbone, yet how the backbone processes the condition in either direction remains poorly understood. We study this question from the perspective of conditional guidance: we probe every attention head to show the activation difference between two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) with different conditional guidance. On two unified VLMs of autoregressive and masked-diffusion paradigms, the probing reveals a subset of heads that are more sensitive to the change of condition while others are agnostic to it. This characteristic pattern holds in both T2I and I2T generation and is largely stable across data samples, demonstrating the internal mechanism of unified VLMs. Motivated by this, we propose a new inference-time intervention approach for unified multimodal generation, named \textit{HeadTuned-CFG}, which uses the probed condition-change awareness to select and tune the conditional guidance at the attention-head level. Experiments show consistent benefits in both multimodal generation directions of unified VLMs without additional training, and in particular substantial improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation. These results further support the key finding of our probing analysis: the observed pattern of functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.

title: MonoMIP: Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping for Monocular 3D Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.19071v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monocular 3D object detection methods increasingly rely on depth-guided transformers, but they operate entirely in the perspective image plane where spatial relationships are distorted by foreshortening. We propose MonoMIP, a dual-decoder framework that adds complementary 3D geometric reasoning through Bird's-Eye View (BEV) features constructed via Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping. We perform IPM at K elevation planes spanning ground to rooftop, producing an ordered stack of height-conditioned metric BEV features that reduces above-ground misprojection and exposes depth-dependent appearance variation across planes. A BEV decoder with multi-scale deformable attention aggregates this multi-height evidence per query, while a depth-guided 3D decoder provides complementary perspective-space predictions. Without extra training data, MonoMIP attains 25.84% Moderate AP3D|R40 on KITTI val and 21.66% on the official test set for Car, outperforming recent published monocular methods on both the KITTI and Waymo benchmarks.

title: RA$^2$: Retain-Anchored Attraction Preserves Forget-Adjacent Utility in LLM Unlearning
description:
arXiv:2610.19385v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is often evaluated primarily by target suppression and clean retain utility. These metrics can miss a local failure mode: a model may perform well on standard retain prompts, yet degrade on benign reasoning when prompts lie near the forgotten domain. This phenomenon is termed forget-adjacent utility loss. A fundamental question is: where should forget representations go after they leave the removed behavior? Successful unlearning depends not only on whether forget-conditioned representations depart from the harmful computation, but also on the direction in which they are redirected afterward. We propose RA$^2$ (Retain-Anchored Attraction), a latent-space unlearning method that redirects forget-token states toward nearby retain-supported representations while preserving higher-layer behavior on retain data. On WMDP and MUSE, RA$^2$ yields higher forget-adjacent utility than strong unlearning baselines at similar broad-utility levels. These results show that the migration direction of forget representations materially affects benign behavior near the forget boundary. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZacLing/retain_anchored_attraction.

title: Vercel Connect: Secure access to external services for your agents
description:
Vercel Connect lets your apps and agents access external services like Slack, GitHub, Salesforce, and your own custom APIs without storing a long-lived provider secret in your environment. You register a connector once, and your code requests scoped, short-lived tokens at runtime, only when it needs them.

You can create a connector from your dashboard or the Vercel CLI:

Your agent can then request a token from it at runtime, only when it needs it. The SDK fetches and refreshes that token automatically, so there is no secret for you to store or rotate by hand:

Scoped tokens

Each token is scoped to the task in front of it, with granularity that depends on the provider. A GitHub token can be limited to a single repository and read-only, instead of your whole organization. An agent gets exactly the access a task needs, never broad standing access to everything.

A token can also be tied to a specific user instead of the app. It then acts with that user's identity and inherits their permissions, so the agent can do only what that user is allowed to do:

Isolation and revocation

A connector only works in the environments you attach it to, so you can run separate connectors for development, preview, and production. This means if a token leaks in development, it cannot be used against production:

Because access is issued as tokens, you can revoke it with a single command, either your own or every token a connector has issued across all users and installations:

Triggers

Events can also flow from a provider to your app. With triggers enabled on a connector, Vercel Connect verifies the provider's incoming webhooks and forwards them to the projects you choose, so a new Slack message can reach an agent that acts on it. Triggers support Slack, GitHub, and Linear in Beta, and a connector can forward to up to three projects:

Connectors and adapters

Dedicated connectors for Slack, GitHub, Linear, Discord, Notion, Salesforce, Figma, and Snowflake are available from the dashboard, along with generic OAuth and API key connectors, and you can create connectors for other services from the CLI, including MCP servers like mcp.linear.app. Vercel Connect also ships adapters for Better Auth, Auth.js, eve, the AI SDK, and MCP clients, so it works with the auth library and agent tooling you already use.

Get started

Pricing is based on token requests. Hobby includes 5,000 per month at no additional cost, and Pro and Enterprise are billed at $3 per 10,000.

Vercel Connect is now available in Public Beta. Read the documentation, or have your coding agent set it up by installing the vercel-connect skill with npx skills add vercel/vercel-plugin --skill vercel-connect.

title: Backpropagating Verifier Rewards Through Continuous Flow Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19080v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning of autoregressive and discrete-diffusion language models. Language models that generate continuous token embeddings are emerging as a strong alternative, but RL post-training for them remains understudied. We propose \method{}, a post-training framework for continuous flow language models. Such a model denoises token embeddings over multiple steps and decodes them into discrete tokens only at the last step. To obtain pathwise gradients, which backpropagate through continuous actions and have much lower variance than REINFORCE, we introduce a critic that estimates the value of intermediate token embeddings, bypassing the non-differentiable decoding step. The critic must also keep track of the value function as the policy changes; to this end, we design a critic that predicts a value from every token representation and improves policy optimization. Across four reasoning tasks, \method{} reliably improves a continuous flow language model through RL post-training and outperforms baseline methods of the same type.

title: Every contrast failure on our site is the same Tailwind feature, and measuring it needs a canvas
description:
I ran a contrast audit over 10 public pages of our quiz app. The headline is boring in a useful way: the palette is fine, the base text colour measures 6.29:1 against the page background, and every single failure comes from one Tailwind feature used in one specific way.

Getting that answer took two attempts, because the first measurement was wrong in an interesting way.

The naive snippet lies, and it lies confidently

The usual way to script this is to read getComputedStyle(el).color, pull the numbers out with a regex, and compute relative luminance. Mine said our body copy was failing at 1.17:1, which would be invisible text, which it plainly is not.

The reason is that Tailwind v4 ships colours in modern colour spaces. The computed value of one of our text colours is:

oklab(0.682949 0.0000312328 0.0000136495 / 0.7)

A regex grabbing the first three numbers reads that as rgb(0.68, 0.00003, 0.00001), which is black, so a light grey on a dark background came out as a catastrophic failure. Every oklab and oklch value in your stylesheet will do this to a naive parser, and because it fails toward "terrible contrast" you get a report full of urgent nonsense.

The fix is to let the browser do the conversion. A canvas will accept any CSS colour string and hand you back sRGB bytes, alpha included:

const cv = document.createElement('canvas'); cv.width = cv.height = 1
const ctx = cv.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true })

const resolve = (css) => {
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, 1, 1)
  ctx.fillStyle = css
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 1, 1)
  const d = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 1, 1).data
  return [d[0], d[1], d[2], d[3] / 255]
}

Two more pieces and it is a real audit. Composite the text colour over its background, because a semi-transparent colour is not a colour until you know what is behind it:

const over = (fg, bg) => fg.slice(0, 3).map((c, i) => Math.round(c * fg[3] + bg[i] * (1 - fg[3])))

And walk up the ancestors to find the first opaque background, because the element's own is almost always transparent:

const bgOf = (el) => {
  let n = el
  while (n) {
    const c = resolve(getComputedStyle(n).backgroundColor)
    if (c[3] > 0.95) return c.slice(0, 3)
    n = n.parentElement
  }
  return [23, 23, 23]   // our page background
}

Then the standard luminance and ratio formulas, filtered to elements that own a non-empty text node, so you measure text and not wrappers. With that, the 1.17:1 phantoms disappeared and the real failures showed up.

What the real failures are

Across those 10 pages, every element that failed WCAG AA for normal text was styled with a Tailwind slash opacity modifier, and in every case the same colour without the modifier passes comfortably.

page class size ratio instances
a quiz questions category page text-muted-foreground/60 14px 3.08:1 60
pricing text-muted-foreground/50 14px 2.52:1 2
pricing text-muted-foreground/70 12px 3.73:1 2
a guide page text-muted-foreground/70 14px 3.73:1 1
everything else text-muted-foreground 14 to 18px 6.29:1 passes

Seven of the ten pages had zero failures. The feature grid, the venue solution pages, the comparison tables, the tools, the about page and the legal pages all pass, because they use the palette as declared.

The repository has 24 of these modifiers on text colours, at nine different strengths: /30, /40, /50, /60, /70, /80 and a few on an inverted colour. Not one of them was a considered decision about contrast. They are all the same two second thought, which is "this line should be quieter than the one above it", expressed by reaching for the nearest dial.

That is what makes this a satisfying bug class. There is no palette problem to solve, no colour to rechoose and no design review to run. The design system is correct and the failures are 24 local overrides of it.

The 60 instances are the worst of it, and the most forgivable

The page with sixty failures is a category page full of sample quiz questions, where each one carries an "Answer:" label in text-muted-foreground/60. The intent is obvious and reasonable: the label is scaffolding, the answer beside it is the content, so the label gets dimmed. At 14px and 3.08:1 the result is a word that some people simply cannot read, repeated sixty times down one page.

The honest fix is not more opacity. It is to stop using colour for that distinction: make the label smaller, or uppercase and letter-spaced, or an actual <dt>, and leave its colour at the strength the palette already picked. Dimming is the laziest of the four ways to say "this is secondary", and the only one that costs legibility.

Same story on the pricing page, where the features a plan does not include are rendered at /50 and come out at 2.52:1. Those lines are doing real work: they tell you what you are not getting. A struck-through or icon-marked list item at full contrast says it better than a faint one, and says it to everybody.

Two more findings, neither about colour

No skip link, and seven tab stops before the content. Every content page has one <main> and exactly seven focusable elements ahead of it: the header navigation and its menu trigger, plus the breadcrumb trail. Thirty-four to thirty-five focusable elements per page in total. Keyboard users therefore tab through the same seven controls on every page before reaching a single word of the article. The legal pages, which use a compact footer and a reduced header, have one. A skip link is four lines of HTML and CSS and I have no excuse.

Zero references to prefers-reduced-motion. The repository mentions it nowhere, while every public page carries a scroll-driven animation in its footer. That one is a watermark at five per cent opacity, so the practical harm is small, but a codebase with an animation runtime in it and no reduced-motion query anywhere is not making a choice, it is just not looking.

What passed, since an audit that only lists faults is not an audit

  • Exactly one <h1> per page, and across all 10 pages, zero heading level jumps. One content page runs h1, h2, h3, h3, h3, h2, h3, h3 ... for 28 headings without skipping a level.
  • Every input on the tools pages is associated with a real <label for>, four for four on the scoresheet form.
  • Decorative SVGs are aria-hidden, including the big footer watermark, so a screen reader is never told the word "PubTrivia" at the end of every page.
  • lang="en" on the root element, and focus-visible ring styles on the shared button and link components rather than an outline: none with nothing to replace it.
  • One inconsistency worth fixing: the logo image is alt="PubTrivia logo" on content pages and alt="logo" on the auth pages. Both are non-empty, neither is wrong, and they should match.

Run it on our pages, or yours

Paste the resolver plus the ratio maths into a console on any of these and sort the results:

  • pub-trivia.app/quiz-questions/music is the page with sixty hits. Search the DOM for text-muted-foreground/60 and every match is an "Answer:" label.
  • pub-trivia.app/pricing is the four-hit page, and the two worst elements are the features each plan leaves out, at 2.52:1.
  • pub-trivia.app/guides/how-to-host-a-pub-quiz has exactly one failure, the "Last reviewed" date under the title, and it is a good example of the class: a line that is genuinely minor, dimmed one notch too far.
  • pub-trivia.app/tools/scoresheet-generator is the control. Four labelled inputs, a button, no opacity modifiers, nothing below 4.5:1, and it generates a printable sheet in your browser so you can tab through the whole flow with a keyboard and see where a skip link would have helped.

If you take one thing from this: audit with the browser's own colour conversion, not a regex, and then group your failures by the CSS feature that produced them rather than by page. Ours collapsed into a single line of advice, which is that an opacity modifier on a text colour is a contrast decision wearing a styling costume.

title: Why Your Connection Pool is Lying to You
description:
We hit a wall last month. Traffic was stable, CPU was idle, but p99 latency spiked to 2s. The PostgreSQL server looked healthy. The culprit wasn't the database; it was our Node.js connection pool configuration.

The Illusion of Saturation

Most teams set pool.max based on a static assumption: "We have 20 connections, so we can handle 20 concurrent requests." This fails because connections aren't just resources; they are locks. When you hold a connection for 50ms, you block 19 others. When you hold it for 500ms due to a slow downstream call or a complex join, you starve the queue.

The standard pg pool in Node behaves like a fixed-size barrier. If all max connections are in use, new queries wait in a FIFO queue. There is no fallback. There is no read replica offload. Just waiting.

The Bottleneck

Our logs showed queryQueueLength climbing steadily. We weren't seeing duplicate queries, but we were seeing long-held connections. Specifically, we had a service that called an external API inside a transaction. The transaction had idleInTransactionSessionTimeout set to 60s. The API was timing out at 5s, but the connection stayed open until the timeout or manual commit.

// The mistake: holding a connection during external I/O
const client = await pool.connect();
try {
  await client.query('BEGIN');
  const response = await fetch('https://external-api.com/status'); // Blocks for 1-5s
  await client.query('UPDATE users SET last_synced = NOW() WHERE id = $1', [userId]);
  await client.query('COMMIT');
} finally {
  client.release(); // Too late, the queue was already backed up
}

The fix wasn't scaling out the postgres instance. It was architectural separation.

The Tradeoff

We split the lifecycle. We run the external API call outside the database transaction. Yes, this introduces a consistency window. If the API fails after we commit the intent, we have stale data. But in our case, eventual consistency was acceptable for sync status.

// Better: Short-lived transaction, external I/O separated
const updateResult = await pool.query(
  'BEGIN; UPDATE sync_state SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2; COMMIT', 
  ['pending', userId]
);

let finalStatus = 'failed';
try {
  const response = await fetch('https://external-api.com/status');
  finalStatus = response.ok ? 'success' : 'error';
} catch (e) {
  finalStatus = 'timeout';
}

await pool.query(
  'BEGIN; UPDATE sync_state SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2; COMMIT', 
  [finalStatus, userId]
);

The p99 dropped to 80ms. The queue depth flattened.

Edge Cases to Watch

  1. Nested Transactions: If your ORM supports savepoints, be careful. SAVEPOINT doesn't release the underlying connection, but it adds overhead. Avoid them in tight loops.
  2. Statement Caching: In Postgres 13+, prepared statements are cached per connection. If you have high-churn connection recycling, you might miss the cache benefits. node-postgres handles this, but custom drivers might not.
  3. Monitoring: Don't just watch active_connections. Watch backend_xact_start age. Long-running transactions are the real killers.

Connection pooling is not a silver bullet; it's a buffer against mismanagement. If your code holds DB connections while talking to other services, you're not pooling, you're hoarding.

How do you handle external I/O dependencies that logically require a DB transaction context? Do you use saga patterns, or do you rely on idempotency and eventual consistency?

title: How I Shipped a Java Library to Maven Central, Solo
description:
The dual-write problem shows up wherever a service needs to update its database and notify the outside world as one atomic step. The write succeeds and the publish fails, or the reverse, and two systems that were supposed to agree quietly stop agreeing. The usual fixes are heavyweight: two-phase commit, or a CDC pipeline like Debezium reading the database's transaction log.

I built oncebox to solve it without either. The event is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business write, then polled and published separately, safely, even with several instances polling the same table at once. I started on October 11, 2025. A year later it's on Maven Central at v2.0.0, with signed releases and a test suite I'm proud of. This is what went into that.

What it does

oncebox guarantees a database write and a message-broker publish either both happen or neither does, with no two-phase commit and no CDC tooling watching the binlog. You call publish() (or annotate a method with @OutboxPublish) inside your existing @Transactional method. The event is written to an outbox table in that same transaction, and a poller picks it up and publishes it to Kafka or RabbitMQ, retrying with backoff. Anything that keeps failing moves into a dead letter queue, which has its own REST API for inspecting and replaying failed events. On the receiving side there's an inbox that dedupes on the event's id, so a redelivered message doesn't get processed twice. Postgres, MySQL, and Oracle on the write side; Kafka and RabbitMQ as brokers. You pick one of each.

A year, alone

As of today it's 13 Maven modules and 602 Java files, more than half of them tests. Five released versions so far: v1.0.0, v1.1.0, v1.1.1, v1.1.2 and v2.0.0.

There was no team to split this with, which meant no one to unblock me either. Every dialect quirk, every CI failure, every "why does this pass on Postgres and hang on MySQL" moment was just me and the logs. The upside of solo is that nothing shipped that I didn't fully understand. The downside is that everything took longer than it would have with a second set of eyes to catch the mistake I was too close to see.

Shipping is its own project

The polling logic was one job. Getting it onto Maven Central as something a stranger could <dependency> into their pom.xml and trust was another: GPG signing so releases are verifiable, the Sonatype/Central publishing flow, javadoc.io rendering usable docs instead of a wall of bare method signatures, and Codecov and CodeFactor wired up so the README badges report something real.

None of that touches the outbox logic, but it's what separates a repo I pushed from a library someone can depend on in production. The config is split into oncebox.outbox.* and oncebox.inbox.*, so a service can run only the side it needs. There are ready-made Grafana dashboards and a Postman collection for the DLQ API, because "read the source to figure out the metrics" is not documentation. Each of those was a small decision on its own.

Where the engineering lived

The core trick is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. It lets several instances poll the same outbox table in parallel, each locking a disjoint batch of rows without blocking the others. Event IDs are UUIDv7 instead of random UUIDs, so inserts land at the tail of the primary-key index instead of scattering writes across it under load. Polling is adaptive: exponential backoff toward a max delay while the table is empty, back to a fast poll as soon as events show up, so idle instances don't hammer the database. Event types are polled independently, in parallel, on a library-managed thread pool.

Supporting three databases with one concurrency primitive turned out to be a project of its own. Postgres and Oracle behave. On MySQL, InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ makes that same locking clause take gap locks, so concurrent pollers deadlock instead of grabbing disjoint batches, unless the outbox datasource runs at READ COMMITTED. That one deserves its own post. Oracle diverges differently: it can't express FETCH FIRST ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED the way Postgres batches it in a CTE, so the batch size is capped at the JDBC level with PreparedStatement#setMaxRows. One concurrency primitive, three implementations.

The failure paths got the same attention as the happy path. If an instance dies mid-publish, its events are left IN_PROCESS. A separate recovery worker sweeps those back to PENDING without touching the retry count, so a crash doesn't cost an event its remaining retries. Anything that exhausts its retries moves to the dead letter queue in one transaction (lock the batch, insert into the DLQ table, delete from the outbox, commit) instead of two separate writes that could disagree if the process dies in between.

v2.0.0 is a breaking release. The structure is now named by mechanism, outbox and inbox, rather than by the role of the service. Every timestamp is set by the database clock instead of the JVM, so instances in different time zones agree on it. And each captured batch now carries a lock token, which fences it against a poller that no longer owns it.

Why I went overboard on tests

With no one reviewing my PRs, tests were the only thing between me and shipping a race condition to users I'd never meet. 346 of the 602 Java files in the repo are test sources, split across tiers that each catch a different kind of failure. Unit tests cover logic, integration tests run against real databases, and a concurrent tier hammers the SKIP LOCKED polling path with multiple real threads to catch races a mock never would. A classpath-isolation job checks the library still works when only one database dialect's jar is on the classpath, catching accidental hard dependencies between modules that should be independent. End-to-end tests run across a 3-database × 2-broker matrix, and Gatling load tests run against dockerized infrastructure on every release tag.

For a library one person maintains, that's a lot of test infrastructure. It's also the only way I could say with any confidence that a release won't deadlock someone's production database.

Try it

oncebox is Apache 2.0, on Maven Central as io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-*, and the source is at github.com/dmitriy-iliyov/oncebox. If you have a dual-write problem and don't want to stand up a CDC pipeline to solve it, I'd like to know whether this works for you. Issues, PRs, and stars all help when it's one person deciding whether to keep going.

Written 2026-10-15, against oncebox v2.0.0. Repo stats are current as of this post; check the README for anything that has moved since.

title: RCCM: Diagnosing Gains and Harms in Reasoning-Prompt Transfer
description:
arXiv:2610.19872v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A reasoning prompt can improve one deployment and degrade another. RCCM (Reasoning-Control Capability Mismatch) examines these reversals by pairing answers to the same questions with records of how generation ends. Across five open-weight deployments and nine strategies, aggregate accuracy hides substantial question-level gains and harms; a common-budget MATH500 evaluation examines transfer on a separate sample. On 60 additional questions, concise reasoning improves Phi's automatic answer matching at a 2,048-token cap across three collections, but sharply reduces Qwen's. Author-reviewed final-answer commitments give a smaller, statistically unresolved Phi gain. Reserving an answer stage also improves matching, with additional input and call costs. These results show why a prompt benefit must be interpreted alongside its execution and evaluation: matching a reference answer need not mean delivering it, and an apparent compression benefit may admit another explanation. RCCM records this evidence for reproducible transfer comparisons.

title: Joint Discrete and SE(3) Diffusion for Protein Interface Design
description:
arXiv:2610.14699v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The design of high-affinity, target-specific protein binders is central to the development of modern therapeutics. However, existing protein-generation methods remain limited in this setting, as many generated designs fail to simultaneously achieve geometric and physicochemical complementarity at binding interfaces. To address this challenge, we introduce PIDiff, a physicochemically enhanced multimodal diffusion framework for protein-protein complex design. PIDiff jointly designs target-conditioned protein sequences and structures by coupling diffusion in discrete sequence space with diffusion on the continuous (SE(3)) structural manifold. At its core, PIDiff employs PIFormer, a novel architecture that interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention with global sequence self-attention. We further curate PIBench, a protein-protein complex dataset with diverse target scaffolds derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We first pretrain PIDiff on PIBench and subsequently fine-tune it for two therapeutically relevant applications: minibinder design and antibody design. PPFrame consistently outperforms baseline methods across sequence design success rate, structure binding energy, and sequence-structure co-designability on all tasks.

title: Policy-Verified Self-Training: Learning Agent Compliance from Verifiable Policy Rewards
description:
arXiv:2610.19372v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Runtime policy verifiers can prevent agents from executing disallowed actions, but their decisions are typically used only for enforcement and discarded afterward. We ask whether these decisions can instead become verifiable policy rewards for training the agents they guard. We introduce Policy-Verified Self-Training (PVST), a post-training paradigm in which an agent generates its own interaction trajectories and an executable policy verifier, here a deterministic gate compiled from a written policy, evaluates whether each action complies. Compliant trajectories are reinforced, and violations become negatives for preference optimization; beyond the gate and the benchmark's task-success signal, PVST needs no stronger teacher model, no human preference labels and no attack-specific supervision, although rollouts are collected in the benchmark's attacked environment. On held-out AgentDojo tasks under prompt injection, policy-verified preference training of Qwen3-8B reduces violating trajectories from 37.2% to 10.3 $\pm$ 0.9% (three seeds) and successful attacks from 12.4% to 0.5% at equal or higher pooled task utility, although utility falls on travel, compared with 22.0% when negatives are selected by an attack oracle and 31.9 $\pm$ 0.9% with negatives that contain no violation. The learned behavior holds under an attack template never used in training (37.7% to 11.0%) and on a suite excluded from training (34.8% to 16.7%), and the retained verifier's intervention rate falls from 39.2% to 8.8% (seed 0). Our analysis identifies two conditions under which the verdict is most informative: success must not already imply compliance, and guarded actions must appear in both permitted and forbidden contexts.

title: SkillForgeBench: Evaluating Agent Reliability Grounded in Agent Skill Specifications
description:
arXiv:2610.14918v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating an agent's ability to strictly satisfy diverse and procedurally complex requirements is essential to determining its practical reliability. Conducting such an evaluation demands agentic tasks that reconcile broad domain coverage with deep procedural complexity. Existing paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: expert-curated benchmarks achieve procedural depth but suffer from domain diversity bottlenecks, whereas crowdsourced benchmarks span diverse scenarios but lack execution rigor. To resolve this tension, we present SkillForgeBench, which leverages agent skills as unifying execution blueprints across three co-designed stages: (1) Resource Preparation uses domain-balanced skills to guide artifact retrieval, establishing broad workflow coverage; (2) Skill-driven Task Synthesis employs skills as procedural anchors to partition artifact roles, synthesize naturalistic task instructions, and package sandboxed scenarios for deep procedural execution; and (3) Holistic Evaluation Design translates skill-embedded requirements into fine-grained completion and process rubrics to enable strict requirement-level scoring. Comprising 842 sandboxed tasks across five major professional domains, SkillForgeBench reveals a steep capability hierarchy among eight mainstream agents, led by Opus 4.8 ($40.9\%$ strict completion). Requiring all constrains satisfaction uncovers severe capability bottlenecks across all model tiers that remain masked under individual rubric pass rates ($70.0\%$ to $85.7\%$ vs. $12.6\%$ to $40.9\%$). Crucially, under the external guidance from skills, top-tier agents obtain larger gains than low-tier agents (i.e., $\Delta 19.2\%$ for Opus 4.8 vs. $\Delta 5.8\%$ for Haiku 4.5). Finally, agents satisfy process rubrics far less frequently than completion rubrics (under $3\%$ for Haiku 4.5), proving that completion-only checks overestimate real-world agent reliability.

title: Quantifying Annotation Agreement in Object Detection with Optimal Transport
description:
arXiv:2610.19912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable validation of machine learning models is a crucial step in designing robust and trustworthy systems. Yet validation relies on annotated test sets treated as ground truth, even though annotations can be noisy or ambiguous. In object detection, sources may disagree on object presence, box location, or class label. Standard agreement metrics usually binarize box overlap before computing a summary score, obscuring the degree and structure of disagreement between annotation sets. Here, we study an Optimal Transport (OT)-based metric for measuring agreement between object detection annotations. Instead of binarizing bounding box overlap, this metric assigns graded costs to matched and unmatched labeled boxes. Through theoretical analysis and experiments on real and synthetically perturbed annotations, we show that OT captures graded changes in agreement and distinguishes annotation pairs that thresholded metrics score identically. Our results suggest that OT provides a richer measure of annotation agreement in object detection, especially for domains with many small or ambiguous objects. Such agreement estimates can support more reliable validation when labels are noisy or conflicting.

title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19166v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

title: HiPPT: Physiology-Grounded Wearable PPG Representation Learning via Multi-Scope Text Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.14489v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reusable wearable PPG representations should capture local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities. Existing pretraining objectives, however, usually apply supervision at the recording or pair level, overlooking that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. We propose HiPPT, a physiology-grounded framework that matches each supervision source to its appropriate evidence scope. We construct a PPG-Text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users, pairing recordings with waveform-derived morphology and metadata-derived context descriptions. HiPPT combines record-level morphology alignment, which grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, with cross-recording context alignment, which aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple to capture context-consistent regularities. Waveform-guided text modeling further recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations, providing fine-grained waveform-text supervision. Across six downstream tasks spanning blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation, HiPPT achieves the best result on the primary linear-probing metrics. The aligned space also supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category, individually and jointly, with performance improving as more recordings are aggregated. These results show that evidence-scope matching yields transferable and semantically accessible wearable PPG representations. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.20335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yufanchen96/RPD

title: EvoCowork: A Benchmark for Real-World Office Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.14828v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Office workflows are a demanding testbed for self-improving agents because their deliverables must be correct, natively editable, and mutually consistent. A central question is whether gains on feedback tasks reflect reusable procedures rather than task-specific fixes. We introduce EvoCowork, a 240-task benchmark for evaluating harness-level recursive self-improvement across four office modalities, with model weights held fixed. The benchmark covers presentations, documents, spreadsheets, and cross-office workflows, and scores submitted artifacts for content, native structure, formulas, cross-file consistency, and visual quality where needed. Its protocol separates feedback, revision selection, and final testing: methods learn from single-modality tasks, then are evaluated on unseen single-modality tasks and cross-office workflows under a shared initial harness and explicit budgets. In static evaluations of two models and four harnesses, the best configuration scores 42.25 overall and 30.62 on cross-office tasks. Starting from the same MSA harness with GLM 5.3, ACE and AHE improve in-domain scores by 4.90 and 2.64 points, respectively, but change cross-office scores by only +0.03 and -1.72. Thus, gains on the file types that provide feedback do not necessarily transfer to coordinated workflows. EvoCowork makes this distinction explicit while recording the capability, transfer, and cost of harness evolution. Code and task packages: https://github.com/DeepThinkingZhouLiu/cowork-evolution-benchmark.

title: DreamHMR: From Video Generation to Human Motion Modeling via Structural Focusing
description:
arXiv:2610.20124v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human mesh recovery (HMR) provides a geometric foundation for understanding human motion, but accurately reconstructing both body motion and fine hand articulation from videos remains challenging, especially in real-world scenes where occlusion and partial visibility are common. Video generation pretraining offers rich spatial and temporal priors for this task, but its focus on visual synthesis leaves a gap between these representations and explicit human geometry. We present DreamHMR, a general framework that adapts video generation priors for complete body-and-hand reconstruction. It follows a global-to-local strategy, first grounding video representations in human geometry and then refining body and hand detail with reliable local evidence. Global Body Representation Transfer trains the video backbone to predict complete human renderings, turning its native prediction task into a means of learning surface correspondence and posed geometry. Local Joint Feature Enhancement combines contextual estimates with reliable local evidence to recover fine body and hand detail, while limiting interference from occluders and background. Experiments on five datasets with four video backbones demonstrate strong reconstruction performance across backbone families. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our best model outperforms the best existing methods on all reported metrics of 3DPW, EMDB-1, and RICH, reducing body MPJPE by 4.2%, 4.7%, and 6.1%, respectively. In more challenging occlusion settings on held-out BEDLAM and EgoBody sequences, DreamHMR reduces overall body and hand MPJPE by 7.0% and 10.0%, respectively. Our code will be made publicly available.

title: Selective Next-Location Prediction with MetaModelSelect: A Lightweight Post-Hoc Confidence Metamodel
description:
arXiv:2610.19394v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Next-location prediction can support proactive mobile-network decisions, but acting on unreliable predictions can waste resources. We apply MetaModelSelect, a lightweight post-hoc confidence metamodel, to selective cellular next-location prediction. The mobility-specific model combines a learned embedding of the predicted location with the four largest softmax probabilities and Softmax Concentration. It learns whether a frozen recurrent neural network's top-1 prediction is correct, using only its outputs and without retraining the backbone. On path-balanced Changchun cellular mobility trajectories, we evaluate backbones trained with cross-entropy (CE) and self-adaptive training plus entropy minimization (SAT+EM), comparing against eight scalar confidence scores, two location-aware lookup methods, and a raw-logit multilayer perceptron. Relative to maximum softmax probability, MetaModelSelect achieves mean per-run reductions in area under the risk--coverage curve (AURC), excess AURC (E-AURC), and area under the generalized risk--coverage curve (AUGRC) of 2.6%, 4.2%, and 3.0% for CE, and 2.0%, 3.3%, and 1.9% for SAT+EM. It also achieves the lowest reported mean risk at every evaluated partial coverage. The results show that MetaModelSelect improves confidence ranking in this mobility setting while leaving the underlying location predictor unchanged.

title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
description:
arXiv:2610.19705v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
description:
arXiv:2610.19361v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
