title: RTAformer: Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer for Video Scene Graph Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.20091v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video scene graph generation (VidSGG) aims to capture objects and their evolving relationships in videos. This requires accounting for both the persistence of object identities and abrupt changes in relationships. Existing methods aggregate information across frames to exploit temporal context, but an emphasis on consistency can obscure these changes. As a result, a model may retain its previous prediction even after the underlying relation has changed. We refer to this failure mode as relational semantic inertia. To address this issue, we propose Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer (RTAformer), a one-stage framework that separately models entity persistence and relation changes. It injects calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries to guide predicate updates, while cross-frame instance alignment during training helps reduce cross-frame representational drift. Experiments on Action Genome show improvements in recall and mean recall over existing methods, with ablation studies supporting the contributions of the proposed components and comparisons using matched backbones showing larger gains on relation-transition frames than on non-transition frames.

title: Protecting against token theft
description:
HTTP requests are inexpensive. Vercel charges ~$2/million, a fraction of a cent per call. But a single prompt to an agent on a frontier model can cost $2, making AI a million times more expensive, and inference theft one of the highest-margin businesses an attacker can run. We have seen this type of attack on our own APIs.

If you have AI endpoints exposed to the internet, the risk of abuse is high and can easily run up bills in the tens of thousands of dollars or more.

Protecting those endpoints requires verification to run on every AI request, not on the session or signup. Rate limits and auth walls aren't sufficient on their own because checks that run once per session get amortized away across thousands of stolen calls.

At Vercel, we gate every AI request through BotID deep analysis, and you can do the same on your own endpoints with a few lines of code.

What inference theft is

Inference theft is the unauthorized use of someone else's paid AI inference, either for free consumption or downstream resale. The operator pays per AI call; the attacker pays nothing for inference and then resells the tokens at a discount. This goes beyond rate-limit abuse to actual resale of a stolen resource in a market.

Which AI endpoints are at risk?

Any internet-facing endpoint that gives a caller meaningful control over an LLM prompt is a target. The more general the endpoint, the higher the payout per stolen call.

AI playgrounds, like the AI SDK Playground, are the most dangerous shape because the caller has maximum control over the prompt, the model, and often the parameters. Stolen calls land cleanly into any standard client.

Support bots and documentation assistants are less exposed when system prompts are fixed server-side, but attackers have learned how to talk the models around system prompts cheaply enough to make resale viable.

Resale value tracks how easily the stolen calls can be dropped into a provider-compatible client.

Why web defenses don't mitigate inference theft

IP rate limits and auth walls were built to defend against attacks with dramatically lower per-call economics, where gaming IPs and accounts weren't worth the cost.

The payoff from stolen inference is high enough that attackers will procure residential proxy IPs by the thousands and register throwaway accounts at whatever scale it takes to defeat your gate. Rate limits get diluted across the fleet of IP addresses, and real accounts pass authentication.

The architecture of abuse

Sophisticated attackers wrap your custom AI endpoint in an OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible adapter and fan calls out through residential proxies.

The adapter is the key component. It is a one-time engineering cost that presents the victim's idiosyncratic API as OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible, so stolen inference can drop into any standard coding agent or SDK. Reselling at even five to ten percent of the list price, with zero marginal inference cost, can make for a generous-margin business.

A recent example is Chipotlai Max, a forked coding agent that ships with a proxy turning Chipotle's customer-support chatbot into an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The project openly solicits help in porting the same inference-theft approach to Home Depot, Lowe's, Target, and Starbucks.

The adapter also serves as the session boundary for the attacker's downstream users. They authenticate to the adapter, not to your endpoint. By the time a call hits your API, it has already crossed the boundary you were planning to defend. The check has to run on the call the adapter proxies, not on the session it sits behind.

The shape of a real attack on our own endpoint

On April 12, 2026, traffic to the Vercel docs AI chat endpoint spiked to roughly ten times normal volume on Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5 model. Traffic rose to 1,300 requests per minute at peak, which would have translated to an inference cost run rate of over ten thousand dollars per day.

The attack came in through residential proxies that obscured the real client IPs. Across hundreds of thousands of bot requests over two days, standard per-IP rate limits had nothing useful to act on.

How to defend against inference theft

Protecting AI endpoints against inference theft requires verification of every request. We use Vercel's BotID with deep analysis, called inside the route handler before the AI request lands.

Verification has to run on every AI request

If our gate had run at session start instead of per request, the attacker would have paid the bypass cost once and walked away with hundreds of thousands of stolen calls. Any check that runs per session amortizes the attacker's bypass cost across every subsequent inference call. Per-request gates force that ratio down to one, and even at high inference prices, defeating a check on every call isn't worth the cost.

This is where the cost asymmetry works in the defender's favor. Inference is the most expensive resource per call that the attacker steals, but verification is one of the cheapest protection costs per call.

Implementing request verification with BotID deep analysis

Traditional image CAPTCHAs no longer hold up against modern attackers because the same AI models that make inference worth stealing can easily bypass them.

We deploy Vercel BotID on our AI endpoints, gating every request. BotID is an invisible CAPTCHA with deep analysis powered by Kasada that uses client-side machine learning to distinguish humans from bots without a visible challenge, so it can run on every request rather than only at session start.

BotID deep analysis detected and blocked more than ten thousand bot requests in the first minutes of the spike. Within twenty-four hours, request volume on the endpoint was flat at normal levels.

Server-side, checkBotId() runs inside the route handler and returns a classification for the request currently being served.

The route also has to be declared on the client. Without this, checkBotId() fails because BotID doesn't attach the challenge headers to the request:

See the BotID docs for the next.config.ts wrapper and the full setup.

Protect inference, not just access

Inference will remain orders of magnitude more expensive than the requests it carries, so resale will remain profitable, and attackers will keep iterating.

To protect your AI endpoints:

  • Audit which of your AI endpoints are exposed

  • Prioritize by attack likelihood: more caller prompt control means an easier target

  • Gate every endpoint on every request

title: SaTPO: Text-to-Image Safety Alignment via Transition Preference Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19563v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety alignment of text-to-image diffusion models aims to suppress harmful content without compromising useful generation capabilities. However, preferences over completed images compress multidimensional generation factors into a coarse signal, potentially driving changes beyond those required for safety. To address this, we propose Safety Transition Preference Optimization (SaTPO), which enforces step-wise alignment during denoising. SaTPO leverages the insight that an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite naturally form a tightly coupled preference pair when conditioned on a shared parent state and noise realization. By anchoring optimization on identical parent states, SaTPO eliminates historical trajectory divergence, confining safety adaptation to an incremental alignment while preserving task-relevant semantics. Multi-scale drift constraints and benign replay further limit behavioral deviation and preserve ordinary generation. We additionally construct CoProPV, a refined dataset ensuring visually verified contrasts. Experiments on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and SDXL demonstrate improved safety-quality trade-offs. Compared with AlignGuard, PerspectiveVision unsafe-detection rates on Inappropriate Image Prompts decrease from 12.70% to 6.00% and from 15.04% to 9.30%, respectively, while FID improves from 32.28 to 25.95 and from 36.50 to 27.51. Warning: this paper includes potentially offensive content.

title: I Built a Faceless Video Factory That Remembers Which Content Actually Pays
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

My side hustle is faceless short-form video. The problem with every tool I tried: they're script runners. Same topic list, same output, run after run. Nothing learns. So I built one that does — a factory that remembers what earned money and steers the next video toward it.

The loop nobody closes

Here's the insight that made this worth building. A faceless-content pipeline has two halves, and everyone only builds the first:

  1. Produce a video from a topic (script → render → post)
  2. Learn which topics paid, so the next one is better

Half 2 is where the money compounds, and it's the half everyone skips. This factory closes it with Backboard's persistent memory:

   recall what paid ──▶ [Brain] ──pick topic──▶ [Script] ──▶ [Assemble] ──▶ [Cashier]
        ▲                    (local LLM +        (local)     (FFmpeg)       (revenue)
        │                     recalled facts)
        └──────────────────── remember the outcome ───────────────┘

Before each video, the brain asks Backboard "what earned money before?" and
lets that steer the pick. After each video, the revenue result is written back
to memory. Run it twice and the second run is measurably smarter than the first.

Why Backboard + a local model

Backboard's memory is the differentiator — facts persist across runs and
sessions, so the factory compounds instead of resetting. But its hackathon
credit covers Memory + RAG, not LLM chat. So generation runs on a local
llama.cpp model on my own machine.

That split isn't a workaround, it's the whole side-hustle thesis: Backboard
supplies the long-term memory that makes the factory smarter; the local model
keeps the per-video cost at zero. No cloud token bill eating the margin.

The learning, measured

I ran the brain cold, then seeded two outcomes, then ran it warm. Here's what
changed:

Run Memory state Topic picked Why
1 (cold) 0 facts recalled What I learned monetizing 40 short videos No history — picked blind
2 (warm) 4 facts recalled The side hustle nobody talks about: faceless video Steered by the $61.30 earner in memory

The seeded facts the brain learned from:

Past video Views Revenue Signal
"Building an income stream that works while you sleep" 14,200 $61.30 🟢 high earner
"From keyword to video in under five minutes" 3,100 $3.10 🔴 underperformed

And the rendered output it produces each run — a real 1080×1920 vertical MP4:

Property Value
Resolution 1080×1920 (9:16)
Codec h264 + aac
Narration espeak-ng (on-device)
Background FFmpeg gradient (generated, not downloaded)

The revenue model behind the cashier is real math, not a mock — YouTube Shorts
RPM, TikTok Rewards RPM, and an affiliate conversion model, all documented and
editable in one file.

What's actually local-first

The whole point of a side hustle is margin, so nothing here phones home for
the expensive parts:

  • Scripts → local llama.cpp on :8080 (falls back to a template if the server's down, so the pipeline never blocks)
  • Narration → espeak-ng on-device
  • Background → FFmpeg gradients filter, generated locally
  • Memory → Backboard (the one cloud call, and it's the free Memory + RAG tier)

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/Reggiebro/faceless-video-factory && cd faceless-video-factory
bash demo.sh        # cold start -> seed -> warm run, the learning in one script
python3 orchestrator.py   # full pass: brain -> script -> video -> cashier

The repo is MIT. The brain (backboard/brain.py) is ~150 lines and readable
end to end — recall, pick, record. That's the whole idea.

Has anyone else used persistent memory to make a content pipeline compound
rather than just repeat? I'm curious whether the recall-steers-the-pick loop
holds up at scale, or whether it starts chasing its own tail after a few dozen
runs. What would you add to the feedback signal beyond revenue?

title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19011v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark standardized evaluation in molecular optimization, but it is built on simple property-based oracles that do not capture structure-based drug design. As the field has moved to docking-based objectives, evaluation practice has become unstandardized, and different methods report results on different docking tasks, often without a shared protocol for fair comparison or sample-efficiency constraints. To address this, we introduce Practical Molecular Optimization for Docking (PMO-Dock), a benchmark and protocol for docking-based optimization consisting of 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task requiring strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development from final evaluation: validation tasks are used for hyperparameter tuning, and test tasks are held out for final evaluation and are not used during development. Evaluation on the test tasks is done under a strict oracle budget to reflect realistic drug-discovery settings. We benchmark four diverse high-performing methods spanning different optimization paradigms, Saturn (reinforcement learning), GenMol (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama (LLM-based evolutionary search). Our results show no universally best method across tasks, additional analyses of hyperparameter transfer (cross-task and cross-category) and sensitivity show that transfer is often limited and varies by method, motivating method-dependent selection strategies. This benchmark provides a concrete standard for evaluating generalization to unseen tasks and sample efficiency under a limited test-time oracle budget.

title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
description:
arXiv:2610.19302v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.

title: ReferFlow: Beyond Final-Target Localization for Complex Referring Expressions
description:
arXiv:2610.20352v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have made significant progress in referring expression comprehension (REC), yet most REC benchmarks still focus on final-target localization. Complex queries often involve intermediate visual references with different dependencies on prior grounding, but final-only evaluation leaves this process unexamined. To address this gap, we formulate trajectory-level REC, in which models receive an ordered sequence of grounding steps constructed from a single complex query and localize the target regions associated with each step. We instantiate this setting in ReferFlow-Bench, which characterizes structured region transitions through four trajectory types, namely Refinement, Shift, Reset, and Mixture. Experiments show that current models struggle to consistently ground intermediate visual references across successive steps. We further propose ReferFlow, which decouples interleaved text-latent trajectory generation from coordinate decoding. Specifically, Stateful Region Latent Reasoning represents each target region as an object-indexed state composed of continuous latents, with explicit visual and spatial supervision to preserve region information for subsequent grounding. Trajectory-Aware Parallel Decoding then recovers all coordinate blocks in parallel through four geometry-constrained refinement rounds, with each block conditioned on its corresponding trajectory prefix, thereby reducing within-box sequential dependencies and eliminating cross-box autoregression. We further apply Grounding-Aware GRPO to promote consistent grounding across steps and learn adaptive trajectory generation from complex REC queries. ReferFlow achieves leading performance on general REC benchmarks and ReferFlow-Bench.

title: Designing a bookmark record that future-you can actually retrieve
description:
A save button creates a record. It does not answer the question that comes a week later: “Where was that example I wanted for the onboarding screen?” For a personal knowledge tool, that question is a useful starting point for the data model.

Store the reason alongside the resource

Consider this proposed record:

{
  "title": "A useful onboarding example",
  "source_url": "https://example.com/onboarding",
  "saved_for": "Compare welcome screens for my side project",
  "intent": "use",
  "keywords": ["onboarding", "welcome", "side project"]
}

The URL identifies the resource. The other fields describe its relationship to the person saving it. Keeping those concepts separate means a later change of project does not require changing the source itself.

Do not make every field mandatory. If capture becomes a form-filling exercise, people will skip it. A reasonable first version accepts the resource immediately and offers one optional prompt: “What will you use this for?”

Show the context in search results

Storing the note is only half the work. Put it beside the title when presenting results. Two nearly identical article titles become easier to distinguish when one says “for the pricing page” and the other says “for the client workshop.”

Treat automatic labels as suggestions. Keep the user's own note available for editing, and avoid silently replacing it with a generated summary.

Test retrieval rather than collection

Ask someone to save five real resources. Later, give them a task that needs one of those resources, without reminding them of its title. Observe the words they search for and the result they choose.

The useful outcome is a resource they can confidently reuse, not a bigger collection of saved links.

This is one of the product questions behind Némos: how can a saved item keep the context that made it useful?

title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
description:
arXiv:2610.19033v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. SQUELCH adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, SQUELCH improves over LoRA by 2.2--3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8--1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.

title: FireGraphNet: Sub-daily wildfire spread prediction with directed graph neural networks
description:
arXiv:2610.19191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wildfire decisions are made in hours, yet most learned spread models predict daily on targets including burned area. We propose FireGraphNet which formulates 12-hour growth as node classification on directed H3 graphs, with candidates ahead of the front and wind alignment, terrain, fuel continuity and barriers on edges. On satellite perimeters it achieves average precision 1.7-1.9x the strongest distance baseline on test California fires and 1.62x out of state. We show this skill comes from message passing rather than cell features or the aggregator, is highest on young fires in state, is carried deep along the wind by its edges, and is hidden by pooling. A convolutional network matches this ranking once trained on new growth, at worse calibration, so candidate construction, target definition, and aggregation shape conclusions about model skill. Editing fuel and barrier attributes reduces predicted spread more under guided than random placement, extending FireGraphNet to operational intervention analysis.

title: Annealed L\'{e}vy Diffusion via Gaussian Surrogate Reverse Dynamics
description:
arXiv:2610.19692v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gaussian diffusion models offer a practical framework for generative modeling. Denoising L\'{e}vy Probabilistic Models (DLPM) introduce heavy-tailed perturbations with a fixed tail index throughout denoising. We introduce Annealed L\'{e}vy Diffusion (ALD). ALD varies the stability index $\alpha(t)$ to combine heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement. Our marginal-first formulation represents stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture. This formulation enables standard Gaussian noise-prediction training with one additional scale input. We study two sampling processes. ALD-renoise estimates the clean sample and injects fresh marginal noise. ALD-posterior preserves dependence between successive states through an accumulated conditional variance and a Gaussian bridge update. Both samplers reuse the same trained predictor with different scalar inputs. We evaluate ALD on four 2D benchmarks and an imbalanced nine-mode mixture. We also examine training efficiency and the effects of prediction perturbations on clipped Holtsmark data. Additional experiments evaluate MNIST and CelebA64 generation and CIFAR-10LT augmentation. ALD preserves local geometry on the evaluated light-tailed and manifold-structured targets.

title: Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
description:
Authors: Nick Rutigliano, Argha C, Samartha Chandrashekar

How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss.

Open Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live.

Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop.

This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform.

Why GPU reliability matters

Netflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners.

All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts. — -

  • Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on.
  • Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work.

Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too.

Why basic health checks are not enough

We start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training.

The next step most teams take is a GPU-level check to confirm that the driver responds and that the GPUs are visible. That catches a dead or missing GPU, but misses the cases that take the most time.

  • A GPU can answer a status query and still be faulty once a workload touches it. A fault in on-chip memory or in the firmware that manages the device can remain invisible until a job allocates memory or runs sustained compute, at which point the job fails or slows.
  • A high-speed network adapter may be present but show fewer links than expected. Collective operations still run, at a fraction of the bandwidth, so the job does not crash. It crawls, and the cause is easy to miss.
  • A check can fail in ways that leave a faulty machine looking healthy. The diagnostic tool can hang when the driver hangs, and a naive check that waits on it hangs too. A binary that the check depends on can go missing after a driver upgrade, causing the check to stop running and report nothing. A check that can silently stop running is worse than no check, because it gives false confidence while the machine keeps working.

Because a job runs as a gang, any one of these on any one machine can degrade or stop the whole job, and none of them shows up in an instance-level check or a driver-responds check. The health system has to assume the hardware can lie and the tools that inspect it can break.

Our approach

We treat reliability as four layers, each catching what the layer below cannot:

1/ Node and hardware health: find bad GPUs, network adapters, interconnects, memory errors, and thermal issues, then taint or recycle the machine.

2/ Scheduler and platform: retry at the task & job level, validate a machine before it takes work, and drain & recycle machines safely.

3/ Training loop: checkpoint and use elastic workers so a job survives losing a machine.

4/ Observability: metrics, service-level objectives, and failure attribution across the other three.

The first two layers keep hardware problems away from jobs. The third accepts that some loss is unavoidable and makes it cheap. The fourth tells us whether the first three are working.

How the health checks work

Checks run in two tiers. Device-level checks look at each GPU. A node-level agent, built on the open-source Kubernetes node-problem-detector, runs on every GPU machine every 30 seconds and turns check results into conditions on the Kubernetes node, the same mechanism Kubernetes uses to mark a node NotReady. Controllers watch those conditions and decide whether the machine can take on work.

GPU device checks are built on NVIDIA’s DCGM for driver-reported error codes, uncorrectable memory errors, interconnect integrity, and thermal state, and networking adapter checks inspect the host state for the count and link state of the Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces that carry cross-machine traffic. A few of these checks deserve detail.

  • Failing closed: if the driver or the diagnostic tool is unresponsive, the check times out and marks the machine unhealthy. A check that cannot reach the hardware reports a problem rather than passing, so a wedged driver takes the machine out of rotation rather than letting it hide behind a hung tool.
  • A fallback path: driver error codes are the strongest signal that a GPU has faulted, but the tool that reads them can itself be broken in certain failure modes! When it does, we read the kernel log dmesg directly for those codes, so no Xid or SXid errors are missed.
  • Our own fatal-error map: vendor driver error catalogs lag newer GPU generations and do not always match what we see in production, so we keep our own mapping of which codes are fatal for each GPU family. A code that means reset-the-GPU in one generation can be benign in another, and one GPU generation emits a burst of normally-fatal code on every healthy boot, which we learned to treat as noise rather than drain fresh machines.
  • No silent no-ops: a check fails when a required dependency is missing. This one came from an upgrade that dropped a binary the network-adapter check relied on. The check quietly stopped running, and machines with the wrong number of adapters shipped for days before the slow jobs were traced back to them. Now a missing dependency fails the check.

Turning a bad machine into healthy capacity, automatically

When a check fails, the machine’s node condition changes, and controllers take over. We distinguish two levels. A problem condition blocks new work from landing while jobs are running, because pulling a job off a machine is disruptive, and many problems clear on their own. If the condition persists beyond a tolerance window, it escalates to a failure condition, which evacuates the machine, drains its tasks (overriding the normal disruption limits to move quickly), terminates it, and replaces it.

Karpenter node auto-repair is used on our compute stack. We have customized it with a policy and a controller that maps each node condition to the duration we tolerate it before acting, so a fast-fatal error is actioned within minutes. At the same time, a flaky signal gets a longer window, and a cap limits how much of a cluster we will disrupt at once, so a bad rollout of the checks themselves cannot cascade into tearing down a whole cluster. We plan to upstream this feature to all Karpenter users.

Not every fault requires a full replacement, and replacement is the slowest way to restore capacity. We match the action to the fault. Killing the offending job clears a software wedge. Resetting a single GPU clears many transient device faults. Rebooting the machine clears the firmware state that has drifted over a long uptime. Terminating and replacing is reserved for hardware that fails a test we trust. For that last case, we record the GPU’s immutable hardware identifier, which stays with the physical device across reboots and relaunches even when the instance changes, report it to the cloud provider, and keep our own list, so a device that fails repeatedly does not quietly rejoin the pool under a new instance.

One subtlety sits between detection and scheduling. A freshly checked machine was handed to the scheduler just as its checks were still settling, so a job could land on it a moment before a slow check flagged it. We now hold capacity until the checks have run and settled, which closed that window.

Validating a machine before it takes work

A machine that just booted is not trusted until it proves itself. Before we release its capacity, it passes system checks, confirms the GPUs and their topology are present, and runs a round of GPU diagnostics. We then wait for the health checks to run twice, because the longer checks, such as counting network adapters, take more than one cycle to fire, and releasing after a single pass would let work land before those checks are reported. Only then do we remove the startup taint. On teardown, we run deeper diagnostics and record the GPU identifiers, which feed the same bad-hardware list, so hardware that failed once does not silently cycle back into service.

Letting long jobs survive machine loss

Even with all of the above, some machines are lost mid-job, so we make that cheap. Jobs checkpoint their state, and on a lost machine, they resume from the last healthy checkpoint rather than restarting from the beginning of a multi-week run. Workers are elastic and retryable, and the scheduler automatically retries platform-caused failures.

Attribution is what makes automatic retries safe. If we retried every failure, we would mask genuine bugs in a job and burn GPU hours looping on an error the platform cannot fix, so we classify each failure as platform or application before retrying. One example of why this matters: a class of timeouts in NCCL, the collective communication library GPUs use to exchange data, appeared to be a network fault and was traced to data-loading stalls at high worker counts. The GPUs and the network were fine, and the fix was in the data pipeline. Treated as hardware failures, those timeouts would have cycled healthy machines without fixing the cause.

Measuring whether it works

We track GPU reliability along three service-level objectives, each split by cause, so a miss points at the layer responsible:

  • Availability: the amount of GPU capacity available for scheduling at any given moment.
  • Job-start success: whether a job starts promptly once its capacity is available.
  • Job success: whether a job finishes without a platform-caused failure.

Each objective is split into hardware, driver, platform, and user causes. Hence, an availability dip from bad hardware reads differently from one caused by a scheduler change or a user misconfiguration. We optimize for goodput, the useful work the fleet completes, because a job held back by one slow GPU can look healthy on an uptime chart while getting almost nothing done. Specific targets for each objective are provided here for illustrative purposes.

A closed remediation loop

These pieces form a loop. Hardware is validated at allocation, before a job starts, with a short collective communication run and pairwise network tests. Hence, any machine that fails within the first minute fails before the job is admitted. During the job, we watch passively for driver errors, memory errors, thermal events, and more. We view each job as a distributed system, which lets us identify a single slow rank dragging the rest, rather than only whole-machine failures. When something is wrong, remediation is automatic and graded. The loop is the same whether a job runs through our batch scheduler, Kueue, or Ray.

Sharing GPUs safely

Not every workload needs a whole GPU, and leaving small inference jobs on dedicated GPUs wastes capacity. We partition GPUs with MIG for memory-level isolation between tenants, so a fault or a memory hog in one partition does not affect another. We also reconfigure those partitions without restarting the machine, so that a pool can shift between many small slices and a few large ones as demand changes. GPU and network adapter allocation is device-plugin-based today, to move to Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation once it is supported in Karpenter. This matters because a GPU talking to a network adapter or working with a CPU on the wrong PCIE root of the machine incurs a bandwidth penalty.

Device-level allocation also changes how we handle a single bad GPU. With DRA support, instead of losing the whole machine, we could isolate the one faulty device and keep the others serving, which matters most for inference, where many small jobs share a machine. And because allocation is expressive, a job can request the capabilities it needs, such as memory or tensor-core support, and the platform matches a suitable GPU type, so users are not pinned to a model they had to choose in advance.

Results

Moving from basic checks and manual draining to layered checks and automatic remediation changed two things users feel. More of the GPU fleet is available for scheduling at any time because bad machines are caught and cycled quickly, rather than sitting in the pool or waiting on an on-call engineer. And fewer jobs fail due to platform issues because most faults are caught before a job lands, and the rest are automatically remediated and retried. Graded remediation also returns capacity in minutes for faults that only require a job kill, a GPU reset, or a reboot, rather than the longer wait for a replacement machine.

Since the above improvements have landed, we’ve seen:

  • Consistently achieving >99.95% availability of our GPU nodes
  • Job success rate has gone from ~98% to above 99.5%

What is next

We are extending active checks to cover additional failure modes under load, widening burn-in so more classes of failures can be cleared before a user encounters them, and making remediation more granular so more error types are cleared in place rather than requiring a full node replacement loop for certain Xid errors. Additionally, we want to do more periodic diagnostics between jobs.

We are working to make placement more topology-aware using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) once it lands in Karpenter, for example, by aligning on Compute/IMEX Domains, PCIe roots, and NUMA nodes.

More on the performance side for multi-GPU training, we plan to run a custom Linux scheduler built on sched_ext. Firstly, we can prioritize processes during collective coordination, such as when GPUs exchange results before the next round of compute, thereby reducing overall GPU idle time by establishing a fleet-wide priority for these tasks. The effect is small on one machine but grows across hundreds of machines, where a few percent of throughput amounts to a large amount of capacity. Secondly, we can prioritize data-loading processes to minimize the bottleneck that sometimes occurs when data is not loaded onto GPUs quickly enough to maintain steady progress.

While we already monitor throttling events, GPUs do not have to report throttling for it to hurt a job. One running ten to fifteen degrees hotter than its peers, even within healthy limits, sets the pace for the gang, so we can treat a large temperature gap as a fault, stop the job, and move it to cooler GPUs.

Additionally, we plan to expand our NCCL RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability) monitoring to identify NCCL issues sooner, such as mismatched collectives or hangs, to more quickly resume work.

Closing

Hardware fails, and at this scale, it fails often enough that the platform has to treat failure as normal. Detecting problems before and during jobs, automatically remediating machines, and allowing long jobs to resume after a loss lets teams run large-scale training and inference without babysitting the hardware. If you like these kinds of problems, we are hiring.

Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Deconstructing Roles with Hiring Managers: A Workshop Guide
description:
• Start with the Outcome, Not the Title
  • Run a Focused Hiring Manager Workshop — 60–90 minutes that produces clarity
  • From Workshop Notes to a Lean Job Description and Interview Scorecard
  • Tie Job Scope Directly to Onboarding, KPIs, and Performance Reviews
  • Workshop Playbook: A 90-minute Hiring Manager Discovery Session
  • Sources

Most hiring failures begin before an interview: a vague role brief. When a hiring manager can’t clearly describe the outcomes they expect, recruiters default to keyword matches, interviewers default to gut checks, and new hires default to guesswork — which erodes time-to-productivity, retention, and team morale.

Hiring symptoms are familiar: job postings rewritten three times, repeated candidate ghosting at late stages, offers accepted then rescinded, new hires whose day‑to‑day tasks don't match the posted responsibilities, and managers surprised at what the hire can't do. Those operational symptoms trace to one root cause: unclear scope and undefined measures of success for the role. You need a repeatable process to deconstruct the work, surface the real success metrics, and translate those decisions into recruitment artifacts the team can act on.

Start with the Outcome, Not the Title

If you want faster hires that stick, stop describing tasks and start describing results. Role deconstruction begins by converting nebulous responsibilities into the handful of outcomes that move the business needle.

  • Define outcomes first: Replace task lists with 3–5 outcome statements (e.g., increase trial-to-paid conversion by 12% in 12 months). Outcomes make job scoping measurable and negotiable.
  • Capture context: team mission, reporting line, key stakeholders, systems the hire must own, and constraints (budget, travel, time zone).
  • Separate must-have from nice-to-have: use a strict two-column rule — if you would cancel the hire without it, it’s a must-have.
  • Use job analysis methods: a short, structured job analysis is not academic fluff — it’s how you map tasks to critical competencies and reduce downstream guesswork.

Contrarian insight: titles rarely predict performance; outcomes do. A “Senior X” that cannot deliver the target outcome is a title, not value. When your job ads and intake briefs prioritize outcomes, your sourcing, screening, and interviewing all get sharply more efficient.

Run a Focused Hiring Manager Workshop — 60–90 minutes that produces clarity

A hiring manager workshop is the fastest way to convert tacit manager expectations into documented hiring artifacts. Keep it compact, focused, and output-driven.

What to invite: the hiring manager (owner), the recruiter (facilitator), one peer from the team, and the HRBP or hiring panel lead (calibrator). No executive committees. Pre-work: hiring manager submits a brief context note (one page) and current team org chart.

Core agenda (timeboxed to 60–90 minutes):

  1. Quick context and priority alignment (5–10 min): business reason for hire and how success maps to the next 6–12 months.
  2. Role deconstruction workshop (20–30 min): identify top 3–5 responsibilities and translate each into a measurable outcome.
  3. Defining success metrics (15–20 min): agree on a 30/60/90 framework and 1–2 KPIs per responsibility (defining success metrics is the deliverable).
  4. Skills & constraints mapping (10–15 min): must-haves, nice-to-haves, blockers, budget, location/remote requirements.
  5. Interview plan & scorecard mapping (10–15 min): choose 3 competencies to score, assign weights, and set debrief rules.
  6. Decisions and next steps (5 min): who writes the job brief, deadline, and interview panel assignments.

Why this works: structured job analysis and consistent interview rubrics increase predictive validity and reduce legal and fairness risk. Use research-backed structure rather than free-form conversation.

Practical facilitation tips:

  • Use a shared whiteboard or live doc and capture evidence-of-success language (exact phrases a manager would say in a 6‑month review).
  • Force decisions: label anything uncertain as hypothesis and assign an owner to validate in hiring.
  • Keep the session to only necessary people to avoid scope dilution.

From Workshop Notes to a Lean Job Description and Interview Scorecard

Translate workshop outputs into two operational artifacts that drive hiring alignment: a lean job description and a calibrated interview scorecard.

Job description skeleton (lean, outcome-first):

  • Role summary: 2–3 sentences emphasizing the team mission and top outcome.
  • Top responsibilities (outcome-based bullets): each bullet begins with the expected outcome and includes the measure and timeframe.
  • Success metrics: explicit 30/60/90 targets and the KPIs you’ll use in hiring and onboarding.
  • Must-have skills vs preferred: list only essentials in the must column.
  • Team & manager profile: who the hire reports to, direct reports, and key stakeholders.
  • Logistics: location, compensation band, required clearances.

Example responsibilities table:

Responsibility (Outcome) Success metric (how measured) 30 / 60 / 90 milestone
Reduce support SLA breaches SLA breaches ≤ 5% month-over-month 30: identify top 3 failure modes; 60: deliver 2 process fixes; 90: SLA ≤ 8%
Increase feature adoption Adoption rate +10% in 6 months 30: baseline adoption; 60: ship onboarding flow; 90: +6% adoption

Convert those bullets directly into interview scorecards. A good interview scorecard contains:

  • Competency name (e.g., Delivery Ownership)
  • Weight (scorecard.weight) as a percentage of final score
  • Behavioral anchors (what a 1/3/5 looks like)
  • Sample evidence you expect (past projects, metrics, artifacts)

Sample interview scorecard in YAML:

role: Product Manager - Growth
competencies:
  - name: Delivery Ownership
    weight: 30
    anchors:
      1: "No clear ownership; missed deadlines without mitigation"
      3: "Delivered with supervision; incremental impact"
      5: "Led cross-functional effort and exceeded targets with measurable outcomes"
  - name: Analytical Rigor
    weight: 25
    anchors:
      1: "No data used in decisions"
      3: "Used basic analysis; needed coaching"
      5: "Built models and demonstrated causal impact"
  - name: Stakeholder Influence
    weight: 20
    anchors:
      1: "Struggles to persuade peers"
      3: "Manages stakeholders with support"
      5: "Built alignment and changed roadmaps through influence"

Evidence basis matters: structured interviews plus behaviorally-anchored rating scales improve selection decisions and fairness. Pair these scorecards with a short work sample or case for mid-senior roles for the best predictive value.

Important: The scorecard is not a feedback form — it’s a decision tool. Score independently, then calibrate evidence in a short debrief.

Tie Job Scope Directly to Onboarding, KPIs, and Performance Reviews

Hiring alignment doesn’t stop at offer acceptance. The same outcomes and metrics you defined during role deconstruction must drive onboarding and early performance conversations.

  • Convert success metrics into a 30/60/90 onboarding plan for the new hire (day 1 deliverables, 30-day learning goals, 90-day outcome targets).
  • Map onboarding tasks to interview evidence: if you weighted stakeholder influence at hire, plan early stakeholder introductions and paired activities to solidify that skill.
  • Feed hiring artifacts into HRIS/ATS and the new-hire checklist so managers have a runbook for ramp. SHRM recommends treating onboarding as an ongoing process (not a single orientation) and aligning it to role outcomes.

Sample 30/60/90 (brief):

  • 30 days: 1) Complete system access + shadowing; 2) Deliver gap analysis of current process.
  • 60 days: Implement one improvement and show metric baseline movement.
  • 90 days: Own a cross-functional deliverable and meet agreed KPI thresholds.

Why this reduces mis-hires: clarity during hiring translates to clarity at Day 1 — managers and new hires know what success looks like, reducing the common "what did I actually hire them for?" problem that drives early attrition. Gallup links declines in role clarity to drops in engagement and retention; making expectations explicit at hire and onboarding is a high-leverage fix.

Workshop Playbook: A 90-minute Hiring Manager Discovery Session

Use this playbook as a repeatable template for role deconstruction and job scoping.

Pre-work (sent 3 business days before):

  • Hiring manager: 1-page context note (team mission, why now, top 3 expected outcomes).
  • Recruiter: current job posting, sample resumes, org chart.
  • Participants: review pre-work and come prepared with one concrete success example for the role.

90‑minute facilitator playbook (timeboxes and scripts):

  1. 0–10 min — Kickoff & framing
    • Script: “We’ll align on one crisp outcome set and leave with a job brief, scorecard, and 30/60/90 plan.”
  2. 10–35 min — Top outcomes & stakeholder map
    • Activity: Whiteboard Top 5 responsibilities; write outcome first.
  3. 35–55 min — Define success metrics
    • Activity: For each top responsibility, list 1 KPI and a 30/60/90 milestone.
  4. 55–70 min — Skills vs. experience & constraints
    • Activity: Move sticky notes into must / nice-to-have columns.
  5. 70–85 min — Scorecard mapping and interview plan
    • Decide 3 competencies to interview against; set weights; list 2 behavioral prompts per competency.
  6. 85–90 min — Decisions & next steps (assign authorship of artifacts)

Deliverables (output within 48 hours):

  • One-page role brief (outcome-first)
  • Job description draft (2–3 sentence summary + outcome bullets)
  • Interview scorecard (YAML/CSV to upload to ATS)
  • 30/60/90 onboarding plan
  • Panel assignments and interview scheduling windows

Calibration protocol (post-interview):

  1. Each interviewer scores independently within 24 hours.
  2. Convene a 30-minute debrief limited to evidence, not opinions.
  3. Tally weights and use a simple threshold (e.g., weighted score ≥ 75) for automatic hiring recommendation or move to reference checks.
  4. If variance > 20 points between interviewers, flag for a calibration retrain.

Quick checklist to attach to the requisition:

  • [ ] Role brief attached to requisition
  • [ ] Scorecard uploaded into ATS
  • [ ] Panel trained on scorecard (5–10 min read)
  • [ ] Offer approval and comp band confirmed
  • [ ] Onboarding owner assigned

A short calibration note: structured, evidence-based interviews and scoring reduce unconscious bias and help panels compare apples to apples. Google’s re:Work guidance and the industrial-organizational research base both recommend this approach for reliability and fairness.

Sources

U.S. Employee Engagement Sinks to 10-Year Low — Gallup - Gallup’s reporting on role clarity and employee engagement; used to support the central role-clarity claim and onboarding alignment rationale.

SIOP: Structured Interviewing and Job Analysis — Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychology - SIOP resources and practitioner guidance on job analysis, structured interviewing, and reducing rating errors; used to justify job analysis and structured interview practices.

The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods in Personnel Psychology — Frank L. Schmidt & John E. Hunter (1998) (summary) - Academic meta-analysis establishing the predictive value of structured interviews plus other assessment tools; cited for the evidence base behind scorecards and selection method validity.

SHRM — New Employee Onboarding Guide - SHRM guidance on treating onboarding as a strategic, ongoing process aligned to role expectations; cited for onboarding alignment and operational recommendations.

Use Structured Interviewing — Google re:Work - Practical guidance and examples from Google on structured interview design, rubrics, and scoring; used to support interview-scorecard design and calibration protocols.

title: Demystifying On-Policy Distillation: Where Does the Teacher's Advantage Live?
description:
arXiv:2610.19145v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly studied as a cheaper alternative to reinforcement learning, yet it remains a form of knowledge distillation (KD) that relies on teacher supervision. We revisit OPD from the KD perspective by asking where the teacher's advantage lies along student-generated trajectories. Controlled token flips at teacher-student disagreements directly measure the accuracy gained from teacher corrections. Single-token flips yield a modest average gain on selected failed trajectories, whereas repeated flips raise accuracy from 28.4% to 74.5%, close to the teacher's 76.9%. Gains continue to accumulate with more flips, but mass- and KL-based selection outperform random flips by 15-18 percentage points at counts of similar magnitude. Selective intervention remains useful after OPD, but greater argmax agreement does not consistently improve accuracy across model pairs. We advocate training schedules that learn more valuable teacher corrections while maintaining distributional stability. Controlled flips and fork-resolution analysis evaluate OPD beyond accuracy by measuring which teacher preferences the student acquires and what further correction can recover.

title: I Tested 3 Free, Open-Source Adobe Clones on My Mac. Here Are the Real Numbers.
description:
ArtCraft just open-sourced free Rust rebuilds of Photoshop, Premiere, After Effects and ten more apps. PhotoCraft alone went past 61,000 GitHub stars in about two weeks.

Stars don't edit videos, though. So I installed three of the apps on my Mac mini M4 (16 GB) and gave them real work. Every number below comes from a log I saved on October 15, 2026.

What ArtCraft actually is

ArtCraft is a family of desktop apps that copy the Adobe and Microsoft playbook, released under the Apache 2.0 license:

  • PhotoCraft: Photoshop
  • VectorCraft: Illustrator
  • FilmCraft: Premiere Pro
  • EffectCraft: After Effects
  • LightCraft: Lightroom
  • Plus clones of InDesign, Figma, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, Pro Tools and AutoCAD

When I took my first screenshot the site listed 12 apps. By the time I finished testing, it listed 13. They run on Mac, Windows, Linux and in the browser.

The price gap: Adobe Creative Cloud Pro is US$69.99/month on adobe.com (about $840 a year). ArtCraft is $0.

The catch: most of these repos were created on September 30, 2026. Every app I checked is labelled early alpha or "in development". So the real question is whether you can use them today.

Test 1: PhotoCraft photo edit (0.23 s)

PhotoCraft looks almost exactly like Photoshop: same toolbar, same panels, same layers. The interesting part is that every action is a command, and the app ships its own MCP server. An AI agent or a small script can drive the real app while you watch.

The edit: auto tone, remove background, yellow fill layer behind the subject, two text layers, drop shadow. From the command line (photocraft-cli 0.9.0), the whole thing took 0.23 seconds and saved a real layered PSD with every layer still editable.

The log, trimmed:

{"command":"image.autoTone","result":null}
{"command":"layer.removeBackground","result":{"bounds":[171,56,587,664],"layer":2}}
{"command":"layer.newFillLayer.solidColor","result":{"layer":3}}
{"command":"type.create","result":{"bounds":[838,244,1155,351],"layer":4}}
{"command":"layer.layerStyle.dropShadow","result":{"layer":5}}
real 0.23

What broke: Remove Background left a blue fringe in the subject's hair from the old backdrop. Photoshop's masking still wins here.

Test 2: batch-edit 20 product photos (1.75 s)

The boring test that actually saves time. Picture a small online shop fixing 20 product photos every week. I gave PhotoCraft one action list: auto tone, more vibrance, unsharp mask, resize to 1080 px.

[["image.autoTone",{}],
 ["image.adjustments.vibrance",{"vibrance":35,"saturation":5}],
 ["filter.sharpen.unsharpMask",{"amount":60,"radius":1.2,"threshold":2}],
 ["image.imageSize",{"width":1080}]]

photocraft-cli batch --actions actions.json --in batch-in --out batch-out --format jpg --quality 90

Result: 20 succeeded, 0 failed, 1.75 seconds. In Photoshop you'd record an action for this. Here it's one line in a terminal.

Test 3: FilmCraft 16-second travel reel (12.5 s export)

FilmCraft is a real Premiere clone: source monitor, program monitor, project bin, timeline. I built a 16-second 1080p30 reel from four free Mixkit stock clips, with three cross dissolves and a title.

What broke: one clip was 720p and showed up small in the middle of the 1080p frame. Premiere does the same thing, and one Fill Frame command fixed it.

The export is the nerdy part. FilmCraft doesn't use FFmpeg; its H.264, HEVC, ProRes and AAC codecs are written from scratch in Rust.

filmcraft-cli --project reel/reel.fcproj export out/travel-reel.mp4 --format h264
"frames": 480, "render_fps": 38.3, "seconds": 12.52, "bytes": 38815510

12.5 seconds for 480 frames. The file is chunky, though: 38.8 MB for 16 seconds, so compress it before you upload it anywhere.

Test 4: EffectCraft animated title (0.99 s render)

This one surprised me most. You script EffectCraft with After Effects-style JavaScript: comps, layers, keyframes, easing, Gaussian blur. Here's part of the title script I wrote:

var comp = app.project.items.addComp("Title", 1920, 1080, 1, 4, 30);
var t = comp.layers.addText("OPEN SOURCE");
var o = t.property("Transform").property("Opacity");
o.setValueAtTime(0.3, 0); o.setValueAtTime(0.8, 100);
var blur = t.property("Effects").addProperty("ADBE Gaussian Blur 2");
blur.property("Blurriness").setValueAtTime(0.3, 40);
blur.property("Blurriness").setValueAtTime(1.0, 0);

A yellow bar wipes in, the text blurs into place, and a subtitle fades up. The script ran in 0.08 s, and the 4-second 1080p title (120 frames) rendered in 0.99 s.

All four results

  • PhotoCraft photo edit: 0.23 s, layered PSD (hair fringe after background removal)
  • PhotoCraft batch, 20 photos: 1.75 s, 0 failures
  • FilmCraft 16 s 1080p reel: 12.5 s export, 38.8 MB file
  • EffectCraft 4 s title: script 0.08 s, render 0.99 s

The real use case: automation

ArtCraft isn't replacing a pro editor tomorrow. The strength is that every app has a command line and an MCP server, so agents like Claude can drive them:

  • Make 50 social posts from a spreadsheet
  • Fix every product photo in one go
  • Turn a script into a rough cut
  • Render a title for every video

Adobe gives you a beautiful app. ArtCraft gives you an app that scripts and AI agents can use too, for free.

So, can you cancel Adobe today?

If you're a professional with client deadlines: no. These apps are days old, labelled alpha, and you will hit missing features.

If you're a student, a Linux user, a small business, or a developer who wants to automate creative work: it's already useful.

And if PhotoCraft keeps moving at 61,000 stars in two weeks, Adobe should be a little nervous.

ArtCraft apps: https://getartcraft.com/apps

Not sponsored by or affiliated with ArtCraft or Adobe. Tested on a Mac mini M4 (16 GB), October 15, 2026. Price checked on adobe.com the same day. This article was written with AI assistance from my own test logs and video script.

title: Signed URLs are now available for Vercel Blob
description:
You can now generate time-bound signed URLs for Vercel Blob. A signed URL is a scoped URL with an expiry that allows you to upload, download, inspect, or delete a specific object without giving access to your entire Blob store.

Each URL is scoped to a single operation (put, get, head, or delete), a single pathname, and an expiry you choose, up to 7 days. The signature covers the operation and constraints, so a URL signed for a GET can't be reused as a PUT.

Direct uploads from the browser

Upload URLs (put) support multipart, so the browser can stream large files straight to Blob storage without round-tripping through your server.

Conditional deletes

Delete URLs accept an ifMatch option so the delete only applies if the object hasn't been overwritten since you signed the URL:

Signed URLs work alongside OIDC. Your server authenticates to Blob via OIDC, generates a signed token, and produces narrowly scoped, time-bound URLs for the browser, so your long-lived BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN never leaves the server.

Update @vercel/blob to 2.4.0 and read the documentation to get started.

title: Healthtech Metering in Go: Provision a Scoped API Key with a Setup Script
description:
TL;DR: A setup job should mint a credential restricted to one customer-usage writer, place it in a secret store without printing it, authenticate with the stored value, and fail unless the returned subject, tenant, and scopes exactly match the request. For a healthtech meter, that identity check matters more than a green “secret written” response: the invoice pipeline must be able to show which workload was allowed to append usage for which customer account, while the credential itself stays out of logs and build artifacts.

Treat bootstrap as a small security transaction with an explicit commit point. Provisioning is not complete when a key exists. It is complete only after the key has crossed into the secret store, the setup process has discarded its plaintext copy, and an authenticated probe proves that the stored value represents the intended machine identity. This framing also forces failure handling into the design: before the commit point, any partial key is untrusted and must be removed; after it, rotation becomes an ordinary lifecycle operation with a known owner and version.

How should a setup script provision and verify a scoped API key?

Imagine the incident review, without inventing an incident: a healthtech platform receives one usage event for customer clinic-042, the event later contributes to a metered invoice, and the audit trail says only that “CI” wrote it. The dashboard is green. The useful questions are less comfortable: which subject authenticated, which tenant boundary applied, which scopes were effective, and did the same credential have permission to read patient data or alter invoices?

If those answers cannot be recovered without exposing the key, the bootstrap design has already failed its primary decision axis: auditability of access. The invariant is straightforward: a credential used to append billable usage must resolve to one stable workload subject, one expected account boundary, and the smallest effective scope set. An environment name such as production is context, not identity.

No identity, no commit.

I would page on repeated identity-verification failures, unexpected subjects, or broader scopes. I would not page merely because a rotation occurred. A rotation is expected state change; an accepted credential that cannot prove its owner is the event that threatens attribution.

Model the handoff before choosing an API

There is no universal API-key provisioning protocol, so keep vendor routes outside the safety logic. The core needs three adapters: a provisioner that returns a secret once, a store that accepts bytes under a versioned name, and an identity endpoint that reports the authenticated principal. That separation lets a team replace an account API or secret backend without weakening the checks that decide whether bootstrap succeeded.

For the example meter, request only an append permission for a single tenant. Do not grant a generic admin scope because setup is convenient. Do not reuse the deployment credential either; deployment and usage submission produce different audit questions and deserve different subjects.

Boundary Required evidence Reject when
Provisioning requested subject, tenant, and scope set the request is ambiguous or overbroad
Secret write versioned secret reference, not plaintext the destination is mutable without version evidence
Authentication returned subject, tenant, and effective scopes any field differs from the request
Audit request ID and secret version the record contains the key or its hash

Do not log a key fingerprint as a consolation prize. A stable fingerprint becomes another correlator, is unnecessary for the decision above, and can encourage teams to treat possession evidence as identity evidence. Log the non-secret subject, tenant, scope set, secret version, and request ID instead. OWASP's secrets guidance recommends centralized storage, least privilege, rotation, expiration where possible, and care to prevent secrets from reaching logs.

That is enough evidence.

Make the verification path executable

The following program is deliberately adapter-driven. Its in-memory implementations make the example runnable with go run, while production adapters would call an account control plane and a secret manager over authenticated, encrypted connections. The safety function does not know their URLs.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/base64"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "slices"
)

type Request struct {
    Subject string
    Tenant  string
    Scopes  []string
}

type Identity struct {
    Subject string
    Tenant  string
    Scopes  []string
}

type Provisioner interface {
    Create(ctx context.Context, request Request) ([]byte, error)
    Revoke(ctx context.Context, credential []byte) error
}

type SecretStore interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, name string, value []byte) (version string, err error)
    Get(ctx context.Context, name, version string) ([]byte, error)
    Delete(ctx context.Context, name, version string) error
}

type Authenticator interface {
    WhoAmI(ctx context.Context, credential []byte) (Identity, error)
}

func bootstrap(ctx context.Context, request Request, name string,
    p Provisioner, store SecretStore, auth Authenticator) (string, error) {

    credential, err := p.Create(ctx, request)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("provision credential: %w", err)
    }
    committed := false
    defer func() {
        if !committed {
            _ = p.Revoke(ctx, credential)
        }
        clear(credential)
    }()

    version, err := store.Put(ctx, name, credential)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("store credential: %w", err)
    }

    stored, err := store.Get(ctx, name, version)
    if err != nil {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("read stored version: %w", err)
    }
    defer clear(stored)

    identity, err := auth.WhoAmI(ctx, stored)
    if err != nil {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("authenticate stored credential: %w", err)
    }
    wantScopes := append([]string(nil), request.Scopes...)
    gotScopes := append([]string(nil), identity.Scopes...)
    slices.Sort(wantScopes)
    slices.Sort(gotScopes)
    if identity.Subject != request.Subject || identity.Tenant != request.Tenant ||
        !slices.Equal(gotScopes, wantScopes) {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", errors.New("verified identity does not match requested boundary")
    }

    committed = true
    return version, nil
}

type memoryBackend struct {
    value    []byte
    request  Request
    version  string
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Create(_ context.Context, request Request) ([]byte, error) {
    raw := make([]byte, 32)
    if _, err := rand.Read(raw); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    m.request = request
    return []byte(base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(raw)), nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Revoke(_ context.Context, _ []byte) error { return nil }

func (m *memoryBackend) Put(_ context.Context, _ string, value []byte) (string, error) {
    m.value = append([]byte(nil), value...)
    m.version = "1"
    return m.version, nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Get(_ context.Context, _, version string) ([]byte, error) {
    if version != m.version {
        return nil, errors.New("unknown version")
    }
    return append([]byte(nil), m.value...), nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Delete(_ context.Context, _, _ string) error {
    clear(m.value)
    m.value = nil
    return nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) WhoAmI(_ context.Context, credential []byte) (Identity, error) {
    if !slices.Equal(credential, m.value) {
        return Identity{}, errors.New("unauthorized")
    }
    return Identity(m.request), nil
}

func main() {
    backend := &memoryBackend{}
    request := Request{
        Subject: "ci-usage-writer",
        Tenant:  "clinic-042",
        Scopes:  []string{"usage:append"},
    }
    version, err := bootstrap(context.Background(), request,
        "healthtech/clinic-042/usage-writer", backend, backend, backend)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("bootstrap verified: subject=%s tenant=%s secret_version=%s\n",
        request.Subject, request.Tenant, version)
}

The compensating path deserves scrutiny. If storage or verification fails, the program deletes the untrusted stored version and attempts revocation. Production code should use a short, separate cleanup context so cancellation of the main setup context does not prevent cleanup; it should also emit a non-secret request ID for reconciliation. The example keeps one context to expose the transaction shape without pretending that generic adapters share retry semantics.

This sample requires Go 1.21 because it uses clear and the slices package.

One subtle limit remains: Go's clear reduces accidental retention in these byte slices, but it cannot promise that no copy exists elsewhere in a runtime, transport, or backend. The stronger controls are architectural: never place the returned value in command arguments, environment dumps, formatted errors, test snapshots, or shell tracing; restrict the setup runner; and make the secret short-lived enough that rotation is routine.

Test the identity mismatch, not only the happy path

A useful test changes the returned identity after the secret write. Make the fake authenticator return clinic-024, add usage:read, or replace ci-usage-writer with a human subject. Each mutation must make bootstrap fail and trigger deletion plus revocation. Also test a store that acknowledges Put but cannot read the exact version back; “latest” is a race-prone reference when two setup jobs overlap.

Test logs too. Feed a recognizable canary credential through every error path, capture process output, and fail the test if the canary appears. This is where a bland success metric stops helping. The check should distinguish these states: provisioning never happened, provisioned but not stored, stored but not authenticated, identity mismatch, cleanup incomplete, and verified.

Retries require idempotency at the adapter boundary. If the provisioning service accepts an idempotency token, derive a new opaque token for one bootstrap attempt and persist its non-secret request ID. If it does not, reconcile by requested subject and tenant before creating another credential, then revoke superseded credentials after a verified replacement exists. Never infer success from an earlier process exit code alone.

Know when a static key is the wrong primitive

This pattern applies when the target service accepts an API key and the CI system must bootstrap it. It does not make a long-lived bearer secret ideal. When both ends support workload federation or another short-lived, audience-bound mechanism, prefer that design: the pipeline exchanges an existing workload identity for temporary access instead of storing a reusable credential. OAuth 2.0 defines bearer-token handling, and RFC 8707 defines resource indicators that can restrict where an access token is intended to be used; neither specification turns an arbitrary API key into a federated identity.

The decision is operational. Static bootstrap is defensible when its scope is narrow, its owner is machine-specific, rotation and revocation are tested, reads from the secret store are auditable, and the authenticated service can report effective identity. The limitation of this pattern is the reusable bearer secret: it is a poor fit when the service cannot expose identity, when all keys inherit account-wide permissions, or when a CI runner cannot keep secret output out of logs. The trade-off is extra setup and rotation work in exchange for compatibility with services that do not accept workload federation; that reason disappears as soon as both sides can exchange a workload identity for short-lived, audience-bound access.

Prefer federation then.

Before enabling the usage writer, run one synthetic event against a non-billable test tenant, verify the authenticated subject in the access record, and confirm that a forbidden operation is actually denied. Then alert on identity drift and cleanup failures, not on dashboard color. The final artifact is evidence of a bounded principal, not evidence that a string was copied successfully.

Sources

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707

title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.18883v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize student-visited positions using diverse signals, including uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, and mismatch direction. We instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself: how much can each position's loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student's predictive distribution? The answer is the utility $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. For reverse-KL it equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio, and for forward-KL it equals the Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence, so the appropriate utility follows from the choice of objective. On shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria, including student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP, concentrate their importance on nearly the same positions as the derived utility at a 50\% selection fraction, while diverging at stricter fractions and for direction-specific criteria. We instantiate the utility as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean-normalized token weighting. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 student-teacher pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD under both reverse-KL (1.35-4.0 macro points) and forward-KL (1.08-2.71 macro points), and is competitive with existing selective methods using a single closed-form score derived from the training objective.
