title: Nobody wants your AI app
description:
The people buying AI are blunt about the fact that the future is intelligence that disappears into existing platforms. Everyone wants it invisible and under their total control at the same time.

We are all racing to build AI apps that nobody wants to open.

Specifically, the standalone AI app, the thing you download, log into, and go to, is a worse idea than almost anyone building in the space wants to admit.

The numbers are brutal. According to RevenueCat’s analysis of more than 115,000 apps, AI apps are fantastic at getting you to sign up and terrible at getting you to stay. They convert free users to paid faster than regular apps, then lose them roughly a third faster.

A year in, only about one in five subscribers is still paying.

The pattern is simple and a little embarrassing. People try the AI app, get their “wow,” and then just stop opening it, because, often, it was just a novelty experience. Venture firm Bessemer has started warning that even business AI tools are heading for the same cliff unless they get themselves embedded into something people already use every day.

This is basically the same problem people had with Google+ (remember that?). Google got hundreds of millions of people to sign up, and then 90 percent of sessions lasted under five seconds.

You can build a gorgeous destination, pour a fortune into it, and get everyone to sign up once, and it still dies if nobody comes back.

Nir Eyal called what these app are missing the Hook Model, that products become habits through a loop of trigger, action, reward, and investment, each pass making the next one more likely. A novelty AI app nails the middle of that loop, you act, you get your clever reward, once, but there’s nothing pulling you back tomorrow and nothing that costs you to simply walk away from it. The loop never closes, so a habit never forms.

On the enterprise side, the rejection is blunter and faster. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard large companies insist they are not taking on yet another tool. At this point, they often already have their own internal AI product and don’t want a new destination, a new login, a new thing for their people to remember to visit.

They want the capability dropped inside the systems they already use, where the work already happens. Snyk, a security firm, studied more than 3,000 enterprise environments and found exactly that. Companies are stitching AI into their existing stack, not buying standalone products to use in parallel.

This is bigger than a retention problem.

The destination is dying. Not AI, AI is everywhere and growing. The app is dying.

The idea that you deliver intelligence by building a place for people to come get it is over. The future is no app at all, intelligence woven invisibly into the tools people already live in, surfacing when it’s useful and getting out of the way when it isn’t.

While that may sound clean, it isn’t. The same companies that want the AI invisible also want it completely under their control. They want it to disappear into the workflow and they want a dashboard, an audit trail, a record of every time it ran and what it touched.

Invisible to the user, totally visible to the owner.

Those two desires are at war, and whoever satisfies both at once is going to win the next decade of AI products.

We need to take stock of why the app model is collapsing, what the people buying AI actually want instead, why “invisible” is so much harder than it sounds, and where the real work, and the real careers, are moving.

The companies still pouring money into beautiful standalone AI apps are building tollbooths on a road people have already started to abandon.

The app everyone downloaded and nobody kept

Surprise, it’s not Quibi!

Malika Aubakirova and Anjney Midha at a16z, working with OpenRouter, analyzed more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world AI usage. Stickiness, they found, doesn’t depend on your product’s interface or features, but rather on the capabilities of the underlying model.

The same study found that fewer than one in ten weekly ChatGPT users ever bothers to try a competing assistant, despite there being zero cost to do it. People plant themselves in one big AI and stay.

They will not leave ChatGPT. They will drop your ChatGPT wrapper in a week. Stickiness lives with the model and churn lives with the destination you built on it.

People aren’t loyal to your app. They’re loyal to the intelligence inside it, and that intelligence is for rent, to everyone, including you.

This is why the AI app graveyard is filling up so fast. Character.AI lost roughly 60 percent of its user base in a year.

Jasper, one of the early AI-writing darlings, watched more than half its revenue evaporate.

Google+ had hundreds of millions of accounts and almost no one who came back. A gorgeous destination nobody had a reason to visit twice.

Yupp, an AI startup that raised thirty-three million dollars and signed up 1.3 million users, shut down anyway, with its founders explaining that the models underneath improved so fast that they never found a durable reason for anyone to keep coming back.

Over a million people used the product and it still wasn’t a business..

If that pattern feels familiar, it should. This is basically the MoviePass story with better branding (and I worked on MoviePass!).

Millions signed up overnight. There was no durable business underneath, and it collapsed in a heap. A lot of AI apps are basically following this same model.

MoviePass got millions of people to sign up almost overnight for something that felt like a cheat code, and the spectacular sign-up numbers meant nothing once it turned out there was no durable business underneath. Massive adoption, a value proposition that dissolved on contact with reality, and a collapse that happened faster than anyone expected.

A lot of today’s AI apps are doing the exact same thing.

Brian Balfour, the founder of Reforge and former head of growth at HubSpot, calls this “product-market fit collapse.” In normal software, customer expectations rise slowly, so a product that nails its market can coast for a while. In AI, he points out, expectations reset almost instantly.

Every time a new model drops, users recalibrate what “good” even means, and dropping your app for whatever is newer, or for the raw model underneath it, costs them nothing. You are not building toward a stable finish line because the finish line keeps moving away from you every few months.

We have a category with astonishing sign-up rates, near-zero switching costs, expectations that reset on a monthly basis, and no loyalty to anything except the model you don’t own.

That same body of research points, almost accidentally, at the way out. The a16z study describes what it calls a “glass slipper” effect. When a user’s actual workflow fits a particular model so precisely that it creates real inertia, a cost, finally, to leaving. The apps that retain are the ones that have wedged themselves so deeply into something a person does every day that walking away would actually hurt.

The answer is quite simple. Stop building a place for people to visit and start building something they can’t easily remove.

What the people buying AI actually want

Larger companies say they aren’t adding another AI tool the way someone declines a second helping at a dinner they’re already full from. These are organizations that have spent two years drowning in AI pilots, logins, dashboards, and Chrome extensions, and they have hit a wall.

Companies do not want another destination. They want the capability, the actual intelligence, dropped inside the systems their people already use, where the work already happens.

The most striking version of it I’ve heard is that you shouldn’t even have to know you’re using a different product. You should just know that the thing you were doing got better.

That is a remarkable thing for a company to say about a product it is paying for, and it is becoming the default expectation rather than the exception. The same instinct shows up outside the enterprise too. A news organization I talked with recently had no interest in building another app for people to download. They wanted their journalism to show up where people already are, in a text message, inside the AI assistant someone is already talking to, with no new place to go.

This is where the measurable center of gravity has already moved, and the infrastructure numbers show it.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard that lets AI reach into the tools and data a company already uses, went from a developer curiosity to something closer to 97 million downloads a month and production use inside roughly 40 percent of technical organizations. Gartner expects that by the end of the 2026, 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents built in.

The designers paying attention have already clocked what this does to the job. Patrick Neeman puts it bluntly, that chat was only ever an interface, and agents are something else entirely.

The design work, he argues, has moved to the contract underneath the product, the rules and handshakes that let one system quietly hand a task to another and get a trustworthy answer back. When the interface disappears, the thing you’re actually designing is the behavior.

Think about what “invisible utility” has always looked like once a technology matures. Mark Weiser, the Xerox PARC scientist who coined the term “ubiquitous computing,” put it in a line that has aged remarkably well. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear. They weave themselves into the fabric of everyday life until they are indistinguishable from it.”

Mark Weiser called it in 1991. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.” He was describing the future of the interface before most of us had one. AI is finally proving him right.

Nobody opens an app to use electricity. You don’t launch a program to get water out of the tap. The most important technologies succeeded precisely by disappearing, by becoming something simply present in the walls, available the instant you need it and invisible the rest of the time.

That is the shape AI is racing toward, and the companies building beautiful standalone AI destinations are, in a sense, trying to sell you a generator and a trip to the well at the exact moment everyone else is wiring the building.

The holy grail is a world where one AI simply calls another. Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation and adopted across more than 150 organizations, exists precisely so that one company’s AI can hand a task to a specialized capability elsewhere and get a usable answer back, with no human opening a separate product to make it happen.

The interface vanishes completely into the workflow. It’s genuinely hard to build well, and the infrastructure is still young, but the direction is set. The companies that understand it are to disappear.

That sounds like a potential answer. Make the intelligence invisible, embed it in the workflow, and, BOOM, you win. The problem is that the people who want it invisible want something else at the very same time, something that pulls in the exact opposite direction, and that contradiction is where most of this is going to get stuck.

Nobody has figured out invisible, but watched

The answer seems to be to make AI invisible. Embed it, dissolve it into the workflow, let it work without anyone having to go anywhere. Simple.

Except it isn’t, and the reason is entirely stuck in humanity. The same companies that demand the AI be invisible to their employees demand that it be completely visible to them.

They want it to disappear into the workflow, and they want a dashboard showing every time it ran. They want it to act without being summoned, and they want an audit trail of everything it touched. They want it woven invisibly into the fabric of everyday life, to borrow Weiser’s phrase, and they want a kill switch they can reach in half a second, a demand that turns out to be mostly aspirational.

In a Writer’s enterprise survey, more than a third of employees said they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent even if they needed to. Invisible to the user, yet totally visible to the owner.

The same leaders who tell me they want our capability to vanish into their systems will, ten minutes later, ask how they’ll track exactly who used it, how often, and what it returned, so they can prove the ROI to their own bosses. One large company essentially wanted the product to be invisible to its workforce and fully instrumented for its executives at the same time.

A recurring, hard stop in these conversations is data. More than one major brand has told me, flatly, that they will not feed their proprietary information into an outside tool, no matter how good it is, and that any vendor has to guarantee the model underneath isn’t quietly learning from what they put in.

Invisible is fine. Ungoverned is a non-starter.

Security researchers now treat this as table stakes.

Becky Brooks describes how organizations need to be able to answer basic questions about every AI action, which tools it called, what data passed through, whether any of it was proprietary, and most of them can’t.

The data behind that fear is genuinely alarming. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, the most-cited study in enterprise security, found that employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a single year, to 45 percent of the workforce, with two-thirds of those people using personal accounts outside any corporate control.

Cyberhaven’s analysis found the average employee now feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach report found that a growing majority of breached companies had no governance in place to manage AI or even detect its unapproved use.

The AI already has disappeared into the workflow.

It gets starker when you look at the actual network traffic. Infrastructure company Kong examined enterprise AI usage running through its systems and found that fewer than 1 percent of organizations had any AI-specific governance controls in place.

Meanwhile, almost 98 percent of their AI requests were flowing out to third-party proprietary services, every one of them carrying prompts, context, and often sensitive data outside the company’s own walls.

OutSystems found 94 percent of organizations worried that AI sprawl is piling up complexity, technical debt, and security risk, while only around 12 percent have any centralized way to manage it. Everyone feels the car accelerating. Almost nobody has their hands on the wheel.

There’s an old piece of political wisdom that fits this moment better than it has any right to. “Trust, but verify.” The companies buying AI have landed in exactly that posture, except the technology has made the two halves nearly impossible to hold at once.

The whole appeal of invisible AI is that you don’t have to watch it. The whole fear of invisible AI is that you can’t.

A thing designed to operate without your attention is, by definition, a thing operating outside your attention, and that is a terrifying property to hand a system that can touch your data, your customers, and your decisions.

This is the actual product problem of the next decade. The winning AI products will be the ones that pull off the paradox of being genuinely invisible to the person doing the work, and genuinely transparent to the person who owns the risk.

Disappear for the user. Light up like a control room for the owner. The teams that treat “invisible” as the whole goal are going to build things no serious company will deploy, because they solved for elegance and ignored accountability. The teams that bury everything in dashboards and approval gates will build something so visible and so clunky that it’s just another tool nobody opens, which puts us right back where we started.

Enterprises want the AI invisible to their people and lit up like this for themselves: every action logged, every data path visible. Invisible to the user, accountable to the owner. Almost nobody has built both.

Getting both right is brutally hard. It’s also the only version of this that actually wins.

Move Up the Stack or Get Buried in It

If you design or build products for a living, this could read like a eulogy for your job. It isn’t. The app dying is not the same as the work dying.

The work moved, and the people who notice where it went are going to be fine. The people who keep polishing the thing that’s going away are the ones who should be nervous.

Nielsen Norman Group has been studying how people actually use software since before most AI founders could type, put it about as plainly as it can be put, AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives.

The interface, the screen, the thing we used to spend all our time perfecting, is becoming a commodity. You can generate a competent one in an afternoon now. What you cannot generate in an afternoon is the judgment about what the system should do, when it should speak up, when it should stay quiet, what it’s allowed to touch, and how a human stays in control of something built to run without them.

Patrick Neeman has a sharp way of framing the trap we have to design our way out of. The reason everyone reached for chat, he argues, is that conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product rather than reveal it.

The thing that feels like the answer, a text box you talk to, is often the thing keeping you from building what the moment actually needs.

The designer’s job used to be drawing the screen. Now it’s deciding the behavior, the rules and handshakes underneath, the contract between systems that no user will ever see but every user will feel.

The hardest, highest-value version of that work is the paradox from a minute ago, made real.

Mangus Eriksen lands on the exact tension this whole piece has been circling. Invisible AI only works if people trust it, and trust requires transparency and real control, without burying that control three menus deep. Read that next to the governance data from earlier and you have the entire job description for the next decade of product work.

Make it disappear for the person using it. Make it accountable to the person who owns it. Hide the machinery, surface the controls. That is a genuinely hard design problem, and it is nothing like designing a prettier chat window.

Think about what happened to the switchboard operator. In the early 20th century, connecting phone calls by hand was one of the most common jobs for young women in America. Then AT&T automated it, and the economists James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross documented what followed. Once a city switched to dial, the operator jobs didn’t shrink, they vanished, dropping 50 to 80 percent and never coming back.

The need underneath, connecting people reliably, didn’t vanish at all. It moved up the stack, into switching systems and the engineers who design them, and it got more valuable. The part that matters is this: the women who were operators mostly didn’t make that jump.

The function moved up, and a lot of the people defined by the old version of it got left behind. The ones who thrived were the ones who moved to the layer underneath before they were forced to.

This connects to something that’s becoming ubiquitous in AI. Nobody is coming to hand you the next version of your job. Not in the broad economy, and not in our corner of it.

The people who make it through every one of these shifts are the ones who stop defending the thing they were good at and start building the thing the new world actually needs, before they’re forced to. In this case, that means letting go of the beautiful destination and getting good at the invisible, accountable system underneath it.

The future of AI is the intelligence woven so completely into the tools people already use that they stop noticing it’s there, with a clean pane of glass that lets whoever is responsible see exactly what it’s doing. Invisible to the user. Accountable to the owner. Almost nobody is building for both yet, which is precisely why it’s the opportunity.

The companies still pouring money into gorgeous standalone AI apps are building elegant tollbooths on a road people have already started to leave. The winners are somewhere else entirely, down in the plumbing, making the intelligence disappear into the work and handing the owner the keys to watch it.

The destination is dead. The infrastructure is where everything now lives.

References and further reading

Why the app model is collapsing

Malika Aubakirova, Anjney Midha, Alex Atallah, Chris Clark, Justin Summerville, State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study. Stickiness depends on the underlying model, not your interface; fewer than 10% of users switch despite zero cost.

RevenueCat, 2026 State of Subscription Apps Report. AI apps churn 30 to 36 percent faster than non-AI apps; only about 1 in 5 subscribers remains after a year.

Bessemer Venture Partners, Seven Product Strategies to Prevent Churn for B2B AI App Leaders. Even B2B AI tools face the churn cliff unless embedded in a daily workflow.

Brian Balfour (Reforge), on product-market fit collapse. In AI, customer expectations reset almost instantly and switching is trivial.

Google+ (Wikipedia). The destination that signed up hundreds of millions and became a ghost town, with 90 percent of sessions under five seconds.

MoviePass (Wikipedia). Spectacular sign-ups, no durable business underneath, fast collapse.

What the buyers actually want

Snyk, State of Agentic AI Adoption. Across 3,000-plus enterprise environments, organizations are embedding AI into their existing stack rather than buying standalone tools; the real AI footprint is roughly 3x the model list.

The Enterprise MCP Guide. The Model Context Protocol’s near-vertical adoption, roughly 97 million monthly downloads and production use in about 40 percent of technical organizations.

Gartner, via OutSystems research. 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents by the end of the year.

Patrick Neeman, Headless AI Will Make Every Product a Platform. The design work has moved to the contract underneath the product.

Mark Weiser (Wikipedia). The father of ubiquitous computing: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.”

Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol (via FifthRow). The Linux Foundation standard that lets one AI hand a task to another, adopted across 150-plus organizations.

Invisible, but watched

Writer, 2026 Enterprise AI Adoption Report. A third of employees say they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent.

The MCP and AI Governance Gap (Techstrong). Enterprises need to answer basic questions about every AI action, and most can’t.

Verizon, 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report. Employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a year to 45 percent of the workforce, two-thirds via personal accounts.

Cyberhaven, shadow AI analysis. The average employee feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM, Cost of a Data Breach Report. A growing majority of breached companies had no governance to manage or detect AI use.

Kong, enterprise AI governance research. Fewer than 1 percent of organizations have AI-specific governance controls; almost 98 percent of AI requests go to third-party services.

OutSystems, State of AI Development. 94 percent worry about AI sprawl; only about 12 percent have centralized management.

Where the work goes

Nielsen Norman Group, on AI-native UX. AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives; the interface is becoming a commodity.

Patrick Neeman, Designing for AI Means Designing Like It’s 1999. Conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product.

UXmatters, The Era of the Invisible User Interface. Invisible AI works only if people trust it, which requires transparency and real control.

James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross, Answering the Call of Automation (Quarterly Journal of Economics). When switchboards automated, the job vanished and the incumbents mostly did not move up with the work.

title: AFCS: Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis for Factual Knowledge Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2610.20086v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly used in language-model pretraining. Existing knowledge-corpus synthesis pipelines, including WRAP and Nemotron-CC, usually take a source passage or document segment as input and generate rewritten or QA-style samples from that text. This can improve surface form and prompt diversity, but it does not explicitly require fine-grained source facts -- especially secondary entities, list/table entries, and precise temporal attributes -- to appear in the synthesized corpus. We propose AFCS (Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis), a pipeline that first extracts source-supported atomic facts and then uses each retained fact to drive generation. AFCS uses structure-aware extraction over the document tree, source-grounded verification, local context expansion, and multi-format generation. In continued-pretraining experiments with OLMo-3-7B and a 32B base on the same FineWiki source corpus, AFCS outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA. Granularity ablations show that fact-level synthesis improves over chunk-level, paragraph-level, and entity-level synthesis; and a 100B-token mid-training integration improves factual benchmarks and raises the 12-task general benchmark average by +1.09.

title: Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability in NLP: A Critical Survey of Recoverability, Interpretability, and Utility
description:
arXiv:2610.20139v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach to mechanistic interpretability by decomposing language-model activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features. However, differences in design assumptions, evaluation objectives, and experimental settings complicate conclusions about their effectiveness. We present a critical survey of 138 studies on SAEs in natural language processing. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) we propose a task-grounded taxonomy connecting dictionary design, feature operations, and NLP functions; (2) we examine how sparsity allocation, geometry, data coverage, and inference affect feature recoverability; (3) we assess evidence for semantic interpretability, mechanistic faithfulness, and behavioral utility; and (4) we synthesize findings across multilingual processing, retrieval, reasoning, classification, and behavioral regulation, highlighting the roles of objectives, baselines, supervision, and intervention pipelines. Through comparative analyses of published results, we reconcile apparent disagreements, identify unresolved questions, and propose directions for more rigorous evaluation. An anonymous research register https://anonymous.4open.science/r/sae-research-register-C331/register.html accompanies the survey.

title: Sort providers by cost, latency, or throughput on AI Gateway
description:
You can now sort the providers behind a model by cost, time to first token (TTFT), or throughput (TPS) in AI Gateway.

The default provider order blends provider reliability, quality of model output, cost, and speed of response. You can now use sort for explicit control over ranking criteria.

For models with many providers and noticeable cost or speed variation, you can use sort to optimize on your dimension of choice. Ranking is computed at request time, so newly added providers, price changes, and shifts in observed latency or throughput flow through automatically without any code changes.

Set sort on providerOptions.gateway to one of the three values:

Value

Description

Direction

When to use

'cost'

Sort by the provider's listed input price per million tokens

Lowest price first

High-volume, cost-sensitive work

'ttft'

Sort by median time to first token, in ms

Lowest latency first

Latency-sensitive workloads where response speed matters

'tps'

Sort by median tokens per second throughput

Highest first

Long-output generation where total response time matters most

Basic usage

Use sort to ensure optimizing for your metric of choice.

In this example, AI Gateway has over five providers for GPT OSS 120B with different prices, so sorting by cost is a useful option for requests that want to route through the lowest price provider.

Providers are tried in sort order. Fallback to the next provider only happens when the higher-ranked one is unavailable.

Combine with other routing controls

sort is compatible with other gateway routing options like Zero Data Retention (ZDR).

The example below uses deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro for an interactive request where latency and data retention matter: AI Gateway filters to only providers for Deepseek V4 Pro that have zero data retention, and then sorts the remaining providers by time to first token (TTFT).

sort also composes with order: providers listed in order are promoted to the front, and the remaining providers follow the requested sort criterion.

Inspecting routing decisions

See exactly why each request landed where it did. Every response includes a sort block in the routing metadata showing which providers were considered, the metric values used to rank them, the order they were attempted, and any that were deprioritized due to degraded health.

For more information on sorting via AI Gateway, read the documentation.

title: Beyond Static Positional Encoding: Bayesian Time-aware Attention for Non-Stationary Long-term Time Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.19603v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformers have demonstrated strong performance in long-term time series forecasting (LTSF), yet modeling non-stationary temporal dependencies remains challenging. In this paper, we interpret self-attention as a Bayesian posterior over attended positions, combining a content-based prior induced by scaled dot-product similarity with a temporal-evidence likelihood induced by positional encoding. This formulation provides a probabilistic interpretation of how positional encoding shapes the temporal dependencies captured by self-attention. Building on this perspective, we derive a population-level evidence lower bound (ELBO) that characterizes the role of positional encoding in forecasting weakly stationary time series. Our analysis further highlights a limitation of static positional encoding: when temporal dependence structures vary across input windows, a fixed temporal bias must accommodate heterogeneous dynamics and can therefore be suboptimal for non-stationary forecasting. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Bayesian Time-aware Attention (BTA), which employs a mixture-of-experts (MoE) router to adaptively combine temporal kernels and generate input-conditioned, head-specific positional biases. Extensive experiments on standard LTSF benchmarks demonstrate that BTA consistently improves forecasting performance across multiple Transformer backbones and achieves competitive overall performance with modest computational overhead and stable training.

title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
description:
arXiv:2610.19380v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.

title: When Pleasing the User Compromises Care: AI Sycophancy in Caregiver-Mediated Healthcare
description:
arXiv:2610.14360v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) alignment often assumes that the user interacting with a model is also the primary beneficiary of its behavior. Yet in many consequential settings, one person directs the system while another bears the consequences. We study this problem in caregiver-mediated healthcare, where parents, pet owners, and caregivers make decisions for children, animals, and older adults. We introduce an evidence-grounded benchmark spanning veterinary, pediatric, and older-adult care, and test whether AI advisors maintain appropriate care when users express clinically inferior preferences. Holding patient facts fixed, we vary stated care preferences and communication styles and evaluate both initial recommendations and multi-turn follow-up. Across frontier and open-weight models, inferior preferences substantially increase switching from appropriate to inappropriate care beyond neutral conversational drift and increase agreement with the requested action, while communication style alone has a smaller effect. These failures accumulate across turns, including on cases models initially answer correctly, and often carry moderate or severe potential harm. In matched eldercare cases, the effect of an inferior preference is similar whether it is expressed by the patient or by a caregiver. Together with models' limited tendency to elicit patient preferences in caregiver conversations, this suggests that current models are highly sensitive to expressed user preferences but less sensitive to whose preferences are represented and who bears the consequences. Our results expose a broader limitation of user-centric alignment in settings with multiple stakeholders.

title: Updates to Legal Terms
description:
The proliferation of agentic workflows means developers now regularly grant AI tools direct access to their infrastructure, use services that act autonomously, and build on platforms that themselves use AI to operate. We’ve updated our Terms of Service and Marketplace terms to clarify shared responsibility when actions on your account may be taken by AI, whether Vercel's own or a third-party tool you've connected, as well as other important updates detailed below.

What is changing?

AI Functionality and Third-Party Tools

Vercel's platform increasingly includes AI-powered services, including v0, Vercel Agent, WAF natural language rules, and AI Gateway. These services may take actions on your behalf. We've introduced two new concepts to make the responsibilities around this explicit:

AI Functionality refers to Vercel services that are AI-powered, that help you build AI products (like AI SDK), or that connect to AI providers (like AI Gateway).

Third-Party Tools refers to any non-Vercel tool, script, service, or automation (AI-powered or not) that you grant access to your Vercel account. This includes CI/CD pipelines, third-party agents, and integration scripts.

The key responsibilities:

  • You control how AI Functionality behaves through your settings. Those settings define the scope of what AI Functionality can do on your behalf.

  • You are responsible for reviewing and authorizing the actions AI Functionality takes, and for evaluating its outputs against your own requirements.

  • If you grant a Third-Party Tool access to your Vercel account (e.g., giving it your API key), you are responsible for what it does, including any costs it incurs.

  • You are responsible for actions taken by AI Functionality or Third-Party Tools on your behalf.

title: Trust Hinders Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.15136v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Trust calibration remains the dominant framing of AI-assisted decision making: the goal is to close the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness of AI systems so that users exhibit appropriate reliance on them. We argue that this approach, while useful for decision problems that are well-defined and clearly scoped, overly restricts what it means to make a decision with AI support. To overcome this limitation, we develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decision making. First, trusting AI is only one of several possible strategies for managing uncertainty. Second, trust calibration is often misapplied when AI models "large-world" decision problems, i.e., ill-defined situations where goals and states are only partially known or unknowable. Third, in such settings human-AI alignment requires addressing higher-order decision processes. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of our observations on the design of process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout the decision-making task.

title: ConicFlow: constrained Inference-time optimal control for flow matching models
description:
arXiv:2610.14307v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose ConicFlow, which frames constrained sampling from a flow matching model at inference time as an optimal control problem that balances deviation from the pretrained trajectory against reward, subject to hard terminal constraints. We discretize this problem and adapt receding-horizon control, optimizing only a short window of the trajectory at each step for computational tractability. We address the resulting sequence of receding-horizon subproblems with a receding-horizon primal-dual algorithm. Its dual multipliers capture the difficulty of satisfying each constraint and are refined throughout sampling, steering generation toward feasible final samples. We further propose a terminal-estimate variant that avoids accumulating local truncation errors by evaluating the reward and constraints at the predicted terminal point rather than at the end of the current horizon. Under standard regularity assumptions, we establish finite-horizon guarantees on suboptimality. Under convex-affine structure, we derive a sharper bound that scales linearly with omitted horizon length, and we show that the terminal-estimate variant is provably tighter when the flow dynamics change slowly. Experiments in both low- and high-dimensional settings with a recent large-scale flow matching model show that ConicFlow achieves high reward and strong constraint satisfaction while deviating less from the pretrained flow than recent baselines.

title: Language Exposure Matters: Distribution and Order in Multilingual BabyLM Pre-training
description:
arXiv:2610.20102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate two aspects of multilingual pre-training with limited data, namely how language exposure is distributed across English, Dutch, and Chinese, and how that exposure is ordered during training. In particular, we compare balanced multilingual exposure to language-dominant exposure, where one language is exposed with more training data than the others. We also compare mixed training, where multilingual training data is used throughout training, with curriculum training, where monolingual exposure of the dominant language is followed by balanced multilingual exposure. Our results show that multilingual BabyLM performance varies with both the amount and order of language exposure. Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning across all 15 matched configurations, indicating that simultaneous multilingual exposure is more effective than staged exposure in our setting. Several language-dominant mixed training configurations achieve higher scores than the balanced configuration, suggesting that a balanced distribution is not necessarily the highest-performing configuration in our setting. Interestingly, the Dutch-primary configurations achieve the best overall performance.

title: Deleting a user's data from backups: crypto-shredding with one key per person
description:
A user asks you to delete their data. You delete the row. Then you remember the replica, last month's backup, the S3 export someone made for analytics, and the log line with their email in it. You can't edit most of those.

Crypto-shredding is the standard way out: encrypt each person's data under their own key, keep the keys in one small keystore, and "delete" a person by destroying their key. The ciphertext can stay wherever it is. Without the key it's noise.

I built a small library for this called aegis-shred: a Rust core, a Python package and a CLI.

from aegis_shred import MasterKey, Vault

vault = Vault.open("keys.db", MasterKey.from_env("AEGIS_MASTER_KEY"), create=True)
blob = vault.seal("user-42", b"alice@example.com", context=b"users.email")  # store anywhere
vault.unseal(blob, context=b"users.email")   # b'alice@example.com'
vault.shred("user-42")                       # erase user-42, everywhere, at once
vault.unseal(blob, context=b"users.email")   # raises aegis_shred.Shredded

How it works 

master key (from your secret manager)
  └─ wraps one data key per subject ───── keystore (SQLite file)
        └─ HKDF → one key per sealed object
              └─ AES-256-GCM, chunked (STREAM)
                    └─ sealed blob/file ── your database, S3, backups, …
  • seal creates the subject's key on first use and returns a self-describing blob. The blob names a random key id, never the user.
  • unseal checks every chunk. A modified byte, a reordered or missing chunk, truncation, or a different context all fail.
  • shred deletes the wrapped key in one transaction, writes a tombstone and a hash-chained audit entry, and returns a receipt. From then on, in every process, that user's blobs raise Shredded.
  • The keystore stores subjects only as HMAC(index_key, subject_id), so the keystore and audit log don't list your users either.

The context argument binds a blob to where it lives, so a ciphertext copied from one column into another won't decrypt.

Large files are streamed in 64 KiB chunks with constant memory, and the output file only appears if every chunk verifies.

Install 

pip install aegis-shred          # prebuilt wheels for Linux, macOS, Windows
cargo add aegis-shred            # Rust library
cargo install aegis-shred-cli    # the aegis command

Honest limits

This is v0.1, alpha. The byte format is specified and versioned, every guarantee has a test, and a second independent implementation in Python runs in CI. But there has been no independent security audit. Read the threat model in the repo before relying on it.

Whether crypto-shredding satisfies GDPR Art. 17, CCPA or India's DPDP Act for your situation is a question for your lawyers. The library gives you the mechanism and an audit trail, not legal cover.

Repo (MIT OR Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Lingikaushikreddy/Aegis

Feedback on the threat model and the file format is the most useful thing you could send me.

title: The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It
description:
The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It

What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

Uncertain rewards. Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

Self-regulation. In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

title: Towards a Data-Centric Understanding of Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.

title: Why One Happy Path Beats a Menu of Options When Your User Is an AI Agent
description:
Give an engineer five ways to deploy an app and they'll pick one. When I gave an AI agent several ways, it tried a few, mixed them together, and left me debugging at midnight.

That's the reason agentic-hosting works the way it does. It's an open-source tool I built that turns a Linux server you own into a place AI coding agents can deploy apps and databases on their own. This post explains its main design rule, one way to do each job, and walks through the API calls an agent makes to go from a git repo to a live URL.

⭐ If this is useful, a star on GitHub helps other people find it.

🤖 Give this to your agent: point it at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dennisonbertram/agentic-hosting/main/llms.txt (or the skill) and it can sign up and get going from that one link.

Why fewer options

I used to think "only one way to do it" was a sign of an unfinished product. Heroku, Kubernetes, Coolify, and Dokku all give you lots of settings, because people running servers have strong opinions about how to build and route things.

Agents don't have opinions. They make a guess, and if the guess fails they retry, sometimes with a different guess. Every extra option is another branch they can wander down that I never tested.

So agentic-hosting has one build system, one router, and one choice per database type. If there's only one path, the agent can't find a creative one I didn't plan for. Here's what that looks like in practice.

Building: git repo in, running app out

Apps are built with Nixpacks, a tool that looks at your code and figures out how to package it into a container without a Dockerfile. It's the only build option. You can't upload your own Dockerfile.

Deploying from git takes two calls. First the agent creates a service. The API requires an image field, so for git deploys it sends the placeholder "pending":

POST /v1/services
Authorization: Bearer <api_key>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "my-app",
  "image": "pending",
  "port": 3000
}

Then it starts a build:

POST /v1/services/{serviceID}/builds

{
  "source_type": "git",
  "source_url": "https://github.com/org/repo",
  "source_ref": "main"
}

source_type has to be "git", and source_ref defaults to "main". Only HTTPS URLs from github.com, gitlab.com, bitbucket.org, sr.ht, and codeberg.org are accepted. Anything else gets rejected before the build starts.

While it builds, the agent can watch the logs:

GET /v1/services/{serviceID}/builds/{buildID}/logs?follow=true

Because there's only one build path, the logs always look the same, and when something breaks there's one place to look. In my experience that helps the agent more than which build tool it is.

Routing: you get one URL

Traefik, an open-source proxy, takes incoming web traffic and sends it to the right app. agentic-hosting writes Traefik's config itself. Apps can't set their own routing rules, so a container can't quietly grab another app's traffic.

The URL follows one pattern:

  • By default: http://{serviceID}.localhost
  • If you start the server with --base-domain example.com (or set AH_BASE_DOMAIN): https://{dns_label}.example.com, where dns_label comes from the service name 
GET /v1/services/{serviceID}
# → includes "url": "http://svc_….localhost"
#    or "https://my-app.example.com"

Custom domains aren't supported yet. That's issue #82.

Databases: Postgres or Redis

The type field takes "postgres" or "redis", and nothing else.

POST /v1/databases

{ "name": "my-db", "type": "postgres" }

It takes about 10 to 30 seconds. Then the agent grabs the connection string, adds it to the app's environment variables, and restarts the app:

GET /v1/databases/{dbID}/connection-string

POST /v1/services/{serviceID}/env
{ "DATABASE_URL": "<connection-string>" }

POST /v1/services/{serviceID}/restart

Environment variables are encrypted on disk and hidden in API responses unless you add ?reveal=true.

The smaller limits

The same thinking shows up in small places. Creating a service accepts name, image, port, and optional env, so the agent can't request more memory or CPU. Images come from Docker Hub or the server's own local registry. And if the agent retries a request with the same Idempotency-Key header within 10 minutes, it won't deploy twice.

None of this limits what you can build. It limits how many ways the agent can get there, which is what I wanted.

Try it

With the server running (see the README, or run ./bin/ah --dev --open-registration --port 8080 on your laptop), the agent's path is:

  1. Register to get an API key.
  2. Create a service with "image": "pending".
  3. Start a build from a git URL.
  4. Watch the build logs, then the app logs at GET /v1/services/{id}/logs?follow=true&tail=100.
  5. Create a Postgres or Redis database, set the env var, restart.
  6. Open the service's url.

If you use Claude Code, the repo also has a skill and /ah-deploy, /ah-db, /ah-logs, and /ah-status commands that do the same steps.

Wrapping up

agentic-hosting gives an AI agent exactly one way to build, route, and add a database, which makes its runs a lot more predictable. You run it on your own server, and the agent does the deploying.

  • ⭐ Star agentic-hosting on GitHub so more people find it.
  • 🤖 Give this to your agent: llms.txt to sign up and set up, or the agent skill for daily use.
  • 📖 Read the docs and try the quickstart.
  • 💬 Open an issue with what you'd want your agent to do next.

And if you hand your agent the keys and something breaks, tell me what it was.

title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
description:
arXiv:2610.19992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.

title: Ephemeral credentials for databases: moving past the shared application account
description:
Ephemeral credentials for databases: moving past the shared application account

A shared database account is a familiar design. An application reads its connection string from configuration, all replicas use the same username and password, and rotation means a coordinated restart across every service that depends on it. Rotation therefore happens rarely or not at all.

Why the static credential persists

The convenience is real. Connection pools assume a stable identity. Database proxies, failover, and read replicas all inherit the same secret. Introducing per-instance credentials appears to add operational risk rather than remove it.

What short-lived credentials change

Dynamic secrets are issued on request and expire on a schedule. Each application instance receives its own credential, so revocation affects one instance instead of the fleet. Auditing becomes concrete: the database log shows which instance connected when.

The lifetime should match the workload. A batch job that runs for two hours needs a credential that outlives the job. A web service that can re-authenticate on each connection can use a much shorter window.

Handling the transition

Connection pools are the practical obstacle. Pools must be configured to refresh credentials before expiry, and the refresh must be tested against database failover. Applications should handle a rejected connection by requesting a new credential rather than retrying the old one indefinitely.

Emergency access needs its own path. If the issuing service is unavailable, operators need a documented break-glass procedure, with the use of that path logged and reviewed.

Verifying the control

A credential system is only as good as what it prevents. Confirm that a revoked credential is rejected within the expected window, that a leaked credential from one instance cannot be used by another, and that the audit trail records the subject rather than a shared account.

References

  • NIST SP 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final
  • NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final

title: Integrated Novelty Detection Systems: From Sensor Networks to Multi-Novelty Computer Vision
description:
arXiv:2610.19347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Novelty detection is crucial in various technological and scientific domains. Its importance spans from ensuring the reliability of sensor networks to enhancing the adaptability of computer vision systems. As AI systems become increasingly sophisticated and complex, effective anomaly detection is essential for maintaining reliability and accuracy. This work addresses novelty detection in weather sensor networks and computer vision. In weather sensor networks, particularly for monitoring rainfall, detecting blocked rain gauges can significantly impact data reliability, food security, and disaster management. This work evaluates four existing quality control methods for detecting blocked rain gauges and demonstrates their limitations, particularly in detecting clusters of faulty sensors. By comparing methods such as the Conditional Mixture Model (CMM), PSWQ (Fz-filter), Kernel Regression, and Gaussian Method, we identify their shortcomings and propose three novel quality control techniques that integrate probabilistic fault detection and consistency-based diagnosis framework to improve timely detection of blocked sensors, while reducing false alarms.
  In the realm of computer vision, current systems often fail to handle multiple types of novelty due to their focus on single-novelty scenarios. We highlight the need for integrated systems capable of handling multiple types of novelty. To support this, we introduce the Novel Snapshot Serengeti (NOVEL-SS) dataset, derived from the Snapshot Serengeti camera trap data, which includes various forms of novelty. We also present the DCA (Detect, Characterize, and Accommodate) baseline system, designed to handle multiple novelty by detecting, characterizing, and accommodating them. This work aims to advance the robustness and adaptability of novelty detection systems across both weather sensor networks and computer vision applications.

title: Why 3D Reconstruction Breaks Down on Under-Ice AUV Video, and How to Predict It
description:
arXiv:2610.19993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstruction of 3D structures using under-ice AUV video footage has been inaccurate, although it is not certain whether this is due to shortcomings in the methods or an inherent deficiency of the capture system. We test four different models for reconstruction on the same Antarctic under-ice AUV video (Icefin, Kamb Ice Stream): classical feature matching SfM, differentiable photometric splatting, volumetric depth fusion, and a pose-free feed-forward foundation model. All four fail, each in a distinct way: near-total registration yielding almost no structure, geometrically broken output despite healthy photometric metrics, a persistent coverage artifact, and unstable cross-chunk scale. We show that all four are consistent with the same capture regime, a small camera-baseline-to-scene-depth ratio. Following our analysis, we propose a detection system that flags this type of failure in minutes, rather than hours of wasted compute.
