title: RepoDNA v1.3.3: Safer WebAssembly CLI, Better Artifact Protection, and Security Fixes
description:
RepoDNA v1.3.3: Safer WebAssembly CLI, Better Artifact Protection, and Security Fixes

Building a developer tool is not just about supporting more programming languages, generating more metrics, or introducing new visualizations.

It is also about what happens when something goes wrong.

What happens when a user supplies an invalid command-line option? What if a report output accidentally points to the analysis file being read? What should a documentation generator do when a link contains malformed encoding?

These are the kinds of questions addressed in RepoDNA v1.3.3, the latest stable release of my open-source, local-first repository intelligence project.

What is RepoDNA?

RepoDNA helps developers understand a software repository through evidence-backed analysis.

It explores repository architecture, module dependencies, Git history, code complexity, security signals, development activity, and more.

It also produces shareable Project DNA cards, reports, and comparisons.

The project is built around Rust, TypeScript, React, and WebAssembly. Its analysis is designed to work locally, without requiring source-code uploads.

  1. Stricter WebAssembly CLI argument validation

RepoDNA includes a WebAssembly distribution that can run analysis and reporting operations without installing a platform-specific native executable.

In v1.3.3, the repodna-wasm command-line launcher has improved validation.

The launcher now rejects invalid input conditions such as missing option values, unsupported report formats, unsupported themes, unsupported privacy presets, flags used with the wrong command, and repeated flags.

These errors are detected before the WebAssembly engine is loaded.

This makes incorrect command-line usage more predictable and easier to diagnose.

  1. Protecting analysis files from accidental replacement

One of the most important changes in this release concerns file safety.

When producing a report or Project DNA card, users specify an analysis artifact and an output destination.

A mistake in those paths should not destroy the original analysis.

RepoDNA v1.3.3 adds safeguards that prevent the WebAssembly CLI from replacing its input analysis file with the generated report or card.

The protection also covers hard links that refer to the same underlying file.

This is a small but meaningful improvement to artifact integrity.

  1. More reliable documentation generation

The documentation-site builder now handles relative paths in raw HTML more consistently.

Links and images using either single-quoted or double-quoted href and src attributes are handled correctly.

The builder also reports malformed percent-encoding in documentation links instead of crashing.

For documentation maintainers, actionable build diagnostics are much more useful than an unexpected termination.

  1. Rust security dependency updates

The release upgrades rustls to version 0.23.46 in both Rust lockfiles.

The update addresses the following advisories:

RUSTSEC-2026-0346

RUSTSEC-2026-0347

RUSTSEC-2026-0348

RUSTSEC-2026-0349

Dependency maintenance is an essential part of maintaining an open-source developer tool, particularly one distributed across several platforms.

  1. Regression tests

The release also adds regression coverage for WebAssembly CLI argument handling and analysis-file preservation.

These tests can run without building the entire WebAssembly engine.

Documentation-site tests now cover raw HTML links and malformed URL encodings as well.

The goal is not simply to fix an issue once, but to make it less likely to return.

Using RepoDNA

The web version is available here:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

You can explore the built-in demonstration or analyze a local folder or archive directly in the browser.

For a command-line installation through npm:

npm install --global @sanskarin/repodna

To use the WebAssembly package:

npx @sanskarin/repodna-wasm analyze .

Platform-specific release downloads are also available for Windows, Linux, and macOS.

What comes next?

RepoDNA continues to evolve as a tool for codebase understanding, architecture exploration, repository history, and evidence-based engineering decisions.

For this release, the priority was correctness, predictable error handling, artifact protection, and security maintenance.

Not every meaningful update needs a large new feature.

Sometimes the most valuable improvement is making an existing tool more dependable.

Links

GitHub: https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA

v1.3.3 Release: https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.3.3

Web version: https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

Documentation: https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/docs/

Source comparison: https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/compare/v1.3.2...v1.3.3

If you work with developer tooling, static analysis, repository architecture, or open-source software, I'd be interested to hear your feedback.

RepoDNA — Understand your codebase. See its DNA.

title: Attention-Based Spatio-Temporal Approach for Fire and Smoke Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.20141v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In various industries, smoke and fire are two of the most important threats in the workplace. One of the common methods for detecting smoke and fire is the use of infrared thermal and smoke sensors, which cannot be used in outdoor applications. Therefore, the use of vision-based methods seems necessary. The problem of smoke and fire detection is spatiotemporal and requires spatiotemporal solutions. This paper presents a method that uses spatial features along with temporal-based features to detect smoke and fire in the scene. It consists of three main parts; the task of each part is to reduce the error of the previous part so that the final model has a robust performance. This method also uses transformer modules to increase the accuracy of the model. The results of our model show the proper performance of the proposed approach in solving the problem of smoke and fire detection and can be used to increase workplace safety.

title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization
description:
arXiv:2610.19344v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.

title: Choosing the Number of Attention Heads from Intrinsic Dimension: A Small-Scale Study
description:
arXiv:2610.19966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The number of attention heads in a transformer is usually set by convention or grid search. We test a simple heuristic for setting it in advance: estimate the intrinsic dimension of token representations without labels, and use roughly that many heads. We estimate intrinsic dimension with a nested-dropout VAE trained on DistilBERT embeddings of WikiText-2, choosing the KL weight at the knee of the VAE's rate-distortion curve rather than by hand. This gives $k^*=9.2$ (95% CI [8.6, 9.8]). In a small 4-layer transformer trained from scratch, 10 heads and 32 heads are statistically equivalent on SST-2 and on MRPC (paired TOST over 10 seeds, $\pm1$ point margin), with 69% fewer attention parameters for the 10-head model. Training 10 heads from the start also slightly outperforms training 32 heads and pruning to 10 (0.6 points, $p=0.008$). The evidence is narrow: two classification tasks, one small architecture, no pretrained models, and no formal link between intrinsic dimension and head count. We present the result as a practical heuristic worth testing at larger scale, not as a general principle.

title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
description:
arXiv:2610.19291v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).

title: Qt, GTK, Flutter, Electron? No: a graphics engine from scratch, entirely in Rust
description:
Llimphi draws every pixel of tawasuyu, even inside an operating system that boots with no Linux underneath. Why it exists, how it works and how true that “from scratch” really is.

Every time you open an application, something has to draw every button, every letter and every window on your screen, dozens of times per second. That something is a graphics engine, and almost nobody builds their own: most of the world’s software is painted with Qt, GTK, Flutter or Electron. Tawasuyu, the software suite with Quechua names being written in the Gioser workshop, chose not to borrow one.

Its engine is called Llimphi, which in Quechua means color, shine, pigment. It draws the whole suite: the desktop, the editor, the video player, the control panels and the interface of the project’s own operating system. Today 276 pieces of the suite are painted with Llimphi.

Fifteen and a half seconds of Llimphi. Everything on screen is drawn by the engine, frame by frame: the controls, the cosmos sky, the supay corridor, the infinite voxel world and the hand.
Why not use one that already exists

Until May 2026, tawasuyu was drawn with GPUI, the engine behind the Zed editor. On May 26 it was removed entirely, and not on a whim: the project has its own operating system, wawa, which boots straight on the hardware, with no Linux underneath. No existing engine knows how to draw there.

Qt, GTK and Flutter take a conventional operating system for granted, with its window manager, its installed fonts and its memory management. Llimphi was designed from day one to paint both in a desktop window and in the video memory of a kernel that has just powered on. That requirement forced it to be written from scratch.
What “from scratch” means

It is worth being precise, because it is the question every programmer asks. Llimphi did not reinvent every piece. Just as Flutter relies on Skia and GTK on Cairo, Llimphi uses four free projects from the Rust community for the most specialized jobs. Everything else is its own: the way an application describes its screen, how it reacts to each click, the components and the paths that lead to the pixels.

Talking to the graphics card: wgpu · community
Drawing curves and fills with antialiasing: vello · community
Working out where each box goes (flexbox and grid): taffy · community
Shaping text: Arabic, Chinese, emoji, ligatures: parley · community
The life cycle of each application: Llimphi
Components, themes, animation, accessibility: Llimphi
Painting without a graphics card, inside the kernel: Llimphi
Isolating an application and painting its drawing from outside: Llimphi

The four community pieces are written in Rust too. That is why the headline says “entirely in Rust”, and stands by it.
How a Llimphi application thinks

Llimphi follows the Elm architecture, named after a language known for applications that almost never crash. The idea is simple: the application does not modify the screen, it describes it. Every time something happens, the engine goes through six steps:

input: A click, a key or a gesture arrives.
update: The application computes its new state.
view: It describes how it should look in that state.
layout: The engine works out the position of each box.
raster: It turns that description into pixels.
present: It shows the finished frame.

Since nothing touches the screen directly, no two parts of the program fight over the same button. It is the same reason this style became popular on the web with React, except here it runs natively, with no browser in between.
One brush, four paths to your screen

The most unusual part of Llimphi is that the same drawing can reach the screen by completely different paths, depending on where the application runs. “Looks about the same” was not good enough: each path was put side by side with the others and the pixels were counted.
With a graphics card

The everyday path on the desktop. It is the reference everything else is measured against.
CPU only

The one the wawa kernel uses, since it has no video driver.
Subscribe to the Medium newsletter

Fills and layers identical bit for bit. Accented text may differ, because the kernel only ships three fonts.
By message

An isolated application doesn’t touch the screen: it sends its drawing as a message and the system paints it on its behalf.

0 pixels of difference across the four test scenes.
For phones

A path that works on mobile graphics chips without general-purpose compute, such as the Mali-G57.

No pixel differs by more than 1/255 out of 19,200.

The “by message” path coming out with zero difference has a practical consequence: an application can live locked away, with no permission at all to touch the screen, and still look exactly the same. Security that costs nothing in appearance.
What it already ships

Close to eighty components: buttons, tables, text editors with multiple cursors, node graphs, panel splitters, calendars and more.
Eleven modules that combine components into complete application pieces.
Real text: right-to-left writing, Chinese characters, emoji, ligatures and input methods for Asian languages.
Accessibility: every element can declare what it is and what it is called, and the tests query it the way a screen reader would.
Image-based tests: a screen is compared with its approved version, and any unexpected change makes the test fail.
A 3D voxel engine that mounts inside the same interface, as just another component.

What it doesn’t do yet

An engine that promises too much loses the trust of whoever tries it, so it is worth saying what is missing too:

The phone path has been tested on real hardware, but no published application uses it yet. The current Android builds take another path that doesn’t work on every chip.
Outside its three built-in fonts, text may look different in the kernel and on the desktop. The cause is known: with no operating system underneath, there is nowhere to get more fonts from.
Part of Llimphi is already published on crates.io, Rust’s official registry, but the release is incomplete and some recent pieces haven’t been uploaded yet.

How to try it

For Rust programmers, the way in is a single package:

cargo add llimphi

The package bundles the core, the themes and the 3D engine. For the rest, the best demonstration is tawasuyu itself: every window in the suite is a Llimphi application.

Originally published at https://gioser.net on October 12, 2026.

title: Why Your Team Needs a Multi-Cloud Database Inventory
description:
Quick question: how many database instances is your team running right now?

Not an estimate. The exact number, across all your cloud providers, all your accounts, all your regions.

If you can answer that in under 10 seconds without opening a console, you have a database inventory. Most teams don't.

TL;DR

A multi-cloud database inventory is a single, always-current list of every database instance your organization runs — across AWS, GCP, MongoDB Atlas, and on-prem. Without one, you're flying blind. 1DataCloud automates this without agents or manual tracking. Try it free →

The Hidden Complexity Problem

Ten years ago, most companies had a simple database setup: a few MySQL or PostgreSQL instances, maybe a replica or two, running in a single data center or a single AWS account. One person knew where everything was.

Today, the landscape looks completely different:

  • Multiple cloud providers. AWS for most workloads, GCP for analytics (BigQuery is hard to replace), maybe Azure for a legacy integration, MongoDB Atlas for flexibility.
  • Multiple accounts per provider. Separate AWS accounts for prod, staging, dev, each product team, each regulated workload.
  • Multiple regions. Latency requirements, data residency laws, disaster recovery — all push toward multi-region deployments.
  • Multiple engine types. Relational, document, key-value, column-family, graph. Often in the same organization, sometimes for the same product.

The result is that "where are our databases?" is no longer a question with an obvious answer. And the consequences of not knowing are real.

What Happens Without a Database Inventory

You forget what you have

Databases created for a project that ended. Test instances that were supposed to be temporary. Replicas that were promoted and then the original was never cleaned up. Without an inventory, these accumulate silently — incurring cost, creating attack surface, and holding data that shouldn't be held.

Security gaps appear

A database that isn't in your inventory isn't in your patching cycle. It isn't reviewed during access audits. It might be publicly accessible. It might have a root password that was never rotated. You don't know, because you don't know it exists.

Onboarding is painful

Every new engineer needs to learn "the landscape" from whoever holds the tribal knowledge. This takes weeks, it's always incomplete, and it walks out the door when that person leaves.

Incident response slows down

When something breaks at 2 AM, you don't want to be asking "which database is connected to which service?" That mapping should already exist. Without an inventory, you're reconstructing it under pressure.

Compliance becomes a project

GDPR, SOC 2, HIPAA — all of them require knowing where data is stored. If you don't have a database inventory, every compliance audit becomes a weeks-long archaeology project.

What a Database Inventory Actually Contains

At minimum, a useful database inventory answers these questions for every instance:

Field Why it matters
Cloud provider Determines which tools and APIs apply
Account / project Determines ownership and billing
Region Affects latency, data residency, DR planning
Engine and version Drives patching and end-of-life planning
Instance size Capacity planning and cost optimization
Status Running? Stopped? Rebooting?
Multi-AZ / HA Risk assessment
Publicly accessible Security posture
Connected services Impact radius for incidents
Schema metadata What data is actually stored there

The last two are the hardest — and the most valuable.

Why Multi-Cloud Makes This Harder

If you were on a single cloud provider with a single account, an inventory is manageable. You can use native tools (AWS Resource Explorer, GCP Asset Inventory) to get a reasonable view.

The moment you span providers, those native tools stop helping. AWS doesn't show your GCP instances. GCP doesn't know about your MongoDB Atlas clusters. Neither knows about your on-prem PostgreSQL.

This forces teams into one of three bad options:

  1. Manual spreadsheets. Updated when someone remembers. Always out of date. Doesn't scale.
  2. Home-built tooling. Scraping APIs from each provider, aggregating results, building a UI. This is weeks of engineering time that solves a problem that isn't your core product.
  3. Ignoring it. Accepting the risk and operational friction as a cost of doing business.

None of these are good options when you're trying to move fast.

What an Automated Inventory Looks Like

The right solution connects directly to each cloud provider's API, discovers instances automatically, and presents them in a unified view that stays current without manual updates.

This is what 1DataCloud does.

Connect once, discover continuously:
Add your AWS IAM credentials, GCP service account, MongoDB Atlas API key, or on-prem connection strings. 1DataCloud queries each provider's management APIs and builds a unified inventory automatically.

What it discovers today:

  • AWS: RDS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server), Aurora, Redshift, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune
  • GCP: Cloud SQL, Spanner, BigQuery, Firestore, Bigtable
  • MongoDB Atlas: clusters across all projects
  • On-prem: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB

Coming soon: Microsoft Azure (SQL Database, Cosmos DB, Azure PostgreSQL)

No agents required:
Everything is read-only and API-based. Nothing is installed on your database nodes. Existing cloud security primitives (IAM roles, service accounts) are used directly.

Schema metadata included:
Click any instance and browse its tables, columns, data types, and indexes. This is the layer that turns an inventory from a list of instances into a map of where your data lives.

The Organizational Benefits

Beyond the operational improvements, a database inventory changes how the organization relates to its data infrastructure:

Engineering teams stop wasting time on "what's running where?" and start spending it on things that matter.

Security teams get a complete surface area to audit — without a months-long discovery exercise before every review.

Data teams know where the data they need actually lives, without filing tickets to find out.

Leadership can make capacity, cost, and risk decisions based on a complete picture, not a best guess.

Getting Started

If you don't have a database inventory today, the fastest path to one is to stop trying to build it manually and connect to a tool that maintains it automatically.

1DataCloud is free to start — connect up to 3 database instances across any provider, no credit card required.

If your team is managing more than that, Pro and Enterprise tiers support unlimited instances across all providers with shared organizational access and RBAC.

👉 1datacloud.ai

👉 Start free

One More Thing

Once you have an inventory with schema metadata, natural language querying becomes possible. Instead of "I know the data exists somewhere in our infrastructure" being the beginning of a long search, it becomes the beginning of a question: "How many active users do we have across all our regional databases?"

That's what Query1AI is for — but you need the inventory first.

Does your team have a database inventory today? How do you maintain it? Genuinely curious what approaches people are using at different scales.

title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
description:
arXiv:2610.19323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.

title: RDCompGS: Rate-Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs
description:
arXiv:2610.19538v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bj{\o}ntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.

title: Exposing AI Inference as a Telco Network API over the 5G User Plane
description:
arXiv:2610.15062v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Supporting edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference as a network service is challenging because current mobile systems can transport tensors but do not expose or understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning. Prior studies have addressed this gap through dynamic partitioning, collaborative inference, and split pipelines; however, these solutions remain application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. This work proposes Inference on Demand (IoD), an inference-on-demand abstraction that exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane path. We evaluate the IoD on a programmable user plane function (UPF)-based testbed using a partitionable visual AI workload, showing that adaptive split selection can operate as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations. Including our findings, split inference becomes more than offloading when the service intent, runtime partitioning, and tensor transport are made visible to the mobile data plane. This opens a path toward network-native AI services, in which programmable telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity for user-facing applications.

title: Qlik QSSA Exam: Why Installation and Configuration Add Up to the 62% Pass Mark
description:
The Qlik Sense System Administrator (QSSA) exam has 50 questions, a 90-minute limit and a 62% passing score. Its two biggest domains, Installation at 30% and Configuration at 32%, add up to exactly 62%, so the pass line sits right where those two domains end.

That one fact shapes how you should study. This post works through what it means in questions, minutes and attempts, using the figures on Qlik's QSSA exam details page, checked on 15 October 2026.

What does the Qlik QSSA exam cover?

The exam tests whether you can plan, install, run and fix a client-managed Qlik Sense Enterprise on Windows site. Qlik splits it into four domains:

  • Installation (30%): planning the infrastructure, installing Qlik Sense Enterprise on Windows with Shared Persistence, and choosing between single-node and multi-node setups.
  • Configuration (32%): streams and apps, automated tasks with triggers, load balancing rules, Active Directory connections with user and group sync, and node settings.
  • Security and Licensing (16%): the Qlik Sense licensing model, user license access, and security rules.
  • Monitor, Troubleshoot, and Maintenance (22%): app issues, system issues and server maintenance.

Qlik states plainly that the exam covers only the client-managed edition. Nothing on it tests Qlik Cloud administration.

How many questions does each domain carry?

Qlik publishes percentages, not question counts. Applying the weights to 50 questions gives a rough split (our arithmetic, not Qlik's):

  • Installation: about 15 questions
  • Configuration: about 16 questions
  • Security and Licensing: about 8 questions
  • Monitor, Troubleshoot, and Maintenance: about 11 questions

At 62%, a pass means about 31 correct answers. Installation and Configuration together come to about 31 questions as well. That is the coincidence in the title, and it is worth reading carefully.

Can you pass on Installation and Configuration alone?

In theory, yes, but only with a perfect score on both, and nobody should plan for that. The real lesson runs the other way: the 19 questions in the two smaller domains are your safety margin.

At the published mark you can get about 19 questions wrong and still pass. If you treat Security and Licensing as a weak spot and miss most of its 8 questions, you have spent a big part of that margin before the clock reaches the halfway point. Qlik also says the passing score "is adjusted to maintain a consistent standard", so treat 31 as a guide and not a promise.

A sensible target is to aim for strong scores in all four domains, with Configuration first, because it is the largest single block.

How much time do you get per question?

Ninety minutes across 50 questions is 1.8 minutes, or 108 seconds, per question. That is enough time to read a scenario twice, but not enough to reason out a load balancing rule or a security rule from first principles.

A practical pace plan:

  1. Take a first pass at about 90 seconds per question and flag anything that needs more thought.
  2. Bank the spare time, roughly 15 minutes, for flagged items.
  3. Leave nothing blank. An unanswered question can only count as wrong, while a guess might be right.

What experience does Qlik expect before you sit it?

Qlik recommends at least six months as an administrator of a Microsoft Windows Server environment. It also lists hands-on work in the Qlik Management Console (QMC): governance, library maintenance, user and app security, server policies, rules and streams.

The less obvious part is the tool list. Qlik names Event Viewer, the Services Console, the DCOM Console and the Windows Registry, plus NSLookUp, Telnet, Ping, NetStat, Fiddler and browser developer tools. Those tools point to the troubleshooting questions in the 22% domain. If you have never traced a proxy or certificate problem with them, that is the gap to close.

For a different view of the exam's scope, the Tier 1 article on why the QSSA leaves Qlik Cloud out explains which skills the client-managed focus rules in and out.

Which installation steps should you know by heart?

The Installation domain asks about single-node and multi-node deployments. For multi-node sites, Qlik's help sets out a fixed order:

  1. Check the pre-installation items: system requirements, supported browsers, ports and licenses.
  2. Prepare the Windows server.
  3. Install Qlik Sense on the central node.
  4. Configure PostgreSQL multi-node connections on the central node.
  5. License Qlik Sense on the central node.
  6. Allocate access to users.
  7. Install the rim nodes.
  8. Connect and configure the rim nodes in the QMC.
  9. Optionally, set a failover candidate for the central node.

Questions often hinge on what has to happen before what. You can walk the same sequence step by step in Qlik's guide to installing Qlik Sense in a multi-node site, which was last updated in October 2026.

What happens if you fail the QSSA exam?

Qlik allows three attempts per exam, and each attempt needs a full payment or a new voucher. The waiting periods are fixed:

  • After a first fail, you wait 48 hours.
  • After a second fail, you wait 14 calendar days before the third and final attempt.
  • After a third fail, you cannot register for that exam again until Qlik releases a new version.

So the quickest path through all three attempts runs from day 0 to day 2 to day 16. Qlik enforces the waits and will not let you book an earlier date. All of this is set out in Qlik Learning's certificates and badges FAQ.

The third-attempt block is the rule to respect. Two fails should send you back to the training and practice work, not straight to a rebooking.

How long does the QSSA certification last?

Your result appears as soon as you finish, and Qlik sends it by email too. After a pass, Credly sends a badge invitation within 24 to 48 hours. Qlik no longer issues certificates; the badge in Credly and in your Qlik Learning history is the record.

The certification is valid for two years from the date you pass. Credly emails you six months before it expires, which is month 18. To keep it, you register for the current exam before the expiry date and pass it. Qlik usually updates its exams every three years, sooner after a major product change.

How should you prepare in the time you have?

A plan that follows the weights:

  1. Build a lab first. A single-node Qlik Sense Enterprise on Windows install teaches more of the 30% Installation domain than any reading.
  2. Spend the most hours on Configuration. Create streams, tasks with triggers, load balancing rules and an AD user sync until you can do them without notes.
  3. Learn security rules and license allocation properly. Eight questions is a small block, but missing most of it eats your margin.
  4. Practise troubleshooting with the Windows tools Qlik lists. Break your lab on purpose and fix it.
  5. Check yourself under time pressure. The QSSA practice exam on AnalyticsExam runs timed sets so you can test the 108-second pace.

If you already run a Qlik Sense Enterprise site at work, you can shorten step 1, but keep the other four.

Before your first study session, the three-minute AnalyticsExam video on how to study for the QSSA exam gives a short overview of the preparation steps. It was recorded for the QSSA2022 version, so check the domain weights above against it.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. How many questions are on the Qlik QSSA exam?

The exam has 50 questions and a 90-minute time limit. Qlik notes that the number and difficulty of questions may change when the exam is updated.

2. What score do you need to pass QSSA?

Qlik lists a passing score of 62%, which works out to about 31 correct answers out of 50. Qlik adjusts the passing score to keep a consistent standard, so treat 31 as a guide.

3. Does the QSSA exam cover Qlik Cloud?

No. The exam covers only the client-managed edition of Qlik Sense, meaning Qlik Sense Enterprise on Windows. It does not test Qlik Cloud administration.

4. How many times can you retake the QSSA exam?

You get three attempts, each paid in full or with a new voucher. You wait 48 hours after the first fail and 14 calendar days after the second. After a third fail, you must wait for a new version of the exam.

5. How long is the Qlik Sense System Administrator certification valid?

It is valid for two years from the date you pass. Credly sends a reminder six months before expiry, and you renew by passing the current exam before that date.

title: Scheduling Stale-Reservation Webhooks — Follow-Up Tasks One Hour Later, Queue or Cron
description:
Short answer: put each reservation's one-hour follow-up in a delayed queue message, then make the consumer idempotent; use cron for a periodic sweep, not for one cron row per reservation.

That choice follows the delivery guarantee you actually need. A reservation is an event with a due time, not a recurring calendar rule. When the hold expires, the worker should re-check the reservation state, emit the webhook if it is still stale, and record that it did so. The scheduling mechanism only gets the work near the right time.

What should a Node.js team schedule for a one-hour webhook hold?

Think in two clocks. The first is the business clock: expires_at = created_at + 3600. The second is the delivery clock: when a worker receives a message and can make the follow-up request. A delayed message joins those clocks without creating a scheduler object for every row. A cron sweep can also work, but it introduces a scan interval and another place to coordinate locks.

The timer is not the business decision.

For a reservation that was created at 12:00, publish an event with a 3,600-second delay. At 13:00, the consumer loads the reservation and checks a version or state transition. If the customer already confirmed payment, the message becomes a no-op. If the hold is still open, the consumer sends the webhook using a stable event id and commits the completion before acknowledging the message.

That last sentence matters more than the word “delayed.” Standard queues are at-least-once. A retry can deliver the same message twice, so the webhook side effect needs a unique key such as reservation_id:hold-expired:v3. Delivery is not exactly-once just because the timer looked precise.

Here is the smallest publish boundary. The request body fields shown are the queue contract used by this example; the public discovery record is the place to verify the current schema before shipping.

import json
import os
import time
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def publish_expiry(queue_name: str, reservation_id: str) -> dict:
    body = {
        "queue": queue_name,
        "message": {
            "reservation_id": reservation_id,
            "event_id": f"{reservation_id}:hold-expired:v3",
        },
        "delay_seconds": 3600,
    }
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.post(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
                "Idempotency-Key": body["message"]["event_id"],
            },
            json=body,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429 and attempt < 4:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(response.text)
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")

The retry loop is intentionally boring. It honors Retry-After, uses an idempotency key, and surfaces non-429 responses instead of treating every HTTP response as success. A one-hour delay is below the seven-day delayed-message limit, and the message is small enough to stay well below the 256KB body cap.

Queue messages, cron sweeps, and specialist schedulers

The comparison is less about brand names than failure boundaries. Before looking at the alternatives, Infrai is a concrete fit for the trigger-and-buffer slice: its public discovery endpoint exposes schemas and runnable examples. Infrai gives this flow one key and one bill for queue, cron, and adjacent backend capabilities instead of another credential rotation path; its one platform spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so the same convention can cover a storage reference or an observability hook without another SDK family. That removes integration friction without changing the reservation state machine.

Here is how I would evaluate the common choices for this reservation flow:

Option Best fit Delivery and operating trade-off
Delayed queue message One follow-up per webhook event Natural per-event delay; at-least-once consumption requires idempotent handling
Cron plus database sweep Holds longer than seven days or a recovery pass Fewer delayed messages, but every run scans due rows and must claim them safely
Celery beat/worker Python teams already operating Celery Mature task routing, with broker and worker operations to own
BullMQ Node.js teams invested in Redis Good queue ergonomics, but Redis durability and topology become part of the design
Temporal Multi-step workflows, timers, and joins Strong workflow model, with a larger platform and programming model than this job needs

Creating a cron entry per reservation is the awkward middle. It turns a one-off event into scheduler configuration, creates cleanup work when a reservation is canceled, and makes a burst of reservations look like a burst of schedule mutations. Cron is still useful: one job every five minutes can sweep long waits, repair missed records, or enqueue work after an outage. It just should not be the primary row-level timer here.

The catch is that a queue is not a workflow engine. There is no native DAG, debounce, throttle, or fan-out join in this boundary. If expiry must wait for three independent services and then aggregate their results, Temporal or Airflow is a better fit. If your team already has Redis and BullMQ expertise, that operational context can outweigh a hosted REST surface. Your mileage may vary when the queue is not the largest integration cost.

How do delivery limits change the Node.js design?

The seven-day delay ceiling defines a clean split. For a 30-day reservation, write expires_at to your database and let a recurring cron sweep claim due rows, then publish ordinary queue messages. In PostgreSQL, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is a practical way to let several sweep workers claim different rows without holding a global lock. The queue remains the execution buffer; the database remains the source of long-lived time.

Large webhook bodies need the same separation. Store the payload in private object storage and put only a reference, reservation id, and event id in the message. A 256KB message cap and a 30-day maximum retention make a queue a poor archive. Acknowledgement deletes the message, and there is no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer-group history to rescue an underspecified audit trail.

Cron has edges too. A cron task can run for at most 900 seconds and calls a public HTTP URL; it does not host your application code. For a long reconciliation, have cron trigger a queue publish and let workers do the work. A paused cron does not replay missed triggers, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. Those are acceptable properties for a sweep, not guarantees for a payment ledger.

I once assumed “the timer fired” meant “the follow-up happened.” It did not. The useful audit record was the reservation state transition and the idempotency key, not the scheduler's run log, whose stored output is limited to the first 4KB. Keep those records in your database. In a real incident review, I would want to answer which worker claimed the row, which downstream status code arrived, and whether a retry reused the same event id; a timestamp in a cron dashboard cannot answer all three, so the database record and webhook receipt belong in the same trace.

That is the operational boundary.

Where does a single REST boundary help?

Infrai is a reasonable option when the queue and cron are only two pieces of a small backend. Its public discovery surface describes a capability's method, path, schemas, and runnable examples, so a team can inspect the scheduling contract before installing an SDK. The practical advantage is one plain REST API and one credential boundary: swapping the service behind a capability does not force a rewrite of the reservation code's interface. The supporting benefit is that queue and cron can share that same key and billing boundary while the application stays in Python, Node.js, or another language.

I would recommend trying Infrai for the trigger-and-buffer portion when you want a self-describing HTTP contract, have a public worker endpoint, and do not need workflow joins or replayable streams. Keep a specialist queue or workflow platform when those semantics are the product requirement, not incidental infrastructure. Infrai does not make an internal endpoint public, and it does not remove the need for consumer idempotency.

The decision rule is short: delayed queue messages for one-off holds, cron for recurring sweeps and long horizons, and a workflow engine for dependencies. Measure the state transition, not just the scheduled timestamp.

If that boundary matches your system, start with the queue capability discovery and verify the request schema before wiring the producer.

References

  • Infrai capability index
  • Infrai queue discovery
  • Celery introduction
  • BullMQ guide
  • Temporal documentation
  • PostgreSQL SELECT documentation

title: AI Gateway production index
description:
Ask which AI model is best, and the answer changes before the ink dries. That's what happens in an industry where new models are released weekly.

Every benchmark measures a different race, and every race crowns its own winner, but Vercel has a unique view of the industry through production workloads. AI Gateway serves tens of trillions of tokens across hundreds of models through real applications and agents.

What we're seeing:

  • Anthropic leads in spend despite a higher unit price, Google leads in volume

  • OSS models are gaining traction, but there is no loyalty to specific labs

  • OpenAI spend share is growing quickly after recent model updates

  • High-volume workloads route across 30+ distinct models on average

  • Agentic workloads carry 59% of all token volume (up 2x over 6 months)

This report is built on data from seven months of production traffic from AI Gateway, with usage from over 200K+ unique teams.

Anthropic leads in spend; Google leads in volume

Cost and volume rankings disagree because they measure two different workloads, even for the same customer.

By spend in April 2026, Anthropic took 61%, Google 21%, and OpenAI 12%.

By token volume, the picture flipped. 38% of April traffic through AI Gateway routed to Google, 26% to Anthropic, 13% to OpenAI, and 10% to xAI. Smaller labs split the rest.

Some models are positioned to win by being cheap enough per token to carry huge volume, while others are priced high enough to make sense only for quality-critical work. The different models are not competing for the same call. In aggregate the same customer base sits on both leaderboards, with premium reasoning calls landing on Claude Opus and cheap fast calls landing on Gemini Flash. Spend follows the high-stakes calls, and volume follows the low-stakes ones, with the labs each holding a different layer of the same applications.

Volume-vs-spend also changes quickly at the lab level. A few specific signals:

  • Gemini Flash helped Google take the lead on volume at a smaller share of spend

  • Claude Opus helps Anthropic lead on spend with less volume than Google

  • OpenAI's spend share tripled from March to April after the GPT-5.4/5.5 releases

  • Google's spend share climbed from 8% in March to 21% in April as Gemini Flash usage scaled

Spend follows the cost of being wrong

The same cost/volume divide exists at a finer grain inside specific kinds workloads:

  • Personal assistants account for 20% of cost on 40% of token volume

  • Coding agents sit roughly balanced at 22% of cost on 20% of tokens

  • Back office agents run at 6% of cost on 15% of tokens

  • App generation runs at 7% of cost on 11% of tokens

What a workload spends per token is a function of how expensive a wrong answer is to the use case. Personal assistants can run on cheap, fast models because mistakes only impact individual users and are quickly corrected. Back-office workflows pay for stronger reasoning because errors can trigger legal, financial, or operational risks that outweigh the per-call savings. The per-token economics are a stake map: applications spend more per token when mistakes cost more.

The same pattern holds in a broader B2C/B2B split. B2C applications generate many low-cost calls, while B2B applications run fewer, more expensive ones. On a per-token basis, B2B costs roughly two times as much as B2C.

No single provider wins across use cases

Cutting the data by use case shows a fragmented provider landscape:

  • Anthropic notably leads in software building

  • Google over-indexes in consumer

  • OpenAI is the most evenly distributed

  • xAI and others are split across coding, consumer, and long-tail use cases

Anthropic's pattern is concentration at the high-stakes layer. As the workload moves from back office to consumer, Anthropic's token share drops from 71% down to 7%. Its cost share follows a much shallower curve and keeps the lead through three of the four categories. The revenue concentrates wherever the answer has to be right, regardless of how much volume passes through.

Google is the inverse shape. Its footprint concentrates in consumer, where Gemini Flash carries 28% of tokens at 15% of cost, and barely appears on the cost chart outside it. The position is a single-SKU bet that rises and falls with Flash adoption.

xAI is a price wedge. Grok carries 20% of building tokens and 18% of outreach tokens at materially smaller cost shares in each. xAI wins on price-to-quality fit, and whoever matches the price closes the wedge.

OpenAI is the most balanced of the four at 6% of building cost, 18% of consumer cost, and 28% of outreach cost. No single layer is load-bearing for OpenAI's overall share, which makes the company the least exposed of the four to disruption in any one layer.

Open-weights families like Kimi, MiniMax, and GLM rotate through the consumer and building tiers where the cost ceiling is lowest. Their cost share stays small, and their token share inside consumer and building is large enough that any cost-only view of the market understates them.

There is no single dominant provider across the whole market because there is no single dominant use case. The right question is not "Who is winning AI?", it is "Which models are winning the use case I care about?" The labs that look closest to even on a blended chart are competing for different layers of the same stack.

Apps are becoming more agentic

The shape of production AI requests has changed underneath all of this. In April 2026, 22.2% of AI Gateway requests ended with a tool call, up from 11.4% in October 2025. Measured by tokens, the shift is bigger. 58.9% of all tokens are now in tool-call requests, up from 31.6% six months ago.

By both measures the agentic share roughly doubled in half a year, but the more telling number is the gap between the two shares. 22.2% of requests carry 58.9% of tokens, which means tool-using requests are about 2.6× more token-heavy than the rest. The cost surface of AI has shifted from chat-shaped to agent-shaped, while headline request counts barely budged.

Every kind of round trip bills against the same meter, whether it's a function execution, an API call, a database query, or a code run, so an agent shipping ten tool calls bills roughly ten times the tokens a chat would. Where a chat bills one round trip per prompt, an agent bills a chain.

Leaderboards rank one model, but production teams use 35+ at scale

At scale, multi-model stops being a choice and becomes standard agent architecture.

Teams running 1K to 10K requests averaged 3 distinct models. By the 10M+ requests bucket, the average is 35 models in regular use. The jump from 18 models in the 1M to 10M bucket to 35 in the 10M+ bucket is the inflection point.

A 35-model fleet runs as a routing graph, with a cheap classifier for intent detection, a frontier model for the reasoning step, an embedding model for retrieval, a fast model for summarization, and a vision model for screenshots. Every one of those models is swappable. If a provider raises prices, degrades quality, or has an outage, traffic redistributes across the rest in hours. At the scale that produces most of the spend on the leaderboards, switching between labs is closer to a config change than to a vendor migration, and the standard story about lab lock-in inverts the higher you go on the request-volume curve.

New models are adopted rapidly

The same fleet design explains how fast new releases get absorbed. When a new version ships inside a model family, traffic moves to it within weeks.

Claude Sonnet 4.6 absorbed most of the Sonnet family's share by its first full month after launch.

The Opus family is moving through the same shape now, with Claude Opus 4.7 taking share from Opus 4.6 on a near-identical curve.

Predecessor models stayed live and routable on AI Gateway throughout both windows, but teams moved anyway. The migration is a config change, and the labs no longer set the upgrade timeline of their own product lines.

Provider outages have a hidden cost

Roughly 3.5% of requests on AI Gateway complete after a fallback. That means the initial route hit an error, a rate limit, or a timeout, and the gateway reissued the request to a healthy alternative fast enough that the user still got a successful response.

Measured in tokens the rescue rate runs at 5.1%, and in dollars at 4.9%. The token-weighted and cost-weighted rates run higher than the request-weighted rate because the requests that get rescued are, on average, bigger and more expensive than the ones that don't. Long context windows hit rate limits more often than short ones, multi-step agent runs accumulate failure across steps, and heavy reasoning calls time out under sustained load. Each of those failure modes targets the expensive end of the workload, which is why the dollar rate sits higher than the request rate.

A provider's SLA measures request-level uptime, but a production application experiences cost-weighted uptime, and the two come apart on exactly the calls that paid for the model.

Conclusion: Build for workload, not the lab

Production workloads are designed for efficiency, reliability, and flexibility, not to match the latest model leaderboards.

Across six cuts of the same data, the shape underneath stays the same. Different labs win different layers of the same applications, and the architecture that handles those layers is the one production teams at scale have already built for.

This echoes the early cloud era. Teams expanded compute first (more instances, regions, redundancy) and squeezed per-unit cost later. The 35-model fleets visible at the top of the spend curve are the same patter at a faster cadence; the optimization that follows happens at the routing layer.

For anyone shipping AI today:

  • Plan for multiple models across providers

  • Assume the need for fallbacks to optimize for uptime and cost

  • Design routing as a core unit of architecture from the beginning

We expect to revisit this data on a recurring cadence as the patterns shift. Live model rankings are available on the AI Gateway Leaderboards.

About this data

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through April 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend uses market-rate pricing (published list price) to provide a normalized view across teams that bring their own API keys.

  • Volume counts tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • B2C, B2B, and use-case classifications are aggregate. No individual team or workload is identified.

title: Cómo construí ora-tui: Un gestor en consola (TUI) en Go sin dependencias para Oracle RAC y Single Instance
description:
Son las 3:15 AM de una guardia de producción. Te conectas por SSH a un nodo de Oracle RAC en Oracle Linux porque ha saltado una alerta crítica. En cuestión de segundos tienes que:

  1. Comprobar si los demonios del cluster (CRS, CSSD, EVMD, ASM) están ONLINE en todos los nodos (crsctl check cluster -all y crsctl status resource -t).
  2. Cambiar del usuario grid al usuario oracle para abrir sqlplus / as sysdba.
  3. Averiguar qué sesión está bloqueando una tabla crítica en gv$session (enq: TX - row lock contention) o qué tablespace acaba de lanzar un ORA-01654 porque llegó al 93% sin AUTOEXTEND.
  4. Si toca mantenimiento de sistema operativo en un nodo, reubicar todos los servicios RAC (srvctl relocate service), parar la instancia local y detener la pila CRS sin provocar ni un segundo de caída en las aplicaciones.

Después de repetir este ritual cientos de veces, decidí construir ora-tui: una herramienta interactiva de terminal (TUI) escrita en Go, empaquetada como un único binario estático (CGO_ENABLED=0) e instalable vía dnf install ora-tui.

En este artículo te cuento cómo funciona por dentro, cómo resolví los retos de arquitectura en servidores Oracle y cómo puedes probar su modo simulador (--mock) en tu propio portátil.

🖥️ El Diseño: Marcos Unicode (┌─┐ y ╔═╗) y Navegación con Flechas

Uno de los objetivos principales era que la herramienta se sintiera rápida y clara sobre cualquier sesión SSH, utilizando una jerarquía visual de marcos Unicode:

  • Borde Simple (┌ ─ ┐ │ └ ┘) para los paneles secundarios y tablas de datos.
  • Borde Doble (╔ ═ ╗ ║ ╚ ╝) para la cabecera principal, el panel que tiene el foco activo, las ventanas emergentes de mantenimiento y los diálogos de confirmación.
  • Barras de progreso por bloques ([█████████░] 93.0%) coloreadas según criticidad (verde $<80\%$, amarillo $80\text{–}90\%$, rojo $>90\%$).

⚙️ Decisiones Clave de Arquitectura

1. ¿Por qué CGO_ENABLED=0 y cero librerías de cliente C?

La mayoría de los drivers de Oracle requieren CGO y enlazar dinámicamente contra libclntsh.so (Oracle Instant Client). En entornos empresariales con RHEL / Oracle Linux 7, 8 y 9 y distintas versiones de glibc, distribuir binarios con dependencias dinámicas es una fuente constante de problemas.

En ora-tui, el binario se compila 100% estático (CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64) y se comunica directamente con las herramientas nativas que ya residen en $ORACLE_HOME/bin y $GRID_HOME/bin (sqlplus -s / as sysdba, srvctl, crsctl, olsnodes, lsnrctl, rman, adrci).

2. Auto-Descubrimiento sin Archivos de Configuración

Nada más ejecutarse, ora-tui descubre qué tipo de instalación Oracle tiene delante sin pedir un solo archivo .yaml o .env:

  1. Topología del Servidor: Lee /etc/oracle/ocr.loc y /etc/oracle/olr.loc:
    • local_only=false $\rightarrow$ ORACLE RAC
    • local_only=true $\rightarrow$ ORACLE RESTART (Standalone Grid)
    • No existe $\rightarrow$ SINGLE INSTANCE
  2. Homes e Instancias Vivas en /proc: Además de leer /etc/oratab e inventory.xml, escanea /proc/[0-9]*/cmdline para localizar procesos ora_pmon_<SID>, db_pmon_<SID> (Oracle 21c/23ai) y asm_pmon_+ASM*. Así detecta bases de datos levantadas aunque nadie las haya registrado en /etc/oratab. 
func ExtractSIDFromPMON(cmdline string) (sid string, isASM bool) {
    fields := strings.Fields(cmdline)
    if len(fields) == 0 {
        return "", false
    }
    proc := filepath.Base(fields[0])
    switch {
    case strings.HasPrefix(proc, "ora_pmon_"):
        return strings.TrimPrefix(proc, "ora_pmon_"), false
    case strings.HasPrefix(proc, "db_pmon_"):
        return strings.TrimPrefix(proc, "db_pmon_"), false
    case strings.HasPrefix(proc, "asm_pmon_"):
        return strings.TrimPrefix(proc, "asm_pmon_"), true
    }
    return "", false
}

3. Cambio Dinámico de Usuario UNIX (root $\rightarrow$ oracle / grid)

En un cluster RAC con separación de roles, grid es dueño de $GRID_HOME y oracle es dueño de $ORACLE_HOME. Ejecutar sqlplus o srvctl como root falla o ensucia permisos.

ora-tui lee el uid y gid propietarios de cada directorio con os.Stat y lanza cada subproceso con las credenciales exactas de ese usuario mediante syscall.Credential, reservando root únicamente para crsctl start/stop crs:

if !asRoot && targetOwner != nil && targetOwner.UID != 0 && currentUID == 0 {
    cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{
        Credential: &syscall.Credential{
            Uid: targetOwner.UID,
            Gid: targetOwner.GID,
        },
    }
}

4. Marcos Simples (┌─┐) y Dobles (╔═╗) en tview

La librería rivo/tview permite definir globalmente los runas de dibujo de cajas, distinguiendo entre ventanas normales y ventanas con foco activo. Configurando tview.Borders, conseguimos que cualquier tabla o menú emergente resalte automáticamente con borde doble cuando el usuario lo selecciona con las flechas:

// Borde simple (┌ ─ ┐ │ └ ┘) para contenedores y tablas estándar
tview.Borders.Horizontal = '─'
tview.Borders.Vertical = '│'
tview.Borders.TopLeft = '┌'
tview.Borders.TopRight = '┐'
tview.Borders.BottomLeft = '└'
tview.Borders.BottomRight = '┘'

// Borde doble (╔ ═ ╗ ║ ╚ ╝) para la ventana con foco y modales emergentes
tview.Borders.HorizontalFocus = '═'
tview.Borders.VerticalFocus = '║'
tview.Borders.TopLeftFocus = '╔'
tview.Borders.TopRightFocus = '╗'
tview.Borders.BottomLeftFocus = '╚'
tview.Borders.BottomRightFocus = '╝'

Además, pulsando la tecla b en cualquier momento, puedes alternar en caliente entre el modo mixto (┌─┐ + ╔═╗), todo borde doble (╔═╗), todo borde simple (┌─┐) o ASCII clásico de 7 bits (+ - = |) si entras desde una consola serie antigua.

🛠️ Los 8 Módulos de Diagnóstico y Mantenimiento Guiado

En lugar de memorizar comandos, te mueves con las flechas del teclado (↑/↓) por las 8 vistas y pulsas Enter sobre cualquier fila para abrir su menú contextual de mantenimiento:

  1. Cluster & DB Estado: Salud de demonios (CRS, CSSD, EVMD, ASM), VIPs, instancias, PDBs y Drenado Seguro de Nodo (Graceful Node Drain) en 4 pasos:
    • Paso 1: Pre-chequeo de nodos failover ONLINE.
    • Paso 2: Reubicación en caliente de servicios (srvctl relocate service).
    • Paso 3: Parada limpia de la instancia local (srvctl stop instance -stopoption IMMEDIATE).
    • Paso 4: Parada opcional de la pila de clusterware (crsctl stop crs).
  2. Usuarios Conectados (gv$session): Detección instantánea de bloqueos TX/TM, SQL_ID, evento de espera y texto SQL actual, con opción para ejecutar KILL SESSION IMMEDIATE o DISCONNECT SESSION POST_TRANSACTION.
  3. Tablespaces & Datafiles: Barras visuales de llenado y asistente para añadir datafiles en ASM (+DATA), activar AUTOEXTEND ON o hacer COALESCE.
  4. Tablas, Segmentos & Objetos Inválidos: Identificación de tablas con estadísticas STALE o alta fragmentación para lanzar DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS, SHRINK SPACE CASCADE, REBUILD ONLINE de índices o recompilar objetos inválidos con UTL_RECOMP.
  5. ASM & Red Listeners: Monitorización de diskgroups (v$asm_diskgroup) y control de listeners locales y SCAN (lsnrctl start/stop/reload).
  6. RMAN, Flashback & Data Guard: Estado de backups RMAN, creación de Guaranteed Restore Points (GRP) antes de un cambio crítico y verificación de lag en réplicas Data Guard Standby.
  7. Alert Log & Errores ORA-: Lectura directa sobre v$diag_alert_ext con salto automático al módulo que resuelve el error y purgado de trazas con adrci.
  8. Centro de Mantenimiento: Catálogo guiado de operaciones DBA con confirmación de seguridad y consola de auditoría en tiempo real.

🚀 Pruébalo en 30 Segundos (Modo Simulación --mock)

No necesitas tener un cluster Oracle RAC instalado en tu máquina para probar la interfaz. ora-tui incluye un modo simulador (--mock) con datos realistas de un cluster RAC en producción (incluyendo sesiones bloqueadas, un tablespace al 93% y alertas ORA-01654):

git clone https://github.com/mario/ora-tui.git
cd ora-tui

# Compilar y lanzar el simulador interactivo en modo Oracle RAC:
make mock

# O ver la captura estática directamente en tu terminal:
make preview

title: Certify the Decision, Not Every Score: Exact Top-k Selection from Few Evaluations
description:
arXiv:2610.14996v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Choosing a few robust algorithms or schedules can require evaluating every candidate under many adverse scenarios, even though an agent only needs to identify the winners. A predictor may suggest those winners, but cannot rule out a surprise in an unevaluated scenario. We introduce Certified Adaptive Selection (CAS), which returns the exact top-$k$ set as soon as remaining uncertainty cannot change it. CAS keeps guaranteed lower and upper bounds on Expected Shortfall (ES), the average loss in the worst scenarios. Its stopping test compares the worst admissible selected candidate with the best admissible excluded one; for information-disjoint Cartesian intervals this one-cut test is necessary and sufficient. Prediction has a separate role: selecting the next outcome to evaluate, never authorizing the decision. For empirical ES with exact unit-cost queries, we compute in polynomial time the fewest evaluations that could have proved the realized decision in hindsight. Our prediction-guided agent CAS-PG is exact for every predictor, including adversarial ones. On two public algorithm-selection matrices, CAS-PG certifies the exact top three after 630 of 3150 and 981 of 2200 replayed queries, or $1.14$ and $1.18$ times that hindsight minimum. Without historical outcomes, its transcript-only variant requires $1.28$ and $1.37$ times the minimum, outperforming the tested non-predictive certified policies. Separately, a prediction-free CAS policy avoids $93.0\%$ of exact recourse solves in synthetic energy scheduling. One certificate thus supports several acquisition policies and separately proved risk/cost extensions: prediction changes the work, not the justified choice.

title: Beyond Reachability: A Relation-Semantic Reasoning Framework for Biomedical Multi-hop QA
description:
arXiv:2610.19754v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Biomedical multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs requires identifying a semantically valid relation sequence that supports the answer. Existing methods can retrieve correct answers, yet often rank them poorly within a large pool of seemingly relevant candidates. Even when a correct answer is retrieved, its associated evidence and reasoning path may fail to support the relation composition required by the question. We term this disconnect between answer reachability and evidential validity the reachable-but-invalid problem. We present ReSemReason, which shares a question-induced distribution over typed, directed relation schemas between candidate discovery and evidence selection. Schema compatibility guides graph search; ReSemAttn then uses relation-conditioned key/value projections and an uncertainty-weighted path prior to attend to candidate-specific evidence. A separate absolute-support score complements normalized attention when all retrieved paths are weak. The reported experiments on BioHopR, PrimeKGQA, and MedReason show improvements in answer ranking and answer-set quality. Path-discrimination analyses examine the distinction between endpoint correctness and evidential support. We also specify matched controls for search, attention, and schema uncertainty.

title: PN-Mix: Pair-Norm Guided Mixed-Precision Key Cache Quantization for Efficient Long-Output LLM Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.19605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. Through attention logit perturbation analysis at the RoPE channel-pair level, we show that quantization errors in channel pairs with large query--key pair-norm products contribute significantly to logit variation. Based on this insight, we propose PN-Mix, a mixed-precision key-cache quantization method for RoPE-based decoder-only LLMs, which allocates higher precision to salient channel pairs identified once during the prefill stage and reused throughout decoding. Across standard reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks, PN-Mix with 2.26-bit average precision achieves comparable or better average accuracy than prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32--2.39 bits. Furthermore, in our Pareto sweep, PN-Mix degrades gracefully down to 1.5 bits, whereas the compared baselines exhibit sharper performance drops below 2.25 bits.

title: ANASSA: From High-Level Framework to Low-Level Architecture for Spatial Agentic AI
description:
arXiv:2610.14382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems operating over geospatial data require more than autonomous reasoning and tool use; they must also support explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, failure handling, and human decision authority. Prior work introduced ANASSA, an agentic AI orchestration framework for spatial intelligence that established high-level components and responsibility boundaries for governed agentic execution (arXiv:2609.14824). However, the framework did not specify how those high-level responsibilities should be systematically decomposed into an implementation-facing low-level architecture. This paper addresses that gap by applying Design Science Research (DSR) to refine the ANASSA framework from high-level architectural (HLA) responsibilities into a low-level architecture (LLA). The resulting design preserves the responsibility boundaries of the foundational framework while translating them into executable architectural structures, including 47 logical roles, versioned task graphs, capability-based agent selection, typed contracts, explicit runtime states, spatial validation mechanisms, governance controls, failure and recovery paths, and provenance records. The architecture is demonstrated through an end-to-end execution trace and analytically evaluated for requirements traceability, internal consistency, responsibility preservation, and technology independence. The resulting high-level-to-low-level design provides an implementation-facing bridge between the ANASSA framework and future system implementations, defining how governed spatial agentic workflows can be made inspectable, reconstructable, and testable without binding the architecture to a specific AI model, geospatial platform, communication protocol, or deployment environment.
