title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space
description:
arXiv:2610.19708v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an
  explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a
  sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our
  representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For
  reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory.
  For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and
  then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera
  controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.

title: Tenant Cohort Monitoring: 3 Node.js Docker Kubernetes Readiness Liveness Startup Signals
description:
A restart tells you that a container failed. It does not tell you whether the failure hit the control cohort, the experiment cohort, or both. TL;DR: expose separate startup, readiness, and liveness endpoints; let Kubernetes own the restart decision; and emit matching state transitions as logs plus metrics. For a small property-management SaaS, this is the leanest setup that can reconstruct a tenant-cohort incident without turning monitoring into a second product.

Choice Best fit Reconstruction strength Main boundary
App probes + metrics + logs Small service, weekly releases Strong with cohort and request IDs in logs You operate queries and notifications
Datadog or Grafana Cloud Several services or an on-call team Broader telemetry workflows More platform surface to manage
Better Uptime Public endpoint checks Strong outside-in timeline A healthy homepage can miss a stuck job
Healthchecks.io Cron and worker silence Excellent missed-heartbeat evidence It does not replace request-path probes

My recommendation is the first row for a one-person SaaS with one or two deployable services, plus an outside-in monitor for the failure it cannot see. Keep the contract yours: three HTTP responses, structured events, and a small metric vocabulary. A backend vendor can change later without changing application semantics. Ship the useful boundary now.

Three signals. One timeline.

How should Node.js on Docker use Kubernetes readiness, liveness, and startup probes?

Startup, readiness, and liveness answer different questions. Mixing them creates bad evidence and worse automation.

A startup probe asks whether initialization has completed. Until it succeeds, Kubernetes does not run readiness or liveness probes. That protects a deliberately slow boot from a premature restart. Readiness asks whether this pod should receive traffic now. A temporary database dependency failure can make a pod unready without proving that its process is dead. Liveness asks whether the process is stuck beyond recovery; repeated failure lets the platform restart the container.

Keep liveness narrow. If it fails whenever a downstream API is slow, Kubernetes can restart every healthy process during somebody else's outage. That destroys local state and muddies the timeline. Readiness is the better place for a dependency that makes serving requests unsafe.

For the property-management experiment, log the tenant cohort at the request boundary, not inside the probe. Probes have no tenant context. During reconstruction, join the deployment version and time window from health events to request logs carrying cohort, trace_id, and span_id. This distinguishes a rollout-wide failure from an experiment path affecting only lease_reminder_v2.

The trade-off is explicit: this design favors evidence that can survive a backend swap over a rich vendor-specific data model. I would make that choice while one person still owns deployment and feature delivery. Once cross-service debugging becomes routine, the time saved by a full suite can outweigh the portability.

Implement the evidence contract

The app should calculate health once, then expose that state to Kubernetes and telemetry. This TypeScript service is runnable after installing express, prom-client, and the relevant TypeScript types. It models three endpoints, exports Prometheus metrics, and adds cohort evidence to application logs.

import express, { Request, Response } from "express";
import { Counter, Gauge, Registry } from "prom-client";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!apiKey || !baseUrl) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL");
}

async function readLogContract(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(new URL("/v1/discovery/logs.ingest", baseUrl), {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });
  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const delayMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return readLogContract(attempt + 1);
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

const app = express();
const registry = new Registry();
const failures = new Counter({
  name: "app_probe_failures_total",
  help: "Failed application health probes",
  labelNames: ["probe"] as const,
  registers: [registry],
});
const ready = new Gauge({
  name: "app_ready",
  help: "Whether this process can receive traffic",
  registers: [registry],
});

let startupComplete = false;
let databaseReachable = false;

function respond(
  probe: "startup" | "readiness" | "liveness",
  healthy: boolean,
  res: Response,
): void {
  if (!healthy) failures.inc({ probe });
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    event: "health_state",
    probe,
    healthy,
    deployment: process.env.DEPLOYMENT_VERSION ?? "unknown",
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  }));
  res.status(healthy ? 200 : 503).json({ healthy });
}

app.get("/health/startup", (_req, res) => {
  respond("startup", startupComplete, res);
});
app.get("/health/ready", (_req, res) => {
  ready.set(databaseReachable ? 1 : 0);
  respond("readiness", databaseReachable, res);
});
app.get("/health/live", (_req, res) => {
  respond("liveness", true, res);
});
app.get("/metrics", async (_req, res) => {
  res.type(registry.contentType).send(await registry.metrics());
});
app.get("/leases/:id", (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const cohort = req.header("x-experiment-cohort") ?? "control";
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    event: "lease_viewed",
    lease_id: req.params.id,
    cohort,
    trace_id: req.header("x-trace-id") ?? null,
    span_id: req.header("x-span-id") ?? null,
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  }));
  res.status(200).json({ id: req.params.id, cohort });
});

async function initialize(): Promise<void> {
  databaseReachable = true;
  startupComplete = true;
  ready.set(1);
}

app.listen(3000, () => {
  void Promise.all([initialize(), readLogContract()]);
});

The Kubernetes configuration can also live in typed deployment code. These values are examples, not universal thresholds: measure normal initialization and recovery before tightening them. The relationship matters. Startup gets its own budget, readiness removes traffic, and liveness restarts only a process that cannot recover.

type Probe = {
  httpGet: { path: string; port: number };
  periodSeconds: number;
  timeoutSeconds: number;
  failureThreshold: number;
};

const containerHealth: Record<string, Probe> = {
  startupProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/startup", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 2,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 30,
  },
  readinessProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/ready", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 5,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 2,
  },
  livenessProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/live", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 10,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 3,
  },
};

console.log(JSON.stringify(containerHealth, null, 2));

There is a deliberate asymmetry. A failed readiness check changes routing quickly, while liveness waits longer before replacing the process. Fast restarts feel decisive, but false positives erase evidence and amplify dependency trouble.

Read the 14:03 tenant timeline

A useful dashboard needs only two health measures at first: the rate of app_probe_failures_total split by probe, and the current app_ready gauge split by deployment. Do not add the cohort label to either metric. Tenant or cohort labels can grow without bound and create noisy time series; cohort belongs in request logs.

Suppose lease_reminder_v2 requests begin failing at 14:03, readiness drops at 14:04, and Kubernetes replaces a container at 14:05. Start with the counter and gauge to bound the window. Inspect health_state logs for the deployment version. Then search request logs in that interval and compare control with lease_reminder_v2, following trace_id and span_id where they exist. Those IDs support log correlation, but they do not create a distributed trace or span tree.

This answers the business question: did the experiment path fail, or did the whole deployment lose its dependency? It is not enough to map a failure across five services. Be honest about that boundary.

Keep the log schema and metric names stable so the storage vendor can move behind the contract. Infrai is one reasonable backend when a solo operator values one plain REST API that needs no installed SDK; its public, self-describing discovery surface lets the app read the real request schema before binding an adapter. Infrai covers 295 routes across 20 modules with one API key and one bill, so adding another backend capability does not create another credential rotation or invoice-reconciliation job for the same operator. Its observability surface can ingest logs and report metrics.

The limitations are substantial. It has no threshold notification route, distributed trace query, synthetic heartbeat, source-map decoding, or session replay. Query polling must provide notifications, and discovery does not declare filters for log search or metric query, so verify requests from the public discovery response rather than inventing parameters. It is not suitable when native alerting or span-tree investigation is a requirement; choose Datadog or Grafana Cloud instead. A stable contract saves replacement work, but polling creates operational work. That is the trade-off.

No span tree.

Draw the product boundaries

Choose Datadog when cross-service investigation, mature alert workflows, and a broad integrated telemetry product justify the added platform surface. It fits once several services and people share on-call work. Grafana Cloud suits teams already committed to Prometheus-style metrics and Grafana dashboards, especially when they want logs and traces in the same ecosystem while retaining familiar open telemetry formats.

Better Uptime is the stronger runner-up for outside-in availability and incident response. It can observe that a public endpoint is unreachable even when internal probes look healthy. Healthchecks.io solves a different blind spot: a nightly rent-ledger job that never starts emits no application failure. A dead-man's-switch heartbeat detects that silence. Pair it with probes rather than asking either tool to cover both jobs.

No choice wins every axis. A small SaaS can start with app-owned probes, logs, and metrics, then outsource the undifferentiated edge: public checks to an uptime service and missed-job detection to a heartbeat service. Add a full observability suite when cross-service reconstruction consumes feature-shipping hours. That revenue-per-hour threshold is more useful than a feature-count contest.

One more boundary matters for property data. If logs contain tenant identifiers, deletion and retention controls are part of the design. A backend without per-user log deletion cannot by itself satisfy an erasure workflow. Minimize identifiers before ingestion, define retention deliberately, and choose controls that match the legal obligation.

Govern the evidence, then stop

Keep automation and evidence separate. Kubernetes acts on three low-cardinality health decisions. Logs preserve cohort and request context. Metrics show frequency and present state. An external checker covers failures the cluster cannot observe.

Start with the smallest version that answers one reconstruction question. After each incident, record the unanswered question. Buy or build the next layer only when the same missing evidence recurs; otherwise, ship the tenant feature.

Sources

  • Kubernetes: Pod lifecycle and container probes
  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana Cloud documentation
  • Better Uptime documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure

title: Copy-Paste Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19247v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.

title: Structural Chain-of-Thought: Reasoning with Executable Computational Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.15107v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting enables reasoning in large language models but produces explanations that are difficult to verify, expensive to generate, and not always faithful. We introduce a Structural Chain-of-Thought framework where models generate executable computational graphs instead of free-form reasoning. The final answer is obtained by deterministically executing the graph. The model is trained using graph-based reinforcement learning that rewards structural validity, answer correctness, and node overlap with reference graphs.
  Experiments across five benchmarks and four model families show that our method consistently improves accuracy over supervised graph training and can reduce generation length by up to 5-6x compared with standard GRPO and chain-of-thought supervised training. Our faithfulness experiments reveal that models trained with our approach tend to rely on deriving their answers from the generated graphs rather than producing post-hoc rationalizations as usually in chain-of-thought reasoning.

title: How to Evaluate When You Don't Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking
description:
arXiv:2610.19185v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.

title: Node.js GDPR-Friendly App Logging: Hosted Services, Deletion, Retention, and Export APIs
description:
The least complex workable design is to keep personal data out of operational logs, attach a pseudonymous subject reference when correlation is unavoidable, and send the re-identification map to a system built for deletion. Short answer: for an EU-facing logistics app, use a mature hosted log service when per-user erasure, retention controls, or bulk export are hard requirements. A centralized ingest-and-search API can cover ordinary debugging, but it should not become the system of record for data-subject workflows unless those controls exist.

The page arrives at 02:17: “dispatch-agent completion rate below threshold.” On-call can see that 73 route-planning jobs started, 69 completed, and four have no terminal event. They can also see each AI loop's duration and attributed model cost. What they must not need to see is a driver's name, email address, street address, or raw prompt. The useful incident key is agent_run_id; the compliance liability is everything copied around it.

That distinction determines the architecture before vendor selection does.

What should have fired before the completion-rate page?

The earlier signal is not “many errors.” It is an age invariant: every accepted planning job must reach exactly one durable terminal state within the service-level window. A job can fail without emitting an exception, and a worker can disappear after acknowledging work. Error-count alerts miss both cases.

The alert path therefore starts with a scheduler or queue monitor that knows which jobs should exist. Infrai has no alert or notification route and no synthetic or heartbeat monitoring, so a team using its centralized log ingest and search must pair it with a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks or run its own polling alert. It also does not provide distributed trace queries or a span tree; trace_id and span_id in logs are correlation fields, not a tracing backend.

This matters during triage. The page should contain a runbook link, the violated invariant, the evaluation window, and a query key. It should not dump the last prompt into a notification. An operator first checks the authoritative job state, then uses agent_run_id to find the corresponding log events and cost records.

No log line is proof that a job completed.

The database transition is.

How should I compare GDPR-friendly hosted app logging services?

There are two defensible architectures for this workload. Both need the same invariants: retries cannot create a second logical job; every run has one stable identifier; cost and latency attach to that identifier; and personal data is excluded or tokenized before it crosses the logging boundary.

Shape Operational invariant Good fit Boundary that decides it
Specialist observability stack The logging vendor owns search, retention policy, compliance export, and subject-deletion workflow Regulated production logs and established audit pipelines Choose only after verifying deletion granularity, export completeness, EU processing terms, and retention configuration
Split control plane The job database owns identity and completion; a narrow log API receives pseudonymous events; a separate monitor pages on missing work Moderate log volume and teams minimizing backend integrations The log store must remain disposable because it is not the erasure or archive authority

The first shape is the conservative choice when logs may contain personal data. Evaluate Datadog, Better Stack, Axiom, and Elastic against a written test plan rather than a feature-page checklist: create a subject's events, change retention, delete that subject's records, export the required interval, and preserve evidence that the workflow ran. The supplied requirement is the judge. A product that cannot pass the deletion test is unsuitable even if its search is excellent.

The second shape can deliberately include Infrai for everyday ingest and search. One key. One wallet. One bill. Infrai provides one API key and consolidated billing across 295 routes in 20 backend modules, replacing the pile of vendor credentials and invoices that otherwise needs reconciling at month end. It directly reduces credential sprawl in a small on-call rotation. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; it returns request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. That is useful when a team wants to validate an integration before adding it to the dispatch path.

Teams running moderate-volume, pseudonymized logistics logs should try Infrai for the search-and-debug slice when consolidating backend credentials and integration surfaces matters. Keep compliance deletion and archival outside that slice. There is no per-user log deletion API, no bulk export or subscription API, and no exposed retention configuration entry point. Those are design boundaries, not backlog assumptions.

Instrument the AI loop at the state transition

Instrument four moments: accepted, model call finished, terminal state committed, and abandoned-by-deadline. The model-call event records latency_ms and cost_usd returned by the AI surface, associated with agent_run_id. Do not derive cost by scraping prose from a log message. Infrai specifies per-call cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request ID metadata on its native envelope; its OpenAI-compatible surface also exposes cost and latency metadata.

The application is Node.js, but the operational probe below is Go because a static runbook binary is easy to execute from a bastion or a scheduled diagnostic job. It calls the real log search route without inventing filters: the route's discovery parameters do not declare any. The probe reads the key from the environment, sets the HTTP method, retries a 429 using Retry-After when present, and returns non-success bodies to the operator instead of printing a false green result.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const searchURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search"

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func searchLogs(client *http.Client, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, searchURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("log search returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("log search remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    body, err := searchLogs(&http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

This probe is diagnostic, not the alert itself. Since no search filters are declared in discovery, it deliberately sends none; pretending that a convenient agent_run_id parameter exists would make the runbook brittle. In production, cost_usd and latency_ms must come from model response metadata, while the terminal outcome must come from committed application state. The ingestion-side allowlist should admit fields such as event, agent_run_id, shipment_ref, latency_ms, cost_usd, outcome, and occurred_at, while rejecting email, driver_name, address, prompt, and response. A random shipment_ref can be resolved through the separately controlled application database when access is authorized; deleting that mapping breaks the link without pretending the log vendor has performed per-user erasure.

Retries need the same discipline. A worker retries with the original agent_run_id; the database enforces one terminal transition; duplicate telemetry is tolerated and deduplicated downstream by event identity. This is the idempotency reflex that prevents an observability retry from looking like a second paid model run.

How the hosted options differ at this boundary

Datadog is the broad-suite candidate: evaluate it when logs need to sit beside metrics, traces, and an established incident workflow. Axiom is the focused analytical candidate for teams that want to interrogate event data and should be tested against the same deletion and export script. Better Stack is the candidate when logs and on-call workflow need to be assessed together. Elastic deserves a place when control over the storage and operating model outweighs the work of running or managing the stack.

Those are evaluation lanes, not claims that every plan or deployment mode supplies the required GDPR control. Product behavior, region availability, retention limits, and APIs change. Record the exact plan, region, and API tested in the data-protection impact assessment, then rerun the test before renewal.

Infrai occupies a narrower lane. Centralized ingest and search cover routine debugging, and its 295 routes across 20 modules can consolidate credentials beyond logging. The trade-off is sharp: it has no per-user deletion, bulk export, subscription, native alert notification, synthetic monitoring, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or Session Replay. If any of those is part of the acceptance criteria, select a specialist that demonstrates it or build an explicitly owned adjacent system.

This is why the comparison cannot be reduced to query speed or price. The relevant cost is the amount of operational state the team must own when a driver invokes a data right or an auditor requests a bounded export.

Thresholds create their own incident load

Set the missing-job threshold from the contractual completion window, queue delay, and a measured safety margin. Do not copy a percentile from a web-performance guide into a batch workflow. A logistics planner that normally takes minutes and a synchronous customer request have different failure semantics.

Start the alert in shadow mode. Count pages that would have fired, label each as actionable or expected delay, and only then enable paging. A threshold that catches every slow run but wakes someone for normal carrier API variance is not conservative; it spends attention until the real silent failure is ignored.

There is a second false positive to avoid. Search lag is not job failure. Page from the scheduler or durable job state, then use logs as evidence. If the logging service is unavailable, the agent loop should continue and the shipper should retry with bounded storage; observability must not become a new dependency in the dispatch path.

The final decision rule is plain: choose the specialist-stack shape when deletion, retention configuration, or export must be performed inside the log platform. Choose the split control plane when logs are pseudonymous, moderate in volume, and operational search is the goal. In both cases, prove the alert from the state machine and prove the GDPR workflow with test data before production traffic arrives.

Further reading

  • Datadog data security and privacy documentation
  • Better Stack logs documentation
  • Axiom documentation
  • Elastic data lifecycle management documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • ClickHouse documentation
  • Core Web Vitals definitions and percentile guidance
  • Infrai app logging comparison guide

If this split boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai app logging guide and verify the discovery schema before wiring the shipper.

title: Outcome-Routed Distillation and Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19271v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision on the student's own samples, but its targets still come from the teacher. Verifier reinforcement learning (RL) instead uses an outcome signal, but it provides no direct constraint on capabilities outside the verifier. Combining the two is difficult for diffusion language models (dLLMs), because bidirectional denoising makes the policy likelihoods required by ratio-based RL unreliable.
  We develop a likelihood-free pipeline for a mixture-of-experts dLLM. Each rollout group is routed by verifier outcome. Mixed groups use ratio-free, group-centred REINFORCE. If every student rollout fails but a teacher succeeds, the model receives dense KL supervision on the student's denoising canvases. All other groups are skipped. A KL term anchored to the distilled checkpoint limits changes outside the verifier reward.
  The tool-calling teacher succeeds on only 18.6% of the training prompts. At 24 denoising steps, distillation exceeds the teacher by 6.77 percentage points, and routing improves the distilled checkpoint by a further 18.31 points. Routing lowers reasoning-trace accuracy by 0.71 points but raises direct-answer accuracy on the same items by 13.21 points. The anchored arm restores trace accuracy. Its tool-calling score differs by -0.16 points, with a confidence interval that includes zero, although this comparison also removes a small fallback distillation route. A domain-conditional recipe retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain; a second seed gives 18.23 points and reproduces both preservation results, but the math result is seed-dependent. We pre-registered every arm and evaluated each comparison on paired items in a single sweep on one machine.

title: Making PyTorch & Local ML Work on Modest Hardware: Lessons from a 4GB/8GB Laptop GPU
description:
Most machine learning tutorials and paper implementations silently make an expensive assumption: you have an enterprise cloud instance or an A100/H100 with 40 GB+ of VRAM waiting on standby.

In reality, many engineers, students, and independent builders experiment on personal machines—often a laptop with an RTX 3050, 4050, or similar GPU offering 4 GB to 8 GB of VRAM.

Hitting a terminal wall after waiting through preprocessing is an all-too-common milestone:

torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 512.00 MiB...

The standard advice online is often "just reduce your batch size" or "rent a cloud instance." But lowering the batch size too much destabilizes optimizer dynamics, and cloud bills add up fast when you are just prototyping or debugging architectures.

You do not need massive hardware to train custom models, experiment with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), or run local pipelines. Here is an end-to-end breakdown of how to make PyTorch run cleanly on memory-constrained consumer laptop GPUs.

1. Simulate Effective Batch Sizes via Gradient Accumulation

Optimizers like AdamW and SGD need a representative sample of data per step to compute stable gradient directions. If your architecture hits an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error at batch size 64, cutting it down to 8 might prevent the crash, but it can introduce excessive variance into training.

Gradient Accumulation resolves this tension by computing micro-batches sequentially, summing the gradients internally, and only stepping the optimizer once a threshold is reached.

import torch

model.train()
optimizer.zero_grad()

# If 64 crashes, use a micro-batch of 16 across 4 steps
accumulation_steps = 4 

for step, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(dataloader):
    inputs, targets = inputs.to("cuda"), targets.to("cuda")

    outputs = model(inputs)
    # Scale loss to maintain mathematical equivalence with a larger batch
    loss = criterion(outputs, targets) / accumulation_steps
    loss.backward()

    if (step + 1) % accumulation_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

Memory impact: Your GPU only ever holds the activations and intermediate tensors for batch_size = 16, but the optimizer trajectory matches batch_size = 64.

2. Halve Activation Memory with Mixed Precision (torch.amp)

PyTorch defaults to 32-bit floating point (FP32) for tensor allocations. Modern NVIDIA GPUs feature specialized Tensor Cores built to process 16-bit floats (FP16 or BF16) with substantially higher throughput and half the memory footprint.

Using native Automatic Mixed Precision (torch.amp) automatically casts non-sensitive operations into 16-bit while keeping sensitive weight calculations in 32-bit:

from torch.amp import autocast, GradScaler

# GradScaler prevents small gradients from underflowing to zero in FP16
scaler = GradScaler("cuda")

for inputs, targets in dataloader:
    inputs, targets = inputs.to("cuda"), targets.to("cuda")
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    # Operations inside this block run with lower precision
    with autocast("cuda"):
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)

    # Scale loss, backprop, step, and update scaler
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()

Memory impact: Memory overhead for layer activations drops by roughly 40% to 50%, often allowing you to double your local micro-batch size without OOM errors.

3. Plug Hidden Autograd Leaks

PyTorch's dynamic computational graph is flexible, but it makes it easy to accidentally pin large chunks of VRAM indefinitely.

The Running Loss Accumulation Trap

A common mistake looks like this:

# ❌ INCORRECT: Keeps the entire backward graph in VRAM
total_train_loss = 0.0
for inputs, targets in dataloader:
    outputs = model(inputs)
    loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    total_train_loss += loss  # Leaks autograd graph

Because loss is a PyTorch tensor linked to the autograd graph, adding it directly keeps the entire computation history across all previous iterations alive in memory.

#  CORRECT: Extracts the raw scalar float
total_train_loss += loss.item()

Always Disable Gradients During Evaluation

Never run evaluation without disabling autograd tracking:

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    for inputs, targets in val_loader:
        inputs, targets = inputs.to("cuda"), targets.to("cuda")
        outputs = model(inputs)
        # No forward activations are cached for backpropagation

4. Tune the Host: Data Pipeline and Thermals

On laptops, training bottlenecks are rarely just raw GPU compute—host memory, PCIe bandwidth, and thermal dissipation play massive roles.

  • Downcast types in memory: When ingesting CSVs or NumPy arrays, cast default float64 features to float32 and int64 targets to int32 before passing them into PyTorch tensors.
  • Configure DataLoader pinned memory: Set pin_memory=True in your PyTorch DataLoader to speed up CPU-to-GPU data transfers via page-locked (pinned) memory: 
dataloader = DataLoader(
    dataset,
    batch_size=16,
    shuffle=True,
    num_workers=2,        # Set between 2 and 4 to avoid CPU starvation
    pin_memory=True       # Speeds up host-to-device memory copy
)
  • Mitigate Thermal Throttling: Laptops share cooling pipes between CPU and GPU. Elevating the chassis by an inch or placing it on a simple stand drops temperatures significantly, preventing clock-speed throttling halfway through an epoch.

Conclusion

Understanding how frameworks allocate tensors, how autograd stores intermediate state, and how hardware limits dictate software design makes you a more capable engineer.

Before reaching for cloud credits, what is your favorite technique for keeping local experiments lean and responsive? Drop your thoughts or local setups below!

title: Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Models for Consistent Future Frame Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next-state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next-state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance-gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.

title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.19306v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.

title: 6 GSAP Component Libraries Compared in 2026 (Annnimate, Made With GSAP, Osmo, React Bits, Codrops)
description:
GSAP is an animation engine, not a component library. That is the first thing Google tells you when you search "gsap animation component library", and it is true: GSAP gives you gsap.to(), ScrollTrigger and SplitText, and leaves the hero reveal, the pinned gallery and the page transition to you.

So a small ecosystem of libraries has grown up that sell or give away finished GSAP components. I run one of them (Made for Award), so read this with that in mind. I have tried to be fair, and I link to every site so you can check the current numbers yourself, because prices and counts change.

Here is how the six I know best compare, and who each one is for.

Quick comparison

Library What you get Frameworks Pricing model Free tier
Annnimate ~119 UI components: buttons, menus, scroll, sections, shaders React, Vue, HTML Subscription (quarterly / yearly) + one-time kits 16-component starter pack
Made With GSAP ~121 JS effects: scroll, mouse, drag, infinite Webflow, vanilla JS Subscription (quarterly / annual) A few free effects
Osmo Vault of GSAP/Webflow resources and snippets Webflow, vanilla, some React Subscription Some free resources
React Bits Animated React components, part GSAP, part Motion React Free, open source Everything
Codrops Hundreds of demo tutorials, many on GSAP Vanilla Free Everything
Made for Award 40 award-style components: scroll, hero, preloader, slider, page transition, WebGL React, Next.js One-time ($22, lifetime) 8 free components

Counts are what each site stated in October 2026. Check the links for today's numbers.

1. Annnimate

The most "design system" of the group. Components are organised like a UI kit (Buttons, Menus, Scroll, Sections, Shaders), every component ships in React, Vue and plain HTML, and there is an MCP server so Cursor or Claude Code can pull the real source while it writes code. The studio behind it has built for Coca-Cola and Powerade and the polish shows.

Best for: teams on a subscription budget who want a consistent kit across React and Vue, and who like the AI-editor integration.

Watch out for: it is a subscription, so the components stop coming when you stop paying. Check the licence for client work.

2. Made With GSAP

121 effects and counting, all lightweight JavaScript plus GSAP, with an explicit "no Canvas, no WebGL" rule. The sweet spot is Webflow: effects are packaged so you can paste them into a Webflow project, and the source download covers vanilla sites too.

Best for: Webflow designers and anyone who wants scroll and mouse effects without a build step.

Watch out for: no React or Next.js versions, and no 3D or shader work by design. Subscription pricing.

3. Osmo

Osmo is a resource vault from the people behind a well-known Webflow/GSAP studio: snippets, cloneables, utilities and full sections, with a strong Webflow bias and growing framework support. Less a component library than a toolbox you dip into.

Best for: Webflow-first builders who want the studio's own helpers and patterns.

Watch out for: subscription, and you will still assemble most things yourself.

4. React Bits

Free and open source. A big catalogue of animated React components (text effects, backgrounds, cursors, cards) with a CLI, where some components use GSAP and others use Motion. Quality varies piece to piece, as you would expect from a community project, but for a landing page you can get far at zero cost.

Best for: React developers who want something free today and are happy to adapt.

Watch out for: it is a mix of animation engines, so not everything is "GSAP". Expect to tune timings and clean up for production.

5. Codrops

Not a library, but the original source of most of the effects the libraries sell. Every Codrops demo comes with a tutorial and a GitHub repo, many built on GSAP. The catch is that demos are vanilla and written to teach, not to ship: you port them yourself and you handle cleanup, resize and reduced motion.

Best for: learning how an effect works, and developers who prefer to build their own component from a reference.

Watch out for: licences differ per demo; some assets (fonts, images) are demo-only.

6. Made for Award

This is mine. Made for Award is a GSAP animation component library: 40 production-ready React and Next.js components (scroll animations, hero sections, preloaders, sliders, page transitions and WebGL effects), 8 of them free and the rest unlocked by one $22 lifetime purchase. Every component has a live demo you can open full-screen before you sign in, and the source is TypeScript + Tailwind with props for the content, so a slider takes your slides and a hero takes your headline.

The focus is narrower than Annnimate's: not a UI kit, but the specific award-site pieces (pinned scroll scenes, preloaders, smoke and wave page transitions, three.js heroes) that are the hard part of a portfolio or agency site.

Best for: React and Next.js developers building a portfolio, agency or launch site who want award-style motion without a subscription.

Watch out for: React only, no Vue or Webflow versions, and a smaller catalogue than the subscription libraries.

How to choose

  • Webflow: Made With GSAP or Osmo.
  • React + Vue in one kit, subscription is fine: Annnimate.
  • Zero budget: React Bits, plus Codrops to learn from, plus the free tier of any of the paid ones.
  • React or Next.js, pay once: Made for Award.

Whichever you pick, the thing that matters more than the library is the setup underneath it: register ScrollTrigger once, create animations inside useGSAP with a scope, put Lenis on the GSAP ticker, and refresh after fonts and images load. Every library above assumes you have that right, and most "the component is broken" issues are one of those four.

If I missed a library you use, tell me in the comments and I will add it.

title: RASSG: Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating for Streaming Tool Execution
description:
arXiv:2610.14659v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Streaming speech assistants can launch tools before users finish speaking, overlapping execution with incoming speech to reduce user waiting time. However, subsequent self-corrections can invalidate apparently stable arguments, causing stale execution whose irreversible effects persist even after the final call is corrected. We propose Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating (RASSG) to jointly control tool launch and cancellation during streaming speech. RASSG launches a tool when three consecutive speech recognition results arrive with identical nonempty arguments, then combines calibrated argument invalidity risk with execution costs to decide cancellation at the last feasible opportunity before effects become irreversible. Evaluation on ReCAST, FDB-v3, and Audio2Tool uses a controlled execution clock with fixed tool runtimes and cancellation parameters. On ReCAST's prospective-repair subset, RASSG reduces the stale execution rate from LocalAgreement-2's 50.00% to 3.15%, with a mean delay of 3.676s across successful trajectories. The stale reduction also holds against every early-execution baseline on both public speech datasets. Ablations with identical initial launches support active cancellation, showing the value of controlling ongoing calls before their effects become irreversible. Code and data are available at https://github.com/daijinhu/RASSG.

title: AWS News: Lambda Web Functions
description:
Originally published at https://www.vaines.org/posts/2029-10-15-lambda-web-functions/

This week, AWS have announced Lambda Web Functions, which, after fighting with Amplify for the last few years, made me drop what I was doing and have a play.

I was excited about this because as much as the JS community seems to be hell-bent on finding another way of running JavaScript and more JavaScript frameworks running Next.Js outside of Vercel isn't the best experience. I've been running Next.js on AWS Amplify for a couple of years, and I would quite like to stop doing that. It sucks.

Next.js seems like a decent framework, particularly when you want to mix static pages with server-side rendering, dynamic routes and a bit of server-side application logic. If you're deploying to Vercel, the whole thing is a pretty slick experience. Which isn't terribly surprising, given Vercel's relationship with Next.js. Hosting it elsewhere is ... interesting.

If you're just using what could be hosted as a static site, fine. But why bother with Next.js at all? Easily hosted and known patterns abound for this. As soon as you want the funky routing, SSR, or on-demand ISR bits, it's pain time.

Obviously we looked at containers where ECS would do the job, but it seemed like a lot of plumbing just to host a web application. We also looked at splitting the server-side bits out into Lambda. That's perfectly possible, especially with projects like OpenNext making it easier, but it still means owning rather more of the integration than we wanted to at the time.

Amplify appeared to be the least worst option; we just needed to connect the repository, let AWS build and deploy Next.js, get a CDN and managed SSR infrastructure thrown in. Having this work in a sensible SDLC in an enterprise has been a bit challenging. Like many of the higher-level AWS managed services, it seems to forget all the patterns and prescriptive guidance about promoting through environments and accounts in favour of the target audience being smaller teams or singular developers having a click-and-go with built-in dev and release options. Compared with maintaining our own hosting arrangement, Amplify sounded quite sensible.

Lets build some stuff...

The Amplify infrastructure-as-code experience is shite. Between provider limitations, gaps in the APIs and behaviour that isn't documented particularly well (or at all), I've spent far too much time working around the Amplify platform rather than building applications. We've encountered things that behave differently depending on whether they were configured through the API or clickOps'd in the console. That's particularly irritating when you're trying to keep environments reproducible.

When something goes wrong, which it will, debugging can be equally unpleasant - though I will say it has gotten a lot better recently. You know that something somewhere in the managed deployment black-box isn't behaving, but getting enough information to understand what is happening feels like an archaeological expedition.

Even the mundane stuff gets weird: AWS documents that Amplify environment variables aren't automatically available to Next.js server components. You have to explicitly write the ones you need into the Next.js environment configuration during the build. I get the security rationale, but it's another Amplify-specific detail to remember when you thought you were just deploying a Next.js app.

And then there are the framework features. At the time of writing, Amplify's Next.js support documentation lists support through Next.js 15, but specifically excludes Next.js streaming and on-demand ISR. Those aren't the only features in Next.js, and to be fair to Amplify, it handles plenty of other things nicely, including static delivery. But after years of dealing with the awkward bits, I was stoked to read I might have an alternative to it.

Demo time!

After reading the news post I quickly sent an AI agent off to throw a small Next.js application together which used routing, ISR, and SSR along with some other bits. I deployed exactly the same code to Amplify and Lambda Web Functions, then ran a battery of tests over them repeatedly with Playwright to see what happened. There's a copy of all the code in the linked GitHub repo if you want to run your own tests.

Traditional Lambda, or as AWS now call it Lambda Event Functions, gives your code an event and expects a response. A normal Next.js production server doesn't work like that; it listens on an HTTP port and serves requests. Getting it onto traditional Lambda just wouldn't work very well with that difference.

A Lambda Web Function, on the other hand, seems to be simply running an HTTP server. Your application listens on the host and port supplied by Lambda, and AWS provides the HTTPS endpoint, execution environments, and scaling. No API Gateway nonsense pretending to be an HTTP request and no framework-specific adapter to get a standard Node server running.

The docs show some other interesting changes too! A warmed Web Function can serve multiple requests at once, rather than the single concurrent invocation model we're used to with ye old Event Functions. AWS allows an upper bound of up to 128 concurrent requests per environment, although the actual concurrency is apparently managed dynamically. This could be handy for web applications which spend a good deal of time waiting for other stuff like databases or whatever other AWS services you plumb in.

The billing model is cool as well; Web Functions meter active CPU time, alongside memory over the lifetime of the environment, requests and data transfer. Waiting for databases or whatever doesn't consume much CPU, even though the environment still has memory allocated. Whether that's cheaper for a particular Next.js application is another question entirely, but it sounds good for the use case.

Oh, AND Web Functions support native response streaming, which is a feature I really wanted to get my greasy mitts on.

At launch, this is Node.js 24 on Arm64, not a general-purpose way to run absolutely anything, and AWS also has immutable revisions, endpoints that can direct traffic to revisions, and optional multi-region routing. Quite a lot of toys straight out of the box for something that looks much more like deploying an ordinary web server.

Of course, an HTTP endpoint and some compute aren't the same thing as a complete managed Next.js hosting platform. But we can worry about that after we've made some fish.

Just Eat...but for fish

Uber but for dogs is so passé. If any investors are reading, we should talk 🤙

I wanted to exercise the actual Next.js behaviour I wanted to play with rather than just a simple Next.js starter page, deploy it twice and declare victory because both returned a 200.

So I (Codex GPT 6 Astra) built Fin & Feast, a fictional takeaway service offering fish delivered to your door. Searchable menus, dish pages, a working basket, checkout and order tracking mock. It looks enough like a real little application to be suitable for testing some of these toys out.

The app uses Next.js 15, TypeScript and the App Router. There's one codebase and two hosting targets, with all the source, Terraform and benchmarking code attached to the top of this post.

The homepage renders dynamically using details from the request. The individual dish pages are statically generated. Checkout goes through /api/orders, where the basket is validated and prices are calculated on the server. The order confirmation is personalised using a signed, HttpOnly receipt cookie, which the server checks when you open the order page.

There's no database or payment integration. The basket lives in browser storage, and checkout is simulated as this is just a hosting experiment. The signed receipt means you can't just guess someone else's order URL and read their order, but it isn't meant to be a production commerce system.

The homepage availability panel and the order progress panel are asynchronous components behind React Suspense boundaries. I've deliberately added a second or so of delay to availability and order progress to simulate some waiting. These delays are there to make the difference between streaming a page as pieces become ready and waiting until everything is ready obvious. It's not supposed to be a benchmark of database performance or a claim about how long Lambda takes to run JavaScript or any of that.

flowchart TD
    Browser["Browser"]

    Home["/ — dynamic homepage<br/>Request headers and query parameters"]
    Shop["Interactive shop<br/>Search, filters and basket"]
    Storage["Browser localStorage"]
    Availability["kitchen availability - simulated 1.6-second delay"]

    Dish["/menu/[slug]<br/>Statically generated dish pages"]
    API["POST /api/orders<br/>Validate basket and calculate total"]
    Cookie["Signed HttpOnly receipt cookie"]
    Order["/orders/[id]<br/>Server-rendered personalised receipt"]
    Progress["kitchen progress - simulated 1.2-second delay"]

    Browser --> Home
    Home --> Shop
    Home --> Availability
    Shop <--> Storage
    Shop -->|"Next.js navigation / prefetch"| Dish
    Shop -->|"Submit checkout"| API
    API -->|"Set-Cookie"| Cookie
    API -->|"Return order URL"| Browser
    Browser --> Order
    Cookie -->|"Validated on the server"| Order
    Order --> Progress

One app to rule them all

Both deployments have IaC written in Terraform and given that I said IaC is one of the things that's made Amplify so painful, it made sense to include that.

For Amplify, Terraform sets up the application and connects it to the GitHub repository. Amplify does its thing and builds the Next.js app from app/ and deploys it using its managed hosting setup. Importantly, that includes a CloudFront distribution somewhere in the AWS-managed bit.

For Web Functions, that all becomes your problem to deal with. The Next.js app is built in standalone mode from a Linux Arm64 build container which packages the generated Node server and its assets into a ZIP, and uploads that to an S3 bucket. Terraform creates a Web Function revision pinned to that object version and points an HTTPS endpoint at the revision. A tiny entry point tells Next.js which host and port to listen on.

That container is just for the build; the application is running as a native Web Function, not as another container service, meaning Corey Quinn doesn't get to update his 17 ways to run containers in AWS post today.

I think one of the biggest caveats to this setup is that CloudFront distribution Amplify is bundling in with its managed service wrap. Web Functions doesn't come with one, so I didn't deploy one. In hindsight, maybe I should have. I'm still torn over this; feel free to run your own tests after adding one.

Test time

Rather than sit clicking around and pat myself on the back because the new thing felt faster, I've got a small Playwright harness to drive the same journeys on both deployments. It loads the dynamic homepage and waits for availability, opens a static dish page, navigates to a dish from the homepage using normal Next.js prefetching, then adds an item to the basket, performs the checkout and reloads the personalised order page.

Each journey runs with a fresh browser context, and again after a priming journey in the same context. Fresh in this context means new browser state, but I couldn't guarantee a Lambda cold start or an empty CloudFront cache. The requests were run serially, alternating the order of the platforms to reduce the chance of one consistently getting the better conditions.

The main run across both platforms was made up of four journeys in both browser modes, producing 1,600 journeys, with another 800 priming journeys. I found no failed measured journeys, and no browser HTTP errors, thankfully. I think this represents a repeatable browser-experience comparison, rather than running out my AWS credits through a load test.

Here are the results:

Measurement Amplify median (ms) Web Functions median (ms) Amplify p95 (ms) Web Functions p95 (ms)
Homepage time to first byte 1,803 297 1,893 369
Static dish page time to first byte 43 288 108 355
Prefetched navigation to dish 44 44 60 60
Checkout click to visible order summary 1,582 244 1,684 296
Direct order reload to visible summary 1,410 121 1,524 171
Order reload: summary-to-progress gap 24 1,192 25 1,288

Amplify is much better at static delivery

A statically generated dish page came back in 43 ms on Amplify, versus 288 ms through the direct Web Function endpoint, which seems like a big difference, but I'm putting that down to Amplify having a CloudFront distribution serving content close to the browser. I haven't isolated the underlying compute or proved anything about the relative speed of the runtimes. We've demonstrated that a CDN is useful, which hopefully isn't a surprise to anyone.

The repeat-browser tests showed the same pattern with roughly 16 ms for Amplify versus 96 ms for Web Functions on that static page.

The big difference seems to be when the pages are doing stuff. After checkout, Web Functions displayed the order summary and progress pages repeatedly quicker than Amplify.

The direct order reload follows the same pattern: the summary appeared far quicker in Web Functions, compared with Amplify. The gap between that summary and the slower progress component was around 1,192 ms on Web Functions and just 24 ms on Amplify. That really short gap from Amplify means the two bits of content arrived together, but only after the user had spent considerably longer waiting to see the first useful byte.

This seems pretty consistent with Web Functions streaming the response and Amplify buffering it in the deployments I tested, which lines up with AWS's documented lack of Next.js streaming support in Amplify.

My colleague thinks the main difference is likely the parallel request model in Web Functions which is effectively what Vercel implemented to make their hosted apps cheaper and more responsive - a Lambda that loads up and connects to some kind of routing layer that sends multiple requests to the same Lambda instance to get better concurrency use out of it. His suspicion is that Amplify still runs one Lambda instance per request, so you hit lots of cold starts as it loads separate resources, etc. via multiple requests.

Navigation to a prefetched dish page took 44 ms on both platforms being the browser rather than either hosting environment. When Next.js has already fetched what it needs, the click-to-navigation measurement is testing a different path from loading a page directly. In the repeat-browser tests, the dynamic homepage continued to show the same general advantage for Web Functions.

Can I finally ditch Amplify?

I'm more interested than I was before running the experiment, put it that way.

The nicest part is that the Web Function is just running the Next.js standalone server. It isn't trying to reinterpret the framework through a different hosting model. The build and deployment are easier, the Terraform describes what we're creating, and the Web Function revision points at a particular versioned artefact. Adding a CloudFront distribution is a few minutes' work and AWS supports using Web Functions as a CloudFront origin, including origin access control, so that's a fairly obvious path.

AWS regularly announces services that seem to solve a problem you didn't know you had and this feels like one that might solve a problem I've been dealing with for ages.

All the application code, Terraform and Playwright benchmarking harness are in the demo repository if you fancy taking it for a swim.

title: GraphRAG-LTM: A Layered Threat Modeling Framework for Attacks on Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19549v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) uses document-derived knowledge graphs to assemble evidence for large language model (LLM) answers. Its security depends on both the seed chunks retrieved for a query and the graph evidence assembled from them, yet attacks on this evidence path remain underexplored. We introduce GraphRAG-LTM, a Layered Threat Modeling framework that tests three nested levels of attacker access. BB Query uses ranking feedback to make query edits under a semantic-similarity constraint and demote relevant seed chunks. WB Query uses retriever gradients for the same objective. Graph-aware WB keeps the white-box adversarial query and deletes bridge triplets from the query-specific evidence graph, disrupting multi-hop evidence propagation through localized graph edits. Across datasets, retrievers, and LLM backbones, rank feedback alone reduces answer quality, gradient access strengthens query attacks, and bridge-triplet deletion further impairs supporting-fact retrieval. Further analyses show how seed retrieval and graph evidence jointly contribute to these failures.

title: DeltaStreamer: Towards Human-Like Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.19849v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change-aware memory with query-driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively.
  Project page: https://bbbbchan.github.io/DeltaStreamer/

title: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.19035v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality. Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.

title: I built a cross-platform Android emulator manager with Tauri 2 + Rust — no Android Studio required
description:
I got tired of three things at once: the Android emulator CLI is tedious, Android Studio is a multi-gigabyte install for just running AVDs, and every decent alternative is either closed-source or expensive. So I built Enmulator — a desktop app that manages Android Virtual Devices end to end, ships on Windows/macOS/Linux, and doesn't need Android Studio installed.

It's Tauri 2 on the backend (Rust, 13 modules), React 18 on the frontend, and it's GPLv3.

What it actually does

  • Create / start / stop / clone / delete AVDs, plus batch operations across multiple devices
  • 66 pre-loaded device profiles across 16 brands (Pixel, Samsung, Xiaomi, OnePlus, realme…)
  • Device identity spoofing: IMEI, operator, phone number, WiFi MAC, timezone, locale
  • Root: adb root for google_apis images, and Magisk via rootAVD for everything else
  • Per-device proxy, GPS mocking, screen recording, clipboard sync, live logcat, a split-panel file explorer
  • A headless REST API (Actix-web) so you can drive it from CI or a script

The whole point was to make emulator setup feel like a product, not a shell-script chore.

Why Tauri instead of Electron

A tool that spawns emulator processes shouldn't eat 300 MB of RAM on its own. Tauri uses the OS webview instead of bundling Chromium, so the installer is small and idle memory is low. The backend being Rust mattered more than I expected: adb calls are blocking Command invocations, and being able to move them off the main thread with plain std::thread — without async ceremony — kept the UI responsive for free.

The tradeoff is real too: the macOS/Windows/Linux build matrix means three toolchains and three sets of platform quirks (more on that below).

Architecture

The Rust side is a flat set of modules, each owning one concern:

  • sdk.rs — locate the Android SDK, adb, emulator, avdmanager binaries
  • avd_manager.rs — create/delete AVDs, write config.ini (resolution, DPI, hardware keyboard)
  • emulator.rs — process management + port allocation (each emulator gets a console port)
  • adb_bridge.rs — the adb shell / install / push / pull wrappers
  • fingerprint.rs — the identity-spoofing engine
  • bypass.rs — build.prop patching for detection bypass
  • extras.rs — GPS, clipboard, screen record, logcat streams
  • api_server.rs — the REST layer

The frontend is a few focused components: a create wizard, per-device cards, an identity panel, the file explorer, quick actions. Nothing clever — state lives in the backend, the UI just calls commands over Tauri's IPC.

The parts that were actually hard

Fingerprint spoofing is a moving target

The naive version is adb shell setprop with the IMEI/operator values. That works for some properties and silently fails for others — and "silently fails" is the worst outcome because the user thinks they're spoofed when they aren't.

The reality on modern Android:

  • ro.product.* (brand, model, manufacturer) are immutable — set at boot by the system image, setprop can't touch them.
  • IMEI/SIM fields (persist.radio.imei, etc.) stopped being settable via setprop around API 29.
  • The reliable route for read-only props is Magisk's resetprop, which patches the property store in memory.

So the identity engine is now Magisk-aware: if the device is rooted with Magisk, it uses resetprop for ro.product.* and ro.build.fingerprint; otherwise it falls back to setprop for the fields that still allow it. The app also reports which fields applied and which failed, instead of one big "success" that might be a lie.

Magisk integration without Android Studio

Rooting an emulator normally means patching the ramdisk. Enmulator bundles rootAVD, which does exactly that: it grabs ramdisk.img from the system image, patches it with Magisk, and pushes it back.

The gotcha I learned: the ramdisk is shared per system image, not per AVD. Root one device on a given image and every AVD using that image is rooted. That's worth documenting loud, because it surprises people.

Also adb root only works on google_apis (non-Play-Store) images — Play Store images reject it outright. So the app offers both paths and tells you which one applies to your image.

Windows wants to show you console windows

Every adb / emulator spawn on Windows popped a black console window. The fix is CREATE_NO_WINDOW (0x08000000) in the process creation flags — one line, but it has to wrap every command invocation, so it went into a shared sdk::new_command() helper used everywhere.

Windows also likes to prepend \\?\ to long paths, which broke resolving the rootAVD submodule. dunce::canonicalize fixed it by stripping the prefix.

Shipping three platforms from one repo

The release pipeline is a GitHub Actions matrix (ubuntu / windows / macos) that produces a .deb, .AppImage, .msi, and .dmg with stable filenames, then uploads them to the release. The thing that bit me: the default GITHUB_TOKEN can't update a release — it needs permissions: contents: write in the workflow. Took a failed run to learn that.

I also did a git history cleanup before open-sourcing: the repo's .git was 483 MB because old target/ and node_modules blobs were stuck in history. git filter-repo brought it to 6.7 MB. Same code, 72× smaller clone.

Honest limitations

  • ARM64 system images only run natively on Apple Silicon — x86_64 everywhere else.
  • The detection-bypass and fingerprint features are for testing on software you own/are authorized to test. There's a disclaimer in the README for a reason.
  • This is a solo project, so some edges (snapshot management, exotic device configs) are rougher than a team-built tool.

Try it

Repo: github.com/engnzdl/enmulator

Installers for macOS / Windows / Linux are on the releases page. If you poke at it and hit something, open an issue — and if it's useful, a star helps others find it.

Built with Tauri 2, Rust, and React. GPLv3.

title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
description:
arXiv:2610.19901v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task-specific adapters achieve a dataset-macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset-macro micro-F1 of 0.6286 for multi-label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset-macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset-macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report-generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task-specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision-language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26-Hexapus.

title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Diagnostic Test for LLM Chemical Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19906v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLMs have achieved strong performance on chemical prediction benchmarks. However, existing evaluation methods typically provide target entity identity information directly, making it difficult to determine whether model predictions arise from transferable structure-property reasoning capabilities or rely on target-related contextual information or memory retrieval. We propose the Identity-Blinded Reasoning Diagnostic framework to evaluate chemical prediction models when target entity identity information is hidden. In this framework, the target is no longer directly defined by its entity identity, but instead by a known source entity and an explicit structural edit operation. This setting preserves the information required to determine the target while reducing the opportunity for models to access target identity cues. We evaluate this framework across six tasks spanning odor prediction, molecular property prediction, retrosynthesis, and reaction yield prediction. The results show that models generally achieve better prediction performance when source and target entity properties are consistent. Providing explicit source entity labels further strengthens this dependence. Moreover, while keeping the target entity, structural change, and ground-truth label unchanged, replacing only the source entity label causes some model predictions to systematically shift toward the substituted source labels. These results indicate that high benchmark accuracy in chemical prediction tasks does not necessarily imply that LLMs possess reliable structure-property reasoning capabilities. Our diagnostic framework provides a controlled evaluation approach for testing whether models can genuinely update predictions according to entity changes. The framework can be extended to other AI for Science tasks, particularly those where targets can be defined through transformations of known entities.
