description:
TL;DR

  • In sustained 5,000 requests-per-second benchmarks, Go-based proxies introduce as little as 11 microseconds of processing overhead per request, whereas Python proxies typically add between 500 microseconds and several milliseconds.
  • Python proxies running on asyncio and Uvicorn encounter severe event loop latency and memory bloat under heavy server-sent events (SSE) streaming concurrency due to Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) contention and per-coroutine object allocations.
  • Bifrost, an open-source AI gateway written in Go, sustained 9.5 times higher throughput and 54 times lower tail latency (p99) than Python-based LiteLLM on identical hardware under saturated load.
  • While Python remains the standard for machine learning prototyping and model training, Go provides the concurrency primitives, memory efficiency, and predictable garbage collection necessary for production AI infrastructure.

Production AI systems routing thousands of requests per second often discover that the proxy sitting between client applications and upstream model providers introduces more latency instability than the models themselves. As teams scale autonomous agents, multi-tenant software platforms, and high-frequency inference pipelines, the programming language chosen for the intermediary routing layer dictates operating costs, tail latencies, and service reliability. Bifrost, a high-performance open-source AI gateway written in Go by Maxim AI, and LiteLLM, a popular Python-based proxy server, represent two divergent architectural philosophies for solving this problem. This analysis examines head-to-head benchmark results across both runtimes, evaluating how Go and Python handle concurrent connection spikes, streaming token delivery, and resource utilization.

Why Runtime Architecture Dictates LLM Proxy Performance

A high-throughput LLM proxy operates primarily as an intelligent network router that intercepts HTTP/2 requests, parses JSON payloads, enforces rate limits, evaluates caching layers, and streams server-sent events across long-lived TCP sockets. Unlike typical REST microservices that complete requests in 10 to 50 milliseconds, an LLM gateway holds open connections for seconds or minutes while upstream providers generate output tokens.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                          Client Application                             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                          HTTP POST /v1/chat/completions
                                     v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        High-Throughput LLM Proxy                        |
|                                                                         |
|  [Authentication & Virtual Keys] -> [Semantic Cache Lookup]             |
|  [Rate Limiting & Routing Rules] -> [Provider Selection & Failover]     |
|                                                                         |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | Concurrency Engine: Goroutines (Go) vs Asyncio Event Loop (Python) |  |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                          Upstream Inference Call
                                     v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|             Upstream Providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock)             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

When handling ten concurrent requests, the performance difference between Go and Python is negligible because upstream inference latency dominates total turnaround time. However, when traffic scales to thousands of concurrent requests across hundreds of internal teams, the runtime characteristics of the proxy become the primary bottleneck.

Under heavy concurrency, Python proxies must navigate the constraints of the CPython runtime, specifically the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) and single-threaded cooperative multitasking. Go, by contrast, compiles directly to native machine code and schedules lightweight execution units across all available CPU cores using an internal runtime scheduler. When a gateway must parse thousands of streaming chunks per second while simultaneously evaluating authentication keys and tracking token quotas, these architectural differences compound into measurable latency penalties.

Concurrency Models: Goroutines vs Python Asyncio

Go uses goroutines, which are user-space execution threads managed by the Go runtime rather than the host operating system. A newly allocated goroutine requires approximately 2 kilobytes of memory stack space, allowing a single binary to comfortably manage hundreds of thousands of concurrent routines simultaneously. The Go runtime scheduler uses an M:N model, mapping M goroutines onto N operating system threads distributed across available CPU hardware cores. When a goroutine initiates network input or output, the Go netpoller parks the goroutine and assigns the operating system thread to other active workloads without blocking.

// Representative Go gateway worker pattern
func handleRequest(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    ctx := r.Context()

    // Non-blocking routing and authentication
    targetProvider, err := router.SelectProvider(ctx, r.Header.Get("Authorization"))
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusTooManyRequests)
        return
    }

    // Forward request upstream using Go's optimized transport pool
    resp, err := targetProvider.RoundTrip(r)
    if err != nil {
        fallbackProvider.ExecuteFallback(w, r)
        return
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    // Stream chunks directly with minimal buffer allocation
    io.Copy(w, resp.Body)
}

Python web proxies depend on the asyncio framework and asynchronous server gateway interface (ASGI) web servers such as Uvicorn or Hypercorn. Python concurrency uses cooperative multitasking executed on a single system thread. The event loop maintains a queue of coroutines and advances each task whenever an await expression yields control during an I/O operation.

# Representative Python asyncio proxy handler
@app.post("/v1/chat/completions")
async def handle_request(request: Request):
    headers = dict(request.headers)
    body = await request.json()

    # Validation and routing logic execute on the event loop
    provider = await router.select_provider(headers.get("authorization"))

    # Upstream call yields execution back to the loop
    async def stream_generator():
        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            async with client.stream("POST", provider.url, json=body) as response:
                async for chunk in response.aiter_bytes():
                    yield chunk

    return StreamingResponse(stream_generator(), media_type="text/event-stream")

The fundamental limitation of Python's model in an LLM gateway is that coroutines yield control only at explicit I/O pause points. Any CPU-intensive operation performed by the gateway, such as JSON serialization, regular expression evaluation, cryptographic signature verification, or token counting, executes synchronously on the event loop thread. If parsing a large JSON payload takes 2 milliseconds of pure CPU execution, every other connection waiting in the event loop is stalled for those 2 milliseconds. Under sustained high throughput, these brief computational pauses cause task queue backups, resulting in connection timeouts and escalating tail latency.

Benchmark Methodology and Test Environment

To measure the real-world overhead introduced by each runtime architecture, benchmarks were structured to isolate proxy processing latency from external cloud variability. External model endpoints introduce jitter, rate limits, and network volatility that skew measurements. Consequently, the test topology substituted upstream providers with a deterministic mock server that replied with consistent token payloads and configurable delays.

The evaluation compared Bifrost, compiled with Go 1.24, against LiteLLM running on Python 3.12 with Uvicorn workers and uvloop enabled. Both proxies were deployed on dedicated AWS EC2 instances running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS within a private virtual private cloud (VPC). Benchmarks were executed across two separate compute profiles:

  1. t3.medium instance: 2 virtual CPUs, 4 gigabytes of memory, baseline network burst performance.
  2. t3.xlarge instance: 4 virtual CPUs, 16 gigabytes of memory, up to 5 Gbps network bandwidth.

Traffic generation was handled by distributed k6 client instances deployed on separate EC2 nodes within the same availability zone to minimize network transit variance. The load profile simulated real-world enterprise traffic patterns, ramping from 500 requests per second (RPS) to a sustained 5,000 RPS. Each request submitted an OpenAI-compatible payload requesting a streaming chat completion, with the mock backend returning a 10-chunk response simulating a total inference duration of 1.5 seconds.

Latency and Throughput Under Sustained Load

The performance metrics collected during sustained load testing highlight a significant divergence between compiled Go infrastructure and interpreted Python services. When traffic was applied at 5,000 requests per second, the gateway overhead, defined as the time added by the proxy exclusive of backend response time, was measured alongside tail latency and error rates.

Performance Metric LiteLLM (Python, t3.medium) Bifrost (Go, t3.medium) LiteLLM (Python, t3.xlarge) Bifrost (Go, t3.xlarge)
Max Sustained RPS 44.8 RPS 424.0 RPS 480.0 RPS 5,000.0 RPS
Success Rate @ Target Load 71.4% (degraded) 100.0% 88.2% (degraded) 100.0%
Gateway Added Overhead (Mean) ~500 µs to 7.5 ms 59 µs ~350 µs to 3.2 ms 11 µs
P90 Latency (Overall) 14.20 s 1.62 s 3.85 s 1.58 s
P99 Latency (Overall) 90.72 s 1.68 s 18.40 s 1.61 s
Average Queue Wait Time 820.00 ms 47.13 µs 145.00 ms 1.67 µs
Peak Resident Memory 372 MB 120 MB 1,480 MB 3,340 MB (configured pool)

On the t3.medium configuration under saturated load, the Python proxy experienced significant event loop contention. As incoming connection rates outpaced the event loop's ability to dispatch coroutines, the request queue backed up, causing the overall p99 latency to climb to 90.72 seconds before connections dropped with HTTP 504 gateway timeout errors. Bifrost on the same t3.medium hardware maintained a 100% success rate, preserving a p99 latency of 1.68 seconds (representing 1.5 seconds of simulated model generation plus only 180 milliseconds of total queueing and transport latency).

On the larger t3.xlarge system, Bifrost scaled smoothly to 5,000 requests per second. At this operating volume, published benchmarks document that Bifrost added only 11 microseconds of internal routing overhead per request. The average queue wait time dropped to 1.67 microseconds, while JSON marshaling took 26.80 microseconds. By contrast, the Python proxy on t3.xlarge hit an architectural throughput wall near 480 requests per second, requiring horizontal pod autoscaling across multiple container replicas to handle equivalent load.

Memory Footprint and Garbage Collection in Streaming Pipelines

In an LLM proxy, memory consumption is largely governed by how the runtime handles streaming response buffers. Server-sent events require the proxy to receive small string fragments from upstream providers, inspect or log them, and flush them immediately to downstream HTTP clients.

Python's memory management introduces high overhead during streaming operations. In CPython, every string fragment, dictionary, and HTTP chunk is allocated on the heap as a complete PyObject. A single 20-character text token wrapped in an SSE data frame generates multiple object allocations, each carrying internal reference counts and type descriptors. Furthermore, Python's memory allocator rarely releases heap memory back to the host operating system immediately; instead, it retains allocated arenas for future Python objects. Under thousands of concurrent streams, memory consumption climbs steadily, increasing pressure on the generational garbage collector. When cyclic garbage collection cycles trigger, they momentarily pause the interpreter thread, compounding event loop delays.

Go Runtime Memory Pipeline:
[Incoming Socket] ---> [Pre-allocated Buffer Pool] ---> [Zero-Copy Parser] ---> [Client Socket]
                                  ^                            |
                                  +----- sync.Pool Reuse ------+

Python Runtime Memory Pipeline:
[Incoming Socket] ---> [C-String] ---> [PyUnicode Object] ---> [PyDict Chunk] ---> [GC Tracked Heap]

Go manages streaming pipelines with significantly higher memory efficiency. The Go standard library and production frameworks allow developers to use memory pools (sync.Pool) to recycle byte buffers across independent requests. Rather than allocating new objects for incoming response chunks, Go reuses fixed-size byte slices, completely bypassing dynamic heap allocation for the steady-state data path.

As detailed in the Bifrost benchmarking documentation, Bifrost allows operators to configure explicit buffer and worker pool sizes to balance memory limits against maximum throughput. While Bifrost used 3,340 megabytes of memory on t3.xlarge during the 5,000 RPS benchmark, that allocation consisted of pre-allocated buffers specifically sized to handle 20,000 queued requests with zero runtime allocations. Under baseline operational conditions on t3.medium, its memory footprint remained at a compact 120 megabytes.

CPU Efficiency, Connection Pooling, and Worker Contention

Efficient network proxying requires extracting maximum throughput from every available CPU cycle. In multi-core server environments, Go and Python take opposing paths to hardware utilization.

Because CPython enforces the GIL, running a Python proxy across a multi-core machine requires spinning up multiple independent worker processes using process managers like Gunicorn. For example, a 4-vCPU instance typically runs 4 to 8 separate worker processes. While this strategy bypasses the GIL across processes, it introduces operational drawbacks:

  • Isolated Connection Pools: Each Python worker maintains its own distinct pool of HTTP/2 connections to upstream providers. Ten workers querying OpenAI cannot share keep-alive connections, resulting in duplicate TCP handshakes, redundant TLS negotiations, and higher connection overhead.
  • Process Memory Duplication: Each worker process loads its own copy of the Python interpreter, imported libraries, routing tables, and in-memory caches, multiplying baseline memory overhead.
  • Inter-Process State Synchronization: Tracking shared state across workers, such as global rate limits, virtual key quotas, or circuit breakers, requires an external caching layer like Redis. Accessing an external Redis store over local sockets introduces additional network round-trips for every incoming request. 
Multi-Process Python Model (Gunicorn / Uvicorn):
[Worker 1 (PID 101)] ---> [Isolated HTTP Pool] ---> Upstream Provider
[Worker 2 (PID 102)] ---> [Isolated HTTP Pool] ---> Upstream Provider
[Worker 3 (PID 103)] ---> [Isolated HTTP Pool] ---> Upstream Provider
(State shared only via external Redis / IPC)

Single-Process Go Model (Bifrost):
[Goroutine Pool] ===> [Shared HTTP/2 Connection Pool] ===> Upstream Provider
(State shared natively in-process via atomic primitives and mutexes)

Bifrost operates as a unified, multi-threaded binary. A single Go process manages connections across all available CPU cores. All incoming requests share a centralized HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 transport pool, maximizing socket reuse and minimizing upstream handshake latency. Internal state, including token bucket rate limits and quota tallies, is tracked in-process using atomic memory primitives and low-contention synchronization constructs, eliminating mandatory dependencies on external caching instances for single-node deployments.

Extending Gateway Control to the Endpoint

As organizations scale their AI infrastructure, governance challenges extend beyond centralized server deployments into local developer environments and endpoint devices. Beyond routing, Bifrost applies governance and security controls (virtual keys, budgets, guardrails, audit logs) centrally, and Bifrost Edge extends that same governance and security to AI traffic on employee machines, with endpoint enforcement on each device.

                                  +---------------------------------------+
                                  |     Bifrost AI Gateway (Go Core)      |
                                  |  - Centralized Control Plane          |
                                  |  - Policy Engine & Audit Logs         |
                                  |  - Virtual Keys & Budgets             |
                                  +---------------------------------------+
                                                      ^
                                                      | Enforces Unified Policies
                                                      | via Local Routing Agent
                                                      v
                                  +---------------------------------------+
                                  |       Bifrost Edge (Endpoint)         |
                                  |  - Desktop Apps (Claude, ChatGPT)     |
                                  |  - Coding Agents (Cursor, CLI tools)  |
                                  |  - Local MCP Server Discovery         |
                                  +---------------------------------------+

When platform teams deploy gateways solely as centralized cloud services, ungoverned AI usage often emerges on client laptops. Developers install desktop chat clients, run terminal coding agents, and connect local tools using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) without configuring proxy base URLs. Bifrost Edge, currently in alpha, operates as a lightweight endpoint agent that transparently routes desktop and CLI traffic through the central Bifrost policy engine. This combined architecture ensures that guardrails, data loss prevention rules, and spend limits apply consistently across cloud microservices, developer terminals, and desktop interfaces.

Feature Matrix: Go vs Python in Production Infrastructure

Choosing between Go and Python for an LLM gateway involves balancing runtime raw throughput against developer ecosystem familiarity. Python excels during initial experimentation, whereas Go dominates high-scale infrastructure deployments.

Capability / Attribute Python AI Proxies (e.g., LiteLLM) Go AI Gateways (e.g., Bifrost) Engineering Impact
Primary Concurrency Primitive Single-threaded asyncio event loop Multi-threaded M:N goroutine scheduler Go eliminates head-of-line blocking on CPU-bound operations.
Execution Format Interpreted bytecode (CPython VM) Statically linked native machine binary Go binaries launch instantly and deploy with zero runtime dependencies.
Per-Request Memory Overhead High (multiple heap-allocated PyObjects) Low (stack allocations, buffer pools) Go reduces memory consumption by 60% to 80% under sustained concurrency.
Multi-Core Scaling Requires multiple Gunicorn OS worker processes Scales natively within a single OS process Go shares connection pools and internal routing state across all cores.
Streaming Pipeline Efficiency Event loop context switching on every chunk Non-blocking zero-copy socket streaming Go maintains flat p99 tail latency during token generation.
Observability Overhead Tracing middleware adds CPU cycles to event loop Native OpenTelemetry and Prometheus exporters Go exports metrics concurrently without stalling the request path.
Ecosystem Extensibility Vast library of Python AI/ML packages Systems-level performance with Go/WASM plugins Python enables faster script prototyping; Go guarantees operational stability.

For organizations evaluating infrastructure investments, the architectural choice correlates with long-term cloud hosting bills. A proxy that handles 5,000 RPS on a single 4-vCPU Go instance requires dozens of scaled Python pods behind an external load balancer to achieve comparable throughput. The LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide provides an expanded framework for evaluating gateway capacity against organizational traffic projections.

Production Capabilities: Beyond Raw Proxying

While high-throughput network proxying is essential, an enterprise gateway must execute complex policy checks on every passing request. If security and governance rules introduce substantial latency, the benefits of a compiled runtime are quickly lost.

Bifrost implements a comprehensive suite of enterprise capabilities directly within its compiled Go core:

  • Drop-in SDK Replacement: Bifrost functions as a drop-in replacement for major AI development kits. Applications migrating from direct provider APIs or Python proxies adjust only their base URL parameters without rewriting application logic.
  • Dynamic Failover and Load Balancing: When upstream providers return rate-limit errors or experience service interruptions, Bifrost executes automatic fallbacks to secondary models or healthy API keys with zero application downtime.
  • Semantic Caching: To cut redundant inference costs, Bifrost provides native semantic caching, evaluating query intent in memory before routing requests upstream.
  • Hierarchical Governance: Security teams configure virtual keys that enforce granular spend budgets, rate limits, and access permissions across projects, departments, and external clients.
  • Model Context Protocol Support: As an enterprise MCP gateway, Bifrost coordinates autonomous tool calls, exposing centralized tools to AI models while managing authentication and filtering permissions.
  • Unified Observability: Comprehensive request logs, distributed OpenTelemetry traces, and native Prometheus metrics are exposed via Bifrost's built-in observability suite without degrading gateway throughput. 
// Example: Initializing the Bifrost Go core with custom routing and fallback policies
package main

import (
    "context"
    "log"
    "github.com/maximhq/bifrost/core"
    "github.com/maximhq/bifrost/core/providers"
)

func main() {
    gateway, err := bifrost.NewGateway(&bifrost.Config{
        Port: 8080,
        RoutingStrategy: bifrost.StrategyLowestLatency,
    })
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Failed to initialize Bifrost: %v", err)
    }

    // Register multi-provider fallback chain
    gateway.RegisterRoute("production-chat", &bifrost.RouteConfig{
        Primary:   providers.AnthropicClaude35Sonnet,
        Fallbacks: []providers.Provider{providers.OpenAIGpt4o, providers.BedrockLlama3},
        TimeoutMs: 2500,
    })

    log.Println("Bifrost gateway listening on :8080")
    gateway.ListenAndServe()
}

Teams migrating from Python-based infrastructure can review specific migration strategies on the Bifrost LiteLLM alternatives page, which details configuration translation and parity benchmarks.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does an LLM proxy need low latency when LLM responses take several seconds?

An LLM proxy handles token streaming across thousands of concurrent clients. If the proxy adds several milliseconds of overhead to every incoming token chunk, streaming jitter increases, client buffers stall, and server connection queues rapidly exhaust available memory. Low gateway latency preserves application responsiveness and prevents the proxy itself from becoming a single point of failure under unexpected traffic spikes.

Can Python's asyncio performance be fixed using multiple worker processes?

Running multiple worker processes via process managers such as Gunicorn allows Python to utilize multiple CPU cores, but it does not resolve per-process event loop bottlenecks. Each worker maintains its own isolated connection pool, multiplying memory consumption and preventing unified connection reuse. Furthermore, coordinating shared state across multiple Python workers requires external caches like Redis, which introduces additional network latency to every request.

When is a Python-based LLM proxy suitable for an engineering team?

Python proxies are suitable for early-stage prototyping, internal proof-of-concept deployments, and environments where total traffic remains below a few dozen requests per second. Teams with dedicated Python platform engineers often prefer Python proxies initially because they can inspect, debug, and patch routing logic directly using familiar scripting tools without needing to compile binaries.

How does Go prevent head-of-line blocking in streaming LLM responses?

Go uses an internal scheduler that multiplexes lightweight goroutines across multiple operating system threads. When a goroutine waits for the next token chunk over a network socket, the Go runtime automatically parks that routine and executes active workloads on the freed thread. This prevents CPU-bound tasks, such as JSON parsing or cryptographic operations, from delaying network packet processing for other active client streams.

What hardware is required to run a high-throughput Go LLM gateway?

A compiled Go gateway such as Bifrost operates comfortably on modest hardware. In published benchmarks, a standard AWS EC2 t3.xlarge instance (4 vCPUs and 16 GB RAM) sustained 5,000 requests per second with only 11 microseconds of internal gateway latency. Even a smaller t3.medium instance (2 vCPUs and 4 GB RAM) reliably handles hundreds of concurrent streaming requests without connection degradation.

How does Bifrost handle upstream provider rate limits?

Bifrost manages provider rate limits through intelligent load balancing, key pooling, and automated fallback rules. When an upstream provider returns an HTTP 429 status code or encounters temporary downtime, the gateway immediately reroutes the pending request to an alternative API key, model tier, or secondary cloud provider without returning an error to the calling client application.

Choosing the Right Infrastructure Foundation

Building scalable generative AI applications requires treating the routing and governance layer as critical production infrastructure rather than an afterthought. While Python remains an exceptional language for model experimentation, data science, and pipeline orchestration, its runtime constraints create significant hurdles when deployed in high-concurrency network proxies.

Go delivers the structural advantages required for modern AI workloads: true multi-core concurrency via goroutines, minimal memory footprints through native buffer pooling, and sub-millisecond request processing. Engineering teams evaluating high-throughput AI gateways can request a Bifrost demo to explore enterprise governance capabilities or review the source code on the Bifrost GitHub repository.

title: Go App Log Alerts: Compare Logging Tools for Silent Import Results
description:
App logging alerts should report a missing business result, so compare logging tools by the page they produce and the operational work left behind. At 02:20, the useful page says supplier import produced no catalog results; on-call can see store 17, the scheduled slot, the last successful completion, and the incident key. An alarm that merely says "log volume is low" leaves the responder to reconstruct the failure while inventory grows stale.

TL;DR: For scheduled e-commerce imports, choose Datadog, Better Stack, or Grafana Cloud when native log-query alerts and notification routing are requirements. Searchable logs plus a Go poller are defensible when the alert set is small and the team will own durable cursors, deduplication, and delivery. Attribute the whole path to each import: ingestion, queries, notification delivery, maintenance, false pages, and the downstream exposure of a missing catalog update. A low storage line item does not make an unreliable page inexpensive.

Infrai fits the narrower searchable-logs boundary. It ingests and searches logs, but its logging capability has no native threshold rule engine or phone, SMS, webhook, or email routing. A poller must provide that control plane, and an independent heartbeat monitor must cover a job that never starts.

How should I compare app logging tools with log alerts?

Start at the page, because it forces an operational definition of success. A scheduled import has not succeeded when a queue accepts work or when a download begins. It succeeds after the catalog write commits and the terminal event records a result.

For one scheduled slot, the responder needs a stable run key, tenant or store identifier, expected completion deadline, last successful result, terminal status, and result count. The incident key should be derived from the store and scheduled slot. Retries can then refer to one incident rather than opening several.

One page. One owner.

Nothing vague.

Keep secrets, payment data, and unnecessary customer fields out of these events. OWASP's logging guidance is a useful minimum for deciding which data should never enter the log pipeline. Cost attribution does not require stuffing a customer record into an alert; store_id, supplier_id, and run_key are enough dimensions for this decision model.

The alert threshold comes from the schedule and the import's observed completion envelope. A five-minute window has no meaning by itself. A small hourly price feed and a nightly catalog rebuild deserve different grace periods, even if both emit the same terminal event shape. Consider store 17: its supplier file is due at 02:00, its grace window closes at 02:15, and its alert key remains fixed even if the queue redelivers the import. A page at 02:20 should say which proof is missing. It should not make the responder compare a burst of retry logs by eye, guess which delivery is authoritative, and then discover that three notifications refer to one scheduled run. The stable key prevents that bookkeeping failure, while the terminal event keeps the threshold tied to a catalog result rather than incidental activity.

Trace backward from the page

At 02:20 the worker evaluates a closed grace window. It finds no successful terminal result for the expected run key, confirms that it has not already handed off this incident, and sends one notification. Work backward another step: the search result exists only because the importer emits its completion event after the catalog transaction commits.

There is an important split here. A started event proves that some scheduling path ran. A completed event with a result count proves that the business result appeared. If the process never starts, a log search sees nothing, and absence in a logging system cannot distinguish a missed schedule from a failed poller. Use a dead-man's-switch service such as Healthchecks for that heartbeat. Infrai has no synthetic or heartbeat monitoring, so it cannot supply this proof by itself.

Instrumentation should therefore produce two independent signals: a schedule check-in and a terminal business result. Progress logs remain useful during diagnosis, but they are a poor paging contract and add ingestion volume without proving completion.

Before binding the importer to a request shape, inspect the live capability contract. This complete Go program calls the public discovery surface with an explicit method, checks the status, and prints the documented method and path for log ingestion. It avoids inventing fields because the returned JSON Schema is the authority.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    req, err := http.NewRequest(
        http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/logs.ingest",
        nil,
    )
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
    if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    }

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s", resp.Status))
    }

    var c capability
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&c); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("%s %s available=%t schema_bytes=%d\n",
        c.Method, c.Path, c.Available, len(c.Params))
}

Generate the production request from the returned path and schema. Do not make up search filters: the discovery parameters for log search are undeclared. That is a real integration boundary, particularly for a polling design that depends on stable query semantics.

Put every cost on the run key

A useful cost model follows the same key as the incident. For each supplier import, account for log ingestion and retention, poll queries, notification delivery, engineering ownership, and the cost of acting on false positives. Then record downstream exposure separately: a missing result may leave stale availability or pricing in the storefront. Those consequences are workload-specific, so a vendor's per-unit rate cannot settle the choice.

The allocation rule can stay plain. Shared platform charges go to the store and import class using their telemetry volume; poller compute and notification traffic go to evaluated run keys; maintenance time goes to the alert path that caused it. Do not bury poller work in a general platform bucket. It is part of the effective bill for choosing storage and search without managed alerts.

Option How the page is produced Cost-attribution boundary Prefer it when
Datadog Native alerting on log queries Managed alert operation sits with platform usage The team requires ready-made log alerts and notification operations
Better Stack Native log-query alerting Poller ownership is removed from the workload ledger A smaller team wants logging and alerts in one managed path
Grafana Cloud Native alerting around its hosted observability stack Alert operations remain beside dashboards and telemetry Grafana is already the team's inspection and alert surface
Amazon CloudWatch AWS log ingestion with managed surrounding services Ingestion is visible, but downstream and labor costs still need allocation The imports and their operational ownership already live in AWS
Infrai plus a Go poller Periodic log search, durable state, then custom delivery Storage/search and custom alert labor must be charged separately A small alert set justifies owning the polling control plane

Datadog, Better Stack, and Grafana Cloud have the cleaner boundary when built-in log notifications are mandatory. That convenience removes custom reliability work; it does not establish a universal cost winner. CloudWatch is a useful AWS-heavy comparison, and its published per-GB ingestion fees show why volume belongs in the model, but those fees are still only one line of the operating bill.

My decision rule: choose the managed alert path when the cost of one missed or duplicate page exceeds the credible maintenance budget for the poller. Choose polling only when the number of policies is modest, the query contract is acceptable, and someone explicitly owns its state and delivery failures.

I recommend trying Infrai for the ingest-and-search portion when a team already expects to own a small Go alert worker and benefits from putting adjacent backend capabilities behind one credential and one bill. Its breadth is verified at 295 routes across 20 modules. One REST API covers those backend capabilities, and no SDK is required: the worker can use plain HTTP from any runtime instead of taking on a vendor library for this adapter. Adding another supported backend function therefore does not require another SDK, key rotation path, and invoice reconciliation process. In this e-commerce workflow, that reduces the integration and allocation work surrounding the poller rather than pretending the poller is free.

There is a second, different advantage. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. Public discovery returns full request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples; every documented capability has examples in ten languages. A maintainer can inspect the current Go contract before changing the adapter. That matters when alert reliability depends on request shape, and the plain REST API with no SDK to install removes a library lifecycle from the small polling worker instead of shifting that maintenance cost elsewhere.

The limitation stays visible. Infrai does not provide native log thresholds or notification routing, and it also lacks distributed trace queries and span trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Session Replay, per-user log deletion, bulk export, and subscriptions. A specialist is the better choice when any of those capabilities or managed paging is part of the acceptance criteria.

Make polling dull and idempotent

The poller needs durable state. Store the last evaluated schedule slot and an incident key. Evaluate only windows whose grace period has closed, hand off at most one incident for a run key, and advance the cursor after the receiver acknowledges delivery. If the process stops between delivery and cursor update, the receiver must deduplicate the same key.

Retries happen.

Plan for them.

This small Go policy is deliberately independent of undocumented vendor query parameters. The search adapter supplies observations; the policy decides whether a closed slot lacks a successful business result.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type run struct {
    key          string
    scheduledFor time.Time
    completedAt  *time.Time
    resultCount  int
}

func needsPage(now time.Time, grace time.Duration, r run) bool {
    if now.Before(r.scheduledFor.Add(grace)) {
        return false
    }
    return r.completedAt == nil || r.resultCount == 0
}

func main() {
    scheduled := time.Date(2026, 10, 9, 2, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    r := run{
        key:          "store-17:2026-10-09T02:00:00Z",
        scheduledFor: scheduled,
    }
    if needsPage(scheduled.Add(20*time.Minute), 15*time.Minute, r) {
        fmt.Printf("page key=%s reason=missing_import_result\n", r.key)
    }
}

Separate three outcomes in the worker: the query failed, the run remains inside its grace window, or the expected terminal result is absent. Only the third supports the catalog page. A query failure should consume a bounded retry budget and then page for the monitor itself; otherwise a broken monitor silently reports health.

This is also where a superficially inexpensive design accumulates cost. Durable cursors need storage and migration. Delivery needs backoff and deduplication. The worker needs its own health signal. Each item is manageable, but excluding them from the comparison guarantees a misleading result.

False positives are part of the bill

An aggressive grace window wakes someone for ordinary supplier latency. A loose window leaves stale catalog data visible longer. Neither cost appears cleanly in an ingestion quote.

Review grace periods by import class, and record acknowledgements, duplicates, and false positives against the run key. Change a threshold through the same review path as the schedule. With real completion observations, the team can adjust the window; before that, an arbitrary threshold converts uncertainty into pager noise.

The sound design ends with two proofs: the schedule checked in, and the import committed a terminal result. Managed logging platforms package more of the route from query to notification. Polling remains reasonable when its state, retries, ownership, and failure alarm are treated as production infrastructure. If that boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet and inspect the live contract before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
  • Datadog log monitors
  • Better Stack log-based alerts
  • Grafana alerting documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing

title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.

title: Three Things I Learned Building a Local-LLM Java Repair Tool
description:
I built a tool that uses AI to fix broken Java projects. One of the biggest lessons? You can't just trust what the AI gives you.

Over the past few days, I've been working on CompileLoop, a Java project that uses local LLMs to try and fix broken Maven builds.

The idea is pretty simple. You give it a broken Java project, it sends the build errors to a local code model, gets back a proposed fix, applies that fix in a temporary copy of the project, and runs the build again to see if it actually worked.

If the fix passes validation, you get a patch to review. Your original source code stays untouched.

I'm building this because I want to explore how far we can take AI-assisted software development without blindly trusting the AI to get everything right. I also wanted to build something that goes beyond just sending prompts to a model and hoping for the best.

While working on CompileLoop, I ran into a few interesting problems. Some were things I hadn't really thought about before, and others made me realise that getting an AI model to produce code is only one part of the problem.

Here are three things I learned along the way.

1. The AI can get the fix right and still get the details wrong

One of the first interesting problems I ran into was with unified diffs.

For anyone who hasn't worked with them before, a unified diff is basically a way of describing the changes between two versions of a file. Git uses this format to show changes, and tools can use it to apply patches.

In one of my benchmark cases, the Java compiler complained about a missing semicolon. The model correctly identified what needed to change and produced a diff that looked something like this:

--- a/src/main/java/bench/Adder.java
+++ b/src/main/java/bench/Adder.java
@@ -5,3 +5,3 @@
 public class Adder {
     public int add(int a, int b) {
-        return a + b
+        return a + b;
     }
 }

The actual fix was correct. The problem was that the model got the line counts in the diff header wrong.

A unified diff uses those counts to tell the patch tool how many lines to expect before and after the change. My original implementation rejected the patch if those counts didn't match.

So here I was, looking at a model that had identified the correct fix, but my tool was rejecting it because of a formatting detail.

It happened repeatedly.

Eventually, I realised I needed to handle this differently. Instead of making the model try again every time it got the counts wrong, I changed the patch-handling logic to recalculate those counts from the diff body, similar to what git apply --recount does.

The important part was that I wasn't relaxing the validation of the actual changes. I was correcting a part of the diff that could be calculated deterministically.

My biggest takeaway here is that not every problem needs to be solved by asking the AI to try again.

Sometimes, the better solution is to identify which parts of the output can be corrected safely by normal code.

2. Just because the AI says it fixed something doesn't mean it actually did

This one was interesting because it showed me how important it is to separate what a model says it did from what it actually changed.

I had a Java method declared to return an integer, but its implementation was returning a string:

public int add(int a, int b) {
    return "x";
}

The compiler correctly complained that a String couldn't be converted to an int.

The model returned a summary saying it would fix the method's return type to int. However, the method was already declared to return int.

What the model actually changed was the method body:

public int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

In this case, the diff was correct, but the explanation of the fix wasn't.

At first, this might seem like a small issue. The code was fixed, so why worry about the summary?

The problem is that if you build a tool around AI-generated output, you need to know which parts of that output you can actually trust.

A model can produce a correct patch and an incorrect explanation in the same response. If your tool relies on the explanation instead of examining the actual changes, you could end up making the wrong decision.

That's why CompileLoop validates the patch itself and checks the result by running the build. The model's summary is useful context, but it isn't proof that the fix worked.

For me, the lesson is simple: AI can suggest the solution, but the evidence needs to come from the actual code and the tests.

3. You need to know when to stop asking the AI for help

Another problem I encountered was the model repeatedly producing the same incorrect fix.

The first attempt would fail. CompileLoop would send the model feedback about the failure, and the model would return another patch.

Except the second patch was identical to the first.

Sometimes the third attempt was identical too.

Technically, the tool was doing what I had designed it to do. It had a maximum number of attempts, and it would eventually stop.

But when I looked at what was happening, I realised it was wasting time.

Each attempt involved another model call and another Maven build. If the model wasn't making progress, repeating the process wasn't giving me anything useful.

So I added two conditions to stop the repair loop early:

  • Repeated patches: If the model produces a patch that has already been attempted, the loop stops instead of applying the same failed solution again.
  • Unchanged errors: If two consecutive attempts fail with the same diagnostic information, the loop recognises that it isn't making progress.

For the patch fingerprints, I used Java's String.hashCode() rather than introducing a cryptographic hash. In this case, the fingerprint is only used to compare patches generated by the same process. A collision could cause the tool to stop early, but it wouldn't allow an unsafe patch through.

In my benchmark runs, these stop conditions were triggered 27 times across 60 runs. That included 21 cases where the tool detected a lack of progress and six where the AI provider was unavailable.

That showed me that stopping early wasn't just a theoretical improvement. It was something the tool was actually using.

The lesson I learned is that an AI repair loop needs more than a maximum attempt count. It needs a way to recognise when another attempt is unlikely to help.

Otherwise, you're just spending more time and computing resources asking the same question.

What happened when I tested different models?

I also wanted to see how different local code models performed rather than assuming that a model with a particular parameter count would automatically be better.

I created 20 small Maven projects, each containing one deliberate defect. These covered syntax errors, type mismatches, missing symbols, assertion failures, and bugs involving multiple files.

I tested three models, with three attempts per fixture.

Here are the results from my benchmark:

Model Successful repairs Repair rate Average latency
Qwen2.5-Coder 7B 9/20 45% 29 seconds
Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B 4/20 20% 12 seconds
DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B 1/20 5% 39 seconds

Qwen2.5-Coder 7B performed best overall in these tests.

What surprised me was the result for DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B. It often identified the correct fix in its summary, but its diffs contained context lines that didn't match the actual source files. CompileLoop rejected those patches because they couldn't be applied safely.

This was a useful reminder that choosing a model isn't just about its size or how good its explanations sound. It also matters whether it can produce output in the exact format your system requires.

I also noticed that Qwen2.5-Coder 7B performed better on the test-failure fixtures than on the compilation-failure fixtures. There were only five test fixtures, so I wouldn't make any big claims from that result, but it's an interesting observation worth investigating with a larger benchmark.

The benchmark isn't perfect, and the sample is small. That's exactly why I wanted the results to be available instead of only sharing the successful examples.

The fixtures, runner, and individual result files are committed to the repository. You can reproduce the benchmark by pulling the required Ollama models and running:

bash benchmarks/run.sh

What I actually enjoyed building

Something I've realised while working on CompileLoop is that the AI integration is only one part of the engineering.

A lot of the work is about making sure everything around the model behaves properly.

For example, I had to build:

  • A process runner that executes Maven, handles its output without deadlocking, enforces timeouts, and terminates the process tree when necessary.
  • A parser that turns Maven's output into structured compilation errors and test failures.
  • A patch validator that rejects dangerous or unsupported changes, including path traversal, symlink escapes, and unexpected file operations.
  • A temporary workspace where patches can be applied and tested without modifying the original project.
  • A repair engine that records attempts, checks whether fixes work, and stops when it detects that progress has stalled.

I also wrote tests around these components, including tests that use a fake Ollama server and scripted model responses. That means the test suite can run without downloading a local model.

The project currently has 233 tests, with CI running on Ubuntu and Windows.

These are the parts that make the difference between a simple AI coding experiment and a tool that attempts to handle failures in a controlled way.

There are still things I want to improve. Regression detection is one of them, because fixing one failing test shouldn't mean accidentally breaking another. I also want to introduce stronger isolation for build execution and eventually support other languages beyond Java and Maven.

CompileLoop currently uses a temporary copy to protect the original source tree, but that isn't a security sandbox. Build scripts can execute arbitrary commands, so proper container isolation is still an important next step.

I've documented these limitations rather than pretending the project is more complete than it is.

Building with AI is still engineering

I used Claude during development for architecture discussions, reviewing code, and working through problems when I wasn't sure which approach made the most sense.

But using AI to help build a project doesn't remove the responsibility of understanding what you're building.

I still needed to test the implementation, investigate failures, compare different approaches, and decide which trade-offs were appropriate.

For example, I needed to understand why recalculating diff counts was safe, why the patch itself mattered more than the model's summary, and why stopping repeated attempts was better than blindly continuing.

Those decisions matter because I need to be able to explain and defend them, not just get the code to compile.

I'm still learning as a software engineer, and that's part of why I enjoy projects like this. They give me an opportunity to work through problems that go beyond implementing a feature and to understand how the different parts of a system fit together.

I also think this is one of the more interesting areas of AI-assisted development: not just getting models to write code, but building systems around them that can verify their work and handle their mistakes.

That's ultimately what I want CompileLoop to explore.

The model proposes a fix. The tool checks it. The developer reviews the result.

And if the model keeps getting it wrong, the tool should know when to stop.

Try CompileLoop

The source code, benchmark fixtures, and results are available on GitHub:

github.com/LambdaJedi/compileloop

You can build the project with Maven and run it using a local Ollama model:

git clone https://github.com/LambdaJedi/compileloop.git
cd compileloop

mvn -B -DskipTests package

ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b

java -jar target/compileloop-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar repair \
  examples/broken-compilation-project \
  --model qwen2.5-coder:7b

If you're working on local LLMs, Java tooling, or AI-assisted software development, I'd be interested to hear what you've been building and what problems you've run into.

I'm still developing CompileLoop, so feedback and ideas for improving the approach are welcome.

title: Do Syntax Heads Influence Model Behavior?
description:
arXiv:2610.19231v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformer language models develop attention heads that specialize in syntactic relations, for example, attending from verbs to their subjects. Do these heads play a causal role in the model's syntactic predictions? Evidence for such a role is mixed to negative: even when we force these heads to attend to a distractor noun other than the subject, the model's syntactic predictions are still more consistent with the subject than with the distractor. Interventions on specialized syntax heads had a significantly stronger effect on syntactic predictions than interventions on random heads, but only in one of the two measures we propose.

title: Team-wide provider allowlist on AI Gateway
description:
AI Gateway now supports a team-wide provider allowlist. Teams can restrict which providers can serve requests, so traffic only routes to approved providers. The allowlist applies to every request through AI Gateway, including Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) traffic.

Regulated teams typically vet AI providers across multiple dimensions with security and legal sign-off, ending up with a vendor set that reflects the specific requirements of their org. The allowlist turns that approved-vendor list into a routing guarantee:

  • Enforcement happens at the gateway level, not at the request level. A developer on the team cannot route traffic to a provider the org hasn't approved.

  • This restriction also applies to coding agents. Even if an agent omits or modifies request-level provider filters, AI Gateway still blocks unapproved providers.

  • Only team owners can modify the provider allowlist, keeping control centralized and auditable.

  • New providers are disabled by default once the allowlist is on, so the approved set doesn't silently expand when AI Gateway integrates a new vendor.

How to configure

Toggle on Provider Allowlist in the AI Gateway Settings tab. All current providers are allowed by default, so existing traffic is unaffected. Disable any providers your team shouldn't use.

The allowlist filters by provider, not by model. AI Gateway falls back to other allowed providers for the same model if the initial provider fails. The allowlist also functions as an and with other restrictions applied to the team, like Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or request-level filtering.

For example, if a team has disabled DeepSeek in their allowlist and a request pins routing to only the DeepSeek provider:

Since DeepSeek is not in the allowlist, AI Gateway rejects the request.

Provider Allowlist works across every API format supported by AI Gateway, including AI SDK, OpenAI Chat Completions API, and Anthropic Messages API.

Read the provider allowlist documentation for more information. For other account-level security and compliance functionality, check the Zero Data Retention and Disallow Prompt Training documentation.

title: PostgreSQL 19 RC 1 Released!
description:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group announces that the first release candidate of PostgreSQL 19 is now available for download. As a release candidate, PostgreSQL 19 RC 1 will be mostly identical to the initial release of PostgreSQL 19, though some more fixes may be applied prior to the general availability of PostgreSQL 19.

The next scheduled update release for supported versions of PostgreSQL, on November 12, 2026, will include a large number of fixes. Because of this, the release team decided to include these fixes in PostgreSQL 19 before its general availability. This means a second release candidate, PostgreSQL 19 RC 2, will be available on the same day as the update release.

The planned date for the general availability of PostgreSQL 19 is November 19, 2026. Please see the "Release Schedule" section for more details.

Upgrading to PostgreSQL 19 RC 1

To upgrade to PostgreSQL 19 RC 1 from earlier versions of PostgreSQL, you will need to use a major version upgrade strategy, e.g. pg_upgrade or pg_dump / pg_restore. For more information, please visit the documentation section on upgrading:

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/19/upgrading.html

Changes Since 19 Beta 4

Several bug fixes were applied to PostgreSQL 19 during the Beta 4 period. These include:

  • Several fixes for REPACK (CONCURRENTLY).
  • Several fixes for pg_plan_advice.
  • Several fixes for new query planner optimizations that rely on whether an expression can be NULL.
  • Several fixes for the automatic enablement of logical replication when wal_level is set to replica.
  • Fix postgres_fdw statistics import to run as the owner of the foreign table instead of the user running ANALYZE.
  • Several fixes for parallel autovacuum.
  • Fix COPY (query) TO ... (FORMAT json) to use the query's column names, including aliases, as the JSON keys instead of the table's column names.

For a detailed list of fixes, please visit the open items page.

Release Schedule

This is the first release candidate for PostgreSQL 19. The release team plans to issue a second release candidate, PostgreSQL 19 RC 2, on November 12, 2026. Unless an issue is discovered that requires a delay or an additional release candidate, PostgreSQL 19 should be made generally available on November 19, 2026.

For further information please see the Beta Testing page.

title: Mastering API Integrations: A Deep Dive with Max Estates
description:
Introduction

In today's interconnected digital landscape, the ability to seamlessly integrate various services and data sources is paramount. APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) serve as the backbone of this connectivity, allowing different software systems to communicate and exchange information. This article will explore the intricacies of API integration, using the real-world example of maxestates.in to illustrate key concepts and best practices. We'll delve into the technical challenges, architectural considerations, and the benefits of robust API integration strategies.

Technical Insights: Building Bridges with APIs

API integration is not merely about making requests and receiving responses; it's about building reliable, scalable, and maintainable connections between disparate systems. For a platform like maxestates.in, which likely deals with real estate listings, property data, and user interactions, integrating with external services can unlock significant value. Consider these common integration scenarios:

Data Synchronization

Maintaining up-to-date property information is critical. This might involve integrating with multiple Multiple Listing Services (MLS) or other data providers. The process typically involves:

  • RESTful APIs: Most modern APIs utilize REST (Representational State Transfer) principles, relying on standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and JSON for data exchange. Understanding these principles is fundamental.
  • Data Mapping: Ensuring that data fields from the source API correctly map to the corresponding fields in your system is crucial. This requires careful analysis of both API schemas.
  • Rate Limiting and Error Handling: External APIs often have rate limits to prevent abuse. Implementing strategies to handle these limits, such as exponential backoff and robust error logging, is essential for preventing service disruptions.

Third-Party Service Integration

Integrating with services like payment gateways, mapping providers (e.g., Google Maps API), or communication platforms (e.g., Twilio for SMS notifications) enhances user experience and operational efficiency. For instance, maxestates.in might integrate with a mapping API to display property locations visually. This involves:

  • Authentication and Authorization: Securely authenticating with third-party services using API keys, OAuth, or other methods is non-negotiable. Proper management of credentials prevents unauthorized access.
  • SDKs and Libraries: Many services provide Software Development Kits (SDKs) or client libraries that simplify the integration process, abstracting away much of the low-level HTTP communication.

Architectural Patterns for Integration

When building complex integration systems, adopting specific architectural patterns can lead to more maintainable and scalable solutions:

  • API Gateway: An API Gateway acts as a single entry point for all client requests, routing them to the appropriate backend services. This can simplify client-side logic and provide centralized cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and logging.
  • Event-Driven Architecture: For scenarios requiring real-time updates or decoupling of services, an event-driven approach using message queues (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka) can be highly effective. When a property listing is updated on maxestates.in, an event can be published, triggering other services to react accordingly.

Conclusion

Effective API integration is a cornerstone of modern software development, enabling platforms like maxestates.in to offer rich functionalities and connect with a broader ecosystem. By understanding REST principles, implementing robust error handling and security measures, and choosing appropriate architectural patterns, developers can build resilient and scalable integration solutions that drive business value and enhance user experiences.

title: Learning after Execution with Action-Specific Credit
description:
arXiv:2610.14573v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Execution is often used as terminal feedback: it scores a generated program, but the resulting state is not used for another learning action. Learning after execution instead uses the execution result as an intermediate state that supports an additional learning interaction for the same policy. This creates a credit-assignment problem because the two actions share the same final objective but play different roles in the trajectory. Accordingly, action-specific credit assigns the initial action credit from the final trajectory outcome and the corrective action credit for improvement over the intermediate state. Image-to-TikZ serves as an executable visual testbed for this setting. On 945 held-out examples, learning after execution strengthens the shared policy under single-call inference and also produces a post-execution corrective capability. Single-call render success reaches 92.70\%, compared with 88.25\% for continued single-stage GRPO after the same number of additional training iterations. This corrective capability is not reproduced by continued single-stage training and depends on the intermediate state. Alternative credit definitions also induce different group-relative preferences over the same trajectories. Together, these results suggest that executable tasks contain useful learning structure beyond a terminal reward. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyufengcn/Learning-after-Execution.

title: UsersTable — the dumb component I copy into every admin panel
description:
Every admin panel I've ever built has a users table. Or a products table. Or an orders table. They're all the same shape: rows of records, a couple of status pills, edit and delete actions on the right. And every time, there's a temptation to build the clever version — sorting, filtering, pagination, inline editing — before the panel even works.

In my starter kit, the users table is deliberately dumb. Here's the entire contract:

export default function UsersTable({ users, onEdit, onDelete }) {

Three props. Data in, callbacks out. The component fetches nothing, authenticates nothing, routes nowhere. It renders a table with name, email, a role pill (indigo for admin, gray for everyone else), a formatted creation date, and Edit/Delete buttons that call the callbacks with the user object.

That's it. And that restraint is the feature.

Because the component knows nothing about where the data comes from, the parent page owns all the interesting decisions: how users are fetched, what the edit modal looks like, what happens after a delete (refetch? optimistic removal? confirmation dialog?). I can reuse this exact component in a demo build that runs against an in-memory mock API — the kit has a demoMock seam for exactly that — and in production against the real Laravel API, without changing a line of it. Props in, actions out. The component doesn't care.

This is also how I keep admin features cheap to add later. When a client asks for a products table next month, I don't build a new abstraction; I copy this file, change the columns, and wire new callbacks. Ninety percent of the code is identical. People call this boring. Boring is what lets me ship an admin panel in an afternoon.

A few small details I do keep in the "dumb" version: overflow-x-auto on the wrapper so the table scrolls horizontally on mobile instead of breaking the layout; whitespace-nowrap on cells so dates don't wrap weirdly; hover:bg-gray-50 on rows because affordance matters even in internal tools. And the role pill — a tiny inline conditional — because the person staring at this table is an admin, and the fastest thing their eyes need is "who here is an admin."

The lesson I keep re-learning: the smartest component in your admin panel is the one that knows the least. Push the knowledge up to the page, keep the table stupid, and you'll thank yourself on every project after this one.

The full admin loop — this table, the Users page that drives it, the API behind it, and the tests proving it — ships in my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit, $19 one-time. The admin panel is done; go build the product.

title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.19427v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.

title: BFHD: Bidirectional Feature Harmonization Decomposition for Heterogeneous Clinical Assessments
description:
arXiv:2610.19352v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical assessments are often collected using heterogeneous assessment systems across centers and time, leading to records that mix different but related sets of measurements. This motivates harmonization beyond total-score linking. We formulate clinical harmonization at the measurement level as a bidirectional recoverability problem: given paired observations from two assessment systems, the goal is to identify which measurements can be reliably translated in both directions within an application-defined tolerance, while separating non-translatable components. We propose Bidirectional Feature Harmonization Decomposition (BFHD), a feasibility-driven framework that enforces bidirectionally coupled translation and uses feature-wise output gating to produce an explicit decomposition in the original measurement space. Experiments on synthetic data and real clinical assessment pairs show that BFHD achieves broader feasible harmonization coverage and improved subset stability compared to baselines.

title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.18880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine-learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single-gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output-based and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow. The code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/OOD.

published_at: "2026-12-28T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [systemdesign, database, scalability, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of system design architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Sharding Keys: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Range-Based Vs Hash-Based Sharding: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Cross-Shard Joins And Distributed Transactions: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Consistent Hashing: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: System design Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Sharding keys, range-based vs hash-based sharding, cross-shard joins and distributed transactions, consistent hashing, and rebalancing shards."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.
