title: SQL Secrets: Crafting Lightning‑Fast Queries in 2024
description:
Introduction

SQL has been the lingua franca of relational data for half a century, yet many developers still write queries that crawl like a snail on a hot day. In 2024 the fundamentals haven’t changed, but the ecosystem - cloud‑native warehouses, modern ORMs, and sophisticated execution engines - offers new levers to squeeze performance out of even the most stubborn statements. This post walks you through a practical toolkit for turning “just works” SQL into “blazing fast” SQL, with concrete examples you can copy‑paste into PostgreSQL, MySQL, or any ANSI‑compatible engine.

1. Start With the Right Schema

Performance begins at the table definition stage. Choose data types that reflect reality; a BIGINT for a flag field is wasteful.

-- Bad: storing a boolean as an integer
CREATE TABLE users (
    id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    is_active   INT NOT NULL   -- 0/1
);

-- Good: proper boolean and compact primary key
CREATE TABLE users (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    is_active   BOOLEAN NOT NULL
);

Why it matters: Smaller rows mean more pages fit in memory, reducing I/O and cache pressure.

1.1 Normalize... but Don’t Over‑Normalize

Normalization eliminates redundancy, but every extra join adds CPU cycles. A common sweet spot is Third Normal Form (3NF) for transactional systems, and Denormalized aggregates for reporting.

-- Normalized: orders reference customers
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days';

If the query is run thousands of times per second, a materialized view or a pre‑joined “wide” table can be a win.

2. Indexing - Your First Speed Boost

An index is a sorted copy of the column(s) you care about. The right index can turn a full‑table scan into an index‑only scan.

2.1 Single‑Column Index 

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders (created_at);

Now the previous query can locate the relevant rows without touching every page.

2.2 Composite (Multi‑Column) Index

When a query filters on multiple columns, a composite index respects the column order.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status 
    ON orders (customer_id, status);

Tip: The most selective column should go first. If status has only a few distinct values, place customer_id ahead of it.

2.3 Covering Index (Include Columns)

PostgreSQL (10+) lets you add non‑key columns to an index for index‑only scans.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cover 
    ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total, created_at);

Now the planner can satisfy the SELECT without reading the heap table.

3. Analyze Your Queries with EXPLAIN

Never guess why a query is slow; let the engine tell you.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2024-01-01';

The output shows:

  • Seq Scan vs Index Scan
  • Cost (estimated) vs Actual time
  • Rows Removed by Filter - a sign of poor selectivity.

If you see a Seq Scan on a large table, it’s a red flag that an index is missing or not being used.

4. Query Refactoring Patterns

4.1 Use EXISTS Instead of IN for Sub‑Queries 

-- Slow: IN with sub‑query
SELECT *
FROM products p
WHERE p.category_id IN (SELECT id FROM categories WHERE is_active = true);

-- Faster: EXISTS
SELECT *
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM categories c
    WHERE c.id = p.category_id AND c.is_active = true
);

EXISTS stops at the first match, while IN may materialize the sub‑query result set.

4.2 Leverage Common Table Expressions (CTEs) Wisely

CTEs improve readability, but they can act as optimization fences in older PostgreSQL versions (pre‑12). Use inline CTEs (WITH ... SELECT ...) when you need temporary result sets, but remember they may be materialized.

-- Inline CTE (materialization avoided in PG 12+)
WITH recent_orders AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
)
SELECT ro.id, ro.total, c.name
FROM recent_orders ro
JOIN customers c ON ro.customer_id = c.id;

If you notice a performance dip, try rewriting the CTE as a sub‑query.

4.3 Window Functions for Ranking & Aggregates

Window functions let you compute running totals, rankings, or percentiles without extra joins.

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    total,
    SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01';

They’re executed after the WHERE clause, so they operate on a reduced data set.

5. Parameterized Queries & Prepared Statements

Hard‑coding literals prevents the planner from reusing execution plans. Use placeholders ($1, ?) and let the driver prepare the statement.

-- PostgreSQL example
PREPARE recent_orders(date) AS
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= $1;

EXECUTE recent_orders('2024-04-01');

Prepared statements reduce parse/plan time and protect against SQL injection.

6. Partitioning for Massive Tables

When a table grows beyond tens of millions of rows, partitioning can dramatically cut scan time.

-- Range partitioning by month (PostgreSQL syntax)
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    total       NUMERIC(12,2),
    created_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_01 PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_02 PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');

Queries that filter on created_at automatically prune irrelevant partitions, turning a scan of 100 M rows into a scan of a single month’s slice.

7. Monitoring & Automation

  • pg_stat_statements (PostgreSQL) or performance_schema (MySQL) captures query frequency and latency.
  • Set up alerts for any query whose average execution time exceeds a threshold (e.g., 200 ms).
  • Automate index recreation during low‑traffic windows if you use BRIN or partial indexes that need refresh.

8. The Cloud Factor

Modern data warehouses like Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift push computation to the cloud. The same SQL principles apply, but you also need to watch:

  • Concurrency scaling - avoid “spilling” to disk by limiting result set size.
  • Cluster keys (Redshift) - analogous to composite indexes.
  • Result caching - repeated identical queries can be served from cache at zero cost.

Conclusion

SQL performance isn’t magic; it’s a disciplined combination of schema design, indexing, query rewriting, and vigilant monitoring. By applying the patterns above you’ll see measurable latency reductions, lower CPU usage, and happier users. Remember: the best query is the one you never have to run because the data you need is already stored in the right shape.

Recommended Tools

  • For a sleek, cross‑platform GUI that makes index inspection a breeze, try DataGrip by JetBrains - it’s packed with visual EXPLAIN plans and smart code completion.
  • If you need a managed, auto‑scaling PostgreSQL instance, ElephantSQL offers one‑click provisioning and built‑in monitoring dashboards, perfect for dev‑ops teams focused on performance.

Happy querying!

title: Stop Hand-Writing a Hundred Characterization Tests: Shrink a Recorded Corpus Instead
description:
Characterization suites usually die of bloat, not of missing cases. Hand-written tests guess at the input space and pin behavior nobody calls. Record real calls at the seam, shrink them with coverage, then extract. That order is the whole article.

This is a corpus budget, not a coverage target. You want the fewest fixtures that still reach every line you are about to move. Everything else is documentary dead weight.

Why the hand-written pass fails

You sit in front of an unfamiliar module and invent inputs. Each invented input encodes your assumptions about the domain. Those assumptions are exactly what a refactor must not change, and exactly why the suite can feel safe while missing production shapes.

The result is a suite with ninety cases and three real ones. Maintenance cost lands on whoever inherits the branch. The suite decays, and the refactor happens anyway.

Recording inverts the direction. Production tells you which inputs exist today. Coverage tells you which subset of them is worth freezing.

Step 1 - Record at the seam

Wrap the function you plan to extract. Log arguments and results in a canonical form.

# recorder.py - illustrative harness; adapt names, then run it locally
import json, functools, pathlib, hashlib

CORPUS = pathlib.Path("corpus/calls.jsonl")

def canonical(obj):
    return json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"))

def snapshot(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        call = {"args": [canonical(a) for a in args],
                "kwargs": {k: canonical(v) for k, v in sorted(kwargs.items())}}
        result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
        payload = canonical(call) + canonical(result)
        call["sha256"] = hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()
        with CORPUS.open("a") as fh:
            fh.write(json.dumps(call) + "\n")
        return result
    return wrapper

Three rules keep the corpus usable. Sort keys, strip timestamps, never log object ids or memory addresses. An unstable corpus turns into a flaky suite within a week.

Redact personal fields at write time. Recording is the last moment where you still control the data.

Step 2 - Score each call by lines reached

You do not need a coverage service to rank cases. The standard library does this.

# score.py - line reach per recorded call
import trace, sys

def lines_touched(target_file, fn, args):
    tracer = trace.Trace(count=1, trace=0, ignoredirs=[sys.prefix, sys.exec_prefix])
    tracer.runfunc(fn, *args)
    return {lineno for (filename, lineno) in tracer.results().counts
            if filename == target_file}

Replay the corpus once and write a small index. Case id maps to a line set and a result hash.

python -m recorder replay corpus/calls.jsonl > corpus/index.json

Now you can answer the only question that matters. Which recorded calls reach lines that nothing else reaches?

Step 3 - Shrink with greedy set cover

Coverage selection is set cover. It is NP-hard in theory and trivial in practice. Greedy lands within a small constant factor in seconds.

# shrink.py - greedy cover over line sets
def shrink(index, universe):
    remaining = list(index.items())
    chosen, covered = [], set()
    while covered != universe and remaining:
        cid, lines = max(remaining, key=lambda kv: len(kv[1] - covered))
        gain = lines - covered
        if not gain:
            break
        chosen.append(cid)
        covered |= lines
        remaining = [(k, v) for k, v in remaining if k != cid]
    return chosen, covered

Two guards matter more than the algorithm. Keep every case that raises an exception. Keep a hand-written edge list as well: empty string, None, non-ASCII text, and the largest value your logs ever showed.

Greedy minimizes line reach only. It is blind to correlated values. Rounding and money math need extra care, which I cover below.

Step 4 - Freeze the survivors as bytes

Fixtures are golden files. One canonical JSON in, one canonical JSON out, plus a hash next to it.

def fixture(case_id, fn, args):
    out = canonical(fn(*args))
    path = pathlib.Path("tests/fixtures") / f"{case_id}.json"
    path.write_text(out, encoding="utf-8")
    path.with_suffix(".sha256").write_text(
        hashlib.sha256(out.encode()).hexdigest())

Byte comparison is the point. Rounding, ordering, and whitespace all surface as diffs instead of silent drift. Run the frozen suite before you touch anything.

pytest tests/characterization -q

Step 5 - Make the smallest safe change

Extract one function. Keep the original public name as an alias at the old import path. Do not rename parameters, reorder arguments, or fix the naming you dislike. Those are separate commits with separate evidence.

# before: billing/invoice.py holds build_totals()
# after
from billing.totals import build_totals  # noqa: F401  (alias keeps call sites stable)

Re-run the frozen suite. Any byte diff is a behavior change, intended or not. Fix the extraction, not the fixture, unless you can write down why the new bytes are correct.

Step 6 - Watch for the line-number trap

Here is the failure that bites people who like this method. Coverage-based selection is valid only for the pre-refactor module. After the move, line numbers shift, so re-running the selection picks a different corpus and a different story.

Never re-select coverage from the refactored module to validate the refactor. Validate with bytes. Coverage chooses the corpus once, at the start.

Add one more alarm. Log when production reaches a line your extracted module never saw during replay. New reachable code after a supposedly pure move means the extraction changed control flow.

Decision table

Situation Record and shrink Hand-write
Large input space, real traffic Yes Too slow to guess
Under about 15 branches Overkill Yes
Money, tax, rounding Yes, plus hand-written edge values Those values still needed
Sensitive payloads Redact at record time Prefer synthetic data
Path you cannot replay offline No Yes
One-line rename Not worth it Yes

Limitations and who should skip this

Recording cannot capture inputs production never sends. It inherits every blind spot of current traffic.

Coverage minimization is blind to value correlation. Two branches may need values that must vary together, and the shrinker will happily keep only one of them.

Exception paths are usually under-recorded. Offline batch jobs and rare error branches still need hand-written cases.

Corpora carry personal data. If you cannot redact reliably, do not record at all.

Skip the whole approach when the target function is small, when traffic is thin, or when a clean rewrite with fresh tests is cheaper than preserving behavior.

Where free tooling fits

The mechanical parts here are boring, and boredom is where free tiers help. I used MonkeyCode's free model access to draft the recorder and shrinker harness, then to triage fixture diffs into "intended" and "suspicious" piles. Its free server option ran long replay sweeps over the recorded corpus while my laptop stayed on code review.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Availability and limits change, so check the current terms before you plan around them. Treat any free tier as a convenience, never as the evidence behind a refactor.

Closing checklist

  1. Record at one seam for a day.
  2. Score every call by lines reached.
  3. Shrink with greedy set cover plus a hand-written edge list.
  4. Freeze survivors as canonical bytes and hashes.
  5. Move one function. Keep call sites stable.
  6. Verify by byte diff, never by fresh coverage.
  7. Alarm on any line production reaches that replay never did.

The suite you keep should be small enough to read and strong enough to argue with. Spend that budget on the code you are actually moving, not on the size of your test folder.

title: Building Custom AI Agents with JavaScript, React, and Ext JS
description:
AI-powered development tools are evolving beyond code completion and conversational assistance. Modern AI agents can be designed to understand project context, interact with external tools, retrieve relevant resources, and coordinate multi-step workflows.

For JavaScript developers, this creates an opportunity to build custom AI-powered experiences directly into existing development environments.

By combining JavaScript, React, agent communication protocols, and reusable UI components, developers can create interfaces that make AI workflows easier to monitor, understand, and control.
This article explores the architecture behind custom AI agents and how React and Ext JS can contribute to the user experience.

  1. What Is a Custom AI Agent?

A traditional AI assistant typically responds to a prompt with generated text or code. An AI agent can be designed to go further by coordinating multiple actions toward a defined objective.
Depending on its implementation and permissions, an agent might:

  1. Inspect project files and documentation.
  2. Retrieve information from external tools.
  3. Help developers investigate errors.
  4. Coordinate multi-step coding tasks.
  5. Display execution progress and diagnostic results.
  6. Support repeatable engineering workflows.

These capabilities depend on the agent's model, available tools, context, permissions, and execution architecture. They should not be assumed to work automatically simply because an application uses an LLM.

  1. Why JavaScript and React Are Useful JavaScript is already widely used for web applications and developer tooling. React provides a component-based approach to creating interactive interfaces. Together, they can provide a foundation for building an AI agent interface that developers can use inside a web application or a Visual Studio Code extension.

A typical interface might contain:

  • A prompt or task-entry panel.
  • An execution-status indicator.
  • A conversation history.
  • A tool activity panel.
  • A structured diagnostic table.
  • A results view for generated recommendations.

Separating these interface elements into reusable components makes it easier to develop, test, and maintain the application.

  1. Understanding MCP and ACP AI agent development often involves more than calling a language model API. Model Context Protocol (MCP)

MCP provides a standardized way for compatible AI applications to interact with tools and contextual resources.

Depending on the implementation, these integrations can expose documentation, project information, external services, and other approved capabilities.

Developers should carefully control which tools are available, what information they can access, and whether an operation requires user approval.

Agent Client Protocol (ACP)

ACP provides a protocol for communication between compatible agent clients and agent backends.

Using an appropriate protocol can help separate the interface from the underlying agent implementation. This can be valuable when developing client experiences that need to work with supported agent backends.

MCP and ACP have different roles: one concerns connections to tools and contextual resources, while the other concerns communication between compatible agent clients and agents.

  1. Building the Agent Interface with React

A useful AI interface should make the agent's activity understandable instead of presenting everything as a stream of generated text.
React components can divide the interface into focused sections.
For example:
Task panel: Allows developers to describe the operation they want the agent to perform.

Conversation panel: Displays messages and relevant explanations.
Activity panel: Shows progress, tool invocations, and execution status.

Diagnostics panel: Presents structured findings, errors, and results.
Approval controls: Allow developers to review sensitive actions before they proceed.
This separation helps developers understand what the agent is doing and where human intervention may be needed.

  1. Where Ext JS and a React Grid Component Fit In

As an agent becomes more capable, it may generate structured information that is difficult to review in a chat window.
Consider an agent that examines a project and reports deprecated APIs, failed checks, file references, or proposed changes. A structured data grid can make this information easier to filter, compare, and inspect.

Sencha's Ext JS provides enterprise-oriented UI components, including data grids. ReExt allows developers to integrate Ext JS components into React applications.

A React Grid component built with an appropriate grid library can be useful for displaying:
Tool execution history.
Diagnostic findings.
Validation results.
File-level analysis.
Task status and timestamps.
Structured output from agent workflows.

The important distinction is that Ext JS is a UI framework, not an AI agent engine. It contributes to the presentation layer; the agent's reasoning, tool execution, and permissions need their own implementation.

ReExt is worth evaluating when an application already uses React and needs Ext JS components within the same interface.

  1. A High-Level Architecture A custom AI agent can be organized into several layers: React interface: Collects tasks and displays progress and results. Extension or application host: Manages the surrounding environment and approved interactions.

Agent orchestration: Coordinates model responses, tool calls, and multi-step execution.

Protocol integration: Uses compatible protocols such as MCP and ACP where appropriate.

Tool and data layer: Provides approved access to files, documentation, and external services.
Governance layer: Enforces permissions, approval requirements, and logging.
Keeping these responsibilities separate makes the application easier to reason about and test.

  1. Security and Reliability Considerations

AI agents that can interact with development environments require careful safeguards.
Before deploying an agent, consider:
Restricting access to sensitive files and credentials.
Validating tool inputs and outputs.
Requiring approval for consequential actions.
Handling timeouts, failed tools, and malformed responses.
Keeping an audit trail for relevant operations.
Treating repository content and external tool responses as untrusted input.
Testing whether the agent follows the intended permission boundaries.
A polished interface is useful, but it cannot replace appropriate controls in the execution layer.

  1. A Practical Development Roadmap

Start with a small, clearly defined workflow rather than attempting to build a fully autonomous coding system immediately.

Step 1:
Choose a task, such as reviewing project configuration or identifying deprecated API usage.
Step 2:
Build a simple React interface for submitting tasks and displaying responses.
Step 3:
Connect the agent to a limited set of tools with explicit permissions.
Step 4:
Add execution status, structured results, and diagnostic reporting.
Step 5:
Evaluate whether a React grid component or Ext JS data grid would improve the presentation of structured output.
Step 6:
Add validation, error handling, approval flows, and automated tests.
Measure the results against a baseline before expanding the agent's responsibilities.

Conclusion

Custom AI agents combine model integration, tool access, orchestration, and a clear user interface. JavaScript and React provide a practical foundation for developing these experiences, while MCP and ACP can support different parts of the integration architecture.

For agent interfaces that display structured diagnostic information, Ext JS and ReExt are worth evaluating alongside other React UI libraries.

The best design makes agent activity understandable, keeps sensitive operations under appropriate control, and gives developers the tools they need to inspect results.

Further reading: Building Custom AI Agents with JavaScript, React, and ReExt — Sencha.

title: How I Cut My Cloud Storage Bill From $240/Year to $10/Year
description:
How I Cut My Cloud Storage Bill From $240/Year to $10/Year

Two years ago, I was paying for three cloud storage services at once. Today, I pay $10/year for one domain, and everything else runs on hardware I own. This is the step-by-step story of how I got here, what went wrong, and what I'd recommend.

The 2024 peak: $240/year on cloud storage

I had:

  • Dropbox Plus ($120/year, 2 TB) — for daily work files
  • iCloud+ ($36/year, 200 GB) — for iPhone photos
  • Backblaze Personal ($99/year, unlimited) — for backups

Total: $255/year. And the worst part? I was running out of space — Dropbox wanted me to upgrade to 3 TB for another $20/year, iCloud was constantly nagging me about being full, and Backblaze was uploading at 4 MB/s over my home connection.

Step 1: cancel iCloud, switch to phone-direct Nextcloud

iCloud's 200 GB was always too small because of Live Photos (each Live Photo is ~3 MB, so 1000 photos = 3 GB, and I take a lot of photos). Switching to Nextcloud with the official iOS app was straightforward:

  • Open the iOS Nextcloud app
  • Settings → Auto Upload → enable for Camera Roll
  • Choose "keep on device" for favorites only

After 3 months I had 47 GB of photos on my Nextcloud, all viewable in the iOS Photos app via the native share sheet. Saved $36/year.

Step 2: cancel Dropbox, move work files to WebDAV mount

This was the harder one. I had 10 years of work files in Dropbox and was deeply integrated with the Dropbox desktop client. The migration:

  1. Set up Nextcloud on my server (Ubuntu 24.04, Nextcloud Hub 9 in Docker)
  2. Set up ScsDriver to mount it as a Windows drive letter (Z:)
  3. rsync the entire Dropbox folder from ~/Dropbox to the Z: drive over 2 nights (~400 GB)
  4. Disable the Dropbox desktop client
  5. Use Z:\work\... paths in all my scripts

The ScsDriver WebDAV mount is the missing piece. Without it, the Nextcloud desktop client syncs one folder at a time, can't be remapped to existing paths, and is slow. With ScsDriver, the entire Nextcloud is just a drive letter.

Saved $120/year.

Step 3: cancel Backblaze, do real 3-2-1 backups

Backblaze was uploading my entire machine continuously, which meant my home internet was constantly saturated. The replacement: proper 3-2-1 backups.

  • Primary copy: on my home server (RAID 1, 16 TB)
  • Secondary copy: rsync nightly to a friend's house (8 TB external drive he keeps plugged in)
  • Tertiary copy: encrypted Backblaze B2 of just the truly critical stuff (financial documents, photos) — about 50 GB, costs $0.50/month

The 3-2-1 setup took one weekend and has been running for 18 months without drama.

Saved $93/year.

What I run now (annual cost)

Item Cost / year
Domain (scsoi.com equivalent, any TLD) $10
Backblaze B2 (50 GB critical stuff) $6
Home server electricity (25W × 24h × 365) $25
Total $41/year

That's a saving of $214/year vs the 2024 setup. And I have 16 TB of usable storage, which is 8x what I had with Dropbox Plus.

What I'd recommend for someone starting from zero

  1. If you have < 200 GB of data and a Mac, just keep iCloud+ ($36/year). Don't self-host.
  2. If you have 200 GB - 2 TB and you're a power user, self-host Nextcloud on a $200 mini PC. Use ScsDriver to mount on Windows.
  3. If you have > 2 TB, definitely self-host. $200 hardware + $10/year domain is unbeatable.
  4. If you have > 10 TB, you're probably already doing this — but the ScsDriver mount trick is the productivity multiplier that most setups miss.

The ScsDriver piece in detail

I keep mentioning ScsDriver because it's the part that most self-hosted cloud guides skip. Without a proper mount, the workflow is:

  • Open Nextcloud web UI → click file → edit → save → re-upload

With ScsDriver:

  • Click file in Windows Explorer → edit in any app → save → automatic

That second workflow is the same as Dropbox. It is what makes self-hosted cloud actually usable on Windows.

Pricing (overseas)

  • $1.5 / month
  • $5.5 / year
  • $5.5 lifetime (limited-time, was $9.99)

CN users: the lifetime price in China is ¥20, separately listed on the official site.

What I would NOT recommend

  • Syncthing only (without a mount). Syncthing is great, but you still have to set up a NAS at the other end.
  • Renting a dedicated server ($50+/month). At that price you're paying for someone else's hardware, and you might as well use Dropbox.
  • Using only the Nextcloud desktop client (without ScsDriver). The Nextcloud client is reliable but slow and clunky on Windows.

FAQ

Q: Is $10/year really all you pay for storage?
A: Yes. $10 for the domain, $6 for Backblaze B2 of 50 GB, $25 for electricity. The hardware ($200) was a one-time cost.

Q: What happens when the server dies?
A: RAID 1 means one disk can fail and I keep going. If the motherboard dies, I move the disks to a new box and import the ZFS pool (or mergerfs in my case).

Q: Is your data safer than on Dropbox?
A: Different tradeoff. On Dropbox, my data is on someone else's redundant infrastructure. On my setup, my data is in my house, but I have 3 copies. Both approaches are reasonable.

Q: Can I do this on a laptop?
A: Not really — you need something that's on 24/7. A mini PC or used desktop is the right form factor.

Disclaimer: I run all this on my own hardware. The ScsDriver link above is the public pricing page.

title: Counterfactual Regret for Reflective Agents with Lean-Verified Guarantees
description:
arXiv:2610.14790v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reflective language agents reuse feedback and memory to adapt across tasks without updating model weights. However, existing guarantees for policy selection and action generation do not by themselves establish when local reflection yields long-term performance guarantees for the complete agent under resource constraints. In this paper, we address this gap by deriving sufficient conditions for sublinear counterfactual regret from local generation and deployment guarantees, while retaining the native controller. Specifically, we establish a resource-sensitive transfer that bounds full-state deployment discrepancies along actual execution paths and preserves the own-history laws of both learner and comparator. Besides, local generation reliability yields a cumulative generation opportunity bound, linking policy acquisition to long-term performance through an explicit quality, coverage, and hard-budget tradeoff. To verify these guarantees, we formalize the conditional proof chain for all thirteen numbered theoretical results in Lean, including a native instance with repeated policy growth and imperfect validation.

title: Action Jets: Learning the Local Shape of the Action-conditioned Data Manifold
description:
arXiv:2610.19007v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models are a powerful means of reasoning and planning, but many of these action-conditioned predictive models are high dimensional and computationally expensive. These challenges limit the number of action candidates that can be evaluated by a planner. We show that this cost is avoidable for planners over short horizons, which only require local information with respect to the current state. For a fixed state, the frames reachable by varying a low-dimensional action (a camera movement or an end-effector command) lie on a low-dimensional manifold. We estimate the local shape of that manifold directly via a network trained to estimate how each image region moves per unit of each action axis supervised by data collected from samples by the generator. A correction head fit to trajectory data estimates the shape of this manifold region up to a third-order Taylor polynomial. We call this network estimating the Taylor polynomial describing the manifold shape an Action Jet and compute its radius of validity in closed form. By traversing this approximation of the local manifold shape, we only have to perform inference once per state for any number of candidate actions. Scoring sixteen candidates from a single extraction is over 300x faster than with either source generator, and this gap widens with the number of candidates a planner evaluates. We measure against state-of-the-art action-conditioned generators, IRASim and WorldGym on BridgeData V2, a real 7-DoF manipulation benchmark, and FrameCrafter on DL3DV scenes, where we chart from the novel-view generators DepthSplat and LagerNVS. Because only the tangent comes from the generator and every other term from the data, the Action Jet also predicts held-out frames more accurately than IRASim, the generator that supplied its tangent, at short horizons and at over 100x less compute.

title: TEX-MEX: Similarity-Guided Temporal Contrastive Learning for Time Series
description:
arXiv:2610.19557v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contrastive learning for time series depends on deciding which pairs of inputs should be treated as similar and dissimilar. Because few augmentations reliably preserve meaning in time series, prior methods have relied on two disjoint notions of similarity between windows: structural similarity, which relates windows with similar morphology, and temporal similarity, which relates windows that occur close together in time. We introduce TEX-MEX, to our knowledge the first approach to unify the two into a single relationship. Given a random batch of windows drawn across the dataset, TEX-MEX uses the encoder to identify which windows are structurally similar or dissimilar to each other. It then pulls each window toward the temporally shifted versions of similar windows and pushes it away from those of dissimilar ones, learning what typically accompanies similar windows in time. Across PPG, EEG, ECG, accelerometry, and continuous glucose monitoring, TEX-MEX broadly achieves state-of-the-art performance against contrastive, reconstructive, JEPA-based, and modality-specific approaches, establishing it as a strong general SSL objective. We further train a 560K-parameter PPG foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of downstream benchmarks while being roughly 50x smaller than the next-best unimodally pretrained PPG foundation model in our evaluation. We will release this foundation model open-source and open-weight to the community to support future work and practical applications.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Character Set Troubleshooting: Fix Chinese Garbled Text
description:
Chinese garbled text is a common issue when working with GBase Database(GBase 8s). The cause may be incorrect database locale settings, client encoding mismatches, terminal configuration, or data that was already corrupted during insertion. This guide covers practical checks to help identify and troubleshoot character encoding problems.

1. Understand Common Character Encoding Problems

Before changing any configuration, identify the symptom.

  • Chinese text displays as question marks (**????**): The original characters may have been lost during data insertion or conversion.

  • Chinese text displays as unreadable symbols: The client and database may be interpreting the same bytes differently.

  • Only one application has the problem: The issue may be related to that application's connection or encoding configuration.

  • Chinese text displays correctly in one tool but not another: Compare the client environments before changing database settings.

The key is to determine whether the problem occurs during storage, transmission, or display.

2. Check GBase Database(GBase 8s) Locale Settings

Start by checking the environment variables used by the database installation and client tools.

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$LANG"
echo "$LC_ALL"
echo "$CLIENT_LOCALE"
echo "$DB_LOCALE"

These values help identify the current environment configuration. Their availability and expected values depend on the installation and client setup.

You can also inspect the database environment using the relevant GBase Database(GBase 8s) monitoring commands available in your version.

Before changing locale settings, verify the database's existing locale and the locale expected by the application. Do not assume that changing an environment variable will convert existing data or repair text that was stored incorrectly.

3. Check the Client and Terminal Encoding

If Chinese text looks incorrect in a command-line session, check the terminal environment first.

locale
echo "$LANG"

Confirm that the terminal, client application, and database connection use compatible character encodings.

If the problem occurs only in one terminal or database client, test the same query using another client. This helps distinguish a display issue from a database storage issue.

4. Test Chinese Data

Use a small test table in a non-production database to check whether Chinese characters can be inserted, stored, and retrieved correctly.

CREATE TABLE charset_test (
    id INTEGER,
    name VARCHAR(100)
);

INSERT INTO charset_test VALUES (1, '中文测试');

SELECT * FROM charset_test;

If the returned text is incorrect, compare the result across different database clients.

Before running this test, confirm that the target database supports the intended characters and that your session is configured appropriately. Use an existing test table if you do not have permission to create tables.

A successful test does not necessarily prove that all existing data is correct. It only helps narrow down the problem.

5. Check Application and JDBC Connections

For Java applications, review the JDBC connection configuration and the encoding settings supported by your specific GBase Database(GBase 8s) driver.

For example, a connection URL may look like this:

jdbc:gbasedbt-sqli://192.168.1.100:9088/mydb:GBASEDBTSERVER=gbase01

Verify the correct JDBC URL format, connection properties, and supported character set settings against the documentation for your installed GBase Database(GBase 8s) driver. Do not copy connection properties from another driver or version without verification.

If command-line clients display Chinese correctly but a Java application does not, focus on the application's connection configuration and data handling before modifying the database.

6. Quick Troubleshooting Checklist

When troubleshooting Chinese garbled text in GBase Database(GBase 8s), check these items in order:

  1. Confirm the database locale and supported character set.

  2. Review CLIENT_LOCALE, DB_LOCALE, and related environment settings where applicable.

  3. Check the terminal and client application's encoding.

  4. Compare query results across different clients.

  5. Test inserting and retrieving Chinese text in a test environment.

  6. Review application and JDBC driver configuration.

  7. Determine whether existing data was already corrupted before attempting any conversion or repair.

Avoid changing locale settings on a production system without understanding the impact and preparing a recovery plan.

Conclusion

Troubleshooting character encoding issues in GBase Database(GBase 8s) starts with identifying where the problem occurs: storage, connection, or display. Check locale settings, compare client behavior, and test with a small amount of Chinese text before making changes.

A systematic approach helps isolate the cause while reducing the risk of disrupting existing data or production services.

title: Why Generate a Click? Plug-in Decision Heads for Web Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.20107v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web agents built on vision language models decide every action by generating text such as click(12), although most of that text encodes a choice among a few action types and a few dozen marked elements. We read these choices directly from the hidden states that the generator computes while it reads the goal and the screenshot. Plug-in decision heads on a frozen generator predict the action type, pool the visual tokens inside each numbered box to pick the target, and point at a listed text option or at a WRITE slot that leaves the writing of new text to the generator. A confidence cascade executes the heads' action when they are sure and otherwise lets the generator decode from the KV cache of the same forward pass. With Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators trained on 213k web steps, a strict threshold keeps the cascade between 0.3 points below and 1.4 points above the generator on seven offline test sets while the heads decide 12 to 64% of the steps. A looser threshold raises step success on unseen Mind2Web websites by 3.1 and 1.8 points, costs up to 2 points on GUIAct and MiniWoB++, and lifts WebArena task success from 12.5 to 13.8% (4B) and from 13.6 to 14.6% (8B) with less than half of the generated tokens. Training the heads jointly with the generator lowers the generator's own step success by up to 4.9 points; heads on a frozen generator avoid this cost.

title: I Looked at Countdown Timers as a Shopper and a Web Developer
description:
I noticed something about the way I shop online: when a website tells me an offer is about to expire, I suddenly feel like I need to make a decision.

A product I wasn't particularly interested in can start looking tempting when a message appears saying, "Only 10 minutes left."

That got me thinking about something beyond shopping. How much can a small element of web design influence the decisions we make online?

I wanted to explore the relationship between countdown timers and impulse buying, look at how these timers work from a web development perspective, and understand what makes an online shopping experience helpful rather than unnecessarily stressful.

The Same Product Feels Different With a Countdown Time

I compared two shopping scenarios to understand how the presence of a timer might affect my thinking.

In the first scenario, I find a jacket online without any special offer or deadline. I can check its price, compare alternatives, read reviews, and decide whether I actually need it.

In the second scenario, I find the same jacket with a countdown timer showing that a discount will soon expire.

Suddenly, my attention shifts. Instead of asking whether the jacket is worth buying, I start thinking about whether I'll miss the deal.

The product hasn't changed. The interface has.

This wasn't a controlled experiment, and I didn't measure actual purchases. It was a way to examine how urgency might influence my own decision-making.

Still, it left me with a useful question: would I want this product just as much if the timer weren't there?

Why Countdown Timers Matter in E-Commerce UX

Countdown timers are widely used in flash sales, seasonal promotions, and limited-time offers. From a web development perspective, they're relatively simple interface elements that can have an important effect on how users experience a website.

They communicate urgency, draw attention to a deadline, and encourage users to consider an offer before it expires.

When the deadline is genuine, that information can be useful. If a promotion really ends at midnight, displaying the remaining time helps shoppers understand the offer's terms.

The problem arises when urgency becomes more important than clarity.

A timer that resets every time someone refreshes a page, or an offer that repeatedly claims to be ending soon, can make it difficult for shoppers to understand whether a deadline is real.

That's where I think developers need to look beyond whether an interface element attracts clicks. They should also consider whether it gives users accurate information and allows them to make informed decisions.

Research published in the Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics has examined the relationship between countdown timers and impulse buying in online group-buying situations. This provides useful context for understanding why urgency deserves attention in e-commerce design.

It doesn't mean every timer causes an impulse purchase, but it does raise an interesting question about the responsibility that comes with designing persuasive interfaces.

A Simple JavaScript Countdown Timer

I also wanted to look at the technical side of the feature.

At its simplest, a JavaScript countdown calculates the time remaining and updates the display at regular intervals. Here's a basic example:

Offer ends in 10:00

let remainingSeconds = 10 * 60;

const countdown = document.getElementById("countdown");

const interval = setInterval(() => {
const minutes = Math.floor(remainingSeconds / 60);
const seconds = remainingSeconds % 60;

countdown.textContent =
  `Offer ends in minutes:`+`{String(seconds).padStart(2, "0")}`;

remainingSeconds--;

if (remainingSeconds < 0) {
  clearInterval(interval);
  countdown.textContent = "Offer period ended";
}

}, 1000);

This is only a front-end demonstration. The timer starts again if the page is reloaded, so it shouldn't be used as the source of truth for a real promotion.

For a production e-commerce website, I'd use a fixed deadline supplied by the server, calculate the remaining time from that deadline, and verify the promotion's validity on the server when the user checks out.

That distinction matters because a timer should accurately represent the offer, not simply create the appearance of scarcity.

What I'd Consider Before Adding a Countdown to a Website

If I were implementing a countdown timer for an online store, I'd consider a few things beyond the visual design.

1. Is the deadline real?

The timer should represent an actual promotion end time. A countdown that resets indefinitely can mislead users.

2. What happens when the timer reaches zero?

The website should clearly explain that the offer has ended and ensure that the displayed price and checkout conditions reflect the actual promotion.

3. Does the timer improve the user experience?

A useful deadline indicator provides information. Repeated pop-ups, flashing messages, or exaggerated warnings can distract users from comparing products and understanding the offer.

4. Is the timer accessible?

Frequently announcing every second to screen readers would be disruptive. The implementation should communicate important changes without creating unnecessary accessibility problems.

These details might seem small, but they influence whether the feature feels informative or manipulative.

How I Apply This Thinking When Shopping

Thinking about the design behind countdown timers also changed the questions I ask myself before buying something.

When I come across a limited-time offer, I try to step back and consider whether I wanted the product before seeing the promotion.

I also compare the final price, check delivery costs, and think about whether the purchase fits my budget.

While exploring ways to make more deliberate shopping decisions, I came across the Impulse Buying Evaluator Tool created by shopping platform RabattDigga. It connects with the question I was exploring: how can shoppers pause and reconsider a purchase instead of reacting immediately to an offer?

For example, if I see a jacket advertised at 30% off, I'd ask myself whether I was already planning to buy one and whether the final price is genuinely competitive.

If I can't answer those questions, waiting is often more sensible than rushing to checkout.

I've found one principle particularly useful to remember: saving money on something unnecessary is still spending money.

Four Questions I Ask Before Buying a Limited-Time Deal

I've started using four simple questions when an online offer makes me feel pressured to act quickly.

1. Did I Want This Before Seeing the Timer?

If the product was already on my shopping list, the discount might be worth investigating.

If I discovered it only because of a countdown banner, I think more carefully about why I want it.

2. Is the Discount Actually Worth It?

A large percentage discount doesn't automatically mean a good price. Comparing similar products, delivery charges, and recent price history can help put the offer into perspective.

3. Would I Still Buy It Tomorrow?

For non-essential purchases, waiting can help distinguish genuine interest from temporary excitement.

4. Does It Fit My Budget?

I consider the total checkout cost instead of focusing only on the advertised savings. A discount isn't useful if it pushes me to spend money I need for something else.

What This Taught Me About Web Development and Shopping

The interesting thing about countdown timers is that they sit at the intersection of technology, psychology, and design.

A developer can implement a timer in just a few lines of JavaScript. But deciding how that timer should behave, what it communicates, and whether it helps users make informed choices requires more thought.

From a shopper's perspective, the lesson is equally simple: urgency isn't the same as value.

A countdown can tell me when an offer ends, but it can't tell me whether I need the product or whether buying it makes financial sense.

I don't think countdown timers are inherently bad. When they're accurate and transparent, they can communicate useful information. The challenge is designing them in a way that respects the person using the website.

Key Takeaway

The next time I see a countdown timer, I'll try to evaluate the product before thinking about the deadline.

I'll compare the price, consider whether I actually need it, and decide whether it fits my budget.

And if the offer expires while I'm thinking, I haven't necessarily missed a bargain. I may simply have avoided an unnecessary purchase.

As someone interested in web development, I also think it's worth remembering that the interfaces we build can influence real decisions. Good UX shouldn't just encourage people to click faster; it should help them understand what they're choosing.

If you build e-commerce websites, how do you approach countdown timers? Do you see them as useful UX elements, or do you think they can create unnecessary pressure? I'd be interested to hear how other developers approach this trade-off.

title: What Information Buys in Active Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.19046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.

title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
description:
arXiv:2610.19625v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.

title: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text
description:
arXiv:2610.19294v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.

title: How Inner Optimizers Shape Replica Scaling
description:
arXiv:2610.19064v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. However, a central challenge remains: it is well known that increasing the number of model replicas (replica scaling) while fixing the total training budget leads to monotonically decreasing performance. Existing work has empirically demonstrated that the choice of inner optimizer (Muon v.s. AdamW) can significantly improve this trend, but offers only limited explanation of the performance difference. In this work, we consider a range of inner-optimizers and identify two important factors that impact replica scaling: (1) the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and (2) the impact of batch size on the pseudogradient's noise scale. Based on these insights, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that whitening-based pre-conditioning is a powerful inner-optimizer desideratum. Our empirical evaluation extends the results to reveal that whitening-based inner-optimizers achieve strong replica scaling (for 8-96 replicas), with performance relative to DP improving as parameters and data are scaled.

title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

title: I built shipshape-cli: a preflight check for JavaScript and React projects before you ship
description:
Most broken builds I've seen weren't caused by hard bugs. They were caused by small things:

  • an import pointing at a file someone renamed
  • an environment variable that never made it into .env.example
  • an empty lint script in package.json
  • a repo with no .gitignore, and node_modules sitting there waiting to be committed

None of these are difficult to fix. They're just easy to miss, and you usually find out at the worst time: when CI goes red, or when a teammate clones the repo and nothing runs.

So I built shipshape-cli, a small preflight check you run before handoff, CI or deployment.

npx shipshape-cli check .

It's on npm now as v0.1.0: shipshape-cli

What it checks

shipshape-cli runs four groups of checks in one pass.

Package configuration. Missing or invalid package.json, invalid package names or versions, empty scripts, no test script, or no build script even though Vite, webpack or Next.js is a dependency.

Import integrity. Relative imports (./ and ../) that don't resolve to a real file. It handles import, export ... from, import(), require() and TypeScript's import type. It also tries the usual extensions and index.* files, the same way your bundler would.

Environment configuration. Variables your code reads through process.env or import.meta.env but that are missing from .env.example, plus entries in .env.example that nothing uses any more.

Project hygiene. No README, no .gitignore, or generated folders like dist or node_modules that aren't ignored.

Here's what it prints for a deliberately broken React app:

IMPORTS
  ✗ IMP001 Cannot resolve import "./components/Footer" (src/App.jsx:2:20)
      Fix: Check the path and file name (including letter case), or create the missing file.

ENVIRONMENT
  ! ENV001 VITE_SENTRY_DSN is referenced but missing from .env.example (src/App.jsx:6:35)
      Fix: Add "VITE_SENTRY_DSN=" with a placeholder value to .env.example.

Summary: 4 errors, 4 warnings, 2 info

Every finding has a rule ID, a file and line, and a suggested fix.

Design decisions

It parses code, it doesn't pattern-match it. Imports and env variables are found with @babel/parser, not regular expressions, so comments and strings that only look like imports don't produce false alarms.

It's strictly read-only. This was the rule I cared about most. A tool you point at your project shouldn't be able to change it, leak it or run it. shipshape-cli:

  • never writes, moves or deletes files
  • never runs npm scripts, installs packages or executes project code
  • never opens your real .env files; it reads only .env.example, and keeps only the variable names
  • makes no network requests and sends no telemetry
  • never prints your source code in its output

All of these are covered by tests.

"Skipped" is not "passed". If a check has nothing to analyse, for example no JavaScript files, it's reported as skipped, never as a green tick. A preflight tool that quietly passes things it never looked at is worse than no tool.

Ignores are never silent. You can leave out intentionally broken folders with a .shipshapeignore file, but every report lists the patterns in use, so nobody can hide a problem without it showing.

Using it in CI

Install it as a dev dependency and add a script:

npm install --save-dev shipshape-cli

{
  "scripts": {
    "preflight": "shipshape check ."
  }
}

The exit codes are built for pipelines: 0 means no errors, 1 means errors were found, and 2 means the scan itself couldn't run. Add --strict to fail on warnings too, or --json for a machine-readable report.

One thing to watch: use npx shipshape-cli, not npx shipshape. The unscoped shipshape package on npm is an unrelated project.

What it doesn't do (yet)

This is a first release, and I'd rather be clear about its limits:

  • Path aliases such as @/components/Button aren't resolved yet, so those imports aren't checked.
  • On macOS and Windows, an import with the wrong letter case still resolves locally, so it isn't caught, even though it will fail on Linux CI.
  • .vue, .svelte and .astro files aren't parsed yet.

Path alias support is the most obvious next step.

Try it 

npx shipshape-cli check .

It needs Node.js 20 or later and works on Node 20, 22 and 24.

  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/shipshape-cli
  • GitHub: https://github.com/Sameera-MHK/shipshape-cli

If you run it on one of your projects, I'd really like to hear what it found, and what it got wrong. Issues and suggestions for new checks are very welcome.

title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.19928v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.

title: Node.js Welcome Email Deliverability: Custom-Domain Evidence for Compliance Notices
description:
A customer-support compliance notice needs an evidence chain, not a prettier mail queue. The practical Node.js design is to block production sending until the branded domain verifies, keep the from-address consistent, make DKIM rotation an owned maintenance task, and pull bounce and complaint events into an audit ledger. That work matters more to welcome and transactional email deliverability than exotic infrastructure tuning.

TL;DR: model DNS state, send acceptance, and later delivery events as separate evidence. A successful API call proves acceptance only. It does not prove delivery.

How can Node.js improve welcome email deliverability on a custom domain?

The support workflow has a concrete question to answer: what happened to the notice sent for case CS-18427? One row saying "sent" cannot answer it. The domain may have been unverified at release time, the message may later bounce, or a complaint may arrive after the case is closed.

Use a ledger with three checkpoints:

  1. Record the sending domain's verification state during deployment.
  2. Record the provider's send result against the support case ID.
  3. Append bounce and complaint observations from subsequent event polls.

Keep those checkpoints distinct. Shortcuts blur the evidence.

The domain should be branded, and the application should use consistent from-addresses. That helps recipient trust and inbox placement while making audit searches predictable. DKIM key rotation belongs in the same maintenance calendar as other credential hygiene, with DNS confirmation captured after a change.

This is an evidence-preservation angle, not a claim that DKIM proves regulatory compliance. The capability fits basic US/EU deliverability work. It must not be cited as proof of mainland China email compliance because the domestic email vendor is still pending. For US commercial email obligations, DKIM is only one technical control; the FTC's CAN-SPAM guidance covers duties outside authentication.

Build the smallest useful ledger

I benchmark integration designs by time-to-first-call and the glue they force into a repository. For this job, a small event collector is more useful than a large orchestration framework. It retrieves the raw observations that close the gap between send acceptance and later delivery evidence.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function wait(milliseconds: number): Promise<void> {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));
}

export async function collectEmailEvents(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(new URL("email/event/list", baseUrl), {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delay = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
      await wait(delay);
      continue;
    }

    const body: unknown = await response.json();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Event collection failed (${response.status}): ${JSON.stringify(body)}`);
    }
    return body;
  }

  throw new Error("Event collection exhausted its retry budget");
}

Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented v1 API base in deployment configuration. This code deliberately does less. It does not invent a delivered state, infer provider time from worker time, or flatten raw events into a lossy boolean. Validate the returned body against the current public discovery schema at the adapter boundary, then append the raw observation to the case ledger.

For an API call, use Authorization: Bearer with a key loaded from the environment, set the HTTP method explicitly, check non-success responses, and surface their bodies. A write retry needs an idempotency key derived from the notice or case ID. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. Those rules prevent an audit worker from becoming the source of duplicates or a retry storm.

The polling worker needs a durable cursor. Because email events are pull-only here, overlap query windows and deduplicate stable event identities when the response supplies them. Store both the provider event time and the collector observation time when available. The difference is operationally important: it separates delivery feedback from polling lag.

No webhook means no instant reaction. If the requirement says "send SMS within seconds of a bounce," this design is the wrong fit.

Put DNS in the release path

Domain verification is a deployment gate. Run it before production launch, confirm DNS health in the checklist, and stop the release if the sending identity is not ready. Application health beside broken authentication records is not a healthy email release.

DKIM rotation is different from initial verification. Treat it as controlled maintenance: request rotation when needed, apply the returned DNS changes according to the current provider response, then confirm the domain state again. Do not hard-code record values or propagation estimates into the application. DNS is the authority.

The specific control is easy to state and easy to neglect: ownership for rotation must exist before an urgent key change. Record who initiated it, which domain was affected, and the verification observation that closed the change. That evidence is far more useful than a screenshot of a dashboard with no case identifier.

Compare evidence paths, not feature totals

Four real options can send transactional email. Their useful differences show up in how the evidence reaches your system and how much surrounding infrastructure you already operate.

Option Good fit Evidence trade-off
Amazon SES Teams already using AWS identity, logging, and operations tooling Strong AWS integration, but the team still designs its own audit ledger and surrounding workflow
Postmark Teams focused on transactional email and message activity A focused email product; other backend services and their credentials remain separate
Resend Teams optimizing for a compact developer-facing email workflow Clean email integration, while cross-service evidence still needs application-owned correlation
SendGrid Teams needing an established, broad email platform Broad email tooling can mean more provider-specific configuration to govern
Infrai Small backends that value one credential and one bill across backend capabilities Email feedback is pull-only, so the application must operate polling and accept its latency

Infrai's relevant operational advantage is narrow: one key and one bill reduce credential sprawl and month-end invoice reconciliation when the backend already uses multiple capabilities.

Infrai uses one plain REST API. It requires no SDK. That lets the deploy check and polling worker share one authentication convention without runtime-specific client configuration. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface needs no key. It returns full request and response schemas, while every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. The broader platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules, but route count is not evidence quality.

There is a separate governance advantage: multi-vendor readiness is transparent per capability through vendors_ready, vendors_pending, default_vendor, and key_status. That visibility matters here because it exposes the pending domestic email vendor before release. It prevents a support team from mistaking API breadth for mainland China compliance evidence. For this compliance-notice workflow, the deciding trade-off is still whether pull-based event review meets the response target.

Amazon SES is a sensible answer when AWS is already the operating boundary. Postmark and Resend are easier to justify when email deserves a focused vendor surface. SendGrid fits teams that need its wider email platform. None removes the need to correlate domain state, acceptance, and later events in application-owned storage.

I'd reject any option whose evidence model is unclear, even if its first send takes fewer lines. DX includes the second week of operation.

What changes when volume and scrutiny grow

Split verification checks, sending, and event collection into separate idempotent jobs. Keep the support case ID as the correlation key, but avoid one giant state machine that overwrites history. Append observations. Derive a current view from them.

Measure polling lag and alert on stale cursors. The interval is a business decision: a five-minute poll may be acceptable for an archive and unacceptable for a live fallback. There is no verified universal number, so write the required response time down before choosing the provider. Benchmark the actual workflow under its expected load rather than borrowing somebody else's latency claim.

At this scale, configuration bloat starts hiding ownership. Keep the deploy gate, rotation runbook, cursor, and retention policy explicit. Idempotency is marked on 171 of 294 capabilities, with a 24-hour default deduplication window, so long-delayed replays still need application-owned duplicate protection. I choose an application ledger over trusting that window because a compliance replay can arrive later. Four obvious controls beat forty vague flags.

Several boundaries remain. There is no managed email OTP interface, so an email-code fallback must be built in the application. Scheduled email has no cancellation capability, although SMS does. There is no SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. Tag-aggregated cost reporting is not available through an API. If any of those is mandatory, change the composition instead of wrapping the gap in more code.

The final rule is blunt: choose the provider whose feedback timing and operating boundary match the evidence requirement. Then verify the domain before launch, maintain DKIM, keep sender identities stable, and retain bounce and complaint events. Deliverability starts with those controls. Compliance still needs its own legal and retention analysis.

Further reading

  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • Amazon SES DKIM guidance
  • Postmark DKIM setup
  • Resend domain documentation
  • SendGrid domain authentication
  • FTC CAN-SPAM compliance guide
  • OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet

title: Learning Across Temporal Graph Representation Silos
description:
arXiv:2610.19576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal graph data are recorded in different representations, but whether these differences also determine the scope of learned knowledge reuse remains unclear. This study investigates whether predictive structure learned from relational histories can be reused between continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) and temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs). Bidirectional reuse emerges while retaining distinct input and prediction interfaces and independent vocabularies, and sources with the same representation are not always more useful. Controlled reorganizations of source histories show that the organization contributing to reuse varies across source-target conditions. We show that learned aspects of Relational Dynamics, the predictive structure present in relational histories, can be reused across conventional representation boundaries. Independently pretrained TKG and CTDG learners can also be fused at the score level to improve prediction on a third dataset without entity or relation-semantic alignment. Two proofs of concept in recommendation and security detection illustrate that external temporal sources without direct alignment can also become useful pretraining resources.

title: AtomSearch: Evidence-Grounded Tree Search for Agent Skill Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19951v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent skills adapt frozen models through editable external instructions. Revising several rules at once makes changes difficult to inspect, while judging each local edit only by its immediate score can discard useful intermediate states. We introduce AtomSearch, which keeps revision actions local while using subsequent skill states to guide search. Contrastive atomic editing links each primitive rule edit to failed and successful executions, a behavioral hypothesis, and an intended scope. Skill-State Tree Search (STS) evaluates short edit compositions and selectively retains them as executable states that can be revisited and extended. Outcome memory supplies later proposals with observed repair and regression statistics. We evaluate AtomSearch across four tasks and five target models. With deepseek-v4-flash, it exceeds SkillOpt on three of four tasks, including a 9.68-percentage-point gain on LiveMathematicianBench, and SkillOpt's final skills contain 2.3-19.7 times as many characters. In 67% of completed searches, the best validation state passes through an ancestor that was not highest-scoring at its depth. These results show how local rule edits can support the exploration of useful revision paths and yield compact skills, with additional offline evaluations used to explore alternative states.

title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
description:
arXiv:2610.19638v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
description:
arXiv:2610.14402v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.

title: StreamErase: Towards Ultra-Fast Streaming Video Erasing
description:
arXiv:2610.20137v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current video object removal methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction. We present StreamErase, enabling sub-second latency with up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU. Our approach first augments a text-to-video model with mask input to generate high-quality videos that erase target objects and synthesize coherent backgrounds, but does not perform inference on the fly. As such, we progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity. Several key challenges arise when generating videos over long, potentially infinite horizons: (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to long horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without increasing computational cost as the context grows. To address these challenges, we carefully designed sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks. By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos. Finally, we establish a dedicated benchmark, LongErase, for streaming long-video object removal. Our model achieves strong performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming. With StreamErase, users can input a mask and see the erasing results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.
