title: Cheap Webhook Task Processing Explained — Node.js SaaS Rate-Limit Retry Backoff
description:
Short answer: for a nightly fintech reconciliation, put the delayed webhook work in a queue and make the worker idempotent. A cron trigger should enqueue a bounded batch, while retries and rate limits live at the worker boundary. That shape is cheap to reason about because the provider's rate limit cannot turn one long cron invocation into a hidden scheduler.

The bill is mostly downstream work, not the timer. Every payment lookup, webhook delivery attempt, and retained message costs attention; a cron job that fires 10,000 calls at once creates a burst of throttled retries. Controlling worker concurrency changes that dominant term. It also gives the team one place to record an idempotency key such as reconcile:2026-09-10:merchant-42:payment-981, so a duplicate delivery cannot post the same ledger adjustment twice.

Bursts hurt.

Suppose the provider allows 20 requests per second and the nightly window contains 2,400 merchants. A cron loop that launches every request immediately will spend its first minutes collecting 429 responses, then create a retry wave that is larger than the original wave. With a queue, the trigger publishes the merchant windows quickly, while workers take 20 tokens per second and attach the same reconciliation key to every attempt. Merchant 17 may fail once and return after a 30-second delay; merchant 18 may succeed on its first call. Those paths do not interfere. The audit row records the provider cursor, attempt count, and final comparison before the message is acknowledged. If the worker dies after the provider accepts the adjustment but before ack, the next delivery still carries the same key, so the database uniqueness check and provider idempotency guard converge on one ledger result. This is the operational reason I care about queue shape more than the timer brand.

There is a retention trade-off. An acknowledged queue message is deleted, and retention tops out at 30 days. I keep the reconciliation result and provider response hash in an audit table before acking; I do not pretend the queue is a replay log. When an auditor asks for a six-month trail, the table is what we query, and the queue's short retention is the deliberate cost of keeping the operational path small.

That boundary is where Infrai can fit: its queue is reachable through a plain REST API, so the nightly trigger and a Python or Node.js worker can share one HTTP contract without an SDK. I would test it for the low-complexity path below, not for workflow orchestration.

Two viable shapes for delayed webhook work

The simple shape is cron plus queue: a nightly trigger finds the reconciliation window, publishes one message per merchant or bounded page, and workers consume at a controlled concurrency. Cron executions are capped at 900 seconds, so long work belongs behind the trigger. The queue's standard delivery is at-least-once; the invariant is that the consumer can safely run the same message twice.

The second shape is a durable workflow engine. Temporal or Airflow can model a multi-step reconciliation with joins, compensations, and a long-lived history. That is the right invariant when a payment run is a graph whose later steps depend on several earlier results. It is more machinery than a single provider sweep needs.

For a small SaaS, I would choose the first shape when the job is “fetch, compare, emit, retry.” Its broader backend surface can also keep storage and scheduling behind the same key, which removes a little integration bookkeeping without changing the queue invariant.

How should Node.js teams model rate limits, retries, and backoff?

Treat a rate limit as state, not as a sleep sprinkled through a cron loop. A worker should reserve a provider token, perform one idempotent operation, and requeue a failed attempt with a bounded delay. Exponential backoff with jitter prevents every merchant from retrying on the same second; Retry-After wins when the provider sends it.

Here is the core decision in Python, kept independent of a vendor client so the behavior is testable:

import requests
import json
import os
import random
import time


def retry_delay(attempt, retry_after=None):
    if retry_after is not None:
        return min(float(retry_after), 604800)
    cap = min(2 ** attempt, 3600)
    return random.uniform(cap / 2, cap)


def reconciliation_key(merchant_id, window_start):
    return f"reconcile:{merchant_id}:{window_start}"


def publish_reconciliation(queue, payload, delay_seconds=0):
    body = {"queue": queue, "message": payload,
            "delay_seconds": delay_seconds}
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
               "Idempotency-Key": payload["reconciliation_key"]}
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            "POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
            json=body, headers=headers, timeout=20)
        if response.status_code < 400:
            return response.json()
        if response.status_code != 429:
            raise RuntimeError(response.text)
        time.sleep(retry_delay(attempt, response.headers.get("Retry-After")))
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after five attempts")

Keep delayed messages at or below 604800 seconds, and attach the reconciliation key to the payload. If a write is retried, send the same client id or idempotency key. The platform convention uses an Idempotency-Key header for operations that support it; your application still owns the provider-side idempotency check.

There is no native debounce or throttle primitive, and FIFO deduplication lasts only five minutes. That is a capability boundary, not a failure mode: use a database uniqueness constraint for a longer business window. For one-to-many delivery, publish to separate queues because there is no built-in topic fan-out.

What do queue, cron, and workflow products actually trade?

Option Best fit Retry and rate-limit shape Retention or orchestration caveat
Queue plus cron trigger Delayed webhook batches and ordinary SaaS reconciliation Worker concurrency, requeue, exponential backoff At-least-once; finite retention; no joins
Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers Short, publicly reachable HTTP trigger You build the queue and retry state A single invocation is capped at 900 seconds
Inngest Event-driven functions with managed retry history Function-level retry and step state More orchestration semantics than a basic queue
Temporal Long-running, branching reconciliation workflows Durable workflow timers and activities Operational and modeling overhead is substantial

The comparison is not a price contest. Cloudflare is compelling when the timer and edge execution are already your platform. Inngest is a better choice when each reconciliation has explicit steps and you want their history attached to the run. Stick with Temporal when you need DAG-like joins or compensation logic. A queue is not suitable when replay across multiple consumer groups is a hard requirement; persist an event log or select a stream system instead.

The small implementation I would ship

Create one queue per independent consumer, publish a bounded batch from the nightly trigger, then let workers claim and ack messages only after the audit row is durable. A failed provider call becomes a delayed republish, with the attempt count and next-attempt timestamp in the message. Keep payloads below 256 KB and delayed work within seven days; a later reconciliation window can be scheduled by the next cron run.

I initially thought a FIFO queue would solve duplicate payments by itself. It does not: the five-minute deduplication window is shorter than a nightly business key, and standard queues can deliver at least once. The invariant belongs in the database and in the provider request, where the same reconciliation_key produces the same result.

One operational wrinkle matters in fintech: cron does not backfill triggers missed while paused, and run output is limited to the first 4 KB. Write a run record as soon as the trigger starts, then store detailed diagnostics in your audit system. Your mileage may vary around provider-specific quotas; confirm the live quota contract before choosing worker concurrency.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want this queue-centered shape and a plain HTTP integration, especially when the same service already needs several backend capabilities under one key. It is not the right choice for a workflow graph, Kafka-style replay, private push endpoints, or native fan-out. In those cases, use Temporal, Airflow, a stream platform, or a specialist queue that states those guarantees directly.

If this boundary matches your reconciliation job, the queue capability details and runnable examples are at docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.push_subscribe
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
description:
arXiv:2610.19728v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.

title: Workflow SDK now runs natively in Nitro v3
description:
Workflow SDK's native Nitro v3 integration is now in beta. Steps run inside the same bundled runtime as the rest of your app, instead of a separate bundle. Nitro's useStorage() and other server-side APIs work directly inside "use step" functions.

The Nitro dev server also serves the workflow web UI at /_workflow. Open it in your browser to inspect, monitor, and debug workflow runs.

Workflow routes are now bundled by Nitro as part of the app build. Dependencies are traced, and unused code is tree-shaken, so the output includes only what runs, with faster builds and smaller bundles.

Get started with Workflow SDK on Nitro.

title: Towards Training and Inference of Graph Neural Networks in Graph Databases
description:
arXiv:2610.19142v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph Neural Networks on large graphs commonly rely on in-memory graph storage with ad hoc data processing pipelines for both training and inference. Graph databases provide scalable storage and efficient traversal for graphs that can evolve over time, but their applicability in GNN training and inference are rarely studied. We show that graph DBs can be used in GNN training and inference directly, executing sampling, feature retrieval, and even the full forward pass. We show different GNN training pipelines can perform on-the-fly sampling and retrieval in graph DBs using Cypher. We further provide optimisations that speed up the training process by \~2.5x while maintaining the same accuracy. We illustrate that fully in-DB inference is possible, independent of how the GNNs are trained. Our inference setup can be >10x faster than cold loading the graph into RAM with no extra memory overhead on real-world graphs. Our work lays the foundation for in-graph-DB GNN training and inference.

title: Keep focus visible (Web HIG tip #10)
description:
Press Tab on your own site. If you can't tell where you are after two or three presses, neither can anyone who navigates by keyboard. Somewhere in the CSS, a focus ring was switched off and nothing replaced it.

Web HIG tip #10 (Quick #72 / HIG-A11Y-006): Focus must be visible on every interactive element — never outline: none without a custom ring.

Why it matters

The focus ring is the keyboard user's cursor:

  • People who use a keyboard, switch device, or voice control rely on it to see which link, button, or field will act next
  • Without it, pressing Enter is a guess, and a wrong guess can submit, delete, or buy
  • outline: none is often added to stop the ring showing on mouse clicks, and that also hides it from everyone who needs it
  • Rings hidden under a sticky header or cookie banner fail the same way

The full HIG (§5.3, Keyboard Focus & Interaction) requires an explicit, high-contrast indicator on every interactive control. The ring must contrast with what's next to it and must not be hidden by other elements. §5.1 sets the contrast floor for focus indicators at 3:1, the figure from WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (AA); Quick #62 is the companion rule. On the WCAG side, this builds on 2.4.7 Focus Visible and 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), both Level AA in WCAG 2.2. WCAG's minimum only asks that the focused element isn't completely hidden; the HIG asks for more and keeps the ring itself uncovered.

The rule of thumb

Ask: if I unplug the mouse, can I always see where I am?

If you removed the default ring, put a better one back.

/* Don't: the ring is gone for everyone */
button:focus {
  outline: none;
}

/* Do: a clear ring for keyboard focus, from one shared color */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Delete the outline: none rule rather than adding a ring next to it. button:focus is more specific than :focus-visible and will still win.

:focus-visible lets the browser decide when a ring helps. It shows for keyboard focus and usually not for a mouse click on a button, which is what most people wanted from outline: none in the first place. Text fields still show it on click, because you need to know where you're typing.

If a sticky header covers whatever is focused, leave room for it:

/* Keep focused elements from scrolling under a 4rem sticky header */
html {
  scroll-padding-top: 4rem;
}

Match it to the header's real height (a custom property helps), and use scroll-padding-bottom for bottom bars and cookie banners.

Do this instead

  • Delete outline: none and outline: 0 unless a visible ring still applies on keyboard focus (for example, suppress only with :focus:not(:focus-visible) and style :focus-visible).
  • Style :focus-visible with one shared focus-ring color (a CSS custom property works well), so it's contrast-checked once, in light and dark mode
  • Prefer outline to box-shadow for the ring: Windows high-contrast (forced colors) mode drops box shadows, so a shadow-only ring can vanish. If you keep a box-shadow ring, add outline: 2px solid transparent as well. Forced colors mode repaints it in a visible system color.
  • Use outline-offset so the ring isn't lost against a button's own border or background
  • Check that sticky headers, footers, and banners don't cover the focused element

Quick check for your app

Put the mouse aside and Tab through a whole page, including a menu, a dialog, and a form. At every stop, you should see where focus is without hunting for it, and, as the HIG asks, nothing should sit on top of the ring. Then repeat in dark mode. A tool can find outline: none in your CSS, but only tabbing through tells you whether people can actually see where they are.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/25
  • Hashnode: https://thewebhig.hashnode.dev/keep-focus-visible-web-hig-tip-10
  • Dev.to: https://dev.to/frozonfreak/keep-focus-visible-web-hig-tip-10-lge

title: SysInfo Viewer, a simple system spec viewer for Linux
description:
I made a small GUI app that shows your system specs in one window: OS, CPU, memory, network, storage plus GPU. It has search and light and dark themes.

I originally built it for ShopnoOS, a Debian-based distro I work on at my work. We needed a simple system specs viewer for our users. The tools I tried were either too detailed (hardinfo2), had a dated UI (CPU-X), or felt more like a task manager (Mission Center). So, I started working on it and thought I’d share. This one just shows basic information.

It is AI assisted, yes. I tested on bunch of systems and VMs. Detection may miss on hardware I don’t own, so reports of wrong or missing values are the feedback I seek most.

Repo: https://github.com/fa-saikat/sysinfo-viewer
.deb package is available on the release page.

Write the agent once. Use the best harness available. Today. In 3 months. A year from now.

Initial harness adapters for this experimental release include Claude Code, Codex, and Pi, with more coming soon.

HarnessAgent is available on the AI SDK canary release. Read the AI SDK harness documentation to get started.

title: Set and forget
description:
Every leap in computing has handed people back a piece of their time by taking one job off their hands. Keeping your application alive after it is written, is the next one to go.

An essay from LILY Labs

The history of computing can be told as a list of jobs that stopped being jobs.

In 1957, John Backus and his team at IBM released FORTRAN, and programmers stopped writing most of their instructions in the language of the machine. They described the calculation, and a compiler worked out the rest. Around 1960, John McCarthy, at MIT, built automatic memory management into Lisp. A whole category of bookkeeping, deciding when each piece of memory could be given back, moved from the programmer to the system. In 2006, Amazon put storage on sale at fifteen cents a gigabyte-month. Now a company could stop buying and managing their own hard drives and keep access to their data anyway.

Each time, people worried that something important was being lost. Each time, the people freed from the job did not sit idle. They built more interesting things on top.

None of these transitions was clean. Compilers produced slow code for years. Garbage collection brought pauses of its own. The cloud swapped buying machines for configuring them. Every handover created some new work alongside the work it removed. But the direction stayed steady. A job that used to fill a day became a thing the system took over automatically.

Writing code has never been faster. Tools that help with it, many of them now built on AI, can produce in an afternoon what used to take a week. The odd thing is how little that has changed the rest of the week.

Writing out the application logic is only one step. After it is written, someone has to package it, choose a machine for it, decide how many copies to run, set rules for when to add more, watch it, patch what sits beneath it, and answer the phone when any of that goes wrong. None of those tasks got meaningfully faster while the output of code exploded.

Komodor, a vendor for Kubernetes troubleshooting tools, reported in its 2025 Enterprise Kubernetes Report that operations teams spend more than 60 percent of their time troubleshooting. Even if discounted by a large margin, that is still a sizeable number. The bottleneck has moved. It used to be in the creation of software. Increasingly it lies in keeping that same software running.

The one-person organization

AI writes the code. Payments, email and sign-in arrive as services. Set and forget takes the servers off the list. Stack those together and one person can do what took a small team a few years ago: build a product, ship it, and keep it running.

And it is leaving the screen. CNC mills, 3D printers and laser cutters now fit in a spare room, and AI can walk a beginner from the first sketch to the finished part. Someone tired of a bike part that keeps breaking can design a better one over a weekend, print three prototypes, mill the final version in aluminium and be selling it a month later. The shop, the order queue and the shipping emails are just software. Set it once, and the attention goes back to the product.

Just open YouTube, the creator economy has exploded with people building things on their own that used to need a workshop and a team: electric conversions in home garages, hand-built instruments, hardware products shipped worldwide, and courses teaching everyone else to do the same. That flood of content is a public record of the new tools at work.

A product for a few hundred customers becomes a real business when all of them can be operated from a single hand. An idea can be tested within a week, not after a funding round. And the most valuable skills shift from depth to range: knowing enough about design, materials, code and customers to connect them, and to spot when the AI is wrong. Deciding what to build is still the hard part. Everything around it is getting lighter.

The freed hours can go in two directions:

The first is to do more. One person directs a small organization of agents, each carrying part of the work: E.g. one writes code, one answers customers, one watches the stock, one drafts the next product page. The person in the middle decides, checks and connects as the central orchestrating node in this network of agents.

The second is quite the opposite: Much of a working day is not work at all. It is clutter: searching five internal tools for one document, filling in the same fields on a contract for the tenth time, photographing a flat and clicking through every menu it takes to list it for rent. Each step is a tiny decision: the click of a button, locating the next textbox to fill out, remembering which note taking tool holds a specific piece of information, etc., etc. Together they can eat hours in front of a screen. That is exactly the kind of work agents are good at. The human in the loop simply needs to track the outputs to deliver. A lot of the workflows, machines can now take over just as well as an actual personal assistant, freeing up the users time.

Most people will mix the two. For decades, software competed for attention: more features, more dashboards, more reasons to log in. The tools that win next may be the ones that ask for the least of it. A product that does its job while nobody is looking stops being one more thing to manage and becomes what infrastructure was always supposed to be: the part underneath that lets everything else happen.

Back in the forest

It would be easy to end on productivity. Ship faster, do more, fill the freed hours with more of the same.

That is not quite the point. The people who stopped writing machine code did not spend the time writing more machine code. They spent it on problems that had been out of reach.

There is a catch. Agents shorten the loop between decisions. A change that once took a week to build now comes back in an hour and asks for the next call straight away. The manual work that used to sit between choices, and quietly gave the mind a rest, is disappearing. What is left is a day made almost entirely of decisions, and decision fatigue grows with it.

The same shift also loosens where work happens. You can walk through a park with a pair of smart glasses, talking an agent through a rewrite of your backend. Some of the freed time should go to nothing at all. Time, to replenish the cognitive resources spent. Deploy with us and rest easy, we will take care of the rest!

You build. We carry.

title: DeepSeek enters the fight for token volume, Anthropic continues to dominate spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — June 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs, giving us visibility into what AI usage actually looks like, separate from leaderboards and benchmarks. We publish the data monthly in the AI Gateway production index.

June 2026 summary

The July index reports on AI Gateway data collected in May 2026.

  • Total AI Gateway tokens grew +20% MoM; total spend grew +43% MoM. Customers paid almost 20% more per token on average than in April.

  • DeepSeek’s share of tokens jumped from under 1% to 17% in a single month, while its share of spend stayed near 1%.

  • Anthropic’s share of spend grew from 61% to 65% in May, holding 70–80% of spend across every high-stakes use case (AI app generation, back office agents, and coding agents).

  • Cost-consciousness meant smarter routing between low-cost and frontier models. Customers got more deliberate about which model did which work, while overall usage kept climbing.

Last month, headlines about blown token budgets dominated tech news: Uber burned through its annual Claude Code budget shortly after Q1 and Amazon shut down KiroRank to curb unproductive tokenmaxxing. While runaway cost is a real problem, this month’s report shows that spend on production use cases still increased.

Two insights emerged from AI Gateway data in May:

  • Low-cost models entered production: New models shipped at price points that made the established labs look even more expensive, and they are capable enough to enter the mix in production.

  • Spend is increasing, but with smarter model mixes: Teams are still increasing token budgets, but they are implementing smarter routing strategies to get more value out of every dollar.

Low-cost models saw significant production volume for the first time

From February to April, volume distribution across labs on AI Gateway changed slowly, but in May, DeepSeek V4's launch completely shifted token share. The low-cost end of the market that barely existed in April became AI Gateway’s third-largest provider by volume in May, without a significant impact on overall spend.

In April, DeepSeek accounted for less than 1% of AI Gateway tokens and less than 0.2% of spend. In May, its volume share jumped to 17% of tokens, putting it in third place, ahead of OpenAI. Almost all of the volume comes from two models: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro, both released in May.

The spend picture tells the other half of the story. Even though DeepSeek’s token share grew to 17% in a single month, its cost share stayed near 1%.

DeepSeek V4 Flash launched at $0.14 input / $0.28 output per million tokens, roughly 20–50× lower than comparable Anthropic models and 8–12× lower than other value-tier flagships like Qwen 3.6 Plus and Kimi K2.6. With a savings gap that big, teams adopted V4 Flash quickly.

Price alone wouldn’t have shifted DeepSeek’s volume that much in a month, meaning teams testing DeepSeek V4 against their existing evals found the output good enough to ship, not just low-cost enough to try.

Value-tier models have always been available on AI Gateway, but have never captured token share at this scale, meaning DeepSeek V4 was the first model at its price point to clear the quality bar for production work.

Frontier labs continued to capture a majority of new spend

Even as the low-cost end of the market grew fastest in volume, the expensive end grew faster in dollars.

Anthropic’s token share grew from 26% to 32%, and its spend share from 61% to 65%. OpenAI’s token share held near 13%, but its spend share ticked up from 12% to 13% on a much larger total, so customers were paying more per OpenAI token in May.

The average token got more expensive in May, even with DeepSeek pulling the average down. That increase happened because the work that demands frontier models grew faster than the work that doesn’t. The AI coding agent use case shows the low-cost/frontier split most clearly:

  • DeepSeek drove 49% of the segment’s token volume, but only 4% of the cost.

  • Anthropic drove 28% of tokens and 70% of the cost.

Lower-cost models are now a meaningful part of production workflows, but frontier model use is still growing, driving the increase in overall spend.

The frontier is getting more expensive per token, and customers are still paying. Anthropic continues to lead on spend, taking 65% of all gateway spend in May, and 70–80% of spend across every high-stakes use case.

Cost discipline became a routing strategy

Increased overall spend showed that demand for AI continued to grow in May, but teams applied more precision to their budgets through routing. They sent the cheap, high-volume work to lower-priced models and used frontier models where quality mattered most. Slow adoption of Google's latest Flash model is a clear example.

Gemini 3.5 Flash launched in May at a higher price point than Gemini 3.0 Flash, but migration didn’t happen at scale. By month-end, 3.5 held only 7% of the Flash family’s tokens while 3.0 held 90%.

Compared to the rapid adoption of Gemini 3.1 Pro across February and March, slower migration to 3.5 Flash shows that teams happy with 3.0 Flash aren't willing to pay the higher cost yet.

Conclusion: Cost-effective, capable options mean smarter model mixes

This month's report signals increased pricing sensitivity in the market, even as overall spend and token volume grow. That means developers are looking for ways to get more out of every dollar.

Data revealed two optimization strategies:

  1. Using DeepSeek's cheap, but capable V4 family for lower-risk, high-volume tasks

  2. Choosing to delay model family upgrades until the ROI makes sense

Routing gives teams the ability to adjust their model mix, and budget, in real time as the labs compete for different layers of production AI workloads.

Appendix

Token vs cost share by B2B classification

B2B applications run fewer, more expensive calls, while B2C applications run many cheap ones. On a per-token basis, B2B cost roughly 60% more than B2C in May.

Agent tool use across tokens and requests

Just under a quarter of requests end in a tool call, but those requests carry well over half of all tokens. Both metrics are roughly flat month-over-month.

Model diversity distribution by request volume

The more requests an app serves, the more models it runs in production. Single-model setups dominate the lowest-volume tier, while at 1M+ requests the majority of apps route across 11 or more models.

Cost vs volume share by use case

Use case cost share indicates how expensive a wrong answer is, not how many tokens it burns. Personal assistants and coding agents run cheap per token, while back-office and recruiting work costs far more.

Previous reports

Read the May 2026 AI Gateway production index.

About this data

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through May 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend uses market-rate pricing (published list price) to provide a normalized view across teams that bring their own API keys.

  • Volume counts tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • B2C, B2B, and use-case classifications are aggregate. No individual team or workload is identified.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as data completes.

title: Node.js Marketplace Recovery: Send and Verify SMS OTP with Cooldowns
description:
TL;DR: For a Node.js marketplace password reset with a short expiry, let a hosted service own SMS code issuance and verification, but keep resend cooldowns, IP and device limits, country policy, and delivery polling in the application. The clean boundary is narrow: your service decides whether an attempt may proceed, the provider decides whether the code is valid, and your service changes the account only after verification. A unified provider is worth considering when the same flow touches auth, email, and SMS because the implementation can keep one HTTP contract, base URL, and key. That reduces integration work; it does not remove abuse controls.

A useful postmortem question is not "did the SMS dashboard look healthy?" It is "what page fired when one buyer requested 400 resets against 40 seller accounts?" A graph of successful sends can be green while the reset endpoint is doing exactly the wrong thing. Application admission control is the invariant.

How should a Node.js backend send and verify SMS OTP?

Start before the SMS call. Normalize the phone number, resolve the marketplace account without revealing whether it exists, check the country allowlist, and evaluate counters for the account, IP, and device. A permitted request enters a cooldown and then calls /v1/sms/otp. A submitted code goes to /v1/sms/verify; only successful verification can mint a short-lived reset grant. The SMS response must never directly change a password.

That split is deliberately boring. Hosted send and verify avoid rebuilding token validation, while the application retains the decisions that depend on marketplace risk. The unified option does not provide built-in geographic fencing or per-country cost circuit breakers, so those checks cannot be delegated. Delivery status and events are pull-based rather than pushed by webhook, which means the application must poll when it needs delivery visibility.

The account-to-message handoff should preserve one internal correlation ID, not a vendor-specific message object. The account result supplies the normalized recipient; email suppression preflight consumes that recipient; SMS becomes the fallback transport. With Infrai, auth, email, and SMS calls use the same https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base URL and Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. Swapping the vendor behind a capability therefore does not force the application contract to change.

Infrai's second, separate integration advantage is its plain REST API, so there is no SDK to install. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. It exposes request and response JSON Schema, billing metadata, and readiness. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. A Node.js gateway and a Go worker can therefore generate the same HTTP contract instead of maintaining two SDK adapters, while paths come from the discovery path field rather than description prose. That removes a concrete upgrade and dependency-review chore from this reset flow.

The page is the test.

I would page on exhausted reset budgets, a sustained delivery-state backlog, and reset grants issued without a matching verification record. I would not page merely because one carrier is slow. That distinction keeps a transport symptom from masquerading as an account-security incident.

Put cooldown policy in code you own

The exact thresholds are business policy, so this sample uses explicit example values rather than pretending they are universal: one attempt every 30 seconds per account, five attempts per 15 minutes per IP, and three per 15 minutes per device. Production counters need a shared store and atomic increments; this in-memory implementation is runnable and useful for tests, but it is not suitable across multiple processes.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type limiter struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    events map[string][]time.Time
}

func (l *limiter) allow(key string, limit int, window time.Duration, now time.Time) bool {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    cutoff := now.Add(-window)
    kept := l.events[key][:0]
    for _, at := range l.events[key] {
        if at.After(cutoff) { kept = append(kept, at) }
    }
    if len(kept) >= limit {
        l.events[key] = kept
        return false
    }
    l.events[key] = append(kept, now)
    return true
}

func admit(l *limiter, account, ip, device, country string, now time.Time) error {
    countries := map[string]bool{"US": true, "CA": true}
    if !countries[country] { return fmt.Errorf("country outside reset policy") }
    if !l.allow("account:"+account, 1, 30*time.Second, now) { return fmt.Errorf("cooldown active") }
    if !l.allow("ip:"+ip, 5, 15*time.Minute, now) { return fmt.Errorf("IP budget exhausted") }
    if !l.allow("device:"+device, 3, 15*time.Minute, now) { return fmt.Errorf("device budget exhausted") }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    l := &limiter{events: make(map[string][]time.Time)}
    fmt.Println(admit(l, "seller-1842", "198.51.100.24", "device-77", "US", time.Now()) == nil)
}

The provider-side half can remain schema-safe without baking undocumented fields into an article. Put the JSON object produced from the live discovery schema in INFRAI_OTP_REQUEST_JSON; this runnable Go caller validates that it is an object, sends it with an explicit method and environment-backed key, honors Retry-After, and reports the real error body. A production service should cap the total retry duration at less than the reset expiry.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_OTP_REQUEST_JSON"))
    var object map[string]any
    if key == "" || json.Unmarshal(payload, &object) != nil || object == nil {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY and a schema-valid INFRAI_OTP_REQUEST_JSON object")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", os.Getenv("RESET_ATTEMPT_ID"))

        response, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { panic(readErr) }
        if response.StatusCode >= 200 && response.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        if response.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("send failed: status=%d body=%s", response.StatusCode, body))
        }
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
}

The order exposes a real pitfall: this compact example consumes the account budget before discovering an exhausted IP or device budget. In production I would evaluate and commit all counters atomically in one server-side operation, so a rejected request cannot burn only part of the budget. Dashboards hide this. Load tests do not.

Provider calls should load the key from the environment, specify the HTTP method, and surface non-success response bodies. A retry on HTTP 429 should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter. Write retries need an idempotency key tied to the reset attempt; Infrai specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities. Stop after a bounded number of attempts. Fast retry loops turn throttling into an incident.

Do not log the OTP. Store the attempt ID, account ID, policy decision, provider request ID when returned, verification outcome, and reset-grant ID. Those fields answer the postmortem question without putting an authenticator into the logging system.

Three integrations or one trust boundary

The obvious alternative is Clerk for the account, Resend for email, and Twilio for SMS verification. It is a sensible specialist arrangement, and each component can be selected independently. It also means three signups, three credential sets, three client conventions, and application glue to reconcile recipient identity and suppression state. The marketplace team owns that glue forever.

Option Integration shape Better fit when Cost of the choice
Clerk + Resend + Twilio Three accounts and credential sets; application joins account, email, and SMS state Specialist controls justify separate operational surfaces More credential rotation and reconciliation code
Twilio Verify SMS verification is isolated behind a specialist Carrier tooling and SMS operations dominate Account and email handoffs stay separate
Clerk Account lifecycle is central Identity features matter more than a shared communications contract Email and SMS retain separate boundaries
Resend Transactional email is primary Email deserves an independent specialist It does not collapse the account-to-SMS handoff
Infrai Auth, email, and SMS share one REST surface, key, and bill Low integration effort and a stable provider boundary matter One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface

My recommendation: a small marketplace team should try Infrai for the auth-to-email-to-SMS handoff when reducing integration code is more valuable than deep channel-specific control; the stable HTTP contract is the primary reason, and public self-describing schemas remove the separate cost of maintaining several SDK-shaped adapters. The discovery index reports 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth is not the decision. The decision is whether one boundary makes the reset path easier to reason about at 3 a.m.

The main limitation and trade-off is concentrated dependency. The specialist stack is a better fit when an organization already has mature Clerk, Resend, or Twilio ownership, needs immediate webhook-driven orchestration, or needs voice, WhatsApp, RCS, or SMTP relay. The unified option does not provide those channels. It also has no managed email OTP endpoint, so SMS failure cannot become managed email-code verification; the application must build that flow.

This is not a fit for every team.

Polling changes the incident model

Without webhook pushes, delivery observation is delayed by the poll interval. That is acceptable for a short reset window only if the product treats delivery state as diagnostic, not as proof of possession. Verification remains the gate. Poll at a bounded cadence, stop at a terminal state or expiry, and attach the admission layer's attempt ID.

A growing set of nonterminal messages is actionable because it can consume the useful lifetime of the reset flow. A single delayed message is usually a support event. Page on sustained queue age or a broad verification drop, not every late carrier update. Choose thresholds from the marketplace's actual expiry and traffic distribution, then test them during a controlled failure exercise.

Email fallback has a second boundary. Check suppression before sending recovery email, but remember that vendors can define suppression differently. In the three-vendor design, the team must reconcile those meanings. In the single-contract design, the handoff is smaller, although the lack of managed email OTP still leaves verification logic with the application. Tencent email support is pending, so this design is not evidence of domestic compliance.

When this design does not apply

SMS OTP is practical for shipping a second factor quickly, but it is not the strongest authenticator. NIST's identity guidance treats the public switched telephone network as restricted and asks verifiers to consider signals such as device swap or number porting. High-risk payouts, administrator recovery, and accounts with meaningful stored value deserve a phishing-resistant recovery design rather than a larger pile of SMS rules.

Short expiry is not a substitute for throttling. Nor does successful delivery prove that the intended person controls the number. Keep account-enumeration responses uniform, bind a verified attempt to exactly one reset grant, expire that grant promptly, and invalidate it after use. Those are application invariants regardless of vendor.

If this boundary fits your system, generate requests from the published schemas rather than assumptions.

Sources

  • NIST SP 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Clerk documentation
  • Resend documentation
  • RFC 7489: DMARC
  • Infrai machine-readable documentation index

title: Pre-Trained Language Models as Zero-Shot Tools for Social Science Research
description:
arXiv:2610.19048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine demands in social science. Most approaches to these problems require labeled training data that are difficult or costly to acquire. I show that pre-trained language models perform both tasks accurately without requiring task-specific training. For record linkage, I introduce EnsembleLink, an algorithm that uses pre-trained embeddings alongside string-based scorers to retrieve a short list of candidates and then identify the likeliest matches. EnsembleLink matches or exceeds the performance of most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats that those methods are unable to handle. For ethnicity inference from names, I show that large language models (LLMs) achieve up to 83.8% accuracy on U.S. voter files, compared to 78.0% for name-supplemented BISG. Open-weight models offer reproducible implementations that approach these models in accuracy. Moreover, LLMs are able to infer group membership for religious, caste-based, and other ethnic group categories outside of the United States, and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps. Where pre-training encodes the world knowledge required by each task, task-specific labels add less information.

title: CAST: History-Adaptive Spectral Clipping for LLM Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2610.19761v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW's previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output's estimated spectral norm sets each matrix's threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline's final smoothed training loss in 7.2\% fewer steps.

title: Beyond Aggregate Accuracy: Item-Level Transitions in Prompt Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19084v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) uses feedback from model responses to improve prompts automatically. However, its effectiveness is usually measured through overall scores, which do not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers become wrong, or whether improvements extend to unseen questions. We introduce Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (RFDPO), a tool that tracks recoveries (incorrect to correct), regressions (correct to incorrect), and churn (all changed outcomes). RFDPO uses this feedback to guide subsequent revisions and records prompt changes throughout optimization. We evaluate RFDPO across five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy, using GPT-5 as the optimizer and GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 Mini as solvers. Our results show that overall accuracy can hide substantial changes: in five of nine configurations, churn was at least five times the absolute net change, and a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes. Average validation gains were 7.9 percentage points, compared with 5.2 points on held-out tests. In a controlled ablation on LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% ($p=0.024$) while maintaining similar net gains. These findings motivate reporting recovery, regression, churn, and performance on unseen data alongside overall accuracy.

title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.14495v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.

title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
description:
arXiv:2610.19210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}

title: On Windows, four processes appending to one file lost 37 of 200 lines
description:
My CI failed with this, only on the Windows runner, on a commit that changed nothing but a few GIFs:

receipts: Unexpected token '\', "\hostedtoo"... is not valid JSON

The same test had passed on that runner a few hours earlier. Here is what it was, because it is a small bug that is easy to ship.

The setup

Receipts runs the tests a change added or edited twice: with the change, and with the changed source files put back the way they were. For pytest it loads a tiny plugin that writes one JSON line per test result into a file, and the Node side reads that file afterwards.

def _emit(record):
    out = os.environ.get("RECEIPTS_PYTEST_OUT")
    if out:
        with open(out, "a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            fh.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")

One file, opened in append mode, one line per record. Fine, until the project uses pytest-xdist. Then several worker processes run the tests, and at the end every one of them writes a record with the list of modules it imported. Those records are long, full of paths like \hostedtoolcache\windows\Python\.... That is the fragment in the error: the start of a line that got torn in half.

The repro

Four processes, each appending the same long JSON line 50 times to one file:

import json, os, multiprocessing as mp

def worker(out, n):
    rec = {"files": [r"\hostedtoolcache\windows\Python\Lib\m%04d.py" % i for i in range(400)]}
    for _ in range(n):
        with open(out, "a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            fh.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = "race.jsonl"
    ps = [mp.Process(target=worker, args=(out, 50)) for _ in range(4)]
    [p.start() for p in ps]; [p.join() for p in ps]
    print(sum(1 for _ in open(out, encoding="utf-8")), "lines")

On my Windows machine: 163 lines instead of 200. 37 writes simply vanished. With records of different lengths you also get torn lines instead of clean losses, which is what CI hit.

Why

On POSIX, O_APPEND means "move to the end and write" happens as one step for each write(), so concurrent appenders don't overwrite each other. On Windows, the C runtime emulates append mode: it seeks to the end, then writes. Two processes can both seek to the same end and the second write lands on top of the first. Nothing errors, data is just gone.

It only showed up now because it needs two xdist workers to finish within the same moment. It had been passing for weeks.

The fix

Stop sharing the file. The controlling process keeps out.json, each xdist worker writes out.json.<worker id>, and the reader picks up all of them:

worker = getattr(_config, "workerinput", None)
if worker is not None:
    out = "%s.%s" % (out, worker.get("workerid", os.getpid()))

While I was there, the reader stopped throwing on a line it can't parse: a run killed for hanging can leave a half-written last line, and the records before it still count.

The regression test doesn't try to reproduce the race (that would be a flaky test about flakiness). It checks the mechanism directly: a worker writes to its own file, the controller to the main one, and a torn line at the end doesn't sink the read. It fails on the old plugin and passes on the new one, which, given what the tool is for, felt like the least I could do.

Takeaway

If several processes append to one file, it works on Linux and macOS and loses data on Windows, quietly and rarely. Give each process its own file, or take a lock.

I drafted this post with an AI assistant. The error, the numbers and the code are from the actual CI run, my machine and the commit: https://github.com/syntaxixr/receipts/commit/70bb9b2

title: AlignPoison: Conditional Targeted Poisoning of Generative Recommenders via Decoding-Aligned Prefixes
description:
arXiv:2610.14487v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation models based on autoregressive decoding have been adopted as alternatives to classical ranking-based systems. While their modeling flexibility has been widely studied, their resilience to data poisoning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we ask: how susceptible are generative recommenders to conditional targeted poisoning? Under a realistic setting where an adversary can inject limited malicious interactions and query a recommendation API as a black box, our empirical study shows that generative recommenders are vulnerable: injecting fewer than 1% synthetic interactions significantly increases the likelihood of promoting malicious targets under the trigger. To characterize this vulnerability, we analyze the synthesis of malicious interactions from two perspectives: (i) decoding alignment and (ii) prefix popularity. We observe that short, context-aligned prefixes that are both common under the model's induced transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger consistently amplify targeted promotion. Motivated by this analysis, we develop AlignPoison, a black-box framework that discovers and samples context-aligned prefixes from API outputs. We conduct experiments on benchmarks in unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation settings. Results show that these prefixes outperform competitive baselines, improving ASR lift by up to 16.3 percentage points and highlighting a decoding-dependent, context-sensitive poisoning vulnerability in generative recommendation models.

title: 7 CSS Myths Beginners Should Stop Believing
description:
If you're learning CSS, you've probably heard a lot of advice.

Some of it is helpful.

Some of it is incomplete.

And some of it is simply a myth.

The problem is that beginners often don't know which is which.

You might hear someone say:

“You need to memorize CSS properties.”

Or:

“CSS is just for making websites look pretty.”

Or perhaps:

“Just add more margin if something isn't aligned.”

So you try it.

And suddenly you're staring at your stylesheet wondering why everything has moved 47 pixels to the left. 😂

CSS becomes much easier to learn when you understand how it actually works, rather than relying on random rules you've heard from other people.

Let's clear up seven common CSS myths beginners should stop believing.

Myth #1: “You Need to Memorize Every CSS Property”

This is one of the first traps beginners fall into.

You see developers writing CSS quickly and think:

“They must have every property memorized.”

Not necessarily.

CSS has a large number of properties, values, layout techniques, and combinations.

Trying to memorize everything isn't the most useful way to learn.

Instead, focus on understanding the important concepts.

For example, learn what these do:

color
background
font-size
margin
padding
width
height
display
position
flex
grid

But don't feel like you have failed because you forgot a property.

Even experienced developers look things up.

The important skill is knowing what you're trying to accomplish and knowing how to find the appropriate CSS solution.

A better learning approach

Instead of:

“I must memorize everything.”

Think:

“I need to understand the concepts and know how to find the details.”

Learn.

Practice.

Build.

Reference documentation when necessary.

That's a much more realistic approach to learning CSS.

Myth #2: “CSS Is Just About Changing Colours”

This myth probably comes from the fact that colour is one of the easiest CSS properties to demonstrate.

You write:

h1 {
color: blue;
}

And immediately see a change.

But CSS goes far beyond colours.

CSS controls many aspects of how a webpage is presented, including:

Layout

How elements are arranged on the page.

Spacing

The space inside and around elements.

Typography

Fonts, sizes, weights, line height, and text presentation.

Sizing

How wide or tall elements are.

Alignment

How elements are positioned relative to one another.

Positioning

Where elements appear within the page.

Responsive design

How layouts adapt to different screen sizes.

Animations and transitions

How visual changes happen over time.

CSS can even dramatically change the layout of the same HTML without changing the underlying HTML structure.

So saying CSS is “just colours” is like saying a house is just paint.

Colour is one part of the presentation.

CSS controls much more.

Myth #3: “Good CSS Means Using Lots of Effects”

This is another common beginner mistake.

You discover:

Box shadows
Gradients
Animations
Transitions
Transforms
Glowing effects

And suddenly you want to use all of them.

😂

The result might look impressive to you for five minutes.

But good CSS isn't about using as many effects as possible.

A website can have:

simple colours
clean spacing
consistent typography
sensible layouts
subtle interactions

…and still look professional.

In fact, adding unnecessary effects can make an interface harder to understand.

Imagine a website where every button moves, every heading animates, every card has multiple shadows, and every section has a different gradient.

There may be plenty happening visually.

But that doesn't automatically mean the design is better.

Good CSS should have a purpose.

Ask:

Does this style improve clarity?

Does it improve usability?

Does it support the visual hierarchy?

Does it help the user understand what to do?

If the answer is no, you may not need the effect.

Sometimes the most professional CSS is the CSS you barely notice.

Myth #4: “You Need a Framework Before You Can Learn CSS”

Frameworks can be extremely useful.

But you don't need a CSS framework before learning CSS itself.

Imagine trying to learn how a car works by only learning how to drive one specific model.

You might get around.

But your understanding of what's happening underneath may be limited.

The same idea applies to CSS.

Before depending heavily on a framework, it's useful to understand fundamental CSS concepts such as:

Box Model

Flexbox

Grid

Positioning

Responsive Design

Cascade

Specificity

Inheritance

Once you understand these concepts, frameworks become easier to understand because you can recognize the CSS ideas behind the tools.

Frameworks aren't the enemy.

The issue is using a tool without understanding the underlying concepts.

Learn the foundation first.

Then use tools to become more productive.

Myth #5: “If Something Doesn't Align, Just Add More Margins”

This one deserves special attention.

Because almost every beginner eventually does it.

Your element is too far to the left.

You add:

margin-left: 20px;

Still wrong?

Try:

margin-left: 40px;

Still wrong?

Maybe:

margin-left: 80px;

😂

Congratulations.

You've moved the problem instead of solving it.

Margins aren't bad.

They're an important part of CSS.

The problem is using them to compensate for an issue you haven't identified.

If something isn't aligned correctly, the real problem might be:

Flexbox
Grid
Padding
Width
Height
Box sizing
Alignment properties
Positioning
Document flow

Instead of asking:

“What margin should I add?”

Ask:

“Why is this element not where I expect it to be?”

That question will take you much further.

Myth #6: “Responsive Design Can Be Added Later”

Imagine building an entire website for a desktop screen.

Everything looks perfect.

Then you open it on your phone.

And suddenly:

The text is too large.

The buttons don't fit.

The navigation breaks.

Images overflow.

The layout becomes difficult to use.

Now you're trying to repair a structure that wasn't designed with smaller screens in mind.

Responsive design is about creating interfaces that adapt to different screen sizes and devices.

That doesn't mean every website needs a completely different design for every device.

It means you should think about how your layout behaves as the available space changes.

A website may be viewed on:

📱 Smartphones

📱 Tablets

💻 Laptops

🖥️ Desktop monitors

Different screen sizes create different layout challenges.

Responsive thinking should happen during development.

Don't treat it as a final decoration you add after everything else is finished.

Think about:

Flexible widths
Relative units
Media queries
Flexible layouts
Responsive images
Mobile navigation
Text scaling
Content hierarchy

The earlier you consider responsiveness, the easier it becomes to build a layout that adapts naturally.

Myth #7: “CSS Is Only for Designers”

This is another misunderstanding.

CSS is certainly important for visual design, but it isn't exclusively a “designer thing.”

CSS is a core part of frontend development.

If you're building websites, you need to understand how HTML structure becomes a usable interface.

A frontend developer might need to understand:

Layout
Spacing
Responsive behaviour
Typography
Component styling
Positioning
Accessibility considerations
Browser rendering
CSS architecture

You don't have to become a professional visual designer to learn CSS.

But understanding CSS can make you a much more capable frontend developer.

A simple way to think about the core frontend technologies is:

HTML → Structure

CSS → Presentation and Layout

JavaScript → Behaviour and Interactivity

Each has a different primary responsibility, but they work together.

So, What Should Beginners Actually Focus On?

If you shouldn't memorize everything, add endless effects, depend immediately on frameworks, or solve every problem with margins…

What should you learn?

Start with the fundamentals.

  1. Understand the Box Model

Learn how:

Content → Padding → Border → Margin

affect the size and spacing of elements.

This alone will help explain many layout problems.

  1. Learn Selectors

Understand how to target elements using:

Element selectors
Classes
IDs
Attribute selectors
Descendant relationships

Selectors are fundamental to writing effective CSS.

  1. Learn Flexbox

Flexbox is extremely useful for arranging elements along one dimension.

Learn concepts such as:

display: flex
justify-content
align-items
flex-direction
gap
flex-wrap

Don't just memorize the properties.

Understand what problem Flexbox is solving.

  1. Learn CSS Grid

Grid is useful for two-dimensional layouts.

Understand:

Rows
Columns
Gaps
Grid areas
Flexible tracks

Again, focus on the concept rather than memorizing every possible combination.

  1. Understand the Cascade and Specificity

This becomes extremely important as your stylesheets grow.

Learn why one rule may override another.

Understanding specificity can save you from repeatedly adding random CSS or reaching for !important.

  1. Learn Responsive Design

Understand how your layout behaves when the available space changes.

Practice building interfaces that work across different screen sizes.

  1. Practice Debugging

This is one of the most valuable skills you can develop.

When your CSS doesn't work, don't immediately rewrite everything.

Ask:

What did I expect?

What actually happened?

Which rule controls this element?

Is another rule overriding it?

What does the browser's Developer Tools show?

The goal isn't simply to make the problem disappear.

The goal is to understand why it happened.

The Bigger Lesson About Learning CSS

Many beginners approach CSS as if the goal is to memorize a huge list of commands.

But CSS isn't really about memorization.

It's about understanding relationships.

You need to understand how:

HTML elements + CSS selectors + properties + values + the cascade + layout systems

work together.

Once you understand those relationships, learning new CSS techniques becomes much easier.

You don't need to know everything.

You need a solid foundation and a willingness to investigate when something doesn't work.

Don't Be Afraid to Break Things

One of the best ways to learn CSS is to experiment.

Change a value.

See what happens.

Remove a property.

See what changes.

Try Flexbox.

Break the layout.

Fix it.

Change the width.

Resize the browser.

Watch the layout respond.

Use Developer Tools.

Inspect the element.

Try something different.

Every experiment teaches you something.

And sometimes the mistake teaches you more than the successful result.

Final Thoughts

CSS has a reputation for being frustrating.

And yes, sometimes it can be.

But many frustrations become easier once you stop relying on myths and start understanding the fundamentals.

You don't need to memorize every property.

CSS isn't just about colours.

More effects don't automatically mean better CSS.

You don't need a framework before learning the basics.

More margins aren't always the solution.

Responsive design shouldn't be an afterthought.

And CSS isn't only for designers.

Instead:

Understand the fundamentals.

Build real projects.

Experiment.

Debug your mistakes.

Use documentation when you need it.

Keep improving.

The goal isn't to become someone who never makes CSS mistakes.

The goal is to become someone who knows how to understand and solve them.

And that is a much more useful skill.

Which CSS myth did you believe when you first started learning?

Share it in the comments. 👇

Someone else learning CSS may be believing the same thing.

title: Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.19587v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? We answer this question with a multi-agent framework grounded in Moral Foundations Theory (MFT). Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.

title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
description:
arXiv:2610.19095v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.

title: CSS-Only Custom Elements for Accessibility (a11y)
description:
In CSS-Only Custom Elements for Layouts, I used undefined custom-element tags to define an API for layout primitives.

That technique can also be used to improve accessibility in your application.

Building visually-hidden

One of the most common accessibility patterns is visually hidden content that remains available to screen readers and other assistive technology.

An element that is merely transparent or moved off-screen is not always equivalent to hidden content. It can still affect layout, receive focus, or be exposed inconsistently. Use a deliberate clipping pattern:

/**
 * Visually hides content while keeping it available to assistive technology.
 */
visually-hidden {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1px;
  height: 1px;
  padding: 0;
  margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip: rect(0 0 0 0);
  clip-path: inset(50%);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border: 0;

  /* Restores visibility while the element or one of its descendants contains focus. */
  &:focus-within {
    position: static;
    width: auto;
    height: auto;
    margin: 0;
    overflow: visible;
    clip: auto;
    clip-path: none;
    white-space: normal;
  }
}

The element can now carry context without changing the visual design:

<button type="button">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 16 16"><!-- icon --></svg>
  <visually-hidden>Open navigation</visually-hidden>
</button>

The button is still the semantic and interactive element. visually-hidden only changes how its child text is presented.

If the element contains a focusable descendant, :focus-within restores the wrapper automatically while that descendant has focus.

NOTE: Do not use this element for content that shouldn't be available to everyone. For that, use the native hidden attribute or display: none.

Building skip-link

Skip links are a useful example because they combine an accessible name, keyboard focus, and visual presentation:

/**
 * A keyboard-accessible link that becomes visible when focused.
 */
skip-link {
  display: block;
}

skip-link > a {
  position: absolute;
  top: 1rem;
  left: 1rem;
  z-index: 1000;
  transform: translateY(-200%);
  padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem;
  background: Canvas;
  color: CanvasText;
  border: 2px solid currentColor;
}

skip-link > a:focus-visible {
  transform: translateY(0);
}

<skip-link>
  <a href="#main-content">Skip to main content</a>
</skip-link>

<header><!-- site navigation --></header>
<main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">
  <h1>Dashboard</h1>
</main>

The target needs a stable id. tabindex="-1" allows a script or a browser to move focus to the main region without adding it to the normal tab sequence.

The custom element does not make the link a skip link. The nested native <a>, its href, and the target relationship do that. The custom element only gives the pattern a discoverable styling hook.

Building reduced-motion

Motion preferences can also be standardized without JavaScript. A common misconception is that prefers-reduced-motion: reduce means every animation and transition must be turned off. The goal is to minimize non-essential motion while preserving information and interaction.

A wrapper can provide a practical boundary for controlling descendant animations, especially in an area of the page that comes from a third-party component or code you do not own:

/**
 * Minimizes non-essential motion for its descendants when requested.
 */
reduced-motion {
  display: contents;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  reduced-motion,
  reduced-motion * {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

<reduced-motion>
  <aside class="toast">Message sent</aside>
</reduced-motion>

This is a policy boundary, not a guarantee that every animation has become accessible. Motion that communicates meaning may need an alternate presentation, and the preference should be respected by JavaScript-driven animation too.

What CSS cannot do

It is tempting to create elements such as <a11y-button>, <a11y-dialog>, or <a11y-live-region> and assume the names communicate their purpose. They do not.

CSS cannot:

  • add a button or other relevant ARIA role, click behavior, or keyboard activation to a generic element.
  • create an accessible name for an unlabeled control.
  • reliably announce changing content to a screen reader.
  • manage focus when a dialog opens or closes.
  • validate a widget's state or keep aria-expanded synchronized.

Use a native element first. Add ARIA only when native HTML cannot express the required relationship or state. Use JavaScript when interaction needs state, focus management, announcements, or event coordination.

Accessibility and the cascade

CSS-only elements have no shadow root, so their styles participate in the global cascade. That makes the API easy to override, but it also means a broad rule can interfere with consumer content.

Keep the base selector low-specificity when possible:

:where(visually-hidden, skip-link) {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

Scope descendant rules narrowly. Target specific interactive elements (a, button, etc.) rather than using broad universal selectors. A small selector surface is easier to audit.

Document the attributes and custom properties as part of the public API. A Custom Elements Manifest can describe CSS-only elements when the stylesheet includes the expected JSDoc comments, even though there is no JavaScript class.

When you should use these

CSS-only accessibility elements are useful when the primitive is about presentation or a reusable styling boundary:

  • A design system can standardize visually hidden content.
  • Templates can make skip links and reduced-motion boundaries discoverable.
  • Native HTML can remain responsible for meaning and interaction.
  • There is no JavaScript cost or custom-element upgrade lifecycle.

Conclusion

CSS-only custom elements can make accessibility patterns visible in markup, but they cannot make an inaccessible structure accessible by naming it.

The strongest design is a division of responsibility: native HTML provides semantics and interaction, ARIA fills specific gaps, JavaScript manages state and focus when required, and CSS handles presentation and user preferences.

When that contract is explicit, a tag and a stylesheet can provide a useful accessibility primitive without pretending to replace the platform.
