title: Scaling Actors and Workers With HPA In Agent Substrate
description:
The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available to consume, digest, and schedule what you need to run. In the case of agentic workloads, that's typically Agents. For example, is there enough memory to run multi-Actor Workers? Or do you need to scale Workers out to schedule Actors accordingly?

In this blog post, you'll learn how to schedule and scale Actors (where Agents run) via Workers and WorkerPools for any number of Actors that need to run within your environment.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this blog post from a hands-on perspective, you will need:

  1. A cluster with Agent Substrate running (e.g., GKE or a local cluster like Kind).
    1. Agentgateway set as the dataplane proxy for your atenet-router.
  2. Worker images built with your underlying isolation layer (e.g., gVisor).
    1. You can build these images via the Agent Substrate repo (you need to clone it down) ./hack/run-tool.sh and see how to do it here.

What Will You Be Deploying?

Going through this blog post, you will be:

  1. Deploying Actors
  2. "Parking" an Actor until a Worker is ready to schedule it.
  3. Scaling out Workers so if you have, let's say 3 Actors but only 2 Workers, HPA can scale out the Worker (a Pod) to schedule the third Actor.

The goal here is to park Actors when there aren't enough Workers, or memory in the Workers, readily available to schedule an Actor. The Workers in this blog have a 1Gi memory limit, and each Actor asks for 768Mi. A second Actor needs 1536Mi, which means it won't fit. If anyone raises the WorkerPool memory or lowers the Template's, Actors will start sharing workers. Once a Worker is made available, the Actor can be automatically scheduled on said Worker so your Agent can run.

To go through the hands-on portion of this blog post in the way that it is configured, you'll want to clone this repo as it has all of the scripts and HPA configurations to run the lab along with Step 1 and Step 2, which is building the images and deploying your Workers.

Deploying Actors

The first step is deploying Actors. All Actors, when deployed, are automatically in a "suspended" state. Because they're in a suspended state, they aren't technically running, which is where the efficiency and overall performance of Agent Substrate come into play. Actors are only running when there is an active session to said Actor. That way, they aren't consuming resources (CPU/memory) for no reason.

Actors sit in a "warm state", which means they don't take seconds to resume. That way, when you create a session to an Actor that's running an Agent, it won't feel like the Actor is in a cold state and takes forever to resume/respond to the request that you're sending to the Actor running an Agent.

  1. Deploy the Actors. The pool caps each worker at 1Gi of memory (manifests/workerpool.yaml.tmpl), and the template asks for 768Mi per actor (manifests/actortemplate.yaml.tmpl). The scheduler only places an actor where its memory still fits, so a second actor never does. 
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  kubectl ate create actor "a$i" -a ate-lab-burst --template burst
done

💡

the burst template is what's created in actortemplate.yaml.tmpl.

All six start in ACTOR_STATE_SUSPENDED. They exist only as records, plus the golden snapshot in GCS.

  1. Confirm that the Actors are in a suspended state and in Agent Substrate. 
kubectl get actors -a ate-lab-burst

You should see an output similar to the screenshot below.

As you're going through the rest of this blog post, an important note to keep in mind is that because six Actors were deployed and there are two Workers, there's a 3:1 ratio here. That means two Actors can be scheduled, but four cannot and therefore sit in a "parked" state until a Worker is available.

Park and Schedule An Actor

With the Actors deployed, let's resume two of the Actors, and then try a third, which will sit in a parked state until a Worker becomes readily available.

  1. Port-forward the router so it's open and accepting requests (for when a client or something like curl needs to reach it). 
kubectl -n ate-system port-forward svc/atenet-router 8000:80
  1. Fill both Workers with Actors. 
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a1" http://localhost:8000
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a2" http://localhost:8000
  1. Check and confirm that both Workers got assigned an Actor. 
kubectl ate get workers -n ate-lab-burst

You'll see an output similar to the below:

NAME                                   POOL    STATE                 ACTORS   CPU      MEMORY      POD                                    AGE
cc852e96-6035-47a1-96e9-1b85d2b47c95   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t26t7   20m
43210b1e-2a85-496c-96e9-497575d4e200   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t7gm6   20m
  1. Try assigning a third Actor. 
curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll get a "request timed out" with a 504. The reason why is that there isn't enough memory on either Worker to schedule the third Actor.

  1. Suspend Actor 1 and then run the curl again. 
kubectl ate suspend actor a1 -a ate-lab-burst

curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll see that Actor 3 can now be scheduled.

Add HPA For WorkerPools

In the previous section, you saw that because there are two Workers available within the WorkerPool, only 2/3 of the Actors could be scheduled on the Worker until a Worker freed up.

As you read in the What Will You Be Deploying? section, multiple Actors CAN be scheduled on one Worker as long as there's enough memory to support it. The scenario we want HPA for WorkerPools is when the Worker runs out of memory and therefore a new Worker (Pod/replica) needs to be created.

Tldr; Where HPA comes into play is scaling out an Actor to another Worker (or as many Workers as are needed based on how many Actors are waiting to be unparked).

💡 Because you created six Actors in the Deploying Actors section and the HPA config allows up to 10 replicas, all six Actors will be deployed onto the Workers as there will now be more Workers available because the replica count in the HPA config goes up to ten.

  1. Use the burst script to wake up all six Actors 
./scripts/burst.sh -m hold -d 120

You'll see 504s (timeouts) for the 4 Actors that aren't scheduled on Workers as they aren't scheduled and therefore, aren't running.

  1. In another terminal, scale your WorkerPool to 6 replicas 
kubectl -n ate-lab-burst scale workerpool burst --replicas=6
  1. Go back to the first terminal and you'll see the scale start to occur (from 2/2 to 6/6). This shows that all six Actors are now up and running with successful 200's.

This proves out that scaling the Workers officially worked!

Wrapping Up

Scale becomes increasingly important in the world of agentic because it impacts so many areas. It's not just one app that impacts a department or a particular functionality of an app that impacts a customer. If an Agent is down, it can potentially impact the entire organization. That's why ensuring that scale can be properly implemented across Agents isn't just about the tech teams; it's everyone from engineering to marketing to HR and all teams that are incorporating AI into daily workflows.

title: Are Multimodal Benchmarks Really Useful? Item-Level Multimodal Benchmark Diagnosis via Structure-Response Co-Calibration
description:
arXiv:2610.14542v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal benchmarks are central to evaluating whether models can reason over information from multiple modalities. However, existing literature has revealed that some benchmarks may contain shortcut items that can be answered from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone, thus failing to reflect models' true cross-modal inference ability. Existing methods for assessing benchmarks typically rely either on intrinsic item structure or extrinsic model response behavior, which are not adequate for a comprehensive diagnosis. To fill in this gap, we propose SRCoD, a structure-response co-calibrated diagnosis framework for item-level diagnosis of modality dependence in multimodal benchmarks. SRCoD estimates sample-wise multimodal information structure from benchmark content and target answers, and uses this signal as a soft structural anchor for modality-conditioned item response modeling. The learned model produces a calibrated item-level diagnostic profile that reflects how strongly an item depends on different forms of modality evidence, enabling fine-grained benchmark analysis beyond aggregate accuracy. SRCoD also provides interpretable attribution of the diagnosis results. Extensive experiments under two complementary protocols, i.e., benchmark-refinement oriented validation and human-labeled item validation, demonstrate that SRCoD outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark diagnosis methods.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Installation FAQ: 10 Questions Beginners Ask
description:
Installing GBase Database(GBase 8s) for the first time can raise questions about Linux users, environment variables, character sets, network connections, and instance startup. This FAQ answers 10 common installation questions and explains how to troubleshoot typical issues without making risky configuration changes.

Q1: Can I install GBase Database(GBase 8s) as the root user?

Answer: Yes. In a typical GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation workflow, use root to install the database software and perform system-level configuration, then switch to the dedicated gbasedbt account to initialize and run the database instance.

Typical Workflow

Step 1: Install the software as root.

Run the installation program according to the instructions provided with your GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation package.

Step 2: Prepare the database environment.

Verify that the required directories, ownership, permissions, and environment variables are configured correctly for the gbasedbt account.

Step 3: Switch to the database user.

su - gbasedbt

Step 4: Initialize the instance.

Run the documented instance initialization command under the gbasedbt account. For example, oninit -ivy may be used when initializing a new instance, provided this matches the procedure for your version and configuration.

Important: Do not run instance initialization commands against an existing database as a troubleshooting shortcut. Confirm the instance state and follow the appropriate startup or recovery procedure.

Q2: Why can't I connect when sqlhosts contains localhost?

Answer: The cause depends on the connection protocol, server configuration, and how the hostname resolves.

In GBase Database(GBase 8s), the sqlhosts entry specifies the server name, connection protocol, host, and service or port. For TCP connections, an entry may look like this:

gbase01 onsoctcp 192.168.1.100 9088

This is an illustrative example, not a universal configuration. Replace the server name, address, and port with the values used by your installation.

When troubleshooting, verify that:

  • The client uses the expected server name.
  • The host resolves to the correct address.
  • The configured protocol matches the intended connection method.
  • The server is listening on the configured port.
  • Firewall rules allow the connection when connecting remotely.

localhost does not automatically mean a connection will fail. Check the actual sqlhosts configuration and connection error before changing it.

Q3: Can I change the character set after installation?

Answer: It depends on which character set or locale setting you need to change.

GBase Database(GBase 8s) environments may use settings such as DB_LOCALE and CLIENT_LOCALE to control database and client character handling. These settings serve different purposes, and changing a client environment variable does not convert existing database data.

Before making changes:

  1. Identify the database's current locale and the application's expected encoding.
  2. Check the requirements for the specific database and client version.
  3. Test Chinese text insertion and retrieval in a non-production environment.
  4. Back up important data before performing any migration or conversion.

If an existing database must use a different database locale, creating a new database with the intended configuration and migrating the data may be necessary. Confirm the supported migration procedure first.

Do not assume that changing DB_LOCALE or CLIENT_LOCALE alone will convert an existing database. Choose the locale based on the application's requirements and the character sets supported by the installation.

Q4: Why does oninit produce no obvious output?

Answer: Limited terminal output does not necessarily mean that startup has failed.

Start by checking the instance status:

onstat -

Then inspect the relevant environment variables:

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$ONCONFIG"

If the expected environment is configured, inspect the message log. For example, some installations use a log under the database installation's temporary directory:

tail -50 "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log"

The actual log location depends on the configuration. Check the configured message-log path if this file does not exist.

Also verify that you are using the correct database account and configuration file. Avoid repeatedly running initialization commands to troubleshoot a startup problem; first determine the instance's current state and read the error messages.

Q5: What is the default port for GBase Database(GBase 8s)?

Answer: Port 9088 is commonly seen in GBase 8s examples, but the actual port depends on the instance configuration.

Check the configured service or port in sqlhosts and the corresponding network configuration. You can inspect listening TCP ports with:

ss -lntp

If you need to change the port, follow the configuration procedure for your version and ensure the client connection settings match the server.

Changing a port may also require updates to firewall rules, monitoring systems, and application connection strings. Do not assume that every installation uses the same port.

Q6: What should I do if dependency installation fails?

Answer: First, identify the missing package or library instead of installing a large, generic list of dependencies.

On a compatible RPM-based Linux system, you can check whether package repositories are available with:

yum repolist

If the installer reports a missing library, check the exact package name and version required by your GBase Database(GBase 8s) release.

Common troubleshooting steps include:

  • Confirming that the operating system version is supported.
  • Checking whether the required repositories are enabled.
  • Verifying package names for the current distribution.
  • Checking library architecture and version compatibility.
  • Using approved offline RPM packages when the environment has no internet access.

Do not assume that packages such as Java, development libraries, or terminal libraries are required for every installation. Follow the prerequisites for your specific release.

Q7: Which operating systems does GBase Database(GBase 8s) support?

Answer: Supported operating systems depend on the product release, package, CPU architecture, and vendor certification.

Before installing GBase Database(GBase 8s), verify the official compatibility information for your exact version. Check:

  • Linux distribution and release
  • CPU architecture
  • Required system libraries
  • Kernel and runtime prerequisites
  • Supported deployment and maintenance configurations

Do not choose an operating system solely because an older installation guide uses it. A distribution that worked for a previous release may not be supported by a newer package.

For production systems, use a supported configuration and confirm the relevant requirements with the official product documentation or vendor support.

Q8: How can I verify that the installation succeeded?

Answer: Verify the instance state, network listener, and database connectivity separately.

Step 1: Check the instance status.

onstat -

Review the output to determine whether the instance is online and operating as expected.

Step 2: Check the network listener.

ss -lntp

Confirm that the expected port is listening. A listening port alone does not prove that database authentication and SQL queries work.

Step 3: Test a database connection.

Use the supported client for your installation, such as dbaccess where available, and connect to the intended database or a designated test database.

Verify that you can execute a simple query with the expected account and permissions.

A successful installation check should cover all three areas: instance status, network connectivity, and an actual database session.

Q9: Where can I download the GBase Database(GBase 8s) installer?

Answer: Start with the official GBase website:

https://www.gbase.cn/

Check the product documentation and download resources available for your version. Access requirements may vary.

Before downloading, confirm the following:

  • The correct GBase Database(GBase 8s) product and release
  • The target operating system
  • The CPU architecture
  • Installation prerequisites
  • Package integrity and any vendor-provided verification instructions

Keep the installer and its corresponding documentation together so that the installation procedure can be repeated consistently.

Q10: How do I configure automatic startup after installation?

Answer: Use the startup mechanism documented for your GBase Database(GBase 8s) release and operating system.

On a system using systemd, database startup may be integrated with a service unit or a vendor-provided startup script. However, the correct service configuration depends on how the instance starts, the required environment variables, and the expected shutdown procedure.

Before enabling automatic startup, verify:

  1. The correct database service account.
  2. The required environment variables and configuration files.
  3. The documented startup and shutdown commands.
  4. Service dependencies and startup ordering.
  5. Behavior after a restart or unexpected shutdown.

Do not copy a generic systemd template into production without validating its ExecStart, ExecStop, process type, and environment settings. An incorrect shutdown command or service definition can interrupt database operations or cause startup failures.

Test automatic startup and shutdown in a non-production environment first, then document the verified procedure for your deployment.

Final Thoughts

Most GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation problems become easier to diagnose when you verify the environment before changing configuration. Check the database account, locale settings, sqlhosts, instance status, and message logs systematically.

For beginners, three habits are especially valuable:

  • Follow the documentation for the exact product version.
  • Verify each installation stage before moving to the next.
  • Diagnose the underlying error before reinstalling or modifying database files.

A careful installation and verification process helps reduce troubleshooting time and makes future deployments more predictable.

title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
description:
arXiv:2610.14224v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

title: Building a 12-axis political quiz with Vite, TanStack Start and Cloudflare Workers
description:
Most political quizzes squeeze you onto one line, left vs right, or a two-axis compass. I wanted something that keeps questions apart: you can want a strong welfare state and still distrust central government, or love new technology and be socially traditional. So I built The 12 Axes, a free quiz that scores you on twelve independent axes, in English, Spanish and Portuguese.

The statements and the scoring model come from the open-source 12Axes quiz (MIT). My part was the product around it: a fast, server-rendered site with shareable results and no accounts. Here is how it fits together.

The stack

  • Vite for the build and dev server.
  • TanStack Start (with TanStack Router) for file-based routes, server rendering and typed search params.
  • Cloudflare Workers to serve every page from the edge. The quiz itself has no backend at all.

There is no database. Everything a result needs fits in the URL.

Scoring in a dozen lines

Each statement belongs to one axis and points toward one of its two poles. Answers run from -2 (strongly disagree) to +2 (strongly agree). An axis score is the average answer, flipped for statements that point the other way and mapped to 0-100%:

export function scoreQuiz(items: QuizItem[], answers: (number | undefined)[]) {
  const sums = new Array(12).fill(0);
  const counts = new Array(12).fill(0);
  items.forEach((item, i) => {
    const answer = answers[i];
    if (answer === undefined) return;
    sums[item.axis] += answer * (item.level < 4 ? 1 : -1);
    counts[item.axis] += 1;
  });
  return sums.map((sum, axis) =>
    counts[axis] ? Math.round(50 + (50 * sum) / (2 * counts[axis])) : 50
  );
}

A skipped axis stays at 50, the neutral middle, rather than breaking the result.

A result that fits in 24 characters

Twelve scores from 0 to 100 need two base-36 digits each, so a whole result is a 24-character string:

export const encodeScores = (scores: number[]) =>
  scores
    .map((s) => Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.round(s))).toString(36).padStart(2, '0'))
    .join('');

That string goes in the result URL as ?r=. Sharing a result is sharing a link: the result page rebuilds every score, match and chart from those 24 characters, so nothing is stored anywhere. Decoding validates strictly (/^[0-9a-z]{24}$/, every value ≤ 100) and anything else falls back to an empty state. TanStack Router's typed search params make this pleasant: the route declares the param, and the page component gets a typed value.

Matching ideologies and historical figures

Two kinds of matches are shown, and both use root-mean-square distance:

  • Ideologies are defined on four classic dimensions (economy, power, diplomacy, culture), so they are compared on the four matching axes. Match = 100 minus the RMS gap.

  • Historical figures have a position on up to twelve axes. Many took no stand on some of them; Aristotle had no view on biotechnology. Skipping those axes would favour figures with few known positions, because they get compared on less. So an unknown axis counts as a fixed gap of 28 points, and a figure needs at least six known axes to be ranked at all.

One bug worth sharing: I had entered one axis backwards for twenty figures, and every match still looked plausible. Now a unit test pins the direction of every axis with figures whose positions are unambiguous. Plausible-looking output is the hardest kind of wrong to notice.

Progress that survives a reload

The full test has 288 statements, so losing your place hurts. Progress lives in localStorage and is restored on load. Answers never leave the browser, which is also why there is no sign-up.

A share card made from the DOM

The share card is a normal React component styled like the rest of the site. To share it as an image, it is rendered off-screen and turned into a PNG in the browser. On phones that support the Web Share API with files, the share sheet gets the image directly:

if (navigator.canShare?.({ files: [file] })) {
  await navigator.share({ files: [file], url, title });
}

Elsewhere you get a download button. Building the card as a component, not a canvas drawing, means it uses the same fonts, translations and layout code as the page.

Three languages, one set of routes

English lives at /, Spanish at /es/ and Portuguese at /pt/. Every page renders hreflang alternates and a canonical URL. Each language also gets its own Open Graph image, so a link shared in a Spanish group chat shows a Spanish preview.

Running on Cloudflare Workers

The Worker's fetch handler is a thin wrapper around the TanStack Start handler. It is also where redirects belong:

  • the old launch domain 301s to the same path on the new one;
  • plain http:// 301s to https://, with a 308 for anything other than GET/HEAD so a request body is never silently turned into a GET.

Both live in a pure function with unit tests, including one that feeds each redirect target back in and expects no further redirect. A redirect loop on the edge is not something you want to discover from Search Console.

Deploys are one wrangler deploy. The custom domain, TLS and caching come with Workers.

SEO for a quiz site

A few things mattered more than I expected:

  • Server-render everything crawlable, including FAQ answers inside collapsed panels: hidden="until-found" keeps them in the HTML while staying collapsed.
  • A sitemap with real lastmod dates and an IndexNow ping after each content change, so Bing and other IndexNow engines hear about new pages without waiting for a crawl.
  • An explainer page per axis, so the site answers "what does this axis mean" and not just "take the quiz".

Try it

The quick test takes 60 statements, about six minutes: 12axes.site. I'd love to hear which axis surprised you, and whether the historical-figure match felt fair.

title: STP-GUI: Spatially-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Web-GUI Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.20390v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the rapid development of vision-language models (VLMs), Web-GUI agents have achieved promising performance in interacting with real-world interfaces through screenshot-based grounding. However, high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn histories introduce excessive visual tokens, causing substantial inference overhead. Existing token pruning methods, mainly designed for natural images, often select tokens independently based on importance scores, which can fragment the local visual structures required for recognizing small GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and hyperlinks. In this work, we propose STP-GUI (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query-guided token pruning framework that preserves fine-grained instruction-conditioned token scoring while performing spatially coherent window-level selection under aggressive token reduction. A lightweight selector is optimized through policy learning while the VLM backbone remains frozen. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web show that \papername achieves a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff under low token budgets. At 21% token retention, it preserves 77.7% of full-token performance while reducing inference latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%. Results on Android in the Wild further suggest that the method transfers to mobile GUI environments.

title: MIPS: Mitigating Mode Collapse in Reinforcement Learning for Large Outcome Spaces
description:
arXiv:2610.19457v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Expected-reward maximization in reinforcement learning concentrates probability mass on a few outcomes, even in tasks that require many distinct, high-quality solutions, a failure known as mode collapse. Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) counters this in group-based policy gradients such as GRPO by dividing each reward by the outcome's probability, estimated from its frequency within the sampled group. When the outcome space is large relative to the group, outcomes rarely repeat and these estimates become uninformative. Since an outcome can be constructed along many trajectories, its probability is a sum over all of them, and computing it directly is intractable. We propose Marginal IPS (MIPS), which performs marginal evaluation by combining the sampled trajectory with a learned model of the trajectories that lead to each outcome. On Hypergrids, where the exact sampling distribution is computable, MIPS stays near the reward-distribution target as the outcome space grows relative to the rollout group, while frequency-based IPS degrades. In molecular synthesis and phylogenetic inference, MIPS sustains diverse, high-quality sampling where GRPO and frequency-based IPS collapse, showing that MIPS serves as a reliable solution to mode collapse in RL.

title: Go Live Captions and Post-Session Transcripts for Video Room Users
description:
Ship the post-session transcript first, then add live captions only when accessibility requirements or in-meeting comprehension make them mandatory. That recommendation is less glamorous than treating captions as a checkbox, but it respects the hard boundary: captions have a live delivery SLO, while a transcript is a file that can be retained, deleted, and audited after the room closes.

Short answer: a few seconds of caption latency is noticeable and can still be acceptable; missed or badly ordered text during the call cannot be repaired for the person who needed it at that moment. A transcript covers most review, search, handoff, and record-keeping value without joining the media fan-out path. Check accessibility requirements before making that trade, because for some rooms the live path is non-negotiable.

For a developer-tools video room, I would keep room admission narrow with scoped tokens, treat captions as an optional live stream with an explicit degraded mode, and store the final transcript as a private session artifact. Infrai is worth trying for teams that want room tokens and private object storage behind one plain REST API and one key, because there is no client SDK version to carry through two integration surfaces; its public discovery surface and runnable Go examples are a useful second advantage when the platform team needs to inspect request schemas before deployment.

Should users get live captions or a post-session transcript?

WebRTC gets people and media into the room. Caption delivery adds another deadline-sensitive path: audio must be processed, partial text must reach the right room, and updates must be presented in useful order while the speaker is still talking. A delay of a few seconds is visible, even when users accept it. Capacity planning therefore starts with concurrent rooms and fan-out recipients, not with the eventual transcript size.

Users notice.

The SLOs should differ. For captions, measure useful text delivered during the session and bound end-to-end delay; do not hide a missed live delivery behind a successful transcript written later. For the transcript, measure durable completion after room close, then verify that retention and deletion behave as promised. One cannot substitute for the other.

This is also where the trust boundary becomes concrete. The RTC provider handles room media and scoped admission. A speech processor may receive audio. The realtime transport carries caption events. Object storage retains the finished artifact. Before enabling captions, identify the region used at every step, the processor receiving audio, its retention behavior, and the deletion mechanism. A general API layer does not create audio-residency or contractual guarantees on behalf of a specialist processor.

No hand-waving here.

If a user needs captions to participate, loss during fan-out is an availability failure. If users mainly revisit decisions after a demo or support session, the transcript is the smaller and more defensible first release.

Choose the boundary before choosing the vendor

The operational decision is not a feature tally. It is ownership of data during the call and after it.

Stack Strong fit Boundary the platform team still owns
LiveKit plus Amazon S3 Teams wanting a specialist RTC layer and a separately controlled object-store account Two signups, two credential sets, token-to-object glue, processor-region review, retention, and deletion policy
Daily plus Amazon S3 Teams prioritizing a managed video-room product with separate storage control Two signups, two credential sets, artifact transfer, and evidence that media and stored data follow the required regions
Twilio Video plus Amazon S3 Teams already operating Twilio and AWS trust boundaries Cross-provider credentials, artifact handoff, processor contracts, lifecycle policy, and independent outage planning
Pusher plus Amazon S3 Teams that already use Pusher Channels and only need caption-event fan-out RTC, speech processing, token scope, transcript assembly, retention, and deletion remain separate work
Ably plus Amazon S3 Teams needing a dedicated realtime messaging layer for caption events It is not a video-room or transcription replacement; media admission and the final artifact pipeline still need owners
PubNub plus Amazon S3 Teams with an established PubNub event-delivery architecture Room media, speech processing, private artifact transfer, and cross-provider credentials remain outside that layer
Infrai Teams that value one REST surface for scoped room access and private transcript storage One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface; specialist audio processing and its contractual guarantees remain separate

The combined Infrai approach reduces integration surfaces, not accountability. Live discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and room tokens and storage use the same bearer key and base URL. That removes an extra account and credential bridge from this particular handoff. It also concentrates risk, so a platform review should demand region, retention, deletion, and processor evidence before approval rather than infer those properties from API consistency.

LiveKit, Daily, and Twilio remain better choices when their specialist RTC controls, media topology, or existing enterprise agreement decide the architecture. Pusher, Ably, and PubNub are narrower alternatives when the missing component is event fan-out rather than the room itself. Amazon S3 is the clearer storage boundary when the organization already has mature AWS residency, lifecycle, and deletion controls. The right answer can be two vendors. On-call load rises, but contractual and failure domains may be easier to separate.

The limitation is deliberate: Infrai is not suitable when a specialist RTC contract, a separately owned storage account, or independently isolated failure domains are mandatory. This trade-off matters more than reducing the number of credentials.

Put the session artifact behind the same authenticated boundary

The safe implementation issues a scoped room token, gives it to the participant, and uploads only the completed transcript to a private object path. The program below deliberately takes the exact token request as JSON from RTC_TOKEN_REQUEST_JSON; token scope fields must come from the current discovery schema rather than copied prose. It then feeds the token response into the stored audit artifact, demonstrating the handoff without claiming that storage performs speech recognition.

Both writes carry an idempotency key, every request has an explicit method, and 429 responses honor Retry-After or use exponential backoff. The upload never exposes a public URL. In production, keep the token response only if policy permits it; otherwise store a stable, non-secret issuance identifier selected from the documented response schema.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func doWrite(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, endpoint, key, idem string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s returned %d: %s", endpoint, resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s remained rate limited after retries", endpoint)
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    tokenRequest := []byte(os.Getenv("RTC_TOKEN_REQUEST_JSON"))
    bucket := os.Getenv("TRANSCRIPT_BUCKET")
    objectKey := os.Getenv("TRANSCRIPT_OBJECT_KEY")
    transcript := os.Getenv("TRANSCRIPT_TEXT")
    if key == "" || len(tokenRequest) == 0 || bucket == "" || objectKey == "" || transcript == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY, RTC_TOKEN_REQUEST_JSON, TRANSCRIPT_BUCKET, TRANSCRIPT_OBJECT_KEY, and TRANSCRIPT_TEXT")
    }
    if !json.Valid(tokenRequest) {
        panic("RTC_TOKEN_REQUEST_JSON must be valid JSON from the discovery schema")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    tokenResponse, err := doWrite(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/rtc/token/issue", key, "room-token-"+objectKey, tokenRequest)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    artifact, err := json.Marshal(map[string]json.RawMessage{
        "room_token_issue": tokenResponse,
        "transcript":       json.RawMessage(strconv.Quote(transcript)),
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    uploadURL := baseURL + "/storage/object/put/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(objectKey)
    if _, err := doWrite(ctx, client, http.MethodPut, uploadURL, key, "transcript-"+objectKey, artifact); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("private transcript artifact stored")
}

The example has one API key and one base URL. The alternative LiveKit-or-Daily-plus-S3 stack needs two signups, two credential sets, a mapping between room identity and object key, and code to cross that provider boundary. Those are manageable costs, but they belong in the on-call estimate.

Verify delivery, retention, and deletion

Verification needs to exercise user outcomes rather than stop at a successful response. Run a room with caption consumers on a stable connection and after a reconnect; observe whether useful live text arrives within the chosen SLO, and keep transcript completion as a separate check. Do not declare caption success because a final file exists.

Storage can wait. Captions cannot.

For the artifact, confirm that an unauthenticated read fails, an authorized read returns the expected session object, and the object sits in the approved region. Then test the documented deletion operation and verify that the object is no longer retrievable. Retention needs an owner, a duration derived from policy, and evidence from the storage boundary; silence is not a retention policy.

Processor review comes last only in this runbook, not in procurement. Record which specialist receives audio, which region it uses, how long it retains inputs and outputs, and how deletion requests propagate. The evidence may force a different stack. That is a valid result.

Capacity tests should cover peak concurrent rooms, speakers per room, and caption recipients per room. Averages are misleading because fan-out load follows the busy room, while transcript storage follows sessions completed over time. Set separate error budgets so dropping captions cannot be disguised by retrying the later upload.

Roll back without losing the meeting record

The rollback switch disables live caption publication while leaving the room and transcript workflow intact. Announce the degraded state in the product, because silently removing an accessibility feature is not an acceptable recovery mode. If captions are required for participation, the rollback is to stop or reschedule the affected session, not to pretend the transcript is equivalent.

Keep transcript uploads idempotent so a retry cannot create competing artifacts. If the combined API boundary is unavailable, queue the completed transcript inside the approved retention boundary and retry later under the same object key; do not move it to an unreviewed public store. Recovery is complete only after the private object is verified and any temporary copy is deleted according to policy.

The decision rule is blunt: default to a post-session transcript for review value, add live captions when in-session need or accessibility makes their delivery SLO worth owning, and select vendors only after their regional, processor, retention, and deletion boundaries survive review. If the single-key boundary fits that review, start with the Infrai documentation.

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Daily developer documentation
  • Twilio Video documentation
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: A Diagnostic Study of World-Space Human Recovery Under High Camera Dynamics
description:
arXiv:2610.19729v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monocular world-space human recovery methods excel on current benchmarks, but these rarely include fast camera motion. We introduce the K-Pop stress test, broadcast dance videos that combine fast, large camera motion with dense multi-person choreography. Leading methods produce plausible per-frame meshes on these videos, yet their world-space trajectories drift far from the performers' stage positions. Through a systematic diagnosis, we show that the camera and human estimates each remain self-consistent, and that the drift appears when they are combined at mismatched scales. Each is recovered at its own scale, so a mismatch between the two can turn camera motion into human drift that grows with camera displacement and becomes severe in broadcast dance videos. We derive a closed-form correction that estimates this mismatch and applies one scale to all performers, removing the drift while keeping their relative positions in one shared world frame. It requires no retraining and works with existing backends. Combined with physical constraints, the correction yields stable world-space reconstruction for choreography modeling, scene editing, data generation, and virtual reshooting.

title: Why your small business WordPress site says "Not secure" (and a small Python script that checks for it)
description:
Most small business sites I look at don't have exotic problems. They have the same four boring ones:

  1. The TLS certificate is expired or about to expire, so browsers show a full-page warning.
  2. http:// doesn't redirect to https://, so old links and some search results land on the insecure version.
  3. The page is HTTPS but still loads images, scripts or stylesheets over http:// (mixed content). Browsers upgrade or block them, and the padlock can disappear.
  4. There's no responsive viewport tag, so phones render a tiny zoomed-out desktop page.

All four can be seen from the outside with a normal page load, so you can check them without any access to the site. Here's a small script that does exactly that, and then the WordPress fix for each one.

The script

Standard library only, so it runs anywhere Python 3.8+ is installed. It loads the homepage like a browser: no scanning, no guessing paths, no logins.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""site_check.py - a quick, polite HTTPS + mobile sanity check for a small business site.

Standard library only (Python 3.8+). It loads the homepage like a normal browser
would: no port scans, no login attempts, no path guessing.

Usage:  python3 site_check.py example.com [another-site.co.uk ...]
"""
import socket
import ssl
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from html.parser import HTMLParser

UA = "Mozilla/5.0 (site_check.py; quick public health check)"
TIMEOUT = 15


class PageScan(HTMLParser):
    """Collects the viewport tag and any http:// sub-resources on the page."""

    # tag -> attributes that make the browser fetch something
    RESOURCE_ATTRS = {
        "img": ("src", "srcset"), "script": ("src",), "iframe": ("src",),
        "source": ("src", "srcset"), "video": ("src", "poster"),
        "audio": ("src",), "embed": ("src",), "object": ("data",),
    }

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.viewport = None
        self.insecure = []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        a = {k.lower(): (v or "") for k, v in attrs}
        if tag == "meta" and a.get("name", "").lower() == "viewport":
            self.viewport = a.get("content", "")
        if tag == "link" and "stylesheet" in a.get("rel", "").lower():
            self._check(tag, a.get("href", ""))
        for attr in self.RESOURCE_ATTRS.get(tag, ()):
            self._check(tag, a.get(attr, ""))

    def _check(self, tag, value):
        # srcset can hold several URLs: "a.jpg 1x, b.jpg 2x"
        for part in value.split(","):
            url = part.strip().split(" ")[0]
            if url.lower().startswith("http://"):
                self.insecure.append(f"<{tag}> {url}")


def cert_days_left(host):
    """Days until the TLS certificate expires, or the error string if the handshake fails."""
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((host, 443), timeout=TIMEOUT) as sock:
            with ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=host) as tls:
                not_after = tls.getpeercert()["notAfter"]
    except ssl.SSLCertVerificationError as e:
        return f"certificate problem: {e.verify_message}"
    except (OSError, ssl.SSLError) as e:
        return f"no HTTPS connection: {e}"
    expires = datetime.fromtimestamp(ssl.cert_time_to_seconds(not_after), timezone.utc)
    return (expires - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).days


def fetch(url):
    """Follow redirects like a browser. Returns (final_url, status, html)."""
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=TIMEOUT) as r:
            return r.geturl(), r.status, r.read(2_000_000).decode("utf-8", "replace")
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.geturl(), e.code, ""


def check(host):
    host = host.replace("https://", "").replace("http://", "").strip("/")
    print(f"\n== {host}")
    problems = 0

    # 1. Does the certificate validate, and when does it expire?
    days = cert_days_left(host)
    if isinstance(days, int):
        flag = "OK" if days > 14 else "WARN"
        problems += flag != "OK"
        print(f"  [{flag}] certificate valid, expires in {days} days")
    else:
        problems += 1
        print(f"  [FAIL] {days}")

    # 2. Does plain http:// send visitors to https://?
    try:
        final, status, _ = fetch(f"http://{host}/")
        if final.startswith("https://"):
            print(f"  [OK] http:// redirects to {final}")
        else:
            problems += 1
            print(f"  [FAIL] http:// stays on {final} (status {status}), no redirect to HTTPS")
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - report, don't crash on one bad site
        print(f"  [INFO] http:// check skipped: {e}")

    # 3. Mixed content and viewport on the HTTPS homepage
    try:
        final, status, html = fetch(f"https://{host}/")
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
        print(f"  [FAIL] could not load https://{host}/ ({e})")
        return problems + 1
    scan = PageScan()
    scan.feed(html)
    if scan.insecure:
        problems += 1
        print(f"  [FAIL] {len(scan.insecure)} http:// resource(s) on an HTTPS page (mixed content):")
        for item in scan.insecure[:5]:
            print(f"         {item}")
    else:
        print("  [OK] no http:// images, scripts or stylesheets found in the HTML")
    if scan.viewport and "width=device-width" in scan.viewport.replace(" ", ""):
        print(f'  [OK] viewport: "{scan.viewport}"')
    else:
        problems += 1
        print("  [FAIL] no responsive viewport tag, so phones will show a zoomed-out desktop page")
    return problems


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    total = sum(check(h) for h in sys.argv[1:])
    print(f"\n{total} problem(s) found")
    sys.exit(1 if total else 0)

Testing it

badssl.com runs deliberately broken test hosts, which makes it a good way to see each check fire:

python3 site_check.py badssl.com expired.badssl.com mixed.badssl.com http.badssl.com wordpress.org

== badssl.com
  [OK] certificate valid, expires in 74 days
  [OK] http:// redirects to https://badssl.com/
  [OK] no http:// images, scripts or stylesheets found in the HTML
  [OK] viewport: "width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"

== expired.badssl.com
  [FAIL] certificate problem: certificate has expired
  [INFO] http:// check skipped: <urlopen error [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: certificate has expired (_ssl.c:1010)>
  [FAIL] could not load https://expired.badssl.com/ (<urlopen error [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: certificate has expired (_ssl.c:1010)>)

== mixed.badssl.com
  [OK] certificate valid, expires in 74 days
  [OK] http:// redirects to https://mixed.badssl.com/
  [FAIL] 1 http:// resource(s) on an HTTPS page (mixed content):
         <img> http://mixed.badssl.com/image.jpg
  [OK] viewport: "width=device-width, initial-scale=1"

== http.badssl.com
  [OK] certificate valid, expires in 74 days
  [FAIL] http:// stays on http://http.badssl.com/ (status 200), no redirect to HTTPS
  [OK] no http:// images, scripts or stylesheets found in the HTML
  [OK] viewport: "width=device-width, initial-scale=1"

== wordpress.org
  [OK] certificate valid, expires in 68 days
  [OK] http:// redirects to https://wordpress.org/
  [OK] no http:// images, scripts or stylesheets found in the HTML
  [OK] viewport: "width=device-width, initial-scale=1"

4 problem(s) found

The expired certificate, the missing redirect on http.badssl.com and the insecure image on mixed.badssl.com are all caught; the healthy sites pass. The exit code is 1 when anything fails, so you can drop it into a cron job or CI step for the sites you look after.

Fixing each one on WordPress

Always take a backup first (your host's backup tool, or wp db export plus a copy of wp-content).

1. Expired or failing certificate

On most shared hosting the certificate is a free Let's Encrypt one that renews automatically, and an expired one usually means the renewal broke: the domain's DNS moved, or a CDN/proxy sits in front of the site. Look in the host's SSL/TLS panel first and re-issue there. If the site is behind Cloudflare, check that its SSL mode matches what the origin actually serves.

2. No redirect from http:// to https://

First make sure WordPress itself knows its address is HTTPS: Settings → General, set both WordPress Address (URL) and Site Address (URL) to https://.... Then add a server-level 301. On Apache, near the top of .htaccess (above the # BEGIN WordPress block):

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTPS} off
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://%{HTTP_HOST}/$1 [L,R=301]

One trap: behind a proxy or CDN, %{HTTPS} can be off even for HTTPS visitors, which gives you a redirect loop. In that case do the redirect at the CDN (Cloudflare's "Always Use HTTPS") instead of in .htaccess. On Nginx it's a return 301 https://$host$request_uri; in the port-80 server block.

It's also worth adding this to wp-config.php so the dashboard is always served over HTTPS:

define( 'FORCE_SSL_ADMIN', true );

3. Mixed content

This almost always comes from old absolute URLs saved in the database (post content, widgets, page-builder data) from before the site moved to HTTPS. With WP-CLI, do a dry run first:

wp search-replace 'http://example.com' 'https://example.com' --all-tables --dry-run
wp search-replace 'http://example.com' 'https://example.com' --all-tables

wp search-replace handles PHP-serialized data, which a raw SQL REPLACE() would corrupt. Some page builders keep generated CSS files with the old URLs, so regenerate those afterwards (in Elementor: Tools → Regenerate CSS & Data). Anything still left is usually hard-coded in a theme or plugin file, or comes from a third-party embed that only supports http://; replace or remove it.

The script only reads the homepage HTML, so it won't see URLs inside CSS files or resources injected by JavaScript. For the full list, open the browser DevTools console: mixed content warnings name each URL.

4. No viewport tag

Any reasonably modern theme includes it, so a missing viewport usually means a very old or heavily customised theme. The real fix is a responsive theme, because the tag alone won't make a fixed-width layout fit a phone. If the layout already uses responsive CSS and only the tag is missing, add it from a child theme's functions.php:

add_action( 'wp_head', function () {
    echo '<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">' . "\n";
}, 1 );

Check the page source afterwards so you don't end up with two viewport tags.

Wrapping up

None of this is hard, but it's easy to miss when nobody is looking after the site day to day. Running a check like this monthly catches a certificate that's about to lapse before customers see the warning.

I'm Shanmukh, a student and solo developer. I fix exactly these issues (HTTPS, mobile layout, forms) on small business sites, and build simple 5-page sites, as fixed-scope freelance work. If you'd rather hand it off, the packages are on Fiverr and Whop. More code is on GitHub.

title: Credential Stuffing Starts With One Reused Login: A Password Setup That Survives a Breach
description:
A small business almost never loses an account because one person picked a lazy password. It loses the account because nobody ever decided how passwords would work. A spreadsheet shared between three people, one password reused across the accounting tool and the inbox, a sticky note under the keyboard — that is the entire attack surface an outsider needs.

This is the practical version of that fix: what makes a setup genuinely safe, where a browser vault is enough, how to audit what you already have, how to hand access to staff without handing them your identity, and how to move everything to a new tool without spilling it on the way.

None of it requires enterprise software or a security budget. It fits in one working session on Windows, macOS, or a phone.

The chain reaction: one leaked login becomes five

The reason password reuse is so damaging is not the first breach. It is the automated retry that follows it.

When a site is compromised, the attacker walks away with a list of email addresses and matching passwords. Those pairs are then replayed against mail providers, banks, marketplaces, and admin panels by software that never gets tired. Security people call this credential stuffing. It works for one reason only: the same string opens more than one door.

Here is how the common habits compare once a leak has already happened.

Habit What a leak exposes Exposure
One password everywhere Inbox, banking, and client files at the same moment Critical
Written beside the machine Anyone standing in the room High
Stored in a shared file Everyone with the file, plus everyone who ever had it High
Unique passwords in one browser The single site that leaked Low
Unique passwords plus a second factor Not enough to sign in Lowest

So the target is not a clever password. The target is that no login shares a secret with another login, and that nobody has to hold those secrets in their head.

Stop treating a password as something you remember

Memorability and strength pull in opposite directions, and for years people were asked to satisfy both. Managers break that trade-off: the machine invents the string, the machine types it back, and the human only has to remember one thing — the key that unlocks the vault.

That single key deserves more attention than any individual site password. If it falls, everything inside falls with it.

What a browser vault really protects

Chrome, Edge, and Firefox all encrypt saved credentials into a local store tied to your operating system account. On Windows that store sits behind the OS credential encryption; on macOS it is tied to Keychain. A different person logging into the same machine with their own account cannot open it.

That protection depends on two conditions, and both are easy to break by accident.

  • The computer account itself has a password. A machine that boots straight to the desktop with no prompt has effectively published every saved login to whoever opens the lid.
  • That account is not shared. A single staff login with saved passwords is the same as leaving a printed list on the counter.

The browser also cannot defend a machine that is already infected. Malware running inside your own user session can read the vault, which is why patch level and working antivirus protection still matter next to any password plan.

The real gap is collaboration. A browser profile is built for one person on one device. It cannot grant a colleague access to one credential, revoke that access when they leave, or tell you who opened what. For a solo operator that is fine. Once two or three people need the same supplier portal or ad account, it stops being fine.

The quarterly check you can finish in one sitting

Chrome and Edge ship a free check that compares your saved logins against known breach data. It is the fastest way to see where the damage already is.

Run it and sort the findings into three buckets:

  • Compromised — that password appeared in a public leak. Replace it today, starting with mail and anything that moves money.
  • Reused — one string guarding several accounts. Split them, at minimum everywhere business-critical.
  • Weak — short or guessable. Replace these wherever customer data or payments are involved.

Then work in order of blast radius, not order of appearance.

  1. Primary email — it can reset almost every other account you own.
  2. Banking, payment processors, marketplaces — direct financial exposure.
  3. Ad accounts, social profiles, the domain registrar — a hijack here damages customers and brand trust.
  4. Supplier portals and rarely used subscriptions — lower stakes, still worth cleaning.

When you replace a password, take the generated suggestion instead of inventing one. Long random strings beat human-chosen ones outright, and since the vault remembers it, you never need to type it from memory. Repeat the exercise every quarter: breach dumps keep arriving, so a clean report this month proves nothing about next month.

Handing access to staff without creating a liability

Sharing is where most small teams quietly fall apart. The usual methods — a spreadsheet, a chat message, a verbal handover — fail in the same way. You cannot say who holds the credential, and you cannot take it back.

If sharing has to happen today, four rules limit the damage:

  • Never send a credential through chat or email. Both keep history forever, and both get compromised regularly.
  • Send a one-time link from a tool built for secrets instead of pasting the password itself.
  • Change the password the moment a role ends. No exceptions, no "we will do it later".
  • Prefer separate accounts over a shared one. Most platforms now support multiple users, which gives you per-person revocation and an actual trail.

For a team where more than a couple of people need the same access, this is where a dedicated manager starts paying for itself. Judge candidates on these capabilities rather than on the price of the cheapest tier:

Capability Why it decides the purchase
End-to-end encryption The provider cannot read your vault either
Shared folders Access is granted per team, not per password
Per-user permissions View or edit rights that can be withdrawn
Access log Who opened which credential, and when
Data export You can leave without losing the vault

Migration follows a fixed order: export from the browser, import into the new tool, confirm a few critical logins actually work, delete the export, then clear those entries from the browser so you are not maintaining two sources of truth.

The export file is the most dangerous thing in your backup folder

A vault can disappear with a failed disk, a Windows reinstall, or a corrupted profile. Back it up — but understand what the backup is. A CSV export holds every password as plain readable text. It is the single most valuable file on the machine to anyone who wants in.

Four rules apply every time you export:

  • Move the file out of Downloads immediately. It is the first place a stranger looks and the first place malware scans.
  • Never send it by mail or chat. Nothing encrypts it on the way.
  • Encrypt it before it sits anywhere long-term — inside a password-protected archive, on an encrypted drive, or in encrypted cloud storage.
  • Delete it after the import, including from the recycle bin.

For routine safety, syncing beats exporting. With sync on, credentials are encrypted before they leave the device and come back automatically when you sign in somewhere new. Keep the CSV route for genuine moves between tools.

Two habits make the whole arrangement sturdier. Turn on a second factor for the account that holds your synced vault, because that account now unlocks everything inside it. And keep recovery codes somewhere offline — a printed sheet in a locked drawer — rather than inside the mailbox those codes are meant to rescue.

A one-page policy for a team under twenty

A policy nobody follows is worse than no policy, because it buys the feeling of security without any of the substance. Keep it short enough to enforce and specific enough to check.

A baseline that holds up:

  • Every business service gets its own password. "Internal only" tools are not exempt.
  • Everyone uses a manager. Browser-based is acceptable at the start; move to a shared tool once more than a couple of people need the same login.
  • A second factor is mandatory on email, banking, ad accounts, and the domain registrar. Those four control everything else.
  • Access is granted to a person, never to a team. When someone leaves, disable their account instead of rotating one shared password.
  • Run the health check every quarter and fix the worst findings within a week.

Two smaller habits close most of what remains. Review active sessions monthly in your mail and cloud accounts — an unfamiliar device or city is the earliest sign of a takeover. And treat a sudden password prompt as a warning: if your browser stops autofilling on a site you visit daily, read the address bar before typing anything, because a lookalike login page is the standard way credentials get harvested.

Write the whole thing on one page and keep it where staff can find it. The point is not paperwork. It is making the safe option also the easy one, so following the rules costs less effort than ignoring them.

Frequently asked questions

Is it safe to let the browser save passwords?

For one person, or a very small team, yes — as long as the computer account has a password and is not shared. Those entries are encrypted and tied to your OS login, which beats reusing one string everywhere. The limit is collaboration: a browser cannot share one credential, revoke it, or produce a log, so move to a dedicated manager once several people need the same login.

A password of mine just leaked. What comes first?

Change that password, then change it everywhere you reused it. Start with the primary email, because it can reset everything else, then banking and payment services. Add a second factor so the leaked string alone is useless, and check active sessions so you can sign out anything you do not recognise.

Are CSV password exports dangerous?

Only if they are handled carelessly — but a CSV holds every password in plain text with no encryption at all. If you must export, get it out of Downloads, encrypt it before storing it, keep it away from mail and chat, and delete it after the import. For ordinary backup, syncing is safer because the data never leaves encrypted.

Should I invent my own passwords or accept the generated ones?

Accept the generated ones. They are long and unpredictable, while anything a person invents follows dates, names, or familiar words that attackers try first. The vault stores and autofills it, so memorising is no longer a requirement. Just protect the account holding your synced vault with a second factor.

How often should a small business review passwords and access?

Run the health check once a quarter and clear the highest-impact findings within a week. Review active sessions in mail and cloud accounts monthly, since an unrecognised device shows up before anything else. Review access every time a role changes or a person leaves. A quarterly rhythm catches new exposure without turning into a task people skip.

title: AegisVox: Factorized Privacy and Clinical Preservation for Long-Form Speech
description:
arXiv:2610.14643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical speech reveals identity through both spoken identifiers and voice, yet its pauses, delivery, and speaker roles can also carry useful clinical evidence. Protecting that speech therefore requires more than preserving its words. We present AegisVox, a factorized framework that assigns consistent surrogate voices and edits identifier-bearing turns using document-consistent replacements. Across 390 public simulated or non-patient conversations totaling 63.6 hours, a matched comparison of two speech renderers separates replacement realization from retained identifiers, speaker linkage, and clinical preservation. Text-to-speech rendering realizes 535/601 planned replacements versus 453/601 for the codec-based speech editor. However, similar aggregate clinical preservation conceals more model-labeled contradictions, and conversation-wide speaker scores conceal greater edited-speech linkage under a score-direction sensitivity analysis. Fresh transcription of original audio provides a reference for interpreting the clinical measurement chain; an independent judge tests sensitivity to model-based assessment. Better replacement realization can therefore coexist with worse clinical or speaker-linkage measurements. AegisVox supports use-specific evaluation of those tradeoffs, not a guarantee of identifier removal or clinical safety.

title: Your test passed on retry. Your report should say so.
description:
Most Java test suites have a retry somewhere: an IRetryAnalyzer in TestNG, @RetryingTest from JUnit Pioneer, or Surefire’s rerunFailingTestsCount. Retries keep pipelines green. They also hide information.

When a test fails, gets retried and passes, most reports show one word: Passed. The failure that happened two minutes earlier, along with its stack trace, its API calls and the screenshot of what the browser showed, is gone. The test is flaky, and the report hides it.

The second problem is quieter. To get a useful report, teams end up writing reporting code inside their tests:

`java
test.log(Status.INFO, "Calling POST /users");
test.log(Status.INFO, "Response: " + response.asString());
Allure.addAttachment("Screenshot", new ByteArrayInputStream(png));`

That code isn’t testing anything. People forget to add it, it drifts out of date, and it lands in every test for the rest of the project’s life.

I built Ace Reports to fix both problems. Here’s what it does in Java.

One dependency, no reporting code
xml

`<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.acereports</groupId>
    <artifactId>acereports-junit5</artifactId>  <!-- or acereports-testng / acereports-cucumber -->
    <version>1.1.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

`

There are no listeners to register, no base class and no annotations. Run mvn test as usual, and a single self-contained HTML file appears in TestResults/.

Every attempt keeps its own history

A test that fails and then passes on a retry is shown as flaky, with one tab per attempt. Each attempt keeps:

its own log lines,
its own error and stack trace,
its own API calls,
its own screenshots.

So when attempt 1 timed out and attempt 2 passed, you can see exactly what was different. Pass, fail, flaky and retried counts sit at the top of the report.

API calls are recorded automatically

This is a typical API test with no reporting code in it:

java

`
class UsersApiTest {
private final HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

@Test
void createsUser() throws Exception {
    HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(
        HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://reqres.in/api/users"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("{\"name\":\"John\"}"))
            .build(),
        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
    assertEquals(201, response.statusCode());
}

}
`

The report’s API tab for this test shows the method, URL, request body, response body (JSON indented), status code and duration.

REST Assured calls are captured the same way, with no code.
Authorization and cookie headers are never stored.
One limitation: a client created inside the test method itself can’t be reached automatically, so you wrap it once with AceHttpClient.wrap(...).
Screenshots before teardown

The failure screenshot is taken before @AfterEach / @AfterMethod runs, so the browser is still open. Ace Reports finds a Playwright Page or Selenium WebDriver in a field of the test class, a base class or a ThreadLocal by itself. A page that never navigated anywhere (about:blank) is skipped, so a failed API test doesn’t get an empty screenshot.

Cucumber: steps are the log

With Cucumber (JUnit 5 or TestNG runner), each scenario is a row and every step is a line in the log:


GIVEN the login page is open
WHEN I log in as "InvalidUser" with password "admin123"
FAIL Step failed. TimeoutError: Timeout 3000ms exceeded.
SKIPPED Then the dashboard is shown
Scenario Outline rows carry their example values.
Tags become categories.
Images you attach with scenario.attach(...) show up as screenshot tabs.
Writing to the report, when you want to

You never have to, but you can:

java


Ace.info("Submitting payment");
Ace.takeScreenshot("After login");

Each line attaches to whichever test is running on the current thread, so parallel runs keep their logs apart.

Same report in .NET, Java and Python

Ace Reports started in .NET (xUnit, NUnit, MSTest, Reqnroll) and Python (pytest, pytest-bdd). The Java version produces the identical report, which helps when one team works across more than one stack.

Try it
Live demo report: **https://harshadlambate.github.io/AceReportsWebsite/demo.html
**Website and docs: https://harshadlambate.github.io/AceReportsWebsite/
Maven Central: https://central.sonatype.com/namespace/io.github.acereports

I’d like to hear how your team handles flaky tests: do you keep the history of each attempt, or only the final result?

title: Your browser agent pays to look at pictures: opencli vs claude-in-chrome token use
description:
We run a lot of clickops through Claude Code: reading dashboards, checking settings, pulling a number out of a web app. There are two ways we do it. claude-in-chrome drives Chrome and can return screenshots. opencli drives the same logged-in Chrome but returns the page as text.

We wanted to know what each one costs in tokens, so we measured it.

What we measured

We went through our own Claude Code session logs: 7,500+ browser tool calls. For each call, we took the token counts the API reported before and after it. The difference is how many tokens that call's result added to the context.

These are real API counts, not character-based estimates.

Screenshots are the bill

claude-in-chrome call type Share of calls Median tokens per call
Returned a screenshot 23% 1,855
Returned text only 77% 373

A screenshot call cost about 5x a text call. The 23% of calls that returned screenshots made up 49% of all claude-in-chrome tokens.

An opencli call had a median of 397 tokens. That is about the same as a claude-in-chrome text call. The difference between the two tools comes from screenshots, not from the text.

Same sites, both tools

Nine websites had at least 10 calls with each tool. Here is the change in median tokens per call when we used opencli instead of claude-in-chrome:

Site claude-in-chrome opencli Change
telegram.org 1,879 275 −85%
github.com 580 336 −42%
cloudflare.com 578 378 −35%
google.com 605 437 −28%
linkedin.com 736 594 −19%
youtube.com 542 470 −13%
lokerdollar.com 432 386 −11%
nvidia.com 363 384 +6%
bing.com 270 353 +31%

opencli won on 7 of the 9 sites, about 27% fewer tokens per call when weighted by call count. The big wins were logged-in web apps like Telegram Web, GitHub and the Cloudflare dashboard. On simple public pages the two tools were even, and on Bing opencli used more. The nvidia.com and bing.com rows have under 30 calls each, so take them loosely.

Our clickops rule now

  1. Use the API or curl when one exists.
  2. Read the page as text with opencli.
  3. Take a screenshot only to check something visual.

Limits of this measurement

The site comparison matches calls by website, not by identical task. We did not run the same task twice with each tool, so this is a field measurement, not a lab A/B. Screenshot results also stay in context and get re-read on later turns. We left that out because session length differed between the tools, so the real cost of screenshots is likely higher than shown here.

title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
description:
arXiv:2610.19685v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes. Matching a local reference distribution keeps those probabilities and also penalizes margin expansions. We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.
