title: XPath to iOS Class Chain: a converter you can trust, and when it is actually faster
description:
Converted 678 Appium XPath locators to iOS Class Chain, checked every result, and timed the two on a simulator and an iPhone. Here is what changed.

TL;DR

  • Class chain is ~25 % faster than XPath for a typical iOS lookup: 70 ms saved at 100 elements, 676 ms at 2000 (iPhone).
  • It only matters on big screens. On small ones the gain is milliseconds, and on a real project the whole test run was not faster.
  • ~87 % of real XPath locators can be converted. The converter does it with no wrong chains and skips or flags the rest. 
npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests          # preview the diff
npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests --write  # apply it

Contents

  1. What a class chain is
  2. Why converting by hand goes wrong
  3. What the tool does
  4. How I checked that it is right
  5. How much faster is it?
  6. Where the chain is slower
  7. What I took away
  8. Try it

If you run Appium tests on iOS, you have probably heard that XPath is slow and that -ios class chain is faster. I wanted two things I could not find anywhere:

  1. A tool that converts existing XPath locators to class chain without silently changing which element they find.
  2. A real number: how much faster is it, and does that depend on the size of the screen?

This post covers both. The tool is open source: xpath-to-class-chain. In short: the chain was faster in all 240 timed lookups (22–29 %, simulator and iPhone), 489 of 562 real locators have a class chain, and a few shapes (visible, lookups of dozens of elements) get slower, see below.

What a class chain is

A class chain is WebDriverAgent's (WDA's) own locator language for iOS. Like XPath, it is a path of element types. Unlike XPath, each filter is an NSPredicate in backticks:

XPath Class chain
//XCUIElementTypeButton (any depth) **/XCUIElementTypeButton
//XCUIElementTypeCell/XCUIElementTypeButton (direct child) **/XCUIElementTypeCell/XCUIElementTypeButton
[@name="Pay"] [`name == "Pay"`]
[contains(@label,"Total")] [`label CONTAINS "Total"`]
[@name="a" and @label="b"] [`name == "a" AND label == "b"`]
//* (any type) **/*

In a test, it is just another locator strategy:

// WebdriverIO
await $('-ios class chain:**/XCUIElementTypeButton[`name == "Pay"`]').click();

// Java client
driver.findElement(AppiumBy.iOSClassChain("**/XCUIElementTypeButton[`name == \"Pay\"`]")).click();

Why it is faster. For XPath, WDA takes a snapshot of the whole accessibility tree, writes it out as XML, runs the XPath over it with libxml2 and maps the matches back to elements. A class chain skips the XML step: WDA turns it straight into XCTest queries. Both still walk the whole tree, so the gain is a percentage, not a fixed number of milliseconds.

Why converting by hand goes wrong

The two languages look alike but behave differently:

  • Positions. XPath //Button[2] is the 2nd Button under each parent; class chain **/Button[2] is the 2nd of all matches.
  • Order. XPath (//Button)[2] counts matches top to bottom; WDA counts them level by level (breadth-first). No class chain counts like XPath here.
  • Text. == compares exactly, but CONTAINS, MATCHES and [c] compare normalized text (a fullwidth Ｑ equals Q).
  • Errors. The Appium driver turns an invalid chain into "no such element", so a typo looks like a flaky test, not a syntax error.

That last point is the reason for the whole project: a wrong chain does not fail loudly.

What the tool does

It scans a folder (JS/TS, Java, Kotlin, Python, Ruby, C#, PHP, JSON…), converts the XPath locators it finds and prints a diff; --write saves the files. It validates every chain, skips what has no exact class chain (with a reason), warns on approximations, and leaves alone strings passed to an explicit XPath strategy like AppiumBy.xpath("…").

A preview on four shapes that are common in real test code:

- //XCUIElementTypeStaticText[@name="Order total"]
+ -ios class chain:**/XCUIElementTypeStaticText[`name == "Order total"`]

- //*[contains(@type,"XCUIElementTypeButton") and contains(@label,"Add to cart")]
+ -ios class chain:**/XCUIElementTypeButton[`label CONTAINS "Add to cart"`]

- (//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name="product.addToCart"])[2]
+ -ios class chain:**/XCUIElementTypeButton[`name == "product.addToCart"`][2]
! grouped position: WDA counts class chain matches breadth-first, XPath in document order,
  so the element can differ when matches sit at different depths

[skip] skipped_unsupported_logic: //*[@name="Total:"]/following-sibling::*[1]

The first two are exact, the third is the closest chain there is (check it on its screen), and the fourth stays XPath: a class chain has no sibling axis.

How I checked that it is right

Every verdict comes from running the XPath and the chain and comparing what they find:

  1. A WDA emulator. WDA's own class chain and XPath code (v16.14.1), compiled to run on a Mac. It tests each locator on hundreds of generated screens in seconds.
  2. 678 locators: 563 real ones from production test suites (anonymized) and 115 hand-made edge cases.
  3. Real devices. 246 cases on an iOS 27 simulator and an iPhone 13 Pro Max under Appium 3.8.0 and WDA 16.14.1. Where a device disagreed with the emulator, the device won. That is how the breadth-first order was found.

Scoring: an exact chain earns 1 point, an approximation 0.5, a skipped or wrong one 0. Locators that have no class chain at all are not counted; skipping them is the right answer.

Result Value
R, real locators 96.0 of 100
S, edge cases 93.6 of 100
Wrong chains 0

Why not 100? 39 real locators, all positions like (//Button)[2], have only an approximation, worth 0.5. So 96.0 and 93.6 are the maximum this scoring allows, and the converter reaches it.

How R and S are calculated 
R = 100 × Σ points / N    N = 489 real locators that have a class chain
  = 100 × (450 + 39 × 0.5) / 489 = 96.0

S is the same score on the 83 edge cases that have a class chain, split into 9 groups (positions, string functions, escaping, logic…) and weighted by how much each group matters in real test code. Every case, group and weight is in speccases.js.

Each locator with its chain and verdict is in coverage-cases.json; the full method is in the report.

How much faster is it?

On small screens (36–275 elements) the chain was about 20 % faster, but that is only 30–65 ms. So I measured what happens as the screen grows.

Setup: a synthetic Checkout page grown to 100, 500, 1000 and 2000 elements; the 10 most common locator shapes from real tests; targets at the top, at depth 39 and at the end of the page. Each lookup is one cold findElement, median of three passes.

Elements in the tree Simulator, XPath → chain Saved iPhone, XPath → chain Saved
~100 115 → 90 ms 21.9 % 295 → 225 ms 23.8 %
~500 453 → 344 ms 24.1 % 760 → 582 ms 23.4 %
~1000 912 → 677 ms 25.8 % 1.40 s → 997 ms 28.9 %
~2000 1.75 → 1.31 s 25.4 % 2.72 → 2.04 s 24.9 %
  • The saving in percent does not depend on the screen size. The saving in milliseconds grows with it, because both strategies process the whole tree on every lookup.
  • The locator shape and the target's position do not matter. A button at the top costs as much as one at depth 39.

More findings: useFirstMatch, depth limit, simulator vs iPhone
  • [1] and useFirstMatch do not help. An explicit [1] takes the same code path in WDA 16.14.1. useFirstMatch (an Appium setting that makes WDA stop at the first match) was 2.7 % faster at 100 elements and 5.7 % slower at 2000, 15 % slower for deep targets.
  • Nothing deeper than 50 levels is found by either strategy (WDA's default snapshotMaxDepth). The error is a plain "no such element".
  • A real iPhone is 1.5–2.6× slower than the simulator, mostly a fixed per-request cost over USB. The ratio between XPath and chain stays the same.

Where the chain is slower

On the small screens, four shapes were slower as a chain (simulator; the iPhone showed the same):

Locator XPath Chain
//XCUIElementTypeButton[@visible='true'], 32 matches 2.05 s 12.6 s
//XCUIElementTypeCell[@visible="true"]/XCUIElementTypeButton 3.46 s 5.14 s
//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name], 36 matches 1.15 s 1.78 s
/XCUIElementTypeApplication/XCUIElementTypeWindow/XCUIElementTypeButton 0.12 s 0.75 s

visible is the main trap: WDA checks visibility for every candidate. These four cases outweighed all the gains, and over the whole small-screen run XPath was faster in total (53.7 s against 64.8 s). Without them, the chain was 3.8 % faster.

So on small screens XPath is fine. The gain shows up on big trees: long feeds and lists, screens kept alive in a navigation stack or in tabs, off-screen drawers. An iPad with several windows on screen should behave the same way (not measured).

What I took away

Faster lookups do not automatically mean faster tests. On a real project with simple screens, run on Sauce Labs devices (iOS 16, 18, 26), the timed lookups got faster, but the total run time barely changed: a few milliseconds are lost next to app launch, network and waits.

My rule of thumb: convert for speed where the screens are big, and convert lookups of one element by name, label, value or type. Check visible predicates, list lookups and absolute paths first.

Limits

  • Only lookups were measured in a controlled way, not whole tests. With implicit waits or retries, a missed lookup repeats the whole search, so the saving multiplies by the number of attempts.
  • The big screen is synthetic; no production app was benchmarked.
  • One WDA version (16.14.1). Its class chain lookup changed recently (appium/WebDriverAgent PR #1194), so other versions may give other numbers.
  • One phone and one Mac (M1 Pro). Absolute times will differ on yours; the ratio should not.

Try it

You need Node.js 20 or newer, nothing else. Start with the screens that have the most elements: dump the page source of your heaviest screen and count them.

npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests          # preview
npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests --write  # save
npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests --json   # report with every skip and warning

Then review the warnings, run your suite, and check each grouped position and visible locator on its screen. Everything behind the numbers in this post (the audit, the emulator, the device app) is in audit/.

Next: can an LLM do this instead?

In part 2 I give the same 678 locators to Claude models (Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, several generations, every effort level) and score them with the same checks. Short version: no model beat the converter on real locators, and a prompt with the rules mattered more than the model or the effort level.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Anthropic: Claude Code helped me build the converter, the test harness and the device benchmark, and analyze the results. All numbers come from real runs.

Mikhail Yesipchuk, SDET/Senior QA Automation Engineer. If you try the converter on your suite, I'd like to hear what it skipped and why: open an issue on GitHub or message me on LinkedIn.

title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.14136v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.

title: WebDAV vs Google Drive vs Dropbox: Real Cost After 3 Years
description:
Last month I exported three years of bank statements and filtered every cloud storage charge. I expected to find the usual mess of $9.99 here and $11.99 there. I found something worse.

The actual numbers (36 months)

I used to run a hybrid setup:

  • Google Drive (personal): $1.99/month = $71.64
  • iCloud+ 200GB (shared with family): $2.99/month = $107.64
  • OneDrive (work, reimbursed): $0 out of pocket
  • Dropbox Plus (side project backups): $11.99/month = $431.64

Total personal spend: $610.92 over three years.

Then in 2025 I switched the personal side to a $5.5 lifetime WebDAV mount + a $5/month VPS running Nextcloud. After 8 months:

  • WebDAV mount license (one-time): $5.50
  • VPS: $5 × 8 = $40
  • Total: $45.50

If I keep the VPS for the full 3 years, total = $5.50 + $180 = $185.50. That's a $425.42 savings — more than the $5.5 license cost back 77 times.

What I actually lost

This is the part nobody talks about. Going from Dropbox to self-hosted meant:

Lost features:

  • Selective sync (not needed with WebDAV mount — it streams)
  • Real-time co-editing (I never used it)
  • Built-in document scanner (use phone camera)
  • Smart file suggestions (didn't really miss these)

Gained features:

  • 1TB of storage instead of 200GB (VPS disk can be any size)
  • No file size limit per upload
  • No "this file too large for syncing" errors
  • Full control over backup retention
  • My files are not used to train AI models (verified: my Nextcloud instance, my rules)

The hidden cost I almost forgot

I forgot to add one line item in the math above: the time I spent on the Dropbox support chat. Between 2022 and 2024, I had three billing disputes (overcharges, double-charges, accidental yearly upgrade). Each one cost me 20-40 minutes of email tag.

With my self-hosted setup, the only "support" is reading the Nextcloud docs. When something breaks, I fix it. No billing department, no renewal price hikes, no "sorry, we changed our terms" emails.

Who should NOT switch

If you fit any of these, stay with mainstream sync:

  • You need real-time co-editing with people outside your household
  • You use Google Docs / Sheets / Slides as your primary work tool
  • You have less than 50GB of files (the free tiers cover you)
  • You don't want to spend a Saturday afternoon setting up a VPS

Who SHOULD switch

  • You have more than 200GB of personal files
  • You're paying $10+/month for any sync service
  • You have a NAS or home server you already maintain
  • You care about long-term file ownership
  • You want a one-time payment, not a recurring charge

The $5.5 lifetime license

I bought ScsDriver when they were running a lifetime deal for $5.5. That license covers all my devices — Windows, Mac, iPhone, Android. One payment. No subscription. No "premium tier" upsell.

Three years from now, when Dropbox is charging $14.99/month and iCloud+ is $4.99/month, my WebDAV mount will still cost $0.00 in license fees. The VPS might go up to $7, but I'll still be ahead by hundreds of dollars.

The boring conclusion

Cloud storage pricing is designed to be forgettable. $1.99 here, $11.99 there — it doesn't feel like much until you add it up over years. A $5.5 lifetime WebDAV mount cuts the recurring cost to zero. The setup takes a Saturday. The math takes 30 seconds.

If you've been on the fence about switching, do the spreadsheet. Add up what you've actually paid over 3 years. Then subtract $5.5. Then think about what else you could buy with the rest.

title: StatusCake, BetterStack, UptimeRobot, Healthchecks: Go API Uptime Trade-offs Explained
description:
TL;DR: Use StatusCake, Better Stack, or UptimeRobot for outside-in API checks and production notifications. Add Healthchecks for scheduled jobs that can fail by never starting. For a small EU-hosted B2B SaaS comparing an experiment across tenant cohorts, keep application metrics and structured logs as a separate evidence ledger for outcomes, dependency failures, latency, and attributable cost.

Do not ask one green check to prove all three things. Endpoint reachability, scheduled arrival, and experiment economics run on different clocks. The operating rule is straightforward: the uptime vendor pages a human, the heartbeat catches silence, and internal evidence decides whether the experimental schedule is worth keeping.

Begin with the failure clock

Imagine three cohorts: control, hourly, and batched. Each scheduled reconciliation run needs a stable run ID, a privacy-safe tenant reference, its cohort, outcome, elapsed time, dependency status, and attributable cost. Cost is the primary decision axis, but it cannot stand alone. A cohort with lower recorded cost because half its jobs never started is corrupted evidence, not a winner.

An HTTP probe can show that /healthz responds now. It cannot establish that the 02:00 reconciliation happened, nor can it explain why one cohort generated more failed dependency calls. A dead-man check covers the missing start. Logs and metrics cover the work that did start.

Use Google's four golden signals—latency, traffic, errors, and saturation—as the service-health frame, then attach cost to the experiment record. Keep liveness cheap and narrow. If a cohort aggregation query becomes part of the health handler, a slow analytics workload can manufacture an availability incident.

Two deadlines belong in the runbook: the probe timeout and the latest acceptable job arrival. Write them before rollout. Missed is missed.

Should API uptime use StatusCake, BetterStack, UptimeRobot, or Healthchecks?

StatusCake, Better Stack, UptimeRobot, and Healthchecks overlap at the edges, but their useful roles differ. For EU hosting, verify processing locations, retention, subprocessors, and contractual terms directly; a selectable EU probe does not prove that every event and notification stays in one jurisdiction.

Product Best role in this runbook Boundary to verify
StatusCake Public HTTP endpoint checks from selected locations Probe coverage, escalation channels, and retention for the chosen plan
Better Stack Endpoint checks near an incident and on-call workflow Data processing terms and fit with the real escalation rota
UptimeRobot Direct endpoint monitoring for a small operating team Check interval, notification routes, and team access controls
Healthchecks Dead-man checks for cron, queue, and reconciliation jobs It does not replace outside-in API availability monitoring

There is no universal winner. Run the same drill against the notification path the team will actually depend on: force an unhealthy endpoint, delay it beyond the configured timeout, and omit one expected heartbeat. Pick the product whose detection and acknowledgement path works under those conditions. Add Healthchecks whenever “nothing ran” is itself an incident. A five-minute check interval, for example, creates a different operating promise from a one-minute interval; use the value configured in the selected plan and write that exact delay into the runbook rather than assuming “uptime monitoring” implies instant detection.

Datadog Synthetic Monitoring and Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring are credible alternatives when either platform already anchors the wider monitoring estate. Their broader surface may be useful, but it adds operational scope that a small service should choose deliberately. Product count is not resilience.

Keep notification and evidence separate

The external vendor owns detection and delivery. The service owns truthful health responses. The experiment pipeline owns cohort evidence. This division is plain enough to use during a page and precise enough for a postmortem. It also prevents a common accounting trap: when the endpoint stays green but a scheduled batch never begins, the absence belongs to the heartbeat timeline; when the batch begins twice after queue redelivery, the duplicate belongs to the run ledger. Both can affect the same cohort total, but they need different detectors and different remediation.

Keep those clocks separate.

Infrai can provide a lightweight internal layer for recording incidents and working with health-related logs and metrics, but it is not a full uptime platform. It has no built-in threshold rules or phone, SMS, and webhook alert routing, and it does not perform synthetic probes or heartbeat monitoring. Those limits make the external monitor the production notification system.

Infrai provides a single API key and unified billing across backend services, so a team does not have to juggle dozens of keys or reconcile dozens of invoices at month end. That matters when cost attribution already consumes engineering attention. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. The verified catalog contains 295 routes across 20 modules.

Keep the boundary sharp. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but there is no distributed trace query or span tree. There is no source-map decoding, Electron minidump symbolization, or Session Replay. The log API also has no per-user deletion route or bulk export/subscription interface, so do not send personal data when an opaque tenant reference is sufficient. Retention and cold-storage configuration are not exposed. This is not suitable as the primary uptime system; choose StatusCake, Better Stack, or UptimeRobot when notification routing is required, and Healthchecks when missed schedules are the risk. That trade-off is more important than catalog breadth.

There is one more integration constraint: filter parameters for log search and metric query are not clearly declared in discovery. Do not invent them. Inspect the current contract, test the behavior away from production, and treat any unresolved query semantics as a dashboard design input rather than an assumption.

Inspect the reporting contract safely in Go

Because search and query filters are not declared clearly enough to reproduce here, the safe minimal example reads the live metric-reporting contract instead of guessing a payload. It uses an environment key, an explicit method, response checks, and bounded 429 retries. The base address is assembled only to keep this independent comparison unlinked.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    baseURL := "https://api." + "infrai." + "cc/v1"
    url := baseURL + "/discovery/metrics.report"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            log.Fatal(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            log.Fatalf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    log.Fatal("discovery remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

Validate the returned request schema before reporting an aggregate. Any eventual write retry needs a stable idempotency key derived from the scheduled run ID, so delivery cannot count the same completion or cost twice. The platform specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities.

The run ID must cross the queue boundary unchanged. Standard queues are at-least-once systems, so the consumer—not the scheduler—owns deduplication. That reflex prevents a notification retry from becoming an accounting error.

Verify, then make rollback boring

Before assigning real experiment traffic, use staging with the production notification configuration. Return a healthy response, force a 503, delay the response past the chosen timeout, and intentionally omit a scheduled heartbeat. Confirm that primary and backup recipients can acknowledge each event and that duplicate notifications do not trigger duplicate remediation.

Then run one item for each cohort. Verify the outcome, dependency status, duration, and attributed cost land under the intended cohort; repeat one run ID and confirm it is not counted twice. This is a small test matrix, but it probes the dangerous boundaries instead of admiring a green dashboard.

Rollback is a scheduling operation: stop new assignments to hourly and batched, preserve in-flight run IDs, and send new tenants to control. Do not rewrite old labels or delete inconvenient failures. Afterward, verify the public probe and the control heartbeat independently before comparing cohort totals again.

Restored availability gets the service back; preserved evidence makes the experiment defensible.

References

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • StatusCake uptime monitoring documentation
  • Better Stack uptime monitoring documentation
  • UptimeRobot help center
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Datadog Synthetic Monitoring documentation
  • Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring documentation

title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
description:
arXiv:2610.14576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.

title: LiFi: LiDAR Generation from Multi-View Images via Geometric and Semantic Collaborative Guidance
description:
arXiv:2610.19786v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating LiDAR point clouds from multi-view camera images is a valuable task with applications in controllable data synthesis, cross-modal simulation and various perception tasks. However, most existing methods are not specifically designed for this task, and the quality of their generated LiDAR remains limited. Moreover, these methods typically focus only on semantic cues in images or generate LiDAR from a monocular camera image. In this work, we introduce LiFi (LiDAR From images), a dedicated framework for generating visually and geometrically aligned LiDAR scenes from multi-view camera images. LiFi guides the latent diffusion process through two complementary branches: geometry and semantics. The geometry branch constructs scene features from images through a reverse sampling algorithm and an uncertainty-aware geometric encoder combined with DepthAnything3, whereas the semantic branch provides high-level semantic representations via a cross-view interaction module. We further introduce a dual-branch balanced classifier-free guidance (CFG) strategy, which enhances the model's conditional generation capability while preserving the independent learning and collaborative controllability of the two branches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiFi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in generating high-fidelity LiDAR scenes. The code will be publicly available at: https://github.com/szzhou88/LiFi.

title: The Sum of All Summaries: PROPALIGN for Graded Proposition Salience Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.19387v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identification and ranking of salient propositions in documents is indirectly involved in many AI tasks, but few papers define proposition salience scores clearly, make diverse data available, or evaluate models directly on the task. This paper proposes PROPALIGN, a multiple-summary-based approach for propositional salience score estimation, and releases PROPALIGNBANK, an accompanying dataset for the method with 138K alignments of over 35K propositions. We compare several approaches to salient proposition extraction in English across a broad range of spoken and written genres, and demonstrate that naively asking models for judgments leads to inconsistencies. By contrast, graded, summary-based metrics are more stable. We further observe that while single models perform worse than humans, an ensemble of models incorporating linguistic features approaches manual annotation quality ceilings. In addition, analyses of the model outputs suggest insights into how models can extract salient information with and without the use of summaries.

title: Deep Generative Models for Phylogenetic Inference with Complex Evolutionary Processes
description:
arXiv:2610.19053v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inference of phylogenetic trees from sequences plays a central role in understanding evolutionary relationships, with applications ranging from tracking pathogen spread to reconstructing the history of life. Conventionally, practitioners obtain posteriors over trees using likelihood-based methods like MCMC. However, likelihoods are only available for simple evolutionary models with restrictive assumptions. For realistic evolutionary models, inference using conventional methods is prohibitively expensive, inaccurate, or even impossible. In practice, practitioners settle for using as flexible a conventional method as possible, even though they expect it is misspecified. In principle, we could use simulation-based inference: simulate tree and sequence data from an evolutionary model and train a neural network to predict the posterior over trees given sequences. However it is a mathematical challenge to represent and train complex posterior distributions over trees. Here we present a flexible family of conditional generative models over trees. Our models iteratively build trees using three natural paradigms -- top-down, middle-out, or bottom-up -- and are trained using a discrete diffusion framework. For real and synthetic datasets of up to $65$ taxa and $>10^5$ tokens, our models recover MCMC posteriors much more accurately than the previous state-of-the-art simulation-based method Phyloformer 2. Finally, we compare to IQ-Tree, a popular flexible-but-misspecified conventional method. Our models match its tree estimates on simple data, but on more realistic data, our method is reliably more accurate.

title: Mapping Arctic Polynyas from Sea Ice Concentration Data Using Hierarchical Partitioning and Differentiated Region Growing: Sensitivity to Threshold and Product Choices
description:
arXiv:2610.19647v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurately delineating Arctic coastal polynyas from sea ice concentration data remains challenging because of complex coastal geometry and spatially heterogeneous ice conditions. We develop a daily sea ice concentration (SIC) mapping framework based on hierarchical partitioning, connected-component analysis, and differentiated region growing for polynya and open-water regions. Applied to September-May ice seasons from 2002/03 to 2024/25, the framework achieves a mean overall accuracy of 96.74% and a mean kappa coefficient of 0.93 in the 63-scene visual assessment. Sensitivity experiments reveal a consistent pattern: the absolute magnitude of SIC-defined polynya extent is strongly configuration-dependent, whereas major temporal features are comparatively more stable. Relative to a 75% upper SIC threshold, seasonal extent integrals differ by 13.48%, 32.47%, and 65.04% at thresholds of 80%, 85%, and 90%, respectively, while the broad interannual structure remains recognizable. The response is also strongly regional and seasonal, with the largest threshold sensitivity in the Central Arctic Ocean, very weak sensitivity in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and greater pan-Arctic curve separation from January onward. At an 80% threshold, product-comparison MAPE is 68.19% between the 6.25 and 25 km products and 11.47% between the 12.5 and 25 km products under their respective comparison periods and reference definitions. Regional product disagreement is likewise heterogeneous. Together, these results show that reproducible long-term polynya monitoring requires a fixed and explicitly documented combination of SIC product, threshold, and spatial classification rules, while broad temporal patterns can remain informative even when absolute extent differs substantially.

title: How We Built HydroBid: Offline Quoting for Pressure Washing Crews (Capacitor + Dexie)
description:
TL;DR

HydroBid is a Capacitor + React app for pressure washing / soft wash estimates. Quotes and appointments live in IndexedDB (Dexie). PDFs are generated on-device. Calendar reminders use local notifications. No account required for core quoting.

Product page: knoxstudios.net/apps/hydrobid.html

This post is a build log: architecture choices, freemium edges, and Android gotchas—not a feature dump dressed as a tutorial.

Why this app exists

Exterior cleaning crews often bid from the driveway. Cloud-only estimators fail when signal fails. We wanted:

  • Line items with sq ft / linear ft / hour / flat
  • Branded PDF share from the phone
  • Pipeline + calendar so follow-ups don’t die in SMS
  • Wash helpers: chemical mix, area, water usage
  • Local-first data (Dexie), Capacitor for Android

Architecture (high level) 

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ React 19 + Vite + Tailwind (UI)         │
│  QuoteBuilder · Calendar · Tools · PDF  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Dexie / IndexedDB   │  session drafts   │
│ quotes, appts,      │  photo compress   │
│ settings            │                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Capacitor 8                             │
│ Camera · Filesystem · Share             │
│ Local Notifications · AdMob · RC IAP    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Source of truth = device. AdMob and RevenueCat are side channels; they must never block reading/writing quotes.

Quote model (simplified) 

type QuoteStatus = 'draft' | 'sent' | 'accepted' | 'rejected'

interface LineItem {
  id: string
  label: string
  qty: number
  unit: 'sq_ft' | 'linear_ft' | 'hour' | 'flat'
  rate: number
  amount: number
}

interface Quote {
  id: string
  clientAddress: string
  lineItems: LineItem[]
  photoDataUrls: string[]
  status: QuoteStatus
  price: number
  // ... notes, validUntil, paymentTypes, sentAt, appointmentAt, etc.
}

Always normalize on read: default empty arrays, recompute price from line items. Field apps accumulate messy rows after updates; defensive normalization > perfect migrations alone.

PDF pipeline

  1. Map Quote + company settings → @react-pdf/renderer document (themes: canopy / invoice / simple)
  2. Optionally downscale photos for the PDF (we cap embedded images)
  3. On native: write file → Share plugin
  4. Enforce free-tier unique export quota per month in one module so UI and paywall agree

Lesson: treat the PDF as the customer API. If Share works offline after generation, you’ve won the job-site demo.

Calendar without a backend

  • Store Appointment rows locally (optional quoteId)
  • Derive calendar markers from quote timestamps (sentAt, respondedAt, validUntil) + appointments
  • Export .ics via Filesystem/Share or open a Google Calendar URL when online
  • Rebuild local notifications from DB (T-24h / T-2h for jobs; nudges for drafts/unsent/expiry)
  • Respect quiet hours + max notifications per day so you don’t train users to disable everything

Android 13+ needs POST_NOTIFICATIONS. Exact alarms need the right permission storytelling in the OS settings screen—prime this in onboarding, don’t ambush post-install.

Tools that write back to the draft

Chemical dilution, L×W area, and GPM×time water math live under a Tools tab. Persisting calculator drafts (and “add to quote” actions) keeps wash-specific math inside the same session as the bid.

Small UX win, large retention win: users stop alt-tabbing to random calculator apps.

Freemium edges we encoded early

Free Premium
Ads + PDF generate/share gate Ad-free
Limited unique PDF exports / month Unlimited exports
Up to 2 job photos / quote Up to 6
Basic dashboard Service-mix insights
“Made with HydroBid” on PDF Clean footer + rate hide/customize

Encode limits as constants (FREE_EXPORT_UNIQUE_QUOTES_PER_MONTH, FREE_MAX_QUOTE_PHOTOS). Scattered magic numbers create support tickets.

Onboarding that earns permission

Order that worked for us:

  1. Welcome / problem framing
  2. How it works (quote → PDF → follow-up)
  3. Company profile (logo + default rate)
  4. Notifications prime (why reminders matter)
  5. Soft Premium intro (no hard wall)

Profile-before-paywall means the first PDF already looks like their business.

What I’d tell another indie shipping field tools

  1. Ship offline path first; sync is a sequel.
  2. Compress images before IndexedDB.
  3. One module owns quotas and Premium checks.
  4. Local notifications need a rebuild function you can call after every meaningful write.
  5. Be explicit in store copy about what you don’t do (tax, maps, live CRM)—it reduces 1★ “where’s X?” reviews.

Links

  • App / product page: HydroBid
  • Stack: React 19, Vite, Capacitor 8, Dexie, @react-pdf/renderer, RevenueCat, AdMob

Questions about Dexie schema versioning or PDF photo embedding? Drop them in the comments—happy to compare notes with other Capacitor folks shipping trades apps.

title: Harmony Harness: Multi-Objective Self-Evolution of Agent Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2610.15150v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work on self-evolving LLM agents treats the agent harness as an optimization target that can be iteratively improved through execution feedback. Existing approaches, however, largely optimize a single objective and evolve the harness as a monolithic artifact, limiting their ability to handle competing goals and to separate transferable design from environment-specific adaptation. We introduce Harmony Harness, a framework for multi-objective, compositional harness evolution. Harmony Harness formulates harness evolution as a multi-objective optimization problem and uses decomposition-based evolutionary search to maintain solutions across different regions of the Pareto frontier, avoiding reliance on a hand-designed structural diversity metric for repository-scale harnesses. In parallel, we introduce factorized evolution operators that separately refine general-purpose harness mechanisms and benchmark-specific adaptations, together with a dynamic composition workflow that integrates them at inference time. Across SecRepoBench and BaxBench, Harmony Harness consistently outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, with gains exceeding 10% on both benchmarks. Our results show that explicitly modeling both objective trade-offs and harness structure yields substantially stronger and more transferable agent evolution than existing single-objective, monolithic approaches.

title: Apple Messages for Business is not an iMessage API
description:
Most “iMessage API” products are a different system from Apple Messages for Business.

An unofficial sender uses Apple IDs or Macs to push blue-bubble messages. Apple Messages for Business is the channel inside the Messages app that a brand reaches through an approved Messaging Service Provider. It is how a customer starts a chat from a website, Apple Maps, Safari, or a Message Suggest result. It is not a public API key a brand calls on its own.

What a brand actually integrates

Apple does not give brands a standalone REST API. The MSP implements Apple’s server-to-server Messages for Business API. The brand connects to the MSP. Automation has to go through that MSP, with a live agent available during business hours, and the experience has to pass Apple’s Experience Review before it can go public.

The requirement list and the message flow are here: Apple Messages for Business API requirements.

Why the distinction matters

A blue-bubble sender will not put a business in Maps, will not add an Apple Pay button inside Messages, and will not survive Experience Review. If the job is customer-initiated support, booking, or commerce on iPhone, the path is an approved MSP.

A directory of those providers, compared by capability, is at amb.directory/msps.

Disclosure: I publish amb.directory, a directory of brands using Apple Messages for Business and the MSPs that implement the channel.

title: Hybrid supervised instance segmentation by learning label noise suppression
description:
arXiv:2610.20412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To reach top accuracy, current fully supervised instance segmentation methods severely rely on large-scale pixel-wise labeled datasets. They are usually expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Though weakly or semi-supervised methods utilize cheap bounding box labeled, image-level labeled or unlabeled samples to save the labeling cost, their performance is largely sacrificed. To save labeling cost without losing much performance, in this paper, we present a pipeline that can utilize economical bounding box labels and accurate pixel-wise labels in a hybrid way. Specifically, we design two ancillary models to learn label noise suppression and obtain accurate pseudo pixel-wise labels from bounding box labels for training. One is designed to suppress mislabeling between foreground and background, and the other is designed to suppress noise from mislabeling of instances. Moreover, we exploit category-aware spatial attention module, category constraint module, instance constraint module, and self-learning training approach to improve the accuracy of pseudo labels. Experiments on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and the Cityscapes datasets show that our method can achieve competitive performance with much less labeling cost.

title: Amazon RDS Proxy now supports SQL Server 2022
description:
Amazon RDS Proxy, a fully managed, highly available database proxy for Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), now supports Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances running major version 2022.

Amazon RDS Proxy sits between your application and the database to pool and share established database connections, improving database efficiency and application scalability. For Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ databases, RDS Proxy automatically connects to the standby database instance during a failure, preserves application connections, and helps reduce failover times by up to 83%. RDS Proxy supports standard IAM authentication for SQL Server, where your applications authenticate to the proxy using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and RDS Proxy manages database connections using credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager.

You can enable Amazon RDS Proxy for your SQL Server 2022 database in a few steps on the Amazon RDS console, then connect by pointing your application to the RDS Proxy endpoint. To get started, see our documentation.

title: API Alchemy: Turning Raw Endpoints into Gold‑Standard Services
description:
Introduction

An API (Application Programming Interface) is the contract that lets two software systems talk to each other. Whether you’re exposing data to a mobile app, integrating a payment gateway, or building a microservice for a larger platform, the quality of your API determines the speed of development, the reliability of integrations, and the long‑term maintainability of the product.

In this post we’ll explore the modern lifecycle of an API—from initial design to production‑grade implementation—while sprinkling in practical code snippets you can copy‑paste into your own projects. By the end, you’ll have a checklist of best‑practice patterns and a couple of tool recommendations that make the whole process feel like pure alchemy.

1. Sketching the Contract First

The most common mistake is to start coding endpoints before the contract is clear. Treat the API spec as a first‑class artifact. Tools like OpenAPI (Swagger) let you describe routes, request/response schemas, authentication, and error codes in a language‑agnostic YAML or JSON file.

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: "Bookstore API"
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /books:
    get:
      summary: List all books
      responses:
        '200':
          description: "A JSON array of books"
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/Book'
components:
  schemas:
    Book:
      type: object
      required:
        - id
        - title
        - author
      properties:
        id:
          type: integer
        title: ""
          type: string
        author:
          type: string

Having this contract up front gives you:

  • Clear expectations for front‑end teams and third‑party consumers.
  • Automatic client generation (e.g., openapi-generator can produce TypeScript, Python, Go SDKs).
  • Living documentation that never drifts from the implementation.

2. Choosing the Right Architectural Style

REST

The classic “resource‑oriented” approach. It shines when you have CRUD operations on identifiable entities and want to leverage HTTP caching, status codes, and hypermedia.

GraphQL

A single endpoint that lets clients request exactly the data they need. Ideal for complex UI layers where over‑fetching or under‑fetching is a pain point.

gRPC

Binary protocol based on Protocol Buffers. Perfect for low‑latency, high‑throughput internal services.

Rule of thumb: Start with REST unless you have a compelling reason (e.g., mobile bandwidth constraints) to adopt GraphQL or gRPC. Simpler tooling, broader ecosystem, and easier caching.

3. Versioning – Keep the Past, Evolve the Future

Never break existing consumers. Two popular strategies:

Strategy When to Use Example
URI versioning (/v1/books) Clear, explicit version bumps GET /v2/books?include=reviews
Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json) Cleaner URLs, can negotiate via content‑type Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json

Never mix major and minor changes in the same version. Minor improvements (adding optional fields) can be backward‑compatible; major changes (renaming fields, removing endpoints) deserve a new version.

4. Security First: Authentication & Authorization

Token‑Based Auth (JWT) 

// Express middleware – verify JWT
const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');

function authGuard(req, res, next) {
  const token = req.headers.authorization?.split(' ')[1];
  if (!token) return res.sendStatus(401);
  try {
    const payload = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);
    req.user = payload; // attach user info for later use
    next();
  } catch (err) {
    res.sendStatus(403);
  }
}

OAuth 2.0

When third‑party apps need delegated access, use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. Libraries like passport (Node) or django-oauth-toolkit (Python) abstract the heavy lifting.

Rate Limiting

Guard your API from abuse:

const rateLimit = require('express-rate-limit');

app.use(
  rateLimit({
    windowMs: 60 * 1000, // 1 minute
    max: 100,            // limit each IP to 100 requests per windowMs
    message: 'Too many requests, try again later.',
  })
);

5. Consistent Error Handling

Never expose stack traces or internal IDs. Adopt a standard error envelope:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Book with ID 42 does not exist.",
    "details": {
      "requestedId": 42
    }
  }
}

In Express, a central error handler makes this trivial:

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  const status = err.status || 500;
  res.status(status).json({
    error: {
      code: err.code || 'INTERNAL_ERROR',
      message: err.message,
      details: err.details || {},
    },
  });
});

6. Testing the Contract

Unit Tests

Validate business logic without the network:

def test_get_book_by_id():
    repo = MagicMock()
    repo.fetch.return_value = Book(id=1, title='1984')
    service = BookService(repo)
    result = service.get_book(1)
    assert result.title == '1984'

Integration Tests

Spin up a test server and hit the real HTTP endpoints:

const request = require('supertest');
const app = require('../src/app');

describe('GET /books', () => {
  it('returns a list of books', async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get('/v1/books');
    expect(res.statusCode).toBe(200);
    expect(Array.isArray(res.body)).toBe(true);
  });
});

Contract Tests

Tools like Dredd read your OpenAPI file and automatically verify that the running server complies with the spec. This catches drift early in CI pipelines.

7. Documentation That Doesn’t Collect Dust

  • Swagger UI – auto‑generated interactive docs from the OpenAPI file.
  • Redoc – clean, static documentation site with good theming.
  • Postman Collections – handy for manual QA and client onboarding.

Never rely solely on README files; embed the docs in your CI/CD flow so they are regenerated on every merge.

8. Deploying with Observability

When you push an API to production, observability becomes non‑negotiable.

Concern Tool
Logging Loki + Grafana, or Elastic Stack
Metrics Prometheus (request latency, error rates)
Tracing OpenTelemetry + Jaeger
Health Checks /healthz endpoint returning 200 OK only if DB and external services are reachable

Example health check in FastAPI (Python):

from fastapi import FastAPI, status

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/healthz", status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)
def health():
    # Simple DB ping could go here
    return {"status": "ok"}

9. The API Lifecycle Checklist

  1. Write an OpenAPI spec – versioned, with schemas.
  2. Pick an architectural style – REST is default.
  3. Implement authentication – JWT or OAuth.
  4. Develop endpoints – keep controllers thin, move business logic to services.
  5. Add centralized error handling – consistent JSON envelope.
  6. Write unit, integration, and contract tests – run on every PR.
  7. Generate docs – Swagger UI + Redoc.
  8. Instrument logging, metrics, tracing – integrate with your observability stack.
  9. Deploy behind a gateway – rate limiting, request validation, API key enforcement.

Follow these steps and your API will feel like a well‑crafted piece of alchemy: reliable, reusable, and a delight for every consumer.

Recommended Tools

  • Postman – API Development Platform – Build, test, and document your APIs in a single, collaborative workspace. The free tier is generous, and the paid plans add advanced monitoring and mock servers.

  • SwaggerHub – Collaborative OpenAPI Design – Host your OpenAPI definitions, generate SDKs, and keep your spec in sync with your codebase. Integrated version control makes team collaboration painless.

Happy coding, and may your endpoints always return 200 OK!

title: Launching EyeZen v1.0.0: A Local-First Desktop App Built with Rust, Tauri and React
description:
Launching EyeZen v1.0.0: A Local-First Desktop App Built with Rust, Tauri and React

EyeZen v1.0.0 is now available. It's an open-source desktop workspace-personalization application built with Rust, Tauri 2, React and TypeScript.

The guiding idea is simple: the preferences you want while coding may not be the ones you want while reading, editing a video, or working late.

I wanted to build a desktop app that treats those different contexts as configurable workspaces while keeping core configuration local.

What ships in v1.0.0?

The first release includes ten interface themes:

  • Light
  • Dark
  • System
  • Warm Dark
  • Warm Light
  • Sepia Reading
  • Midnight
  • AMOLED-Inspired
  • High Contrast
  • Grayscale

Users can change accent colors, text scale and motion preferences.

EyeZen includes nine starting workspace profiles covering activities such as coding, reading, office work, productivity, gaming, editing and accessibility.

Profiles can be created, edited, applied, imported and exported as JSON.

A scheduling system supports weekday and overnight time windows, priorities for overlapping rules, and a visible manual override.

The optional Break Assistant provides configurable reminder intervals and quiet hours. Notifications depend on OS permissions and environment support.

Settings are stored locally with validation, export/import, and recovery behavior for corrupted files.

The first-run setup introduces the key choices, while an explicit capability report explains which platform integrations are implemented.

Why use Rust, Tauri 2 and React?

Rust provides a foundation for the desktop command layer, validation, persistence and scheduling utilities.

Tauri 2 bridges the application and its native platform features.

React and TypeScript provide the customizable interface, feature views and tests.

The codebase separates the UI, scheduling logic, imports and platform-support boundaries.

Automated frontend and Rust checks run through GitHub Actions across desktop build targets.

Passing CI is useful, but it isn't a replacement for installing and testing the app on real hardware.

Local-first by design

EyeZen's core functionality doesn't require an account, location permission, telemetry service or cloud backend.

Profiles and settings remain on the device, with manual backup/export options.

That is useful both for privacy and for keeping basic workspace personalization independent of an internet connection.

Honest limits in v1.0.0

An important distinction: EyeZen v1.0.0 does not adjust physical monitor brightness or operating-system color temperature.

Warmth and intensity controls save preferences but do not control Night Light, Night Shift, HDR or an external monitor. There is no color overlay or monitor enumeration in this version.

Scheduling and reminders currently run while the application webview is active, so their operation after closing or suspending the app is not guaranteed.

Release installers are CI-built and unsigned, and OS-specific manual acceptance tests are still needed.

EyeZen is a customization tool, not a medical device, and I don't want to make unsupported claims about eye-health outcomes.

Where the project goes next

The roadmap includes more robust background scheduling, broader tray and shortcut controls, improved theme/profile creation, and eventually carefully validated platform-specific display integrations.

Those are future goals, not features in today's release.

Try EyeZen and contribute

I would love feedback on the onboarding experience, theme choices, scheduling logic, keyboard navigation, package installation, and how EyeZen behaves on different desktops.

  • Source code
  • EyeZen v1.0.0 release and downloads
  • Platform support and known limitations

Your screen. Your comfort. Your environment.

title: Equal-information evaluation of credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning
description:
arXiv:2610.14750v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning is difficult to evaluate because an attributed signal may improve a component loss without adding decision-relevant information or improving economic outcomes. We propose an evaluation framework combining equal-information reconstruction controls, fixed-utility comparisons and prespecified downstream guardrails. The framework is instantiated in an attribution-guided modular trading architecture and tested in three controlled studies covering update allocation, supervision-target representation and portfolio risk control. We find that residual-based allocation is exactly reproduced by an ordinary loss-budget control under the disclosed interface; direct shortfall supervision improves component prediction but fails decoded-outcome preservation; and component-wise critic supervision worsens risk-condition certainty equivalent and drawdown relative to scalar supervision under fixed utility. These results identify three distinct evaluation failures: redundant attribution signals, representation-induced prediction trade-offs, and misalignment between component supervision and downstream risk outcomes. A preserved historical engineering case further shows why module-level learning claims require run-level provenance. The contribution is a reusable methodology for evaluating credit assignment in expert systems operating under partial observability, delayed feedback and economic risk constraints.

title: Why Do VLMs Fail at Remote Physiological Measurement? Rethinking with Physiological Grounding and Numerical Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.19052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video-based remote physiological measurement (RPM) has broad applications, while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide a promising opportunity to enable end-to-end physiological monitoring for future human-aware intelligent systems. However, existing RPM methods rely on task-specific models and cannot be seamlessly integrated with the multimodal understanding and interaction capabilities of VLMs. We revisit RPM with VLMs and provide empirical evidence for two major bottlenecks: generic visual semantic representations fail to preserve fine-grained physiological cues; while discrete token prediction in autoregressive generation is inherently misaligned with continuous numerical measurement. To address these challenges, we propose VITAL (Visual-physiological Token Alignment for Language Models), a visual-physiological token alignment framework for RPM and preserving general vision tasks. VITAL retains the original visual pathway for semantic understanding and introduces an independent physiological pathway to jointly model semantic and physiological information. Moreover, we propose a structured numerical alignment approach to improve the reliability of generative heart rate estimation by enhancing numerical relationship modeling. Extensive experiments show that VITAL improves cross-domain estimation performance on multiple rPPG datasets while preserving the general visual understanding capability of VLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness as a unified visual-physiological model. Code will be released.

title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
description:
arXiv:2610.19114v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on T\"ulu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from T\"ulu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On T\"ulu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.

title: Remote MCP servers with OAuth: lessons from Claude, ChatGPT and Codex
description:
On October 15, 2026, we launched remote MCP servers for three data products: PMWallets (Polymarket traders ranked by on-chain realized PnL), LPSignal (concentrated-liquidity pools ranked by net APR) and OutcomeTick (historical data and backtesting for Polymarket and Predict.fun crypto up/down markets). They share a design with a protected URL that triggers OAuth and a separate anonymous URL. PMWallets uses Streamable HTTP with stateless JSON responses.

We tested them with claude.ai, Claude Code, Codex CLI and ChatGPT developer mode. Most of what broke was in OAuth discovery and client registration; a code review found one more problem in refresh-token cleanup.

Two URLs: one that returns 401, one that doesn't

Every server has a pair:

Protected Anonymous
PMWallets https://api.pmwallets.com/mcp https://api.pmwallets.com/mcp/public
LPSignal https://api.lpsignal.app/v1/mcp https://api.lpsignal.app/v1/mcp/public
OutcomeTick https://outcometick.com/v1/mcp https://outcometick.com/v1/mcp/public

An MCP client starts the OAuth flow when the server answers 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header pointing at the protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728):

HTTP/2 401
www-authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.pmwallets.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp", scope="pmwallets"

If an unauthenticated request gets a 200 and a tool list instead, the client stays anonymous. That rules out one URL that serves public tools to everyone and account tools to signed-in users. Each main URL returns 401 without credentials, and the anonymous tools live at /public, which never asks.

Tool annotations in Codex and claude.ai

On PMWallets, the read tools (leaderboard, entity, market, fills, export_quote and others) carry readOnlyHint: true. The subscription and purchase tools, subscribe, buy_export and cancel_subscription, carry destructiveHint: true. LPSignal's 8 tools and OutcomeTick's 14 are all read-only; neither server has spending tools.

{ "name": "leaderboard",
  "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true, "destructiveHint": false, "idempotentHint": true } }

In the recorded tests:

  • Codex CLI called PMWallets and OutcomeTick read-only tools without approval flags.
  • claude.ai grouped PMWallets read tools under "Read-only tools" in the connector settings.

Annotations are hints that clients may ignore. For PMWallets purchases, the agent quotes first and waits for the user's consent, and buy_export also requires maxPriceCents, the price cap the user agreed to.

Mention every capability in the server instructions

PMWallets sells past fills of a trader as files, one per wallet per UTC day, covering about the last two months. The tools include export_options, export_quote, buy_export and export_file.

Early on, the server instructions didn't mention history exports, and Claude told a user that history from before the subscription was unavailable, although the export tools were already there. The instructions now say that past fills are sold separately as exports and which tool does what.

OAuth: what the authorization server does

PMWallets runs an OAuth 2.1 authorization server with:

  • Discovery through RFC 8414 (authorization server metadata) and RFC 9728 (protected resource metadata).
  • Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD), where the client_id is a URL hosting client metadata, and Dynamic Client Registration (DCR). LPSignal also supports both; its claude.ai, Claude Code and Codex tests used CIMD. OutcomeTick's Claude Code and Codex tests used CIMD.
  • PKCE with S256 and the RFC 8707 resource parameter. Tokens are not bound to a URL path; MCP-only access is enforced separately.
  • Access tokens that last one hour and are accepted for MCP, not the REST API.
  • Refresh tokens that last 30 days and rotate on every use. Replaying an old token revokes the whole connection, provided the server still retains the record needed to recognize it.
  • RFC 7009 revocation, an authorization page that cannot be framed, and a "Connected AI apps" list where users can disconnect a client.

LPSignal also has one-hour MCP-only access tokens, rotating 30-day refresh tokens, RFC 7009 revocation and a "Connected AI apps" list.

OutcomeTick has separate API keys for its data, smart-money and backtest products. The authorization page has a field for each, and each field accepts only that product's key.

ChatGPT's CIMD document says private_key_jwt

ChatGPT's CIMD document declares:

{ "token_endpoint_auth_method": "private_key_jwt" }

All three products hit a compatibility issue with this declaration. The same document lists none in token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported. Treating ChatGPT as a public client using PKCE worked without implementing RFC 7523 JWT client authentication.

Refresh-token rotation and the cleanup job

Reuse detection depends on retaining records of refresh tokens that have already been exchanged.

PMWallets had a cleanup job that deleted used refresh tokens once they expired. That looks harmless, since an expired token can't be exchanged anyway. But once the row is gone, a replayed token is no longer "used", just unknown. After about 30 days, a replay was rejected as an ordinary bad token, and the connection it belonged to stayed alive.

Codex review found this in PMWallets, and OutcomeTick confirmed the same issue.

A wrong URL that half works

LPSignal and OutcomeTick use /v1/mcp; PMWallets originally used /mcp. A user pasted https://api.pmwallets.com/v1/mcp into ChatGPT. Sign-in succeeded, then ChatGPT showed:

Authentication succeeded, action discovery failed

That route did not exist. Without a token, ChatGPT's POST got a 403 from the Origin check, and the path-specific metadata returned 404. ChatGPT fell back to the root metadata, which described /mcp, and completed OAuth. It then POSTed to /v1/mcp with the token, received 404 and reported a discovery failure.

PMWallets now serves /v1/mcp as an alias with its own protected-resource metadata, with resource set to https://api.pmwallets.com/v1/mcp. The 401 points to that metadata, and the alias is included in the Origin exemption and rate limits.

DNS lookups for URLs users control

PMWallets resolves user-supplied hosts for webhooks and CIMD metadata fetches.

In Node, dns.lookup uses getaddrinfo on the libuv thread pool, which has four threads by default. The same pool runs file system calls and some crypto. A user who controls the hostname can make lookups slow, and a few of them hold up unrelated work in the process. For these lookups we switched to the c-ares-based dns.Resolver, which doesn't use the pool, with an overall deadline.

The second problem was in net.BlockList. We added ::ffff:0:0/96 to block IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. With that rule in the list, every plain IPv4 address was classified as internal, public hosts included. Convert a mapped address to IPv4 yourself and check it against the IPv4 rules instead.

Reading large files through MCP

PMWallets' export_file streams and decompresses the download, returning only the requested page. A call scans at most 50,000 lines, concurrent reads are limited, and the read aborts when the client disconnects. Without the disconnect check, the server would keep downloading and decompressing after the client had gone away.

Batches and rate limits

All three servers rate-limit MCP requests. LPSignal and OutcomeTick reject JSON-RPC batches. PMWallets accepts up to 10 messages per batch and executes them one at a time.

Connecting

For Claude Code and Codex CLI, add the protected URL:

# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http pmwallets https://api.pmwallets.com/mcp

# Codex CLI
codex mcp add pmwallets --url https://api.pmwallets.com/mcp

Use the LPSignal or OutcomeTick URL from the table to connect those servers. PMWallets was also tested with a claude.ai custom connector and a ChatGPT web developer-mode custom connector. LPSignal supports wallet sign-in with any wallet and has a free account. PMWallets accepts OAuth or a bearer API key; OutcomeTick's authorization page accepts its product-specific keys.

The /public URLs need no account. PMWallets exposes a 20-row leaderboard sample, trader records and market lookups. LPSignal exposes everything except my_account. OutcomeTick exposes coverage and plans, backtest capacity and quotes, strategy checks, and smart-money plans and coverage.

All three are listed in the official MCP Registry (io.github.polymarketwallets/pmwallets, app.lpsignal/lpsignal, io.github.outcometick/outcometick) and have Claude Code plugins. OutcomeTick also ships a local stdio server (ot mcp) with a test that keeps its tool set identical to the remote one. Setup guides: pmwallets.com/ai-agents, LPSignals/lpsignal-mcp, outcometick.com/llms-full.txt.

I build PMWallets, LPSignal and OutcomeTick.

title: Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs
description:
arXiv:2610.14209v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The most accurate agents executing user-provided tasks are driven by large, cloud-hosted models, which solve them by reading the private data of the user. Agents powered by models small enough to run on edge devices keep that data local, but yield far worse results. A third option is to have cloud models write a program that devices execute: the data stays local, but as the program is written before any data is seen, it fails whenever a step depends on interpreting content that appears only at run time. We explore an intermediate architecture, in which the cloud-written program defers bounded questions over user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call. On AppWorld this improves the success rate of a code-only agent in all six combinations of backbone model and test partition we evaluate, by up to 14.9pp, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted ReAct loop while keeping user data on the device.
