title: Email coding tasks to your own computer
description:
Send an idea by email

You can remember a signup form problem while you are away from your computer. You can email yourself the task from your phone. You send the message from your own Gmail account to your own address with +agents added. Gmail delivers the message to your normal inbox, so you need no new email account.

You write the task in the email body. You can send plain text or HTML email. You can attach files, and atgent gives the saved attachment paths to the agent.

A signup form task can ask an agent to improve confusing parts of the form and run the relevant checks. Your computer can stay at home while you send the task from another device.

Run the task on your computer

You install atgent on the computer that holds your projects. The runner reads your Gmail Sent folder, not your Inbox. It starts Codex or Claude Code in a configured project with your existing sign-in.

Your repositories and agent sign-ins stay on your computer. Task text and results travel through Gmail and your chosen agent provider. Tasks for different projects can run at the same time.

The runner sends Queued, Started and the result as replies in the task thread. The result is the agent's final message as formatted email. Every reply ends with the task ID and the command to open it in your terminal.

Only mail that you send from your own Gmail account can start a task. Mail from other people lands in your Inbox. The runner does not read your Inbox, so their mail cannot start a task. Anyone who can add mail to your Sent folder can also send tasks, so you must protect your Gmail account and its credentials.

Route work with the subject line

The subject line selects the agent, project, model and run mode. Agent names ignore case. Project names are case sensitive. The task body contains the instruction.

Codex: improve the signup form runs Codex in your default project.

Claude: improve the signup form runs Claude Code in your default project.

Codex/website: fix the footer links runs Codex in the project named website in your config.

Claude [opus]: review the auth flow runs Claude Code with the opus model. Replies in the thread keep that model.

Codex/website [gpt-6.1-sol]: fix the build runs Codex in the website project with the gpt-6.1-sol model.

Claude [opus, terminal]: review the auth flow opens Claude Code in a new Terminal window and uses the opus model.

Without a model in brackets, the configured default model runs. Add headless in the brackets to run the task in the background. Add terminal in the brackets to open the task in a Terminal window.

Continue and control the session

You can reply in the same thread to continue the same agent session. The agent keeps the earlier turns. A reply of status returns progress by email. A reply of stop cancels queued turns and stops the running agent. Changes that the agent already made stay in your project.

Approval emails let you approve or deny a blocked action from your phone. Each approval covers one action. You reply directly to the approval email with approve or deny. Silence becomes a denial after the configured timeout.

With approvals off, Codex uses its configured sandbox and approval policy. Claude Code denies actions that need approval by default. You review the work before you publish or deploy it.

When you return to your computer, run atgent list to see each email task with its agent, model and status. Select a task and press Enter to resume the same session in your terminal. The agent then answers in the terminal instead of by email. A reply resumes a Claude terminal session. Codex terminal sessions are not tracked, so a reply opens a new window.

Set up atgent

Install uv first. Then install Codex or Claude Code and sign in. Install the runner with uv tool install atgent. Run atgent init to enter your Gmail address, sign-in method, project folders, installed agents and default models. The setup writes no secret to the config.

Turn on IMAP in Gmail. Create a Google app password, or use your own Gmail OAuth desktop client when app passwords are blocked. Keep the app password in your OS keychain or in the AGENT_MAILBOX_PASSWORD environment variable. Never put it in the config file.

Run atgent doctor to check Gmail over IMAP and SMTP without sending mail. The command also checks that Codex and Claude Code are installed. Run atgent start to start the runner in the background. Its first check skips old Sent mail, so send your first task after that check.

Requirements and licence

atgent needs Gmail with IMAP access, macOS or Linux, Python 3.11 or later, uv, and a computer that stays awake and online. You need Codex or Claude Code installed and signed in. Claude Code needs version 2.1.259 or later.

HTML email, attachments, concurrent projects, approval email replies with both agents, and the login service were tested live on macOS. Linux and Gmail OAuth are unit-tested only.

atgent is free and MIT licensed. Your existing Codex or Claude Code plan and its limits apply.

https://atgent.dev

title: ELARSpeech: A 30K-Hour Dataset Across 675 Underrepresented Languages for Long-Tail Multilingual Speech Technologies
description:
arXiv:2610.19388v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Massively multilingual speech modeling has made remarkable progress in recent years, yet existing training resources and benchmarks still underrepresent much of the linguistic long tail. To address this gap, we introduce ELARSpeech, a large-scale multilingual speech resource comprising 30,202 hours of speech across 675 underrepresented languages, curated from the Endangered Languages Archive. Combining human-annotated and unlabeled recordings, the corpus spans diverse recording conditions, domains, and language families. Beyond corpus construction, our experiments show how ELARSpeech supports extending ASR and TTS capabilities to diverse underrepresented languages, with further benefits from pseudo-labeling unlabeled data. At the same time, our speech representation analysis reveals remaining limitations in transferring existing multilingual models to the linguistic long tail. Together, ELARSpeech provides both a resource and a testbed for extending multilingual speech technology further into the linguistic long tail. We publicly release the dataset, all trained ASR and TTS models, and the complete data construction pipeline to facilitate research on long-tail multilingual speech technologies.

title: Build in public
description:
While building ShopPilot AI, I’ve been working on a function that checks availability for a requested product color and size.

“Out of stock” and “that variant doesn’t exist” need different answers.

I defined three cases to test:
• The variant exists and has stock.
• The variant exists but has zero stock.
• There’s no matching variant.

The interesting part was the third case.

JavaScript’s .find() returns undefined when nothing matches, so I need to handle that before reading the variant’s stock.

This is a small function, but it’s helping me connect JavaScript fundamentals, TypeScript, and testing to a real customer question.

I’m learning how to use TDD for this logic: define the expected behavior with a failing test, implement it, then refactor.

My main lesson so far: a useful test starts with a clear requirement.
Before checking whether the code works, I need to decide what it should do.

title: Exact Scaling Laws for a Random-Features Bigram Model
description:
arXiv:2610.19281v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding neural scaling laws is increasingly important for theory and practice, yet first-principles explanations remain limited even in simple settings. In this work, we study capacity-limited scaling in a bottlenecked bigram model with power-law (Zipf) token statistics, viewed as an analytically tractable toy model of a large language model. Fixed random embeddings serve as a proxy for representational capacity and induce an explicit bottleneck of width, allowing us to derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. Our results complement recent theoretical accounts based on optimization dynamics by isolating scaling due purely to representational constraints. In the appropriate regime, the theory recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws and suggests that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both optimization- and capacity-driven scaling. Experiments natural language datasets (WikiText2, OpenWebText) closely match the predicted curves.

title: Learning to Select Features with Manifold Deep Unfolding PCA
description:
arXiv:2610.19436v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unsupervised feature selection (UFS) is of great significance in image processing and pattern recognition. Nevertheless, existing model-based methods often rely on manually tuned hyperparameters, while deep learning-based methods generally require massive training data. To address these issues, this paper proposes an efficient manifold deep unfolding feature selection network (MDUFS-Net). Technically, we first incorporate the $\ell_{2,0}$-norm into the classic principal component analysis (PCA) framework, then unfold the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)-based iterative algorithm into an end-to-end trainable network, thereby enabling automatic parameter learning. Moreover, a manifold optimization strategy is developed to improve the numerical robustness. On this basis, we further extend MDUFS-Net into an enhanced variant called MDUFS-Net+ by introducing the $\ell_{0}$-norm for more discriminative feature representations. Extensive experiments validate that our proposed MDUFS-Net and MDUFS-Net+ outperform state-of-the-art methods in the UFS task, with promising performance in clustering. Our code is available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/MDUFS.

description:
When engineering fintech and access control infrastructure for large-scale physical events, standard cloud architectures eventually hit a hard physical wall.

Under the Saudi Vision 2030 events strategy, mega-summits in Riyadh and Jeddah regularly process upwards of 10,000 delegates. At these scales, the operational realities of a crowded convention center break traditional web systems:

  1. Saturated Networks: As thousands of delegates stream through the doors, local cellular macrocells congest and venue Wi-Fi suffers catastrophic packet loss.
  2. Concurrency Bursts: 80% of gate traffic and 60% of food and beverage (F&B) purchases happen during narrow 30-to-45-minute windows (e.g., morning ingress and keynote breaks)[cite: 14].

If your event analytics platform or POS system relies on a synchronous HTTP handshake to a remote PostgreSQL database to open a turnstile or process a payment, it will fail under burst load.

To guarantee sub-second transaction times and zero gate downtime, we redesigned our RFID attendee tracking and cashless event payments architecture entirely around Edge Persistence and Dual-Frequency hardware.

Here is how we built it.

1. Dual-Frequency Credentials (UHF + HF)

The foundation of our architecture is a single physical smart credential (either a sub-3-second on-demand thermal badge or a durable silicone wristband).

We abandoned optical QR codes entirely. Instead, each credential contains a dual-frequency inlay with two distinct memory chips:

  • Passive UHF EPC Gen 2 (865–868 MHz): Used strictly for zero-contact spatial tracking. Overhead RFID portals read these tags at distances up to 8 meters. Using dynamic Q-algorithm arbitration (Frame-Slotted ALOHA), a single portal can resolve up to 400 tag collisions per second, tracking venue capacity and sponsor dwell times without attendees ever breaking stride.
  • Near-Field HF (13.56 MHz / NFC): Used for explicit intent actions, such as tapping to process a cashless payment at a vendor terminal or tapping to access a restricted ministerial VIP lounge.

2. Offline-First POS Architecture with SQLite WAL

If a vendor's Point-of-Sale terminal has to query an external cloud API to verify a wristband's wallet balance, the F&B queue will grind to a halt the moment venue Wi-Fi drops.

We pushed the financial ledger down to the edge. Each physical POS terminal and gate controller runs an embedded SQLite database in Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode[cite: 14].


sql
-- POS Edge Node Initialization
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;
PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;

-- Local Ledger Schema
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS edge_transactions (
    txn_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    wallet_uid TEXT NOT NULL,
    vendor_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    amount INTEGER NOT NULL, -- Stored in base currency units (Halalas)
    epoch_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
    sync_state INTEGER DEFAULT 0
);
Sub-Millisecond Tap-to-PayWhen a delegate taps their wristband to buy a coffee:The local NFC reader validates the cryptographically signed offline balance directly from the HF chip's secure memory sector.   

The transaction is appended to the local SQLite WAL companion file in under 4 milliseconds.   The physical UI updates instantly, completing the transaction.

A background Go daemon running on the terminal continuously monitors network health. When the internet connection is stable, it asynchronously flushes the committed transactions in batches to our central cloud API. If the internet drops, the terminal keeps selling.

3. Cloud Ingestion with Go & Redis StreamsTo handle the asynchronous telemetry bursts coming from hundreds of offline-resilient edge nodes, we use a Go-based ingestion layer backed by Redis Streams[cite: 14].Gopackage main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "[github.com/redis/go-redis/v9](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/v9)"
)

var ctx = context.Background()
var rdb *redis.Client

type SyncBatch struct {
    Transactions []CashlessTxn `json:"transactions"`
}

func ingestEdgeBatch(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    var batch SyncBatch
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&batch); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, err.Error(), 400)
        return
    }

    pipe := rdb.Pipeline()
    for _, txn := range batch.Transactions {
        // Push to in-memory Redis Stream buffer
        pipe.XAdd(ctx, &redis.XAddArgs{
            Stream: "stream:cashless_ingestion",
            Values: map[string]interface{}{
                "txn_id": txn.TxnID,
                "wallet": txn.Wallet,
                "amount": txn.Amount,
                "vendor": txn.VendorID,
            },
        })
    }

    if _, err := pipe.Exec(ctx); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "Ingestion Failed", 500)
        return
    }

    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
}
By pushing telemetry directly into an in-memory stream buffer, we completely decouple our primary PostgreSQL database from the extreme write contention caused by hardware synchronization bursts.4. Live Command via WebSocketsA worker pool consumes the Redis Streams, applies idempotent deduplication logic based on the txn_id, and computes rolling spatial and financial aggregations.

These metrics are then broadcasted via WebSockets directly to our KSA custom reporting dashboard. 

Event directors and financial controllers gain instant visibility into live vendor settlements, peak F&B purchasing windows, and civil defense hall capacities, all without aggressively polling the database.

ConclusionBuilding physical event technology requires acknowledging that venue networks will fail[cite: 1, 14]. By treating cloud connectivity as an eventual luxury rather than a strict requirement, we guarantee continuous ingress and revenue generation.

To explore how these architectures are deployed in the field across GCC exhibitions, review the hardware integration models behind StampIQ's cashless payments for events and their real-time event analytics platform.

title: BOOTH Was Featured in Python Weekly: A Small Milestone for My Open-Source Project
description:
A small milestone for a project I've been building: BOOTH was featured in Python Weekly!

It appears in Python Weekly Issue #767 (October 15, 2026) under Interesting Projects, Tools, and Libraries, described as a lightweight, zero-dependency Python checkpoint layer for structured LLM output reliability.

I started BOOTH only a couple of months ago, and I'm still learning what it takes to turn a small library into something other developers find useful. Seeing it in a curated newsletter is encouraging.

Why BOOTH exists

A few months ago, a person working an airport gate helped me find mine after I'd gotten lost, boarding pass in hand, signs everywhere, still at the wrong gate. She didn't know where I'd flown in from, how the aircraft was built, or anything about my itinerary beyond that one boarding pass. She didn't need to. She knew the airport, and she knew what to check.

That's the idea BOOTH is built around. The industry's default answer to "the model got it wrong" has mostly been to make the model know more: more context, more compute, bigger models, more tools bolted around it. And the problem still happens, because it isn't always a knowledge problem. Sometimes what's missing isn't more information going in. It's something whose only job is checking whether what came out actually meets the bar.

BOOTH doesn't try to know more than your model does. It just knows what to check.

So the question I kept coming back to was:

Before passing an LLM response to the rest of the application, should we check it first?

A response can sound confident and still be ambiguous, fail validation, or disagree with the evidence your application retrieved. That's the problem BOOTH explores.

I wrote the longer version of this idea on Substack: Knowing less, but knowing what matters.

What BOOTH does

BOOTH is a lightweight, provider-agnostic library that sits between an LLM call and your application logic. Instead of raw text, you get a structured result (ACCEPTED, REPAIRED, AMBIGUOUS, UNCERTAIN or BLOCKED) so your app can decide what to do next.

It has three main entry points:

  • check(): a synchronous checkpoint for ambiguity and confidence, with reconsideration retries.
  • acheck(): the async counterpart.
  • check_with_evidence(): checks an answer against evidence your application supplies, such as documents from a RAG pipeline. 
import booth

result = booth.check(call_llm, "What is the capital of France?")

if result.ok:
    print(result.answer)
else:
    print(f"BOOTH returned {result.status}")  # AMBIGUOUS / UNCERTAIN

For evidence grounding, imagine your retrieval pipeline returns a policy saying refunds are available within 45 days, but the generated answer says 90 days:

result = booth.check_with_evidence(
    answer=llm_answer,
    evidence=retrieved_docs,
    compare_fn=your_comparison_function,
)

if result.status == booth.BLOCKED:
    print(result.detail)  # the answer disagrees with the retrieved evidence

You provide the comparison function, and BOOTH makes the checking step explicit.

To be clear about the limits: BOOTH doesn't replace your retrieval pipeline, and agreeing with the supplied evidence doesn't prove the evidence is correct or complete.

Why keep it lightweight?

BOOTH is small on purpose. It has zero runtime dependencies, works with any provider through functions you supply, and returns structured results instead of making decisions for you.

I don't want it to become another framework that forces you to rebuild your application around it. You should be able to try it in an existing Python project without changing your stack.

pip install boothpy

What's next

Testing across providers and models has been the most useful part of building BOOTH. Real integrations expose edge cases that are easy to miss in your own setup. The repo now includes runnable examples with real console output for several providers and local models, including the negative results.

I'm continuing to work on error handling, documentation, integrations, and the behavior of the checkpoint APIs. I'd also welcome contributors who want to test BOOTH, find edge cases, or pick up open issues.

The Python Weekly feature is a nice milestone, but what matters most to me is whether developers find BOOTH useful enough to try in their own applications. If you work with Python, LLMs or RAG, I'd genuinely appreciate your feedback.

Links

  • Python Weekly Issue #767
  • BOOTH on GitHub
  • BOOTH on PyPI
  • Open issues and contributions

Thanks to everyone who has explored the project, reported issues, contributed integrations, or shared feedback. I'm excited to keep building BOOTH in the open.

title: LYNX: Analytical Program Synthesis via Grounding and Closed-Loop Refinement
description:
arXiv:2610.14777v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-powered data analytics aims to translate natural language instructions into executable analytical programs over underlying data. However, existing approaches, whether treating LLMs as intent-to-code translators or as standalone analytical engines, often fail to reliably align domain semantics with complex schemas and heterogeneous metadata, resulting in brittle execution and semantically inconsistent analytical outputs in real-world workloads. We present LYNX, a multi-agent framework that formulates LLM-driven analytics as a schema- and knowledge-constrained analysis problem rather than a single-pass generation task. LYNX organizes analytical synthesis into a closed-loop workflow of planning, generation, verification, and refinement through three role-specialized agents that collaboratively enforce schema grounding, semantic consistency, and execution correctness. To address domain ambiguity and schema misalignment, LYNX integrates Semantic-Structural Distillation and Stage-Aware Allocation (SSD-SAA). A delta-guided iterative revision continuously diagnoses and repairs semantic and execution-level failures, substantially improving synthesis robustness. We evaluate LYNX on two NL-to-SQL benchmarks, BIRD-SQL Mini-Dev and the more challenging Spider 2.0-Lite. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance and efficiency, achieving 10.66% to 59.54% execution accuracy across lightweight and commercial models, while reducing token consumption by 70.53% compared with the prior most efficient method. Our framework displays high generalization over different backbones, from open-source, lightweight models to the latest commercial models. Additional case studies on quantitative finance analytics and complex multi-relational SQL workloads further demonstrate the framework's robustness, scalability, and practical applicability in real-world analytical scenarios.

title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.

title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19138v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.

title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
description:
arXiv:2610.19331v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.

title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.14721v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.

title: The 8 tests I ship in a starter kit (and why I stop at 8)
description:
Most starter kits ship with one test: test_that_true_is_true. It's the Laravel default, and almost nobody replaces it. When I started packing my SaaS kit for other developers, I decided the test suite had to earn its place — a buyer should be able to run php artisan test, watch green, and trust that the auth layer they just bought actually works.

So the kit ships tests/Feature/AuthTest.php with eight real tests. Here's what they cover and why each one exists.

The register tests. test_register_returns_token_and_user posts to /api/auth/register and asserts a 201 with a user object (shaped through the API resource) and a token. It also asserts the database row was created with role => 'user' — because the register endpoint hardcodes the role. Which leads to the second test: test_register_cannot_self_assign_admin_role. You can POST role: admin all day; you still get created as a user. That's a security property, and security properties are exactly the things that deserve tests — they're the ones that silently regress when someone "refactors" the controller six months later.

The login tests. test_login_returns_token_and_user creates a user via the factory and asserts a 200 with the token and user. test_login_with_wrong_password_returns_401 asserts the failure shape: 401, message Invalid credentials. Testing the sad path matters more than the happy path here — frontend devs build their error UI against the exact status code this endpoint returns.

The contract tests. test_me_requires_authentication hits /api/auth/me with no token and expects a 401. test_me_without_accept_header_returns_json_401 is the sneaky one: it checks that even without an Accept: application/json header, you get JSON back, not a redirect to a login page that doesn't exist. If you've ever debugged a SPA that got HTML back from an API and choked, you know why this test exists. It's a one-line regression test for a bug I hit on a real client project.

The authorization tests. test_non_admin_cannot_list_users and test_admin_can_list_users — a regular user gets 403 on the user index, an admin gets 200. Two tests, the entire role system proven end to end.

And here's the deliberate part: I stop at 8. There is no test for password reset, no test for email verification, no test for Stripe webhooks — because the kit doesn't ship those features. I won't write tests for code that doesn't exist to make the suite look bigger. A starter kit is a foundation, not a framework, and its tests should mirror its actual scope. What it does ship, it proves.

All eight run against a fresh database (RefreshDatabase), take a couple of seconds, and are written against the public API of the app — routes and JSON — not internals. That means a buyer can refactor my controllers freely and the tests still guard the contract their frontend depends on.

If you want the whole thing — Sanctum auth, role middleware, the admin user management loop, and these 8 tests proving it all works — I packed it into the Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit, $19 one-time. Skip the three days of wiring and start on the part that's actually yours.

title: A Go Small-App Observability Stack for Health Monitoring Without Sentry or Datadog
description:
A marketplace import page should fire when scheduled imports stop producing results, not merely when the API process dies. TL;DR: use an external heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks or Better Stack to detect the missing completion, then use errors, logs, and metrics to explain it. For a small Go service, that is the least complex stack that covers silent scheduler failures and still lets the on-call roll back safely.

The page should say which import is late, when it last completed, and how far it is beyond its expected interval. It should not begin with a graph titled “host CPU.” If the 02:00 supplier import normally finishes by 02:20, the actionable event is the absent successful completion after a deliberate grace period.

The page at 02:25 UTC

Start at the pager and work backward. A useful alert reads like this: supplier-catalog-import has not completed; last success 01:58 UTC; grace period 25m. The runbook then asks three questions in order: did a run start, did it fail, and did it finish with a plausible result count?

That order protects rollback safety. If a newly deployed parser started producing zero records, the operator can compare the deployment time, error group, and rows_imported metric before reverting. If no run started, rolling back application code may be pointless; the scheduler or queue path deserves attention first. If the run started twice, the response shifts again: stop duplicate delivery from causing duplicate marketplace writes, using an idempotency key derived from the schedule and supplier.

One signal cannot answer all three questions. An uptime probe proves an HTTP target responds. A heartbeat proves the expected job reached a checkpoint. Logs and errors preserve diagnostic context. Metrics show whether “success” produced 18,000 listings or zero.

That last distinction matters.

What should health monitoring prove without a full observability stack?

A job that never starts emits no fresh error, log, or metric. Querying the observability store can reveal that absence, but somebody still has to run the query on schedule, maintain threshold state, and deliver the notification. That is a monitoring system built beside the monitoring system.

External heartbeat products own that negative-space problem. Healthchecks exposes ping URLs and documents start, success, and failure signals. Better Stack combines uptime monitoring with heartbeat monitoring and incident escalation. Either can watch for a missing completion independently of the process and scheduler being watched.

The threshold needs operational slack. Set it from the schedule plus the observed upper end of normal runtime, then add a grace period for queue delay and upstream variance. Do not invent a universal “two missed runs” rule: for a daily catalog import, waiting for a second miss means discovering the failure a day late; for a five-minute enrichment job, paging on one slightly slow execution may create noise.

Page on missing useful work, not missing telemetry. A metrics backend can still alert on rows_imported == 0 after a run reports, but the external heartbeat is what catches a worker that never got far enough to report anything.

Build the Go integration around completion

The heartbeat should surround the real unit of work. This runnable Go program sends a start signal, runs an import, and sends success only after the result is committed. Set HEALTHCHECKS_URL to the private ping URL supplied by the heartbeat service.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func ping(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, url, suffix, body string) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url+suffix, strings.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        message, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        return fmt.Errorf("heartbeat returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(message)))
    }
    return nil
}

func queryErrorGroups(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) error {
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/errors/groups", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("error groups returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        log.Printf("error groups response received: bytes=%d", len(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("error groups remained rate limited after retries")
}

func importCatalog(context.Context) (int, error) {
    return 18000, nil
}

func main() {
    pingURL := os.Getenv("HEALTHCHECKS_URL")
    if pingURL == "" {
        log.Fatal("HEALTHCHECKS_URL is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    if err := ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/start", "supplier=catalog-a"); err != nil {
        log.Printf("start heartbeat failed: %v", err)
    }

    rows, err := importCatalog(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        _ = ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/fail", err.Error())
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if rows == 0 {
        err = fmt.Errorf("import committed zero rows")
        _ = ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/fail", err.Error())
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    if err := ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "", fmt.Sprintf("rows_imported=%d", rows)); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if err := queryErrorGroups(ctx, client); err != nil {
        log.Printf("diagnostic query failed: %v", err)
    }
    log.Printf("import complete: rows_imported=%d", rows)
}

In production, the import itself also needs an idempotent commit boundary. A deterministic key such as supplier-id + scheduled-window lets an at-least-once queue retry without publishing the same listings twice. Send the success heartbeat after that transaction commits, never when the message is merely dequeued.

The sample treats heartbeat delivery failure differently at the start and the end. A failed start ping is logged because the import can still do useful work. A failed final ping fails the process so the queue can retry; that retry is safe only because the import commit is idempotent. This is a conscious trade-off: monitoring delivery becomes part of completion semantics, which is appropriate when the page depends on that completion record.

OpenTelemetry metrics can add duration, attempted rows, committed rows, and queue age using vendor-neutral instruments. Keep a stable supplier_id only if its cardinality is bounded. Do not put order IDs, listing IDs, or raw error messages in metric labels.

Compare failure coverage, not feature counts

The right choice depends less on dashboard polish than on which failure modes must wake somebody up. These products overlap, but they do not substitute for one another.

Option Strong fit here Boundary that changes the decision
Healthchecks Focused cron and heartbeat monitoring with start, success, and failure signaling Pair it with a separate store for searchable logs, errors, and metrics
Better Stack Uptime and heartbeat monitoring with an incident-management path Broader workflow means more surface area than a heartbeat-only tool
Grafana Cloud Metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, and alerting around an OpenTelemetry-oriented stack A missed job still needs an explicit heartbeat or absence rule
Datadog Integrated logs, metrics, traces, synthetic monitoring, and alerting Capability breadth and its ingestion/indexing model deserve review before adoption
Sentry Application error diagnosis, source maps, tracing, and session replay It is not the primary proof that a scheduled backend import ran

Infrai can be the errors, logs, and metrics component when a team wants a self-describing plain REST API whose public discovery response supplies schemas and billing metadata, whose documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, and whose single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one bill. For this import worker, that means one credential to rotate and one access boundary to review when another backend capability is added. It does not provide synthetic uptime checks, heartbeat monitoring, native alert delivery, distributed trace querying, source-map processing, crash symbolication, or session replay. Its logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a span-tree UI. For this use case it belongs beside a heartbeat monitor, not in place of one.

For the smallest service, I would begin with Healthchecks plus structured application logs and OpenTelemetry metrics. Move toward Better Stack when the same team wants the alert escalation workflow in that layer. Choose Grafana Cloud or Datadog when cross-signal querying, managed dashboards, and wider infrastructure visibility justify the extra operational surface. Add Sentry when frontend stack traces, source maps, or replay are the diagnostic gap.

This is not a permanent architecture decision. Keep the heartbeat call isolated and the application telemetry in OpenTelemetry-compatible instruments; then changing a backend does not require changing the definition of a successful import.

Plan rollback and migration before the alert

A page needs evidence that separates deploy regression from data and scheduler failures. Record the deployed revision in logs, attach it as a bounded metric attribute, and include it in the import result. Then define the rollback trigger before the incident: for example, a new revision fails across multiple suppliers while the previous revision completed the same scheduled window. The exact trigger must come from the service's own baseline; no honest generic article can manufacture it.

The runbook should preserve the failed payload reference, verify the idempotency key, roll back the worker, and replay the same scheduled window. A rollback that loses the input or changes the deduplication key is not safe. It can turn one missed import into duplicated listings.

Also test the monitor. Disable a staging schedule, verify that the missing heartbeat reaches the intended channel, then restore it and confirm recovery. A green dashboard is weak evidence if nobody has exercised the delivery path.

Account for the cost of a noisy threshold

A short grace period detects a stalled supplier feed quickly, but routine upstream slowness will page the on-call. A long grace period preserves sleep while stale inventory remains visible to buyers. The threshold is therefore a product decision expressed as an SRE setting: how long can this marketplace tolerate stale availability before a human must act?

Review that setting using actual completion durations and queue age, especially after schedule or supplier changes. Keep warning and paging thresholds distinct when the business window permits it. And avoid automatic rollback on one late heartbeat: absence tells you the result is late, not that the newest deployment caused it.

The compact architecture is deliberate: external heartbeat for detection, telemetry for diagnosis, idempotent replay for recovery. More tooling is justified only when it closes a named failure mode. Consider the specific 02:00 supplier run: no start ping points toward scheduling, a start followed by failure points toward execution, and a success with zero committed rows points toward validation. Those three states lead to different actions, so collapsing them into a single “job unhealthy” event makes rollback riskier and the page slower to resolve.

Keep those states separate.

title: FinGREAT: Evaluating LLMs on Financial Graph-guided Retrieval And Typing
description:
arXiv:2610.19240v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial disclosures express the underlying relationships of double-entry accounting through unstructured text. While financial LLM benchmarks predominantly emphasize question answering and classification, schema-guided evidence discovery remains relatively under-explored. We investigate whether open-weight LLMs can extract and classify evidence corresponding to predefined double-entry accounting relationships underlying the text. Using a financial accounting graph comprising 11 nodes (accounts) and 11 edges (transaction types), we evaluate mid-sized models from 5 open-weight families across 1,300 SEC 10-K Item 7 filings spanning 26 years, comparing their extraction performance against three proprietary models. Results reveal substantial differences in extraction volume, edge distributions, and cross-model agreement. Building on this study, we introduce a human-annotated relation classification benchmark comprising 483 passages across three financial accounting categories, evaluating 34 open-weight and 10 proprietary models. The strongest open-weight and proprietary models achieve 84.1\% and 92.8\% accuracy, respectively, with considerable variation across accounting categories. Our findings highlight the importance of evaluating evidence discovery and relation understanding separately, while investigating locally deployable models for scalable, privacy-sensitive financial analysis.

title: How KIKO Milano scales for Black Friday
description:
KIKO Milano on Vercel:

  • Eliminated 3 weeks of Black Friday infrastructure prep

  • 75% decrease in app build times

  • Went from minimal releases to deploying multiple times per day

KIKO Milano’s ecommerce team used to treat peak traffic as an operations project. Weeks before Black Friday, they had to manually scale AWS infrastructure and adjust application configuration, knowing that if demand exceeded forecasts, their site could slow down or even break, costing them real revenue.

After migrating to Vercel, they removed manual prep from their playbook. Instead of provisioning infrastructure, their team now ships campaigns and tests daily.

The Black Friday problem: manual scaling and stressful failure modes

Before Vercel, KIKO ran their ecommerce app on AWS EC2 instances sized for normal traffic, then scaled by hand ahead of peak periods.

This was their previous process leading into Black Friday:

  • Manual scaling window:

    Black Friday prep began 2–3 weeks ahead of the event, then had to be unwound after the traffic spike passed.

  • Infrastructure configuration:

    The infra team manually adjusted AWS EC2 capacity to support expected traffic.

  • Application configuration:

    Scaling also required application-side changes, making peak readiness more than just an infrastructure task.

  • War room prep:

    Chat channels and conference rooms were set up for teams to triage performance and downtime problems.

Beyond the manual prep work, KIKO’s dev team had to anticipate failure modes that hurt the business. Slow navigation and site instability made it hard for users to purchase, and, in Ant’s words, they knew that at any point, “everything could break.”

Worry-free delivery and automatic scaling

Vercel changed the work from preparation to execution. With environments available on demand, faster builds, and automatic scaling during traffic spikes, Ant’s team stopped planning around infrastructure limits and focused on the ecommerce experience itself.

Environments without the bottleneck

KIKO's old setup ran on a fixed number of shared environments, which constrained how the team handled dev, test, pre-prod, and prod work in parallel. On Vercel, Ant described provisioning new environments as "snapping your fingers," including spinning them up on the fly when a project calls for it. Cloning environment variables is quick, and many changes that used to require code edits now "just require redeployment."

Shipping faster without the operational tax

The dev team’s old pipeline took around 20 minutes to run, which meant they had to keep releases to a minimum. Builds on Vercel finish in under four minutes on average, even with many locales and a large catalog of pre-rendered pages. The deployments view in the Vercel dashboard gives the team one place to check build status and surface failures without digging through logs.

No more performance variability during traffic spikes

Performance used to swing with traffic, which meant the team felt every spike. Ant said that on Vercel, "everything scales automatically."

That’s possible because their Next.js app runs on infrastructure that separates static delivery, cached pages, and dynamic compute, so each part can scale independently during traffic spikes, instead of forcing the team to size and tune servers ahead of time.

Beyond Black Friday: velocity, SEO, and innovation

The infrastructure migration didn’t just change how KIKO prepares for traffic spikes, it changed how much operational work the team carries every week.

Ant estimates that Vercel saves his team almost an entire day per week when all of the friction is added up, and that time savings has made the team more confident: the platform works, they can ship quickly, and when they need support, they know Vercel is there with them.

About KIKO Milano: KIKO Milano is a global beauty brand delivering cosmetics and ecommerce experiences to customers worldwide.

title: Prepare Email-Safe Images: A 4-Step Convert, Compress, and Host Pipeline
description:
TL;DR: Convert generated promotional images to a conservative format, compress them aggressively, store them privately, and put a time-limited hosted link in the email instead of attaching the bytes. Treat moderation as a separate release gate before delivery. For a team also generating short promo videos from prompts, that boundary matters more than an attractive dashboard: the page should fire when unsafe media can escape or recipients cannot load an asset, not merely because a conversion job took a little longer than usual.

This is a four-step delivery pipeline, but the operational question is narrower: what will the person carrying the pager actually see? A useful alert says that an email campaign contains an unmoderated asset, that signed links are failing, or that output size has crossed the team's tested ceiling. A weak alert says only that a media dashboard turned red. At 3 a.m., the first kind leads to an action; the second leads to tab hunting.

Infrai is an early candidate when the same team needs conversion, compression, private storage, and email behind one REST contract. That can remove three SDK and credential boundaries from the incident path, but it does not choose a format, set a size budget, or define moderation policy for you.

What should the first page say?

Start at the failure visible to a recipient: an image is absent, rejected, or mishandled by the mail client. Work backward. The stored object may be healthy while its signed URL has expired; the URL may be valid while the converted file is too large; and the conversion may have succeeded while a generated promotional asset never passed the required moderation policy. Those are different incidents with different owners, so collapsing them into one “image pipeline failed” counter discards the information needed to respond.

The signal that should fire earlier is a per-campaign release invariant. Before a message can be sent, every referenced image should have a successful conversion, a compression result, a private object key, a usable signed URL, and the moderation decision required by the publisher's policy. This is also the right place to stop an unsafe still derived from a prompt-generated video. It keeps moderation coverage explicit instead of assuming that a successful generation request implies approval.

Instrument the transitions, not the dashboard. Record a correlation ID, campaign ID, source media ID, output format, output bytes, moderation state, object key, link expiry, and send state. Do not log the signed URL itself. Then alert on broken invariants near the send boundary and include the failed transition in the page. “Campaign 8f2 has 17 messages ready and one asset without a moderation decision” is actionable; “media errors > 0” is not.

No single byte threshold is universally correct. Establish it from the clients and templates you actually test, then keep it as configuration rather than folklore embedded in code. A threshold set too high allows slow or rejected mail through. Set it too low and harmless variation in generated imagery pages the on-call, encouraging people to mute the alert that later matters.

How should Node.js prepare and convert email-safe images?

Even when an application is written in Node.js or Express, the safest first integration step is to inspect the live contract rather than copy a stale request body. The following Go utility calls Infrai's public discovery surface for image.convert, prints the full JSON Schema and runnable examples, handles HTTP errors, and backs off on rate limits. It uses the required environment-based bearer credential convention even though public discovery itself does not require a key. This is intentionally a contract-discovery example: the supplied API facts do not establish conversion payload fields, and guessing them would make a copyable sample actively harmful.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := discover(ctx, os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    if err != nil { fatal(err) }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, apiKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    if apiKey == "" { return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/image.convert"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay): continue
            case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited")
}

func fatal(err error) { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }

Run this during integration, use the returned schema and runnable example to implement the conversion request, reject a result that violates your tested size policy, and retain the source media ID beside the object metadata so an incident responder can trace the artifact without searching a campaign by filename. The distinction is deliberate: discovery can be generic and safe to automate, while conversion parameters should remain schema-driven.

For remote processing, I would not fabricate payload fields in a sample: the public discovery response supplies the full request and response JSON Schema plus runnable examples, so production code should generate or validate requests against the discovered contract. This is where a broad service surface is useful. Image processing, private storage, and email sit behind one REST contract rather than three unrelated SDKs and credential sets; the supporting advantage is that each documented capability has runnable examples in ten languages, which shortens the path from discovery to a first valid request.

Teams that want one contract for conversion, compression, private storage, and email delivery should try Infrai for this pipeline, because reducing credential and SDK sprawl leaves fewer integration boundaries to diagnose during a send incident. The public discovery surface reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules. That breadth does not remove the need to test recipient clients or define a moderation policy.

Choosing the processing boundary

There are at least four defensible choices. They are not interchangeable.

Option Setup and credentials Best fit Boundary to watch
Sharp An application dependency and no hosted-service credential Teams that want conversion in their own Node.js worker The team owns capacity, patching, storage, signed delivery, and moderation integration
Cloudinary A specialist media account, delivery model, and SDK or API integration Rich managed image and video transformation workflows Email and the rest of the backend remain separate integrations
Imgix A specialist image-delivery integration connected to an origin URL-driven transformation and image delivery It is narrower than a combined processing, storage, and messaging surface
ImageKit A specialist account with media delivery and transformation APIs Teams centered on managed image and video optimization Messaging and broader backend operations use separate contracts
Infrai One REST contract and credential across multiple backend modules A small team minimizing SDK and credential sprawl Use discovery schemas rather than assuming fields; specialist media workflows may deserve specialist tooling

Sharp is the cleanest starting point when the worker already runs Node.js, the input set is controlled, and the team is prepared to operate the surrounding queue and storage path. Cloudinary is a reasonable specialist choice when sophisticated media lifecycle and transformation features dominate the architecture. Imgix fits particularly well when there is already an origin and delivery-time image transformation is the center of the problem. ImageKit belongs on the shortlist when managed image and video optimization is the dominant concern. A specialist is the better answer when its media-specific controls, delivery network, or workflow depth matter more than consolidating backend contracts.

The platform's advantage is integration shape, not an assertion that one abstraction wins every comparison. Its API is self-describing; GET /v1/discovery/{capability} returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That is concrete friction removed: an engineer can inspect the exact contract before installing anything or distributing credentials. It also reports readiness per capability, including vendors that are ready or pending, which is relevant to media teams that must prove coverage rather than infer it from a product landing page.

Store privately, then link

An email should reference a hosted result rather than carry the image as an attachment. Byte size matters acutely in email, and clients can reject or mishandle modern formats, so conservative encoding is a reliability decision rather than nostalgia. Hosting also makes open observation possible, provided it is disclosed and implemented consistently with the sender's privacy obligations.

Keep the object private or signed-only and issue a presigned URL. Never put an Infrai bearer token into that URL request: a presigned URL is already the scoped authorization mechanism, while the API key belongs only on calls to the API host. Avoid public-read buckets and static-hosting patterns for generated campaign assets. The object key should be stable enough for traceability but should not contain recipient data.

There is a real trade-off here. Short link lifetimes reduce exposure but can break an old message when a recipient opens it later; very long lifetimes preserve rendering but expand the authorization window. Pick the duration from the promised lifetime of the campaign, document it, and page on signing failures before sending. Do not page merely because an individual recipient opens after the documented expiry.

Moderation is a release gate, not a generation feature

For prompt-generated promotional video, moderation coverage needs to be stated as a matrix: original prompt, generated video, extracted poster frame, resized email image, and any user-supplied overlay. A product name in the architecture does not prove that each artifact was reviewed. The release record should show which policy and which artifact version produced the decision.

This matters during retries. If conversion changes the actual pixels, decide whether policy requires the derived asset to be checked again; do not silently reuse an approval for a different byte sequence. Likewise, a send retry must refer to the same approved object rather than regenerating content. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities, but idempotency is still not a substitute for recording the moderation decision attached to the released artifact.

Keep the stop condition boring: no decision, no send.

Stop there.

The false-positive cost deserves equal attention. If a moderation alert fires on every reviewable item rather than on an unresolved item approaching release, responders learn that the page has no immediate consequence. Alert when the invariant is broken at the action boundary; send routine review volume to a work queue or report. The same discipline applies to image size and link expiry. Pages are for a response, not for displaying anxiety.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Sharp documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • Imgix rendering API
  • ImageKit documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the discovery schema for each capability before writing the integration.

title: Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories
description:
arXiv:2610.19614v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. To exploit this signal across tasks, we introduce Precog-RM, a transformer-based model that meta-learns a representation in which outcome prediction can be performed in a few-shot setting. We show that Precog-RM generalizes to unseen tasks and models, and gives confident predictions of trajectory success long before termination. Deployed as an early stopping controller for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Tau2-Bench, Precog-RM cuts training FLOPs by up to 47.3\% while maintaining performance comparable to baseline GRPO.

title: TreeSpark: Learning to Draft the Trees You Verify for Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.20175v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parallel drafters such as DFlash and DSpark reduce proposal latency, but early mismatches limit how much of each block can be accepted. Retaining alternatives introduces parent states and candidate choices that reference-conditioned training does not directly supervise. We introduce TreeSpark, a unified training and inference framework extending the semi-autoregressive DSpark architecture. It constructs parent-conditioned candidate trees from one backbone pass and replays their expansion, pruning, and budgeted packing during training. Survival negative log-likelihood weights retained edges by reference-derived path mass, while a capped coverage hinge promotes target-important alternatives near local selection boundaries. Both objectives reuse reference-chain target distributions without additional target forward passes. We evaluate greedy decoding with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on nine general benchmarks and six writing domains. Across targets and suites, TreeSpark improves mean acceptance length over DSpark by 23.4% to 31.6% and mean single-request throughput by 15.1% to 25.0%. Batched Qwen3-4B throughput improves by 12.6% to 17.2%. At fixed attention capacity and inference policy, the proposed supervision further improves mean acceptance length by approximately 6.4% and mean system throughput by 4.2% to 5.0% on Qwen3-4B.

description:
Orchestrating the Cloud: A Hands‑On Guide to Mastering Kubernetes in 2024

Kubernetes has become the de‑facto standard for container orchestration, yet many developers still feel like they’re navigating a maze of YAML, controllers, and networking quirks. This post walks you through the most practical bits-setting up a local cluster, deploying a real‑world service, and mastering rolling updates-so you can start shipping production‑grade workloads today.

1. Why Kubernetes Still Matters

  • Declarative Desired State - You describe what you want, not how to get there. The control plane constantly reconciles reality with your spec.
  • Self‑Healing - Pods that crash are automatically rescheduled.
  • Scalability - Horizontal Pod Autoscalers (HPA) let the cluster react to CPU, memory, or custom metrics.
  • Ecosystem - From service meshes (Istio) to GitOps (Argo CD), the platform is a launchpad for modern cloud‑native tooling.

If you’ve ever manually SSH‑ed into a VM to restart a service, you already know the pain Kubernetes solves.

2. Spin Up a Local Cluster in Minutes

For learning and CI, two tools dominate:

Tool When to Use Quick Start
Minikube Mimics a single‑node cluster with most cloud‑provider add‑ons minikube start --driver=docker
kind (Kubernetes IN Docker) Fast, CI‑friendly, multiple nodes via Docker kind create cluster

Below is a kind example that creates a three‑node cluster:

# Install kind (if you don’t have it)
GO111MODULE="on" go install sigs.k8s.io/kind@v0.22.0

# Create a cluster with a custom config
cat <<EOF > kind-config.yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
  - role: worker
  - role: worker
EOF

kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml

Verify everything is alive:

kubectl get nodes
# NAME                 STATUS   ROLES                  AGE   VERSION
# kind-control-plane   Ready    control-plane,master   1m    v1.29.0
# kind-worker          Ready    <none>                 1m    v1.29.0
# kind-worker2         Ready    <none>                 1m    v1.29.0

3. Deploy a Sample Application

Let’s deploy a tiny Go microservice that returns the current time. The Dockerfile is intentionally simple:

# Dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o server .

FROM alpine:3.19
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

Build and push the image (replace your-registry with a real registry):

docker build -t your-registry/time-service:v1 .
docker push your-registry/time-service:v1

Now the Kubernetes manifests. Keep everything in a single file for readability.

# time-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: demo

---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: time-deployment
  namespace: demo
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: time
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: time
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: time
          image: your-registry/time-service:v1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "256Mi"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: time-svc
  namespace: demo
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: time
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

Apply the manifest:

kubectl apply -f time-service.yaml

Check the rollout:

kubectl rollout status deployment/time-deployment -n demo

You now have a load‑balanced service reachable inside the cluster at http://time-svc.

4. Expose the Service to the World

For local testing, kubectl port-forward is handy:

kubectl port-forward svc/time-svc 8080:80 -n demo
# Now curl http://localhost:8080

In production you’ll likely use an Ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, or cloud‑native LB). A minimal Ingress resource looks like:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: time-ingress
  namespace: demo
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  rules:
    - host: time.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: time-svc
                port:
                  number: 80

Deploy the Ingress controller of your choice, point your DNS to the external IP, and you’re live.

5. ConfigMaps & Secrets - Keeping Config Out of Code

Separate configuration from the container image:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: time-config
  namespace: demo
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  TZ: "UTC"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: time-secret
  namespace: demo
type: Opaque
stringData:
  API_KEY: "super‑secret-key"

Consume them in the pod spec:

# Add to the container spec in time-deployment
envFrom:
  - configMapRef:
      name: time-config
  - secretRef:
      name: time-secret

Now you can change logging level or rotate secrets without rebuilding the image.

6. Rolling Updates & Rollbacks

Kubernetes shines when you need zero‑downtime deployments. Increment the image tag:

docker build -t your-registry/time-service:v2 .
docker push your-registry/time-service:v2

Patch the deployment:

kubectl set image deployment/time-deployment time=your-registry/time-service:v2 -n demo

Watch the progress:

kubectl rollout status deployment/time-deployment -n demo

If something goes sideways, rollback in a single command:

kubectl rollout undo deployment/time-deployment -n demo

7. Autoscaling with HPA

Enable the metrics server (required for HPA):

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml

Create an HPA that scales based on CPU:

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: time-hpa
  namespace: demo
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: time-deployment
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 50

kubectl apply -f time-hpa.yaml
kubectl get hpa -n demo

The controller will now spin up additional pods as traffic spikes.

8. Debugging Tips

Situation Command
Pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff kubectl logs <pod> -n demo
Networking mystery kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl -s http://time-svc
Resource pressure kubectl top nodes & kubectl top pods -n demo
Event history kubectl describe pod <pod> -n demo

Don’t forget kubectl describe-it surfaces events that often pinpoint the root cause faster than logs.

9. Best‑Practice Checklist

  • Namespace per environment - dev, staging, prod.
  • Pod‑Disruption‑Budget - guard against accidental mass evictions.
  • Read‑Only Root Filesystem - enforce security at container level.
  • Use helm or kustomize for templating and version control.
  • Enable PodSecurityPolicy / OPA Gatekeeper to enforce compliance.

10. Wrap‑Up

Kubernetes is a powerful abstraction layer, but its real strength shines when you treat it as a platform, not just a scheduler. By mastering declarative manifests, leveraging built‑in controllers, and integrating the rich ecosystem, you can ship resilient, scalable services with confidence.

Happy orchestrating!

Recommended Tools

  • K9s - Terminal UI for Kubernetes - Navigate your clusters faster than ever. Grab it at the official site and support the project: https://k9scli.io?ref=affiliate123

  • Lens - The Kubernetes IDE - Visualize workloads, edit resources, and get instant diagnostics. Install through their website and enjoy a 30‑day premium trial: https://lens.dev?utm_source=affiliate&utm_medium=blog

These tools aren’t required, but they dramatically improve day‑to‑day productivity when working with complex clusters.
