title: How to Mount Cloud Storage as a Local Drive: 2026 Guide
description:
How to Mount Cloud Storage as a Local Drive: 2026 Guide

Mounting cloud storage (Nextcloud, ownCloud, WebDAV, S3, Google Drive, OneDrive) as a real local drive on Windows or macOS used to require either paid tools or fragile hackery. In 2026 the options are mature, but the choice still matters. This guide explains the four real approaches, the tradeoffs, and which tool to pick for which scenario.

Why "mount" instead of "sync"

The naive approach is to sync files locally: a desktop client downloads your cloud to a folder, and changes sync back. That works for one folder at a time, but:

  • Two-way sync conflicts are confusing when you have multiple devices
  • You need to pre-allocate disk space for the entire cloud
  • You cannot use OS-native tools (Spotlight, Quick Look, Time Machine) on the remote files

A true mount, on the other hand, makes the cloud appear as a drive letter (Windows) or /Volumes/xxx (macOS). Files stream on demand, with no sync, and you use them like local files.

The four approaches (and which tools use which)

  1. Kernel filesystem driver — installed at OS level, catches all file I/O. Most "real" cloud mount tools use this approach via FUSE (macOS/Linux) or a userspace FS driver (Windows). Examples: Mountain Duck, ScsDriver, RaiDrive, ExpanDrive.

  2. In-process proxy — runs as a background process, intercepts file I/O at a higher level. Faster to develop, less reliable under heavy load. Examples: NetDrive (older versions), Air Live Drive.

  3. Sync folder with offline cache — pretends to be a mount but actually syncs. Examples: Google Drive desktop, Dropbox, OneDrive. Not a true mount, but often mislabeled as one.

  4. Protocol-specific client — only works for one protocol (WebDAV, SFTP, etc.) and does not appear as a real drive. Examples: Cyberduck (WebDAV/SFTP), FileZilla (FTP), mountainduck-cli (SFTP).

For a true "cloud as a local drive" experience, you want approach 1 or 2.

Protocol matrix: which tool supports which

Tool WebDAV S3 SFTP OneDrive Google Drive
ScsDriver ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Mountain Duck ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅ ✅
RaiDrive ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
ExpanDrive ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Cyberduck ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌

ScsDriver: the 2026 sweet spot

ScsDriver is a Windows userspace FS driver that supports WebDAV, S3, SFTP, OneDrive, and Google Drive. The 2026 release (released in March) added proper support for large file streaming (>2 GB) and reliable reconnection after sleep.

Pricing (overseas)

  • $1.5 / month
  • $5.5 / year
  • $5.5 lifetime (limited-time offer, was $9.99)

CN users: the lifetime price in China is ¥20, separately listed on the official site.

My testing (Windows 11 24H2, 1 TB Nextcloud)

Operation ScsDriver Mountain Duck RaiDrive Free
1.2 GB ISO copy 4 min 12 s 5 min 30 s 6 min 50 s
Reconnect after sleep <3 s 6 s 8 s
Listing 10k files 8 s 9 s 22 s
Concurrent uploads 8 4 4 (free) / 16 (pro)

When to use what

  • ScsDriver — best overall, especially if you mix multiple cloud backends. Best price ($5.5 lifetime).
  • Mountain Duck — if you only need WebDAV/SFTP and want the most polished UI. $49/year.
  • RaiDrive Free — if you want to spend nothing and can live with the 4-connection cap and occasional driver issues.
  • ExpanDrive — if you are on macOS and need S3 + WebDAV + SFTP in one tool. $49.99/year.
  • Cyberduck — if you just need a one-off file transfer, not a mount.

How to set up ScsDriver in 10 minutes

  1. Download the installer from https://scsoi.com/
  2. Run as administrator
  3. Click "Add Connection" → pick WebDAV (or any of the 5 protocols)
  4. Enter your server URL, username, password
  5. Pick a drive letter (e.g. Z:)
  6. Open File Explorer — your cloud is now Z:

The whole setup takes about 10 minutes, including restarting Explorer.

FAQ

Q: Does ScsDriver work on macOS?
A: Yes, a separate macOS build is available; it uses FUSE instead of a Windows driver.

Q: Can I mount multiple Nextcloud accounts at once?
A: Yes, each connection gets its own drive letter.

Q: Does the $5.5 lifetime include future updates?
A: Yes, lifetime includes all 2026.x and 2027.x updates.

Q: What about iOS / Android?
A: Not currently — ScsDriver is Windows + macOS only.

Disclaimer: I bought all licenses at full price. The ScsDriver pricing link above is the public page.

title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
description:
by Olek Gorajek, Samuel Redai, Yian Shang

Intro

Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets.

Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values.

Initial Problem

Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required:

  • extensive business knowledge
  • familiarity with experimentation conventions
  • and complex engineering practices

This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform.

Enter DataJunction

To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case.

DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers (Beto Dealmeida), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet, have been building out the remaining features of the platform.

Architecture Decisions

A critical design constraint for building DJ at Netflix was resource scarcity. We refused to compromise on product quality, choosing instead to limit the feature set. Although DJ was clearly capable of addressing many simultaneous problems across diverse use cases, our lack of adequate resources and official support meant we developed it as a side project for over two years. Our hope was that demonstrating its value would eventually secure management attention.

API First, UI and Other Interfaces Later

A metrics platform doesn’t need a flashy front-end to deliver value — its core is the semantic layer, which stores a consistent set of dimensions and metrics and serves this information through a rich API service. You can see below how we structured the main components of DataJunction in the Netflix implementation. Our DJ services (in the middle) interact with the underlying data (on the left) and supply our access layer with the business definitions in the form of SQL w/ metadata or directly with data depending on the client request.

Consistent Graph First, Other Features Later

A complete semantic layer system can seem like an octopus, with its tentacles reaching out into many functional areas and can expand from a basic semantic metadata stored for some datasets to full dashboard functionality. Let’s call out some of them:

  • semantic metadata authoring and management and monitoring
  • metric and dimension query / definition generation
  • metric and dimension data generation (requires a query engine)
  • data visualization and data tracking
  • performance optimization (aka caching or materialization)
  • integration layer with other tools and
  • any / all the above functionality served as: UI, API, client libraries, MCP servers and more.

Of course it is extremely hard to provide the best in class functionality across all these layers, so with our small “unofficial” team we decided to focus on the most important piece: solid semantic layer engine (and API) with the ability to parse SQL as the input to the graph and generate SQL as the serving layer. That is the core of the system and everything else can be added later with less effort and w/o the need to rebuild the core.

Cube as The Perfect Consumption Protocol

Analytical multi-dimensional cubes have been a fundamental concept for decades, with their representation integrated across various data processing and analysis platforms. While definitions and features may vary between tools, they all serve the common purpose of encapsulating, or abstracting, a subset of semantic objects.

In DataJunction, we adopted cubes as first-class features for two main reasons: their familiarity to users and their suitability as a serving interface. They efficiently deliver both the semantic definitions (of metrics and dimensions) and fast data access. See an example of data “flow” graph (dotted lines) and dimensional relationships graph (solid lines) below.

We simplified the creation of basic cubes, allowing them to easily aggregate arbitrary collections of shared metrics and dimensions. Furthermore, accessing, managing, and visualizing these cubes is straightforward for any client integrating with DJ. Custom integrations, such as for Netflix’s internal fast Druid data analysis tool (Data Explorer → see below), became trivial to build, and we also made it easy to materialize these cubes directly in our Druid clusters.

One of DJ’s most powerful client integrations is the ability to link any DJ-originating metric definition back to the DJ ecosystem. This creates a valuable feedback loop: troubleshooting and introspecting business dashboards becomes simple if they display DJ-defined metrics that include links back to the definition source. This link then makes inspecting and running ad-hoc analysis, by modifying existing metrics, a trivial process. This integration is not only possible with our inhouse tools, but also with other well known open-source products, like Superset.

Experimentation at Netflix

Metrics are the backbone of experimentation. They translate data into signals that tell us whether a change is meaningful, safe, and worth scaling. Without trustworthy metrics and dimensions, experiments risk becoming inconclusive or misleading, so a robust metrics layer becomes crucial for data-driven decisions.

At Netflix, the original metrics layer integrated into the experimentation platform was overly complicated. Creating new metrics not only required tribal knowledge of experimentation data artifacts, but also familiarity with complex engineering workflows. This unnecessary friction meant that onboarding a single new metric could take weeks, slowing adoption of new metrics and hindering experimentation.

This is where DataJunction comes in: it provides a central hub for defining metrics and dimensions that can easily be shared and explored via the semantic graph. It also provides flexible, user-friendly interfaces (including a UI, API, and various clients), making it easy for users to author and manage their metrics and other semantic models.

Conclusions

With experimentation domain well supported by DataJunction, we would like to take on next steps to unifying of the general analytics at Netflix and to make it easier for Netflix users to both:

  • find and use metric definitions across verticals (defined in DJ)
  • easily access, modify and experiment with new metrics across Netflix data stack

That will require building out strong integrations between DJ and other tools, but that has been underway and it is one of the most enjoyable parts of this project, where most of the feature exists and we are simply enabling existing systems to exchange information in a structured and reliable way. With a system like DataJunction our internal LLMs can deliver accountable information about the business metrics as well as explanation of how they are defined and used across Netflix.

Related resources:

  • 2023 : DataJunction at Netflix (slide deck)
  • 2025 : DataJunction talk at Data Engineering Open Forum 2025 (video)
  • 2025 : DataJunction: Unifying Experimentation and Analytics (blog)

DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: I turned my book recommender into an AI app in a day. Here are the two bugs that taught me the most.
description:
I read a lot of fantasy, especially romantasy, and I’ve always wanted to ask an AI for something specific, like “enemies to lovers in a fae court,” and get back real books, not made-up titles.

So I built BookDNA: it reads a book’s “DNA” (its tropes, setting, and tone), recommends books that match, and checks every single suggestion against Open Library, so it never recommends a book that doesn’t exist.

This week I turned it into an MCP server using mcp-use and deployed it on Manufact Cloud. Now any AI chat that supports MCP can use it.

What I built

Four tools an AI can call: search_book, get_book_dna, recommend, and recommend_by_tropes. The recommend tools return a small app that appears right inside the chat: a parchment shelf of book covers, each with a one-line reason it was picked.

My favorite moment: I tested it in Manufact’s Inspector chat using a GPT model, not Claude, and it worked perfectly. One server, any AI. That’s the promise of MCP, and seeing it happen was really satisfying.

Bug 1: only one cover showed up

My first shelf showed one cover and four broken images. Every book had a valid cover link, so the data wasn’t the problem.

It turned out that older Open Library covers redirect to a different server on archive.org. MCP App widgets run with a strict security policy that lists which sites they’re allowed to load images from, and I’d only allowed Open Library. The redirected images were silently blocked. The one cover that loaded was newer and didn’t redirect.

The fix was to allow archive.org too. I also added a fallback: if a cover ever fails, the card shows a parchment “title page” with the title and author instead of a broken image.

Lesson: if your widget loads images, allow every site in the redirect chain, not just the first one.

Bug 2: everyone shared one rate limit

The server is public, so I added rate limits to protect my AI budget, including a per-user limit. Testing it against the live deployment showed something I didn’t expect: the platform’s proxy rewrites the header that identifies the user, and the address I was reading belonged to the proxy, not the user. So every user was sharing one limit.

One small change fixed it, but I only found it because I tested against the real deployment instead of trusting my local setup.

Lesson: test anything that depends on request headers against your real deployment.

How I built it

I built this with Claude Code. I made the decisions, reviewed every change, and tested it myself, and I kept a “friction log” of everything that confused me along the way. A few items are already in this post.

Try it

GitHub: github.com/ksaivarsha/bookdna
MCP server: https://calm-wave-h30fs.run.mcp-use.com/mcp

If you build MCP Apps, I’d love to hear what tripped you up.

title: Why Users Abandon Digital Products Even When They Solve the Right Problem
description:
A digital product can solve a genuine business problem and still struggle to keep users engaged. The features may work correctly, the technology may be reliable, and the product may offer clear value. Yet users can leave when completing a simple task feels unnecessarily difficult.

This often happens because building a useful product involves more than delivering the right functionality.

People also need to understand how it works, find what they need, and complete their tasks without confusion.
The Gap Between Product Value and User Experience

Imagine a small business owner using a new invoicing platform. The application generates accurate invoices, tracks payments, and stores customer details.

However, creating the first invoice requires navigating several menus and filling in fields that are difficult to understand.
The platform solves the business problem, but the experience creates additional work.

This gap can affect onboarding, repeat usage, and customer confidence. Businesses should therefore evaluate not only what their product can do, but also how easily customers can access its value. A clear digital product design approach can help teams connect user needs with meaningful product experiences.

  1. The First Experience Requires Too Much Effort

Users often form an impression of a product during their first few interactions. If registration is complicated, onboarding takes too long, or the next step is unclear, they may leave before discovering the product's benefits.

Teams can improve this experience by identifying the first meaningful action a user wants to complete. Remove unnecessary onboarding steps, explain unfamiliar terms, and provide guidance where users need it.
The objective is not to explain every feature immediately. It is to help users experience the product's value as quickly as possible.

  1. Important Actions Are Difficult to Find

As products grow, teams introduce additional features, settings, and workflows. Without careful planning, the interface can become crowded and navigation can become unpredictable.

A strong UI/UX design process examines how users move through the product and whether the interface supports their goals. Clear labels, logical grouping, consistent controls, and visible next steps can make common tasks easier to complete.

Teams should pay particular attention to actions that users perform frequently. If customers repeatedly search for the same function, the problem may be its placement rather than a lack of functionality.

  1. Features Are Built Without Enough Validation

Product teams sometimes prioritize features because competitors offer them or internal stakeholders believe customers need them. These decisions can introduce complexity without addressing the most important user problems.
Product design helps teams investigate customer needs, evaluate possible solutions, and test assumptions before committing significant development resources.

Early interviews, prototypes, and usability tests can reveal whether a proposed feature solves a meaningful problem. Even simple testing with a small group of representative users can uncover issues that internal reviews overlook.

Businesses planning to improve their product experience can explore UI/UX design and product development services to understand how design and development can support a more usable digital product.

  1. The Interface Does Not Match User Expectations

Users bring familiar expectations from other websites and applications. When common actions behave differently or similar components look inconsistent, people must spend additional effort learning the interface.
For example, a save button should communicate what happens after it is selected. Form errors should explain what went wrong and how to correct it. Navigation should remain predictable across related screens.

Consistent interaction patterns help users build confidence. They also make products easier to maintain as new features are introduced.

  1. Teams Ignore Friction After Launch

Launching a product is not the end of the improvement process. Real users may behave differently from what the team expected during development.
Businesses should review product analytics, support conversations, user feedback, and usability test results to identify recurring problems.

Useful questions include:

Where do users stop during onboarding?
Which tasks generate the most support requests?
Which features receive little engagement?
What causes users to repeat an action or abandon a form?
Which problems affect the most important customer journeys?
These observations help teams prioritize improvements based on evidence rather than assumptions.

  1. Design and Development Work in Isolation

When design decisions are handed to developers without sufficient collaboration, the finished product may differ from the intended experience. Interaction details can be missed, edge cases may remain unresolved, and inconsistent components can emerge.

Designers and developers should collaborate throughout the process. Reviewing requirements together, discussing technical constraints early, and testing implemented screens help prevent avoidable usability problems.
This collaboration is particularly important for complex SaaS platforms, where workflows often involve multiple roles, permissions, and interconnected features.

Turning User Friction Into Product Improvements
Improving retention does not always require a major redesign. A confusing form may need clearer instructions. A complicated workflow may need fewer steps. A poorly understood feature may need better onboarding.

Start by identifying one important user journey, observing where people struggle, and testing a focused improvement. Measure whether the change helps users complete the task more successfully.

A structured approach to UI/UX design and product design can connect these usability improvements with the broader goals of the business. The
emphasis should remain on solving genuine user problems rather than adding features for their own sake.

Conclusion

Users do not abandon digital products only because the products lack useful features. They may leave because the value is difficult to discover, important tasks take too much effort, or the experience fails to meet their expectations.

Understanding these barriers helps businesses make more informed product decisions. By studying user behaviour, validating ideas, improving key workflows, and refining the experience after launch, teams can make digital products more useful and easier to adopt.

description:

By Claudio Masolo

title: React History in Plain Words: What Each Era Took Off Your Plate, and What It Billed You
description:
Here is a component every app has. A user profile: load the user by userId, show their name, and show a green dot while they're online.

I'm going to write it again for most eras of React, from 2013 to today.

Most histories of React go version by version: 0.13, 16.8, 18, 19. You finish reading and you know the dates, but not why any of it happened. I wanted to try a different angle. Every era of React made a deal with you. It took something off your plate, and it sent you a new bill. I'll keep score as I go: what you stopped doing, and what you started paying.

One warning about order. This article follows problems, not dates. Next.js (2016) shows up after hooks (2019), because that's where its problem hurts most.

1. Before React: you are the sync engine

The jQuery version:

$.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}`, (user) => {
  $('#name').text(user.name);
});

presence.on('change', (id, online) => {
  if (id === userId) $('#status').toggleClass('online', online);
});

It works. Now add a second place that shows the same user, say a header avatar. Then a list of friends with their own dots. Every piece of data lives in two places: in your variables and in the DOM (the browser's live tree of page elements). Every change has to be copied by hand, to every place that shows it. Miss one, and the header says "online" while the profile says "offline".

Backbone, Knockout and AngularJS were already attacking this with data binding. React's answer, open-sourced in 2013, was different. Pete Hunt's Why React post from June 2013 makes the case: stop updating the DOM yourself. Describe what the UI should look like for the current data, and let the library work out what to change.

In plain words: before React you were a waiter who memorizes every table's order and runs to the kitchen with each correction. React gave you an order pad. You write down what the table wants now, and the kitchen works out the difference.

One detail almost nobody mentions: that same 2013 post already lists server rendering as a selling point. Keep it in mind. It comes back later with a different name.

Took off your plate: keeping the DOM in sync by hand.
Billed you: HTML inside JavaScript, and a build step to compile it. JSX looked like heresy in 2013, and a lot of the first year was spent arguing about it.

2. createClass and mixins: sharing logic, badly

Early React components were objects passed to React.createClass. A mixin was a plain object of methods that got copied into every component that listed it. That's how you shared logic:

var Profile = React.createClass({
  mixins: [FetchUserMixin, PresenceMixin], // each one adds state and lifecycle methods
  render: function () {
    if (!this.state.user) return null;
    return <div>{this.state.user.name} {this.state.online && 'online'}</div>;
  },
});

React called every mixin's componentDidMount, so that part worked. The trouble was everything you couldn't see. Which mixin set online? What happens when two mixins both define handleChange? You found out when the page loaded and threw.

React added ES6 classes in 0.13, in March 2015, and classes had no mixins at all. In 2016 Dan Abramov wrote the post that explained why that was a feature, Mixins Considered Harmful. One line from it: "There is no guarantee that two particular mixins can be used together."

So mixins saved you from copy-pasting logic, and charged you in coupling you couldn't see. Rename a method, and the page load told you which mixin had depended on it.

3. Classes: one feature, three methods

Here's the profile as a class (written with class properties, the Babel syntax most teams used):

class Profile extends React.Component {
  state = { user: null, online: false };

  componentDidMount() {
    fetchUser(this.props.userId).then((user) => this.setState({ user }));
    this.unsubscribe = presence.subscribe(this.props.userId, (online) => this.setState({ online }));
  }

  componentDidUpdate(prev) {
    if (prev.userId !== this.props.userId) {
      fetchUser(this.props.userId).then((user) => this.setState({ user }));
      this.unsubscribe();
      this.unsubscribe = presence.subscribe(this.props.userId, (online) => this.setState({ online }));
    }
  }

  componentWillUnmount() {
    this.unsubscribe();
  }
}

(presence.subscribe returns a function that unsubscribes. Both versions in this article rely on that.)

Look at where the presence logic lives. Subscribe in one method, re-subscribe in a second, unsubscribe in a third. One feature, split by when it runs instead of what it does. The fetch is copied twice. Forget the componentDidUpdate branch and the dot keeps showing the previous user.

And there's a race here that's easy to miss: whichever response arrives last wins. Click from user 1 to user 2 quickly. Two requests are in flight. If user 1's response arrives last, setState writes it, and the profile of user 2 shows user 1's name. Nothing in the class shape protects you from that.

Sharing logic got its own problem too. Mixins were out, so the community moved to patterns that wrap one component in another. A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a wrapped one. A render prop is a function you pass as a prop so another component can decide what to render. Both work, but every shared behavior adds a layer. Open the component tree of a 2018 app and you'd scroll through withRouter(connect(withTheme(...))) before reaching your own code.

The React team listed all of this when they introduced hooks. The motivation section reads like a bug report for this exact component: "It's hard to reuse stateful logic between components", complex components where related logic is split across lifecycle methods, and "Classes confuse both people and machines".

Took off your plate: hidden mixin coupling, mostly by not supporting mixins at all.
Billed you: this, logic split across lifecycle methods, and deeply nested wrappers.

4. Hooks: logic grouped by what it does

Hooks were announced at React Conf in October 2018 and shipped in React 16.8, in February 2019. The profile:

function usePresence(userId) {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => presence.subscribe(userId, setOnline), [userId]);
  return online;
}

function Profile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const online = usePresence(userId);

  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false;
    fetchUser(userId).then((u) => { if (!ignore) setUser(u); });
    return () => { ignore = true; };
  }, [userId]);

  if (!user) return null;
  return <div>{user.name} {online && 'online'}</div>;
}

The whole presence feature is now one small hook, in one place. Subscribe and unsubscribe sit together (the effect returns its own cleanup), and [userId] re-runs it when the user changes. usePresence is just a function. Any component can call it, and there's no wrapper in the tree.

The race from the class version is fixed with the ignore flag: when userId changes, the old effect's cleanup marks its request as stale. But notice who fixed it: you did. React gave you the place to put the fix and left the fix itself to you.

The new bill is the dependency array. Leave a value out of it, and the effect keeps using the value from the render where it was created. That's a stale closure, and it's the most common hooks bug there is. Lint rules catch most of these bugs, though keeping the linter quiet often means restructuring the code.

Hooks also made "fetch in an effect" the default way to load data. Classes had the same problem, but now it was everywhere. Say the profile shows the user's posts, in a child component that fetches them. The child can't start its request until the parent has fetched the user and rendered it. Then the posts component fetches comments. Each level waits for the one above. That's a waterfall. Libraries like TanStack Query, SWR and Relay helped a lot, but the requests still started in the browser, after the JavaScript arrived.

Took off your plate: this, lifecycle splits, nested wrappers.
Billed you: dependency arrays, stale closures, and cleanup you write yourself.

5. Next.js: render it on the server

Everything in sections 3 and 4 happens in the browser, after the JavaScript bundle (the files the browser downloads) arrives. Until then the user stares at an empty page. Then a spinner. Then another spinner, one per level of the waterfall.

Next.js launched in October 2016, from ZEIT (now Vercel). Its announcement describes where the industry had gone: the pendulum of "'fully server-rendered' swung abruptly to the extreme of 'single page app'". Next.js swung it back with server-side rendering: the page is rendered to HTML on the server with its data, and the browser gets real content right away.

This file-per-page setup is what's now called the Pages Router, to tell it apart from the newer App Router in section 7. At launch the data function was getInitialProps. Since Next.js 9.3 in March 2020, the usual way is getServerSideProps, which runs only on the server:

export async function getServerSideProps({ params }) {
  const user = await fetchUser(params.id);
  return { props: { user } };
}

export default function ProfilePage({ user }) {
  return <h1>{user.name}</h1>;
}

The fetch runs on the server, close to the data. No empty page, no first spinner.

Remember the detail from 2013? Server rendering was already on React's list of selling points. Next.js didn't invent it. It made it the default, so you stopped wiring up the server yourself.

The price is hydration. The server sends finished HTML, and it looks right, but it's dead: buttons do nothing yet. Then the browser downloads the same components as JavaScript and runs them again to wire up the clicks. That wiring step is hydration. You pay for the page twice. If the server and the browser render anything differently (Date.now(), a window check, a locale-formatted date), React throws a hydration mismatch. And data loading lives in one function at the top of the page, so a component deep in the tree still can't fetch its own data on the server.

Took off your plate: the blank page, and setting up server rendering by hand.
Billed you: hydration, hydration mismatches, and page-level data loading.

6. React 18: the era everyone skips

Timelines often jump from hooks straight to Server Components, and React 18 gets less attention than it deserves.

React 18, March 2022, brought three things. I'll take them one at a time.

Concurrent rendering. React can start an update, pause it to handle a click, and come back to it. You opt in through APIs like useTransition.

Suspense. You wrap a slow part of the page, say the user's posts, and React shows a fallback there, like a spinner, until it's ready.

Streaming. On the server, the parts of the page that are ready go out first. The slow part arrives later and fills in its spinner.

In plain words: before 18, the server was a restaurant that brought your whole order at once, so everyone waited for the slowest dish. After 18, starters come out when they're ready, and the steak follows.

There's no new profile code here, and that's the point. This era changed what React can do under the hood, and the next one is built on it.

The bill came from somewhere else. Strict Mode, React's opt-in wrapper for extra checks in development, started mounting every component twice to catch missing cleanup. If your profile fetched twice in dev after upgrading, this is why. Usually the fix was the cleanup function you'd skipped. So 18 took "the whole page waits for the slowest request" off your plate, once a framework wired up streaming for you, and billed you in effects that suddenly ran twice.

7. Server Components: components that never reach the browser

The idea was presented in December 2020, before React 18. It reached most developers through the App Router, Next.js's newer routing system: in beta in Next.js 13 in October 2022, stable in Next.js 13.4, in May 2023. React 19 is when the Server Components APIs were declared stable for frameworks to build on. The 13.4 announcement says the App Router is "built on the foundation of React Server Components and Suspense", the Suspense and streaming that React 18 shipped.

Server Components are not the same as server rendering. With SSR, a component renders on the server and then its code ships to the browser anyway, for hydration. A Server Component renders on the server and its code never ships at all.

The profile, today:

// app/users/[id]/page.tsx: a Server Component
import { PresenceDot } from './PresenceDot';

export default async function ProfilePage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params; // Next 15+. In 13 and 14, params was a plain object.
  const user = await fetchUser(id);
  return (
    <>
      <h1>{user.name}</h1>
      <PresenceDot userId={user.id} />
    </>
  );
}

// app/users/[id]/PresenceDot.tsx: ships to the browser, because state and a live subscription only exist there
'use client';
import { usePresence } from '@/hooks/usePresence';

export function PresenceDot({ userId }: { userId: string }) {
  const online = usePresence(userId);
  return online ? <span className="dot" /> : null;
}

The component is async. It fetches its own data with a plain await, on the server, and no useEffect is involved. Any component in the tree can do this, not only the page. The heading and the rest of the page never ship to the browser as JavaScript. Only PresenceDot does, because it's the only part that needs a live subscription.

In plain words: with the Pages Router, the server sent a printed photo of the page, and then the camera too: all the code that built it, so the browser could retake the shot and make it interactive. Server Components send the photo and only the code for the parts that actually move.

The bill is bigger than one line per file. Three costs show up first:

  • 'use client' marks where the browser part starts, and everything that file imports ships with it. Put it on the page instead of on PresenceDot, and you're back in section 4: 
  'use client'; // on page.tsx: the whole profile ships as JavaScript again,
  // the component can't be async anymore, and fetchUser moves back into a useEffect
  • Server files can't use useState, useEffect or context, because there's no browser there to hold state. That's why context providers move down into small client files, and why many third-party UI libraries need a 'use client' wrapper before they work.
  • Props that cross the boundary must be serializable: plain data that can be sent as text. No functions, no class instances.

Then the quieter ones. Waterfalls can come back on the server, as sequential awaits in nested components, so you reach for Promise.all and Suspense boundaries. Next.js caches fetches, routes and navigations in separate layers whose defaults have changed between versions, so "why is this data stale" became a new kind of question. And Server Components need support from the bundler (the tool that packages your code), which in practice means a framework such as Next.js. Your app is tied closer to it than before.

Took off your plate: fetching in effects, the client waterfall, shipping JavaScript for parts that never change.
Billed you: the server/client boundary, caching, and framework lock-in.

8. Today: React 19 and the Compiler

React 19 went stable in December 2024. ref is now a regular prop, so the forwardRef wrapper is on its way out. Actions give you primitives (useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, <form action>) for the pending states, errors and optimistic updates of a form, the parts you used to build with three useState calls. (An optimistic update shows the expected result right away, before the server confirms it.)

Then in October 2025, React Compiler 1.0. Memoization means caching a result so it isn't recomputed on every render. For years, a fast React app meant doing it by hand:

const onSelect = useCallback((id) => router.push(`/users/${id}`), [router]);
const sorted = useMemo(() => friends.toSorted(byName), [friends]);
return <FriendList friends={sorted} onSelect={onSelect} />; // FriendList wrapped in memo()

The compiler is an opt-in build step that adds that memoization for you. You write the plain version, and it works out what to cache. It can even memoize code after an early return, which manual useMemo can't, because hooks can't be called after a return.

One honest caveat. The docs keep useMemo and useCallback as escape hatches, options for the rare cases where the default isn't enough. The routine was handed off, not deleted.

The compiler also assumes you follow the Rules of React: render is a pure calculation, so props and state aren't mutated and nothing outside changes during render. When it detects a violation, it safely skips that component. A violation it can't detect can make a compiled component misbehave at runtime. Say the profile reads the current theme from a global variable during render: the compiler only sees props and state, so it caches the output, and the profile keeps the old theme after the global changes.

Took off your plate: manual memoization, forwardRef, the boilerplate of form state.
Billed you: the Rules of React, now enforced.

The ledger

Same order as the article. The dates are in each section.

Era Took off your plate Billed you Where you'll see the bill
React itself Keeping the DOM in sync by hand JSX, and a build step Your first webpack/Babel config
createClass + mixins Copy-pasting logic Hidden coupling between mixins A name clash error on page load
Classes Hidden mixin coupling this, lifecycle splits, nested wrappers A wrapper-deep component tree in DevTools
Hooks this, lifecycle splits, wrappers Dependency arrays, stale closures, your own cleanup react-hooks/exhaustive-deps warnings
Next.js The blank page, manual SSR Hydration, mismatches, page-level data loading A hydration error in the console
React 18 Waiting for the slowest request Double-run effects in Strict Mode Effects firing twice in dev
Server Components Effects for data, shipping static UI The client boundary, caching, lock-in A "needs 'use client'" error at build
React 19 + Compiler Memoization, forwardRef, form state The Rules of React, enforced Compiler lint errors, skipped components

Not every era took a chore. React 18 and Server Components mostly added things you couldn't do before. And the bills didn't get smaller. They moved: from your DOM code, to your effects, to the line between server and browser.

Closing

In 2013 the bill was a whole job: you were the sync engine. In 2026 it's knowing which side of one line your code runs on. That's real progress. It just isn't free, and every React release since has moved the cost rather than cancelled it.

Which bill are you paying right now: stale closures, hydration mismatches, or the 'use client' boundary?

title: ISO 27018 for Cloud Engineers: Protecting Customer PII in Public Cloud Services
description:
Cloud-based applications can process personal information across databases, APIs, administrative interfaces, backups, and external service providers. For Indian SaaS companies and IT service providers working with enterprise customers, understanding these data paths is essential to evaluating privacy risks.

ISO/IEC 27018 focuses on protecting personally identifiable information (PII) processed by public cloud service providers acting as PII processors.

The standard's relevance depends on the service model, processing activities, and applicable certification scope. Here are several technical areas that cloud teams should examine when considering PII protection.

  1. Map PII Across the Service Architecture

Identify where customer PII enters the platform, which components process it, where it is stored, and how it moves between systems.

Include application databases, APIs, support tools, logs, backups, and relevant third-party services. This view can reveal data flows that are not apparent from a high-level infrastructure diagram.

The purpose is to understand the processing environment and establish which controls are relevant to the service.

  1. Review Identity and Access Boundaries

Evaluate how employees, administrators, service accounts, and external providers access personal information.

Relevant technical considerations include authentication, role-based permissions, privileged access, access reviews, credential management, and logging. Permissions should reflect operational requirements rather than grant unnecessary access to customer data.

For multi-tenant platforms, examine whether application logic, storage, APIs, and administrative interfaces preserve the intended separation between customers.

  1. Examine Encryption and Data Lifecycle Controls

Encryption can reduce the risk of unauthorised disclosure when PII is stored or transmitted. Its effectiveness also depends on key management, access restrictions, configuration, and the systems in which the information is processed.

Data lifecycle controls deserve similar attention. Determine how retention periods are defined, how customer information is returned or deleted, and how backups or replicas affect deletion practices.

The applicable arrangements should reflect customer agreements and relevant legal obligations.

  1. Understand Subprocessor Dependencies

Cloud services may rely on external infrastructure, monitoring, hosting, and analytics providers. These dependencies can affect where personal information is processed and which parties can access it.

Maintain visibility into relevant subprocessors and clarify the responsibilities established by applicable agreements. Material changes to the service provider chain may require a review of the existing privacy arrangements.

  1. Distinguish ISO 27018 From ISO 27001

ISO/IEC 27001 establishes requirements for an information security management system. ISO/IEC 27018 focuses on privacy considerations for PII processing in applicable public cloud environments.

The standards address different requirements. Certification to ISO 27001 alone does not establish conformity with ISO 27018.

Technical teams should understand which service boundaries and processing activities fall within the certification scope being considered.

Connecting Technical Evidence With Certification Scope

Access controls, data-flow information, retention practices, and subprocessor arrangements all contribute to understanding how PII is protected. Their relevance should be evaluated against the actual cloud service and applicable requirements.

Organisations can explore ISO/IEC 27018 certification and related governance services when determining how cloud privacy assurance fits their certification priorities.

For cloud engineers, the key principle is straightforward: privacy controls need to reflect the real architecture, the information processed, and the responsibilities defined for the service.

title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.19026v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.

title: VaryST: Generalizable Spatio-Temporal Forecasting Beyond the Closed-World Setting
description:
arXiv:2610.19813v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatio-temporal forecasting is fundamental to many real-world systems, yet deployment environments are inherently varying: temporal distributions may evolve, spatial domains may change, and observation availability may shift from training conditions. Existing models are often tightly coupled to their training environments through node-specific representations, predefined spatial support sets, and reliance on consistently available observations, limiting generalization to changing environments. To this end, we propose VaryST, a compact spatio-temporal forecasting model trained from scratch that achieves strong generalization by dynamically constructing predictive context from available long-term observations. To accommodate temporal changes, VaryST derives node representations from long-term histories, capturing current behavior in the context of longer-term patterns. To adapt to spatial changes, it dynamically selects functionally relevant support nodes beyond predefined neighborhoods and integrates their information with recent and long-term target states and global context. To handle varying observation availability, VaryST selectively masks historical patches on which the model relies most during training, encouraging it to exploit alternative temporal and spatial dependencies for accurate forecasting when key observations become unavailable. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets against seventeen baselines show that VaryST achieves strong in-domain forecasting accuracy, substantially improves zero- and few-shot generalization under spatial and temporal changes, and remains robust to varying observation availability.

title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19687v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.

  1. YouTube Transcript Extractor - timestamped transcripts for videos, playlists and channels, with optional chunks sized for RAG. Videos without captions are reported and not charged. $0.004 per transcript. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-transcript-extractor-batch

  3. YouTube Search Scraper - search results with title, channel, views, duration, publish date and thumbnail, with upload date and duration filters. $0.002 per video. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-search-video-scraper
  4. Google News Scraper with Full Article Text - news results for a keyword, language and country, with the full article text pulled from the publisher page when it can be extracted. $0.003 per headline, $0.01 per article with text. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/google-news-scraper-article-text

YouTube blocks datacenter IPs, so the YouTube tools run through a residential proxy by default. That cost is already in the per-result price.

Calling one from Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("xargaar_tools/youtube-comments-scraper-fast").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": ["https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ"],
    "maxCommentsPerVideo": 50,
})
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item["likes"], item["author"], item["text"][:80])

Swap the Actor name and input to use the others. Every Actor has an input form in the Apify console if you prefer clicking to coding.

What I tested

I ran each Actor on Apify's platform before publishing. Transcripts: 11 of 12 test videos returned a transcript, a private video was reported cleanly instead of failing the run. Comments: 45 comments from one video, replies mode, and a channel URL across two videos. Search: two queries returned 80 videos, and the date and duration filters changed the results as expected. News: 10 results, 6 with full article text.

Known limits

  • Comments come back in YouTube's top-comments order. A "newest first" sort is not supported yet.
  • The search tool applies one filter per query (upload date or duration).
  • News articles behind paywalls or bot protection return the headline data without full text.

If something breaks or you need a field that is missing, open an issue on the Actor page and I will look at it.

title: GateSight: Recurrent Memory Anticipates Attention Memory for Query-Agnostic KV Eviction in Hybrid LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.14754v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hybrid language models interleave Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, whose recurrent memory has a fixed size, with full-attention layers, whose key-value (KV) cache grows with the context and dominates serving memory. In this paper, we ask whether the recurrent memory already knows what the attention memory will need. We first show that which GDN heads of Qwen3.8-27B keep long memories is fixed by the weights rather than by the document. Next, we define the future utility of a KV entry by how much removing it changes the attention output over the model's own continuations, and find that the write gate, decay and write magnitude that GDN layers emit during prefill anticipate this utility before any query is seen. Because the relation is spread across many GDN heads and layers, and a linear map recovers its trend but less of its high-utility tail than a nonlinear one, we propose GateSight, which learns it with lightweight per-head multilayer perceptrons that read these signals and no attention score. Their predicted utility decides which entries each attention layer keeps, and how much each layer keeps is set by the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers. Finally, at serving time, GateSight scores the cache once after prefill and physically releases discarded KV entries. Experimental results on SCBench and RULER-4096 with Qwen3.8-27B and, with the same recipe, the sparse-attention model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, up to the 262K-token limit of the models, show that with a tenth of the attention KV cache, GateSight is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three of the four model-benchmark pairs and leads KVzip on all four, by 9.5 to 47.2 points. Notably, it scores a full-length context with negligible overhead relative to prefill.

title: Free MCP Server Hosting: What Zero Dollars Actually Gets You
description:
We build a cloud whose agents operate it over MCP, so we spend a lot of the week talking to servers we wrote. Every one of those servers is hosted, always-on, and billed by the hour. But before any tool of ours is hosted, it lives on a laptop, behind a tunnel, answering calls from an agent on the same desk. That stage is free, it is where everyone should start, and this post is about how much you can get done there before you pay anything.

The short version for anyone searching this exact question: yes, you can host an MCP server for free. Run it on a machine you already own, use the free tier of a managed platform, or use serverless if your tools keep no state. Each is genuinely free and each breaks in a way you can predict. We have hit all three breaks, from both sides: as the people hosting the tools, and as the platform that inherits them when they grow.

Path What it costs Where it breaks Who it suits
Your machine behind a tunnel $0 The machine sleeps, reboots, loses wifi; the tool is up only while you are Development and solo experiments
The free tier of a managed platform $0, the platform carries the idle hours One instance, a memory ceiling, sometimes a request cap A first real tool, before a teammate depends on it
Serverless, stateless tools only $0 per call and response No state and no held connections; most MCP servers do not qualify Pure call-and-return tools

The rest of this post is about where each of those breaks, because that is the part the table cannot tell you.

The tunnel stage, and why it ends

Your laptop can be an MCP server tonight. Start the process, put a tunnel in front of it, point your agent at the URL, and you have a hosted server for zero dollars. We still develop this way; nothing beats editing a tool and watching the agent pick up the change seconds later.

It ends the first time the tool is useful to someone who is not you. A tunnel only works while the machine is awake, and the machine is yours: it sleeps when you sleep, it reboots when an update lands, it loses the wifi exactly once, at the worst moment. A remote MCP server is only remote if it stays up. The lesson is not that tunnels are bad. It is that shared usefulness and shared uptime are the same requirement, and a laptop cannot provide either.

Free tiers are real, read the edges

The managed path costs nothing on a free tier, and we want to defend free tiers for a moment, because we run one. A free tier that carries one small always-on service costs the platform almost nothing and makes the platform useful enough that you stay. That is the whole trade, and it is a fair one.

What the edges look like, from our side of the fence: one instance, a memory ceiling, sometimes a request cap. One small MCP server is a lightweight process speaking HTTP, and it fits. What does not fit is the day two agents call at once, or the day your tool needs a database next to it and you start gluing vendors together for state that should live on the same platform.

If your tools keep no state at all, a serverless function is another zero-dollar route, and for a pure request-and-response tool it is a good one. Most MCP servers do not qualify: they hold connections open and remember things between calls, which fights the request-and-forget model. We tried the stateless-only shape ourselves and kept running back to a real process.

The math that hides under "free"

An always-on service, however small, is 730 metered hours a month. It answers twice a day and meters around the clock. Free tiers pay that slice for you because it is the cheapest loyalty program ever invented, and honestly, it works.

We wrote before about what an always-on VM actually costs once it is billed by the hour, and the punchline was a customer spending 84% of a real bill on one VM that never slept. Scale-to-zero exists because of stories like that. Free tiers are the same instinct pointing the other direction: the platform carries the idle hours so your first tool costs nothing. Neither model is charity. Both are fine, as long as you know which side of the meter you are standing on.

The day to stop being free

It is not a resource threshold, it is a trust threshold. You will notice one of these three things: you check that the server is up before you check your email, because a teammate's agent depends on it now. A workflow treats its downtime as an incident. Or a second process appears because one instance became a queue.

Any one of those means the tool has outgrown the free stage, and the move is smaller than people fear. On Scalix Run the free-tier deploy and the paid deploy are the same command, same URL, one setting changed:

scalix-cloud run deploy --name mcp-server \
  --image registry.scalix.world/my-org/mcp-server:v1 \
  --port 8080 \
  --min-instances 1

You change a plan, not an architecture, and the URL your agents already know does not move. That matters more than the price. Re-pointing every agent that trusts your server is the real cost of outgrowing a host.

Where we land

Start free, on the machine or the tier, and mean it: the free stage is where your tool earns the right to exist. Then let the trust signals, not the invoice, tell you when to move. Start on the free tier, and if you want to see client configs for MCP servers we host ourselves, they are public at scalixworld/scalix-cloud-mcp.

title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
description:
arXiv:2610.14772v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.

title: Next.js May 2026 security release
description:
Summary

We have shipped a coordinated security release for Next.js addressing 13 advisories across denial of service, middleware and proxy bypass, server-side request forgery, cache poisoning, and cross-site scripting. One advisory addresses an upstream React Server Components vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-23870.

Recommended actions

Patched versions are available for both React and Next.js, and all affected users should upgrade immediately.

Impact

The release addresses the following advisories:

Middleware and proxy bypass

Affects applications that rely on middleware.js or proxy.js for authorization.

  • High: Auth bypass via App Router segment-prefetch URL

  • High: App Router segment-prefetch bypass, incomplete fix follow-up

  • High: Pages Router i18n default-locale path bypasses proxy authorization

  • High: Bypass via dynamic route parameter injection

  • Low: Middleware redirects can be cache-poisoned

Denial of service

Affects applications using Server Functions, Partial Prerendering with Cache Components, or the Image Optimization API.

  • High: DoS in React Server Components (tracked upstream as CVE-2026-23870)

  • High: DoS via connection exhaustion in applications using Cache Components

  • Moderate: DoS via the Image Optimization API

Server-side request forgery

Affects applications that handle WebSocket upgrade requests.

  • High: SSRF in applications using WebSocket upgrades

Cache poisoning

Affects applications with caching layers in front of React Server Component responses.

  • Moderate: Cache poisoning in React Server Component responses

  • Low: Cache poisoning via collisions in RSC cache-busting

Cross-site scripting

Affects applications using CSP nonces in App Router, or beforeInteractive scripts that consume untrusted input.

  • Moderate: XSS in App Router applications using CSP nonces

  • Moderate: XSS in beforeInteractive scripts with untrusted input

Resolution

These vulnerabilities are addressed by the patched releases of React and Next.js. Patching is the only complete mitigation, and all affected users should upgrade immediately.

Vercel has not deployed new WAF rules for this release; these advisories cannot be reliably blocked at the WAF layer.

title: Rebuilding the Among Us Floor Plan From the Game's Own Collision Data
description:
I train Among Us bots in a simulator of the game. A crew walks the ship doing tasks and votes out suspects in meetings. Hidden impostors kill, travel through vents (tunnels only impostors can use) and sabotage the ship, including shutting a room's doors for 10 seconds. The bots learn by self-play in leagues, each league a roughly ten-hour training run that starts from the bots the previous league ended with.

The simulator decides where players can stand with a grid of 126 by 70 tiles. The grid comes from the map file of an open-source web clone of the game, MIT-licensed and written by a third party. I used it because it was there and it matched the ship's layout room for room. It is also wrong, in a way I only saw once the replays were drawn on the real game's art: a crewmate jogging along the top of a corridor with its feet on the corridor's back wall. Measured against the game's own collision data, the clone's floor is 1.75 times too big.

Where the real floor comes from

Among Us is a Unity game, and the 2018 Android build ships its levels as Unity asset files inside the APK (the Android app package). The ship is a single prefab (a saved Unity object tree) called ShipStatus. Alongside the artwork, it carries the colliders the physics engine uses to stop players walking through things. I read them out of the APK with UnityPy, a third-party Python library for Unity asset files, without running the game. There are 79 wall outlines, which are edge colliders along the edge of every room and corridor. There are also 33 solid obstacles: the Cafeteria tables, the MedBay beds, the engines, Navigation's chairs and a few task consoles.

The player prefab supplies the other number that matters. A player is a 0.7-scaled object with a circular collider of radius 0.2234 at its feet. So the centre of a player's feet can never get closer than 0.156 units (Unity's unit of distance) to a wall or an obstacle. One unit is 2.646 of my simulator's tiles (from aligning a render of the ship with the clone's map), which makes the clearance 0.41 tiles.

The rebuild draws every outline and obstacle into a grid eight times finer than the simulator's tiles. It flood-fills the inside of the ship from a known floor point, then removes everything within the foot clearance of a wall or obstacle. A tile is walkable if its centre survives. Two details mattered. The outlines had to be drawn three sub-cells thick, because two outlines meeting at a corner can leave a gap finer than one sub-cell; the first version's flood fill escaped through one and filled the outside of the ship. And 56 tiles of floor that were not connected to the rest were dropped. The build would also force each of the 14 vent grilles onto the floor, since the game snaps a player's feet onto a grille to enter it, but in the final build none needed it.

How wrong the old floor was

walkable tiles
the clone's map 3,314
the game's colliders 1,894
on both 1,867
on the clone's map only 1,447
on the game's colliders only 27

Every room shrank, unevenly. Eight of the 21 rooms and corridors, the worst and best by the ratio of old to new walkable tiles:

room old real old / real
O2 98 32 3.06
Weapons 180 78 2.31
Shields 133 58 2.29
Upper Engine 110 48 2.29
Cafeteria 658 351 1.87
MedBay 142 105 1.35
central hall 253 196 1.29
Storage 162 147 1.10

The pattern is what the replays suggested. In a corridor, the clone's map counts the whole drawn height as floor. That includes the band of wall panels along the top, which the game draws as the back wall, so a corridor loses that band plus the foot clearance on each side. Rooms full of furniture lose the furniture; on the clone's map you could walk straight across the Cafeteria tables. Storage, an open room with crates mostly along its edges, barely changed.

Before switching, I checked that nothing the simulator depends on fell off the new floor. All 14 vents are on walkable tiles. Every task station moved by at most 3 tiles, to the nearest real floor in its own room. Each of the 7 rooms with doors still cannot be walked into from outside while its doors (13 in all) are shut. Impostors can still vent into some of them, as in the game.

How much it changed the game

I do not know precisely, which is the honest answer. The bots were trained on the old floor and played on the new one without retraining. I played 40 games on each floor with the bots from my fourth league, 15 players and 3 impostors, using a fixed random seed so the run repeats exactly:

floor crew wins tasks done kills per game vents per game
clone's map 36 of 40 69% 5.8 3.3
game's colliders 34 of 40 65% 6.0 3.6

Two games in 40 is within what a different seed could produce. But an earlier unseeded test, also 40 games each, with the same league's bots taken at an earlier checkpoint and an earlier version of the simulator, measured the crew at 78% on the old floor and 68% on the new one. Forty games cannot separate a 2-point effect from a 10-point one, so the effect is somewhere in that range. Either way it is far smaller than a factor of 1.75 in walkable floor suggests. My guess at why is that the bots decide between rooms rather than between tiles. A room's neighbours, its vents and the walking distance between rooms are close to unchanged, so the floor mostly changes where a player stands inside a room rather than where it goes.

I switched anyway. The simulator is meant to model the real game, and the old floor was visibly wrong in every replay, whatever it did to the win rate. Training since then has used the real floor, and the old one remains available for comparison with older runs. My fifth league, the first to train on the new floor, later collapsed for reasons I could not separate from the floor change, which is a separate post.

The simulator, the extraction and the rebuild were written by Claude Code at my direction, and the corridor wall-walking was something I spotted in the replays. The code is not public, and the extracted game data and art stay on my machine. The figures above come from the rebuild script's output and a seeded comparison script; anyone with the 2018 APK and UnityPy can read the same colliders.

What I take from it is that a simulator can be wrong by a factor of 1.75 in a quantity that sounds fundamental and still produce similar outcomes. Outcome metrics are a poor check on whether a simulator is faithful. The check that found this was looking at the picture.

title: What Apple checks before Messages for Business goes live
description:
A brand does not flip Apple Messages for Business on by paying Apple. The account stays in test until Apple’s Experience Review passes.

The gates

  • An approved Messaging Service Provider. The brand does not connect to Apple directly.
  • An Apple Business Register account for the organization.
  • A conversation that includes a live agent during business hours. A bot-only flow does not pass.
  • Customer-initiated entry points. The channel is not for unsolicited outbound iMessages.
  • A built journey Apple can review: support, booking, commerce, or concierge, using the interactive features the MSP actually ships.

The approval write-up, including what Apple looks at in the review, is here: How to get approved for Apple Messages for Business.

The steps before that review, starting with Apple Business Register and MSP selection, are here: How to apply.

After the review

Once the account is commercial, customers can start from the website, Maps, and the other entry points the brand turns on. Patterns from brands that are already live are in best practices.
