title: Engineering manager : le 1:1 et le suivi individuel
description:
Cet article a été publié initialement sur mon blog.

C'est le deuxième article de ma série sur ce que le rôle d'engineering
manager m'a appris. Comme pour le premier épisode, ce qui suit n'est ni une
méthode ni une vérité générale : c'est un retour d'expérience personnel,
structuré autour des citations et des principes que des personnes qui ont
compté dans mon parcours m'ont transmis, et de ce qu'ils m'apportent au
quotidien.

Le premier épisode portait sur le rôle et la posture
d'engineering manager ; si vous
ne l'avez pas lu, c'est une bonne entrée en matière avant celui-ci. Vous
pouvez aussi retrouver tous les articles de la série sur la page du tag
engineering-management.

Ce billet-ci se concentre sur le 1:1 et le suivi individuel : ce temps
dédié, régulier, en tête-à-tête avec chaque personne de l'équipe, et tout ce
qui se joue autour pour accompagner les individus dans la durée.

Le paradoxe de la porte ouverte

« Ma porte est toujours ouverte. » (une phrase que j'ai entendue de la
bouche de plusieurs managers, que je ne citerai pas ici)

Annoncer que sa porte est ouverte, ce n'est pas si généreux qu'il n'y
paraît. Au fond, cela ne fait qu'ériger en principe le « venez me déranger
quand vous en avez besoin » : la charge de provoquer l'échange repose
entièrement sur le managé. Dans une petite équipe, ça peut suffire. Passé
une certaine taille, ça ne tient plus.

En cas d'urgence ou de situation qui le réclame, votre porte doit
évidemment rester ouverte. Mais une disponibilité permanente n'est pas un
dispositif de suivi : c'est un modèle qui ne passe pas à l'échelle, et qui
laisse de côté ceux qui ne viennent jamais frapper.

La réponse, c'est d'instaurer un rendez-vous régulier avec chaque personne
de l'équipe : un temps dédié, qui vous revient d'initier, pour échanger,
prendre la température et vous donner mutuellement du feedback.


La porte ouverte laisse les sollicitations arriver n'importe quand ; le 1:1 régulier les rassemble dans un temps prévu pour ça.

Une régularité par individu

« Tu veux qu'on se voie à quelle régularité ? »
(Florent Dubost,
mon manager pendant plusieurs années)

Tout est affaire d'individu. Chacun a besoin de voir son manager à une
fréquence et pour une durée qui lui sont propres. Décréter « je vois
tout le monde trente minutes toutes les deux semaines », c'est la garantie
de ne répondre au besoin de personne : certains étoufferont, d'autres
tourneront en rond faute de matière.

Cette cadence se négocie donc avec chaque managé. Elle n'a rien de figé et
peut évoluer au fil du temps, mais une fois posée, elle devient un
engagement : on ne l'annule pas, on la décale.

Concrètement, je recommande de fixer explicitement, en échangeant avec la
personne, la fréquence et la durée du 1:1, puis de les consigner quelque
part. Un accord tacite se perd ; un accord écrit se relit et se révise
quand le besoin change.

Le cas des alternants, stagiaires et profils juniors

« Je ne sais pas si je suis suffisamment à l'aise pour prendre un
alternant… » (un collègue, en pleine crise de confiance)

Le suivi des profils en apprentissage fait souvent peur : celle de mal s'en
occuper, ou celle d'être sollicité en permanence. J'ai eu la chance de
donner des cours, et l'expérience d'une classe de quarante étudiants qui
vous demandent chacun à leur tour « il faut faire quoi, monsieur ? » forge
assez vite l'envie de se doter d'une stratégie.

Comme pour n'importe quel managé, la réponse passe par un suivi régulier,
mais nettement plus soutenu. Ce que j'ai appliqué le plus souvent : deux
créneaux d'une heure par semaine, bloqués dans le calendrier, généralement
un le mardi et un le jeudi, pendant lesquels je leur consacre du temps pour
avancer ensemble sur leur sujet. Ces points réguliers créent des
respirations dans la semaine : la personne sait qu'un moment est prévu pour
poser ses questions et ses blocages, ce qui évite les sollicitations
permanentes. C'est aussi ce qui rend possible l'accompagnement de plusieurs
apprenants en parallèle : votre capacité, c'est le temps que vous êtes prêt
à bloquer chaque semaine.

Un autre réflexe utile : confier deux sujets à la fois. Le premier, « l'os »,
est le sujet difficile, celui sur lequel la personne peut rester coincée.
Le second est un sujet sans blocage connu, sur lequel elle peut continuer à
avancer librement quand l'os résiste. Elle n'est jamais complètement à
l'arrêt, et vous n'êtes pas le seul goulot d'étranglement de sa semaine.

L'arrivée d'un alternant ou d'un stagiaire, ça se prépare. J'y reviendrai
plus en détail dans un article dédié à l'onboarding, l'offboarding et le
recrutement.

Avec Jules Poissonnet, mon ancien alternant, sur la scène de LyonJS 100
pour un talk sur les stratégies de test. Accompagner un profil junior, c'est
aussi l'amener jusqu'à partager devant une salle.

Étaler ses 1:1 dans la semaine

Qu'il s'agisse des 1:1 de vos managés ou de vos apprenants, placez-les dans
un agenda partagé. Pourquoi pas un agenda dédié, avec sa propre couleur,
pour visualiser d'un coup d'œil comment vos entretiens se répartissent. Le
but est d'éviter la journée entièrement remplie de 1:1. Certains préfèrent
tout enchaîner ; pour moi, ce serait un vrai cauchemar.

Un 1:1 demande une écoute pleine et entière. En enchaîner cinq dans la même
journée, c'est arriver au dernier vidé de son attention, à écouter à moitié
la personne qui n'y est pour rien si elle passe en fin de liste. Chaque
entretien laisse aussi du travail derrière lui : une note à prendre, une
relance à faire, un sujet difficile à digérer avant de pouvoir passer à
autre chose. Il faut un peu d'air entre deux pour ça. Enfin, espacer les
1:1 leur laisse la souplesse de déborder : si l'un a besoin d'un quart
d'heure de plus, il ne fait pas s'effondrer les quatre suivants.


Une semaine type : un 1:1 par jour, à des horaires différents, plutôt qu'une demi-journée entière d'entretiens enchaînés.

Des besoins qui ne s'équilibrent pas

« Il est normal que certaines personnes de vos équipes nécessitent un
accompagnement plus fort que d'autres. » (Sarah Drasner, dans le livre
cité dans l'article
précédent)

Ça peut être frustrant quand on débute dans le rôle, mais avec l'expérience,
ça devient une évidence. Chaque personne de l'équipe est différente, et
l'accompagnement que vous lui apportez n'est ni le même ni comparable d'un
individu à l'autre. Oui, vous aurez peut-être quelqu'un qui occupera à lui
seul la moitié de votre temps de management sur une semaine. Avec le recul,
ça ne me choque plus.

Et tout cela évolue. Une personne que vous suivez de loin à un moment donné
sera peut-être bien plus demandeuse l'année suivante. Rien n'est
nécessairement corrélé à l'expérience ou à l'autonomie du managé : un profil
junior vous mobilisera souvent davantage, mais vous croiserez aussi des
juniors qui gagnent très vite en autonomie et se jettent dans les ronces
avec appétit pour apprendre. Dans ce cas, laissez-les faire.

Ne soyez donc pas surpris que les besoins soient déséquilibrés dans
l'équipe. Cherchez l'équité, pas l'égalité : donnez plus à celles et
ceux qui en ont le plus besoin. C'est à vous de vous adapter à l'équipe,
pas l'inverse.


Un exemple : sur une semaine, une personne peut mobiliser la moitié de votre temps de management, une autre à peine 5 %. C'est normal.

Le syndrome du sauveteur compulsif

« Des fois j'y arrive, souvent j'me trompe, donc j'recommence, et puis
j'apprends. » (Orelsan — et pourquoi pas Dorothée tant qu'on y est ? je
cite qui je veux, hein)

Quand on reçoit la responsabilité de manager, on a envie de protéger son
équipe, de lui éviter les erreurs dans lesquelles on est soi-même tombé.
L'intention est louable, mais elle prive l'équipe de l'essentiel de son
apprentissage. L'image que je me fais du rôle, c'est plutôt : « je dois
laisser mon équipe échouer pour qu'elle progresse. » C'est frustrant.

Certains managers se diront « si je le fais moi-même, j'en ai pour dix
minutes ». En réalité, vous en avez pour dix minutes plus vos années
d'expérience. La personne que vous managez, elle, n'a pas ces années :
elle est en train de les construire. Laissez-la échouer.

Vous allez me trouver vilain, mais il m'est arrivé de créer sciemment des
situations où je « soulève légèrement le tapis » pour qu'une personne de
l'équipe s'y prenne les pieds. Rassurez-vous, c'est une image : mon équipe
n'est pas sponsorisée par les crèmes à l'arnica. Provoquer des situations
qui font grandir l'équipe fait partie du rôle. C'est dans une certaine zone
d'inconfort que vos managés apprennent et progressent, pas en refaisant ce
qu'ils maîtrisent déjà.

Votre alarme interne doit évidemment continuer de sonner : il s'agit
d'éviter que l'équipe échoue trop fort, ou se fasse vraiment mal. Pour
distinguer l'incident formateur du vrai problème, je me sers d'un test
simple : si je m'imagine y repenser dans deux ans et que je le trouve
encore grave à ce moment-là, alors il est grave aujourd'hui et je dois
intervenir. Sinon, je laisse faire.

Tenir un journal de bord

« Journal de bord : mer calme, embarquement de 4 passagers, vent NE
force 3… » (pas la citation d'un mentor cette fois, juste l'image qui m'a
servi de modèle)

L'image en tête de cet article est une double page du livre de bord de la
frégate néerlandaise Medea, tenu en 1786 par son commandant A.A. Buyskes
(Nationaal Archief, domaine public). On y
voit des profils de côtes dessinés à main levée et le relevé quotidien de la
navigation : cap, vent, mouillages, incidents. Des siècles avant nos outils
de suivi, la pratique était déjà là — noter chaque jour, factuellement, ce
qu'on observe, pour pouvoir s'y reporter plus tard. C'est exactement l'usage
que je vous propose d'en faire avec votre équipe.

Avant même de parler du document qui me sert à structurer le suivi de mes
managés, il y a un préalable : disposer quelque part d'un espace de notes.
Vous observez votre équipe en continu, dans ses réussites comme dans ses
ratés, à l'échelle collective comme individuelle. Avec une petite équipe, on
a vite envie de s'en remettre à sa mémoire ; elle finit toujours par être
débordée.

Je conseille donc de tenir un journal de bord : un endroit où consigner les
événements de la vie de l'équipe. Il vous est strictement personnel, et sa
seule contrainte est de vous obliger à rester factuel.

On peut y noter la mise en production d'une fonctionnalité, un incident, la
réussite marquante d'une personne, une communication qui est mal passée, un
oubli de standup, ou encore une période où quelqu'un s'est visiblement
beaucoup investi. Relus quelques semaines plus tard, au moment d'un 1:1 ou
d'un point de carrière, ces faits datés valent bien mieux qu'une impression
générale.

Je vous montrerais bien le mien, mais comme je l'ai dit, il est privé. À
vous de faire le vôtre.


Des entrées courtes, datées et factuelles : ni interprétation ni jugement, juste ce qui s'est passé.

Le brag document : se souvenir de ses réussites

« Si on me demande quels sont mes succès de l'année, c'est très dur d'être
exhaustif. » (Anne-Laure de Boissieu, une ancienne collègue et amie)

Dans une conférence que je recommande
vivement, mon ancienne
collègue et amie Anne-Laure présente un concept que je ne connaissais pas et
qui m'a beaucoup servi depuis : le brag document.

C'est un document proche du journal de bord, à ceci près qu'il ne recense
que les fiertés, les sujets que l'on considère personnellement comme des
succès. Notre cerveau fonctionne ainsi : on oublie très vite ce dont on
devrait être fier, pendant que le problème sur lequel on bloque depuis deux
semaines occupe presque tout l'espace.

D'où l'intérêt de tenir un brag document avec chaque managé, et un autre
pour l'équipe dans son ensemble. Chaque personne y historise avec vous, au
fil de l'année, les fiertés qu'elle a eues : un titre, une date, une courte
description. À vous de faire le même exercice à l'échelle de l'équipe.

À quoi bon, me direz-vous ? Ce document se révèle précieux dans plusieurs
situations :

  • accompagner un membre de l'équipe en questionnement, qui n'a pas l'impression de progresser ou qui traverse un syndrome de l'imposteur ;
  • préparer les périodes d'évaluation annuelle en s'appuyant sur tous les succès de l'année, et pas seulement sur ceux des deux derniers mois ;
  • défendre l'impact et la vision de votre équipe dans l'entreprise.

Je ne rends pas justice ici à la richesse du talk d'Anne-Laure. Il vaut
vraiment le détour :

Donner du feedback

« Praise in public, feedback in private. » (Sarah Drasner)

Un manager passe une part énorme de son temps à donner du feedback. Je ne
vais pas détailler ici comment le formuler : le sujet mérite un article à
lui seul. Je m'en tiens à quelques clés que l'expérience, et la lecture du
livre de Sarah, m'ont fait comprendre.

Commençons par le feedback positif. Quand quelqu'un de votre équipe fait
quelque chose que vous trouvez franchement bien, vous devez le dire,
positivement, devant toute l'équipe. Et le redire lors du 1:1 suivant.

Pourquoi deux fois ? Parce que chacun des deux canaux, seul, laisse un
doute. En privé uniquement : « il me dit ça pour me faire plaisir, il ne le
pense pas vraiment ». En public uniquement : « il le dit devant tout le
monde, mais je ne sais pas ce qu'il en pense réellement ». Les deux
ensemble lèvent l'ambiguïté.

Tout cela suppose d'avoir noté ce qui s'est passé — c'est l'un des usages de
mon journal de bord. Des faits consignés factuellement, ce sont des
occasions de feedback prêtes à l'emploi. Et vous verrez qu'une personne
ajoute bien plus facilement une ligne à son brag document quand vous avez
commencé par reconnaître la chose vous-même.

C'est quand, la dernière fois que vous avez dit à quelqu'un de votre équipe
qu'il ou elle avait fait du bon travail ?

Vient ensuite le feedback plus difficile : les rectifications, les axes
d'amélioration.

Sur ce terrain, l'expérience m'a appris qu'il existe très peu de situations
qui justifient un feedback direct, sur le moment. La principale exception :
le danger immédiat. Si quelqu'un dit ou fait quelque chose qui peut nuire
directement à une autre personne, là, j'interviens tout de suite.

En dehors de ça, laisser le feedback mijoter est plutôt une bonne chose.
Qu'est-ce qui vous empêche de noter les faits et d'en reparler à froid lors
d'un prochain 1:1 ? Ce délai vous laisse réfléchir à la manière d'amener les
choses, et, la plupart du temps, il fait retomber la pression : « en fait,
ce n'est pas si grave ». Si un feedback ne vaut pas la peine d'attendre
une à deux semaines pour être donné, est-ce vraiment un feedback
pertinent ?

À l'inverse du feedback positif, celui-ci se donne uniquement en privé, dans
un échange en tête-à-tête avec la personne.

Les valeurs et les préférences

« Tu verras que la source première des conflits dans une équipe, ce sont
des conflits de valeurs. Et l'ego, bien sûr. »
(Kenny Dits)

Si les frictions naissent surtout d'un désaccord sur ce qui compte, alors
une partie du travail de suivi consiste à savoir ce qui compte pour chacun,
avant que ça ne coince.

Sarah Drasner propose pour cela un exercice tout simple dans son livre :
poser directement la question à vos managés, en 1:1. Trois questions
suffisent :

  • Dans ton travail, quelles sont les trois choses les plus importantes pour toi ?
  • Qu'est-ce que tu préfères faire ?
  • Qu'est-ce que tu aimes le moins faire ?

Rien qu'en posant ces questions, vous découvrirez que tout le monde ne
classe pas les choses dans le même ordre que vous. L'un vous parlera des
collègues et de l'ambiance, l'autre de la qualité du code, un troisième de
l'impact pour les utilisateurs, un quatrième de cohérence. C'est très varié.
Cet exercice vous fait mieux connaître les personnes de votre équipe et vous
évite de leur plaquer un archétype construit sur vous-même ou sur un autre
collègue.

Vous remarquerez aussi que certaines personnes n'évoquent pas du tout
certaines thématiques dans leur top 3. Ça ne veut pas dire que ça ne compte
pas pour elles, seulement que ce n'est pas leur priorité. Et ces
non-équivalences de priorité sont souvent à la racine des problèmes
d'équipe.

Imaginez Alex, « j'aime quand on règle vite les soucis des utilisateurs sans
trop débattre », et Sam, « j'aime quand on prend le temps de réfléchir au
problème pour trouver une solution qui répond parfaitement au besoin ».
Inutile de faire un dessin : Alex et Sam finiront par se retrouver en
tension. Mais si vous le savez, et que vous savez maintenant comment chacun
fonctionne, vous pouvez mettre un peu d'eau dans leurs vins respectifs et
trouver des compromis qui ménagent les valeurs des deux.


Le même exercice, deux classements très différents — et une préoccupation commune qui ne pèse pas du tout le même poids d'une personne à l'autre.

Cet exercice se fait en 1:1. Mais quand l'équipe est suffisamment à l'aise,
il devient aussi un bon jeu collectif : chacun arrive avec ses trois post-it
par question, on mélange le tout, et l'équipe doit retrouver quelle réponse
va à qui, et dans quel ordre.

Connaître les préférences, ensuite, ce n'est pas pour ne distribuer que des
tâches que chacun adore et cloisonner l'équipe. C'est pour savoir ce que les
gens aiment et ce qu'ils détestent. On a tous une jauge intérieure : elle se
vide quand on fait des choses qui nous pèsent, elle se recharge quand on
fait des choses qui nous plaisent. En connaissant les deux, vous pouvez
aider chacun à tenir cet équilibre.


Chacun porte cette jauge. Le travail de suivi, c'est de faire en sorte qu'elle ne tombe pas durablement à zéro.

Toutes ces réponses se rangent dans la page de suivi de la personne, et vous
y reviendrez : pour répartir les sujets, pour comprendre une tension, pour
vérifier de temps en temps que ce qui comptait il y a un an compte encore.

Suivre et encourager l'apprentissage

« Un jour j'ai monté un truc, les Last Friday Talks : une demi-journée
de conférences tech internes, le dernier vendredi du mois, pour que les
gens racontent ce qu'ils font. Dès la deuxième édition ce n'était plus le
dernier vendredi, mais peu importe. »
(Kenny Dits — encore lui)

Le manager a le devoir d'accompagner l'apprentissage de son équipe, sur deux
axes qui vont ensemble : s'assurer que chacun a le temps et les moyens
d'apprendre, et s'assurer que personne ne se disperse.

J'ai fini par en faire un petit rituel. On liste ensemble, dans un tableau,
les sujets de veille technique que la personne veut explorer, avec pour
chacun : le sujet, son état, la date de départ, une durée estimée, une
courte description et un pourcentage d'avancement. Tout y passe : des
conférences à voir en replay, des articles à lire, des proof of concept
d'outils ou de technos, des formations, des certifications.

Un extrait, colonne description mise de côté pour la lisibilité :

Sujet État Départ Durée est. Avancement
Talk « Local-first » dotJS partagé 2026-02-10 2 h 100 %
PoC OpenTelemetry terminé 2026-01-15 1 j 100 %
Rust pour l'embarqué en cours 2026-03-02 3 j 60 %
Certification CKA demandé — 5 j 0 %

Une seule règle : on ne démarre un sujet que s'il n'y en a pas déjà deux en
cours. Autrement dit, pour en commencer un nouveau, il faut d'abord en
terminer un, ou l'abandonner assumé.

Les états possibles : demandé, rejeté (très rare — sauf si quelqu'un
vous annonce qu'il aimerait apprendre le saut en parachute), en cours,
terminé, et partagé.

Ce dernier état est le plus important. Pour moi, un apprentissage n'est
vraiment terminé que lorsqu'il a été partagé : à l'équipe, à la guilde, à
la communauté. C'est là que la citation de Kenny prend tout son sens — un
espace de partage régulier, même bancal, même plus vraiment le dernier
vendredi du mois, donne une destination à tout ce travail de veille.

Je dois avouer qu'une fois le principe bien ancré et adopté par l'équipe, le
suivi dans le tableau n'est plus vraiment nécessaire. Mais il aide à poser
les bases.

Le template de page de suivi individuel

Tout ce qui précède se range quelque part. Ce que j'ai fini par construire,
c'est une page unique par managé — un hub de suivi. Chez moi elle vit dans
Confluence, mais Notion, un Google Doc ou n'importe quel autre outil font
tout aussi bien l'affaire. Le point important : elle n'est accessible qu'à
deux personnes, la personne concernée et moi.

Elle rassemble, au même endroit :

  • l'identité et la date d'arrivée ;
  • les valeurs et préférences : le top 3 de ce qui compte, les sujets préférés, les sujets moins aimés ;
  • le brag document : titre, date, description ;
  • l'apprentissage supervisé : le tableau vu plus haut.

Voici un squelette que vous pouvez copier tel quel :

# Suivi — Prénom NOM

- **Date d'arrivée :** AAAA-MM-JJ

## Valeurs et préférences

- **Ce qui compte le plus (top 3) :**
  1. …
  2. …
  3. …
- **Sujets préférés :** …
- **Sujets moins aimés :** …

## Brag document

| Titre | Date       | Description |
| ----- | ---------- | ----------- |
| …     | AAAA-MM-JJ | …           |

## Apprentissage supervisé

<!-- États : demandé · rejeté · en cours · terminé · partagé -->
<!-- Règle : jamais plus de 2 sujets « en cours » en même temps -->

| Sujet | État | Départ     | Durée est. | Description | Avancement |
| ----- | ---- | ---------- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| …     | …    | AAAA-MM-JJ | …          | …           | … %        |

Ce hub, c'est en quelque sorte le résumé matériel de cet article. Et les
notes de chaque 1:1 deviennent des pages enfant de cette page : le suivi
dans la durée d'un côté, le fil des échanges de l'autre.

Ce que je ne détaille pas ici, c'est ce qu'on se dit réellement en 1:1 et ce
qu'on cherche à y adresser
: c'est un sujet à part entière.

Et la suite ?

Il reste d'autres aspects du 1:1 et du suivi que je n'ai pas abordés ici. Si
vous voulez que je précise un point ou que j'aborde un thème en particulier,
mes réseaux sont accessibles depuis ce blog : écrivez-moi, je serai ravi de
vous lire.

Ce thème des citations et principes reçus se poursuivra dans un prochain
article consacré à « Donner des objectifs et de la vision ». Comme
toujours, vous pouvez retrouver l'ensemble de la série via le tag
engineering-management.

title: Diagnosing Low-Confidence Patient Profiles via Localized Harmful Covariate Shift Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.19178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Before deploying clinical prediction models, their reliability must be assessed to ensure safe use. Errors may arise from distribution shifts between training and deployment or from heterogeneous performance where the model systematically underperforms for certain patient subgroups. Yet most post-hoc diagnostic methods evaluate reliability only at the population level, checking whether the deployment data resemble the training data and whether the model performs well on average, without accounting for heterogeneity that may cause some patients to be disproportionately affected. We propose a unified diagnostic pipeline that combines both perspectives. MED3pa first discovers interpretable low-confidence patient profiles, and Detectron is then applied within each profile to test whether its degradation is associated with a detectable harmful covariate shift. Across three clinical prediction tasks and three injected subgroup shifts in MIMIC-IV, we find that shift detectability itself is informative. An injected age shift, undetectable at the population level, was nonetheless localized to specific degraded profiles, whereas sex- and race-related shifts were detected broadly and therefore offered little guidance for identifying the most affected patients.

title: What We Learned Building Cross-Channel Message Routing
description:
Cross-Channel Message Routing for Chatbots: What We Learned Building It Across WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram

Every chatbot starts simple: one channel, one webhook, one reply. Then a customer asks, "Can you also answer on Instagram?" and suddenly you're maintaining three webhook formats, three rate-limit models, and three definitions of what a "message" even is.

At Botsailors, we hit this wall while building our omnichannel automation layer. This post is a behind-the-scenes look at how to route messages across WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram without turning your codebase into a pile of if (channel === ...) statements. You'll learn the architecture we settled on, the mistakes that shaped it, and code you can adapt.

Note: This is a build post, not a product pitch. Where we compare approaches, we include alternatives so you can pick what fits your stack.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites
  • What is cross-channel message routing?
  • Lesson 1: Normalize before you route
  • Lesson 2: Make every inbound event idempotent
  • Lesson 3: Separate routing rules from channel adapters
  • Lesson 4: Respect each channel's limits on the way out
  • Lesson 5: Design human handoff early
  • Build vs. buy: alternatives to consider
  • Conclusion

Prerequisites

Before you follow along, you should have:

  • [ ] Working knowledge of Node.js and TypeScript
  • [ ] Basic familiarity with webhooks and REST APIs
  • [ ] A developer account on at least one messaging platform (WhatsApp Business Platform, Meta for Instagram, or the Telegram Bot API)
  • [ ] A queue or job runner (we use Redis-backed queues, but any works)

What is cross-channel message routing?

Cross-channel message routing is the layer that receives messages from many channels, decides what should handle each one (a bot flow, an AI agent, or a human), and sends the reply back through the correct channel in the correct format.

It sits between channel-specific webhooks and your business logic:

WhatsApp ─┐
Instagram ─┼─> Adapters ─> Normalizer ─> Router ─> Handler (bot / AI / human)
Telegram ─┘                                            │
                                    Outbound queue <───┘

The goal: your business logic never knows or cares which channel a message came from, unless it explicitly needs to.

Lesson 1: Normalize before you route

Our first version routed on raw payloads. It worked for about two weeks.

Each channel describes the same event differently. A text message is messages[0].text.body on one platform and message.text on another. Routing on raw payloads means every new rule has to understand every payload.

The fix was a single internal message shape:

type Channel = "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "telegram";

interface NormalizedMessage {
  id: string;              // our internal ID
  externalId: string;      // the channel's message ID
  channel: Channel;
  contactId: string;       // channel-specific user ID
  conversationId: string;
  type: "text" | "image" | "audio" | "location" | "button_reply";
  text?: string;
  mediaUrl?: string;
  receivedAt: Date;
  raw: unknown;            // keep the original payload for debugging
}

Each channel gets a small adapter that converts into this shape:

function telegramAdapter(update: any): NormalizedMessage {
  const m = update.message;
  return {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    externalId: String(m.message_id),
    channel: "telegram",
    contactId: String(m.from.id),
    conversationId: `tg:${m.chat.id}`,
    type: m.text ? "text" : "image",
    text: m.text,
    receivedAt: new Date(m.date * 1000),
    raw: update,
  };
}

Tip: Always keep the raw payload. When a customer says "your bot ignored my message," raw payloads are the fastest way to find out why.

Lesson 2: Make every inbound event idempotent

Webhook providers retry. If your server is slow or returns a non-200, the same message can arrive two or three times, and your bot happily replies to each one.

We deduplicate at the door using the channel's own message ID:

async function acceptOnce(msg: NormalizedMessage): Promise<boolean> {
  const key = `seen:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`;
  // SET NX with a TTL: only the first writer wins
  const result = await redis.set(key, "1", "EX", 60 * 60 * 24, "NX");
  return result === "OK";
}

app.post("/webhooks/:channel", async (req, res) => {
  res.sendStatus(200); // acknowledge fast, process async
  const msg = adapters[req.params.channel](req.body);
  if (await acceptOnce(msg)) {
    await inboundQueue.add("route", msg);
  }
});

Two rules we now treat as non-negotiable:

  1. Acknowledge first, process later. Slow handlers cause retries.
  2. Deduplicate on the external ID, not on message content. Customers legitimately send "ok" twice.

Lesson 3: Separate routing rules from channel adapters

Routing decisions (who handles this message?) should be pure functions of the normalized message plus conversation state. They should never import a channel SDK.

type Target = "flow" | "ai_agent" | "human";

interface ConversationState {
  assignedTo?: "human" | "bot";
  activeFlowId?: string;
  lastIntent?: string;
}

function route(msg: NormalizedMessage, state: ConversationState): Target {
  // 1. A human owns the conversation: bots stay quiet
  if (state.assignedTo === "human") return "human";

  // 2. A flow is mid-execution: continue it
  if (state.activeFlowId) return "flow";

  // 3. Explicit escalation keywords, on any channel
  if (msg.text && /\b(agent|human|representative)\b/i.test(msg.text)) {
    return "human";
  }

  // 4. Default: let the AI agent handle it
  return "ai_agent";
}

Because route is pure, we can unit test it with plain objects, no mock webhooks required:

test("human-owned conversations never reach the bot", () => {
  const msg = { text: "hello", channel: "instagram" } as NormalizedMessage;
  expect(route(msg, { assignedTo: "human" })).toBe("human");
});

Lesson 4: Respect each channel's limits on the way out

Inbound is only half the problem. Outbound is where channels differ most:

Concern What varies by channel
Messaging windows Some platforms restrict free-form replies after a time window and require approved templates
Rate limits Different per-second and per-user throughput
Rich content Buttons, carousels, and quick replies differ in shape and limits
Message length Text limits vary

Check each platform's current documentation for exact numbers, because they change. Our approach is an outbound adapter per channel plus a shared queue with per-channel rate limiting:

const limiters: Record<Channel, RateLimiter> = {
  whatsapp: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 20 }),   // example values: verify against current docs
  instagram: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 10 }),
  telegram: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 30 }),
};

async function send(channel: Channel, contactId: string, reply: Reply) {
  await limiters[channel].acquire();
  const payload = outboundAdapters[channel](contactId, reply);
  return channelClients[channel].post(payload);
}

Heads up: The numbers above are placeholders. Always confirm current limits in each platform's official docs before relying on them.

A shared Reply type (text, buttons, media) that each outbound adapter degrades gracefully is the key. If a channel can't render a carousel, fall back to a numbered text list rather than failing silently.

Lesson 5: Design human handoff early

We treated handoff as a "later" feature. That was a mistake, because handoff changes your routing model.

Once a human can take over a conversation, you need:

  • A conversation owner field that the router checks first (see Lesson 3).
  • A way to hand back to the bot when the human is done.
  • Idle timeouts so a conversation doesn't stay "owned" by an agent who went home. 
async function handoff(conversationId: string, to: "human" | "bot") {
  await db.conversations.update(conversationId, {
    assignedTo: to,
    assignedAt: new Date(),
  });
}

Adding ownership after the fact meant rewriting every handler. Adding it up front costs one column.

Build vs. buy: alternatives to consider

Building your own router is not always the right call. Depending on your team and requirements, you could consider:

  • Open-source frameworks such as Botpress or Rasa if you want self-hosting and full control.
  • Managed omnichannel platforms if you'd rather not maintain webhooks, templates, and compliance yourself.
  • Direct platform APIs (as in this post) when you need custom routing logic or tight integration with your own backend.

Build your own if routing logic is core to your product. Otherwise, evaluate what already exists before writing adapters.

Conclusion

Cross-channel message routing for chatbots comes down to a few durable decisions:

  • Normalize every inbound message into one internal shape.
  • Deduplicate at the door and acknowledge webhooks fast.
  • Keep routing pure and separate from channel SDKs.
  • Treat outbound limits as first-class, with a per-channel queue and graceful degradation.
  • Plan human handoff from day one.

None of this is exotic, but skipping any one of them creates bugs that only show up in production, usually on a Friday evening.

If you're building something similar, I'd love to hear how you handle routing across channels. What did you wish you'd known earlier? Share it in the comments.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Silent Installation Automation: A Practical Guide
description:
Installing GBase Database(GBase 8s) manually on multiple Linux servers is time-consuming and increases the risk of configuration inconsistencies. Automating silent installation and deployment verification helps database administrators streamline repetitive tasks and manage larger server environments more efficiently.

In this guide, we'll explore how to organize a batch deployment workflow for GBase Database(GBase 8s) using Bash, SSH, and installation response files.

1. Deployment Architecture

A simple deployment project can use the following structure:

gbase-deploy/
├── deploy_gbase.sh
├── bundle.properties
├── server_list.txt
├── verify_gbase.sh
└── logs/

Each file serves a specific purpose:

  • deploy_gbase.sh: Coordinates remote deployment tasks.
  • bundle.properties: Stores silent installation options supported by the installer.
  • server_list.txt: Defines the target servers.
  • verify_gbase.sh: Checks deployment status.
  • logs/: Stores execution logs for troubleshooting.

2. Prepare the Target Servers

Maintain a server inventory containing the connection details for each target machine.

# IP address SSH user SSH port
192.168.1.101 root 22
192.168.1.102 root 22
192.168.1.103 root 22

Before deploying GBase Database(GBase 8s), verify operating system compatibility, available disk space, network connectivity, and required system dependencies.

For unattended deployment, SSH key-based authentication is preferable to storing passwords in scripts.

3. Automate the Installation Workflow

The master script should coordinate the deployment process rather than hard-code every installation detail.

A typical workflow includes:

  1. Read and validate the target server list.
  2. Transfer the GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation package and configuration files.
  3. Execute the supported silent installation procedure remotely.
  4. Configure the database environment and initialize instances as required.
  5. Record execution results and identify failed deployments.

The exact response-file parameters, installation commands, and instance initialization procedures depend on the installed GBase Database(GBase 8s) release. Always validate them against the documentation accompanying your installation package.

For multi-server deployment, control parallel execution and maintain separate logs for each target. This makes failures easier to identify without interrupting unrelated deployment tasks.

4. Verify Deployment Results

Successful software installation does not necessarily mean the database instance is ready for production.

Your verification workflow should check:

  • Whether the installation completed successfully.
  • Whether the database instance starts and reaches the expected state.
  • Whether the required network listener is available.
  • Whether database connections and basic queries work.
  • Whether locale settings and application connectivity meet requirements.

Tools such as onstat and dbaccess can help validate GBase Database(GBase 8s), provided they are used with the correct environment and permissions.

5. Production Best Practices

When extending GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment automation to more servers, keep these principles in mind:

  • Test first: Validate the workflow on a single server before scaling out.
  • Protect credentials: Use secure authentication and least-privilege access.
  • Keep deployments repeatable: Avoid duplicate configuration changes and unintended instance reinitialization.
  • Maintain logs: Record deployment status and errors for troubleshooting.
  • Plan recovery: Back up important data and prepare a rollback procedure before production changes.

Conclusion

Automating GBase Database(GBase 8s) silent installation can reduce repetitive administration work and improve deployment consistency across Linux servers.

A reliable automation workflow combines installation, environment configuration, instance initialization, and verification into clearly separated stages. By validating version-specific commands and monitoring every deployment, database teams can build a more maintainable process and prepare for future integration with CI/CD pipelines.

The key takeaway: Automate repetitive tasks, but keep version-specific installation logic and production validation explicit. That's the foundation of reliable GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment at scale.

title: "css-slop-detector v0.2: from detecting AI slop to fixing it with one command"

tags: css, python, ai, opensource

v0.1 of css-slop-detector
scored your CSS/HTML for AI-generated design cliches — the "AI slop" look:
oversized border radii, glassmorphism on everything, purple gradients, neon
glows, pure-black dark mode with no light toggle, giant centered hero titles.

v0.2 closes the loop: --fix detects AND fixes. One command rewrites the
flagged patterns for you.

pip install css-slop-detector

# preview first — writes nothing
css-slop --dry-run styles.css
# styles.css: 7 fixes (big-radius x1, glass x1, glow-shadow x1,
#   hero-center x1, no-light-mode x1, pure-black x1, purple-gradient x2)
#   — score 100 -> 0 [dry-run, nothing written]

# apply (original backed up to styles.css.bak first)
css-slop --fix styles.css

# changed your mind?
css-slop --restore styles.css

What the fixer does — only patterns the scanner flags, nothing more:

  • big-radius → clamp border-radius ≥ 20px to 12px
  • glass → remove backdrop-filter: blur(...)
  • purple-gradient → swap purple/violet stops for neutral slate
  • glow-shadow → replace neon glow with a soft neutral shadow
  • pure-black → lift #000 surfaces to soft #1e1e1e
  • hero-center → shrink giant centered titles to 32px, left-align
  • no-light-mode → append a prefers-color-scheme: light hook block

It de-slops; it doesn't redesign. Works on .css and .html
(<style> blocks + inline styles), still stdlib-only, still CI-friendly
(--json, --fail-over).

Why not just prompt better?

Tools like pbakaus/impeccable work on
the generation side — they teach AI to design better, improving the prompt.
css-slop-detector works on the detection+fix side: it scores the finished
product's AI fingerprints, then rewrites them for you in one step. Different
ends of the same pipeline.

  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/css-slop-detector/ (0.2.0)
  • pip install css-slop-detector → css-slop --fix styles.css

21 smoke tests, all green. MIT licensed. Feedback welcome — what's the next
AI-slop fingerprint I should detect?

title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
description:
arXiv:2610.19043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.

title: How I Built a 100% In-Browser Instagram Chat Analyzer (Zero Cloud Uploads)
description:
Direct messages contain our most intimate conversations, jokes, memories, and photos. Yet, when searching for tools to visualize chat history or generate Spotify Wrapped-style stats for group chats, virtually every existing tool asks for your Instagram login or forces you to upload your sensitive ZIP archives to their cloud servers.

I wanted to change that. I built Stats Insta — a completely free, 100% client-side Instagram Chat Analyzer where your data never leaves your device.

In this article, I will share the engineering challenges behind parsing multi-megabyte JSON exports in the browser, decoding escaped Unicode emojis, computing deep conversational metrics, and generating 9:16 Instagram Story cards directly from the DOM.

🔒 The Architecture: 100% Client-Side Privacy

The core philosophy behind Stats Insta is Local-First Processing:

  1. Zero Server Uploads: The application does not have a backend parsing server or database for chat messages.
  2. Native HTML5 FileReader: When a user drops a message_1.json file, the browser reads the file directly into client-side RAM using FileReader.readAsText().
  3. Session-Only Memory: Once you refresh or close the browser tab, the data is instantly garbage-collected by the browser engine.

You can verify this in Chrome DevTools (F12 > Network Tab): dropping a 50MB conversation file triggers 0 network POST requests.

⚙️ Technical Challenge 1: Decoding Instagram's Unicode Escapes

When Meta exports your message history in JSON format, emojis and special characters are not stored as standard UTF-8 strings. Instead, they are encoded as escaped byte sequences (e.g., \u00e2\u009d\u00a4 for a red heart).

If rendered directly in React, emojis appear as garbled characters (Mojibake). To resolve this, I implemented an in-memory Unicode normalization pipeline:

const decodeUnicode = (unicodeString: string): string => {
  try {
    return decodeURIComponent(
      unicodeString.replace(/\\u([0-9a-fA-F]{4})/g, "%u$1")
    );
  } catch (error) {
    return unicodeString;
  }
};

This converts raw escaped sequences into native browser-rendered emojis at runtime without lagging the main thread.

📊 Technical Challenge 2: Calculating Deep Conversational Metrics

Simple message counts are boring. People care about the hidden dynamics of their friendships. We compute several unique behavioral metrics in browser memory:

1. The "Night Owls" Tracker (12:00 AM – 4:59 AM)

We parse the Unix millisecond timestamps (timestamp_ms) on each message and isolate activity occurring in the late-night window:

const hour = new Date(msg.timestamp_ms).getHours();
if (hour >= 0 && hour <= 4) {
  nightOwlCounts[msg.sender_name] = (nightOwlCounts[msg.sender_name] || 0) + 1;
}

This immediately reveals who stays awake sending reels and memes while everyone else is asleep.

2. The Conversation Starter Algorithm

Who puts in the effort to keep the conversation alive? We sort the timeline chronologically and scan for silence gaps exceeding 12 hours:

const TWELVE_HOURS_MS = 12 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
if (lastTimestamp === 0 || msg.timestamp_ms - lastTimestamp > TWELVE_HOURS_MS) {
  starterCounts[msg.sender_name] = (starterCounts[msg.sender_name] || 0) + 1;
}
lastTimestamp = msg.timestamp_ms;

3. The Swear Jar

We scan message strings against a local tokenized dictionary of 100+ global curse words and slang to generate a friendly group chat leaderboard of who has the dirtiest mouth.

📱 Technical Challenge 3: Generating 9:16 Instagram Story Wrapped Cards

People love sharing aesthetic visual summaries with their friends. To make the tool virally shareable, I built an in-browser Story Card generator that renders a 1080x1920 (9:16 Full HD) graphic using HTML5 Canvas:

  • Glassmorphism gradient backgrounds with radial glowing orbs
  • Rounded progress bars showing conversational dominance percentages
  • Dynamic badges and highlights
  • 1-Click Native Share: On mobile devices, we invoke the Web Share API (navigator.share({ files: [pngFile] })), which opens the native iOS/Android share sheet directly into Instagram Stories!

🚀 Try It Live & Explore the Code

The project is completely free to use, and I have published detailed guides on understanding Meta's export architecture:

  • 🌐 Live Application: https://stats-insta.vercel.app/
  • 📘 Guide: How to Open & Read Instagram message_1.json Files
  • 📙 Guide: Activity Heatmaps & Peak Texting Hours

I would love to hear feedback from the DEV community! What other client-side analytics or visual metrics would you like to see added?

title: Two-stage Residual Learning for Modelling Strength-Informed Optimisation of Thermal Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.19539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aggregate performance metrics do not identify local modelling inaccuracies in machine learning (ML) surrogates used for thermal-system optimisation. This study assesses local modelling strength through validation-based reliability screening and post-optimisation residual assessment. A two-stage residual learning (TSRL) framework, built on artificial neural networks (ANNs), is developed for modelling-strength-informed and domain-constrained optimisation of thermal systems. Within the TSRL framework, a base ANN predicts the process output, and a residual ANN learns the signed residuals left by the base ANN. The TSRL framework is implemented on two case studies of thermal systems, including 817 simulation observations of a crude distillation unit and operating records from a 395 MW industrial gas turbine. The TSRL framework reduces the test root mean square error (RMSE) from 10.3 g/s to 4.7 g/s for Fuel Oil in the refinery dataset and from 151 kJ/kWh to 105 kJ/kWh for turbine heat rate (THR). The base ANNs trained within TSRL are embedded in domain-constrained optimisation problems, and the modelling strength at each computed solution is assessed using the locked residual-score threshold. Each computed solution receives a good modelled region (GMR) or weak modelled region (WMR) label to inform ML model-based decision-making for safety-critical operation of thermal systems.

title: Agronomic Characterization and Time-Series UAV Phenotyping to Support Field Pea Breeding in Iowa
description:
arXiv:2610.19154v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Field pea has gained interest in the Midwest U.S. and has the potential to benefit Iowa cropping systems. This study evaluated 17 accessions and 7 Canadian varieties for agronomic and seed yield performance. This study found that PI accession trials exhibit genetic diversity in phenology and canopy traits, whereas the Canadian elite varieties demonstrated great yield potential under Iowa conditions. The accession genotypes matured between 75 DAP (late June) and 95 DAP (late July) across six site-years. The top-yielding Canadian varieties averaged 1961 kg/ha across two site-years. To comprehensively assess field pea performance, this study extracted time-series Unmanned Aerial Vehicle(UAV)-derived traits, assessed UAV-derived traits, and evaluated their correlations with multiple agronomic traits and yield. The results found that UAV-derived time-series canopy area was the most yield-relevant trait (r = 0.63) among all UAV-derived canopy features, vegetation indices, and manually collected measurements. Compared with yield, UAV-derived canopy area showed higher selection reliability (H2 = 0.87, CV = 13.46%), making it suitable for phenotypic selection and accelerating Midwest field pea breeding programs. This study identifies useful UAV-derived features for pea breeding and demonstrates the value of integrating diverse germplasm, elite commercial varieties, and time-series UAV phenotyping. Combining genetic variation from the accession trial with the yield potential of high-performing commercial varieties provides valuable breeding materials and phenotyping strategies for developing locally adapted, high-yielding field pea varieties for future production in the Midwest.

title: Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents
description:
Today we are introducing Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, a platform that gives your entire company the ability to ship with AI safely, behind your access and security boundaries.

Over the past year, employees across Vercel shipped hundreds of agents and internal apps. Getting to production was the easy part, because we built them with eve on top of the Agent Stack and deployed them on Vercel.

The difficult questions came after those agents were being used by our employees across the company:

  • Who is allowed to use each agent?

  • How do we keep internal agents internal?

  • Which data and systems are agents allowed to touch?

  • Which models are agents using, and how much are they costing us?

Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to answer these questions for ourselves. It makes ownership, access, and security the defaults your builders inherit instead of the projects your platform team queues.

Platform components

Security implementation

Vercel Passport

Puts every internal app and agent behind your identity provider by default

Vercel Connect

Gives agents short-lived, scoped credentials for the systems they use, like Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Salesforce, and Linear

Enterprise Managed Users

Full lifecycle control over every Vercel and v0 user through your existing directory

Bring your own cloud on AWS

Runs apps and agents inside your own AWS account (currently in Private Beta)

Vercel Passport: Keep internal apps and agents internal

The first agents we built were internal tools for our employees, not our end users, and that's a common starting point for many of our customers.

Vercel is the fastest way to publish software to the web, but that previously meant "internal" was a setting someone had to configure on every project. One employee forgetting to make one deployment private risked exposing access to sensitive company systems and data.

Vercel Passport puts every internal app and agent behind your identity provider by default, so you can control access with Okta, Microsoft Entra, Auth0, or any other OpenID Connect-compatible provider.

App and agent deployments are private from the moment they exist, access is authenticated against your employee identity, every entry is auditable, and admins set the policy centrally rather than relying on each builder to configure it correctly.

Vercel Connect: Give agents secure access to your systems

Passport governs who can access internal agents, but just as the employees who use them do, those agents need access to your data and systems. That business context makes them both useful and dangerous, because most agents are given long-lived credentials, sitting in environment variables, provisioned for everything the agent might need to do.

Vercel Connect consolidates OAuth, OIDC, and secret injection into one product that replaces those static keys. Instead of storing a secret, an agent requests short-lived credentials as it works. Tokens are granted per task rather than once and forever, and expire when the task is complete. Connect provides agents with secure access to Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Salesforce, and Linear, as well as other systems accessible via OAuth or API.

Enterprise Managed Users: Manage every builder from your identity provider

When everyone in the company is a builder, account sprawl is a silent failure mode. Seats appear to have been provisioned by no one, access lingers after someone changes teams or leaves, and there is no single record of who did what across the entire platform.

Enterprise Managed Users gives administrators full lifecycle control over every builder using Vercel. Built on SAML SSO and Directory Sync, it provisions seats automatically through your existing directory, so an account exists the moment your identity provider says it should and off-boarding removes access the moment the directory does.

Group-based access controls, deployment protection, and MFA enforcement on Vercel apply org-wide, and every action lands in a single audit trail. The identity system your company already runs, whether it is Okta or another SAML or OIDC provider, can now govern Vercel and v0, too.

Enterprise Managed Users is in Private Beta.

Democratize data with v0 and Snowflake

v0 is Vercel's AI app builder. You describe what you want, and it generates a working application. v0 now connects to Snowflake, so you can let anyone safely build data apps backed by your warehouse without an engineering ticket. Access to v0 and Snowflake is controlled through your IDP, so data stays internal. You decide who gets a seat, and apps can deploy directly to your Snowflake account.

Bring your own cloud on AWS

For large enterprise companies, the boundary question goes past private deployments. The workloads themselves have to run on infrastructure they control, inside an account the security team owns and audits.

With bring your own cloud (BYOC) on AWS, your compute, build artifacts, and data run inside your own AWS account and VPC, and Vercel runs the control plane on top of it. Your apps and agents reach private backends and internal systems the same way anything else in your AWS account does, and your source code never leaves your CI.

BYOC on AWS means your engineers keep the Vercel developer experience, and your security team keeps the network controls, audit evidence, and account it already owns. Bring your own cloud is in Private Beta on AWS.

Ship at the speed of AI, safely

Traditionally, ideas died in security review for good reason: the risk of a data breach wasn't worth the potential gain of innovation. Vercel Enterprise Apps and Agents builds safety controls into the platform and tools themlseves, meaning everyone in your company can ship apps and agents at the speed of their ideas, without your CISO losing sleep.

This is what building looks like when the safe path is the default:

  • Secure prototyping at scale: Anyone in the company can prototype with v0 on governed rails, so experimentation stops being a security exception and becomes the default way to explore work.

  • Domain experts building their own tools: The people closest to a problem build the thing that solves it instead of filing a ticket and waiting a quarter for someone else to.

  • An immediate graduation path to production: When a prototype proves it matters, engineering takes it into production on the same platform it was prototyped on, rather than rebuilding it from scratch or banning it outright.

FAQ

What is Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents? It is the platform for deploying, governing, and connecting the apps and agents your employees build, across the whole organization. It brings ownership, access control, identity, and security to everything your company ships, whether someone prototyped it in v0 or an engineering team built it from the ground up. The platform includes Vercel Passport, Vercel Connect, Enterprise Managed Users, and the option to run inside your own AWS account.

Do I need to use a particular framework to use Passport, Connect, and Enterprise Managed Users? No. Passport, Connect, and Enterprise Managed Users govern anything you deploy to Vercel, regardless of how it was built. They apply to your existing projects the same way they apply to new ones.

Which identity providers and external services are supported? Enterprise Managed Users works with Okta and any SAML or OIDC identity provider. Vercel Connect gives agents secure access to Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Salesforce, and Linear, plus anything else reachable over OAuth or an API.

What is available today? Vercel Passport and Vercel Connect are in Beta. Enterprise Managed Users and BYOC on AWS are in Private Beta.

title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
description:
arXiv:2610.19074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.

title: See every Google ad a competitor runs, from just their domain (cURL, Python, n8n)
description:
Google's Ads Transparency Center lists the ads that advertisers run on Google Search, YouTube, Shopping, Play and Maps, with the dates each ad was first and last shown. For media buyers, agencies and B2B sales teams, that is a goldmine: what are my competitors running right now, since when, and in which format?

Getting it into a pipeline is the annoying part. Some tools ask you to open the Transparency Center, find the advertiser by hand and paste its URL. That is fine for one brand. It is not fine for 50 competitors or a list of 1,000 prospects.

So I built a small tool that takes plain domains (nike.com, adidas.com) and returns the ads as JSON.

What it does

The Google Ads Transparency Scraper runs on Apify:

  • Domains in, ads out. No advertiser IDs, no copy-pasting Google URLs.
  • No browser, no proxies. It reads the data through an API backend, so runs take seconds.
  • Two output modes: ads returns one record per ad, for swipe files and monitoring. summary returns one compact record per domain (does it advertise, how many ads, which formats, latest ad), for lead lists, Clay tables and AI agents.
  • "Only new ads" monitoring: schedule it daily or weekly with only_new_ads: true, and each run returns only ads you have not seen before.
  • Every advertiser behind a domain: results include every advertiser whose ads lead to the domain, not only the brand itself. When I looked up adidas.com, the advertisers included "Adidas America, Inc", the media agency "MediaCom L.L.C" and an individual advertiser name I did not recognize. That is useful for brand protection too.

1. Quick start with cURL 

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/hirepulse~google-ads-transparency-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "domains": ["nike.com"], "country": "US", "max_ads_per_domain": 5 }'

2. Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("hirepulse/google-ads-transparency-scraper").call(run_input={
    "domains": ["gusto.com", "rippling.com"],
    "country": "US",
    "platform": "google_search",   # all, google_search, youtube, google_shopping, google_play, google_maps
    "format": "all",               # all, text, image, video
    "max_ads_per_domain": 40,      # up to 120
    "mode": "ads",
})

for ad in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if ad.get("ad_id"):
        print(ad["domain"], ad["advertiser_name"], ad["format"], ad["days_running"], "days", ad["transparency_url"])

3. n8n: weekly "new competitor ads" alert

title: Improving Category-Aware Active Domain Adaptation via Uncertainty-Guided Region Coverage
description:
arXiv:2610.19803v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Active domain adaptation researches focus on alleviating the annotation cost, which comprises source data and target data labelling, as well as enhancing the performance of unsupervised domain adaptation. However, optimizing the adaptation model based on the average accuracy can lead to the drop in performance of some difficult categories. To overcome this issue, a point-wise selection strategy built upon the influence function can be used to improve domain adaptation performance. In our work, we first address the sensitive and redundant aspects of point-wise selection, which can lead to overfitting of the acquisition function. We thus introduce a region-based approach that ensures the improvement of the adaptation model by maximizing a positive manifold coverage. An uncertainty score is further introduced to the selection mechanism to learn a better decision boundary for the target domain. In comprehensive experiments, our proposed method surpasses the first category-aware active domain adaptation baseline as well as existing active domain adaptation methods across multiple domain adaptation benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://github.com/nhtm2702/WHO IS NEXT.

title: Warm, Ordered, Dirty: Replay an Agent Patch's Test Suite Cold Before You Trust the Green
description:
A green suite is evidence about one process, not about the diff. Agent patches tend to pass in whatever environment the agent last left behind: warmed caches, leftover sqlite files, a module that happened to be imported in a convenient order. The cheap counter-move is to replay the same patch in a clean sandbox, with caches off and test order shuffled, K times, and to read a per-node status matrix instead of the final exit code.

This is not a correctness check. It is an honesty check on the environment. A patch that survives it has earned a weaker but real claim: the green was not produced by residue.

1. Three residue classes that manufacture warm greens

Process and cache residue. Pytest writes .pytest_cache/lastfailed, which --lf and --ff consult; CPython writes __pycache__. An agent that reruns on failure can inherit failure position from the previous attempt. Disable the cache provider and bytecode writing for the replay:

python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python -m pytest -q

Filesystem residue. Golden files, *.sqlite, uploaded fixtures, and tmp/ directories from attempt 4 satisfy assertions in attempt 5. The only reliable detector is a fresh directory per run plus a before/after file listing (Section 2, Step 4).

Import and collection residue. An untracked conftest.py, sitecustomize.py, pytest.ini, or *.pth the agent created can make an import resolve or a collection hook fire. git status --porcelain must be part of your patch freeze, or the patch you test is not the patch you merge.

2. Build a cold sandbox from the diff

Four steps, all reproducible.

Step 1 — freeze the patch as a diff, including new files. Untracked files are invisible to git diff; git add -N (intent to add) makes them appear without staging content. It is reversible with git reset.

cd "$REPO"
git add -N .
git diff HEAD > /tmp/agent.patch
sha256sum /tmp/agent.patch | cut -c1-12

Step 2 — export HEAD and apply the patch, with no untracked residue and no build artifacts.

SANDBOX=$(mktemp -d)
git archive HEAD | tar -x -C "$SANDBOX"
patch -d "$SANDBOX" -p1 --batch < /tmp/agent.patch

Step 3 — run K times with a closed environment and a shuffled order. pytest-randomly gives you a seeded shuffle via --randomly-seed; if you do not want another plugin in the loop, collect the node IDs once and shuffle them yourself into an args file.

K=${K:-5}
mkdir -p "$SANDBOX/runs"
for i in $(seq 1 "$K"); do
  HOME="$SANDBOX/home-$i" TMPDIR="$SANDBOX/tmp-$i" \
  PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
  python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q -rA \
    --randomly-seed="$i" 2>&1 | tee "$SANDBOX/runs/run-$i.log"
  echo "exit=$?" >> "$SANDBOX/runs/run-$i.log"
done

Plugin-free variant, which also proves that collection itself is order-independent:

python -m pytest --collect-only -q | grep '::' > "$SANDBOX/nodes.txt"
for i in $(seq 1 "$K"); do
  shuf -n "$(wc -l < "$SANDBOX/nodes.txt")" "$SANDBOX/nodes.txt" > "$SANDBOX/nodes-$i.txt"
  xargs -a "$SANDBOX/nodes-$i.txt" python -m pytest -q -rA \
    2>&1 | tee "$SANDBOX/runs/nodes-$i.log"
done

Step 4 — record what the run wrote. A marker file plus -newer gives you the residue list per run.

touch "$SANDBOX/.replay-start"
# ... run the suite ...
find "$SANDBOX" -newer "$SANDBOX/.replay-start" -type f \
  | sed "s|$SANDBOX/||" | grep -v '^runs/' | sort > "$SANDBOX/runs/wrote-$i.txt"

3. Read the matrix, not the exit code

-rA prints one status line per test, which is enough to build a node-by-run matrix. Roughly forty lines of Python:

import collections, glob, json, re

PAT = re.compile(r"^(PASSED|FAILED|ERROR|SKIPPED|XFAIL|XPASS)\s+(\S+)")
matrix = collections.defaultdict(dict)
counts = {}

for path in sorted(glob.glob("runs/*.log")):
    run = re.search(r"run-(\d+)\.log$", path).group(1)
    seen = 0
    for line in open(path):
        m = PAT.match(line)
        if m:
            matrix[m.group(2)][run] = m.group(1)
            seen += 1
    counts[run] = seen

print("collected per run:", json.dumps(counts, sort_keys=True))
for node, runs in sorted(matrix.items()):
    if len(set(runs.values())) > 1:
        print("UNSTABLE", node, json.dumps(runs, sort_keys=True))

Three signatures matter. A node that alternates PASSED/FAILED across seeds is order coupling. A node missing from some runs was never collected, which points at collection-level state. A node that fails in every cold run, when the agent reported green, points at cache residue rather than at your code.

4. From matrix to verdict

Cold replay outcome Reading Action
All runs green, identical collected count, no files outside TMPDIR Patch is order- and residue-independent for this suite Eligible for review, not proof of correctness
One node flips in exactly one of five runs, not reproducible under a pinned seed Flake-class Quarantine with an expiry (Section 5)
One node flips in two or more seeds, or a specific seed reproduces it Order coupling, not flake Block; require isolation through fixtures
Collected count differs between runs Collection side effects in conftest or imports Block; collection must be pure
Files written outside HOME/TMPDIR Hidden state inside the worktree Block; route writes through tmp_path

5. Keep the quarantine honest

The quarantine list is the easiest place to hide a real defect behind the word "flaky". Make it a machine-read file with an expiry and an evidence pointer, and hash the whole file into the verdict record so entries cannot be appended after the replay:

{
  "nodeid": "tests/test_cache.py::test_eviction_order",
  "class": "flake",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-14",
  "evidence": "runs/run-3.log"
}

sha256sum flakefreeze.json >> "$SANDBOX/runs/verdict.txt"

Two rules keep this from rotting. Only a flake-class exit may enter the file; an order-coupling verdict has no path into it. And an entry that reaches expires_at without a new cold replay is treated as a failing test on the next run, because the default outcome of an unreviewed freeze must be failure.

6. Where the free compute fits

The replay loop is K independent suite runs plus one log parser. Every run needs its own sandbox anyway, so the work is trivially parallel and does not want your main CI runner's disk.

That is the gap MonkeyCode's free server option fits into for this workflow: a separate host to run shuffled replays without spending K times your CI minutes, while its free model access covers the tedious part of Section 3 — drafting the status-line parser and the residue classifier. Treat any generated parser as a proposal. It reads build logs and has no way to know whether your -rA output matches the format it assumed, so hand-check one run before you trust the matrix.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The availability claims above (free model access, a free server option) are operator-supplied; I have deliberately not stated quotas, hardware, model names, or durations, because I have no verified numbers for them. Check the current terms before you build a schedule around either.

7. Limitations and who should not use this

Cost scales linearly. K cold replays of a twenty-minute suite is a hundred minutes, and the sandbox export plus patch application adds per-run overhead. Replay the full suite only when the patch touches broad surface; otherwise scope the node list to what the diff can plausibly reach.

Shuffling is a sampler, not a proof. It finds order coupling that a random permutation happens to trigger. Pairwise dependencies between two specific tests can survive every seed you try.

External state is untouched. A shared staging database, a live API, a clock, or a network-dependent fixture is not reset by a fresh sandbox. Cold replay helps only where the state lives in the worktree, the process, or the interpreter cache.

Skip this approach if your suite has legitimate serial ordering with no markers to express it, if you cannot reconstruct the patch as a diff because the agent committed straight to a branch, or if the suite is slow enough that nobody will ever run it K times. A gate that is too expensive to run is a gate that will be switched off within a month.

If you run the loop once, keep the first log where a cold run disagrees with the agent's warm run. That disagreement — not the green — is the artifact worth keeping.

title: Scaling Cheap Synthetic Pretraining Improves Indoor Radio-Map Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19015v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real measurements are too limited to train an accurate indoor pathloss predictor that works across a wide range of buildings. Large-scale synthetic pretraining offers a way forward, but real building layouts are also scarce, and accurate ray-tracing simulators are slow, expensive, and often proprietary. We address both problems by introducing a generator that automatically creates diverse indoor layouts and a fast, open-source approximate ray tracer that computes radio maps for them. Using this pipeline, we generate 128M synthetic samples, pretrain ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders, and fine-tune them on high-quality benchmark data. Despite simulator mismatch, our ResNet-101 model reduces error by 15% on average relative to the best known methods across five indoor radio-map prediction tasks and improves transfer on a small real-measurement dataset. Both architectures show predictable data-scaling trends: power laws fitted on 2M-16M samples predict the mean normalized downstream RMSE at 32M-128M with 3.33% mean absolute percentage error for ResNet-101 and 7.10% for Swin-T. These results show that pretraining on large amounts of cheap simulated data can improve indoor radio-map prediction, even when real measurements and high-quality simulations are limited.

title: Robust Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation with Insole-Based Sensor Fusion
description:
arXiv:2610.19494v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-time monocular human pose estimation is an important sensing component for human-centered intelligent systems. While recent camera-based methods have achieved impressive accuracy, fundamental challenges persist, particularly when visual observations are incomplete, such as during lower-body occlusion or short out-of-frame intervals. In these challenging but common scenarios, vision-only systems often struggle to reconstruct physically plausible lower-limb motion and reliable foot-ground contact. Due to the highly unobtrusive and wearable nature of smart insoles, this paper investigates whether simple plantar pressure and acceleration sensors can effectively resolve these visually induced limitations. To systematically investigate this, we first collect a synchronized multimodal dataset and then propose a part-decoupled temporal fusion framework. The proposed model fuses foot-sensing features into the lower-body branch to compensate for incomplete visual evidence, while a lightweight coordinator exchanges information between the upper- and lower-body temporal representations to maintain whole-body consistency. The framework is evaluated with three representative real-time visual backbones based on 2D keypoints, 3D landmarks, and SMPL-based human mesh recovery. We evaluate our framework on three representative real-time visual backbones. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that incorporating simple foot sensors consistently improves pose accuracy, motion smoothness, and gait-related measurements over vision-only baselines, with the most significant gains observed under occlusion and short visual-dropout conditions. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that unobtrusive foot sensing provides vital and complementary physical observability when camera observations are temporarily unavailable.

title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
description:
arXiv:2610.14605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

title: StateCraft: Augmenting Video World Models with Abstract-State Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.19795v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video world models aim to simulate complex environments with realistic appearance and dynamics. Maintaining consistency over long interactions requires tracking past actions and understanding how those actions affect the environment. Video world models can only generate partial observations of the entire world at a time. Remembering past observations alone may not be sufficient in every scenario, as they may no longer reflect the world after a sequence of actions. We introduce a paradigm that decouples a persistent, updatable abstract state from the visual state. The abstract state keeps track of the entities' changes as the world evolves, and is used to condition the visual state, which represents the current view. We propose StateCraft, a novel architecture that pairs a language model with a video diffusion model to evolve the dynamic world. We evaluate our approach on generative interfaces, which pose a substantial challenge because a single action may change parts of the state that are not currently visible. To support training and evaluation, we develop a data collection pipeline that produces informative, densely annotated trajectories at scale without human or agent supervision, together with a benchmark measuring generation quality, memory, and controllability. On this benchmark, our approach improves surpasses the state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate that StateCraft maintains high self-consistency and strong generation quality over long trajectories. Because the abstract state is explicit, it can be edited directly, and generation follows edits to states never observed in the data. Finally, a proof-of-concept 3D experiment, in which actions change the illumination of an unobserved room, shows that the paradigm can also be applied to spatial environments. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/StateCraft/.
