title: DeBoneDiT: Depth-Driven Conditional Bridge Diffusion Transformers for Bone Suppression in Chest X-Ray Images
description:
arXiv:2610.19466v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chest X-Ray (CXR) is a primary modality for diagnosing pulmonary diseases, yet the overlap of bony structures often obscures critical radiographic findings, increasing the risk of diagnostic uncertainty. While Dual-Energy Subtraction (DES) is the clinical benchmark for bone suppression, its widespread adoption is primarily hindered by specialized hardware requirements and increased radiation exposure. Recently, diffusion-based generative models have shown promise for this task, yet they are still constrained by reconstruction-biased latent compression, prior-induced domain gap, and a scarcity of high-quality paired datasets. To address these challenges, we propose DeBoneDiT, a depth-driven conditional bridge diffusion Transformer architecture for efficient high-resolution bone suppression. We first introduce Depth Auto-Encoder (DAE), a structure-aware vision tokenizer for latent compression. By incorporating a multi-level depth feature loss derived from the pretrained Depth Anything V2 encoder, DAE preserves both visual fidelity and structural consistency. Second, we formulate bone suppression as a source-conditioned Brownian bridge diffusion process, leveraging CXRs as both the diffusion prior and structural guidance to narrow the source-to-target domain gap and maintain anatomical plausibility. Furthermore, we have constructed and released SZCH-X-Rays, the largest publicly available high-quality paired dataset for bone suppression to date, comprising 741 pairs of CXR and DES soft tissue images. Extensive experiments and downstream evaluation demonstrate that DeBoneDiT achieves superior bone suppression performance with reduced computational overhead.

title: OPC UA in action: the SLX GridPilot industrial digital twin
description:
OPC UA becomes easier to understand when a command produces an observable response. A power request, a valve opening, a rotating machine and an alarm connect the protocol to process behavior. With SLX GridPilot, Silicon LogiX presents a desktop application for exploring that path: from the nodes of an OPC UA server to the control of two reversible hydroelectric units and their 3D representation.

The starting point is precise: OPC UA communication and the control runtime are real; the plant is simulated. The computer runs clients, three independent servers and the Eclipse 4diac FORTE runtime. Water, rotating machinery, electrical power and equipment faults belong to the numerical model. This software laboratory serves both people approaching industrial automation and engineers evaluating interfaces, information models and diagnostics without connecting physical equipment.

What is OPC UA, and why does it matter in industrial automation?

OPC Unified Architecture is a platform-independent interoperability architecture. In the client-server model, a server exposes information and services that a client can discover and use: variables, objects, methods and events. For industrial automation, its value includes communicating the meaning of data through types and relationships, beyond a list of numeric values.

A unit's speed, for example, can be presented together with its data type, engineering unit, quality and timestamp. A client can browse the model, read a measurement, call a method and receive notifications. GridPilot applies these operations to a visible scenario: two reversible units, U1 and U2, generating electricity or moving water toward the upper reservoir in pumping mode.

A digital twin demonstrator built around OPC UA

The initial OPC UA Studio workspace displays connected servers, monitored items and notifications received in the current sessions. A live operation map distinguishes the client, servers, FORTE control, simulated equipment and feedback path. These indicators help explain which part of the system is working and where the displayed data comes from.

OPC UA Studio in version 0.4.2. Counters describe actual client connections and notifications; the guided tour verifies server responses.
The three local endpoints represent plant services and the two units: opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4840, opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4841 and opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4842. An external OPC UA client can explore the same model and call its methods. The 3D scene receives state through OPC UA, just like the interface indicators. Selecting U1 or U2 highlights the corresponding unit and lets the operator locate it in the plant view.

From command to feedback: what actually happens

Requesting power does not mean that power has already been delivered. Calling SetPower(1.2) on U1's endpoint requests 1.2 MW of generation. The method's initial response confirms that the request has been queued. LastCommand then reports acceptance or rejection, while power, state and actuator positions show the observed outcome. Hydraulic availability and interlocks can limit the result even when a command is accepted.

The coordinator presents the request to FORTE control logic, which manages sequences and operating limits. The numerical model evolves from the actuator targets; the resulting state is published by the servers and returns to the client through subscriptions. The interface therefore distinguishes request received, command accepted and behavior achieved. The same principle applies to Stop(): confirming a stop requires feedback such as zero speed and closed flow-control devices.

Functional architecture of the demonstrator. OPC UA connects the supervisor to the servers; the coordinator uses local connections to control and model components. Calculated state returns to the servers and client, which also updates the 3D scene.

Exploring OPC UA nodes, types and information models

The integrated browser performs actual Browse and Read operations. Users can search for a node, inspect its type, copy its NodeId and examine quality, timestamps and engineering units. Persistent watchlists follow selected variables, while filters help locate measurements whose quality differs from Good.

A NodeId identifies a node within a namespace. GridPilot's application namespace is urn:siliconlogix:gridpilot:v1. A client must resolve its index on the server instead of assuming that a fixed number always identifies the same namespace. This is a practical detail to understand when moving from an example to integration between different applications.

NodeSet2 XML export, alongside JSON and CSV, documents browsed instances, types and method arguments. It describes the information model: it is neither an executable server backup nor a complete recording of its events.

Subscriptions, quality and timestamps: reading data in context

An OPC UA subscription lets a client receive notifications for configured monitored items. The sampling interval concerns observation of the data; the publishing interval governs notification delivery. A numeric deadband defines a change threshold. The server can revise the requested intervals, and GridPilot exposes those values together with the status of individual monitored items.

Watchlists use a dedicated subscription. Coherent plant state arrives in the Snapshot variable, so indicators and the scene do not have to reconstruct a process snapshot by combining independent reads. SourceTimestamp refers to the sample's UTC publication time; SimTime represents simulated process time. Pausing the simulation therefore does not stop the communication clock.

Quality and freshness have visible consequences: uncertain measurements are identified, and state that no longer receives updates is marked stale. Machine animations do not advance beyond the latest confirmed pose. Motion thus helps users read the available telemetry.

OPC UA faults and alarms: acknowledgement is separate from recovery

The demonstrator supports repeatable actuator, sensor, communication and electrical faults. A simulated speed-sensor error also produces an observable quality change on the OPC UA node. Injecting communication loss for a unit actually shuts down its endpoint, allowing users to examine disconnection, reconnection and the controller's response.

The servers expose standard OPC UA OffNormalAlarmType conditions with severity, message, active state and acknowledgement. An operator can acknowledge a condition and add a comment. Acknowledgement does not remove the fault's cause or automatically release the controller latch: recovery must restore the required conditions. This release uses the experimental Alarms & Conditions support in open62541 1.4.14 and makes no claim of OPC UA conformance certification.

Learning through a guided path and observable checks

The OPC UA Studio tour moves from browsing U1 to requesting power, confirming a stop and injecting a sensor fault, followed by alarm acknowledgement and recovery. Each step advances when the expected feedback is observed. Missing or stale data cannot confirm an outcome.

The plant view complements the experience with overview, cutaway and unit-detail modes. Rotation, flow-control devices, flow indicators and electrical activity make it easier to connect a variable to the relevant machine. Graphics represent received state; the numerical model and control logic determine process evolution.

The Plant view places the 3D model beside operator requests and confirmed values. U1 and U2 labels connect each unit card to its location in the plant.

The technology stack: Rust, Slint, Bevy, open62541 and FORTE

The architecture gives each technology a distinct role. Rust is used for coordination, supervision and the numerical engine. Slint provides the desktop interface; Bevy, together with wgpu, handles the 3D scene and glTF models. Interface and visualization share confirmed process state.

open62541 is the C OPC UA stack used for the servers and client adapter. Eclipse 4diac FORTE is a runtime for function-block applications based on IEC 61499. In GridPilot it executes the application block governing startup, stop, reversal and fault handling. The coordinator maintains a fixed 100 ms step and connects control to the numerical model; supervisor-to-device communication goes through OPC UA.

The hydraulic model is lumped and quasi-steady, with constant efficiencies, actuator limits and water/energy accounting. It is suitable for studying the demonstrator and its interfaces. Designing an actual hydro plant requires further modeling and validation: water hammer, cavitation, electrical-grid transients and qualified electrical protections are examples of phenomena outside this model.

Trends, replay and tests for comparing behavior

The Workbench brings together sequence diagnostics, local numeric history, multivariable charts and CSV export. Commands and alarms can be read alongside measurement trends. Recording, replay, pause and temporal seeking support session review, while test plans define scheduled actions and expected results checked against observed feedback.

For industrial software developers, these functions offer a basis for discussing concrete requirements: how to represent unreliable data, when to declare a command complete, what information to export and what conditions to verify after an interruption. Project checks concern the software and demonstrator model; they do not replace commissioning tests on a real plant.

Download GridPilot and discuss a custom OPC UA project

The SLX GridPilot 0.4.2 release provides a portable Windows x64 package. Download the Windows ZIP, extract the complete folder and launch SLX GridPilot.exe. No compiler, package installation, cloud service or field hardware is required. A Vulkan-capable graphics driver is required. The release also includes SHA-256 checksums for checking the download.

Demonstrator endpoints are limited to the local computer, with anonymous access and SecurityPolicy None. OPC UA provides security mechanisms, but configuring certificates, identities, roles and protected communication for production requires dedicated engineering and verification. The package does not include a preconfigured connection to a physical PLC.

The public repository contains operator documentation, selected screenshots, licensing information and publication checks. The Windows ZIP includes the required runtime data, dependency licenses and corresponding third-party sources. GridPilot's application implementations are proprietary and distributed in compiled form; SDK headers and application sources are excluded from the public distribution. The product license permits study and business evaluation; production integration and redistribution of modifications require written permission. Dependency licenses remain independent.

For an industrial application, a next step may be designing an OPC UA information model, integrating devices and PLCs, developing dedicated supervision, or defining interoperability and recovery tests. These are extensions to agree within a specific project, starting with the actual equipment, security requirements and acceptance criteria. To discuss a project with Silicon LogiX, contact us with the process, the data to expose and the operations the software must support.

Further reading and official documentation

These references lead directly to the respective projects and official specifications for the concepts and technologies discussed:

  • OPC UA: the OPC Foundation introduction and online OPC UA specifications.
  • Security and alarms: OPC UA Part 2: Security Model and OPC UA Part 9: Alarms & Conditions.
  • Clients and servers: open62541 1.4.14 documentation, for the version used in the demonstrator.
  • IEC 61499 control: the Eclipse 4diac FORTE runtime.
  • Language: the official Rust website.
  • Desktop interface: the Slint framework.
  • 3D visualization: the Bevy engine.

Originally published at Silicon LogiX.

title: A Reference Architecture for Integrating Agentic AI into Enterprise Software: Responsibilities, Interactions, and Variability
description:
arXiv:2610.14818v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI moves generative AI applications toward systems that coordinate reasoning, enterprise context, model inference, and external actions. Integrating these capabilities into enterprise software introduces diverse architectural concerns, from orchestration, knowledge and memory, and model access to tools and actions, security, runtime infrastructure, and evaluation. Existing research and industry architectures address many of these concerns but differ in scope, abstraction, responsibility organization, interaction representation, and assumptions about which capabilities are required. This paper presents a technology-neutral reference architecture for enterprise agentic AI integration. We synthesize architectural capabilities from research publications, industry architecture guidance, and interoperability specifications by architectural purpose, organize them into ten responsibilities, and define boundary invariants, typed cross-responsibility interactions, and variation points that distinguish responsibilities from condition-dependent capabilities and replaceable realization mechanisms. We instantiate the architecture as an ESG portfolio-analysis and pre-trade compliance agent over an existing service-oriented ESG metric computation and reporting system, and complement the case with a mapping of an independently published agentic architecture. The case realizes seven of the ten responsibilities; different questions take different interaction paths, controls activate only under their conditions, and the probed boundary invariants hold. The independent architecture maps onto the proposed responsibilities without requiring an additional one. These results provide initial evidence for the architecture's organization and applicability rather than its completeness. The deployment and recorded results are available as a replication package.

title: Actionable Meta-Requirements for AI Robustness Auditing
description:
arXiv:2610.14356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI-enabled systems must remain dependable when the conditions under which they operate change (e.g., due to input perturbations, distribution shifts, or changes in external dependencies). This makes robustness auditing of such systems important for judging whether the available evidence is sufficient to support a defined robustness conclusion. However, designing an AI robustness auditing framework is challenging. A key unresolved issue is determining the requirements such a framework should support; these requirements have not yet been consolidated. We address this gap through meta-requirements: higher-order requirements specifying what a class of auditing frameworks should support. In design science research, literature and domain experts are common sources of meta-requirements; accordingly, we derive the initial set from literature and validate and refine it with practitioners. Our systematic literature review retained 74 of 2,890 records and derived 43 meta-requirements across 16 categories. We evaluated them with 128 practitioners, obtaining 5,504 ratings and 586 substantive comments. Overall, 81.20% of ratings indicated agreement or strong agreement. In particular, 41 of the 43 literature-derived meta-requirements were classified as strongly supported. Practitioner feedback refined the requirements and identified an additional requirement concerning external components and supply chain dependencies. The final set comprises 44 meta-requirements across 16 categories, of which 43 received quantitative validation. These meta-requirements can help organizations implement AI robustness auditing frameworks, assess existing frameworks for completeness, and refine them.

title: Refactoring a Distributed Cache for Strong Reads When Eventual Consistency Fails
description:
we hit a subtle bug in our order‑service after a recent traffic surge: occasional duplicate invoices appeared in the admin UI. the root cause? a cache layer that was designed for eventual consistency but was being used for read‑after‑write scenarios.

The Problem

our stack uses a Node.js API gateway, a PostgreSQL write store, and a Redis cluster as a read‑through cache. writes go through a transaction, then an async job publishes an order.updated event to a Kafka topic. the consumer updates the Redis entry. under low load the latency between the DB commit and the cache refresh is negligible, but under load the lag grows to several seconds. the UI, which reads directly from Redis for latency reasons, sometimes shows stale data, leading to duplicate processing downstream.

Why Not Just Switch to Strong Consistency?

we could have forced every read to hit the DB, but that defeats the purpose of the cache. another option is to use Redis' wait command to block until replicas acknowledge the write, but that only helps with replication lag, not with our asynchronous event pipeline. the real challenge is to preserve the low‑latency read path while guaranteeing that any read immediately after a write sees the latest state.

A Pragmatic Refactor

instead of treating the cache as a fire‑and‑forget layer, we turned it into a write‑through store for critical entities. the API now performs the DB write and updates Redis in the same request, using a transaction‑like pattern. we still keep the async Kafka flow for eventual propagation to other services, but the cache is now authoritative for the write‑through path.

// write‑through helper – keeps DB and Redis in sync
async function updateOrder(id: string, payload: Partial<Order>) {
  // 1️⃣ start DB transaction
  await db.transaction(async trx => {
    await trx('orders').where({ id }).update(payload);
    // 2️⃣ update Redis inside the same logical unit
    const cacheKey = `order:${id}`;
    const fresh = { ...(await trx('orders').where({ id }).first()), ...payload };
    await redis.set(cacheKey, JSON.stringify(fresh));
  });
  // 3️⃣ fire async event for downstream consumers
  await kafka.produce('order.updated', { id, ...payload });
}

Trade‑offs & Edge Cases

  • Latency vs. Consistency – the write‑through path adds a few milliseconds to the request, but the UI now reads correct data.
  • Cache Invalidation – if another service updates the order directly in the DB (bypassing the API), the cache can become stale. we mitigated this by adding a TTL of 30 seconds and a background poller that reconciles mismatches.
  • Failure Scenarios – if Redis is unavailable, the transaction still commits to the DB, but we must decide whether to fail the request or proceed without caching. in our case we fail fast, returning a 503, because a stale cache is worse than a brief outage.
  • Memory Pressure – keeping a large write‑through cache can increase memory usage. we tuned Redis maxmemory-policy to volatile-lru and scoped the cache to only high‑traffic entities.

The Takeaway

by moving from an eventual‑only cache to a write‑through model we regained strong read guarantees without sacrificing overall performance. the pattern does introduce extra complexity around failure handling and cache hygiene, but those concerns are manageable with clear contracts.

how do you handle read‑after‑write consistency in your high‑traffic services, and what patterns have you found most sustainable?

title: DSABench: Benchmarking Source Discovery, Coordination, and Execution for Multi-Database Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.14700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most text-to-SQL benchmarks provide the target database. In a large data catalog, however, choosing the sources is part of the problem: an agent must find every database needed for a request, determine how their results fit together, and execute the resulting workflow. We present DSABench to evaluate these capabilities jointly. Its 815 human-reviewed tasks draw on Spider, BIRD, and LiveSQLBench; 618 require several databases to contribute, and 105 allow more than one interpretation of the required sources. Executable contracts define source participation, cross-source dependencies, and source-local execution, while RouteEnv lets agents inspect public catalog evidence without revealing the gold annotations. In our routing-only study across seven model backends, the highest RA-Set score is 60.55%, compared with a highest RA-Graph score of 34.66% when coordination requirements are included. The gap becomes more pronounced when execution is required. Across four backends, median non-privileged Route+Exec-Graph success ranges from 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification and from 11.44% to 13.25% with one clarification; the best observed clarified configuration reaches 16.99%. On ambiguous tasks, clarification improves exact branch-source recovery by 39.8-43.2 percentage points. These findings illustrate why retrieving plausible databases or producing correct local SQL is not enough: an agent must carry the right information through the entire multi-database workflow.

title: When Pairwise Preferences Cycle: A Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk for Video GRPO
description:
arXiv:2610.20089v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pairwise preference feedback has become a widely adopted supervision signal for reinforcement learning in video generation models, as pairwise comparisons provide a more reliable alternative than pointwise scalar ratings for evaluating the quality of generated videos. Specifically, we define a preference graph for each GRPO group under a pairwise evaluator, where nodes represent sampled rollouts and edges encode pairwise preferences. Auditing 6,976 on-policy comparison graphs, we find that cyclic preferences are prevalent and persist throughout training. Naive pairwise reward aggregation based on average win rates discards the underlying comparison structures and treats each rollout independently, which may introduce unreliable advantage estimates for certain rollouts and consequently affect reinforcement learning optimization. Therefore, we propose the \emph{Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk} (\ours{}), a graph-aware advantage aggregation method that strengthens the global preference signal from win rates with reliable relational evidence from cyclic preference graphs through a reliability-guided preference walk. Under matched evaluator, comparison protocol, group size, prompt schedule, and query budget, \ours{} requires no additional evaluator queries beyond the observed comparisons within each rollout group and improves over Pairwise-GRPO across controlled comparisons, transfer settings, and blind human evaluations.

title: Eloquent vs Query Builder in Laravel: When to Use Each
description:
Use Eloquent when you are working with individual records that have behavior: validation rules, casts, relationships, events, soft deletes. Use the query builder when you are working with rows as data: reports, joins, aggregates, bulk writes and large exports. That rule covers most cases, but the details are where bugs come from, because the two do not behave the same on updates, deletes and inserts. I ran both against a 50,000-row MariaDB table using the real framework code (Laravel 13.35.0) to measure the cost and to check every claim below.

They are the same engine

An Eloquent builder is a wrapper around the query builder. The same fluent methods exist on both, and the SQL is nearly identical. The only difference in this example is the soft delete condition the model adds on its own:

DB::table('posts')
    ->where('status', 'published')
    ->orderByDesc('id')->limit(5)->toSql();
// select * from `posts` where `status` = ? order by `id` desc limit 5

Post::where('status', 'published')
    ->orderByDesc('id')
    ->limit(5)
    ->toSql();
// select * from `posts` where `status` = ? and `posts`.`deleted_at` is null order by `id` desc limit 5

So the choice is not about SQL features. It is about what happens to the rows before you see them and when you write them back.

What Eloquent adds, and what it costs

The query builder returns plain stdClass objects with the values exactly as the database driver gives them. Eloquent turns every row into a model: it applies casts, attaches the original attributes for dirty tracking, fires a retrieved event and registers the model with its relations. In the test, the same row looked like this from each side:

Column DB::table() Model
meta (JSON) string: '{"tags":["a","b","c"],"score":1}' array (cast)
published_at string: '2026-10-14 13:38:00' Carbon instance (cast)
Row type stdClass Post

That convenience has a price, and it shows when you load many rows. I loaded all 50,000 rows with each approach, in a fresh PHP process each time, three runs per row, taking the median:

Approach (50,000 rows, all columns) Time Extra memory
DB::table('posts')->get() about 160 ms 59 MB
Post::get() about 980 ms 103 MB
Post::get() then reading the casts on every row about 1,900 ms 105 MB
Post::query()->toBase()->get() about 200 ms 60 MB
DB::table() with select('id', 'title') about 65 ms 28 MB
Post::select('id', 'title')->get() about 880 ms 76 MB
DB::table()->chunkById(1000) about 180 ms 2.3 MB
Post::chunkById(1000) about 1,200 ms 4.2 MB
DB::table()->cursor() about 255 ms 8.4 MB
Post::cursor() about 2,900 ms 9.4 MB

Hydrating 50,000 models took about six times longer than reading the same rows as plain objects, and used less than twice the memory. Selecting only the columns you need helps both sides, but does not remove the hydration cost. Nobody renders 50,000 models in one request, so this matters for exports, reports and background jobs, not for a paginated page of 25 rows. The numbers are from one machine with MariaDB on localhost; a network hop would add the same cost to both sides, which would shrink the percentage gap but not the absolute one.

Two practical notes from the table. First, toBase() is the bridge: it keeps your model's query scopes and gives you plain rows. Second, cursor() keeps memory flat but is the slowest option for models. The Laravel documentation also notes that PDO still buffers the raw results, so for very large result sets it recommends lazy(), and chunkById when you update the column you are filtering on.

Three places where they behave differently

This is the part that causes production bugs. I ran each operation inside a transaction and rolled it back, with listeners registered on the model:

Operation Model events Result
$post->update([...]) saving, updating, updated, saved updated_at changed
Post::where(...)->update([...]) none updated_at changed
DB::table('posts')->where(...)->update([...]) none updated_at unchanged
$post->delete() (soft deletes on) deleting, deleted Row kept, deleted_at set
Post::where(...)->delete() none Row kept, deleted_at set
DB::table('posts')->where(...)->delete() none Row permanently deleted
Post::insert([...]) none created_at is NULL
Post::create([...]) saving, saved (the create events fire as well) Timestamps filled

Read it as three rules:

  1. A mass update or delete through Eloquent fires no model events. The Laravel documentation says this directly: the models are never retrieved, so events such as updating and deleting are not dispatched. If you have an observer that clears a cache, writes an audit log or syncs a search index, a Post::where(...)->update() silently skips it. Load the models and save them, or accept that the observer will not run.
  2. The query builder ignores soft deletes. DB::table('posts')->delete() removes the row for good, while the same intent through the model only sets deleted_at. Counts differ too: on my data Post::count() returned 49,000 while DB::table('posts')->count() returned 50,000. A report built on DB::table() will include soft-deleted rows unless you filter them yourself.
  3. Bulkinsert()does not set timestamps, even on a model. Post::insert() goes straight to the query builder, so created_at and updated_at stay NULL unless you supply them. Post::upsert() is different: as documented, it sets the timestamps. In my test it updated updated_at, while DB::table('posts')->upsert() left it untouched.

Mass assignment follows the same split. A model only fills attributes you allow ($fillable in my test; the 13.x documentation shows a Fillable attribute for the same job), and extra keys are silently discarded. In my run, Post::create() with id and an unknown key ignored both, whereas DB::table()->insert() with an unknown column failed with a QueryException. The query builder does protect against SQL injection through parameter binding, but the documentation warns that PDO cannot bind column names, so never let user input pick a column or an order by field.

Which one to use

Task Use Why
Show, create or edit one record in a form or API Eloquent Casts, validation flow, mass-assignment protection, events
Anything with relationships (with(), whereHas()) Eloquent Relationships are the main reason to have models
Rules that must always run (observers, soft deletes, global scopes) Eloquent The query builder skips them
Reports, dashboards, joins across several tables, groupBy aggregates Query builder You want rows and numbers, not objects
Exporting or processing tens of thousands of rows Query builder, or toBase() with chunkById or lazy Roughly 6x faster here, with less memory
Inserting thousands of rows insert() or upsert() Next section
Changing one column on many rows (increment, status flips) One mass update query Next section

Mixing them safely

You rarely need to choose one for a whole application. These patterns use each where it fits.

Read big sets as plain rows but keep the model's scopes (soft deletes included):

Post::query()
    ->where('status', 'published')
    ->toBase()                       // stdClass rows, no model hydration
    ->orderBy('id')
    ->chunkById(1000, function ($rows) {
        foreach ($rows as $row) {
            // $row->title, $row->views ...
        }
    });

Write a report with the query builder and filter soft deletes yourself:

$top = DB::table('posts')
    ->join('users', 'users.id', '=', 'posts.user_id')
    ->whereNull('posts.deleted_at')
    ->groupBy('users.id', 'users.name')
    ->selectRaw('users.id, users.name, count(*) as posts, sum(posts.views) as views')
    ->orderByDesc('views')
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

Insert in bulk and fill the timestamps yourself:

$now = now();

foreach (array_chunk($rows, 1000) as $chunk) {
    Post::insert(array_map(fn ($r) => $r + ['created_at' => $now, 'updated_at' => $now], $chunk));
}

The speed difference is large. Inserting 5,000 rows took about 2,700 ms with Post::create() in a loop (5,000 queries), and about 120 ms with Post::insert() in chunks of 1,000. Updating the same 5,000 rows one model at a time took about 3,000 to 3,200 ms; one Post::where(...)->increment('views') query took about 15 ms. On a remote database each saved round trip is worth more, so the gap grows. The trade is the one from the table above: the fast version skips events, so only use it where nothing depends on them.

Frequently asked questions

Is Eloquent slow?

Not for normal page work. In my test, loading models with get() cost about 0.02 ms per row, including the query itself. It becomes a problem when you load tens of thousands of rows, or run thousands of single-row queries in a loop, which is more often an N+1 or batching problem than an Eloquent problem.

Can I mix Eloquent and the query builder in one project?

Yes, and most mature Laravel apps do. Keep models for your domain objects and use DB::table() or toBase() for reporting and bulk work. Just remember the three differences above.

Does the query builder protect against SQL injection?

Values are bound as PDO parameters, so you do not need to escape them. Column names and order by fields cannot be bound, so whitelist them if they come from user input.

References: Laravel: Eloquent ORM and Laravel: Query Builder.

Originally published on DEV Talk.

title: Don't judge Nano Banana 2.1 character consistency from the first picture
description:
People and series · NANO BANANA 2.1

A good first character picture is usually enough to make a good impression. The difficulty shows up in the second one. Change the background, and the eyes change. Change the clothes, and the face shape changes. Pull the camera back a little, and an accessory disappears. For a serial story, a character design, or brand content, those shifts are more trouble than one failed generation. What you need is not many similar people. It is a set of pictures in which the viewer can recognize the same subject.

Nano Banana 2.1 has improved multi-round character consistency, and it can use reference images to describe a person or an object. “Consistent” has to be read inside the actual task. Keeping hair color, clothing, and overall presence is a different demand from making the facial proportions identical from every angle. The official model card still notes limits on character consistency, so a review should not rest on the single most successful picture.

A set of pictures says more than one picture

A practical approach is to give the same subject a few small changes. Change the background first, then the light, then a camera distance that is not extreme. Look at the pictures side by side and check the outline of the face, the hair, the collar, the accessories, and the subject’s proportions. That shows which features stayed, and where the result is most likely to slip. The test does not have to be complicated, but the changes should have a clear order.

The prompt should also separate what stays fixed from what changes. For example: “Keep the person’s appearance and the dark coat, change the background to a bright studio, and do not change the pose.” If the next round only needs slightly warmer light, do not also add a new hairstyle, a new expression, and a new camera angle. A clear boundary for the model is also a comparable version for you.

Reference images can add another view, but they are worth choosing before you upload them. A clear, unobstructed photo with ordinary color is better for conveying appearance. A photo with a heavy filter or strong lens distortion may make the model treat the camera effect as part of the subject. A maximum of 14 reference images is a capability limit, not a number every character task has to reach.

A real series also involves style. The person can look similar while one picture looks like a studio shot, one like an oil painting, and one like a low-contrast film still, and the series still falls apart. Light, color, aspect ratio, and clothing should be managed the way appearance is managed. When a style change is needed, confirm that the character is still recognizable, then widen the change step by step, instead of releasing every control at once.

Do not forget the small places

Hands, earrings, and small structures on clothing are usually easier to miss than the face as a whole. A difference that disappears when the picture is small can matter in a 4K output, or when several pictures sit next to each other. Higher resolution gives more room to check. It does not replace the check. For a character you will keep using, it is especially useful to keep a confirmed set of references.

If you want to try series work in Nano Banana 2.1, start with three pictures: one base scene, one background change, and one lighting change. Do not immediately ask for a dozen complicated story frames. First confirm whether the features you care about can stay, then decide whether this workflow fits your content. Also look at the platform’s current trial terms and output sizes before you start.

A good character tool should make revisions more manageable, not ask the creator to stop looking. The value of Nano Banana 2.1 can be tested in continuous work: which changes go through cleanly, which ones need another reference, and which ones are better stopped for a manual fix. Knowing those boundaries makes it easier to produce a set that actually holds together.

Leave a little room for the next picture. Open the creation workspace

title: Big Tech Is on Track to Spend $800B on AI in 2026. Can the Economics Hold?
description:
One hot inflation report. A sell-off in AI infrastructure stocks. And a question the whole industry can no longer dodge.

For the last few years, the AI conversation has mostly been about capability.

Can a model write code? Can it answer questions? Can it generate images? Can it browse the web? Can it act like an agent?

Those are important questions. But in October 2026, another question has become impossible to ignore:

Can the AI industry turn massive spending into sustainable, measurable value?

This is no longer only a technology question. It is now a business, energy, infrastructure, policy, and investment question. And the answer will shape which companies lead the next decade.

⚡ TL;DR (save this)

  • Markets wobbled. AI and AI-infrastructure stocks fell after hotter-than-expected US inflation data.
  • The spending is enormous. The largest US hyperscalers are on track for about $800B of capex in 2026 and around $1.1T in 2027.
  • There is a gap. An Axios-reported analysis found a ~$1T gap between AI-related spending since 2024 and AI revenue so far.
  • Power is a hard limit. Data-center electricity demand grew 17% in 2025 versus about 3% for overall demand.
  • The next winners will not simply spend the most. They will deliver trustworthy execution.

📉 The Market Just Sent a Warning

This week, major AI and AI-infrastructure stocks fell after the United States released hotter-than-expected inflation data.

Why does inflation matter to AI? Because AI at scale is capital-intensive.

Building and running AI systems requires:

  • Advanced GPUs and specialized chips
  • Large data centers
  • High-speed networking
  • Massive storage systems
  • Reliable electricity
  • Cooling infrastructure
  • Skilled engineering teams
  • Continuous model training and inference capacity

Many companies fund this buildout through debt, future revenue expectations, and investor confidence.

When inflation rises, markets begin to expect higher interest rates. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive. When borrowing becomes more expensive, every large infrastructure project becomes harder to justify.

That is why AI stocks reacted sharply.

Reuters reported that shares of debt-heavy AI infrastructure companies fell as investors became more concerned about the financing of the industry's massive buildout. CoreWeave, Nebius, Oracle, and Dell were among the companies affected.

This does not mean AI is failing. It means the market is asking a fair question:

Is the spending producing enough real value to justify the cost?

💰 The Scale of AI Spending Is Enormous

To understand why this matters, look at the numbers.

Goldman Sachs has estimated that the largest US hyperscalers are on track to spend about $800 billion on capital expenditure in 2026. Consensus expectations suggest this could rise to around $1.1 trillion in 2027.

Capital expenditure, or capex, means money spent on long-term assets such as:

  • Data centers
  • Servers
  • GPUs
  • Networking equipment
  • Land and buildings
  • Power infrastructure
  • Cooling systems

This is not ordinary software spending. This is industrial-scale investment.

Alphabet, for example, reported $80.6 billion in capital expenditures during the first half of 2026 and guided to $195-205 billion for the full year.

That is an extraordinary amount of money being committed to compute, data centers, and AI infrastructure.

At the same time, an analysis reported by Axios found a gap of nearly $1 trillion between hyperscaler AI-related spending since 2024 and the AI revenue generated so far.

This does not mean AI companies have "lost" $1 trillion. It means there is a difference between:

  • Money invested in AI infrastructure
  • Money earned from AI products and services

That difference matters. Investors can support long-term investment when they believe future revenue will arrive. But if spending keeps rising faster than revenue, confidence can weaken.

🏗️ AI Is Becoming an Infrastructure Industry

AI used to feel like a software industry. Now, it increasingly looks like an infrastructure industry.

Why? Because modern AI depends on physical resources: electricity, land, water, fiber networks, chips, cooling systems, data centers, and power grids.

A powerful model is not just an algorithm. It is an algorithm running on expensive hardware, inside a data center, connected to a power grid, supported by supply chains, and maintained by engineers.

This changes the conversation. The question is no longer only:

"How smart can the model become?"

It is also:

  • "Can we power it?"
  • "Can we cool it?"
  • "Can we afford it?"
  • "Can we deploy it responsibly?"
  • "Can it create value for customers?"

AI is becoming similar to railways, electricity grids, telecom networks, and cloud computing. Infrastructure industries create enormous value, but they also require enormous capital, planning, and discipline.

🔌 Electricity Is Becoming a Core AI Constraint

One of the most important facts in this debate is energy.

According to IEA data cited in recent reporting, data-center electricity demand grew by 17% in 2025, while overall electricity demand grew by around 3%.

That is a major difference.

AI data centers need continuous power. They cannot simply switch off during peak hours. Training large models and serving millions of users requires stable, high-capacity electricity around the clock.

This creates several challenges:

1. Power availability

Many regions already face grid constraints. Adding a large data center is not as simple as buying land and installing servers. It requires access to sufficient electricity capacity.

2. Grid upgrades

New data centers may require new transmission lines, substations, and grid upgrades. These projects can take years to approve and build.

3. Energy costs

If data centers increase demand faster than supply, electricity prices can rise for nearby communities and businesses.

4. Environmental impact

AI infrastructure affects carbon emissions, water usage, land use, and local communities.

5. Public policy

Governments are beginning to ask who should pay for the infrastructure required to support AI growth.

In the United States, the House passed a bipartisan bill designed to encourage state utility regulators to protect consumers from rising energy costs linked to large data centers. The bill still needs further approval to become law, but the direction is clear.

In Europe, regulators are preparing stricter disclosure requirements for data centers, including water use, clean-power adoption, and energy efficiency.

The message is simple:

AI growth must be matched by responsible energy planning.

🎯 The Shift From Demos to Business Outcomes

The first phase of enterprise AI was about experimentation.

Companies asked:

  • Can we build a chatbot?
  • Can we connect an LLM to our documents?
  • Can we create a proof of concept?
  • Can we show leadership an AI demo?

That phase was necessary. But demos do not pay for data centers. Business outcomes do.

The next phase is about production AI:

  • AI that reduces manual work
  • AI that improves decision-making
  • AI that accelerates customer response
  • AI that automates repeatable workflows
  • AI that improves quality and compliance
  • AI that creates measurable ROI

This is where agentic AI becomes important.

An AI agent is not just a chatbot. It is a system that can understand a goal, plan steps, use tools, interact with systems, and complete a task.

For example, instead of asking:

"What is our leave policy?"

An employee may ask:

"Apply for two days of leave and confirm my balance has updated."

An agent may need to:

  1. Understand the request
  2. Find the correct application screen
  3. Fill in the required details
  4. Submit the request
  5. Verify the outcome
  6. Report success or failure with evidence

This is much more valuable than a simple question-and-answer system. But it is also more demanding. An agent that takes action must be accurate, safe, observable, and accountable.

🛡️ Why Agentic AI Needs Governance

As AI agents become more autonomous, governance becomes essential.

A chatbot that gives a wrong answer is frustrating. An AI agent that submits the wrong form, sends the wrong email, updates the wrong record, or triggers the wrong workflow can create real business damage.

That is why enterprises need:

Human approval for high-risk actions

Not every action should be automatic. Deleting records, making payments, changing production configurations, or sending external communications may require human confirmation.

Least-privilege access

An agent should only have the permissions required for its task. It should not automatically receive broad access to every system.

Audit trails

Every important action should be logged: what the agent saw, what it decided, what it did, and what evidence supports the result.

Clear success and failure states

A good AI system should say:

  • "Task completed successfully."
  • "Task failed because of a product defect."
  • "Task could not be completed because a required screen or precondition was unavailable."

It should not pretend everything is fine when it could not verify the outcome.

Monitoring and observability

Teams need to monitor agent behavior in real time, detect unusual actions, and stop an agent if needed.

This is especially important as agents move from answering questions to operating inside business systems.

🏆 The Real Competitive Advantage: Trustworthy Execution

Many people think AI competition is only about who has the biggest model. That is no longer the full picture.

The next competitive advantage will come from trustworthy execution.

A company may have access to a powerful model, but if it cannot connect that model safely to its data, workflows, permissions, and business processes, the value remains limited.

The companies that win will be those that can deliver:

  • Reliable AI systems. The system should work consistently, not only in a demo.
  • Measurable ROI. Every AI initiative should answer: What time, cost, risk, or quality improvement did we create?
  • Safe automation. AI should automate the right tasks, with the right controls, in the right environments.
  • Evidence-based results. Users should be able to see why the AI reached a conclusion or completed an action.
  • Responsible infrastructure. AI growth should consider power, water, emissions, and community impact.
  • Human-centered design. AI should assist people, not confuse them or remove accountability.

🏢 What This Means for Businesses

For business leaders, the message is clear: do not evaluate AI only by model benchmarks. Evaluate it by business impact.

Ask questions like:

  • Which workflow are we improving?
  • How much time or cost are we saving?
  • How are we measuring quality?
  • What happens when the AI is wrong?
  • Who approves high-risk actions?
  • How do we audit decisions?
  • What data does the AI access?
  • How do we protect customer information?
  • What is the total cost of ownership?
  • How does this affect our energy and infrastructure needs?

AI strategy should not be "adopt AI everywhere." AI strategy should be:

Adopt AI where it creates clear, measurable, responsible value.

👩‍💻 What This Means for Engineers

For AI engineers, developers, and architects, the skills that matter are changing.

It is no longer enough to know how to call an LLM API.

The most valuable engineers will understand:

  • System design
  • Retrieval and context management
  • Tool use and function calling
  • Agent orchestration
  • Evaluation and testing
  • Observability
  • Security and permissions
  • Cost optimization
  • Human-in-the-loop workflows
  • Production deployment

The best AI systems will not be built by prompt engineering alone. They will be built by combining models, data, tools, policies, tests, monitoring, user experience, and business understanding.

That is where real engineering value lies.

🚀 What This Means for Startups

For startups, this is actually good news.

When AI becomes expensive, companies cannot afford vague experiments. They need focused solutions that solve specific problems.

The best startup opportunities will be in areas such as:

  • AI quality assurance and testing
  • Agent governance and auditing
  • AI cost optimization
  • Enterprise workflow automation
  • Domain-specific AI assistants
  • Data readiness and governance
  • AI security
  • Model evaluation
  • Human-in-the-loop review tools
  • Industry-specific automation

A startup does not need to build a foundation model to create value. It can build the layer that makes AI usable, safe, measurable, and trustworthy inside real organizations.

🔭 The Bigger Picture

AI is not disappearing. It is maturing.

The first phase was about possibility. The next phase is about responsibility.

The first phase asked: "What can AI do?"

The next phase asks: "What should AI do, at what cost, with what safeguards, and for whose benefit?"

That is a healthier phase. Because real transformation does not come from hype. It comes from systems that work reliably in the real world.

AI will create enormous value, but only when companies treat it as more than a trend. They must treat it as:

  • A product
  • A system
  • An infrastructure investment
  • A business process
  • A governance responsibility
  • A long-term commitment

The companies that understand this will build durable advantage. The companies that only chase demos may find that the cost of AI is much easier to measure than its value.

💡 Final Thought

The AI race is no longer only about who can build the most powerful model. It is about who can build the most useful, efficient, safe, and economically sustainable AI systems.

The next winners will not simply spend the most.

They will convert compute into clarity.

They will convert automation into accountability.

They will convert data into decisions.

And they will convert AI into measurable business value.

The future of AI belongs to those who can make it work in the real world.

💬 Your turn

What will matter more in the next phase of AI: model capability or practical, trustworthy execution?

Tell me in the comments. If this helped you think about AI beyond the hype, a reaction and a share help other engineers and leaders find it. Follow for more on AI systems, agents and the economics behind them.

  • Reuters - AI infrastructure firms slumped as rate-hike expectations rose: https://www.reuters.com/business/ai-infrastructure-firms-slump-us-rate-hike-bets-rise-2026-10-14/

title: My custom AI bot keeps giving bad advice because it cannot retain feedback from past calls
description:
Your support bot tells a customer that a sync error goes away if they clear the app cache. It does not. The customer writes back, a person on the team finds the real fix, re-authorising the integration, and the ticket closes. Next Tuesday another customer reports the same error, and the bot recommends clearing the cache again, with the same confidence.

The short answer: each call ends before anyone knows whether its advice worked, so the feedback arrives with nothing to attach to. Keep a record of every call with the ids of the stored notes the answer was built on. When the verdict comes in, from the user, the ticket or the person who took over, send it back as a rating on those notes, and have the bot recall from a memory that reads ratings when it ranks. Next time, the advice that failed and the advice that worked are no longer equals. Nothing is erased: the failed advice stays on record, with its outcome attached.

Why the bot does not learn from its own calls

A typical custom bot is a model call wrapped in retrieval: a system prompt, a search over help articles or stored notes, and the question. The verdict on last week's answer is in none of those. It is in the customer's reply and the helpdesk.

Teams usually try three fixes, in this order.

Edit the system prompt. Add "do not suggest clearing the cache for sync errors". A prompt is the right home for policy, but it scales like any document edited by hand: every bad call adds a line, nobody prunes them, and important rules compete with stale ones for the model's attention.

Store answers and corrections in a memory. The correction now survives the call, but so does the cache advice, and similarity search ranks by closeness to the question. Both notes match, both come back, and the model picks one in context. A wrong note is as similar to the question after ten failures as after none.

Attach the outcome to the note. When a call's result is known, record it on the notes that shaped the answer. The failed note now carries its failure and the working one its success, and a recall that weighs outcomes can tell them apart. Only this fix has a path from what happened back to what gets recalled next.

What to keep from each call

The answer is written during the call. The verdict arrives after it, sometimes days later, in another process. So the call must leave something for the verdict to find:

Call record: what a bot keeps from each call so that a verdict arriving later can find what to judge: the question, the answer, and the ids of the stored notes the answer was built on, under a key the verdict will carry.

The ids are per note, not per conversation. One piece of advice failed, not the exchange. If the model can say which recalled notes it relied on, keep those; otherwise keep every note that was in the prompt and accept that they move together.

The key is one the verdict will carry: a ticket id, a thread id, the session id your feedback button already sends. When one key covers several answers, the code below keeps the latest.

Keep call records in your own database, apart from the notes the bot recalls. Written into the same memory, every logged answer becomes one more candidate in the next recall, the bad ones included.

Where the verdict comes from

Explicit ratings are rare. Other outcomes are often already recorded somewhere, and wiring those places in works better than waiting for a thumbs-down.

signal when it arrives what it says about the advice what to send
thumbs up or down on the answer seconds later, if at all how the answer looked, often before it was tried positive or negative
the user says it did not work the next message, or the next day it was tried and it failed negative
a person takes over and solves it another way when the handover closes it failed, and here is what worked negative, plus the fix as a new note
the same user returns with the same problem hours or days later the first answer did not hold negative, smaller
the ticket closes and stays closed after a quiet period you choose it probably worked positive, smaller
nothing happens never nothing nothing

Two rows need care. A handover for a reason the bot was never meant to handle, a refund or an angry customer, says nothing about the advice. And silence, the commonest row, is not a verdict.

The third row does the most work. A rating can lower the advice that failed, but only a note can supply the advice that worked, so the person's fix goes into the memory the bot recalls from.

What a rating changes, and what it does not

A rating cannot change the answer already given. It changes the order of what the next recall brings back.

Keep the failed note rather than deleting it. Clearing the cache is right for a different error, and a deleted note cannot answer "why did the bot tell customers to clear the cache in October?".

Ratings tune ranking, not truth. If a help article is wrong, fix the article. The loop needs no particular product: a list of failed advice the bot checks approximates it, a store you run can carry an outcome field, a managed memory layer keeps the bookkeeping. What matters is the path from outcome back to recall.

A minimal version in code

This uses mnemoverse 0.4.0, the Python SDK of Mnemoverse (the author's company), set up as on the Python SDK page. The model call is a placeholder, and call records live in SQLite.

import json
import sqlite3

from mnemoverse import MnemoClient

memory = MnemoClient()  # reads MNEMOVERSE_API_KEY
DOMAIN = "bot:support"
db = sqlite3.connect("calls.db")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS calls "
           "(call_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, question TEXT, answer TEXT, used TEXT, concepts TEXT)")


def answer(call_id: str, question: str) -> str:
    recalled = memory.read(question, domain=DOMAIN, top_k=5)
    reply, relied_on = bot.reply(question, recalled.items)  # your model call
    used = [str(item.atom_id) for item in relied_on]
    db.execute("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO calls VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",  # latest answer per key
               (call_id, question, reply, json.dumps(used), json.dumps(recalled.query_concepts)))
    db.commit()
    return reply


def on_verdict(call_id: str, outcome: float, fix: str | None = None) -> None:
    row = db.execute("SELECT question, used, concepts FROM calls WHERE call_id = ?",
                     (call_id,)).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        return  # no call record: the verdict has nowhere to land
    question, used, concepts = row[0], json.loads(row[1]), json.loads(row[2])
    if used:
        result = memory.feedback(atom_ids=used, outcome=outcome,  # -1.0 to +1.0
                                 query_concepts=concepts, domain=DOMAIN)
        print("updated:", result.updated_count)
    if fix:  # what actually worked, from the person who solved it
        note = memory.write(f"Problem: {question}\nWhat worked: {fix}", domain=DOMAIN)
        if not note.stored:
            print("Not stored:", note.reason)


on_verdict("ticket-1042", -1.0, fix="Re-authorise the integration under Settings, Connections.")
on_verdict("ticket-1043", 1.0)  # the customer confirmed it worked

feedback gets the same domain as the read; the SDK page notes that without it the SDK sends "general". A write that is too similar to the nearest memory in the same domain is not stored, so the code checks stored.

The API docs state the effect in one line: "Ratings re-rank what comes back next." The overview says what stays: "feedback changes the order of the next read, not the stored text". A bot on an MCP client rates through the memory_feedback tool instead.

Check it with a control

  1. Seed notes about two different problems, answer one question about each through answer(), and check that the two call records share no id. Print the valence of the notes each call relied on, "Outcome polarity [-1, +1]" in the API reference, and stop the process.
  2. In a new process, send a negative verdict for the first call only. updated_count, "Number of atoms updated" in the reference, should equal the number of ids recorded for that call. If it is zero, check the ids and the domain first.
  3. Read both questions again and print valence for the same notes. What to look for is the first call's notes moving toward -1 since step 1.
  4. Control: the second call got no verdict, so its notes are the comparison for step 3. If they moved and the first call's did not, look at the key the verdict was filed under. If both moved alike, step 3 does not show the verdict's effect.

The library page follows the same loop for coding agents, where the verdict is a build or a test run, with the limits of outcome memory in more detail. Where does the verdict on your bot's answers end up today?

title: Secure Marketplace credentials with Production-only access
description:
You can now secure native integration resources by restricting where they can be used. Setting a resource to Production only removes non-production access and protects credentials as sensitive environment variables. This makes it so secret values or no longer readable from the dashboard or CLI

From the integration resource Settings, select Allowed Environments → Production only and save. We recommend that you rotate the secrets of the integration resource after saving.

Once applied:

  • Development and Preview connections are removed

  • New non-production connections are blocked

  • Connections without a Production target are disconnected

  • Credentials are protected and no longer readable

Reverting this setting requires Owner permissions for your Vercel team. Owners can re-enable Development and Preview environment from Settings and reconnect projects if needed. You may be prompted to reauthenticate with an MFA challenge depending on your settings. Learn more in the Vercel documentation.

title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
description:
arXiv:2610.19890v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test-Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length-conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine-tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length-based and confidence-based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model-agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.

title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function
description:
arXiv:2610.14186v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? In this work, we apply counterfactual interventions which hold everything about a state fixed, besides a targeted change, to explore if the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization agent forms a world model of the Crafter environment. Despite only being trained to optimize reward, we discover that the value function learns concepts such as the rules governing when a diamond is collectible, water and food having an impact on health, heuristics regarding inventory, and more. Finally, we discuss the safety implications of our visualizations and some shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that will prevent us from building truly advanced machine intelligence.

title: MoMaTune: Model, Match, Then Tune Language Models for Numerical Records
description:
arXiv:2610.15235v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in language understanding and generation, decoder language models continue to exhibit striking failures on numerical data. Numerical examples are typically serialized as text by concatenating feature names with their values (e.g., fat:3.4), while conventional task adaptation applies loss only to the downstream prediction target. This leaves two structures weakly supervised: within-value sensitivity, where digit position determines numerical magnitude, because token cross-entropy contains no explicit numerical metric; and across-field structure, where measurements in the same record are statistically dependent, because target-only tuning provides no direct loss on the measurements or their dependencies. We introduce MoMaTune (Model, Match, then Tune), a two-stage post-training strategy organized around these supervision gaps. Stage 1 applies Model, ordinary next-token prediction densely over label-free serialized records, and optionally adds Match, a same-record consistency objective that aligns representations of different partial views of the same example. Stage 2 applies Tune, supervised fine-tuning for downstream target prediction. We evaluate MoMaTune on 169,285 records from eight public datasets, with 339 of 340 input fields numerical. At 1.5B parameters, Model raises the eight-dataset masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401, while the three-dataset correct-context gain rises from 0.058 to 0.167. On diagnostics, Model also increases sensitivity to numerically consequential digit changes, while Match improves robustness to informative partial views. Adding Tune yields higher target-supervised embedding aggregates for each tested Stage-1 parent, and the two-stage recipes obtain higher aggregate scores than Tune alone. The same pattern is observed at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters when model embeddings are used for downstream prediction.
