title: React Memoization Techniques: Master useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo
description:
React applications become more complex as components grow, state changes, and data flows through the component tree. Sometimes, a small state update causes expensive calculations or unnecessary child component renders, making the interface feel slower than it should.

React provides several memoization techniques to help developers avoid unnecessary work. The most commonly used tools are React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback, each designed to solve a different performance problem.

However, memoization is not a magic performance switch. Understanding when to use it, how dependency arrays work, and when memoization adds unnecessary complexity is essential for building fast and maintainable React applications.

Understanding React Memoization Techniques

Memoization is an optimization technique that stores the result of a previous computation so it can be reused when the relevant inputs have not changed. In React, memoization can reduce repeated calculations, prevent unnecessary component renders, and preserve function references between renders. Three important techniques are React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback.

React.memo is a higher-order component that can skip rendering a component when its props are unchanged according to React's default shallow comparison. It is particularly useful for expensive child components that receive the same props across frequent parent renders. However, a memoized component can still render when its own state or consumed context changes, and React does not guarantee that memoization will always prevent a render.

The useMemo hook caches a calculated value between renders while its dependencies remain unchanged. It works well for expensive filtering, sorting, transformations, and derived data calculations. The useCallback hook serves a related purpose by caching a function definition between renders, which can help when passing callbacks to memoized children or when a stable function reference is required by another hook.

Consider a dashboard containing a searchable list of products. Typing in a search field may trigger repeated renders, and filtering thousands of products can become expensive. You can use useMemo to recalculate filtered products only when the products or search query change, useCallback to preserve event-handler references, and React.memo to skip unnecessary renders of individual product rows. The following runnable example demonstrates these concepts using plain JavaScript to simulate their behavior; the actual React APIs should be used in React components.

const products = Array.from({ length: 1000 }, (_, index) => ({
  id: index + 1,
  name: `Product ${index + 1}`,
  price: (index + 1) * 10,
  category: index % 2 === 0 ? "Electronics" : "Accessories"
}));

// Track how often the expensive filtering operation executes.
let filterCalculationCount = 0;

function filterProducts(items, query, maxPrice) {
  filterCalculationCount++;
  console.log(`Step 1: Filtering products (calculation ${filterCalculationCount})`);

  // Simulate a costly operation using realistic product filtering.
  return items.filter((product) => {
    const matchesName = product.name
      .toLowerCase()
      .includes(query.toLowerCase());
    const matchesPrice = product.price <= maxPrice;
    return matchesName && matchesPrice;
  });
}

// A small memoization helper for demonstrating cached values.
// This is an educational simulation, not React's useMemo implementation.
function createMemoizedFilter() {
  let previousItems;
  let previousQuery;
  let previousMaxPrice;
  let previousResult;

  return function memoizedFilter(items, query, maxPrice) {
    const dependenciesChanged =
      previousItems !== items ||
      previousQuery !== query ||
      previousMaxPrice !== maxPrice;

    if (dependenciesChanged) {
      console.log("Step 2: Dependencies changed; recomputing results.");
      previousResult = filterProducts(items, query, maxPrice);
      previousItems = items;
      previousQuery = query;
      previousMaxPrice = maxPrice;
    } else {
      console.log("Step 2: Dependencies unchanged; reusing cached results.");
    }

    return previousResult;
  };
}

// Create one memoized function and reuse it across simulated renders.
const getFilteredProducts = createMemoizedFilter();

function renderDashboard(query, maxPrice, theme) {
  console.log("\n--- Rendering dashboard ---");
  console.log(`Search: "${query}" | Maximum price: ${maxPrice}`);
  console.log(`Theme: ${theme}`);

  // The result is reused when its inputs remain unchanged.
  const filteredProducts = getFilteredProducts(
    products,
    query,
    maxPrice
  );

  console.log(`Step 3: Found ${filteredProducts.length} matching products.`);

  // A theme change does not invalidate the filtering cache.
  console.log(`Step 4: Dashboard displayed using the ${theme} theme.`);
  return filteredProducts;
}

console.log("Starting React memoization demonstration...");

// First render: no cached result exists, so filtering runs.
renderDashboard("product", 500, "light");

// Second render: only the theme changes, so filtering is skipped.
renderDashboard("product", 500, "dark");

// Third render: the query changes, so filtering runs again.
renderDashboard("electronics", 500, "dark");

// Fourth render: the price limit changes, so filtering runs again.
renderDashboard("electronics", 300, "dark");

console.log("\n--- Performance summary ---");
console.log(`Total filtering calculations: ${filterCalculationCount}`);
console.log("Unchanged dependencies allowed cached results to be reused.");

// In a real React component, useMemo would cache the filtered array.
// const filteredProducts = useMemo(
//   () => filterProducts(products, query, maxPrice),
//   [products, query, maxPrice]
// );

// useCallback would preserve a function reference between renders.
// const handleSelect = useCallback((id) => {
//   setSelectedProductId(id);
// }, []);

// React.memo could skip rendering ProductRow when its props are unchanged.
// const ProductRow = memo(function ProductRow({ product, onSelect }) {
//   return <button onClick={() => onSelect(product.id)}>{product.name}</button>;
// });

Conclusion

React memoization is most effective when you understand what work is expensive and which inputs actually affect the result. Use useMemo for costly calculations, useCallback for function-reference stability when it matters, and React.memo for components that can benefit from skipping renders when their props remain unchanged.

Avoid adding memoization to every component or value by default. Each optimization introduces dependencies and additional complexity, while simple calculations and inexpensive components often perform perfectly well without it. Incorrect dependency arrays can also produce stale values or unexpected behavior.

Start by measuring performance with the React Developer Tools Profiler, identify the components or calculations responsible for slow interactions, and apply the smallest useful optimization. With careful profiling and appropriate memoization, you can build React applications that remain responsive without sacrificing readability or maintainability.

title: Two new x402 APIs for AI agents: x402 payment receipt parser + on-chain verifier + OWASP API Top 10 (2023) one-call audit (2026-10-15, cycle 151)
description:
We just shipped 2 new paid x402 endpoints on our URL metadata API — both $0.0005/call, USDC on Base, x402 settlement via pay.openfacilitator.io.

Endpoints:

  1. GET /api/x402-receipt-parse?receipt_b64=<BASE64> OR ?tx_hash=0x... OR POST JSON — x402 payment receipt parser + on-chain tx verifier
  2. GET /api/owasp-api-top10-audit?url=<TARGET> — OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) one-call composite audit

Why these matter for AI agents

1. /api/x402-receipt-parse is the post-settlement companion to /api/x402-payment-trace (c142, pre-send decoder). When an x402 server returns an X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE base64, the AI agent needs to verify on-chain that the payment actually went to the right address, for the right amount, with enough confirmations. The endpoint accepts either the base64 receipt OR a raw tx hash (0x + 64 hex) and fetches it via the Base public RPC (base.gateway.tenderly.co with 1rpc.io/base + base.drpc.org fallbacks), then decodes the USDC Transfer event from the receipt logs (USDC on Base = 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913).

The function-selector decode distinguishes transfer vs transferWithAuthorization (EIP-3009) vs approve — so the agent knows whether the payment was a settled transfer (good) or just an approval (not a payment). It also computes confirmations = latest_block - block_number and warns if <12.

Returns receipt_summary (tx_hash + block_number + from + to + value_atomic + value_usdc + asset + status_is_success + confirmations + function_selector + function_name) + verification (to_matches_our_wallet [0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c] + value_matches_amount + transfers_to_our_wallet_count + total_received_usdc) + findings + x402_receipt_score 0-100 A-F.

2. /api/owasp-api-top10-audit is the one-call composite that answers the single most-asked question by an AI agent deciding whether to use a paid API: "is this API safe to call?". Fetches the target + probes 24 conventional API paths in parallel via ThreadPoolExecutor, then runs all 10 OWASP 2023 category checks:

  • API1 BOLA: compare /api/users/1 vs /api/users/2 response equality (identical = no per-object authz)
  • API2 Broken Auth: no-auth + no-bearer on /api/me + /api/users/1
  • API3 BOPLA: PII keywords in unauth response (password/ssn/credit_card/secret/token/api_key) + over-exposure >=15 top-level fields
  • API4 Unrestricted Consumption: no RateLimit-* headers + huge response >5MB
  • API5 BFLA: /admin returns 200 + dangerous methods PUT/DELETE/PATCH open on /api/users/1
  • API6 Sensitive Business Flow: /api/checkout /api/payment/api/cart open without CAPTCHA
  • API7 SSRF: live test /api/fetch/api/proxy/api/avatar with internal URL http://127.0.0.1/ + http://169.254.169.254/ (AWS metadata) + http://localhost:8080/
  • API8 Security Misconfiguration: X-Debug + X-Powered-By + X-AspNet-Version disclosure + ACAO=* wildcard + stack trace in 404 body
  • API9 Improper Inventory: multiple /api/v1+/v2`+ /openapi.json publicly exposed + staging subdomain returns 200
  • API10 Unsafe Consumption: 3p scripts from risky TLDs .tk/.ml/.ga + http:// subresources on https:// page

Returns per_category[10] {id, name, status pass/warn/fail, score, findings[]} + summary {fail_count, warn_count, pass_count} + composite api_top10_score 0-100 A-F + verdict (production_hardened / standard / weak / vulnerable).

The full catalog is now at 217 paid x402 routes

The service runs at https://mins-alternatively-meanwhile-lauderdale.trycloudflare.com and accepts USDC on Base via the standard x402 flow (payTo: 0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c, asset: 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913, network: eip155:8453). Discovery at /.well-known/x402 (217 endpoints), GET /openapi.json (213 paths), GET /llms.txt (116KB), GET / (landing HTML 119KB).

The first 2 endpoints are free (just GET /api?url=... returns JSON metadata). Everything else is $0.0005–$0.005 per call.

Test self-settle still works: a buying agent signs a real EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization envelope, the Flask server POSTs to pay.openfacilitator.io/verify + /settle, and the wallet 0xCa0a6c... receives real USDC on Base.

Categories: 24 API path probes, 10 OWASP checks, 2 base JSON-RPC endpoints (tenderly + 1rpc + drpc fallback chain).

Designed for AI agents that need to make trust decisions before paying for a tool.

title: Glance Forcing: Making Bidirectional Diffusion Autoregressive at a Glance
description:
arXiv:2610.20220v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive generation underlies real-time, causal video synthesis and is the backbone of video world models. Today's dominant approach distills a bidirectional diffusion model into a causal few-step student, but existing pipelines make this conversion prohibitively expensive, requiring offline Probability Flow ODE} (PF-ODE) trajectories that cost tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of storage. We show it can be made dramatically more efficient. Pushing this efficiency to its extreme, we reduce trajectory supervision to a single sample, the strictest setting possible, and find that it causes severe quality collapse. We trace this to the teacher's trajectory geometry: the high-noise regime, governing semantic layout and motion, and the low-noise regime, governing fine texture exhibit fundamentally different curvature and optimization behavior, so a single monolithic student cannot jointly fit both, causing severe representation interference. Motivated by this, we propose Glance Forcing, a lightweight distillation framework that decouples the denoising trajectory into two complementary slow and fast experts, each guided by a tailored, stage-specific objective, while keeping the pretrained teacher entirely frozen. This decoupling further reveals a general mechanism underlying few-step distillation: PF-ODE distillation mainly straightens the few-step trajectory geometry, while the subsequent distribution-matching stage independently governs distributional quality. Using only one PF-ODE trajectory, Glance Forcing already surpasses the fully-trained state-of-the-art baseline, raising the VBench Total score from 84.04 to 84.22 while cutting trajectory-collection cost from thousands of GPU-hours to about one A100-GPU-hour, with markedly larger gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, and instruction-following, and consistent preference from human raters over strong baselines.

title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
description:
arXiv:2610.19801v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn.
  We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job.
  The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.

title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19327v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.

title: Building Scalable APIs with Node.js: A Developer's Guide
description:
Introduction: The Rise of Node.js for Backend Development

Node.js has become a powerhouse in the backend development landscape, lauded for its non-blocking, event-driven architecture that excels at building fast and scalable network applications. Its JavaScript-first approach allows developers to use a single language across the full stack, streamlining development workflows and fostering collaboration. Whether you're crafting a simple REST API or a complex microservices architecture, Node.js offers a robust and efficient platform.

Core Concepts for Scalable Node.js APIs

Understanding Asynchronous Operations

At the heart of Node.js's performance lies its event loop and asynchronous I/O model. Unlike traditional threaded models, Node.js handles multiple requests concurrently without blocking the main thread. This is achieved through callbacks, Promises, and the increasingly popular async/await syntax. Mastering these asynchronous patterns is crucial for building APIs that can handle high traffic volumes efficiently.

Leveraging Express.js for Robust Routing

Express.js is the de facto standard framework for building web applications and APIs in Node.js. Its minimalist and unopinionated nature provides a flexible foundation for routing, middleware, and request handling. Setting up a basic Express server involves defining routes for different HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and handling incoming requests and outgoing responses. Middleware functions allow you to execute code at various stages of the request-response cycle, enabling tasks like authentication, logging, and data validation.

Database Integration and ORMs

Scalable APIs often require efficient data persistence. Node.js has excellent support for various databases, including relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL) and NoSQL (MongoDB) options. For relational databases, Object-Relational Mappers (ORMs) like Sequelize or TypeORM can significantly simplify database interactions by mapping database tables to JavaScript objects. For NoSQL databases like MongoDB, libraries like Mongoose provide a schema-based solution to model your application data and offer powerful querying capabilities. Choosing the right database and integration strategy is key to performance. When considering various service providers, it's useful to look at established players in different sectors, for example, understanding the market dynamics by exploring Top Real Estate Companies in Delhi NCR can offer insights into how different entities manage their operations and customer reach, which can indirectly inform strategies for API scaling and service delivery.

Performance Optimization Techniques

To ensure your Node.js API scales effectively, several optimization techniques should be employed:

  • Clustering: Node.js's cluster module allows you to create child processes that share the same server port, effectively utilizing multi-core processors.
  • Caching: Implementing caching strategies (e.g., using Redis or Memcached) for frequently accessed data can drastically reduce database load and improve response times.
  • Load Balancing: Distributing incoming traffic across multiple Node.js instances using a load balancer (like Nginx or HAProxy) is essential for handling peak loads.
  • Code Profiling: Regularly profiling your code to identify bottlenecks and areas for improvement is a proactive approach to maintaining performance.

Conclusion: Building for the Future

Node.js provides a powerful and flexible environment for building scalable backend APIs. By understanding its asynchronous nature, leveraging frameworks like Express.js, integrating databases effectively, and employing performance optimization techniques, developers can create applications that are not only performant but also maintainable and ready to handle future growth. Continuous learning and adaptation to new best practices within the Node.js ecosystem will ensure your APIs remain robust and competitive.

title: MCPDisCo: Seesaw-Mitigated Tuning for MCP-Native Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.14956v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Model Context Protocol provides a shared interaction substrate for the agentic web, allowing heterogeneous services to expose capabilities through a standardized interface. Learning to use this ecosystem entails a hierarchy of capabilities: tool-format skills, server-level transfer, and cross-server composition. We present MCPDisCo, an ecosystem-scale reinforcement learning framework for MCP-native agents. Using a Thought-Markov Decision Process (Thought-MDP), the framework explicitly represents internal reasoning alongside routing, execution, and termination and trains on real-server, long-horizon interactions spanning 70 MCP servers and 527 tools across six domains. We study the reasoning--tool seesaw, a joint-learning failure mode in which improvement in one objective can accompany deterioration in the other. To mitigate potential interference, MCPDisCo combines token-masked reward attribution with bidirectional gradient surgery: the former separates direct supervision for reasoning and action spans, while the latter removes conflicting components from both objective gradients in shared parameters. MCPDisCo achieves higher success with fewer chain-of-thought tokens. On the out-of-distribution MCP-Atlas and the GAIA benchmark, MCPDisCo maintains monotone gains, confirming that the learned behavior generalizes beyond the training server distribution and broader agentic tasks. Model weight and implementation are available.

title: No Bootstrap, No Principal: The Day My Audit Log Became Fiction
description:
My v0.1.0 series couldn't talk about authorization, because there wasn't any. v0.2.0 shipped RBAC-lite, scoped API keys, and an encrypted secret vault on HivePlane — and the first thing the field test taught me is that attribution has a cold-start problem.

I shipped a control plane with roles, permissions, and an audit trail — and for an hour, none of it was reachable, because there was no way to mint the first API key.

This is the article about the prerequisite for every governance claim I made in the earlier series: a principal. Without one, your audit log is fiction.

The cold start

The finding was D-10. RBAC was wired. /auth/login existed. Scoped keys were implemented. And the entire model was unreachable end-to-end, because there was no HTTP bootstrap to mint the first admin key. The roles existed; nobody could assume one.

The fix was a dev-grade env admin key — boot the first principal from the environment, then issue scoped keys from there:

# the first principal has to come from outside the API
export HIVEPLANE_AUTH__ENABLED=true
export HIVEPLANE_AUTH__ADMIN_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
# now you can POST /keys to issue scoped, tenant-bound keys

The lesson is that authn is the admission gate for the operators. Until there's a principal, every "who did this" question is unanswerable, and every other governance feature is theater.

The audit log that named the wrong person

Then I found the worse one. Pause, resume, stop, kill-switch, quarantine — every privileged operator action — was attributed to a client-supplied actor field. The caller put --operator alice in the request. The audit log recorded alice. Any caller could sign an action as anyone.

tip: A who column populated by the request body is a confession that you don't know. The actor must come from the authenticated principal, not the payload. A client-supplied actor is repudiation by construction.

Findings #560, #561, and #541 were all the same shape: the action was real, the attribution was a string the caller chose. The fix is that the principal resolves the actor; the field is read-only. You can attribute an action to yourself. You cannot attribute it to someone else.

The endpoints that had no permission at all

Then the field test found the gaps RBAC was supposed to cover and didn't:

  • #537 — registry mutation endpoints had no permission checks. A viewer could DELETE /workloads.
  • #526 — destructive immune-system endpoints (quarantine, kill-switch) were ungated.
  • #563 — pause/resume/stop had no permission gate; a viewer could stop any run.
  • #566 — the UI session secret shipped a hardcoded public default.

A role system that doesn't gate the destructive verbs is a role system in name only. The fix is server-side authorization on every privileged action: approve, promote, kill-switch. A viewer cannot approve. A viewer cannot stop. A viewer cannot delete a workload. The 401/403 is the product.

HMAC-first, not bearer-first

The one I didn't see coming was #515. With auth enabled, GitHub and Alertmanager webhooks got 401 before the HMAC signature was verified. The bearer-first model broke event ingest from ≥3 sources — which is a release gate. Triggers are the autonomy layer; if they can't authenticate, the fleet doesn't run itself.

The fix is that webhook ingest is HMAC-first, not bearer-first. The signature is verified before any bearer token is required; the trigger source is trusted by its HMAC, not by a login. Autonomy and authorization have to coexist, or you've secured the plane against its own purpose.

What I learned

Bootstrap the first principal, or none of it exists — the env admin key is the admission gate for operators. Attribution comes from the principal, never the payload: a client-supplied actor is repudiation by construction. Gate the destructive verbs — a viewer who can delete a workload doesn't have a role, they have root. And webhooks are HMAC-first: bearer-first auth breaks event ingest, and autonomy and authorization have to coexist or you've secured the plane against its own purpose.

The v0.2.0 field test asserts per-tenant budget/policy/key isolation with a viewer who cannot approve, and a secret that never appears in logs/traces/agent context (verified by test). Full evidence in the field-test report; the auth bootstrap and key-rotation runbook is at docs/runbooks/auth-bootstrap-and-key-rotation.md.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Auth bootstrap & key rotation runbook
  • Secrets, RBAC & access audit design
  • Secrets, RBAC & access audit (User Guide)

Open your audit log. Pick one privileged action. Is the who populated by the authenticated principal — or by a field the caller wrote? If it's the second, your audit log is a story someone else is telling you.

title: Bridging Risk Approximation Gaps in Model Predictive Task Sampling via In-Context Modeling
description:
arXiv:2610.14913v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is essential for adaptive decision-making, e.g., robust Meta-RL and domain randomization (DR), and efficient post-training of large language models (LLMs), where tasks are commonly structured as Markov decision processes or prompts. A central bottleneck in all these settings is the cost of agent-environment interactions required for task selection and policy optimization. Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. However, existing RPMs suffer from two failure modes: (i) sparse optimization histories, which limit RPMs' generalization across the task space, and (ii) a one-step lag in risk approximation, which causes biased difficulty estimation as the policy evolves. This work formalizes these failure modes, derives lagged-risk decompositions that expose the resulting temporal bias, and recasts risk prediction as an in-context sequence modeling problem. The developed RPM integrates a one-step look-ahead mechanism with a temporal-weighted sliding window to mitigate data non-stationarity and scarcity, without requiring additional rollouts. Empirically, our approach yields more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent performance gains across robust Meta-RL, DR, and prompt curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.

title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19408v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

title: PAWA: Panoramic Action-conditioned World Modeling for Multiple Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.20240v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A multiplayer world model must predict how the independent actions of several players change a shared environment, including changes outside a player's current field of view. A point-of-view (POV) video captures such changes only after they enter its field of view, whereas panoramic video records the surroundings in every viewing direction and has served as an intermediate representation of the world state in recent world models. Learning this task therefore requires synchronized POV and panoramic videos of interacting players together with their actions, yet no existing dataset provides this combination in Minecraft, an established testbed in which players act independently in a shared, modifiable 3D world. We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling. The dataset pairs each player's POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions. Its distributed pipeline decouples CPU gameplay capture from GPU rendering, scales beyond 64 simultaneous players, and re-renders each recorded session under new observation configurations without replaying the gameplay. On this dataset, we develop a dual-tower model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video and couples the two streams through cross-attention that aligns tokens observing the same direction in a shared world frame. We further introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that provides many more player codes than existing rotary codes at the same embedding dimension. Experiments show that PAWA outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV prediction quality while also producing high-fidelity panoramic predictions. The dataset and collection pipeline are open source to support further research on multiplayer world models.

title: Four ways I tried to ingest data for my League of Legends hobby project
description:
Intro

Hello fellow devs! This is my first post on dev.to. My name is Rinat, I'm a senior full stack developer and I'm developing professionally and for fun for more than 11 years now.

This spring I started my hobby project Riftmind - a web application that analyzes raw data from videogame League of Legends and extracts useful information. Most of you probably heard of that game - it's one of the most popular multiplayer games with very big esports community (by the way Worlds 2026 starts today!). There's a public Riot API that serves a lot of data that we can use - which champions were picked, which champions were banned, who dealt the most damage, who were dying the most, etc. Currently Riftmind calculates winrates by role, rank and region and shows synergies, counterpicks, analyzes draft.

Every 2 weeks Riot releases new patch with changes to the game - from small to very significant. So for our calculations we constantly need large amount of fresh data, desirable balanced by each rank and this brings me to the point I wanted to talk about in this post. The thing is - in order to find the useful effect - we need a lot of data, so for example to say that champion A is statistically confirmed to be stronger than champion B we need to have at least data from 1000 matches between them (and even then the margin of error is about ±3%), while the effect itself is small - for most matchups it's 1-2%, and only the strongest counterpicks reach 5-8%. Riot API has rate limits for small projects like mine - about 100 calls per 2 minutes for each server. And all the match data goes through only 4 regional servers, so it's roughly 200 match API calls per minute for the whole world (calls about players and ranks go to 14 other game servers, like EUW or NA, each with its own limit). And the worst part - there's no endpoint to fetch matches from certain rank directly, we can only get matches of a certain player and we can also get players from certain rank.

So my goal was to ingest as many matches as possible by making as less API calls as possible.

Architecture

As it is my hobby project that was never intended to bring any money I wanted to minimize my monthly spending on the infrastructure. That's why I split the project into 3 applications - Ingestion, Processing and Published Web App. Ingestion is running 24/7 constantly gathering data from RiotAPI and writing it raw to its own database. Processing is executed by schedule or on demand and it calculates aggregates and copies them to the production database at the end of each run. The published app is running on Render and only has small database that only contains aggregated data. Ingestion and processing I was running at my local PC first (the gathered data could reach about 150GB) and then I moved it to the cheap VPS.

Attempt 1 - crawling the players

So the first idea was simple as the idea but turned out to be very complex at execution - I manually went to the website that had some info about players in each rank, manually selected ones that had many games and used them as seeds - my ingestion worker then fetched all their games, saved info and then moved to the other players from these games (each game always has 10 players). It worked and first month or two the ingestion used this approach. But with time some problems became obvious:

  • I couldn't reliably balance games between ranks. When we fetch the game - we don't know the ranks of all players, we only know the rank of the player whose game we're fetching. And the ranks in the same game can vary quite significantly. And if on the lower ranks it worked fine - on the higher ranks our queue would constantly drift to lower ranks. And making additional calls for each player would be very inefficient for our goal
  • It wasn't clear how to pick who we crawl next - each game adds 10 candidates, how do we maximize the "useful" calls? I had to introduce some scoring for players - considering how many games do we play.

Eventually the logic of crawling grew more and more complex while introducing little to none improvements.

By the time I gave up, the crawler was 1,790 lines of code with 17 settings to tune, and the queue of players had to be capped at 250,000 so it wouldn't grow forever.

Attempt 2 - random sampling from the ladder

This time I tried different approach - Riot API has endpoint to fetch players from any rank - the ladder, a list of all players in a rank, about 200 per page. So we don't need to crawl, we already have list of players we can fetch directly. So algorithm was simpler:

  1. Fetch players from the least represented rank in our data
  2. For every player - fetch their 20 recent match ids, download games from the current patch and stop at the first older-patch game
  3. Put these players on 48-hour cooldown, to wait until they play more games

This approach was way simpler - twice less code, games are ingesting, crawler logic was deleted at the same day.

The problem - most of the players we fetch didn't have any new games. So our ingestion was basically looking at the ladder, taking a random player and asked "did you play any games?" and answer was "no" most of the times.

In numbers: over the last full patch with this approach (16.19, two weeks) a random player gave us only 0.66 new matches on average, and only about 38 of every 100 match API calls brought a new match. That's about 2,900 new matches per hour.

Attempt 3 - catching live games

Before the next ladder idea, I tried one more thing. Riot API has a Spectator endpoint - you can ask if a player is in a game right now, and if they are, you get the game id. When the game ends, you download it with a single match API call. And Spectator calls go to those 14 game servers, whose limits I barely used. So the plan was to use these "free" calls to find games, and spend the expensive match calls only on downloading them.

I didn't want to break the working ingestion, so I ran it for an hour and a half as a side experiment - it only recorded the games it found, without downloading anything.

The games it found were perfect - every game I checked was a ranked game from the current patch. But there were too few of them: 5,340 calls found only 156 players in a game, which gave 62 unique games. Even if I used the whole spare limit of all 14 servers, it would find under 500 games per hour, while random sampling was already ingesting about 1,700 per hour at that time. Random players are rarely in a game right at the moment you ask. So I dropped the idea, but it showed me what I actually needed - a cheap way to know which players played recently.

Attempt 4 - Ladder, but better

This time instead of asking random player from the ladder - I requested 200 players from ladder in a single call (ladder calls go to the same 14 game servers with spare limits, so they're basically free), waited for 30 minutes, requested again and checked which player's game number (wins + losses) changed. And only fetched games from players who have played some actual games.

Before switching, I ran it for 7 hours as a side experiment, the same way as Spectator. The ladder turned out to be very precise: if a player's wins + losses grew by 1, they had on average 0.95 new games for us, by 2 - 1.95, by 3 - 2.91. So I switched to it the same day. Now the ingestion re-reads 20 ladder pages for every division every 2 hours (every 30 minutes was too heavy for my small VPS database), fetches games of the players with the most new games first, and only falls back to random players when the ladder runs out of active ones.

The results for the first week:

  • 1.7 new matches per checked player, against 0.66 for random players
  • about 62 of every 100 match API calls bring a new match, instead of about 38
  • about 7,100 new matches per hour instead of 2,900 (together with a couple of other fixes I made the same day)
  • the current patch got more matches in 9 days (1.23 million) than the previous one in two weeks (0.98 million)

Takeaways

  • Write down what you actually need before picking an algorithm. I needed "many recent games in every rank", and the ladder already had players sorted by rank. Crawling was a solution looking for a problem.
  • Find your bottleneck and measure everything against it. For me it was match API calls, so I compared every approach by how many new matches 100 calls bring.
  • Use what's cheap to save what's expensive. Ladder calls were almost free, and they turned out to be the signal that tells me where to spend the expensive match calls.
  • Try new ideas on the side first. Both Spectator and ladder ran next to the working ingestion and wrote to their own tables, so a bad idea couldn't break anything.

If you play League - check out Riftmind. And if you solved a similar problem differently - I'd love to hear about it in the comments!

title: PersEvalBench: Can LLM Evaluators Judge Contextually Appropriate Use of Persona Information?
description:
arXiv:2610.19314v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluators are increasingly used to assess personalized assistants, yet whether they can reliably judge personalization has rarely been tested. We introduce PersEvalBench, a benchmark testing whether an evaluator can recognize appropriate and inappropriate uses of user history. It contains 403 multi-episode scenarios where user information should persist, transfer, or cease to apply. The benchmark covers nine controlled error subtypes across three families: under-personalization, over-personalization, and misapplied-state errors. Human audits confirm that generated errors match their intended types and that the prescribed uses of user information are reasonable.
  Across five LLM evaluators, recognition of controlled personalization errors remains limited even with the full dialogue history. On the human-evaluated subset, under-personalization shows the largest gap: humans recognize 94.4% of these errors, compared with 63.9% for the strongest reported evaluator. Evaluators often recognize that a response is problematic but reverse the error direction, mistaking failure to follow an applicable preference (UNDER) for use of an inapplicable preference (OVER). Easier evidence access offers little help: highlighting the relevant history turns raises error recognition only slightly, suggesting that the remaining difficulty lies in judging what role that information should play in the response.

title: A/B tests your coding agent can run
description:
Your coding agent can change a headline in seconds. Finding out whether that headline helps people sign up takes an experiment.

I built SplitHub to keep that experiment in the same workflow as the code. You declare variants and a goal in splithub.config.ts, render the assigned value in your app, and read results from the CLI or an MCP client.

Start in your app

SplitHub needs Node.js 22.13 or newer. Run:

npx splithub init

For your own database, use:

npx splithub init --mode self

The React SDK provides SplitHubProvider, useVariant, useValue and useTrack. The Next.js package adds middleware and server component helpers. Assignment uses a local hash, so choosing a variant doesn't require a network request during rendering.

Give your agent the tools

To connect the MCP server in Claude Code:

claude mcp add splithub -- npx -y @splithub/mcp

For another MCP client, the configuration is:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "splithub": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@splithub/mcp"]
    }
  }
}

You can then ask it to create a headline test, start or pause an experiment, push config, or read results. The server uses the same project config and credentials as the CLI.

For example:

Test a shorter headline on the pricing page, using signup as the goal.

Later:

Read the results for the pricing headline test. Is there enough evidence to choose a variant?

The CLI also lets you inspect results directly:

npx splithub status
npx splithub results hero-title

Replace hero-title with your experiment key.

Cloud or your own storage

SplitHub Cloud returns statistical verdicts. Self-hosted storage returns raw visitors, conversions, conversion rates and revenue. The public SDK is MIT licensed; the cloud analysis is separate.

You still need real visitors and a measured goal. An agent can help operate a test, but it can't replace evidence with a confident answer.

The repository includes complete Vite + React and Next.js examples.

Explore the SDK on GitHub · Documentation

Questions or feedback: info@splithub.io

title: Belief Embedding Tree Search
description:
arXiv:2610.15046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.

title: Your HTML-to-PDF Invoices Look Different in Every Tool. Here's Why.
description:
The first time I generated invoice PDFs from HTML, the staging version looked perfect and the production version quietly moved the totals block to page two, alone, like it had been exiled. Same HTML, same CSS, different converter. That day I learned the fact that governs all HTML-to-PDF work: there is no single "HTML to PDF." There are several rendering engines with different subsets of CSS, different default margins, and different ideas about when a page should break. The output differences are not bugs in your markup. They are the engines, being themselves.

The three families you will actually meet

  • Browser engines (headless Chromium via Puppeteer/Playwright, or hosted tools built on it) render your page the way Chrome does — modern CSS, flexbox and grid, web fonts — then print it. If your invoice looks right in Chrome's print preview, this family will treat you best.
  • Dedicated layout engines (WeasyPrint, Prince) implement the CSS paged-media spec more faithfully — running headers, page counters, cross-references — but lag on newer layout CSS.
  • Legacy converters (older wkhtmltopdf builds and friends) use ancient WebKit. Flexbox is partial, grid is a rumor, and every project eventually has the "why is this column the whole page" incident.

My current one-off jobs go through an HTML-to-PDF converter built on a browser engine; in pipelines I pin one engine in the dependency file and treat changing it as a migration, with visual diffs, not an upgrade.

The CSS that actually controls a printed page

Most invoice-print bugs are five properties wearing trench coats:

  1. @page { size: A4; margin: ... } — set the paper and margins in CSS, or accept each engine's defaults, which differ. US Letter vs A4 alone explains a class of "it fits here but not there."
  2. break-inside: avoid on blocks that must not split — totals, signature areas, table rows groups. Without it, every engine breaks content where the page happens to end.
  3. thead repetition — browsers repeat a table's header group on each printed page if you use real thead markup; divs pretending to be headers do not repeat, which is how invoices end up with a page of orphan numbers.
  4. Print color — backgrounds vanish by default in print CSS (print-color-adjust: exact restores the ones you actually want, like a shaded header row).
  5. Fonts the engine can see. A webfont your page loads from a CDN may or may not be fetched by the converter; self-hosting the font or embedding it removes the coin flip, and invoices are not the place for coin flips.

The discipline that ends the surprises

Keep one golden sample — the nastiest invoice you produce: multi-page, long item descriptions, a discount, a tax line, a note in small print — and render it with your pinned engine on every change. Compare page count and eyeball page two; totals drift is visible in seconds. And generate the PDF at the moment of issue with the same engine that renders your preview, so the customer never sees a layout you have not.

HTML-to-PDF is a good architecture — one template, styled with skills your team already has. It just punishes the assumption that print is a screenshot of the screen. Treat the page as a separate medium with its own five rules, pin your engine, and the exiled totals block stays home.

title: Crossing the Gender Binary: Modelling Gendered Reference in Science Fiction and General Fiction
description:
arXiv:2610.19028v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Science fiction is widely credited with unsettling gender. This article asks whether that holds at the linguistic level, in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or other social category, and whether it separates the genre from general fiction. It does so by masking man/men, woman/women, and person/people across same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora and classifying RoBERTa's five likeliest substitutes by gender. Retention and displacement are permutation-tested over five resampling rounds, and the underlying sentences are read closely. Both corpora cross the gender binary in both directions, but unequally: where woman is masked, the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked. Each mismatch marks a statistical surprise, a word the corpus did not expect there. Against this shared pattern, science fiction shows greater gender permeability than the general fiction corpus, placing man in feminine contexts more often than general fiction while the reverse rate holds steady. Its degendering tendency is stronger too, drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral. Beyond the binary, a masked woman also draws substitutes naming a social category and no gender far more often than a masked man does. In measuring the gender permeability of man, woman, and person in linguistic distribution and testing whether genre changes it, the study gives science fiction studies linguistic evidence for thematic claims and computational literary studies a pipeline applicable to other category vocabularies, such as race and class.

title: Dynamic Graph World Modelling: Learning Future Dynamics from Temporal Context
description:
arXiv:2610.19364v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dynamic graph learning models how entities and their relations evolve from historical observations to predict future graph states. Existing methods do not fully address dynamic graph world modelling, which requires learning transitions from temporal context to future latent graph states. This is difficult for three reasons: nodes and relations rely on different historical evidence, structural evolution is path-dependent, and future snapshots provide sparse and realization-specific targets. We propose Dynamic Graph World Modelling (DyG-WM), the first framework to jointly predict future node and relation representations from temporal context by answering three questions: what has evolved, how it evolved, and what will evolve next. To capture what has evolved, a historical node-relation context encoder summarizes node-neighborhood trajectories and pair-specific histories. To characterize how it evolved, a node-relation path-signature encoder captures ordered structural changes. To predict what will evolve next, a dual-level joint-embedding objective predicts target-snapshot node and relation representations without reconstructing the raw graph. Experiments on 12 link-prediction and two node-classification datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DyG-WM across both tasks.

title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.19571v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.

title: Explore Microsoft Azure: How to Get Started with Azure
description:
1. Introduction

  • Brief Overview of Microsoft Azure:

    • Microsoft Azure is a comprehensive cloud computing platform offered by Microsoft, providing a range of services including computing power, storage solutions, and networking capabilities. Azure is significant in the cloud computing industry because it allows businesses to build, deploy, and manage applications and services through Microsoft-managed data centers globally. With its extensive infrastructure and integration capabilities, Azure supports a wide variety of programming languages, tools, and frameworks, making it a versatile choice for developers and enterprises alike.
    • Azure is one of the most popular cloud platforms in the world, competing with Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud. It is known for its extensive range of services, from basic virtual machines to complex artificial intelligence tools, and its ability to cater to businesses of all sizes, from startups to large enterprises.

  • Why Get Started with Azure?

    • Azure offers scalability, allowing businesses to adjust their resources according to their needs without upfront investments in physical hardware. This flexibility means you can scale up during high-demand periods and scale down when demand decreases, all within a cost-effective framework.
    • Azure’s pay-as-you-go pricing model, extensive support for open-source technologies, and seamless integration with Microsoft products like Office 365 and Dynamics 365 make it an attractive option for various industries, including healthcare, finance, and retail.
    • Professionals such as developers, system administrators, and data scientists can benefit from Azure by leveraging its tools to build, test, and deploy applications more efficiently.

2. Setting Up Your Azure Account

  • Creating a Microsoft Account:

    • If you don't already have a Microsoft account, visit account.microsoft.com and click "Create a Microsoft account." You can sign up using an existing email address or create a new one. Follow the on-screen instructions to complete the account creation process.

  • Signing Up for Azure:

    • Once you have a Microsoft account, go to azure.microsoft.com. Click on "Start for free" to begin the sign-up process. During sign-up, you'll need to provide some basic information and a payment method, even if you're using the free trial. Azure typically offers a 30-day free trial with $200 in credits, which you can use to explore various services.
    • After signing up, you'll be directed to the Azure Portal, where you can start managing your cloud resources.

  • Understanding the Azure Portal:

    • The Azure Portal is the central hub for managing all your Azure services. Upon logging in, you'll see a customizable dashboard where you can pin resources for quick access. The "All Services" section gives you access to all available Azure services, while "Cost Management" allows you to monitor your spending and set budgets to avoid unexpected costs.

3. Navigating the Azure Portal

  • Overview of the User Interface:

    • The Azure Portal interface is designed to be intuitive. The left-hand menu provides access to services, subscriptions, resource groups, and more. The top bar features a search function, notifications, and settings. Notifications will keep you updated on the status of your resources and any potential issues.

  • Creating Your First Resource:

    • For your first resource, let's create a Virtual Machine (VM). In the Azure Portal, click on "Create a resource" and select "Virtual Machine" from the options. Follow the guided steps to configure your VM, such as selecting an operating system, instance size, and region. Once configured, click "Review + Create" to finalize your VM setup.

4. Exploring Core Azure Services

  • Introduction to Key Services:

    • Compute: Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) allow you to run applications in the cloud with your preferred operating system. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) helps you manage containerized applications using Kubernetes.
    • Storage: Azure Blob Storage is ideal for storing unstructured data, while File Storage and Disk Storage offer file-level and block-level storage solutions, respectively.
    • Networking: Azure Virtual Networks enable you to create isolated networks for your Azure resources, while Load Balancers and Azure DNS ensure high availability and optimized performance.
    • Database: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed relational database service, while Cosmos DB offers multi-model database capabilities for global distribution.

  • Use Cases and Examples:

    • Provide practical examples, such as hosting a website using Azure VMs, storing backups using Blob Storage, or setting up a scalable microservices architecture with AKS.

5. Managing and Monitoring Your Resources

  • Resource Management:

    • Group related resources using Resource Groups to manage them collectively. For instance, if you have a VM, storage account, and network all related to a single application, you can organize them under one Resource Group.
    • Use tagging to categorize resources by department, project, or environment, which helps with organization and cost management.

  • Monitoring and Alerts:

    • Azure Monitor offers insights into the performance and health of your resources. Set up alerts to notify you of potential issues, such as high CPU usage or low available memory, allowing you to respond proactively.

6. Learning and Certification

  • Azure Learning Resources:

    • Microsoft offers a wealth of learning resources, including free online courses through Microsoft Learn, extensive documentation, and hands-on labs. Consider exploring tutorials and joining Azure communities to stay updated on the latest features.
    • Engage with Azure blogs, podcasts, and forums to gain insights from other professionals and Azure experts.

  • Certification Pathways:

    • Starting with Azure Fundamentals (AZ-900) is recommended for beginners. From there, you can pursue role-based certifications, such as Azure Administrator (AZ-104) or Azure Solutions Architect (AZ-305), to validate your skills and advance your career.

7. Conclusion

  • Recap of Getting Started:

    • In this guide, we walked through the essentials of getting started with Microsoft Azure, beginning with setting up an account and navigating the Azure Portal. We also explored creating your first resource, understanding core Azure services, and managing and monitoring your resources effectively. These initial steps are designed to provide a solid foundation for leveraging Azure's powerful cloud computing capabilities.

  • Call to Action:

    • Now that you have an overview of how to get started with Azure, it's time to take the first step. Create your Azure account today and start exploring the platform’s vast array of services. Whether you're deploying your first virtual machine or experimenting with Azure's AI tools, the possibilities are endless. Don't hesitate to dive in and discover how Azure can enhance your projects and business operations.
    • We encourage you to share your experiences or ask questions in the comments section below. Your insights and inquiries can help foster a supportive community where we can all learn and grow together in our Azure journeys.
