title: TextVerifier: Seeing Beyond Recognition to Verify Chinese Text Rendering
description:
arXiv:2610.19551v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-image models increasingly generate readable Chinese text that still contains local rendering defects, such as a character with an extra or missing stroke or a malformed component. Such errors are invisible to OCR and vision-language models, which are trained for recognition and are therefore invariant to the very structural deviations that define a rendering error. We formalize text rendering verification as a target-conditioned problem: given a target character and an image crop, decide whether the crop is a correct rendering of that character. Our verifier TEXTVERIFIER feeds the text tower a character's Ideographic Description Sequence (IDS) rather than a single-character symbol, and is trained on 12.7M crop-IDS pairs plus label-free "same-character, different-quality" hard pairs sampled from the training trajectory of a text-region inpainting model. To evaluate this ability we build TEXTRENDERBENCH-ZH, the first per-character benchmark for generated Chinese text, annotating position, identity, and correctness for 7,358 characters. TEXTVERIFIER reaches an F1 of 0.844, far above OCR confidence (0.526), a general VLM (0.329), and TextPecker (0.590). Used as a per-character reward for Flow-GRPO post-training, it further reduces rendering errors, showing that its score can both detect and correct errors.

title: Efficient contextual partial monitoring with general function approximation
description:
arXiv:2610.19804v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study finite stochastic partial monitoring (PM) games with side information, a paradigm of sequential learning with partial feedback. On each round $t \in [T]$, both player and environment observe a context and player chooses an action and environment simultaneously chooses an outcome. The player neither observes the outcome nor the loss; instead, they only observe a feedback symbol which is partially informative about the outcome. We utilize the Estimation-to-Decisions (E2D) meta-algorithm of Foster et al.(2021) to design E2D.PMSide, a computationally efficient framework for contextual partial monitoring, which uses an online regression oracle to efficiently estimate the outcome distributions based on historical (context, action, feedback symbol) tuples. Since the exploration rule given by the original E2D algorithm is intractable to compute, we propose two computationally efficient exploration rules that achieve optimal regret orders in $T$: in the globally observable setting, our exploration rule is based on $\epsilon$-greedy, while in the locally observable setting, our exploration rule uses inverse gap weighting (Foster & Rakhlin, 2020), which was previously only known to be effective in the bandit setting. We show that a variant of E2D.PMSide named OE2D.PMSide can be combined with offline regression oracles to give an efficient algorithm with optimal regret when the contexts are drawn independently from a fixed distribution. We evaluate our algorithm on a synthetic label-efficient prediction game and an LLM routing task, in which a learner decides from prompt, uncertainty, and internal state features whether to escalate a query from a weak model to a strong one. We show that our method has superior performance to prior approaches.

title: Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
description:
By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen Mareddy

Stratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more.

Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions.

Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts, live events, sports, ads, or regional ingests like TF1 in France.

To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below:

functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1
resources:
  numCpus: 8
  memoryInMB: 18000
  diskSizeInMB: 50000
  networkInMbps: 1000

Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners.

In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong.

The Challenge: Over-Provisioning

When engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution.

Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons:

  • High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task.
  • Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1, AV2, and spatial audio). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released.
  • Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts, sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats, and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise.
  • Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste.
  • Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform.

To understand the scale of the challenge, we analyzed historical usage across Stratum’s workloads. The telemetry confirmed our hypothesis: over-provisioning was frequent, wasted compute was compounding, and the sustainable path forward required a fundamental re-evaluation of how resource configurations are managed.

Meet the Stratum Resource Tuner

To address the challenges listed above, we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) to automatically right-size Stratum containers. Our north star is to ensure that users never have to manually specify the resource configurations. We started with a handful of high-throughput workloads with relaxed latency requirements, which account for the majority (70%–80%) of resource usage.

As a quick note on terminology, we use “right-sizing” and “tuning” interchangeably in this post. “Downsizing” means decreasing resource limits, while “upsizing” means increasing them. Since our goal is to optimize for cost, this post focuses on downsizing.

Automatic right-sizing is not enabled by default. Function owners must manually opt in on a per resource type basis (e.g., CPU, memory, network, or disk). Once enrolled, SRT operates without a human in the loop across five steps:

  1. Collect resource usage metrics across all executions of that function.
  2. Generate a recommendation for each resource type (e.g., CPU or memory).
  3. Verify the recommendation through experiments.
  4. Apply or reject the recommendation based on the results of experiments.
  5. Monitor post-apply metrics, watching for anomalies after applying the recommendation.

“Recommendation” is a key construct in SRT and serves as the primary unit of operation. As SRT executes its steps, it promotes the recommendation through several stages:

  • CREATED: A scheduled workflow generated the recommendation.
  • EVALUATING: Recommendation verification is running, and SRT is analyzing the results.
  • APPLIED: All experiments passed, and SRT automatically rolled out the recommended configuration.
  • REJECTED: At least one experiment failed, leaving the function configuration untouched.
  • MONITORED: SRT monitors the recommendation during a post-apply soak period to verify stability.

The sections below examine each of these stages in detail. To illustrate the flow, we will follow the real-world lifecycle of the VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function — a high-throughput video encoding function whose over-provisioned memory and CPU footprints were successfully tuned.

Note that all operational thresholds and safety limits discussed below are fully configurable per function to accommodate varying workload characteristics and risk tolerances.

Metrics Collection

To make these recommendations possible, we need a solid metrics collection mechanism. Every Stratum container reports its function execution metadata, infrastructure dimensions, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk, and network) at sub-minute resolution.

These metrics flow through Keystone, Netflix’s real-time event streaming platform, and land in two separate datastores:

  • Execution summaries store: Stores execution-level summary metrics indexed in Elasticsearch for fast point lookups, serving as our short-term datastore for querying and inspecting individual runs.
  • High-resolution long-term store: Stores raw, high-resolution usage metrics in Iceberg tables. While slower to query, it serves as our long-term datastore, holding months of history for resource utilization trend analysis.

One record is written per execution, which is represented as a span. Here is how these records look for a single span of our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function.

In Elasticsearch, the record captures the high-level summary of the completed span, identified by tags.stratum.spanId:

{
  "tags.stratum.spanId": "38536313f65f060a",
  "tags.functionName": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "tags.stratum.phase": "run",
  "tags.stratum.success": true,
  "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false,
  "tags.stratum.function.execDurationSecs": 26,
  "tags.cpuCount": 8,
  "tags.memoryInMB": 18000,
  "tags.diskInMB": 50000,
  "tags.networkInMbps": 1000,
  "tags.titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107",
  "tags.instanceType": "r7a.24xlarge",
  "tags.nf.region": "us-east-1",
  "ts": 1780743028000
}

In Iceberg, the record contains the same metadata, but adds the sub-minute resource utilization timeseries tracked during that span:

{
  "span_id": "38536313f65f060a",
  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "phase": "run",
  "success": true,
  "start_epoch_secs": 1780743002,
  "end_epoch_secs": 1780743028,
  "runtime_secs": 26,
  "cpu_requested": 8,
  "memory_mb_requested": 18000,
  "disk_mb_requested": 50000,
  "network_mbps_requested": 1000,
  "titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107",
  "instance_type": "r7a.24xlarge",
  "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false,
  "env": "prod",
  "resource_usage": [ 
   { "cpu_usage": 1.13, "memory_mb": 3701.37, "disk_mb": 20120.4, "net_in_mb": 221.09, "net_out_mb": 0.12 },
   { "cpu_usage": 2.25, "memory_mb": 3584.09, "disk_mb": 25410.1, "net_in_mb": 0.02, "net_out_mb": 0.05 },
   { "cpu_usage": 4.16, "memory_mb": 6750.79, "disk_mb": 30400.5, "net_in_mb": 165.90, "net_out_mb": 0.38 },
   ... 
  ]
}

Recommendation Generation

A scheduled Conductor workflow runs daily, reading the past month of usage data from Iceberg and generating recommendations for every function and resource type. The workflow also generates recommendations for functions that have not opted into automatic right-sizing to preview potential savings.

Each recommendation is saved in the recommendations datastore, enabling us to query and filter recommendations by function, resource type, or status on an ad hoc basis.

For each function and resource type, the workflow applies the following generation logic:

  • Filter by workload type: We only tune high-throughput workloads. This focuses our efforts on right-sizing, which yields the most meaningful fleet-wide savings.
  • Aggressively tune CPU and network: We target p99 usage with no extra headroom. CPU and network are compressible resources; if a container occasionally hits these limits, the function might execute slightly slower.
  • Conservatively tune memory and disk: We target p99.9 usage and include a safety buffer. Running out of physical memory or disk space causes hard failures — such as Out of Memory (OOM) or Out of Disk (OOD) crashes — making a protective margin essential.
  • Apply safeguards to changes: We discard recommendations if the absolute reduction is too small to justify operational effort. For memory and disk, we clamp the maximum reduction allowed in a single cycle to 15% — a safety limit introduced after learning from early production runs.

The workflow creates new recommendations in the CREATED state. If a recommendation already exists in this state for a given function and resource type, SRT overwrites it with updated calculations. Once a recommendation advances past the CREATED state, its recommended_value and stats fields become immutable. Subsequent daily runs generate a new recommendation with a unique ID instead of modifying the existing record.

Here is how these recommendations look across resource types in their initial CREATED state for our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function:

  • CPU recommendation
{

  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "env": "prod", "resource_type": "CPU",
  "current_value": 8, "recommended_value": 4,
  "status": "CREATED",
  "resource_cost_usd_per_hour": ***,
  "stats": {
    "usage": { "p99": 4.16, "p999": 4.57 },
    "execution": {
      "total_fn_executions": 748762182,
      "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75,
      "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723
    },
    "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" }
  },
  "experiment_inputs": null,
  "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null,
  "outcome_message": null,
  "finalized_at": null
}
  • Memory recommendation (15% reduction in one step)
{
  "id": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7",
  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "env": "prod", "resource_type": "MEMORY_MB",
  "current_value": 18000, "recommended_value": 15300,
  "status": "CREATED",
  "resource_cost_usd_per_hour": ***,

  "stats": {
    "usage": { "avg": 5296.43, "p99": 6750.8, "p999": 7820.3 },
    "execution": {
      "total_fn_executions": 748762182,
      "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75,
      "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723
    },
    "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" }
  },
  "experiment_inputs": null,
  "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null,
  "outcome_message": null,
  "finalized_at": null
}

As the recommendation moves through its lifecycle, SRT populates the remaining parameters.

When proceeding to the verification stage, SRT transitions the recommendation status to EVALUATING, records the target experiment settings, and links the active workflow execution tracking the experiment.

Finally, once verification runs complete, the status changes to APPLIED or REJECTED, storing the outcome details and completion timestamp for analysis.

Retry with More Resources

We take a conservative approach to generating recommendations, prioritizing system stability over extreme efficiency. Because recommendations rely on historical usage data, they cannot always anticipate sudden spikes or novel workload profiles when functions encounter heavy, unseen requests.

To handle these unexpected spikes, we developed a fail-safe mechanism. A watcher process running in each tuned container tracks memory and disk usage during function execution. If the container exceeds the pre-set thresholds, 85% for non-cached memory usage or 95% for disk usage, the watcher flags the execution as high risk, cancels execution, and re-queues the task onto a larger container:

new_container_size = original_container_size * 1.5

This 1.5 multiplier only applies to memory and disk dimensions.

This “retry with more resources” mechanism serves as our safety net: larger container configurations are applied only when retrying tasks to self-heal from edge cases. Although these infrequent retries incur additional compute costs and latency, they allow us to keep day-to-day configurations highly optimized without having to size for rare, costly outliers up front.

For our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function, if a heavy run causes memory usage to exceed the 85% threshold (15,300 MB) within its current 18,000 MB container, the system aborts the execution and reruns it on a 27,000 MB container.

While we prefer to trigger retries based on actual OOM or OOD events rather than pre-set thresholds, technical constraints in our current architecture make true event detection challenging. Using pre-set thresholds serves as a reliable stopgap while we develop improved detection capabilities.

SRT automatically enables the retry mechanism for any function opted into memory or disk right-sizing. Each Stratum container reports retry events, which flow into Elasticsearch and Iceberg alongside standard performance telemetry.

Recommendation Verification

Every recommendation must pass a two-stage verification process managed by a Conductor workflow before rollout. During this EVALUATING stage, SRT executes two distinct experiment types:

  1. Synthetic experiment: A low-cost, low-risk test to catch obvious regressions before production rollout.
  2. Production experiment: A live evaluation that validates changes across diverse production workloads to increase confidence.

A recommendation advances to production testing only after passing the synthetic experiment. When an opted-in function has multiple pending recommendations, SRT prioritizes and evaluates the candidates with the highest estimated savings first.

Synthetic experiment:

  • Runs in a test environment isolated from production traffic.
  • Sets up two clusters: one for the current and one for the recommended config.
  • Replays identical request sets across both clusters simultaneously without splitting traffic, exposing both configurations to 100% of test requests.
  • Typically runs for 1–2 hours.
  • Runs to completion without early termination checks.

Production experiment:

  • Runs in production on real user traffic, split three ways:
    ◦ ~90% remains on the main cluster (current production config).
    ◦ ~5% goes to a baseline cluster (current production config).
    ◦ ~5% goes to an experimental cluster (recommendation config).
  • Evaluates recommendations against a similarly sized baseline cluster rather than the main cluster to preserve comparable traffic profiles.
  • Typically runs from one day to one week, depending on traffic volume.
  • Fails fast: cancels the experiment early if regressions are detected.

The Stratum platform executes other experiments alongside SRT experiments. To avoid over-splitting traffic, SRT experiments run at lower priority and yield resources to active, higher-priority experiments.

Traffic arrives in irregular bursts separated by multi-day or multi-week lulls. The verification pipeline accommodates these variable arrival patterns rather than expecting steady traffic.

Back to our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 memory recommendation (18,000 MB → 15,300 MB), verification is triggered with:

{
  "recommendationId": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7",
  "syntheticExperiment": { "numberOfExecutions": 3000 },
  "productionExperiment": {
    "enabled": true,
    "maxContainers": 20, // max containers shift to baseline & experimental clusters
    "upGateTimeoutMinutes": 10080, // time to wait for traffic to start flowing
    "maxRunDurationMinutes": 1240, // max time to run the experiment once traffic starts
    "minSamples": 500 // min executions needed on both clusters before evaluating
  }
}

Both verification stages evaluate recommendations against two sequential checks, terminating immediately if either fails:

  • Retries with more resources: Restricts memory and disk downsizes to a maximum 1% retry threshold over the experiment duration.
  • Execution time: Compares median runtimes to prevent outlier distortion, permitting up to a 10–15% slowdown relative to baseline, depending on workload, and is configurable by function.

If a recommendation passes both verification stages, SRT updates its status to APPLIED and rolls out the configuration to the main production cluster. If a check fails at any point, SRT marks the recommendation as REJECTED and preserves the existing configuration. SRT sends notifications for both outcomes.

For VideoEncoder.encodeV1, both stages passed cleanly:

{
  "outcome": "APPLIED",
  "syntheticExperiment": {
    "result": "SUCCESS",
    "samples": { "baseline": 3000, "experimental": 3000 },
    "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 59.0, "experimental": 59.0 },
    "slownessIncreasePct": 0.0,
    "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 }
  },
  "productionExperiment": {
    "result": "SUCCESS",
    "samples": { "baseline": 50361, "experimental": 49790 },
    "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 196.0, "experimental": 198.0 },
    "slownessIncreasePct": 1.0,
    "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 }
  }
}

The recommendation moved to the APPLIED state, permanently setting the memory allocation for VideoEncoder.encodeV1 to 15,300 MB. We observed similarly clean results for the CPU recommendation, which reduced CPU allocation from 8 cores to 4.

Post-Apply Monitoring

Passing verification experiments does not mark the end of the recommendation lifecycle. Updated function code, modified input parameters, or underlying changes in the compute environment (Titus/EC2) can alter production behavior over time. To ensure configuration safety and foster feature adoption, we instituted continuous post-apply monitoring for applied changes.

We monitor metrics for 90 days across two rolling time windows: a 30-minute fast window and a 24-hour slow window. Each window maintains specific alert thresholds: a 3% retry rate over 30 minutes or a 2% rate over 24 hours triggers an automated notification.

At steady state, workloads exhibit baseline retry rates around 0.1%, with rates up to 2%–3% falling within acceptable operational variances. Most applied recommendations remained stable over the past three months.

VideoEncoder.encodeV1 has operated on its tuned configuration for months without breaching thresholds. However, VideoEncoder.encodeV2 presented a challenging edge case: a 50% memory reduction passed all verification checks and ran stably for two weeks before an unexpected traffic shift drove retry rates above 60%.

Because early versions lacked automated rollback capabilities, engineers manually triaged exception cases. This incident highlighted the need for automated mitigation, prompting us to construct self-healing rollback functionality.

Today, the two auto-revert windows look like this:

  • Last 30 minutes: 3% retries warn us; 10% triggers an auto-revert.
  • Last 24 hours: A 2% retry rate triggers both an alert and an automatic revert.

Breaching an auto-revert threshold immediately restores the function configuration to its pre-recommendation baseline.

We intentionally maintain straightforward revert logic — restoring the last known stable configuration rather than attempting dynamic resource adjustments during an incident.

The VideoEncoder.encodeV2 incident also reshaped our recommendation generation rules for memory and disk allocations. Rather than applying full target reductions immediately, SRT now applies smaller, incremental 15% step changes, advancing only after confirming stability at each step. Additionally, we introduced a global kill switch to disable automated right-sizing across all functions in case of unexpected issues or side effects.

Additionally, we enforce a mandatory cooldown period — typically one week — before initiating new experiments on a function. Pausing adjustments allows us to observe performance across diverse production traffic patterns, identifying potential risks before applying subsequent recommendations.

Where Are We Today

Oversized containers and config drift don’t have to be an accepted tax of running serverless workloads at scale. By building the Stratum Resource Tuner, we transformed manual, risk-averse resource sizing into an automated, self-healing pipeline. Through real-world workloads and hard lessons from unexpected spikes, we’ve proven that continuous right-sizing can safely deliver significant gains in infrastructure efficiency.

We initially focused on right-sizing high-throughput video encoding workloads, aiming for an initial 5% reduction in overall Stratum compute costs. For instance, VideoEncoder.encodeV1 achieved a 50% reduction in CPU usage and 40% in memory usage without compromising performance or retry rates.

However, edge cases like VideoEncoder.encodeV2 highlighted key lessons: large single-step reductions can introduce hidden risks, and manual incident response slows recovery. These insights led us to enforce stricter safety guardrails in the Stratum Resource Tuner, including capping memory and disk reductions at 15% per cycle and adding automated rollbacks when retry thresholds are breached. Guided by these safeguards, re-tuning VideoEncoder.encodeV2 yielded a stable 20% memory reduction with zero subsequent incidents.

Looking ahead, our key priorities include:

  • Expand SRT beyond high-throughput encoding workloads to support a wider variety of functions and workload types.
  • Further tune the resources in regions with constrained resource availability.
  • Move from reactive alerts to proactive, automated upsizing for under-provisioned functions.
  • Experiment with intentional upsizing for latency-sensitive workloads to evaluate performance gains and reduce function execution time.
  • Upgrade our failure signals for OOM/OOD events from lagging indicators to leading indicators to improve tuning precision.

If solving problems like this sounds exciting, we are hiring in our Warsaw office. Check out open roles here.

title: A Hybrid Kinematic GCN and Elastic Transformer for Efficient Indian Sign Language Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.14680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.

title: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit
description:
arXiv:2610.19373v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.

title: AWS HealthOmics introduces resource fallback order for Nextflow workflows
description:
Today, AWS HealthOmics introduces the resource fallback directive for tasks in your Nextflow workflows, enabling you to define an ordered list of preferred accelerator types, including an option to fallback to CPU instances. Researchers and bioinformaticians can use this directive to reduce time spent diagnosing and resubmitting runs due to accelerator constraints and keep production workflows running. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows. 

With resource fallback for Nextflow workflows, you can prioritize your preferred accelerator for your task. When your preferred accelerator is unavailable, HealthOmics automatically moves through your specified alternatives in the fallback without resubmission. Each accelerator profile has a configurable timeout, giving you control over how long HealthOmics searches for that accelerator before moving to the next. Shorter timeouts help you move quickly through the fallback order, while longer timeouts increase the probability of reserving your preferred accelerator. You can also include a CPU profile as a final fallback to increase the likelihood of your task reserving an instance. 

You can now use resource fallback for Nextflow workflows in all AWS HealthOmics Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Seoul, Singapore, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the advanced resource configuration and Nextflow specifics documentation.

title: Generative World Simulation with DAO and JING
description:
arXiv:2610.19726v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a Generative World Simulation framework that couples persistent shared world state with continuous first-person audiovisual generation. The framework integrates DAO, a computable world engine, and JING, an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model, to support sustained interaction for humans and agents. DAO maintains the states of characters, objects, and spaces and their relationships, advancing the world according to interaction rules and world time while preserving the consequences of past actions. From this evolving state, DAO derives observer-specific conditions for JING, which combines these conditions with character, object, and scene references, observation history, and current actions to generate each observer's audiovisual experience. Users can explore environments, manipulate objects, and communicate with characters through viewpoint control and text instructions, with their actions shaping both the shared state and subsequent experiences. By connecting world-state evolution with experience generation in a continuous interaction loop, the framework offers an approach to building interactive worlds that retain their history, evolve through action, and persist beyond any individual observer.

title: I Built an AI Financial Advisor. Now I Need You to Break It.
description:
Vicquant is open for beta testers: pick a frontend design, run four short tasks, and tell me exactly what feels wrong.

The problem with asking "What do you think?"

When I first put Vicquant in front of beta testers, I asked the question every builder asks:
"What do you think?" The answers I got back were polite and vague. "Looks good." "Nice app."
Not one of them told me where someone got stuck, what confused them, or what they expected to happen and didn't.
That is my mistake, not theirs. Open-ended questions produce open-ended politeness.

So this time I am doing it differently: I am giving you specific things to do, a short way to report what
happened, and a say in how the app looks. If you have ever wanted to shape a product while it is still early, this is that chance.

What is Vicquant?

Vicquant is an AI-assisted personal finance and market-analysis app. It started as a small local chatbot that helped people plan debt repayment and savings, and it has grown into something much bigger. One rule shaped it from day one: the AI never does the arithmetic. All the
money math (balances, payoffs, risk numbers) is computed by normal, testable code, and the language model only explains the results. That way a language model's confident guess cannot quietly become your budget.

What you can try in the beta:

• AI Advisor and Budget: ask questions about debt, savings and spending in plain language.
• RAG Vault: upload your own financial documents and get answers with citations back to the source, so you can check the answer instead of trusting it.
• Stocks and Portfolio: track holdings and see risk measures such as Sharpe, Sortino, VaR and CVaR, without needing a finance degree to read them.
• Market regime detection and alerts: a statistical model that tries to tell calm markets from turbulent ones.
• Proof ledger: trading signals are recorded in a tamper-evident, hash-chained log with fixed rules set in advance, so results cannot be quietly rewritten after the fact. No win rate is shown until at least 30 signals have been resolved, because a handful of lucky calls proves
nothing.

Honest status: what is rough right now

A beta invitation is only useful if it is honest, so here is where things stand:
• The AI currently runs through a hosted model service rather than fully on your own device.
Running it locally again is on the roadmap, but it is not the current setup.
• The mobile web experience is not good enough. A native Android and iOS app is planned, so please judge the layout with that in mind.
• Vicquant gives information and analysis. It is not licensed financial advice, and nothing in it is a guarantee of returns.
• Some features are still being tuned, and speed can vary. If something feels slow, I want to know exactly when it happened.
• The frontend UI and UX design also needs working on. This is my first time on working on something of this scale.
Please, I need your honest review and contribution, so i can improve on it

Please use sample numbers. During the beta, enter made-up balances and debts rather than real account details.You can test everything that matters without exposing anything
personal.

Help me choose the design

I have three frontend designs and I do not want to choose alone. The feedback I got earlier was that the interface needs to feel easier for someone who is not a finance expert, so this is where your eyes matter most. The UI design is okay for laptop size screen but for the mobile, i am still working on it.

When you vote, do not only tell me which one you like. Tell me which one you understood fastest. In a finance app, "pretty" matters less than "I knew what to tap."

Your 15-minute mission

Four tasks. Do them in order, and write down anywhere you hesitated, even for a second.

How to send feedback (it takes two minutes)
After the four tasks, answer these five questions in the feedback form:

• Which design did you pick, and which one did you understand fastest?
• Where did you get stuck or confused? Name the screen.
• What did you expect to happen that did not?
• Did any AI answer feel wrong, vague or untrustworthy? Paste it if you can.
• Would you use this again? What single change would make you say yes?

Bug reports are gold. A screenshot, your device and browser, and one sentence about what you were doing is all I need.

Join the beta
If you are a developer, a student, a finance enthusiast, or simply someone who gets confused by money apps, you are exactly who I need. Beginners are especially welcome, because they
find the problems experts forgive.

• Beta link: https://budget-planner-advisor-rho.vercel.app/
• Reply here or message me with questions.

Thank you for reading, and for being willing to break something so it can be built better. Tell me what is wrong with it, and I will make sure the next version is better because of you.

title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
description:
arXiv:2610.19651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.

title: Building a DICOM Import Pipeline With AWS HealthImaging
description:
Medical imaging platforms must move large volumes of DICOM data without losing track of image identity, metadata, or import errors. AWS HealthImaging Solutions provide a managed foundation for storing and retrieving medical imaging data, but the ingestion workflow still needs careful engineering.

A production-ready pipeline involves more than uploading .dcm files and starting an import job. It needs source validation, secure S3 staging, a scoped IAM role, job orchestration, manifest processing, and post-import verification.

This guide explains how to build a DICOM import pipeline using AWS HealthImaging, from preparing source files to making imported image sets available to downstream applications.

Understand the DICOM Import Architecture

AWS HealthImaging imports DICOM P10 files from an Amazon S3 input location into a data store. During import, it performs pixel-data verification and transforms source files into image sets containing metadata and image frames.

A typical workflow looks like this:

PACS / VNA / Scanner Export
|
v
Source Validation
|
v
Amazon S3 Input
|
v
StartDICOMImportJob
|
v
AWS HealthImaging
|
+-------------------+
| |
v v
Image Sets S3 Job Results
|
+----------+----------+
| | |
v v v
Success Warning Failure
Manifest Manifest Manifest
|
v
Reconciliation and QA
|
v
Imaging Viewer

In this architecture, S3 holds incoming files and import results, while HealthImaging manages the resulting image sets. Your application handles workflow state, reconciliation, access policies, and readiness checks.

For teams implementing AWS HealthImaging Solutions, this separation helps keep ingestion logic independent from the applications that consume the data.

Start with the official AWS HealthImaging import guide.

1. Define the Source Data Contract

Before moving files, establish exactly what the source system will deliver. DICOM environments vary in export conventions, metadata quality, transfer syntaxes, and directory structures.

Document these details:

Source system and export method

Expected DICOM SOP classes

Supported transfer syntaxes

Study, Series, and Instance identifiers

Approximate file count and total data volume

Whether metadata overrides are required

How duplicate or corrected studies should be handled

Which system owns the authoritative identifiers

HealthImaging supports specific DICOM elements, SOP classes, and transfer syntaxes. Check the dataset against the current DICOM support documentation before starting a large migration.

An uploaded file is not necessarily a valid import candidate. It may reach S3 but fail validation or produce warnings during processing.

A reliable AWS HealthImaging Solutions implementation should validate representative files early, including data from different modalities and source systems.

2. Stage DICOM Files in Amazon S3

Use a dedicated S3 bucket or prefix for each ingestion environment. Keep source files separate from job outputs so that the pipeline can identify exactly which data belongs to each batch.

For example:

s3://imaging-ingestion-prod/
incoming/
batch-2026-10-15/
study-a/
instance-001.dcm
instance-002.dcm
study-b/
instance-001.dcm

s3://imaging-import-results/
jobs/
batch-2026-10-15/

The folder structure helps with operational organization. HealthImaging uses DICOM metadata, including Study, Series, and Instance UIDs, when organizing imported data.

Consider these controls:

Assign a unique batch identifier to each import.

Maintain a manifest of source object keys and checksums.

Prevent files from changing after a batch is approved.

Restrict bucket access to the required roles and services.

Enable encryption and appropriate access logging.

Define retention rules for source data and import results.

Avoid patient names or other sensitive information in resource names and job labels.

These controls make retries, troubleshooting, and audits easier. They also prevent an upload from silently changing the input associated with a previously submitted job.

For AWS HealthImaging Solutions that handle clinical data, treat source files and processing manifests as sensitive assets throughout the pipeline.

3. Configure the Data Store and IAM Role

Create a HealthImaging data store before starting the import. Decide on the storage format at creation time because it affects how lossless image frames are stored. HTJ2K is the default, and JPEG 2000 Lossless is also available as a configuration option.

Confirm that the selected format works with the applications that will retrieve and decode the images. See the data store creation guide for the available configuration options.

Next, configure the IAM role used by the import job. It needs permission to read the input files and write processing results to the designated output location. Its trust policy must allow HealthImaging to assume the role.

Follow least-privilege principles:

Grant read access only to the approved input location.

Grant write access only to the job-results location.

Avoid broad wildcard permissions where narrower resource permissions are possible.

Separate deployment permissions from runtime import permissions.

Review role trust policies and bucket permissions during testing.

The import role is a key part of the security boundary. A production pipeline should not rely on a developer's personal credentials or broad administrative access.

Refer to the AWS HealthImaging setup guide for the required S3 buckets, permissions, and role configuration.

4. Start an Import Job

The StartDICOMImportJob action starts the bulk import. Its request identifies the target data store, S3 input and output locations, and the data-access role.

The following AWS CLI example illustrates the command structure. Replace the sample values with the identifiers and locations from your environment.

aws medical-imaging start-dicom-import-job \
--datastore-id "$DATASTORE_ID" \
--input-s3-uri "s3://imaging-ingestion-prod/incoming/batch-2026-10-15/" \
--output-s3-uri "s3://imaging-import-results/jobs/batch-2026-10-15/" \
--data-access-role-arn "$IMPORT_ROLE_ARN" \
--job-name "batch-2026-10-15"

Check the current AWS CLI reference for the exact options supported by your installed version. In application code, use an AWS SDK and store the returned job identifier with your internal batch ID.

For example, an application-level batch record might look like this:

{
"batchId": "batch-2026-10-15",
"dataStoreId": "replace-with-datastore-id",
"jobId": "returned-job-id",
"inputPrefix": "incoming/batch-2026-10-15/",
"status": "SUBMITTED"
}

This is an illustrative internal record, not the exact AWS API response. Store only the operational information needed to manage the import.

If a worker times out after submitting a job, the orchestration layer should check the stored job state before attempting another submission. This reduces accidental duplicate processing and makes recovery more predictable.

5. Track Job Status and Parse the Manifests

An import job's status describes job execution. It does not guarantee that every file imported successfully. AWS documents that a job can reach COMPLETED even when file-level validation issues occurred.

Use GetDICOMImportJob to check job status. Once the job reaches a terminal state, inspect the output location and reconcile individual file results.

The output can include:

success.ndjson for successfully imported instances

failure.ndjson for instances that could not be imported

warning.ndjson for instances imported with warnings

The results are stored in an output structure that also includes a job manifest. Each NDJSON line is a separate JSON record, so process the file line by line instead of parsing the entire file as one JSON document.

For every input file, record its outcome, image-set identifier when available, warning details, and any follow-up action. Make reconciliation idempotent so that processing the same manifest twice does not create duplicate application records or trigger downstream actions repeatedly.

The official import-job documentation explains the result structure and how HealthImaging organizes imported instances.

6. Handle Warnings, Failures, and Conflicting Data

Import results should not be reduced to a simple success-or-failure flag. A warning may indicate that an instance was imported but has a data-conformance issue or a limitation affecting later retrieval.

A practical handling policy is:

Outcome

Recommended action

Success without warnings

Record the image-set ID and continue verification

Success with warnings

Store warning codes and route for review based on impact

Failure

Capture the error, correct the source if possible, and retry under controlled conditions

Conflicting metadata

Review primary and non-primary image-set behavior before releasing data

HealthImaging organizes instances using DICOM Study, Series, and Instance UIDs. If newly imported data conflicts with existing primary image sets, HealthImaging may place the new data in non-primary image sets.

Therefore, do not assume that every imported file automatically becomes part of the expected primary image set. Build explicit rules for repeat imports, corrected studies, and data arriving from multiple source systems.

Maintain a source-to-target mapping and avoid treating filenames as unique clinical identifiers. Familiar filenames do not prove that two files represent the same image instance.

Consult the HealthImaging warning codes reference when defining warning categories and remediation procedures.

7. Verify Image Sets Before Releasing Data

A completed import job does not mean the data is ready for an application. Add a verification stage before marking a batch as available to downstream users.

Depending on the use case, checks can include:

Confirm that every expected source file has a recorded outcome.

Compare success, warning, and failure counts with the source manifest.

Confirm image-set identifiers exist for successful imports.

Retrieve metadata for representative image sets.

Retrieve selected image frames and verify that the consuming application can decode them.

Check expected Study and Series relationships.

Test permissions for authorized and unauthorized users.

Record unresolved warnings and failures for follow-up.

Choose representative studies across relevant modalities, file sizes, and transfer syntaxes. A small test import is useful, but it should not replace validation against the actual production dataset.

Pay particular attention to image decoding. HealthImaging may store lossless frames in HTJ2K or another configured format, so the viewer or downstream service must support the transfer syntaxes it receives.

For AWS HealthImaging Solutions connected to a viewer, test the complete retrieval path—not just whether the metadata API returns a response.

8. Orchestrate Large Imports for Recovery

For large archives, avoid relying on a single long-running script to upload files and wait for every job to finish. Separate the workflow into stages so failures can be diagnosed and retried independently.

A pipeline may coordinate:

Batch registration

Source-file validation

S3 upload completion

Import-job submission

Job-status tracking

Manifest parsing

Post-import verification

Exception review

Completion notifications

Persist each stage's state. If a worker stops after an import job starts, another worker should recover the job using the stored identifier. If manifest processing fails, rerun that stage without resubmitting the import.

Use bounded retries with backoff for transient errors. Do not repeatedly retry permanent validation failures without correcting the source or configuration. Account for service quotas, API throttling, and the time required to process large batches.

This staged approach makes AWS HealthImaging Solutions easier to operate because each step has a clear input, output, and recovery procedure.

9. Monitor the Pipeline and Protect Clinical Data

Monitor infrastructure metrics alongside file-level outcomes. Useful operational measurements include:

Files discovered and uploaded

Import jobs submitted and completed

Successful imports

Imports completed with warnings

Failed-file counts and error categories

Time from upload to job completion

Time spent reconciling manifests

Batches awaiting manual review

Retry counts and age of pending batches

Alert on unexpected failure rates, jobs that remain pending too long, missing output manifests, and growth in the manual-review queue.

Keep logs useful for troubleshooting without copying DICOM payloads or unnecessary patient information into general application logs. Define who can access source files, image sets, manifests, and operational dashboards.

Apply least-privilege permissions and follow your organization's retention, audit, and incident-response requirements. The exact controls depend on the deployment and applicable healthcare obligations.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Assuming COMPLETED means every file succeeded. Reconcile the output manifests and investigate failures and warnings.

Skipping DICOM compatibility checks. Verify supported SOP classes, elements, and transfer syntaxes before importing a large dataset.

Using broad IAM permissions. Scope access to the required input and output resources.

Ignoring warnings. Some warnings can affect downstream retrieval and require a documented review process.

Treating filenames as unique identifiers. Use DICOM identifiers and maintain a source-to-target mapping.

Retrying an entire batch without checking its state. Persist job identifiers and make processing stages idempotent.

Releasing data before verification. Confirm metadata, representative image frames, and application access before declaring a batch ready.

Production Readiness Checklist

Before deploying the pipeline, confirm that:

The dataset has been checked against current HealthImaging DICOM support.

S3 input and output locations are separated and access-controlled.

The import role follows least-privilege principles.

The data store's storage-format choice matches downstream requirements.

Each batch has a stable identifier and source manifest.

Import job IDs and terminal states are persisted.

Success, warning, and failure manifests are reconciled.

Duplicate and conflicting image-set behavior is understood.

Representative metadata and image-frame retrieval tests pass.

Alerts, retries, audit logs, and manual-review procedures are defined.

These controls turn a basic import script into a pipeline that can be operated, monitored, and audited over time.

How Oodles Approaches AWS HealthImaging Integration

At Oodles, we approach AWS HealthImaging Solutions as part of a complete medical imaging workflow rather than an isolated storage task. The implementation can include DICOM ingestion, S3 staging, import-job orchestration, manifest processing, secure APIs, viewer integration, monitoring, and operational tooling.

The architecture depends on the source environment, data volume, supported DICOM formats, identity model, and applications that consume the imported studies. We begin by mapping these dependencies, then define a staged workflow with clear recovery paths and verification checks.

If your team is planning a DICOM migration or building a medical imaging platform, let's connect to discuss the import workflow, integration points, and technical requirements.

title: Webhook Hub with Spring Boot: Strategy Pattern, Sub-Strategies and Collection Injection
description:
Introduction

When webhooks are received from third-party systems, technical challenges arise quickly. This article shows how to solve them with the Strategy Pattern in Spring Boot and how a second Strategy Pattern ("Sub-Strategy") represents the event level.

The code in this article comes from a real project and is reduced to the essentials. I left out configuration, error handling, the actual persistence and further details to focus on the integration of the pattern. The starting point is a production hub that receives webhooks from around 20 platforms with more than 25 million requests per month.

The starting point

The hub has a simple task: receive webhooks from third-party systems, validate and store them and, depending on the event, forward them to other systems or execute actions. The platforms differ in many ways:

  • Payload: Every platform has its own JSON format. One puts the event name in event, another in type.
  • Verification: Some sign the body, some send a token, some require a challenge response when the URL is registered.
  • Events: A platform often knows many event types (meeting.ended, recording.completed, ticket.created). Each one has different follow-up actions.
  • Follow-up actions: Some events are only stored, others trigger a download, a call to a CRM or forwarding to a data platform such as Foundry.

In addition, I had my own requirement for the architecture. It should be possible to add new platforms (strategies) and new events (sub-strategies) without changing existing code. The tests should stay simple and clear. Conversely, a strategy or sub-strategy must be removable without affecting the rest of the application.

The challenge

The obvious first approach is a controller with a switch:

switch (platformName) {
    case "zoom" -> zoomHandler.handle(body, headers);
    case "gohighlevel" -> goHighLevelHandler.handle(body, headers);
    // ... 18 more
}

This works for two platforms. With twenty platforms, it becomes a class that knows every platform and has to be changed with every modification. Within a platform, the next branch by event is added, followed by the branch by follow-up action. The result is nested conditions that are hard to understand and hard to test.

Even if every platform is in its own class, like zoomHandler above, the switch remains and still knows every platform. With the second level (event), its complexity would be very high. For this reason I decided against a switch.

The actual challenges were:

  1. Extensibility: A new platform should be a new class, not a change to existing code.
  2. Two levels of branching: First by platform, then by event within the platform.
  3. Multiple follow-up actions per event: An event can be stored, sent to a CRM and forwarded at the same time.
  4. Testability: Every platform and every follow-up action must be testable on its own.

The idea

The solution consists of two levels that use the same mechanism.

Level 1: Strategy per platform. Every platform is a strategy. The strategy stores the received raw data via a RawDataSaveService. The controller only knows an interface and a factory.

Level 2: Sub-Strategy per event. Inside the platform strategy there is a second group of strategies that react to platform and event. The sub-strategies take care of further processing: they often fetch dependent data and store it, for example in Foundry. They are not exclusive: several sub-strategies can match the same event and all of them are executed.

The connecting element: Collection Injection. Spring injects all beans of an interface type as a List<T> into the constructor. The factory therefore does not know any concrete strategy. A new class with @Component is all that is needed.

The first level: Strategies

The interface

The strategy answers two questions: "Am I responsible?" and "What do I do with the payload?".

public interface PlatformStrategyInterface {

    boolean supported(String platformName);

    void handle(String payload, HttpHeaders headers);

    ResponseEntity<String> getResponse();
}

Source: PlatformStrategyInterface

supported is the key. It replaces switch/case and moves the decision into the strategy itself.

The base class

Shared behavior moves into an abstract class. The concrete strategy only passes on its name.

public abstract class PlatformStrategyAbstract implements PlatformStrategyInterface {

    private final String platformName;

    protected PlatformStrategyAbstract(String platformName) {
        this.platformName = platformName;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean supported(String platformName) {
        return this.platformName.equals(platformName);
    }

    @Override
    public ResponseEntity<String> getResponse() {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.OK).build();
    }
}

Source: PlatformStrategyAbstract

The concrete strategies

A platform is a small class:

@Component
public class ZoomPlatformStrategy extends PlatformStrategyAbstract {

    public static final String NAME = "zoom";

    public ZoomPlatformStrategy() {
        super(NAME);
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(String payload, HttpHeaders headers) {
        // platform-specific processing
    }
}

A new platform is another class of this form. There is no central place where it has to be registered.

The factory with Collection Injection 

@Component
public class PlatformStrategyFactory {

    private final List<PlatformStrategyInterface> strategies;

    public PlatformStrategyFactory(List<PlatformStrategyInterface> strategies) {
        this.strategies = strategies;
    }

    public PlatformStrategyInterface getPlatformStrategy(String platformName) {
        for (PlatformStrategyInterface strategy : strategies) {
            if (strategy.supported(platformName)) {
                return strategy;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }
}

Source: PlatformStrategyFactory

Spring fills strategies at startup with all beans that implement PlatformStrategyInterface. The factory does not have to be changed again.

The controller

The controller is deliberately slim. It knows neither Zoom nor any other platform:

@RestController
public class WebhookPlatformStrategyController {

    private final PlatformStrategyFactory platformStrategyFactory;

    public WebhookPlatformStrategyController(PlatformStrategyFactory platformStrategyFactory) {
        this.platformStrategyFactory = platformStrategyFactory;
    }

    @PostMapping("/{platformName:[a-z]{1,16}}")
    public ResponseEntity<String> save(
        @PathVariable String platformName,
        @RequestBody(required = false) String requestBody,
        @RequestHeader HttpHeaders headers
    ) {
        PlatformStrategyInterface strategy = platformStrategyFactory.getPlatformStrategy(platformName);

        if (strategy == null) {
            return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(String.format("{\"error\":\"PlatformStrategy [%s] not found\"}", platformName));
        }

        try {
            strategy.handle(requestBody, headers);
        } catch (JacksonException e) {
            return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(String.format("{\"error\":\"PlatformStrategy [%s] with JSON error\"}", platformName));
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(String.format("{\"error\":\"PlatformStrategy [%s] handle failed\"}", platformName));
        }

        return strategy.getResponse();
    }
}

Source: WebhookPlatformStrategyController

getResponse() is intentionally part of the strategy. Some platforms expect a specific response, for example when verifying a new webhook URL with a challenge. In this case the strategy overrides the method and the controller remains unchanged.

The second level: Sub-Strategies

Up to this point it is the classic Strategy Pattern. However, the platform strategy often has to differentiate further, namely by event. Instead of adding a switch to ZoomPlatformStrategy, the same pattern is repeated one level deeper:

public interface SubStrategyInterface {

    boolean supported(String platformName, String eventName);

    void handle(String payload);
}

Source: SubStrategyInterface

The name stays deliberately generic: Sub only says that the class sits below a platform strategy and is called by it. The platform is not part of the type name because the technique does not depend on it. Here the binding happens through supported(platformName, eventName), and the event is part of the concrete class name (ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy).

Here too, the supported(...) check would be in every class. To avoid writing it again and again, there is a base class, as on the platform level. It holds a map platform -> events and answers supported(...) for all sub-strategies in the same way:

public abstract class SubStrategyAbstract implements SubStrategyInterface {

    // platform -> events the sub-strategy is responsible for
    private final Map<String, Set<String>> supported;

    // Short form: exactly one platform and one event
    protected SubStrategyAbstract(String platformName, String eventName) {
        this.supported = Map.of(platformName, Set.of(eventName));
    }

    // Multiple platforms and/or events
    protected SubStrategyAbstract(Map<String, Set<String>> supported) {
        this.supported = supported;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean supported(String platformName, String eventName) {
        return supported.getOrDefault(platformName, Set.of()).contains(eventName);
    }
}

Source: SubStrategyAbstract

A concrete sub-strategy only passes on to the base class what it is responsible for and implements handle(...):

@Component
public class ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy extends SubStrategyAbstract {

    public static final String STRATEGY = "zoom";
    public static final String EVENT = "meeting.ended";

    public ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy() {
        super(STRATEGY, EVENT);
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(String payload) {
        // follow-up action for this event
    }
}

Source: ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy

The corresponding factory differs in one important point: it returns all matching strategies, not only the first.

@Component
public class SubStrategyFactory {

    private final List<SubStrategyInterface> strategies;

    public SubStrategyFactory(List<SubStrategyInterface> strategies) {
        this.strategies = strategies;
    }

    // returns ALL matching strategies (not just the first)
    public List<SubStrategyInterface> getAllSubStrategies(String platformName, String eventName) {
        return strategies.stream()
            .filter(strategy -> strategy.supported(platformName, eventName))
            .toList();
    }
}

Source: SubStrategyFactory

Where does the event name come from?

So that the factory finds the matching sub-strategy, the platform strategy has to read the event name from the payload. This is the actual difficulty, because every platform names it differently: Zoom sends it in event, GoHighLevel in type and for other platforms it is nested on the second or third level of the JSON.

Instead of searching the JSON manually in every strategy, each platform gets a minimal DTO that only knows the event name. A common interface makes them interchangeable:

public interface EventNameInterface {

    String getEvent();
}

Source: EventNameInterface

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
public class ZoomRootDto implements EventNameInterface {

    @JsonProperty("event")
    private String event;

    @Override
    public String getEvent() {
        return event;
    }

    // setter
}

Source: ZoomRootDto

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
public class GoHighLevelRootDto implements EventNameInterface {

    // GoHighLevel sends the event name in "type"
    @JsonProperty("type")
    private String event;

    @Override
    public String getEvent() {
        return event;
    }

    // setter
}

Source: GoHighLevelRootDto

Two details make this robust:

  • @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) makes Jackson ignore all other fields. The DTO stays small and new fields of the platform do not break anything.
  • @JsonProperty("type") maps the platform-specific name to the uniform getEvent(). The difference between the platforms is encapsulated in exactly one place.

The platform strategy stores and calls the sub-strategies 

@Component
public class ZoomPlatformStrategy extends PlatformStrategyAbstract {

    public static final String NAME = "zoom";

    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;
    private final SubStrategyFactory subStrategyFactory;
    private final RawDataSaveService rawDataSaveService;

    public ZoomPlatformStrategy(
            ObjectMapper objectMapper,
            SubStrategyFactory subStrategyFactory,
            RawDataSaveService rawDataSaveService) {
        super(NAME);
        this.objectMapper = objectMapper;
        this.subStrategyFactory = subStrategyFactory;
        this.rawDataSaveService = rawDataSaveService;
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(String payload, HttpHeaders headers) {
        // Read the event name from the payload
        ZoomRootDto dto = this.objectMapper.readValue(payload, ZoomRootDto.class);

        // Store raw data
        this.rawDataSaveService.save(NAME, dto.getEvent(), payload);

        // Call all sub-strategies that support platform + event
        for (SubStrategyInterface subStrategy
                : this.subStrategyFactory.getAllSubStrategies(NAME, dto.getEvent())) {
            subStrategy.handle(payload);
        }
    }
}

Source: ZoomPlatformStrategy

The GoHighLevelPlatformStrategy looks identical except for the name and the DTO. This is intended: the difference between the platforms is in supported(...) and in the DTO, not in the flow. If the pattern is this uniform in practice, it is worth checking whether the flow can be moved into the base class and the strategy only provides the DTO (Template Method).

This has a side effect that is very useful in practice: a sub-strategy can be cross-platform. It does not have to belong to one platform. The platform strategy does not know anything about it.

Example: Multiple sub-strategies for the same event

In addition to the ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy, another action should be executed for meeting.ended (and meeting.started), for example forwarding to Foundry. This is a separate class. ZoomPlatformStrategy and ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy remain unchanged. Because it covers several events, it uses the constructor with the map:

@Component
public class FoundrySubStrategy extends SubStrategyAbstract {

    // platform -> events this sub-strategy is responsible for
    private static final Map<String, Set<String>> SUPPORTED = Map.of(
        "zoom", Set.of("meeting.ended", "meeting.started")
    );

    public FoundrySubStrategy() {
        super(SUPPORTED);
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(String payload) {
        // action for this event
    }
}

Source: FoundrySubStrategy

supported(...) is data-driven instead of hard-coded: which platforms and events are covered is defined in the map. Another platform or event is an additional entry, the check logic in the base class remains the same. Unknown platforms return false via getOrDefault.

If meeting.ended is received, both sub-strategies match. getAllSubStrategies("zoom", "meeting.ended") returns both and ZoomPlatformStrategy calls each one:

ZoomPlatformStrategy.handle(payload)
   ├─ rawDataSaveService.save("zoom", "meeting.ended", payload)
   └─ getAllSubStrategies("zoom", "meeting.ended")
        ├─► ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy.handle(payload)
        └─► FoundrySubStrategy.handle(payload)

That there is no order and a sub-strategy must not influence another is the prerequisite for this (see Pitfalls).

What worked well

New platforms are additive changes. A class is added. No existing class is changed, which reduces the risk of regressions.

Follow-up actions are decoupled. Storing, forwarding to the CRM, downloading a file: each of these is its own sub-strategy. They can be tested individually, added and removed.

Tests are small. A strategy can be instantiated without a Spring context:

class ZoomMeetingEndedStrategyTest {

    private final ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy strategy = new ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy();

    @Test
    void test_supported() {
        assertTrue(this.strategy.supported("zoom", "meeting.ended"));
        assertFalse(this.strategy.supported("zoom", "meeting.started"));
        assertFalse(this.strategy.supported("gohighlevel", "meeting.ended"));
    }

    // Further tests
}

The platform strategy is tested with a mocked SubStrategyFactory and a mocked RawDataSaveService. This also covers reading the event name, including the platform-specific property, and storing the raw data:

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class ZoomPlatformStrategyTest {

    @Mock
    private SubStrategyFactory subStrategyFactoryMock;

    @Mock
    private RawDataSaveService rawDataSaveServiceMock;

    @Mock
    private SubStrategyInterface subStrategy1;

    @Mock
    private SubStrategyInterface subStrategy2;

    private ZoomPlatformStrategy strategy;

    @BeforeEach
    void beforeEach() {
        this.strategy = new ZoomPlatformStrategy(new ObjectMapper(), this.subStrategyFactoryMock, this.rawDataSaveServiceMock);
    }

    @Test
    void test_handle_calls_all_sub_strategies() {
        when(this.subStrategyFactoryMock.getAllSubStrategies("zoom", "meeting.ended"))
            .thenReturn(List.of(this.subStrategy1, this.subStrategy2));

        String payload = "{\"event\":\"meeting.ended\",\"payload\":{}}";

        this.strategy.handle(payload, new HttpHeaders());

        verify(this.subStrategy1, times(1)).handle(payload);
        verify(this.subStrategy2, times(1)).handle(payload);
    }

    @Test
    void test_handle_stores_raw_data() {
        when(this.subStrategyFactoryMock.getAllSubStrategies("zoom", "meeting.ended")).thenReturn(List.of());

        String payload = "{\"event\":\"meeting.ended\",\"payload\":{}}";

        this.strategy.handle(payload, new HttpHeaders());

        verify(this.rawDataSaveServiceMock, times(1)).save("zoom", "meeting.ended", payload);
    }
}

The factories are tested with a manually created list:

class PlatformStrategyFactoryTest {

    private PlatformStrategyFactory strategyFactory;

    @BeforeEach
    void beforeEach() {
        this.strategyFactory = new PlatformStrategyFactory(List.of(new TestStrategyDummy()));
    }

    @Test
    void test_getPlatformStrategy() {
        assertInstanceOf(TestStrategyDummy.class, this.strategyFactory.getPlatformStrategy("foobar"));
    }

    @Test
    void test_getPlatformStrategy_not_found() {
        assertNull(this.strategyFactory.getPlatformStrategy("dummy"));
    }
}

For the WebhookPlatformStrategyControllerTest a @WebMvcTest with a mocked factory is sufficient. It only tests the HTTP behavior (200, 400, 404, 500) and whether the factory is called.

The pitfalls

The pattern is simple, but in production there were a few things that are good to know in advance.

The base class becomes a god object

In practice, more and more moved into PlatformStrategyAbstract: verification, persistence, error handling, parsing, several overloaded handle methods. As a result, concrete strategies got five or six constructor parameters that they only pass through.

Solution: Keep the base class small (name and supported). Cross-cutting concerns like verification and persistence belong in their own services or interfaces. Composition is better than inheritance here.

Order is not guaranteed

The List<T> from Collection Injection has no defined order. This is not a problem as long as strategies are independent. As soon as a sub-strategy needs the result of another, it becomes a bug.

Solution: Keep strategies independent. If an order is required, use @Order or Ordered and document it.

Errors in a sub-strategy

If three sub-strategies run one after another and the second throws an exception, the question is: Does the third still run? If the webhook is answered with a 500 and repeated by the sender, the first and third run twice.

Solution: Decide deliberately. Either each sub-strategy catches and logs its own errors, or the payload is persisted first and the follow-up actions run asynchronously via a queue with retry. In production, the latter has partly proven itself: store first, then process.

When the pattern is worthwhile, and when not

For two platforms, a switch is simpler and more straightforward. The pattern is worthwhile when

  • the number of variants grows and new variants are added regularly,
  • variants have different dependencies (their own HTTP client, their own repositories),
  • several teams or people work on different variants,
  • every variant should be testable on its own.

It is less worthwhile when there are two or three fixed variants that never change. In this case an enum map or a switch is easier to read.

Conclusion

  • Strategy Pattern replaces the central switch: every platform decides for itself whether it is responsible (supported).
  • Collection Injection (List<PlatformStrategyInterface>) makes the factory immutable. New strategies register themselves with @Component.
  • Sub-Strategies repeat the pattern on the event level. Multiple matches are allowed there and every match is an independent follow-up action.
  • The pitfalls are not in the pattern itself, but around it: a bloated base class, unclear order and error handling with multiple sub-strategies.

Full example on GitHub

title: Dimension-Free Scaling Laws for Size Generalization: An Exponential Separation
description:
arXiv:2610.19279v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern machine learning models increasingly operate on variable-size structured data, such as sets and graphs. A central requirement is \emph{size generalization}: the ability of a model trained on inputs of one size to generalize to inputs of a different, potentially much larger, size. Classical statistical learning theory, however, primarily considers fixed input domains, and its guarantees often deteriorate with input dimension. Although extensive work has established when models on sets and graphs can be transferred across input sizes, such results do not characterize the statistical cost of doing so: the sample complexity of size generalization, and its relationship to classical in-domain learning, remain largely unknown. We develop a statistical learning theory of size generalization and establish a sharp exponential separation in sample complexity. Letting $n$ denote the number of training samples, we show that polynomial source decay is insufficient for efficient size generalization: while it yields error $n^{-\Theta(1)}$ and hence polynomial sample complexity for in-domain learning, size-generalization error decays only as $(\log n)^{-\Theta(1)}$, yielding an exponential separation. Thus, polynomial in-domain sample complexity can become exponential across sizes. We then identify an exponential source condition under which size generalization achieves error $n^{-\Theta(1)}$, recovering polynomial sample complexity. These guarantees are independent of input dimension and depend only on the number of training samples, yielding dimension-free scaling laws. We also provide matching minimax lower bounds, establishing optimality. To our knowledge, this work provides the first dimension-free minimax theory of size generalization and a rigorous characterization of when, and at what statistical cost, learning can transfer across input sizes.
