title: Understanding Paint Containment and Composite Layers for Smooth Animations
description:
You’re building a slick UI with smooth animations. You add a subtle transform here, a fade there. But then, boom , your animations stutter. Frames drop, interactions feel sluggish, and your user experience tanks.

You tweak your CSS, add will-change: transform, and suddenly things get smoother. But why? What actually happens under the hood when you add that mysterious CSS property? Or when you add contain: paint? How do those tiny CSS hints help the browser decide to offload rendering work to the GPU?

Let me share what I learned digging into paint containment and compositing layers , the quiet heroes behind buttery smooth animations and frustrating jank.

The moment you realize something’s wrong

I was working on a dashboard with complex nested components and animations. Some animations were jittery, especially when scrolling or interacting with other UI parts.

Opening Chrome DevTools, I checked the Performance tab and noticed a lot of layout and paint work every frame. The GPU wasn’t getting a break.

I suspected compositing layers weren’t being created smartly. If each animated element had its own layer, the browser could push rasterization to the GPU, freeing up the CPU and enabling smooth 60fps animations.

But how does the browser decide what gets its own compositing layer?

What is a compositing layer anyway?

Imagine the browser’s rendering pipeline like an assembly line:

  1. Style: The browser figures out what styles apply to each element.
  2. Layout: Positions and sizes are computed.
  3. Paint: Elements are drawn into bitmaps.
  4. Composite: These bitmaps (layers) are combined to produce the final image.

Most elements are painted into a shared bitmap. But some elements get their own bitmap , a compositing layer. This bitmap can be handed off to the GPU to be transformed or animated independently without repainting the entire page.

When a layer is created, animations like transforms or opacity changes on that layer become super cheap , the GPU just moves or blends that bitmap.

Paint containment: telling the browser to isolate painting

You can hint to the browser when an element should get its own compositing layer by using CSS containment. The contain property lets you declare what aspects of rendering are confined to a subtree.

contain: paint means “hey browser, this element and its subtree won’t affect anything outside their bounding box when painting.”

Why does this matter? Because if the browser knows an element is paint-contained, it can safely create a compositing layer for it. Changes inside won’t force repaints outside.

Consider this example:

.card {
  contain: paint;
  will-change: transform;
}

Here, .card is paint-contained and hints it will be transformed. The browser can create a separate layer for .card and push its rendering work to the GPU.

How paint containment creates layers under the hood

Under the hood, the browser’s rendering engine tracks containment properties during the paint phase.

  • When it hits an element with contain: paint, it creates a new paint layer.
  • This layer is a bitmap snapshot of that subtree.
  • Because it’s isolated, the browser knows repainting this layer won’t affect siblings or ancestors.
  • The compositor can now handle that layer independently.

This is a big win for animations.

If you animate a transform on that element, the browser only needs to update the layer’s position on screen , no repaint or re-layout.

Without containment, the browser might have to repaint a large part of the page every frame.

The GPU angle: why compositing layers matter

Compositing layers are the boundary between CPU-bound painting and GPU-accelerated compositing.

Your browser’s GPU can move, scale, rotate, or fade whole layers very efficiently.

But creating too many layers is also bad , each layer consumes GPU memory and overhead.

The browser tries to balance:

  • Too few layers: More repaint work on CPU, animations jank.
  • Too many layers: GPU memory pressure, possible thrashing.

You can influence this balance with contain, will-change, and other CSS properties.

Debugging paint containment and layers in DevTools

If you suspect your animations are slow due to missing layers, here’s how to check:

  1. Layers panel in Chrome DevTools:

    • Open DevTools > More Tools > Layers.
    • You’ll see a visual map of compositing layers.
    • Animated elements should have their own layers.

  2. Rendering tab > Paint flashing:

    • Enable "Paint flashing" to see what parts of the page repaint during interactions.
    • If large areas repaint during a transform animation, you lack proper containment.

  3. Performance tab:

    • Record a profile while animating.
    • Look for "Recalculate Style" and "Paint" tasks.
    • Excessive painting per frame hints at missing layers.

Practical tips to avoid jank

  • Use contain: paint or contain: layout paint on animated elements or their parents when possible.
  • Add will-change: transform (or whatever property you animate) to hint the browser early.
  • Avoid animating properties that force layout or paint (like width, height, top).
  • Keep your layer tree manageable: don’t paint-contain everything blindly.
  • Test on real devices with DevTools profiling.

Real-world gotchas

  • Not all browsers support all containment types equally.
  • Overusing will-change can backfire and cause memory bloat.
  • Complex shadow DOM or web components might not behave as expected without explicit containment.
  • Sometimes, a parent’s overflow or opacity settings affect layer creation unexpectedly.

Why understanding this matters

When you grasp how paint containment and compositing layers work, you can:

  • Write CSS that helps the browser optimize rendering.
  • Debug tricky animation jank by spotting missing layers.
  • Balance GPU memory usage and CPU load.
  • Build smoother, more responsive UIs.

Next time your animation stutters, pause and inspect your layers. Your GPU will thank you.

Helpful learning resources

  • MDN Web Docs
  • web.dev performance guidance
  • OpenAI developer resources Originally published at Under The Hood. Get the next deep dive in your inbox: subscribe to Under The Hood.

title: Dataset-Level Regularization for Joint-Embedding Self-Supervised Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.20158v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised joint embedding learning aligns representations of augmented views while regularizing their distribution to prevent collapse. Regularization aims to shape the overall representation distribution, but most joint embedding methods restrict its computation to the active minibatch. We propose out-of-batch regularization, which maintains a dataset-level state in CPU memory and uses globally constructed per-instance targets during minibatch training. Evaluated on natural images and biomedical datasets, these anchors approximate the full-dataset regularization gradient more faithfully than conventional minibatch estimation at small batch sizes. Applications to contrastive (SimCLR) and non-contrastive (SIGReg) approaches show consistent improvement over the corresponding in-batch objectives for image classification, minority-class performance under controlled imbalance, instance retrieval, and continued self-supervised pretraining, with the largest gains at small batch sizes. These results suggest that dataset-level regularization can be decoupled from minibatch optimization, making batch size an optimization choice that does not affect the geometry of the regularizer.

title: Your Pixel-Perfect Tests Have a Trust Problem
description:
Someone updates the product page. The visual test reports 47 differences.

Most of them are timestamps, an animated banner, and a font rendering change. One is a Buy button that moved below the fold on a common laptop size.

Guess which issue gets lost in the noise.

Visual regression testing sounds beautifully simple: take a screenshot, compare it with yesterday's screenshot, flag what changed. But once you use it on a real product, you discover that detecting differences is the easy part.

Deciding which differences deserve attention is the job.

A diff is not a bug report

A screenshot comparison can tell you that pixels changed. It generally cannot, by itself, tell you whether the change was intentional, harmless, or a customer-facing problem.

Think about a page with live prices or stock levels. A strict pixel comparison may generate a new difference on every run even when the interface is behaving correctly.

Now imagine the opposite: the page renders almost identically, but an important button doesn't respond to a click. The visual check may happily pass.

These tests need context. What content was dynamic? Which viewport and browser did you use? What build produced the baseline? Who approved it, and why?

This benchmark plan for visual platforms gets specific about dynamic-content tolerance, review workflow, and keeping evidence. Those are the questions I'd ask before buying another clever image diff tool.

The baseline is a decision, not a file

A baseline isn't automatically correct because it was approved last Tuesday.

I've seen teams design processes where the easiest way to clear a red build is to click "Accept all changes." That's a dangerous habit. It turns the comparison system into a machine for normalizing whatever the latest build happened to render.

A useful review should make it easy to answer:

  • Which component actually changed?
  • Was the change linked to a known product decision?
  • Did the difference affect a critical workflow?
  • Can reviewers inspect the old and new images side by side?
  • Will the decision still make sense to someone investigating it next month?

You can use a hosted review workflow or keep baselines close to your Git history. Both have benefits. The Katalon Visual Testing vs Reg-suit comparison frames that tradeoff as managed review versus Git-first control. It's a more useful debate than asking which product takes the sharpest screenshot.

The workflow that makes good review decisions easiest is the one I'd favor.

Your screenshots have an expiration date

Suppose a release introduces a visual defect. Two weeks later, customer support forwards a complaint. The responsible engineer asks for the original screenshot and browser details.

They're gone. The CI job expired its artifacts after seven days.

Now the team has to reconstruct a browser state that may no longer exist. The app has changed. The data has changed. The third-party content has changed.

Evidence retention sounds like paperwork until you need yesterday's evidence to explain today's bug.

You don't necessarily need to keep every screenshot forever. But important failed runs should retain enough context to support a useful investigation: baseline and actual images, diff, build ID, browser and viewport, test data identifiers where appropriate, and the approval history.

It's worth deciding retention rules deliberately instead of inheriting whatever your CI provider does by default.

Test output should be readable by someone who didn't write the test

Now for the part I think gets ignored most often: handing a finding to another human.

"Visual difference detected" is a notification. It isn't a reproducible bug report.

A stronger report says something like:

On the checkout page, at 1366 × 768 in Chrome, the order summary overlaps the payment button after the shipping estimate loads. Seen on build checkout-1842. Expected: both sections remain visible and independently clickable. Attached: before image, after image, diff, and reproduction steps.

No mystery. No digging through raw logs to discover what page failed. No requirement that the reader know the testing platform's private vocabulary.

This benchmark plan for turning raw findings into reproducible reports measures an outcome many teams forget to track: how quickly evidence becomes something actionable.

That's especially important as AI-assisted testing discovers more issues. Discovering ten times as many potential problems won't help if people spend ten times as long interpreting them.

I'd measure review effort before counting diffs

If I were improving a visual testing process, I wouldn't start with "How many differences did we catch this month?"

I'd start with three smaller questions. How many alerts were dismissed as harmless? How long did a reviewer spend understanding an alert? How often did someone approve a baseline only to find out later that it contained a defect?

Those answers tell you whether the system helps the team notice real problems or merely gives the team another inbox.

The goal is not a perfectly clean diff report. It's confidence that when a meaningful visual regression happens, the team can recognize it, explain it, and fix it without conducting an archaeological dig through last week's CI jobs.

title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.19686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00-4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20-6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89-4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.

title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection
description:
arXiv:2610.18881v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

title: Single-Sample Decoding of a Two-Layer Sound-Word Canvas Model for Thai Klon Pad
description:
arXiv:2610.14980v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a generator of Thai klon pad verse, one stanza from a short topic, and evaluate it against human verse on held-out topics. The generator is a masked language model initialised from WangchanBERTa over a fixed canvas with two layers: a sound layer of pronounced syllables, where rhyme, tone and syllable count are enforced as hard masks, and a word layer of whole words, so that no word is cut into written pieces. Decoding commits one cell at a time and samples at temperature 0.4; one sample is drawn per topic, with no selection, reranking or repair. On 78 held-out topics never used in development, judged by three independent runs of a frozen LLM judge in the same pools as the human stanzas from which the topics were written, 70.5% of the generated stanzas pass form, lexical cleanness of all four lines and topic alignment together, against 76.9% for the human stanzas (difference -6.4 points, 95% CI [-19.2, +6.4]). Cleanness is level with human (85.9% vs. 87.2%), and the stanzas pass form and cleanness together slightly more often than the human ones (+3.8 points, [-6.4, +14.1]); the difference lies in alignment (84.6% vs. 91.0%), on topics that were written from the human stanzas. The low temperature matters: at higher temperatures the same model passes clearly fewer of the same topics, because lexical errors lie in the model's lower-probability choices; sharpening the sampling distribution removes most of them, at a cost in vocabulary (7.5% rare words against 16.5% in the human stanzas) and diversity. The pre-registered target, all-three within 5 points of human, is missed by 1.4 points. KlonSuphap-LM, the only public klon pad generator we know of, passes none of the 78 held-out topics when judged in separate pools together with the method's and the human stanzas (form 19.2%, cleanness 3.8%).

title: Optimistic Locking vs. Pessimistic Locking — Handling Concurrent Updates in SQL Databases
description:
What happens when two users try to update the same database row at exactly the same time? Without proper concurrency control, one update can silently overwrite the other, leading to inconsistent or incorrect data (the classic lost update problem). SQL databases solve this with two main concurrency control strategies: Optimistic Locking and Pessimistic Locking.

✅ Optimistic Locking (Version-Based)

Instead of locking the row up front, each transaction reads the current version number along with the data. When updating, the database verifies the version hasn't changed since it was read:

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = ?, version = version + 1
WHERE id = ? AND version = 5;

If another transaction already modified the row (and bumped the version), this UPDATE affects zero rows — the version check fails immediately, and the application detects the conflict via the affected-row count and can retry.

Key characteristics:

  • ✔ No row-level lock held while "thinking" — the row stays fully available to others.
  • ✔ Better throughput for read-heavy systems, since nothing blocks concurrent readers/writers.
  • ✔ Conflicts are detected at UPDATE time, not up front.
  • ✔ The application is responsible for retrying on failure (re-read the row, reapply the change, try again).

Mental model: "Try first. If someone already changed the data, fail fast and retry."

🔒 Pessimistic Locking (Row-Level Lock)

Before modifying data, the transaction explicitly locks the row so no one else can touch it:

SELECT * FROM accounts
WHERE id = 101
FOR UPDATE;

While one transaction holds the lock:

  • Other transactions requesting the same row wait in a queue rather than failing.
  • They execute only after the lock is released (commit/rollback).
  • No version conflict ever occurs, because updates to that row are forced to happen sequentially.

Key characteristics:

  • ✔ Row locked immediately — guarantees exclusive access for the duration of the transaction.
  • ✔ Other requests wait instead of failing outright.
  • ✔ Strong consistency, even under heavy contention on the same rows.
  • ✔ Lower concurrency (more waiting/blocking) but highly predictable execution order.

Mental model: "Wait your turn before making changes."

📌 When Should You Use Each?

Choose Optimistic Locking when:

  • Conflicts are rare.
  • The application is read-heavy.
  • High throughput matters more than avoiding occasional retries.
  • Retries are acceptable at the application layer.

Examples: e-commerce product catalogs, user profiles, content management systems.

Choose Pessimistic Locking when:

  • Data integrity is critical and lost updates are unacceptable.
  • Many users frequently update the same records (high contention).
  • Predictable, sequential execution is more valuable than raw throughput.

Examples: banking transactions, digital wallets, inventory management, ticket booking systems.

💡 Key Takeaway

There isn't a universally "better" approach. The right choice depends on your application's contention level, consistency requirements, throughput goals, and user experience. Understanding this trade-off is essential for designing scalable, reliable, high-performance backend systems — it's a decision made per use case (or even per table/operation), not a single global choice for the whole system.

In practice, each strategy carries a distinct failure mode worth watching for in production:
retry storms under optimistic locking when contention is higher than expected, and lock contention or deadlocks under pessimistic locking when transactions hold locks longer than intended.

title: Running Hermes Agent on Cursor and Google Antigravity Without Third-Party Proxies
description:
Most developers using autonomous agent harnesses like Hermes Agent already have developer subscriptions: Cursor Pro for coding and Google Antigravity for Gemini/Claude access. But pointing an external agent at them usually means either paying twice for metered API keys, or piping session tokens through third-party reverse proxies.

I built two open-source plugins that drive the official local CLIs instead:

  • hermes-antigravity-oauth (wraps Google's agy CLI)
  • hermes-cursor-acp (wraps Cursor's agent acp server)

Here is how both work and the engineering problems they solve.

1. Cursor ACP: Tool Fencing and Call Recovery

Cursor doesn't expose a chat completions API, but the Cursor CLI includes an ACP server (agent acp).

Connecting Hermes to it required three fixes:

A. The Security Fence

Cursor's CLI has native tools (Read, Write, Shell, WebFetch). When running an external agent harness, Hermes must control all file and shell execution under its own approval rules.

Without intervention, Cursor's native Read can read any file on disk. The plugin creates a private workspace at $HERMES_HOME/cache/cursor-acp-workspace and rewrites .cursor/cli.json every turn:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [],
    "deny": [
      "Read(**)", "Read(/**)", "Write(**)", "Write(/**)",
      "Shell(*)", "WebFetch(*)", "Mcp(*:*)"
    ]
  }
}

This forces Cursor to refuse its internal tools and emit tool calls through Hermes instead.

B. Tool-Call Parser Fixes

Hermes injects tool schemas into the prompt and expects <tool_call>{...}</tool_call> blocks in the output. Standard regex parsers break when:

  1. The model mentions <tool_call> in conversational prose before the actual block.
  2. The model outputs a flat {"name": "...", "arguments": {...}} object instead of a nested function call.

Our parser scans each tag, decodes JSON using raw_decode, and normalizes both shapes so Composer and GPT calls execute reliably.

C. Compression Preservation

Cursor returns no token counts over ACP. If a plugin reports 0 tokens, Hermes assumes real usage has completed and stops proactive compression. Emitting usage=None tells Hermes the provider is usage-less, preserving context compression.

2. Antigravity OAuth: Keychain and Claude Tool Bridging

For Google Antigravity, hermes-antigravity-oauth talks to the agy binary:

  • No Token Handling: The plugin never touches Google credentials. hermes auth add antigravity-oauth runs agy's browser sign-in, and credentials remain in the OS Keychain.
  • SOUL.md Delivery: The Hermes persona is written to GEMINI.md in the private workspace, which agy respects as top-level instructions.
  • Claude Native Tool Re-routing: Claude models on Antigravity often emit native run_command or view_file calls. The plugin intercepts these and re-issues them as Hermes terminal and read_file commands, preserving user approvals.

3. One-Command Setup

Both plugins ship with npx installers:

# Cursor models
npx hermes-cursor-acp
hermes --provider cursor -m claude-opus-5-5

# Google Antigravity models
npx hermes-antigravity-oauth
hermes --provider antigravity-oauth -m gemini-3.8-flash

Links & Provenance

Both are MIT licensed, covered by CI unit tests, and published to npm with GitHub Actions OIDC provenance:

  • hermes-cursor-acp: GitHub · npm · Catalog PR #138835
  • hermes-antigravity-oauth: GitHub · npm · Catalog PR #126041

title: Accessibility in React: What Most Developers Skip
description:
Most React accessibility guides tell you to add alt text to images and call it done. That's table stakes. The gaps that actually hurt users with disabilities — and quietly fail WCAG 2.1 AA — are in the dynamic, interactive parts that every modern React app is built on.

This covers focus management, keyboard navigation, ARIA live regions, and a real screen reader testing workflow. Code examples are TypeScript.

Why alt text isn't enough

Static content is easy. Screen readers handle it fine without any developer intervention. The problems start the moment your UI changes without a page reload — a modal opens, a route changes, a toast fires, a combobox filters. At that point, keyboard and screen reader users are on their own unless you handle it explicitly.

The four areas below are where React apps consistently fail audits.

1. Focus management after dynamic content changes

Modals

When a modal opens, focus must move into it. When it closes, focus must return to the trigger element. Neither happens automatically.

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

interface ModalProps {
  isOpen: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
  triggerRef: React.RefObject<HTMLButtonElement>;
  children: React.ReactNode;
}

export function Modal({ isOpen, onClose, triggerRef, children }: ModalProps) {
  const dialogRef = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (isOpen) {
      dialogRef.current?.showModal();
      // Focus moves to the first focusable element inside
      const firstFocusable = dialogRef.current?.querySelector<HTMLElement>(
        'button, [href], input, select, textarea, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])'
      );
      firstFocusable?.focus();
    } else {
      dialogRef.current?.close();
      // Return focus to the element that opened the modal
      triggerRef.current?.focus();
    }
  }, [isOpen, triggerRef]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={dialogRef} onClose={onClose}>
      {children}
    </dialog>
  );
}

Use the native <dialog> element. It handles focus trapping and Escape to close by default, and its accessibility semantics are built in. Don't build a <div role="dialog"> unless you have a specific reason — you'll spend twice the effort reproducing what <dialog> gives you for free.

Route changes

Single-page apps are invisible to screen readers on navigation unless you tell them something changed. The browser doesn't announce route transitions the way it announces full page loads.

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { useLocation } from 'react-router-dom';

export function RouteAnnouncer() {
  const location = useLocation();
  const announcerRef = useRef<HTMLParagraphElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (announcerRef.current) {
      // Small delay lets the new page content render first
      setTimeout(() => {
        const pageTitle = document.title;
        if (announcerRef.current) {
          announcerRef.current.textContent = `Navigated to ${pageTitle}`;
        }
      }, 100);
    }
  }, [location.pathname]);

  return (
    <p
      ref={announcerRef}
      aria-live="polite"
      aria-atomic="true"
      className="sr-only"
    />
  );
}

Mount this once at the app root. Every route change announces the new page title to screen reader users.

2. Keyboard navigation in custom components

The browser handles keyboard navigation for native elements (<button>, <a>, <input>). The moment you build a custom interactive widget — a combobox, a tab panel, a date picker — you own the keyboard contract entirely.

Tabs (ARIA pattern)

The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide defines the keyboard contract for tabs: Arrow keys move between tabs, Tab moves into the panel, Home/End jump to first/last tab.

import { useState, useRef, KeyboardEvent } from 'react';

interface Tab {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  content: React.ReactNode;
}

interface TabPanelProps {
  tabs: Tab[];
}

export function TabPanel({ tabs }: TabPanelProps) {
  const [activeIndex, setActiveIndex] = useState(0);
  const tabRefs = useRef<(HTMLButtonElement | null)[]>([]);

  function handleKeyDown(e: KeyboardEvent<HTMLButtonElement>, index: number) {
    let nextIndex = index;

    switch (e.key) {
      case 'ArrowRight':
        nextIndex = (index + 1) % tabs.length;
        break;
      case 'ArrowLeft':
        nextIndex = (index - 1 + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
        break;
      case 'Home':
        nextIndex = 0;
        break;
      case 'End':
        nextIndex = tabs.length - 1;
        break;
      default:
        return;
    }

    e.preventDefault();
    setActiveIndex(nextIndex);
    tabRefs.current[nextIndex]?.focus();
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <div role="tablist" aria-label="Content sections">
        {tabs.map((tab, index) => (
          <button
            key={tab.id}
            ref={el => { tabRefs.current[index] = el; }}
            role="tab"
            aria-selected={index === activeIndex}
            aria-controls={`panel-${tab.id}`}
            id={`tab-${tab.id}`}
            tabIndex={index === activeIndex ? 0 : -1}
            onClick={() => setActiveIndex(index)}
            onKeyDown={e => handleKeyDown(e, index)}
          >
            {tab.label}
          </button>
        ))}
      </div>
      {tabs.map((tab, index) => (
        <div
          key={tab.id}
          role="tabpanel"
          id={`panel-${tab.id}`}
          aria-labelledby={`tab-${tab.id}`}
          hidden={index !== activeIndex}
        >
          {tab.content}
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

The tabIndex={-1} on inactive tabs is critical. It means Tab lands on the active tab only — from there, Arrow keys move between tabs and Tab moves into the panel. Without this, keyboard users tab through every tab before reaching the content.

3. ARIA live regions — when to use them and when not to

Live regions announce content changes to screen readers without moving focus. They're useful for status updates (form validation, search results count, toast notifications). They're overused everywhere else.

A reusable announcer 

import { createContext, useCallback, useContext, useState, type ReactNode } from 'react';

type Politeness = 'polite' | 'assertive';

interface AnnouncerContextValue {
  announce: (message: string, politeness?: Politeness) => void;
}

const AnnouncerContext = createContext<AnnouncerContextValue | null>(null);

export function AnnouncerProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [politeMessage, setPoliteMessage] = useState('');
  const [assertiveMessage, setAssertiveMessage] = useState('');

  const announce = useCallback((message: string, politeness: Politeness = 'polite') => {
    // Clearing first lets the same message announce twice in a row
    if (politeness === 'assertive') {
      setAssertiveMessage('');
      setTimeout(() => setAssertiveMessage(message), 50);
    } else {
      setPoliteMessage('');
      setTimeout(() => setPoliteMessage(message), 50);
    }
  }, []);

  return (
    <AnnouncerContext.Provider value={{ announce }}>
      {children}
      <div className="sr-only">
        <p aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">{politeMessage}</p>
        <p aria-live="assertive" aria-atomic="true">{assertiveMessage}</p>
      </div>
    </AnnouncerContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useAnnouncer() {
  const context = useContext(AnnouncerContext);
  if (!context) throw new Error('useAnnouncer must be used within AnnouncerProvider');
  return context;
}

Use polite for non-urgent updates (search results loaded, item added to cart). Use assertive only for errors that require immediate action — it interrupts whatever the screen reader is saying.

When NOT to use live regions:

  • Don't put them on content that already gets focus (error messages next to inputs — just move focus to the error or use aria-describedby)
  • Don't use them for decorative animations or loading spinners with no meaningful status
  • Don't nest live regions — only the outermost one fires

4. Screen reader testing workflow

Browser DevTools axe checks catch about 30% of real accessibility issues. The rest only surface with a screen reader. Here's a minimal workflow that catches the critical gaps.

Tools:

  • NVDA (free) + Chrome on Windows
  • VoiceOver (built-in) + Safari on macOS/iOS

What to test manually:

  • Tab through every interactive element on the page. Confirm focus order is logical and focus is always visible.
  • Open every modal, drawer, and dropdown with the keyboard. Confirm focus moves in, is trapped, and returns on close.
  • Navigate every custom widget (tabs, combobox, date picker) using only arrow keys and Tab. Confirm the keyboard contract matches the ARIA pattern.
  • Trigger every dynamic state change (form error, toast, search results). Confirm the screen reader announces it.
  • Navigate by headings (NVDA: H key, VoiceOver: Control+Option+Command+H). Confirm the heading structure makes sense out of context.

Chrome DevTools shortcut: Accessibility tree panel (Elements → Accessibility tab) shows you exactly what the screen reader sees for any element. Use it before reaching for a screen reader to catch obvious issues faster.

Practical audit checklist

Run through this before every release that touches interactive UI:

  • All modals use <dialog> or have focus trap + Escape handler
  • Focus returns to trigger element when modal/drawer closes
  • Route changes announce the new page title
  • Custom widgets implement the correct ARIA keyboard pattern
  • tabIndex={-1} on all inactive items in composite widgets (tabs, listbox, menu)
  • Live regions use polite by default; assertive only for blocking errors
  • No nested live regions
  • Every interactive element reachable and operable by keyboard alone
  • Visible focus indicator on every focusable element (not removed by outline: none without a replacement)
  • Heading hierarchy: one <h1>, logical <h2>/<h3> nesting, no skipped levels
  • Form inputs have associated <label> elements (not just placeholder text)
  • Error messages linked to inputs via aria-describedby
  • Tested with NVDA+Chrome or VoiceOver+Safari at least once per release

Key takeaways

  • Static content is the easy part. Dynamic UI — modals, route changes, toasts, custom widgets — is where React apps fail screen reader users.
  • Use <dialog> for modals. It handles focus trap and Escape for free.
  • Every custom interactive widget needs an explicit keyboard contract matching the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide pattern.
  • ARIA live regions announce changes without moving focus — use polite by default, assertive only for blocking errors.
  • A single AnnouncerProvider at the app root handles all live region announcements cleanly.
  • axe DevTools catches ~30% of real issues. Manual screen reader testing with NVDA or VoiceOver is non-negotiable before release.

Originally published at https://suprabhat-dev.com/blog/accessibility-in-react-what-developers-skip/

title: Adaptive Observation Control for Active Visual Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.19624v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual recognition models usually process a fixed view under a fixed computation budget, although images often benefit from different scales and amounts of spatial evidence. Active vision can adapt by observing a coarse scene and then selecting informative fixations, but the public AdaptiveNN-DeiT-S pipeline still fixes both field of view and observation count. We extend this fixed-step recognizer with a controllable observation interface that adapts both the field of view and the number of fixations to the input. Specifically, the model predicts a per-fixation scale that sets its field of view, refines each selected crop with optional scale-gated foveation and a residual high-resolution detail-token branch, and uses label-grounded stop heads for input-dependent early termination. Experiments across fine-grained benchmarks, full ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-A/R-derived classification splits show that the interface remains competitive with fixed-step references while exposing a controllable observation budget. The same checkpoint enables threshold-controlled accuracy-compute trade-offs without per-threshold retraining. On sequential ImageNet-1K, the learned stop rule outperforms fixed-step truncation of the same checkpoint, sustaining 81.9% top-1 using 2.45 of the four focus steps and exceeding three-step truncation at lower cost. On each benchmark, a variant combining scale control and detail-token fusion achieves the highest accuracy among the tested component-added non-exit variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/LI-Dikai.

title: A Gradient-Regularized Deep Learning Method for Restoring Image in Myopic Vision
description:
arXiv:2610.19218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Myopic vision degrades the quality of human vision due to spherical eye defocus aberrations that impair the perception of fine spatial details. To address this limitation, this work proposes a deep learning-based approach to computationally design transformed images that allow individuals with myopia in fixed distance to perceive scenes with enhanced clarity. The method trains a neural network to counteract defocus aberrations modeled using the second-order Zernike polynomial $Z_2^0$. The approach employs a U-Net architecture trained with a loss function combining reconstruction error minimization with spatial difference structural preservation through $\ell_1$ regularization. Training is carried out exclusively on the KITTI dataset, while testing is performed on DIV2K and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating generalization across diverse image distributions. Under myopic conditions modeled by $Z_2^0$, baseline performance shows visual degradation with PSNR values ranging from 19.47 to 27.42 dB across datasets and severity levels. The proposed gradient-regularized method achieves consistent improvements, delivering PSNR gains ranging from 1.48 to 7.34 dB and significantly lower perceptual compared to classical baselines.

title: HankelKANet: Lightweight Path Loss Estimation via Physics-Inspired Hankel Convolution
description:
arXiv:2610.19524v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate path loss (PL) estimation is essential for wireless network planning and optimization. This paper proposes HankelKANet, a lightweight physics-inspired network for PL estimation that structurally embeds electromagnetic propagation characteristics into the neural architecture. Built on a single residual UNet backbone, the proposed model integrates urban layout features with a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network(KAN). Specifically, the convolutional kernels are parameterized by the radial amplitudes of the zeroth- and first-order Hankel functions. This formulation acts as a physics-inspired nonlinear distance encoding, enabling the network to capture dominant attenuation characteristics directly without requiring additional physics-based loss terms. Experimental results demonstrate that HankelKANet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on both the simulated RadioMapSeer dataset and the real-world Huawei RSRPSet. Compared with the leading baseline, PEFNet, it reduces the parameter count by 78% and lowers the RMSE by 16.96% on the simulated data, while further exhibiting robust cross-dataset transferability and high data efficiency during target-domain adaptation. To interpret these empirical gains, we mathematically establish a parameter-conditional spatial gradient bound. Using discrete Dirichlet energy (DDE) and Jacobian sensitivity heatmaps, we empirically verify that this physical encoding intrinsically constrains the network's spatial derivatives. This structural smoothness effectively eliminates non-physical spatial ripples, preventing overfitting to simulator artifacts and serving as the fundamental driver for robust real world generalization.

title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.19439v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.

title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?
description:
arXiv:2610.19399v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. Its 4,271 entries support KoAGE, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition and two generation tasks---the latter, to our knowledge, the first to compare model coinages with attested neologisms under their original materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: in a five-model temporal analysis, models define only 13-30% of cutoff-year words, yet can infer meaning from one usage. However, structural understanding remains limited: even correct definitions barely improve formation analysis of pre-cutoff neologisms. Given word-building materials, single models often follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on interaction framing. KoAGE thus separates what models know, learn from use, and coin.

title: Hosted Metrics Query API for React Dashboard Cards — A Startup Backend Pattern
description:
TL;DR: Put a hosted metrics query API behind the Node.js backend when the job is to fill React cards and time-series charts while retaining enough evidence to reconstruct a marketplace incident. Keep reporting separate from querying, attach a stable incident correlation key to every measurement, and record cost attribution at ingestion time. This is the least complex option for a small team that does not need a full monitoring stack.

For this narrow job, Infrai's concrete advantage is a single API key and one REST API spanning 295 routes in 20 modules; a startup can add other backend capabilities without collecting another provider SDK, credential, and invoice each time. Its public discovery surface requires no key and every documented capability includes runnable examples in 10 languages.

It is not a complete observability system. You still need a separate alerting loop, and you should choose a specialist when distributed traces, session replay, source-map processing, configurable retention, or a downstream export stream is part of the requirement. That boundary matters more than a long feature list.

Should a React dashboard use a hosted metrics query API?

Start with the reconstruction question, not the chart library. For a marketplace, an aggregate saying "checkout failures rose" is useful, but an operator also needs to narrow the event by seller, workflow, region, and a correlation identifier. The raw customer identifier should stay out of metric dimensions; keep a pseudonymous incident key that can be joined to access-controlled application records instead.

The flow is small: jobs and request handlers report measurements to the hosted service; the Node backend queries aggregates for a bounded time range; React receives a deliberately narrow view model. The browser never receives the provider key. During an incident, the same backend query can populate a chart and capture the evidence envelope used in the incident timeline. Picture the concrete recovery path: support reports that seller payouts stalled shortly after a deployment, the operator opens a card scoped to the payout operation and seller tier, and the backend requests the same bounded window shown on screen. The saved correlation key links that aggregate to protected application records. The card establishes when volume changed; the application record establishes which workflow instance needs repair. Neither system is forced to do the other's job, and the evidence envelope preserves the exact window and card definition that informed the decision.

That is enough for many admin panels.

Cost attribution belongs in that model from day one. A useful card is not merely "requests per minute." It can show work by marketplace tenant, operation class, or AI feature, using bounded dimensions that let the founder explain which workload created the bill. Avoid order IDs as metric labels. They make aggregation expensive and turn a metrics store into a poor event database.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for this narrow layer when a startup already wants several backend capabilities behind one REST contract. Its self-describing contract reduces integration work when metrics are one part of the backend, rather than a new platform the team wants to operate.

I would try Infrai for the report-and-query portion of a small marketplace admin panel when minimizing provider glue matters and the team is willing to own alert polling. The primary advantage is breadth behind one consistent contract. The supporting benefit is operational: discovery lets the backend validate the live request shape instead of pinning an undocumented payload in application code.

Implementation walkthrough: discover, validate, then query

The request fields for metrics.query are not declared in the supplied discovery parameters, so guessing names such as from, to, or step would produce confident-looking code that may fail. Use the capability document's JSON Schema as the contract, fail during startup if required fields cannot be satisfied, and keep the provider-specific mapping in one server module.

This TypeScript example is intentionally small and runnable. It fetches the public capability description, prints the live request schema, and verifies that the route is available before your adapter accepts traffic. It does not invent a query payload.

type Capability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: unknown;
};

async function loadMetricsQueryContract(): Promise<Capability> {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/metrics.query",
    { method: "GET" },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
  }

  const capability = (await response.json()) as Capability;
  if (!capability.available || capability.method !== "GET") {
    throw new Error("The metrics query capability is not ready for this adapter");
  }

  return capability;
}

const capability = await loadMetricsQueryContract();
console.log(JSON.stringify({
  id: capability.id,
  path: capability.path,
  requestSchema: capability.params,
}, null, 2));

Run it with Node 20 or newer after compiling as an ES module. The output is the input to the only provider-specific code you should write: validate the desired card query against that schema, call the returned path, check the HTTP status, and convert the response into your internal Series type. Do not forward the upstream envelope directly to React. A stable application contract makes switching providers possible without rewriting every card.

For reporting, use the documented write route and the standard Authorization: Bearer convention, with the key read from process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY. A write retry needs an idempotency key. Rate-limited requests should honor Retry-After and then use exponential backoff; retries without either rule can duplicate measurements or amplify an outage. The platform specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities, but the capability schema should still be checked before treating any individual operation as idempotent.

Keep evidence separately from presentation. Persist an incident record containing the query window, normalized dimensions, correlation key, provider request ID when returned, and the exact card definition version. Seven fields can be more valuable than seven more charts. They tell the next person why a graph looked the way it did.

Failure recovery comes before vendor comparison

Treat the dashboard as an operational client, even if only five people can see it. Give every query a timeout and a bounded retry budget. Retry 429 responses only after respecting Retry-After; retry transient failures with jittered exponential backoff; do not retry ordinary validation failures. Surface stale data with its capture time instead of quietly drawing it as current.

Alerting needs its own worker because query access is not alert delivery. The worker can evaluate a small set of thresholds on a schedule, store the last evaluated window and notification state, and send through the team's chosen notification system. Make its state transition idempotent so a retry cannot page twice. For "the settlement job never ran," add a heartbeat product such as Healthchecks.io; absence is difficult to infer from a stream that was never written.

There is another boundary: live data movement. Without export or subscriptions, polling is acceptable for admin cards and a few thresholds, but it becomes custom plumbing for downstream BI synchronization. Choose a provider with a supported streaming or export path when that pipeline is already on the roadmap.

Short paths win.

The React layer should know only value, series, capturedAt, and an explicit freshness state. The Node layer owns authorization, schema validation, provider errors, attribution dimensions, and query limits. This split prevents a card refresh storm from becoming an unbounded provider workload and keeps credentials out of browser bundles.

Compare five operating models, not five price rows

The fair comparison is about operating model and recovery depth, not a single price row. Published prices change, and a startup can spend more engineering time debating units than it spends running the first month of a small admin panel.

Option Best fit for this marketplace job Trade-off to accept
Infrai A thin report/query layer when metrics sit beside other backend API capabilities No built-in alert delivery, export/subscription stream, distributed trace query, synthetic checks, or session replay
Datadog Teams that want a broader commercial monitoring product and are prepared to manage its ingestion and indexing model More platform and billing concepts than a few internal dashboard cards may justify
Grafana Cloud Teams that want managed dashboards around the Grafana ecosystem and familiar telemetry backends The application still needs a deliberate tenant-cost model and incident evidence contract
Honeycomb Engineers whose investigation depends on high-cardinality event exploration and tracing workflows A specialist investigation model can be more than an admin panel's aggregate cards require
Prometheus Teams that value an open metrics model and are comfortable owning or separately hosting collection, storage, and operations Running it directly conflicts with the goal of minimal infrastructure work

Datadog is the sensible comparison when the admin panel is likely to grow into a company-wide monitoring program. Its pricing page explicitly separates log ingestion and indexing, which is a reminder to model evidence volume and retained searchable data independently. Grafana Cloud deserves a look when the team already thinks in Grafana dashboards and standard telemetry components. Honeycomb is stronger territory when an incident starts with an unknown question and trace-shaped, high-cardinality exploration is central.

Prometheus remains a sound choice when ownership is the point. It is less attractive when the actual requirement is "give three React cards a series by Friday" and there is no one available to operate the stack.

Infrai occupies a narrower spot here. The write/query split is approachable, and one contract can reduce the number of SDKs, credentials, and bills around a small backend. Its limits are concrete: there is no alert or notification route, no metrics export or subscription model, and no synthetic heartbeat monitor. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but there is no distributed trace query or span tree. It also does not provide source-map deobfuscation, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or session replay.

Pick based on the incident you must reconstruct. If the question is "which tenant and operation drove this spike, and what did it cost?", the thin hosted API can be enough. If the question is "which span across six services caused this user-visible failure?", use a tracing specialist. No amount of dashboard polish closes that gap.

Operational checklist before launch

Before launch, verify the live discovery schema in CI and again at service startup, then refuse traffic if the adapter no longer matches it. Send metrics from the backend, never the browser. Keep label cardinality bounded; tenant tier and operation class are useful, while order ID and raw user ID belong in the incident record. Define the evidence retention requirement with legal review because there is no user-scoped log deletion interface and no configurable retention entry point described here.

Exercise three failure cases: a 429 with Retry-After, an upstream timeout after a report may have succeeded, and a query response too old for the card's freshness budget. Confirm that writes cannot double-apply, charts show stale state, and operators can recover the correlation key. Then test the silent case by withholding a scheduled heartbeat and checking that the external monitor notices.

Finally, write down the exit condition. Move to Datadog or another broad suite when integrated alerting and a deeper monitoring surface outweigh simplicity. Prefer Honeycomb or another tracing specialist when span-level investigation is mandatory. Reach for Grafana Cloud when managed ecosystem compatibility is the priority, or Prometheus when your team explicitly wants to own the metrics path. A hosted query API is a focused decision, not an observability strategy in disguise.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the public Infrai discovery document and use its schema-driven examples to shape the server adapter.

Further reading

  • Infrai public discovery example
  • Datadog pricing and log ingestion model
  • Grafana Cloud documentation
  • Honeycomb documentation
  • Prometheus documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation

title: AcrossVAM2.0: Conflict-Aware Point Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Video Diffusion Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2610.14693v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. ACROSSVAM2.0 combines a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad that removes only the auxiliary component opposing the primary flow-matching gradient on shared LoRA parameters. The design preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects its primary update during adaptation. In a four-way ablation trained for 1,000 steps with three independent seeds, the full method lowers KLT forward-backward cycle error in all three seeds relative to a matched flow-only continuation (mean seed-level difference -0.00711, SD 0.00505), while robust sharpness remains positive in all three. An expanded 24-prompt evaluation (216 videos) yields 9.7% lower aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error than the matched control and near-matched performance on six VBench dimensions; however, the seed-level tracking effect is heterogeneous and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022. These results support a bounded claim: conflict-aware adaptation improves correspondence consistency without broad perceptual degradation, but does not uniformly improve video quality. We release equations, pseudocode, matched outputs, source tables, and artifact provenance.

title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.

title: Yandex problems didn't stop automated programs, according to Cloudflare
description:
Cloudflare analysis reveals that following data center disruptions at Yandex, malicious bot traffic and automated scanning dropped significantly on the affected infrastructure.

However, operators quickly migrated workloads to alternative hosting ASNs like Radist and Selectel, resulting in flat overall attack volumes across targeted sectors.

After the attacks, traffic on Yandex's search and infrastructure services remained at 10% to 15% of normal levels, indicating that the network remains disrupted. While there was a drop in activities such as checking systems for problems, automated systems did not disappear.

This was clearly seen in the case of a gaming company that works with Cloudflare. While attacks from Yandex's systems dropped to zero, the exact same activity began to flow through other networks.

Overall, requests for gaming accounts remained stable over the week, increasing slightly from 167,7 million to 170,1 million. The people behind these programs simply moved their work to other hosting companies once Yandex stopped functioning properly.

title: Database Indexing: The Performance Trick Nobody Explained Properly
description:
Here's a scenario I've seen dozens of times.

A developer builds an app. It works great in development with 100 users. Then it goes to production, gets 100,000 users, and suddenly everything is slow. Pages timeout. The database CPU is at 100%. Users are complaining.

The developer starts optimizing code. Caching everything. Adding more servers. Nothing helps.

Then someone looks at the database and says, "Have you tried adding an index?"

One line of SQL later, queries that took 30 seconds now take 30 milliseconds. Problem solved.

Database indexing is the single highest-leverage performance optimization most developers ignore. It's not sexy. It's not a new framework. But it can make your app 100x faster with almost no code changes.

This guide explains how indexes actually work, when to use them, and the mistakes that destroy performance. By the end, you'll understand indexes well enough to speed up any slow query.

Let's make your database fast.

What Is an Index?

An index is a data structure that makes finding data faster.

Think of it like a book index. If you want to find every mention of "authentication" in a 500-page book, you have two options:

  • Without index: Read every page, looking for "authentication" (slow)
  • With index: Look up "authentication" in the back, get page numbers, go directly there (fast)

Databases work the same way.

-- Without index: Database scans EVERY row
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';
-- Checks row 1... nope
-- Checks row 2... nope
-- Checks row 3... nope
-- ... 999,997 more checks ...
-- Checks row 1,000,000... found it!

-- With index: Database jumps directly to matching rows
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';
-- Look up 'john@example.com' in index → Row #847,293
-- Go directly to row #847,293 → Found it!

The difference? O(n) vs O(log n). For a million rows, that's a million operations vs ~20 operations.

How Indexes Work (B-Tree)

Most database indexes use a B-tree (balanced tree) structure.

How a B-tree lookup works:

  1. Start at root node
  2. Compare value, go left or right
  3. Repeat until you find the value
  4. Follow pointer to actual row data

Why it's fast: Each step eliminates half the remaining data. With a million rows:

  • Step 1: 1,000,000 → 500,000
  • Step 2: 500,000 → 250,000
  • …
  • Step 20: Found it!

20 steps instead of 1,000,000. That's the power of indexes.

Creating Indexes

Basic Index 

-- Create index on single column
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

-- Create index on multiple columns (composite)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at);

-- Create unique index (also enforces uniqueness)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email_unique ON users(email);

When Indexes Are Created Automatically 

-- Primary keys automatically get an index
CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,  -- Index created automatically
    email VARCHAR(255)
);

-- Unique constraints automatically get an index
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT unique_email UNIQUE (email);
-- Index created automatically

-- Foreign keys do NOT automatically get an index in PostgreSQL!
-- (They do in MySQL)
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id)  -- NO automatic index!
);

-- You should create one manually
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);

Which Columns to Index

Always Index These 

-- 1. Foreign keys (JOIN performance)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_comments_post_id ON comments(post_id);

-- 2. Columns in WHERE clauses (filter performance)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_status ON users(status);
CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON products(category_id);

-- 3. Columns in ORDER BY (sort performance)
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_created_at ON posts(created_at);

-- 4. Columns in GROUP BY (aggregation performance)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_product_id ON orders(product_id);

Don't Index These 

-- 1. Tiny tables (full scan is fast enough)
-- A table with 100 rows doesn't need indexes beyond PK

-- 2. Columns with low cardinality (few unique values)
-- Boolean columns, status with only 3 values
CREATE INDEX idx_users_is_active ON users(is_active);  -- Usually not helpful

-- 3. Columns that change frequently
-- Index must be updated on every change
CREATE INDEX idx_users_last_seen ON users(last_seen_at);  -- Expensive to maintain

-- 4. Columns rarely used in queries
-- Indexes have storage cost and write overhead

The Selectivity Rule

An index is most useful when it narrows down results significantly.

-- HIGH selectivity (good for indexing)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';
-- Returns 1 row out of 1,000,000 = 0.0001% of table

-- LOW selectivity (index might not help)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active = true;
-- Returns 950,000 rows out of 1,000,000 = 95% of table
-- Full table scan might actually be faster!

Composite Indexes (Multi-Column)

Composite indexes cover multiple columns. Order matters!

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at);

How Composite Index Order Works

Which Queries Can Use This Index? 

-- ✅ Uses index (matches left-to-right)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND created_at > '2024-01-01';
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at;

-- ❌ Cannot use index (skips first column)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01';
-- Would need separate index: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date ON orders(created_at);

The Left-Prefix Rule

A composite index can be used for queries that filter on:

  • First column only ✅
  • First + second columns ✅
  • First + second + third columns ✅
  • Second column only ❌
  • Third column only ❌ 
-- Index: (a, b, c)

WHERE a = 1                     -- ✅ Uses index
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2           -- ✅ Uses index
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c = 3 -- ✅ Uses index
WHERE b = 2                     -- ❌ Cannot use index
WHERE c = 3                     -- ❌ Cannot use index
WHERE b = 2 AND c = 3           -- ❌ Cannot use index
WHERE a = 1 AND c = 3           -- ⚠️ Partial: only uses 'a' part

EXPLAIN: See How Queries Execute

The EXPLAIN command shows you exactly how the database executes a query.

Basic Usage 

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';

Output (PostgreSQL):

Seq Scan on users  (cost=0.00..1834.00 rows=1 width=72)
  Filter: (email = 'john@example.com')

Seq Scan = Sequential Scan = Full Table Scan = SLOW!

Now add an index:

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';

Output:

Index Scan using idx_users_email on users  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=72)
  Index Cond: (email = 'john@example.com')

Index Scan = Using the index = FAST!

EXPLAIN ANALYZE (With Actual Timing) 

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';

Output:

Index Scan using idx_users_email on users
  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=72)
  (actual time=0.025..0.026 rows=1 loops=1)
Planning Time: 0.085 ms
Execution Time: 0.043 ms

Now you can see actual milliseconds!

What to Look For

Common Index Problems

Problem 1: Index Not Being Used 

-- You created an index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

-- But this query doesn't use it!
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'john@example.com';
-- Seq Scan!

Why? The index is on email, not LOWER(email).

Fix: Create a functional index.

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users(LOWER(email));

-- Now it works
SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'john@example.com';
-- Index Scan ✅

Problem 2: Wrong Column Order in Composite Index 

-- Index created
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date_user ON orders(created_at, user_id);

-- This query is slow!
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- Seq Scan! The index can't help (wrong order)

-- Fix: Create index with correct order
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at);

Problem 3: Too Many Indexes 

-- Every index has a cost:
-- • Storage space
-- • Slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (must update all indexes)
-- • Query planner overhead

-- Don't do this!
CREATE INDEX idx_users_a ON users(a);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_b ON users(b);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_c ON users(c);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_ab ON users(a, b);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_bc ON users(b, c);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_abc ON users(a, b, c);
-- 6 indexes to maintain on every write!

-- Instead, analyze your queries and create minimal covering indexes

Problem 4: Type Mismatch 

-- Column is VARCHAR
CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    phone VARCHAR(20)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_phone ON users(phone);

-- But you query with INTEGER
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = 1234567890;
-- Index might not be used! (type conversion)

-- Fix: Use correct type
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = '1234567890';

Problem 5: LIKE with Leading Wildcard 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_name ON users(name);

-- This uses the index ✅
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'John%';

-- This CANNOT use the index ❌
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%John%';
-- Must scan entire index/table because we don't know starting point

-- For full-text search, use proper full-text indexes instead
CREATE INDEX idx_users_name_gin ON users USING gin(to_tsvector('english', name));

Index Types

Different index types for different use cases.

B-Tree (Default) 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
-- Same as:
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users USING btree(email);
  • Best for: Equality (=) and range queries (<, >, BETWEEN)
  • Use when: Most cases. This is your default choice.

Hash 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_hash ON users USING hash(email);
  • Best for: Equality only (=)
  • Use when: You only do exact matches, never ranges.

GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) 

-- For array columns
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_tags ON posts USING gin(tags);

-- For full-text search
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_content ON posts USING gin(to_tsvector('english', content));

-- For JSONB
CREATE INDEX idx_users_metadata ON users USING gin(metadata);
  • Best for: Arrays, full-text search, JSONB
  • Use when: You query inside complex data types.

GiST (Generalized Search Tree) 

-- For geometric data
CREATE INDEX idx_locations_coords ON locations USING gist(coordinates);

-- For range types
CREATE INDEX idx_events_duration ON events USING gist(duration);
  • Best for: Geometric/spatial data, range types
  • Use when: PostGIS, geometric queries.

Partial Indexes

Index only rows that match a condition.

-- Full index: includes all 1,000,000 rows
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);

-- Partial index: only includes pending orders (maybe 1,000 rows)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders(status)
WHERE status = 'pending';

-- Much smaller index, faster to search and maintain!

Use cases:

-- Only index active users
CREATE INDEX idx_users_active_email ON users(email) WHERE is_active = true;

-- Only index recent orders
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_recent ON orders(created_at)
WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01';

-- Only index unprocessed items
CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_unprocessed ON background_jobs(queue, priority)
WHERE processed_at IS NULL;

Covering Indexes (Index-Only Scans)

A covering index contains all columns needed by a query, so the database doesn't need to access the table at all.

-- Query needs: email, name, created_at
SELECT email, name, created_at
FROM users
WHERE email = 'john@example.com';

-- Regular index (must access table for name, created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
-- Index Scan → then fetch name, created_at from table

-- Covering index (includes all needed columns)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_covering ON users(email) INCLUDE (name, created_at);
-- Index Only Scan → no table access needed!

PostgreSQL syntax:

CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table(search_columns) INCLUDE (extra_columns);

Real-World Examples

Example 1: E-Commerce Orders 

-- Common queries:
-- 1. Get user's orders
-- 2. Get orders by status
-- 3. Get recent orders
-- 4. Get user's orders by status

-- Recommended indexes:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status) WHERE status IN ('pending', 'processing');
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created ON orders(created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status ON orders(user_id, status);

Example 2: Blog Posts 

-- Common queries:
-- 1. Get posts by author
-- 2. Get published posts by date
-- 3. Search posts by title
-- 4. Get posts by category

-- Recommended indexes:
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_author ON posts(author_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_published ON posts(published_at DESC) WHERE is_published = true;
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_title_search ON posts USING gin(to_tsvector('english', title));
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_category ON posts(category_id) WHERE is_published = true;

Example 3: User Sessions 

-- Common queries:
-- 1. Get session by token
-- 2. Get user's active sessions
-- 3. Delete expired sessions

-- Recommended indexes:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_sessions_token ON sessions(token);
CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_user_active ON sessions(user_id) WHERE expires_at > NOW();
CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_expires ON sessions(expires_at) WHERE expires_at < NOW();

Index Maintenance

Check Index Usage 

-- PostgreSQL: See which indexes are being used
SELECT
    schemaname,
    tablename,
    indexname,
    idx_scan,      -- Times index was used
    idx_tup_read,  -- Rows read from index
    idx_tup_fetch  -- Rows fetched from table
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
ORDER BY idx_scan DESC;

-- Find unused indexes
SELECT indexname, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0
AND indexname NOT LIKE '%_pkey';

Check Index Size 

-- PostgreSQL: Index sizes
SELECT
    indexname,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexname::regclass)) as size
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'users'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexname::regclass) DESC;

Rebuild Bloated Indexes 

-- PostgreSQL: Rebuild index
REINDEX INDEX idx_users_email;

-- Rebuild all indexes on a table
REINDEX TABLE users;

-- Concurrent rebuild (doesn't lock table)
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_email;

Quick Reference

The Bottom Line

Database indexing is not optional for production systems. It's the difference between "fast" and "unusable."

Remember:

  1. Indexes make reads faster, writes slower. Balance is key.
  2. Use EXPLAIN. Don't guess, look at the query plan.
  3. Index your WHERE clauses. Especially foreign keys.
  4. Composite index order matters. Left-prefix rule.
  5. Monitor index usage. Remove unused indexes.
  6. Start simple. Add indexes based on actual slow queries.

One well-placed index can do more for performance than weeks of code optimization. Learn to use them well.

Your turn 👇

What's the worst slow query you've ever fixed with a single index? I'd like to hear your stories in the comments.

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.

title: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers
description:
arXiv:2610.19407v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.

title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
description:
arXiv:2610.18877v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.
