title: When POST becomes GET: a redirect bug in a Node.js fetch wrapper
description:
A POST followed a 302 redirect and became a GET. Its body disappeared, but its Content-Type header stayed behind.

That showed up while extending the client comparisons in ssrf-lab, a testing harness I maintain. The affected package was @tak-ps/node-safeurl@1.8.0, a Node.js fetch wrapper that checks URLs and redirect destinations.

This is a functional redirect-conformance bug. The proposed fix is upstream PR #4, submitted and awaiting review as of October 14, 2026. These tests do not demonstrate an SSRF bypass.

The response looked fine. The request told the story.

The comparison uses a small HTTP server on 127.0.0.1. One route returns a redirect; the destination echoes the method, body, and headers it actually receives. That exact local origin is explicitly allowed in the wrapper's configuration.

Both native fetch and the wrapper successfully completed this request:

{
  method: 'POST',
  body: 'hello',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'text/plain' }
}

After a 302 redirect, the destination observed:

Client Method Body Content-Type
Native fetch GET empty absent
node-safeurl 1.8.0 GET empty text/plain

The same difference appeared for 301 POST and 303 PUT. Checking only the final status or whether the fetch promise resolved would miss it.

The Fetch redirect algorithm changes POST to GET for 301/302, and changes methods other than GET/HEAD to GET for 303. When it discards the body, it also removes the request-body headers: Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Content-Location, and Content-Type.

The wrapper already handled the method and body changes. It was missing the corresponding header cleanup.

The fix belongs in the method-rewrite branch

The patch adds Headers to the existing Undici import, then extends the existing switchToGet branch:

if (switchToGet) {
  fetchInit.method = 'GET';
  fetchInit.body = undefined;

  const headers = new Headers(fetchInit.headers);
  for (const name of [
    'content-encoding',
    'content-language',
    'content-location',
    'content-type',
    'content-length',
  ]) {
    headers.delete(name);
  }
  fetchInit.headers = headers;
}

Content-Length is removed as well, because caller-supplied framing for the discarded body should not carry into the GET. It is separate from the standard's four named request-body headers.

Copying through Headers supports object, tuple-array, and Headers inputs without changing the caller's original headers. Unrelated headers survive. The URL validation logic is unchanged.

The condition matters: a 307 or 308 should preserve the method and body, so stripping these headers on every redirect would introduce another bug.

Prove both the fix and the unchanged cases

The upstream regression test records actual incoming requests and checks seven cases:

Redirect cases Before patch After patch
301 POST, 302 POST, 303 PUT All three fail All three pass
307 POST, 308 POST, 301 PUT, 302 PUT All four pass All four pass

It also checks that an unrelated header is preserved and the caller's headers are not mutated. The full patched upstream suite passes 198 tests on each of Node 22.23.3 and 24.21.0, alongside lint and build.

The recorded evidence includes the original failures, fixed tests, full-suite logs, and published-package comparison.

Run the comparison

With Node 22.19 or newer and npm:

git clone https://github.com/roshan-amble/ssrf-lab.git
cd ssrf-lab
git checkout 41659cda6825b2f7e324294d7242ef1b076b6cce
npm ci --ignore-scripts --prefix integrations/community
node integrations/community/check-redirects.mjs

This prints JSON for native fetch and the unmodified published package across five redirect cases. The HTTP comparison stays on the explicitly allowed loopback origin. The broader SSRF suite has separate network-isolation requirements.

The practical testing lesson is to assert what reached the destination: method, body, and headers. A successful response alone cannot establish that a wrapper preserved fetch semantics.

The harness, adapters, and reproduction are in ssrf-lab. Which redirect or URL-handling edge case would you add to this coverage?

AI disclosure: Codex assisted with the investigation, implementation, and test execution, and drafted this article from the linked code and recorded results.

title: When Occupation-derived Skills Don't Help: On the Limits of Skill-Augmented Career Path Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.20186v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Skills are widely assumed to play a central role in career transitions, motivating their use in career path prediction (CPP) systems. In this work, we critically examine whether explicit skill representations provide complementary signal beyond text-based job representations. We evaluate multiple strategies for incorporating skills into CPP models, including score fusion and neural architectures, under two conditions: predicted skills and ground-truth ESCO annotations. Surprisingly, across two benchmark datasets, none of these settings yield substantial improvements over strong text-only baselines. Even when using ground-truth skills, gains remain marginal and inconsistent. Through detailed analysis, we identify key factors underlying this result: high redundancy between textual and skill representations, limited discriminative power of ESCO's taxonomy, and representational collapse in skill embeddings. Furthermore, we find that skill prediction difficulty correlates with overall sample difficulty, limiting the potential for complementary signals. Our findings challenge the common assumption that explicit skill modeling inherently benefits career prediction and suggest that dense text representations already capture most skill-relevant information.

title: How Conductor moved parallel coding agents from the laptop to the cloud with Vercel Sandbox
description:
Conductor on Vercel

  • Multiple parallel coding agents running at scale in the cloud

  • Model-agnostic, works with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents

  • Used by engineering teams at Notion, Linear, Ramp, and Life360

Interacting with a single coding agent feels natural, and Conductor makes directing a fleet of agents just as intuitive.

It's a GUI for spinning up multiple coding agents in parallel, each working on an isolated branch of your codebase at once. You review their work, merge what works, and redirect the agents that need to keep iterating.

Engineering teams loved it, but hardware was a real limitiation. Every agent ran on your machine, so the fan climbed, the CPU ran hot, and if you closed your laptop, the agents stopped.

Charlie Holtz, co-founder and CEO of Conductor, spent time at Vercel before starting the company. He understands what developers lose when their environment imposes rules on how they can work. Cloud Workspaces, Conductor's remote execution layer built on Vercel Sandboxes, removes the local hardware constraint. Developers can now spawn multiple agents and close the lid without interrupting work.

The journey from local to cloud

Developers who adopted Conductor early felt the power. Notion's engineering team said, "It makes you feel like an octopus, where each one of your arms is working on something separately."

The demand for remote execution came quickly. Developers wanted more agents running longer, and local hardware was the ceiling. For a six-person startup, going from local to cloud is a huge technical leap, and when the developers using Conductor work at companies like Linear and Ramp, provider choice is a matter of building trust with engineers choosing to run their code on infrastructure they don't own.

The team evaluated several sandbox providers, weighing fast spin-up and snapshot support alongside longevity and the depth of the support relationship.

Running parallel agents in the cloud

Conductor built Cloud Workspaces on Vercel Sandboxes. When a developer opens a new workspace, agents spin up on a remote server instead of their local machine. The interface doesn't change.

Holtz describes the result: "To our users it feels just like the local version of Conductor. They don't know the difference, which is amazing, and that's because Vercel Sandboxes are super fast."

Conductor already supports Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents, but they are model agnostic. That means that no matter how often labs release updates, or what the next popular harness is, they can keep the same cloud layer underneath. As Holtz puts it: "The vibes shift every 3 months. Right now GPT-5.5 has the vibes on its side, but that's going change in another few months. Being agnostic to the providers is the key, and we get that with Vercel."

One interface, whatever the frontier looks like next

Conductor's bet is on the interface: the one place to direct your agents, review their work, and decide what to merge. With Vercel Sandbox, that interface goes wherever developers go.

About Conductor: Conductor is a multi-agent IDE for running coding agents in parallel, each on isolated branches of your codebase. Model-agnostic by design, it works with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents.

title: Implementing Distributed Tracing in Go with OpenTelemetry
description:
When a request fails in a distributed system, you end up grepping through five different log files across five services trying to figure out what happened. Logs tell you what, but not where — which service added 800ms of latency, or where an error actually originated across the call chain. Distributed tracing solves this by recording the full lifecycle of a request across service boundaries, and OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for doing it without locking into a specific backend.

What OpenTelemetry Is (and What It Isn't)

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is not a backend — it's an instrumentation framework. It standardizes how you collect traces, metrics, and logs, and ships with:

  • An API — the interface your code calls
  • An SDK — the implementation (samplers, exporters, propagators)
  • A Collector — optional intermediary that receives, processes, and routes telemetry
  • Exporters — Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog, Grafana Tempo, and others

You instrument your code once against the OTel API. You can route data to any backend by swapping the exporter. The instrumentation stays the same.

Initializing the Tracer Provider

Install the necessary packages:

go get go.opentelemetry.io/otel
go get go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace
go get go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracegrpc
go get go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/net/http/otelhttp

Then initialize the tracer at startup:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "log"

    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracegrpc"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/resource"
    sdktrace "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace"
    semconv "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.21.0"
    "google.golang.org/grpc"
)

func initTracer(ctx context.Context) (func(context.Context) error, error) {
    exporter, err := otlptracegrpc.New(ctx,
        otlptracegrpc.WithEndpoint("localhost:4317"),
        otlptracegrpc.WithInsecure(),
        otlptracegrpc.WithDialOption(grpc.WithBlock()),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    res, err := resource.New(ctx,
        resource.WithAttributes(
            semconv.ServiceName("order-service"),
            semconv.ServiceVersion("1.2.0"),
        ),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
        sdktrace.WithBatcher(exporter),
        sdktrace.WithResource(res),
        sdktrace.WithSampler(
            sdktrace.ParentBased(sdktrace.TraceIDRatioBased(0.1)),
        ),
    )
    otel.SetTracerProvider(tp)
    return tp.Shutdown, nil
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    shutdown, err := initTracer(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer shutdown(ctx)

    // start your HTTP server here
}

A few details worth noting:

  • WithBatcher is what you want in production — it buffers spans and sends them in batches rather than flushing on every span end
  • WithInsecure() is fine when the Collector runs on the same host; use TLS everywhere else
  • The resource is metadata attached to every span emitted by this service — service name and version at minimum

Instrumenting Business Logic

The OTel API follows a simple pattern: create a tracer once per package, call Start to open a span, and End it when the operation is done.

package handler

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"

    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/codes"
)

var tracer = otel.Tracer("github.com/yourorg/order-service/handler")

func ProcessOrder(ctx context.Context, orderID string) error {
    ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "ProcessOrder")
    defer span.End()

    span.SetAttributes(
        attribute.String("order.id", orderID),
        attribute.String("order.region", "eu-west-1"),
    )

    if err := validateOrder(ctx, orderID); err != nil {
        span.RecordError(err)
        span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "order validation failed")
        return fmt.Errorf("validate: %w", err)
    }

    span.AddEvent("order validated")

    if err := chargePayment(ctx, orderID); err != nil {
        span.RecordError(err)
        span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "payment failed")
        return fmt.Errorf("charge: %w", err)
    }

    span.SetStatus(codes.Ok, "")
    return nil
}

func validateOrder(ctx context.Context, orderID string) error {
    _, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "validateOrder")
    defer span.End()
    // validation logic
    return nil
}

func chargePayment(ctx context.Context, orderID string) error {
    _, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "chargePayment")
    defer span.End()
    // payment logic
    return nil
}

The critical discipline: pass ctx down through every function call. OpenTelemetry stores the active span in the context. Drop the context and child spans lose their parent — you end up with disconnected orphan spans instead of a coherent tree.

HTTP Middleware and Outbound Calls

For HTTP servers, the contrib package handles span creation automatically per request:

import (
    "net/http"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/net/http/otelhttp"
)

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("/orders", ordersHandler)

    handler := otelhttp.NewHandler(mux, "http-server",
        otelhttp.WithMessageEvents(otelhttp.ReadEvents, otelhttp.WriteEvents),
    )
    http.ListenAndServe(":8080", handler)
}

This creates a span per request, attaches standard HTTP attributes (method, route, status code), and — crucially — extracts incoming trace context from headers. If an upstream service already started a trace, your service joins that trace rather than starting a new one. That's what makes cross-service tracing work.

For outbound calls, wrap the HTTP client transport:

client := &http.Client{
    Transport: otelhttp.NewTransport(http.DefaultTransport),
}
resp, err := client.Get("https://inventory-service/items/42")

The transport injects the current trace context into the outgoing traceparent header automatically.

Sampling Strategy

Recording every span in a high-traffic service is expensive. The options in order of practical usefulness:

AlwaysSample — every request is traced. Fine for development or low-traffic services. Not for production at scale.

TraceIDRatioBased(0.05) — traces 5% of requests. Inexpensive, but you can miss rare events.

ParentBased(TraceIDRatioBased(0.1)) — respects the sampling decision of the upstream service. If the caller sampled this trace, you continue it. If not, you don't start one. This is the correct default for production: it keeps traces coherent across service boundaries without every service independently deciding whether to sample.

One real-world wrinkle: you want to always trace errored requests regardless of the base sample rate. The OpenTelemetry Collector supports this with its tailsampling processor, which can override the head-based decision after a trace completes. This is more complex to operate but gives you both cost efficiency and full fidelity on failures.

One operational note: span attributes can easily capture sensitive data — JWT fragments, query parameters, internal IDs. Before deploying to production, check what your instrumentation is recording. A security hardening checklist for your environment is a practical starting point for what to review.

The Takeaway

Distributed tracing in Go with OpenTelemetry breaks down to four steps: initialize a TracerProvider with a batching exporter, propagate ctx everywhere, use contrib middleware for protocol-level spans (HTTP, gRPC, database drivers), and configure ParentBased sampling for production.

The diagnostic value comes from the attributes and events you attach to spans — not just the default fields. span.SetAttributes(attribute.String("order.id", id)) is what turns "payment service returned an error" into "payment failed on order #4521 in eu-west-1 at 14:03:22." That's the difference between tracing and useful tracing.

I run AYI NEDJIMI Consultants, a cybersecurity consulting firm. We publish free security hardening checklists — PDF and Excel.

title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation
description:
arXiv:2610.19330v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.
